Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the $lang translation.
5. The target language is $lang.

p.seg: *Mù Tiānzǐ Chuán*
The *Mù Tiānzǐ Chuán*
is a book discovered by a resident of Jí Xiàn during the Tàikāng 2nd year, while excavating an ancient tomb.
King [Mù] loved to go on inspection tours.
He acquired the steeds Dàolí and Lǜ'ěr,
and Zàofù was his charioteer,
with whom he observed the four wildernesses.
Northward, he crossed the Liúshā,
westward, he ascended Kūnlún,
and met Xīwángmǔ.
The bamboo slips and plain silk
are all ancient books,
quite readable.
I respectfully transcribe them onto two-chi yellow paper,
and request them to be submitted to the Secretariat,
stored in the Central Archives,
with a copy in the Three Pavilions.
Respectfully submitted.
The seven elite warriors
drank with the Son of Heaven on mount Juānshān.
On the northern expedition,
they cut off the Zhāngshuǐ and toasted on Pánshí.
Then grand music was performed,
and they stayed standing without rest.
Arriving at Quǎnróng,
the Hu toasted the Son of Heaven on the south bank of the Dāngshuǐ.
They then had entertainment,
and bestowed gifts upon the seven elite warriors.
They hunted beasts in the Shènzé,
obtaining black foxes and black badgers.
Hézōng Bǎiyāo met them at Yānrán zhī Shān,
and offered a welcoming gift of woven silk and added a *bì* jade disk.
He was about to lead the Six Armies.
On an auspicious day,
the Son of Heaven wore his grand ceremonial robes, a *miǎn* crown, *yī* vestment, *fú* belt,
tucked in his *hù* tablet, wore his side ornaments,
held a *bì* jade disk, and stood facing south at Hánxià.
Hézōng received the *bì*,
faced west, submerged it in the river,
and bowed twice, kowtowing.
The Son of Heaven held a grand audience at Huáng zhī Shān,
displaying maps and inspecting records to view the Son of Heaven's treasured artifacts:
jade fruit,
stone companions of beautiful jade,
what are called "patterned fruits."
*Xuánzhū* pearls, *zhúyín* silver,
the silver has a brilliant luster like a candle.
Golden paste.
Golden paste is also like jade paste.
Bǎiyāo rode the Qúhuáng chariot,
going ahead of the Son of Heaven.
Eight Steeds
The Son of Heaven's steeds:
Chìjì, Dàolí, Báiyì, Yúlún, Shānzǐ, Qúhuáng, Huáliú, Lǜ'ěr.
All eight steeds are named after their coat color.
Dogs:
Chónggōng, Chèzhǐ, Guānjū, Kǒuhuáng, Nánkǒu, Láibái.
All are names of excellent dogs,
similar to Huáng'ěr, Hánlú, Sòngquè, and so on.
Gold Deer, Silver Roe Deer
When the Son of Heaven campaigned in the north,
the people of Cáonú toasted the Son of Heaven on the Yángshuǐ,
and presented gold deer and silver roe deer.
Nowadays, silver pigs and gold dogs are found underground;
these are all ancient bribes and exotic goods for the Yi and Di.
Cèfǔ
The Son of Heaven returned east,
enfeoffing Chánggōng west of the Hēishuǐ.
These are the long-armed people,
whose arms are three *chǐ* long.
The country of long-legged people
is also east of the Chìhǎi.
Following the Hēishuǐ, they reached Qúnyù zhī Shān,
where Xīwángmǔ resides.
This is what the former kings called the Cèfǔ.
It was an ancient treasury for books and records,
said to be hidden in famous mountains.
The Son of Heaven took three loads of jade tablets and jade utensils and clothing,
and then loaded ten thousand *jí* of jade.
Lèchí
The Son of Heaven rested by the Xuánchí,
where grand music was performed,
lasting three days,
hence it was called Lèchí.
The Son of Heaven then bestowed bamboo,
hence it was called Zhúlín.
Shíkǔ
The Son of Heaven rested and hunted on Kǔshān,
where he ate *kǔ*.
*Kǔ*
is the name of a plant
that is edible.
Xīwángmǔ Toasted at Yáochí
On the auspicious day of Jiǎzǐ,
the Son of Heaven, holding a white *guī* and a black *bì*, met Xīwángmǔ,
and offered one hundred rolls of brocade and silk,
and three hundred rolls of white silk.
*Chún*
is a measure word for a bolt of fabric.
Xīwángmǔ bowed twice to receive them,
and toasted him by the Yáochí.
Xīwángmǔ sang a folk song, saying:
"White clouds are in the sky,
mountains and hills rise by themselves.
The journey is long and distant,
separated by mountains and rivers.
May my lord not die,
you can still return."
The Son of Heaven replied:
"I will return to the Eastern Lands,
and bring peace and order to all the Huáxià states.
When all the people are equal and just,
I will come to see you again."
Mùhé
The Son of Heaven campaigned east to the Hēishuǐ River,
where there were wild wheat and *língdǒng*,
which the Western Xīmò call *mùhé*.
It is a type of millet,
five *xún* long.
There is Cǎishí zhī Shān.
Stones with beautiful patterns.
They drank at the foot of Wénshān.
The people of Wénshān
presented ten teams of fine horses,
three hundred horned cattle,
ninety guard dogs,
and three hundred bulls,
to cross the Liúshā.
The Son of Heaven gave them excellent horses, dragon dogs, and excellent cattle.
The Son of Heaven's bow,
when shot, can pierce men, foot soldiers, swords, cattle, horses, and rhinoceroses,
and its mouth opening is worth a thousand *jīn*.
The Son of Heaven's horses
can run a thousand *lǐ*,
surpassing men and fierce beasts.
The Son of Heaven's dogs
can run a hundred *lǐ*,
and catch tigers and leopards.
Zàofù Sānbǎi
The Son of Heaven's charioteer,
Zàofù Sānbǎi.
Below, it says three hundred were charioteers.
Gěng Xún had many contradictory statements.
Zàofù was a skilled charioteer,
but I have not heard of others.
Zuǒ Pèi Huá
The Son of Heaven said:
"Alas!
I, the lone one, am not rich in virtue,
but distinguished in music.
Will later generations count my faults?"
The seven elite warriors said:
"What later generations hope for
is that you do not deviate from the constant principles of Heaven.
When farmers and artisans are successful,
the common people will be wealthy.
Officials attend to their duties,
sharing benefits with the people;
this will be regarded as a norm for generations."
The Son of Heaven praised them,
and bestowed upon them the *zuǒ pèi huá*.
The *yù huá zhī pèi*
is the finest among pendants.
Large Trees, Gigantic Grasses
The Son of Heaven ascended Wángjū in the southwest,
and conversed about ancient virtuous and sagely rulers.
There were large trees and gigantic grasses,
and the people of Chóukǒu presented one hundred containers of wine to the Son of Heaven.
Below "hundred", the name of the wine vessel is missing.
Zhūzé
The Son of Heaven campaigned in the north,
and stayed at Zhūzé.
They offered three hundred meals,
suitable for dining.
Three thousand sheep and cattle.
Xuánpǔ
The marsh of Chūnshān,
where clear water springs forth,
warm and without wind.
This is what the former kings called Xuánpǔ.
The Son of Heaven obtained *yùróngzhī*,
its essence,
broomcorn millet.
The Son of Heaven campaigned west,
reaching Chìniǎo.
They presented a thousand hú of wine,
and a hundred zǎi of millet.
Millet is similar to broomcorn millet but not sticky.
The Son of Heaven bestowed Mò with a yellow horse with golden fittings and a belt,
and he prostrated himself to receive it.
The Son of Heaven took back auspicious grasses and trees,
and planted them in the Central Plains.
The people of Chìniǎo also presented two women to the Son of Heaven,
saying they were from the Chìwū clan.
The blood of a white crane.
The people of Jùsōu presented the blood of a white crane,
for the Son of Heaven to drink.
They provided an ablution of ox and horse
to wash the Son of Heaven’s feet.
Gambling with Fēigōng.
The Son of Heaven gambled with Jǐnggōng,
and it was decided after three days.
He stayed at a platform,
to hear the administration of the world.
Horses spitting jade.
The Son of Heaven traveled east to Huángzé,
and lodged at Qǔlù.
He commanded the court musicians to sing:
"When passing through Huáng,
its horses spit sand;
the August One is majestic.
At the marsh of Huáng,
its horses spit jade;
the August One has a long lifespan."
The Song of Yellow Bamboo, Three Chapters.
The Son of Heaven traveled south to the hills of Huángshì,
to observe where Xià Hòu Qǐ had resided.
He hunted in Píngzé,
and there was heavy cold rain and snow.
He composed three chapters of poetry,
to lament the people, saying:
"As I traveled to Yellow Bamboo,
the mouth of the pass was sealed by cold.
The Emperor gathered the Nine Ranks.
Alas, my dukes and marquises,
all the lords and prime ministers,
may they protect my myriad people,
and never forget, morning or evening."
Shèng Jī’s Jade Platform.
The Son of Heaven stayed in the marsh.
Shèng Jī reported an illness,
and took medicine to administer.
This was called húzhuǎn.
Zhuǎn is the same as chuán.
He arrived at the platform of Lěibì.
She was interred at the temple of Gǔqiū,
and buried at Xuánchí.
Her posthumous title was "Āishú Rén."
The Son of Heaven raised a mound for her,
which was called the Mound of Shú Rén.
The Son of Heaven, after ending mourning, began to enjoy himself,
and returned in plain clothes.
He rested beneath two cypresses,
forever holding sorrow in his heart.
The Seven Elites admonished him, saying:
"Since ancient times, there has been life and death;
why only Shú Rén?"
The Son of Heaven campaigned south,
entering Nánzhèng.
The purple orchid maiden.
Wǔdì suddenly saw a maiden in green clothes,
who said:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month,
the Queen Mother will briefly come."
The Emperor asked Dōngfāng Shuò:
"Who is this person?"
Shuò replied:
"She is the purple orchid maiden of the Queen Mother of the West,
conveying messages back and forth."
On that day,
the Emperor dressed in splendid attire and stood at the foot of the stairs.
At night, he heard the sound of flutes and drums from the clouds.
The Queen Mother rode in a purple cloud carriage,
drawn by nine-colored spotted dragons.
There were other heavenly immortals,
all a zhàng tall.
The Queen Mother ascended the hall,
and personally set out exquisite dishes,
serving seven peaches on a tray.
The Emperor ate them;
they were sweet and delicious.
The Mother said:
"These peaches bear fruit only once every three thousand years."
Commanding the serving maidens to play music.
The Queen Mother commanded the serving maiden Wángzǐ Dēng to play the bāláng’s áozither,
Dǒng Shuāngchéng to play the yúnhé flute,
Xǔ Fēiqióng to play the língxū’s sheng,
Ān Fǎyīng to sing the xuánlíng曲.
Begging for the art of transcending the world.
The Emperor kowtowed and said:
"Chè
— the Emperor’s personal name was Mǐ.
I am born with an untalented nature,
sunk in common customs.
My governance has many shortcomings,
and the people are not harmonious.
I admire the spirit immortals,
and am fortunate to behold the Most Holy.
It is my predestined fate to attain transcendence."
The Mother said:
"You indulge in lust and debauchery,
killing and extravagance.
To release yourself from the Three Corpses,
and keep your body permanently,
is difficult to achieve, my son.
But if you cherish your essence and hold it firm,
hold your breath and swallow the fluid.
Qi transforms into blood,
blood transforms into essence,
essence transforms into fluid,
fluid transforms into bone.
If you practice tirelessly,
in one year your qi will change,
in two years your blood will change,
in three years your脉 will change,
in four years your flesh will change,
in five years your marrow will change,
in six years your sinews will change,
in seven years your bones will change,
in eight years your hair will change,
in nine years your form will change.
With transformation, the Way will be achieved;
when the Way is achieved, you will be ranked among the immortals,
exhaling and inhaling the Six Qi,
with sweetness and fragrance in your mouth."
Shàngyuán Fūrén.
The Queen Mother sent a serving maiden to convey a message to Shàngyuán Fūrén, saying:
"Liú Chè is fond of the Way.
I just came to see him,
and found Chè to be quite clear,
seemingly capable of progress.
However, his form is sluggish and his spirit impure,
his five viscera are not harmonious.
He has much flesh and little essence,
and the Three Corpses are causing trouble.
I fear he is not immortal material.
Guest and host sit facing each other,
melancholy and unhappy.
Can you come for a moment, Fūrén?"
A moment later, the serving maiden returned, saying:
"Āhuán bows again,
inquiring about your well-being.
Separated by the Crimson River,
and disturbed by palace affairs,
my complexion has thus diminished,
for nearly five thousand years.
I was previously ordered by the Great Emperor Lord to go to Xuánzhōu,
to rectify the Heavenly Cycle.
I am just now momentarily going there,
and will return afterwards."
After a short while, Fūrén arrived,
accompanied by over a thousand civil and military officials,
all women.
Fūrén appeared about twenty-odd years old,
dressed in a crimson frost robe,
with a three-cornered bun,
the rest of her hair hanging down to her waist.
She wore a crown of Nine Spirits and Nightglow,
a pendant of Six Origin Fire Jade,
a sash with phoenix patterns and Lin-Hua,
and a sword of Flowing Yellow and Glittering Essence at her waist.
The Five Natures.
Shàngyuán Fūrén (上元夫人) said to Dì (帝):
“Do you truly love the Dao (道)?
You frequently summon alchemists to climb mountains and sacrifice to gods,
which is indeed diligent.
However, your innate nature is violent,
your innate nature is lustful,
your innate nature is extravagant,
your innate nature is cruel,
your innate nature is treacherous.
These five (natures) constantly reside within your circulation
and inside your five viscera.
If from this day forward you abandon these five natures of yours,
and return to gentleness and kindness,
constantly perform hidden virtues,
and rescue those in mortal peril;
do not leak seminal fluid,
observe fasts and precepts, be diligent and frugal;
strike the celestial drum,
drink jade nectar,
cleanse the glorious pond,
and knock the golden bridge,
and practice these things,
you may then have hope.
Today, Āmǔ (阿母) takes the weighty chariot of the Great Dao (大道),
descending to the abode of the cicada,
bending the spiritual phoenix of the lofty void,
to visit the sacrificial table of a lone bird.
Exert yourself diligently!”
Lower-realm Corpse Release
Wángmǔ (王母) said:
“This child has been diligent for a long time,
but has not met a good teacher.
I am not at all reluctant
for him to achieve lower-realm corpse release.
However, the Xiōngnú (匈奴) are not yet subdued,
and there are matters on the frontier.
Why must he, while still in the prime of life, abandon the reverence of the world
and immediately enter the forests and mountains?
If he truly changes,
I will come often.”
True Forms of the Five Sacred Mountains Diagram
Dì (帝) saw a small scroll in Wángmǔ’s (王母) cloth box,
enclosed in a purple-gold pouch.
Dì (帝) begged to examine it.
Mǔ (母) said:
“This is the True Forms of the Five Sacred Mountains Diagram (Wǔyuè Zhēnxíng Tú, 五岳真形圖).
Yesterday, the immortals of Qīngchéng (青城)
came to me to request it.
It was issued by Sāntiān Tàishàng (三天太上),
and its text is secret and forbidden.
How can your defiled body be suitable to wear it?
For now, I will give you the Spiritual Master’s Scripture (Líng Xiānshēng Jīng, 靈先生經),
which can communicate with spirits.”
Dì (帝) kowtowed unceasingly.
Mǔ (母) said:
“I am pleased that you have such a heart.
I will now give it to you.”
Twelve Matters
Shàngyuán Fūrén (上元夫人) said:
“Āmǔ (阿母) has issued the Purple Terrace Text (Zǐtái zhī Wén, 紫臺之文)
and bestowed the Eight-fold Script (Bāhuì zhī Shū, 八會之書).
Although the True Forms of the Five Sacred Mountains (Wǔyuè Zhēnxíng, 五岳真形) reveal profound principles,
without the Talismans of Spiritual Flight (Língfēi zhī Fú, 靈飛之符) of the Five Emperors and Six Jiǎ (Wǔdì Liùjiǎ, 五帝六甲),
the Records of the Tàiyīn (太陰) Six Dīng (六丁) Jade Maidens (Yùnǚ, 玉女),
the Books of the Tàiyáng (太陽) Six Wù (六戊),
the Texts of the Left Yǐ (乙) Eastern Elephant (Dōngxiàng, 東象),
the Laws of the Right Gēng (庚) for Subduing and Slaying (Shèshā, 攝殺),
the Eight Arts of Yín (壬) and Guǐ (癸) for the Six Paths and Hidden Earth (Liùdào Yǐndì Bāshù, 六道隱地八術),
the Nine Red Stripe Talismans (Jiǔchì Bānfú, 九赤班符) of Bǐng (丙) and Dīng (丁) for Entering Fire,
the Methods of the Six Xīn (辛) Moon’s Radiance (Yuèhuá, 月華),
the Formulas of the Six Sì (巳) for Transformation (Huàxíng, 化形),
the Eight Bǐng (稟) and Ten Jué (決),
the Purple Book of Longevity (Chángshēng Zǐshū, 長生紫書),
and the Inner Zhen (內昣) Central Formulas (Zhōngfāng, 中方)—
a total of twelve matters—
how can one comprehensively control myriad spirits
and command hundreds of ghosts?”
Dì (帝) said:
“I wish to be granted instruction.”
Fūrén (夫人) said:
“The Young Lad Qīngzhēn (青真 Xiǎo Tóng) of Fúguǎng Shān (扶廣山)
possesses these golden books of secret characters.
He has told me their chapter titles.
You are fortunate; go search for them.”
Dì (帝) kowtowed and earnestly pleaded unceasingly.
Wángmǔ (王母) said:
“Since I have bestowed the complete true forms,
and Fūrén (夫人) has informed him of the twelve matters,
we should bring them to fruition for him.”
Fūrén (夫人) said:
“Āhuán (阿環) first learned the Dao (道) at the Hill of Guǎngdū (廣都之丘).
Dàojǐng Jūn (倒景君) and Wúcháng Xiānshēng (無常先生) taught her the twelve matters.
The two lords said:
‘A beginner in the Dao (道) hears it transmitted once every forty years;
one who attains the Dao (道) transmits it once every four hundred years;
one who attains immortality transmits it once every four thousand years;
one who attains truth transmits it once every forty thousand years.’
Since Āhuán (阿環) received the texts,
she has transmitted them to sixty-eight women in total,
but they cannot be given to a man.
The texts received by Young Lad Qīngzhēn (青真 Xiǎo Tóng) are the same.
Qīngzhēn (青真)
is a male official.”
Immediately, she ordered a maidservant to go to Fúguǎng Shān (扶廣山)
and command Qīngzhēn (青真) to bring the Six Jiǎ (Liùjiǎ, 六甲) Twelve Matters,
to bestow upon Liú Chè (劉徹).
A moment later, the maidservant returned,
holding an eight-colored jade casket and a phoenix-patterned pouch, saying:
“Disciple Āchāng (阿昌) has received your command.
The Golden Books of Secret Characters (Jīnshū Mìzì, 金書祕字), the twelve matters,
have each been sealed into one copy.
Āchāng (阿昌) has recently been near the emperor,
and has seen many refer to him as Liú Chè (劉徹).
Mountain ghosts weep in the thickets,
and lonely souls wail in foreign lands.
His lust and cruelty run wild,
and he will surely not transcend this world.
How can such arts be transmitted to a walking corpse?
However, the True Venerable One has commanded it,
and I dare not disobey.”
Wángmǔ (王母) smiled and said:
“This child is indeed very presumptuous.
However, one who loves the Dao (道) should be sincere, observe fasts and precepts,
correct oneself and return to goodness,
preserve the truth, and guard the One.
If this is practiced for one month,
it will remove the transgressions of one year.”
Shàngyuán Fūrén (上元夫人) left her seat and stood up,
holding the eight-colored casket to show Dì (帝).
Mǔ (母) said:
“If you turn away from evil and cultivate goodness,
come again three years and seven months later,
and I will tell you the essential Dao (道).”
Dōngfāng Shuò (東方朔) Peeping Through the Window
Someone was peeping from under the south window.
Dì (帝) was surprised and asked:
“Who is that?”
Wángmǔ (王母) said:
“That is your chamberlain, Dōngfāng Shuò (東方朔),
a young boy from my neighborhood.
He is very humorous by nature.
He has stolen peaches three times.
This child was formerly an immortal official of Tàishàng (太上).
Tàishàng (太上) ordered him to Fāngzhàng Shān (方丈山),
but he only indulged in games,
arbitrarily manipulated thunder and lightning,
stirred waves and raised winds,
causing dragons and water lizards to walk on land,
mountains to collapse, and seas to dry up.
Tàishàng (太上) banished him,
and made him dwell among humans.
Recently, two immortals from Jīnhuá Shān (金華山) and Chén Qǐ (陳乞), a man from Jiǔyí (九疑),
begged for his pardon.”
Dì (帝) then realized that Shuò (朔) was not an ordinary mortal.
Cloud Forest Zither
Shàngyuán Fūrén (上元夫人) played the Cloud Forest Zither (Yúnlín zhī Áo, 雲林之璈) herself,
and sang the Melody of Stepping into the Profound (Bùxuán zhī Qǔ, 步玄之曲).
Thereupon, the banquet, fueled by wine, concluded.
She and Wángmǔ (王母) rode off together.
Fāng Shuò (方朔) flew away on a dragon.
Dì (帝) then believed that there were indeed gods and immortals in the world,
yet he remained lustful and cruel by nature,
and his killings never ceased.
After receiving the texts for six years,
his mind became complacent.
He believed that since true gods had descended,
he would surely attain transcendence.
He erected terraces and pavilions,
exhausting the common people,
and in every matter, he failed to follow the profound words of Wángmǔ (王母) and the exquisite admonitions of Shàngyuán (上元).
The two true beings thus never came again.
In the second year of Tàichū (太初)
(103 BCE), the Bǎiliáng Tái (柏梁臺) suffered a fire.
The True Forms Diagram (Zhēnxíng Tú, 真形圖), the Six Jiǎ (Liùjiǎ, 六甲) Five Emperors Spiritual Flight Twelve Matters (Wǔdì Língfēi Shí'èr Shì, 五帝靈飛十二事),
and the Spiritual Radiance Living Scripture (Língguāng Shēng Jīng, 靈光生經)
were all burned and lost.
However, Dì (帝) had previously, following Wángmǔ’s (王母) words,
bestowed the Five Sacred Mountains Diagram (Wǔyuè Tú, 五岳圖) upon Dǒng Zhòngjūn (董仲君),
and also, following Shàngyuán Fūrén’s (上元夫人) words,
bestowed the Six Jiǎ (Liùjiǎ, 六甲) upon Lǐ Shǎojūn (李少君).
These two books thus circulated in the world.
After Dì (帝) burned the books,
he knew that he had lost the Dao (道).
Thereafter, Dōngfāng Shuò (東方朔) suddenly flew away on a dragon one day,
and Dì (帝) grew even more regretful.
Fire-patterned Mirror
During the time of Zhōu Mùwáng (周穆王),
the State of Qú (渠國) presented a fire-patterned mirror (huǒqí jìng, 火齊鏡) as tribute.
It was two chi and six cun in size.
When viewed in darkness, it was as bright as day.
If a person spoke towards the mirror,
the mirror would echo in response.
— From Shíyí Jì (拾遺記).
《Zhào Hòu Wài Zhuàn》 by Líng Xuán, Commandant of Hédōng in the Hàn dynasty.
Líng Xuán's courtesy name was Zǐyú.
He was learned in all things,
and skilled at writing.
His style was simple and valued naturalness.
Yáng Xióng alone recognized his talent.
Yáng Xióng was greedy for fame and overly passionate,
so Zǐyú declined to be friends with him.
Zǐyú served as an inspector and governor successively,
and was the Chancellor of Huáinán.
His comings and goings had a certain charm.
He bought a concubine, Fán Tōngdé,
and doted on her as a sister.
She had both talent and beauty,
and was knowledgeable in books.
She was quite eloquent in recounting the stories of the Fēiyàn sisters.
Zǐyú said:
“These people have all turned to dust.
When they were at their peak,
exhausting their energy in pursuits of desire and bewitchment,
how could they have known they would return to desolate fields and wild grass?”
Tōngdé pulled up her sleeves, looked at the candle's shadow, and used her hand to hold up her hairbun,
then, weeping, said:
“Infatuation with beauty is not something that happens to a wise man, unless he is truly wise.
If one is wise, one understands;
if one understands, one flows;
if one flows without finding its barrier,
then all things change their forms,
becoming ditches and hollows, going everywhere without restraint.
The doctrines of ritual and righteousness, of success and failure, cannot stop its flow.
Only by impressing upon it the idea of prosperity and decline can its corruption be prevented.
You are melancholy, touched by the sorrow of desolate fields and wild grass.
I, your maidservant, stroke my form and cling to my shadow;
even a Jiéyú, hearing this,
would not be unmoved, would she?
I hope my lord will write their biography,
and allow your maidservant to hold the inkstone and grind the ink,
and recount what is recorded.”
Thereupon, he compiled the 《Zhào Hòu Bié Zhuàn》.
The above is Líng Xuán’s self-preface.
Yízhǔ and Hédé
Féng Wànjīn was skilled in singing.
She served the Prince of Jiāngdū.
The prince's granddaughter married Zhào Màn, the Commandant of Jiāngdū.
Wànjīn also served Màn,
and consequently had an affair with the Princess.
Màn was ill and could not approach women.
The Princess became pregnant,
and, fearing discovery,
feigned illness and resided in the princely palace.
She gave birth to two daughters,
and gave them to Wànjīn.
The elder was named Yízhǔ,
and the younger Hédé.
They then falsely assumed the surname Zhào.
Yízhǔ was intelligent and astute.
Her family possessed the medical texts of Péngzǔ,
and she was skilled in Qì-cultivation techniques.
As she grew, she was slender and delicate,
her movements graceful,
and she was called Fēiyàn.
Hédé's skin was smooth,
remaining dry after a bath.
She was skilled in singing and discerning music.
Both were unparalleled beauties.
Xīnxīng Jì and Yōnglái Zhuāng
Fán Nì spoke to the Emperor,
praising Hédé’s beautiful appearance.
The Emperor summoned her into the palace.
Hédé had just bathed,
applied a nine-layered agarwood fragrance,
and styled her hair into a coiled bun,
called the Xīnxīng Jì;
she drew thin eyebrows,
called the Yuǎnshān Dài;
and applied a light red lipstick,
called the Yōnglái Zhuāng.
Those around her exclaimed in admiration.
During the reign of Emperor Xuān, the scholar of perfumes, Náo Fāngchéng,
who had white hair and taught in the palace,
was called Madam Náo by the palace residents.
Standing behind the Emperor, she spat and said:
“This is a water of calamity;
it will surely extinguish the fire.”
Yuǎntiáo Guǎn
The Emperor opened the Yuǎntiáo Guǎn for the Empress,
and bestowed upon her a purple velvet cloud-patterned canopy, a jade table, and a nine-layered red gold Bóshān incense burner.
Wēnróu Xiāng
The Emperor called Hédé Wēnróu Xiāng (Tender Home/Village),
saying:
“I will grow old in this home;
I cannot imitate Emperor Wǔ in seeking the Bái Yún Xiāng (White Cloud Home).”
Fán Nì congratulated him, saying:
“Your Majesty has truly found an immortal.”
Hédé was granted the title of Jiéyú.
Tuò Xiù (Spitting on the Sleeve)
The Empress and the Jiéyú were seated,
when the Empress accidentally spat on the Jiéyú's sleeve.
She said:
“My sister's saliva has stained your dark blue sleeve,
it truly resembles a flower on a rock.
Even if the Imperial Workshop were to make it,
they might not be able to achieve such a beautiful pattern on the clothing.”
This was called Shíhuá Guǎngxiù (Rock Flower Wide Sleeve).
Jiéyú Yìhù (Jiéyú's Protection)
The Empress had many affairs with imperial attendants and eunuchs who had many children.
The Jiéyú wholeheartedly protected her.
She often said to the Emperor:
“My sister's nature is strong,
she might be framed by others,
which would lead to the extinction of the Zhào clan.”
Each time, tears flowed sorrowfully.
Because of this, anyone who reported the Empress's illicit affairs
was immediately killed by the Emperor.
The Empress ultimately had no children.
Qī Xiāng Dòukòu Tāng
The Empress bathed in Wǔyùn Qīxiāng Tāng (Five Essences Seven Fragrances Bath).
The Jiéyú bathed in Dòukòu Tāng (Cardamom Bath).
The Emperor said:
“Though the Empress has a unique fragrance,
it is not as good as the Jiéyú's natural body fragrance.”
The Empress burned Jiàngshén Bǎiyùn Xiāng (Descending Spirit Hundred Essences Incense).
The Jiéyú applied Lùhuá Bǎiyīng Fěn (Dew Flower Hundred Blossoms Powder).
Wànnián Há and Bùyè Zhū
The kingdom of Zhēnlà presented Wànnián Há (Ten-Thousand-Year Clam) and Bùyè Zhū (Nightless Pearl).
Their radiance was like the moon,
making everyone beautiful, regardless of their original appearance.
The Emperor gave the clam to the Empress,
and the pearl to the Jiéyú, saying:
“When I see the Empress by day,
she is not as beautiful as you are when I see you by night.
And it makes one feel strangely lost.”
The Jiéyú immediately presented the Bùyè Zhū to the Empress as a birthday gift,
and never spoke of the Emperor's words.
Èrshíliù Wù (Twenty-Six Items)
When the Empress was first granted a higher title,
the Jiéyú presented twenty-six items to congratulate her:
one set of gold-flecked brocade patterned mats,
one agarwood lotus-heart bowl,
one sash with a five-colored concentric knot,
one bolt of Wànjīn brocade,
one glazed screen,
one Bùyè Zhū for the pillow,
one mat of fragrant musk-lined fur,
one fragrant tiger-patterned sandalwood elephant statue,
two dragon-scented fish-shaped hand-warmers,
one set of self-waving jeweled fans,
one jar of seven-layered glowing animal-fat hair oil,
three purple-gold bed-warming incense burners,
one plum-blossom mirror compact,
four gold finger rings,
one suit of crimson silk gauze clothing,
three pieces of patterned silk gauze hand-towels,
two pairs of patterned rhinoceros horn poison-detecting chopsticks,
and one green jade ointment box.
The Empress reciprocated with a five-layered cloud brocade canopy,
and an agarwood bath jar.
The Jiéyú complained to the Emperor, saying:
“If not for my noble sister's gift of death to me,
I would not have known about these items.”
The Emperor decreed that Yìzhōu should contribute taxes for three years,
to make a seven-layered brocade canopy for the Jiéyú,
and to decorate her chamber with agarwood.
Hégōng Zhī Zhōu (Boat of United Palaces)
The Emperor built a boat for a thousand people on the Tàiyè Pond,
named “Hégōng Zhī Zhōu.”
Rising from the Yíngzhōu pavilion,
the Empress sang the song “Guī Fēng Sòng Yuǎn” (Returning Wind Sending Afar).
The Emperor struck a jade bowl with rhinoceros horn chopsticks.
As the wine deepened and a wind arose,
the Empress unfurled her sleeves and exclaimed, “Immortal!
Immortal!
Leaving the old and embracing the new!”
The Emperor ordered his attendants to hold her skirt.
After a while,
the wind stopped,
and her skirt was wrinkled.
The Empress said:
“Your Majesty’s grace
prevented me from departing as an immortal.”
Later,
other palace women pleated their skirts into wrinkles,
calling them “Liúxiān Qún” (Immortal-Retaining Skirts).
The Jiéyú became even more favored,
and was granted the title of Zhāoyí.
Liúxiān Qún
See above.
Chìfèng (Red Phoenix) came for her sister
striking a jade bowl with chopsticks
The palace eunuch Yàn Chìfèng
whom the Empress secretly consorted with
was swift and agile, able to leap over pavilions.
He also consorted with the Zhāoyí.
On the fifth day of the tenth month,
it was customary in the palace to make offerings to the Língnǚ Shrine.
They played the xūn, beat drums,
and performed a group tàgē,
singing "The Song of the Vermilion Phoenix's Arrival" (Chìfènghuáng Lái Qǔ).
The Empress asked:
"For whom does the Vermilion Phoenix come?"
The Zhāoyí replied:
"The Vermilion Phoenix comes for you, elder sister;
would it come for anyone else?"
The Empress was enraged,
and threw a cup at the Zhāoyí's skirt, saying:
"Can a little mouse bite people?"
The Zhāoyí replied:
"If one's clothes are pierced,
and one's private parts are seen, that is enough;
where is the biting of people?"
The Zhāoyí had always served the Empress humbly,
and did not expect such a violent retort.
Fán Nì helped the Zhāoyí bow and weep, saying:
"Elder sister, have you forgotten the bitter cold of the long nights we shared a bed,
unable to sleep,
and how Hégé embraced your back?
Now that you are fortunate enough to be noble,
and there is no struggle outside,
how can you bear to fight amongst yourselves within?"
The Empress then took out a purple jade nine-chicks hairpin and placed it in the Zhāoyí's bun.
Then they stopped.
The Emperor vaguely heard of the incident
and questioned the Zhāoyí about it.
The Zhāoyí replied:
"The Empress is just jealous of me.
Given that the Hàn dynasty follows the Fire Element (huǒdé),
she therefore likens His Majesty to a vermilion phoenix."
The Emperor believed her,
and was greatly pleased.
Shàopín Guǎn (Pavilion of the Lesser Consort)
The Emperor built the Shàopín Guǎn for the Zhāoyí,
as well as the Lùhuá Diàn, Hánfēng Diàn, Bóchāng Diàn, Lái'ān Diàn,
and also the Wēnshì, Níngquē Shì, and Yùlán Shì.
The curved verandas were connected,
and the walls were adorned with gold and jade.
It connected to the Yuǎntiáo Guǎn,
and was named the Tōngxiān Mén.
Níshāng Yǔyī Qǔ (Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Robe Song)
In the fourth year of Tiānbǎo,
the palace woman and female Daoist of Tài Zhēn, Lady Yáng, was enfeoffed as Guìfēi,
wearing half the regalia of an Empress.
On the day of her first audience,
the "Níshāng Yǔyī Qǔ" was performed.
Note:
Liú Yǔxī's poem says:
"The Son of Heaven of Kāiyuán had everything he desired,
only regretting the fleeting swiftness of those times.
From the paths of Sānxiāng, he gazed at the Immortal Mountains,
and upon returning, composed the 'Níshāng Yǔyī Qǔ'.
From then on, his immortal heart was in the Jasper Pool,
the Sānqīng and Bājǐng accompanying him.
Suddenly, he rode away on white clouds in the heavens,
leaving behind only 'Autumn Wind' poems in the world."
According to the Yì Shǐ,
in the early autumn of Tiānbǎo,
Luó Gōngyuǎn said:
"Can Your Majesty follow your subject to tour the moon?"
He took a cassia branch and threw it into the air, forming a great bridge,
the color of white gold.
The Emperor ascended to the Moon Palace,
where hundreds of female immortals,
dressed in white,
danced gracefully in the vast courtyard.
The Emperor asked:
"What曲 is this?"
They replied:
"It is 'Níshāng Yǔyī'."
That evening,
he was presented with a golden hairpin and a gold-inlaid box,
a rùyì scepter to ward off summer heat,
a mica folding screen with flowers and dust-repelling incense,
a censer with dancing phoenixes emitting smoke,
a bracelet of smooth jade for connubial bliss,
a purple qióng cup,
and a bamboo mat with jade water patterns,
— and a white flower-patterned stone inkstone.
The Emperor also took a purple-gold double bàngyáo and personally inserted it into her hair bun,
happily saying:
"I have obtained the daughter of the Yáng family,
as if I have obtained a supreme treasure."
He composed a tune called "Débǎo Zǐ".
A Thousand Huàn of Powder and Jade
Seven years later,
Guìfēi's cousin, Guózhōng, was promoted to Yùshǐ Dàfū,
and Xiān Hónglú Qīng.
Her three sisters—Hánguó, Gúoguó, and Qínguó—all received
a thousand huàn of powder and jade annually.
Dù Fǔ's poem
Lady Gúoguó did not apply powder and makeup,
but possessed her own beauty and charm.
Dù Fǔ's poem says:
"Lady Gúoguó received imperial favor,
mounting her horse at dawn to enter the palace gates.
She disliked rouge and powder marring her complexion,
and with lightly swept moth-eyebrows, attended the Supreme One."
The Emperor bestowed a seven-treasure crown upon Gúoguó,
and a linked gold belt upon Guózhōng,
both rare treasures of their time.
Linked Gold Belt
Both mentioned above.
Secretly Playing the Jade Flute of Níng Wáng
Seven-treasure crown
Mínghuáng previously had five princes' tents set up,
for his brothers to reside in.
The Consort secretly played Níng Wáng's jade flute,
hence Zhāng Yòu's poem says:
"In the quiet courtyard of small flowers, unseen by anyone,
she idly played Níng Wáng's jade flute."
Because of this, she incurred imperial displeasure and was expelled.
The Consort wept and told the palace eunuch:
"My crime deserves ten thousand deaths.
Except for my clothes, all else was bestowed by Your Majesty's grace.
Only my hair and skin
came from my parents."
She drew a knife and cut off a lock of her hair, presenting it.
The Emperor immediately recalled her.
Do Not Grieve Over Bearing Daughters
On the Yuánxiao Festival of the tenth year,
the Yáng family's five households toured at night,
and in a procession with Princess Guǎngníng,
they contended over the West Market gate.
A servant of the Yáng family struck the Princess, causing her to fall from her horse.
The驸马 (Princess's husband) Chéng Chāngyì helped the Princess up,
and in turn received several blows.
The Princess tearfully reported it.
The Emperor ordered the Yáng family's servant to be executed,
and Chāngyì's official post was suspended.
Thereupon, the Yáng family became even more arrogant.
A popular rhyme at the time went:
"Do not grieve over bearing daughters;
do not rejoice over bearing sons."
It also said:
"Men are not enfeoffed as xiá, while women become consorts;
behold how women instead become the pillars of the family."
Zǐyún Huí (Return of Purple Clouds)
The Emperor once dreamed of more than ten仙子 (immortal maidens),
descending on auspicious clouds,
each holding a musical instrument.
An immortal said:
"This is the divine immortal tune 'Zǐyún Huí'.
We now bestow it upon Your Majesty,
as the music of true beginning."
Língbō Qǔ (Floating on Waves Tune)
The Emperor also dreamed of a beautiful maiden,
with a jiāoxīn jì hairstyle,
and wide sleeves and robes.
She said:
"I am the dragon maiden from Your Majesty's Língbō Pool.
I guard the palace and protect the imperial carriage;
I truly have rendered service.
Your Majesty thoroughly understands the music of Jūntiān;
I beg you to grant me a tune."
In the dream, he played the húqín for her, composing the "Língbō Qǔ".
Later, when the new tune was performed in Língbō Palace,
waves surged in the pool,
and a divine maiden emerged from the center of the pool;
it was the woman from his dream.
The Emperor then built a temple by the pool,
and sacrificed to her annually.
Xiè Āmán
Xiānfēng presented a female entertainer, Xiè Āmán,
who was skilled in dance.
The Emperor personally directed her in the Qīngyuán Diàn.
Níng Wáng played the flute,
the Emperor played the jiégǔ,
the Consort played the pípa,
Mǎ Xiānqī played the fāngxiǎng,
Lǐ Guīnián played the bìlì,
Zhāng Yěhú played the kōnghóu,
and Hè Huáizhì played the clappers.
Lady Qínguó sat properly observing.
The Emperor joked:
"Āmán, a courtesan,
is fortunate today to be able to perform for the Lady.
Please give her a缠头 (gift for entertainers)."
She replied:
"How can the aunt of the Great Táng Emperor have no money to spend?"
Thereupon, she produced three million coins for one performance.
Green Jade Chime
The imperial consort was skilled at playing the stone chimes.
The Emperor ordered Lántián green jade to be carved into chimes.
For her pípa, the consort used a dragon-incense wood board as a plectrum.
Peonies
During the Kāiyuán era,
the tree peony (mùsháoyào) was initially highly esteemed;
this is the modern-day peony (mǔdan).
When the flowers bloomed,
the Emperor rode Zhàoyèbái,
while the consort followed in a palanquin to the Chénxiāng Pavilion.
The Emperor commanded Lǐ Guīnián to carry a golden flowered paper document and proclaim an imperial bestowal upon Lǐ Bái,
who immediately composed three poems of the "Qīngpíng Diào."
The Emperor ordered Guīnián to sing,
while the consort held a seven-jeweled glass cup,
pouring grape wine from Xīliángzhōu.
After drinking,
she folded her embroidered kerchief and bowed twice.
Gāo Lìshì always felt humiliated by the incident of his shoes.
On another day,
the consort was reciting the previous poems again.
Lìshì said:
"I thought the consort resented Tàibái to the bone,
why then is she so devoted to these?"
The consort said:
"Which scholar could insult someone like that?"
Lìshì said:
"To liken the consort to Fēiyàn is extremely demeaning."
The Emperor had thrice intended to appoint Lǐ Bái to an official position,
but ultimately the palace's obstruction stopped it.
"Let the wind blow how much it may"
The Emperor was reading the "Hàn Wǔ Nèichuán."
The consort arrived later,
and with her hand adjusted the Emperor's collar, saying:
"What document are you reading?"
The Emperor smiled and said:
"Don't ask.
If you knew, you would again need to... ah."
She went to look for it,
and it was about Fēiyàn's lightness of body,
for whom a crystal tray was made,
on which palace women were ordered to sing and dance in her palm.
Also, a seven-jeweled wind-sheltering platform was made.
The Emperor said:
"Then you can let the wind blow how much it may."
This was because the consort was slightly plump.
The consort said:
"One tune of the 'Nícháng' can eclipse all of antiquity."
Crystal Screen
On a crystal screen, beauties of previous generations were carved,
about three inches tall.
The artifacts and ornaments were made with various precious jewels.
The consort bequeathed it to Guózhōng,
who placed it upstairs,
often resting beneath it.
One day,
all the women on the screen descended,
each stating her name:
The Woman by the Stove,
The Lotus-Stepping Woman,
The Feather-Plucking Woman,
The Golden House Woman,
The Jade-Dispensing Woman,
The Cloud-Transforming Woman,
The Eyebrow-Painting Woman,
The Perfume-Stealing Woman,
The Flute-Playing Woman,
Xǔ Fēiqióng,
The Golden Valley Woman,
The Silk-Tying Woman,
The Linchūn Woman.
There were also more than ten slender-waisted courtesans who said:
"We are the Zhānghuá 'Tàyáoniáng' of the Chǔ Palace."
And three more courtesans said:
"We are the slender-waisted women of the Chǔ Palace."
Then they performed their respective arts.
After presenting,
one by one they returned to the screen.
Guózhōng fled downstairs in fear,
and not long after, he indeed suffered defeat.
Harmonious Orange
Jiānglíng presented sweet mandarin oranges,
which the Emperor planted in Pēnglái Palace,
bearing one hundred and fifty fruits.
There was one fruit that was a "harmonious fruit."
The Emperor and the consort held it and admired it, saying:
"This fruit seems to know human intentions.
I and you are one body,
hence this harmony."
Snow-Clad Maiden
Guǎngnán presented a white parrot,
called the "Snow-Clad Maiden."
The consort taught it the "Mìduō Xīnjīng" (Prajñāpāramitāhṛdaya Sūtra),
which it recited skillfully and perfectly.
One day, it suddenly dreamed of being seized by a raptor.
When the Emperor and the consort were visiting a side palace,
they placed the Snow-Clad Maiden on a palanquin pole.
Suddenly an eagle seized and killed it.
It was buried in the imperial garden,
and called the "Parrot Mound."
Luminous Camel Messenger
Jiāozhǐ presented borneol incense,
which had the shape of cicadas and silkworms.
The Persians said
it was only found in the nodes of old borneol trees.
In the Forbidden City, it was called "Auspicious Dragon Borneol."
The consort secretly dispatched a Luminous Camel Messenger,
carrying three pieces to give to Ān Lùshān.
Luminous Camels
have hair under their eyes,
glow at night,
and can travel five hundred *lǐ* a day.
Proper Tower
In Huáqīng Palace, there was the Proper Tower,
which was the consort's dressing and washing place.
There was also the Lotus Flower Bath,
which was the consort's bathing room.
Lychee Fragrance
On Guìfēi's birthday,
the Emperor ordered the lesser musical troupe (xiǎobù yīnsheng) to perform a new song in the Chángshēng Palace.
It had no name yet.
Coincidentally, lychees arrived from the South Sea,
and so the song was named "Lychee Fragrance."
The lesser troupe
was an establishment of the Lírgyuán Fǎbù (Pear Garden Department of Music).
Weighing 350 Jīn
In his later years, Ān Lùshān became increasingly obese.
He weighed himself at 350 *jīn*.
Before the Emperor, he danced in circles like the wind.
The Emperor set up a large golden rooster screen at Qínzhèng Tower,
and placed a large couch,
ordering Lùshān to sit beneath it.
Sùzōng remonstrated:
"Throughout history, no minister has ever sat with the sovereign."
The Emperor said:
"He has an unusual appearance,
so I am trying to avert disaster."
Another time, during a night banquet,
Lùshān lay down
and transformed into a pig with a dragon's head.
His attendants immediately reported it.
The Emperor said:
"A pig-dragon
can do no harm."
He ultimately did not kill him,
and Lùshān eventually brought chaos to China.
"To perish along with the lady"
When Lùshān rebelled,
the Emperor wanted the crown prince to oversee the state
and personally lead the expedition.
Guózhōng was greatly afraid.
His sisters said:
"We will die within days.
Now if the Eastern Palace oversees the state,
we will perish along with the lady."
The sisters tearfully complained to the consort,
and the matter was thus stopped.
"Born in a good place"
When the Emperor traveled to Shǔ,
upon reaching Mǎwéi,
the soldiers killed Yáng Guózhōng.
The Emperor ordered Lìshì to give the consort death.
The consort wept and said:
"I wish everyone well!
I have indeed failed the nation's grace,
and have no regrets in death.
I beg permission to pay respects to the Buddha."
The Emperor said:
"May the consort be born in a good place."
Lìshì then strangled her beneath a pear tree in the Buddhist hall.
As soon as she died,
lychees from the south arrived.
The Emperor cried out mournfully
and ordered them to be offered to her.
The consort was thirty-eight years old at the time.
The Emperor said to Zhāng Yěhú:
"From here to Jiànmén,
birds crying, flowers falling,
water green, mountains blue—
none but adds to my sorrow and grief."
Daoist Priest's Poem
The geomancer Lǐ Xiá-zhōu (李遐周) first had a poem that said:
“In Yānshì (燕市) people all leave;
At Hánguān (函關) horses do not return.
If you meet a ghost below the mountain,
Tie a silk robe to its ring.”
“In Yānshì (燕市) people all leave,” refers to Lù Shān (祿山) taking all the soldiers from Jìmén (薊門) and coming.
“At Hánguān (函關) horses do not return,” refers to Gē Shū’s (哥舒) defeat at Tóngguān (潼關).
“Ghost below the mountain,” refers to Mǎwéi (馬嵬).
The imperial consort’s (妃) pet name was Yù-huán (玉環).
When she died,
the eunuch Lìshì (力士) strangled her with a silk scarf.
Furthermore, the consort often wore a wig as a head ornament,
and liked to wear yellow skirts.
A folk song at the end of the Tiānbǎo (天寶) era said:
“The ornamental wig is thrown into the river,
The yellow skirt flows with the water.”
This was fulfilled at this time.
“Rain on the Bells” (雨霖鈴曲)
Upon leaving Mǎwéi (馬嵬), the Emperor saw a pomegranate tree by the roadside.
He loved it,
and so called it the “Upright Tree” (端正樹),
for he had someone in mind.
When he arrived at Xié Valley (斜谷),
heavy rain lasted for over ten days.
On the plank road, he heard the sound of bells echoing from across the mountains.
The Emperor adopted its sound to compose the song “Rain on the Bells” (《雨霖鈴曲》),
to express his sorrow.
Brocade Sachet (錦香囊)
In the second year of Zhìdé (至德),
the Retired Emperor (上皇) returned from Chéngdū (成都).
He secretly ordered a palace eunuch to move the consort’s (妃) clandestine burial to another location.
When she was first buried,
she was wrapped in a purple blanket.
By this time,
her flesh had dissolved,
but a brocade sachet was still on her chest.
Pear Garden Disciples (梨園弟子)
The Retired Emperor (上皇) resided in the Nánhǎi (南海) inner palace.
One night, he ascended the Qínzhèng (勤政) Tower.
Smoke and moonlight filled his eyes,
and he sang:
“The jade tree in the courtyard is already ripe for climbing,
But the soldiers beyond the frontier have not yet returned.”
He faintly heard singing from within the neighborhood.
He looked at the eunuch Lìshì (力士) and said:
“Is that not an old Pear Garden performer?”
The next day,
Lìshì (力士) secretly summoned and questioned him.
He said:
“It was indeed a Pear Garden disciple.”
That night,
the Retired Emperor (上皇) and Hóng-táo (紅桃), a maid of the consort (妃), sang the “Liángzhōu (涼州) Song” composed by the consort.
The Emperor then expanded its melody.
Today, the version circulating in Liángzhōu (涼州) is even more extensive.
Carved Wood Pulled by Threads as an Old Man (刻木牽絲作老翁)
The Retired Emperor (上皇) again visited Huáqīng (華清) Palace.
Most of the accompanying officials and concubines were not the old ones.
Below the Wàngjīng (望京) Tower,
he ordered Zhāng Yě-hú (張野狐) to play the “Rain on the Bells” (《雨霖鈴》) melody.
The Emperor looked around at the cool and desolate surroundings.
From then on, the Emperor’s heart was deeply troubled.
He only recited: “Carved wood pulled by threads makes an old man,
Chicken skin and crane hair, just like the real thing.
Soon the dance ends, and there is nothing,
Just like a human life in a dream.”
Jade Consort Tàizhēn (太真) Court (玉妃太真院)
The alchemist Yáng Dào-yōu (楊道幽) claimed to possess the arts of Lǐ Shào-jūn (李少君).
The Retired Emperor (上皇) ordered him to summon the spirit of Guìfēi (貴妃).
He went out to the celestial realm,
and descended to the underworld,
but could not find her.
He crossed the vast Eastern Sea,
and traversed Pénghú (蓬壺),
where there was a cave entrance with a sign that read “Jade Consort Tàizhēn (太真) Court” (玉妃太真院).
A maid in green interrogated him about his origin.
The alchemist claimed to be an envoy of the Son of Heaven.
He was ushered in,
and the consort (妃) appeared,
wearing a golden lotus crown,
clad in purple gauze,
and trailing phoenix slippers.
She asked about the Emperor’s well-being.
She took a golden hairpin and a gold box, broke them in half, and said:
“This is for a reunion of our old affection.”
The alchemist requested an event from that time that was not known to others as proof,
otherwise he feared being accused of Xīn Yuán-píng’s (新垣平) deception.
The consort (妃) said:
“At the Qīxī (七夕) festival in Líshān (驪山) Palace,
the Emperor was moved by the story of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl,
and we secretly swore an oath in our hearts,
wishing to be husband and wife for generations.
This is known only to the Emperor.”
She then said with self-pity:
“Because of this single thought,
I cannot remain here either,
I will descend to the lower realm,
and conclude our next缘.
Whether as a god,
or as a human,
we will definitely meet again.
The Retired Emperor (上皇) will also not stay long in the human world.
I hope he will take good care of himself,
and not suffer needlessly.”
Cherry Sugarcane Juice (櫻桃蔗漿)
The Retired Emperor (上皇) moved into the Dànèi (大內) Palace.
He daily mourned the consort (妃子).
Empress Zhāng (張后) presented cherry sugarcane juice,
but he did not eat any.
He often played a purple jade flute.
After a few notes, a pair of cranes descended into the courtyard,
circled, and then left.
The Retired Emperor (上皇) said:
“I have received the command of the Supreme Deity (上帝) to become Yuánshǐ Kǒngshēng Zhēnrén (元始孔昇真人).
This is the time I can reunite with the consort (妃子).
The flute can be given to Dà-mù (大牧).”
Dà-mù (大牧)
was Dàizōng’s (代宗) pet name.
He immediately ordered a bath to be prepared,
saying:
“When I go to sleep,
be careful not to disturb me.”
Soon, a sound was heard in his sleep,
and he had already passed away.
Brocade Socks (錦襪)
An old woman at Mǎwéi (馬嵬) obtained a pair of brocade socks.
Each traveler who viewed them paid a hundred coins,
and she subsequently acquired countless coins.
Consort’s Dropped Pond (落妃池)
Guìfēi (貴妃) was born in Shǔ (蜀).
She once accidentally fell into a pond.
Later generations called it “Consort’s Dropped Pond” (落妃池).
Pearls and Kingfisher Feathers Could Be Swept (珠翠可掃)
The Emperor ordered palace dancers to wear jeweled necklaces,
and dance the “Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Robe” (《霓裳羽衣曲》).
When the music ended,
pearls and kingfisher feathers could be swept from the ground.
Bird Craftsman Departs (鳥工往)
Gǔsǒu (瞽叟) ordered Shùn (舜) to plaster the granary.
Shùn (舜) told his two wives:
“Should I go?”
His two wives said:
“Go!
A bird craftsman will repair your clothes and depart.”
He employed the skill of birds flying to go,
the meaning of "鹊" (què, magpie) is wrong here.
Upon his return,
Gǔsǒu (瞽叟) ordered Shùn (舜) to dredge the well.
Shùn (舜) told his two wives:
“Should I go?”
His two wives said:
“Take off your clothes, a dragon craftsman will go.”
Dragons know the pulse and patterns of water springs.
Prenatal Education (胎教)
When Dà-rèn (大任) was pregnant with King Wén (文王),
her eyes did not look at evil colors,
her ears did not listen to evil sounds,
her mouth did not utter evil words.
She was able to practice prenatal education.
A Woman Has No Two Heavens (婦人無二天)
Before a woman marries,
she considers her parents her heaven.
Once married,
she considers her husband her heaven.
When her parents die,
she lowers her mourning attire by one grade,
which reflects the principle of having no two heavens.
Liǔ Xià-huì’s (柳下惠) Eulogy (柳下惠誄)
Liǔ Xià-huì’s (柳下惠) wife composed a eulogy for her husband.
His disciples could not change a single word.
Mother Shī-lǔ (母師魯)
was the widowed mother of nine sons.
Duke Mù (穆公) bestowed upon her the title “Mother Shī” (母師).
Qú Bó-yù’s (蘧伯玉) Carriage Sound (蘧伯玉車聲)
Lady of Duke Líng (靈公) of Wèi (衛) heard the sound of a carriage approaching at night.
She said:
“This must be Qú Bó-yù (蘧伯玉).”
The Duke playfully said:
“It is not.”
The Lady congratulated him, saying:
“Previously, I alone thought Wèi (衛) had only Bó-yù (伯玉).
Now there is another who equals him,
this means you have two virtuous men,
which is why I congratulate you.”
The Duke was greatly pleased,
and then told her the truth.
Nǚzōng
Sòng Bāosū's wife was not jealous.
Dù. Duke Sòng proclaimed their neighborhood "Nǚzōng."
Neighboring States with Shared Walls
Zāng Wénzhòng's mother said:
"Lǔ and Qí
are neighboring states with shared walls."
End of Juàn zhī Yī.
When Kǒngzǐ praised and promoted hermits, the world submitted to him.
Hóngyá Xiānshēng achieved greatness in the era of the Shànghuáng.
Xǔ Yóu and Shàn Juàn did not condescend to serve in the court of Táng Yú.
The Yì has the ceremony of bundles of silk,
the Lǐ has the system of black and crimson silk,
the poets composed the song of the white colt,
and the Chūnqiū showcased Zǐzāng's integrity.
Therefore, the Yuèyáng stipulated that in the last month of spring, renowned scholars should be invited,
and worthy individuals should be honored.
Thus, gentlemen who valued loftiness and humility
were prioritized by royal governance.
Shǐ Bān's writings
were often incomplete.
Liáng Hóng extolled hermits,
Sū Shùn narrated about noble scholars,
but some of them recorded those who compromised their integrity,
making it mixed and impure.
Furthermore, they were close to the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
and did not extend to ancient times.
If one thinks of the person, one still loves their tree;
how much more so when praising their virtue and verifying their deeds?
Mì collected information on gentlemen from ancient and modern times,
whose persons were not subservient to kings and dukes,
whose names did not fade with the passage of time.
From Yuán Yáo to Wèi,
there were over ninety people.
Even those whose integrity and righteousness were equal,
whose comings and goings were like the two Gōngs,
were not recorded.
Preface.
Jiǔlóng Jǐng
Lǐ Ěr composed over five thousand words,
becoming the patriarch of the Daoist school.
Because he wrote a book in his old age,
his work was titled Lǎozǐ.
In Bózhōu, south of the palace, is Jiǔlóng Jǐng.
In front of the well is the Shēngxiān Guì and Lǎojūn Liàndān Jǐng.
North of the well is Xūwú Táng,
where the Dàodé Jīng is carved on a stone wall.
After Xiántōng,
for nearly fifty years, there were wars,
yet there was no burning or destruction.
This was Lǎojūn's spiritual response.
Duke Huán's Five Visits
Xiǎochén Jì was someone Duke Huán visited three times but could not see.
The Duke sighed, saying:
"A commoner."
Thus, he went five times,
and finally managed to see him.
Soot Falls into the Rice
Yán Huí.
When Kǒngzǐ was without provisions,
Zǐgòng informed a countryman,
and obtained one shí of rice.
It was cooked in a dilapidated house.
Soot fell into the rice,
and Huí took and ate it.
Zǐgòng suspected Huí of stealing food.
He went in and asked Kǒngzǐ:
"Do benevolent and honest gentlemen
change their principles when in distress?"
The Master said:
"If they changed their principles,
how could they be called benevolent and honest?"
Zǐgòng then told the Master about Huí eating the rice.
The Master summoned Huí and said:
"Last night I dreamt of my ancestors cooking rice.
I intended to offer it as a sacrifice."
Huí replied:
"Soot fell into the rice.
I wanted to leave it, but it was unclean;
I wanted to throw it away, but it was a pity.
So, Huí ate it.
It cannot be offered as a sacrifice."
After Huí left,
Kǒngzǐ said:
"My trust in Huí is not just from today.
What I trust is my eyes,
but even eyes cannot be entirely trusted.
What I rely on is my heart,
but even the heart cannot be entirely relied upon.
My disciples, remember this:
knowing people is indeed not easy."
The Grand Historian says that Huí died young at twenty-nine, with white hair.
Only Jiāyǔ says thirty-two years old.
If twenty-nine,
it would be the seventh year of Dìnggōng,
fourteen years after the hardship in Chén.
Huí had not yet died then.
Therefore, Jiāyǔ should be considered correct.
Deep Wheel Marks Outside the Gate
Lù Tōng, courtesy name Jiēyú.
The King of Chǔ sent an envoy to invite him, saying:
"I request that you govern Jiāngnán."
Tōng laughed and agreed.
His wife came from the market
and asked:
"Why are the wheel marks outside our gate so deep?"
Tōng said:
"The king sent an envoy with a hundred yì of gold,
ordering me to govern Jiāngnán."
His wife said:
"Your concubine serves you, sir.
I personally farm for food,
and personally embroider for clothes.
We act according to righteousness,
and our joy is already sufficient.
Now, if we accept heavy emoluments from others,
ride their fine four-horse carriages,
and eat their rich and fatty foods,
how shall we respond to this?"
Tōng said:
"I have not agreed."
His wife said:
"To not obey the ruler is disloyal;
to obey him
violates righteousness.
It is better to leave."
Therefore, they changed their names,
traveled to famous mountains,
ate mushrooms and wild fruits,
and consumed huángjīng.
They lived in reclusion on Mount Éméi in Shǔ,
living for several hundred years.
Locals commonly believed them to be immortals.
The Comfort of a Space for the Knees, the Taste of One Piece of Meat
Chén Zhòngzǐ, courtesy name Zǐzhōng.
The King of Chǔ sent an envoy with a hundred yì of gold to invite him to be prime minister.
Zhòngzǐ said:
"I have a humble wife;
please allow me to go in and consult with her."
Then he said to his wife:
"Today I become prime minister,
tomorrow I will have a team of four horses, a string of riders,
and a table full of food before me."
His wife said:
"With a qín on the left and books on the right,
joy is found therein.
Even with a thousand carriages in a string,
the comfort is no more than a space for the knees;
with a table full of food before one,
the sweetness is no more than one piece of meat.
Now, for the comfort of a space for the knees
and the taste of one piece of meat,
one bears the worries of the state of Chǔ.
In troubled times, there is much harm;
I fear, sir, you may not preserve your life."
Zhòngzǐ and his wife fled,
and became gardeners for others.
Tilting His Quilt
Qián Lóu xiānshēng 先生 passed away.
Zēng Xī 曾西 came to offer condolences.
He saw the corpse beneath the window,
covered with a cloth quilt,
but it did not completely cover his hands and feet.
If the head was covered, the feet were exposed;
if the feet were covered, the head was exposed.
Zēng Xī 曾西 said:
“If you lay the quilt diagonally, it will cover him entirely.”
His wife said:
“Though laying it diagonally might provide a surplus,
it is not as good as the insufficiency of laying it straight.
My husband lived without being crooked;
to lay him crooked in death
is not his intention.”
Zēng Xī 曾西 asked:
“What will be his posthumous name?”
His wife replied:
“Kāng 康.”
Zēng Xī 曾西 said:
“When your husband was alive,
he never ate his fill,
and his clothes did not cover his body.
How can he be given the posthumous name Kāng 康 (peaceful, healthy)?”
His wife replied:
“In the past, my husband,
when the ruler wished to employ him as prime minister of the state,
declined and did not accept;
this shows he had a surplus of honor.
When the ruler bestowed grain, he declined to accept;
this shows he had a surplus of wealth.
He found the blandest tastes in the world sweet,
and was content with the lowest positions in the world.
To give him the posthumous name Kāng 康,
is it not appropriate?”
The Four Whiteheads Composed a Song
The Four Whiteheads (Sì Hào 四皓) saw that Qín Zhèng 秦政’s rule was tyrannical,
so they fled into Lántián Shān 藍田山
and composed a song which said:
“Vast, vast high mountains,
deep valleys winding.
Bright, bright purple ganoderma,
can relieve hunger.
The era of Táng Yú 唐虞 is far off,
where shall I return?
Four-horse carriages with high covers,
their worries are very great.
The fear that wealth and honor bring,
is not as good as being poor and humble and following one’s will.”
Then they entered Shāngluò Shān 商洛山
to await the world to be settled.
Qīan Jūshì 岍居士
Zhì Jùn 摯峻, courtesy name Bólíng 伯陵,
lived in seclusion on Qīan Shān 岍山.
Sīmǎ Qiān 司馬遷 sent a letter saying:
“The highest is to establish virtue,
next is to establish meritorious deeds,
next is to establish words.
I humbly believe your talent surpasses others,
your ambition is noble,
you are as pure as ice and jade,
and you do not allow trivial matters to tarnish your name.
However, you have not yet fully achieved what is meant by the highest (i.e., establishing virtue).”
Zhì Jùn 摯峻 replied:
“A gentleman acts after estimating his capabilities,
and dwells after assessing his virtue;
thus, regret is kept far from him.
Benefits cannot be received in vain,
and fame cannot be maintained falsely.
Since the rise of the Hàn 漢 dynasty,
the way of emperors and kings has begun to manifest.
Those capable see the benefits,
while the unworthy withdraw themselves.
This is also the right time.”
From then on, the two followed their own desires.
Sīmǎ Qiān 司馬遷 indeed suffered humiliation due to regret.
Zhì Jùn 摯峻 died on Qīan Shān 岍山,
and the people of Qīan 岍 built a shrine for him,
calling him Qīan Jūshì 岍居士.
My Sickness is My Ear, Not My Insufficiency
Yán Zūn 嚴遵,
courtesy name Jūnpíng 君平,
sold divinations in the city.
There was a rich man in Shǔ 蜀, Luó Chōng 羅沖,
who asked him why he did not enter officialdom.
Yán Zūn 嚴遵 replied:
“I have no means to promote myself.”
Luó Chōng 羅沖 provided him with a carriage, horses, clothes, and provisions.
Yán Zūn 嚴遵 said:
“My sickness is my ear,
not my insufficiency.
I have a surplus, while you have an insufficiency.
How can one who has an insufficiency serve one who has a surplus?”
Luó Chōng 羅沖 said:
“I have ten thousand gold pieces,
while you have not even a single dàn shí 擔石 (a small measure of grain).
Yet you say you have a surplus.
Is this not absurd?”
Yán Zūn 嚴遵 said:
“Not so.
I stayed at your house the night before last.
When people had settled down for the night, your servants had not yet rested;
day and night they toiled,
never having enough.
Now, I make a living by divination.
Without leaving my bed, money arrives,
and I still have several hundred in surplus,
with dust an inch thick (on them),
not knowing what to use them for.
Is this not that I have a surplus and you have an insufficiency?”
Luó Chōng 羅沖 was greatly ashamed.
Yán Zūn 嚴遵 sighed:
“What increases my wealth harms my spirit;
what creates my fame kills my body.”
He never entered officialdom.
Jūnfáng 君房 is Always Foolish
Yán Guāng 嚴光.
Shìzǔ 世祖 (Emperor Guāngwǔ 光武) invited him with an anzhē 安車 (a comfortable carriage).
Hóu Bà 侯霸 sent his aide Hóu Zǐdào 侯子道 to deliver a letter.
Hóu Bà 侯霸 instructed Hóu Zǐdào 侯子道, saying:
“Zǐlíng 子陵 (Yán Guāng 嚴光) is always lofty and superior,
so you should humble yourself before him.”
Yán Guāng 嚴光 opened the letter
and said:
“Jūnfáng 君房 (Hóu Bà 侯霸) has always been foolish.
Now he is one of the Three Ducal Ministers.
Is he a little better or worse?”
Hóu Zǐdào 侯子道 replied:
“His position is like the legs of a tripod (i.e., one of the highest);
he is not foolish.”
Hóu Zǐdào 侯子道 said:
“His Excellency (Hóu Bà 侯霸) heard that you, Sir, had arrived
and immediately wished to visit.
He was constrained by his official duties,
which is why he could not.”
Yán Guāng 嚴光 said:
“You say he is not foolish.
Are these not foolish words?
The Son of Heaven has summoned me three times.
The sovereign has not yet seen me,
let alone his minister?
My hand cannot write.”
He gave a wooden tablet from the side of his bed to Hóu Zǐdào 侯子道 to engrave the reply.
Yán Guāng 嚴光 dictated a few words,
and Hóu Zǐdào 侯子道 said:
“Why is the letter so short?
It could be lengthened.”
Yán Guāng 嚴光 said:
“How can it be lengthened?”
Crossing the Sea and Encountering a Storm
Guǎn Níng 管寧 encountered a storm while crossing the sea.
All his companions drowned,
but Guǎn Níng’s 管寧’s boat alone survived.
Everyone said it was due to his accumulated good deeds.
One Gourd
Xǔ Yóu 許由 lived on Jī Shān 箕山.
He had only one gourd for drawing water,
which he hung on a tree branch.
The wind blew the gourd, making it rattle,
which he found annoying,
so he threw it away.
The Hermit’s Straw Sandals
Zhū Táo 朱桃, a hermit from Shǔ 蜀, made his living by making straw sandals.
He placed his sandals at the corner of a road.
People recognized them and said:
“These are Jūshì Zhū’s 居士朱 (Hermit Zhū) sandals.”
They would exchange them for rice and take them away.
A Hundred-Patched Robe
Dǒng Wēi 董威 resided in Luòyáng 洛陽,
living in seclusion at Báishè 白社.
He made his clothes from remnants of floss and silk threads,
which were called “a hundred-patched robe” (bǎi jié yī 百結衣).
Girls’ Faces are Seared
In Zhāojūn Cūn 昭君村, even today, if a girl is born, her face must be seared.
Bái Lètiān’s 白樂天 poem says:
“To this day, the village girls’ faces
are burned and form scars.”
Lice entered a pigsty
and discussed choosing food, saying:
“A fat pig will not last through the twelfth lunar month.”
They then proceeded to eat the skinny ones.
Spirit Becoming Ganoderma
King Xiāng of Chǔ 楚襄王 journeyed to Yúnmèng 雲夢.
He dreamed of a woman,
named Yáo Jī 瑤姬,
who said:
“I am
the youngest daughter of Xià Dì 夏帝.
I was enfeoffed on Yángtái 陽臺 of Wū Shān 巫山.
My spirit has become ganoderma.
If you charm and consume it,
then we will meet in dreams.”
Qiānyáng Tán
There is a Qiānyáng Tán in Xiāngyáng.
When the Cìshǐ first arrived,
they would certainly lead a sheep to circle the altar,
using the number of times it circled to predict the years of their governorship in the prefecture.
When Jìn Wéndì was the Cìshǐ,
he circled six times and did not stop.
Someone forcefully stopped him.
Indeed, he was transferred after eight years.
Zhú Yīng
Jūshì Xīn Xuānzhòng cut bamboo to make a vessel (yīng) for serving wine.
He said:
“I am very fond of bamboo and wine by nature.
I wish for these two things to be together.”
Chátóu Suōxiàng Biān
The bream (biān) fish in the Hànshuǐ river are very delicious.
People were often forbidden from catching them.
Logs (chá) were used to block the water,
hence they were called Chátóu Biān.
When Sòng Zhāng Jìng'ér was the Cìshǐ,
he made a six-oared boat and presented it to Qí Gāodì, saying:
“I respectfully offer one thousand eight hundred Chátóu Suōxiàng Biān.”
Yù Jìng Yù Jī
In the Jiàn​yuán era of Qí,
robbers plundered the tomb of the King of Chǔ,
obtaining a jade mirror (yù jìng) and jade clogs (yù jī).
They also found ancient books,
bound with green silk slips.
Hūyīng Tái
When Liú Biǎo was the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu,
he built Hūyīng Tái,
and composed the song "Yě Yīng Lái".
Lóng Zhǒng Lái Guī
When Páng Huàn resigned from office and returned to his hometown,
the villagers said:
“The dragon's offspring (lóng zhǒng) in our pond has returned.”
Qiāntóu Mù Nú
Lǐ Héng built a residence
and planted a thousand orange trees.
Before his death, he instructed his son, saying:
“I have a thousand wooden slaves (mù nú),
so you can avoid poverty.”
Bài Páng Dé
Zhūgě Liàng bowed to Páng Dégōng from beneath the bed.
The Duke, however, did not allow him to stop.
Sāngōng Fēng
At Cén Shān,
the three eastern peaks are named Sāngōng,
the nine western mountains are named Jiǔqīng,
and the next mountain is named Zhǔbù.
Guāngài Shān
At the end of the Hàn dynasty, there were four Jùnshǒu, seven Dōuwèi, two Qīng, two Shìzhōng, one Huángmén Shìláng, three Shàngshū, and six Cìshǐ.
Their vermillion carriages and lofty canopies (zhū xuān gāo gài) gathered at the foot of the mountain,
hence their village was named Guāngài Lǐ,
and the mountain was named Guāngài Shān.
Qīngqīng Dōngmén Liǔ
Mì was intelligent and quick-witted in his youth.
He wrote a poem to satirize Yáng Guózhōng, saying:
“Green, green the willows at the eastern gate;
when the year ends, they must wither.”
Guózhōng complained to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
“If a poem about willows is to satirize you,
then a poem about plums (Lǐ) would satirize me.
Is that acceptable?”
Dézōng Dāněr Lóng
When Mínghuáng fled to Shǔ,
Dézōng was fifteen years old.
An elder said:
“The Crown Prince (Tàisūn) is a Dāněr Lóng;
why fear the bandits?”
Liùhé Dàtóng Yìn
When Sùzōng was in Língwǔ, he cast a seal to summon troops.
Its inscription read “Liùhé Dàtóng” (Great Unity of the Six Harmonies).
Zhěn Tiānzǐ Xī Shuì
Mì said to Sùzōng:
“Your servant abstains from grain and has no home.
Rank and emolument, and even territory (máotǔ) are not what I desire.
After recovering the capital,
I only wish to sleep a nap with my head on the Son of Heaven’s lap (zhěn tiānzǐ xī shuì),
and have the officials report that a 'guest star has trespassed on the Emperor's seat' (kè xīng fàn dì zuò).
A single astrological omen (tiānwén) will suffice.”
Wǔ Bù Kě Zhù
After Sùzōng returned to the capital,
Mì resigned and left,
saying:
“Your servant has five reasons why he cannot stay:
Your servant met Your Majesty too early, Your Majesty used your servant too heavily,
the grace is too deep,
the merit is too high, and the traces are too extraordinary.”
He strongly insisted on leaving,
and indeed left.
Xiāng’àn Qián Zòushì
Mì lay beside Sùzōng, separated by a brazier,
earnestly requesting to retire,
saying:
“Today, Your Majesty considers separation by a brazier to be far,
so I cannot make my request now.
On another day, when I present memorials before the incense table (xiāng’àn qián zòushì),
how could I possibly get my wish?”
Chá Shī
The imperial grandson, Fèngjié Wáng, brewed tea,
adding butter, pepper, and the like.
He asked Mì to compose a poem.
Mì said:
“The swirling foam turns into a jade-green pond;
added butter scatters to form agate eyes.”
Fèngjié Wáng was indeed Dézōng.
Duānjū Shì
Mì received permission to live in seclusion on Mount Héng.
An imperial decree ordered the construction of a Duānjū Shì (Room of Serene Dwelling) at his residence.
Suǒzǐ Gǔ
When Mì was young, his body was extremely light;
he could walk on a screen and stand on an incense burner.
A strange person said:
“This child will certainly ascend (shēngténg) at fifteen.”
His parents feared this.
Suddenly, they smelled an unusual fragrance in the air,
and poured garlic juice to prevent him from flying away.
When he grew up,
he practiced辟榖 (bìgǔ, abstaining from grains).
Whenever he performed Dǎoyǐn (Daoist exercises),
his bones and joints rattled (shānrán).
People called this Suǒzǐ Gǔ (chain bones).
Bāgōng Shī
There were eight reclusive scholars,
whose attire was very unusual.
They visited Mì for several days,
speaking exhaustively about matters of immortals and spirits.
Before leaving,
they sighed:
“Worldly ties are ultimately not exhausted;
it is a pity for his heart and bones.”
Mì requested to go with them.
They said:
“No,
you must serve as prime minister (xiàng) for ten more years.”
They went out the door and were never seen again.
Thus, he composed the Bāgōng Shī to record this event.
It is also unknown whether they were true immortals
or mountain spirits.
Hán Nèi Hēishí
A recluse came with a boy of six or seven,
saying:
“I have a reason;
I must travel south.
This boy has dysentery.
Since we are both fellow Daoists,
I wish to entrust him to you.”
He then left a box (hánzi) and said:
“If he does not recover from his illness,
bury him with this.”
He then asked the boy:
“Bùjiāo,
is it acceptable to stay here?”
The boy said:
“Yes.”
Then he left.
After eight or nine days, the boy died.
He was buried in the courtyard beneath a rose trellis, placed in the box.
After several months,
the person did not return.
They tried to open the box;
there was only a black stone,
square in shape,
with characters like chisel marks on it, saying:
“The true divine has not yet completed the years of refining his form,
transformed into my son, his功 (gōng) continues.
The Prime Minister buried him with inscribed black jade;
how long is the immortal path, how short is death!”
Hòu Zhào Yǐ Yín Wéi Xìn
Later, he was summoned, and silver was used as a token.
Dài Zōng wanted to appoint Mì as chancellor.
Yuán Zǎi ordered his partisans to slander and obstruct him in every way.
The Emperor had no choice but
to send Mì out as the Judge of Jiāngxī Circuit.
He said:
“When I summon you again, I will use a silver token as a sign of trust.”
Later, Lù Sìgōng replaced Wèi Shàoyóu as the Commissioner of Jiāngxī Circuit.
Zǎi wrote a letter to Lù saying:
“Do not let Mì be in the south,
nor let him be in the north.”
Lù then memorialized to appoint Mì as the Deputy Prefect of Qiánzhōu.
The following spring,
an imperial edict was issued,
appointing him as Silver-Green Grand Master of Guanglu.
Upon seeing him,
the Emperor was extremely pleased and
said:
“I have been separated from you for eight years.
Only now have I been able to deal with this villain,
and I almost fell for his scheme.
To see you again,
what comfort could compare?
Thanks to the crown prince's benevolence and filial piety,
who exposed his plot;
otherwise,
I would not have been able to see you again.”
Mì replied:
“Last year, I already memorialized that
if the great ministers or Your Majesty thought it was unacceptable,
he should be removed.
However, due to the need for certain matters, the villain was overly tolerated,
allowing his wickedness to reach this point.”
The Emperor said:
“Do you know that all officials above the third rank are villains?”
And he personally instructed you before leaving,
yet he took Zǎi's intention and memorialized to appoint you as Deputy Prefect of Qiánzhōu,
claiming that you desired it.
His deception of me was like this.
Moreover, when Lingnán was pacified,
a nàolì plate,
nine inches wide, was presented.
I considered it a treasure.
But when Zǎi's house was raided,
one a foot wide was found,
which was what he had kept.
If he is not a villain, then what is he?”
Gate Masters
During the Táng dynasty, when transporting grain by river,
from Jí Jīn Shàng to Sānmén,
each raft of boatmen pulled one boat,
and hundreds of people from nearby were hired to tow it.
The river flowed like a rushing arrow,
and Sānmén often had waves.
Fewer than one or two hundred boats could pass daily.
If a boat struck a hidden rock,
it would shatter into pieces
and be swept into the whirlpool,
never to be seen again.
The pole-workers who navigated the Sānmén upstream
were called 'Gate Masters' (ménjiàng),
and they were all commoners from the plains.
They held a staff and gestured,
and with the sound of wind and water,
people's voices could not be heard.
People from Shǎnxi said:
“From ancient times, there has been no tomb of a Gate Master.”
Meaning they all drowned.
Therefore, below Sānmén,
there are mountains in the river named Mǐduī and Gǔduī.
Whenever a raft passed Sānmén upstream,
without damage,
it still took nearly a hundred days to complete.
This is why water transport was so difficult.
Drunkard as an Auspicious Omen
When Dézōng was displaced,
many people lacked food,
and no one brewed wine.
Later, when the capital became somewhat peaceful,
there was a drunkard,
and people gathered to watch, considering it an auspicious omen.
Chancellors Cannot Divide Their Duties
After Dézōng appointed Mì as chancellor,
he ordered him to divide duties with his colleagues.
Mì said:
“Chancellors govern affairs on behalf of Heaven,
and the duty of assisting the emperor
cannot be divided.
As for the imperial secretaries and attendants, they divide their duties and oversee matters.
Thus, the imperial secretaries are called 'Six-Oversight Peacemakers.'
Matters should be handled jointly.
If each manages his own department,
then they are mere department officials,
how can they be called chancellors?”
The Emperor agreed.
The Reign Title Zhēnyuán
Dézōng initially discussed changing the reign title.
The Emperor said to Mì:
“The prosperity of our dynasty
was unsurpassed by Zhēnguān and Kāiyuán;
let's take one character from each.”
So, the reign title was changed to Zhēnyuán.
Langguan Rode Shu Horses, Yí Bǔ Rode Donkeys
Dézōng listened to Mì's advice
and first increased the stipends for all officials.
Initially,
in the capital, those who rode large horses in the streets
were recognized by passersby by their status.
They were officials from the imperial secretaries, attendants, secretaries, langguān, grand ministers, and censors upwards;
otherwise, they were noblemen or sons of regional commanders.
The langguān all rode Shu horses,
while the yíbǔ sometimes rode donkeys.
Two months after the increase in stipends,
all langguān rode large horses and even had escort horses.
Lǐ Shèng's Merits Differed from Guō Zǐyí's
Initially,
Lǐ Shèng was about to establish an ancestral temple.
According to regulations, officials of the second rank and above worshipped four temples; those with named enfeoffments worshipped five temples;
those of the fifth rank and above worshipped three temples;
and those of the third rank and above did not need to hold concurrent titles.
At that time, Mì believed that four temples were not in line with ancient practice,
and that there were distinctions in rites.
The Son of Heaven had seven temples,
and feudal lords had five temples;
this was the ancient system.
The Emperor permitted the establishment of five chambers,
but only for worshipping four generations,
leaving the chamber for the founder empty,
awaiting a fifth-generation descendant to worship and move out previous ancestors,
then Lǐ Shèng could be regarded as the founder whose chamber would not be moved out.
The intention was to allow meritorious officials to have a long-term plan.
Mǎ Suì said:
“Grand Mentor Guō also only established four temples.”
Mì said:
“Lǐ Shèng's merits differed from Guō Zǐyí's.
During the recovery in Zhìdé,
although Xuánzōng fled to Shǔ,
Sùzōng went from Língwǔ to Fèngxiáng.
At that time, the late emperor was marshal
and personally commanded the army.
Foreign tribes and armies from various circuits numbered over 100,000.
Zǐyí came from Tóngzhōu to join the battle,
but he was only the Military Commissioner of Shuòfāng.
In the victory and recovery,
the功 of the Huíhé and the Four Garrisons was greater.
As for Shèng's recovery,
Your Majesty again fled to Liángyáng.
Beside him, Huái Guāng, with the strength of Shuòfāng, also rebelled.
Troops from various circuits had already withdrawn.
On the day of the recovery,
Hún Jiān was in Xiányáng
and did not come to join.
At that time, there was no marshal.
Luò Yuánguāng and others all had their own commands.
This recovery
depended entirely on Shèng.
How could Zǐyí compare?”
The Emperor said:
“Indeed, as you say.”
Thereupon, he allowed the establishment of five temples, leaving the western chamber empty.
Received a Hundred Lions
There was a commoner, Zhāng Zǐlù, who submitted a memorial criticizing Mì.
Dézōng executed him
and said to Mì:
“I found all his accusations to be false and baseless.
Moreover, he claimed you received a hundred lions from Yán Zhèn,
valued at 20,000 strings of cash.
I estimated they must have been sugar lions.
The Shānnán region is poor;
where could there be so much gold?
And what would a family do with a hundred gold lions?
I tried to send someone to secretly investigate,
and the envoy who delivered the sugar was still in the city.
You avoid suspicion;
when envoys from various circuits send tea and delicacies,
you always open and bring them in.
This villain dared to make such false accusations,
so I dealt with him.”
Commentary on the Analects
Mì was promoted to Jíxián Xuéshì,
and memorialized, saying:
