"The Analects are the words of the Sages.
The disciples recorded them,
but the titles and order of the chapters are often unreasonable,
and moreover very jumbled.
Hé Yàn's collected commentaries also contain many errors.
When I was young, I wanted to compile and annotate them, but I never had the time.
Now that I have been made a Xuéshì,
my duties in the privy council are somewhat simplified,
and I wish to fulfill my long-cherished ambition."
The Emperor said:
"When I was young, I loved the Analects.
Because its chapter titles are shallow and simple,
and the commentaries are also sparse,
I intended to work on it with great scholars.
Since you already have this intention,
please immediately establish a hall for discussion and lectures.
Once the hall is complete, I will discuss it with you day and night."
Mì said:
"This is not yet advisable."
The Emperor said:
"Previous emperors liked to use their subjects' writings as imperial compositions,
but my intention is not like that.
Since childhood, I have read books and developed a certain understanding of principles.
Now I wish to collaborate on compiling and annotating.
If my interpretation is superior, the commentary will be called an imperial composition.
If your interpretation is superior, it will be attributed to your subject.
This will let later generations know that ruler and subject were of one mind,
proficient in ancient teachings,
a glorious achievement of the time,
not that I wish to appropriate your insights."
Mì said:
"Your Majesty is sagacious and wise,
heaven-endowed with innate knowledge,
truly on par with Yáo and Shùn.
Xuānní was
one who followed the ways of Yáo and Shùn.
My understanding is shallow and limited;
I am merely trying to interpret the words of the Seventy Disciples.
How could I worry about you appropriating my insights?
The reason I said it is not yet advisable is that
we see that Emperor Wǔ of Liáng,
when Hóu Jǐng and the Zhōu army arrived,
still lectured on the Lǎozi without interruption.
Hence, Yǔ Xìn's rhapsody says:
'The gentry treat war as child's play,
and the chief ministers regard pure conversation as state strategy.'
What good did Gāo Guì Qīnggōng and Zhōng Yáo and others comparing subtle meanings do
to save them from defeat?
Now the Tǔbō have broken the alliance,
and their encampment is less than five hundred Lǐ from the capital.
If Your Majesty were to discuss and lecture with your subject,
I fear the border generals would become complacent,
and we would also be ridiculed by later generations.
I am honored to be a Xuéshì;
it is acceptable for me to fulfill my long-cherished ambition on my own.
But for ruler and subject to annotate together
is not an urgent matter.
I wish to wait until peace is restored before planning this."
The Emperor said:
"For you to be so profound and meticulous in all matters,
you can truly be called a genuine chancellor.
However, you cannot proceed with your own annotation immediately either.
I will ultimately wait until peace is settled to do it with you."
Thereupon, it was stopped.
Zhōnghé Jié
Dézōng said:
"In previous dynasties, the three nines (third day of the third month, ninth day of the ninth month) all had public gatherings,
but the Shàngsì and Hánshí festivals often coincided.
Next year, Hánshí will fall on the second day of the third month,
meaning there will be no public gathering in spring.
I wish to establish a new festival in the second month.
What day would be suitable?"
Mì said:
"After the fifteenth day of the second month,
although it is flower season,
it coincides with Hánshí,
and is also close to the last day of the month.
Making the last day a festival
is not a good name or occasion.
The first day of the second month is precisely when peach and plum trees blossom.
Please designate the first day of the second month as Zhōnghé Jié.
On that day,
grant rulers to ministers, regional commanders, and honored relatives,
calling them 'Cáidù' (measures for tailoring).
Let families exchange gifts of various grains and fruits in green pouches,
calling them 'Xiàn Shēngzǐ' (offering of new sprouts).
Brew wine,
calling it 'Yíchūn Jiǔ' (wine for suitable spring).
Villagers will sacrifice to the god Gōumáng to pray for grain,
and all officials will present agricultural books to show their focus on fundamentals."
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and immediately ordered it to be put into practice.
Together with Shàngsì and Chóngyáng, these were called the 'Three Auspicious Festivals,'
and both inside and outside the capital, money was granted, scenic spots were visited, and banquets were held.
Lú Qǐ's Caution
Mì considered Lú Qǐ to be treacherous and evil,
but Dézōng praised his caution.
Mì said:
"Caution is precisely the demeanor of a treacherous minister."
Shoes are 'Xié'
Before Mì became a chancellor, he stayed in the inner court.
One morning,
Qǐ secretly took Mì's shoes and sent them to the Emperor's residence.
The Emperor said:
"Shoes (xié) are 'harmonious' (xié);
he will surely assist and harmonize,
and affairs will soon be harmonious."
Burning Pears
Mì abstained from food.
Sùzōng personally roasted two pears and bestowed them upon him.
Yǐng Wáng requested to compose linked verses for a future story.
Yǐng Wáng said:
"How old is the master?
His complexion rivals a child's."
Xìn Wáng said:
"At night, he embraces the bones of nine immortals;
in the morning, he dons a first-rank robe."
Another prince then said:
"He eats not a thousand measures of grain,
but only two pears."
The Emperor said:
"Heaven gave birth to this qi here,
to help me achieve non-action."
Láncán
When Mì was at Héngyuè,
there was a monk named Míngzàn,
known as Láncán.
Mì observed that he was an extraordinary person,
and went to visit him in the middle of the night.
Láncán bade him sit,
started a fire, roasted taro, and offered it to him, saying:
"Speak not much.
Accept ten years as chancellor."
Wáng Dàn,
courtesy name Zǐmíng,
was a Hànlín Xuéshì.
Once, after reporting on affairs and descending the hall,
Zhēnzōng watched him leave and said:
"He who will bring great peace to朕
must be this man."
Later, he was appointed Píngzhāngshì,
calming the four barbarian tribes externally,
and harmonizing the common people internally.
Officials obtained their positions,
and the empire became prosperous and abundant,
with songs of praise overflowing.
This was due to Dàn's efforts.
Wáng Zēng
Wáng Zēng, courtesy name Xiàoxiān.
Zhēnzōng was fond of immortals,
and built the Zhāoyìng Jǐnglínggōng.
He used ministers to lead the project,
appointing Zēng as Jǐnglínggōng Shǐ.
Zēng did not accept the appointment,
which displeased the Emperor's will,
and he was dismissed from his position as Cānzhèng.
Later, he was recalled to be chancellor.
During Zhēnzōng's lingering illness,
he obstructed the proposal for Míng Xiàn to oversee court affairs,
and requested the crown prince to supervise the state,
clarifying the great principle to stabilize the ancestral temples and the state.
The empire relied on him for this.
Kòu Zhǔn
Kòu Zhǔn,
courtesy name Píngzhòng, in his youth governed Bādōng County.
He penned the lines: "Wild waters no one crosses,
a lone boat drifts all day long."
At the time, people believed that if he were to be employed,
he would surely manage a great river.
Later, he became the Surveillance Commissioner of Yùnzhōu.
When summoned for an audience,
Tàizōng said:
"I know, my lord, that you have deep strategies and far-reaching thoughts.
Try to decide one matter for me.
The Crown Prince's actions are unlawful,
and in the future, he will surely become a Jié or Zhòu.
If I wish to depose him,
there are soldiers and weapons within his palace,
and I fear this might cause a rebellion."
Zhǔn replied:
"Invite the Crown Prince to perform a ceremony at a certain place,
and instruct all his close attendants and guards to follow him.
Your Majesty can then search his palace;
if indeed there are unlawful instruments,
show them to him upon his return.
Isolate his close attendants,
and let no one else in.
To depose him then
would require only the strength of one eunuch."
The Emperor considered this correct.
When the Crown Prince left,
they searched and found instruments of torture,
including those for gouging out eyes, severing tendons, and plucking out tongues.
The Crown Prince admitted his guilt
and was subsequently deposed.
Zhāngshèng was established as the Crown Prince.
At the beginning of the Jǐngdé era,
he was appointed Prime Minister.
At that time, the Qìdān attacked Chányuān,
and the high ministers discussed a plan to flee southwest.
Zhǔn said:
"Wáng Qīnruò is from Jiāngnán,
hence he urges Your Majesty to flee to Jīnlíng.
Chén Yáosǒu is from Shǔ,
hence he urges Your Majesty to flee to Chéngdū."
He then requested the Emperor to lead the campaign in person,
and they greatly defeated the barbarians.
The peace treaty that exists to this day
is thanks to Zhǔn's effort.
Once, while dining in the Central Secretariat,
some soup stained his beard.
Dīng Wèi brushed it off for him.
Zhǔn said:
"You are a high minister participating in governance,
and yet you brush a superior's beard?"
Zhāngshèng grew weary of governing,
and Wèi plotted to align with the Empress Dowager to rule from behind the curtain.
Zhǔn memorialized, saying:
"The Crown Prince's sagely virtue
is sufficient to undertake the affairs of the realm.
Dīng Wèi relies on his talent to harbor treachery,
and Cáo Lìyòng relies on his power to act presumptuously;
neither can assist the young ruler."
The next day,
Wèi's faction falsely accused Zhǔn of rebellion,
and for this, he was dismissed from his prime ministerial post
and demoted to judicial clerk of Léizhōu.
His route passed through Gōng'ān,
where he cut a bamboo and stuck it in front of a spirit temple, saying:
"If Zhǔn has ever betrayed the court,
this bamboo will surely not grow.
Otherwise,
this withered bamboo will regenerate."
The bamboo indeed grew.
Later, Fàn Zhòngyān wrote the "Yàoshí" poem,
stating Zhǔn was innocent.
The Emperor was about to restore his position,
but in that very month, he died in his place of exile.
The world compared him to Wèi Zhènggōng and Dí Liánggōng.
Yàn Shū,
courtesy name Tóngshū,
could write prose at seven sui.
When Zhāngshèng was presiding over the Southern Bureau,
Empress Zhāngxiàn, having gained favor in her humble days,
considered Zhāng Qí a great supporter.
During the Tiānshèng era,
the Empress Dowager appointed Qí as Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Shū said:
"Although the court lacks worthies,
it should still place those of moderate talent in such positions.
As for Qí,
it is enough to grant him wealth and nobility."
He thus defied the Empress Dowager's will
and was punished by being made to strike a servant with his ritual tablet,
and was sent out to govern Nánjīng.
He was recalled to serve as Councilor.
When the Empress Dowager visited the Imperial Ancestral Temple,
she wished to wear the Emperor's ceremonial robes.
Shū argued:
"The Rites of Zhōu prescribe the robes for a Queen,
and one cannot violate these laws and regulations."
During the Qìnglì era, he became Prime Minister.
Upon his burial,
he was granted a stele inscribed "Stele of the Old Scholar."
Dīng Wèi,
courtesy name Wèizhītiān.
During the Xī era, he was appointed Prime Minister
and concurrently served as the commissioner for Zhāngshèng's imperial tomb.
He and the eunuch Lěi Yǔngōng presumptuously altered the tomb's boundary.
When the matter was exposed,
he was demoted to judicial clerk of Yázhōu.
While in Zhūyá,
he taught the locals how to build houses
and composed one poem daily,
calling the collection "Zhīmìng Jí."
He once used tens of thousands of his family's wealth to trade with the locals,
taking no profit.
When the people asked what he desired,
Wèi said:
"I wish for someone to trouble themselves to carry a family letter to Luòyáng."
He then wrote a memorial of appeal and a family letter,
ordering him to send it to the Defender-in-Chief of Xījīng,
and await a high-ranking eunuch to arrive in Luò to feast with the Defender-in-Chief,
then hand it over.
"You will be arrested and imprisoned,
but later you will be rewarded."
The man followed his instructions.
The Defender-in-Chief was greatly alarmed upon receiving the letter,
dared not open it,
and thus reported it to the throne.
His memorial recounted his services in establishing the Crown Prince, stating:
"Your servant has sins that cover the heavens,
but also merits that cover the heavens."
The Emperor released the man,
rewarded him generously, and sent him back.
Wèi was then transferred to Léizhōu.
Censor Liú Suí memorialized:
"He presumptuously altered the imperial tomb's boundary,
which would be detrimental to the heir.
He rightly deserves to have his head taken
and displayed in the suburban temples."
When he was still a commoner,
he met a Daoist priest who said:
"In the future, you will resemble Lǐ Déyù but be slightly superior."
It turned out exactly as he said.
Zhào Zhěn,
courtesy name Zhòngwēi.
He served as the Transport Commissioner for Yìzhōu Circuit.
During the Tiānshèng era,
he was summoned to court.
The Emperor said:
"During the previous emperor's time, an edict ordered the market in Yìzhōu to purchase six thousand bolts of brocade.
At that time, a prefect named Zhào only purchased one thousand bolts.
Was that you, my lord?"
Zhěn replied:
"It was."
Soon after, he was greatly promoted.
Shí Yánnián,
courtesy name Mànqīng.
Zhēnzōng said:
"I have long known your talent, my lord,
but I hear you are fond of drinking,
and I fear you might be too drunk to attend to matters."
Yánnián replied:
"Your servant is not fond of drinking;
it is merely for self-release.
However, even when your servant is drunk,
in dealing with affairs,
I am superior to those who are not drunk."
Cài Qí,
courtesy name Zǐsī.
Zhēnzōng was assessing scholars from the imperial veranda
and dreamt that night of "cài qí" (vegetables arranged) below the palace hall.
The Emperor saw his dignified demeanor
and said:
"We have found our man."
He specially decreed that seven Imperial Guards clear the way for him.
This practice began with Qí.
Fàn Zhòngyān
Fàn Zhòngyān, courtesy name Xīwén.
He was appointed Zhī Kāifēng Shì (Prefect of Kāifēng Prefecture),
and made decisions with divine swiftness.
The people of the capital sang a ballad:
"The imperial court has no worries with Lord Fàn,
The capital has no troubles with Xīwén."
Each time he presented a memorial,
he often discussed matters of governance and disorder,
and criticized the illegal conduct of high officials.
Those who spoke against him accused Zhòngyān of alienating the emperor and his ministers,
and he was dismissed from office and made Zhī Ráozhōu (Prefect of Ráozhōu).
The supervising censor, Gāo Ruònà, said the demotion was still too light.
Ouyáng Xiū submitted a memorial to defend him,
and also incurred punishment.
Yú Jìng and Yǐn Zhū were both dismissed for factionalism.
Cài Xiāng composed the "Poem of Four Sages and One Scoundrel,"
the scoundrel referring to Ruònà.
During the Baoyuán reign,
Yuán Hào rebelled.
The emperor, knowing his talent in both civil and military affairs,
appointed him to lead troops in Yán'ān.
Day and night, he trained elite soldiers.
When the rebels heard of it, they said:
"Do not pay attention to Yánzhōu;
now, the younger Lord Fàn has tens of thousands of soldiers in his belly,
unlike the elder Lord Fàn, who could be deceived."
The barbarians called a Zhīzhōu (prefect) "Lǎozi" (old master).
The "elder Lord Fàn"
referred to Yōng.
Later, when he was Zhī Qìngzhōu (Prefect of Qìngzhōu),
after the imperial army's defeat at Dìngchuān,
it was proposed to conscript local militia.
Zhòngyān ordered them to be tattooed on the hand.
When the war ended,
all the people in the Huánqìng circuit were able to return to farming.
The emperor entrusted him with the position of four-circuit Dū Zhāotǎo (Overall Commander of Pacification).
Zhòngyān and Hán Qí conspired together,
determined to recover the lands of Líng, Xià, and Héngshān.
A ballad on the frontier said:
"In the army there is a Hán,
when the western rebels hear him, their bones turn cold;
in the army there is a Fàn,
when the western rebels hear him, they are scared out of their wits."
Yuán Hào was greatly terrified,
and consequently declared himself a vassal.
Chén Yáozuǒ,
courtesy name Xīyuán.
He revised the "Shī Zhēnzōng Shílù" (Veritable Records of Emperor Zhēnzōng),
and was specially appointed Zhī Zhìgào (Drafting Official).
According to the old system,
one had to be summoned for examination.
Only Yáng Yì and Yáozuǒ were appointed without examination.
During the Jǐngyòu reign, he was appointed prime minister.
There were celestial anomalies and an earthquake.
Yáozuǒ submitted a memorial saying:
"Wáng Suí's position is above mine,
but he is ill and unable to perform his duties;
Chéng Lín's position is below mine,
yet all the blame for these anomalies rests with me."
He petitioned to be relieved of his post,
and was sent out to govern Zhèngzhōu.
He passed away,
and was posthumously given the epithet Wénhuì.
His elder brother, Yáosǒu,
eventually became Píngzhāngshì (Grand Councilor);
his younger brother, Yáozī, was a Jiédùshǐ (Military Governor).
Both ranked first in the imperial examinations.
The brothers were noble and prosperous,
rarely paralleled in their time.
Yáozuǒ, after retiring to Zhèngpǔ,
was particularly fond of poetry.
Zhāng Shìxùn, who was governing Xījīng,
sent him peony flowers and wine.
Yáozuǒ replied:
"With flowers but no wine, my head is too lazy to lift;
with wine but no flowers, my eyes are too lazy to open.
Just as I was thinking of the desolation in the western garden,
the Luòyáng flowers and wine arrived simultaneously."
Yáozī was skilled in archery,
and was known throughout the land as a divine archer,
calling himself Xiǎo Yóujī (Little Yóujī).
Dí Qīng,
courtesy name Hànchén.
When Yuán Hào rebelled at that time,
he frequently led troops to battle.
In four years,
he fought twenty-five battles, large and small,
and was hit by stray arrows eight times.
People called him Dí Tiānshǐ (Angel Dí).
The emperor observed his demeanor,
and said:
"He is my Guān Yǔ and Zhāng Fēi."
Thus he earned the moniker "Dí Wàn" (Dí Ten Thousand),
meaning one of him was enough to rival ten thousand.
Initially,
when Qīng was among the military ranks,
Hán Wèigōng and Fàn Wénzhèng, upon seeing him,
both praised him as having the potential of a general and prime minister.
He indeed was able to achieve meritorious service for the nation,
and became a renowned general of his time.
After returning from suppressing the Nóng rebels,
he became somewhat conceited and arrogant,
and many of the imperial guards became attached to him.
Public opinion at the time became quite suspicious of him.
Xiè Jiàng,
courtesy name Xīshēn.
Empress Zhāngxiàn had been overseeing the court for a long time,
and somewhat believed in geomancers,
who frequently entered and exited the palace.
Jiàng submitted a memorial saying:
"These are all unorthodox ways,
the root of political disorder.
Since ancient times in periods of decline and chaos,
when female favorites held sway,
such things occurred."
He also cited Bāo Sì's destruction of the Zhōu dynasty to advise against deposing Empress Guō,
all in accordance with classical principles.
He was promoted to Zhī Zhìgào (Drafting Official).
His writing had the style of Yuán Jiǔ and Bái Jūyì.
When he governed a prefecture, his focus was on moral education.
At the time, he was compared to Dù Fǔ's poetry.
Zhèng Jiǎn,
courtesy name Tiānxiū.
He was appointed Zhī Kāifēngfǔ (Prefect of Kāifēng Prefecture).
A prefectural official named Féng Yuán was cunning and deceitful,
and had connections with powerful magnates,
so the capital nicknamed him "Lìdì Jīngzhàoyǐn" (Instant Jīngzhào Commander).
Jiǎn thoroughly investigated his crimes,
and exiled him to an island.
Later, he was transferred to guard Cháng'ān,
and submitted a memorial stating:
"Listening to the bells and drums of the stern imperial court,
I cannot predict what time it will be;
planting strong cypresses in snow and frost,
I shall observe their integrity in old age."
The emperor praised and recited this several times.
He replaced Fàn Zhòngyān as the four-circuit Zhāotǎo (Pacification Commissioner),
establishing his headquarters in Jīng.
He often greatly admired the achievements of Guō Dàigōng.
When Yuán Hào gathered his troops and approached Hēishān,
Jiǎn commanded his soldiers to patrol the border,
and hurried to Liánhuābǎo.
The weather was cold and the wind strong.
He held a grand feast with wine,
with banners crimsoning the fields,
and cymbals and drums resounding to the sky.
The ten thousand barbarian troops
looked at each other, not daring to move.
Yuán Hào said:
"I have already sent an envoy to declare myself a vassal,
why does the imperial court still use this lord to protect its generals?"
Such was his fear.
Shí Jiè,
courtesy name Shǒudào,
was a hermit of Cūlái Shān.
His writings and scholarship were revered by all under heaven,
and everyone called him Cūlái Xiānshēng.
He authored "Sòng Sòng" (Eulogies of the Sòng Dynasty) in ten chapters,
which were considered
no less excellent than "Yī Nuó" and "Qīng Miào" (ancient odes).
In the third year of the Qìnglì reign,
all those considered virtuous scholars and officials in the realm were employed in the two administrations (Zhōngshū and Shūmì), as imperial attendants, or as censors.
The Sòng dynasty's appointment of officials
reached its peak at this time.
Jiè composed the "Qìnglì Shèngdé Shī" (Poem on the Sacred Virtue of Qìnglì).
Dù Yǎn,
courtesy name Shìchāng.
In the fourth year of Qìnglì, he was appointed prime minister,
and he forcefully stopped the abuses of internal imperial decrees.
At that time, if a powerful and favored person made a request,
the Emperor would say:
"It is not difficult for me to issue an internal decree,
but Chancellor Yǎn is just and upright,
and will certainly not issue the edict."
If there was no alternative but to issue an imperial decree,
Yǎn would collect them all,
and wait until there were ten or more,
then seal and return them.
The Emperor once said:
"Yǎn has helped me greatly."
However, the powerful and favored officials turned against him,
and soon after,
he was dismissed from his post as prime minister.
Initially,
after Yǎn became prominent,
he had a daughter,
and his wife doted on her,
insisting on finding a good son-in-law.
Yǎn considered Sū Shùnqīn to be the foremost in literary talent and scholarly achievements in the realm,
so there was no one like him,
and thus he gave his daughter to him in marriage.
When Yǎn was in the Central Secretariat,
the powerful and favored officials wanted to remove him,
so they accused Shùnqīn, who was supervising the Zhīnzòuyuàn (Bureau of Memorials), of buying old paper
and embezzling while in charge,
and dismissed him from office.
This was done to shake Yǎn,
and Yǎn also used this to request retirement.
Wáng Zhì,
courtesy name Zǐyě.
When Fàn Zhòngyān was demoted to Ráozhōu for speaking out,
Zhì was then the Prefect of Kāifēngfǔ,
and went to see him off at the east gate.
Someone said:
"Why do you implicate yourself in factionalism?"
Zhì replied:
"In the past, Xú Huì did not fail Yáng Línhè;
now, I, Zhì, wish to associate with Fàn Ráozhōu."
During the Qìnglì reign,
when gentlemen Dù, Hán, Fù, and Fàn were in the two high offices,
and famous scholars were spread throughout the Censorate,
those who held different views
were accused of factionalism.
Soon after, all these gentlemen were sent out to provincial posts,
and Sū Shùnqīn and his associates,
due to excesses in drinking and feasting,
were imprisoned and exiled.
Zhì wept bitterly and said:
"The reason the realm is governed
is because of the support of many virtuous people.
Now the virtuous are daily retreating,
this is cause for concern.
A human life is but a fleeting moment,
I no longer enjoy being in this world."
He then died of sorrow and indignation.
Zhì was born on the twenty-sixth day of the seventh month,
and died on the same day;
everyone found it extraordinary.
End of Volume 2.
Playing the sheng to imitate the phoenix's call
Wángzǐqiáo
was Jìn, the crown prince of King Líng of Zhōu.
He loved to play the sheng to imitate the phoenix's call.
After meeting Fúqiū Gōng and attaining immortality,
he told Bǎiliáng:
"Tell my family
to wait for me on the east side of Mount Gōushì on the Qīxī festival."
He arrived riding a white swan.
Nòngyù playing the xiao
Xiāoshǐ was
a man from Qín,
skilled at playing the xiao.
King Qín had a daughter named Nòngyù,
who loved him,
so he married her to him.
He taught Nòngyù to play the xiao to imitate a phoenix's call,
and a phoenix came to their chamber.
They then built a Phoenix Terrace to live in.
One night, as they played the xiao, phoenixes gathered,
and they rode them to ascend to immortality.
Subsequently, a Phoenix Maiden Shrine was built.
Seeking Yǎnyuèzǐ
Xǔ Què traveled all over famous mountains,
and wherever he went, he inscribed, "Seeking Yǎnyuèzǐ, I reached here."
He composed a poem:
"Before the flowers of Lángyuàn is the land of intoxication,
mistakenly overturning the Queen Mother's nine-colored jade wine cup.
The immortals clapped their hands, finding me frivolous,
and banished me to the human world to be a wine maniac."
He wrote it in a wine tower,
and rode on a cloud to depart.
Golden bed and jade table
In the stone chamber of Dàizōng,
hanging high above and deep below,
there is a golden bed and a jade table.
Carrying a bureau and grinding mirrors
Fùjú Xiānshēng lived in seclusion by grinding mirrors.
Jade Maiden's hair-washing basin
On the summit of Huàshān, there is a stone mortar,
called the Jade Maiden's Hair-Washing Basin.
Inside, there is clear water,
which never increases or decreases.
Jìqiū Jūn
Jìqiū Jūn, a Taoist priest from the foot of Tàishān,
met Emperor Wǔ of Hàn during his eastern tour.
He held his zither and came for an audience.
Practicing the art of Yùzǐ
The Grand Mystery Maiden practiced the art of Yùzǐ,
her hair was black as a crow's.
Jade City and Jasper Towers
Shùn traveled south,
and there was a state called Yángzhōu.
He entered the Gate of a Thousand Dragons
and floated on the River Zhāohuí.
There were Jade Cities and Jasper Towers,
called "the capital of Jiǔyí."
Ascending with the entire household
Xǔ Zhēnjūn ascended to immortality with his entire household,
only the wheel hub and brocade canopy fell back down.
Consuming hydrous quartz
Chìsōngzǐ,
the Rain Master during Shénnóng's time,
consumed hydrous quartz.
Calling chickens by name
Zhùjī Wēng lived north of Hùxiāng,
raising chickens.
All the chickens had names,
and would come when called by name.
Azure bird
Wú Zhēnjūn encountered a great storm,
wrote a talisman, placed it on the roof,
and an azure bird carried it away,
whereupon the wind immediately ceased.
Five-colored smoke
Níngfēngzǐ was the potter for the Yellow Emperor.
A person visited him
and helped him tend the fire,
able to produce five-colored smoke.
After a long time, he taught it to Fēngzǐ.
Fēngzǐ accumulated fire and burned himself,
able to ascend and descend with the smoke.
Sealing the door with a ball of clay
Fāng Huí was robbed by someone
and confined to a room,
begging for the Dao.
Huí transformed and departed,
and moreover sealed the door with a ball of clay,
stamping it with Fāng Huí's seal.
At the time, it was said that if one received a ball of clay from Huí sealing the door,
it could never be opened.
Unclasping the pendant on the Hànjiāng River
Zhèng Jiāofǔ traveled along the Hànjiāng River
and saw two maidens wearing two bright pearls as pendants.
Jiāofǔ was pleased by them,
not knowing they were divine beings,
and humbly requested their pendants.
The maidens unclasped their pendants and gave them to Jiāofǔ.
After walking several tens of paces,
the maidens suddenly disappeared.
Lady Gōuyì
Lady Gōuyì's right hand was curled.
Emperor Wǔ opened her hand
and found a jade hook.
Soon after, he had her killed.
During her funeral,
her body was not cold and emitted a fragrance.
One month later,
Emperor Zhāo ascended the throne
and reburied her.
The coffin was empty,
containing only silk slippers.
Therefore, her palace was named Gōuyì,
later changed to Yì to avoid a taboo name.
Five-colored mica
Wèi Shūqīng served on cloud mica and achieved immortality.
His son, named Dùshì,
traveled extensively through mountains and seas,
seeking to meet his father.
One day, he saw him in the mountains,
gambling with several gentlemen,
sitting on a white stone couch.
Dùshì asked who the gamblers were,
and his father replied:
"They are Hóngyá Xiānshēng,
Xǔ Yóu, Cháo Fù, and Wáng Zǐjìn.
I have an elixir formula beneath a pillar in my dwelling."
Dùshì left,
returned home and dug for it,
and obtained a jade casket,
sealed with the seal of a flying immortal.
It contained five-colored cloud mica.
Dùshì consumed it,
and indeed ascended to immortality.
Emerald Lotus Roots and White Oranges
King Mù of Zhōu met the Queen Mother of the West at Yáochí,
and ate plain puffballs, black dates, emerald lotus roots, and white oranges.
Qín Gāo Riding a Red Carp
After Qín Gāo ascended to immortality,
a shrine was established to worship him.
From time to time, he would come to partake of offerings, riding a red carp.
Gale Chariot and Feathered Wheels
At Kūnlún Pǔ and Lángfēng Yuàn, there are twelve jade towers and nine layers of profound chambers.
To the right is Yáochí,
to the left is Cuìshuǐ,
encircled by nine layers of Ruòshuǐ,
with vast, towering waves.
It is unreachable without a gale chariot and feathered wheels.
This is the dwelling of the Queen Mother of the West.
Compiling the Materia Medica
Táo Yīnjū met the immortal Báikāi, who said:
"Your hidden merits are manifest.
However, in the Materia Medica you compiled, you used horseflies and leeches as medicine.
Although this benefited humans,
it harmed living creatures.
Because of this,
you will only be able to shed your form and depart after twelve years."
A Rendezvous with Hànmàn
Lú Áo saw a scholar
with deep-set eyes and a prominent Adam's apple,
hawk-like shoulders and a long neck,
broad above and slender below,
sitting on a tortoise shell and eating clams and crabs.
He said to Áo:
"I have a rendezvous with Hànmàn beyond the nine heavens,
and cannot linger long."
Then he departed.
Nine Meals a Day
Qīngjīng Xiānshēng was a thousand years old,
with the complexion of a child.
He could go a whole year without eating,
and also eat nine meals a day.
White Stones as Sustenance
Báishí Xiānshēng cooked white stones as sustenance.
Péng Zǔ asked:
"Why do you not take elixir and ascend to immortality?"
He replied:
"Those who are most revered in heaven
are difficult to serve,
and they inflict more suffering on people."
At that time, he was called the Reclusive Immortal.
He often traveled in all directions,
curing people's illnesses.
Gathering Flowers of a Hundred Herbs
Fèng Gāng gathered the flowers of a hundred herbs,
boiled them nine times,
and consumed them, ascending to immortality.
Bìluò Shìláng
Shěn Xī was about to ascend when
suddenly there appeared a white deer, a green dragon chariot,
and a feathered official holding a staff,
who, with a green jade tablet bordered with cinnabar, conferred upon him the title of Bìluò Shìláng.
Twelve Jade Flasks
Wáng Yuǎn, courtesy name Fāngpíng,
once stayed at Cài Jīng's house.
After more than ten years,
he returned on the seventh day of the seventh month.
His bearing was like that of a great general.
He carried twelve jade flasks,
all sealed at the mouth with wax.
Wáng Yuǎn sent a letter to Chén Wèi.
The letter was broad and expansive,
grand but not artful.
A Woman Whipping an Old Man
A Hàn envoy passed through Hédōng
and saw a woman
whipping an old man.
The old man received the blows very respectfully.
When asked,
she said:
"This is my son.
Formerly, my maternal uncle Bóshānfǔ taught me a divine formula.
I made him take it,
but he did not apply himself,
which led to this decline and aging,
so I whip him."
When asked her age,
she said:
"I am one hundred and thirty years old,
and my son is only a little over seventy."
One Person Becomes a Thousand
Liú Zhèng possessed magical arts.
He could make one person appear as a thousand,
and a thousand people appear as ten thousand.
He could also breathe water to raise clouds,
gather soil to form mountains,
and pierce ponds to create abysses.
Red Pills Cause Fire
Sūn Bó threw red pills into the army,
and in an instant, fire erupted.
He then threw in green pills,
and the fire was extinguished.
He could also transform a mirror into a knife,
and bend it back into a mirror.
Mud Horses
Zhāng Zhèn, styled Yùzǐ,
could make horses out of mud
that could travel a thousand *lǐ* a day.
His disciple, styled Tàiyángzǐ,
was fond of drinking.
When asked about it,
he said:
"I am a late learner, and my worldly habits have not yet been eliminated,
so I use wine to drive myself."
Stone Marrow
Wáng Liè obtained stone marrow.
According to the *Xiānjīng*, it says:
"The divine mountain opens once every five hundred years,
and marrow emerges.
If one consumes it,
one's lifespan will be equal to that of heaven and earth."
Liè first consumed white stones,
cooked them until soft, and gave them to people.
They tasted like taro.
Riding a Red Dragon
Máo Yíng rode a red dragon to ascend to heaven.
Before this,
a children's rhyme went:
"The divine immortal attained by Máo Chūchéng,
rides a dragon to ascend to the Grand Purity of heaven,
sometimes descends to Zuǒzhōu to frolic at Chìchéng,
his successor and the next generation is Máo Yíng,
the Emperor wishes to learn it in the twelfth month."
Elixir Manual in the Sleeve
Zhāng Dàolíng's disciple Zhào Shēng
passed all seven trials,
and was then granted the Elixir Manual in the Sleeve.
Liú Ān Ascends to Immortality
Liú Ān invited sorcerers,
whereupon the Eight Immortals came to see him.
They transformed into children,
with complexions like peach blossoms.
They then imparted the Elixir Manual.
After Liú Ān ascended to immortality,
his medicinal vessels remained in the courtyard.
When chickens and dogs licked them,
they all ascended to immortality.
Nine-Jointed Staff
Wáng Yáo encountered rain,
and had his disciple carry a basket with a nine-jointed staff,
and it did not get wet.
Eight-Hundred-Year-Old Square Pupils
Lǐ Gēn had square pupils in both eyes.
The *Xiānjīng* says:
"At eight hundred years of age, one's pupils become square."
Nine-Jointed Calamus
The Nine Peaks Immortal saw Emperor Wǔ and said:
"I heard there is a stone calamus,
one inch with nine joints,
which can be consumed as food.
Therefore, I came to gather it."
Seen Jì Zixùn in Twenty-Three Places
Jì Zixùn possessed magical arts.
When he arrived at the capital,
many noblemen invited him.
He promised them all that he would visit on a certain day at noon.
On that day,
Jì Zixùn was seen in twenty-three places,
his clothes and conversation identical in each.
Making Elixir
Wèi Bóyáng and three disciples made elixir.
When the elixir was made,
he first gave it to a dog.
The dog died.
One disciple, together with the master, took it.
He also died.
The two went down the mountain to seek burial items.
Bóyáng immediately rose,
and again placed the elixir into the mouths of the dog and the disciple.
They all rose,
and ascended to immortality.
Inscription for the New Palace
Cài Shàoxiá dreamt of someone entrusting her with a book, "Inscription for the New Palace."
It said it was composed by Zǐyáng Zhēnrén Xuánqīng.
Its summary read:
"Jade-green steps, like scales, are staggered;
Jade-white stairs are carved smoothly.
Pearl trees are linked in order;
Jade springs flow in standard measure.
Immortal elders stand like cranes;
Daoist masters are pure as ice.
Three transformations of dark clouds;
Nine layers of crimson snow."
Six Jiǎ Traveling Kitchen
Zuǒ Cí summoned the Six Jiǎ,
able to command ghosts and spirits,
and by sitting, conjure a traveling kitchen.
Dividing the Cup
Zuǒ Cí said to Cáo Gōng:
"I am about to travel far,
I wish to divide this cup and drink wine."
Cí pulled out his hairpin and drew a line on the cup.
The wine immediately broke in the middle,
dividing into two directions.
Four-Hundred-Year-Old Child
Lǐ Bābǎi called Zhì Zhèng a four-hundred-year-old child.
Intently Gazing at a Stone Wall
Bó Zǔ went to Xīchéng Shān to serve Wáng Jūn,
who ordered him to intently gaze at a stone wall.
At first, for one year,
he saw nothing.
In the second year,
gradually there were characters.
In the third year,
he obtained the inscribed divine elixir formulas and the Five Peaks map.
Luòhé Shān
Wáng Cìzhòng transformed seal script into clerical script.
Shǐhuáng summoned him,
but he did not come.
Shǐhuáng intended to kill him.
Cìzhòng transformed into a large bird,
flapping its wings and rising.
The envoy bowed and said:
"I have nothing to report,
I fear being executed."
Then three large feathers fell to the envoy.
Shǐhuáng then named it Luòhé Shān (Falling Feathers Mountain).
Flesh Ganoderma
Xiāo Jìngzhī dug the ground and found a human hand,
moist and white.
He cooked and ate it.
When people asked what it was,
he said:
"It is flesh ganoderma."
Péng Zǔ's Wives
Péng Zǔ, at eight hundred years old,
lost forty-nine wives
and fifty-four sons.
Queen Mother's Jade Ring
The Queen Mother (Wángmǔ) bestowed a white jade ring upon Wǔ,
and also presented a white jade tube,
to be blown to harmonize the eight winds.
Lǎozi's Servant Xú Jiǎ
Lǎozi traveled west past the pass.
The pass official Yǐn Xǐ knew he was no ordinary person,
and followed him to inquire about the Dao.
Lǎozi was greatly surprised,
and stuck out his tongue, which was flat (dānrán),
hence he was called Lǎo Dān.
Lǎozi had three openings in his ears,
and ten characters in his hand.
His servant Xú Jiǎ had agreed to a daily wage of one hundred coins.
He claimed to have followed for two hundred years,
calculating a debt of seven million two hundred thousand coins.
Jiǎ went to the pass official to demand the arrears.
The official asked Lǎozi,
who replied:
"Jiǎ should have died long ago.
I saved him with the Tàixuán Qīngshēng Fú (Talisman of Supreme Mystery and Pure Life),
allowing him to live until today."
He made Jiǎ open his mouth towards the ground.
The talisman came out,
its crimson characters fresh as new.
Jiǎ immediately became a pile of withered bones.
The official, knowing Lǎozi's divine power,
knocked his head and begged for his life.
Lǎozi again threw the talisman onto the bones,
and Jiǎ was revived.
Jade Maidens Playing Touhu
Dōng Wángfù played Touhu with jade maidens.
Every throw,
twelve hundred "xiāo" (points).
If one failed to enter,
it was a "xū".
The sound "hū jiān qiè"
means "open mouth laugh."
Péng Zǔ Jīng
Jiān Kēng
is Péng Zǔ.
He possessed the art of Daoyin.
Whenever he was ill,
he would hold his breath to attack the ailment.
His breath would flow like clouds through his body,
reaching down to his fingertips.
Immediately, his body would be harmonized.
He once said:
"Superior people have separate beds,
middling people have different blankets.
Taking medicine for a hundred li
is not as good as sleeping alone."
Later generations compiled his techniques of absorption,
calling it the "Péng Zǔ Jīng."
Wèiyāng Wán
Mòzǐ lived in the mountains
and met a divine being who bestowed upon him plain books and the Wèiyāng Wán,
granting him eternal life.
Man in the Moon Wearing Armor
Jūn Sī,
a Jìn person.
On the fifteenth night of the first month, while sitting in his room,
he sent his child to see if there was anything unusual in the moon.
The child reported:
"This year there will be floods.
There is a man in the moon wearing a straw cape and carrying a sword."
Sī went out to look,
and said:
"It is not floods;
there will be military unrest.
The man in the moon is wearing armor and holding a spear."
It happened just as he said.
Ability to Govern People Leads to Taming Tigers
Guō Wén attained the Dao
and could tame fierce tigers.
The Jìn Emperor summoned him to ask about his art.
He replied:
"Humans have no intention to harm tigers,
and tigers have no intention to harm humans;
what art is there?
If you treat me kindly, I will become your tiger,
just like the people;
if you abuse me, I will become your enemy,
the people are like tigers.
One who can govern people can tame tigers."
Lǐ Chángzài
There was a man named Lǐ
who attained the Dao and lived in the mountains, never growing old.
People, generation after generation, called him elder brother.
They did not know his name,
so they called him Lǐ Chángzài (Li the Ever-Present).
Spitting into a Plate to Form Carp
Liú Gāng spat into a plate and it formed carp.
His wife Fán Fūrén spat into a plate and it formed otters.
They ate them.
Shrinking the Earth's Meridians
Fèi Chángfáng met Hú Gōng,
who possessed divine arts,
and could shrink the earth's meridians,
making a thousand li appear right before one's eyes.
When released,
they returned to their former state.
Immortal Art
Liú Shāng lived in the mountains.
There was a seller of arts,
who obtained them at a good price.
Later, a strange person said:
"Lord Liú has already been bestowed the immortal art.
Take it and become an immortal."
Turtle Cup
Nánjí Zǐ Liǔ Róng took powder and applied it to a cup,
cursing it to become a turtle.
He boiled and ate its meat.
He cursed its shell,
and it reverted to a wine cup.
A Tree Ascends and Breaks the Heavens
Wáng Dūn (王敦) plotted rebellion.
He dreamt of holding a tree that ascended and broke the heavens.
He inquired of a diviner.
Xǔ Zhēnjūn (許真君), who was then the magistrate of Jīngyáng (旌陽), saw Dūn (敦) and interpreted it, saying:
“This is the character ‘未’ (wèi, meaning ‘not yet’ or ‘future’).
The Jìn (晉) dynasty’s mandate has not yet ended,
so you should not make a move yet.”
Song of the Fisherman
Zhāng Zhìhé (張志和), styled Xuánzhēnzǐ (玄真子),
once composed a song of the fisherman, saying:
“White birds fly by Xīsàishān (西塞山),
peach blossoms drift on the water, mandarin fish are plump.
A green bamboo-leaf hat,
a green straw cape,
in slanting winds and fine rain, there’s no need to return home.”
Later, while at the banquet of Yán Zhēnqīng (顏真卿), the Prefect of Húzhōu (湖州),
clouds and cranes gathered and soared,
and he ascended into the sky and departed.
The Tàtà Gē (踏踏歌)
Lán Cǎihé (藍彩和) often wore a tattered robe,
a black wooden belt with six flaps,
one foot in a boot,
one foot bare,
begging in the marketplace.
He sang:
“Tàtà gē (踏踏歌),
Lán Cǎihé (藍彩和),
how much more can the world hold?
Rosy cheeks are but a spring tree,
passing years are thrown like a shuttle.
Ancient people endlessly depart, never to return,
modern people incessantly arrive, ever more numerous.
In the morning, riding a luánfèng (鸞鳳) to the blue sky,
in the evening, seeing mulberry fields turn into white waves.
The long, bright radiance hangs in the void,
golden and silver palaces stand tall and majestic.”
Later, he ascended into the sky from a wine tower in Háoliáng (濠梁),
leaving behind his robe, boot, belt, and the large clapper he held.
Digging for Lycium chinense
Zhū Rúzǐ (朱孺子) as a youth served the Daoist Wáng Yuánzhèng (王元正),
residing at Dàruòyán (大若巖).
One day,
while drawing water by the stream,
he saw two flowered dogs chasing each other.
He pursued them,
and they entered a patch of lycium chinense (gǒuqǐ 枸杞).
He dug there,
and the root was shaped like two dogs.
He cooked and ate it,
and suddenly felt his body become light.
He flew to the peak,
and was carried away by clouds and mist.
Yuánzhèng (元正) ate the remainder,
and also attained immortality.
Hence, the peak was named Tóngzǐfēng (童子峰).
Hearing Threshing in the Air
Old Wáng (王), living in a village,
aspired to the Dao.
An old Daoist visited him,
staying for over a month.
Suddenly, his whole body was covered in sores.
He told Old Wáng (王):
“If I can immerse myself in several measures of wine,
I will recover immediately.”
So, Wáng (王) prepared a full jar of wine.
The Daoist sat in the jar,
emerging only after three days.
His beard and hair were all black,
and his face was like that of a child.
He told Old Wáng (王):
“If you can drink this wine,
you can ascend to immortality.”
At that time, they were threshing wheat.
Old Wáng’s (王) whole family drank it,
and in an instant, they were all drunk.
Suddenly, wind stirred and clouds steamed,
and they all lightly ascended at once.
Their house, chickens, and dogs all departed,
and the sound of threshing could still be heard in the air.
Dragon Palace Prescriptions
Sūn Sīmiǎo (孫思邈) once saved a green snake,
which was a dragon prince.
Later, he was summoned by the Dragon King to his aquatic palace,
and obtained thirty Dragon Palace prescriptions.
He wrote the "Qiānjīnfāng" (千金方),
secretly hiding one prescription in each scroll.
Jiànxiányuàn (集賢院) Wine Cask
Mínghuáng (明皇) summoned Zhāng Guǒ (張果) and
asked about his age.
He said:
“I was born in the bǐngzǐ (丙子) year during Yáo’s (堯) reign,
and when I grew up, I served as a Shìzhōng (侍中).”
The Emperor offered him wine.
He said:
“My disciple is able to drink.”
He ordered him to be summoned.
Suddenly, a small Daoist descended from the eaves of the palace,
sixteen years old,
with a beautiful demeanor,
and skilled at witty conversation.
The Emperor offered him a drink,
and he drank one dòu (斗) without getting drunk.
Guǒ (果) said:
“You must not drink more,
lest something be lost.”
But he was forced to drink more,
and the wine suddenly poured from the top of his head,
splattering onto the ground,
transforming into a wine cask,
which was an item from the Jiànxiányuàn (集賢院).
Guǒ (果) was appointed Yínqīng Guānglù Dàfū (銀青光祿大夫)
and styled Tōngxuán Xiānshēng (通玄先生).
Pénglái (蓬萊) is separated by Ruòshuǐ (弱水) by Three Hundred Thousand Lǐ (里)
Xiè Zìrán (謝自然) sought the Dao from Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn (司馬承禎),
but he merely nodded and did not reply.
Zìrán (自然) sighed, saying:
“Every time I ascend Yùxiāofēng (玉霄峰), I see the vast sea,
Pénglái (蓬萊) should not be far.”
Thereupon, she departed,
entering the sea.
She reached a mountain,
met a Daoist, and asked where she was going.
She said:
“To Pénglái (蓬萊) to seek a master.”
The Daoist laughed and said:
“Pénglái (蓬萊) is separated by Ruòshuǐ (弱水),
three hundred thousand lǐ (里) from here.
Unless you can fly, you cannot reach it.
Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn (司馬承禎) of Tiāntái (天台) resides in Chìchéng (赤城),
his name is recorded in Dāntái (丹臺),
he is a truly good master.”
Zìrán (自然) returned to see Chéngzhēn (承禎),
who then transmitted to her the methods of Shàngqīng (上清).
Record of White Clouds
Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn (司馬承禎) was skilled in seal script,
creating a unique style,
named "Jīn Jiǎn Shū" (金剪書).
He lived in reclusion on Yùxiāofēng (玉霄峰) of Tiāntái (天台),
and was styled Báiyúnzǐ (白雲子).
Ruìzōng (睿宗) summoned him for an audience.
After his return,
court officials composed poems to bid him farewell,
filling a compilation,
which he titled "Báiyúnjì" (白雲記).
Lánggān (琅玕) Tree
Xiè Xuánqīng (謝玄卿) encountered an immortal,
and saw crimson branches and emerald leaves.
When a gentle breeze struck them,
five musical notes harmonized,
which were said to be a Lánggān (琅玕) tree.

He was also served phoenix-crown millet, dragon-eye rice, white lin (麟) fat, patterned chī (螭) marrow, Xuánzhōu (玄洲) white náishù (奈樹) fruit, Kōngdòng (空洞) spiritual claws, fúsāng (扶桑) boat mulberries, and Qīnghé (清河) literary algae.
There was also Qióngyí (瓊飴) wine, guìnǎo (桂腦), and yúnyīng (芸英).
He played the bāláng zhī áo (八琅之璈), cóngxiāo zhī shēng (叢霄之笙), and dòngyīn zhī qìng (洞陰之磬),
performed the Yuánjūn Gē (元鈞歌),
and danced the Huílúan Zhuǎnfèng zhī Wǔ (回鸞轉鳳之舞).
Grain Father and Silkworm Mother
The Three Mountains suffered famine.
A blue-clad youth said:
“People have scorned the five grains;
the Earth Officials have already collected their seeds.
You should lead one another to pray and express gratitude to the Gǔfù Cánmǔ (榖父蚕母) (Grain Father and Silkworm Mother),
and there will be abundant harvest.”
Sleeping Immortal
Xiàhóu Yǐn (夏侯隱) always ascended Shuǐdùshān (水渡山)
with his eyes closed, in a deep sleep.
His companions heard his snores,
but he never stumbled or fell.
People called him the Sleeping Immortal.
Planting Melons
Mǎ Xiāng (馬湘),
courtesy name Zìrán (自然).
Possessed Daoist arts.
Once, at the banquet of Mǎ Zhí (馬植), the Prefect of Jiāngnán (江南),
he filled a wine cup with soil and planted a melon,
and in an instant, it grew vines, flowers, and fruits,
which were very delicious to eat.
He could also rub his body and produce bronze coins,
which he threw into a well,
and they would emerge when called.
The Hair Maid
Her name was Yù Jiāng.
Because her body was covered in hair,
she was called the "Hairy Woman."
She claimed to be a palace woman of Qín Shǐhuáng.
When the Qín dynasty fell, she entered the mountains.
She met a Daoist priest
who taught her to eat pine needles,
and she subsequently attained the Dao.
Liǎng Chén
Yìrén Dīng Yuē was living in obscurity among the soldiers.
Wéi Zǐwēi served him as a master.
One day, he took his leave,
saying to Zǐwēi:
"It will still be two 'dusts' before you, young master, attain the Dao."
When asked why,
Yuē said:
"Confucianists call it 'shì' (ages),
Buddhists call it 'jié' (kalpas),
and Daoists call it 'chén' (dusts)."
Lǐ Bābǎi
Lǐ Zhēnduō was
a man from Shǔ.
After becoming an immortal,
he often traveled among mortals.
He was approximately eight hundred years old,
hence he was called Lǐ Bābǎi.
Yīn Qīqī,
whose given name was Wénxiáng.
Whenever he was drunk, he would sing:
"The zither plays the jade tune,
medicines refine the white cinnabar.
Able to brew instant wine,
and make flowers bloom in a moment."
At that time, there were azaleas at Hèlín Sì,
which bloomed profusely every spring.
When the Double Ninth Festival was approaching,
someone asked Qīqī:
"Can you make these flowers bloom?"
Qīqī said:
"They can be a nine-day spectacle."
Two days before,
he went and stayed beneath them.
The next day, the flowers bloomed,
and on the ninth day, they were as luxuriant as in spring.
On ordinary days when these flowers bloomed,
a red-clad woman was often seen protecting them.
When Qīqī wished to make these flowers bloom,
the woman suddenly appeared,
saying:
"I am the guardian of these flowers.
Today, I shall join the Daoist in making them bloom."
Qīqī once attended a banquet hosted by an official.
He scattered chestnuts among the courtesans.
All smelled a strange fragrance,
except for those who laughed at Qīqī; the chestnuts stuck to their noses and could not be removed,
and they only smelled a foul odor.
Soon, they danced wildly,
their makeup in disarray.
When they collectively admitted their faults,
the chestnuts fell off.
Qīqī could also turn water into wine,
carve wood into dried meat,
make a boat stop with a gesture,
and birds descend with a call.
Tán Qiào's Poem
Tán Qiào's poem says:
"Refining into a long river, fanning into the sky,
my slippers tossed towards the eastern sea.
Pénglái is indeed not much land,
just before Tán Shēng's staff."
Wūlóng
Wéi Shànjùn carried a dog
named Wūlóng.
Later, it transformed into a dragon,
and he rode it away.
Dragon Bed
Hán Zhìhé possessed Daoist arts.
During Xiànzōng's reign, he presented a dragon bed.
When one sat on it, its scales, mane, claws, and horns all moved.
Also, before the emperor, he took dozens of jumping spiders
and made them dance the Liángzhōu tune in formation,
all in perfect rhythm.
Rice Grains Becoming Bees
Gé Xuán served Zuǒ Cí as a master.
While eating with a guest,
he rinsed his mouth,
and the rice in his mouth all turned into large bees.
Slowly, he put them into his mouth,
whereupon they reverted to rice grains.
Immortal Terrace Official
Hóu Dàohuá rose in the morning
and flew to the top of a pine tree,
waving his hand to the crowd and saying:
"The Jade Emperor has summoned me to be an Immortal Terrace Official.
I am leaving now."
Green Cloud Ganoderma
Yáng Xīmèng dreamed he entered a grotto,
and something very long flew out of a stone cave.
It was very long.
A spirit person said:
"This is the Green Cloud Ganoderma."
Zhǒngzhēn Zhēnrén
Wáng Yuǎn,
courtesy name Fāngpíng.
He understood astronomy and prophecies,
and could foresee good and bad fortune.
Emperor Huán of Hàn asked about disasters and auspicious signs,
but he did not answer.
Instead, he wrote over four hundred characters on the palace gate,
predicting future events.
The emperor disliked this
and ordered people to erase it.
Although the outer characters were erased,
the inner characters reappeared,
the ink having penetrated through the plank.
He stayed at the home of Grand Commandant Chén Dān for over forty days.
One day, he said:
"My fated time to depart has come;
I cannot stay any longer."
Three days later,
his body suddenly disappeared.
Dàshàng Lǎojūn bestowed upon Fāngpíng seven-turn spiritual talismans,
making him the Zhǒngzhēn Zhēnrén,
leading fifteen thousand immortal gentlemen.
Traveling east to Kuòcāng,
he passed by the home of the Daoist follower Cài Jīng.
Knowing that his skeletal structure was suited for the Dao,
he said:
"You are destined to attain salvation and
become an immortal official.
However, you have insufficient knowledge of the Dao,
with too little 'qi' and too much flesh.
You can only achieve 'shījiě' (liberation by means of a simulated corpse).
This method is fleeting,
like passing through a dog's hole."
Jīng suddenly felt hot and desired water.
When water was poured on him, it was like watering a parched object,
and he subsequently lost his body.
More than ten years later, he suddenly returned home,
saying:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month,
Lord Wáng will come.
Prepare a hundred 'shí' (stones/units) of drink
to provide for his attendants."
On that day, he indeed arrived,
and then sent someone to summon Má Gū.
When Gū arrived,
she was eighteen or nineteen years old,
with a topknot on her head,
and the rest of her hair hanging to her waist.
Once seated,
they each began to serve the feast.
Golden cups, jade plates,
phoenix脯 (dried meat) and immortal delicacies,
not found in the human world.
Gū said:
"Since I began attending upon you,
I have seen the Eastern Sea turn into mulberry fields three times.
Just now, I arrived at Pénglái,
and the water is shallower than before;
perhaps it will soon return to being dry land?"
Fāngpíng said:
"Indeed, dust will again be stirred in the sea."
Gū requested a little rice,
and when she threw it on the ground, it all turned into pearls.
Fāngpíng laughed and said:
"Gū is young and performs such transformations.
I am already old
and do not enjoy doing so."
Hearing the Dao is Easy, Cultivating the Dao is Difficult
Guǐgǔ Wáng Xiānsheng,
given name Xǔ,
received the Dao from Lǎojūn and
resided in Guǐgǔ of Qīngxī.
Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí sought the Dao.
The master said:
"Hearing the Dao is easy,
cultivating the Dao is difficult.
The hearts of you two are not yet attuned to the world beyond.
You can learn the art of persuasion
and you will surely become chancellors of your respective states.
If not,
you will die.
If you are not afraid,
I will transmit it."
The two requested to learn it,
and three years later, they took their leave.
The master said:
"These two slight the eternal longevity of Sōng and Qiáo,
valuing fleeting worldly glory above all.
What a pity!"
Yǎngshén Zhī
During the reign of Qín Shǐhuáng,
many people in Dàyuān died of plague.
There was a bird that carried a blade of grass and covered their faces with it, upon which they would revive.
Guǐgǔ Xiānshēng said:
“Among the ten continents in the sea,
Zǔzhōu has the Herb of Immortality,
which grows in the Qióng fields.
It is also called Yǎngshén Zhī.
One stalk can revive one person.”
Zéxiè Wán Fāng
Wáng Tàn,
at the beginning of the Hàn dynasty, withdrew to Nánshān,
residing in Lóuguān.
He valued his reputation less than his person,
and considered virtue the root of the Dao.
He widely practiced generosity and charity,
and cared for all living beings.
Zhào Xiānshēng taught him the method of Huángtíng Nèijǐng and the formula for Zéxiè Wán.
Later, he met Tàixuán Xiānnǚ,
who could transform her body and change scenes,
manifesting myriad forms in an instant.
He then became a disciple of Sīmǎ Jìzhǔ
and obtained the art of infinite divine transformations.
Suddenly, he would rise up and dissipate into clouds and mist;
or standing on flat ground, it would become a towering mountain.
His appearance remained exactly the same,
staying in the old spot.
Taking Huánglián
Wáng Chuán,
courtesy name Gōng,
studied the Dao.
He took huánglián for 140 years,
and his strength was like that of a forty-year-old.
Zhǔbù Huā
Wáng Xīng served as the zhǔbù of Pújiāng.
After resigning from office,
he lived as a recluse on Qiūcháng Shān.
In a cave at the foot of the mountain lived a thousand-year-old golden toad,
and those who saw it would attain the Dao.
On the peak of the mountain was a qióng flower,
whose leaves resembled white sandalwood.
When the flower bloomed, someone would ascend to heaven.
Xīng cultivated himself on this mountain for nine years.
Suddenly, he saw the qióng flower emit its radiance
and the golden toad leap.
A cloud chariot came to welcome him,
and he ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Later generations passed it down as Zhǔbù Huā.
Wèiyāng
Wáng Jiā, courtesy name Zǐnián,
had long resided at Dōngyáng Gǔkǒu.
When Fú Jiān campaigned against Jìn,
he sent someone to ask about his fortune.
Jiā said:
“The adamantine fire is too strong for Jiān to resolve.”
Jiā rode his horse slowly,
then dismounted, abandoned his clothes,
and rode his horse back.
Jiān still did not understand.
He further asked about the duration of the dynasty's reign.
Jiā replied:
“Wèiyāng (not yet ended).”
Jiān considered it an auspicious sign.
The next year,
which was the guǐwèi year,
Jiān suffered a great defeat at Shòuzhōu,
and subsequently perished.
This meant the disaster was in the wèi year.
He took the west of Qín as gold
and the south of the Jìn capital as fire,
as fire can melt gold.
When Yáo Cháng stabilized Cháng'ān,
he asked Jiā:
“Do I correspond to the Nine-Five position?”
He replied:
“Barely.”
Cháng was enraged
and executed Jiā and his two disciples.
Cháng had previously sent someone to Lǒngyòu.
They met Jiā with his disciples,
already over a thousand *lǐ* away.
It was precisely the day Jiā was executed.
Cháng ordered his coffin to be opened,
but there was no corpse,
only a bamboo branch for each.
Wáng Qiáo Yǒu Sān
On Běipíng Shān in Yìzhōu, there was a white toad,
called Ròuzhī.
Only immortals with spiritual bones
could obtain it.
Wáng Qiáo ate it
and attained the Dao.
Today, in Wǔyáng, there is a shrine to Immortal Qiáo.
There were three Wáng Qiáo,
with the same name.
There was Prince Jìn Wáng Qiáo,
and Yè Lìng Wáng Qiáo.
The Wáng Qiáo who ate the Ròuzhī
was a divine immortal from Shǔ.
Tāixī Shù
Wáng Zhēn,
at the age of seventy-nine, began to study the Dao.
He practiced the art of tāixī (embryonic breathing),
abstaining from grains for over thirty years.
His strength was equal to that of several men.
Shuǐmǔ
Wáng Xuánzhī saw a Daoist priest at night,
and followed him.
They were at the bottom of the Xījiāng River.
In the moonlight, no mud or sand was seen.
The water parted by itself as they walked.
By the path was an object like a dragon,
yet also like a snake,
about ten zhàng long.
The Daoist priest said:
“This is the shuǐmǔ (jellyfish/water-mother).
Those who see it will live long.”
Méi Shàng Ròukuài
Wáng Shǒuyī,
at the beginning of the Zhēngguān era, called himself Wáng Bùyī, a man from Zhōngnán Shān,
and sold medicine in Luòyáng market.
A wealthy man, Liǔ Xìn,
had only one son,
who had a fleshy lump on his eyebrow.
Bùyī took a pill from his gourd and gave it to him.
In a moment, the lump broke,
and a small snake squirmed out,
resplendent in five colors,
gradually growing to about one zhàng.
Bùyī yelled at it,
and the snake leaped up.
Clouds and mist darkened,
and Bùyī rode the snake away.
Táo Hén Dà Rú Shù Dǒu
Wáng Chú served as the magistrate of Wángwū.
He often recited the Huángtíng Jīng six thousand times,
but had not yet grasped its profound meaning.
After resigning from office,
he abstained from grains and swallowed vital essence.
He entered a cave,
where there was a stone chamber and a stone bed,
and an ancient scripture scroll on a table.
Chú bowed twice and said:
“This subject has presumptuously entered the grotto-heaven,
a rare encounter in myriad kalpas.
Now I behold the profound scripture;
I wish for my mortal eyes to peruse it once.”
Suddenly, a person appeared and said:
“I am the True Person of the Eastern Pole, Wáng Tàixū.
The Huángtíng Jīng was annotated by me;
I bestow it upon you.
I also give you peach pits,
each as large as several dòu.
Grind and consume them;
they will cure illnesses and prolong life.
You cannot stay here yet;
you have another twenty-year term.”
Chú took the pits and the scripture and returned.
Tán Yī Xián Qín
Tàizhēn Wáng Fūrén,
the young daughter of Wáng Mǔ.
Whenever she played a one-stringed zither,
hundreds of birds would fly and gather.
She often rode a white dragon,
traveling throughout the four seas.
Zhào Bǔ Xiānguān
The niece of Chancellor Wáng Huī,
as a child, she yearned for the Dao,
holding scriptures and playing the zither.
She often said:
“The grotto palace has called me;
I am to be appointed a celestial official.”
She wrote a poem:
“Playing by water and climbing mountains, there’s never enough time;
The immortals frequently descend to listen to my zither and poetry.
This heart does not yearn to dwell in the human world;
I only see a pair of cranes flying in the sky.”
That evening,
she passed away suddenly.
The next day,
paired cranes and music,
and exotic fragrance filled the fields.
When they moved her body to the wood,
only her empty clothes remained.
Xuánzhōu Gōngzhǔ
Nǚxiān Wáng Bàotái 女仙王抱臺 attained the Way,
residing in the palace of Xuánzhōu 玄洲.
The island was surrounded by dark, surging waves that reached the sky.
Bàotái 抱臺 was the maidservant of Zhǔxiān Dàojūn 主仙道君.
Dàojūn 道君 commanded her to wear a green brocade with a jade satchel,
and to bring out the hidden scripture Lóngwén Bālíng Zhēnjīng 龍文八靈真經,
to bestow upon Qīngxū Wáng Zhēnrén 青虛王真人.
Bái Yún Rú Bǎichǐ Lóu 白雲如百尺樓
The two Daoist adepts lived in the Bǎitái 柏臺 of Guǐgǔ 鬼谷.
White clouds often emerged from the platform,
appearing like a hundred-foot tower from a distance.
Dàozhēn 道真 often rode on these clouds, playing on the mountain peaks.
At dusk, when he returned,
the clouds would also retract into the platform.
Héngwēi Xiāng 蘅薇香
The mother of Zhāng Dàolíng 張道陵
was given Héngwēi xiāng 蘅薇香 by a celestial being from the Kuíxīng 魁星.
She became pregnant by this sensation.
Huàchū Yùjú 化出玉局
During the Yǒngshòu 永壽 reign of Huán Dì 桓帝,
Tàishàng 太上 descended upon Chéngdū 成都.
From the ground there, a jade stand emerged,
upon which he ascended and sat.
He imparted essential doctrines to Dàolíng 道陵.
Jiàngxuě Dān 絳雪丹
During the Kāiyuán 開元 reign,
the palace attendant Zhào Yúnróng 趙雲容 asked Wáng Yuánzhī 王元之 for medicine to prolong life.
Yuánzhī 元之 gave her one pill of Jiàngxuě Dān 絳xuě丹,
saying:
"If you take this,
you will surely not perish when you die,
and will be reborn after a hundred years."
By the end of the Yuánhé 元和 reign,
a hundred years had passed,
and Yúnróng 雲容 was indeed reborn.
Xiǎo'ér Sòngjīng Shēng 小兒誦經聲
During the Kāiyuán 開元 reign,
Wénjìng Tiānshī 文靖天師 and Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn 司馬承禎 each lay on their pillows.
Suddenly, they heard the sound of a small child chanting scriptures,
clear and melodious like jade and metal.
Tiānshī 天師 peered at it,
and saw a small sun, like a coin, shining brightly on Chéngzhēn's 承禎 forehead, illuminating the entire room.
He drew closer to listen,
and it was the sound from Chéngzhēn's 承禎 brain.
Báilǘ 白驢
Zhāng Guǒ 張果 often rode a white donkey.
When he rested, he would fold it like paper
and store it in a box.
When he sprinkled water on it,
it would become a donkey again.
Bái Biānfú Jīng 白蝙蝠精
Mínghuáng 明皇 asked Yè Fǎshàn 葉法善:
"Who is Zhāng Guǒ 張果?"
Fǎshàn 法善 replied:
"He is a white bat spirit from the initial division of chaos."
End of Juǎn Zhī Sān 卷之三.
End.
Tí Jǐ 綈几
According to the Hàn 漢 system,
the emperor's jade armrest was covered with brocade in winter,
called a tí jǐ 綈几.
Ivory was used for braziers,
wine for water droppers,
and jade for inkstones,
all chosen because they would not freeze.
In summer, feather fans were provided,
and also silk fans.
Chángmǎn Dēng 常滿燈
Dīng Huǎn 丁緩, a skilled artisan from Cháng'ān 長安, made a Chángmǎn Dēng 常滿燈.
It featured seven dragons and five phoenixes,
interspersed with lotus flowers.
He also made a portable incense burner for use under covers,
with a mechanism that rotated all around,
while the burner body remained level.
He also made a seven-wheeled large fan,
which, when operated by one person,
caused the whole hall to shiver with cold.
Qīxī Chuānzhēn 七夕穿針
During Qīxī 七夕 in the Hàn 漢 palace, needle threading
was done in the Kāijīn Lóu 開襟樓.
The needles all had seven holes.
Jiǔzhī Dēng 九枝燈
In Qín Xiányáng 秦咸陽, there was a nine-branched lamp of green jade.
Beneath it was a coiled dragon,
and when lit, its scales and armor all moved.
Xiàng Yǔ 項羽 entered the pass and took it.
Zhūrú Yùxiá 珠襦玉匣
According to the Hàn 漢 system,
all imperial tombs contained pearl shirts and jade caskets,
shaped like armor,
connected with gold threads.
On Wǔ Dì's 武帝 casket, there were also carved dragons.
Jújiǔ 菊酒
According to Hàn 漢 custom,
on the ninth day of the ninth month, people wore sprigs of cornelian cherry,
ate Artemisia cakes,
and drank chrysanthemum wine.
The method was to mix chrysanthemum with millet to brew wine,
seal it in a room,
and open it on the Chóngyáng 重陽 day of the following year
to drink the aged wine.
Hàn 漢 system,
in the ancestral temple, aged wine was drunk in the eighth month,
using jiǔyùn jiǔ 九醞酒 (nine-fermentation wine).
Liánzhī Cǎo 連枝草
In the Lèyóu Yuàn 樂遊苑, rose bushes grew naturally.
Beneath the trees, there was much alfalfa,
also called Huáifēng 懷風,
and also Guāngfēng 光風.
The wind among them was always rustling.
The sunlight shone on its flowers with splendor.
The people of Màolíng 茂陵 called it liánzhī cǎo 連枝草.
Yuǎnfāng Yìguǒ 遠方異果
Guīlì 瑰栗 (chestnuts of extraordinary quality), wénxìng 文杏 (figured apricots), xiānghétáo 緗核桃 (deep yellow walnuts), qīngfánglǐ 青房李 (green-chambered plums)
were all rare fruits from distant lands,
planted in the Shànglín 上林 park.
Zǐní Xīshì 紫泥璽室
The Zhōngshū 中書 (Central Secretariat) of Hàn 漢 used purple mud from Wǔdū 武都 for their seal chambers,
all covered with green brocade.
Bǎofū 寶跗
The imperial writing brushes presented
were inlaid with precious hilt ornaments (bǎofū 寶跗),
interspersed with decorations of jade bi 璧 and kingfisher feathers.
Jīn Kōuhuán 金彄環
Qī Fūrén 戚夫人 was skilled at the 'raised sleeves and bent waist' dance,
and sang the songs "Chūsài" 出塞, "Rùsài" 入塞, and "Wàngguī" 望歸.
She also wore bracelets (kōuhuán 彄環) made of a hundred-refined gold,
which allowed the finger bones to be seen through them.
The emperor disliked this,
and gave them to his serving maids Míngyù 鳴玉 and Yàoyù 耀玉, etc.
Jíguāng Qiú 吉光裘
During Wǔ Dì's 武帝 time,
the Western Regions presented a Jíguāng Qiú 吉光裘 (auspicious light fur coat),
which would not get wet in water.
A foreign country presented short people.
Dōngfāng Shuò 東方朔 asked:
"Jùlíng 巨靈,
how did you rebel?
Is Āmǔ 阿母 well now?"
Jīnwū Zhù Ājiāo 金屋貯阿嬌
When Wǔ Dì 武帝 was a prince,
just a few years old,
Chén Chángzhǔ 陳長主 wanted to marry her daughter to the emperor.
She asked:
"Is Ājiāo 阿嬌 good?"
The emperor replied:
"If I get Ājiāo 阿嬌,
I will keep her in a golden house."
The princess was pleased,
and immediately had her married to the emperor.
Ājiāo 阿嬌
was the small name of Empress Chén 陳.
Yù Sāotóu 玉搔頭
Wǔ Dì 武帝 visited Lǐ Fūrén 李夫人
and bestowed upon her a jade hairpin (sāotóu 搔頭).
He also bestowed an ivory mat.
Suìxīng Bùjiàn Shíbā Nián 歲星不見十八年
Before Dōngfāng Shuò 東方朔 died,
he said:
"No one in the world knows me,
only the calendar official Dàrèn Gōng 大任公 knows."
The emperor summoned and asked him,
and he said:
"The Jupiter star has not been seen for eighteen years,
and it will appear this evening."
Tūn Wénshí 吞文石
Hóngchéng Zǐ 弘成子,
when young, was given a patterned stone,
as large as a swallow's egg.
He swallowed it,
and his mind became clear and enlightened,
whereupon he became a learned scholar.
Later, when ill,
he vomited out the stone,
and gave it to his disciple Wǔlù Chōngzōng 五鹿充宗,
who also became a great scholar.
Lóng Shēng Jiǔ Zǐ 龍生九子
When Hùzǐ 瓠子 first breached,
there was a flood dragon with nine offspring,
which swam upstream from the breach,
splashing waves and foam for several li.
Xiāng Lián’ài
On the Qīxī of the Hàn palace,
facing the hundred sons,
the pond was bound with five-colored threads,
called xiāng lián’ài (mutual love and pity).
Under the Bamboo, Playing Chess for Divination
On the fourth day of the eighth month,
they played chess under the bamboo for divination.
The winner would have good fortune all year,
the loser would fall ill.
Jiǔyì
When Emperor Wén was in the Dài mansion,
he had nine excellent horses,
named Jiǔyì (Nine Steeds).
These included Chìdiàn, Línjū, Zǐyànliú, and Lǜchīcōng.
Xìxiàng
Júdàolóng.
In ancient times, there was Huáng Gōng,
whose art could control tigers.
He could also instantly raise clouds and mists,
and sitting, transform mountains and rivers.
Later, as he aged and weakened,
he drank excessively,
and his art lost its divine power.
He was eaten by a tiger.
Therefore, among the Sānfǔ, this was taken as a xìxiàng (warning omen).
Dōnggé Sānguǎn
When Gōngsūn Hóng was Chancellor,
he opened the Dōnggé and divided it into
three halls:
one was called Qīnxián,
to receive great worthies;
the next was Qiáocái,
to receive great talents;
the last was Jiēshì,
to receive national scholars.
Better to meet a bad guest than an old friend
Gōngsūn Hóng fed his old friend Gāo Hè with coarse grain rice,
and covered him with a cloth quilt.
Hè said:
"What use is an old friend's wealth and status?
Coarse grain rice and a cloth quilt,
I have these myself.
Hóng has five cauldrons in his inner kitchen,
but only one dish for his outer meal.
This is deceit."
Hóng said:
"Better to meet a bad guest,
than to meet an old friend."
Jiāchéng
When Téng Gōng went to the Eastern Capital,
as he left the gate, his horse neighed,
crouched, and would not advance.
It pawed the ground, forming a pit.
The Duke ordered it dug,
and a stone sarcophagus was found,
with ancient and unusual inscriptions.
Shūsūn Tōng said:
"It is Tadpole Script."
The text read:
"The beautiful city is verdant,
after three thousand years, it sees the white sun.
Alas, Téng Gōng resides in this chamber."
The Duke sighed:
"It is fate!
When I die, shall I rest here?"
Later, he was buried there.
Dragon Entering the Bosom
Dǒng Zhòngshū dreamed of a dragon entering his bosom,
whereupon he wrote the Chūnqiū Fánlù.
Words Containing Wind and Frost
Huáinán Wáng Ān wrote the Hóngliè,
and said:
"The words within all contain wind and frost."
Dust Falling and Cap Flying
Whenever Dōngfāng Shuò whistled,
dust fell and his cap flew off.
Sùshuāngqiú
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú and Wénjūn grew poorer over time,
and pawned his sùshuāngqiú (heron-feather cloak) for wine.
Báitóu Yín
Xiāngrú wanted to take a woman from Màolíng as a concubine.
Wénjūn wrote the Báitóu Yín (White Head Chant) to cut ties with him,
and Xiāngrú stopped.
Writing the Měirén Fù
Wénjūn's brows needed no darkening makeup,
like distant mountains,
her cheeks were always like hibiscus,
her skin like fat.
Chángqīng (Xiāngrú) had long suffered from xiókě (wasting and thirsting disease).
He wrote the Měirén Fù (Rhapsody on the Beautiful Woman) to mock himself,
and eventually died of this disease.
Wénjūn composed an elegy for him,
which was passed down through the generations.
Dreaming of a Yellow-Robed Elder
As Xiāngrú was about to present his rhapsody,
unsure what to write,
he dreamed of a yellow-robed elder who said:
"You may write the Dàrén Fù (Rhapsody on the Great Man)."
He then composed it.
Méi Mǎ Wénzhāng
Méi Gāo's writing was quick,
but sometimes contained redundant phrases;
Chángqīng's was slow and deliberate,
with a warm and beautiful beginning and end;
thus, it is known that hurried action leaves no good traces.
Yáng Xióng said:
"During military campaigns,
for urgent letters and rapid manifestos,
use Méi Gāo;
in the halls of the court,
for lofty essays and grand treatises,
use Xiāngrú."
There is much in here
When Huì Zhuāng debated with Zhū Yún,
he stuttered and could not respond.
He pointed to his chest and said:
"Though my mouth cannot speak eloquently,
there is much in here."
Twitching Eyes Bring Wine and Food
Lù Jiǎ said:
"Twitching eyes bring wine and food,
lamp flowers bring money,
magpie chirps mean travelers arrive,
spiders gathering mean all things are joyful."
Arithmetic
Sōng Zhēn and Cáo Yuánlǐ both loved arithmetic.
Zhēn calculated that he would die at 73,
on the twenty-fifth day of the first month at dusk.
He died on the twenty-fourth day at dusk.
His wife said:
"I saw Zhēn Cháng deduct one from his calculation.
I suspected there was another meaning,
so I didn't say anything.
Indeed, he died one day earlier.
What a regret!"
Chén Guǎnghàn stored two granaries of rice.
He asked Yuánlǐ to calculate the amount.
Yuánlǐ took a pair of chopsticks, made a few calculations,
and said:
"Each contains such and such."
When the granaries were opened and checked,
the eastern one's amount matched, but the western one
was off by one shēng.
There was a dead mouse inside.
Yuánlǐ was ashamed and said:
"I didn't know that the mouse wasn't rice.
I might as well have flayed my face!"
Another day,
Yuánlǐ visited Guǎnghàn,
who offered a very meager meal.
Guǎnghàn said:
"There are unexpected guests,
but no unprepared host."
Yuánlǐ used seven chopsticks to calculate and said:
"There's steamed pork on the chopping block,
and lychees in the kitchen.
Why aren't they served?"
Guǎnghàn was greatly astonished.
Wet Nurse Appeals for Help
Emperor Wǔ wanted to kill his wet nurse.
She appealed to Dōngfāng Shuò for help.
Shuò said:
"When you leave, just look back at me repeatedly;
I will come up with a clever way to provoke him."
The wet nurse did as instructed.
Shuò, standing beside the Emperor, said:
"You should leave quickly.
The Emperor is already grown now.
How could he still think of when you nursed him?"
The Emperor then spared her.
Wǔhóu Qīng
The Five Marquises were not on good terms,
and their guests could not visit each other.
Lóu Hù arranged a gathering,
pleasing each of them,
and they competed to bring exotic dishes.
Hù combined them into a dish called qīng,
which the world called "Wǔhóu Qīng,"
considering it an extraordinary delicacy.
Golden Slingshot Pellet
Hán Yān loved to play with slingshots,
using golden pellets,
losing hundreds each day.
At the time, a saying went:
"Suffering from hunger and cold,
chasing golden pellets."
Huái Qián Tí Qiàn
Yáng Xióng carried lead tablets and held wooden slips,
following the record-keeping officials,
inquiring about dialects from all directions,
to compose the Fāngyán.
Dān Hú Guǎ Fú
Liú Dàojiāng was skilled at playing the guqin,
performing the melody "Dān Hú Guǎ Fú."
Listeners were overcome with sorrow.
Mèng Bái Fèng
When Yáng Xióng was writing the Tài Xuán,
he dreamt of a white phoenix landing on it.
He once said:
"Chángqīng's rhapsodies don't seem to come from the human world."
His friend asked:
"How good are they?"
He replied:
"They combine woven patterns to form text,
and arrange brocades to form the essence."
Thus, the "Hé Zǔ" song
and the "Liè Jǐn" rhapsody
were created.
Pú Táo Jǐn Sàn Huā Líng
Huò Guāng's wife gifted Chún yú Yǎn fifty bolts of Pú Táo Jǐn Sàn Huā Líng.
The绫 (líng) came from Chén Bǎoguāng's family in Jùlù.
Huò Xiǎn summoned him to her mansion to make it.
It took sixty days to complete one bolt.
Each bolt was worth ten thousand coins.
She also gave her pearl ornaments, gold, and money,
built her a mansion,
and gave her innumerable servants.
Yǎn said:
"What功 (gōng) have I achieved for you
to reward me like this?"
Chún yú Yǎn
was a female physician.
Huò Guāng's wife had her use poison to kill Empress Xǔ.
Later, all were executed,
implicating several thousand families.
Dú Fù Qiān Shǒu
Someone asked Yáng Xióng about writing rhapsodies.
Xióng said:
"One must read a thousand rhapsodies
before one can write them."
Zhì Chéng Jīn Shí Wèi Kāi
Lǐ Guǎng was hunting on Míngshān
when he saw a sleeping tiger.
With one arrow, he killed it.
Another day, he saw another sleeping tiger.
He looked at it;
the arrow had pierced to the fletching.
He went closer to look,
and it was actually a stone.
He retreated and shot again,
but the arrowhead broke and the shaft snapped, yet the stone was unharmed.
Gé Hóng asked about this.
Yáng Xióng said:
"Extreme sincerity can penetrate metal and stone."
Hóng said:
"Once, there was a traveler in the East Sea
who encountered a storm and his boat drifted
to a solitary islet.
He moored his boat, went ashore to cook,
but before the food was cooked, the boat sank.
The islet was a giant fish,
which swallowed the waves, exhaled them, and departed."
"Also,
Chén Gǎo went into the mountains to gather firewood
and saw a stone horse in front of a tomb.
He mistook it for a deer.
His axe chipped and its handle broke,
but the stone horse was unharmed.
Both these cases involved extreme sincerity,
so why was the effect on metal and stone biased?"
Xióng had no answer.
Sān Yún Diàn
Emperor Chéng set up cloud curtains, cloud canopies, and cloud screens in the Zǐdiàn palace at Gānquán.
The world called it the "Sān Yún Diàn."
Jīn Yī Jú Shāng
A yellow swan descended to the Tàiyè pool,
singing:
"A yellow swan flies down to Jiànzhāng,
with gold for its clothes and chrysanthemums for its skirt."
Diāo Hú
Gù Áo served his mother with extreme filial piety.
His mother loved to eat diāo hú,
which is the grain of the wild rice.
Yōuwáng's tomb
had a very large entrance.
More than a hundred corpses were piled up,
but only one man's appearance was lifelike.
Bìng Fāng
The Supervisor of the Mìshūshěng
was called the 'Chancellor's Bìng Fāng';
the Shǎofǔ
was called the 'Palace Attendant's Bìng Fāng';
the Chéng and Dàzhuó
were called the 'Provincial Official's Bìng Fāng';
the Mìshūláng and Xiǎozhuó
were called the 'Censor's Bìng Fāng'.
Shā Lóng Zhōng Rén
Before Lǐ Fān passed the examinations,
a monk told him:
"You are a shā lóng zhōng rén."
Fān asked for the reason.
The monk said:
"All chancellors
in the underworld have their images erected,
protected by a gauze cage."
Later, he indeed rose to the position of a senior minister.
Zétiān Gǎi Xīn Zì
Zétiān liked to change characters.
Someone said there was a "huò" in the "guó,"
and that "huò"
meant bewilderment,
requesting to suppress it with "wǔ."
So, "guó" was changed to "武."
Again, it was said that "wǔ" inside "kǒu"
was no different from a prisoner.
So, it was changed to "囧."
Míng Jiān Liè Bǎng
Cuī Shào died suddenly.
He revived
and saw lists in the underworld,
with people's names written in full.
Generals and chancellors were on golden lists;
the next rank was on silver lists;
minor officials from prefectures and counties were all on long iron lists.
Niàn Zhū Tīng
The Jīngzhào Shìcáo handled a hundred and eight judicial cases,
calling it the "Niàn Zhū Tīng."
Fó Páo Jí
Zhāng Tián Gǔ said to his colleague:
"Recently, I bought Sēng Rǔ Jí."
He was referring to Niú Sēngrǔ.
His colleague said:
"I also obtained Fó Páo Jí."
Qín Jīng Zá Jì
Chàng Zhàng
According to the ordinances of Kāiyuán:
When punishing people through official examination,
only governors and magistrates were allowed to order flogging;
other officials were not.
Fó Yá
Five temples in the capital city had Fó Yá:
Zǒngchí Sì on the right street,
Ānguó Sì on the left street,
Chóngshèng Sì,
Jiànfú Sì,
Ruìshèng Sì.
Fasts were set up in sequence,
lasting up to half a month.
By the seventh or eighth day, envoys were sent to bestow incense,
and the city's populace gathered in great numbers.
Bào Luó Shǐ
After the jinshi examination results were announced and before the spring pass,
