there had to be one person who died,
named the "Bào Luó Shǐ,"
meaning to report to Dà Luó Tiān.
Shéng Jué Zhī Xì
On the Cold Food Festival,
the chariots of the Nèipúsī and the various military commanders played a game called "Shéng Jué Zhī Xì."
They drove chariots to both ends of a road, hammered in large stakes,
and stretched a rope between the stakes,
about two feet high.
It had to be tightly secured.
The chariots would turn and circle,
rolling their wheels over the rope.
Those who didn't fall won;
those whose wheels fell below the rope lost.
All adorned their chariots and oxen,
betting items numbering in the thousands.
Nèi Rén Kē
The old wall inside Xiányáng
was called Nèi Rén Kē,
also written as Xié.
Deceased palace women were buried there.
It was two or three lǐ long.
In wind and rain, songs and cries could be heard.
**Yīnshēng Shù**
After all the provinces,
outside the gate of the Dūtáng, there was a large locust tree,
called the **Yīnshēng Shù**.
If someone was to be appointed as a **púshè**,
this locust tree would surely emit sounds like songs.
**Hànbō**
**Hànbō** was named for its delicious fish.
**Shíqiáo Shàng Bǔ Xíngmǎ**
When the **Jīngzhàoyǐn** was newly appointed,
his subordinates often watched the horses cross the stone bridge
to divine his future actions.
If the horses crossed the bridge quickly,
this **Yǐn** would surely be benevolent;
if the horses moved slowly and with difficulty,
this **Yǐn** would surely be severe and wicked.
It was very accurate.
**Yājīng Qián**
When Lǐ Ài was the **Yǐn**,
it was customary
for various departments like **Yányīng Zhōng Xiè Gémén** to use
a total of three thousand strings of cash,
funded by public service money.
When Ài arrived,
only a few strings of cash were found to be present.
He asked his clerk how they managed to get enough.
The clerk asked to consult with **Hán Zhū**, the officer for catching thieves.
Zhū said,
"This is easy.
Tomorrow, during the morning court,
drag **Zhū** into the courtyard,
and question him about the mingling of Persian and Han merchants in the West Market,
then release him after a long time."
Ài, being a scholar,
did not understand the reason behind this.
The next day,
he reproached **Zhū** as instructed.
When **Zhū** was released,
about two hundred households of foreign merchants each sent "fright-calming money,"
amounting to several thousand strings of cash.
Three thousand strings of cash were then supplied to the treasury,
with a substantial surplus.
**Shìyǔ**
The market people of Cháng'ān spoke differently,
there were gourd talk (**húlu yǔ**), lock talk (**suǒzi yǔ**), knot talk (**niǔ yǔ**), chain talk (**liàn yǔ**), and three-fold talk (**sānzhé yǔ**),
collectively called **shìyǔ**.
**Jīsù**
During a general amnesty,
a golden rooster was erected,
and a victory ornament was placed in its mouth.
When the **Xuānzhèng** court drum sounded,
the rooster on the tower crowed.
Six people would, on that day, simultaneously climb the rooster pole with ropes,
competing for the ornament in its mouth.
The winner
received a monthly salary of three **shí** of grain,
called **jīsù**.
**Suígà Lǎoyā**
During imperial progresses and inner banquets,
flocks of crows often soared and gathered,
known as "imperial escort old crows" (**suígà lǎoyā**).
Later, they were driven away with bows, arrows, and pellets.
**Wǔyáng**
The two mountains of Pānyú
gave Guǎngzhōu its name.
In the past, five immortals rode sheep and arrived,
hence the name **Wǔyáng**.
**Huǒzhái Sēng**
Monks who had families
were called **huǒzhái sēng**.
**Léicáng**
Villagers dug caves in the mountains,
offering various items to the thunder god,
hoping the thunder god would enjoy them.
This was called "**Léicáng**."
**Léiláng**
If a commoner's daughter was possessed by a spirit,
she was called a **Léiláng**,
and her children were called "thunder children" (**léizǐ**).
**Kàncháo**
When the magistrate of Pānyú first arrived, after three days,
he would visit the tide god.
By observing how many gods appeared,
he would know how many years he would serve in office.
If the person governed well,
the gods would rise majestically
and descend slowly,
their number often reaching seven.
**Gētáng**
Southerners valued folk songs.
They would often gather in one place to sing together,
calling it **gētáng**.
**Làyī Fú'èr**
Festivals highly regarded in Lǐngbiǎo:
the first of **Là** (the 12th lunar month), the second of **Fú** (the hottest days of summer), the third of Winter, and the fourth of the New Year.
**Shuǐyī**
Killing oxen to sacrifice to ghosts for treating illness
was called **máoyào**.
Whenever a fever occurred,
water was poured over the patient's head from the top,
called **shuǐyī**.
**Dàngfēng**
According to Guǎng custom,
before meeting the wife's parents,
the bride first drank a large cup of wine,
called **dàngfēng**.
**Zhānbǔ**
There were many forms of divination in Lǐngbiǎo:

rat divination (**shǔbǔ**), chopstick divination (**zhùbǔ**), ox divination (**niúbǔ**), bone divination (**gǔbǔ**), snail divination (**tiánluóbǔ**), chicken egg divination (**jīluǎnbǔ**), and bamboo strip divination (**mièzhúbǔ**).
This was due to their belief in ghosts.
**Zhàngmǔ**
Sometimes a substance would be seen descending from the sky,
initially like a pellet,
gradually growing to the size of a carriage wheel,
then scattering.
If a person was struck by it, they would fall ill.
This was called "**Zhàngmǔ**."
**Guǐshì**
Ghost markets (**guǐshì**) sometimes appeared by the sea,
forming at midnight
and dispersing at cockcrow.
Those who attended
often obtained strange objects.
**Huìjī**
Róngzhōu people liked to eat **jī** (pickled vegetables),
but the locals considered it taboo.
Some say
it was made from earthworms.
**Yù Dǐ Què** People of Lídòng
used incense instead of firewood;
below Jīngshān,
they used jade to repel magpies.
**Hòufān**
The horseshoe crab has a bone on its back like a fan.
It travels with the wind,
thus called **hòufān**.
When they gather in large numbers like rafts,
they are called **hòupái**.
**Liànfēng**
When a hurricane (**jùfēng**) was about to strike,
there would be a light breeze and fine rain,
starting slowly then intensifying,
called **liànfēng**.
There was also the **Shíyóu Fēng**,
also a type of hurricane.
**Qīcháo**
When the morning tide receded
and the evening tide rose,
the two waters merged,
called **qīcháo**.
**Cháotián**
Fields irrigated by tidal water
were called **cháotián**.
**Tiānhá**
The **tiānhá** (sky frog) was as large as a common frog.
Whenever there was heavy snow,
it would descend from the sky,
thus named **tiānhá**.
**Dàosūn**
Rice that regrew after being harvested
was called **dàosūn**.
**Héhuāncài**
Its leaves were like fingernails,
with four leaves opposing each other at each node.
It closed at night and opened during the day,
called **héhuāncài**.
**Yúzǐcǎo**
In streams and lakes,
grass often bore fish eggs.
The grass was collected and dried,
and in spring,
planted in ponds,
quickly transforming into fish.
**Jìnghuǒshù**
There was a plant called **jìnghuǒshù** (fire-competing tree),
meaning fire could not burn it.
Many were planted to ward off fire.
It was also called **huǒhéyán**,
meaning like a river separating fire.
**Chuánjiǎo**
Emperor Yángdì (Yángdì) went to Jiāngdū (Jiāngdū).
He commanded the Dragon Boat from Luòkǒu (Luòkǒu).
It was forty-five *chǐ* (chǐ) high,
fifty *chǐ* (chǐ) wide,
and two hundred *chǐ* (chǐ) long.
It was divided into four decks.
The top deck had a main hall,
the next deck had one hundred and sixty rooms,
and the two lower decks housed the palace attendants and boatmen.
Boatmen was the name for the water-workers.
Agarwood Hall
Yáng Sù (Yáng Sù) built a residence in the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū),
which was extravagantly and ingeniously designed to the extreme.
In its center, he erected an Agarwood Hall (Chénxiāng Táng).
After its completion, it was sealed.
Three days later, when it was opened,
the four walls were splattered with fresh blood,
and a foul smell permeated the air.
Illustrated Gazetteer
Emperor Yángdì (Yángdì) ordered Dù Bǎo (Dù Bǎo) to compile a fifteen-volume Illustrated Gazetteer of Water Chambers (*Shuǐshì Tújīng*).
On the Shangsi (Shàngsì) Day, he gathered his ministers at Qūshuǐ (Qūshuǐ).
There was a divine turtle carrying the Eight Trigrams (Bāguà),
a yellow dragon carrying a map,
two yellow fish leaping,
white fish entering the boat,
Lǚ Wàng (Lǚ Wàng) fishing at Pánxī (Pánxī),
a golden figure holding a sword,
Zhōu Chǔ (Zhōu Chǔ) slaying a dragon,
Xǔ Yóu (Xǔ Yóu) washing his ears,
Zhuāng Zhōu (Zhuāng Zhōu) observing fish,
and Qū Yuán (Qū Yuán) sinking into the Xiāng (Xiāng) River.
A total of seventy-two such scenes
were all carved in wood.
Four Seasons Drink
Xiè Fěng (Xiè Fěng) created the Four Seasons Drink (*Sìshí Yǐn*):
in spring with peaches,
in summer with kumiss,
in autumn with lotus seeds,
and in winter with wolfberries.
Five Fragrances Drink
During the Rénshòu (Rénshòu) era,
Chan Master Chóu (Chóu) created the Five-Colored Drink (*Wǔsè Yǐn*).
He used hibiscus leaves for the green drink,
*báxiēchéng* (báxiēchéng) for the red drink,
kumiss for the white drink,
dark plums for the black drink,
and river bamboo for the yellow drink.
*Guì* (Guì) is the sound of *gūi* (gūi).
He also used agarwood, clove, *zélán* (zélán), and *gānsōng* (gānsōng) for the Five Fragrances Drink (*Wǔxiāng Yǐn*).
Auspicious Ganoderma
Auspicious ganoderma grew in the Eastern Capital (Dōngdū),
resembling towers and palaces.
Some even appeared to have characters emerging from them.
Two Dragons
Cài Yōng (Cài Yōng) and Cuī Shí (Cuī Shí) were known as "Paired Phoenixes."
Shí (Shí) and Xǔ Shòu (Xǔ Shòu) were also known as "Two Dragons."
Wáng Zhòngxuān (Wáng Zhòngxuān) was known as "Frog潛 Under the Mud."
Embroidered Tiger
Cáo Zhí (Cáo Zhí) composed a poem in seven paces,
earning him the moniker "Embroidered Tiger."
Hidden Phoenix, Concealed Swan
Dèng Ài (Dèng Ài) was known as "Hidden Phoenix,"
and Lù Yún (Lù Yún) as "Concealed Swan."
Throwing Jade at the Gate
Lǐ Shèng (Lǐ Shèng), while serving as the Administrator of Ānnán (Ānnán),
dreamed of someone throwing jade at his gate.
Shèng (Shèng) said,
"'Gate' (mén) and 'jade' (yù) combine to form the character 'rùn' (rùn),
meaning a leap month.
Surely there will be glorious prosperity."
Indeed, he became immensely wealthy and noble.
Sorrowless Wine
Emperor Wǔ of Han (Hàn Wǔdì) made "Sorrowless Wine" (*Wúchóu Jiǔ*);
whoever drank it became free from worry.
Three Times Flourishing, Three Times Withering
To the north of the capital city of Yángdū (Yángdū) in the Jìn (Jìn) dynasty,
there was a huai tree.
Within a single day,
it would flourish three times and wither three times.
Hidden Hook
Consort Gōuyì (Gōuyì Fūrén) was said to have clenched her fist, which was a national beauty.
The game of "hidden hook" originated from this.
Wèi Yě (Wèi Yě) Presents a Poem
Wáng Wéngōng Dàn (Wáng Wéngōng Dàn) served as prime minister to Emperor Zhēnzōng (Zhēnzōng) for nearly twenty years.
The recluse Wèi Yě (Wèi Yě) presented a poem:
"Year after year, prime ministers of great peace emerge;
You have been in the Central Secretariat for fourteen autumns.
The Western Sacrifices and Eastern Investiture are all completed;
Perhaps you can come and accompany Chìsōng (Chìsōng) on his travels."
Ōuyáng Gōng (Ōuyáng Gōng) wrote in Dàn's (Dàn) spirit-path stele inscription:
"When the state faces major affairs,
and affairs involve great doubts,
without relying on divination or milfoil,
the Duke serves as the *shīguī* (shīguī) [diviner]."
Emperor Zhēnzōng (Zhēnzōng) often relied on Dàn (Dàn) to resolve difficult matters.
Poetry with Medical Plant Names
Chén Yà (Chén Yà) rose to the position of Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Shàocǐng),
and was a master of wit.
He once composed poems using medical plant names,
for example: "The wind and moon are near the front lake,
the verandas and windows are cool with *bànxià* (bànxià)."
"Chess fears the cold of winter to *hēzǐ* (hēzǐ) down,
clothes dislike the warmth of spring to tailor with *suōshā* (suōshā)."
In "A Poem for a Monk Praying for Rain," he wrote:
"If there's no rain after *bànxià* (bànxià),
you and the master will be dried into *húluobā* (húluobā)."
He once said:
"With a rough gown, a sleeve full of invitations,
everywhere I go, I delay those who demand *húsǔo* (húsǔo)."
This line could be given to poor scholars who travel to seek patronage. Yà (Yà) was good friends with Zhāng Xún Gōng (Zhāng Xún Gōng),
and wrote "Shēngcházǐ" (*Shēngcházǐ*) to express his feelings:
"The court frequently grasps the worthy,
then occupies the path to the heavens.
It is naturally for a melancholy person,
that in peril and difficulty there is no place to move.
I also know there is no *mòyào* (mòyào) to cure loneliness and cold,
why misunderstand the eating of *bò* (bò)?
Large sheets of paper are pasted together,
the 'Ode to Returning to the Fields' of *gāncǎo* (gāncǎo)."
He once wrote three poems of boudoir sentiment in "Shēngcházǐ" (*Shēngcházǐ*):
"My longing is already deep,
white paper is insufficient to write it all.
Every character is like Cān (Cān) and Shēn (Shēn) [stars],
so I especially want my beloved to read them.
I clearly remember the promise to *dāngguī* (dāngguī),
and the ripe *yuǎnzhì* (yuǎnzhì) cherries.
Why, at the time of chrysanthemums,
have you not yet returned to our village?"
The second reads:
"After the rain, the small courtyard is cool,
the wind rustles the pinks on the steps.
Setting aside the fan, she is quite composed,
sleeping in a gauze curtain with *bànxià* (bànxià).
Rising, she sits idly in the north pavilion,
shedding pearls of tears.
She thinks of her husband's toil,
going to pluck the cassia in the Toad Palace."
The third reads:
"Wandering back and forth,
the azalea flowers frequently change.
Alas for the pomegranate skirt,
half of its orchid and musk fragrance has faded.
After idle thoughts, she plays the pipa again,
surely plucking the vermilion strings until they break.
She intends to mend the broken strings,
waiting for that scoundrel to see."
Yà (Yà) also made a riddle about his own name "Yà" (Yà):
"If it were allowed to have a mouth, it would be 'mute' (yǎ),
and it certainly wants to be 'heartless' (wúxīn) for evil.
Completely lacking intestines in the middle,
it forcibly grows sharp edges on the outside."
There are over a hundred other poems,
titled "Chéngyuán Jí" (*Chéngyuán Jí*).
In his poem "Suìdàn" (*Suìdàn*), he wrote:
"Coldness retreats to the earth's depths,
old age is distributed among mankind."
In his poem "Sending off Magistrate Wáng (Wáng) of Guīhuà (Guīhuà)," he wrote:
"Officials' farewells are like days of congratulations,
the people's send-off is like a welcoming."
In his "Jiāoyóu Shī" (*Jiāoyóu Shī*), he wrote:
"Horses whinnied where they once reached a temple,
dogs barked as they first entered a village."
Looking Down, the Yangtze Appears Small
Cáo Yǎn (Cáo Yǎn), a *lángzhōng* (lángzhōng), was also a wit.
A monk presented a volume of poems to Yǎn (Yǎn).
The first poem, "Ascending the Ganlu Pavilion (Gānlù Gé) in Rùnzhōu (Rùnzhōu)," read:
"Looking down, the Yangtze (Yángzǐ) appears small."
Yǎn (Yǎn) said,
"A lowly dog is fat."
Another poem, bidding farewell to a monk, read:
"Monkeys cry, travel thoughts are bleak."
Yǎn (Yǎn) said,
"Dogs bark at Third Sister-in-law Zhāng (Zhāng Sānsǎo)."
Fifth Watch Three Sevens on Eight
Liú Yè (劉瞱) Longtú (龍圖) was also a jester.
He often drank tea with Liú Jūn (劉筠).
He asked his attendants,
"Is the water boiling?"
Before his attendants could all answer,
"It's already boiling,"
Jūn (筠) said,
"You all say 'gǔn' (鯀)!"
Yè (瞱) said,
"I was asking about 'diǎn' (點)."
Another time, he rode side-by-side with Jūn (筠) to court.
Jūn's (筠) horse had a sore leg.
Yè (瞱) said,
"Why is your horse so slow?"
Jūn (筠) said,
"It's just 'wǔ gēng sān' (五更三)."
He meant 'diǎn tí' (點蹄), referring to its limping.
Yè (瞱) immediately replied,
"Why don't you give it 'qī shàng bā' (七上八)?"
He meant that Jūn (筠) should dismount and walk.
Official positions belong to the state.
When Chén Zhízhōng (陳執中) became chancellor,
his son-in-law sought an appointment.
Zhízhōng (執中) said,
"Official positions belong to the state,
they are not items in a bedroom chest.
How can my son-in-law expect to have one?"
He ultimately did not grant it.
During Rénzōng's (仁宗) reign,
censors repeatedly said,
"Zhízhōng (執中) is unlearned and without skill;
he is not fit to be a chancellor.
Your Majesty's continued favor,
is it not because Zhízhōng (執中) once, in the previous reign, pleaded for Your Majesty to be made crown prince?
The late emperor had only two sons,
and King Zhōu (周王) had already died.
If not Your Majesty, then who else could be established as heir?"
The Emperor said,
"It is not for that reason.
It is simply that Zhízhōng (執中) does not deceive me."
Féng Dào's (馮道) Poetry
Féng Dào's (馮道) poetry, though simple and direct,
reaches profound principles.
He has a poem that says:
"Poverty and prosperity are all determined by fate,
why bother to sigh?
Just know to do good deeds,
do not ask about the future.
When winter goes, ice must melt,
when spring comes, grass naturally grows.
I ask you, sir, to observe this principle,
the Way of Heaven is very clear."
He also wrote:
"Do not be disheartened in times of danger,
the future often holds opportune circumstances.
One must know that seas and mountains return to enlightened rulers,
how could Heaven and Earth entrap good people?
When has virtue ever departed the world?
Where do boats and carriages not find a crossing?
As long as your heart is free from evil,
you can stand firm even amidst wolves and tigers."
On Féng Dào (馮道)
The world ridicules Féng Dào (馮道) for serving four dynasties and eleven emperors,
unable to die a martyr's death.
Examining what he said and did,
he never acted deceitfully or compliantly.
To escape the chaotic times was,
perhaps, a blessing from Heaven.
At the end of the Shí Jìn (石晉) dynasty,
when a conflict arose with the barbarians,
no one dared to serve as envoy.
The young ruler ordered the chancellor to select someone.
Dào (道) wrote a memorial, saying,
"I, Dào (道), will go myself."
The entire court paled,
all believing he would fall into a tiger's mouth,
yet Dào (道) returned alive.
Initially, Guō Wēi (郭威) sent Dào (道) to welcome the Xiangyīn (湘陰) envoy.
Dào (道) said,
"I do not know if this matter is justified.
I, Dào (道), have never spoken falsely in my life,
do not make me a person who speaks falsely."
When Zhōu Shìzōng (周世宗) wanted to reclaim Hédōng (河東),
he boasted that this campaign would be like a mountain crushing an egg.
Dào (道) said,
"I do not know if Your Majesty can become a mountain."
In all these instances,
he showed sincerity and entrusted himself to fate,
never considering evasion or flattery.
Also, when the barbarian chieftain asked,
"The myriad people are in disarray,
who can save them?"
Dào (道) responded with a single sentence,
which was no less effective than saving a million lives.
Common people only see Dào's (道) outward actions,
but do not understand his heart.
Fù Wénzhōng Gōng (富文忠公) commented on Dào's (道) character, saying,
"This is what Mencius called a great man."
Losing Demeanor during the Birthday Celebration
Zhāng Wéndìng Gōng (張文定公) Qíxián (齊賢) served as chancellor under Tàizōng (太宗) and Zhēnzōng (真宗),
and was praised for his uprightness and reliability.
In his later years, he married a woman from the Xuē (薛) family,
which displeased Zhēnzōng (真宗).
At the New Year's court celebration, Qíxián (齊賢), already slightly tipsy,
lost his composure in his movements and deportment.
Because of this,
he was demoted to Ānzhōu (安州).
His dismissal edict stated:
"Moreover, he indulged in wine,
and his cap tilted."
This was indeed the reason.
Zhāng Qíxián's (張齊賢) Poetry
Zhāng Qíxián's (張齊賢) poem says:
"Do not fear speaking cautiously,
what harm is there in enduring things?
The laws of the state must be obeyed,
do not publicize others' faults.
Be selfless and overcome yourself,
be upright and harmonize with the light.
If this is truly achieved,
Heaven will surely send auspicious blessings."
Chǔhòu (處厚) expanded on this into eight chapters.
One of them says:
"One must believe in the method of the pivot,
how can a four-horse team pursue it?
The matter of three seals can be seen,
the karma of two tongues should be known."
Two says:
"How lamentable is the pāramitā,
how pitiful is King Kāli (歌利王).
From the heart and also from the blade,
the meaning of the words has detailed explanations."
Three says:
"If even a single hair is offended,
three feet will not be spared."
Four says:
"What is truly lacking in others,
what advantage is there in oneself?"
Five says:
"Being public and clear often invites resentment,
being high and proud easily attracts danger."
Six says:
"One must assist with harmony,
and harmony relies on direct interaction.
Relying on directness often leads to offense,
being overly harmonious lacks firmness."
Seven says:
"Forever rely on the strength of a cane,
and leave strategies for your descendants."
Eight says:
"Though expansion and contraction are not fixed,
flourishing and withering have their constant patterns."
Wanghuoma (望火馬) and Riyoushen (日遊神)
During the Huángyòu (皇祐) and Jiāyòu (嘉祐) eras,
there was no prohibition on visiting the palace,
and many scholars rushed to seek favors.
One person was called Wànghuǒmǎ (望火馬),
and another was called Rìyōushén (日遊神),
which was due to the daily scrambling and competing.
Incense Seal
The given name of Tàizǔ (太祖) (Xiāngyìn (香印)),
when mispronounced, sounded like 'xiāngyìn' (香印), or 'incense seal'.
Therefore, those selling incense seals were not allowed to call out their product explicitly,
but only rang a gong.
Rénzōng's (仁宗) given name, when mispronounced, sounded like 'zhēng' (蒸), or 'steamed'.
Today, steamed cakes are called 'cuībǐng' (炊餅),
to avoid the taboo.
Qián Wǔsù Wáng's (錢武肅王) given name was Liú (鏐).
To this day, in Wúyuè (吳越), pomegranates are called 'jīnyīng' (金櫻),
and the Liú (劉) family is called the Jīn (金) family.
'Liúzhù' (留住) (to stay) is called 'zhùzhù' (駐住).
Yáng Xíngmì (楊行密) controlled Jiānghuái (江淮).
To this day, 'mì' (蜜) (honey) is called 'fēngtáng' (蜂糖).
Father's Name Yuè (岳), Did Not Listen to Music
Liú Wēnsǒu's (劉溫叟) father's name was Yuè (岳).
Throughout his life, he did not listen to music,
nor did he visit Sōng (嵩) or Huà (華) mountains.
Whenever he attended an imperial banquet,
hearing the court music, he would weep for a long time.
He said,
"If not for the emperor's command,
I would not be here."
This is quite similar to Lǐ Hè (李賀), whose father's name was Jìnsù (晉肅), and thus he could not take the imperial examination.
Taboo Against Accepting Unlawful Bribes
Dù Qígōng Yǎn often said:
"The taboo names of one's parents
are my concern alone;
how do they relate to others?"
When the Duke was military governor of Bìng,
the gate official requested his family's taboo names.
The Duke said:
"This humble official has no names to taboo,
except for taking bribes that bend the law."
Later, the Duke retired from office
and wrote a poem saying:
"I am often deeply ashamed, like a pair of wild ducks riding wild geese;
wild horses and yellow sheep also cause excessive worry."
Zhāng Shuō of the Táng dynasty said:
"My flesh is not that of a yellow sheep,
so I need not fear being eaten;
my blood is not that of a wild horse,
so I need not fear being stabbed."
The Duke's poem likely used this allusion.
Poem on Reading the Shàngshū
During his leisure from governing, Emperor Zhēnzōng
only busied himself with reading books;
upon finishing a book, he would immediately compose a poem.
There were imperial compositions like "Three Chapters of Poems on Reading the Shàngshū" and "Three Chapters on the Chūnqiū".
He can be called a lord who loved literature in recent times.
Water ferry called bù
Hán Tuìzhī's "Stele for Luóchí Temple" says, "At the ferry (bù), there are new boats."
This is because in Lǐngnán, a water ferry is called bù.
Therefore, zēngbù (net-bù) is where fishermen set their nets,
and chuánbù (boat-bù) is where people cross the river.
Examples: Guābù in Yángzhōu,
Guānbù in Hóngzhōu.
In Mǐnzhōng, a riverside is called xībù (stream-bù).
Village market called xū
In Lǐngnán, a village market is called xū.
Liǔ Zǐhòu's "Biography of Tóng Qū Yǐ" says:
"He went to the market (xū)
and sold it."
Another poem says:
"Mountain dwellers return, salt wrapped in green bamboo leaves;
People hurrying to the market, rice packed in green lotus leaves."
Where there is a market,
if there are people, it is full;
if there are no people, it is empty (xū).
Lǐngnán village markets are more often empty than full,
so calling them xū (empty/market)
is not unfitting, is it?
Intermittent market
In Shǔ, there is an intermittent market (jiēshì),
which gathers every other morning,
like the onset of tertian malaria (jiēnüè).
Their custom also uses the ebb and flow of 'cold' and 'heat' to describe markets;
this is a metaphor.
The scholar can pass through the low place
The villager Wēi Xù went to take the imperial examination
and checked the provincial exam results.
A few steps out the door, he encountered mud.
An old woman pointed and said:
"Scholar, you can pass through the low place."
Wēi immediately followed her advice.
When he looked at the list,
his name was at the very bottom;
that year, he indeed passed the examination.
This is similar to what is recorded in "Zhīyán": "Later, one will surely attain a position."
Head chopped, neck remains inside
Liú Xiànghàng repeatedly failed the examinations.
During the Tiānshèng era, as he was about to take the provincial exam,
he dreamt that his head was chopped off,
and he was greatly disturbed by it.
A villager explained:
"The top scholar isn't for Shí'èr Láng to achieve;
he will only be the second-place candidate."
He questioned him,
and the reply was:
"Although the head is chopped off,
the neck (xiàng) remains inside."
This is because in the southern dialect, xiàng (neck) is pronounced hàng.
Indeed, he passed in second place.
Hair on the tongue
Mǎ Liàng was the prefect of Jiāngníng Fǔ.
As he was about to be replaced,
he dreamt that hair grew on his tongue.
A monk explained:
"Hair on the tongue
cannot be shaved off,
so you will be reinstated."
Indeed, it happened.
On physiognomy
Judging by external appearance is not as good as judging by the heart;
there are thirty-six good qualities of the heart.
My wife once said,
"Even if one does not seek office,
one must naturally be like this:
first,
possess both firmness and gentleness;
second,
admire goodness and draw close to gentlemen;
third,
share delicious food with others;
fourth,
do not associate with petty people;
fifth,
constantly perform hidden good deeds;
be helpful in every matter;
sixth,
be able to manage the household;
seventh,
do not dislike those who beg or seek things;
eighth,
benefit others and overcome oneself;
ninth,
do not pursue evil, greed, or killing;
tenth,
do not panic when hearing news;
eleventh,
keep promises made to others;
twelfth,
do not easily change one's conduct or principles;
thirteenth,
do not fall asleep easily at night;
fourteenth,
leave immediately without looking back;
fifteenth,
do not incur hatred or anger from others;
sixteenth,
do not gloss over mistakes or whitewash wrongs;
seventeenth,
be thorough in one's work;
eighteenth,
do not forget people's kindness;
nineteenth,
possess great magnanimity;
twentieth,
do not harm the good or encourage evil;
twenty-first,
aid those in urgent need;
twenty-second,
do not assist the strong in bullying the weak;
twenty-third,
do not forget old acquaintances;
twenty-fourth,
act in a way that is useful to the multitude;
twenty-fifth,
do not speak excessively or utter wild words;
twenty-sixth,
always feel ashamed when receiving things from others;
twenty-seventh,
speak in an orderly manner;
twenty-eighth,
do not leave before others finish speaking;
twenty-ninth,
always speak of good deeds;
thirtieth,
do not dislike coarse clothing or simple food;
thirty-first,
be adaptable to circumstances;
thirty-second,
never tire of doing good; thirty-third,
understand people's hunger, thirst, toil, and suffering; thirty-fourth,
do not dwell on past grievances;
thirty-fifth,
exert oneself to rescue those in peril;
thirty-sixth."
Those who possess all thirty-six good qualities
will reach the highest positions among ministers,
live long lives, and have a good end.
If not all are complete, then misfortune and fortune will balance each other out.
Those who possess twenty
will attain the rank of Cìshǐ.
Those who possess ten or more
will hold the office of Lìngzhǎng.
Those who possess five
will also be very wealthy.
Heart physiognomy
A proverb says:
"If one has the heart (virtue) but no (corresponding) appearance,
the appearance will follow the heart and manifest;
if one has the appearance but no heart,
the appearance will follow the heart and perish."
Recognizing noble persons
Ancient people said:
"Once one reaches the third official rank,
one does not need to read physiognomy books
to recognize noble persons."
This is because they have much experience.
The virtue of Wǔ and Yǔ's division of the land
When Lóngtú Liú Yè 劉燁 had not yet passed the imperial examination,
he married the eldest daughter of Shàngshū Zhào Huǎng 趙晃.
She died young.
There were still two younger sisters,
and the family again wished to marry one to him.
Liú Yè 劉燁 said:
"If this is a virtue of Wǔ 武,
I would not dare to be related;
if it is like the province where Yǔ 禹 separated,
I might perhaps comply with the command."
This was because he wished to marry the ninth sister [jiǔ yí 九姨],
and did not wish to marry the seventh sister [qī yí 七姨].
His wife said:
"The proverb says:
'One peels a thin cake from the top.'
Liú Láng 劉郎 has just passed the examination,
how can he already be picky about a family's daughter?"
Liú Yè 劉燁 said:
"It's not that I dare to choose,
but the seventh sister's bone structure is cold and thin,
not a match for me."
So he married the ninth sister,
who later gave birth to seven sons,
all of whom became high officials.
The seventh sister later married Guān Shēng 關生,
but he never passed the examinations.
They were destitute and cold,
and the Liú 劉 family supported them for the rest of their lives.
Literary Style with Courtly Air
Xià Yīnggōng 夏英公 paid a visit to Shèng Wénsù 盛文肅.
Shèng Wénsù 盛文肅 said:
"Your literary style has a courtly air;
in the future, you will surely become prominent."
Later, it turned out as he said.
Official Literary Style
There are two kinds of literary styles:
the literature of mountains and wilderness,
whose spirit is dry and withered,
esteemed by those who write books and establish doctrines;
and the literature of the court and governmental offices,
whose spirit is warm and moist,
esteemed by those who draft edicts and official documents.
Wáng Ānguó 王安國 said:
"The style and tone of literature
must be official."
Today, there are also two types of music and art:
those taught are graceful and charming,
while those outside the norm are crude and discordant.
Village songs and communal dances
are even more so,
also similar to literary styles.
On Wealth and Nobility
Yàn Yuánxiàn 晏元獻 read Lǐ Qìngsūn's 李慶孫 "Song of Wealth and Nobility" and said:
"The scroll-mounted score with golden characters,
the jade-engraved stele recording flower names."
The Duke said:
"This is a beggar's perspective;
he does not understand wealth and nobility."
The Duke's poems have lines such as:
"Willow catkins drift past the side of the pavilions,
swallows fly amidst the screens."
"A soft moon in the pear blossom courtyard,
a gentle breeze across the willow-strewn pond."
The Duke said:
"Do poor families have such scenery?"
The Duke did not like meat,
especially disliking fatty and rank meat.
He always loved Wéi Sūzhōu's 韋蘇州 poetry,
saying:
"It has not a trace of greasiness."
Collected Lines
Yàn Yuánxiàn 晏元獻 collected lines, such as "Helplessly, the flowers fall,
unknown, the swallows return" and "Quietly seeking where woodpeckers hide,
idly watching gossamer reach the ground" and "Pavilions desolate on the night lanterns are put away,
alleys deserted on a snow-swept day" and "Already settled but again stirring, the spring water's hue,
like red, like white, the crabapple blossoms."
Sòng Jǔgōng 宋莒公 said:
"These few couplets,
later poets will have no words to add."
Yáng Wéngōng's Memorial
When Yáng Wéngōng's 楊文公 mother was ill,
he requested leave to return home,
and lived with his younger brother,
remaining unappointed for over a year.
He wrote a memorial of thanks saying:
"Jiè Tuī's 介推 mother and son
wished to return to their fields in Miánshàng 綿上;
Bó Yí's 伯夷 brothers
willingly endured starvation on Shǒuyáng 首陽 Mountain."
Later, he was appointed Prefect of Rǔzhōu 汝州,
but those who spoke on affairs of state attacked him relentlessly.
The Duke again wrote a memorial saying:
"Already pushed into a gully,
they still throw stones without cease;
already trapped in thorns,
they still bend their bows and shoot at each other."
Memorial on Restoring Original Surname
When Fàn Wénzhènggōng 范文正公 was young,
as an orphan, he followed his mother who married into the Zhū 朱 family,
and thus assumed the surname Zhū 朱.
Later, he restored his original surname,
and his memorial of thanks said:
"With the ambition to serve Qín 秦,
upon entering the territory, one is called Zhāng Lù 張祿;
not aspiring to dominate Yuè 越,
on a boat, one emulates Táo Zhū 陶朱."
This refers to Fàn Suī 范睢 and Fàn Lí 范蠡 having changed their surnames.
Fàn Yǔchēng 范禹偁 of the False Shǔ 蜀 also once assumed the surname Zhāng 張,
and his memorial of thanks said:
"In former years, upon passing the highest examination,
I mistakenly bore the name Zhāng Lù 張祿;
today, in my old home,
I am again a descendant of Fàn Suī 范睢."
However, it was not as precise and apt as Fàn Wénzhènggōng's 范文正公.
Xià Wénzhuāng's Poem
When Xià Wénzhuānggōng Sǒng 夏文莊公竦
passed the Imperial examination [zhì kē 制科],
after the palace examination,
he met Yáng Huīzhī 揚徽之.
Seeing his youth,
Yáng Huīzhī 揚徽之 said:
"I wish to beg for one piece from the 'Worthy and Good' section,
to divine your future ambitions."
The Duke's poem said:
"On the palace hall, the imperial robes illuminate the sun and moon,
in the inkstone, the banner's shadow stirs dragons and serpents.
Three thousand characters of ceremonies and music arranged horizontally and vertically,
standing alone facing the vermilion steps until the sun has not yet set."
Yáng Huīzhī 揚徽之 sighed in admiration, saying:
"Truly a talent for a prime minister or general."
"Xǐ Qiān Yīng" Lyric
During the Jǐngdé 景德 era,
Xià Wénzhuāng 夏文莊 was first appointed to a court position.
It was early autumn,
and the Emperor was in the Gǒngchén Diàn 拱宸殿 watching a dance.
He ordered a palace eunuch to seek a new lyric.
The Duke immediately presented "Xǐ Qiān Yīng 喜遷鸎," saying:
"Hues scatter like brocade,
the moon sinks like a hook,
curtains are rolled up in Wèiyāng Lóu 未央樓.
Cool night, the Milky Way cuts across the sky,
palaces enclose the new autumn.
Yáojiē 瑤階
violates the personal name of Yīngzōng 英宗.
golden dew,
phoenix marrow incense mixes with clouds and mist.
Three thousand pearls and jades surround the imperial excursion,
in the water pavilion, 'Liángzhōu' 梁州 is played."
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
Huái Yīn Temple Poem
Among the poems inscribed at the temple of the Marquis of Huái Yīn 淮陰,
only Qián Kūn's 錢昆 is the most outstanding,
saying:
"Building an altar and bowing to him was a great favor,
but suspicions were already deep when he was made marquis with a foot on his back.
The prominent nose (of Liú Bāng 劉邦) he should have long known was like a bird's beak,
the general (Hán Xìn 韓信) should have had the heart for the Five Lakes."
Fifty Rhymes of "Old Man's Poem"
Táng Lù Déyán had fifty rhymes of "Poem for Children,"
and Attendant Minister Zhāng Shīxī composed a poem in the same rhyme, titled "Poem for the Aged," which says:
"Hair entirely hoary,
eyebrows parted, as fresh as white snow.
Shielding themselves, they prolong conversations with guests,
stooping to dote on their grandchildren.
Without illness, they are constantly served gruel,
not cold, yet they wear cotton.
They feign warmth, their backs embraced by quilts,
borrowing strength from staffs supporting their shoulders.
Their appearance resembles a guest from Sānfēng,
their age surpasses the Four White-Haired Immortals (Sìhào).
They are called just as they leave their pillows,
helped to reach the doorway.
They always love brewing mountain tea,
often dislike being served stone lotus.
Ears deaf as if plugged with silk floss,
eyes dim as if veiled by smoke.
When sitting in meditation, they lean weakly on a low table,
when riding, tiredly drop the whip.
Heads shake as if turning,
lips move as if twitching.
Bones chilled, they fear leaving the fire,
teeth aching, they dread rinsing with water.
Their physical forms are nearing the coffin,
yet their money bags still covet wealth.
Sticky eyelids are dry and crusted,
clinging whiskers drip cold snot.
When donning a fur coat, they are too lazy to tie the waist,
when washing hands, too weary to roll up sleeves.
Carried and lifted, their clothes are frequently changed,
supported and assisted, medicine is repeatedly decocted.
Sitting too much, cushions easily wear out,
walking too little, shoes are hard to wear through.
They are happy when maids cut cloth for skirts,
angry when wives buy cosmetics and hairpins.
Rooms are instructed to have deep-drawn curtains,
beds are ordered to be thickly covered with felt.
Listening to the qín, they pity the 'three joys,'
unrolling a painting, they laugh at the 'seven worthies.'
When reading scriptures, they dislike the small characters,
when striking the qìng, they rejoice in its round sound.
After eating, soup
(one version reads 'stains')
drips on sleeves,
after drinking, wine leaves saliva on the cup.
When entertainment comes, it must be dismissed,
when doctors arrive, they are kept waiting a long time.
Wrapping hats, they sweep their hair haphazardly,
combing hair, they tie it up carelessly.
They sigh often, thinking of past events,
feeling many emotions, listening to mournful strings.
Qi accumulates, making their waists heavy,
wind pulls, making their mouths more askew.
Tomb pines are planted by prior command,
epitaph stones are engraved in advance.
When guests arrive, they only ask for medicine,
when monks come, they suddenly ask about Zen.
Roasting tea, they hang it on the stove wall,
drying mugwort, they spread it on the eaves rafters.
Angrily, servants only stare with wide eyes,
furiously, young attendants vainly clench their fists.
Startled, they dislike playing cùjú,
with weak legs, they fear swings.
Curled up, like a cold macaque,
hunched, like a satiated kite.
When gazing, they often feel dizzy,
when moving, their heads spin.
For daughters' marriages, they seek red candles,
for sons' weddings, they beg for colorful paper.
They have already heard of being granted a table and staff,
how could they still wear leather straps (for humility)?
Guests are no longer personally received,
family affairs are already handed over to children and grandchildren.
Cultivating harmony, screens serve as companions,
ruyi scepters and whisks are intertwined.
Long ago, they discarded their mountain climbing clogs,
retaining only their fields by the city wall.
Moaning, they are unhappy in the morning,
tossing and turning, sleepless at night.
Calling children to their bedside,
reading books by their pillow.
Suspecting that a container holds water,
vainly warning, they hear the cold cicada.
Bolts of silk are not without their share,
a comfortable carriage indeed has a destiny.
Fú Shēng (伏生) gladly sits at the end,
Jiàng Lǎo (絳老) yields precedence.
Embracing urgency, in a windy night,
hazy and dim, on a day threatening rain.
Chicken-skin-like wrinkles are quickly stained with dust,
decaying teeth are frequently filled with food.
They often recall dwelling in the court office,
constantly thinking of fishing by the Wèichuān.
Happily, they meet Buddhist gatherings,
ashamed, they avoid flower-viewing feasts.
Paths are narrow enough to move fences,
steps are dangerous, so they ask for bricks to be removed.
They love life, burning bird nets,
hate killing, breaking fishing boats.
Already feeling the 'mulberry and elm' days (old age),
often lamenting the 'poplar and willow' years (frailty).
They constantly think of when they were at their 'weak cap' (twenty years old),
regretting not having been more unrestrainedly wild."
Obstacles in Poetry
Lǐ Gòu from Jiāngnán wrote a poem saying:
"People say the setting sun is the end of the world,
looking to the horizon, I see no home.
Already regretting the emerald mountains obstructing the view,
the emerald mountains are further obscured by evening clouds."
Those who understood said:
"The meaning of this poem has layers upon layers of obstruction,
Mr. Lǐ fears his fate is unlucky."
Afterwards, it came true as they said.
Expressing Ambition in Poetry
Sòng Jǔ Gōng Xiáng, when he was the Prefect of Xǔzhōu, wrote a poem for "Opening Xīhú" (West Lake), saying:
"Dug open, a place where fish and birds forget their feelings,
stretching out, a sky where rivers and lakes reach the eye's limit."
Those who understood knew that his position would reach the highest rank (first grade).
Mèng Jiāo's poem "Failing the Examination" says:
"Twice on the streets of Cháng'ān,
vainly shedding tears at the flowers."
His poem "Passing the Examination" says:
"In one day, I saw all the flowers of Cháng'ān."
Progress and setbacks are common affairs,
failing the examination and suffering a downfall,
to the point of shedding tears;
when passing, his ambition overflowed,
in a single day,
all the flowers were seen,
how swift!
He eventually died as the Magistrate of Lìyáng.
Poetic Prophecy
Kòu Láigōng, when young, wrote a poem saying:
"To the sea, only ten *lǐ*,
over mountains, there must be ten thousand layers."
When he arrived in Léizhōu,
he asked how many *lǐ* the prefecture was from the sea.
The official said:
"Ten *lǐ*."
Thus, his exile to the south was already prophesied.
Zhāng Guāiyá's poem "Governing Huáiyáng Prefecture in Old Age" says:
"Only now do I believe there is nothing to do in times of peace,
Old Minister is idly killed in Huáiyáng."
A year later, he passed away,
also a poetic prophecy.
Sū Gōng's early "Inscription for Jīnshān Temple" says:
"Monks dwell in the light of the jade mirror,
people walk on the back of the great turtle (áo)."
Those who understood said:
"This is an omen of glorious entry into the Jade Hall."
Afterwards, he only reached the position of internal minister,
also a poetic prophecy.
The Poems of Bái and Mèng
Bái Jūyì's poem says:
"Without affairs, days and months are long,
as a sojourner, heaven and earth are vast."
These are the words of a broad-minded person.
Mèng Jiāo's poem says:
"Stepping out, there are immediate obstructions,
who says heaven and earth are wide?"
These are the words of a narrow-minded person.
How could heaven and earth ever obstruct Jiāo?
Jiāo obstructs himself.
Peonies Accomplish Nothing
Wáng Wénkāng Gōng's poem says:
"Jujube flowers, though tiny, can bear fruit,
mulberry leaves, though soft, can yield silk.
What a laugh, peonies as big as dippers,
accomplishing nothing, just empty branches."
These are also the words of a serious and profound person.
Seeking Food
The "Zǎoshì Zhuàn" of the "Chūnqiū" states:
"Three rebels went out with their land,
merely seeking food."
They were lowly yet their names were recorded,
because of their utter lack of shame.
Today, courtesans are called "seeking food,"
which originated from this.
The Three Terraces
Sūzhōu has Gūsūtái,
hence it is called Sūtái.
Xiāngyáng has Tóngquètái,
hence it is called Xiāngtái.
Huáxiàn has Cèjǐngtái,
hence it is called Huátái.
Relay Post Vouchers
Before the Táng dynasty,
guest houses and relay posts provided travel for those coming and going.
During the Kāiyuán era,
aiming for simplicity and convenience,
paper vouchers began to be issued. The issuance of vouchers by relay posts started from this time.
Fán Tái
Tiānqīng Sì Fán Tái
was originally Liáng Wáng's drum-and-wind-instrument terrace.
Liáng Gāozǔ changed it to the Drill Ground Terrace.
Later, the Fán clan lived beside it,
and the local people called it Fán Tái.
Huìchóng's Poems
The Chǔ monk Huìchóng was skilled in poetry.
In his "Shū Yáng Shì Biéshù" (Writing about Yáng's Villa) he said:
"The river divides, the hill's momentum broken,
Spring enters, the burn-marks turn green."
In "Sài Shàng" (On the Frontier) he said:
"River ice is firm enough for horses to cross,
Frontier snow is thick enough to hide eagles."
In "Sù Dōnglín Sì" (Lodging at Dōnglín Temple) he said:
"Birds return, mountains shed snow,
Monks settle in meditation, rocks sink into clouds."
In "Shàng Yáng Hànlín" (To Chancellor Yáng) he said:
"Dew is cold, the golden palm is heavy,
Heaven is near, the jade cord hangs low."
In "Liǔ Shì Shūzhāi" (Liǔ's Study) he said:
"Writing books, I am surprised the day is short,
Playing the sword, I lament the deep spring."
In "Qiū Xī" (Autumn Evening) he said:
"Dew falls, cattle and sheep are still,
The river brightens, mulberry and zhe trees are empty."
In "Zhōu Xíng" (Boat Journey) he said:
"Forest ends, city walls emerge,
River divides, islands turn back."
In "Yóu Yǐnjìng Sì" (Visiting Yǐnjìng Temple) he said:
"Empty pond hears deer drinking,
Sparse trees see monks walking."
In "Sòng Qián Gōngfèng" (Sending off Attendant Qián) he said:
"Sword and pendant gleam like mountain snow,
Banners and flags are damp with sea clouds."
In "Háoliáng Yè Pō" (Night Mooring at Háoliáng) he said:
"Night is quiet, tide moves the boat,
Autumn is distant, moon hangs over the city."
In "Zǎo Xíng" (Early Travel) he said:
"Thick frost accumulates on clothes,
Fading moon hangs low before the horse."
In "Huái Zhǎnggōng" (Remembering Zhǎnggōng) he said:
"Autumn nears, grass insects are restless,
Night is long, frosty moon hangs low."
In "Xià Yè" (Summer Night) he said:
"Fan's sound still carries the heat,
Well's air suddenly brings autumn."
In "Hè Liú Shèrén" (Congratulating Assistant Minister Liú) he said:
"Sun's orbit is far along the Yellow Path,
Spring enters deeply into the Purple Palace."
In "Shǎnxī Dào Zhōng" (On the Road in Shǎnxī) he said:
"Passes and rivers turn my temples white,
Wind and snow, a single lamp glows green."
Erecting Temples for Chéng Yīng and Chǔ Jiù
During the reign of Shénzōng,
the imperial succession was often lacking.
Wú Chǔhòu submitted a memorial,
requesting the erection of temples for Chéng Yīng and Gōngsūn Chǔjiù,
hoping that ghosts would not cause harm,
and the national lineage would be continued.
The emperor ordered Hédōng to search for their traces,
and their family was found in Jiàngzhōu.
An imperial edict conferred the title of Marquis upon Yīng and Chǔjiù,
and then ordered the construction of temples.
Chǔhòu's memorial,
in essence, stated:
In the "Shǐjì Shìjiā",
when examining the rise and fall of the Zhào clan,
only Chéng Yīng and Gōngsūn Chǔjiù risked death without hesitation,
to preserve the orphan of the Zhào clan.
Thus, it is known that the nation's transmission of sovereignty to this day
is all due to the efforts of these two men.
Deathbed Verses
Yáng Wéngōng and Wáng Xiāngsuí, these two gentlemen, both had a deep understanding of the nature of reality.
Wéngōng's deathbed verse said:
"Bubbles rise and bubbles perish,
These two phenomena are fundamentally the same.
To know the true destination,
It is west of Zhàozhōu's east courtyard."
Wáng Xiāng's verse said:
"The lamp in the painted hall is already out,
To whom can I speak, snapping my fingers?
Coming and going are inherently commonplace,
Spring wind sweeps away residual snow."
That evening he died,
and at dawn there was a heavy snowfall.
Zhāng Fāngpíng's Verse
Minister Zhāng Fāngpíng
had an especially profound understanding of the nature of reality.
Someone asked about the meaning of the Patriarch's coming from the West,
and Zhāng composed a verse saying:
"Since the beginningless thousands of kalpas,
The myriad dharmas are fundamentally without a single dharma.
The Patriarch's coming meaning I do not know,
One night, the west wind swept away yellow leaves."
Seeking Hèzé's Portrait
Fù Zhènggōng left a letter to Wú Chǔhòu,
entrusting him to find portraits of the various Zen masters of Hèzé.
Wú composed a verse saying:
"This body is like a bubble, an illusion,
Entirely not a true form.
What more of this shadow on paper,
Adding delusion upon delusion.
No need for a boat when you reach the shore,
If there's no wind, don't stir up waves.
Only by observing with clarity and stillness,
Can the wondrous dharma be understood as imageless."
The Duke replied:
"To cling to form is indeed wrong,
To break form is also delusion.
Neither clinging nor breaking,
This is called the true form."
Péi Jìnggōng's Fu
One's aspirations can be seen in poetry,
and also in fu (rhapsodies).
Jìnggōng composed "Zhù Jiànjǐ Wèi Nóngqì Fù" (Rhapsody on Casting Swords and Halberds into Agricultural Implements) saying:
"Our Emperor has ascended the throne for thirty years,
The whole realm is clear as a mirror,
All corners are smooth as a whetstone.
He urged all within his domain to dedicate their strength to farming,
And showed the world that weapons would no longer be used."
Then, pacifying Huáixī,
and unifying the realm,
was already foreseen in this fu.
Fàn Wénzhèng's Fu
Fàn Wénzhènggōng composed "Jīn Zài Róng Fù" (Rhapsody on Gold in the Crucible) saying:
"If it means distinguishing beauty from ugliness,
I wish to be Xuān Yuán's mirror;
If it means pacifying disaster and rebellion,
Please let me be Gān Jiàng."
Thus, the Duke's capacity for premiership and generalship,
and his complete civil and military talent,
were already apparent in this fu.
The Duke also composed "Shuǐchē Fù" (Rhapsody on the Waterwheel) saying:
"Currently, with the Sage on the throne,
One wind every five days,
One rain every ten days,
Then this waterwheel,
I would not take it."
This means the waterwheel is only useful during drought,
and without drought, it serves no purpose.
During the Bǎoyuán and Kāngdìng eras, the Duke,
when there were troubles at the borders,
was rapidly promoted and employed;
but when things were peaceful, he was set aside and not used,
which was no different from the waterwheel.
Wáng Yígōng's Fu
Wáng Yígōng's "Yǒu Wù Hùnchéng Fù" (Rhapsody on Something Undifferentiatedly Formed) said:
"It neither shrinks nor overflows,
How can its form be confined by breadth or narrowness?
Neither carved nor hewn,
Its flowing shape is not limited by fullness or emptiness."
Thus, the Prime Minister's intention of cosmic regulation can be seen.
It also said:
"Those who receive a small portion of me,
scatter and become grasses and trees;
Those who receive a large portion of me,
gather and become mountains and rivers."
Thus, his selection and appointment of various talents,
allowing the small and large to each find their proper place,
can also be seen.
Palace Poems
Wáng Gōngsuí had a "Gōngcí" (Palace Poem) that said:
"A single bird cry, the palace gate is still,
Flowers fall across the ground, the spring day is long."
Another "Yě Bù" (Stroll in the Fields) said:
"Mulberry axes open up spring colors,
Fishermen's songs chant with the setting sun."
All were composed when he was taking the imperial examinations.
Volume 4
End.
Suppression and Aversion Ritual
Every year on the first day of the first lunar month,
glutinous rice is cooked into a meal,
and mixed with white lamb marrow to form balls,
the size of a fist.
Forty-nine balls are scattered in each imperial temporary palace tent,
as a suppression and aversion ritual.
The barbarians call this "Nǐ Dānlí."
Nǐ means "ding" (nail or peg),
Dānlí means "day."
Xiāo Clan Invites Yélǜ Clan
On the first day of the second lunar month,
those of the Xiāo clan among the barbarians all invite those of the Yélǜ clan to a banquet at their homes.
The barbarians call this festival "Xiālǐ Jié."
Xiālǐ means "invite,"
Jié means "time."
Wooden Rabbit
On the third day of the third month, wooden rabbits are carved.
They are divided into two teams.
Riding horses, they shoot at them.
The first to hit wins.
The losing team dismounts and kneels to offer wine to the winning team.
The winning team receives the goblet on horseback and drinks.
The Fān people call this festival "Táo Lǐ Huà".
Táo Lǐ is rabbit,
Huà is shoot.
Mugwort Clothes
On the fifth day of the fifth month, at noon,
mugwort is gathered and its leaves picked.
Mixed with cotton, it is used to stuff seven items of clothing,
which the Róngzhǔ wears.
Fān and Hàn officials are each given three items of mugwort clothing.
Bóhǎi cooks present mugwort paste.
The Fān people call this festival "Tǎo Sài Lí".
Inviting those with the Xiāo surname
On the eighteenth day of the sixth month,
those with the Yēlǜ surname invite those with the Xiāo surname.
It is also called "Xiā Lǐ Dì".
Three Festivals
From the thirteenth to the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
the Welcome Festival, the Farewell Festival, and the Weeping Festival.
The Great Fān people call them "Sài Lí Shě".
Sài Lí is moon,
Shě is son.
Burying the Dog
On the eighth day of the eighth month, a white dog is killed.
Its head is buried seven paces in front of the sleeping tent,
with its muzzle exposed.
Seven days later, the sleeping tent is moved to the ground where the dog's head is buried.
This festival is called "Dān Hè Nǐ".
Dān Hè is dog,
Nǐ is head.
Beating the Garden and Shooting Tigers
On the ninth day of the ninth month, the garden is beaten,
and tigers are shot.
The younger ones who lose must provide a banquet for the Double Ninth Festival.
After shooting, a tent is pitched on high ground,
and chrysanthemum wine is drunk.
Rabbit liver is brought out, cut raw,
mixed with deer tongue sauce and eaten.
This festival is called "Yī Shí Sài".
Yī Shí is nine,
Sài is nine.
Mùyè Shān
In the tenth month,
small paper armor, model spears, swords, and weapons are sent to Mùyè Shān to be stored in a vault.
It is called "Dài Là".
Dài is burn,
Là is armor.
Offering to Hēishān
On the Winter Solstice, a white sheep, a white horse, and white geese are killed.
Their fresh blood is mixed with wine,
and offered to the gods, facing Hēishān.
It is said that the souls of the deceased Qìdān are governed by the god of Hēishān.
Whirlwind
When Qìdān people see a whirlwind,
they close their eyes and strike the air forty-nine times with a whip,
saying "Kūnbù Kè" seven times.
Drinking in Military Attire
In the twelfth month,
they drink wine in military attire.
It is called "Shānlí Dì".
Shānlí is battle,
Dì is time.
Farming
The Fān people call farming "Zhuō Liè".
Punishing Thieves
On the thirteenth day of the first month,
Qìdān people are allowed to be thieves for three days.
If a theft involves more than ten strings of cash,
they are punished according to the law.
It is called "Hú Lǜ Dì".
Hú Lǜ is steal,
Dì is time.
Beating Drums
The Róngwáng has sixteen additional drums.
They are beaten when the watch is set,
stopping at the second watch.
They are beaten again at the third watch.
It is called "Bèi Qí Bù Lí Gǔ".
It is to startle ghosts.
Shèlì
Wealthy Qìdān commoners who wish to wear headscarves
must offer seventy oxen and camels,
and one hundred horses,
and are given a Qìdān designation.
This is called Shèlì.
Marching an Army
The Qìdān do not choose an auspicious day for marching an army.
They burn mugwort and horse dung on the shoulder blade of a white sheep.
If it breaks, they depart.
If it does not break, they do not depart.
Great Shout on Wǔ Days
Every Wǔ day, Fān soldiers,
even if they do not encounter enemy troops,
must form ranks,
and shout loudly seven times towards the west.
They say Wǔ is the day of the Fān royal lord.
Ten-Li Nose
The Hàn people in the northern territories,
when subjected to humiliation by the Qìdān,
are cursed as "Ten-Li Nose".
Ten-Li Nose
means slave.
Chèdé Yífēng
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn sat in a small warm room.
A young girl,
with a jade complexion,
dressed in green,
entered through a carved lattice window,
and knelt before the Emperor, saying:
"The Venerable Hòutǔ
has sent your servant to deliver a jade talisman to Your Majesty."
The talisman read:
"Chèdé Yífēng."
The Emperor then deliberated on the matter of the Fēngshàn sacrifices.
Nine-Colored Phoenix Chick
Dōngfāng Shuò wandered in the wilds of Fánglín,
and captured a nine-colored phoenix chick.
Mr. Carrying-a-Basket
Lǐ Gǔn arrived carrying the True Form Map of the Five Sacred Mountains,
and was called Mr. Carrying-a-Basket.
Sleep-Repelling Grass
The people of Shànyǔ Guó drank a red dew,
saying:
"When the sun first rises, there is a dew like vermilion."
There was also a grass,
eating it prevented sleep,
called Sleep-Repelling Grass.
Divine Horse
Dōngfāng Shuò traveled to the land of Jíyún,
and obtained a divine horse.
Riding it, he circled the sun three times,
departing in the morning and returning in the evening.
Jiaorén Weeping Pearls
A person from Báhè Guó once hosted a Jiaorén in their dwelling.
When it departed, it wept in farewell,
and all the tears it shed turned into pearls.
Yīlán Diàn,
the palace where Emperor Wǔ of Hàn was born.
Queen Mother Descends
During Emperor Wǔ's time,
the Queen Mother descended.
Her song was heard but she was not seen,
her voice echoed around the beams and pillars.
Jade Branch
Dōngfāng Shuò obtained a jade branch from Xīnà Guó and presented it.
Emperor Wǔ bestowed it upon senior trusted officials.
It was said:
"If one is ill, the branch sweats;
if one dies, it breaks.
Lǎo Dān obtained it,
and did not sweat for seven hundred years;
Wò Quán obtained it,
and it did not break for three thousand years."
Tortoise Shell Screen
Emperor Wǔ built the Shénmíng Tái.
On the platform, a golden bed and an elephant-hide mat were placed,
and a tortoise shell screen was made of various jades.
Sword Transforms into a Red Magpie
Emperor Wǔ bestowed a sword upon Dōngfāng Shuò.
Later, it transformed into a red magpie and flew into the clouds.
Cassia Pillars
At Gānquán Gōng, there was the Língbō Diàn,
with cassia wood pillars.
When the wind came, it brought a fragrance.
Green Grass
On Yáo Kūn Shān there was green grass,
the fruits of the grass were like water caltrops.
Used to brew wine,
one drink would keep one intoxicated for three decads.
Singing "Huífēng Qǔ"
Hàn gōngrén Lìjuān 善歌，
體弱殆不勝衣。
常居瑠璃帳，
帶琥珀佩。
恐隨風輕舉，
常唱迴風曲，
庭葉翻落如秋，
Lóngjiào Chí
Hàn gōng Lóngjiào Chí yǒu duōyuè zhōu，
Tàiyī Chí yǒu liánqián xìng，
Fān Jīlíng
Xuándū Guān yǒu Cuìshuǐ，
水中有菱，
狀如飛雞，
謂之 Fān Jīlíng。
又有鴨，
丹毛而輕，
登芙蕖唼食朝露，
號 Shēngqú Yā，
Nièkōng Cǎo
Niǎobēn Guó yǒu cǎo rú jièyè，
食之能行空中，
號 Nièkōng Cǎo，
Xiègāo
Shànhuà Guó gòng xiè，
長九尺，
有百足四殼。
煮其殼為 Xiègāo，
勝於 Fèngzhuó，
Huáimèng Cǎo
Zhōnghuǒ Shān yǒu xiāngcǎo，
Wǔdì sī Lǐ Fūrén，
Dōngfāng Shuò xiàn。
Dì huái zhī jí mèngjiàn，
名 Huáimèng Cǎo，
Téngguāng Tái
Jiàn Yuán zhōng qǐ Téngguāng Tái，
臺上設樂，
有 xuánlí zhī qìng，
吹 shuāngtiáo zhī chí，
唱 lái yún yī rì zhī qǔ，
Hányān Zhōu
Hàn gōng Hányān Zhōu，
以 mùlán、wénqí wéi lǔ，
Yùchī
Chéngdì wēixíng，
見一 yùchī yóu yú lù，
Yùyàn Chāi
Zhào Hòu yùchāi huà wéi báiyàn fēiqù，
後人因作釵，
名 “Yùyàn Chāi”，
Guī èrqiānnián yī chūtóu
Huáng Ān zhě，
為 Dàijùn zú。
服 zhūshā，
舉體皆赤。
嘗坐一龜，
廣長三尺。
曰：
“Cǐ guī Fúxī chū zào wǎnggǔ dé zhī。
性畏 rìyuè，
每 èrqiānnián yī chūtóu，
我坐 cǐ，
見 wǔ chūtóu yǐ。”
Huájī'ér
Dì hū Dōngfāng Shuò wéi “Huájī'ér”，
Yǐng'é Chí
Wàngquè Tái yǒu chí，
廣 qiānchǐ。
Dì yù shǐ xiānrén chéng zhōu nòng yuèyǐng，
因名 Yǐng'é Chí，
Shízhōu Jì
Shízhōu zhě，
Zǔzhōu、Yíngzhōu、Xuánzhōu、Yánzhōu、Chángzhōu、Yuánzhōu、Liúzhōu、Shēngzhōu、Fènglínzhōu、Jùkūzhōu，
Bùsǐ Cǎo
Zǔzhōu yǒu bùsǐ cǎo，
出 Qióngtián，
又名 Yǎngshén Zhī。
人 yǐ sǐ sānrì zhě，
以 cǎo fù zhī jí huó。
採服 zhī chángshēng，
Jíxián Jiāo
Fènglínzhōu yǐ línjiǎo zuò jiāo，
名 Jíxián Jiāo，
能 shǔ lián duànxián，
又名 Xùxián Jiāo，
Gēyù Rúní
Liúzhōu yǐ Kūnwú Shí zuò lì，
冶tiě zuò jiàn，
割 yù rú xuē ní，
Bìhǎi
Fúsāng dōng yǒu Bìhǎi，
水色 shēnbì，
Huǒhuàn Bù
Yánzhōu yǒu Huǒlín Shān，
山 yǒu huǒshǔ，
鼠毛為 huǒhuàn bù。
有 gòu，
燒 jí chú，
Xiānzhěn
Fúsāng Dǎo yǒu mù rú sāng，
實 rú zhěn，
xiānrén yǐwéi zhēnguǒ。
jiǔshí nián yī shí，
Péngqiū
Pénglái Shān yīmíng Péngqiū。
別有 Yuánhǎi，
黑色，
無fēng ér hóngbō bǎizhàng，
不可 dé wǎng，
Shí'èr Yùlóu
Kūnlún Shān jīnjīn wéi chéng，
名 Tiānyōng Chéng。
面 fāng qiānlǐ，
上有 shí'èr yùlóu，
Kūnlún Gōng
Kūnlún Shān yǒu sānjiǎo：
一jiǎo zhèngběi，
名 Làngfēng Diān；
一jiǎo zhèngxī，
名 Xuánpǔ Tái；
一jiǎo zhèngdōng，
名 Kūnlún Gōng，
Guǎnghán Gōng
Dōngzhì hòu，
yuè yǎng pò yú Guǎnghán Gōng，
Qīngyún Qiāngǔ
Hàn Wǔ shí，
Xīyù yuǎnyí lái gòng，
云：
“Cháng zhān：
‘Dōngfēng rù lǜ，
shíxún bù xiū。
Qīngyún Qiāngǔ，
liányuè bù sàn。’
意 Zhōngguó yǒu hàodào zhī jūn，
gù sōu qí yùn yǐ xiàn。”
Shénwán
Yuèzhī Guó xiàn Wǔdì xiāng sìliǎng，
dà rú què'luǎn，
léi rú sāngzhěn。
Shǐzhě yuē：
“Cǐ gēngshēng zhī Shénwán。”
Wǔdì Sì Duō
Yuèzhī shǐzhě jiàn Wǔdì，
tuì ér yǔ rén yuē：
“Dì yǒu sìduō：
mù duō gù zé tānrěn，
kǒu duō yán zé fànnán，
shēn duō dòng zé yínzéi，
xīn duō shì zé shēchǐ。
Wèi yǒuyòng cǐ néng chéng tiānxià zhī zhì zhě yě。”
Fēngshēng Shòu
Yánzhōu yǒu Fēngshēng Shòu，
似 bào，
qīngsè，
dà rú lí。
在 huǒzhōng bù fén，
qí máo bù jiāo，
zhuó cì bù rù。
以 tiězhuī zhuī qí tóu nǎi sǐ，
以 kǒu xiàng fēng biàn huó。
Shíshàng Chāngpú sè qí ěr bí zé sǐ，
取 qí nǎo hé jú fú zhī，
chángshēng，
Língjiāo
Rìxī Guó wáng gòng Língjiāo sìliǎng，
jíguāng qiú èrlǐng qiú。
Rùshuǐ bù chén rùhuǒ bù jiāo，
Fúsāng
Fúsāng dìfāng wànlǐ，
多 shēng línmù，
葉 rú sāngshù，
長zhě shùqiān zhàng，
兩liǎng tónggēn ǒu shēng，
故名 Fúsāng，
Fēng Shān
Xuánzhōu shàng yǒu Fēng Shān，
聲xiǎng rú léi，
Qīnghóng
Chūnhuáng was
a separate appellation for Fúxī,
who resided in the state of Huáxū.
Initially,
Shénmǔ (Divine Mother) journeyed on an island.
A green rainbow encircled Shénmǔ,
and she immediately became pregnant.
After twelve years, she gave birth to Fúxī.
Dānqú Xiájiāng
During Shénnóng's time,
Dānqú grew on land,
clustering together like a carriage canopy.
There was also flowing cloud-sprayed liquid,
named Xiájiāng.
Kūntái
Huángdì grew weary of the world at Kūntái.
This was the place of Dǐnghú Jùnjí.
Summoning a hundred lords to receive instruction
When Huángdì summoned a hundred lords to receive virtuous instruction,
he first arranged jade tablets on Lántái,
and burned incense of chén’yú (agarwood).
Níngfēng eating flying fish
Huángdì had Fēnghòu carry books
and Chángbó carry a sword.
They journeyed by day along Huánliú
and returned to Yīnpǔ by night,
covering ten thousand Lǐ in a single breath.
In Huánliú, there was a stone channel
where one stem had a hundred leaves,
and flowered once every thousand years.
This place was also called Shālán,
as the sand surged up to form waves.
It contained many divine dragons, fish, and turtles,
all capable of flying.
The immortal Níngfēng ate flying fish and died,
but was reborn after two hundred years.
Therefore, Mr. Níng's eulogy for his travels in the sand sea says:
"Green lotuses shimmer brightly, blooming after a thousand years,
a hundred years temporarily dead, bait for flying fish."
Lone Mulberry
Shǎohào's mother was called Huáng'é.
She resided in Xuángōng, weaving at night,
or sometimes floated on a raft to the shores of Qióngsāng.
There was a divine youth called the Son of the White Emperor,
who was the essence of Tàibái (Venus),
who would frolic with her.
Qióngsāng was
on the shore of the Western Sea,
where there was a lone mulberry tree
reaching straight up a thousand rén (fathoms).
It bore fruit once every ten thousand years.
Those who ate it would grow old after heaven.
The sound of bells and chimes vibrating for a hundred Lǐ
Zhuānxū possessed a bell of floating gold
and a chime of sunken brightness.
A flick of a feather would make their sound vibrate for a hundred Lǐ.
He also played the music of Hányīng.
Dreaming of swallowing the sun and giving birth to a son
The consort of Dìkù,
daughter of the Zōutú clan.
She did not tread the ground when she walked,
but always walked on wind and clouds.
She dreamed of swallowing the sun and gave birth to a son.
Cinnabar Stone
In the wilds of Dānqiū,
there was much ghost blood,
which transformed into cinnabar stones,
which are agate.
Dānqiū burns once every thousand years.
The Yellow River clears once every thousand years.
Precious Dew
An agate jar from Huángdì's time
still existed in Yáo's time.
Sweet dew was within it,
full and inexhaustible,
called "Precious Dew."
It was bestowed upon the officials.
By Shùn's time,
the dew gradually decreased.
When the times were pure, the dew was full;
when the times were corrupt, the dew was exhausted.
Three Gourd Mountains
The three mountains in the sea were called the "Three Gourd Mountains."
Fānghú was Fāngzhàng,
Pénghú was Pénglái,
and Yínghú was Yíngzhōu.
Their shape was like gourds.
Green Pheasant
North of Yǔshān,
there was a bird called "Qīngdì" (Green Pheasant).
Its sound was like bells and chimes.
A common saying went:
"When the Qīngdì calls,
the times are peaceful."
Moon-piercing Raft
In Yáo's time,
a giant raft floated on the Western Sea,
glowing like the moon.
The raft floated across the four seas,
completing a cycle every twelve years,
circling back and forth.
It was named "Guànyuè Chá" (Moon-piercing Raft),
also known as "Guìxīng Chá" (Cassia Star Raft).
Birds emitting five-colored qi
When Shùn was buried at Cāngwú,
there were birds that emitted five-colored qi,
named "Píngxiāo."
They carried soil to form the grave mound,
and accumulated pearls to form a ridge.
River Spirit
Gǔn worked to control the waters for nine years without success,
then drowned himself in Yǔyuān,
transforming into a dark fish.
Yellow Dragon and Dark Turtle
Yǔ exerted his utmost effort in dredging irrigation channels.
A yellow dragon dragged its tail in front,
and a dark turtle carried blue mud behind.
Jade Tablet
When Yǔ journeyed to Lóngmén,
eight spirits presented him with a jade tablet.
It was one chí and two cùn long,
and was used to measure heaven and earth.
Yǔ held the tablet to bring peace to the waters and land.
Fùyuè dreaming of riding clouds
Fùyuè was hired as an ochre-clad worker in Chūnyán.
He dreamed of riding clouds and traveling around the sun.
Divination yielded "beneficial to establish a marquis," and he was enfeoffed.
The emperor invited him.
Bee Boat
When Wǔwáng attacked Zhòu,
there was a large bee, like a cinnabar bird,
that flew and gathered on the king's boat.
He then painted it on a flag
and named the boat "Fēngzhōu" (Bee Boat).
Nílí State coming to court
In Chéngwáng's time,
the state of Nílí came to court.
Its people, setting out from their own country,
often traveled in the clouds,
hearing thunder from below.
Sometimes they entered submerged caves,
with waves above.
They observed the sun and moon to know the directions of states,
and calculated cold and heat to know the years and months.
Phoenix Kite
Zhāntú State presented a Fèngyào (Phoenix Kite).
It was transported in a jade chariot,
drawn by red elephants.
It drank qióngjiāng (jade nectar)
and was fed cloud-fruits.
When Chéngwáng died,
it flew away.
Pills and powders in a green pouch
When Zhāowáng was seated on the Zhīmíng Terrace,
he dreamed that white clouds arose.
A feathered person pointed and drew on the king's heart.
It immediately tore at his touch,
saying:
"First, I wish to change the king's heart."
Then he produced a square-inch green pouch,
containing "Xùmài Míngwán" (Pulse-Continuing Bright Pill)
and "Bǔxuè Jīngsǎn" (Blood-Replenishing Essence Powder).
The king stored them in a jade jar
and sealed it with a golden cord.
When the king applied them to his feet,
he could fly ten thousand Lǐ through the sky,
as if traveling a mere zhǐchǐ.
Shī Yán playing music
Shī Yán
was a musician.
When he struck a single-stringed zither,
the earthly deities all ascended;
when he blew the jade pitch-pipe,
the celestial gods all descended.
During the time of Xuānyuán,
he was already several hundred years old.
He could discern the rise and fall of states by listening to music.
Zhòu wanted to kill him.
Shī Yán played the sounds of qīngshāng, liúzhǐ, and díjué.
Zhòu said:
"Such pure, ancient, and distant music
is not for me to listen to."
He then played a melody that confused the souls,
and thus escaped disaster.
Bǐyìniǎo
The kingdom of Ránqiū presented a Bǐyìniǎo,
kept in a jade cage.
Its envoy traveled through over a hundred kingdoms before reaching the capital.
Bājùn
King Mù toured the world,
driven by eight dragons among steeds:
The first was named "Juédì,"
its feet never touching the ground;
the second was named "Fānyǔ,"
it moved faster than flying birds;
the third was named "Bēnxiāo,"
it traveled ten thousand *lǐ* by night;
the fourth was named "Chāoyǐng,"
it chased the sun as it moved;
the fifth was named "Yúhuī,"
its coat shimmered brightly;
the sixth was named "Chāoguāng,"
one form with ten shadows;
the seventh was named "Téngwù,"
it galloped amidst the clouds;
the eighth was named "Jiáxì,"
its body had wings.
Yùzhàng Gāohuì
King Mù gathered *fāngshì* at the Chūnxiāo Palace,
setting up lamps of eternal life,
lamps of phoenix brain,
and lamps of *fán* ointment.
There were also ice lotuses,
emerging from an ice gorge.
The Queen Mother of the West (Xīwángmǔ) arrived in a phoenix carriage.
At the jade tent high gathering,
they presented scarlet blossoms from Dòngyuān,
sweet snow from Qiáozhōu,
flowing white lotuses from Kūnlún,
black dates from Yīnqí,
ten-thousand-year-old ice peaches,
and thousand-year-old green lotus roots.
Each pod of the white lotus contained a hundred seeds,
the black date tree was a hundred *xún* tall,
its fruits two *chǐ* long,
ripening once every hundred years.
Rénwū
Duke Wén of Jìn set fire to the forest to find Jiè Zǐtuī.
There was a white crow circling and cawing around the crow,
calling it "Rénwū" (benevolent crow).
It is popularly said that crows with white breasts are "Cíwū" (filial crows),
so this was of that kind.
Shuǐjīng zhī Zǐ
On the night Kǒngzǐ was born,
three azure dragons descended from heaven,
and two divine maidens held fragrant dew in the air to bathe Zhēngzài,
while the Emperor (Dì) played the music of Jūntiān.
Five elders were arrayed in the courtyard,
who were the essences of the Five Planets.
Before this, a *lín* had spat out a jade book at a household in Quēlǐ,
saying:
"The Son of the Water Essence,
is connected to the declining Zhōu and is a 'Plain King'."
Therefore, two dragons circled the room,
five stars descended into the courtyard,
and Zhēngzài tied an embroidered sash to the *lín*'s horn.
When the Master (Fūzǐ) was about to die,
he embraced the *lín*, untied the sash, and wept.
Huángfà Wǔlǎo
Lǎo Dān dwelled on the mountain of the Fǎnjǐng Rìshì,
where there were five yellow-haired elders (Huángfà Wǔlǎo),
who were the essences of the Five Directions.
Some rode swans or cranes,
some wore feathered garments.
Their ears emerged from the top of their heads,
their pupils were all square.
They held staffs of green bamboo,
and discussed with Dān the numbers of heaven and earth.
Bǎojǐng
Fàn Lǐ collected rare treasures from all four directions,
some of which he stored in wells and moats,
calling them "Bǎojǐng" (treasure wells);
beautiful women filled his chambers,
which he called "Yóugōng" (wandering palaces).
Xuántiān Nǚ
During the time of the King of Yān,
the kingdom of Guǎngyán presented two excellent dancers.
One was named Tímò,
the other was named ____.
Some moved without casting a shadow,
others did not feel hunger for years.
Their dances were called Yíngchén
and Jíyǔ.
The king was fond of immortals.
The Maidens of Xuántiān (Mysterious Heaven) took on these two forms.
Zhǒujiān Jīnhú
The kingdom of Fútí presented two persons skilled in writing,
who produced a golden pot from their elbows,
containing a liquid like lacquer.
When sprinkled on the ground, it formed seal and clerical scripts.
They assisted Lǎo Zǐ in writing the *Dàodé Jīng*, totaling tens of thousands of words.
Lǎo Zǐ edited and deleted from it,
leaving five thousand words.
Zhǐduān Chūfútú
Shī Luó, a Daoist from Xiūxū kingdom,
could produce a ten-storied *fútú* (stupa) from his fingertip,
three *chǐ* high,
with people five or six *fēn* tall,
holding banners and canopies,
walking around the pagoda.
Luózhōu
Qín Shǐhuáng was fond of immortals.
There were people from Wǎnqú,
who arrived in a "Luózhōu" (snail boat).
The boat was shaped like a snail,
and traveled submerged at the bottom of the sea,
with no water seeping in.
Its people were ten *zhàng* tall,
and spoke of the time when heaven and earth first opened,
as if they had witnessed it firsthand.
Zǐwǔtái
Shǐhuáng erected the Yúnmíng Terrace,
gathering rare woods from all four directions,
and searching for skilled artisans throughout the realm.
Construction began at *zǐ* hour,
and was completed by *wǔ* hour.
The people of Qín called it "Zǐwǔtái" (Midnight-Noon Terrace).
Zhào Gāo Huáizhōng Qīngwán
Qín Zǐyīng suspended Zhào Gāo over a well,
and he did not die for seven days;
he was boiled in a cauldron of hot soup,
and it did not boil for seven days;
then he was executed.
The prison official said:
"When Gāo was first imprisoned,
he had a green pill in his bosom,
the size of a sparrow's egg."
A *fāngshì* said:
"Gāo's ancestors received the elixir method from Hán Zhōng,
sleeping on solid ice in winter,
and on a furnace in summer,
without feeling cold or heat."
After Gāo died,
a green sparrow flew from his corpse into the clouds,
a verification of the nine transmutations.
Zǐliúlí Zhàng
Huáng Yǎn used jade essence as a tray,
stored ice in front of it,
set up a purple glazed curtain (Zǐliúlí Zhàng),
a fire-glazed screen,
and arranged candles of spirit hemp.
Yúnléi Gōng
Emperor Chéng of Hàn built a flying palace,
one *zhàng* square,
which moved as swiftly as wind and thunder,
called the Yúnléi Gōng (Cloud Thunder Palace).
Kōngtóng Língguā
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
Dūnhuáng presented an unusual melon,
said to be a Kōngtóng Língguā (Kōngtóng spirit melon),
bearing fruit once every four *jié*.
Qióngshù Jīnxué
At the home of Guō Kuàng, younger brother of Emperor Guāngwǔ's empress,
the sounds of construction were incessant.
It was said that within the Guō clan's residence, it thundered without rain.
People in the Eastern Capital called Kuàng's home "Qióngchú Jīnxué" (Jade Kitchen, Golden Lair).
Liǎngshé Chóngyīn
To the west, there was the country of Yīnxiāo.
All the people of that country were good at whistling.
Men's whistles could be heard for a hundred *lǐ*,
women's for fifty *lǐ*,
like the sound of pipes and flutes.
The tip of a person's tongue was inverted towards the throat.
It was also called a double tongue sound.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* says:
"The country of those with 'reversed tongues and peculiar customs'" refers to this.
Yèshūhé
Emperor Líng of Hàn built a thousand-room Nude Bathing Pavilion.
A canal of water wound around the steps.
The lotuses were as large as canopies,
and a *zhàng* long.
The lotuses unfolded at night and closed during the day,
named Yèshūhé (Night-Unfolding Lotus).
Court ladies, exquisitely dressed,
would remove their outer garments and wear inner clothes,
or bathe nude together.
The Western Regions presented Yīnchí incense.
It was boiled to make a soup,
and the remaining liquid was poured into the canal,
which was then called the Liúxiāng Qú (Flowing Fragrance Canal).
The Essence of Tài Yī
Liú Xiàng was collating books in the Tiānlù Gé.
At night, an old man wearing yellow clothes,
holding a staff of green *lí* wood,
gave Liú Xiàng the *Wǔxíng Hóngfàn*.
He said:
"I am the essence of Tài Yī.
The Heavenly Emperor heard that the son of Jīnmǎo was a great scholar,
and descended to observe him."
He took out a jade tablet from his bosom,
which contained books of astronomy and geography.
Tongue Plowing
Jiǎ Kuí mastered the classics.
His disciples came to study,
not deterred by thousands of *lǐ*,
and offered so much grain that his granary was full.
Some said:
Jiǎ Kuí did not plow with strength,
this was what is called "tongue plowing."
Scripture God, Scripture Garden
Zhèng Kāngchéng was called the "Scripture God."
Rèn Mò was called the "Scripture Garden."
Hé Xiū was called the "Sea of Learning."
Walking Corpses, Moving Flesh
Rèn Mò said:
"If a person loves learning,
even if dead, they are as if alive.
But one who does not learn, even if alive,
is merely a walking corpse and moving flesh!"
Book Granary
Cáo Lǔ piled up stones to make a granary,
to store books,
named "Cáo Shì Shūcāng."
Needle God
Empress Wén of Wèi had a beautiful concubine, Xuē Língyún,
whose beauty was peerless.
She was skilled in needlework,
able to cut and dye in the dark,
and was called the "Needle God."
Cold-Repelling Gold
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Wèi,
the country of Kūnmíng presented a cough-gold bird.
It was fed with pearls
and given turtle brains to drink.
It often spat out gold dust like millet.
The bird's nature was to fear the cold,
so it was housed in a small room.
The doors were made of crystal,
allowing light to pass through inside and out,
and it was named Pìhán Tái (Cold-Repelling Terrace).
Court ladies adorned their hairpins with the gold spat out by the bird,
calling it Pìhán Jīn (Cold-Repelling Gold).
Loom-Skill Marvel, Needle-Skill Marvel, Silk-Skill Marvel
Lady Zhào of King Wú was able to weave brocade between her fingers,
and was called the "Loom-Skill Marvel."
She could embroider the Five Sacred Mountains, rivers, and seas on a square inch of silk,
and was called the "Needle-Skill Marvel."
She used divine glue to join hair,
weaving and cutting it into curtains.
Moreover, she could split a single hair into several strands,
and was called the "Silk-Skill Marvel."
Sleep Talk Understanding the *Zhōuyì*
Lǚ Méng dreamt of reciting the *Zhōuyì*.
Suddenly, he awoke and exclaimed:
"Just now I dreamt of seeing Fúxī, Zhōu Gōng, and Wén Wáng,
discussing matters of the rise and fall of imperial fortunes,
and the way of the constant brightness of the sun and moon."
The crowd said:
"Lǚ Méng's sleep talk understands the *Zhōuyì*."
pronounced *yú jì fǎn*,
means sleep talk.
Nine Tripods
Yǔ cast the Nine Tripods.
Five corresponded to the Yang numbers,
and four symbolized the Yin principles.
Female metal was used for the Yin tripods,
and male metal for the Yang tripods.
The tripods were always full,
used to divine good and ill fortune.
When Xià Jié perished,
the water in all the tripods boiled.
Coolness-Summoning Pearl
Black clam pearls could repel heat.
King Zhāo of Yān carried one during the summer months,
calling it the "Heat-Dispelling Coolness-Summoning Pearl."
White Otter Marrow
Sūn Hé, dancing with a crystal *rúyì* under the moon,
accidentally injured Lady Dèng's cheek.
The great physician said:
"If white otter marrow is obtained,
mixed with jade and amber powder,
the scar will disappear."
A fisherman from Fùchūn said:
"This creature knows when people want to catch it,
and then enters a stone cave.
Wait until it sacrifices fish;
there will be some that die in battle.
In the cave are withered bones;
these can be combined with jade spring to make a powder,
and sprinkled on the wound."
Sūn Hé then mixed this ointment.
There was too much amber,
and when she recovered,
there was a red spot,
which even enhanced her beauty.
All the favored concubines then began to dot their cheeks with cinnabar rouge,
to seek favor.
Hundred Washes Fragrance
Sūn Liàng made a fragrance for his four concubines,
which would not fade after a hundred washes,
and was called Bǎizhuó Xiāng.
Blue-Clad Firefighters
Mí Zhú's house had a hidden corpse.
At night, weeping was heard.
Mí Zhú ordered a coffin to be made,
and placed a blue cloth garment in the tomb.
Later, he saw a woman who said:
"You will suffer a fire calamity,
now I repay you with a blue reed staff."
Mí Zhú's wealth was like mountains,
with large pearls like eggs,
which he called "Treasure Court."
Later, a fire broke out,
and dozens of blue-clad youths were seen putting out the fire.
The fire was extinguished.
The youths said:
"Gather many storks to ward off fire,
