because storks can store water on their nests."
Nine Brews Wine
Zhāng Huà made a "Nine Brews Wine."
If one got drunk
and did not shout, laugh, or move,
it would cause the intestines and stomach to rot away,
and was called "Intestine-Rotting Wine."
Pínsī Guó
During the Wèi Dynasty, people from Pínsī Guó came to pay tribute.
They wore clothes made of five-colored jade
and carried golden gourds.
Inside the gourds was a paste-like liquid;
one drop tasted would grant a thousand years of life.
Their country had a large stone
that could accommodate ten thousand people,
on which were carved images of the Three Sovereigns.
The Heavenly Sovereign had twelve heads,
the Earthly Sovereign eleven heads,
and the Human Sovereign nine heads,
all with dragon bodies.
The people of this country did not eat the five grains,
had no shadows at midday,
drank cassia juice,
and wore clothes made of feathers.
Cèlǐ Paper
Zhāng Huà presented the *Bówù Zhì*,
and was bestowed with Yútián green iron inkstones,
Liáoxī unicorn horn brushes,
and Nányuè Cèlǐ paper.
People of the South used moss to make paper.
Their paper had vertical, horizontal, and slanted lines,
hence its name.
Later generations pronounced it "Zhìlǐ."
Fáng Lǎo
Shí Jìlún's concubine was named Xiángfēng.
She was skilled at discerning the sound of jade
and adept at observing the color of gold.
There were ten women whose voices and appearances were similar to hers.
Their attire and adornments were all of the same quality.
Sandalwood dust was scattered
upon an ivory mat.
Those who walked on it without leaving a trace were rewarded with a hundred strings of pearls.
Those who left traces had their food and drink rationed.
Within the boudoir, they would playfully say:
"If you don't have slender bones and a light physique,
how can you obtain a hundred strings of pearls?"
When Xiángfēng's beauty faded,
she was retired to become an old woman of the chambers.
Twelve Yaótái:
On Kūnlún Shān there are twelve Yaótái,
each a thousand *bù* wide,
all made of five-colored jade.
The ninth level has a *zhī* field and a fragrant orchid garden.
Fāngchén:
Shí Hǔ erected a forty *zhàng* high building.
He made curtains of strung pearls
and hung five-colored jade pendants.
Mixed treasures and rare fragrances were ground into dust.
When the wind blew, it would scatter them.
This was called Fāngchén.
When the dust was thick,
wine was sprinkled on it,
which was called Nián Yǔ.
He also built four seasonal bathhouses.
*Wūfū* served as the embankments,
and amber as the ladles.
A hundred various fragrant sachets were steeped in the water of the pools.
After bathing, the water was drained outside the palace,
and this was called Wēnxiāng Qú.
Jīnwù:
Dàiyú Shān has a thousand *lǐ* of flat sand,
the color of gold.
When the wind stirs the sand,
it is called Jīnwù,
also known as Jīnchén.
There is a beast called Sòuyuè,
which emits light like the moon.
There is also Yaocǎo grass,
whose flowers and leaves are all fragrant.
Pōléng:
A Western country vegetable named Pōléng.
Because a monk brought its seeds to China,
it was mispronounced as Bōléng.
Yuànbēi:
Qín Shǐhuáng built his tomb,
and also sealed the artisans inside.
The artisans carved their grievances into the stones inside the tomb.
Later, when the tomb was opened,
people called it Yuànbēi.
Dì Xīn's Pillow:
When the Hàn dynasty executed Liáng Jì,
they obtained a jade tiger-head pillow.
Under its jaw, an inscription read:
"Dì Xīn's pillow,
on which he slept with Dájǐ."
Nífēng:
During the Yuánfēng era,
the state of Fúxīn presented *lánjīn* clay.
This clay was always used to seal boxes, chests, and palace gates.
Ghosts and demons dared not interfere.
Wèi Qīng, Zhāng Qiān, and others
all received seals made of *jīnní*.
Quán:
In Rìnán, there is a spring with sweet and soft water.
When men and women drink it, they become
called Quán.
Lóngjū Dǎo:
In the East Sea, there is an island
named Lóngjū Chuān.
It is where Mù Wáng raised his eight steeds.
There is a grass named Lóngchú there.
Pénglái Shān:
Pénglái Shān is also called Fángqiū,
and also Yúnlái.
Yíngzhōu is also called Húnzhōu,
and also Huánzhōu.
Fire spirits are hung as the sun,
black jade as the raven,
water spirits as the moon,
and blue jade as the toad and rabbit.
Bùzhōu Millet:
Yuánjiǎo Shān has many large magpies
that carry Bùzhōu millet.
The millet stalks are three *zhàng* high.
Eating it prevents hunger for a month.
The *Lǚshì Chūnqiū* also states:
"Among the finest millets,
there is Bùzhōu millet."
Bīngcán:
Yuánjiǎo Shān has ice silkworms,
seven inches long,
with scales.
Covered with snow and frost,
they spin cocoons one *chǐ* long.
Woven into brocade,
it does not get wet when immersed in water.
Jīntáng:
Dòngtíng Shān floats on the water.
Beneath it are hundreds of Jīntáng chambers,
where dragon maidens reside.
The sounds of metal, stone, strings, and bamboo
reach the mountain peak.
Yùqián:
During the Jìn dynasty, the state of Yīnchí presented jade coins.
Their inscription read:
"Heaven's longevity, eternal prosperity."
Bìshuāng:
In Guǎngtíng Guó, the frost is a deep blue-green.
Yùrén:
The Former Ruler of Shǔ kept a jade figure beside Gān Hòu to admire it.
The palace women were jealous of the empress,
and also jealous of the jade figure.
Yèmíngtái:
In the Tàishǐ era of the Jìn dynasty,
a foreign country presented gold moss.
Palace women who gained favor were given it.
It illuminated the entire room.
It was called Yèmíngtái.
Two Swords Forged from Rabbit Kidneys:
Gānjiàng and Mòyé.
Kūn Wú Shān has beasts resembling rabbits
that eat copper and iron.
Their gallbladders and kidneys are all like iron.
The weapons in Wú Guó's armory were all gone,
but the seals remained as before.
They found two rabbits,
killed them,
and found iron like gallbladders and kidneys.
Only then did they realize that the weapons had been eaten by the rabbits.
So they forged the kidneys into two swords:
the male one was Gānjiàng,
and the female one was Mòyé.
Yuèjìng:
During the reign of Zhōu Líng Wáng,
a foreign country presented a stone mirror.
Its whiteness was like the moon.
When it shone on people, they felt cold.
It was called Yuèjìng.
Shénguī:
Kūnlún Shān has divine turtles.
After ten thousand years, they can climb trees
and speak.
Bāhóng:
The eight directions are called Bāhóng.
Hóng
means 'great'.
Xuán Gōng:
The imperial harem is called Xuán Gōng.
Shén Shí Bù Jìn:
Sòng Wáng Guànzhī did not believe in Buddhist teachings.
He often said, "Both body and spirit are extinguished.
How can there be three lives?"
Later, he fell ill, stopped breathing, and then revived.
He attributed this to the power of the Dao.
Someone asked:
"Your Excellency's usual arguments were not like this.
What have you seen now that makes you different?"
Guànzhī furrowed his brow and replied:
"The spirit truly does not perish.
Buddhism cannot but be believed."
After speaking, he passed away.
Wearing Scriptures as Clothing
Sòng [Sòng] bhikṣuṇī Zhìtōng [Zhìtōng],
in her youth, her faith was not firm.
After her teacher died,
she left [the order]
and married Liángfǔ [Liángfǔ] of Wèijùn [Wèijùn],
giving birth to one son.
Their family was poor and had no clothes.
The bhikṣuṇī had the Fǎhuá [Fǎhuá] and other sūtras,
which she entirely processed to make clothes.
Her son fell ill at one year old,
his entire body became rotten,
appearing like fire sores.
There were small white worms,
emerging more than a sheng [shēng] a day,
crying out day and night.
She heard a voice from the sky saying:
"You made clothes from the sūtras,
and this is your retribution!"
In a little over ten days, he died.
Āliàn [Āliàn]
Wáng Mín [Wáng Mín], Central Secretariat Director of Jìn [Jìn],
had a Hu [Hú] śramaṇa [shāmén],
who would often gaze at Mín's [Mín] elegant demeanor
and say:
"If I were to be reborn,
and could be a son to this person,
my wish would be fulfilled."
Shortly thereafter, he fell ill and died.
Mín [Mín] had a son,
and as soon as he could speak,
he understood foreign languages and recognized precious items from distant lands,
identifying things he had never seen in his life.
His name was Xián [Xián],
and he was the śramaṇa's [shāmén] previous incarnation.
Therefore, Mín [Mín] gave him the courtesy name "Āliàn [Āliàn]".
A Daughter Remembers a Knife from Her Previous Life
Xiàng Jìng [Xiàng Jìng] had a daughter who
died at a few years old.
When she first fell ill, she was playing with a small knife.
Her mother took it away from her,
and did not give it back,
hurting her mother's hand.
Later,
she gave birth to another daughter.
When she was four years old,
she said:
"Where is the knife from last time?"
Her mother said:
"There isn't one."
The daughter said:
"Previously, we fought over the knife,
and I hurt Mother's hand.
How can there not be one?"
Jìng [Jìng] searched for several knives,
placed them together,
and asked the daughter to identify it herself.
The daughter was overjoyed at the sight,
and immediately picked up the original one.
Eating Minced Turtle
In Jìn [Jìn], there was a woman named Má Gū [Má Gū]
who liked to eat minced meat;
Huá Běn [Huá Běn]
liked to eat stewed turtle.
The two were good friends.
Má Gū [Má Gū] saw a turtle as large as a cauldron,
with a tail like a huge snake.
She tied it up for a month,
and it completely transformed into a turtle.
She took it to make a stew,
and invited Běn [Běn] to eat it.
It was extraordinarily plump and delicious.
Běn [Běn] insisted that Má Gū [Má Gū] eat some.
Gū [Gū] ate one piece,
and something got stuck in her throat and would not go down.
She opened her mouth and saw Běn [Běn].
Běn [Běn] saw a snake's head
opening its mouth and sticking out its tongue.
Běn [Běn] was startled and fled.
Later, Běn [Běn] caught a large snake,
minced it,
and called Gū [Gū] to eat.
It was very delicious,
and she strongly requested this "fish".
Běn [Běn] became drunk,
and her family brought out the remaining snake meat.
When Gū [Gū] saw it,
she vomited blood and died.
Needling Swelling
There was a Fàn Guānglù [Fàn Guānglù] who
suffered from abdominal distension and swollen legs.
Suddenly, a person
entered his study without announcing his name,
saying:
"Buddha sent me to treat your illness."
He then needled the swelling,
drawing out about three sheng [shēng] of yellow pus, and then left.
The illness subsequently healed.
White Otter
Xú Miǎo [Xú Miǎo] of Wèi [Wèi] was skilled in painting.
Emperor Míng [Míng] was touring the Luòshuǐ [Luòshuǐ]
and saw white otters.
He loved them but could not catch them.
Miǎo [Miǎo] said:
"Otters crave gray mullet [cíyú],
and will not fear death."
So he painted gray mullets on a board and hung it by the bank.
A group of otters competed to come,
and were all caught at once.
The Emperor said:
"Your painting is truly divine!"
End of Volume Five
Gold Phoenix Chariot-axle Caps
Emperor Xuān [Xuān] of Hàn [Hàn] bestowed a dark-canopied chariot upon Huò Guāng [Huò Guāng].
At night,
the gold phoenixes on the chariot-axle caps would invariably fly away,
only returning at dawn.
Huáng Jūnzhòng [Huáng Jūnzhòng] from Nánjùn [Nánjùn] captured a phoenix on Beishan [Běishān].
He presented it to the imperial court.
The Emperor placed it on a dew-collecting plate,
but it soon flew into Guāng's [Guāng] family chariot.
The Emperor took his chariot,
and it would always be driven when he traveled.
When the Emperor died,
the phoenix flew away,
and its whereabouts were unknown.
Dividing the Purple Bauhinia
Tián Zhēn [Tián Zhēn] and his two brothers from Jīngzhào [Jīngzhào] divided their property.
The purple bauhinia tree in front of their hall was about to be split into three.
The next morning,
the tree withered and died.
Zhēn [Zhēn] said:
"The tree, originally one trunk,
when about to be split and cut,
became withered.
Humans are not even as good as wood!"
Consequently, they did not divide the tree,
and the tree immediately flourished.
The brothers were moved and pooled their wealth,
thus becoming a filial family.
Lù Jī [Lù Jī]'s poem says:
"The three bauhinia rejoice as one trunk."
Yellow Bird Jade Rings
Yáng Bǎo [Yáng Bǎo] saw a yellow bird being attacked by an owl.
Bǎo [Bǎo] then took it and placed it on a beam,
feeding it yellow flowers.
When its feathers grew,
it would leave in the morning and return in the evening.
Suddenly, one night, a yellow-clad boy appeared and said:
"I am an envoy of the Queen Mother of the West [Wángmǔ],
formerly on a mission to Pénglái [Pénglái],
attacked by an owl.
I received your rescue."
He gave four jade rings to Bǎo [Bǎo],
saying:
"May your descendants be pure and noble,
attaining the rank of the Three Dukes [Sāngōng],
just like these rings."
Bǎo [Bǎo] begot Zhèn [Zhèn],
and four generations became renowned dukes.
A Thousand-Year Huábiǎo [Huábiǎo]
In front of King Zhāo [Zhāo] of Yān's [Yān] tomb, a striped civet transformed into a scholar.
He asked the huábiǎo [huábiǎo] in front of the tomb:
"I wish to see Zhāng Huá [Zhāng Huá],
what do you think?"
The huábiǎo [huábiǎo] said:
"With your subtle understanding,
there is nothing you cannot do.
However, Zhāng Gōng's [Zhāng Gōng] wisdom and measure
might be difficult to ensnare.
You would lose your thousand-year essence,
and also mislead this old man."
The civet did not heed this,
and went to discuss literature with Huá [Huá].
After he left,
Huá [Huá] sent someone to investigate,
but he could not be found.
Léi Huàn [Léi Huàn] said:
"A thousand-year-old spirit [jīng],
only by illuminating it with thousand-year-old withered wood
will its form be revealed."
The huábiǎo [huábiǎo] in front of King Zhāo's [Zhāo] tomb was already a thousand years old.
He sent someone to cut it down,
and burned it to illuminate the scholar,
who was then revealed to be a striped civet.
A Scholar Spits Out a Woman
Xǔ Yànshān was traveling
when he met a scholar
who said his foot hurt
and asked to be allowed to ride in his goose cage.
The scholar entered the cage and sat alongside the goose.
After traveling a while, they rested under a tree.
The scholar emerged from the cage,
and from his mouth he spat a bronze tray,
laden with dishes and delicacies.
After a few rounds of wine,
he spat out a woman,
whose beauty was unparalleled.
The woman said,
“Bring the man here too.”
He spat out a man,
who was intelligent and lovely.
Then he spat out a brocade screen.
The scholar kept the woman to sleep with,
and the man then spat out another woman to drink with them.
As evening approached,
the scholar swallowed everything back into his mouth,
leaving the bronze tray for Yàn.
Zhāng Chǎng said:
This happened in the second year of Yǒngpíng.
Cornel Sachet and Chrysanthemum Wine
Fèi Chángfáng told Huán Jǐng:
“On the ninth day of the ninth month,
your household will suffer misfortune.
Quickly tell your family members to each make a crimson sachet,
fill it with cornel, tie it to their arm,
climb a high place, and drink chrysanthemum wine.”
Jǐng did as he was told.
When he returned that evening,
he saw that his chickens, dogs, cows, and sheep were all dead.
Three Days of Winding Water
Emperor Wǔ asked Zhì Zhòngzhì:
“What is the meaning of the ‘three days of winding water’?”
He replied:
“Xú Zhào of Hàn had three daughters born in the third month,
and all three died on the third day.
The entire village considered it an ill omen.
They went together to the waterside to wash themselves,
and thus the custom of floating wine cups down the winding stream began.”
Cì Zhé said:
“The Duke of Zhōu built Luòyì,
and floated wine cups on the winding stream.
Also, King Zhāo of Qín, on the third day of the third month (Shàngsì),
held a feast by the river bend,
and saw a golden man presenting a sword from the heart of the water.
Thus, the custom of winding water was established.”
The Weaver Girl Visits the Cowherd
Chéng Wǔdīng had achieved immortal powers.
Suddenly he told his disciples:
“On the seventh day of the seventh month, the Weaver Girl crosses the river to briefly visit the Cowherd.
All immortals return to their palaces,
and I will part from you.”
The next day, Wǔdīng was indeed gone.
Eye-Brightening Bag
Dèng Shào entered Huà Shān on the first day of the eighth month
and saw a boy holding a five-colored sachet filled with dew from cypress leaves.
He said:
“Chìsōng Xiānshēng takes this to brighten his eyes.”
Today, people make eye-brightening bags on the first day of the eighth month.
Minister Sānlǘ
Qū Yuán cast himself into the Mìluó River on the fifth day of the fifth month.
On this day, the people of Chǔ threw bamboo tubes filled with rice into the water as an offering.
Qū Qǔ of Chángshā saw a man who claimed to be Minister Sānlǘ.
He said:
“I am grateful for your offerings,
but they are always stolen by dragons.
You should stop them with liàn leaves [Melia azedarach]
and tie them with colorful ropes;
these two things are feared by dragons.”
Grease Porridge
Zhāng Chéng saw a woman south of his house
who said:
“I am the Earth God.
On the fifteenth of the first month, you should make white porridge,
float grease on top,
and offer it to me.
This will ensure your silkworms yield a hundredfold.”
Today, the custom of offering grease porridge on the fifteenth of the first month
began from this.
Legend of the Qīngxī Spirit
Zhào Wénsháo lived by Qīngxī.
One moonlit night, he sang “Qī Yè Niǎo Xī Fēi” (Night Birds Flying West).
Suddenly, a girl in green appeared and said:
“Lady Wáng’s message is that
upon hearing your singing,
she finds it rather moving.”
Soon after, the lady arrived,
her appearance enchanting.
Wénsháo sang for her,
which deeply touched the lady’s heart.
She then said:
“As long as there is a bottle,
why worry about lack of water?”
She took a kōnghóu (harp) and played it,
telling her maid to sing “Fán Shuāng” (Heavy Frost).
She herself untied her skirt sash to bind the kōnghóu,
and sang:
“At dusk, the wind blows,
leaves fall, clinging to branches.
My true heart’s feeling,
I worry you do not know.”
After they had slept together, she left.
The next day,
he went to the Qīngxī Temple,
and saw the statue of the Goddess Nǚ Gū,
with the girl in green standing before it.
They were all those he had seen the night before.
Pán Shān
On Xī Shān, a large rock (pánshí)
constantly makes a sound like a turning millstone.
If it turns quickly, the year will be abundant;
if it turns slowly, the year will be lean.
Door Gods
On New Year’s Day (Suìdàn),
two gods are painted and pasted on the left and right sides of the door.
The left god is Shéntú,
the right is Yùlèi.
Commonly, they are called Door Gods (Ménshén).
According to the Kuòdì Tú:
“On Dùshuò Shān, a large peach tree twists and turns for three thousand lǐ.
Beneath it are two gods,
one named Lěi,
one named Yù.
Both hold reed ropes
to tie up inauspicious ghosts,
capturing and killing them.”
Originally, there was no mention of Shéntú.
Firecracker Dawn
Setting off firecrackers in the courtyard
is commonly believed to be the ritual of the courtyard bonfire (tíngliáo),
but this is incorrect.
The Shényì Jīng says:
“In the mountains of the West,
there is a creature a foot tall.
When people see it, they immediately fall ill with fever and chills.
It is called ‘Shānsāo’.
By placing bamboo in the fire,
the popping sound of firecrackers
startles it and makes it flee far away.”
Bone Rope
During the Spring Festival, a long rope is hung from a tall tree.
Men and women in splendid attire sit or stand on it and swing it.
This is called qiūqiān (swing).
The custom in Chǔ calls it shī jūn.
The Nièpán Jīng calls it gǔsuǒ (bone rope).
Cold Food Ban on Smoke
One hundred and five days after the Winter Solstice,
there is the Cold Food (Hánshí) with strong winds and heavy rain.
Jiè Zǐtuī was burned to death by fire on the fifth day of the third month.
The people of the state mourned him,
and every late spring, they refrained from lighting fires,
calling it the ban on smoke (jìnyān).
Violating it would result in hailstones damaging the fields.
Apricot Kernal Paste and Wheat Porridge
Sūn Chǔ offered sacrifices to Zǐtuī, saying:
“One plate of wheat cakes,
two bowls of sweet fermented paste,
twenty measures of clear spring water,
to fill your kitchen.”
Today, during Hánshí, there are apricot kernel paste and wheat porridge,
which are of the same kind.
As-You-Wish Record
The Yì Jì says:
A merchant crossed Qīng Hú
and met Lord Qīng Hú.
The Lord asked what he desired.
Someone advised him, saying:
“Just ask for ‘as you wish’ (rúyuàn).”
The Lord granted it,
and indeed, he obtained a maidservant,
whose name was Rúyuàn (As-You-Wish).
Whatever the merchant desired,
she could bring about.
Later, on New Year’s Day,
Rúyuàn woke up late.
The merchant beat her,
and she ran into the manure pile and disappeared.
Today, on New Year’s Day, people tie a small string to a doll and throw it into a manure pile,
calling it rúyuàn.
Seven Kinds of Vegetables
On Rénrì (Human Day),
seven kinds of vegetables are picked to make soup.
Evil-Warding Cake
On *Fú* days,
one eats *tāngbǐng* (soup cakes),
named "evil-repelling cakes."
On *Rénrì*
the first day of the first month is for chickens,
the second for dogs,
the third for pigs,
the fourth for sheep,
the fifth for cattle,
the sixth for horses,
the seventh for humans,
the eighth for grain.
The abundance or scarcity is foretold by whether it is cloudy or clear.
Chewy candy
On the first day of the year, one eats chewy candy (*jiāoyáxíng*),
taking the meaning of "firmly bonded."
Long-life threads
On the fifth day of the fifth month, one wraps one's arms with five-colored silk threads,
called "long-life threads" (*chángmìnglǚ*).
One makes human figures from mugwort
and places them above the door to ward off evil.
The *Shīkuàng Zhàn* says:
"In a year with many illnesses,
the 'illness grass' (*bìngcǎo*) grows first."
The 'illness grass' (*bìngcǎo*)
is mugwort (*ài*).
On this day, one catches toads to ward off weapons.
Immortal art
Peaches (*táo*)
are the essence of the five elements
and can control all ghosts.
They are called "immortal art" (*xiāanshù*).
Bean flower rain
Rain in the eighth month
is called "bean flower rain" (*dòuhuārǔ*).
Flying teal
Those who compete in boat races prepare their boats
to make them light and swift.
These are called "flying teal" (*fēifú*).
They are also called "water chariots" (*shuǐchē*),
and also "water horses" (*shuǐmǎ*).
*Qiāanniú* borrows money from the Celestial Emperor
A Daoist text says:
"When *Qiāanniú* married *Zhīnǚ*,
the Celestial Emperor lent him twenty thousand coins for the betrothal gift.
He did not repay it for a long time,
and was expelled to the *Yíngshì* constellation."
*Bāngniú*
The *Jīnwú* guards, holding *shuò* spears, lead the way,
and all officials make way.
The *Ěryǎ* says:
"This is the *bāngniú*."
This beast is good at butting and striking,
so its head is carved on a pole,
adorned with dragon and tiger insignia (*jié*),
and carried in an oiled bag.
Plucking flowers
When entertaining the *jìnshì* (advanced scholars),
their first gathering in the Apricot Blossom Garden (*Xìnghuāyuán*)
was called the "flower-plucking banquet" (*tànhuāyàn*).
Two young, outstanding men were appointed as "flower-plucking envoys" (*tànhuāshǐ*).
They would visit all famous gardens.
If others had already picked the famous flowers,
then both envoys would be punished.
Gathering vegetables
On the second day of the second month, vegetables were gathered at *Qūjiāng*,
and the festive sightseeing was very grand.
Purple bamboo shoot tea
On *Qīngmíng* day,
Húzhōu presented purple bamboo shoot tea (*zǐshǔnchá*).
Poem on white peonies
At *Cí'ēnsì* (Temple of Great Kindness), there is Péi Lín's "Poem on White Peonies" (*Báimǔdānshī*), which says:
"The powerful and noble of Cháng'ān regret the departing spring,
vying to admire the purple peonies of *Kāiyuán*.
Separately, there are jade cups holding cold dew,
no one rises to look at them by moonlight."
Fan market
Two days before *Duānwǔ*,
the East Market was called the "fan market" (*shànshì*),
and there was an extraordinary profusion of carriages and horses.
*Nuó* old man, *Nuó* old woman
On New Year's Eve, during the *nuó* exorcism,
people assumed the appearance of ghosts and spirits.
Among them, two elders were designated the *Nuówēng* (Nuó old man) and *Nuómǔ* (Nuó old woman).
Fire city
On the first day of the first month, before the dawn clepsydra,
the Grand Chancellor (*zǎixiàng*), the Three Judicial Commissioners (*sānsī*), and the *Jīnwú*, with several hundred birchwood torches,
surrounded their horses like a city.
This was called the "fire city" (*huǒchéng*).
*Zhōnghé* Festival
On the first day of the second month, the *Zhōnghé* Festival,
all officials presented agricultural books.
From the palace came the *Zhōnghé Lì* (Zhōnghé Calendar),
which was bestowed upon the assembled officials by imperial decree.
*Túmí* wine
During the *Hánshí* inner court banquet, the Grand Chancellor (*zǎixiàng*) drank *túmí* wine (*túmíjiǔ*).
Cherry bamboo shoot kitchens
On the fifteenth day of the fourth month,
from the White Hall kitchen (*Báitángchú*) to the kitchens of all offices (*bǎisīchú*),
they were collectively called "cherry bamboo shoot kitchens" (*yīngsǔnchú*).
Poem for *Chóngyáng* by imperial command
Wáng Wéi's "Poem for *Chóngyáng* by Imperial Command" (*Chóngyáng Yìngzhì Shī*) says:
"Peace reigns throughout the Four Seas,
the three autumns bring a great harvest year.
The endless chrysanthemum festival,
long serves the *Bǎiliáng* verses."
Many *jìnshì* were poor scholars
In the eighth year of *Tàihé*, when the *jìnshì* list was published,
many were poor scholars.
An anonymous person wrote a poem saying:
"Even beggars have a year of great prosperity;
twenty-three men are complete with bowl and staff.
Xuē Shù, as before, rides a lean horse,
Fàn Cuó, as always, covers a sleeping mat."
The Four Stubbornnesses of the Ministry of Personnel
The Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù*) had four stubbornnesses: At the beginning of winter, when submitting documents,
they would say, "The election gate is closed."
When affairs were concluded in the fourth month,
they would say, "The election gate is open."
If a person's name was before the 'division of history' (*fēnshǐ*) [part of the document],
it was called "such-and-such family's commoner statement" (*mǒujiābǎixìngzhuàng*).
If it was after the judgment (*pàn*),
it had to be affixed before the judgment.
Practicing characters
Emperor Xiàowén of the Later Wèi dynasty gathered his officials.
While in their cups,
the Emperor raised his goblet and said:
"Three threes horizontal,
two twos vertical,
who can discern it will be granted a golden goblet."
The Commandant of the Guards (*Zhōngwèi*), Lǐ Biāo, said:
"An old woman selling wine, her jar's spigot is firm,
a butcher cutting meat is like the scale."
The Attendant of the Left (*Zuǒyòu*), Zhēn Chēn, said:
"A man of Wú floating in water calls himself skilled,
a performer throwing a rope into empty space."
Prince Péngchéng, Xié, said:
"This is practicing characters (*xízì*)."
Broken bricks
Lǐ Yánjiǎn, the maternal uncle of Emperor Zhuāng of Wèi, was appointed Inspector of Qīngzhōu.
The Emperor said:
"The custom of 'broken bricks' (*huàizhuān*) is known to be difficult to govern.
My uncle should employ good trusted subordinates
to assist in the trust placed by the court."
Formerly, Prince Péngchéng served as the Governor of Qīngzhōu.
He inquired about its customs,
and his guests said:
"The land of Qí is superficial and fickle.
When a governor first arrives,
they all break bricks and kowtow to show their intentions.
But when his term ends,
they strike him with bricks."
This referred to their initial support and eventual betrayal.
A saying in the capital (*jīngshī*) goes:
"No prisoners held in jail,
no Qīngzhōu people near the house.
Even if the family is poor,
there is no sorrow in the heart."
Whey slave
When Wáng Sù of Qí returned to Wèi,
he initially did not eat mutton or drink whey.
He always ate crucian carp soup
and drank tea when thirsty.
Emperor Gāo said:
"How does mutton compare to fish soup?
How does tea compare to whey?"
Sù replied:
"Sheep
are the best of land produce;
fish
are the chief of aquatic creatures.
Sheep are comparable to the great states of Qí and Lǔ;
fish are comparable to the small states of Zhū and Jǔ.
Whey is not fit to be a slave to tea."
Prince Péngchéng, Xié, said:
"You do not value the great states of Qí and Lǔ,
but you love the small states of Zhū and Jǔ.
Tomorrow, I will arrange a gathering for you in the style of Zhū and Jǔ,
and there will also be 'whey slaves'."
Thus, tea was called "whey slave" (*làonú*).
Water calamity
Wáng Méng 濛 loved tea.
Whenever guests arrived, he would make them drink it,
which the literati found very vexing.
Whenever they wanted to visit Méng,
they would always say:
"Today I have a 'water calamity'."
An Old Woman Playing the Chí
King Héjiān's 河間 servant girl was named Zhāoyún 朝雲,
and she was skilled at playing the chí.
When the Qiāng 羌 rebelled,
the King ordered Zhāoyún 朝雲 to disguise herself as an old woman and play the chí.
The Qiāng 羌 all shed tears
and surrendered again.
The saying goes:
"Fast horses and strong men
are not as good as an old woman playing the chí."
Painting Eggs and Carving Wood
Yuán Chēn 元琛 was extravagant.
He once said:
"Shí Chóng 石崇 was of common descent,
yet he could still paint eggs and carve wood."
Wild Goose Vassals
The chiefs of the northern barbarians would send their sons to serve at court.
They would usually come in autumn and leave in spring,
to avoid the heat of the central plains.
They were called "Wild Goose Vassals."
Jade Phoenixes and Golden Dragons
Yuán Chēn's 元琛 windows had jade phoenixes holding bells in their mouths,
and golden dragons spitting out banners.
The Miáocí 苗茨 Stele
The one hundred stone steles south of Nàilín 奈林,
erected by Emperor Míng 明 of Wèi 魏,
were inscribed with "The Miáocí 苗茨 Stele."
Gāozǔ 高祖 built the Miáocí 苗茨 Hall.
During the Yǒng'ān 永安 reign,
Emperor Zhuāng 莊 was shooting arrows in the Huálín 華林 Garden.
The hundred officials read the stele,
and doubted the character "Miáo 苗" was correct.
Yǎnzī 衍之 explained:
"Because it refers to artemisia and ganoderma,
it is called Miáocí 苗茨.
What error is there?"
Historical Records Are Not True Accounts
The hermit Zhào Yì 趙逸,
who said he was a Jìn 晉 man,
said:
"From Yǒngjiā 永嘉 onwards, for over three hundred years,
sixteen rulers founded states and claimed kingship.
I witnessed all these events with my own eyes.
After the fall of states,
the historical records were all not true accounts.
Even today, people are foolish in life and wise in death;
the confusion is extreme!
While alive, they are ordinary people.
But when they die,
their epitaphs and tomb inscriptions extol their great virtues to the heavens
and exhaust the abilities of mankind.
In life, they were bandits like Dào Zhí 盜跖,
but in death, they become saintly like Yí Qí 夷齊.
Sycophantic words harm righteousness,
and flowery language diminishes truth."
One Meal from the King of Gāoyáng 高陽 Worth a Thousand Days of Mine
When Yōng 雍, the King of Gāoyáng 高陽, was chancellor,
one meal cost tens of thousands of cash.
Jì Chóng 季崇 said:
"One meal from Gāoyáng 高陽 is worth a thousand days of mine."
Chóng 崇 was the Grand Secretary,
rich enough to rival the world but stingy by nature.
He often had no meat with his meals,
only chives and scallions.
People said:
"Lord Jì 季 eats eighteen kinds of food in one meal."
This was because two nines make eighteen.
Báiduò's 白墮 Spring Brew
Liú Báiduò 劉白墮, a man from Hédōng 河東 in Jìn 晉, was skilled at brewing wine.
Those who drank it would get drunk and could not sober up.
During the Yǒngxī 永熙 reign,
Máo Hóngbīn 毛鴻賓, the Administrator of Qīngzhōu 青州, carried this wine to his fief.
He encountered bandits who robbed the wine.
They all drank it and became drunk,
and were captured.
Therefore, the wine was named "Capturing Traitors Wine."
The wandering heroes had a saying:
"We do not fear drawn bows and unsheathed swords,
only Báiduò's 白墮 spring brew."
Word Prophecy
Emperor Yáng 煬 once held a drinking party,
and played a word game,
taking the meaning of separation and combination of characters from those present.
He said to Yǎoniáng 杳娘:
"I take the character 'yǎo 杳' to mean 'eighteen days' (十八日)."
At that time, the palace maid Luólúo 羅羅 was attending.
Yǎoniáng 杳娘 broke down the character 'luó 羅' into 'four directions' (四維).
The Emperor said to Empress Xiāo 蕭:
"Can you break down my character?"
The Empress replied:
"Moving the left stroke to the right,
is it not the character 'yuān 淵'?"
This was a prophecy of the rise of Táng 唐.
Flower-Controlling Girl
The Emperor had a concubine, Yuán Bǎo'ér 袁寶兒,
who had many charming and silly ways.
At that time, Luòyáng 洛陽 presented an auspicious conjoined-stemmed flower to greet the imperial carriage.
The Emperor ordered her to hold it,
calling her the "Flower-Controlling Girl."
The Emperor said to Yú Shìjī 虞世基:
"Bǎo'ér 寶兒 has many silly charms.
You try to tease her."
Shìjī 世基 composed a poem saying:
"Learning to paint a raven, half undone,
shoulders drooping, sleeves dangling, a big silly creature.
Yet because of her silliness, she gains the emperor's favor,
always holding a flower branch, walking by the imperial carriage."
Jiàngxiān 絳仙 Can Relieve Hunger
The palace woman Wú Jiàngxiān 吳絳仙, who served in the Fènggě 鳳舸 Palace,
was skilled at painting long moth eyebrows.
The Emperor favored her,
and because of this, everyone competed to draw long moth eyebrows.
The palace officials supplied five hu (斛) of conch shell black paste daily,
calling it "moth green."
The Emperor often looked at Jiàngxiān 絳仙 through the curtain,
not moving for a long time,
saying:
"The ancients said that beauty is like food.
If it is someone like Jiàngxiān 絳仙,
she can relieve hunger!"
Female Sīmǎ Xiāngrú
The Emperor bestowed a harmonious fruit upon Wú Jiàngxiān 吳絳仙.
Jiàngxiān 絳xiān presented a poem on red paper in thanks.
The Emperor said:
"Jiàngxiān's 絳仙 talent and style
make her a female Sīmǎ Xiāngrú 司馬相如."
Keep Me
The Emperor wrote a poem to the palace woman Luólúo 羅羅:
"My beloved has irresistible captivating eyes,
brows painted dark on a high forehead, clustering like small moths.
How lucky if you would keep me to sleep by my side,
what if you don't keep me here?"
The Maze Tower
The Emperor built the Mílóu 迷樓 (Maze Tower).
On the upper floors, four precious chambers were set up:
one called "Singing Spring Sorrows,"
the second "Forgetting to Return Soberly,"
the third "Containing Night,"
and the fourth "Extending Autumn Moon."
Dream-Bringing Child
The Emperor indulged excessively and lost all restraint.
Every time he slept, he needed shaking and exertion
before he could fall into a dream.
His maid, Hán Jùn'é 韓俊娥, was particularly favored.
Every time he lay down, he would order her to shake and massage his limbs,
and he would often have a good sleep.
He therefore called her "Dream-Bringing Child."
Encounter with the Former King Chén
One day, the Emperor felt disoriented and encountered the former King Chén 陳 (Emperor Hòuzhǔ 後主).
One person to the left and right of Hòuzhǔ 後主 was very beautiful.
He pointed and said to the Emperor:
"This is Lìhuá 麗華.
I often recall crossing the river northward with her in front of Peach Leaf Mountain.
At that time, Lìhuá 麗華 was leaning on Línchūn 臨春 Pavilion,
trying out a purple rabbit-hair brush from the eastern capital,
writing on small polished red silk to answer Commander Jiāng's 江 'Poem on the Bright Moon.'
Before she finished,
Hán Qínhǔ 韓擒虎 came straight to press upon them,
leaving no room to escape."
Hòuzhǔ 後主 poured new Hóngliáng 洪梁 brew into a green-veined shell cup that measured the sea, to offer to the Emperor.
The Emperor asked Lìhuá 麗華 to dance "Jade Tree Backyard Flower."
Lìhuá 麗華 declined, saying that since she had come out of the well (i.e., had been resurrected),
her waist and limbs no longer had their former grace.
The Emperor requested her repeatedly,
so she rose and performed one tune.
Hòuzhǔ 後主 asked:
"How does Empress Xiāo 蕭 compare to this person?"
The Emperor replied:
"Spring orchids and autumn chrysanthemums
each have their own time of splendor."
Hòuzhǔ 後主 recited dozens of poems,
but the Emperor particularly loved the one titled "Small Window":
"Waking late from a midday nap,
alone, startled by a dream.
The setting sun, as if with purpose,
shines especially bright by the small window."
He also recited "A Poem Sent to Maid Bìyù 碧玉":
"My heart must break from separation,
my bones surely melt from lovesickness.
If my sorrowful soul disperses,
I trust it to beckon you."
Jīn Jī Yù Kuài
The capital of Wú presented Sōngjiāng perch.
Yángdì said,
"This is what is called Jīn Jī Yù Kuài,
the finest flavor of the southeast."
Shǎndiàn Chuāng
Where the Emperor read,
the windows were exquisitely arranged facing each other.
With golden frames and jade-like views,
their brilliance filled the eye.
It was called Shǎndiàn Chuāng (Lightning Window).
Wénzhāng Zǒngjí
The Emperor ordered Yú Shìnán and forty others to select writings.
From the Chǔ Cí to the Dàyè era, they compiled a work in five thousand volumes,
titled Wénzhāng Zǒngjí (Compendium of Literature).
He also selected two thousand skilled calligraphers to be imperial scribes,
who copied books in shifts.
Fēnbēi Fǎ
Originated with Chóu Chánshī.
All the medicines were put into a common tube,
which was inserted into a hat for seven days,
then taken out and stuck into the head.
When drinking with guests,
a hairpin was used to draw in the wine.
When one side was completely drunk,
the other side remained full.
This was called Fēnbēi Fǎ (Method of Dividing the Cup).
Xí Bào
Lǐ Mì proclaimed himself Wèi Gōng,
and issued a proclamation to the commanderies and counties,
denouncing the wickedness of Yángdì, saying:
"The late emperor's consorts
were all presented with silver rings;
all the princes' children
were kept in golden houses."
He also said:
"He secretly went to the nine markets,
personally driving four donkeys.
He likened himself to a merchant,
and accepted invitations from inns."
Tóngjìng Píng
Yángdì loved luxury.
When he visited Jiāngdū,
Wáng Shìchōng presented a bronze mirror screen.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and promoted him to Grand Administrator of Jiāngdū.
Zài Xí
Lǐ Mì again said in a proclamation:
"Hèruò Bì was executed as a supreme general,
Gāo Jǐng was strangled despite his great merits.
Xuē Dàohéng, a literary master and scholar,
was subjected to capital punishment.
Pain is tied in people's hearts,
sorrow entangled in Huáxià."
He also said:
"He built many palaces,
and erected vast ponds and terraces.
He exhausted the treasures of pearls and jades,
and squandered the exquisite decorations of painting.
Singing girls and dancing women
indulged in debauchery all day long;
racing dogs and flying hawks
roamed without restraint.
Between Sāngjiān and Púshàng,
he listened to the music of a dying state;
at糟丘 and the酒池,
he drank through endless nights."
He also said:
"When the stars moved in the Hàn dynasty,
did it speak of toiling people?
When rocks spoke in the Jìn kingdom,
it was not considered a troublesome task."
He also said:
"In one moment he collected ten years' rent,
in one day he wasted a thousand gold's worth of expenses.
Husbands went, wives became widows;
fathers departed, children became orphans.
A hundred rivers boiled,
ten suns appeared simultaneously."
Liáodōng zhī Yì
After Dàyè year seven,
there was first the campaign in Liáodōng.
Then able-bodied men were conscripted as Xiāoguǒ,
and donkeys and horses were sent to Zhuójùn.
Then men in yellow clothes were mobilized to tow boats into the Cānghǎi.
Then grains, various seeds, ox hides, iron, and charcoal were dispatched,
transported by flying carts for a thousand *lǐ*.
Zhīshìláng
At the end of the Dàyè era,
Sòng Kòu rose first.
Wáng Báo of Zōupíng gathered a multitude and occupied Chángbái Shān,
calling himself Zhīshìláng (Gentleman Who Knows the World).
He meant that the affairs of the world could be known.
He composed a song to recruit conscripts.
The song said:
"On Chángbái Shān is Zhīshìláng,
wearing only a red silk brocade back-covering.
His horizontal spear invades half the sky,
his whirling saber shines with sunlight.
Up the mountain he eats deer and elk,
down the mountain he eats oxen and sheep.
Suddenly hearing the arrival of the government army,
he raises his sword and charges forward.
Like a pig from Liáodōng,
what injury is there in having its head cut off?"
Many people joined him.
Later, when Yáng Xuángǎn rebelled,
Shāndōng consequently fell into great chaos.
In Héběi, there were Zhāng Chēng, Wáng Báfū, and others, totaling twenty-seven groups,
many reaching over a hundred thousand,
the smallest no less than ten thousand people.
They garrisoned commanderies and counties,
and established camps in mountains and marshes.
Their subordinate chieftains
also had names,
some called "Qǐ Jiàn Dí" (Beg to See the Enemy),
some called "Xián Tóu Fāng" (Dislike Head Square),
some called "Chè Juàn Wán" (Thoroughly Stubborn Dependents) or "Wù Xī Sǐ" (Don't Pity Death).
They also gathered in villages,
hundreds and tens forming groups,
with names like "Hēi Shè" (Black Society), "Bái Shè" (White Society), "Qīng Tè" (Green Special), "Hú Lǘ" (Barbarian Donkey),
"Fúyún Zéi" (Floating Cloud Bandits), "Hūlǜ Zéi" (Tiger Bandits).
Finally, Lǐ Mì rose and the Suí dynasty fell.
Zhìgōng Shī
The poem by the Daoist Zhìgōng of Liáng says:
"One *tǔ* (earth) will disorder ten *zhōu* (prefectures)."
When Shìchōng usurped the throne,
his state was named Zhèng.
He then used the character "土" (earth) to form the character "王" (king).
It also says:
"Disorder (亂),
is explained as governance (理)."
He made this into a prophecy,
and changed Luòzhōu to Shízhōu (Ten Prefectures).
Pósuōluó Shù
North of Luòchéng Shan is called Máng Shān.
There are no trees on it,
only an ancient Ailanthus tree on the northern ridge,
spreading four or five *mǔ*.
Yáng Sù, when building the capital city,
used this tree as the north-south standard.
Disliking the ill-omened name of the Ailanthus,
he called it Pósuōluó Shù.
Buddhist scriptures say the Pósuōluó Shù is the place of Tathāgata's Nirvāṇa,
which implies ill omen.
Later, when Yáng Xuángǎn rebelled,
Lǐ Mì besieged the city,
and when Tàizōng campaigned against Shìchōng,
they all parked their chariots by this tree
to look down upon the city.
Yǔ Wèi Gōng Cáng Zhuō
Liáng sent Xú Líng as an envoy to Qí.
At that time, Wèi Shōu's literature was considered the best in the Northern Dynasties.
His writings were recorded and shown to Líng.
When Líng crossed the river,
he threw them into the water.
He said:
"I will hide my clumsiness with Wèi Gōng."
Nánshì Zhǒng Míng
Luòyáng's Nánshì was
the Fēngdū market of the Suí dynasty.
A tomb was unearthed,
and in the coffin was a flat-topped cap and a scarlet robe.
The inscription read:
"Divination said to reside at court,
tortoise shell said to reside in the market.
After five hundred years,
it is seen here."
Comparing the dates,
it was during Wèi Huángchū year two.
Wèi Zǐ Zuò Zhōu
When Lǐ Yīnggōng's elder sister was ill,
he personally made porridge for her,
accidentally singeing his beard.
His sister stopped him,
and he said:
"Sister is old,
Jì is also old.
How can one make this porridge for long?"
Mén Jìn Liù Quē
Zhū Jìngzé compiled the Xiàoyì (Filial Piety and Righteousness).
From Wén Zhōu to Táng,
all were honored with six ceremonial gates at their entrances.
Flying cavalry.
During the Zhēngguān
period, swift and agile horsemen skilled in archery were selected
and called Fēijì.
They wore robes of five colors,
rode six-stallion horses,
and accompanied the emperor on his excursions.
Buddha's Tooth
During the Zhēngguān period, a monk said that nothing hard could withstand the Buddha's tooth.
Chuán Yì said,
"I've heard that diamonds are extremely hard,
and only antelope horn can break them."
When tested,
it crumbled instantly in hand.
Zhāng Dǐ became Zhōngshū Lìng.
Zhāng Jiāzhēn was a Shèrén.
Shí looked down on him,
always calling him Zhāng Dǐ.
Later, Jiāzhēn's deliberations on matters surpassed expectations.
Shí, surprised, said to his colleagues,
"Zhāng Dǐ is a person like us.
He deserves to sit here."
Indeed, he later became Zhōngshū Lìng.
Zhāng Family's Ox
Jiě Fèngxiān, a painter from Luòyáng, painted for the household of Sī Jiāng Wáng
and overcharged for his work.
The Prince reprimanded him.
He then swore before the Buddha, saying,
"If I am deceitful,
may I die and become an ox for the Prince's family."
Shortly after, he died suddenly.
A dun calf was born in the Prince's household,
with white markings on its back that read,
"Jiě Fèngxiān."
Xuē Dàohéng's Poem
In the Suí dynasty, Xuē Dàohéng was sent on a mission to Chén.
He wrote a poem on the day of his departure, saying,
"Spring has barely begun for seven days,
yet I have been away from home for two years."
Southerners mocked him for it.
He also said,
"People return after the wild geese,
thoughts emerge before the flowers."
Then they said,
"No empty scholar under a great name."
Fúróng Yuán
The Fúróng Yuán in the capital
was originally named Qǔjiāng Yuán.
Emperor Wén of Suí, considering "Qǔ" an improper name,
changed it.
Běitáng Shūchāo
Yú Shìnán, in the back hall of the provincial office,
collected materials from various books that could be used for writing.
It was titled Běitáng Shūchāo.
Guō Zhèngyī's Amusing Incidents
Guō Zhèngyī served as the chronicler for Lǐ Yīnggōng's campaign in Liáo.
Upon his return, Jī said,
"This journey,
I recorded Guō Zhèngyī's amusing incidents.
Even if they filled ten scrolls, I still couldn't finish."
Liú Chén and Ruǎn Zhào
During the reign of Emperor Míng of Hàn,
Liú Chén and Ruǎn Zhào entered Tiāntái together.
They saw two women
who offered sesame rice,
goat jerky,
peaches, and wine,
all very delicious.
They returned over a year later.
Their hometown had all changed.
Upon searching for their families,
they found that seven generations had already passed.
Scholars
Xiūwén Guǎn Scholars were
established in the second year of Jǐnglóng.
There were four Grand Scholars, symbolizing the four seasons;
eight Scholars, symbolizing the eight seasons;
and twelve Direct Scholars, symbolizing the twelve hours.
They all participated in banquets and gatherings.
Rìjiù Diàn
Made from fragrant juniper, brocaded cypress, and other materials.
Intercalary Ninth Day
On the Ninth Day, a banquet was held, and poems were composed.
Lǐ Qiáo said,
"The intercalary festival opens the double Ninth."
Guó Yà
Dòu Cóngyī was appointed Yùshǐ Dàfū.
Emperor Zhōngzōng said,
"I will arrange a marriage for you."
The New Year's Eve banquet was grand.
In the middle of the banquet, his bride was brought in.
When the fan was removed and the flowers taken away,
it was an old woman.
Later, it was learned that she was the Empress's wet nurse,
known in the palace by the title Guó Yà.
Diémǎ Xì
At a banquet for Tǔfān envoys,
the Diémǎ Xì (horse dancing show) was performed.
The saddles were adorned with five-colored silk threads and metal fittings,
and augmented with qílín heads and feathered wings.
When the music played,
the horses all tapped their hooves to the sound,
turning gracefully in rhythm.
The "Hu" people were greatly astonished.
Four Divisions of Books
Xuē Jì was in charge of the Jí Kù,
Mǎ Huáisù of the Jīng Kù,
Shěn Quánqí of the Shǐ Kù,
and Wǔ Píng of the Zǐ Kù.
Collectively, they were called "Sì Bù Shū."
Táohuā Xíng
Lǐ Qiáo and others composed peach blossom poems.
The Emperor ordered twenty pieces to be inserted into the Yuèfǔ
and called Táohuā Xíng.
Bānjīng Zhī Xì
On the Qīngmíng Festival, court officials were ordered to perform the Bānjīng Zhī Xì (tug-of-war).
A large hemp rope had over ten smaller ropes tied to its ends.
Several people held each rope, vying for the main rope.
The side with weaker strength lost.
At that time, ten prime ministers and two imperial sons-in-law formed the Eastern team,
while three prime ministers and five generals formed the Western team.
Púyè Wéi Jùyuán
and Shàoshī Táng Xiūjǐng, due to their old age, stumbled with the rope and fell,
unable to rise for a long time.
The Emperor found this amusing.
Fine Willow
On the Shàngsì Purification Rite,
fine willow branches were bestowed upon court officials,
saying:
wearing them would avert centipede venom and plague.
Hésheng
Hésheng songs were played in the palace,
their lyrics shallow and vulgar.
Wǔ Píngyī admonished, saying,
"Sorcerers, prostitutes, street children, and market women
discuss the emotions and appearances of imperial consorts and princesses,
and list the names and qualities of princes and dukes,
singing and dancing.
This is called Hésheng,
and should not be performed within the palace."
Màizhōu
On Hánshí, oat porridge, pasted colorful balls, and carved eggs were bestowed.
Each Person Composed Four-Couplet Poems
The preface to the imperial poem for "Banquet at Báilù Guān" stated:
Each person composed four-couplet poems,
after which three cups of wine were penalized.
Lǐ Zōngchǔ and others bowed and said,
"Having enjoyed imperial joy,
we dare not not get drunk."
They also said,
"Respectfully we raise the imperial cup and drink."
Pines Gate and Ivy Tent
At Wéi Sìlì's estate, the banquet poem said:
"At the pine gate, banners halt;
Within the ivy tent, officials' attire is arrayed."
Jiǎncǎi Huā Shī
Zhào Yànruò's "Jiǎncǎi Huā Shī" said:
"Flowers blossom with red intentions,
Leaves freshen with green feelings."
Lúnshěng Tuī Gāo
When Zhōngshū Shèrén Lǐ Yì was appointed Scholar,
the imperial edict stated, "Lúnshěng pushes him high."
Nánchuáng
The Shìyùshǐ were called Zádān,
being the most powerful and severe.
When they gathered at the Censorate,
a horizontal couch was set up south of the seats,
called Nánchuáng,
also known as Chīchuáng,
meaning that those who sat on this couch were arrogant as if foolish.
Yùshǐ Běncǎo
Jiǎ Zhōngyán compiled the Yùshǐ Běncǎo (Materia Medica of Censors),
likening the Lǐxíng to "closed-mouth peppercorns,"
the most poisonous;
the Jiānchá to "open-mouth peppercorns,"
slightly poisonous;
the Diànzhōng to "radishes";
the Shìyù to "crisp pears,"
meaning they gradually entered a pleasing taste;
and those promoted to Nánshěng Láng to "licorice,"
meaning they could enjoy long-lasting peace.
Wǔmò Sānyīng
Three Palace Censors (Yùshǐ) were transferred to provincial ministries (nánsheng láng) but retained their former posts.
Five were appointed by imperial edict (mòchì).
At the time, they were called “Five by Edict, Three Retained.”
The Materia Medica of Officials
Hóu Wèi Xū authored "The Materia Medica of Officials."
It said of the Censor (Yùshǐ): "It is very hot and poisonous,
primarily to expel evil and sycophancy,
block treachery,
redress injustices,
and stop excess;
it is especially effective against greed and corruption,
is wary of being distanced or used,
and dislikes being on night duty.
It is adverse to powerful bullying.
Those from outer provinces are especially commendable for re-use,
and those dried and broken by sun exposure are excellent.
Taking it enhances mental clarity,
diminishes charm and beauty,
and prolonged use makes one cold and aloof."
The Six Paths
There were six paths for Capital Prefects (Jīwèi) in the Táng dynasty:
entering the Censorate (Yùshǐ) was the path of a Buddha (fódào),
entering the Reviewing Office (Píngshì) was the path of an Immortal (xiāndào),
entering the Capital Prefecture (Chìwèi) was the path of a Human (réndào),
entering the Capital Assistant (Jīchéng) was the path of Bitter Sea (kǔhǎidào),
entering the County Magistrate (Xiànlìng) was the path of Beasts (chùshēngdào),
and entering the Judicial Clerk (Pànsī) was the path of a Hungry Ghost (èguǐdào).
The Ao-fishing Guest
Wáng Yánguāng had talent but was unrecognized.
He styled himself "The Ao-fishing Guest."
He traveled through cities and towns,
seeking funds for hemp and iron to build fishing gear.
If anyone did not respond,
he would record their name and place it in a basket,
saying:
"When I cast my line, I will use these simpletons as bait."
His extravagance was of this kind.
Zhāng Yòu visited Lǐ Shēn,
also calling himself "The Ao-fishing Guest."
Lǐ angrily asked:
"Since you can fish for the Ao,
what do you use for a rod?"
He replied:
"I use a rainbow for a rod."
"What do you use for a hook?"
He replied:
"I use the moon for a hook."
"What do you use for bait?"
He replied:
"I use the 'short Li' prime minister (duǎnlǐ xiàng) as bait."
Lǐ Shēn fell silent,
then gave him a generous gift.
Ten Times Ten Thousand Words
In the early Kaiyuán reign,
Cháng Jìngzhōng, at fifteen, submitted a memorial,
able to recite a thousand words in one reading.
Zhāng Yàngōng summoned him and asked:
"Can you memorize ten thousand words in ten readings?"
He replied:
"Yes."
He was tested with ten thousand characters,
and by the seventh reading, he had mastered them.
Forging an Ancient Calligraphy
Lǐ Yōng never approved of Xiāo Chéng's calligraphy.
So Xiāo made a fake ancient calligraphy,
deliberately darkening the paper,
and showed it to Lǐ Yōng, saying:
"This is a genuine work by the Right General (Yòujūn)."
Lǐ Yōng happily exclaimed:
"This is truly authentic; I have never seen its like in my life!"
Xiāo Chéng then told him the truth.
Lǐ Yōng took it back and looked again, saying:
"Upon closer inspection,
it's not actually that good."
Large Sticks and Small Sticks
Yán Ānzhī and Cuī Tán were both Capital Prefects (Chìwèi).
Yán Ānzhī ordered his bailiffs (wǔbó) to carry large sticks,
while Cuī Tán made his sticks even smaller,
to the size of chopsticks.
Yán Ānzhī then ordered his bailiffs to go empty-handed,
but Cuī Tán could not imitate this.
Two Woks
At the Buddhist temple in Qīngzhōu's southern city, there were two large woks.
The larger held forty dàn,
the smaller thirty dàn.
It was traditionally believed that the temple was Mèng Cháng's former residence,
and the woks were used to cook food for guests.
Lǐ Pī destroyed them to make weapons.
The People of Lǔ are Ruined
During the Guǎngdé reign,
Censor Lǐ Jìqīng visited the Temple of Confucius (Wénxuān Miào) in Qūfù.
His attendant led the way,
and at each spot,
would point and say:
"This is Yán Zǐ's humble alley,
this is the mausoleum of the Língguāng Diàn."
Upon reaching a pond, he said:
"This is where the people of Lǔ fished at Língguāng."
Lǐ laughed and said:
"The people of Lǔ are ruined!"
The Yìshān Stele
It says that Yuè Lè carved this stone,
but many people do not understand.
Yán Shīgǔ said it was a stele made from a floating chime (fúqìng) from the Sì River bank.
Fifteen Chapters of Whistling
There are fifteen chapters of whistling,
including "Tiger of the Deep Stream,"
"Cicada of the Tall Willows,"
"Ghost of the Empty Forest,"
"Gibbon of Wū Xiá,"
"Descending Swans and Geese,"
and "Kite of the Ancient Tree."
The Zhìgǔzi records them in detail.
Painting Landscapes
During the Dàlì reign,
a scholar from Wú named Gù Zǐ painted landscapes that were very strange.
He would first spread silk on the ground,
grind and mix colors,
and have dozens of people blow horns, beat drums, and shout.
Gù Zǐ would wear a brocade robe and turban,
drink until half-drunk,
pour ink onto the silk,
then pour various other colors,
and use a large brush to spread and define them,
creating shapes of peaks, ranges, islands,
mastering their subtleties completely.
Tail-burning Scholars
When scholars first passed the imperial examination,
they would hold celebratory banquets,
called "burning the tail" (shāowěi).
Some say:
"A tiger transforms into a human,
but only its tail does not transform;
it must be burned off before it can fully become human."
Another saying:
"When a new sheep enters the flock,
the other sheep butt and do not bond with it;
only by burning its tail does it settle."
Yet another: "When a fish leaps the Dragon Gate and transforms into a dragon,
its tail must be burned by lightning before it transforms."
Leopard Duty
According to old Censorate (Yùshǐ) custom:
the first fifteen days of accompanying duty upon entering the Censorate were called "prostrate leopard" (fúbào),
taking the meaning of "not yet emerged."
It was also called "leopard duty" (bàozhí),
with the same meaning.
Taking the jīndēnghuā as a magical herb (zhīcǎo)
Xīmén Huán, as the Magistrate of Hándān,
regarded the jīndēnghuā as a magical herb (zhīcǎo),
and submitted a memorial detailing it.
The provincial administration (shǐsī) knew it was preposterous,
but did not question him further.
Those Who Sinned Were Made to Wear Green Turbans
Lǐ Fēng, as the Magistrate of Yánlíng,
did not punish officials with floggings when they sinned,
but merely made them wear green turbans to humiliate them.
The prefecture and local community considered this a great disgrace.
He never flogged a single person.
The Moon Laurel Descends
During the Chuígǒng reign,
a moon laurel (yuèguì) descended in Táizhōu.
According to the theory that the sun and moon each have limited cities,
how could they be a bottomless void,
allowing a laurel to descend?
How could creatures like toads and rabbits
not fall?
Dàn Tumor
Someone loved drinking tea,
drinking up to two dòu.
One day, he drank excessively
and vomited a mass resembling a cow's lung.
When tea was poured on it,
it held one hú and two dòu.
A guest called it a "dàn tumor" (hú jiǎ).
Long Whistle
Daoist Chén of Mount Éméi
was skilled in the long whistle,
producing a thunderous sound,
which startled those who heard it.
The Noble Consort (Guìfēi) Painted Liú Yàn’s Eyebrows
Liú Yàn was eight years old
when he presented the "Book of the Eastern Sacrifices."
Míng Huáng ordered the prime minister to set a topic,
and tested him in the Department of the Central Secretariat.
He brought Yàn into the inner palace,
where the Six Palaces watched.
He seated Yàn on Guì Fēi's lap,
and the Emperor personally painted his eyebrows,
and tied his twin topknots.
The palace maids gave him flowers and threw fruit.
White Mule General
When the Emperor ascended Tàishān for the Feng Sacrifice,
a white mule arrived from Yìzhōu.
It was gentle, accustomed to riding, and comfortable.
After the ceremony was completed, it died.
It was posthumously titled "White Mule General."
Golden Celestial King
When Míng Huáng passed Huáyīn,
he saw the god of Mount Huà welcome and greet him.
He asked his attendants,
but they saw nothing.
The old shamaness Ā Mǎ Pó said:
"The Third Son
is by the roadside,
with red hair and purple robes."
When the Emperor arrived before the temple,
a figure with a quiver and bow case stood in the courtyard.
He was then enfeoffed as "Golden Celestial King."
New Melody of Liángzhōu
A new melody was composed in Western Liángzhōu,
called "Liángzhōu."
Níng Wáng said:
"The sound begins with gōng,
disperses at shāng,
and culminates in jué, zhǐ, and yǔ.
This is a new melody,
but the gōng is discordant and weak,
and the shāng is chaotic and violent.
I fear there will be a disaster of displacement and dispersal."
When the An-Shi Rebellion broke out,
it confirmed the subtlety of Níng Wáng's understanding of music.
Yán Gōng's Boundary
The Emperor held a grand feast at Qínzhènglóu,
where people thronged and packed the area.
The white staffs of the Jīnwú guards rained down like water.
The Emperor summoned Yán Ānzhī, the Governor of Jīngzhào, to manage the crowd.
Ānzhī walked around the square,
drawing lines on the ground with his handboard,
saying:
"Those who transgress this will die!"
People pointed to his drawing and said:
"Yán Gōng's Boundary,"
and no one dared to cross it.
Rabbit Poem
Sū Huán initially did not know Tíng,
and kept him in the stable.
Tíng once recited a poem about a Kūnlún slave:
"Ten ink-sticks for fingers,
two spoons for ears."
He also wrote a "Rabbit Poem" which said:
"The rabbit is utterly dead,
brought and hung on a bamboo pole.
If you try to shine a bright mirror on it,
how is it different from looking at the moon?"
Huán was greatly surprised,
and from then on, Tíng's writings surpassed his contemporaries.
When the Emperor quelled internal troubles,
all edicts were written by Tíng overnight.
He was called "Little Xǔ Gōng" by his generation.
Melon Seed
When Hè Zhīzhāng requested to return to Wúzhōng,
the Emperor summoned him and asked what he desired.
Zhīzhāng said:
"Your servant has a son who has not yet been named.
I hope Your Majesty will bestow a name."
The Emperor said:
"Without trustworthiness, a person cannot stand.
Fú means trustworthiness,
so he should be named Fú."
Zhīzhāng later realized and said:
"Why did the Emperor mock me?
Because I am from Wú,
Fú (孚) is composed of 'child' (子) under 'claw' (爪), which looks like 'melon' (瓜) without the top, forming the character '瓜子' (guāzǐ, melon seeds).
He called me 'melon seed'!"
Purple Cloud Returns
The Emperor dreamt he traveled to the Moon Palace,
heard the music of the Supreme Purity,
remembered the melody,
and sought it out with a jade flute.
It was named "Purple Cloud Returns."
White Stone Seal Script
At Hángǔguān, a white stone was found with the seal script character "sāng."
Interpreters said:
"It means forty-eight."
This precisely matched the number of years the Emperor was on the throne.
Yī Xíng Presents Dāngguī
When Chan Master Yī Xíng was about to die,
he left an item to be presented to the Emperor.
It was Shǔ dāngguī (angelica root).
When the Emperor returned from his journey to Shǔ,
he then understood its meaning.
Mr. Qū's Flavor
Yè Fǎshàn possessed Taoist arts,
and resided at Xuánzhēnguān.
One day, he gathered several court officials;
everyone present yearned for wine.
Suddenly, someone knocked on the door,
calling himself "Scholar Qū,"
and burst in to sit.
He was young and handsome,
and his discourse was extraordinary.
Fǎshàn secretly struck him with a small sword;
it instantly fell to the ground and transformed into a wine bottle and flask,
containing exquisite wine.
They then drank it together.
All said:
"Mr. Qū's flavor
is unforgettable."
Péi Yǐn's Judgments
Péi Xǔ was the Governor of Hénán.
Once, someone submitted a petition with the writing mistakenly on the back of the paper.
Xǔ ruled:
"This side has that side,
that side resembles this side.
I would not refuse to judge it for you,
but the boot-wearing fellows at the gate would laugh themselves to death."
Another time, a woman submitted a complaint disputing ownership of a cat.
The complaint said:
"If it is a child cat,
then it is a child cat.
If it is not a child cat,
then it is not a child cat."
Xǔ ruled:
"A cat that doesn't know its place,
it stands by me and catches mice.
The two families need not argue,
bring it to Péi Xǔ."
So he took the cat.
Killing the Buddha's Son
Sānzàng Wú Wèi relied on Vinaya Master Xuān.
Wú Wèi drank wine and ate meat,
and his words and actions were crude and easygoing,
which displeased the Vinaya Master.
Once, he made him sleep outdoors.
In the middle of the night, the Vinaya Master felt lice and threw them under the bed.
Wú Wèi immediately called out:
"You've killed the Buddha's son!"
The Vinaya Master found this unusual.
Prince Názhà
protected Vinaya Master Xuān.
The Vinaya Master once traveled at night.
When he was about to step onto a stair, he lost his footing,
but someone held him up.
He saw a young man,
and the Master asked who he was.
He replied:
"I am Prince Názhà, son of Bishāwáng,
and I have been protecting the reverend monk for a long time."
The Master said:
"This poor monk cultivates himself,
there is no need for Your Highness,
your divine power is free."
The deity then presented a Buddha tooth,
which is the one now stored in Chóngshèngsì.
Jade Chime
Yáng Fēi was skilled at striking the chime.
Thus, a chime was carved from Lántián green jade.
Rebuking Wǔ Yōujì
When the Emperor was a grandson,
he rebuked Wǔ Yōujì in the court hall, saying:
"This is my family's court hall;
how dare you look around like a bee or wasp?"
Zétiān said:
"This child will eventually be the Peaceful and Prosperous Son of Heaven for our family."
Wàn Huí
Master initially seemed foolish.
Even his parents treated him like a pig or dog.
His elder brother was conscripted for military service in Ānnán,
and communication was cut off.
Suddenly, one day,
his brother went there in the morning and returned in the evening,
saying that his elder brother was safe and well.
They opened the letter and saw
it was his brother's handwriting.
His family called him "Wàn Huí" [Ten Thousand Li Return]
because he returned from ten thousand li.
Poem on Jiànmén
The Emperor went to Shǔ and returned,
passing through Jiànmén.
The Emperor said:
“The natural defenses are like this,
yet from ancient times until now, defeat and destruction have followed one after another.
Is it not because success lies in virtue, not in danger?”
He composed a poem, saying:
“The Jiàngé is lofty, spanning the sky;
The imperial carriage returns from the hunt.
Green screens of a thousand *rèn* close in,
Crimson peaks are cleft open by Wǔdīng.
Shrubs entangle the turning banners,
Immortal clouds brush against the arriving horses.
To seize the opportune moment lies in virtue;
Alas for you who engrave inscriptions!”
Zhānrán
When the Emperor was to perform the Fēng sacrifice on Mount Tài,
he advanced to the Zhānrán River in Xíngyáng.
He saw a black dragon,
and ordered it shot with a bow and arrow.
After that, the Zhānrán flowed underground.
It was originally the Jì River,
which overflowed and formed a winding course,
thus it was named Zhānrán.
The *Zuǒ Zhuàn* says:
“The Chǔ army crossed the Zhānrán,” which refers to this.
Wèngdù Fēng
At the Yúntái Guān of Mount Huá,
a mountain rises abruptly from the central platform,
shaped like half an urn,
and is named Wèngdù Fēng.
The Emperor wanted to carve the two characters “Kāiyuán” deeply into the belly of the peak,
and fill them with white stone,
but a censor memorialized, and he stopped.
Mocking Liú Wénshù
Liú Wénshù, a general in the Ānxī protectorate, was skilled at answering imperial questions.
He had a beard growing under his chin,
and his appearance resembled a monkey.
The Emperor ordered Huáng Fānchuò to mock him.
Wénshù intensely disliked being called a monkey,
and secretly bribed Fānchuò,
begging him not to mention it.
Fānchuò presented his mockery, saying:
“Pitiable good Wénshù,
His beard and chin live separately.
His face does not resemble a monkey,
A monkey is a strong companion to Wénshù.”
The Emperor laughed greatly.
Seeing a Hairy Man in the Yuètáng
Lǐ Línfǔ saw a creature in the Yǎnyuètáng,
its entire body covered in hair, standing like a pig,
with hooked tusks and claws over three *chǐ* long.
Línfǔ repeatedly shouted at it, but it did not move.
He hastily ordered a bow and arrow,
but the hairy man laughed and leaped into the front hall.
Not many days later, Línfǔ fell from power.
Rhapsody on Visiting the Hot Springs
When the Emperor visited Huáqīng Gōng,
Liú Zhāoxiá presented the *Rhapsody on Visiting the Hot Springs*,
which roughly said:
“As for the second year of Tiānbǎo,
After the tenth month, before the twelfth,
The heavenly gate creaked open,
Revealing a converging multitude of immortals;
The imperial carriage swept out,
Driving forth a dense array of armored guards.
One team green, one team yellow,
Bears stepping on backs, leopards stepping on backs;
One mass of rice, one mass of embroidery,
Jade carved on bridles, gold carved on saddles.”
In describing virtue, it said:
“Directly grasping Pángǔ’s marrow,
Plucking Nǚwā’s gourd,
Regardless of the Five Emperors of ancient times,
Are they equal to our Five Lords of today?”
The self-preface said:
“Poor and stumbling,
Lost and wild.
Though the bone-flag is short,
Artistic skill can be long.
How many times rich and noble in dreams,
Awakening still miserable and desolate.
Today is a once-in-a-thousand-year encounter,
Prostrate yourself, do not be disheveled and agitated.”
The Emperor ordered the phrase “wǔjiǎo liùzhāng” to be changed,
but the memorial responded:
“When your servant drafted this *fu*, it was as if aided by spirits.
Without adding a single dot,
I do not wish to change it at the command of heaven.”
The Emperor said:
“Truly a person of meager fortune.”
Method of Invisibility
Luó Sīyuǎn was skilled in the method of invisibility.
The Emperor learned it from him,
but not all its essentials.
When Sīyuǎn performed it with him,
he would disappear completely.
When the Emperor tried it himself,
sometimes a sash would remain,
sometimes the corner of his head wrap would show.
The Emperor was angry,
and ordered strongmen to wrap him in an oiled sack,
place him under a coffin, crush him to death, and bury him.
Ten days later,
a palace envoy returning from Shǔ
met Sīyuǎn on the road, who smiled
and said:
“How cruel was the Emperor’s prank?”
Manual of Cultivation
The *Cáizhí Jīng* in three volumes is handed down through generations,
saying:
“Many trees suffer from a 'sour heart' disease.
Its symptom is
that both the bark and sap are sour.
If someone can cure it,
hook out the borers,
and the tree will flourish.”
Ink Stains on Clothes
If ink stains clothes,
hold your breath over water and write white characters,
then wash it immediately.
It will be clean in no more than seven washes.
Sījiǎ
A military general saw Emperor Liáng Yuándì,
and described himself as foolish and dull, mispronouncing it as “sījiǎ.”
The Emperor laughed and said:
“‘Sī’ is not a cool breeze,
‘Jiǎ’ is not dry wood.”
Accepting a Gift of Squatting Taro
Someone mistakenly read “yù” (taro) as “yáng” (sheep).
When someone gave him taro,
he thanked them saying, “I have received your gift of squatting taro.”
My Riddle Swallowed Your Riddle
Cáo Zhù was quick-witted.
A guest tested him,
and made a riddle, saying:
“One thing, when sitting, it sits;
When lying, it sits;
When standing, it sits;
When walking, it sits;
When running, it sits.”
Zhù immediately responded:
“On public land, on private land.”
Then the guest made another riddle, saying:
“One thing, when sitting, it lies;
When standing, it lies;
When walking, it lies;
When running, it lies;
When lying, it lies.”
The guest could not understand.
Cáo said:
“My riddle swallowed your riddle.”
The guest was greatly ashamed.
Jùzhī
I found it troublesome for guests to compose linked verses and pass them around,
so I took a striped bamboo,
and wrapped its top with white gold like a tea pod,
to pass around linked verses.
This was called *jùzhī*.
Sometimes, one might compete with bad rhymes,
or compose an eight-rhyme poem for a bowl of tea.
All these were called *zálian*.
If one aimed for immortality,
one would select guests,
choose stable rhymes,
and stop if nothing suitable was found.
This was called *kǔliánjù*.
When all verses rhyme with a level tone
and the good rhymes are not obscure,
they are written on bamboo slips
and called *yùndié*.
Crab Named Hǔxún
The large sea crabs with tiger-striped patterns
are called *xún* because
they are submerged and carried away by the waves.
Small crabs,
whenever the tide is about to come in,
emerge from their holes and raise their claws to meet it,
and are called Zhāocháozǐ.
Another kind of small crab sheds its shell with the tide.
When the tide recedes,
it slowly moves through the mud,
and is called Tāntú.
Lìnú
Inside oyster shells, there are small crabs,
which emerge to feed,
then return into the oyster shells.
They are called "oyster slaves" (lì nú).
The bird thief mud loach
refers to a type of loach that has eyes like a monkey, hence its name "mud loach" (ní hóu).
Also, the Ěryǎ states:
“Xīqiū.”
There is also the "army fish" (jūnyú).
Therefore, people by the sea have a drinking game saying:
“The army fish goes to sea to fight the cuttlefish,
and if successful, it is enfeoffed as a mud loach.”
Truthful Gull
A distinct species of gull,
they cry in groups, jījiē,
and move with the tides.
They are called "truthful gulls" (xìngōu).
White Egret Cloak
People from Jiāngdōng take the feathers from the heads and necks of white egrets
to make attached decorative pieces,
which they call "white egret cloak" (báilù suō).
Sometimes, red cranes are interspersed among them.
Jellyfish
Its clear ripples extend its substance,
and congealed pearls form its shape.
Its name is Xī,
which is the jellyfish (shuǐmǔ).
Officials' Minced Fish
People from Jiāngnán make minced fish
called "officials' minced fish" (lángguān kuài).
It is said to have been named after Zhāng Hàn.
Cicada Gauze
Silk gauze woven by the Spring Maidens (Quánnǚ),
so fine and thin like cicada wings,
is called "cicada gauze" (chánshā).
Eight-Silkworm Cotton
Made by eight silkworms,
sharing one large cocoon.
Seagull Boat and Crab-Apple Oar
When the Yuè people engage in naval warfare,
they rush to the enemy, treading on the waves,
they have the "seagull" (hǎioū),
which is a boat name.
It is also called "fish flowing through" (chuānxíng yúliú).
To bathe in waves without drowning,
they have the "crab-apple oar" (tánglǔ),
which, like the crab-apple, does not sink.
Heavenly Luan Roast
The geckos (wǎlóngzǐ) are also called "heavenly luán" (tiānluán).
Shrimp Whiskers
Sea shrimp whiskers can be one zhàng long,
and can be made into walking sticks.
Litchi Slave
People in Lǐngnán call longans "litchi slaves" (lìzhī nú).
End of Scroll Six.
End.
Eight Treasures
During the Kāiyuán era,
there was a woman surnamed Lǐ who married into the Huò family.
Her husband died,
and she became a nun,
named Zhēnrú.
Her conduct was noble and pure.
On the seventh day of the seventh month of Tiānbǎo first year,
she suddenly saw five-colored clouds fall to the ground,
and a pouch containing five objects.
Zhēnrú hid them.
During the An Lùshān rebellion,
she migrated to Ānyí County, Chǔzhōu.
In the first year of Sùzōng, in the month of Zǐ,
Zhēnrú was summoned by a divine being to Huàchéng,
where she saw the Heavenly Emperor,
who bestowed upon her eight treasures,
and commanded her to present them to the court,
to dispel the cold qi.
Zhēnrú then presented all eight treasures, along with the previous five objects.
When the treasures were placed in the sun,
their radiance connected to the sky.
Sùzōng, afflicted by illness,
summoned Dàizōng and said:
“You, from Prince of Chǔ, became Crown Prince.
Now Heaven bestows treasures upon Chǔzhōu.
Heaven blesses you.
You should carefully preserve them.”
Dàizōng received the gifts
and changed the era name to Bǎoyīng.
From then on, military conflicts diminished,
and the empire enjoyed relative peace.
The first is called "Profound Yellow Heavenly Talisman" (Xuánhuáng Tiānfú).
Its shape is like a ceremonial tablet (hù),
round at the top and square at the bottom,
made of yellow jade.
Its color is like a chestnut,
and it repels the qi of war and pestilence among humans.
The second is called "Jade Chicken" (Yùjī).
Its feathers are all complete,
made of white jade.
It appears when the ruler governs the world with filial piety.
The third is called "Grain Bi-Disk" (Gǔbì).
It is also white jade.
Its pattern is like grains of millet,
not from carving.
If a ruler obtains it,
all five grains will ripen.
The fourth is called "Queen Mother's Jade Ring" (Wángmǔ Yùhuán),
two pieces.
It is also white jade.
If a ruler obtains it,
all foreign nations will submit.
The fifth is called "Wish-Fulfilling Jewel" (Rúyì Bǎozhū).
It is as large as a chicken egg.
When placed in a room,
it shines like a full moon.
The sixth is called "Red Mòhé" (Hóng Mòhé).
It is as large as a huge chestnut,
and intensely red like a vermillion cherry.
Looking at it, one doubts if it can be touched,
but striking it, it is extremely hard and unbreakable.
The seventh is called "Lánggān Pearl" (Lánggān Zhū).
The eighth is called "Jade Seal" (Yùyìn).
It is as large as half a hand,
and its pattern is like a deer.
The ninth is called "Empress's Mulberry Hook" (Huánghòu Cǎisānggōu),
two pieces.
They are as thin as chopsticks,
and can be bent like gold.
The tenth is called "Cloud Duke Stone" (Yúngōng Shí),
two pieces.
They are shaped like axes,
and as smooth as green jade.
Names of Waters
The Yellow River (Huánghé) has different names for its waters in each month:
The first month is called "Ice Breaking Water" (Língjiěshuǐ).
The second and third months are called "Peach Blossom Water" (Táohuāshuǐ).
The fourth month is called "Wheat Yellow Water" (Màihuángshuǐ).
The fifth month is called "Melon Vine Water" (Guāmànshuǐ),
as melons are just vining.
The sixth month is called "Plank Mountain Water" (Bǎnshānshuǐ).
The seventh and eighth months are called "Reed Sprout Water" (Dímáoshuǐ),
as reed flowers are just opening.
The ninth month is called "Ascending High Water" (Dēnggāoshuǐ).
The tenth month is called "Returning Trough Water" (Fùcáoshuǐ),
as it flows back into its old channel.
The eleventh and twelfth months are called "Crushed Ice Water" (Cùlíngshuǐ),
as ice breaks and refreezes,
piling up in layers.
Discussing Ancient and Modern Painting
Ancient paintings
are simple in execution and subtle in meaning;
works by Gù and Lù are examples of this.
Medieval paintings
are meticulous and refined;
works by Zhǎn and Zhèng are examples of this.
Recent paintings
are brilliant and seek completeness.
Contemporary paintings
are chaotic and lack purpose.
Difficulty in Painting
Gù Kǎizhī said:
“Painting people is the most difficult,
followed by landscapes,
then dogs and horses.
As for pavilions and towers,
they are fixed objects.”
Cháo Zǐ said:
“Dogs and horses are difficult,
ghosts and spirits are easy.
Dogs and horses are seen by ordinary people,
while ghosts and spirits are strange and grotesque forms.”
Landscapes, Trees, and Rocks
Wú Dàoxuán often painted walls in Buddhist temples,
always with strange rocks and collapsing torrents.
The transformation of landscape painting began with Dàoxuán,
and was perfected by the two Lǐs.
General Lǐ (Lǐ Jiāngjūn)
was the son of Sīxùn,
and Zhāodào was his mid-secretariat official (zhōngshè).
The depiction of trees and rocks
was exquisite with Wéi Yǎn,
and reached its peak with Zhāng Tōng.
Also, there is the profound depth of Wáng Yòuchéng,
the extraordinary richness of Minister Yáng (Yáng Púshè),
the intricate skill of Wáng Zǎi,
and the symbolism of Liú Shāng.
Painting Ailments
Wú Dàozǐ painted Zhòngyóu,
wearing a wooden sword.
Yán Lìnggōng painted Zhāojūn,
wearing a veiled hat.
Little did they know that the wooden sword originated in the Jìn dynasty,
and the veiled hat flourished in the current dynasty.
Citing this common example,
it is also a flaw in painting.
For instance, the fú jīn (headcloth) was transmitted in the Hàn and Wèi dynasties;
the mùlí (veil) arose from the Qí and Suí dynasties;
the pútóu (headscarf) was used in the Zhōu dynasty;
the jīnzi (cap) was created in the Wǔdé era.
How can Hú clothing and boots be arbitrarily applied to ancient portraits?
And robes, caps, sashes, and ribbons should not be commonly used for contemporary people.
Straw sandals are not suitable for the northern frontier,
and ox-carts are not found in the Lingnán region.
One must distinguish clearly between ancient and modern objects,
and inquire into what is suitable for local customs and climate.
By referring to specific things and depicting their forms,
one can verify the era.
If one grew up in the Southern Dynasties
and has not seen people from the Northern Dynasties;
or is accustomed to the northern frontier
and does not recognize the mountains and rivers of Jiāngnán—
hence Lǐ Sìzhēn criticized Dǒng and Zhǎn, whose locales were plains,
lacking the aid of rivers and mountains;
whose lives involved military affairs,
lacking the decorum of officials.
Just as Zhèng Xuán did not distinguish between zhā and lí pears,
Cài Mó did not recognize crabs,
Emperor Wèi ultimately cut 《Diǎnlùn》,
and the recluse was ignorant of the names of northern medicines.
What I do not know,
I leave blank.
Only by thoroughly understanding the traces of both North and South,
and discerning clearly the names of ancient and modern things,
can one then discuss painting.
Huángchū, because he had no fire-retardant cloth,
published 《Diǎnlùn》 and engraved it in the university.
Later, foreign countries offered fire-retardant cloth,
and so he cut and discarded 《Diǎnlùn》.
Táo Yǐnjū's 《Běncǎo》
often did not comprehend the names of northern medicines.
Tracing Paintings
