Those who are fond of such things should always prepare a hundred sheets of Xuān paper,
waxing them according to the method,
to be ready for tracing.
In ancient times, tracing paintings was common,
achieving seven or eight out of ten
without losing the spirit, expression, or brushwork.
There were also imperial tracings,
called "official tracings."
Kǎizhī had a marvelous method for tracing.
Painting Vimalakīrti's Admonition
Having observed all paintings,
only Gù Shēng's paintings of ancient sages captured their profound principle,
and he also first created the image of Vimalakīrti,
with a slender and sickly countenance,
leaning on a table, speechless.
Lù and Zhāng imitated him,
but ultimately could not surpass him.
The Canonical Nine Classics and Three Histories
For any family that collects,
it must have famous scrolls by Gù, Lù, Zhāng, and Wú
before it can claim to possess paintings.
If one claims to have books,
how can one not have the Nine Classics and Three Histories?
Gù, Lù, Zhāng, and Wú are the Nine Classics;
Yáng, Zhèng, Dǒng, and Zhǎn are the Three Histories;
other paintings are the Hundred Schools.
Hánjù
Those who are not aficionados should not carelessly pass around calligraphy and paintings.
Do not view calligraphy and paintings near fire.
When facing wind,
or spitting directly,
or without washing hands, one must not view calligraphy and paintings.
In the past, Huán Xuán greatly cherished books and paintings.
Whenever he showed them to guests,
there was a non-aficionado who was eating hánjù.
Hánjù
are today's huánbǐng (ring-shaped cakes),
deep-fried items.
He touched the painting with his hand,
greatly staining it.
Huán Xuán sighed with regret for a long time.
Thereafter, whenever he brought out calligraphy,
he would order people to wash their hands.
Cloud-River and North Wind Paintings
Liú Bāo,
a man of the Hàn Huán Dì era,
painted a cloud picture;
people who saw it felt hot.
He also painted a wind picture;
people who saw it felt cold.
Bā Shòu Tán
In the mountains of Pǔchéng County, Jiànzhōu, there is a beast called "Xiàn,"
with the body of a pig and the head of a human,
ugly in appearance.
It likes to come out on rocks by the water's edge.
Zhāng Píngzǐ went to paint it,
but the beast entered the deep pool and did not come out.
Someone said it feared the painting,
which is why it would not come out;
so the paper and brush were removed.
The beast indeed came out.
Zhāng Píngzǐ clasped his hands and did not move,
secretly drawing with his foot.
This place is now called Bā Shòu Tán.
According to 《Èr Qí Jì》, it says:
"Qín Shǐhuáng saw a sea god and
ordered his attendants to draw it with their feet."
《Fēngsú Tōng》 says:
"Gōngshū saw the shape of a snail on the water,
and also drew it with his foot."
Wáng Méng's Painting
Wáng Méng's painting was exquisite.
He himself said:
"I love wine, enjoy meat, and am skilled in painting.
But if people have fine wine, delicious food, excellent silk, and good brushes,
all these please my heart.
Why should I leave?"
Painting Dragons Without Dotting the Eyes
Zhāng Sēngyáo painted four dragons in Ānlè Temple in Jīnlíng,
but did not dot their eyes.
He always said:
"If I dot them, they will fly away."
People thought he was exaggerating,
so they asked him to dot them.
In a moment,
thunder broke the wall,
and two dragons ascended to heaven on clouds.
The two dragons whose eyes were not dotted are still there.
The Two Paintings of Dǒng and Zhǎn
Dǒng Bórén and Zhǎn Zǐqí were both people of the Suí dynasty.
Lǐ Sìzhēn said:
"Dǒng has Zhǎn's carriages and horses,
but Zhǎn does not have Dǒng's terraces and pavilions."
Hán Gàn's Teacher, the Imperial Stable Horses
Hán Gàn was residing quietly, having nothing to do,
when suddenly someone came to his door claiming to be a ghost envoy,
asking for a horse.
Gàn painted a horse and burned it.
Another day,
he saw the ghost envoy riding the horse to thank him.
The Emperor once asked Hán what he took as a model for painting horses,
to which he replied:
"The horses in the imperial stables are all my teachers."
Greatly Vulgar in Spirit
Dài Āndào painted Buddhas.
Yǔ Dào'ān said:
"The spiritual expression is greatly vulgar.
This is probably because your worldly desires are not yet exhausted."
Zhuāngyán Temple
The monk Lú Léngqí,
a disciple of Wú Dàoxuán.
Once painted the three gates of Zhuāngyán Temple.
Wú Dàoxuán said:
"This child's brushwork is usually not as good as mine,
but now it resembles mine.
His vital energy is all poured into this."
Not long after, he indeed died.
Zhāng Zǎo's Pines and Rocks
Someone collected Zhāng Zǎo's painting of a screen with pines and rocks.
When he later sought to buy it,
his wife had already laundered it into clothes.
He only obtained a double-width piece of pines and rocks.
The world considered it a famous work.
Tuózǐtóu
The three Tuózǐs of the Táng dynasty
were skilled in landscape painting.
The world called it "Tuózǐ's head,
Dàozǐ's feet."
Yuèbēi
The two music academies, left and right.
The right was mostly good at singing,
the left mostly skilled in dancing.
Outside the academy was a pond,
colloquially called Yuèbēi (Moon Pond),
because its shape was like a reclining moon.
Lost and Fallen
The emperor favored the left section,
hence the saying, "Below the building, the right section plays;
poles and wood are often lost and fallen."
This is its hidden meaning.
The people in front
Prostitutes entering the Yíchūn Yuàn
were called "Nèirén,"
also "Qiántóu Rén,"
always being at the forefront.
Their families were allowed into the Jiàofāng
and were called "Rénjiā,"
receiving rice rations seasonally.
Those who received imperial favor were called "Shíjiā,"
were given residences,
and their rewards were of a different class.
Initially, there were ten families who received imperial favor,
and subsequent entrants received rewards equivalent to the Shíjiā.
Though there were dozens of families, they were still called Shíjiā.
On the second and sixteenth days of each month,
the Nèirén were allowed to meet their mothers;
if without a mother, then one sister could meet them.
When the Yúnsháo
performances exited below the tower,
if there were few people in the Yíchūn Yuàn,
then people from Yúnsháo would be added.
Yúnsháo
were lowly palace women.
Not only was it easy to distinguish between beautiful and ugly,
but Nèirén wore fish pendants,
while palace women did not.
Chōután Jiā:
Ordinary women selected for their beauty to enter the palace
and taught to play the pípa, wǔxián, kōnghóu, and zhēng
were called Chōután Jiā.
In the eleventh year of Kāiyuán,
the Shèngshòu Yuè was first composed.
The emperor ordered the women to wear five-colored clothes and sing and dance.
Those from the Yíchūn Yuàn could perform after just one day of practice.
The Chōután Jiā could not succeed even after a full day.
The emperor personally encouraged them, saying:
"Excellent, excellent,
do not disgrace Sānláng."
Ending a dance to the finish was called "Héshā,"
it was particularly important for it to be swift and vigorous,
which is why further skill was required.
Ruǎnwǔ and Jiànwǔ:
Pieces like "Huíbō Yuè," "Chūnyīng Zhuàn," and "Wūyè Tí"
were called Ruǎnwǔ (soft dances).
Pieces like "Zhèzhī," "Dà Wèizhōu," and "Dámózhī"
were called Jiànwǔ (vigorous dances).
Drumming:
Lǚ Yuánzhēn played the drum
with a bowl of water placed on his head.
At the end of the piece, the water did not spill.
Everyone praised his ability to keep his head steady.
When the emperor, while still a prince, summoned him,
Yuánzhēn, relying on his skill, often did not arrive on time,
and would say, "I need a yellow paper."
Yellow paper referred to an imperial edict.
The emperor governed through it.
Therefore, all his peers received titles and appointments,
only Yuánzhēn remained common.
Polo and Falling from Horse:
The emperor once played polo in the Sān Diàn.
Polo caused King Róng to fall from his horse and faint,
not recovering for some time.
Huáng Fānchuò then reported:
"Your Majesty, your age is no longer young,
and your sacred body is heavy;
it is not fitting for you to exert yourself.
Why not have your sons-in-law and others do it for you?
Like me, sitting opposite the food tray,
my mouth and eyes are both satisfied;
this is enjoyment.
Watching Your Majesty rushing and toiling,
how can there be time for enjoyment?"
The emperor said:
"Your words are very reasonable."
He never played it himself again.
Yágōng, Xiǎndǒu, Chángrù:
Sanlè performers called heaven "Yágōng,"
joy "Xiǎndǒu,"
and being constantly by the emperor's side "Chángrù."
Acrobatics:
The emperor set up a tent-palace south of Tiānjīn Qiáo,
and held a three-day feast.
A small boy from the Jiàofāng performed acrobatics peerlessly.
He was dressed in colorful silks,
bathed and groomed,
and mingled among the palace actresses.
He stood on a long pole,
upside down,
then released his hands,
and after a long time, lowered his hands to embrace the pole,
flipping down.
The musicians and others all abandoned their instruments,
rolling on the ground,
shouting "Wànsuì!"
All officials bowed in celebration.
An imperial envoy proclaimed:
"This skill is particularly difficult,
recently mastered by the Jiàofāng."
In reality, it was just a small boy.
Shēngjì'ér:
Within the district, the Grand Music Bureau musicians were called Shēngjì'ér.
Four Daughters Good at Singing:
Rèn Zhìfāng had four daughters good at singing.
Among them, the two older ones' vocal delivery was mournful and plaintive,
while their breathing was controlled and harmonious.
The two older ones' demeanor was serene and gentle,
their focus not on the singing.
The four children's voices were strong and mellow,
as if coming from a place of calm.
Seller of Fake Gold:
Páng Sānniáng was good at singing and dancing.
Her dancing was somewhat heavy-footed,
but she was especially skilled at dressing up.
She was also old,
with many wrinkles on her face.
She would cover them with light gauze,
mixing mica with powder and honey to apply,
thus appearing youthful.
Once, during a great feast in Biànzhōu,
an envoy was sent to hire her by name.
He arrived at her door.
Upon seeing her,
he called her "wicked old woman"
and asked where Páng Sānniángzi was.
Páng deceived him, saying:
"Páng Sān is my niece,
she's temporarily not here.
Come tomorrow,
I will leave a message for her."
The envoy returned as told the next day.
Páng then prepared a grand meal.
The guest did not recognize her.
He then said:
"Yesterday I already met the young lady's aunt."
Such was her transformation.
Therefore, people in the district called her "Seller of Fake Gold."
Lady's Eye Ruined:
There was also Yán Dàniáng, who was good at singing and dancing.
Her eyes were heavy and her cheeks deep,
different from others.
She could manage them
to appear like undulating waves,
even her family members did not notice.
Once, when her child died, she wept bitterly and wiped away tears.
Her maid saw her face
and exclaimed, "The lady's eye is ruined!"
Left Turn:
Wèi Èr's appearance was roughly beautiful,
but her singing and dancing were very clumsy.
Once, when she was gathered with others of her kind for a feast and got up to dance,
a person named Yáng Jiāshēng laughed as he watched her.
Soon after, it was time for a song.
A parrot on a perch first shifted its foot and turned right,
then immediately turned left again.
Jiāshēng looked and said:
"A left turn!"
He meant the parrot,
and truly had no other intention.
Wèi thought he was referring to her,
stopped singing and cursed vehemently.
After the entertainment,
people called a performance error "Left Turn."
Sū Wǔnú:
His wife was good at singing and dancing,
and also beautiful.
She was skilled at performing "Tà Yáoniáng."
When someone invited her,
Wǔnú would always follow her.
People, wanting him to get drunk quickly,
often urged him to drink.
Wǔnú said:
"Just give me more money;
even if I eat dumplings, I'll get drunk,
no need for wine."
Now, those who sell their wives are called "Wǔnú,"
starting from Sū.
Tà Yáoniáng:
In Northern Qí, there was a man surnamed Sū,
with a large nose.
He did not serve in office,
but self-proclaimed himself as a Lángzhōng.
Whenever he got drunk, he would beat his wife.
His wife, holding back her sorrow, complained to the neighbors.
People at the time would tease him
by having a man wear women's clothing,
slowly enter the stage and sing.
With each repetition of the chorus,
the bystanders would all chime in, saying:
“Tà Yáoniáng,
why such bitterness?”
Because he walked and sang at the same time,
it was called Tà Yáoniáng.
Because she cried out her grievances,
they spoke of bitterness.
When her husband arrived,
they would mimic the scene of a fight for amusement.
Nowadays, women perform this.
Pénchéng.
Qīngpénshān has a shape like a water basin,
hence the city is called Pénchéng,
and the inlet is called Pénpǔ.
Kuāng Yù Xiānshēng.
Kuāng Yù's
surname was Kuāng and his given name was Yù.
During the transition between the Shāng and Zhōu dynasties, he withdrew from society and lived in seclusion,
making his hut on this mountain.
Bìxū Shàngjiān.
Dǒng Fèng would often treat people's illnesses.
Once cured, he would instruct them to plant five apricot trees,
which eventually formed a forest.
Fèng later ascended to heaven,
becoming the Bìxū Shàngjiān.
Jǐnglàng.
The well opened by Guàn Yīng was extremely deep.
The local people called it Làngfēi.
When there were waves in the Pénjiāng River,
the well water would often move.
Jiǔtiān Cǎifǎng.
Emperor Míng had a dream of an immortal,
who called himself Jiǔtiān Cǎifǎng,
patrolling and investigating the human world.
He wished to build a palace on Lúshān Mountain,
and the timber needed no seeking, as it was sufficient.
Yǒngquán.
Yǔan Shī wished to build a temple,
but there was no water.
He struck the ground with his staff,
and a spring immediately gushed forth.
Later, during a drought,
he prayed and a dragon emerged.
Shényùn Diàn.
Yǔan Gōng dreamed that a spirit told him:
“This pond is serene and quiet,
sufficient for a divine dwelling.”
Suddenly, in the middle of the night, there was thunder and rain.
The next morning, white sand covered the ground,
and fine trees stood luxuriantly.
Hence, the hall was named "Shényùn".
Sānxiào Tú.
Yǔan Gōng and the eighteen worthies cultivated Pure Land Buddhism together in the Báilían Shè.
When seeing guests off, they would cross the stream,
and tigers would gather and roar.
While discussing the Way with Táo Yuánliàng and Lù Xiūjìng,
they unconsciously crossed Hǔxī Stream
and all burst into laughter.
Thus, the Sānxiào Tú was painted.
Pìshé Xíngzhě.
When Yǔan Gōng first arrived,
the mountain had many snakes and insects.
A traveler was skilled at driving away snakes,
and the snakes would draw lines for him.
Hence, he was called Pìshé Xíngzhě.
He was actually a mountain god.
Yóushān Hǔ.
There was a tiger on the mountain
that never harmed anyone.
Its tracks were occasionally seen,
and it was called Yóushān Hǔ.
Cōngmíng Quán.
Yīn Zhòngkān discussed the Yìlín with Yǔan Gōng by the side of the spring and admired his eloquence.
Yǔan Gōng said:
“You are like this gushing spring.”
Hence, it was named Cōngmíng Quán.
Lìlǐ.
Yuānmíng's residence was in Lìlǐ.
Between two mountains, there was a large rock
that could seat a thousand people.
Luánxī.
Guīzōng Sì Temple has the posture of a soaring luán bird spreading its wings,
hence its stream was named Luánxī.
Shísān Rén Xuédào.
During the chaos of Qín,
thirteen people abandoned their official posts to study the Way.
Passing through this mountain,
three of the martial artists among them wished to reside there.
Ten people said:
“Our initial aspiration was to return to Qúnyù Dòngfǔ,
how can we stop midway?”
One night, there was thunder and rain,
and they transformed into two streams.
In the middle was a large rock,
on which were jade slips with celestial characters that read:
“Divine transformation into Lóngxī,
golden slips mark the title.
True Immortals guide and instruct,
hidden dwelling in the jade grotto.”
Tíngxiá Bǎoniǎn.
Lù Xiūjìng was buying medicine in the capital.
Emperor Wén built the Tíngxiá Bǎoniǎn
and sent Xú Xuānzhǐ to persuade him to stay,
but he could not be persuaded.
Later, the emperor had the affair of Dàhé.
Emperor Míng strongly invited him,
building the Chóngxū Guǎn and Tōngxiān Táng,
and had him expound the Way.
Shāndài.
Xiānglú Fēng Peak stands alone and precipitous,
its qi swirling like incense smoke.
When it is about to rain,
white clouds crown the peak,
hence it is called Shāndài.
Quáncháo.
Below Jīlóngshān Mountain, there is a gully stream
where a spring gushes like a tide,
never ceasing for a moment.
Húshén Gōngtíng.
The Húshén god could split winds and divide currents.
Nǚ'érguān Cí.
Zhāng Gōngzhí, the Grand Administrator of Wújùn, passed by the Nǚ'érguān Cí.
He liked to point at the statues of the maiden-play-consorts.
That night, he dreamed of receiving betrothal gifts.
Frightened, he immediately set off.
Mid-stream, his boat would not move.
His family exclaimed in surprise:
“Could it be that loving one daughter will cause the whole family to suffer misfortune?”
Gōngzhí could not bear it,
and his wife substituted his elder brother's daughter for her.
Gōngzhí angrily said:
“How can I face the world?”
He then threw his own daughter into the water again.
As they were about to cross,
they saw two girls remotely on the bank.
An official said:
“I am the Registrar of the Lord of Lúshān Mountain.
Respecting your righteousness,
I return both daughters to you.”
They were all unharmed.
Lù Rú Fǔcǎo.
Héngyáng Wáng Yìjì asked Zōng Bǐng:
“I wish to prevail upon you, Master, with great emoluments.”
He replied:
“Emoluments are like rotten grass,
how long do they flourish or decay?”
Jīnmén Yǔkè.
During the Bàotài reign,
the Daoist Tán Zǐxiāo was bestowed the title "Jīnmén Yǔkè".
Wǔyí Jūn.
Wǔyí Shān has a divine being,
named Wǔyí Jūn.
One day,
he spoke to people, saying:
"You all shall gather on the mountain peak on the tenth day of the eighth month."
On that day, the villagers all assembled.
They saw splendid banners, houses, and utensils grandly set up.
They heard human voices in the air,
but could not see their forms.
Men and women were ordered to sit separately to eat and drink.
After a short while, music began.
It was announced:
"Zhāng Ānlíng is striking the leading drum,"
which was in the shape of today's zhànggǔ;
"Zhào Yuánhú is tapping the副鼓 fùgǔ;
Liú Xiǎojīn is beating the kǎndágǔ;
Lǔ Shàozhòng is shaking the táogǔ;
Qiáo Zhīmǎn is rattling the cáogǔ;
Gāo Zǐchūn is holding the duǎngǔ."
"The pipe master, Bào Gōng, is playing the héngdí;
Hé Fèng'ér is tapping the jiébǎn."
"The string master, Dǒng Jiāoniáng, is plucking the kǎnhòu,"
which is a kōnghóu;
"Xiè Yīngfēi is strumming the chánglí,"
which is a large zhēng;
"Lǚ Héxiāng is scraping the yuánfù,"
which is a pípa;
"The pipe master, Huáng Kǎngū, is wailing sadly and tremblingly,"
which is a bìlì;
"Hán Jì is blowing the dòngxiāo;
Mǐ Xiǎo'é is resonating the jūcháo,"
which is a large shēng;
"The metal master, Luó Miàoróng, is clanging the liáodiào,"
which is bronze cymbals;
"Hǎo Yòuxiān is striking the yèxuàn,"
which is a flat-bottomed sīluó."
They only saw the musical instruments, but not the people.
Wine was served, then food was commanded.
Some said,
"yīnrúan,"
which is water moss;
some said "xiāngruí,"
which is water chestnut;
some said "shíyí,"
which is a small crab;
some said "shājiāngzhǎ,"
which is shrimp;
some said "hézhīfǔ,"
which is dried fish.
All tasted sweet and delicious,
only the wine tasted somewhat thin.
After the immortals had departed,
everyone joyfully exclaimed:
"We ordinary mortals
have gathered with the divine lord in the幔亭 màntíng!"
Thus, they named that place Tóngháo.
Bǎihuā Pǔ
The Táng Chancellor Jiǎ Dān authored the 《Bǎihuā Pǔ》,
and considered the haitang as a divine immortal among flowers.
Huāmù Hǎiwàilái
Lǐ Zànhuáng said:
"Flowers and trees named 'sea'
all come from overseas."
Chén Mínghuànhǎi
《Xiānzhuàn Shíyí》 says:
A Daoist told Yán Zhēnqīng, saying:
"You, Zǐjué, can transcend the world,
and should not sink into the sea of fame and officialdom."
Mìng Xiàng Jué Shì Zhòngshì
On the twenty-seventh day of the sixth month of the seventh year of Dàhé,
Wénzōng wanted to appoint Déyù as Píngzhāngshì.
He had already issued the edict on hemp paper,
saying:
"Appointing a chancellor is an extremely important matter.
I just checked the calendar,
and the day's auspiciousness is not good.
The edict shall be announced on the twenty-eighth."
Lǐ Déyǔ
The capital had suffered a long drought.
When Déyù was appointed chancellor,
there was a heavy rain that very day.
The Púmìshǐ said:
"Inside the palace, they are delighted by this rain,
and call the chancellor by a name with one character changed,
calling him Lǐ Déyǔ."
Xíng Zhōngshū
Wénzōng detested factions,
and pointed to Yáng Yúqīng as the leader.
He was actually introduced by Chancellor Lǐ Zōngmǐn.
The Emperor now ordered him to take charge of Chángzhōu.
Zōngmǐn, seeing the Emperor's anger,
immediately complied, saying:
"Outsiders call Yúqīng's residence, the South Pavilion, the Xíng Zhōngshū (Acting Central Secretariat),
where daily meetings are held.
That is why I did not give him a good official post."
Déyù said:
"Are Gěishìzhōng
and Zhōngshū Shèrén not good official posts?
What other official posts are good then?"
Zōngmǐn paled.
Bà Gěishílì Wénjié
The two departments previously issued official documents to wealthy people from Jiānghuái,
who traveled throughout the realm,
calling themselves tángchú (hall kitchens),
and people profiting from this privilege monopolized trade,
with profits flowing into wealthy households.
I judged, saying:
"Ten thousand coins are already abundant;
one should always live simply.
The common people are still poor;
how can it be proper to compete for profit?
This differs from the principle of 'uprooting mallows'
and moreover harms the reputation of 'eating coarse grain.'
To lead others,
it is right to rectify the root.
The issuing of documents for profiting from official meals should all be abolished."
Bù Suǒ Guìfāng
A few days after Déyù became chancellor,
the high-ranking official Yán Cóngyuē was given plums by a god,
who said:
"No need to lock the safe-houses."
I asked why,
and he said:
"Since the Chancellor entered office,
the prices of maidservants and fine horses in the capital have become immeasurable,
and the two markets do not lock their safes."
Pàn Tíng Wèisòng
When Déyù first became chancellor,
the officials of the two streets requested, according to precedent,
that soldiers escort him every morning during court attendance.
I judged, saying:
"In a position where all eyes are upon him,
there is already the nation's dignified appearance.
In times of peace,
why bother with military preparations?
The escort should be stopped."
Xuānzōng Dé Rénjūn Fǎ
The Emperor governed the realm
according to the methods of a true monarch.
Whenever a chancellor reported to him at Yányīng Hall,
there was not a single person standing around him.
As soon as he gave instructions,
his imperial majesty was awe-inspiring and unapproachable.
After three or four kè (approximately 45-60 minutes) of reporting,
the dragon's face suddenly became joyful,
saying:
"Now we can chat casually."
He would inquire about trivial matters in the villages
and speak of palace entertainments,
covering all subjects.
After about one kè,
his imperial majesty would become stern and solemn again,
indicating he was about to return to the palace.
There would certainly be words of warning and admonition:
"Every day I worry greatly that you all will violate the laws and regulations,
and we will not be able to meet."
Such were the laws and regulations.
Línghú Táo said:
"For ten years, I held political power.
Whenever I reported at Yányīng Hall,
even in the depths of severe winter,
sweat would flow down my back."
Jīnliánhuā Jù
The Emperor was about to appoint Línghú Táo as chancellor.
In the middle of the night, he summoned him for an audience at Hánchūntíng,
and bestowed a golden lotus torch to escort him back to the Xuéshìyuàn.
Those in the academy were startled, saying:
"His Majesty is coming!"
Jiāng Rénchén Bǐ Wǒ Dé Fǒu
During his leisure from governing, the Emperor enjoyed writing poetry,
and ordered the academicians to compose matching verses.
Xiāo Zhì wrote a memorial of thanks, saying:
"This poem's line, 'The Guì River a thousand li a day,'
cannot be surpassed."
Wéi Ào reported, saying:
"It is like the poetry of Shěn Yuē, who was the tutor to the Sòng Crown Prince.
Xiāo Zhì merely uses his clear imperial talent to compare himself to Shěn Yuē."
The Emperor was displeased,
saying:
"Can a minister be compared to me?"
He was dismissed to become the Governor of Zhèjiāng.
Sānchǐ Jiēqián Biàn Shì Wànlǐ
Yánlíng was appointed Jìanzhōu Cìshǐ.
The Emperor asked how far Jìanzhōu was from the capital.
He replied:
"Eight thousand *lǐ*."
The Emperor said:
"Many people from Jìan are among my attendants.
The prefecture is not bad at all.
If you are honest and serve the public,
comfort the distressed,
it will be no different than staying by my side.
But if you bend the law,
and the distant people have no one to rely on,
then three feet before the steps
will feel like ten thousand *lǐ*."
Yánlíng was startled and trembled.
The Emperor patted him and sent him off.
Míng Cónghuì's Thin Ears
The monk Cónghuì's conduct was lofty and pure,
and he was also skilled in literature, composing pieces to imperial command.
The Emperor often chose difficult rhymes for him to compose poems.
Cónghuì had served for many years,
hoping for a purple robe.
The Emperor said:
"I do not begrudge a purple *jiāshā*,
but the master's ears are a bit thin,
I fear they cannot bear it."
Mistakenly Written Memorials
A memorial from the Dùzhī stated that some bolts of cloth had been 'stained and defiled' (*zìwū* 漬污),
but it mistakenly wrote 'slippery and defiled' (*huáwū* 滑污).
The Emperor was surprised upon seeing it.
The Shūmì Chéngzhǐ, Sūn Yǐnzhōng, thinking the Emperor had not yet noticed,
added the character *zì* (漬) to complete it.
When it was resubmitted by the Zhōngshū,
the Emperor was furious.
He investigated those who added or altered memorials,
and they were punished according to the severity of their offense.
Lǐu Gōngquán Mistakenly Said the Imperial Title
On the first day of the first month of Dàzhōng 11th year,
the Emperor held court in the Hányuán Diàn.
The Tàizǐ Shàoshī, Lú Jūn, was eighty years old.
His voice and demeanor were calm and slow,
and the entire court respected him.
By the New Year's Day of the 12th year, when congratulations were received,
the Tàizǐ Shàoshī, Lǐu Gōngquán, was also eighty years old,
and again led the hundred officials.
The palace hall was vast,
and his strength was already exhausted.
After offering congratulations,
when the imperial title "Shèngjìng Wénsī Héwǔ Guāngxiào Huángdì" was proclaimed,
Gōngquán mistakenly said "Guāngwǔ Héxiào."
The Yùshǐ impeached him,
and he was fined a quarter's salary.
Retiring at seventy
was an old custom.
Gōngquán did not adhere to the etiquette,
and was humiliated in his old age.
Wēn Tíngyún's Degradation Edict
"Edict to Wēn Tíngyún, a tribute scholar from the countryside:
Early he followed the tax officials,
and long bore a great name.
He merely possessed unbridled talent,
rarely putting it to timely use.
Like banishing the poet to the Xiāng Pǔ,
or moving Jiǎ Yì to Chángshā.
There is still hope for a seat before the Emperor,
and no loss of thought for drawing the brush.
He may be appointed Wèi of Suíxiàn, Suízhōu."
This was the composition of Shèrén Péi Tǎn.
Tíngyún's poetry and *fù* were unsurpassed at the time,
but he repeatedly failed the *jìnshì* examinations.
At this point, he was demoted to a ninth-rank official.
The *jìnshì* Jì Tángfū presented a poem saying:
"Though receiving the phoenix edict by imperial command,
the parrot's high talent yet harms its person."
The Emperor
was a wise ruler,
yet Tíngyún was instead ruined by his talent.
The edict's reference to the poet and Chángshā was criticized by commentators.
Construction of the Jīngyǐn's Residence
According to custom:
The Jīngzhào resided in his private mansion.
On odd-numbered days, he entered the prefectural office;
on even-numbered days, he entered the Déiyuàn.
When Cuī Yǐng was the Yǐn,
prisoners escaped from prison.
The Emperor then ordered the construction of a residence for the Jīngyǐn.
Advising Against a Visit to Huáqīng Gōng
The Emperor was about to visit Huáqīng Gōng.
Both provinces (Zhōngshū Shěng and Ménxià Shěng) strongly advised against it.
The Emperor said to the prime ministers:
"Huáqīng
is an old palace of the ancestors.
The sacred portraits of the Sage Ancestors
are in the Cháoróng Gé,
which I have never seen or bowed to.
Now the arrangements do not trouble the prefectures and counties.
You should instruct the remonstrance officials not to deliberate on this further."
The prime ministers summoned both provinces to convey the imperial message.
Soon, remonstrance memorials were submitted again.
The Emperor said:
"The remonstrance officials say that since Mùzōng's tour,
none of the successive emperors have left the palace.
Living in peace, they worried about danger,
begging me to reconsider.
When I heard these words,
I decided against the visit to Huáqīng.
You should summon the officials from both provinces
and explain my intention."
Bì Tàiyuán Presents a Beautiful Woman
Bì Chéng was originally a merchant's son.
The Emperor intended to appoint him as prime minister,
but Lìnghú Táo was jealous of him,
and had him transferred to three different frontier garrisons.
Bì Chéng thought of a way to curry favor with Táo
and sent him a beautiful woman.
Táo's heart was stirred, but he said:
"A rare beauty will surely harm people.
Bì Tàiyuán has no personal connection with me,
and offers this as bait,
intending to ruin my family."
He did not accept her.
Bì Chéng then sold her to the imperial physician Xuán Bó,
who was close to the Emperor,
and Xuán Bó presented her to the Emperor for 700,000 *qián*.
The Emperor was greatly enamored by her,
and her favor surpassed that of all the other women in the six palaces.
Xuán Bó prepared and offered cinnabar treated with 'fire' (伏火丹砂),
which caused the Emperor to develop sores.
When Yìzōng ascended the throne,
Xuán Bó, along with the hermit Wáng Yuè and the Daoist Yú Zǐzhī, were all executed in the marketplace.
Record of Imperial Examinations
The Emperor particularly valued scholarly achievements.
When Zhèng Hào was in charge of the imperial examinations,
the Emperor requested a record of the examination subjects.
Zhèng Hào compiled thirteen volumes,
covering the period from Wǔdé to Dàzhōng.
He also requested that from now on, after the results were published,
the names of the successful candidates,
and the titles of their poems and *fù* be recorded and submitted.
He ordered the relevant authorities to continue the compilation.
Summoned to the Palace Examination for Writings
Zhāozōng summoned Wò to the palace
to be tested on five essays:
《Wàn Bāng Xiánníng Fù》, 《Yǔ Bài Chāngyán Shī》, 《Wǔ Chén Shòu Dōngchuān Jiédù Zhì》, 《Dá Fóshì Guówáng Jìngòng Shū》, and 《Pī Sān Gōngchén Ràng Túxíng Biǎo》.
His memorial stated:
"Your servant's talent does not surpass the masses,
nor is his character extraordinary.
His waiting for the right price is unlike that of a jade in a box,
and his profound study is ashamed before one who reads by the light of a firefly.
He has encountered a clear era,
and been nourished by sagely benevolence.
Wearing a tall cap and jingling pendants,
he has already received his place at the elephant-carved gate;
sharpening his brush and mixing lead,
he has further been honored with a summons to the Golden Gate.
Though praised for his composition,
his weaving is not skilled;
gazing at himself and examining his limitations,
he takes honor as a source of fear."
Refusing to Draft an Edict
During the siege of Fèngxiáng, Cuī Yífàn
used Lǐ Màozhēn to force his reappointment as prime minister.
Wò was supposed to draft the edict,
but he submitted a strongly worded memorial arguing against it.
At midnight, he handed it to the Hànlín Yuànshǐ,
who was an inner palace attendant.
He said to Wò:
"Scholar, do not play with your life."
Wò did not reply,
but locked his door and went to sleep.
The next day,
no imperial edict was announced.
Lǐ Màozhēn said:
"Your Majesty appointed a prime minister,
but the scholar refused to draft the edict.
How is this different from rebellion?"
Zhāozōng said:
"You recommended Yífàn,
and I dared not refuse;
Wò refused to draft the edict,
and I also dare not refuse.
What can be done when the reasoning is so clear?"
Lǐ Màozhēn's Disrespect
Zhāozōng hosted a banquet for his court officials,
and had fish caught from the pond to be served.
Mào Zhēn said,
"These fish were originally raised
to await the Imperial carriage."
He then offered the Emperor wine in a large cup,
but the Emperor did not wish to drink.
Mào Zhēn raised the cup and tapped it against the Emperor's chin.
Everyone at the table was outraged by his impudence.
Hastily making peace with Liáng.
The magistrate of Biàn set up over ten palisades to besiege Qíchéng,
and dug tunnels to attack the city.
The city was in great distress,
with people burning human excrement to boil and eat human flesh.
Mào Zhēn was unwilling to make peace with Liáng.
The Emperor instructed, saying,
"Quán Zhōng's troops have not yet withdrawn,
and the city is in dire straits. Among the sixteen households of princes,
reports come daily of two or three people dying,
all due to freezing and starvation.
Inside, princesses, concubines, and others eat porridge one day,
and unbaked cakes the next;
now even these are exhausted.
I wish you would quickly make peace with Liáng."
Bǎiyè Shānrén
Tián Luán entered Huàshān,
and saw a yellow-robed Daoist master who pointed at cypress leaves and said,
"This is the elixir of immortality."
He taught him the method of consuming it,
and later he attained the Dao,
ascending to Shàngqīng to become an immortal,
and was called "Bǎiyè Shānrén."
Sōnghuā Jiǔ
An old man visited Cuī Xīzhēn in the snow.
Xīzhēn offered him Sōnghuā Jiǔ (pine flower wine).
The old man said,
"The flowers are astringent and tasteless."
He threw a pill into the wine,
and the wine immediately tasted delicious.
Dān Zào Bái Tù
Wáng Qīng guarded the alchemy furnace for the Heavenly Master.
He secretly broke the seal and peeked inside.
A white rabbit leaped out.
Everyone said,
"The elixir is gone!"
A Daoist transformed into a crane and flew away.
After a short while, he captured the rabbit and returned,
throwing it back into the furnace.
Qiānlìn Wèi Chú
Hé Zhīzhāng visited the medicine-selling elder Wáng Lǎo,
and asked about the art of transmuting base metals into gold.
He presented a large pearl as a gift.
When the old man saw the pearl,
he immediately instructed him to exchange it for cakes to share.
Zhīzhāng wondered why a precious pearl would be used to buy cakes,
but dared not speak.
The old man said,
"If your stinginess is not yet eliminated,
how can you obtain the art?"
Bǎo Mǔ
There was a man named Wèi Shēng,
who obtained a beautiful stone.
Later, a Hu person saw it and said,
"This is a treasure mother.
On the full moon of each month,
set up an altar by the sea,
place the stone upon it,
and it can gather precious pearls."
Luófù
Wú Kān of Yìxīng was a county official,
and his home was near the Jīngxī stream.
Suddenly, there was a large snail,
which later transformed into a woman,
known as Luófù (Snail Woman).
The county magistrate heard of this and sought her,
but Kān did not comply.
So the magistrate used various pretexts to persecute Kān.
The magistrate said,
"I require two things: frog's hair and a ghost's arm.
If you fail to obtain them, you will be punished."
Kān told Luófù,
who immediately produced them.
The magistrate then falsely said,
"I further require a guādòu (snail-dipper)."
Kān again told Luófù,
and the woman said,
"This is a beast."
In a short while, she led it forth.
It resembled a dog but ate fire,
and its excrement also turned into fire.
The magistrate tried it with fire.
Suddenly, it discharged excrement, burning down the county office,
and the magistrate died there.
Yǔ Shēn Rì Shǒu Sān Shī
Liú Wúmíng regularly observed "Yǔ Shēn Rì Shǒu Sān Shī" (guarding the Three Corpses on the day of Gēngshēn),
and ate realgar.
Later, he saw a ghost envoy
who said,
"I am Tàishān Zhífú (Duty Officer of Mount Tai),
come to seize you.
But I see a yellow light several feet high above your head,
and cannot approach.
Is this not due to the efficacy of realgar?"
He then said,
"One gold and one stone are called 'elixir.'
You have consumed the stone,
if you further ingest the gold,
then your name will be removed from the register of mortals,
and permanently recorded in the Qīnghuá register."
Liú later encountered Qīnghuá Zhēnrén,
who imparted to him the elixir formula:
using lead as the sovereign,
mercury as the minister,
eight stones as envoys,
and huángyá (yellow sprouts) as assistants.
Mèng Zhū Cǐ
During the Jiànzhōng era,
a market vendor in Jīngxī dreamed of arriving at a government office.
There was a nobleman in purple robes seated at a desk,
with three or four attendants holding leaf-bound registers.
In the central courtyard was Zhū Cǐ,
his body shackled and neck locked,
with his head exposed and bowing,
as if pleading with sorrow.
The nobleman said,
"You are destined for this matter.
The Emperor's command has already been issued,
and your plea will be of no avail."
Zhū Cǐ pleaded incessantly.
The nobleman angrily said,
"Why do you not know Heaven's mandate?"
He ordered an opening to a courtyard in the east corridor.
Inside the gate were over thirty people,
all dressed in scarlet and purple.
The nobleman pointed and said,
"These are awaiting your wealth and status."
This person looked at them
and saw they were of the likes of Lǐ Shàng and Wéi Luò.
He then angrily told Zhū Cǐ to enter a courtyard in the west corridor.
This person asked the attendants,
"When will this happen?"
They replied,
"In the seventh month,
Fèngtiān will be thus."
Afterwards, it indeed came to pass.
Dài Wén Sǐ Wèi Niú
During the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a man named Dài Wén in Hǎiyán County.
His family was wealthy, but he was greedy.
Whenever villagers borrowed money,
he would collect several times the interest.
A neighbor paid interest,
being exploited greatly.
Several years later,
Dài Wén fell ill and died.
In the neighbor's home, a cow gave birth to a black calf,
and on its flank, white hair formed the characters "Dài Wén."
Whenever "Dài Wén" was called,
the ox would respond and come.
It died several years later.
Shè Yì Jiāng
Yáng Yōngbó often provided free drinks to travelers.
One day,
someone, after drinking,
took out a pint of pebbles from his bosom and gave them to him,
saying,
"If you plant these, beautiful jade will grow,
and you will also obtain a good wife."
He planted them as instructed.
There was a remarkably beautiful woman of the Xú clan.
He tried to seek her hand in marriage.
Xú Gōng said,
"A pair of white jade discs will suffice."
He then found the jade discs where he had planted them,
and subsequently married her.
Chì Hóng
Kǒngzǐ (Confucius) edited the Chūnqiū (Spring and Autumn Annals)
and composed the Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety).
After their completion,
he purified himself through fasting and abstinence,
and reported to the Big Dipper in the north.
Suddenly, a red rainbow descended from the heavens,
transforming into a yellow jade with carved characters.
Kǒngzǐ knelt and received it.
Zǐ Mǔ Qián
The qīngfú 青蚨 resembles a cicada but is slightly
larger. It lays its offspring among the grass,
like silkworms.
If one takes its young,
the mother will immediately fly to it.
Smear eighty-one coins with the mother's blood,
and eighty-one coins with the young's blood.
Whenever purchasing goods,
whether the mother coins are used first
or the young coins are used first,
they will all fly back,
returning in an endless cycle.
Golden belt hook
A man named Zhāng 張 of Cháng'ān 長安
had a dove fly into his bosom,
which transformed into a golden belt hook.
His grandson, Fùshèng 富盛,
was born with a divine glow.
Yīngyù 应嫗
was a woman whose son was born with a divine light shining upon the altar to the local god.
All four of her sons became renowned for their talents.
Āxiāng 阿香 pushes a cart
One evening, a person traveling
sought lodging in a thatched hut by the roadside.
Only a single woman lived there.
In the middle of the night, a child called from outside the door:
"Āxiāng 阿香,
the official summons you to push a cart."
The woman then left.
By dawn, a great thunderstorm broke out.
Looking at the hut, it was merely a tomb.
Ant hole
Lú Fén 盧汾 dreamt he entered an ant hole
and saw a grand hall, dilapidated and cavernous.
It was inscribed "Shěnyǔ Táng 審雨堂."
Commander of Fate of Tài Shān
Jiǎ 賈, whose courtesy name was Wénhé 文合,
fell ill and died.
An official led him to Tài Shān 太山.
The Commander of Fate said:
"We should summon Wénhé 文合 of a certain commandery,
why was this person summoned?
He must be quickly sent back."
It was dusk,
and they rested under a tree outside the city wall.
Wénhé 文合 saw a young maiden walking alone.
He asked her name and surname.
She said:
"I am from Sānhé 三河.
My father is currently the magistrate of Yìyáng 易陽.
Yesterday I was summoned here,
but today I am permitted to return.
Meeting dusk,
I feared being suspected of impropriety,
so I stopped here,
relying on a virtuous person."
Wénhé 文合 said:
"My heart is pleased with you,
and I wish to enjoy this evening together."
The maiden said:
"I have heard from my aunts
that women take purity and integrity as their virtue."
Wénhé 文合 spoke with her repeatedly,
but she ultimately remained unmoved.
At daybreak, they parted ways.
Wénhé 文合 had already been dead for two nights,
his coffin prepared for burial,
when he revived.
Wishing to verify the matter,
he went to Yìyáng 易陽 to visit the magistrate,
saying:
"Did your daughter die and then revive?"
He fully recounted the maiden's appearance, clothing, and the entirety of their conversation.
The magistrate went in to ask his daughter,
and what she said was identical.
The magistrate was greatly astonished and admired it,
and married his daughter to Wénhé 文合.
Thunderbolt
Yáng Dàohé 楊道和 was in the fields during a summer thunderstorm.
He went under a mulberry tree,
and a thunderbolt struck down upon him.
Dàohé 道和 blocked its arm with his hoe,
and it fell to the ground, unable to leave.
Its color was like cinnabar,
its eyes like mirrors,
its hair and horns more than a foot long,
its form like a domestic animal,
and its head resembled a macaque.
Long whistle calling wind
Zhào Bǐng 趙炳 begged a boatman for passage.
He did not get it,
so he sat down and whistled loudly,
calling the wind to cross the water.
Ascended a tower and self-immolated
Zhāng Huàn 張奐 was the Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi 武威.
His wife dreamt she wore Huàn's Huàn 奐 official seal and ribbon,
ascended a tower, and sang.
Huàn 奐 ordered someone to divine it.
The diviner said:
"Your wife is about to give birth to a son,
who will again govern this commandery,
and his life will end in this tower."
Later, his son Měng 猛 was born,
and indeed became the Grand Administrator of Wǔwēi 武威.
When Shāngzhōu 商州 troops besieged the city urgently,
Měng 猛 was ashamed to be captured,
so he ascended a tower and self-immolated, dying.
A green dog and an attendant cause mischief
At Zāng Zhòngyīng's 臧仲英 house,
cooked food would disappear from the pot,
bows and crossbows would move by themselves,
and fire would start from within a chest,
burning all the clothes while the chest remained as before.
His granddaughter, four years old,
went missing,
and could not be found.
Three days later, she was found crying in the garden under manure.
Such incidents were not isolated.
Xǔ Lǐshān 許李山 divined it, saying:
"There is a green dog in the house,
and an attendant named Yìxǐ 益喜 within,
who are responsible for these occurrences.
If you truly wish to stop them,
kill this dog
and send Yìxǐ 益喜 back to his hometown."
Zhòngyīng 從仲英 followed this advice,
and the troubles ceased.
Volume Seven
End.
Pángǔ Shì 盤古氏
was the ancestor of heaven, earth, and all things.
When he died,
his head became the Five Sacred Mountains,
his eyes the sun and moon,
his fat and grease the rivers and seas,
and his hair and fur the grass and trees.
One account says:
His head was the Eastern Peak,
his belly the Central Peak,
his left arm the Southern Peak,
his right arm the Northern Peak,
and his feet the Western Peak.
Another account says:
His weeping became rivers,
his breath the wind and thunder,
joy was clear weather and anger was cloudy weather.
Ghost Mother
In Xiǎo Yú Shān 小虞山 in Nánhǎi 南海, there is a Ghost Mother.
She gives birth to a thousand ghosts at a time,
bearing them in the morning
and eating them in the evening.
The Ghost Aunt Goddess in Cāngwú 蒼梧 today is she.
She has a tiger's head,
dragon's feet,
python's eyes,
and jiaolong's eyebrows.
Turtle Calendar
During the era of Táo Táng 陶唐,
the state of Yuèshāng 越裳 presented a thousand-year-old divine turtle.
On its back were tadpole-script writings,
recording events since the creation of the world.
The Emperor ordered them recorded,
and they were called the Turtle Calendar.
Running mountains and weeping stones
In the time of Jié 桀,
Mount Tài 太 ran,
and stones wept.
King Wǔ of Zhōu 周武王 said to Duke of Zhōu 周公:
"Jié 桀 was unprincipled,
causing mountains to run and stones to weep."
Ten auspicious omens in Yáo's time
In the time of Yáo 堯,
fodder in the palace transformed into grain,
phoenixes rested in the courtyard,
divine dragons appeared in the pond,
"calendar grass" grew on the steps,
birds had five colors,
crows turned white,
divine grain grew,
bamboo shoots grew in the kitchen,
an auspicious star shone in the sky,
and sweet dew descended to earth.
These were the ten auspicious omens.
Yáo's stele and Yǔ's tablet
On Kōngtóng Shān 崆峒山 there are Yáo's 堯 stele and Yǔ's 禹 tablet,
both in ancient seal script,
recounting the emperors' merits and virtues.
Bān Zhú 班竹
Shùn made a southern tour,
and was buried in Cāngwú.
Yáo's two daughters, Éhuáng and Nǚyīng, wept, their tears staining the bamboo,
and all the bamboo became speckled because of it.
Xiāngsī Mù (Acacia Tree)
Wèi lamented the difficulties of Qín,
as people conscripted for war never returned.
A wife, longing for her husband, died.
On her grave grew a plant,
whose branches and leaves all leaned towards where her husband was.
Thus, it was called Xiāngsī Mù.
Now, between Qín and Zhào, there is Xiāngsī Cǎo (Acacia Grass),
which resembles a carnation.
It is also called Duàncháng Cǎo (Heartbreak Grass).
Lǎnfù Yú (Lazy Woman Fish)
In Huáinán, there is the Lǎnfù Yú.
Once, a woman of the Yáng clan was drowned by her mother-in-law,
and transformed into this fish.
Its fat can be burned in lamps and candles;
it gives light when illuminating musical instruments or board games,
but gives no light when illuminating spinning and weaving.
Lóngxiāo Gōng (Dragon Gauze Palace)
In Nánhǎi, there is Lóngxiāo Gōng,
the place where the fountain-dwellers weave gauze.
Nǚ Shānhú (Female Coral)
During the reign of Emperor Guāngwǔ,
Nánhǎi presented a coral figure of a woman.
The Emperor planted it in front of the palace,
and called it Nǚ Shānhú.
During the reign of Emperor Líng, the tree died,
which was an omen of the impending fall of Hàn.
Yìnglóng (Winged Dragon)
A water serpent becomes a jiāo after five hundred years.
A jiāo transforms into a lóng (dragon) after a thousand years.
A lóng becomes a jiǎolóng (horned dragon) after five hundred years,
and then an yìnglóng (winged dragon) after another five hundred years.
Xuánlù (Black Deer)
A deer turns grey after a thousand years,
then white after another five hundred years,
and then black after another five hundred years.
During the reign of Emperor Chéng of Hàn,
a person from Zhōngshān obtained a xuánlù.
When cooked,
its bones were all black.
An immortal said:
"If xuánlù is made into dried meat
and eaten, one will live for two thousand years."
Língguī (Spirit Tortoise)
A Língguī grows hair after two thousand years.
One that lives for five thousand years is called a shénguī (divine tortoise),
and one that lives for ten thousand years is called a língguī.
When a tiger lives for a thousand years, its teeth fall out and horns grow.
Fēng Shào Huà Hǔ (Fēng Shào Transforms into a Tiger)
Fēng Shào, the governor of Xuānchéng during the Hàn dynasty, transformed into a tiger,
and preyed on the people of the commandery.
At the time, there was a saying:
"Do not be Magistrate Fēng;
while alive he did not govern the people, and after death he ate them."
Xiāojiàng (Owl and Jaxartes)
The beasts xiāo and jiàng,
resemble tigers and leopards but are smaller.
Upon birth, they devour their own mothers.
Thus, they are called xiāojiàng.
Jīnjī Yùquǎn (Golden Rooster and Jade Dog)
On Jìyáng Shān, there is the place where Mágū ascended to immortality.
On the mountain, there is a golden rooster crowing,
and a jade dog barking.
Jīncán Yùyàn (Golden Silkworms and Jade Swallows)
In the tomb of Hélv̈'s wife,
there were over a thousand each of golden silkworms and jade swallows.
Wúwáng Chūnxiāo Gōng (King of Wú's Palace of Spring Nights)
King Fūchāi of Wú built the Chūnxiāo Gōng
for endless nights of drinking.
He commissioned a wine vessel holding a thousand stones,
and also created a Tiānchí (Heavenly Pool).
In the pool, he built a Qīnglóng Zhōu (Green Dragon Boat).
He spent his days in water games with Xīshī.
There was also a separate lodge in Jùróng,
where catalpas and parasol trees formed a forest.
An ancient yuèfǔ poem says:
"The parasol palace, the catalpa,
causes the King of Wú to worry." This is it.
Shètáng (Archery Hall)
The Wúwáng Shètáng [Archery Hall of the King of Wú] had
pillar bases all resembling crouching tortoises.
Yuán Hóng's "Gōngfù" says:
"the bases of sea turtles," and this is it.
Xiàozhú Sòng (Ode to Filial Bamboo)
In the third year of Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
mother-and-child bamboo shoots grew in front of the Báihǔ Diàn (White Tiger Palace).
At the time, they were called xiàozhú (filial bamboo),
and the assembled officials presented the "Xiàozhú Sòng."
Jújí (Orange Register)
In Yuè, there were many oranges and pomelos,
and each year there was much orange tax.
This was called Chéngjú Hù (Orange and Pomelo Households),
also known as Jújí.
There were also Wáng Shì Júyuán (Wang Family's Orange Orchard),
Hú Shì Méishān (Hu Family's Plum Mountain),
Hè Shì Cháqiū (He Family's Jujube Hill).
Báilían Bānzhú (White Lotus and Speckled Bamboo)
In Wú, there were Lù Jiā Báilían (Lu Family's White Lotus)
and Gù Jiā Bānzhú (Gu Family's Speckled Bamboo).
In Zhào, there was Hán Shì zhī Suānzǎo (Han Family's Sour Jujube).
Zhīfěntáng (Powder and Rouge Pond)
In the old Wú palace, there was the Xiāngshuǐ Xī (Fragrant Water Stream).
The common saying was that it was where Xīshī bathed,
and people called it Zhīfěntáng.
Mójìng Shí (Mirror-Polishing Stone)
The common legend in Jìnghú is that Xuānyuán Shì cast mirrors here.
Today, there is the Mójìng Shí;
no creeping plants grow on this stone.
Quèchén Xī (Dust-Repelling Rhinoceros),
a sea beast,
whose horn repels dust.
Xuánhè Zhòngjiàn (Black Crane Shot by Arrow)
Kuài Cān was extremely filial in raising his mother.
When a xuánhè was shot by an arrow,
Cān took it in and treated its wound.
Once it healed, he released it.
Later, a pair of cranes, male and female, arrived,
and presented luminous moon pearls at night as a token of gratitude.
Yùnǚ Dǎoliàn Zhēn (Jade Maiden's Pounding Block)
In the mountains of Lángyá Jùn, there is a square stone.
A divine maiden pounded clothes here,
and it is called Yùnǚ Dǎoliàn Zhēn.
Shénrén Qūshí (Divine Being Drives Stones)
Shǐhuáng built a stone bridge over the sea,
wanting to watch the sunrise.
Someone was driving the stones,
but not fast enough.
A divine being whipped him until blood flowed.
Today, the stone bridge still has a reddish color.
Wǔsè É (Five-Colored Moth)
Yuánkè, a person from Jìyīn,
planted five-colored fragrant herbs for over ten years,
and consumed their fruits.
There were always five-colored moths gathering on the herbs.
When it was silkworm season,
a maiden came to help raise silkworms.
They obtained one hundred and twenty cocoons,
as large as urns.
Each cocoon took six or seven days to reel completely.
The maiden and Yuánkè both became immortals and departed.
Jiǎnnǚ Quán (Silkworm Maiden Spring)
In Bìngzhōu, there is the Jiǎnnǚ Quán.
If women wearing beautiful makeup and colorful clothes come to this place,
it will surely cause clouds and rain.
It is also said to be Jiè Tuī's sister.
Lànkē (Rotten Axe Handle)
On Shíshì Shān in Xìn'ān Jùn,
during the Jìn dynasty, Wáng Zhì went there to cut wood.
He saw several boys playing chess.
They gave Wáng Zhì an object like a date pit,
and when he held it in his mouth, he felt no hunger.
He looked at his axe handle, and it had completely rotted away.
When he returned,
there were no people from his time left.
Luótíng (Snail Pavilion)
In Nánkāng, there was a woman
who made a living by collecting snails.
One night, she lodged in a pavilion
and heard the sound of wind and thunder. She saw a multitude of
snails approaching with their mouths open,
devouring her flesh chaotically.
The next day, only her bones remained.
Therefore, the pavilion was called Luótíng.
Qīchǐ Zǎo Sānchǐ Lí (Seven-Foot Jujube, Three-Foot Pear)
In the north, there are seven-foot jujubes,
and in the south, there are three-foot pears.
If a person sees and eats them,
they will immediately become an earthly immortal.
Huánghè Lóu (Yellow Crane Tower)
Xún Huán toured on the Huánghè Lóu in Jiāngxià.
Looking southwest, he saw something floating gracefully.
It was a guest riding a crane,
wearing feathered robes and rainbow-colored skirts.
Host and guest conversed joyfully.
Soon after, he bid farewell and departed,
straddling the crane and soaring into the sky,
disappearing into the distance.
Báiyī Sùnǚ (White-Clad Plain Maiden)
In Jìn'ān, a scholar named Xiè Duān
found a large conch on the seashore.
It was as big as a *shí* (斛) of rice.
When he opened it,
inside was a beautiful woman,
who said:
“I am the White-Clothed Maiden from the Tiānhàn (天漢).
The Heavenly Emperor pities your uprightness
and bids me be your wife.”
Xiè Duān thought she was a demon
and cursed her.
The woman sighed and ascended into the sky,
riding on a cloud, and departed.
In Qín’s prison land
along the Gānquán (甘泉) road, there was a worm
with a fully formed head, eyes, mouth, and teeth.
Dōngfāng Shuò (東方朔) said:
“This is ancient Qín’s prison land,
and this is caused by accumulated sorrow.”
The Emperor ordered a check against a map,
and it was indeed Qín’s prison land.
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
“Accumulated sorrow can be dispelled by wine.”
He placed the worm in wine,
and it immediately dissolved.
Life-Reviving Grass
During the reign of Hàn Guāngwǔ (漢光武),
the Yuèzhī (月支) Kingdom offered life-reviving grass.
If a person died,
covering their face with this grass would revive them.
Dragon-Liver Melon
It was one *zhàng* (丈) long,
growing in an ice valley.
Benevolent Bamboo
In Nánzhōng (南中) grew mother-and-child bamboo,
which is today’s Benevolent Bamboo.
Xièzhì (獬豸)
It is a one-horned goat.
By nature, it knows when a person is guilty.
When Gāoyáo (皋陶) administered justice,
if a crime was doubtful,
he would order the goat to butt the suspect.
Yuánjué (猿玃)
An ape transforms into a *jué* (玃) after five hundred years.
A *jué* transforms into an old man after a thousand years.
Swallows grow a barbarian beard after a thousand years.
Turtles Grow Hair
During the reign of Yīn Zhòu (殷紂),
large turtles grew hair and rabbits grew horns,
a sign that military conflict was about to erupt.
The Sky Rains Gold and Other Things
During the time of Xià Yǔ (夏禹),
the sky rained gold for three days.
During the reign of Zhōu Chéngwáng (周成王),
Xiányáng (咸陽) rained gold.
In Wáng Mǎng’s (王莽) palace, *wǔzhū* (五銖) coins rained down,
turning into turtles upon reaching the ground.
Hàn Wēng Zhòngrú (漢翁仲孺) was poor,
and the sky rained ten *hú* (斛) of gold into his home.
In Hàn Huìdì’s (漢惠帝) palace, gold and black tin rained down.
During the time of Empress Lǚ (呂后),
millet rained.
During the reign of Xuāndì (宣帝),
Jiāngnán (江南) suffered famine,
and grain rained for three days.
Qín (秦) and Wèi (魏) lands rained grain over two thousand *qǐng* (頃).
During the reign of Chéngdì (成帝),
a blue deer rained down in the palace.
During the time of Dà Yǔ (大禹),
the sky rained rice.
An ancient poem says:
“How can the heavens rain rice
to feed my people throughout the land?”
During the reign of Wú Huánwáng (吳桓王),
Jīnlíng (金陵) rained five grains into the homes of the poor.
During the Wèi (魏) period,
Yè (鄴) rained five-colored stones,
and Hénèi (河內) rained jujubes.
In the home of Hèjiān (河間) Prince Yuán (子元), it rained,
and eight or nine small children fell into his courtyard.
They said their home was in Hédōng (河東)
and they were blown there by the wind.
Between the Zhōu (周) and Qín (秦) periods,
Hénán (河南) rained jujubes,
which is why Suānzǎo (酸棗) County got its name.
Wheat Transforms into Moths
In the middle of Jìn Yǒngjiā (晉永嘉) reign,
on a rainy day in Liángzhōu (梁州),
all the wheat transformed into moths.
Also, in Jīngzhōu (荊州), after prolonged rain,
the millet transformed into worms.
Zhōngláng (中郎) Wáng Yì (王義) submitted a memorial, saying:
“Regarding the moth-wheat and worm-millet,
what do you, Your Majesty, think of your own sagely virtue?”
The Emperor showed a look of shame.
Spirits of Water and Wood
On a beam in Hàn Wǔ’s (漢武) Wèiyāng (未央) Palace,
an old man, eight or nine inches tall,
hobbled to the Emperor,
bowed his head but said nothing,
looked up at the roof,
then looked down at the Emperor’s feet,
and suddenly vanished.
The Emperor was alarmed and frightened.
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
“These are the spirits of water and wood.
Your Majesty has greatly expanded the palaces,
cutting down their homes,
so they came to complain.
Looking up at the roof and then looking at Your Majesty’s feet
means they wish the palace construction would suffice here
and not be built anew.”
The Emperor then halted the labor.
Later, the Emperor visited the Hùzi (瓠子) River
and heard string music from under the water.
The old man from the beam earlier emerged, treading on the waves.
The Emperor said:
“The music I just heard,
was it performed by you and your kind?”
He replied:
“After our previous complaint,
Your Majesty graciously ceased the axe work,
allowing us to preserve our homes,
so we are celebrating and making music.”
Then they performed music
and presented luminous red pearls from a cave’s clam.
Separating and Joining Wind
Liè Yùkòu (列禦寇) rode the wind.
He always returned to the eight wildernesses on the day of Lìchūn (立春),
and roamed the wind caves on the day of Lìqiū (立秋).
When the wind came, all plants and trees grew;
when it left, plants and trees withered.
This is called the Separating and Joining Wind.
Yún (蝹) Resembling Pigs and Sheep
During the time of Qín Mùgōng (秦繆公),
a person from Chéncāng (陳倉) dug the ground and found a creature
that looked like a pig or a sheep.
Mùgōng encountered two boys who said:
“This creature is called *yún*;
it eats the brains of dead people underground.
If you pierce its head with a cypress leaf, it will die.
That is why cypress trees are now planted on graves
to prevent its harm.”
Thirty-Six Grotto-Heavens
Among the thirty-six grotto-heavens in the human world,
only ten are well-known.
The rest are found in the *Jiǔ Wēizhì* (九微志),
which has not yet circulated in the world.
Mermen’s Chambers
In the South Sea are mermen,
who dwell in water chambers,
like fish,
and do not neglect weaving.
Their eyes can weep pearls.
Divine Gong
In Dòngtíng (洞庭) Mountain, there is a stone tower.
Below the tower are two stones.
When struck, their sound resonates like a gong,
thus it is called the Divine Gong.
Heavenly Rooster
On Táodū (桃都) Mountain, there is a peach tree.
On the tree is a heavenly rooster.
When the rooster crows, the human world’s roosters crow.
Fragrant Commander
Hàn Yōng Zhòngjìn (漢雍仲進) presented southern sea incense
and was appointed Luòyáng (洛陽) Commander,
nicknamed Fragrant Commander.
Crystal Palace
Chānghé (閶闔) built a crystal palace.
Golden Plums
Dùlíng (杜陵) has golden plums.
Zhōngshān (中山) has azure plums,
as big as a fist,
one plum with two colors.
Cold-Dispelling Incense
Hàn Wǔdì (漢武帝),
foreign countries offered cold-dispelling incense.
When burned in a room,
even during severe cold,
people would certainly wear fewer clothes.
Patterned Water
The Suī (濉) and Huàn (渙) Rivers,
their wave patterns are all five colors.
Called Patterned Water,
it is also called Jīshuǐ (績水).
Confusing Grain
There is a grain like the fruit of a paper mulberry tree.
Wearing it prevents hunger.
It is called mígǔ.
Lǎnfùcǎo
In Guìlín there is a sleeping grass.
Seeing it makes one sleep.
It is also named Zuìcǎo,
and also Lǎnfùcǎo.
Jīngjīngxiāng
In Jùkūzhōu there is a soul-returning tree.
Cut out its root-heart,
and boil its juice in a jade cauldron.
It is called Jīngjīngxiāng.
Dead bodies smell its scent and immediately revive.
Zǐxuān
Xuāncǎo is also named Liáochóuhuā,
and also Zǐxuān,
and also Wàngyōucǎo.
Xiānrénxìng
On Tiāntáishān there are apricot blossoms.
They have six petals and are jade-colored.
They are called Xiānrénxìng.
Língfēng
In the south there are Fēngzǐguǐ,
which are old maple trees
that transform into human form.
They are also called Língfēng.
Luángē Fèngwǔ
In the South Sea there is Xuānyuánqiū.
Luán birds sing and Fèng birds dance.
This is the music of the Tiāndì.
Jiāojiē
In Xià Jié's palace,
there was a woman who transformed into a dragon.
Soon after, she reverted to a woman.
She was very beautiful but ate people.
Jié named her Jiāojiē.
She informed Jié of good and bad omens.
Digging up Tàisuì ground
Cháo Liángzhèng had a strong, unyielding nature and did not fear ghosts.
Every year he would dig up the Tàisuì ground.
Later, he dug again.
Suddenly, he saw a fleshy object.
Liángzhèng struck it three hundred times
and threw it into the river.
That night, he sent someone to watch it.
After the third watch,
many chariots and horses
arrived at the location of the flesh.
They asked the Tàisuì:
"Brother, why did you endure such humiliation
without seeking revenge?"
The Tàisuì said:
"He is currently flourishing.
There's nothing that can be done."
The next morning, it was gone.
Imprisoned Father Repays Kindness
During the Qiányuán era,
Zhāng Shǒuyī served as Táilǐ Shàoqīng.
He reversed misjudged cases and corrected wrongful imprisonments,
and many death row inmates were released.
Later, an old man with white hair came forward and bowed.
He thanked him, saying:
"I am not a living person.
I am the father of a death row inmate whom you, honored sir, released.
I have no way to repay your kindness.
If you should have any urgent personal request,
I might be able to fulfill it."
Soon after, an imperial decree granted a general amnesty and celebration.
People in the city watched the festivities freely.
Shǒuyī saw a daughter of a gentry family who was very beautiful.
He was attracted to her.
Having no way to approach her,
he tried calling out to the former ghost, asking if he could bring her to him.
The ghost said:
"This is easy,
but it cannot last long,
only about seven days."
So, he prepared a quiet place
and set up curtains.
A short while later, she arrived.
The woman was startled and said:
"Where is this?"
Shǒuyī and the ghost, standing by, replied:
"This is Heaven."
Thus, they became intimately affectionate,
and their love was very deep.
After seven days,
the ghost covered her eyes again and sent her back.
Shǒuyī secretly observed the woman's home,
and it was said that the young lady had suddenly fallen ill,
not recognizing anyone.
After seven days, she woke up.
Apes and Dogs as Wonders
When Wèi Yuánzhōng had not yet achieved prominence,
his family was poor,
and he only had one maidservant.
As she was cooking,
she saw an old ape watching the fire.
His wife was startled and told Yuánzhōng.
Yuánzhōng said:
"The ape pities us for having no one
and is cooking for us.
This is very good."
Another time, he called for his servant,
who did not answer,
and a dog called in his stead.
He again said:
"This is a dutiful dog,
it can even work on my behalf."
Another time, as he sat alone,
a group of rats stood before him with clasped paws.
He again said:
"They must be hungry,
seeking food from me."
So, he ordered them to be fed.
At night, an owl hooted on the rooftop.
His family was about to shoot it,
but he stopped them, saying:
"Owls cannot see in the daytime,
so they fly at night.
These are nurtured by Heaven and Earth.
They cannot be made to run south to Yuè,
or north to Hú.
How can you harm them?"
Afterwards,
no wonders occurred.
Wealth and Rank Come from Heaven
When Wèi Yuánzhōng was still obscure,
he visited Zhāng Jǐngzàng.
The latter treated him very poorly.
When asked about success and failure,
he also did not answer.
Yuánzhōng then became greatly angry and said:
"I traveled a thousand *lǐ*, carrying provisions, to come here;
it was not just for this.
I surely thought you would have some teaching for me.
But you meet me with a 'golden mouth and wooden tongue' (unresponsive).
Wealth and rank come from Heaven above.
What concern is it of yours?"
With that, he brushed his clothes and left.
Jǐngzàng quickly stopped him
and said:
"Your facial features show you are currently in a state of anger.
Later, you will achieve the highest wealth and rank among subjects."
It turned out exactly as he said.
Silver Mine Turtle
Liú Yànhuí's
father was the governor of Húzhōu.
A subordinate official found a turtle in a silver mine,
one foot long.
He presented it to the governor.
All the officials congratulated him, saying:
"Having this turtle means a lifespan of a thousand years."
The governor thanked them.
He was already not that kind of person (who would accept such a gift).
He personally rode his horse to return the turtle to the mine and released it.
Later, the governor died.
Yànhuí became the judicial officer of Fángzhōu.
When he was going to his official post,
the mountains and waters overflowed,
and the flat ground was completely submerged.
His whole family was terrified.
Soon, a large turtle led the way.
Following the turtle,
all the places were shallow.
After passing through more than ten locations,
they escaped the danger of the flood.
That evening,
Yànhuí dreamt that the turtle said:
"Formerly in the silver mine,
I received the kindness of your late father, the governor.
Therefore, I am repaying that grace."
Zhīpǔ
Xiāndū has a mushroom garden.
All kinds of auspicious fungi are planted there.
Some are like chariots and riders,
some like imperial canopies,
some like tall buildings,
and some like flying birds of five colors.
Mountain Cave Chūpú
Someone was riding a horse in the mountains
and saw two old men playing chūpú in a cave.
He propped his whip on the ground and watched.
A short while later,
his whip had rotted and his saddle had decayed.
Golden Sheep, Jade Horse
There was accumulated snow that did not melt for a long time.
When the ground was dug, a golden sheep and a jade horse were found,
about two *chǐ* high.
Wáng Bì guards the gate.
In Chénzhōu, someone shot a pig,
and it entered a stone chamber.
He saw an old man,
who asked why he shot the pig.
He replied that it was damaging the crops.
The old man immediately called a boy and reprimanded him:
"Why were you not careful with the gate,
allowing the pig to escape?"
The shooter asked who they were.
The boy said:
"This is Hèshàng Wēng,
the Emperor sent him to lecture on the *Yì* for the immortals,
and I am Wáng Bì.
I have not fully understood the *Yì* after receiving it,
and so I am punished to guard the gate."
Módǐng Sōng
Xuánzhuāng went to the Western Regions
and saw a pine tree.
He stroked its branches with his hand and said:
"I am going west to seek Buddhist teachings.
You may grow westward.
When I return, you should turn eastward,
so that my disciples may know."
After he left,
the pine branches pointed westward year after year.
One year, they suddenly turned eastward.
His disciples said:
"The Dharma Master has returned."
Soon after, he indeed came back.
To this day, it is called Módǐng Sōng.
Xǔ Jīngyáng's蛟-slaying sword
Wǔ Shèngzhī saw the Duke of Thunder chasing a yellow snake on a river beach.
Someone threw a stone at it,
and there was a metallic clang.
The Duke of Thunder flew away.
A bronze sword was found,
with an inscription saying "Xǔ Jīngyáng's second蛟-slaying sword."
Yùyīngfěn
A Daoist priest held some soup noodles
and told people:
"These are Yùyīngfěn.
Eat them, and on the seventh day of the seventh lunar month, you will ascend to immortality."
Crab Claws
A sea merchant suddenly saw two mountains facing each other,
emerging several *zhàng* from the waves.
Soon they disappeared.
The boatmen said:
"These are crab claws."
Old Man Playing the Flute
Lǚ Jūnqīng anchored his boat by Jūnshān on a moonlit night,
drinking wine and playing the flute.
Suddenly, a fishing boat came alongside.
An old man held a flute,
as large as two hands clasped together,
and showed it to Lǚ, saying:
"This is a heavenly instrument,
it cannot be played."
Next, he produced a flute
like those used in the world,
and said:
"This is an immortal instrument from a grotto-heaven."
Then another smaller one,
like a brush handle,
he said:
"This is a human flute."
Thereupon, he played the small one.
After one or two notes, the waves surged.
After three to five more notes, the boats and oars danced wildly.
Lǚ was greatly frightened.
The old man stopped playing the flute
and recited aloud:
"An old man from Xiāngzhong reads Huáng and Lǎo,
leaning on purple vines, sitting on green grass.
When spring arrives, he knows not the depth of the Xiāng River;
at dusk, he forgets the road to Bālíng."
Poem by a Descending Deity
A deity descended to Zhèng Jiàng's house
and recited a poem:
"Suddenly, a patch of cloud flew over the lake;
unaware, the rain wet my clothes in the boat.
Having picked lotus flowers, I completely forgot them,
and returned with only a lotus leaf covering my head."
Dàojūn Clips the Tongue
Wáng Fǎláng, a Daoist priest from Kuízhōu,
had a long tongue,
and could not pronounce words correctly.
So he recited the *Dàodé Jīng* daily.
Suddenly, he dreamt that Lǎozi clipped his tongue.
When he awoke,
his speech became correct.
One-legged Mountain Imps
Shānxiāo [mountain imps]
are found throughout Lǐngnán.
They have one foot,
reversed heels,
and three fingers on both hands and feet.
Males are called "Shānzhàng" [mountain elders],
females "Shāngū" [mountain maids].
At night, they knock on people's doors.
Males ask for gold and silk,
females ask for rouge and powder.
Monk of Jìng'ài Temple
At the beginning of the Kāiyuán era,
Qíwáng Fàn had no son,
so he asked the Daoist priest Yè Jìngnéng to petition the Celestial Bureau
to take a monk from Jìng'ài Temple as his son.
The ghost mistakenly went to the chamber of a great virtue monk at Shèngshàn Temple.
The great virtue monk said:
"I am cultivating the karma for the Tusita Heaven,
I should not be a noble's son.
It must be a certain monk from Jìng'ài Temple."
The ghost then did not take him.
A year later,
Qíwáng had a son.
From a young age, he came to Jìng'ài Temple to worship.
When he was over ten years old,
he did not perform good deeds at all;
he only enjoyed holding a slingshot,
and shot all the pigeons in the temple courtyard until none were left.
Lone Crane Struck by an Arrow
Mínghuáng was hunting in Shāyuàn.
Among the clouds was a lone crane.
The Emperor personally took his bow and arrow.
With one shot, he struck it.
The crane, with the arrow, flew southwestward and departed.
Xú Zuǒqīng, a Daoist priest from Qīngchéng at Míngyuè Guān in Yìzhōu,
one day suddenly arrived from outside and said:
"I was walking in the mountains
and was accidentally struck by a flying arrow.
Soon I was well again.
This arrow is not of the human world.
I will leave it on the wall.
Next year, when the arrow's owner arrives here,
it should be given to him."
He also recorded the month and day.
Mínghuáng, on his journey to Shǔ, arrived at this temple
and was greatly astonished.
The date Xú Zuǒqīng inscribed
was precisely the day of the hunt in Shāyuàn.
Indeed, it was the lone crane struck by an arrow.
Píngděng Gé
During the Kāihuáng reign of the Suí dynasty,
the Buddhist monk Chéngkōng cast an iron statue in Jìnyáng,
seventy *chǐ* high.
It took twenty years to gather the materials.
On the day the furnace was opened,
the statue was not completed.
Chéngkōng reaffirmed his previous vow.
Twenty years later,
the pouring of the statue again failed.
He cried out to heaven in sorrow,
knocking his head in repentance.
Another twenty years passed,
and the efforts were gathered again.
People from near and far gathered.
Chéngkōng ascended to the top of the furnace, a hundred *chǐ* high,
and said:
"I vowed in my youth to cast a great Buddha.
This year I am eighty,
and twice it has failed.
If this again goes against my wish,
I shall sacrifice my life,
and perhaps the statue will be complete.
Fifty years from now,
I will build a grand pavilion."
Immediately, golden liquid was injected,
and Chéngkōng threw himself into it.
When the furnace was opened,
the iron statue was exquisite.
From then on, the people of Bìngzhōu wished to build a pavilion to cover it,
requiring great effort and resources.
At the beginning of the Kāiyuán era,
Lǐ Hào served as the military governor of Tiānpíng.
He donated seventy thousand *mín* of money, and the grand pavilion was completed.
This is the present Píngděng Gé.
Counting from the day the monk died and the statue was completed to Lǐ Hào's time,
it was exactly fifty years.
Was it not Chéngkōng's later incarnation?
Robbers Plunder Xiāowáng's Tomb
Xiāo Yǐngshì 濟 Guāzhōu,
among them were two youths who said:
“This person greatly resembles the loyal and valiant King of Póyáng.”
Yǐngshì said:
“I am his great-grandson.”
The two men said:
“We have known your ancestor for a long time.”
They hurriedly took their burdens and departed.
The following year,
he stopped at the office of the Yìzhǎng of Gǎnyí,
where an official had captured five or six tomb robbers,
and the two youths from the river were among them.
Yǐngshì said:
“These two are either immortals or spirits.”
He fully recounted the previous incident,
and the Yìzhǎng questioned them closely,
and they confessed, saying:
“We once opened the tomb of the King of Póyáng,
and obtained a large amount of gold and jade.
At the entrance, there was a nobleman lying as if alive,
who was identical to Yǐngshì.
How could we have any other method?”
I once heard that among the descendants of a person,
every three to five generations, there must be one who resembles their ancestor,
could this be proof of that?
White Dragon
During the Yuánhé era,
Wéi Yòu was appointed governor of Wēnzhōu.
He traveled by boat along the riverbank.
In the shallow sands and turbulent currents,
a reed branch had a new silk zither string.
Yòu pulled the reed and extended the string,
which was twice as long as a xún,
and it immediately tied itself back together.
Yòu gave it to a zither musician,
and soon it stretched out, wriggling,
and after a short while, it stirred and moved,
its two eyes clear.
Yòu was startled and said:
“Could it be a dragon?”
He burned incense and paid his respects,
then threw it into the river.
Winds and waves rose,
clouds steamed, and lightning flashed,
and within a咫尺 (a short distance), it became dark and gloomy.
There was a white dragon over a hundred zhàng long,
clutching and rising into the sky,
and it disappeared after a long time.
Collecting Feathers Fur Coat
During the reign of Zétiān,
the Nánhǎi region presented a Collecting Feathers Fur Coat.
The Empress then bestowed it upon Zhāng Chāngzōng.
Dí Rénjié came to report on matters,
and was ordered to play liùbó with Chāngzōng.
Zétiān said:
“What shall you wager?”
Liáng Gōng said:
“I will wager Chāngzōng’s fur coat,
and use my purple silk robe as the counter-wager.”
Zétiān said:
“This fur coat is worth over a thousand gold coins.”
Liáng Gōng said:
“My robe is the attire of a high official when attending court,
while Chāngzōng’s is the favored garment of a pampered minion.
To wager against my robe,
I am still discontent.”
Chāngzōng was crestfallen and disheartened,
losing game after game.
The Duke, in the presence of the Empress, removed the fur coat,
bowed in thanks, and departed.
When he reached Guāngfàn Mén,
he immediately gave it to his household slave to wear,
and rode off on his horse.
Wáng Wéi Passes the Examination
Wáng Wéi was renowned for his literary talent,
and naturally skilled in music.
Qí Wáng held him in high regard.
When Wéi was about to take the imperial examination,
there was Zhāng Jiǔgāo, who frequented the Ninth Princess’s residence,
and he had sent a letter to the examiner of Jīngzhào,
asking for Wéi to be made the top candidate (jiě tóu).
Qí Wáng said to Wéi:
“You can select ten of your clearest poems,
and compose one new pípa melody.
Go together to the Princess’s residence.”
The various musicians entered in succession,
and Wéi stood in the front row,
playing his new melody alone.
The Princess asked:
“What is the name of this piece?”
He replied:
“《Yùlúnpáo》.”
He then presented his scroll of poems.
The Princess said:
“I have long recited and studied all of these,
believing them to be fine works of ancient poets.
Are they truly by you?”
She ordered him to change his clothes
and sit to her right.
The Princess said:
“If the Jīngzhào official can have this student as the jiě tóu this year,
it would truly be a national glory.”
He replied:
“I have already received the esteemed Princess’s endorsement to Jiǔgāo.”
The Princess said:
“Initially, he was entrusted by someone else.”
She then summoned the examiner for Wéi and conveyed her message,
and Wéi thus passed the examination in one attempt.
Singing Girls Recite Poems
During the Kāiyuán era,
the poets Wáng Chānglíng, Gāo Shì, and Wáng Huànzhī went together to Qítíng for a small drink.
There was a gathering of Liyuán musicians celebrating,
and four singing girls arrived afterward,
all famous performers.
Chānglíng and the others said:
“We are renowned for our poetry,
but our superiority has not yet been determined.
We can observe which poets’ verses the singing girls sing the most,
and the one with more will be deemed superior.”
One singing girl sang two jueju by Chānglíng, saying:
“The cold rain over the river enters Wú at night,
at dawn, a solitary Chu sail bids farewell to guests.
If friends and relatives in Luòyáng ask about me,
my pure heart is like ice in a jade vase.”
“Sweeping the floor, the golden palace opens at dawn,
reluctantly holding a round fan, I linger.
My jade countenance is not as good as the color of a cold crow,
still bringing the sunlight from Zhāoyáng.”
Another singing girl recited a jueju by Gāo Shì, saying:
“Opening the chest, tears wet my bosom,
seeing your letter from the other day.
How lonely is the netherworld,
it is still like Zǐyún’s dwelling.”
Huànzhī said:
“The songs sung by the musicians are all vulgar words.
If the songs sung by the fine singing girls are not my poems,
I will never dare to compete with you all my life.
But if they are my poems,
you all must bow before the bed.”
A moment later,
a fine singing girl said:
“Yellow sand stretches far up to the white clouds, still,
a solitary city within ten thousand ren of mountains.
Why should the Qiāng flute lament the willows?
The spring breeze does not cross Yùmén Guān.”
Huànzhī ridiculed the two men, saying:
“You country bumpkins,
was I boasting idly?”
The other musicians did not understand the reason,
and bowed in unison, saying:
“Our mundane eyes failed to recognize an immortal,
please deign to join our banquet.”
The three men complied,
