and drank merrily all day.
Zhāng Yì Is Appointed Prime Minister
Dàizōng orally promised Zhāng Yì the position of prime minister.
Suddenly, he dreamed:
“Zhùdiào (stay tuned) for appointment as prime minister.”
Yì pondered, thinking there was no such person among those inside or outside the court.
His nephew, Lǐ Tōnglǐ, said:
“Zhùdiào is a reverse wordplay for ráotián ráotián (sweet, sweet).
None is like gāncǎo (licorice),
which is uniquely a precious medicine (zhēnyào).
The reverse of 'precious medicine' (zhēnyào)
is precisely your name.”
Shortly after, a report came that the imperial edict (bái má) was issued,
and the Duke was indeed appointed Píngzhāngshì.
Zhēnyào Zhen Bì,
Zhāng Yāng Yǎng Yàng,
Yàojiàn.
Mountain Spirit Avenges
The Magistrate of Xiāoshān, Wéi Zhīwēi,
found his county plagued by many mountain spirits (shānxiāo).
Previous officials had treated them as gods.
Zhīwēi burned and killed almost all of them.
Suddenly, Xiāo Zào came to visit,
saying:
“I obtained an adorable monkey cub in Xiázhōu.”
He then took out a small box,
which contained a monkey the size of a chestnut.
Immediately, it transformed into a tiger,
devouring everyone in the house, leaving no one behind.
Duke Dí’s Wonderful Needle
Dí Liánggōng’s nature was attuned to medicine and
he was especially skilled in acupuncture.
During the Xiǎnqìng period,
he was summoned to the capital.
By the roadside, a large notice read:
“Whoever can cure this child
shall be rewarded with a thousand bolts of silk.”
There was a wealthy family’s child whose nose had a growth like a fist-sized stone,
attached to the root of the nose,
with a stalk like a tendon,
causing severe and critical pain.
The Duke inserted a needle behind the child’s head,
and the growth fell off instantly.
The parents presented a thousand bolts of silk in a carriage,
but the Duke left without a glance.
Wáng Jīxīn Hears a Mother-in-Law and Daughter-in-Law Playing Go
Wáng Jīxīn, a Go player in the Hánlín Academy, followed Mínghuáng on his western journey.
He lodged in a remote mountain family’s home,
where there were only a mother-in-law and a daughter-in-law,
who merely provided water and fire.
As soon as it was dark,
they closed the door.
Jīxīn heard the mother-in-law say to the daughter-in-law:
“This beautiful night, there’s nothing to do for entertainment.
Shall we play Go together?”
There was no candle in the hall,
and the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law were in separate rooms, east and west.
The daughter-in-law said:
“Place a stone at east five, south nine.”
The mother-in-law said:
“Place a stone at east five, south twelve.”
The daughter-in-law said:
“Place a stone at west eight, south nine.”
The mother-in-law said:
“Place a stone at west nine, south ten.”
By the fourth watch of the night,
they had only placed thirty-six stones.
The mother-in-law said:
“You’ve gone too far north!
I’ve only won by nine intersections.”
At dawn,
he inquired of the old woman,
who looked at the daughter-in-law and said:
“This child can be taught the common strategies.”
The daughter-in-law then demonstrated methods of attack, defense, capture, taking, response, refusal, prevention, and rescue,
very briefly.
The old woman said:
“Just this,
and she will be unrivalled in the world.”
Jīxīn walked a few steps,
then looked back, and the house he had been in was gone.
From then on, his skill was unmatched.
He exhausted his mind trying to analyze the strategies of the nine intersections,
but could never fully grasp them.
He then named it “Dèng Ài’s Strategy for Attacking Shǔ.”
《Shǐ Yí》 also records this.
Wénchāng Becomes a Chancellor; Yǔxī Turns to His Original Department
Duàn Wénchāng was talented but arrogant.
In Jiānglíng, there was a large mansion
whose gate faced a stream.
The Duke, while drunk, said:
“When I become the Military Governor of Jiānglíng,
I will surely buy this residence.”
All who heard him laughed at his madness.
Later, he indeed became the defender of Jīngnán
and bought this residence.
He also once served Wéi Gāo as an inspecting official in Chéngdū,
but suddenly fell out of favor,
and was made acting county magistrate of Língchí.
He rushed to the county seat.
Six or seven *lǐ* later, it was already dark,
and the road was devoid of travelers.
Suddenly, two torches appeared, leading the way,
and a voice called out:
“Grand Commandant is coming!”
When he reached the city gate,
the torches extinguished.
Liú Yǔxī was previously a supernumerary official in the Ministry of Rites.
A diviner once said:
“Your promotion is far off.
Ten years later, when Lord Duàn becomes a chancellor,
you will then be transferred back to your original department as a principal secretary.”
From then on, Yǔxī was continuously appointed to outer official posts for over ten years.
When Wénchāng became a chancellor,
Yǔxī was then appointed as a Director of the Ministry of Rites.
Mysterious Origin Statue
The essence of the planet Venus fell to the west of Guīfēng in Zhōngnán,
and was therefore named Tàibái Mountain.
Its essence transformed into a white stone,
covered by a purple aura.
Xuánzōng erected the Xuányuán Temple in Cháng’ān
and dreamt that a divine being said:
“The Tàibái jade stone can be carved into a statue.”
The emperor sent an envoy to dig, and they unearthed the jade stone.
It was carved into the Xuányuán statue.
It was about two *zhàng* tall,
depicting two true immortals,
two attendant boys, and the forms of Lǐ Línfǔ and Chén Xīliè,
about six *chǐ* tall.
Sand Fleas
In Tán, Yuán, and other prefectures, there are sand fleas,
which are lice found among the scales of poisonous snakes.
They are tiny and invisible.
In summer,
when snakes are tormented by these fleas,
they lie belly-up in the swift currents of riverbanks,
allowing the water to wash off the fleas;
or they lie in the sand,
grinding the fleas into the sand.
When travelers are afflicted by them,
it feels like a needle prick or a grain of millet,
with five-colored patterns all around,
which is their poison.
If a sorcerer can use an incantation to treat it,
and a small piece of flesh is cut out, it will heal.
Otherwise, one will die in two or three days.
Gu Poison
The *shǔinǔ* insect is shaped like a dung beetle,
black with eight legs,
and a tail several inches long;
this is the *nǔ*.
From the first day of the fourth month, the *nǔ* emerges,
and it retreats in the eighth month.
It shoots when it sees a human shadow.
Where the shadow is hit,
a sore and swelling appear on the body.
Its poison is similar to that of the sand flea.
It is necessary to quickly suppress the *qì* [with an incantation]
and cut out the poisoned flesh.
There is also *gǔ* poison.
Whenever entering a house with *gǔ* poison,
one must forewarn the host, saying:
“Your house has *gǔ* poison;
do not easily harm me.”
If done this way, the poison will not act.
Green Pig and Fierce Beast
Huáng Wànyòu practiced cultivation in Qiánnán.
King Jiàn of Shǔ welcomed him into his palace
and asked his age.
He replied:
“I only remember being invited out in the year when the Marquis of Yèláng ruled Shǔ and when the Cáncóng clan established their capital in Pí.
Later, the sun and moon raced,
flowers bloomed and withered,
and I do not remember the *jiǎzǐ* cycle.”
Later, he firmly declined and returned to the mountains.
After he left,
he wrote on the wall of his dwelling:
“Do not let the green pig’s foot be moved;
if moved, it will burn fiercely and cannot be extinguished.
The fierce beast does not wish for both ends to be yellow;
if they turn yellow, that year the world will weep.”
By the *yǐhài* year,
there was a fire in the inner palace,
and the treasury was completely reduced to ashes.
Only then was it known that the *Tàisuì* *yǐhài* [year]
was the time for the green pig’s burning.
Later, in the *wùyín* year, associated with earth, Jiàn died.
*Yín* is the fierce beast,
and both the celestial stem and the *nàyīn* are earth,
which is why it said ‘both ends yellow.’
Fish of the Hàn River
Táng Huánjūn was traveling at the Lèyào Pool of the Hàn River.
He caught a fish
several *chǐ* long,
with words on it saying:
“Thrice have I crossed the sea,
twice ascended the Hàn.
Having reached Lè Pool,
my fate belongs to Huánjūn.”
Three Bandits Executed on the Same Month and Day
On the first day of the eleventh month of Xiànzōng’s first year, Liú Pì was beheaded.
On the first day of the eleventh month of his second year, Lǐ Qí was beheaded.
On the first day of the eleventh month of his twelfth year, Wú Yuánjì was beheaded.
The three bandits were executed on the same month and day.
Yuánzhèn’s Two Parents Alive
Lǐ Yōng’s epitaph for Guō Yuánzhèn states:
“Among Tang chancellors,
Yuánzhèn was the only one whose two parents were still alive.”
Three Generations of Chancellors
Zhāng Jiāzhēn’s son Yánshǎng,
and Yánshǎng’s son Hóngjìng,
succeeded as chancellors.
Thrice Appointed to Zhōngshū
Zhāng Yuè was thrice appointed to Zhōngshū,
and remained untainted throughout;
this had never happened in ancient times.
Became Chancellor Three Years After Starting His Career
Zhāng Hào was first appointed Zuǒ Shíyí,
then Yòu Bǔquē,
then Probationary Yùshǐ,
then Jiànyì Dàfū,
and finally Zhōngshū Shìláng Píngzhāngshì.
He rose from a humble background to govern in three years,
a feat unprecedented in history.
Shèrén Appointed Shìláng
Zhāng Shuō's son Jūn and grandson Méng,
across three generations, were appointed Shìláng from Zhōngshū Shèrén.
Tiānshuǐ Bì
In the final years of Lǐ Hòuzhǔ,
palace maids competed to wear blue-green clothing.
They extracted indigo flowers,
filled them with rainwater,
clarified it, and dyed the fabric with it,
calling it Tiānshuǐ Bì.
A Daoist Sings the Ci Poem "Gǎntíng Qiū"
In Shǔ, there was a mad Daoist
who went to the Zǐjí Gōng to visit Master Dù Guāngtíng, seeking lodging.
Morning and evening, he would drink himself drunk
and sing the Ci poem "Gǎntíng Qiū".
One evening,
the lamps and candles glowed brightly,
and many were seated.
The Daoist sat upright,
attended by two green-clad boys.
Guāngtíng peeked through the door and said:
"My knowledge is shallow and ordinary;
I did not expect an celestial being to descend.
I prostrate myself at your gate,
hoping to pay homage to your divine presence."
The Daoist replied:
"Why should you bother, esteemed Master, with such diligent study?"
He then ordered the two boys to gather and fold the banquet utensils.
As they did so, the items shrunk in their hands,
like talismans.
He then combined the two boys into a single wooden puppet,
about an inch tall,
and placed them all inside his hat.
Then he opened the door.
Guāngtíng joyfully entered,
but nothing was to be seen;
only the four walls remained.
Táo Gǔ's Eye Change
When Táo Gǔ was young,
he dreamed that several officials said:
"We are commanded to change your eyes."
An official whispered in his ear, asking for 100,000 cash
to install the first eye, but
Gǔ did not respond.
The official then said 50,000 cash
for the second eye,
but again he did not answer.
The official said:
"We will just install the third eye."
Immediately, he placed two pellets into Gǔ's eyes.
When he awoke,
his eyes were a deep blue-green.
Later, a skilled physiognomist, the Daoist Chén Zǐyáng, said:
"You have a noble and aristocratic aura,
but what can be done about your pair of ghost eyes?
You will certainly not reach a high position."
Lǐ Yù Becomes King of the Sīzi Guó
When Jiǎ Huángzhōng was guarding Jīnlíng,
a person vaguely appeared and presented a calling card saying:
"The former ruler, Lǐ Yù, respectfully visits."
When he appeared,
he was a thin Daoist.
Jiǎ understood his intention
and said:
"How could the Grand Tutor reach such a state?"
Lǐ replied:
"When I was young, I chose the Buddhist path,
but I did not achieve complete understanding;
I had some mistaken perceptions.
Now I am the king of Sīzi Guó.
Just now I was thinking of Zhōngshān,
so I came to see you."
He took a poem from his bosom and handed it to Jiǎ,
then suddenly disappeared.
The poem read:
"A foreign land is not my will,
the weariness and toil never cease.
Ten thousand miles of wind and waves,
I will never again see Zhōngshān."
Jiǎ read it,
and it instantly turned to ash and vanished.
The Qin Woman Punished to Be a Ewe
Liú Dàofāng served as the Magistrate of Péngxī.
After his term, he returned to the capital,
spending the night at the home of a wealthy man named Qín in the county.
Suddenly, he saw a red-clad woman weeping and saying:
"I was originally the daughter-in-law of the Qín family.
My husband bought a concubine,
and as my nature was strong, I could not tolerate her.
So I was beaten by my son and died.
That concubine appealed to the underworld to apprehend him,
and my son has already paid with his life.
My remaining karma is to be punished as a ewe,
and I am now in the Qín family's pen.
Because of your visit, Your Excellency,
they are about to cook me for your meal.
While I am willing to endure death as a sheep,
I have a lamb in my womb.
If I am cooked now,
my karma will become even heavier.
I beg to die after I have given birth, without regret."
Dàofāng warned the host to come out
and conveyed his wishes,
saying that he privately abstained from meat and blood,
and insisted that no animals be cooked.
At dawn,
someone came out to tell him,
smiling, "We have already cooked the sheep."
Dàofāng sighed in surprise
and recounted the events of the night.
The entire Qín family was deeply moved
and buried the lamb within its mother's belly.
Poem Inscribed on a Paulownia Leaf
Zhāng Shìjié was a guest in Shòuyáng.
Having had some wine, he walked along the Huái River
and entered the Dragon Temple.
He saw the exquisitely beautiful statue of a dragon maiden behind the curtain
and, inscribing a poem on a paulownia leaf, threw it behind the curtain,
saying:
"I am the one who paints with a gifted brush in dreams,
inscribing this on a leaf to send to the morning clouds."
Suddenly, he saw a beautiful woman in the house,
so Shìjié went to her.
Wine was served,
and the woman recited:
"Lower the sail and moor by the small sandbank,
the frosty moon casts no ripples, the Huái River is cold.
If you get news from the rivers and lakes,
please send word of the wind and water to Cháng'ān."
Shìjié became heavily drunk.
When he awoke,
he was sitting alone on a stone by the temple gate.
A small maidservant said:
"My mistress sends word,
returning your paulownia leaf.
Do not dwell on it further."
Dragons Have Genders
Liú Dòngwēi was skilled at painting dragons.
One day,
a couple came to his door and said:
"Dragons have genders,
and their forms differ.
The male has sharp horns, concave waves (on its body),
deep eyes, a flared nose,
large mane, dense scales,
is robust above and slender below,
with fiery red glow.
The female has soft horns, flat waves,
wide eyes, a straight nose,
a round mane, sparse scales,
a tail more robust than its belly,
and is completely transparent and awe-inspiring."
Liú Dòngwēi asked:
"How do you know this?"
The person replied:
"We ourselves are dragons."
They then transformed into two dragons and flew away.
Crane-Transformation Elixir
Xǔ Áo possessed magical arts.
Whenever he refined elixirs for people,
he would always take a substantial amount to buy herbs and build a furnace,
asking the person to guard it themselves.
Each refining took
forty-nine days to complete.
As it was about to be finished, there would always be a large wildcat
that would break the furnace,
and two cranes would fly away.
This happened every time,
so people called it the "Crane-Transformation Elixir".
Poem on the Wall of the Secret Chamber
During the Chúnhuà reign,
on a high wall in the Secret Chamber, there was a couplet of poetry that read:
"Cool breezes send away the heat,
the courtyard trees' leaves all fall."
A little over a month later,
Sòng Yán, Yè Qí, and Qí Zhíshū
all departed due to various matters.
Silkworm Flight
During the Duāngǒng [reign era],
in Chángrùn, after the silkworms of the common people had completed their major sleep,
one day,
there were insects like locusts,
obscuring the sun as they flew,
passing north of the river.
Those that were unable to continue and fell
were indeed silkworms.
That year,
among the common people of Tōngtài, some households' silkworms yielded dozens of times [the usual amount].
Later, there was a great famine in Wúzhōng,
and most of the people died.
Wáng Shēng did not eat.
Zhāng Shēng,
a notorious thief in the capital,
knew a certain Yùshānrén [Jade Mountain Man]
with whom he had a close acquaintance.
[Yùshānrén] knew that [Zhāng Shēng] had not eaten cooked food for fifty years.
Zhāng sought [help from Wáng Shēng].
Wáng used two items spread in three layers,
and took them for two days.
"On the first day, you will feel very hungry;
be sure not to think of eating.
On the second day, you will still be hungry;
you must not think of eating.
After the third day, you will never eat again."
Shēng took them,
and it indeed worked.
Several years later,
he suddenly saw Wáng Shēng looking weak and frail.
Shēng, feeling pity, said:
"My brother, you have abstained from food for so long,
how can you have this illness?"
Wáng said:
"It is because the drug's poison accumulated and was never dispelled.
Your own medicine will act up someday,
and you will also be like this."
Shēng wanted to prevent the medicine from acting up.
Wáng said:
"Go home and eat mallow soup,
and take bàdòu [croton seeds].
Then the medicine in your belly will cause no future trouble."
Shēng went home and took it,
and had diarrhea for several days.
Its odor was all fragrant,
and later he passed a lump of yellow fat,
glistening brightly,
with a small hole in the middle,
large enough to fit a hairpin.
This was the passage for air to move up and down.
In total, three lumps were passed,
which were the two items he had spread out previously.
Later, he suddenly met Lord Wáng,
whose complexion was as before.
Shēng happily asked him,
and he said it was due to the former medicine,
which, if not dispelled, would also not harm people.
Shēng greatly regretted [his actions],
then realized that Wáng Shēng had been testing him.
End of volume eight.
Essays Selected
Reading *Wénxuǎn* in the boat,
I regret its disordered arrangement
and improper selections.
The writings of the Qí and Liáng dynasties are weak and crude,
and Xiāo Tǒng's in particular are inferior and weak.
For instance, the five-character poems attributed to Lǐ Líng are all forgeries.
Today, upon reading Táo Yuānmíng's collection, many pieces are delightful,
yet [Xiāo Tǒng] only selected a few.
Táo Yuānmíng's composition of "Xiánqíng Fù" [Rhapsody on Idle Emotions]
is precisely what is meant by *Guófēng* being fond of beauty without being licentious.
Even if it does not reach the level of *Zhōunán*,
how is it different from what Qū Yuán presented?
Yet Tǒng greatly ridiculed it;
this is a child pretending to understand affairs.
Three premature deaths
Lǐ Shàn's commentary on *Wénxuǎn* is detailed and comprehensive from beginning to end.
The so-called five commentators
are truly ignorant and crude scholars.
The poem "Yǒng Zhāng Zǐfáng" [Ode to Zhāng Zǐfáng] says:
"The cruelties and evils inflicted three premature deaths."
This refers to the three premature deaths—upper, middle, and lower—mentioned in the *Lǐ* [Book of Rites],
meaning that the Qín dynasty was without the Way,
and its killings extended even to the young.
However, the commentary quotes: "Harsh government is fiercer than a tiger;
my father, my husband, and my son all died."
To refer to husband and father as "prematurely dead" is a great fallacy.
Solar and lunar eclipses
Yùchuānzi's "Yuèshí Shī" [Poem on a Lunar Eclipse] states that the one who eats the moon is the toad in the moon.
Méi Shèngyú's "Rìshí Shī" [Poem on a Solar Eclipse] says
that the one who eats the sun is the three-legged crow.
These are based on folk legends to convey meaning.
*Zhànguócè* [Strategies of the Warring States] says:
"The sun and moon shine externally,
but their enemies are within."
Thus, the folk legends are also correct.
Central Palace Tàiyǐ
Dù Zǐměi's poem says, "Since the pacification of the Central Palace's Lǚ Tàiyǐ."
The world does not understand its meaning,
and some mistakenly believe that there was a "Central Palace" in the Táng dynasty.
I happened to read *Xuánzōng Shílù* [Veritable Records of Emperor Xuánzōng],
which mentions, "Tàiyǐ of the Central Palace rebelled in Guǎngnán."
Dù's poem says, "Since the pacification of Lǚ Tàiyǐ in the palace."
The text below it contains a line about collecting pearls in Hǎinán.
Not having read widely,
and lightly changing words,
few avoid being laughed at.
Eight Battle Formations Poem
My son once dreamed that Dù Zǐměi said:
"People in the world misunderstand the 'Bāzhèntú' [Eight Battle Formations] [poem].
The lines 'The river flows, but the stones do not turn; the lingering regret is for failing to swallow Wú.'
They believe that the Former Lord [Liú Bèi] and the Martial Marquis [Zhūgě Liàng] wanted to avenge Guān Yǔ,
and therefore regretted not destroying Wú.
This is incorrect!
My intention was that Wú and Shǔ were like lips and teeth to each other,
and should not have plotted against one another.
The reason Jìn was able to conquer Shǔ
was because Shǔ harbored the intention of swallowing Wú.
This is the regret."
Sincerity without malice believed by other species
When I was young,
bamboo, cypress, and various flowers grew in front of my study,
and many birds nested there.
Lord Wǔyáng detested killing,
and his maids and servants were not allowed to catch [the birds].
After several years,
birds nested on low branches,
and their chicks could be observed from above.
This was due to nothing else
but the sincerity of not being malicious,
which was trusted by other species.
Three repetitions of Yángguān
It was formerly said that "Yángguān Sāndié" [Three Repetitions of Yángguān]
meant that the singer repeated each line twice and that was it.
If understood as the entire song,
it would be four repetitions,
neither of which is correct.
If each line were sung three times to correspond to "three repetitions,"
then it would become a jumble without rhythm.
A certain Wén Xūn
obtained an ancient version of "Yángguān,"
where each line was sung twice,
but the first line was not repeated.
Thus, it is known that the Táng version of "three repetitions" was like this.
Bái Lètiān's poem says:
"When we meet, do not refuse wine,
listen to the fourth verse of Yángguān being sung."
"I urge you to drink one more cup of wine,"
using this to verify it.
If a line were repeated twice,
then this line would be the fifth verse.
Now it is the fourth,
so it is certain that the first line is not repeated.
Capricorn as the Dangers Palace
Hán Tuìzhī's poem says:
"At the time of my birth,
the moon lodged directly in Dǒu."
From this, it is known that Capricorn was Hán Tuìzhī's shēngōng [Dangers Palace].
I have Capricorn as my mìnggōng [Life Palace],
and throughout my life, I have suffered much slander and defamation.
We are probably afflicted by the same condition.
Treating eyes and teeth
Zhāng Wénqián said:
"For eye diseases, avoid applying drops and washing.
When the eye is ill, it should be preserved;
when the tooth is ill, it should be treated.
Treating the eyes is like governing the people;
treating the teeth is like commanding the army.
Governing the people is like Cáo Cān governing Qí;
commanding the army is like Shāng Yāng governing Qín."
Explanation of *Lǎozǐ*
Zǐyóu sent his *Lǎozǐ Xīnjiě* [New Explanations of Lǎozǐ].
If this book had existed during the Warring States period,
there would have been no Shāng Yāng or Hán Fēi.
If this book had existed in the early Hàn dynasty,
then Kǒng and Lǎo would have been one.
If this book had existed between Jìn and Sòng,
then Fó and Lǎo would not have been two.
Three Grand Poems
Shí Jiè 史介 composed "Ode to the Three Heroes," saying:
"Màn Qīng 曼卿 is heroic in poetry;
Yǒng Shū 永叔 is heroic in history;
Dù Diǎn 杜點 and Shī Xióng 師雄 are heroic in song."
Yǒng Shū 永叔 also presented Diǎn 點 with a poem, saying:
"I presented them with the 'Three Heroes' poem,
and I wrongly took one of the names."
Diǎn's 點 songs are rarely seen in the world,
but some say:
"An old dragon in the waves of the sea of learning,
a great tiger at the Master's gate."
All such phrases.
Yǒng Shū 永叔 did not criticize him
because this gentleman disliked contending for fame
and also out of respect for Jiè 介.
Diǎn's 點 heroic spirit was precisely that of a scholar from Jīngdōng 京東,
drinking private wine,
eating beef from animals that died of malaria,
and speaking what came after being sated and drunk.
His poetry was wild and bizarre,
reaching its extreme with Lú Tóng 盧仝 and Mǎ Yì 馬異.
If one were to seek such a person further,
they would become Dù Diǎn 杜點.
Wànhuā Huì 萬花會
The peonies of Yángzhōu 揚州 were the best in the world at the Wànhuā Huì 萬花會.
When Cài Jīng 蔡京 was the prefect,
he first established the Wànhuā Huì 萬花會.
Over ten thousand branches of flowers were used,
which distressed the local officials,
who then engaged in corruption.
I was the first to abolish it.
The Wànhuā Huì 萬花會 was originally a custom in Luòshī 洛師,
which also harmed the people.
When Qián Wéiyǎn 錢惟演 became the留守 liúshǒu,
he first set up post stations to tribute Luò 洛 flowers.
The discerning scorned this,
which was merely a gesture of palace maids' love for their lord.
Nòng Húsūn 弄猢猻
Chén Dūn 陳敦 said:
"Monkeys wear human clothes,
bending, turning, bowing, and rising according to measure.
If one looks closely,
their contempt is quite severe.
People speak of playing with monkeys,
unaware that they are being played with by monkeys."
This statement has some truth.
Zhì Dàfēng Fāng 治大風方
Wáng Yóu Yuánlóng 王游元龍 said:
"Sūn Zǐfēi 孫子飛 had a highly effective remedy for leprosy (dàfēng 大風),
which he often administered to people.
One day he dreamt a person said:
'The celestial beings caused this illness.
If you, a ruler, defy Heaven's wrath,
and continue to administer it without ceasing,
you will contract this disease,
and medicine will not save you.'
Zǐfēi 孫子飛 was afraid
and consequently stopped administering it."
I believe that if an illness is caused by Heaven,
is it incurable?
Then the medicine should not be effective.
If the medicine is effective,
then Heaven cannot cause the illness.
It must be that the affliction respects and fears the medicine,
and merely uses Heaven to forbid people.
Zǐfēi 孫子飛 did not discern this
and was threatened by ghosts.
I am not like that;
if the patient can be cured,
I would willingly bear their suffering.
My family has a remedy
that can purge internal filth,
which I should now often administer to people.
Jiǔ Míng 酒名
Tuì Zhī 退之's poem says:
"One can diligently buy 'Pāo Qīngchūn 拋青春' ."
The Guóshǐ Bǔ 國史補 says:
"Wines include Yǐng Zhī Fùchūn 郢之富春,
Wū Chéng Zhī Ruòchūn 烏程之若春,
Xíngyáng Zhī Tǔkūchūn 滎陽之土窟春,
Fùpíng Zhī Shídòngchūn 富平之石凍春,
and Jiànnán Zhī Shāochūn 劍南之燒春."
Dù Zǐměi 杜子美 said:
"I hear of Yún'ān Qūmǐchūn 雲安麴米春."
Péi Xíng 裴鉶's Chuánqí 傳奇
also has a wine named Sōngláochūn 松醪春.
Thus, it is known that many Tang people named their wines with "chūn 春."
Lùn Shī 論詩
When the culture and artifacts of Tang, Song, and the Five Dynasties declined,
poetry had a concrete form,
and calligraphy had Yà Qī 亞栖.
The rustic and vulgar atmosphere
was generally similar.
Sū Zǐměi 蘇子美 had a long letter saying:
"Behind the screen, the song is already beautiful;
sitting opposite, the appearance is even more refined."
The language is both ordinary and bad,
and the calligraphy style is truly of Yà Qī's 亞栖 lineage.
Zēng Zǐgù 曾子固 compiled the Lǐ Tàibái Jí 李太白集,
which contains "Song on Huáisù's 懷素 Cursive Script" and "Smile."
Several pieces were by Guàn Xiū 貫休 and later,
with humble and crude styles.
Zǐgù 子固 was known as discerning and knowledgeable,
so this is deeply strange.
Such as Bái Lètiān 白樂天's gift to Xú Níng 徐凝,
and Tuì Zhī 退之's gift to Jiǎ Dǎo 賈島,
these were all fabricated by ignorant common people,
and are not too surprising.
Jìn Tóng Shěng Wǎnglái 禁同省往來
In the first year of Yuányòu 元祐 (1086),
I was a Zhōngshū Shèrén 中書舍人.
The presiding officials worried that many matters of the department were being leaked,
and wanted to build a fence behind the Shèrén 舍人 hall,
to forbid movement between colleagues in the same department.
I said:
"Presiding officials should be simple, essential, clear, and open.
Why must they erect fences and plant thorns?"
The gentlemen laughed and stopped.
The next year, however, it was built.
One idle day, I happened to read Bái Lètiān's 白樂天 poetry,
which contained:
"In the newly built small pavilion in the north court of the Western Department,
bamboo is planted, and windows are opened.
Lǐ Chángshì 李常侍 from the Eastern Department drinks a little wine and composes poetry through the window."
Thus, I learned that in the Tang dynasty, the Western Department was allowed to have windows opening to the Eastern Department for communication,
but now, in this very department, movement is forbidden.
Alas!
Liú Yuánfù Yǔ 劉原父語
Liú Yuánfù 劉原父 once said while in a drunken state:
"Chén Jìbì 陳季弼 said to Chén Yuánlóng 陳元龍:
'The opinions near and far
say that you, my lord, are arrogant.'
Yuánlóng 元龍 replied:
'Within the family, harmonious and solemn,
virtuous and upright,
I respect Chén Yuánfāng 陳元方 and his brothers;
profoundly clear and pure as jade,
observing rites and laws,
I respect Huá Zǐyú 華子魚;
pure and upright, abhorring evil,
discerning and righteous,
I respect Zhào Yuándá 趙元達;
broadly learned and strong in memory,
I respect Kǒng Wénjǔ 孔文舉;
heroic and outstanding,
I respect Liú Xuándé 劉玄德.
My respects are thus.
What arrogance is there?
As for the rest of the trivial men,
why bother recording them?'
Then he sighed to the heavens."
This was Yuánfù's 原父 refined taste.
I once wrote a poem saying:
"In my life, I too scorned other men;
in old age, who remembers this old man?"
It records Yuánfù's 原父 words.
Yuánfù 原父 died,
but Gòngfù 貢父 was still alive,
and every word of his was compelling.
Now he too is dead.
When will I ever see such outstanding men again?
Alas!
Xī Dòng Huà Lǐ Shīzhōng Xiàng 溪洞畫李師中像
Guō Xiángzhèng 郭祥正 followed Zhāng Dùn 章惇 into the Měishān Xī Dòng 梅山溪洞.
They saw a portrait in the home of Sū Gān 蘇甘, the cave king,
which was revered with great solemnity.
They said it was Lǐ Dàfū 李大夫 from Guìfǔ 桂府.
When asked his name,
they said:
"How can this be named?"
They kowtowed and confessed to capital crimes several times,
but ultimately dared not name him.
They then examined the dates
and indeed it was Lǐ Shīzhōng Chéngzhī 李師中誠之.
He had once served as Tíxíng 提刑
and temporarily held the post of Guìfǔ 桂府.
The barbarians and savages were thus in awe and trust of him.
Hán Yùrǔ Lǐ Jīnwú 韓玉汝李金吾
When Hán Zhěn 韓縝 was in Qínzhōu 秦州,
he lost his official post due to killing innocents as a bandit.
The people of Qín 秦 said:
"Better to encounter a nursing tiger
than Hán Yùrǔ 韓玉汝."
Sūn Lín 孫臨 was most witty.
Someone asked:
"If 'better not to encounter Hán Yùrǔ 韓玉汝,'
what should be the response?"
Lín 臨 said:
"Why fear Lǐ Jīnwú 李金吾?"
Shū Gōng Fēng Jīng Gōng
Wáng Jièfǔ was first enfeoffed as Shū Gōng,
then enfeoffed as Jīng Gōng.
A poem says:
“The Róng and Dí are struck down,
Jīng and Shū are chastised.”
Those who knew said:
“This is the prime minister’s fault for not studying.”
Changing Texts by Conjecture
In recent times, people lightly change texts by conjecture.
Shallow-minded people,
whose likes and dislikes are often similar,
then echo them,
causing ancient texts to become increasingly erroneous and incorrect.
Kǒngzǐ said:
“I can still refer to the historian’s omissions.”
The Shǔ edition of the *Zhuāngzǐ* says:
“When one’s will is undivided,
one then doubts the spirits.”
This is similar to the *Yì*’s “Yīn doubts Yáng” and the *Lǐ*’s “making others doubt you about the Master.”
Now, all editions from the four directions render it as “níng” (congeal).
Táo Qián’s poem:
“Picking chrysanthemums beneath the eastern hedge,
I leisurely behold the southern mountain.”
While picking chrysanthemums,
he accidentally saw the mountain,
the scene and the sentiment coinciding.
Now, all editions render it as “gazing at the southern mountain.”
Dù Zǐměi said:
“White gulls disappear into the vast expanse.”
This means they vanished into the mist and waves.
But Sòng Mǐnqíu said, “Gulls cannot disappear,
so it should be changed to ‘bō’ (waves).”
Changing these two characters in these two poems,
makes the whole piece feel spiritless and diminished.
Writing the Autumn Rain Poem
Mǎ Zhèngqīng from Qǐ copied Dù Zǐměi’s “Tàn” (Lament on Autumn Rain) in its entirety.
Originally, there was no intention to display it on the wall.
Zhèngqīng immediately resigned and retired, never to return to public life,
remaining white-haired to this day,
steadfastly adhering to his principles in poverty.
Dù Zǐměi’s Poems
When I was in Qíshān,
I saw a horse presented from Qínzhōu;
its mane was like an ox’s,
with a heavy, inverted dewlap under its neck,
and hair growing from fleshy protrusions.
The Barbarians said:
“This is a fleshy mane.”
Then I realized that Dèng Gōng’s “Cōngmǎ” (Dappled Horse) poem’s line “ròu zōng wěi lěi lián qián bù” (fleshy mane, rugged and resembling linked cash)
should be “ròu jùn” (fleshy steed).
“Bēi Chéntáo” (Lament for Chéntáo) says:
“Loyal warriors from all four directions died on the same day.”
This refers to Fáng Guǎn’s defeat.
The *Táng Shū* writes Chéntāo;
it is unknown which is correct.
After Guǎn’s defeat,
he still wished to maintain his strength and await an opportunity,
but the palace eunuchs urged battle,
leading to a crushing defeat.
Therefore, a later section says:
“How can I send a letter to our army,
to endure and wait for next year, not to rush?”
The “Běizhēng” (Northern Expedition) poem says:
“The valiant General Chén,
wielded his axe and displayed loyalty and valor.”
This refers to Chén Xuánlǐ,
who assisted Xuánzōng in quelling the internal rebellion,
and also followed him in his flight to Shǔ,
proposing the plan to execute Guózhōng.
“Xǐ Bīngmǎ” (Washing Weapons and Horses) says:
“Minister Zhāng was a wanderer by rivers and seas his whole life.”
This refers to Zhāng Hào.
Although Mínghuáng executed Xiāo Zhìzhōng,
he always cherished his memory.
“Hóu Jūnjí” says:
“To be thwarted to this extent.”
Was Zhìzhōng also thwarted?
Therefore, Dù Zǐměi also lamented him, saying, “The illustrious Xiāo Jīngzhào,
is now pitied by the times.”
The “Hòu Chūsài” (Later Expedition to the Frontier) poem says:
“I was originally from a good family,
and there were many ways for me to join the army.
Having ridden horses for thirty years,
I feared I might fail to repay the wise lord’s grace.
Sitting, I watched the Yōuzhōu cavalry,
charging far and wide until Héluò grew dim.
At midnight, I returned via a side path,
only to find my old village desolate.
Fortunately, I escaped ill repute,
and grew old without sons or grandsons.”
Carefully savoring this poem,
it describes how, when Lùshān rebelled,
one of his generals escaped and returned to the country,
but Lùshān killed his wife and children.
His name is not mentioned,
which is regrettable.
The “Yì Xī” (Recalling the Past) poem says:
“A small boy from Guānzhōng ruined the order.”
This refers to Lǐ Fǔguó.
“Empress Zhāng was unhappy, the emperor was busy on her behalf.”
This refers to Empress Zhāng of Sùzōng.
“Leaving fierce warriors to guard Wèiyāng.”
This refers to Guō Zǐyí seizing military command and entering the palace guard.
Things Beyond Dù Zǐměi’s Poems
Dù Zǐměi compared himself to Jì and Qiè;
it is not certain he truly meant it.
However, his poem says, “Shùn appointed sixteen ministers,
how noble his person, how lofty his Dao.
In Qín times, Shāng Yāng was employed,
laws were as numerous as ox hair.”
These are words from the mouths of people like Jì and Qiè.
It also says:
“Being known is not enough to be called worthy,
like the confined old men of Shāngshān.”
And it says:
“Kings and marquises, like ants,
all perish and become mounds of ruins.
I wish to hear the ultimate truth,
to return to the original mind.”
Thus, we know there were other matters beyond Dù Zǐměi’s poems.
Mèng Jiāo’s Poems
Ōu Yǒngshú said:
“Mèng Jiāo’s poem says, ‘Though there are threads by my temples,
they are not enough to weave a winter garment.’
Even if they were enough to weave,
how much could one get?”
Bái Lètiān’s Poems
Bái Lètiān was slandered by Wáng Yá,
and demoted to Sīmǎ of Jiāngzhōu.
During the Gānlù Incident,
Bái Lètiān had a poem that said:
“When you return with white hair on the same day,
it is the time I alone go to the green mountains.”
Those who did not understand thought he was rejoicing at their misfortune.
How could Bái Lètiān rejoice at others’ misfortune?
He was lamenting them.
Chéng Xiāng
In Xún Qīngzǐ’s writings, there are rhymed passages;
their language is vulgar and simple,
often saying “chéng xiāng,”
but no one understood its meaning.
In the poetry and rhapsody section of the *Qián Hàn·Yìwén Zhì*,
there are ten chapters of “Chéng Xiāng Zácí,”
thus “chéng xiāng” was the name of an ancient song or ballad.
It is suspected to be what is called “sàng chūn bù xiāng.”
Also, the *Yuè Jì* says:
“Order and disorder are governed by xiāng,”
which may also have derived its name from this.
Imitations
Liú Zǐxuán argued that the “Lǐ Líng yǔ Sū Wǔ” (Lǐ Líng to Sū Wǔ) letter recorded in *Wén Xuǎn*
was likely an imitation by a literati from Qí or Liáng.
Consequently, I realized that Líng and Wǔ’s five-character poems were also later imitations.
In *Liènǚ Zhuàn*, Cài Yǎn’s two poems,
their words are clear and full of emotion.
They rather resemble the *Mùlán Shī*;
such a style did not exist in the Eastern Hàn.
Even the Seven Masters of Jiàn’ān were restrained,
not fully expressing their feelings,
let alone Bójiē’s daughter?
Yǎn’s wanderings
must have been after her father’s death.
After Dǒng Zhuó was executed,
Bójiē met with misfortune.
This poem, however, says she was driven out by Dǒng Zhuó,
and captured by the Hú,
which further confirms its inauthenticity.
It is probably that Fàn Huá was careless and shallow,
and thus included it in the main biography.
Eating too much ginger harms intelligence.
Wáng Jièfǔ (王介甫) was given to much thought and liked to dig deeply into things.
He would often put forth a new theory;
then, later realizing its error,
he would put forth another theory to explain it.
This is why his scholarship contained many errors.
Once, while eating with Liú Gòngfù (劉貢父),
he said:
“Confucius (孔子) never went without ginger when he ate.
Why is that?”
Gòngfù (貢父) replied:
“It is said that eating much ginger harms intelligence.
If the Way (道) does not enlighten the people,
it will instead make them ignorant.
Confucius (孔子) was one who taught people with the Way (道),
therefore he never went without ginger when he ate,
this was for the purpose of making them ignorant.”
Jièfǔ (介甫) was delighted and laughed.
After a long while, he realized it was a joke.
Although Gòngfù’s (貢父) words were a joke,
Wáng’s (王) scholarship was truly very much like this.
Stone Ink
Lù Shìhéng (陸士衡) wrote in a letter to Shìlóng (士龍):
“I ascended the Tóngquè Tái (銅雀臺)
and obtained several jars of stone ink stored by Cáo Gōng (曹公).
I am now sending you a piece.”
The Dàyè Shíyí (大業拾遺) says:
“In the palace, moth-green (蛾綠) was used to paint eyebrows,”
which is also a type of stone ink.
Shěn Cúnzhōng (沈存中) served as a military advisor in Fūyán (鄜延).
He made ink from stone candles,
which was hard, heavy, and black,
superior to pine soot.
Could the item Cáo Gōng (曹公) stored be this material?
Peach Sedge Mat
Liǔ Zǐhòu (柳子厚) wrote in a poem:
“In times of prosperity, once wealth is lost, one becomes lowly.
How can peach sedge mats and sunflower fans last forever?”
I did not know what a peach sedge mat (桃笙) was.
Upon reading the Fāngyán (方言),
it states that between the Jìn (晉) and Wèi (魏) dynasties,
mats (簟) were called shēg (笙).
Then I realized that a peach sedge mat (桃笙) was a mat made of peach bamboo.
Pond Fish
In Méizhōu (眉州), there was a household that kept several hundred fish in a deep pond.
It was built with bricks,
and surrounded by houses.
This went on for over twenty years.
One day, the weather was clear with no thunder,
when suddenly a great sound like wind and rain erupted from the pond.
All the fish leaped up,
ascending like a whirlwind,
and disappeared.
An old saying goes,
if you do not guard them with turtles,
they will be taken by jiāolóng (蛟龍).
I believe that jiāolóng (蛟龍) must rely on wind and rain.
I suspect these fish were confined for over thirty years,
had thoughts of ascending every day,
their spirit did not wane,
and after a long time, they attained it naturally.
This explanation might be true.
Ears Whiter than Face
Ōu Gōng (歐公) once said:
“When I was young, a monk read my fortune:
‘Ears whiter than face,
fame will fill the world;
lips not covering teeth,
unjust slander will arise.’
His words proved quite accurate.”
That his ears were whiter than his face
is something everyone has seen;
as for lips not covering teeth,
I dare not ask His Excellency how that was.
Rúmèng Cí
Below the Yōngxī Tǎ (雍熙塔) in Sìzhōu (泗州),
I playfully composed two quatrains of Rúmènglìng (如夢令), saying:
“When did dirt ever impart itself?
Look closely, both are without it.
A message for the back-scrubber:
All day you toil, waving your elbows.
Lightly!
Lightly!
The layperson is originally without dirt.”
And also said:
“Only by being clean oneself can one wash others.
I myself am sweating and sighing.
A message for the bath attendant:
Let's just play with this physical body.
Just wash!
Just wash!
Originally for all humanity.”
This was originally composed by Táng Zhuāngzōng (唐莊宗),
named Yìxiānzī (憶仙姿).
Finding it inelegant,
he changed it to Rúmènglìng (如夢令),
“Rúmèng!
Rúmèng!
With tears, seeing you off at the gate.”
He took this as its name.
Discussing Physical Principles
Lǐ Wéixī (李惟熙), a physician from Shūzhōu (舒州), was good at discussing physical principles.
He said:
“Water caltrops (菱) and foxnuts (芡) are both aquatic plants.
Water caltrops (菱) are cold and foxnuts (芡) are warm because
water caltrop (菱) flowers open away from the sun, while foxnut (芡) flowers open towards the sun.”
He also said:
“Peaches (桃) and apricots (杏) with double kernels always kill people because
their flowers are originally five-petaled,
and six petals must mean double kernels.
The flowers of all plants are five-petaled,
only willows (柳) and snowflakes (雪花) have six petals.
This is probably the principle of yin (陰) and yang (陽).
Now, peaches (桃) and apricots (杏) with six petals and double kernels
all kill people,
because this is abnormal.”
Wood Borer
Wood that is infested with borers will definitely not rot into sand;
that which rots will definitely not be infested with borers and can float.
That which does not float also kills people.
I once investigated its principle:
once it rots into sand and scatters,
it cannot accumulate and breed insects.
Gourds (瓜) are extremely sweet yet not infested with borers
because they are sandy.
Child Inhales Toad’s Qi
Fù Yánguó (富顏國) was in Qīngshè (青社).
There was a great famine north of the Yellow River,
and people vied to go to him.
A husband and wife, carrying an infant on their back,
abandoned it in an empty tomb by the roadside and left.
Later, returning to their village and passing this tomb,
they wanted to retrieve its bones.
But the child was still alive,
fatter and healthier than when they abandoned it.
Looking into the tomb,
there was a large toad like a cartwheel,
puffing air.
They thought the child was breathing this air,
which is why it could be healthy without eating.
From then on, it did not eat.
At six or seven years old,
its skin was like jade.
Its father carried the child to the capital
to show it to Zhāng Jīngkuāng (張荊筐), a pediatrician.
Zhāng (張) said:
“Creatures that can hibernate,
swallows (燕), snakes (蛇), and toads (蝦蟆) are such examples.
If they can hibernate, they do not eat.
If they do not eat, they live for a thousand years.
If you let him not eat and not marry,
he will certainly attain the Dao (道) in the long run.”
The father happily took him away,
and now his whereabouts are unknown.
Slave as an Apparition
Shí Pǔ (石普) liked to kill people,
never feeling shame or regret.
While drunk, he tied up a slave
and ordered his attendant to throw him into the Biànhé (汴河).
The attendant, out of pity, released him.
After waking up, Shí Pǔ (石普) regretted it.
The attendant, fearing his violence,
dared not tell the truth.
After a long time,
Shí Pǔ (石普) fell ill,
seeing the slave as an apparition,
and believed he would surely die.
The attendant called the slave and showed him.
The apparition was no longer seen,
and Shí Pǔ (石普) also recovered.
Appended Remarks
In the world, there are those possessed by voices,
mostly lowly maidservants and concubines,
or those who are frail and sick, soon to die.
Their voices and gestures all resemble those of the deceased.
Could it be that some extraordinary ghost is capable of such things?
Once, a man went on a long journey,
took a golden hairpin and hid it in the wall,
forgetting to tell his wife.
Later, he fell ill and was on the verge of death,
and told others about it.
However, he did not die.
His wife heard a voice in the air,
which was truly her husband's.
It said:
"I have already died.
You do not believe it.
The golden hairpin is in a certain place."
She retrieved it,
and then held the funeral.
Later, her husband returned,
and she mistakenly thought he was a ghost.
Jìn Rén Shū (Calligraphy of the Jìn People)
Táng Tàizōng sought Jìn calligraphy,
acquiring nearly a thousand scrolls from the Two Wángs onwards,
all kept in the imperial archives.
During Wǔ Hòu's time,
they were plundered by Zhāng Yìzhī's brothers,
and thus scattered among the common people,
many ending up in the homes of Wáng Yá and Zhāng Yánshǎng.
When Wáng Yá fell,
soldiers looted and snatched the golden and jade scrolls,
but discarded the books.
I saw several帖 (albums) of Jìn calligraphy at the residence of Commander Lǐ Wěi,
all bearing a small seal with the character "Yá."
I suspect they were Wáng's property.
There were works by Xiè Shàng, Xiè Kūn, and Wáng Yǎn, among others,
all extraordinary.
Wáng Yǎn alone was supremely aloof,
like a flock of cranes with wings raised, poised to fly but not yet taking off.
The Recluse Yáng Pǔ
Zhēnhuáng made the Eastern Pilgrimage,
seeking recluses throughout the realm.
He found Yáng Pǔ from Qǐ.
The Emperor asked:
"Did anyone compose a poem for you before your departure?"
Yáng Pǔ replied:
"My wife composed one, which says:
'No more must you be down-and-out, indulging in cups of wine;
Absolutely no more must you be wild and fond of composing
poems. Today, they'll seize you and take you to the official's office,
This time, your old head will be forfeit.'"
The Emperor laughed heartily,
and sent him back to the mountains.
Stone Mirror
During the Yuánfēng era,
I traveled from Qí'ān through ancient Huángzhōu,
and obtained a mirror.
Its back bore an inscription that read:
"In the Hàn dynasty, fine copper came from Báiyáng,
forged into a mirror,
clear and bright."
To its left was a dragon, to its right a tiger, assisting it.
Its characters were like beans,
in Large Seal Script,
and the inscription was extremely exquisite.
Báiyáng,
I suspect, means the sunny side of Báishuǐ.
Its copper was black like lacquer,
and when it reflected a person, they appeared slightly smaller;
ancient mirrors were all like this.
This is a Daoist method of gathering forms.
Cutting Open a Peach Pit to Find Realgar
Wáng Xǔ of Qítíng dreamt he saw a person by the water,
who had been beaten and wounded,
and was already dead.
Seeing Wáng Xǔ, the person cried out,
and Wáng Xǔ saved him from death.
The next day, by the water, he saw a deer caught by a hunter.
It had several wounds.
Wáng Xǔ redeemed it for several thousand (coins).
The deer followed Wáng Xǔ in his daily life,
never leaving for a moment.
Wáng Xǔ lived in a dense forest.
One day,
a village woman in the forest saw an overripe and exceptionally large peach,
alone at the top of a tree.
She picked it and ate it,
and discarded the pit.
Wáng Xǔ was greatly surprised,
took it and cut it open,
and found a piece of realgar like a peach kernel.
He then chewed and swallowed it,
finding it very sweet and delicious.
From then on, he abstained from meat,
lived a vegetarian life,
and never again took a life in his entire lifetime.
Polished Silk Hat
Xu Cùi Lǐ Táo
had a son, seventeen or eighteen years old,
who suddenly recited a poem about plum blossoms:
"Flowing water is hard to view exhaustively,
The setting sun easily breaks one's heart.
Who shares the polished silk hat,
Dancing a melody of 'Mountain Fragrance'?"
His father, startled, asked him about it.
As if possessed by something, he [the son] said:
"The Queen Mother of the West feasted the immortals.
There was a dancer wearing a polished silk hat,
with flowers pinned on the hat,
who danced a piece called 'Mountain Fragrance.'
Before the music ended, all the flowers fell off."
Dài Sōng's Fighting Bulls
Someone possessed Dài Sōng's painting of fighting bulls.
He kept it in a brocade bag tied to his elbow, carrying it with him.
He took it out to show a guest.
A nearby shepherd boy said:
"A fighting bull's strength is in its front,
and its tail is tucked between its hind legs.
Now, the painting shows them fighting but with tails swinging.
Why is that?"
Huáng
Quán saw
a painting of flying wild geese,
with necks and legs both extended.
He said:
"Flying birds retract their heads and extend their legs,
or retract their legs and extend their heads.
None extend both."
Upon verification,
it was indeed true.
Geese Have Two Abilities
People of Qiántáng loved killing,
slaughtering a hundred geese daily.
One night, I returned from the lake,
and at the butcher's door, a hundred geese were all crying out,
their voices shaking the streets,
as if protesting something.
Geese can alert to thieves,
and also ward off snakes.
Their droppings kill snakes.
When people in Shǔ kept geese in their gardens and ponds,
snakes would immediately move away.
They possessed these two abilities, yet could not escape death!
They also suffer the calamity of being sacrificed for rain.
Alas!
How can one find a person like Yìshǎo?
Cessation of Killing
Aquatic creatures are foolish and ignorant,
and people easily kill them.
Some say they cannot repay grievances,
which is to bully the good and fear the evil.
Lǐ Gōngzé said:
"If a hen lays eggs,
and one incubates them, though they can break the shell and hatch,
they invariably die within a few days.
These eggs can be eaten;
it is not killing."
I said:
"All that can move are children of the Buddha.
Bamboo aphids first appear like powder dusted on bamboo leaves;
after a while, they can move,
hundreds and tens forming groups,
all are children of the Buddha.
When Liáng Wǔ painted the 'Water and Land' images,
those outside the Six Realms [of existence] were depicted with faint ink as human, animal, bird, fish, and other forms,
dimly suspended in the air.
These are the wandering children of the Buddha,
extremely lowly and inferior.
As for those born from dampness, like bamboo aphids,
they are even harder to discern,
appearing as if existing or not existing in the netherworld.
How then can one say that aquatic creatures and chicken eggs can be killed?
As soon as a thought of killing arises,
hell is already established.
It does not depend on whether they can protest or not."
On the Difficulty of Understanding Medical Pulses
What has always troubled people
is when extreme deficiency presents with signs of repletion,
and great repletion presents with signs of debility.
In such ambiguous situations,
there lies the difference between life and death.
Officials and scholars often conceal their ailments
to fully test the doctor's ability.
This forces the doctor to seek out the illness in obscurity,
and distinguish deficiency from repletion, and cold from warmth, amidst ambiguity.
If the doctor unfortunately fails,
he will never admit his own fault,
but will cleverly blame the patient
to protect his reputation.
Occasionally, there are cautious and compliant doctors
who, although they might listen to the patient's words,
also incorporate their own observations,
and treat with both, leading to mixed remedies.
This is why the medicine is ineffective.
In my life, whenever I seek a doctor,
I usually silently assess their skill beforehand.
When I fall ill and seek treatment,
I always fully disclose my ailments,
so that the doctor clearly knows the location of the problem,
and only then does he examine me.
The primary determination of deficiency or repletion, cold or warmth, is made internally (by my own knowledge),
and the ambiguity of the pulse cannot mislead me.
Therefore, even an average doctor
can usually cure my illness.
I merely seek recovery from my illness;
how could I make it my business to trouble doctors?
Lí Jiǎzi
My old friend Lí Chún (字 Zì Xīshēng),
studied the 《Chūnqiū》,
and Ōugōng liked him.
He was honest, slow, and a bit dull.
Liú Gòngfù jokingly called him Lí Jiǎzi (黎稼子, meaning Lí the Farmer's Son, but also homophonous with 黎茄子, Lí the Eggplant).
Lí thought it referred to his virtuous character,
unaware that there really was a fruit with that name (eggplant).
One day, as they were riding together,
they heard someone shouting "eggplant for sale!"
Lí laughed so hard he almost fell off his horse.
Drinking well-flower water
When it rains,
I place many containers in the wide courtyard;
the water collected is indescribably sweet and smooth.
It makes tea and boiled medicine
both delicious and beneficial.
Next best is sweet and cold well water.
Qián transforms by its 'nine-two' line,
Kūn uses its 'six-two' as kǎn,
and 'heaven one' is water.
If a person can drink well-flower water,
its sweetness and heat are comparable to realgar, stalactites, etc.
If an unsuitable person drinks it,
it can also cause carbuncles on the back and brain.
Furthermore, if water is collected and stored on the equinoxes or solstices,
after seven days, creatures will invariably appear,
resembling mica.
Fèi Xiàoxiān's Gua-shadow
In the first year of Zhìhé (1054),
Fèi Xiàoxiān of Chéngdū traveled to Qīngchéng,
and visited an old man's village,
where he broke his bamboo bed.
Xiàoxiān wanted to compensate him,
but the old man smiled and said:
"Look at the inscription underneath it:
'This bed was broken by Fèi Xiàoxiān in such-and-such a year, month, and day.'
It was truly destined,
why would you compensate me?"
Xiàoxiān recognized his extraordinary nature,
and stayed to become his disciple.
The old man taught him the 《Yì》 and the methods of 'gua-shadows' (卦影).
Several years later,
Xiàoxiān's name became famous throughout the land.
Scholars from all directions who studied his methods
were found everywhere,
all claiming to be disciples of Xiàoxiān,
making it impossible to distinguish genuine from fake.
Watching tea and sipping ink
Genuine ink made from pine soot and distant smoke
naturally possesses the fragrance of dragon musk and musk deer.
Those in this world who are addicted to it include Téng Dáodào, Sū Hàorán, and Lǚ Xíngfǔ.
On leisurely, clear, and warm days,
they grind a few measures of ink water,
and after playing with their brushes,
they sip it.
Cài Jūnmò was fond of tea,
but when he was old and ill, he could not drink it,
only handle and appreciate it.
Watching tea and sipping ink
are also amusing activities.
Zhèngxiàn Gōng burns the Imperial Edict
When Dù Zhèngxiàn Gōng was chancellor,
Cài Jūnmò and Sūn Zhīhàn were remonstrance officials,
and repeatedly requested to be transferred out.
Rénzōng said:
"If you truly wish to receive a prefecture,
you should submit what you desire."
Thereupon, Cài was appointed to Fúzhōu,
and Sūn to Ānzhōu.
Zhèngxiàn Gōng said:
"For remonstrance officials to leave without cause
is ultimately not a good thing.
I request that they remain in their original posts."
The emperor agreed,
and then wrote an imperial edict.
At that time, Chén Gōnggōng was a chief councilor,
but he refused to transcribe it,
saying:
"I never heard about this in the first place."
Zhèngxiàn was afraid,
and so he burned it,
and was consequently dismissed from his chancellorship.
Commentators said that Zhèngxiàn should have clearly reported and sought confirmation,
and should not have hastily burned the document.
Jiǎ Pópó
Empress Wénchéng's wet nurse, née Jiǎ,
was called Jiǎ Pópó in the palace.
Jiǎ Chāngcháo befriended her,
calling her 'auntie.'
The Censors denounced her for her treachery,
and Wú Chūnqīng wanted to uncover the truth but could not.
A close attendant who had an audience with the emperor said:
"The Censors' recent pronouncements
are half truth, half fabrication.
Regarding the matter of Auntie Jiǎ,
how could such a thing be true?"
Rénzōng was silent for a long time,
then said:
"Madam Jiǎ did indeed recommend Chāngcháo."
If it were not for Rénzōng's great virtue,
how could he have spoken the truth to his subordinates?
There are prominent people in the world
Lǐ Shìhéng's father
was arrogant and unlawful,
and was executed.
When Shìhéng was promoted,
Wáng Qīnruò wanted to speak about this but found no opportunity.
It happened that Rénzōng was discussing the flaws of contemporary literary style,
and Wáng Qīnruò took the opportunity to say:
"Lù Zhèn is a literary man,
but he does not understand propriety."
The Emperor asked:
"Why?"
"Lǐ Shìhéng's father was executed,
yet Zhèn wrote a eulogy for him saying:
'There are prominent people in the world.'" The Emperor nodded, and because of this, Shìhéng was not greatly employed.
Discussion on Liǔ Zōngyuán
He dared to speak exaggerated and improbable things,
and believed them without doubt.
When Lǚ Wēn served as governor of Dàozhōu and Héngzhōu,
and when he left,
the people of the two prefectures cried for over a month.
Beggars along the riverbanks would certainly wail noisily to the passing boats.
Even Zǐchǎn would not have inspired such a reaction,
so how did Wēn achieve it?
He (Liǔ Zōngyuán) also claimed that Wēn's younger brother, Gōng, was also an exceptional and heroic man.
Moreover, he said
that Gōng's wife was the daughter of Péi Yánlíng;
what noble gentleman would be willing to be a son-in-law of Yánlíng?
Zōngyuán's association with Pī and Wén
probably meant he was not ashamed to be associated with Yánlíng either.
Discussion on gold and soil having the same value
Qí Gāodì said:
"Gold and soil should be made to have the same value."
His intention was good,
but how could things truly operate on such a principle?
Mèngzǐ said:
"The inequality of things
is their natural disposition.
If large shoes and small shoes had the same price,
would people bother to make them?"
Mèngzǐ himself forgot these words
when he spoke of grain and pulse being as abundant as water and fire.
Gold cannot be as cheap as soil,
just as soil cannot be as valuable as gold.
The people under Yáo could all be enfeoffed,
while the people under Jié could all be executed.
If one believes this saying,
then during Yáo's time, feudal lords would have filled the world,
and during Jié's time, capital punishment would have been widespread across the four seas.
Qīngmiáoqián
Lí Zǐyún (黎子雲), a *jìnshì* from Dān'ěr (儋耳), said:
North of the city, there was an old man from Tángcūn (唐村) named Yǔn (允).
His followers asked Zǐyún:
"Why does the chancellor so bitterly trouble us with the 'Green Sprouts' loan?
Is it beneficial to the government?"
Zǐyún said:
"The government is concerned that the people's wealth is unevenly distributed.
The rich pursue ten-to-one profits,
becoming richer,
while the poor take double the rate,
even to the point of selling their land and pledging their children.
Therefore, this law was enacted to equalize it."
Yǔn's followers said:
"The disparity between rich and poor
has existed since ancient times.
Even Heaven itself cannot equalize it.
That people have rich and poor
is like utensils having thick and thin parts.
If you wish to grind down the thick to equalize it with the thin,
the thick part will not yet have moved,
but the thin part will have already been perforated."
Is this a woodcutter who can discuss the Kingly Way?
Wūgǔ (巫蠱)
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn (漢武帝) detested *wūgǔ* as if it were a sworn enemy,
for it caused anguish and made life unbearable
between husband and wife, lord and minister, father and son.
However, the *Shǐjì·Fēngshàn Shū* (史記·封禪書) states:
"Lady Dīng (丁夫人) and Yú Chū (虞初) of Luòyáng (雒陽), among others,
used ritual sacrifices to curse the Xiongnú (匈奴) and Dàyuān (大宛)."
If this was already *wūgǔ*,
how could he blame his subordinates?
This is most laughable.
Zìmí (字謎)
Bào Míngyuǎn's (鮑明遠) poems contain three *zìmí*.
"Springs flowing upward"
is traditionally said to be the character *jǐng* (井).
And "One nine of *qián* (乾),
standing alone without a mate.
Two six of *kūn* (坤),
appearing as a pair."
This is said to be the character *xiǎo* (小).
And "Head like a knife,
tail like a hook,
four corners horizontal in the middle, six.
On the right side, carrying two blades,
on the left side, double attached to ox."
This is the character *guī* (龜).
Lùn Mò (論墨)
When modern people discuss ink,
they do not value its luster.
If it is lustrous but not black,
it is considered discarded ink.
If it is black but without luster,
it is dull and lacks spirit;
of what use is it then?
It must have a blue luster that is not superficial,
deep and profound like the eyes of a small child,
only then is it good.
Fó Púsà Yǔ (佛菩薩語)
Sòng Bǎoguó (宋保國), the supervising prefect of Jǐnán (濟南),
brought out his collected annotations of Wáng Jīnggōng's (王荊公) *Huáyán* (華嚴).
I said:
"The *Huáyán* has eighteen scrolls;
why have you only explicated one of them?"
He told me:
"This is the Buddha's (佛) teaching,
profound and subtle.
The rest are merely the Bodhisattvas' (菩薩) teachings."
I said:
"Among the Buddhist scriptures,
I have taken Buddha's teachings mixed with Bodhisattva's teachings,
and then taken Bodhisattva's teachings mixed with Buddha's.
Can you distinguish which is which?"
He said:
"No, I cannot."
"Not only can you not,
Jīnggōng (荊公) cannot either.
Once, when I was in Qíxià (岐下),
I heard that the pigs from Héyáng (河陽) were exceptionally delicious.
I sent someone to procure one.
The messenger got drunk,
the pig escaped during the night,
and he bought another pig to substitute.
I did not know,
and all the guests greatly praised it,
thinking it incomparable to other local produce.
Later, when the deception was exposed,
all the guests were greatly ashamed.
Now, Jīnggōng's (荊公) pig
has not yet been exposed.
Butchers sell meat,
and courtesans sing songs;
perhaps this can enlighten you.
If one's mind is pure,
walls and rubble all speak of the Dharma (無法).
To say that Buddha's teachings are profound and subtle,
and Bodhisattvas cannot compare,
is this not a dream-like utterance?"
Bǎoguó (保國) said:
"Indeed."
Lǐ Chì Shī (李赤詩)
The poem "Yǒng Xīagǔ Shútáng (詠姑孰堂下)"
is strange in that its language does not resemble Tài Bái's (太白).
Wáng Píngfǔ (王平甫) said:
"This is Lǐ Chì's (李赤) poem.
Chì (赤) compared himself to Lǐ Bái (李白),
hence his name Chì (赤).
Later, he was misled by a toilet ghost and died."
Now, looking at his poem,
it is only thus.
To compare himself to Tài Bái (大白) (Lǐ Bái),
his mental illness had already been long-standing.
How could it be the fault of a toilet ghost?
Lùn Chá (論茶)
To remove vexation and grease,
tea is indispensable.
However, it secretly harms many.
I have a method:
After every meal,
gargle with strong tea.
All vexation and grease are expelled,
and the spleen and stomach remain unaware.
Meat stuck between the teeth shrinks and falls off,
without the need for picking,
and the teeth naturally become firm and dense because of this.
Generally, use medium or low-grade tea;
high-grade tea is not always available.
Drinking a sip every few days
does no harm.
This is very reasonable.
Lǔzhí Shīwén (魯直詩文)
Huáng Lǔzhí's (黃魯直) poems and essays are like fiddler crabs and river pilings,
their style and rhyme are exceptionally lofty,
making all other meals seem tasteless.
However, they should not be consumed in large quantities,
or they will cause wind and agitation.
Lùn Qī (論漆)
Lacquer fears crabs.
I once had a worker making lacquerware.
The worker cleaned his hands with steamed buns and ate them,
then twisted as if poisoned.
I quickly gave him crab to eat,
and he recovered.
Adding ink to lacquer is good for writing,
but it must be spoiled with a little crab roe.
Otherwise,
it will be hard and stubborn, unusable.
Èrhóng Fàn (二紅飯)
This year Dōngpō (東坡) harvested over twenty *shí* of barley.
It sold for a very low price,
and our *jīngmǐ* (粳米) had just run out.
So, at night, I instructed the servants to hull it for rice.
When chewed, it made a "pēn pēn" sound.
The children teased each other,
saying they were chewing lice.
However, when hungry at noon,
we mixed it with fermented rice water and ate it.
It was naturally sweet, sour, light, and smooth,
with the flavor of a northwestern village.
Today, I again had the cook mix it with adzuki beans to make rice;
it was even more flavorful.
My old wife laughed loudly, saying:
"This is the new-style *èrhóng fàn* (二紅飯)."
Dà Yǔ Zhōugōng (大禹周公)
When Dōngpō (東坡) was about to depart,
he asked Xú Zhòngchē (徐仲車) for a piece of advice.
Xú Zhòngchē (徐仲車) said:
"Since ancient times, many have had achievements,
but only Dà Yǔ's (大禹) achievements are singularly praised.
Since ancient times, many have had talent,
but only Zhōugōng's (周公) talent is singularly praised.
This is because they possessed virtue to lead it."
Volume Nine
End.
Lùn Shèlǐ (論設醴)
King Yuán of Chǔ, for Mù Shēng, set out a feast.
When Wáng Wù succeeded to the throne,
he forgot to do so.
Mù Shēng then pleaded illness and left.
Shēn Gōng and Bái Gōng stayed.
Wù became increasingly immoral and tyrannical.
The two remonstrated,
but he did not listen.
Officials in red robes mingled with prostitutes in the market.
Shēn Gōng was ashamed of this,
and returned to Lǔ.
Later, Zhào Wǎn and Wáng Zàng spoke to Emperor Wǔ,
who summoned him with a carriage with straw-padded wheels.
He ultimately lost his position due to Zhào Wǎn's embezzlement case.
Mù Shēng distanced himself before the crisis occurred.
Shēn Gōng clung on after the crisis had begun.
To say that good and bad fortune are all Heaven's will
and cannot be avoided or cut off
is not necessarily true.
Taking pine resin
Pine resin that has a calming effect is good.
Place it in a fine cloth bag,
soak it in water,
and boil it in hot water.
Those that float to the surface,
take them out with a skimmer,
and put them into fresh water.
Those that do not come out after prolonged boiling should be discarded.
Add powdered Bái Fúlíng.
Pound and sift into a powder.
Take three qián daily.
Place seven of these into the mouth,
rinse with a little warm water,
then brush the teeth as usual,
and further sip a small amount of hot boiled water to warm them,
then rinse the teeth again.
This strengthens the teeth, preserves the complexion, and blackens the beard.
Kǒng Běihǎi
Wáng Gǒng said:
"Zhāng Āndào said Sū Zǐzhān was comparable to Kǒng Běihǎi and Zhūgě Kǒngmíng."
Sū Zǐzhān said: "Kǒngmíng
I would not dare hope to be like,
but Běihǎi might be somewhat similar,
though not to the extent of being so foolish."
Now, Kǒngmíng was preeminent in loyalty, righteousness, spirit, and integrity throughout the world.
His power was sufficient to contend with Cáo Cāo,
and they could certainly not coexist.
Běihǎi died defending the Hàn.
How could he be called one who regarded death as lighter than a swan's feather?
Why is he called foolish?
The merchant from Liáng
A merchant from Liáng traveled south.
He returned after seven years.
He consumed seaweed,
breathed the essence of mountains and rivers,
drank the fragrant spring water,
and ate the pure soil.
The cool breeze seemed to be always around him.
Tired of traveling, he returned home.
He even claimed to have attained the Dao,
and strolled through the old capital,
thinking no one was his equal.
He entered his house,
ascended his hall,
looked at his wife,
and was shocked into fleeing.
His wife tried to comfort him,
but he said:
"What concern is it of yours?"
He spat and ignored her.
He said:
"How are you worthy of me?"
He eventually drove his wife away.
Three years after the merchant returned,
his neighbors disliked his conduct
and did not arrange marriages with him.
When the local climate and atmosphere gradually changed his hair,
and sipping beans and drinking water loosened his rough skin,
his former ugliness slowly returned to its original state.
Then he returned to his wife's chamber,
and they treated each other as before.
A gentleman would say that in this action,
the merchant was gravely lacking in righteousness.
He changed his friends when he became rich,
and did not consistently uphold his principles.
He was a sinner against moral teaching.
Those who do not understand scholarship
act like this without shame.
In the arena of conflicting interests,
and the realm of right and wrong,
loyal ministers often become enemies of their country,
and filial sons become captives.
Such incidents are numerous throughout history,
why should it be unique to the merchant from Liáng?
The crowing of a rooster
In Guāng and Huáng prefectures, people gather in groups during the second and third months to sing folk songs.
They are not in tune with musical scales,
but rather resemble the crowing of a rooster.
It is similar to the faint singing of palace women at the water clock,
but extremely crude and rustic.
The Hàn Guān Yí says:
"No chickens are kept in the palace.
Long-crowing roosters are produced in Rǔnán.
Guards wait outside the Zhūquè Gate,
specifically to relay the rooster's crowing."
Yīng Shào also said:
"This refers to the Jī Gē."
The Jìn Dàkāng Dìdào Jì says:
"Guards of the Later Hàn learned this tune,
and sang it below the pass.
This is the present Jī Chàng."
Yán Shīgǔ did not consult ancient texts,
and rashly dismissed this claim.
What I hear now,
could it be a remnant of the Jī Chàng?
Today, local people call it 'mountain song'.
Wáng Jìnqīng's ink
Wáng Jìnqīng's posthumous ink was made with gold and cinnabar.
When the ink was finished,
its value was equal to gold.
Cài Liú from Sānqú, besides using his own glue made from soot,
used no other materials.
It was solely due to his skillful compounding methods
that his ink was extremely black and lustrous,
hardly inferior to Wáng Jìnqīng's.
The Hu people say that rhinoceros horn is dark,
and elephant is white.
This can be used to describe ink,
and can also be used to describe tea.
Xú Zhòngchē's two contradictions
Xú Jī,
courtesy name Zhòngchē,
was a man of independent conduct from ancient times;
even Yúlíng Zhòngzǐ could not surpass him.
However, his poetry and prose were strange and unrestrained,
like Yùchuānzǐ.
This is his first contradiction.
His hearing was extremely poor.
He would draw characters on the ground
before communication was possible.
He sat facing the wall all day,
not interacting with people,
yet he knew everything happening in all four directions.
This is his second contradiction.
Discussion on Emperor Wǔ of Hàn
He was without principle;
there is nothing worth observing.
Only that he met Wèi Qīng while sitting on the toilet,
and met Jí Àn without wearing a cap,
is noteworthy.
As for Wèi Qīng, a mere slave,
it was quite fitting for him to lick ulcers.
To meet him while sitting on the toilet
was exactly appropriate.
Tracing with hard yellow paper the calligraphy of the Two Wángs
The surviving calligraphy of the father and son from Huìjī, Wáng Xīzhī and Wáng Xiànzhī,
is perhaps only a handful.
The Tang dynasty calligraphers, such as Xuē and Chǔ,
tracing and imitating with hard yellow paper,
is also quite valuable.
Lǔzhí's poems
Reading Huáng Lǔzhí's poems
is like seeing Lǐ Zhònglián and Lǐ Táibái.
One dares not speak of trivial matters again.
Although they might seem not practical,
they are not without benefit to the world.
A commoner from Bǎoyīng
Qín Dàxū said,
there was a commoner from Bǎoyīng who hosted guests for a wedding.
Halfway through the feast,
one guest suddenly rose and walked out the door.
The host chased after him.
The guest was about to jump into the water.
The host quickly held him back.
The guest said:
"A woman summoned me with a poem,
its words were:
'Below the long bridge, there is a perfumed boat,
breaking through the moon and rushing through the mist, floating freely.
What is the use of gold and jade filling the hall?
How can it compare to a young man coming and going freely?'
I rushed to her in a daze,
not realizing it was the water."
Buddha receiving precepts to redress grievances
Lǐ Rú-sǔn's younger sister,
when she reached womanhood, fell ill.
She saw her karmic enemies from a past life
who scourged her daily.
Thus, she wholeheartedly took refuge in the Buddhadharma.
In a dream, she saw the Buddha grant her precepts
and send away her enemies.
Lǐ therefore ate vegetarian and did not marry.
Cài Jūn-mó's Calligraphy
I have often argued that Cài Jūn-mó's calligraphy is the finest of our dynasty,
but many disagree.
Some say Jūn-mó's calligraphy is weak,
which truly shows they do not understand calligraphy.
If it were like Lǐ Zhǔ of Jiāngnán,
outwardly strong and dangerous, but inwardly hollow,
that could truly be called weak.
If Lǐ Zhǔ is considered strong,
then Jūn-mó should be considered weak.
Zhāng Zǐ-yě's Poetry
His brushwork is old and marvelous,
but his lyrics are merely a secondary effort.
His "Huāzhōu Xīxī" says:
"Where duckweed breaks, mountain shadows appear;
A wild boat comes across, and the sound of grass is heard."
My poem matching it says:
"Grief is like a lone fish, knowing the night is long;
Laziness is like a butterfly, busy for spring."
Such lines as these
can all be compared to the ancients.
Yet the common folk only praise his lyrics.
In the past, Zhōu Fǎng's paintings of figures were divine,
but people only knew of Zhōu Fǎng's ladies.
Can this be said to be seeing those who love virtue as much as those who love beauty?
Wild Apple Tree Poetry
Zǐ-mài, when young, wrote a poem about a "wild apple tree" saying:
"Ripe fruits fall on their own when there's no wind,
Half a cheek facing the sun competes in fresh redness."
Among his peers, this was considered to have thoughtful artistry.
He also had a poem saying:
"Leaves follow the flowing water, where do they go?
An ox carries a cold crow past a late village."
This is also admirable.
Phoenix Beak Inkstone
I like to use a Phoenix Beak stone inkstone,
but many critics have differing opinions,
as few obtain a genuine one.
The dim, shallow beach stones confuse them.
Táng Yàn-yóu considered Qīngzhōu red-silk stone to be excellent,
but some say it is only fit for making dice bowls,
as they have not seen a good one.
Lǐ Shí-bā's Cursive Script
Liú Shí-wǔ commented on Lǐ Shí-bā's cursive script,
calling it "parrot's娇" (charm/coquetry),
meaning that parrots can speak,
but only a few sentences,
mostly mixed with bird sounds.
Shí-bā later improved somewhat,
and wrote to me asking:
"How is it now compared to before?"
I replied:
"It can now be a Qín Jí-le (talking mynah bird)."
Yáng Níng-shì's Calligraphy
In the late Táng and Five Dynasties,
literature was vulgar and base,
and calligraphy followed suit.
However, Yáng Níng-shì's calligraphy was strong and powerful,
often comparable to Yán's running script.
Today, many praise Lǐ Jiàn-zhōng and Sòng Xuān-xiàn.
As for these two's calligraphy,
I do not understand it;
Sòng's is cold and Lǐ's is vulgar,
they probably gained their fame for nothing.
Only Cài Jūn-mó's poetry and calligraphy
are both of high style and form,
and his scholarship is also most appropriate,
making him the finest of our dynasty.
Dù Fǔ's Poetry
His poetry is indeed unmatched,
yet the lines from "Zhì Yuǎn" onwards
are very rustic and crude.
The world blindly follows along,
no longer criticizing them,
which is excessive!
However, this also cannot conceal its beauty.
Singing and Harmonizing with Tán Xiù
When I was in Guǎnglíng,
seeing a guest off at Shānguāng Sì,
Tán Xiù wrote a poem saying:
"A small boat, carried by inspiration, reaches Shānguāng,
The ancient temple by the stream conceals its supreme energy.
Ashamed that the south wind knows my mind,
It blows the grass and trees to make a heavenly fragrance."
I harmonized it saying:
"Amidst the clamor, a pure excursion borrows a sliver of light,
In drunkenness, a true realm reveals its celestial hiddenness.
Awakening from the dream, I picked up the blown-in lines,
Ten miles of south wind, the fragrance of grass and trees."
Wén Yǔ-kě's Poetry
Once, I recited Wén Yǔ-kě's poem to Ōu Gōng:
"The beauty holds a fan and sits,
Ashamed, the flowers beneath the courtyard fall."
Ōu Gōng said:
"Such lines originally existed in the world,
Yǔ-kě merely picked them up."
On Dǒng Qín
Yùchuānzi's "Poem on a Lunar Eclipse" says:
"The Jupiter star presides over blessings and emoluments,
Official ranks are bestowed upon Dǒng Qín."
Carefully tasting these words,
it suggests one who enjoys high emoluments without merit.
Dǒng Qín was originally a loyal subject;
at the end of Tiānbǎo, he repeatedly fought and established merit,
and also largely understood righteousness.
During Dài-zōng's reign,
Tǔbō invaded the capital.
When troops were summoned,
Dǒng Qín immediately went to face the danger.
Someone advised him to choose an auspicious day,
to which he replied:
"When the emperor and father are in danger, should one choose a day?"
Later, he was executed under Zhū Cǐ's false command.
Examining his beginning and end,
he was not one who enjoyed emoluments without merit.
I wonder why Yùchuānzi had this line?
Lètiān Burning Elixirs
Bái Lètiān built a thatched hut on Lúshān,
and was burning elixirs, which were about to be completed when the furnace and tripod failed.
The next day, the appointment letter as Cìshǐ of Zhōngzhōu arrived,
thus he knew that worldly affairs cannot coexist.
Eating "Pán-yóu Fàn" and "Gǔdǒng Gēng"
People in Jiāngnán like to make "Pán-yóu Fàn" (lit. "plate-roaming rice"),
where all kinds of cured meats, dried fish, and minced raw fish are buried in the rice.
A local saying goes:
"It's like digging up a cellar."
Luófú Yǐng Lǎo took all sorts of food and cooked them together,
calling it "Gǔdǒng Gēng" (lit. "antique soup" or "miscellany soup").
The poet Lù Dàoshì offered a couplet saying:
"Pouring fermented rice into the Gǔdǒng Gēng pot,
Digging up a cellar in the Pán-yóu Fàn bowl."
Cān Liáo's Poetry
One night, I dreamt Cān Liáo came over with a scroll of poems.
When I awoke, I remembered two lines from his "Poem on Drinking Tea":
"Hánshí and Qīngmíng have all passed,
Stone springs and huái-wood fires are fresh all at once."
In the dream, I asked:
"The fire is certainly fresh,
but why is the spring fresh?"
He replied:
"It is customary to clean wells on Qīngmíng Day."
Ode to Boiled Pig's Head
Clean the pot,
add shallow water,
press the firewood deep, do not let it rise.
In Huángzhōu, it's as cheap as dirt.
The rich refuse to eat it,
the poor don't know how to cook it.
Sometimes I'll make a bowl myself,
full and knowing it myself, you need not bother.
Qián Cǎo Poetry
Dù Zǐ-měi has a piece titled "Removing Qián Cǎo."
In Shǔ, it is called máo qián (hairy qián);
its hairs and awns are formidable,
touching it is like being stung by a bee or scorpion.
To treat urticaria, this grass is used to dot the affected area,
and the whole body loses it.
Those with purple backs of leaves are used in medicine.
Dù's poetry notes say:
"Qián is pronounced qián,
it is mountain leek."
Gathering Āi on Duānwǔ Day
On Duānwǔ Day,
before sunrise,
one should intentionally seek out āi (mugwort) that resembles a person,
gather it and use it for moxibustion,
it is remarkably effective.
I saw this in a book,
but have forgotten which one.
No āi truly resembles a person;
it is simply by intention in the dim light that one designates it as such.
All phenomena are illusory,
none are real;
