what is there to doubt about this?
Treating Internal Eye Diseases
《Běncǎo》 says:
"Shú Dìhuáng, Mài Mén Dōng, Chēqiánzǐ mixed together,
taken internally, are effective in treating internal ophthalmic conditions."
Repeated trials prove it true.
The method is:
Pound them finely and sift them,
then make honey pills the size of parasol tree seeds.
All three herbs are difficult to pound and sift,
but when combined, they are exceptionally sweet and fragrant,
truly a miraculous medicine.
Wasp nest,
snake slough,
tangled hair,
each burned to ash, retaining their original properties,
taken with wine, a monetary unit's worth,
treat chronic sores that do not heal.
Pān Gǔ's Ink
His ink was exquisite,
yet its price was not doubled.
One day,
he suddenly took all the promissory notes for ink he was owed and burned them,
then drank wine for three days,
went mad, rushed to a well, and died.
People looked down
and saw him sitting cross-legged in the well,
still holding a string of prayer beads.
Xuětáng Yìzūn
During the Yuányòu era,
Fùmǎ Dōuwèi Wáng Jìnqīng obtained over ten types of ink,
ground them together,
and wrote dozens of characters
to observe the depth of their colors.
If they were truly excellent,
they should be pounded and blended into a single type.
The harmonious blend of wine was called "Xuětáng Yìzūn,"
but now it is "Xuětáng Yìmò," is it?
Yán Lǔgōng Imitating Yìshǎo's Calligraphy
Yán Zhēnqīng's stele inscriptions,
among them, the "Dōngfāng Shuò Huàzàn" is the most clear and majestic.
Later, upon seeing Yìshǎo's original,
I realized that Lǔgōng had imitated every character from it.
Although there was a great difference in size,
the intent was truly there,
and it is not easy to describe it as self-derived from his calligraphy.
It is not easy to speak of it.
Ōugōng's Calligraphy
Ōugōng used a pointed brush to create square and broad characters,
with a brilliant and elegant spirit,
endlessly rich and lustrous.
Later generations who saw it
felt as if they saw his clear and dignified, full cheeks,
and his serene and abundant charm.
Jīnggōng's Calligraphy
Wáng Jīnggōng's calligraphy
attained the method of no method,
yet it cannot be learned;
to learn it is to have no method.
When I intentionally seek to write,
it somewhat resembles Cài Jūnmó's;
when I am a bit more free, it resembles Yáng Fēngzi's;
when I am even more unrestrained, it resembles Yán Fǎhuá's.
The Heart of a True Person
Daoists say:
"The heart does not leave the field,
the hand does not leave the house."
They also say:
"The heart of a true person
is like a pearl in the deep.
The heart of ordinary people
is like a gourd on the water."
The Bānyùn Method
In Yángzhōu, there was a military official
who served in the Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī regions for over ten years,
yet never contracted malaria.
His face was rosy and lustrous,
his waist and feet light and nimble.
He never took medicine,
only every day, at the fifth watch, he would rise and sit,
rubbing the Yǒngquán points on his soles together countless times,
until he sweated.
Ōugōng usually did not believe in immortals or Buddhas,
and laughed at people who practiced Qìgōng.
In his later years, he said:
"For several years, I had a small sore on my foot,
the pain was unbearable.
Recently, someone taught me a method,
and after using it for three days,
the pain imperceptibly disappeared."
The method is to sit with feet dangling,
close eyes, clench fists, contract the anus,
and shake the feet as if kicking a ball,
then the Qì settles;
when the Qì is calm, do it again.
Do it eight or nine times a day,
whenever free,
it is a quick Bānyùn method.
Wénzhōng's pain has ceased,
but he does not discard it,
it must be beneficial.
Diligently Cultivate Good Karma
The Buddha said that in the three thousand great thousand worlds,
empty flowers rise and perish in confusion,
and how much more so am I within the rising and perishing of these empty flowers?
Dwelling here for a moment,
what do nobility and lowliness, longevity and short life, gain and loss, wisdom and foolishness, amount to?
Only by diligently cultivating good karma,
to elevate the spirit,
to illuminate and dispel illusions,
and to sincerely know one's true nature,
is the most important matter for one's life.
The Dogs Are Displeased
Huìzhōu City is desolate,
yet still, one sheep is slaughtered daily.
I dare not compete with officials to buy meat,
so I sometimes instruct the butcher
to sell me the backbone.
Occasionally, there is a little meat on it;
cook it thoroughly,
then thoroughly rinse it with well water,
if not thoroughly cooked, the bubbles will not disappear.
Use wine as desired,
lightly salt and roast it until slightly charred,
then eat it.
Picking and scraping all day,
I find tiny bits of meat between my teeth,
like eating crab claws.
Eating it once every three to five days
feels very nourishing.
In the kitchen of Shānniántáng,
the fodder and meat consumed
are eaten without leaving bones,
how could they ever know this taste?
Although this is a jest,
it can be put into practice.
If this method is used, the dogs will be displeased!
Three Old Men Ask Ages
Once, three old men met,
and someone asked them their ages.
One said:
"My age cannot be calculated,
but I only remember that when I was young, Pángǔ and I were distantly related."
Another said:
"When the sea turns into mulberry fields,
I always place a tally,
and already ten houses are full."
The third said:
"My master ate蟠桃Pántáo peaches,
and discarded their pits beneath Kūnlún,
and now they are as tall as Kūnlún."
In my opinion,
how are they different from mayflies or morning glory fungi?
Dreaming of Hán Wèigōng
One night, I dreamed of ascending Héjiānglóu,
the moonlight was like water.
Hán Wèigōng came riding a crane,
and said:
"I have been ordered to jointly manage a difficult official post,
so I came to inform you."
Another day, when I return north to the central plains,
it should not be long.
Zhēnyī Wine
When I was in my new residence, Báihè,
Daoist Dèng suddenly knocked on the door.
It was already the third watch,
all my family members were asleep.
The moonlight was like frost.
Behind him,
there was a great man dressed in Areca palm leaves,
carrying a dipper of wine,
with a handsome and heroic bearing,
like Lǚ Dòngbīn.
He said:
"Have you ever tasted Zhēnyī wine?"
He sat down.
The three of us each drank several cups,
tapping out a rhythm and singing loudly.
Below Héjiānglóu,
the sea wind stirred the water,
and all the large fish came out.
He took out a book from his sleeve and handed it to me;
it was the Zhēnyī method and nine characters for cultivation,
at the end of which it said:
"Written by Jiǔxiá Xiānrén Lǐ Jìng."
After he left, I was in a trance.
The Three Bodies of Dharma-Nature and Retribution
Recently, I read *Liùzǔ Tánjīng* which explains the three bodies: *fǎshēn*, *bàoshēn*, and *huàshēn*,
which opens people's minds and clarifies their understanding.
However, there is another analogy:
"What the eye sees is the *fǎshēn*;
the ability to see is the *bàoshēn*;
what is seen is the *huàshēn*."
What is meant by "what the eye sees is the *fǎshēn*"?
The nature of seeing in the eye,
is neither existent nor non-existent.
A person without eyes
cannot avoid seeing darkness.
Even if the eyes wither and perish,
the nature of seeing does not cease.
This means the nature of seeing does not depend on the eye.
But it has no coming or going,
no arising or ceasing.
Therefore, it is said that what the eye sees is the *fǎshēn*.
What is meant by "the ability to see is the *bàoshēn*"?
Although the nature of seeing exists,
if the eye organ is incomplete,
then one cannot see.
If one nourishes this organ,
and it is not obstructed by objects,
always keeping its light clear and penetrating,
the nature of seeing is then complete.
Therefore, it is said that the ability to see is the *bàoshēn*.
What is meant by "what is seen is the *huàshēn*"?
Once the nature of the organ is complete,
in an instant,
there are a thousand changes and ten thousand transformations.
All vertical and horizontal changes and destructions are wondrous functions.
Therefore, it is said that what is seen is the *huàshēn*.
Poem on Steamed Pork
When Wáng Zhōnglì had pacified Shǔ,
he was very hungry.
He entered a village temple.
The monk was very drunk and
sat sprawled out.
The Duke wanted to execute him,
but the monk replied without fear.
The Duke was surprised by this.
The Duke asked for vegetarian food,
but the monk said there was meat but no vegetables.
He served a steamed pig's head,
which was very delicious.
The Duke was pleased,
and asked:
"Do you only drink wine and eat meat?
Or do you have other skills?"
The monk said he could compose poetry.
The Duke ordered him to compose a poem on "Steamed Pork,"
which he completed immediately,
saying:
"Long snout, short hair, lightly holding its jowl,
Long accustomed to eating medicinal herbs in the mountains.
When steamed, it's already wrapped in banana leaves,
When cooked, it's also basted with apricot syrup.
Its fresh red color perfectly adorns a golden platter,
Its tender softness is truly worthy of jade chopsticks.
If compared to a smelly root,
The smelly root itself deserves to be beaten with a rattan cane."
The Duke was greatly pleased
and granted him a purple robe and a monastic title.
Dān'ěr Hell
West of Dān'ěr city,
a maiden of the common people died of illness.
Two days later, she revived,
saying:
"At dusk, someone led me to the curtained court of an official.
They said I was mistakenly summoned.
An officer in the courtyard said,
'She has no sin; she can be sent back.'
I saw the prison in a cellar,
and those bound were all Dān'ěr people.
There were sixteen or seventeen monks and nuns.
There was an old woman whose body was entirely covered in yellow hair,
like a donkey or horse,
shackled and seated.
The maiden recognized her;
she was the wife of a Dān'ěr monk.
Another monk had died two years prior,
and his family was just celebrating a great memorial.
Someone brought a platter of food and several thousand coins to give to the monk.
The monk gave several hundred to the gatekeepers.
When the food was brought in,
the gatekeepers and those bound scrambled for it,
and the monk ate little.
Another monk arrived,
and all who saw him knelt and bowed in reverence.
The monk said,
'This person can be sent back by someone.' " The maiden awoke in surprise.
Was this monk not the one called Dìzàng Púsà?
Grain Depletes Earth's Energy
I once had land in Qíshuǐ.
I only planted one *dòu*,
and harvested ten *hú* of rice.
When asked why,
it was said that the continuous mountains were all wild grass and scattered trees,
where no grains grew.
The earth's energy was not depleted,
thus it yielded so much.
From this, I know that grains deplete the earth's energy most severely.
At the end of Wáng Mǎng's reign,
there were early locust plagues throughout the land.
One *jīn* of gold was exchanged for one *dòu* of rice.
By the sixth year of Jiànwǔ,
wild silkworms formed cocoons,
covering mountains and marshes.
After five years, they gradually decreased,
while agricultural work increasingly flourished.
This is because when the soil did not produce grain,
the earth's energy had no means of depletion;
it accumulated over a long time,
and manifested as wild silkworms and abundant grain.
Where the earth does not produce grass and water,
it often yields gold and tin;
this is also the same principle.
Méi Xún Is Not a Gentleman
During the reign of Zhēnzōng,
someone recommended Méi Xún.
The emperor said:
"Lǐ Kàng said he is not a gentleman."
At that time, twenty years had passed since Kàng's death.
Ōu Gōng once asked Sū Ziróng:
"A chancellor has been dead for more than twenty years,
yet he can make the emperor trust his words.
By what means?"
Ziróng replied:
"Because he was without ulterior motives, that's all."
Wú Yù Not Appointed Chancellor
When Chén Zhízhōng was dismissed from his chancellorship,
Rénzōng asked who could replace him.
Zhízhōng recommended Wú Yù.
The emperor immediately summoned him.
It happened to be the Qianyuan Festival banquet,
and Yù, being somewhat drunk, fell asleep while sitting.
Suddenly, he startled awake, looked around,
and patted the bed, calling his attendant.
The emperor was astonished,
and immediately appointed him Commissioner of the Western Capital.
Although Zhízhōng was a common official,
he could also be considered virtuous.
Yù's failure to become chancellor
was fate.
In his later years, he suffered from heart disease,
which also made him difficult to be greatly employed.
No Heroes at the Time, So a Mere Lad Became Famous
My former friend, Shǐ Jīngchén, said:
"Ruǎn Jí ascended Guǎngwǔ and sighed, saying:
'There are no heroes at the time,
so a mere lad becomes famous.'
Did he mean Pèi Gōng was a mere lad?"
I replied:
"No,
he lamented the absence of Liú Xiàng-like figures at the time.
'Mere lad' refers to the people of the Jìn and Wèi period."
Lǐ Tàibái's poem *Guǎnglíng Wǔ* says:
"Sinking into wine, he calls the mere lads,
His wild words are not truly impartial."
Thus, I know that Tàibái also misunderstood Sìzōng,
no different from my former friend.
Although Sìzōng was unrestrained,
he originally had aspirations for the world.
Due to the many troubles during the Jìn and Wèi periods,
he merely indulged in wine.
Why would he call Pèi Gōng a mere lad?
The Battle of Yǒngluò
Zhāng Shùnmín said:
"In the Battle of Yǒngluò,
Lǐ Shùnjǔ, Xú Xǐ, and Lǐ Jì were all among the captives.
The emperor sent a handwritten edict to the four men,
saying:
'If you can preserve the officers and soldiers,
I will fully recover the lost territory.'
Before the edict arrived,
Shùnjǔ and others had already died.
The emperor's intention can be said to value a single scholar lightly over a thousand *lǐ*.
It is a pity that these men did not receive his bounty,
alas!"
The Merits and Demerits of the Two Lǐs
The eunuch Lǐ Shùnjǔ died at Yǒngluò.
Before dying, he wrote on half a piece of old paper:
"Though Shùnjǔ dies,
there is nothing to regret.
I only wish Your Majesty not to take these rebels lightly."
A clever messenger rushed to report this.
At that time, Lǐ Jì was also about to die,
and he wrote at the end of a piece of paper:
"Jì dies."
The emperor was deeply saddened.
However, the merits and demerits, and the worth and unworthiness of the two men,
were already evident.
The Grand Chancellor's Fragrant Feet
When Lǐ Xiàn ēn was in power,
gentlemen sometimes served him like slaves.
Mù Yǎn and Sūn Lù went so far as to hold his robes and sashes.
When Wáng Zhōngzhèng was at his peak,
Yú Chōng made his wife hold a clapper to accompany his drinking.
Péng Sūn was originally a bandit.
After being recruited out,
he lorded over high officials and noblemen.
Hán Chígúo even visited his residence,
where Péng Sūn brought out courtesans to drink.
When he was drunk,
he treated Hán Chígúo disrespectfully,
but Chígúo dared not confront him.
However, Péng Sūn once washed Lǐ Xiàn's feet
and said:
"How fragrant are the Grand Chancellor's feet!"
Xiàn then stepped on his head with his foot, saying:
"Isn't your flattery a bit excessive, slave!"
When Péng Sūn was in Xǔxià,
he secretly captured three hundred runaway soldiers and forced them into service.
I was about to be appointed to Xǔ,
and was told to come after he had been executed in the commandery.
The appointment to Yǐng, which came later, made me desist.
Poetry on the Western Campaign
Zhāng Shùnmín was well-versed in matters of the west
and somewhat skilled in poetry.
Returning from the western campaign with Gāo Zūnyù,
he composed a poem on the way, saying:
"Underneath Língzhōu city, a thousand willows,
All cut into firewood by the imperial army.
When I return from Yángguān another day,
With what shall I break off a branch to give to travelers?"
"On the road to Wéizhōu through Qīnggāng Gorge,
Ten went to war, nine never returned.
White bones like mountains, mountains like snow,
General, do not ascend the Terrace of Longing for Home."
He was impeached by Lǐ Chá,
and demoted to supervisor of taxes in Chēnzhōu.
Shùnmín said:
"The imperial army besieged Língwǔ,
but failed to take it.
With provisions exhausted, they retreated."
The Westerners on the city wall asked the imperial army:
"Are the Han people 'wācā'?"
They replied:
"Wācā."
Everyone on the city wall laughed."
"Wācā" means
ashamed and flustered.
Inviting Gāolì
Wáng Bǐng zhī said:
Once, when I was an investigator in the Bureau of Military Affairs,
I saw a Gāolì case.
It began when Zhāng Chéngyī was an envoy to Qìdān,
and met a Gāolì person in the barbarian tent,
who privately spoke of his king's admiration for China.
Upon returning, Zhāng Chéngyī reported this,
and the late emperor first had the idea of attracting them.
The Grand Commissioner of Military Affairs, Lǚ Gōngbì, adapted to this,
personally wrote a memo requesting to invite them,
and so the Transportation Commissioner Luó Jí was ordered to send merchants to invite them.
The world knows Luó Jí's fault,
but not Gōngbì's fault.
As for Chéngyī,
he is hardly worth mentioning.
On the Book of Changes and Analects
The ancient texts from the Kǒng family wall and the Jí Tomb bamboo slips, written in tadpole script,
were all written in lacquer,
and eventually succumbed to decay.
The Han bronze bells and stone drums are much more enduring.
The ancients' plans for immortality were indeed great.
However, the subtle meaning which prevents them from being lost
is transmitted solely by people.
The *Yìjīng* states, "Spiritual and intelligent,
it rests with the person."
My own *Yìshūzhuàn* and *Lúnyǔshuō*
are also roughly complete.
Alas!
What more can be done?
Perfected One of the Great Ultimate
Xú Zé of Dōnghǎi,
lived in seclusion in Tiāntái,
abstaining from grain to cultivate his nature.
The Perfected One of the Great Ultimate, Master Xú, descended and said:
"When you are eighty, you will become the teacher of a king,
and then attain the Dao."
When Jìn Wáng Guǎng heard of his reputation and summoned him,
Xú Zé said:
"I am now eighty-three years old.
The King has come to summon me,
Master Xú's words have been verified."
So he went to Yángzhōu.
The King asked him to impart the Dao,
but he declined, citing unfavorable timing.
A few days later, he died.
People on the road all saw him walking back to the mountains,
saying:
"I have been released to return."
He then took his scriptures, distributed them to his disciples, and left.
Soon after, his funeral arrived.
Everyone believed he was a man transcending the world,
who would not be defiled by an emperor,
and chose to die rather than transmit the Dao.
Were Master Xú's words
merely a means to avoid disaster?
Was this what is meant by 'acting with caution and speaking with humility'?
If not,
Yángdì's conduct
was spat upon by ghosts.
And how could the Perfected One of the Great Ultimate
have placed him between his teeth?!
Discussion on Gold and Salt
When Wáng Mǎng was defeated,
there were three hundred thousand catties of gold in the palace treasury;
Chén Píng used forty thousand catties to sow discord in Chǔ;
Dǒng Zhuó's Méiwù also had much gold;
as for others who were bestowed thirty or fifty catties,
they are countless.
In recent times, gold is not measured by the catty;
even the sovereign has not given a hundred catties to anyone.
Why was there much in ancient times and little now?
Mining mountains and sifting sand never ceases,
where has the gold gone?
I rather suspect that precious goods undergo divine transformations.
How could it be unknown that they return to mountains and marshes?
I once heard that salt is similar.
The Dàníng Salt Bureau in the Gorges boils salt;
there is a fixed daily output.
If a large merchant ship capsizes, the amount of salt suddenly increases.
Thus, I know that the outflow of ordinary flows
does not depend on distance,
but all returns to its source.
Tablet of the Pond for Releasing Life
In Húzhōu, there is a tablet for the Pond for Releasing Life,
which records a memorial submitted to Sùzōng, saying:
"Three audiences a day
demonstrate the filial piety of an enlightened ruler;
inquiring about his health and personally serving meals
do not alter the rites of a family member."
Did Lǔgōng know that Sùzōng felt ashamed of this?
Who would say that Lǔgōng was merely concerned with releasing life?
Three Excellent Horses
In the Tang dynasty, General Lǐ Sīxùn painted *Emperor Mínghuáng Picking Melons*.
Amidst the mountains and waters of Jiālíng,
the Emperor rides a dappled horse,
with three excellent horses rising,
and a dozen or so princes, consorts, and attendants on horseback.
Emerging from under Fēixiānlǐng,
upon first seeing flat land,
all the horses seemed startled,
but the Emperor's horse would not advance when it saw a small bridge,
precisely in this state.
I did not know what the three excellent horses were.
Now I see Cén Cān's poem,
*Song of the Red Dappled Horse Guarding the Emperor*, which says:
"Red dappled horses, Hú-style grooms, golden scissors,
At dawn, three excellent horses are clipped high."
Thus I know that many imperial horses of the Tang were clipped and groomed,
and the 'three excellent horses' were their ornamentation.
Reciting the Diamond Sūtra
In recent years, someone went to retrieve a silver sickle.
Reaching a deep spot,
he heard someone reciting scriptures.
He dug it open and found a person,
who said:
"I was also one who came to retrieve a sickle.
The mountain collapsed, and I could not get out.
I have lived here for I don't know how many years.
All my life, I have recited the *Jīngāngjīng*.
I always kept the scripture with me.
Whenever I felt hungry or thirsty,
someone would give me cakes and provisions from below my navel.
This must be a manifestation of this Sūtra."
Daoists speak of "guarding the One":
if hungry,
the One provides food;
if thirsty,
the One provides drink.
Did this person perhaps attain what is called "the One"?
Shénqīngdòng
Cáo Huàn (曹渙) traveled to Sōngshān (嵩山).
Midway, a Daoist priest sat on a rock and called out,
“Are you not Cáo Huàn (曹渙), the son-in-law of Sū Zhé (蘇轍)?”
He looked at his companions and asked,
“Who is this?”
They replied,
“It is old Liú (劉) the Daoist priest, who resides here.
He has never spoken to anyone before.”
The Daoist priest said,
“Sū Shì (蘇軾)
was a disciple of Ōu Yǒngshú (歐永叔).
What kind of person do you consider Yǒngshú (永叔) to be?”
Huàn (渙) replied,
“In literary talent and loyal righteousness, he is number one under Heaven.”
The Daoist priest said,
“What the world knows is merely that.
I,
Yǒngshú’s (永叔) contemporary,
received this robe from Yǒngshú (永叔).
It has been torn but never mended,
and never soiled but washed.
Recently I received a letter; I am quite well.
Do you not know Shénqīngdòng (神清洞)?
You and I shall meet on a certain year, month, and day at a certain place.
That year, I will transform into an immortal on a rock on a certain month and day.”
He sat down again and spoke no more.
Huàn (渙) also continued into the mountains.
Indeed, as scheduled, he transformed into an immortal on a rock.
Dù Fǔ’s (杜甫) Cuckoo Poem
Wáng Yìbó (王誼伯) of Nándū (南都) said that Dù Zǐměi’s (杜子美) poems, having passed through the wars of the Five Dynasties,
were mostly damaged and incomplete.
For example, “In Xīchuān (西川) there are cuckoos,
in Dōngchuān (東川) there are no cuckoos.
In Fúwàn (涪萬) there are no cuckoos,
in Yún’ān (雲安) there are cuckoos.”
This was a note under the title,
starting from “I once traveled to Jǐnchéng (錦城)” as the first line.
Yìbó (誼伯) was mistaken.
Zǐměi’s (子美) poems encompass all forms;
how can one harm the words with the writing,
or harm the meaning with the words?
Examining his original intent, they all contain a sense of emotion,
which is the allegorical and evocative style of poetry,
and the meaning of the *Lísāo* (離騷).
According to the *Bówùzhì* (博物志):
Cuckoos lay their eggs
in other nests,
and hundreds of birds feed them.
In Jiāngdōng (江東), it is said, “The character ‘Dù (杜)’ was formerly a king of Shǔ (蜀),
who transformed and flew away, leaving his old city desolate.”
Its subtle reverence for the exalted is well known.
Thus, Zǐměi (子美) said, “It is the reanimated spirit of an ancient emperor,”
and also said, “The rites are like serving the supreme one,”
criticizing the prefects of the time for not treating birds respectfully.
After the Míng Táng (明唐) era,
the imperial path became fraught with difficulties;
the prefects who could, in an emergency, not forget their sovereign were few.
Yán Wǔ (嚴武) in Shǔ (蜀),
though harsh in levying taxes,
indeed provided resources to the central plains.
This is “In Xīchuān (西川) there are cuckoos.”
But when he defied the imperial command,
usurped military authority,
and cut off tributes,
like Kèxùn (克遜) in Zǐzhōu (梓州) causing worry to the imperial court,
this is “In Dōngchuān (東chuān) there are no cuckoos.”
The prefects of Fúwàn (涪萬) and Líng’ān (靈安)
are too obscure to investigate.
Generally, those who uphold the sovereign
are “having” [cuckoos];
those who harbor disloyalty
are “without” [cuckoos].
Yìbó (誼伯) also said,
“Zǐměi (子美) should not have repeated rhymes.”
Zǐměi (子美) created his own style;
how can repeated rhymes harm poetry?
Stirring the Cauldron
When Gāozǔ (高祖) was in humble circumstances,
he passed by his elder brother's wife's (his sister-in-law's) house to eat.
The sister-in-law, weary of her brother-in-law and his guests,
pretended that the soup was finished by stirring the empty cauldron.
From then on, he broke off relations with her.
When he later established the Qí (齊) Crown Prince,
his elder brother's son alone did not receive a marquisate.
The Grand Supreme Emperor (his father) spoke about it,
and Gāozǔ (高祖) said,
“It’s not that I dare to forget,
but her mother was not a benevolent person.”
He then enfeoffed him as Gēngxié Hóu (羹頡侯) (Marquis of Stirred Soup).
Gāozǔ (高祖) was known for his magnanimity,
not remembering people’s faults.
Yet, he did not let go of the grudge of stirring the cauldron.
Did he not feel ashamed of the Grand Supreme Emperor’s words about “sharing the cup”?
On Chúnyú Kūn (淳于髡)
Chúnyú Kūn (淳于髡) got drunk with one *dǒu* (斗) [of wine],
and also got drunk with one *shí* (石) [of wine].
Among the villagers,
men and women mingled,
almost in revelry.
What was there to admonish?
There was likely a subtle intention.
By the varying amounts, he understood impermanence,
understood that drinking was not inherently “me” (his true self),
observed changes to recognize delusion.
His lifelong fondness for it also gradually diminished.
Therefore, by using words of indulgence,
he was able to admonish the extravagant ruler against prolonged night drinking.
The world has yet to understand his true meaning.
Male and Female Bamboo
Bamboo has male and female plants.
Female bamboo produces more shoots.
Therefore, when planting bamboo, one should plant female ones.
From the root upwards to the tip,
those that sprout from a single node are female.
No thing escapes yin and yang;
this is truly credible!
Forbidding the Taking of Life
I killed little in my youth,
but could not completely stop.
In recent years, I began to be unable to kill pigs and sheep.
By nature, I am fond of crabs.
Whenever I see someone sending them as a gift,
I release them all into the river.
Although I know they have little chance of survival,
I hope for one to live.
Even if they do not survive,
it is still better than being cooked.
To personally face misfortune
is no different from chickens and ducks in the kitchen.
I cannot bear, for the sake of my appetite,
to make living creatures suffer immeasurable fear and pain.
I still regret that I cannot forget the taste
and eat only self-dead things.
Summoned by Guǎnglì Wáng (廣利王)
One day, I fell asleep drunk.
There came from the sea a creature with a fish head and a ghostly body,
who said,
“Guǎnglì Wáng (廣利王) invites Duānmíng (端明).”
I donned a coarse robe, wore grass sandals, and a yellow Daoist cap, and departed.
I was unaware of my body stepping into the water,
only hearing the sound of wind and thunder.
After a moment,
it suddenly became clear and bright.
It was truly what is called the Crystal Palace.
Below it were black pearls, luminous pearls, patterned rhinoceros horns, foot-long jade bi-discs, southern gold, and fire-red quartz,
too brilliant to look directly at.
Corals and amber, I know not how many.
Guǎnglì (廣利) came out, wearing a sword, crown, and robes,
followed by two young green-clad attendants.
I said,
“I am an exile on the sea; it is too much trouble to invite me.”
After a moment,
Dōngpéng Zhēnrén (東蓬真人) and Nánmíng Fūrén (南溟夫人) arrived.
They brought out a piece of fine silk gauze, more than a *zhàng* (丈) long,
and commanded me to write a poem.
I composed:
“Though Heaven and Earth are vast and empty,
only the sea is the greatest.
All sagely kings worship it,
its position revered, even the River God bows.
Zhùróng (祝融) is another name for it,
a mystical gathering of myriad strange beings.
The two cosmic forces transform into flowing light,
wind and clouds swift over ten thousand *lǐ* (里).
Spirit banners wave with rainbow pennants,
red *qiú* (虬) dragons spray forth in torrents.
Its home is near the Jade Emperor’s (Yùhuáng) (玉皇) palace,
crimson light shines without bounds.
If I could obtain a moon pearl,
it could repay the exile’s debt.”
After writing, I presented it.
A turtle prime minister (biē xiànggōng) (鱉相公) said,
“Sū Shì (蘇軾) does not avoid taboos.
The character ‘Zhùróng (祝融)’ infringes upon the king’s personal name taboo.”
The king was greatly angered.
I withdrew and sighed,
“Everywhere I go, I am ruined by a turtle prime minister.”
Volume Ten
End.
Tianci (天賜) Slip-Bamboo (簡策)
In the Hàn dynasty, Hé Bǐqiān had an old woman
of about eighty years of age
seek shelter from the rain.
The rain was heavy, but her clothes were not wet.
Bǐqiān invited her in to wait,
and she then said:
"Your ancestors originate from Hòujì.
From Yáo to Jìn, they accumulated hidden merits.
Now Heaven bestows upon you a strategy."
It was like a bamboo slip,
nine cùn long,
and she handed it to him, saying:
"Your descendants who can wear this will be rich and noble."
After speaking, she disappeared.
Headache
Yáng Hù suffered from headaches.
When treated,
Hù said:
"When I was three days old,
my head faced the northern door.
I felt the wind blowing,
and was greatly troubled by it,
though I couldn't speak.
Since the root of the illness is so ancient,
it cannot be cured."
Zhèng Xuán, the old slave
Wáng Fǔsì, in his commentary on the 《Yì》,
ridiculed Zhèng Xuán, saying:
"The old slave is truly without insight."
Late one night, he suddenly heard the sound of clogs outside,
and in a moment, someone entered.
He introduced himself as Zhèng Xuán
and said:
"Young man, why do you so arbitrarily interpret and criticize my writings,
and wantonly mock this old man?"
After speaking, he departed.
Fǔsì died suddenly.
Ashamed to compete with魑魅 for light
Jī Kāng was playing the qín under a lamp
when suddenly a person, over ten chǐ tall,
with a black face,
wearing a single garment and a leather belt, appeared.
Kāng stared intently,
then blew out the lamp and said:
"I am ashamed to compete with chīmèi for light."
People say ghosts are repulsive
Ruǎn Déru once went to the latrine
and saw a ghost over ten chǐ tall,
black-faced with large eyes,
wearing a white single garment,
groping with its hands.
They were but a chǐ apart.
Déru remained calm and composed,
and laughed, saying:
"People say ghosts are repulsive;
it is indeed so."
The ghost blushed and retreated.
Guō Chángshēng
In the Sòng Jiāzhōng period,
Mr. Cháo from Tài Shān resided in Jìnlíng.
His household maid was gathering firewood
when suddenly a man followed the maid back home,
not allowing others to see him.
When drinking and feasting with the maid, he would often play the flute and sing.
The song went:
"The night is quiet and clear;
the long flute sounds bright.
If you wish to know me,
my surname is Guō, and my courtesy name is Chángshēng."
Poverty in Gāohuāng
Dù Zǐjuàn was down on his luck,
his assets completely exhausted.
An old man gave him three million cash,
without stating his name, and left.
Within a period of ten days, it was mostly spent.
He went from owning a horse to a donkey,
then to walking.
The old man again gave him ten million cash.
Several years later, he was poorer than before.
The old man again gave him thirty million cash,
saying:
"If this does not cure you,
then poverty is in your gāohuāng."
Zǐchūn said:
"I am grateful to the elder.
What is not yet attained is forgotten,
and I love only this.
If you make no sigh,
my medicine will be complete,
and you too will become an immortal."
He pointed the way for him to return.
He sighed with regret and left.
General Wū Marries a Wife
Guō Yuánzhèn failed the imperial examination during the Kāiyuán era
and traveled from Jìn to Fén.
He lost his way while traveling at night.
There was a residence,
the characters on the gate were very grand.
Inside the hall, there were lamps and candles, but no one was present.
Soon, he heard a woman weeping.
He asked:
"Are you human
or ghost?"
She replied:
"In my village, there is General Wū,
who can bring misfortune or fortune to people.
Every year, the villagers choose a beautiful woman to marry him.
My father, coveting the villagers' money,
secretly chose me for the selection,
and left me drunk in this room.
The General is due to arrive at the second watch."
He was greatly angered and said:
"If I cannot save you by my strength,
I will sacrifice myself for you."
Before he had spoken long,
carriages and horses arrived in a throng.
Officials in purple robes entered,
then rushed out again, saying:
"The Grand Councilor is here."
Soon after, the General entered.
He stepped out to greet him, saying:
"I hear of a auspicious ceremony tonight;
I wish to act as a junior officiant."
The General was pleased and invited him to sit.
Then, a dried venison was offered.
He took his saber, grabbed the General's wrist, and cut it off.
The General cried out and fled.
At dawn,
he looked at the severed hand;
it was a pig's trot.
Soon, he heard crying sounds approaching.
It was the woman's parents carrying burial clothes,
intending to collect her body.
He explained everything to them.
He then instructed the villagers to take bows and arrows and follow the blood trail.
They entered a large tomb
and found a large pig missing its front left trot,
which ran out and died.
He took the woman as his concubine.
Lady Wéi Marries Old Zhāng
Zhāng Lǎozhě
was a gardener from Liùhé County.
His neighbor, Wéi Shù, had a daughter.
When she came of age,
she summoned a matchmaker to seek a good husband.
Zhāng Lǎo said,
"Please do me the favor of finding one."
The matchmaker cursed,
"How could a refined lady consent to marry a gardener?"
The old man said,
"Just mention it to her.
If she doesn't agree, then so be it."
The matchmaker went in and told her.
Wéi Shù said,
"If he can come up with five hundred ǒu of money today, then it's acceptable."
The old man said,
"Agreed."
In no time, the money arrived.
Wéi was greatly astonished and said,
"I assumed he wouldn't be able to, so I said it.
Now what shall I do?"
Having no other choice, he agreed.
His daughter showed no shame,
but her relatives all disapproved of it.
The old man said,
"Since you are now displeased with each other,
what difficulty is there in leaving?
There is a small estate at the foot of Wángwū Shān.
I shall return there tomorrow morning.
If you miss me someday,
you can have your elder brother visit me south of Tiāntán Shān."
After he left,
there was no further news.
Several years later,
Wéi Shù sent Yìfāng to Tiāntán Shān to visit him.
He met a Kūnlúnnú who said,
"Why has Dàlángzǐ not come for so long?"
He led him to a grand mansion,
where flowers bloomed beautifully and mist hung enchantingly,
and luán and hè birds lingered.
Upon reaching the gate,
he heard the sound of jade pendants.
A servant in green led someone out,
wearing a yuǎnyóuguān and
a crimson silk robe.
He led Wéi to bow before him.
It was Zhāng Lǎo.
He said,
"Human life is full of toil and hardship,
as if in a blazing fire,
with the flames of worry growing fiercer each day.
You, my brother, have been away for so long; how do you amuse yourself?
Your esteemed sister will comb her hair briefly and then come to see you."
He led them into the hall,
where the beams were made of agarwood,
the doors inlaid with tortoiseshell,
the windows of emerald,
and the blinds of pearls.
The sister briefly exchanged greetings and nothing more.
Zhāng Lǎo said,
"Brother, you cannot stay long."
He presented him with twenty yì of gold and an old straw hat,
saying,
"If you have no money,
you can go to the home of the elderly physician Wáng Lǎo in Yángzhōu and collect ten million coins,
using this as proof."
Wéi returned, took the hat, and went to Wáng Lǎo's home.
Indeed, he received the money.
The Fox Reciting the Tōngtiān Jīng
Péi Zhòngyuán's home was north of Hù.
Once, chasing a rabbit, he entered a large tomb.
There was a fox leaning against a coffin, reading a book.
Zhòngyuán struck at it but missed.
He took the book and returned home.
The characters were unrecognisable.
Suddenly, a scholar named Hú Xiùcai, who called himself Xíngzhōu, asked to see him.
He was
the one who had been reading by the coffin.
Péi asked,
"What book is it?"
He said,
"It is the 《Tōngtiān Jīng》.
It is not something practiced by humans.
You truly have no use for it.
I wish to offer a hundred gold coins to redeem it."
Péi did not respond.
He then said,
"A thousand yì."
Still, he did not respond.
The guest became angry
and rose, flicking his sleeves.
Péi's maternal elder brother, Wéi Duānshì, who had already died,
suddenly appeared and said,
"I heard you got a book by chasing a rabbit.
I recognize its characters."
He then showed it to him.
Wéi said,
"It is for Hú Xiùcai to take."
Then it was lost and seen no more.
Péi also died soon after.
Shēn Lán and Shēn Chūn
The nun Miàojì,
whose surname was Yè,
was initially married to a great merchant, Rèn Huá.
Her father, Shēng, went to Chángshā with Huá.
Suddenly, she dreamt her father wept, saying,
"Your husband and I encountered bandits in the lake.
The one who killed me was 'monkey in the carriage,'
and 'grass east of the gate'."
She dreamt her husband said,
"The one who killed me was 'running in the grain,'
and 'one day husband'."
Miàojì did not understand.
There was a Lǐ Gōngzuǒ,
who could decipher riddles.
He told her,
"The one who killed your father was Shēn Lán,
and the one who killed your husband was Shēn Chūn.
'Monkey' (申生) is 'Shēn'.
'Carriage' (車) with two 'heads' (兩頭) removed forms 'Shēn' (申);
'Grass' (草) and 'east of the gate' (門東) form 'Lán' (蘭);
The character 'Lán' (蘭);
'Running in the grain' (禾中走者) means passing through fields (穿田),
which also suggests 'Shēn' (申);
Adding 'one day' (一日) to 'husband' (夫) forms
'Chūn' (春)
The character 'Chūn' (春)."
Miàojì then changed into men's clothing,
and roamed the jiānghú as a hired laborer.
She heard there was a Shēncūn in Mín Huáng,
and in Shēncūn, there were the Shēn Lán brothers.
She secretly went to seek work there.
For over a year, no one knew she was not a man.
When the two bandits were drunk,
Miàojì rushed to inform the authorities and they were captured.
They confessed and were brought to justice.
Thereafter, she adopted Buddhism.
The Human Mine
Què Huán,
the son of Sī Róng Xuānláng,
fell ill.
He saw two yellow-clad officials arrest him and take him into a city.
Its gate was inscribed with "Pànguān Yuàn,"
and thousands were shackled.
The officials went in to report,
then came out and said,
"The Pànguān sends word:
'You have not diligently built up your family,
but indulged in wine and lust.
You are released with a light beating.
If you repeat your former wrongs,
there will be no forgiveness.'"
Huán asked,
"Who is the Pànguān?"
He replied,
"It is Sī Róng Láng."
Huán said,
"If this body does not enter,
how can it receive punishment?"
The official said,
"If it enters, it cannot leave.
Every person has three souls:
one soul stays at home,
and one soul receives punishment.
West of this street is a gate,
inscribed with 'Rénkuàng Yuàn.'
Huge rocks, several li in circumference,
and thousands of great demons are there.
East of the rocks, thousands of people are shackled.
Their names are called, and they are dragged and thrown onto the rocks to be crushed,
then handed over to the mill prison,
the fire prison,
or the boiling water prison."
As they reached the city gate, he saw
an official running south,
who said,
"The Huáng Hé wishes to divert a branch.
Previously, Heaven commanded that one in three men be taken,
but the labor collected was insufficient.
Now, it is requested that one in two men be taken."
Huán awoke.
His family had been weeping and waiting for him for seven days.
Several months later,
Xuē Gōng, the Jìdùshǐ of Hézhōng, memorialized to divert a branch of the river,
to reduce the force impacting the city.
Initially, he proposed taking one in three men.
Later, he requested taking one in two men.
It turned out exactly as he had seen.
Jūnshān Yīngwǔ
Suí Liǔ Guīshùn
journeyed by boat from Bālíng.
He encountered a storm and arrived at Jūnshān.
He disembarked and walked for several *lǐ*,
where he saw thousands of parrots
calling out each other's surnames and given names.
There were those named Wǔ Yóuláng, Ā Sū'ér, Wǔ Xiānláng, Zìzài Xiānshēng,
and Tà Liánlù.
Wǔ Yóuláng said:
"Once I saw Emperor Wǔ of Hàn riding an yèjīnjí (turmeric oar boat),
floating on the Jīcuì Chí (Piled Jade Pond),
playing a biāoyùdí (floating jade flute) himself."
Wǔ Xiānláng said:
"Liǔ Shí'èr encountered a storm and managed to reach this extraordinary place.
This is what is called 'beauty achieved through illness.'
We, humble birds,
cannot exert ourselves
to convey a message to Guìjiā Niángzi."
They called out from afar:
"Hé Chūn,
we have a guest!"
Immediately, someone appeared, bearing a crystal bed.
Hé Chūn called out:
"Fènghuātái, why do you not see the guest?"
Immediately, a parrot flew over,
reciting some recent poems by Yù Shù.
Guīshùn then recited several pieces by Xuē Dàohéng and Jiāng Zǒng.
Fènghuātái said:
"Modern works are not without their magnificence and beauty,
but they greatly lack *gǔqì* (spirit and vigor)."
Suddenly, two Daoists appeared and said:
"Your boat has a favorable wind;
why do you not return quickly?"
They handed him a foot of brocade, saying:
"Cover your eyes with this,
and you will be gone."
Guīshùn suddenly flew back to his boat.
Wángmǔ Yùzhī Niángzi
There was a scholar named Cuī.
He saw a young woman at Luógǔ Kǒu in Dōngzhōu.
He made all arrangements for marriage.
Cuī Mǔ said:
"This new daughter-in-law is enchantingly beautiful;
she must be a fox spirit
who will harm you."
The woman said:
"I serve Kījì (my husband's parents),
hoping to stay for life.
But your esteemed mother treats me as a fox spirit.
I will leave tomorrow."
The next day, she entered the mountains
and was never seen again.
Later, a Hu Monk said:
"The wife you took
was Wángmǔ's third daughter, Yùzhī Niángzi.
If she had stayed for one year,
your whole family would have become immortals."
Cuī Shēng sighed and lamented incessantly.
Wēiwū Huò
Lái Jūnchuò traveled at night
and sought lodging at a commoner's house.
The host introduced himself as Wēiwū Huò,
and his servant as Guā'ér.
The room was square,
and both land and water delicacies were fully displayed.
The next morning, when he looked at the place,
there was only a muddy pond,
with large earthworms several feet long,
and extremely large snails and conches.
He then vomited several *shēng* of the green mud and filthy water he had eaten last night.
Qīngsù and Qīnghóng, Two Underworld Figures
Cáo Huì,
was a Cānjūn (staff officer) in Jiāngzhōu.
In his official residence, there were wooden puppets.
One said:
"I am Qīngsù.
Qīnghóng and I were burial figurines from Xiè Xuānchéng's family,
belonging to the old servant of Yǐnhóu's family.
In the past, while in the tomb,
I was holding water for Lèjiā Niángzi to wash her feet.
Suddenly, two bandits arrived, holding lamps.
The lady, barefoot, transformed into a white cricket.
The bandits saw that Qīnghóng and the other two underworld figures were not bad,
and could serve as playthings for their children.
Since then, we have been passed through several households.
If a person from Lúshān wants Qīngsù to be a dancing girl,
I shall bid farewell."
The Deceased Liú Zhēn Protects the Living Gù Zǒng
Gù Zǒng was a county official
who was frequently whipped.
He fled to a cemetery.
Two men in yellow clothes said:
"Mr. Liú, do you still remember our past acquaintance?
We two are Wáng Càn and Xú Gàn;
your previous incarnation was Liú Zhēn."
Then, they produced a book from their sleeves and said:
"This is your collected works."
Gù Zǒng glanced at it
and suddenly understood clearly.
He then took the collected works to the county magistrate.
The magistrate was greatly surprised and said:
"Liú Gōnggàn should not be made a minor official."
He immediately treated him with the courtesy due to a guest.
At that time, it was said that the deceased Liú Zhēn still protected the living Gù Zǒng.
The Young Woman's Lúan Nǎo Líng (Phoenix Brain Game)
Liú Fěng, a clerk in Jìnglín,
sought lodging in an empty hall at night.
Four young women arrived.
The one in green said:
"Zǐshòu,
please bring Liújiā Liù Yí, Jiùmǔ, and Nánlíng Qiáoqiáo, along with Yìnú.
The moon and wind here are delightful;
playing the *qín* and reciting poetry would be wonderful.
The Jìnglín Pànsī (Vice-magistrate) need not avoid us."
A moment later, three women arrived,
carrying a small child.
They set out a rhinoceros horn wine *zūn* (goblet)
and an ivory ladle.
One young woman recited a verbal game:
"Lúan Nǎo Lǎo Tóu Nǎo Hǎo,
Hǎo Tóu Nǎo Lúan Lǎo."
She then laughed and said:
"In the past, Hèruò Bì teased Chángsūn Luán Shìláng
because of his old age, stammer,
and baldness.
Therefore, this game was created."
She then sang:
"Bright moon, clear breeze,
a good night for gathering.
The Milky Way easily overturns;
joy and pleasure do not last.
Green *zūn*, emerald ladle,
pour for you.
If not drunk tonight,
when will there be joy?"
She sang again:
"Jade door, golden lamp,
wish to accompany the king.
In Hándān Gōng,
metal, stone, silk, and reed instruments.
Wèi Nǚ, Qín É,
in rows on either side.
Fine silk fluttering,
emerald eyebrows, red makeup.
The king's joy turns his gaze,
for the king they sing and dance.
May the king's joy be obtained,
and long be free from disaster and suffering."
When the song ended, it was already the fifth watch.
She then said:
"Willow branches sway gently with the strong wind,
the beauty on the western perch is in a spring dream,
the emerald curtain is obliquely rolled up, letting in a thousand rays."
Suddenly, a man in yellow clothes said:
"Pótí Wáng summons the ladies to come quickly."
All the young women rose.
The next morning,
two emerald hairpins were found.
Sān'ěr Xiùcai
Dǒng Shèn, an aide to the governor of Yǎnzhōu,
was visited by a yellow-robed messenger who said:
"Tàishān Fǔjūn summons you to resolve a difficult case."
Shèn was put into a cloth sack,
and with water and mud sealing both his eyes,
he was carried away.
Suddenly, a voice said:
"Fàn Shèn is pursuing Dǒng Shèn."
The Lord laughed and said:
"To send Fàn Shèn to pursue Dǒng Shèn,
and take the cloth sack from the Left Scribe's office to hold the record keeper of the Right Scribe's office,
can truly be called a prudent precaution!"
He ordered Shèn to identify the record keeper of the Right Scribe's office.
Shèn said:
"The clerks do not understand writing; Zhāng Shěn Tōng, a xiùcái from this prefecture, could be used."
A moment later, Fǔjūn summoned Shěn Tōng and appointed him as the record keeper of the Left Scribe's office.
Each was bestowed with a silk garment,
a fish-beard hu tablet,
leopard-skin boots,
and a ride on a black fox.
Fǔjūn said:
"Without you, this case cannot be set right.
I will plug your two ears
and give you
a third ear."
When the matter was concluded,
he said to Shèn:
"Thanks to your recommendation of a worthy person,
I will repay you with an additional year of life."
Again, mud was used to seal both their eyes,
and they were sent back in cloth sacks.
His wife and children said:
"Your spirit has been gone for more than ten days."
Shěn Tōng had an ear emerging from his forehead,
and he became especially sharp of hearing.
People at the time said:
"In the heavens there is a nine-headed bird,
and on earth there is a three-eared xiùcái."
In Dōuxuán Guó,
Xuē Jūn Cáo suddenly saw two green-clad figures
riding a red calf out of the market.
There was another realm,
with lush flowers and trees.
They said:
"This is Dōuxuán Guó."
Téng Liù sends snow, Xùn Èr raises wind.
Xiāo Zhìzhōng, the governor of Jìnzhōu, intended to hunt on the Làyuè day.
A woodcutter saw a tall man on Huòshān.
Suddenly, tigers, rhinoceroses, deer, pigs, foxes, and hares gathered around.
The tall man said:
"I am Xuánmíng Shǐzhě,
sent by the Northern Emperor's command.
On the Làyuè day, Governor Xiāo will hunt.
Such-and-such a number of you will die by falcon,
and such-and-such a number by arrow."
An old elk bent its knee and begged for help.
The messenger said:
"Yán Sì of the Eastern Valley is skilled in strategy."
The beasts followed,
and the woodcutter secretly followed them.
In a thatched hut, there was a yellow-robed Taoist.
The old elk pleaded mournfully.
The yellow-robed Taoist said:
"If Téng Liù causes snow to fall
and Xùn Èr raises the wind,
then Lord Xiāo will not hunt again."
The woodcutter returned.
Before dawn,
wind and snow lasted the entire day,
and Xiāo indeed did not go out.
Yellow Stone Transforms into Gold.
Hóu Shì,
outside Jiànmén, saw four yellow stones as large as dippers.
When he collected them, they all transformed into gold.
Shì traded them for a million cash,
bought over ten beautiful concubines,
a grand mansion, and much fertile land.
Suddenly, an old man carrying a satchel said:
"I have come to claim payment from you.
You took my gold,
do you not remember?"
He gathered all the entertainers and concubines and put them into his satchel.
It did not feel cramped at all.
In a short while, they were gone.
Several years later,
Hóu Shì saw the old man traveling with his entertainers.
When asked, they all laughed and did not speak.
When pressed,
they suddenly disappeared.
The Joy in the Orange is No Less Than on Shāngshān.
In Bāqióng, in an orange grove,
after the frost, two oranges were as large as three-dǒu jars.
When cut open, two old men were inside, facing each other, playing xiàngqí.
They chatted and laughed naturally.
One old man said:
"You owe me ten liǎng of the Sea Dragon King's wig,
nine hú of Yíngzhōu jade pots,
and eight pairs of dragon silk stockings."
The other old man said:
"The joy in the orange
is no less than on Shāngshān.
It's just that they couldn't take deep root and solidify their base,
and so were picked by foolish people."
One old man took dragon liver jerky and cut it to eat.
A moment later, the four old men together rode a dragon,
and clouds rose beneath their feet as they departed.
A macaque in a goiter.
The entertainer Diāo Jùncháo's wife, Bā Yù,
had a goiter on her neck.
Initially, it was like a chicken egg,
gradually growing to the size of a several-dǒu sack.
Inside, there were sounds of zithers, lutes, flutes, and chimes.
The wife said:
"This illness is truly hateful.
I can cut it open
to see what is inside."
As she raised her blade to strike,
the goiter suddenly split open,
and a macaque leaped out.
His wife immediately fell gravely ill.
A yellow-robed Taoist knocked on the door and said:
"My macaque child in the goiter
was originally an old monkey spirit,
able to bring wind and rain,
and frequently interacted with the old dragon of Guǐchóu Tán in the Hànjiāng River.
Heaven executed the dragon and
searched for its associates.
Therefore, it hid in your wife's beautiful neck.
Now I have obtained the 'Cloud-Rising Ointment' from the deity of Fènghuáng Shān.
Apply it and it will immediately heal."
Jùncháo applied it as he was told.
The wound closed instantly.
Héshén Guó.
Lǐ Yuánzhī suddenly fell ill.
He saw a robed figure who said:
"I am Gǔ Bì,
your distant ancestor.
I wish to go to Héshén Guó,
and have no one to carry my sack.
You may accompany me."
They flew very swiftly.
In that country, all kinds of fruits grow,
ripening once a year,
secretly transforming from flower to fruit.
Large gourds are filled with the five grains,
without the need for farming;
tree branches produce five-colored silk threads,
without the need for silkworms or looms.
There are no mosquitoes, gnats, nits, lice, bees, or scorpions;
no owls, crows, or magpies;
no tigers, wolves, or foxes.
The climate throughout the four seasons is like February or March.
People have two sons and two daughters.
Neighbors marry across generations.
People live to one hundred and twenty years,
without premature death or illness.
No privies are built.
People have no private granaries.
Surplus grain rests in the fields,
and those who need it take it.
It rains once every ten days,
always at night.
Gǔ Bì said:
"Although this country is not a realm of immortals,
its customs are not bad.
When you return, tell this to the people of the world."
Lǒngyòu Shānchuān Lüèshèng Shǐ.
Wéi Yuánfāng's maternal cousin, Péi Pú, died.
Yuánfāng saw a military officer riding a horse.
It was indeed Pú.
He said:
"I am the Lǒngyòu Shānchuān Lüèshèng Shǐ.
Every drink and morsel a living person takes is predetermined.
Moreover, wealth and treasures are recorded in the netherworld.
There is a limit to what one can obtain.
If one exceeds this number, the netherworld officials report it to the messenger,
who then seizes it.
Your encounter with me is also predetermined.
You are destined to receive two catties of white gold.
Anything beyond this would be seized,
hence not a greater amount.
Human life has its fate;
it is fixed and unchangeable.
Observe it calmly with the Dao,
and you will no longer be restless or disturbed.
Strive for this!"
Míng Huáng Observes the Làyuè Festival in Yángzhōu.
On the fifteenth day of the first month of the Kāiyuán
era, Mínghuáng said to Master Yè Xiānshī:
“Of all the places in the four directions on this evening,
where is the most splendid?”
He replied:
“Nowhere under heaven is as splendid as Guǎnglíng.”
The Emperor desired to see it.
Suddenly, a rainbow bridge rose before the palace hall.
The Master reported:
“Please proceed,
but do not look back.”
The Emperor stepped onto it,
accompanied by Gāo Lìshì and several tens of court musicians.
In a short while, they arrived in Guǎnglíng.
The men and women looked up and said:
“Immortals have appeared in the clouds.”
The Master said:
“Please command the court musicians to play a piece of the Níshang Yǔyī.”
After the Emperor returned to the palace,
it was reported:
“On the night of the Lantern Festival in Guǎnglíng,
immortals riding on colorful clouds came from the west,
descended upon Xiàogǎn Sì,
played the Níshang Yǔyī Qǔ,
finished one piece, and then departed.”
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
A Foreign Monk Curses the Seawater
Yè Jìngnéng lectured in Fènghuà, Míngzhōu, during the Kāiyuán era.
An old man, dressed in white and bearded, wept and bowed,
identifying himself:
“I am the dragon guardian of the treasure,
my duty is in the small sea.
For a thousand years, I have not failed,
and so I am about to be slightly promoted.
If I fail, I will suffer the punishment of burning sand.
Now, it has been over nine hundred years.
A foreign monk, whose magic will be perfected at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month,
will come to curse the water.
When the water dries,
the treasure will have nowhere to hide,
and the burning sand will truly be unavoidable.”
The Immortal Master then sent a person in green clothes with an inked talisman.
At the edge of the sea, black curses rose everywhere.
There was a Brahmin, wielding a sword and chanting curses.
The seawater diminished by half,
and the person in green clothes immediately fell from his horse.
He then sent a person in yellow clothes, carrying a cinnabar talisman.
The Brahmin cursed again,
and seven or eight tenths of the seawater dried up.
A white dragon leaped in the shallow waves.
Again, he sent a person in vermilion clothes, carrying a yellow talisman.
Despite repeated curses, he did not fall.
The person in vermilion clothes threw the talisman,
and the seawater returned to its original state.
The Brahmin sighed and said:
“How can a Daoist priest be so capable?”
The waves stilled and the wind subsided.
The old man tearfully thanked the Immortal Master,
pledging allegiance forever.
From then on, he paid his respects morning and evening,
as if he were a disciple.
A Tomb Fox Cultivates Dao and Becomes an Immortal
Dǎng Chāoyuán lived as a recluse on Huà Shān.
One night, a woman knocked on his door and said:
“I am a fox from the southern tomb.
I have cultivated the Dao and become an immortal.
My karma is complete and my wish fulfilled.
The day after tomorrow, I am destined to die by an arrow.
Tomorrow morning, when the passing hunters arrive,
they should be asked to hunt a fox.
After my Dao cultivation is complete, I will surely repay you.”
The next evening, hunters indeed arrived and sought lodging.
He treated them generously,
and requested them to hunt a fox.
The next day, the hunters indeed encountered a fox,
which was killed by an arrow.
They brought it to Chāoyuán.
Chāoyuán secretly sent it back into its den.
He again saw the former woman, who tearfully thanked him and said:
“Although my Dao cultivation is complete,
according to custom, I must die
by being torn apart and eaten.
There is no way to be reborn.
Now, by your profound kindness,
my deceased form has been preserved.
The path of immortality is long,
and from this point, I bid you farewell forever.
In the burning house,
the flames of sorrow are raging.
If one can contemplate tranquility,
and momentarily quell worldly desires,
even in a single thought,
one can temporarily reach a cool place.
I offer fifty *jīn* of alchemical gold as thanks.”
Later, a foreign merchant came
and said:
“You have celestial liquid gold.”
He paid a high price for it and left.
The Woman Leaves a Blue-Flowered Felt Shoe
Yǐn Zòngzhī studied on Zhōngtiáo Shān.
On a moonlit night, a woman arrived,
graceful and extraordinary,
but her ears were slightly black.
She stayed the night, and they had great joy.
Zòngzhī kept one blue-flowered felt shoe.
The woman bowed deeply, expressing boundless gratitude.
When he would not return it,
she wept and left.
Clotted blood was on the ground.
The felt shoe
was a right hoof.
He went down the mountain
and saw a large pig without its rear right hoof,
which ran with angry eyes,
and as it ran, it died.
Marrying the Naizhòng Ghost
Wáng Huáng traveled from Luò [yáng] to Gōushì Zhuāng.
By the roadside, there was a woman in white,
setting out offerings and weeping very sadly.
Two maids beside her said:
“Our young mistress married Péi Láng,
who has already died.
She was orphaned young
and has no home to return to.”
Huáng traveled with her to a villa
and performed the marriage ceremony.
A Daoist priest, Rèn Xuányán, said:
“The one you married is a ghost of a powerful deity.
It is still possible to break it off quickly.”
A few days later, he said again:
“You will surely die!
You didn’t believe my words until now.
What a pity!
Tomorrow, throw this talisman at her,
and you will see her true form.”
Huáng threw the talisman,
and she immediately transformed into a Naizhòng ghost,
saying:
“Our affection was like this,
why did you listen to that demonic Daoist priest
and reveal my form?”
She seized Huáng and threw him onto the bed,
trampled him once, and he died.
Xuányán said:
“This is a Naizhòng from under the right hoof of the Northern Heavenly King.
Every three thousand years, one is replaced.
It transforms into human form
to choose and replace itself.
If Huáng had died sitting,
he would have completed three thousand years and
would also seek replacement.
Now that he died lying down,
he will never be replaced again.”
《Zhītián Lù》
Ashamed of the Rat Prison, Lacking the Wisdom of the Chicken Stele
An elder’s poem says:
“After the book, three hundred fruits are inscribed,
Dòngtíng must wait for the trees to be full of frost.”
Later generations mostly said it was spontaneously composed,
not knowing that someone in the Southern Dynasties wrote “three hundred Dòngtíng frosted oranges” at the end of a paper.
I am ashamed of the rat prison,
lacking the wisdom of the chicken stele,
and thus, pondering the words of former worthies
related to human affairs,
I compiled five volumes.
Giving Sòng Jǐng Stalactites
On the fifth day of the fifth month,
stalactites were bestowed upon Sòng Jǐng.
He was ordered to have a physician prepare and refine them.
His children and nephews said:
“The emperor’s gift must be precious,
and others will surely cheat or exchange it.
It is better to process it at home.”
Jǐng said:
“Even by showing sincerity and trustworthiness,
I still fear being suspected.
How can one act with distrust towards others?
Is it possible?
You must not treat people this way.”
What Kind of Face Did Lù Zhì Have?
When Chancellor Lù Xuāngōng arrived in Zhōngzhōu,
earth blocked his gate,
and salt and vegetables entered through a dog hole.
He sat upright, copying medicinal prescriptions.
His children and nephews rarely spoke with him either.
It happened that the transport commissioner arrived in the capital.
The Emperor asked:
“When you passed through the gorges,
what kind of face did you hear Lù Zhì had?”
He reported the situation in detail.
The Emperor felt saddened.
He was appointed Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince,
but he had already died.
Fáng Guǎn Is Not the Hand to Annihilate the Bandits
In the Tiānbǎo era,
the bandits captured the two capitals.
Xuánzōng fled west,
and Sùzōng ascended the throne.
The emperor, acting as the master, looked at the list of appointments
and said to Péi Shìyān:
"There is a new prime minister."
Shìyān asked who it was.
The emperor said:
"Fáng Guǎn,
but he is also not the hand to annihilate the bandits."
Shìyān said:
"Your Majesty does not need to say this."
The emperor felt a little ashamed.
Lǐ Línfǔ Envies the Worthy and Hates the Capable
The retired emperor said:
"Lǐ Línfǔ's talent is hard to come by,
but envying the worthy and hating the capable will surely lead to his downfall."
Shìyān said:
"Since Your Majesty knows this,
why did you keep him in office for so long?
Today's troubles
are Línfǔ's doing."
The emperor was displeased.
After several *lǐ*,
holding his whip, he remained silent.
Wèi Zhēng's Illness
The emperor said:
"Since you will surely not recover,
do you have nothing to say?"
Zhēng said:
"The weaver neglects the woof."
The emperor said:
"Truly a remedy!"
Open Your Eyes and Recognize Your New Daughter-in-law
When Wèi Zhēng's illness was critical,
the emperor led his young daughter and said:
"I have no way to repay your meritorious service.
Force your eyes open
and recognize your new daughter-in-law."
Zhēng said:
"All important matters are done;
I will ultimately be unable to manage her."
Several years later, the princess was married to Bóyù.
King Wǔ Bestowed Dájǐ upon Duke of Zhōu
When Cáo Tàizǔ captured Jìzhōu,
Yuán Xī's wife was beautiful,
and Emperor Wén took her as a concubine.
Kǒng Běihǎi admonished, saying:
"When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he bestowed Dájǐ upon the Duke of Zhōu."
Cáo Gōng said:
"I don't recall this matter in the histories or traditions?"
Róng said:
"I only see that Duke Míng is doing it today,
so it must have been fitting at that time."
The Duke was displeased for a long time.
Paper Kites Carrying Edicts
When Hóu Jǐng besieged Táichéng,
Emperor Liáng Wǔ had no solution.
A young boy offered a plan:
make kites out of paper,
attach edicts to them,
and release them with the wind,
hoping for outside aid.
Hundreds of kites flew,
but no aid arrived,
and Táichéng subsequently fell.
Wooden Geese Carrying Edicts
When Emperor Yáng was in Dōngdū,
the King of Dài remained to guard Cháng'ān,
and bandits rose like swarms of bees.
Someone offered a plan:
carve wooden geese, attach edicts to their necks,
and place them in the Wèihé River,
hoping for rescue troops from Guāndōng to arrive.
A hundred or so were released daily,
drifting downstream,
but ultimately no rescue arrived.
What Surname is Mài?
Qiě Wēi, a Shangshū, saw General Mài Tiězhàng in the chancellery
and jokingly said:
"What surname is Mài?"
Tiězhàng said:
"How far apart are Qiě and Mài?"
At the time, this was considered a perfect retort.
I Grant You the Entire Tree
Lǐ Yìfǔ was presented as a child prodigy at the age of eight.
When Emperor Wén was in the Shànglín Park,
someone captured a crow.
Yìfǔ presented a poem about the crow, saying:
"In the sun, it displays its morning colors;
in the zither, it accompanies night cries.
The Shànglín Park has so many trees,
but grants not a single branch for rest."
The emperor smiled and said:
"I grant you the entire tree."
Your Father's Face Was Like Yours
Lù Suí lost his father at a young age.
His mother asked:
"Do you remember your father?"
He said:
"No."
His mother said:
"He was just like your face."
Suí, until adulthood,
never looked in a mirror throughout his life.
Gāozōng Punctured Bǎihuì
Emperor Gāozōng had a brain carbuncle.
The imperial physician Mínghè said:
"It requires acupuncture at Bǎihuì."
Empress Zétiān said:
"Is the Son of Heaven's head a place for bleeding?"
She ordered him to be executed.
The emperor said:
"Let him try needling it."
Immediately, his eyes brightened,
and all his suffering ceased.
Empress Zétiān personally rewarded him with gold and silk.
Holding a Bowl to Judge Selections
When Emperor Dézōng fled,
Qiáo Lín followed him to Zhōuzhì.
He said:
"Your subject wishes to become a monk at Xiānyóu Temple for Your Majesty,
to ward off the bandits."
The emperor regretted his departure
but could not prevent it.
Later, he entered the capital holding a bowl to seek alms,
saying:
"There is always something, there is always giving."
Later, he served Zhū Cǐ as Shàngshū of the Ministry of Personnel
and managed the selection process.
When a candidate for office said it was not convenient,
Lín jokingly said:
"Is this selection convenient or not?"
When Cǐ was defeated,
the emperor said:
"Our bond is deep,
how could you hold a bowl and judge selections?
Your words are still in my ears.
When you were making light jokes,
it was precisely when I was in distress."
Pushing Down the Ping Huaixi Stele
In the Yuánhé era,
an old soldier pushed down the Píng Huáixī Stele.
The emperor was enraged
and ordered him to be bound and brought, saying: "I will personally hack him to death."
When the prisoner arrived,
he said:
"The stele only praises Péi Dù's achievements,
but does not mention Lǐ Suò's efforts.
Your humble subject therefore felt it was unfair."
Because of this, the emperor ordered his pardon
and commanded Duàn Wénchāng to compose a new text.
Huìshān Spring Water Delivery
Grand Commandant Lǐ was by nature simple and frugal.
While in the Central Secretariat,
he did not drink water from the capital,
but used only Huìshān spring water.
At the time, he was known as "Water Delivery."
A monk said:
"Water delivery damages your eminent virtue."
The Duke said:
"Among latter-day commoners, who is without desires or cravings?
I do not seek wealth,
nor do I draw near to sensuous pleasures.
If I am to be condemned merely for water,
then what of those who accumulate riches,
or extensively collect singing and music?"
The monk said:
"Behind the Hàotiān Temple in the capital, there is a spring
whose water source is connected to Huìshān."
They then took water and weighed it.
It was equal to Huìshān water,
so he ceased the water delivery.
Using Small Bushels in the Market
In the Chángqìng era,
a person was struck dead by lightning.
On his back was written in white powder:
"Using small bushels in the market."
Materials for Hányuán Hall pillars
When Hányuán Diàn was replacing its pillars,
in Shèyángjiè's poor mountains there were several hundred feet of giant timber that could be used.
A commoner in the mountains said:
"This timber will carry the palace away in a future year,
shocking and shaking the universe.
You should saw and cut it to verify this now."
They cut it,
and indeed red blood flowed out.
The commoner said:
"This is blood.
Send it quickly to the Wèishuǐ river,
otherwise, it will be a calamity for the entire prefecture.
Deep mountains and vast marshes
truly give birth to dragons and serpents.
This wood grew in an uninhabited place;
a python was within it.
Fifteen years from now, it will collapse mountains and overturn valleys.
How can it be used as timber?"
Avoiding the Character "Lè" (Joy) Prevents Laughter
Wéi Yǒuyì, a Shàngshū,
had a great reputation.
Throughout his life, he did not drink alcohol,
nor did he engage in joyful laughter.
This was because his family avoided the character "lè" (樂).
A Man Named Tán Seeks Office
Xiè Tiào of the Jìn dynasty was in charge of selecting officials in the Língbù.
A man named Tán requested an official post.
Xiè Tiào said:
"Qí Huán destroyed Tán.
How can there be a gentleman like you?"
The man replied:
"Tánzǐ fled to Jǔ,
that is why I exist."
Consulting Húlú Shēng about Fate
Bái Zhōngjīn repeatedly failed the imperial examinations.
He went to Húlú Shēng to inquire about his fate.
Húlú Shēng would not permit it at all.
Later, as Bái Zhōngjīn entered Ānshàng Mén,
a woman, with a new purple silk handkerchief sealed around her hair bun,
had her slave girl, exhausted from the effort,
place it on the gatepost.
Carriages and horses gathered.
As the gate was about to be opened,
both the woman and the slave girl disappeared.
The handkerchief remained by the gatepost,
and the gentleman (Bái Zhōngjīn) guarded it.
Until late in the day,
the owner did not appear.
Suddenly, he saw the woman crying, saying:
"I have committed a crime.
If anyone can rescue me,
I only desire a precious belt.
I lost it this morning,
and my husband will not escape punishment."
The gentleman returned the belt to her.
The woman thanked him tearfully and left.
The next day, Bái Zhōngjīn saw Húlú Shēng again,
who said:
"Xiùcái, you have recently accumulated hidden virtue.
Next year you will pass the examinations
and reach the highest official position."
Bad Writing and a Relative's Name Offered at Once
Lú Jūn was appointed as Mù (governor) of Qúzhōu.
A scholar presented a letter of introduction.
The governor opened the scroll
and read ten of his essays,
all of which had been written by the governor himself.
He secretly said:
"This is not your writing, Xiùcái."
The man replied:
"I have worked hard on my studies,
and my understanding is not unique,
so I did not borrow from others."
The governor said:
"These are essays I wrote.
Can you also recite them by heart?"
The guest was at a loss for words
and confessed:
"I obtained these essays without a name,
and did not know they were composed by Yuánwài."
He was terrified and wished to leave.
The governor said:
"Although these were written by me,
I did not show them to others.
Just keep them, Xiùcái."
He detained him and treated him generously.
Before he left,
the governor asked where he was going.
He replied:
"To Biànzhōu, to Liáng Shàngshū.
He is my maternal uncle (qīn zhàngrén),
and I must stay for ten days."
The governor said:
"Dàliáng Shàngshū is my cousin (qīn biǎo).
If you are his relative by marriage,
then I and you must be close relatives.
This statement is probably false again."
The man trembled with fear,
as if there was no place for him.
The governor said:
"There's no need to be like this.
Earlier, your bad writing and the claim of being a relative of Dàliáng were
both offered at once."
He Will Certainly Not Lose His Title of Guīmìng Hóu
Emperor Wén of Suí asked Hèruò Bì:
"Do you recognize the Son of Heaven of Chén?"
Hèruò Bì replied:
"I do not know him very well."
The Emperor summoned him.
The Lord of Chén, knowing Hèruò Bì's great reputation,
bowed to him first upon meeting him,
showing such respect and caution that he sweated.
Hèruò Bì jested:
"You don't need to be so terrified.
You will certainly not lose your title of Guīmìng Hóu."
Eulogy for Tàigōng Encountering King Wén
Wáng Bó's ancestor, Wénzhōngzǐ,
saw Wáng Bó playing with his brush,
and bade him compose "Eulogy for Tàigōng Encountering King Wén,"
saying:
"Jī Chāng favored virtue,
Lǚ Wàng praised his brilliance.
Though the palace gates are near,
wind and clouds are still distant.
The fishing boat leans on the stone,
the fishing bank lies across the sand.
The path is secluded in the mountain valley,
the stream is deep, the banks are steep.
The leopard's tactics ward off evil,
the dragon's bell repels misfortune.
Though they meet intimately,
they still await the emperor's carriage.
When the king clasps his hand,
how late it is!"
Selling Rice to Relieve Drought
Lìnghú Wéngōng was appointed governor of Yǎnzhōu.
The prefecture was experiencing a drought,
and the price of rice was very high.
When the welcoming officials arrived,
the governor first asked the price of rice,
how many granaries the prefecture had,
and how many *shí* each granary held.
He counted on his fingers and muttered to himself:
"The old price was such-and-such.
If so much rice is released from the granaries
and sold at a fixed price,
then it can relieve the distress."
His attendants secretly overheard,
and the words reached the wealthy people in the commandery.
They subsequently released their hoarded grain,
and the price of rice immediately stabilized.
Secretary Dù Is Well
Niú Qízhānggōng was the commander of Wéiyáng.
Dù Mù was serving in his retinue.
At night, Dù Mù would go out in plain clothes to roam freely.
The Duke secretly sent several street patrols to follow him
to prevent any unforeseen incidents.
Later, Dù Mù was summoned to serve as Shíyí.
The Duke warned him against his unrestrained behavior.
Dù Mù initially tried to conceal it.
The Duke took out a casket
containing all the reports from the street patrols,
which all read:
"Secretary Dù is well."
Imperial Plums
Wèi Wǔ moved Emperor Xiàn of Hàn to Xǔchāng.
There were yellow plums,
as large as plums (literally, "containing peaches," likely referring to a specific type of large plum or a fruit similar in size to a peach pit).
The Emperor ate them.
To this day, they are called Imperial Plums (Yù Lǐzǐ).
Yuán Gōng Starved to Death in an Empty Valley
Yuán Déxiù retired to Ānlù,
dozens of *lǐ* from his home.
Heavy rain caused flooding,
and for seven days, communication was cut off.
He starved to death in an empty house.
Lú Zài composed a eulogy saying:
"Who served as the Prefect's assistant?
The great ones must eat meat.
Who served as the Prefect's colleagues?
Their horses must eat grain.
Yet my Yuán Gōng
starved to death in an empty valley."
Using a *Shì* Board to Divinate a Lost Ox
Jiǎ Dān (賈耽) was skilled in divination.
An old man had lost his ox
and went to the Duke to report it.
The Duke took a divining tray from his hat case and cast a hexagram,
saying:
“Your ox is in the magpie’s nest in the locust tree behind the three gates of Ānguó Guàn (安國觀).”
The old man went to investigate. Below the nest,
he saw a neighbor’s ox tied up.
Thus he recovered it.
Brothers Litigating Over Property
In Xīshǔ (西蜀), there were brothers litigating over property.
The case had dragged on for a long time without resolution.
Bì Gòu (畢搆) became the Liánchá (廉察),
and he called the brothers,
had them drink human milk.
They were all awakened and enlightened,
and lived together again.
Fish Keys
Door keys must be made in the shape of a fish,
taking its characteristic of not closing its eyes,
symbolizing keeping watch through the night.
Volume 11
End.
Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) of Táng’s Dream
When Emperor Gāozǔ (高祖) of Táng was about to raise his righteous army,
he dreamt at night that his body died and fell from his bed,
and was eaten by a swarm of maggots.
Zhìmǎn Chánshī (智滿禪師) said:
“You will obtain the empire.
Moreover, ‘death’ is ‘bi (斃)’ (to fall),
and ‘falling from the bed’ is ‘xià (下)’ (below).
Your Majesty (Bìxià 陛下)
is the form of the supreme.
‘Eaten by a swarm of maggots’ means
that myriad people will flock to you.”
He also dreamt of countless armored horses,
flying full in the sky,
and said:
“These are the spirits within your body.”
After speaking,
the armored horses flew into the Emperor’s body.
He awoke and summoned Tàizōng (太宗), saying:
“My enterprise is accomplished.”
Calendar Off By One Day
Xuánzōng (玄宗) decreed Yīxíng Chánshī (一行禪師) to cast a celestial sphere and compile the Tàiyǎn Lì (《太衍曆》) calendar.
Before this,
during the reign of Hàn Wǔ (漢武), Luòxià Hóng (洛下閎) had said:
“This calendar,
after a thousand years, will be off by one day.
A sage will appear and correct it.”
It was indeed a thousand years by this time.
Dàyuān (大宛) Presents Six Sweating Horses
During the Tiānbǎo (天寶) era,
Dàyuān (大宛) presented six sweating horses.
The first was called Hóng Chìbō (紅叱撥),
the second Zǐ Chìbō (紫叱撥),
the third Qīng Chìbō (青叱撥),
the fourth Huáng Chìbō (黃叱撥),
the fifth Dīngxiāng Chìbō (丁香叱撥),
and the sixth Táohuā Chìbō (桃花叱撥).
The Emperor then renamed them Hóngyù Niǎn (紅玉輦), Píngshān Niǎn (平山輦), Língyún Niǎn (凌雲輦), Fēixiāng Niǎn (飛香輦), and Bǎihuā Niǎn (百花輦).
He ordered them to be painted in Yáoguāng Diàn (瑤光殿).
Golden Casket and Dāngguī (當歸)
When Mínghuáng (明皇) was in Dàmíng Gōng (大明宮),
Yīxíng (一行) said:
“Your Majesty will have a journey of ten thousand *lǐ*.”
He then gave the Emperor a golden casket,
to be opened in an emergency.
When Lù Shān (祿山) attacked the capital,
the Emperor opened it,
and found a piece of Dāngguī (當歸) (Angelica sinensis, literally “should return”).
The Emperor then went to Shǔ (蜀).
Civil and Military Officials Given Separate Food
After Xuānzōng (宣宗) finished a banquet,
he saw the officials and guards bowing and dancing,
leaving behind fruits and food.
The Emperor was surprised.
They all said:
“We are taking it home to present to our parents and to give to our young children.”
The Emperor commanded the chief cook:
“From now on, at grand banquets,
civil and military officials shall be given two portions of food,
one for their parents,
and separate fruits for their children.
Any leftover food
may be wrapped in a handkerchief and taken home.”
This then became a custom.
Phoenix Perch Pears
In the mountains of Shǎnzōu (陝州), there was a wild pear tree.
At the beginning of the Zhēngguān (貞觀) era,
a phoenix perched there.
Its fruit was plump and delicious,
and thus it was called “Fèngqī Lí (鳳棲梨).”
Two Elephants of Gold and Jade
Lǐ Déyù (李德裕) was fond of consuming cinnabar.
A Daoist priest, who called himself Lǐ Zhōngnán (李終南) and lived on Luófú Shān (羅浮山),
said:
“Chancellor, you have long consumed cinnabar pills.
This is very good,
but it shortens life.”
From his bosom, he produced a small jade elephant, about the size of a fist,
and said:
“You should seek a pure one from Gōulòu (勾漏),
place it under the elephant’s trunk.
The elephant must consume the cinnabar and then spit it out before it can be taken.
This is the essence of the great yang,
condensed for thirty thousand years.
Now I lend it to you.
Remember loyalty and filial piety,
so as not to incur calamity.”
He also produced a golden elephant,
saying:
“This is the female,
to be a pair with the jade.”
Zànhuáng (贊皇) verified each one, and they were without error.
After consuming it,
his complexion became younger,
his hair and temples like lacquer.
He then sought out beautiful and extraordinary women,
numbering several hundred.
Later, when he returned south,
he met the Daoist priest at Guǐmén Guān (鬼門關).
The priest angrily demanded the two elephants,
saying:
“You did not heed my words,
so it must come to this.”
The Duke reluctantly refused to give them.
When he reached Èyú Tán (鱷魚潭),
the wind and rain became dark and gloomy.
The jade elephant flew out of the boat by itself,
its light illuminating the sky.
The golden elephant followed it into the water.
