The Duke reached Zhūyá (朱崖),
and died of resentment.
Then it was known that the elephants
were fire beasts of the south;
Gōulòu (勾漏) was the treasure of Zhūyá (朱崖);
Luófú (羅浮) was a mountain by the sea;
and Lǐ Zhōngnán (李終南)
was Zànhuáng (贊皇) who would not return.
Yán Lǔgōng’s (顏魯公) *Shījiě* (屍解)
Yán Zhēnqīng (顏真卿) went to admonish Lǐ Xīliè (李希烈).
Everyone, both inside and outside, knew the Duke would not return.
His relatives saw him off at Chánglè Pō (長樂坡).
The Duke, drunk,
leapt onto the front pillar of the hall, saying:
“I met a Daoist priest early on,
who said his name was Táo Bābā (陶八八).
He bestowed upon me the elixir Bìxiá Dān (碧霞丹),
and I have not declined since then.”
He also said:
“At seventy, if there is a calamity, it will be auspicious.
On another day, carry me to Luófú Shān (羅浮山).
Is it not today’s calamity?”
The Duke arrived at Dàliáng (大梁).
Xīliè (希烈) ordered him to be strangled to death,
and he was buried south of the city.
When Xīliè (希烈) was defeated,
his family opened the coffin,
and found his appearance as if alive,
his whole body golden,
his nails extending from the back of his hands,
and his beard several *chǐ* long.
He was reburied on the northern mountain of Yǎnshī (偃師).
Later, a merchant arrived at Luófú Shān (羅浮山).
Two Daoist priests were playing *wéiqí* under a tree.
One said:
“Who comes here?”
He replied:
“A small guest,
a man from Luòyáng (洛陽).”
The Daoist priest smiled and said:
“Please deliver a letter to my family.”
He sent a boy to fetch paper and brush to write the letter.
When he arrived at the northern mountain,
Yán’s (顏) descendants received the letter and were greatly surprised,
saying:
“It is our late Grand Preceptor’s (Tàishī 太師) own handwriting.”
They opened the tomb and coffin,
which were already empty.
They went directly to Luófú (羅浮) to search for him,
but found no trace.
They also said:
“Our late Grand Preceptor’s (Tàishī 太師) calligraphy had the style of ‘cán tóu mǎ wěi (蠶頭馬尾)’ (silkworm head and horse tail),
this is truly becoming an immortal.”
The Scarlet-Robed Official Leapt Out
Yuán Zhěn was sitting alone in his private residence.
A crimson-robed official entered and said,
"Xiànggōng is to be appointed today."
After speaking, he hurried out.
Yuán Zhěn ordered his attendants to pursue him,
but they all said no one was there.
When he went to court, there was indeed an imperial decree.
Several months later, he again saw the crimson-robed official,
who said he was dismissed from his premiership.
At dawn,
a report came out from the Department of the Central Secretariat.
The "Tuó-Há" character puzzle:
The *jìnshì* Gù Fēixióng
heard Línghú Xiàngguó Chǔ's quick wit,
so Línghú Chǔ changed one character puzzle,
saying:
"Take a *tuó* (alligator) from the water,
take a *tuó* (camel) from the shore.
Use this *tuó* (camel) to carry this *tuó* (alligator),
which is *tuó tuó tuó* (camel carries alligator)."
Fēixióng said:
"Take a *gē* (pigeon) from the rooftop,
take a *há* (clam) from the water.
Use this *há* (clam) to close this *gē* (pigeon),
which is *gē hé há* (pigeon closes clam)."
The Duke greatly admired him.
Zhèng Tián is appointed Prime Minister:
When Zhèng Tián was an academician,
he suddenly heard the imperial procession's clearing signal.
He quickly went out to welcome and bow.
The Emperor had already ascended to the Yùtáng,
took a stack of papers from the desk and wrote, "Concurrent Deputy Director of the Central Secretariat and Grand Minister of State."
Tián bowed in thanks.
The Emperor smiled and said,
"I was just joking."
Tián said,
"The Duke of Táng clipped a paulownia leaf,
and the Duke of Zhōu considered the Son of Heaven incapable of joking.
How much more so Your Majesty's imperial handwriting,
how can it be a joke?"
So the Emperor had no choice
and appointed him Prime Minister.
Tián was demoted to Wúzhōu after serving as Imperial Edict Attendant.
When Xīzōng ascended the throne,
he summoned him as a Regular Attendant,
and he was appointed Prime Minister,
which differs from this account.
The hemp in Zhèng Hé's courtyard:
Zhèng Jué and Lǐ Yú were both academicians.
In Zhèng Hé's courtyard, there was a patch of hemp.
Lǐ Yú said,
"The Imperial Edict Attendant will become Prime Minister.
I wish to draft the imperial decree
and complete the desolation."
At that time, there had been a severe drought for a long time,
but the hemp alone flourished.
When frost descended, it bore fruit,
which was the white hemp.
That night, the decree was issued,
and Zhèng indeed took office.
The "Three Nines Prime Minister":
Zhèng Tián took the imperial examination at the age of nineteen,
passed it at nineteen,
and became Prime Minister nineteen years later.
At that time, he was called "Sānjiǔ Xiànggōng."
The "White Sand Prime Minister":
There was a heavy rain at Lǐ Yú's residence,
and the entire courtyard became white sand.
When he passed away,
the sand in his younger brother's courtyard turned black.
At that time, he was called "Báishā Xiànggōng."
No more mood to remember Lǎojūn:
The poet Shǐ Jūnshí saw a female Daoist returning to secular life,
and presented a poem saying:
"Shedding the rosy skirts for embroidered ones,
Immortal and mortal paths diverge from this day.
Her moth-like brows repainted like the moon of old,
Her cicada-like temples re-combed like the clouds of yesteryear.
Her jade countenance slowly reflected in the phoenix mirror,
Her brocade quilt scented with musk.
Within the screen, she finds the love of Xiāo Láng,
And has no more mood to remember Lǎojūn."
Mouth like a measureless *dǒu*:
Gāo Pián, while garrisoned in Chéngdū,
ordered his wine assistant Xuē Táo to create a one-character puzzle, saying:
"It must be a character resembling a shape,
and it must rhyme."
The Duke said:
"Kǒu (mouth),
resembles a measureless *dǒu* (bushel)."
Táo said:
"Chuān (river),
resembles three rafters."
The Duke said:
"Why is one of them crooked?"
Táo said:
"Xiànggōng, as the Military Governor of Xīchuān,
still makes one *dǒu* measureless.
As for a poor wine assistant,
having three rafters,
with one of them crooked,
what is there to marvel at?"
Red silk mooncakes:
Xīzōng ate mooncakes
and found them delicious.
When *jìnshì* graduates had their celebratory banquet,
the Emperor bestowed upon each a serving of red silk mooncakes.
Xú Yín's poem says:
"Do not mock my missing and broken teeth,
For I once ate red silk mooncakes."
"Dǎqiú one stroke for 'fierce entry'":
Zhuāngzōng summoned Mèng Zhīxiáng to garrison Chéngdū.
Previously, when people in Shǔ played *dǎqiú*,
the one who got the ball into the hole with one stroke was called *měngrù* (fierce entry).
The pronunciation became corrupted to *Mèng rù* (Mèng entry),
earning one point.
Later, the Mèng clan gained control of both Shǔ regions,
down to his son Chǎng.
"One point"
indeed refers to one son.
Children with shaved heads:
At the end of Guǎngshùn era,
a rumor spread in the capital:
"The underworld needs tens of thousands of children with topknots."
Consequently, all families with children who had topknots shaved their heads.
A discerning person said:
"Children with shaved heads
are a sign of a new ruler."
Soon after, Shìzōng ascended the throne.
Shāhú Lín:
The Qìdān King was angry that the young Emperor of Jìn did not heed his command
and arbitrarily ascended to the imperial throne.
He personally led his forces south,
seized the young Emperor, his empress mother, and his ministers, and returned.
Upon reaching Yè, he fell ill at Chóusǐ Gāng,
and died at Shāhú Lín in Luánchéng.
As for the *Gāng*,
it was originally where Chén Sī Wáng, not tolerated by Wéndì,
grieved and chanted,
thus named Sīgāng, corrupted to Chóusǐ.
Shāhú Lín
was named because villagers killed a fox inside the forest.
Héng'é is very ugly:
Shěn Sōng and Luó Yǐn served under the military governor of Zhéxī.
When the princess appeared,
the crowd exclaimed:
"Her beauty is truly that of Héng'é!"
Sōng said:
"Cháng'é is very ugly;
how can she compare to the princess?"
They were startled and asked:
"Does the scribe know Héng'é?"
He replied:
"Sōng has twice been to the Moon Palace to pluck cassia branches;
how could I not know her?"
Sōng intended to surprise Yǐn,
hence his remark.
Possessing the talent of *hòupǔ*:
Lú Duān was the archivist for Zhuāngzōng.
At the time, the imperial physician Chén Xuán was appointed Professor of Excavation Studies for Tàiyuán Prefecture.
Duān drafted the decree saying:
"Possessing the talent of *hòupǔ* (magnolia bark, also 'thick and plain'),
he is suited for the position of leisure and dignity."
Visiting the old Buddhist nunnery:
Yáng Níngshì was facetious.
The old nun of the monastery was the wet nurse of Wáng Línggōng's family.
When Yáng arrived,
she refused to show proper courtesy.
So he wrote on the wall:
"On a leisurely day, I visited the old Buddhist nunnery,
and was received with exceptional warmth."
The nun was very touched.
Later, understanding the words "old Buddhist nun,"
she immediately plastered over it.
Poem on Tàiháng Shān:
Gōng Lín submitted a collection to Hé Níng.
His poem "Dēng Tàiháng Shān" (Ascending Tàiháng Mountain) says:
"As long as there's a path to climb,
however high, people will still go."
Poem on morning clouds:
Zhào Lín’s poem “Zhāoxiá” (Morning Glow) says:
“Not because of the red sun’s light,
it forever flies as white clouds.”
However, once the sun shines,
it is not a lasting image.
Later, he passed the imperial examination and rose to court,
was granted scarlet robes, and then died.
Summoning the Owner to Redeem
In the last years of Mèng Chǎng’s reign,
a pawnbroker collected officials' goods.
A large sign was placed in front of the pawnbroker, saying:
“By imperial decree,
the owner is summoned to redeem within one month.”
Not long after, the royal army marched west.
People then realized that “summoned” (zhào 召) was Zhào (趙, referring to Sòng Tàizǔ, Zhao Kuangyin),
and “redeem” (shú 贖) was Shǔ (蜀, referring to the Later Shu kingdom),
Mèng Chǎng,
was a subject of Sòng (宋).
Transmitting Robe and Bowl, Gaining the Mind-Seal
Fàn Zhì was a disciple of Hé Níng; he had been his disciple before.
Those whose names appeared on the same examination roster as their patron teacher,
were called “robe and bowl” (yībō 傳衣缽).
Fàn’s name appeared interspersed with Hé’s,
and Fàn inherited from him again;
Hé became chancellor,
was enfeoffed as Lǔ Gōng,
and ended as Tàifù;
Fàn was also enfeoffed as Lǔ Gōng,
and ended as Tàifù;
this was truly a transmission of the robe and bowl,
and gaining the mind-seal.
Falsely Appearing as Mutton at the Banquet
The prefectural vice-magistrate of Shè,
whose name is forgotten,
when his principal was practicing archery,
ordered the cook to slaughter a pig.
The vice-magistrate asked to go and strike it himself,
saying:
“I’ve hated it for more than a day!”
The guests all asked him,
and he said:
“I can’t stand it pretending to be mutton on the prefect’s banquet table.”
From then on, the principal treated him with great respect.
A Couplet about Tiānhàn
Wáng Yú was famous for his poetry.
He once had a couplet that said:
“If Tiānhàn (天漢, the Milky Way) is not straight,
how can the source of the river be clear?”
Prime Minister Cuī Yìn heard it,
and was very displeased.
He eventually wandered and died.
Observing Yǔshēn and the Poem
The Daoist Chéng Zǐxiāo
once attended a night gathering of court officials at the Tàiyī Temple in Zhōngnán.
They pulled the Master to observe Yǔshēn (庾申).
The Master wrote a poem:
“Not observing Yǔshēn, nor doubting,
this heart is truly fitting with the Dao.
The Jade Emperor already knows one’s conduct,
let the Sān Péng speak of right and wrong.”
Forbidding Pine Torches, Cutting Off Moonlight
During the time of Emperor Zhāo’s Zōngjiàofāng official Ān Pèixīn, who had recently studied under Qí Shī Xú Mào Zhēn, military expenses were insufficient.
So, official oil was still monopolized and sold.
Someone said:
“Recently, no official oil can be sold at all.”
This was because pine torches were being let in through various gates,
infringing upon official profits,
and should be quickly prohibited.
Mào Zhēn immediately ordered a notice to be posted.
Ān Pèixīn said:
“This is excellent.
It would be even better if it could cut off the moonlight as well.”
Mào Zhēn laughed heartily,
and subsequently withdrew the previous notice.
To Properly Console the Afflicted
Wéi Chāng was a recorder in Xīchuān.
At that time, Wáng Jiàn was gathering people,
and expenses were particularly high.
A county magistrate, by illicit means, extorted and collected,
and was accused by a sub-official.
Zhuāng drafted a petition for Wáng Jiàn, which said:
“It is precisely the autumn of affliction,
so it is good to properly console the afflicted;
do not let the aftermath of wounds
become wounds again.”
Pípá Legs and Bìlìtóu
The Left Street Monk Registrar Huì Jiāng
and the majestic Chéng Zǐxiāo were both quick-witted,
and often ridiculed each other.
Huì Jiāng was naturally plump.
Once, in the heat, he bared his chest.
Chéng Zǐxiāo suddenly saw him and
said:
“Monk Registrar has pípá (lute) legs.”
Huì Jiāng replied:
“And you, sir, have a bìlì (oboe) head.”
Later, they saw several camels.
Chéng Zǐxiāo saw a large one and said:
“This must be a dhūta.”
Huì Jiāng said:
“These creatures reproduce,
and there is also a sequence of seniority.
This one is older than you, sir,
not a dhūta.”
Three Not Open
Mǎ Chè Sūn became a prime minister.
He never extended invitations to his relatives and old friends,
and was at the time called “Three Not Open.”
When the prime minister went to court,
his seal was not open;
when he met guests,
his mouth was not open;
when he returned home,
his door was not open.
Therefore, he was called “Three Not Open.”
Dreaming of Marrying a Wife
Cuī Yuánzōng served as the Staff Officer in Yìzhōu.
Wishing to marry a wife,
he suddenly dreamt that someone said:
“The daughter of this family is not your wife.
Your wife is born today.”
Then, in the dream, he was led to a house north of the road in the Lǚxìn Fāng of Dōngjīng (Luoyang),
where he saw a woman giving birth to a daughter,
and was told:
“This is your wife.”
Cuī woke up,
and did not believe it at all.
Soon after, the girl he was supposed to marry suddenly died.
Later, he rose to a fourth-rank official.
At fifty-eight years old,
he married Wéi Shè’s younger sister,
who was only nineteen,
and lived in Lǚxìn Fāng.
Upon checking the years and months,
she was born exactly on the day of his dream.
Lù’s Estate Laid Waste
Cuī Qún was in charge of the imperial examinations.
As the time approached,
his wife advised him to acquire land.
Cuī Qún said:
“I have thirty beautiful estates;
the thirty people I select on the roster are they.”
His wife said:
“Are you not a disciple of Lù Zhì?”
“When you are in charge of writing,
if you forbid your son to submit informal letters,
and if it is truly as you believe, like good fields,
then Lù’s estate would be laid waste.”
Cuī Qún had no words to reply.
Daoists Playing Chess in a Cave
In the two caves of Gōng Shān in Wùyuán,
there was a hole like a well.
In the late Xiántōng era,
a Daoist named Zhèng Dàoqī used a rope to descend over a hundred zhàng.
There was light beside him.
He went to look,
but the path ended blocked by water.
Across the bank, there was light,
and flowers and trees on the bank.
Two Daoists were playing chess.
A young attendant rowed a boat over
and asked:
“Do you wish to cross?”
He replied:
“I shall return.”
The attendant turned the boat and left.
Zhèng Dàoqī ascended again using the rope.
The next day,
a stone stalagmite blocked the mouth of the well,
and since then, no one has entered.
Five Hundred Coins Upright and Leaning on the Urn
In the mountains of Jiàn'ān,
there was a villager who traveled by small boat,
making a living by cutting firewood.
Suddenly, a few coins flowed down from the foot of the mountain.
Following them up to halfway,
under a tree was a large urn,
full of coins.
The urn was slightly tilted,
which was why the coins were flowing out.
So, he righted it,
covered it with a stone,
and took over five hundred coins home.
He led his family there,
intending to take all of them,
but they could not find the urn.
They lingered for several days and then left.
That night, he dreamt a person said:
"The money has an owner;
you cannot take it.
Before, because the urn was tilted,
I hired you with five hundred [coins] to right it."
Woman in the Waves
Xiè Zhòngxuān was boating northwest
when he saw a woman appearing and disappearing in the waves.
From her waist down, she had transformed into a fish.
People did not know whether it was a person turning into a fish,
or a fish turning into a person.
Yuanzhōu Yǎngshān Deity
In a village in Yuánzhōu,
there was an old man of a cautious and honest nature.
One day,
a purple-clad youth with a large retinue of carriages
asked him for food,
saying:
"I am the deity of Yǎngshān."
The old man bowed twice and said:
"The deity of Yǎngshān receives sacrifices daily;
why seek food?"
The deity said:
"Whenever people sacrifice to me,
they seek blessings from me.
If I have the power but cannot grant them,
or if it is not the right person,
or they are not worthy of receiving blessings,
I do not eat any of it.
Since you are an elder,
I ask for your food."
After eating, he left,
disappearing in a moment.
Deceased Wife Blames New Wife
In Jiàn'ān, there was a man whose wife died, and he remarried.
The new wife mistreated the former wife's child,
and the husband could not control her.
Suddenly, the deceased wife appeared, entering the house,
and reproached the new wife, saying:
"Who does not die?
Who is without maternal affection?
Why do you mistreat the child I bore?
If you continue like this, I will report it to the underworld
and be granted ten days.
I command you to repent;
if you do not change again,
I will surely kill you."
The couple bowed repeatedly
and prepared wine and food.
After ten full days, she was about to leave,
her reprimands and warnings very stern.
The whole family escorted her into a cypress grove,
and then she vanished.
Mining Silver at Dènggōngchǎng
At Dènggōngchǎng in Ráozhōu,
it was a place for mining silver.
In the mountains, there was a stream
flowing from the base of the mountain.
At the end of Tiānyòu era,
over ten silver miners dug a tunnel beside the stream.
They went in several steps,
and it became spacious and bright.
At the top of the mountain was a hole like a skylight.
Sunlight shone down,
and pavilions and towers wound around.
All the natural stones were white silver.
The silver miners came out again,
then went back in with axes,
intending to take it.
Suddenly, the mountain collapsed,
and all who entered were crushed to death.
After a short while,
blood flowed out from the stream,
uninterrupted for several days.
From then on, no one dared to enter.
Saving a Cat from Drowning
In Jiànchāng, there was a person who kept a cat,
which was very handsome and strong.
When the cat died, he could not bear to discard it,
still keeping it by his seat.
After several days, it began to rot and smell,
so he carried it and abandoned it in the Qínhuái River.
The cat suddenly came back to life,
and tried to save itself,
but then drowned.
The cat climbed ashore,
and a Jīnwú officer tied it up.
The cat bit through the rope and escaped.
Cooking Chicken to Remove Gamey Taste
Liú Zuì, a man from Héféi,
loved to eat chicken.
Each time, he would sever the two feet and place them in a wooden cabinet.
Only after all the fat and blood had dripped out would he cook them,
calling this "removing the gamey taste."
Later, Liú Zuì fell ill with sores that appeared on his temples.
After they healed,
small chicken feet grew in the scars of the sores.
Every time he used a towel or comb, he would injure them,
and blood would flow over his face.
He suffered in agony for years and then died.
Maid Eats Huángjīng
In Línchuān, there was a scholar
who mistreated his maid.
The maid could not bear it
and fled into the mountains.
Her provisions ran out, and she suffered from hunger.
By the water, she saw wild grass with lovely branches and leaves.
She pulled it up, roots and all, and ate it,
finding it very sweet and delicious.
From then on, she was not hungry,
and her body became lighter and stronger.
Wherever she intended to go,
she would float away lightly.
Several years later,
her family members, while cutting firewood, saw her
and reported it to her master.
The master tried to capture her but could not.
One day, he encountered her at the base of a sheer cliff.
He surrounded her with a net,
but she instantly soared to the mountaintop.
Her master was determined to catch her.
Someone said:
"This maid does not have immortal bones;
it is likely she got some spiritual medicine and ate it."
They tried placing a lavish feast on her usual path.
The maid indeed came to eat.
After eating, she could no longer leave,
and was consequently captured.
She fully recounted her story.
When asked about the shape of the grass she ate,
it was huángjīng.
They sent people to look for it again,
but could not find it again.
The maid also died several years later.
Lǐ Bái's Old Residence Wine Vessel
Inspector Lǐ of Cāngzhōu
lived in an empty house in Luòyáng.
One night, his son was reading when
a short, fat person in a black robe,
reeking of alcohol, pushed open the door and entered.
The son, frightened, ran away.
The person in black robe angrily said:
"Lǐ Bái still considers me a friend;
who are you?"
The son suspected he was an immortal,
bowed twice, and invited him to sit.
The person in black robe said:
"I have wine for us to drink."
Then he brought wine in a straw hat.
After drinking several cups,
his father, peeking from outside the door,
thought it was a demon,
and threw a brick at him.
The person in black robe fled.
They looked at his hat,
and it was the lid of a wine vessel.
The next day,
they found a wine vessel in the dung heap.
The old folk said:
"This was the old residence of Academician Lǐ."
Old Ape Steals a Woman
In Hánshān in Jìnzhōu there was a demon-ghost,
fond of stealing women.
Once a scholar traveled to Hánshān,
and at night lost his wife.
At dawn, he searched for her,
entering deep into the mountains.
By a large rock,
there were five or six women sitting together.
They asked:
"Sir, why have you come here?"
He fully explained his reason.
The women said:
"Your esteemed wife arrived here last night,
and is in a stone chamber.
We all passed by and were stolen by him.
The general steals people and brings them here,
performing the technique of Róngpéng.
Every day he tries once,
taking plain white silk and wrapping it around his body, hands, and feet,
performing a ritual to circulate his energy,
and the silk all breaks.
Each time he tries, he adds one bolt.
Tomorrow it will be five bolts.
Tomorrow morning, you should come here and wait for him.
We will tightly wrap six bolts around his body,
and when you arrive, we will all kill him together.
Can we do this?"
The man went as agreed,
and saw a person
whose appearance was very frightening.
The women had wrapped him with six bolts.
So he went straight forward and fought him,
and killed him.
It was an old ape.
Thereupon, he recovered his wife,
and all the women were able to escape.
The monster then ceased.
The wife was reburied.
Pān Xí, the magistrate of Jìn'ān,
sent a strong man with a document to the countryside.
At night, he arrived at a straw hut and sought lodging.
There was only one woman.
She said:
"Tomorrow I will be moving,
and have no time to receive guests."
The strong man, because there were many tigers on the road,
earnestly pleaded.
The woman invited him in,
and he slept on the ground.
The woman was tying up straw and bundling boxes and similar items.
At dawn,
the strong man said his goodbyes and left.
A few li away, he realized he had lost the document he was carrying,
so he returned to look for it.
The place where he had stayed was a tomb.
He then saw her family reburying her.
When the coffin was opened,
a book was found under the mat,
which was the lost document.
An ill-omened house where a vault of silver was dug up.
Zhào Lín was a great general in Shòuzhōu.
In his prefecture, there was an ill-omened house
which no one dared to live in.
Lín went to live in it,
occupying the main hall alone.
At night, something pushed the bed down, saying:
"We have been here for a long time.
You are pressing down on us,
which is very unpleasant.
You should leave quickly."
The ghosts then moved his bed together to the courtyard,
but Lín still slept soundly.
The next day,
a vault of silver was dug up at the place where the bed had been in the hall.
The house then became peaceful.
The "Leftover-Looting Ghost" of Yángzhōu.
Mínchǔ, a monk at Guǎnglíng Temple,
was close friends with the merchant Zhāng Qí.
A few months after Zhāng died,
Chǔ suddenly met him in the market.
Zhāng said:
"Because of a minor offense,
I was assigned to be a 'Leftover-Looting Ghost' in Yángzhōu.
For all market transactions and trading,
there is a fixed profit margin.
Anything exceeding it can be looted.
There are many like us in the human world."
He then pointed to men and women on the street and said:
"Such and such people are all like this." He also saw a woman selling flowers. Zhāng said:
"This is also a ghost.
The flowers she sells are also for ghost use.
They are useless to humans."
Zhāng bought flowers and gave them to Chǔ, saying:
"Whoever smiles upon seeing these flowers
is a ghost."
Chǔ returned home,
and many passersby smiled when they saw the flowers.
He threw the flowers into a ditch,
and the splashing water made a sound.
When he looked at the flowers again,
they were dead human hands.
Chǔ was also unharmed.
Holding a register to inspect the dead.
When the royal army campaigned against Yuè,
it was defeated at Lín'ān.
Bìjiàng Liú Xuān was seriously wounded and lay among the dead.
At night,
several officials came, holding a register and inspecting all the dead.
When they reached Xuān, they helped him up,
saying:
"This fellow is not one of them."
They led him out a few steps,
and placed him by the side of the road.
The next day, the bandits retreated,
and he was able to return.
Earthworms covered the navel of a mistakenly killed person.
In a village in Jiāngxī, there was a thunderclap,
and an old woman's arm was burned by the lightning.
Afterwards, a voice from the sky said:
"A mistake!"
Immediately a bottle fell,
and in the bottle was medicine like an ointment.
The voice said:
"Apply this and she will recover."
As instructed, it was applied,
and she indeed recovered.
There was also a villager who was killed by lightning.
A voice from the sky cried:
"A mistake!
Take earthworms, pound them thoroughly,
and cover his navel."
As instructed, it was covered,
and he revived.
A sweat-shirt came out of a bull's mouth.
During the Tàihé reign,
a village boy in Máoshān was herding a bull.
He washed the sweat-shirt he was wearing,
and spread it out on the grass to dry.
He lost it,
and suspected that a neighbor's child had stolen it.
His father angrily said:
"If my son is a thief,
what use is he?"
And immediately threw him into the water.
The neighbor's child crawled out, reaching with his hands,
crying out to Heaven and proclaiming his innocence several times.
The father again wanted to throw him in.
Suddenly, a violent thunderstorm arrived,
striking and killing his bull.
The sweat-shirt then came out of the bull's mouth.
Rabbit Ghost.
Yáng Mài was fond of hunting.
He released his hawk in the wilderness.
He saw a rabbit in the grass,
but when the hawk struck, there was nothing.
This happened three times.
He then cut the grass to search for it,
and found a complete set of rabbit bones.
It was the ghost of the rabbit.
Inscription on the wall of the Zǐwēi Palace.
In Jiànyè city, there was a fortune-teller
who suddenly inscribed on the wall of the Zǐwēi Palace, saying:
"Yesterday I passed through Zǐwēi on my way to the Heavenly Court,
the jade altar was cold and the apricot blossoms sparse.
The green peach suspected I was conveying news,
why is it that in the human world one is certain not to return?"
From then on, he vanished without a trace.
Everyone said he had ascended to the upper realm.
If you have gold, why not provide for your mother?
In Pǔchéng, a man died on the road.
His family had one pound of gold.
His wife hid it and did not let her mother-in-law know.
Suddenly, at night, there was a knocking at the door.
Crying and wailing, he returned.
He then sat on his mother's lap,
speaking as if alive,
but his hands and feet were cold as ice.
He scolded his wife, saying:
"I died with gold;
why did you not provide for my old mother but hide it?"
Thereupon, he wept and bid farewell to his mother, and left,
sending his wife back to her father's home.
By dawn, he was suddenly gone.
A wife died, and her head was sold as meat.
In Chíyáng, Hú Chéng's wife died.
The officials provided a coffin for her burial.
All the clothes and food she had used in her lifetime were placed in the coffin.
Several years later, Hú Chéng saw someone selling head-garments and food in a row of shops,
which turned out to be the items buried with his wife.
The seller said a woman had deposited them,
agreeing to retrieve them on a certain day.
Hú Chéng went back at the appointed time,
and indeed saw his wife taking the payment and leaving.
Hú Chéng followed her,
catching up to her outside the city.
His wife said:
"When I was buried,
the officials provided the burial implements.
Although I avoided exposure of my bones,
I have since been pressed by the authorities to pay for them.
With no other way,
I sold these to repay the debt."
After speaking, she disappeared.
Lián Pó's Precious Sword
A butcher in Shòuchūn
once had a person claim to be Lián Pó,
saying:
"You can dig in the ground east of your house to find my precious sword;
it will make you rich."
Following his words,
the butcher indeed found it.
In little more than a year, he became rich.
Later, he revealed the matter,
and then lost the sword.
Throwing Food into the Ditch
Qián Chǔshì once saw a man
who said:
"Heaven's punishment is about to befall you;
you must quickly confess and apologize."
Qián said:
"I have committed no fault." After a long pause, the man said:
"Yesterday, your food was not to your liking, and you threw it into the ditch." Qián said:
"That is precisely it!
Quickly retrieve the food you threw away and eat it."
So he rinsed it with water to remove the filth.
Suddenly, there was a great thunder and lightning.
Qián said:
"Quickly eat the filthy food as well!"
He did as told, and the thunder and lightning indeed ceased.
Běidà Xiānshēng
Gěng Xiānshēng's wife was beautiful,
skilled in Daoist arts,
and could control ghosts and spirits.
During the Bǎodà era,
the Emperor summoned her into the palace.
She often wore a green-blue shawl,
had hands like bird's claws,
and called herself Běidà Xiānshēng.
She could turn snow into silver.
She would take snow and fill something with it,
then carve it into silver ingots,
and throw them into hot coals.
When they cooled,
they shone brilliantly as silver ingots.
Later, Běidà Xiānshēng became pregnant.
One day she said to the Emperor:
"I shall give birth tonight."
At midnight, there was wind and thunder.
The next morning, her abdomen had disappeared.
She said:
"Last night I gave birth to a child,
but a divine being has already taken it away."
Later, she died of illness.
Leaves Turning into Fish
Pān Yǐ moored his boat on the Qínhuái River.
An old man asked to share the boat,
and Pān Yǐ agreed. At that time,
there was heavy snow.
The old man took a small gourd from his topknot,
poured it out, and drank endlessly from it.
He could scoop mercury into his hand and rub it to turn it into silver.
Once he saw fallen leaves in the pond,
scooped them out and placed them on the ground.
According to their size, all the leaves turned into fish.
Ordering Two Concubines to Practice Weeping
In the late Táng dynasty,
Shěn Fén, an imperial censor, retired to Lèdào.
He had two concubines in his household.
One day he said to them:
"When I die,
will you be able to weep?"
The concubines said:
"How can you speak such inauspicious words?"
He insisted on asking,
and they replied:
"If it were so,
how could we not weep?"
Shěn Fén said:
"You try weeping,
I wish to observe it."
At first, the concubines refused,
but Shěn Fén held them and forced them.
Having no choice, the concubines
covered their faces with their sleeves and wept.
When they finished weeping,
Shěn Fén had already died.
Holding Flowers Through the Four Seasons
Yú Dà lived in Xīshān, Hóngzhōu,
always holding flowers through the four seasons.
A young man who loved the Dao
bowed and said:
"I wish to follow you, Master."
Yú Dà led him,
traversing mountains and crossing waters without stopping.
He asked the young man:
"Are you thirsty?"
He took out tea from his bosom
and scooped water to brew it.
Soon, the young man fell into a deep sleep.
When he woke up, Yú Dà was gone.
The Delicious Oranges of Fēngchéng
Chén Yǔnshēng entered Lónghǔshān.
During the Tiānyòu era,
people saw him on Mágūshān.
It was estimated that seventy years had passed since he left home,
yet his appearance was as before.
The Cìshǐ welcomed him and placed him in the commandery.
Sitting at night,
he often said:
"The oranges of Fēngchéng are delicious;
I really miss them."
A short while later, Chén Yǔnshēng brought several hundred oranges.
Fisherman Presents Fish
Wú Tàizǔ, as the Dūyán of Lúzhōu,
once came to the riverside.
A fisherman presented him with fish and said:
"Like your noble grandsons,
they will rise in succession and become hegemons."
The Emperor Takes Away the Yì Zǒng
During the Shàngyuán era,
Wáng Yuǎnzhī, a Daoist priest from Táizhōu, was skilled in the Yì (Book of Changes).
He knew people's life, death, misfortune, and fortune,
and wrote fifteen scrolls of the Yì Zǒng.
One day, during thunder and rain,
an old man in the mist and clouds shouted at Wáng Yuǎnzhī:
"Where is the book you revealed?
The Emperor has ordered me and the six Dīng spirits with thunder and lightning to retrieve it."
Wáng Yuǎnzhī was terrified and fell to the ground.
Six men stood nearby,
dressed in green,
already holding the book.
The old man reprimanded him:
"Heaven forbids this text;
there are flying celestials protecting it,
and its golden precepts are secretly stored in Xuándū.
Who are you,
to dare conceal a volume?"
Wáng Yuǎnzhī replied:
"It was transmitted to me by Qīngqiū Yuánlǎo."
The old man said:
"The Emperor has issued an edict:
your immortal rank has already been conferred,
and your appointed period has been extended by four years and two cycles more."
Wáng Yuǎnzhī passed away during the Guāngzhái era.
Later, someone crossing the sea
was swept by the wind
and suddenly saw a leaf boat approaching from the horizon.
It was Wáng Yuǎnzhī.
He said:
"Why have you come to such danger?
This ocean
is a hundred thousand *lǐ* east of the sea.
I will lend you a swift wind;
you can reach Dēngzhōu in one night."
After he left,
the boat was like a flying feather;
the traveler only felt the wind carrying him along.
The next day,
he indeed reached Dēngzhōu.
Dreaming of Cáo Zǐjiàn Asking for an Introduction to His Collected Works
Hán Zhòngqīng dreamt of a young man with a bird-shaped cap,
who said:
"I am Cáo Zǐjiàn. My writings are at the home of the Xiù clan in Jiàndū.
You are highly renowned today;
would you be willing to write an introduction for me?"
Hán Zhòngqīng agreed.
When he awoke,
he found Cáo Zǐjiàn's collected works,
divided them into ten scrolls,
and wrote an introduction for them.
Plum Blossoms of Luófú
During the Kāihuáng reign of the Suí dynasty,
Zhào Shīxióng arrived at Luófú.
One day,
the sky was cold and the sun was setting.
Beside a wine shop among the pines,
he saw a beautiful woman with light makeup and plain clothes come out to greet him.
It was already dark,
the remnant snow had not melted,
and the moonlight was dim.
Shīxióng spoke with her;
her words were extremely clear and beautiful,
and a fragrant scent assailed him.
He then knocked on the wine shop's door with her and they drank together.
After a short while,
a green-clad boy came,
laughing, singing, and dancing.
Shīxióng became drunk and fell asleep,
only feeling the fragrance surrounding him.
After a long time,
the east was already white.
He got up and looked,
and found himself under a large plum blossom tree,
with noisy emerald birds chirping and looking at each other above.
The moon had set and the Shēn constellation had crossed the sky,
leaving him only with a feeling of melancholy.
Tàibái Riding a Red Qióu
In the early Yuánhé period,
someone saw Lǐ Tàibái on the sea, laughing and talking with a Daoist priest on a high mountain.
After a long time,
the Daoist priest rode away on a red qióu amidst the blue mist.
Tàibái sprang up and swiftly pursued, catching up,
and they rode together towards the east.
Dream of Swallowing a Cinnabar Scroll
When Hán Tuìzhī was young,
he dreamt of a person giving him a scroll of cinnabar writing,
ordering him to forcefully swallow it.
A person beside him clapped his hands and laughed.
After waking, he felt as if something was lodged in his chest,
and it was several days before he felt well again.
He still remembered one or two characters from it,
and the brushwork was not like writing in the human world.
Later, he met Mèng Jiāo,
who was the one laughing beside him in the dream.
Six Horses Rolling in Dust Painting
Níng Wáng was skilled at painting horses.
On the wall of the Huā'è Lóu there was a painting of six horses rolling in the dust.
Mínghuáng particularly cherished the jade-faced floral dappled horse,
with its wind-swept mane and dew-kissed bristles,
all depicted with utmost detail.
Later, there were only five horses on the wall;
one of them was missing,
which truly shows that divine skill is inherently accompanied by transformation.
Mínghuáng's Visit to the Moon Palace
In the sixth year of Kāiyuán,
the Supreme Emperor (Mínghuáng) and the Daoist priest Shēn Tiānshī were traveling as guests.
On the Mid-Autumn night,
they traveled together to the moon.
They passed a large gate,
and in the jade light, they saw a grand palace,
with a plaque that read "Guǎnghán Qīngxū zhī Fǔ".
The guards at the gate were very strict,
and all three were stopped below it, unable to enter.
Tiānshī led the Supreme Emperor to leap up,
and in the mist, they looked down upon the towering jade city,
below which was like a field of ten thousand miles of glazed tile.
Immortals and Daoist priests rode clouds and cranes, coming and going between them.
They slowly stepped forward,
feeling the emerald color and cold light
dazzling their eyes,
and it was too cold to proceed.
Below, they saw more than ten fair maidens,
dressed in white and riding white luán,
laughing and dancing under a large cassia tree in a spacious courtyard,
with chaotic yet clear and beautiful music.
When the Supreme Emperor returned,
he composed tunes and rhythms,
creating the "Níshang Yǔyī Wǔqǔ".
Flying Essence Precious Mirror
In Cháng'ān, Rèn Zhòngxuān's family possessed a precious mirror,
called "Flying Essence".
Those who knew said it was an artifact from the Three Dynasties period.
On its back were eight characters,
which were recent zhuan script,
saying: "Quicksilver, yin essence,
a hundred refinements make a mirror."
Later, Zhòngxuān journeyed south to Dòngtíng,
and his boat was anchored due to winds and waves.
He dreamt of a Daoist priest in red clothing riding a dragon,
taking the mirror and leaving.
He also said:
"This mirror is a supreme treasure of the water palace,
its appearance in the world has a set time,
and now it must return to me."
Upon waking from the dream,
he quickly checked the chest,
and it was already gone.
Fireflies as a Prodigy
Jū Huì once sat up late at night,
and Tuìzhī and I, the other two, discussed ghosts and divine transformations.
At that time, the wind and snow were extremely cold,
when suddenly there were flowing fireflies outside the window.
In a moment, there were tens of thousands,
countless,
coming and going, separating and uniting,
then changing into a loud sound and departing.
Even Tuìzhī, with his upright and resolute character, was moved,
and Jū Huì and I prostrated ourselves, covering our eyes.
A folk poem says:
"Do not talk about people during the day,
for talking about people harms life;
do not talk about ghosts at night,
for talking about ghosts brings prodigies."
The three of us all fared unfavorably afterward.
Five-Power Ghost
Liǔzhōu formerly had a ghost
called the Wǔtōng Ghost.
I initially did not believe in it.
One day, as I opened a chest to change clothes,
all the clothes had turned to ashes.
I then wrote a memorial and offered a jiaosù sacrifice to the Emperor,
and Longchéng thereafter was free of strange occurrences.
Jíxián Yuàn Books
Among the Táng dynasty, only the Kāiyuán period had the most complete collection of literary works.
The Jíxián Yuàn housed up to seventy thousand scrolls.
At that time, forty-seven scholars including Zhāng Yuè were assigned to manage the collection,
and there were no missing texts.
Since the military conflicts,
both capitals were reduced to ashes,
and alas, nothing remains.
Double-Headed Peony
Gāozōng hosted a banquet for his officials,
admiring a double-headed peony.
They composed poems,
and only Shàngguān Zhāoróng's couplet was exceptionally beautiful,
which was: "Their power is like linked jade friends,
their hearts are like people who smell of orchids."
Línglù Cuìtāo
The Left Chancellor Wèi was skilled at making wine,
and its names included Línglù and Cuìtāo.
He once stored it in a large golden urn for ten years,
and its flavor did not spoil.
Tàizōng once bestowed a poem saying:
"Línglù surpasses Lánshēng,
Cuìtāo exceeds Yùxiè.
A thousand days drunk and not sober,
ten years and its flavor does not spoil."
Lánshēng
is the hundred-flavor fine wine of Hàn Wǔdì.
Yùxiè
is the name of Yángdì's wine.
This wine was originally learned from brewing by Hú people from the Western Regions.
Could it not be that they obtained the method from Dàyuān,
what Sīmǎ Qiān called the rich storing ten thousand shí of grape wine,
which does not spoil for decades?
Unbroken Line of Scholars
Péi Lìnggōng once instructed his son:
Our family should only ensure an unbroken line of scholars;
as for those who succeed and become prime ministers to the Son of Heaven,
that is up to Heaven.
Lǐ Línfǔ Struck Dead by Lightning
A prostitute in Huìzhōu was struck dead by lightning in the market street.
On her ribs were vermilion characters that read:
"Lǐ Línfǔ used cruelty and abuse of power;
the Supreme Emperor commanded him to be struck dead by lightning."
Was this woman the reincarnation of Yǎnyuègōng?
This was in the sixth month of the first year of Yuánhé.
Liú Zhòngqīng's Hidden Immortal Cave
North of the Shuangxī stream in Jīnshān, there is an immortal cave,
containing thirty-two palaces,
totaling thirty-six lǐ.
When illuminated with pine torches, the stone inscription
reads:
"Liú Yán,
courtesy name Zhòngqīng,
a Han Dynasty Shooting Cavalry Commandant,
was demoted for his forthright remonstrance during the time of Gōngxiǎn.
He hid his traces here,
and his end is unknown."
This was recorded by the Daoist priest Xiāo Zhì.
It is popularly believed that Zhòngqīng returns to the cave every Zhongyuán Festival,
and people from the prefecture pray for blessings.
Slaying the Jiaolong
Zhào Yù followed the Daoist Lǐ Jué and lived in seclusion on Qīngchéng Shān.
Suí Yángdì, knowing his worthiness,
appointed him as the Grand Administrator of Jiāzhōu.
At that time, an old flood dragon in a deep pool in Qiánwéi was causing harm.
Yù had been in office for five months,
and 700 boats had been submerged.
Yù was greatly enraged,
and led a thousand armored soldiers
and ten thousand men,
who lined the riverbanks, beating drums and shouting,
their sound shaking heaven and earth.
Yù, holding a knife, plunged into the water.
After a moment,
the river water turned completely red,
and the rock cliffs roared and crumbled like thunder.
Yù, holding the flood dragon's head in his left hand
and his knife in his right,
burst forth from the waves.
At the end of the Suí dynasty, there was great chaos,
and he went into seclusion, his whereabouts unknown.
Later, when the Jiālíng river rose,
people in Shǔ saw Yù, riding a white horse amidst a blue mist, accompanied by several hunters,
crossing over the surface of the waves.
Tàizōng bestowed upon him the title of Shényǒng Dàjiāngjūn (Great General of Divine Valour)
and offered sacrifices to him at Guànjiāngkǒu.
The Shànghuáng (Emperor Emeritus) visited Shǔ
and further enfeoffed him as Chìchéng Wáng.
When Yù slew the flood dragon,
he was twenty-six years old.
The flower master
Sòng Dānfù, courtesy name Zhòngrú,
was skilled in cultivating artistic peonies,
transforming them into a thousand varieties.
The Shànghuáng summoned him to Líshān,
where he planted ten thousand flowers,
each with a different color and style.
The palace women called him the flower master.
Volume Twelve
concludes.
Distinguishing Texts with Dates
states in its preface:
"I dare to join in the discussion of distinguishing texts with dates,
and roughly compare it to composing thoughts on planting daylilies."
A Solitary Oar West of Wild Magpie Shoal
The Xiangchuān Jì states:
"The spirit altar of Zhūlíng,
the treasure grotto of Tàixū,
lies within the constellations Yì and Zhěn.
Its altitude corresponds to Jī and Héng,
hence it is called Héngshān.
The mountain has five peaks:
Zǐgài, Yúnmì, Zhùróng, Tiānzhù, and Shílǐn."
The mountain has many literati;
woodcutters and boatmen are often capable of composing poetry.
Once, an official from Guǎngzhōu was traveling by boat
and heard someone reciting a poem:
"A solitary oar west of Wild Magpie Shoal,
the moonlight remotely connects to Dòngtíng Hú.
How hateful to pass before Huíyàn Fēng,
gazing until the family mountains vanish without a trace of a character."
Four Old Men All Transform into Apes
Wáng Jìn studied at Sōngyáng Guàn when he was young.
One day,
four old men carrying wine jars came to visit.
One was named Mùcháo Nán, the second Lín Dàjié, the third Sūn Wénwèi, and the fourth Shí Mèiqíu.
They conversed loftily and drank heartily.
When they were drunk,
they all transformed into apes
and ascended the trees and departed.
The Bottle Recluse
Shēntú Yǒuyá
was unconstrained and lived among clouds and springs.
He once carried a bottle.
One day, he leapt into the bottle.
At the time, he was called the Bottle Recluse.
A Blue-Clad Woman Recites a Poem
Zhāng Què once traveled along Bái Pín Xī above Zhà.
He saw two blue-clad women holding hands and reciting poems.
One poem said:
"The green water's color is fit for dyeing,
the white lotus's fragrance is truly rich.
Flying apart, both have regrets;
when will we meet again after this parting?
The lotus root hides its exquisite jade,
the flower conceals its ethereal form.
When can I borrow a pair of wings,
and for a moment, follow your voice and shadow?"
Què pursued them,
but they transformed into kingfishers and flew away.
The Divine Woman Bequeaths a Bolt of Dragon's Whisker Silk
Lǐ Yí met a divine woman who bequeathed him a bolt of silk,
saying:
"It was woven in the flood dragon's chamber."
Later, he met a Hú person who exchanged it for three million coins,
saying:
"This is woven from the small whiskers of a dragon's jaw;
it takes thirty minor kalpas to complete one strand."
Taking a Zither to Play "Dominating the Western Rong"
Wéi Fán,
in the early Xiántōng era, traveled along the Jīng River.
Arriving at a dilapidated pavilion,
he met a scholar who introduced himself as "Zhībái."
He invited Fán to stay the night,
saying:
"Fifty segments of splendid discourse
can resolve over a thousand years of doubtful history."
Late at night,
he took out a zither and played it,
saying:
"Qín Mùgōng cultivated virtue and military might,
and all the feudal lords came to congratulate him.
Thus, this composition was made,
titled 'Dominating the Western Róng.'
It is rarely heard in the world;
only I received it from Wūchóu Bó."
In a moment,
both the person and the zither disappeared,
and in the room, there was only a tomb.
Meeting a Woman Reciting a Poem at Night
Zhèng Púyè of Pānyú
once traveled in Xiāngzhōng
and stayed overnight in an inn tower.
At night, he met a woman reciting a poem, saying:
"Red trees send off autumn colors,
green streams pluck night strings.
The good time cannot be repeated;
wind and rain seem like a year. "
In an instant, she disappeared.
The Wú Divine Music Department
A jinshì from Jīnlíng, surnamed Huáng,
dreamed of meeting a former courtesan of Táichéng,
who composed a poem saying:
"After the singing, the jade tower moon;
after the dancing, the golden thread robe.
Evenly set ornaments gather scattered hairpins,
lowered eyebrows bid farewell to heavy palace gates.
The web broken, the spider still weaves;
the beam empty, the swallow does not return.
How can I bear to look back at the place
where wild crabapples flew by the riverbank."
Patrons' Votive Incense
A langguān dreamed he visited an old monk in a pine forest.
In front of him was an incense burner,
with very faint incense smoke.
The monk said:
"This is the patrons' votive incense.
The incense smoke still lingers.
The patron has already had two lives,
and achieved three honors of scarlet and purple robes."
Two Old Men Transform into White Egrets
Jiǎ Chuán of Shàn, moored his boat on Jìng Hú.
Under the night moon,
he strolled amidst the clear water and fragrant lotuses,
and saw two old men standing and talking.
One called himself Bìjì Wēng,
the other Huángqī Sǒu.
They recited poems to each other.
Jiǎ immediately shouted at them,
and they transformed into white egrets and flew away.
The Master of Zhaochanguan
Lǐ Liánggōng, while garrisoning Shuòfāng,
had a peasant's garden.
Under a tree, a single mushroom grew,
several feet tall in total.
On it were towers and platforms,
and inside, two old men were playing chess.
Three characters were carved,
which read:
"Zhāoróng Guān."
The Duke ordered the peasant to dig several feet into the ground,
where there was a giant python with eyes like mirrors,
whose spittle formed the mushroom.
That night, the Duke
dreamed of a yellow-clad man delivering a message, saying:
"Huánglú Gōng was just playing chess with the Master of Zhāoróng Guān,
and was presented to you by a foolish person."
Lǐ Yōng Sees Xú Jìngyè
The monk Dào Xiāng of Tiānzhù Temple on Mount Nányuè,
lived in a dead tree on the western ridge of the temple.
His disciples often numbered several hundred.
Lǐ Yōng saw him and said,
"Formerly, Xú Jìngyè was defeated and fled into the sea.
Lǐ Yì sent a different general to pursue him,
but he was not found.
So, he beheaded someone resembling Jìngyè and presented his head.
Does the reverend recognize this person?"
The master replied,
"Initially, I took you to be thoroughly enlightened about the principles of things,
but now you are so ignorant of circumstances!"
When the master was about to die,
he summoned his disciples and said,
"My original surname was Xú.
I had great merit at the beginning of the dynasty,
and fled here to escape disaster."
After speaking, he died.
It was indeed Xú Jìngyè.
Shěn Shíyí composed a stele inscription for him,
but dared not state the truth directly.
Instead, he wrote that Xú Jìngyè's brothers...
rhinoceros horn
placed amidst heavy fog and dew,
will never become wet.
It can also be made into a hairpin.
Peacocks do not mate,
but merely by the contact of sound and shadow, they become pregnant.
Just as white egrets, male and female, become pregnant by merely looking at each other.
white peacock
During the time of Sòng Wǔdì,
someone presented white peacocks.
Elephants are burned for their tusks,
musk deer die for their fragrance.
Peacocks also suffer because of their feathers.
owl
During the day, it sees nothing,
but at night, its eyes are very bright.
If people cut off their fingernails and toenails and leave them exposed on the ground,
the bird will come to people's homes at night,
pick them up and inspect them,
then know whether there will be good or ill fortune.
The unfortunate ones will suffer its calamity.
Chén Zàngqì quotes the *Wǔxíng Shū*:
"Remove fingernails and toenails,
and bury them inside the door."
This is probably to prevent them from being obtained by this bird.
The owl is similar to the *gūhuò* and *guǐchē* classes of spirits.
Heavenly maiden
*Gūhuò*,
the *Xuánzhōng Jì* says:
"Flies at night and hides by day.
Also named Heavenly Maiden,
also named Night Traveler,
also named Hidden Flyer.
It likes to take small children from people's homes to raise them.
Today, children's clothes should not be exposed to the night dew,
as this creature marks their clothes with blood as a sign,
and then takes the child."
Nine-headed bird
*Guǐchē*,
also named ghost bird.
It has nine heads,
and can enter people's houses to collect souls and vital energy.
One head was bitten off by a *dàsuǒ*.
It often drips blood into people's homes,
which brings misfortune.
Today it is called the Nine-headed Bird.
Making owl soup on the fifth day of the fifth month
The owl,
is as large as a dove,
and has an unpleasant cry.
If the bird enters a person's house,
it is a bad omen.
Its meat is very delicious,
and can be roasted.
The *Shuōwén* says:
"The owl is
an unfilial bird.
On the winter solstice,
capture an owl and dismember it."
On the fifth day of the fifth month of the Hàn dynasty,
owl soup was bestowed upon all officials.
The ancients valued roasted owls,
this was to exterminate their kind,
not because of its deliciousness.
Also, the *Huáinán Fāngbì Shù* says:
"If you hear an owl hooting on a tile,
take a broken pot and throw it at the owl,
it will stop on its own."
parrot
Guǎngnán has many parrots,
with green chests and red beaks,
skillfully imitating human speech.
The small ones are inferior to those from Lǒngyòu.
Each flight involves thousands of birds.
When raising them,
it is popularly taboo to frequently touch their backs with hands.
Those who violate this often suffer from epilepsy and die.
Scholars call this 'parrot miasma.'
Parrot is also written as *yīnggē*.
When Sūn Quán held a grand assembly,
a white-headed bird gathered in the palace hall.
Quán asked,
"What bird is that?"
Zhūgě Kè replied,
"A white-headed old man (*Báitóuwēng*)."
Zhāng Zhāo, being the oldest in the assembly,
suspected Kè was making fun of him,
and said with a look,
"I have never heard of a bird named 'white-headed old man.'
Please ask Zhūgě to go find a 'white-headed old woman' (*Báitóumǔ*)."
Kè replied,
"I couldn't identify the bird named 'parrot' (*yīngwǔ*).
Please ask Zhōng Wú to go find a 'parrot father' (*yīngfù*)."
red and white *jíliǎo* birds
The people of Liánzhōu caught red and white *jíliǎo* birds.
The red ones soon died.
The white ones survived for a long time and could speak,
imitating human laughter and speech.
They are rare birds.
feathered creatures and hairy creatures
The *Lóutàn Jīng* says:
"There are four thousand five hundred types of birds,
and two thousand four hundred types of beasts."
The *Báihǔ Tōng* says:
"There are three hundred and sixty-six feathered creatures,
with the phoenix as their chief;
there are three hundred and sixty-six hairy creatures,
with the qílín as their chief."
red crabs
Dànzhōu produces red crabs,
which are *móuxiú*, *péngqí*, *yǐwàng*, *niáncháo*, *jiépiáo*, *shāgǒu*, *lúhǔ*, and *shǔjiǔ* — nine types in total.
The crab is called the 'gentleman without intestines.'
A crab is also called *guǐ*.
The *Guǎngyǎ* says:
"The male is called *lángyǐ*,
the female is called *bódài*."
The *Bàopǔzǐ* says:
"Among the mountain deities, it is called the 'gentleman without intestines' (*wúcháng gōngzǐ*)
on the middle day of the month; it is a crab."
There are small crabs in the sea,
attaching themselves like elm pods.
They are called 'crab slaves.'
tree-born children
The kingdom of Dàshí borders the great sea to the west.
They once sent people on a ship,
which after eight years had not reached the western shore.
In the midst of the sea was a square stone,
and on the stone was a tree,
with a red trunk and green leaves.
Children six or seven *cùn* long hung on the tree,
all laughing upon seeing people,
moving their hands and feet,
their buttocks attached to the branches.
When the envoy plucked a branch,
the child on it immediately died.
red bat
Found in Lóngzhōu.
A pair roosts among red banana flowers.
If one is caught,
the other will not leave.
Southerners collect them as love potions.
love potions
The leg and neck bones of the cuckoo,
are love potions.
Men wear them on the left, women on the right.
Placed in water, they can follow each other.
magpie brain
Modern people suffering from lovesickness,
stir-fry and crush a pair,
and place them in the pillow,
to make husband and wife fond of each other.
*jīngcǎo* (stem grass) The daughter of the Dì (God) of Gūyáo Mountain died,
and transformed into *jīngcǎo*.
Consuming it makes one charming.
*zuǒxíngcǎo* (left-moving grass) makes people amorous.
Spiritual Water
Southwest of Jīnyì is Pánlóng Mountain.
The mountain has a milky cave,
diagonally traversed by a stream,
named Spiritual Water.
There are thirty-six named caves.
There are thirty-six famous grottoes under Heaven,
and Dòngtíng and Línwū rank among the top nine.
This is where Wú Wáng sent Lóngwēi Zhàngrén to obtain the Yǔ Shū.
The Yǔ Shū is also called the Língbǎo Jīng,
in three scrolls.
In its grottoes, there is gold with dragon basins for fish,
all four-footed.
When there are three hundred and sixty fish heads, a jiāolóng will become their chief.
Táo Zhūgōng's Yǎng Yú Jīng says:
"To breed fish,
create several islets in the pond,
so that the fish can endlessly follow the currents,
as if in rivers and seas.
Every second month, on the upper gēng day,
place carp with roe into the pond.
In the fourth, sixth, and eighth months,
each time release a divine guardian,
the divine guardian being
a turtle.
When the fish reach three hundred and sixty heads,
a jiāolóng will become their chief,
and it will fly away with the wind and rain.
Only if the turtle guards them will they be unable to leave."
Wénmǔ Niǎo (Mosquito Mother Bird)
In Duānzhōu, there is a bird
that catches and eats fish.
Every time it makes a sound,
mosquitoes swarm out of its mouth.
The Guǎng Yǎ says:
"The wings of the Wénmǔ Niǎo
can be made into fans
to ward off mosquitoes."
Goose Feather Quilt
South of Yōngzhōu,
chieftains in the stream grottoes use goose feathers for quilts.
They take the fine, soft feathers from the head and neck,
sewing them like rice paddies.
Their warmth and softness are no less than cotton floss.
Writing Brushes
In various commanderies of Pānyú,
most use blue goat hair for brushes,
or chicken or duck feathers,
or mountain pheasant feathers,
lovely in their five colors.
Could this not be what Jiāng Yān obtained in his dream?
Sometimes fox hair,
tiger hair,
rat whiskers, sheep wool, musk deer hair, civet hair, goat whiskers, or fetal hair are used,
but none are as good as rabbit hair.
According to Bó Wù:
"Méng Tián invented the brush."
Dǒng Zhòngshū, in response to Niú Xiǎng's question, said:
"Méng Tián used dry wood for the handle,
deer hair for the core,
and goat hair for the outer bristles.
This is what is called cāngháo (dark bristles),
not rabbit hair and bamboo shafts."
The principle of the brush
originated at the same time as writing.
The Shàngshū Zhōng Hòu says:
"A turtle carried a diagram,
and Zhōu Gōng took up a brush to copy it."
Its origin is ancient.
Zǐgū Divination
Various forms of divination are seen in books and traditions:
tiger divination, Zǐgū divination, ox hoof divination, bone burning divination, bird divination.
Though not conforming to milfoil and turtle shells,
some are still commendable.
Yì Yuàn says:
"There was a woman named Zǐ Nǚ,
also called Zǐgū,
said to be a concubine of a family,
who was hated by the principal wife,
and was constantly forced to do filthy tasks.
On the fifteenth day of the first month, she died of grief.
Therefore, people make her effigy on that day
and welcome her at night in the latrine or by the pigsty."
Méng Gōng, Méng Lǎo
In the south, on New Year's Eve and when setting sail,
chickens are killed and their bones are chosen for divination,
a tradition of ancient custom.
If the omen is auspicious, the meat is offered to the boat gods,
who are called Méng Gōng and Méng Lǎo.
Their origin is ancient.
Guāngláng
The wood is like the skin of a sǎ tree,
like the bark of a ráng tree.
It yields flour that is edible.
The wood grain has patterns
suitable for making qíjú (Go boards).
Ink and Paper
The Southern Dynasties called food "head" (tóu),
and fish "dou" (dǒu, a measure).
The Liáng Code and Laws stated:
"So many dòu of raw fish."
They called brushes "pair" (shuāng), "bed" (chuáng), or "piece" (méi).
Liáng Jiǎnwén, in a letter replying to Xú Chī, wrote: "Sometimes discoursing on books,
occasionally placing a brush bed."
Four brushes constituted one "bed."
They called ink "snail" (luó), "measure" (liàng), "pill" (wán), or "piece" (méi).
Lù Yún, in a letter to his elder brother, wrote:
"Sending two 'snails' of ink."
The Liáng Code and Laws stated:
"One 'measure' of imperial ink, twelve 'pills'."
The Hàn Guān Yí says:
"The Língpú Céngláng were granted one 'piece' of ink."
They called paper "bundle" (fān), "width" (fú), or "piece" (méi).
Xiāngdōng Wáng presented ten thousand "widths" of Jīng Wǔ paper
and four hundred "pieces" of brushes;
Jiǎnwén Dì offered three thousand "bundles" of red and green notepaper;
it also says,
three hundred thousand "pieces" of four-colored paper were sent,
in response to Xiāngdōng Wáng.
Juǎnzhǐ (Cocoon Paper)
Between the Jìn and Sòng dynasties, there was a kind of paper,
over a zhàng (ten feet) long,
that was scooped from boats.
The world called it juǎnzhǐ.
The character "zhǐ" (紙) is composed of "sì" (糸) and "shì" (氏).
Cài Lún used "jīn" (巾).
Tuányóu Fàn (Round Oiled Rice)
Among the common customs of Guǎngzhōu,
when wealthy families' wives give birth, on the third day or at full term,
after washing the baby or grandchild,
they prepare tuányóu fàn.
It is made by frying shrimp, fish, chicken, goose, sheep, sausages, scorched nuts, ginger, cinnamon, salt, and fermented beans.
Yǐzǐ Jiàng (Ant Larva Sauce)
The people of Guǎngzhōu dig up large ant larvae in the mountains to make sauce,
called yǐzǐ jiàng.
Háhuò (Frog Stew)
In Guǎngnán, háhuò is made;
há here means wā (frog).
The stew is made in the usual way.
Táo Hóngjǐng's commentary on Běncǎo says:
"Those with green backs are called tǔyā (earth ducks),
and those with black backs are called házi (frogs)."
Huò is made from the fresh animal.
The Hàn Shū says:
"Between È and Dù,
the waters have many guīyú (salmon)."
The Sòng Shū says:
"Zhāng Chàng's younger brother was bitten by a rabid dog,
and the physician said to eat xiāmá kuài (minced frog).
When the kuài was prepared,
the brother showed reluctance.
Chàng ate it first, and only then did his brother eat,
and indeed he recovered."
Thus, we know that people have been eating frogs for a long time.
Bào Pǔzi says:
"A frog that lives for ten thousand years
has eight characters inscribed in red under its jaw."
The Nán Shǐ quotes Qiū Jié as saying:
"Frogs are poisonous.
In a dream, three people enjoyed them,
and then discharged several shēng of parasitic larvae."
East Family Plants Bamboo, West Family Prepares Land
Whenever planting bamboo,
in the first or second month, cut off the southwest roots
and plant them in the northeast corner.
The nature of bamboo is to extend towards the southwest.
The proverb says:
"The east family plants bamboo,
the west family prepares the land."
Biàngān (Transformed Orange)
Xīnzhōu produces biàngān;
its peel is larger than a shēng.
It was transplanted from Gāoyào.
Within a few hundred lǐ,
its shape and taste changed,
hence its name.
Húgān (Barbarian Orange)
The Fēngtǔ Jì says:
"Oranges that are ochre-colored
are called húgān."
Lǐ Héng, the Administrator of Dānyáng, built a residence
and planted a thousand orange trees,
saying:
"I have a thousand 'wooden slaves'."
Hú Jú (Pot Mandarin)
Luófú has ten kinds of hú jú,
and also coconut jelly.
Coconuts have two 'eyes',
popularly called Yuèwáng Tóu (King of Yuè's Head).
Hú Jié Bēntáo (Hu-Jie Fleeing)
Liǔ Shìlóng's *Xiè Lèyóu Hútáo* says:
"The Hújié flee,
this is an auspicious omen."
Red Vine Mushroom
Qióngzhōu produces red vine mushrooms,
the local dialect calls it *shēng*,
or *qúchú*,
or *Xíngtáng*.
Shěn Yuē's *Tánzòu Shè Lìng Zhòngwénxiù Zìhèng* says:
"The clerical official delivered forty *lǐng* of six-foot *shēng*."
Xí Záochǐ's letter to Grandee Secretary Xiè says:
"Here there is safflower,
northerners pick its flowers to make rouge."
Rouge,
used by women to color their cheeks when applying makeup,
about the size of a bean,
rub it to cover the entire cheek,
it appears exceptionally vivid."
The Xiōngnú call their wives *Yānzhī*,
meaning they are as lovely as rouge.
A song in *Xīhé Jiùshì* says:
"We lost our Qílián Shān,
causing our livestock not to multiply;
we lost our Yānzhī Shān,
causing our women to be without color (beauty)."
Pomegranate Used to Make Rouge
Zhèng Qián said:
"Pomegranates can be used to make rouge,
Ruìzōng's daughter, Princess Dàiguó, once made it.
She discarded its fruits within the palace,
and they grew in clumps, forming a forest."
Centipede
Kāiníng County has many centipedes,
the large ones have skin that can cover drums.
Sòng Wǔdì's Princess Shòuyáng,
had a plum blossom fall on her forehead,
forming a five-petal flower.
Later generations imitated it, creating plum blossom makeup.
Forehead Decorations to Cover Scars
Shàngguān Zhāoróng made her own forehead decorations to cover a dark spot.
Whenever Empress Tiānhòu met with her prime ministers,
she ordered Zhāoróng to lie under the bed skirt,
to record the matters presented.
One day,
she secretly peeked at the prime ministers.
The Empress noticed,
and after the court session, she was extremely angry.
She took a nail knife and pierced her face,
not allowing it to be pulled out.
Zhāoróng immediately composed the poem *Qǐ Bá Dāozǐ Shī*.
Later, she made forehead decorations to cover the scar.
There is a collection of twenty volumes,
the poem is in the collection,
Emperor Míng ordered Zhāng Yuè to write a preface.
Covenant Sacrifice with White Dog and Red Rooster
Whenever the Yuè people become friends,
they build an altar at the foot of the mountain,
and offer a white dog and red rooster as sacrifice.
They look up to the sky and swear an oath, saying:
"On a certain month and day,
A and B become friends,
may all above, below, and on the four sides bear witness.
If you ride in a cart,
and I wear a bamboo hat,
when we meet again in the future, you will get out of your cart and bow;
If I walk,
and you ride a horse,
when we meet again in the future, your horse should be dismounted."
Such oaths comprised several thousand words,
taken from their local *Fēngtǔ Jì*.
Swallowing Paper and Embracing Fire
Máo Qǐn,
*Jiāxùn* says:
"Zhū Zhān was poor yet fond of learning.
When hungry, he would swallow paper;
when cold, he would embrace fire,
and he never stopped reading."
A Certain Number of Slaves
"Princess Ānjí presented a *Húzǐ* (bearded man)."
Local dialects and foreign customs are very worth observing,
high mountains and deep seas,
as if in their very appearance."
Also, *Liáng Lǜ* says:
"A certain number of slaves."
Móu Yǐng of Luòyáng,
buried a skeleton outside the city.
He dreamed a person came to thank him, saying:
"I was originally a powerful bandit,
and was killed by my peers.
Grateful for your burial of me,
I wish to secretly protect you.
If you are in urgent need,
just call Chìdīngzǐ,
and I will arrive immediately."
Afterwards, there were several fulfillments.
White Phoenix Bearing a Letter
Consort Yáng once sat alone,
when a white phoenix came before her,
bearing a letter in its mouth.
She took and saw that it was an imperial decree from the Heavenly Emperor,
calling the consort a banished immortal,
blaming her for her allure,
and describing in detail the affair at Mǎwéi.
Spirits of Seven Trees
During the reign of Shùnzōng,
the scholar Jiǎ Mì encountered seven people drinking together in an abandoned garden in Luòyáng,
who called themselves the Qī Xián.
They invited Mì to sit,
and slowly questioned them.
They were actually the spirits of seven trees: pine, willow, pagodatree, mulberry, jujube, chestnut, and Ailanthus.
When Mǎ Jǔ governed Huáinán,
an old man visited Jǔ,
and spoke of military strategy, saying:
"First, govern troops with discipline;
only after troops are disciplined can commanders and officers be skilled,
and soldiers be brave.
He (Jǔ) asked:
"What about being a commander?"
The old man said:
"First, seize strategic locations;
next, confront the enemy army.
Charging through passes and repelling them (the enemy),
must not be forgotten.
Furthermore, there is sacrificing the small to preserve the great,
stopping killing and frequently retreating,
occupying strategic terrain,
deploying deceptive troops,
the key lies in swift attack,
one must not hesitate.
If perchance one is undecided on speed (pace),
and the terrain varies greatly between difficult and easy,
unable to advance and attack,
the situation demands seeking survival.
Frequent victories will surely lead to defeat;
caution lies in deceiving the enemy."
Jǔ said:
"Sir, where are you from?
How profound is your learning!"
He said:
"I am the Nánshān Mùqiángrén,
with the reputation of concealing jade and containing pearls.
A temporarily conjoined body,
it is not at all firm,
how can it last long?"
The Duke kept him at the guesthouse,
but by night he was gone.
Inside the room, only a chessboard was seen.
Suddenly, it leaped up, fell to the ground, and shattered.
Dōután Dálà
It originated from foreign music.
Being a drum of the Róngjié tribes,
it is therefore called *jiégǔ*.
Its pitch matches the *tàicù* mode.
Both Qiūcí and Gāochāng used it.
It ranks below the Dōután drum and the Dálà,
and above the Nánlóu drum.
The Dōulǜ resembles a drum, and the Dálà is also a *kāigǔ* (friction drum).
The Dálà is like a lacquer bucket,
supported on a rope frame,
played with two sticks,
its sound is sharp and urgent,
under the bright moon and clear breeze,
it is especially unique among all music.
The *Jiégǔ* as the Leader of the Eight Sounds
Míng Huáng 尤其喜愛羯鼓 (jiégǔ) 和玉笛 (yùdí),
將它們視為八音之首。
春雨初霽，
景色明媚，
皇帝說：
「面對此等景物，豈能不與之相應和呢？」
他命人取來羯鼓，
臨窗縱情擊奏，
曲名為《春光》 (Chūnguāng)。
回顧窗外柳樹和杏樹，
都已微微綻放。
皇上笑道：
「此事若不是我來做天公，
又該是誰呢？」
他又創作了《秋風高》 (Qiūfēng Gāo)，
到了秋日天空清澈開闊時演奏，
必然有遠風徐徐吹來，
庭院樹葉緩緩飄落。
花奴 (Huānú)
是汝陽王 (Rǔyáng Wáng) Lǐ Jìn (李璡)，
即寧王 (Níng Wáng) 的長子。
他曾戴著壓花輕絹帽子擊鼓奏曲，
皇上親手摘下紅色的木槿花，
放到他帽子上扁平處。
這兩樣東西都極其光滑，
過了很久才安穩下來。
一曲奏罷，花朵不曾墜落。
本色演奏中所謂的「定頭項」 (dìngtóuxiàng)，
難就難在不能有絲毫搖動。
皇帝說：
「花奴 資質聰明透徹，
必定是謫降凡間的神仙。」
寧王 聽後隨即貶損他。
皇上說：
「大哥 (Dàgē) 你不在意這些，
但阿瞞 (āmán) (指他自己) 自會看相。
帝王的儀表，
必須具備英武特異的氣概，
和深沉內斂的神情。
花奴 只是容貌端莊秀麗勝過常人，
常能得到公卿們的讚賞。」
羯鼓解穢 (jiégǔ jiěhuì)
皇上不喜歡琴，
聽人彈奏還沒結束，
就說：
「快點召見花奴，
帶羯鼓來為我解穢 (jiěhuì) (消除厭煩或不快)。」
奉勑豎金雞 (fèngchì shù jīnjī)
黃幡綽 (Huáng Fānchuò) 精通音律，
皇上召見他，
他卻沒有按時到達。
皇上非常憤怒。
黃幡綽 趕到時，
聽到皇上正在擊鼓，
便阻止謁者不要通報。
曲子奏罷，
黃幡綽 快步走入，
皇上問：
「你去了哪裡？」
黃幡綽 說：
「送親戚朋友去了郊外。」
皇上說：
「幸好你來遲了些。
剛才我正生氣，
你若到了必定要挨打。」
恰巧他的長子進來供職，
皇上暫時放過他，說：
「他出去了就不能放過他。」
內官們笑著說：
「黃幡綽 聽完鼓聲才進來的。」
皇上厲聲說：
「我心底的感受，
豈是一個宦官聽鼓聲就能預料到的？
現在你來告訴我如何？」
黃幡綽 走下台階鞠躬，
大聲說：
「奉勑豎金雞！」 (意指皇上心情轉好，如同金雞報曉，指令可以頒布了)
皇上笑了，怒氣也就平息了。
漢第二鼓 (Hàn dì'èr gǔ)
宋璟 (Sòng Jǐng) 尤其擅長羯鼓，
他所作的《南山起雲》 (Nánshān Qǐyún) 和《山起雨》 (Shān Qǐyǔ) 兩曲，
就是宋璟 所作。
皇帝和唐 (Táng) 討論鼓樂之事時說：
「不是青山的石末，
就是魯山的花磁，
這是漢震 (Hànzhèn) 的第二鼓。
然而，使用石末 (shímò) 或花磁 (huācí) 製作的，
固然是腰鼓。
堂上十個指頭能清晰發聲，
是用手拍擊的，
顯然不是羯鼓。
第二鼓的演奏方法，
左手用杖，
右手拍擊。」
宋璟 又說：
「鼓槌的頭部像青山之峰，
拍擊的手法像白雨點；
山峰取其不動如山，
雨點取其急促碎密，
這就是羯鼓演奏的精髓。」
明皇供御捲 (Míng Huáng gōngyù juǎn)
嗣曹王 (Sì Cáo Wáng) Gāo (皋) 善於巧思，
有人獻上兩卷 (juǎn)。
Gāo 說：
「想不到今日能獲遇至寶。」
他命人取來盤子。
選了一個平坦的盤子，將其中一卷放在盤子中央，
將油注滿捲中，
而油卻沒有滲透，
原來是它們契合得天衣無縫。
Gāo 說：
「這必定是明皇 曾經御用的卷子。」
問及它的來源，
那人說他父親在黔中 (Qiánzhōng) 從高力士 (Gāo Lìshì) 那裡得到的。
無結尾聲 (wú jiéwěi shēng)
廣德 (Guǎngdé) 年間，
蜀地有個李宛 (Lǐ Wǎn) 擅長羯鼓。
一天晚上他聽到鼓聲，
便敲門對鼓工說：
「您所敲奏的，
莫非是《耶婆色雞》 (Yépósèjī) 嗎？
為何沒有結尾？」
鼓工說：
「按照舊譜沒有結尾的樂聲，
所以我晚上才四處尋訪 (以求解決)。」
李宛 說：
「曲中意境已盡了嗎？」
鼓工說：
「已盡。」
李宛 說：
「意境已盡，那麼曲子也就該結束了。」
鼓工說：
「那樂聲未盡怎麼辦？」
李宛 說：
「可以與你談談了。
曲中有意猶未盡之處，
可以用其他曲子來銜接，
這首曲子應當用《掘柘急遍》 (Juézhè Jíbiàn) 來銜接。」
鼓工照他的話去做，
果然非常和諧，
樂聲和意境都完美結束了。
註解說：
例如《柘枝》 (Zhèzhī) 用《渾脫》 (Húntuō) 來銜接；
《甘州》 (Gānzhōu) 用《吉了》 (Jíle) 來銜接之類。
琵琶 (pípá)
琵琶 象徵三才 (天地人) 和四時 (春夏秋冬)，
它本是胡人 (Hú Rén) 在馬上敲奏的樂器，
向前推手撥弦叫「琵」 (pí)。
向後卻手撥弦叫「琶」 (pá)。
漢朝 (Hàn Cháo) 派遣烏孫公主 (Wūsūn Gōngzhǔ) 出嫁，
念及她路途遙遠會思念故鄉，
便命精通音律者在馬上彈奏琵琶來慰藉她。
曹綱右手興奴左手 (Cáo Gāng yòu shǒu Xìngnú zuǒ shǒu)
元和 (Yuánhé) 年間，
有王芬 (Wáng Fēn) 和曹保 (Cáo Bǎo)。
曹保 的兒子叫善才 (Shàncái)，
曹保 的孫子叫曹綱 (Cáo Gāng)，
他們都擅長琵琶。
裴興奴 (Péi Xìngnú) 與曹綱 同時。
曹綱 擅長連撥，
不常用提絃；
裴興奴 擅長攏撚 (lǒngniǎn)。
當時的人們說曹綱 有「右手」 (指撥弦技巧高超)，
裴興奴 有「左手」 (指按弦技巧精妙)。
蕤賓鐵 (Ruíbīn tiě)
樂工廉郊 (Lián Jiāo)，
師從曹綱。
曹綱 說：
「我教過很多人，
從未見過如此有靈性的弟子。」
廉郊 曾在池邊彈奏蕤賓調 (Ruíbīn diào)，
忽然聽到芰荷叢中跳出一個東西到岸上，
竟是一片方響 (fāngxiǎng)。
有識貨的人辨認出那是蕤賓鐵 (一種樂器)。
這是因為他的指撥精妙，
能使音律相應和，
連物類都能受到感動啊。
鄭中丞大小忽雷 (Zhèng Zhōngchéng dàxiǎo Hūléi)
During Emperor Wénzōng's
reign, there was a palace attendant named Zhèng Zhōngchéng,
who played the húqín.
The imperial treasury had two pípa,
named "Dà Hūléi" and "Xiǎo Hūléi."
An old official, Liáng Hòuběn,
while fishing in his villa in Zhāoyìng,
suddenly saw an object pass by,
about five or six chǐ long,
wrapped in brocade.
He ordered his servant to retrieve it from the bank,
and it was indeed a secret vessel.
When opened, it revealed a young woman,
beautifully adorned and composed,
with her neck bound inside it,
and still breathing.
After nurturing her for about ten days,
it turned out she was an imperial disciple,
and Hòuběn took her as his wife.
She spoke of the pípa,
mentioning that the peg had come loose,
and it had been sent to the Nán Zhàojiā for repairs.
During the upheaval of the Xùnzhù Rebellion,
no one knew of this.
Hòuběn acquired it,
only daring to play it softly after midnight.
Later, on an auspicious day,
drunk with wine under the flowers,
he played several tunes.
A eunuch passed by and said:
"This is the sound of Zhèng Zhōngchéng's pípa!"
The next day, this was reported to the emperor.
Emperor Wénzōng, who had previously regretted this matter,
was now both surprised and delighted.
He sent for Hòuběn,
pardoned his offense,
and allowed them to remain a couple.
There was a palace attendant, Hú Èrjiě,
whom Bái Xiùcái took as a concubine.
She was originally a palace maid.
She suddenly sang a new tune,
which startled Bái,
and she never sang it again.
Later, when Bái traveled to Língwǔ,
at the banquet of Lǐ Língyào Shàngshū,
a guest sang "Hémǎnzǐ,"
and everyone praised its beauty.
Bái said:
"I have a concubine
whose voice and tune are quite different from this."
When she was summoned,
she appeared in simple clothes, elegant and refined,
and her playing was spirited and soaring.
The guest said:
"Could this be Hú Èrjiě from the palace?"
Hú replied:
"Could this be Luò Gòngfèng from the Líyuán?"
They faced each other and wept.
Original skill with a discordant sound.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Kāng Kūnlún was the foremost pípa player.
When both markets prayed for rain,
a musical contest ensued.
Kūnlún ascended the Green Tower on the east side of the street,
and played a new barbarian "Yǔdiào Lǜyāo" tune.
The text notes:
"Lǜyāo" is "Lùyào,"
originally a tune presented by a musician,
which the emperor ordered to be recorded for its important parts.
He was certain there was no rival on the west side of the street.
When the tune ended,
a young woman emerged from the West Market tower,
carrying a musical instrument, and said:
"I also play this tune,
and moreover, I can transpose it into the 'Fēngxiāng' mode."
Then she struck the plectrum,
and the sound was like thunder,
wonderfully exquisite, as if by a spirit.
Kūnlún bowed,
acknowledging her as his teacher.
The young woman changed her clothes and came out,
revealing herself to be the monk Shàn běn,
whose secular surname was Jiǎ.
The next day,
Emperor Dézōng summoned him
and ordered him to teach Kūnlún.
Jiǎ Shī said:
"Please play a tune."
Jiǎ said:
"How is your original skill so mixed?
And tinged with a discordant sound?"
Kūnlún replied:
"Jiǎ Shī,
you are a divine being!
When I was young, I learned from a neighboring female shaman,
who taught me the first-grade string.
Later, I changed several teachers."
Jiǎ said:
"First, let Kūnlún stay away from musical instruments for over ten years,
to forget his original habits,
then he can be taught."
The emperor approved this,
and later Kūnlún indeed inherited all the teacher's skills.
Mǐ Héláng
During the Xiántōng era,
there was Mǐ Héláng,
also known as Jiāróngzi.
Tián Cóngdào was especially excellent,
and later there was Wáng Lián'ér,
whose appearance was very serene.
Yáng Dànián was playing chess with a guest,
when Shí Zhōnglì arrived from outside,
and playfully said:
"He stops at the corner of the seat,
his appearance very serene."
Shí replied:
"My mouth cannot speak,
so please let me reply by instinct."
Boots worth nine hundred
Féng Dào and Hé Níng were both in the Zhōngshū.
One day,
Hé asked Féng:
"Your new boots,
how much do they cost?"
Féng raised his left foot and said:
"Nine hundred."
Hé was irritable by nature,
so he glared at his attendant and scolded:
"Why do my boots cost one thousand eight hundred?"
Féng slowly raised his right foot and said:
"This one is also nine hundred."
Era names containing the character 'Bǎo'.
The currency of the state during the "Kāibǎo" era
bore the inscription "Sòng Tōng Yuánbǎo,"
while that during the "Bǎoyuán" era bore "Huáng Sòng Tōngbǎo."
In recent times, the inscriptions on coins all include the era name,
but these two coins do not,
because their era names already contained the character "Bǎo."
Changing the era name to "Zhádé"
In the sixth year of Jiànlóng, Tàizǔ discussed changing the era name,
telling his chief ministers not to use old names from previous dynasties.
After the era name was changed to Zhádé,
the name Zhádé was found on the back of a mirror belonging to a palace attendant.
The Academician Táo Gǔ said:
"This is the era name of the false Shǔ kingdom."
Because of this, Tàizǔ esteemed literati even more.
Where in life does one not meet again?
Guàn Zhōngmǐn Gōng Zhǔn was repeatedly demoted to Sīhù of Léizhōu.
At that time, Dīng Jìnggōng and Féng Zhěng were both in the Zhōngshū.
Dīng, holding the brush,
wanted to demote him to Yázhōu.
Someone questioned:
"Yázhōu is beyond the whale-waves again;
how can this be?"
Féng merely assented,
so Dīng then proposed Léizhōu.
When Dīng himself was demoted,
Féng then proposed Yázhōu.
At that time, people said:
"If you meet Guàn Sīhù in Léizhōu,
where in life does one not meet again?"
Several baskets of drafts
Yáng Wéngōng Yì was in the Xuéshì Yuàn,
when he was suddenly summoned late at night.
The emperor calmly brought out several baskets of drafts and said:
"You criticize my writings,
but all these manuscripts are my own drafts;
I have never ordered my subordinates to write for me."
Dànián knew he must have been slandered by someone,
so he feigned madness and ran onto the balcony.
If favor goes to oneself, who bears the resentment?
Wáng Wénzhèng Gōng once said that high officials should not monopolize favor,
often remarking:
"If favor goes to oneself,
who bears the resentment?"
A scholar seeking office.
Táo Gǔ, as an academician,
was once summoned for an audience late in the evening.
Tàizǔ was in the imperial private hall.
When Gǔ saw the emperor,
he made to advance but feigned retreat repeatedly.
Tàizǔ laughed heartily and said:
"A scholar seeking office!"
He looked to his attendants, asking them to bring a robe and belt.
The emperor had already tied his belt.
Gǔ quickly departed.
Yellow silk quilt and bedding
Rénzōng was unwell.
The high ministers came to his bedchamber daily.
They saw the Emperor using a plain lacquer spittoon and a porcelain cup.
On the imperial couch, the quilts and mattresses were all of yellow silk gauze,
already old and dim.
