The palace maids hastily brought new quilts to cover them,
which were also yellow silk gauze.
Skillful Hands
Chén Kāngsù Gōng Yáozī was skilled in archery.
A oil seller said:
"It's nothing else,
just skillful hands."
The Duke angrily said:
"How dare you slight my archery!"
The old man said:
"I know it from how I pour oil."
He took a gourd,
covered its mouth with a coin,
and ladled oil through the coin's hole,
without wetting the coin.
Then he said:
"I also have nothing else,
it's just skillful hands."
The Duke smiled and dismissed him.
The Two Chancellors Wén and Fù
At the beginning of Zhìhé reign,
Lord Wén and Lord Fù were both appointed chancellors.
The Emperor sent a eunuch to listen to their discussions among the ranks of officials.
The court gentlemen often congratulated each other.
The Emperor said:
"In ancient times,
people were sometimes appointed based on dreams or divination.
If one does not truly know a person,
one should follow public opinion.
How can divination be relied upon?"
I wrote in "Wén Gōng Pīdá":
"Seeking to be recorded by Shāng and Zhōu,
one resorts to dreams and divination to seek out worthies;
if one uses the public opinion of the gentry,
it is to follow the hopes of both inside and outside the court."
Friendly Neighboring Lands
Yáng Dànián's letter responding to the Qìdān read:
"Friendly neighboring lands."
Zhēnzōng commented:
"Rotten land,
dung land."
Dànián changed it to "neighboring regions."
The next morning,
citing a Tang dynasty precedent,
he requested to be dismissed for not being competent.
The Emperor said:
"Yáng Yì does not accept discussion,
he really has a temper."
Scholar of Zǐchén Hall
Dīng Dù, after being dismissed as Administrator,
became a Scholar of Zǐchén Hall.
Because of "Wénmíng,"
Zhēnzōng's posthumous title,
Zǐchén was changed.
Those who deliberated considered Zǐchén inappropriate for a subject to hold,
so it was changed to Guānwén.
It was the name of Suí Yángdì's palace,
and it was proper to avoid it.
At the time, this was not known.
Therefore, the officials of the court
must not neglect their studies.
Five Phoenixes Soar into the Hanlin Academy
During Tàizōng's reign,
Sòng Bái, Jiǎ Huángzhōng, Lǐ Zhì, Lǚ Méngzhèng, and Sū Yìjiǎn, five men, were simultaneously appointed Hanlin Academicians.
Chéngzhǐ Hù Méng presented a poem:
"Five phoenixes soar into the Hanlin Academy."
They all later became famous ministers.
Censors Reporting Matters Must Inform the Vice Censor-in-Chief
According to the traditions of the Censorate:
Censors of the three bureaus, when reporting matters,
must first inform the Vice Censor-in-Chief.
Since Liú Zǐyí became Vice Censor-in-Chief,
he posted a notice in the Censorate:
"If a Censor has anything to report,
there is no need to inform beforehand."
This has remained the practice ever since.
Duke Dīng's Fasting for Monks Edict
Dīng Jìngōng, when exiled south,
composed "Fasting for Monks Edict," saying:
"To mend Zhòngshān's imperial robe,
though drawn with skillful intent,
and to harmonize Fù Yuè's broth,
is indeed difficult to adjust to all tastes."
He also had a poem that said:
"Grass forgets sorrow, what is there to sorrow about?
Flowers named 'containing smiles,' at whom do they smile?"
Minister Zhāng's Food
Zhāng Púshè Qíxián
always loved several catties of fatty pork.
For Tiānshòu Yuàn's Fēngyào Hēishén Pills,
an ordinary person would take no more than one pill,
but the Duke took five or seven liǎng as a large dose.
He ate them with húcake.
After being dismissed from chancellorship and knowing Ānzhōu,
when dining with guests,
the kitchen clerk placed a large bucket,
secretly observing what the Duke ate,
and threw similar items into the bucket.
By evening,
the bucket was full of soaked items.
Yàn Yuánxiàn was thin as if carved,
always breaking a half-cake and rolling it with chopsticks,
and putting a single strand of yóuzi inside the twisted head.
This, too, was unusual compared to others.
A Good River
Cáo Shìzhōng Lìyòng was in the Privy Council,
determined to eradicate opportunism,
and eunuchs were particularly suppressed.
Later,
Cáo Ruì was executed,
and Cáo was again demoted to Fángzhōu.
Upon reaching the Xiāngyáng crossing,
the supervising eunuch Yáng Huáimǐn said to him:
"Shìzhōng, what a good river!"
Presumably wishing him to throw himself in.
He repeated it again and again,
but Cáo did not understand.
Upon reaching Xiāngyáng驛,
he was then forced to hang himself.
Three Times an Imperial Edict Was Not Carried Out
During the war at Chányuān,
Cáo Shìzhōng was sent as an envoy to the Qìdān,
and an alliance of friendship was settled.
During the time of Zhāngxiàn Míngsù Tàihòu,
he considered himself an old meritorious official,
and the Empress Dowager also greatly feared and respected him,
addressing him as Shìzhōng and not by name.
All imperial favors granted by the palace
were held back by him and not implemented.
Since many were held back,
there were instances where after being held back three times, they were issued again,
and he had no choice but to implement them.
This caused him to be eyed askance by petty individuals.
Whenever an edict was not implemented after three issuances,
the petitioners would again report to the Empress Dowager, saying:
"Your servant has told the wet nurse in Shìzhōng's residence or his close confidants to speak of it,
and he has agreed."
Thus, it would be re-issued.
Cáo, having held it back three times,
had no choice but to implement it.
The Empress Dowager was greatly angered,
which led to the disaster of Cáo Ruì.
Thus, it is known that when a great minister has high achievements and heavy influence,
calamities are beyond what foresight can anticipate.
The Two Sòngs
Sòng Zhènggōng Xiáng,
originally named Jiāo,
and his brother, originally named Dòng Tiānxià,
were known as "The Two Sòngs."
Rénzōng wanted to employ them greatly,
but there was a slanderous report saying that their surname matched the national dynastic title (Sòng),
and the name Jiāo corresponded to the suburban sacrifice to Heaven (jiāotiān).
Jiāo (郊) means jiāo (交, to interact), thus Sòng Jiāo's words were inauspicious.
The Emperor ordered them to change their names,
and the Duke had no choice but to do so.
The Duke later served in two high offices,
and retired as Sīkōng.
He enjoyed both blessings and longevity,
while the slanderer was never employed.
Returned from an Imperial Assignment to Supervise Affairs in Jiāngnán
Cáo Wǔhuìwáng Bīn's achievements were very great.
He once said:
"As a general, I have never killed anyone out of anger or joy."
His residence's hall was dilapidated,
and his children wanted to repair it.
The Duke said:
"It is winter;
hundreds of insects are hibernating between the walls and tiles.
Their lives must not be harmed."
Such was his love for living things.
After pacifying Jiāngnán and returning,
he went to the palace gate to request an audience.
His signboard read: "奉勑江南勾當公事回" (Returned from an Imperial Assignment to Supervise Affairs in Jiāngnán).
Such was his humility.
Rhapsody on Casting Tripods and Portraying Objects
Although Emperor Zhēn Zōng selected scholars based on their literary talent,
he invariably considered their character and insight.
Each time he bestowed the title of *jìnshì* upon successful candidates,
he would summon the top three or four individuals to stand in the court.
After further observing those whose presence and spirit were grand and unconstrained,
he would then bestow the title of *dì yī rén jídì* (first-place successful candidate).
Sometimes, he would choose based on the essays they submitted that possessed logical appeal.
Xú Shì’s “Zhù Dǐng Xiàng Wù Fù” says:
“The feet are merely for uprightness below;
how could one hear of the *gōng sù* (duke’s porridge) tilting?
The handles are positioned above;
they truly embody the gravitas of a king’s minister.”
He was then made first place.
Cài Qí’s “Zhì Qì Fù” says:
“To bring peace to the world under an overturned bowl—
its merit can be great.”
He was then made first place.
Coral Pen Holder
Qián Sī Gōng was by nature frugal.
His children could not take a single coin unless it was specifically granted.
The Duke had a coral pen holder,
which he cherished throughout his life.
When his children wanted money,
they would secretly take it.
The Duke would then post a notice in the household,
offering to buy it back for ten thousand cash.
His children would pretend to find it and present it,
and the Duke would gladly give them ten thousand cash.
This happened five or seven times within a year,
and the Duke never caught on.
Decorated Candles
The decorated candles of Dèng Zhōu,
it is said, were in the style of Guān Lái Gōng.
The Duke had been wealthy and esteemed since childhood;
he did not light oil lamps.
Even in the latrine,
candle wax would pile up.
Dù Qí Gōng, when in office,
never burned official candles.
A single oil lamp,
and he would sit facing guests.
Both Dukes were famous officials,
but their extravagance and frugality differed thus.
Qí Gōng lived a long life and ended well,
while Lái Gōng suffered the calamity of being banished south.
Though his misfortune,
it can also serve as a warning.
Academicians Using Surnames
According to custom,
when academicians were in the inner court,
they were led by two scarlet-robed palace officials.
During the reign of Tài Zǔ,
when Lǐ Fǎng was an academician,
Tài Zōng was in the Southern Administration (Nán Yá).
He was led by one scarlet-robed official.
Lǐ Fǎng removed one of them.
In earlier times, academicians submitting memorials did not include their surnames,
but merely said, “Your humble servant, Academician So-and-so.”
Shèng Dù and Dīng Dù both served as academicians,
so they began including their surnames to distinguish themselves.
Thereafter, all included their surnames.
Wáng and Zhāng Taunting Each Other
Yàn Yuán Xiàn, after being dismissed as Vice Chancellor,
became the Grand Administrator of Nán Jīng.
He was thirty-eight years old at the time.
Among his staff were Wáng Qí and Zhāng Kàng.
Zhāng Kàng was exceptionally large-bodied,
and Wáng Qí called him an ox.
Wáng Qí was so thin he looked like bones standing,
and Zhāng Kàng called him a monkey.
Wáng Qí taunted him, saying:
“Zhāng Kàng bumps into a wall and forms the character ‘eight’ (八).”
Zhāng Kàng replied:
“Wáng Qí gazes at the moon and shouts three times.”
Virtue Surpassing the Nine Emperors
Yáng Wén Gōng admonished his disciples that when writing essays, they should avoid colloquialisms.
Subsequently, the Duke composed a memorial that said:
“I humbly submit that Your Majesty’s virtue surpasses the Nine Emperors.”
His disciple Zhèng Jiǎn asked:
“I wonder when one can sell fresh vegetables?”
The Duke laughed and changed it.
Memorial on an Envoy Mission to Qìdān
Xià Wú Gōng Sǒng’s
father was an official in Hé Běi.
When the Qìdān invaded Hé Běi,
he died in battle.
Later, after the Duke rose from mourning his mother,
he was sent as an envoy to the Qìdān.
The Duke’s memorial stated:
“My father died for the state,
and I am in mourning for my mother.
Righteously, I cannot live under the same sky [as my father’s enemies]; it is difficult to bow in a humble dwelling.
According to ritual, I should be sleeping on an earthen pillow;
how can I bear to hear the sounds of barbarian music?”
At the time, this was considered an exquisitely crafted parallel couplet.
Lí Shān Poems
Sūn Jǐn, while serving as the Transport Commissioner of Shǎn Xī,
composed two “Lí Shān Poems.”
The later poem said:
“When the Qin Emperor’s tomb was finished, Chén Shèng rose;
when Emperor Míng’s palace was completed, Lù Shān came.”
At that time, the Yù Qīng Zhāo Yìng Palace was being built.
Someone who disliked Sūn Jǐn
recorded the poem and presented it.
Emperor Zhēn Zōng read the first poem, which said:
“Scarlet-robed officials lead the way up Lí Shān.”
He immediately said:
“Jǐn is a man of shallow capacity.
What is there to boast about here?”
He then cast it aside and did not read further,
so the words about Chén Shèng and Lù Shān were ultimately not heard.
People considered this fortunate.
Well-Expressed Wealth and Nobility
Yàn Yuán Xiàn said:
“‘I feel the golden sash heavy in my old age,
and lazily find the jade pillow cool’—
these are not truly expressions of wealth and nobility.
Better is: ‘Sheng and song return to the courtyard,
lamps and fires descend from the towers’—
these are truly excellent expressions of wealth and nobility.”
Famous Paintings
Recent famous paintings:
Lǐ Chéng and Jù Rán’s landscapes,
Bāo Dǐng’s tigers, and Zhào Chāng’s flowers and fruits.
Lǐ Chéng rose to the rank of Shàng Shū Láng;
many people possess his landscapes and winter forests.
Only the north wall of the Yù Táng (Jade Hall) retains a work by Jù Rán.
The Bāo clan,
from Xuān Zhōu,
was famous for painting tigers;
Bāo Dǐng was exceptionally skilled.
His descendants could never quite match him.
Zhào Chāng’s lifelike paintings were very realistic,
but his brushwork was soft and vulgar,
utterly lacking the ancient masters’ style and composition.
Matching Couplets
Guān Lái Gōng playfully said:
“The sun under the water is the sun in the sky.”
Yáng Tài Nián said:
“The person in my eye is the person before me.”
This Time, It Really Is Sending a Lampstand
The proverb says:
“Old Zhào sends a lampstand—
once it’s gone, it never returns.”
During the Tiān Shèng era,
there was a Shàng Shū Láng named Zhào Shì Cháng.
He was old
and sought to be the Acting Administrator of the Western Capital.
A frivolous person sent him a poem that said:
“This time, it really is sending a lampstand.”
Afterward, he indeed died while serving as Acting Administrator.
Laughed Until His Face Was Like Boot Leather
Tián Yuán Jūn, when in the Three Departments,
deeply disliked solicitations.
Not wanting to refuse them harshly,
he would always send them away with a warm expression and a forced smile.
He once said:
“After serving as Commissioner of the Three Departments for several years,
I’ve literally laughed until my face is like boot leather.”
Discussing Chess
Hú Dàn said:
“To consider chess easy to understand,
even with my intelligence, I might still fail;
to consider it difficult to understand,
then often foolish and lowly people are exquisitely skilled.”
Writing Essays on the “Three Uppers”
Qián Sī Gōng would read classics and histories when sitting,
read novels when lying down,
and peruse short poems when on the toilet.
Zōng Gōng Chuí always carried a book when going to the toilet,
and people far and near heard his recitations.
As for the essays I have written throughout my life,
many were composed on the “three uppers”:
on horseback, on the pillow, and on the toilet.
Unable to Inscribe Name on Yellow Paper
Qián Sī Gōng held both military and prime ministerial posts,
and he himself said:
“In my life, my only regret,
and a deep one, is that I never got to inscribe my name on yellow paper (for an imperial edict).”
On Teaching Without Discrimination
In the provincial examination for jinshì, the rhapsody titled "There is education for all, without discrimination" (有教無類賦) was submitted.
Wáng Yígōng (王沂公) was ranked first.
It contained the lines: "Even divine dragons with extraordinary innate abilities
still have desires that can be sought;
What do delicate grasses know,
yet they borrow from each other's fragrance."
A frivolous fellow remarked:
"In front of Xiàngguó Sì (相國寺),
bears perform somersaults;
Outside Wàngchūn Mén (望春門),
donkeys dance the zhè zhī."
Commentators said:
"Though the words are crude and vulgar,
the matter is pertinent to the topic."
Golden Belts
Tàizōng (太宗) said:
"Jade does not leave the stone,
rhinoceros horn does not leave the horn;
What is truly precious is gold."
He created golden buckles and bestowed them upon his officials.
Round, ball-patterned ones were given to officials of the two courts (liǎng fǔ),
while imperial fairy-flower patterns were given to academicians and above.
Today, common folk refer to the ball-patterned ones as "hù tóu" (笏頭, tablet head),
and the imperial fairy-flower patterns as "lì zhī" (荔枝, lychee).
Monkey in a Cloth Sack
Huán Shèngyú (桓聖俞) was renowned for his poetry,
but for thirty years, he never obtained an official post.
In his later years, he received an imperial order to compile the "History of the Táng Dynasty" (唐書).
He told his wife:
"My compilation of this book
can be likened to 'a monkey entering a cloth sack'."
His wife replied:
"Your official career,
how is it different from 'a catfish climbing a bamboo pole'?"
Shèng is Fat, Dīng is Thin
Shèng Wénsù Gōng (盛文肅公) was corpulent,
while Dīng Jìngōng (丁晉公) was as thin as a catfish.
Hànlín attendant reader Méi Xún (梅詢) was fond of burning incense.
Every morning when he rose to attend to his duties,
he would burn incense,
cover it with his official robe,
gather his sleeves, and step out.
When he sat down and spread his robe,
a rich fragrance would emanate.
There was a staff member of the academy, Dòu Yuánbīn (竇元賓),
who disliked elaborate food
and went for a long time without bathing.
At the time, people would say: "Shèng is fat, Dīng is thin;
Méi smells fragrant, Dòu smells foul."
Ancient Mirror that Shines Two Hundred Lǐ
Lǚ Wénmù Gōng Méngzhèng (呂文穆公蒙正) was a prime minister.
A court official had an ancient mirror
that could illuminate two hundred lǐ.
He wanted to offer it through his younger brother, seeking a position.
The Duke said:
"My face is no larger than a plate;
What use do I have for shining two hundred lǐ?"
Those who heard this marveled and admired him,
considering him far more virtuous than Lǐ Wèigōng (李衛公).
Zházi (劄子)
What Táng (唐) people submitted to the emperor other than formal memorials were called bǎng zǐ (榜子)
or lù zǐ (錄子).
Today, they are called zházi (劄子).
Crabs but No Tōngpàn (通判)
During the present dynasty, the position of tōngpàn (通判) for all prefectures was established.
They often vied for power with the zhīzhōu (知州, prefect).
There was a man named Qián Kūn (錢昆),
a native of Háng (杭),
who was fond of crabs.
He once sought an outer prefecture.
Someone asked him which prefecture he desired.
Qián Kūn (錢昆) replied:
"Any place with crabs but no tōngpàn (通判) will do."
Censorate Officials Use Rare Surnames
During the Jǐngyòu (景祐) era,
there was a director, Pí Zhòngróng (皮仲容),
whom a frivolous fellow playfully teased, saying:
"I heard you have been appointed to the Censorate (Táixiàn, 臺憲)."
Pí Zhòngróng (皮仲róng) was ashamed and declined,
asking how he knew.
He replied:
"Newly appointed Censorate officials
must use rare surnames;
I know it by your surname."
At that time, the Censorate officials of the three departments were Zhòngjiǎn (仲簡), Lùn Chéng (論程), and Zhǎng Yǔxī (掌禹錫).
Errors in Temples' Names
Popular transmission of errors is most prevalent
in the names of temples and shrines.
The Mǎnchí Sì (滿池寺) in the capital
is now mistakenly called Pútí Sì (菩提寺).
The Dàgūshān (大孤山) and Xiǎogūshān (小孤山) in Jiāngnán (江南),
now mistakenly call gū (孤, lonely/isolated) as gū (姑, paternal aunt/maiden).
On the side of the river, there is Pénglàng Jī (澎浪磯),
now mistakenly called Péngláng Jī (彭郎磯),
and it is said to be the husband of Xiǎogū (小姑).
At Lóngmén Shān (龍門山) in Xī Jīng (西京),
when viewed, it resembles twin gate towers.
At the mouth of the mountain, there is a temple with a statue
holding a butcher knife,
sitting with knees pressed down.
It is called Huōkǒu Dàwáng (豁口大王),
which is even more laughable.
Speech Errors
Among the common errors passed down through generations,
the word "dǎ" (打) is one where the entire world shares the same mistake.
Its original meaning refers to the sound of striking or hitting.
Therefore, people beating each other,
or striking objects,
are all called dǎ (打).
However, artisans making gold and silver ornaments also say dǎ (打),
which still retains the meaning of beating or hammering.
But as for building boats and carriages, they say "dǎ chuán" (打船, beat a boat) and "dǎ chē" (打車, beat a cart);
Netting fish is "dǎ yú" (打魚, beat fish);
Drawing water is "dǎ shuǐ" (打水, beat water);
Serving food to laborers is "dǎ fàn" (打飯, beat rice);
Pasting paper is "dǎ hú" (打糊, beat paste);
Measuring land is "dǎ liàng" (打量, beat measure);
Testing one's eyes is "dǎ shì" (打試, beat test).
After examining all dictionaries,
this character is not found.
Its original sound was "zhé gěng" (謫耿);
I don't know how it transformed into "dīng yǎ" (丁雅).
Zhāng Déxiàng (章得象)
Zhāng Xún Gōng Déxiàng (章郇公得象) was on good terms with Shí Zīzhèng Zhōnglì (石資政中立).
Shí (石) teased Zhāng (章), saying:
"In the past, there was Dài Sōng (戴嵩)'s oxen and Hán Gàn (韓幹)'s horses;
Now we have Zhāng Déxiàng (章得象)'s elephants."
Jùn dāo (俊叨)
Food stalls in Jīngshī (京師) sold sour pastries (suān xiàn, 酸餡),
with large signboards.
Common folk mistakenly pronounced suān (酸) as shī (食),
and xiàn (餡) as yǎo (舀).
Some said that family sold "jùn dāo" (俊叨),
not knowing what it was.
Soup noodles (tāng bǐng, 湯餅),
Táng (唐) people called them "bù tuō" (不托),
nowadays called "bó tuō" (餺飥).
Jìn (晉) period Cì Xī (朿皙)'s "Bǐng Fù" (餅賦) mentions mántou (饅頭), bó chí (薄持), qǐ sōu (起溲), and láo jiǔ (牢九).
The name mántou (饅頭) still exists,
but qǐ sōu (起溲) and láo jiǔ (牢九),
no one knows what they were.
Bó chí (薄持),
Xún Shì (荀氏) also called it "bó yè" (薄夜),
also unknown what it was.
Literary Tiger (Wénzhōng Hǔ)
Xiè Xīshēn (謝希深) first raised to prominence as Fèng Lǐbù Láng (奉禮部郎) through a closed-door examination.
He wrote a memorial to visit Dànián (大年), saying:
"If one drags out their empty thoughts,
there will be no gentlemen;
If one is unwilling to resign,
what will the Duke do for the common people!"
Dàzhōng (大中) said:
"This is a literary tiger."
Records of Flowers and Trees
Táng (唐) Prime Minister Shí Quán Gōng Wáng Fāngqìng (石泉公王方慶) authored "Huā Mù Shū" (花木疏).
Zàn Huáng Gōng Lǐ Déyù (贊皇公李德裕) authored "Huā Mù Lù" (花木錄).
One Leaf, A Hundred Shadows
In Yíngzhōu (瀛州), there is a shadow tree.
When viewed at noon, one leaf casts a hundred shadows.
Its flowers bear fruit,
which at night resemble a host of stars.
It fruits once every ten thousand years,
and its size is like a melon.
Northern Capital Imperial Garden
Běi Qí (北齊) Emperor Wǔ (武帝) renamed Qínlín Yuán (芹林園) to Xiāndū Yuán (仙都苑).
He planted famous fruits,
including the Héhuān Xìng (合歡杏, united joy apricot)
and Tóngxīn Lǐ (同心李, united heart plum).
Flower Maiden (Huā Gū)
Madam Wèi (魏夫人)'s disciple Lǐ (李)
was skilled in planting,
and was called Huā Gū (花姑).
Flower Stem (Huā Dì)
When peonies are about to bloom,
they should not be watered excessively.
If the soil is cold, they will bloom late.
When cutting flowers, one should be swift;
if swift, the flower stem will not be damaged.
Cutting a Horse's Liver
When the reception envoys, Yēlǜ Yǒngxīng and Vice-envoy Yáo Qí returned,
Zhāng asked:
"Northern horses have had their livers cut out.
It is said that this makes them able to travel without illness.
Is this true?"
They replied:
"It is true.
The method is to give them strong wine to drink,
then make an incision in the armpit,
and remove a small amount of flesh.
However, eight or nine out of ten cases fail."
He then asked:
"Are hunting dogs born in eagle's nests
true?"
They replied:
"That also happens,
but it is extremely rare to obtain them.
Currently, there are two such dogs before the Emperor's carriage,
and their nature and perception are quite extraordinary.
Each hunt yields ten times more prey than with ordinary dogs."
Blowing Leaves into Music
The Hú people blow leaves to make music,
harmonizing with foreign songs.
The tunes are very harmonious.
Hunting
Northern people hunt,
each having their designated activities throughout the year.
In the first month, they fish at sea,
catching large fish from the seabed.
In the second and third months, they release falcons,
called Hǎidōngqīng,
to hunt geese.
In the fourth and fifth months, they hunt elk and deer.
In the sixth and seventh months, they reside in cool wetlands.
In the eighth and ninth months, they hunt tigers, leopards, and similar animals,
and this continues until the end of the year.
It is like the southerners tilling and planting according to the season.
Austere Southerners
Qí returned and said:
"Since serving as an envoy to the Northern court,
the generosity of the reception has been unmatched, particularly when Wáng Gǒngchén participated in fishing and falconry events.
The Emperor personally played the pípa to accompany the wine.
At that time, my late father was the host,
and they got along very happily.
Gǒngchén said to my late father:
'Among the austere men of the Southern court, only you stand out.'
On another day,
my late father recounted these words to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
'Gǒngchén's replies to questions contained many such remarks.
His talent and capability are not inferior to others,
but his discernment and breadth of mind are insufficient,
making it difficult for him to achieve great things.
Among the envoys I have seen,
only Fù Bì is immeasurable.
I once asked how many talents like him the Southern court possessed.
Bì replied:
'Your servant is merely a small vessel, not worth mentioning.
Our court possesses talents superior to me in wagonloads and bushelfuls;
how can they be counted?'
Observing this man,
he is truly immeasurable."
Silver Plaque
It is shaped like a square,
engraved with the foreign script for "xuān sù" (swift dispatch).
An envoy holding this plaque would gallop on horseback,
traveling hundreds of lǐ in a day.
Wherever he arrived, it was as if the Tartar ruler himself had come.
Any demands for change or replacement
no one dared to disobey.
Black Mountain
Among the Tartars, Hēishān
is like Dàizōng in China.
It is said that the souls of deceased Tartars
all return to this mountain.
Every year,
the Five Capitals present over ten thousand paper effigies of people and horses,
which are sacrificed to the mountain and burned.
The ritual is extremely solemn.
Unless it is for the sacrifice,
no one dares to approach it.
Buddha Makeup
Hú women apply a yellow substance to their faces, making them gold-like.
This is called Fózhuāng.
Crossing a River by Cart
When crossing the Lúgōu River,
the accompanying envoy said:
"I fear riding in a sedan chair would be dangerous.
Crossing by cart is extremely safe and swift."
I did not understand the method.
Cloud Feet, Milk Surface
If there is little tea and much water,
the "cloud feet" will disperse.
If there is little water and much tea,
the "milk surface" will gather.
Waiting for the Water
The Chájīng says:
"One is 'chá',
two is 'jiǎ',
three is '',
four is 'míng',
five is 'chuǎn'."
Guō Pú said:
"Tea picked early is called 'chá';
tea picked late is called 'chuǎn'."
There are also three stages for waiting for the water:
when it boils like fish eyes,
with a faint sound,
that is the first boil;
when all sides resemble surging springs in a string of pearls,
that is the second boil;
when waves surge and billow,
that is the third boil.
At this point, the water is old.
Tea Battle
People in Jiàn call tea competitions "míngzhàn."
Before Fire, After Fire
On Mount Méngdìng in Yǎzhōu, Shǔ, there is "huǒqián chá,"
meaning tea picked before the fire ban.
The later one is called "huǒhòu chá."
There is also "shíhuā chá."
Spring Reporting Bird
Gù Zhǔ's Shānchájì says:
In the mountains, there is a bird.
Every first and second month, it sings, "Spring has begun."
In the third and fourth months, it sings, "Spring is leaving."
Tea pickers call it "bàochūnniǎo."
Toad's Back, Shrimp's Eyes
Xiè Zōng commented on tea, saying:
"How can it be merely a servant to cream?
It should rightly replace wine as the principal companion."
He also said:
"Observe the fragrance on the toad's back,
and the bubbling like shrimp's eyes.
Fine foam flowers float,
surging froth clouds rise.
The dull dust and toil of the mundane world,
with one sip, they disperse."
Gentle Heat
Gù Kuàng's Lùnchá says:
"Boil with gentle heat and fine smoke,
in a small tripod with long springs."
Bitter Tea
Táo Yǐnjū said:
"Bitter tea transforms bones and lightens the body.
Dānyuè Huángshíjūn consumed it and ascended to immortality."
Secret Water
The water in the Táng Dynasty's Mìshū Shěng was the best,
named Mìshuǐ.
Tea Poetry
Ancient tea poems:
"If you wish to know the pure, cool taste of floral cream,
you must be one who sleeps in clouds and rests on stones."
Dù Mù's Cháshī says:
"The fruits of the mountains are the finest of Dōngwú,
tea is known as the king of auspicious herbs."
Liú Yǔxī's Shìcháshī says:
"How much more so the spring tea of Méngshān and Gù Zhǔ,
whose white clay and red seals send forth fragrant dust."
Volume Thirteen
End.
Straddling a Horse and Wielding a Whip Beside the River, Pulling a Boat
In the Jìn Dynasty, Liú Dàozhēn encountered chaos,
and by the river, he pulled a boat for someone.
He saw an old woman sculling,
and Dào mocked her, saying:
"Why do you not adjust the loom and ply the shuttle?
Why are you by the river sculling?"
The woman replied:
"Why does a husband not straddle a horse and wield a whip?
Why are you by the river pulling a boat?"
Missing the Target
Táng Dynasty Duke Sòng Xiāo Yǔ was unable to shoot.
Tàizōng granted him an archery session,
but he missed the target every time.
Ōuyáng Xún composed a poem to ridicule him, saying:
"A strong wind blows a slow arrow,
a weak hand wields a strong bow.
Wishing to go high, it instead falls low;
aiming west, it turns even further east.
Ten times it all hit the ground,
both hands held empty.
May I ask who did this?
Most likely it was Duke Sòng."
Reciting Poetry on a High Seat
In the Táng dynasty, there was a monk named Fǎguǐ,
who was short in stature.
He held a lecture at a temple.
Lǐ Róng went,
and debated with him.
The monk, from his high seat, recited a poem, saying:
"Your surname Lǐ certainly should be Lǐ,
but your given name Róng is not 'flourishing' (róng)."
Lǐ Róng immediately responded:
"Your body is three and a half feet tall,
and the hair on your head has not yet grown."
Juǎněr and the Virtue of a Queen
Wéi Qìngběn's daughter from the Táng dynasty
was chosen to be a imperial concubine.
When she went to the court, she sat down, intending to thank the emperor.
Qìngběn had curly hair on both ears,
so many court officials called him "Juǎněr" (Curly-ears).
Sōngshòu, the magistrate of Cháng'ān, congratulated him, saying:
"I knew for sure that your daughter would become a concubine."
Qìngběn asked:
"How did you know?"
Sōngshòu replied:
"The juǎněr (dockweed) signifies
the virtue of a queen."
Boiling Bamboo Mats into Bamboo Shoots
A Hàn man traveled to Wú.
The Wú people served him bamboo shoots.
He asked what it was.
They said:
"It's bamboo."
When he returned, he boiled his bamboo sleeping mat (zhú zé),
but it didn't cook through.
He said:
"The Wú people are treacherous (línlù),
they tricked me like this."
A Sheep Trampling the Vegetable Garden
Someone, who usually ate vegetables,
suddenly ate mutton.
He dreamt that the gods of his five zàng-organs said:
"A sheep has trampled our vegetable garden."
Riddle of Fried Cakes
Gāo Zǔ of Qí made a riddle about fried cakes (jiānbǐng).
Zúlǜ Gě answered:
"It's the character 'bìng' (并) reversed, with 'huǒ' (火) inside."
Áocáo's Poetry
Gāo Áocáo's poem says:
"Tombs on the ground play wòshuò,
Stars in the sky play wéiqí.
Opening the door, the house gapes its mouth,
Rolling up the mat, the bed peels its skin."
"Peaches grow hairy pellets,
Gourds grow long clubs.
Walls lean with concave bellies,
Rivers freeze with skin growing on the water."
Black Face and Red Eyes Mocking Each Other
In the early Táng dynasty,
Liáng Bǎo was fond of witty banter.
He once went to Bèizhōu,
where there was a Zhào Zhòngdé who was very good at mocking,
so he ordered him to be summoned.
Bǎo's face was very black,
and he leaned on a table to wait.
Zhòngdé entered,
with both eyes red.
Bǎo said:
"Since there are no clouds in the sky,
why is the lightning so erratic?"
Zhòngdé replied:
"As I entered the door,
behind the table I only saw an inkstick."
Bǎo then said:
"The court distributes cinnabar,
and half an eye can cover a whole country."
Zhòngdé again replied:
"Grind your little finger,
and you can paint the north of the Grand Altar."
Bǎo had no response.
Ode to Blackness
Lǐ Shúshèn and Hèlán Sēngjiā of Táng had very black faces.
Dù Shànxián, when he was the magistrate of Cháng'ān,
was also black.
Liú Xíngmǐn wrote an ode to them, saying:
"Shúshèn rides a black horse,
Sēngjiā draws a lacquer bow.
Summon the Magistrate of Cháng'ān,
to hunt the black bear of the North Mountain."
An Old Junior Minister
Sūn Shào of the Later Wèi dynasty served as the Junior Minister (shǎoqīng) of the Grand Treasury.
Emperor Gāo asked:
"Why are you so old, Minister?"
He replied:
"Although I am old,
my 'qīng' (minister) is indeed 'shǎo' (junior/young)."
He was then promoted to Senior Minister (zhèngqīng).
Mocking the Bamboo in the Courtyard
Wēn Yànbó and Dù Rúhuì served together as Prime Ministers (púshè).
A man named Fěi Lüè came to plead a case,
but the two lords did not respond for a long time.
Lüè introduced himself, saying he was articulate,
and skilled in mockery.
Yànbó told him to mock the bamboo in the courtyard.
Lüè said:
"Bamboo,
bamboo,
a dense green clump.
Its leaves don't wither in the cold,
its fruits don't ripen in summer.
With an empty heart, it cannot await a national talent,
why does its skin need to grow joints and knots?"
Then he was asked to relay a message,
and he ran to the screen wall.
Arriving at the wall, he said:
"Currently, there is a sagacious and enlightened ruler,
who opens the four gates to await scholars,
what are you,
that you dare obstruct the path of the worthy?"
Known from Under the Hat
In a certain county in Shāndōng during the Táng dynasty,
there was an old clerk (xū) who was good at insult.
When a new county magistrate arrived,
he tested him with an incident,
and immediately knew what kind of person he was.
Another magistrate had just arrived,
and was about to assign duties for preparing the registers.
The clerk changed the names or nicknames (xiǎozì)
to make them amusing when called out in succession.
He loudly called out:
"Zhāng Bùdài (Zhang Cloth Bag),
filled with mice (lǎoshǔ).
Sòng Lángjūn (Song Young Master),
going to the underworld (míngfǔ)."
The magistrate did not question him.
When the clerk left,
he said to his associates:
"Known from under the hat."
Thereafter, he had no scruples.
Mocking the Buttocks
Fēng Dàohóng, a director (lángzhōng) of the Left Bureau,
was large-bodied and had broad buttocks.
Lǐ Jì said to him:
"Fēng Dàohóng,
your buttocks should be considered before sitting,
why do they need to be so large?"
If the Master is Present, How Dare Huí Die?
Hóu Bái of Suí was quick-witted and eloquent.
He once rode side-by-side with Yáng Sù.
By the roadside, there was a huái tree,
withered and on the verge of dying.
Yáng Sù said:
"Scholar Hóu's reasoning surpasses others.
Can you make this tree live?"
He replied:
"Hang huái seeds on the tree branches, and it will live."
Yáng Sù asked for the explanation.
He replied:
"The Analects say:
'If the Master is present,
how dare Huí die?'"
Three Bald Men Cannot Match One Lú
Lú Jiāyán of Suí went to a Buddhist temple.
He exchanged responses several times with three monks.
Lú Jiāyán laughed and said:
"These three bald masters don't even know how to play chūpú."
The monks didn't understand.
Lú Jiāyán said:
"Haven't you heard the proverb 'three bald men (tū) cannot match one Lú (surname)'?"
Ordering Ministers to Boast
Hàn Wǔdì set up a banquet,
and ordered his ministers to make grand pronouncements,
while those who made small ones would drink wine.
Prime Minister Gōngsūn said:
"Your servant Hóng is arrogant yet fierce, and also resolute.
My teeth interlock, my voice is loud,
and I shout across ten thousand *lǐ*, making a generation clamor."
The other four Dukes could not respond.
Dōngfāng Shuò requested to take their place and make a grand pronouncement.
First, he said:
"Your servant sits unable to rise,
pressed from above by heaven and earth,
worried about not growing tall."
Second, he said:
"Your servant traverses the nine provinces,
with no room for a toe,
swallowing the world,
wishing to dry up the four seas."
Third and fourth,
he said:
"The world is not enough to hold your servant sitting down,
the four seas are not enough to hold your servant's spittle.
Your servant chokes not from food,
but goes out to lie down beyond the heavens."
The Emperor said:
"How grand!
Hóng's words were the smallest;
he must drink."
This Hu Has No Tail
Sùzōng repeatedly spoke of Ān Lùshān's disloyal behavior.
One day, Mínghuáng summoned the Crown Prince and other princes to play polo.
The Crown Prince secretly intended to injure him with a saddle horse.
The Emperor secretly told the Crown Prince:
"It's not that I don't suspect him,
but this Hu has no tail.
You should just leave him be for now."
If Not Foolish, Not Deaf, One Cannot Be a Family Elder
Guō Ài once had marital discord with Princess Shēngpíng.
Ài cursed the princess:
"You rely on your father being the Son of Heaven.
My father disdained being the Son of Heaven and didn't take it."
The princess was enraged
and reported it to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
"His father indeed disdained being the Son of Heaven and didn't take it.
Even if he didn't disdain it,
could the empire belong to your family alone?"
The Shàngfù detained Ài
and brought him to the imperial court to await punishment.
The Emperor said:
"If not foolish, not deaf,
one cannot be a family elder.
These are just private words between young husband and wife.
Why should a high minister listen to them?"
He was given gifts and sent away.
The Shàngfù flogged Ài several tens of times.
Furs Are Worn Starting in the Tenth Month
Dézōng,
in late autumn, felt a slight chill.
The Emperor said:
"In the ninth month, one wears a shirt;
in the tenth month, one wears a robe.
This doesn't match the season.
How about moving it forward by a month?"
Hànlín Chéngzhǐ Lǐ Jífǔ, believing that a sage can conform to the heavenly seasons above
and fully understand the principles of things below,
requested to proclaim this to the four directions
and codify it into law.
Prime Minister Lǐ Chéng said:
"Respectfully, according to the 'Monthly Ordinances,'
furs are worn starting in the tenth month.
Xuánzōng revised and set this,
and it cannot be changed."
The Emperor then stopped.
Selected a Good Magistrate
Dézōng personally managed all government affairs,
paying careful attention to
every appointment and dismissal, both inside and outside the court.
Zhào Cǎn was appointed Magistrate of Gāolíng County from his post as Surveillance Commissioner.
Later, while strolling in the park,
he met a servant.
The Emperor asked where he was from.
He replied that he was a commoner from Gāolíng.
The Emperor said:
"I have now selected a good magistrate for you.
Do you know?"
Cockfighting and Wrestling
Wénzōng had an event for the Southern Suburban Sacrifice.
The department in charge presented wrestlers.
The Emperor said:
"I am currently fasting and purifying myself.
How can I watch this?"
His attendants said:
"It's an old custom."
The Emperor said:
"This is probably just to get rewards.
They can wrestle outside,
give them their rewards, and let them go."
He also once watched cockfighting.
A performer praised it greatly, saying it was excellent.
The Emperor said:
"Since the chicken is good,
I will bestow it upon you."
Bestowing upon Noblemen and Petty People Not on the Same Day
Wénzōng bestowed official robes upon the Hànlín Academicians.
Afterwards, there were court attendants who had requested gifts earlier.
The Emperor said:
"Bestowing upon noblemen and petty people cannot be on the same day.
Wait for another day."
Often Called Chén Bóyù
Wénzōng discussed literature with various academicians.
Attendant Pèi repeatedly mentioned the name of the Supervising Censor Chén.
Attendant Liǔ Jǐng gave him a look,
but Pèi didn't notice.
The Emperor looked at Liǔ and said:
"His courtesy name is Bóyù,
so it is also appropriate to often call him Chén Bóyù."
Fényáng Requests a County Official
Guō Fényáng was in Bīnzhōu.
He once requested a county official,
but the imperial edict was not issued.
Someone said:
"Given the Duke's (Lìnggōng) meritorious virtue, to be obstructed in requesting a single official shows how utterly the Prime Minister misunderstands the situation."
The Prince (Wáng) said:
"Since the difficult times,
the court has indulged the regional governors (fāngzhèn),
and military officials have obtained whatever they sought.
The regional governors' arrogance
has made the court suspicious of them.
Now, Zǐyí requests a subordinate official;
it's merely that the request was inappropriate,
and the Emperor does not treat Zǐyí as a mere military official.
Gentlemen, you can congratulate me on this."
All of Fényáng's Sons Are Like Servants
Guō Fényáng was in Hézhōng.
He prohibited unauthorized galloping of horses;
offenders would be executed.
The son of his wife's wet nurse violated the prohibition.
The Chief Commandant (Dūyúhóu) flogged him to death.
His sons wept and accused the Chief Commandant of being tyrannical.
The Prince (Wáng) the next day, facing his guests and officials, sighed and said:
"All my sons are like servants!
They don't praise their father's Chief Commandant,
but pity their mother's wet nurse's son.
If not servants, then what are they?"
Southern Zhèng and Northern Zhèng
Grand Tutor Zhèng Yīn's residence was in the south,
from the Southern Ancestry.
Minister of Education Zhèng Zhēn Gōng's residence was in the north,
from the Northern Ancestry.
At the time, they were called Prime Minister Southern Zhèng
and Prime Minister Northern Zhèng.
The Minister of Education's elder cousin, Duke Wénxiàn,
successively served as Prime Minister for Dézōng,
and was also called Grand Prime Minister Zhèng
and Junior Prime Minister Zhèng.
Hán Gāo Is Hard
Executive Assistant Hán Gāo had a small sore.
He ordered the doctor to apply an ointment.
The ointment was not pliable.
The Duke (Gōng) asked about it.
The doctor said:
"It's cold, so the ointment is hard."
The Duke (Gōng) smiled and said:
"Hán Gāo is indeed hard."
In the end, he did not blame him.
His Disciples Continuously Became Prime Ministers
Quán Wéngōng Déyú,
though he did not achieve his position through the imperial examinations,
was in charge of the imperial examinations for three years.
His disciples (zhūshēng) subsequently became Prime Ministers.
Lotus Cup
Junior Tutor Móu and his guests were feasting.
On a hot day, by the water,
they used lotus leaves as cups.
He poured a full measure of honey, held it close to the person's mouth,
and pricked it with a chopstick.
If it wasn't finished, they had to drink again.
After the banquet,
someone spoke of how joyful the drinking had been yesterday.
The Duke (Gōng) said:
"To speak of joy today
implies that yesterday was not joyful.
Regardless of good or bad,
do not mention it."
Drinking and Calling Out Names
Jiǎ Xiāngwénchāng's nature was narrow-minded.
In Xīchuān,
there was a *jìnshì* Xuē Tàibái.
He drank and called out too many names.
The next day, he was not invited again.
A Good Footprint Disciple
Lǐ Féngjí was in charge of the imperial examinations.
The results were published, but before he had been released from the examination duty, he was appointed Grand Councilor.
The successful candidates went to the Central Secretariat to see their examiner.
At the time, this was called a "good footprint disciple."
Completing One's Own Duty
Liú Qīchǔ was the *Jīngzhào Yǐn*.
He said to his subordinates:
"Gentlemen, each of you should complete your own duty.
On sunny days with beautiful scenery, feel free to travel and enjoy yourselves.
Do not feel constrained."
Resounding Spring and Resonant Chime
Lǐ Qiān Gōng owned two exceptionally fine *qín*s,
known as "Resounding Spring" and "Resonant Chime."
His two favorite courtesans, Xiùcái and Qīqī,
were skilled at playing the *qín* and *zhēng*.
They composed their own *qín* scores.
A Gibbon Named Shān Gōng
Lǐ Yuē excelled in the art of the *qín*, the virtue of wine, and the style of poetry.
Throughout his life, he did not associate with women.
He collected many ancient artifacts.
He once obtained a piece of stone and iron,
which, when struck, produced a clear and melodious sound.
He also kept a gibbon,
named Shān Gōng.
Yuē
was the son of Qiān Gōng.
When he first arrived in Jīnlíng,
he sat with the Prefectural Lord, the Commoner Qí,
and repeatedly praised the beauty of Zhāoyǐn Sì.
One day,
the Commoner hosted a banquet in the temple.
The next day, he said,
"Shíláng often praises Zhāoyǐn Sì.
Yesterday, when we feasted there,
I looked closely, what was so different from within the prefecture?"
The gentleman laughed and said,
"What I appreciate is its rustic wilderness!
If distant mountains are covered with green curtains,
ancient pines are wrapped in colorful fabrics,
foul odors pollute the deer-trodden springs,
and music disrupts the calls of mountain birds,
it is truly not as good as being in my uncle's grand hall."
Live Fire to Brew Tea
Lǐ Yuē was passionately fond of tea.
He once said,
"Tea must be roasted over a slow fire,
and brewed over a live fire."
"Live fire" refers to a charcoal fire with flames.
Able to Speak of the Zhāng Family's Ancestry
Zhāng Hóngjìng's family held the position of writing imperial edicts in the Censorate for three generations,
which was unprecedented in previous dynasties.
Yáng Jùyuán gifted him a poem, saying:
"Yī Zhì had no famous ancestor,
Wéi Xián's descendants did not reach such a level."
At the time, he was praised for being "able to speak of the Zhāng family's ancestry."
Jùyuán was old,
his head often shook,
caused by strenuous poetic composition.
When the Time Comes, Depart
Péi Jìng Gōng did not believe in divination,
nor was he fond of taking elixirs.
He once said,
"Chicken, pork, fish, garlic,
if I encounter them, I eat them;
birth, old age, sickness, death,
when the time comes, I depart."
Ode on Casting Swords and Halberds into Farm Implements
Xiànzōng bestowed an jade belt upon Péi Jìng Gōng.
The Duke, nearing his end, sealed and returned it,
with a memorial that read:
"A treasure of the imperial treasury,
bestowed by the former emperor.
I dare not take it with me to the underworld,
nor is it appropriate to leave it in the human world."
The Duke's "Ode on Casting Swords and Halberds into Farm Implements" from the Zhēnyuán era stated:
"Thirty years since the Emperor ascended the throne,
the realm is clear as a mirror,
all corners are smooth and level.
The people from the cities are all sent to devote their efforts to agriculture,
showing the world that weapons will no longer be used."
Later, when he became a Grand Councilor,
he indeed achieved extraordinary merits.
Looking at the spirit and breadth of his poetic prose,
how could there not have been a future event foreseen?
Composing an Ode to Tears
The *jìnshì* Lǐ Wéi composed "Ode to Tears" and the four odes of Light, Thin, Dark, and Small.
Lǐ Hè composed *yuèfǔ* poetry,
mostly focusing on flowers, grasses, bees, and butterflies.
Neither of these two individuals achieved greatness in their careers.
Hán Tuìzhī's Poem
Hán Tuìzhī traveled to Lúshān.
Passing by Xiāo Jīnbù's mountain dwelling,
he wrote in a poem:
"Zhōngláng has a daughter who can carry on his work,
Bódào has no son to manage the household.
Today, I pass by the old hermitage in Kuāngshān,
emptily facing the misty clouds with sorrowful tears."
Female Conduct
The wife of Lángzhōng Yuán Pèi, née Liú,
was learned,
and authored a piece titled "Female Conduct,"
also known as "Direct Admonition."
Two Clear, Two Creaking
Jiāngnán had many famous monks.
In Yuèzhōu, there were Qīngjiāng and Qīnghuà;
in Wùzhōu, there were Gāhòu and Gāfǔ.
At the time, they were called the "Two Clear of Kuàijī"
and the "Two Creaking of Dōngyáng."
Presenting a Poem to Wéi Sūzhōu
The monk Huàzì Jiǎorán from Wúxīng,
was skilled in regulated verse.
He composed more than ten pieces expressing his thoughts,
and presented them to Wéi Sūzhōu.
Wéi did not commend them at all.
The next day,
he copied out some of his old compositions and presented them.
Wéi greatly admired and praised them.
He said,
"You almost lost your reputation!
Why did you not just present what you are skilled in,
but instead presumptuously sought to please this old man?"
Each person has their own strengths,
which cannot be achieved by mere haste.
Great Virtuous of Literature
Since the Yuánhé era,
many Buddhist and Daoist monks were given the title "Great Virtuous One."
If they happened to receive an official appointment,
they became the head of their order.
Each was crowned with the title "Great Virtuous One" based on their profession,
to the extent that some were called "Great Virtuous of Literature."
Should Not Seek Fame and Advancement Section
In ancient times, there was a virtuous decree
to search for and recruit those with talent and ability,
who did not seek fame and advancement.
Someone encountered a scholar rushing into the capital,
and asked what he was seeking.
He replied,
"I am going to apply for the 'Should Not Seek Fame and Advancement Section'."
Jiàn Xū's Method for Cooking Meat
During the Yuánhé era,
the monk Jiàn Xū did not know the taste of meat.
There was a monk who had always lacked spiritual cultivation,
who then created "Jiàn Xū's Method for Cooking Meat."
Later Generations Falsely Attributed
"On Talent and Fate" is attributed to Zhāng Yāngōng,
"Biography of Changing Flowers" is attributed to Hán Wéngōng,
"Song of the Old Ox" is attributed to Bái Lètiān,
"Poem on the Buddha's Relics" is attributed to Zhèng Sītú,
all of which were falsely attributed by later generations.
One's Own Child Is Loved
Xuánzōng asked Huáng Fānchuò:
"Which child
is loved?"
He replied:
"One's own child is loved."
At that time, Sùzōng was in the Eastern Palace and often in danger.
In the palace, Lùshān was called "son."
The Emperor bowed his head for a long time.
Another time, he ascended a tower,
and saw a drunk man lying by the water.
He asked who it was.
Fānchuò said:
"It's a clerk who has reached the age limit."
The Emperor asked how he knew.
He replied:
"After one more rotation, he will enter the ranks."
The Emperor also ate with the various princes.
Níng Wáng accidentally spat food directly onto the Emperor's face.
The Emperor said:
"Níng Gē, why did you get choked?"
Fānchuò said:
"This was not choking;
it was a sneeze."
Lǐ Guòtíng
Yáo Xiàn 姚峴 was witty.
Yáo Nánzhòng 姚南仲, as an imperial commissioner, inspected the outskirts of Shǎnjīng 陝京.
Xiàn 峴, being a distant relative, went to see him.
Suddenly, someone presented a calling card, identifying himself as Lǐ Guòtíng 李過庭.
Nánzhòng 南仲 said:
"The name Guòtíng 過庭 is quite new;
I wonder whose family's son he is?"
Xiàn 峴 replied:
"Perhaps it is Lǐ Qū'ér 李趨兒."
Āoxiàng Qiáo 拗項橋
There is a bridge in the eastern corner of the Shàngshū Shěng 尚書省 [Department of State Affairs],
named Āoxiàng Qiáo 拗項橋 [Neck-Craning Bridge].
It is said that attendant censors and those in the Diànzhōng 殿中 [Palace Chamber] who had served for a long time,
upon reaching this point, would crane their necks to gaze at the Nángōng 南宮 [Southern Palace].
Yīnshēng Shù 音聲樹
In the Dūtáng 都堂 [Grand Secretariat], there was an old locust tree.
Late at night, the sounds of stringed and bamboo instruments could be heard from it.
Soon after, someone from the Shěngzhōng 省中 [Department] would be appointed prime minister.
The common people called it the Yīnshēng Shù 音聲樹 [Sound Tree].
Bīngtīng 冰廳
The Cíbù 祠部 [Ministry of Rites] was called Bīngtīng 冰廳 [Ice Hall],
meaning it was cool and clear.
The seals of the Twenty-Four Bureaus
were, whenever the Lángguān 郎官 [bureau directors] rotated duties,
hung by the clerks on their arms to transfer to one another,
which was quite troublesome.
Yáng Yúqīng 楊虞卿 first placed them in a cabinet with a lock,
which people found convenient.
Initially, Chéng Zhōu 成州, perhaps as a Lìbù Láng 吏部郎 [Personnel Bureau Director],
playfully wrote a performance review,
saying, "After enduring a thousand and ten thousand times,
one cannot help but be examined from top to bottom."
Yùshǐ Sānyuàn 御史三院 [Three Censorate Bureaus]
One is the Táiyuàn 臺院 [Bureau of the Censorate],
its officials are called Shìyùshǐ 侍御史 [Attendant Censors],
addressed as Duāngōng 端公.
Those in charge of miscellaneous affairs are called Zádūan 雜端 [Miscellaneous Censor],
while those not in charge of such affairs are called Sǎnduān 散端 [Loose Censor].
The second is the Diànyuàn 殿院 [Palace Bureau],
its officials are called Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ 殿中侍御史 [Palace Attendant Censors],
addressed as Shìyù 侍御.
Newly appointed ones are in charge of the Yòuxún 右巡 [Right Patrol],
and then the Cí Zuǒxún 左巡 [Left Patrol] in sequence,
called the Liǎngxúnshǐ 兩巡使 [Two Patrol Envoys].
The third is the Cháyuàn 察院 [Investigative Bureau],
its officials are called Jiānchá Yùshǐ 監察御史 [Investigative Censors],
also addressed as Shìyù 侍御.
Whenever there was a communal meal in the public hall,
the Zádūan 雜端 sat on the south couch,
and the Zhǔbù 主簿 [Registrar] sat on the north couch.
All refrained from laughing or talking.
If the Zádūan 雜端 laughed inadvertently,
then all three bureaus would laugh,
which was called Hōngtáng 哄堂 [a burst of laughter throughout the hall].
Cháyuàn Tīngmíng 察院廳名 [Names of the Cháyuàn Halls]
Each of the various halls in the Cháyuàn 察院 [Investigative Bureau] had other names.
The Lǐchá 禮察 [Censor of Rites] was called Sōngtīng 松廳 [Pine Hall],
because there were ancient pines to its south;
the Xíngchá 刑察 [Censor of Punishments] was called Yǎntīng 魘廳 [Nightmare Hall],
as many suffered nightmares when sleeping there;
the Bīngchá 兵察 [Censor of Military Affairs] was in charge of the tea in the courtyard,
the tea necessarily being excellent quality from Shǔ 蜀,
stored in earthenware,
and was called Chápíng Tīng 茶瓶廳 [Teapot Hall];
the Lìchá 吏察 [Censor of Personnel] was in charge of the registry of officials attending court,
and was called Cháobù 朝簿 [Court Registry];
above the Lìchá 吏察 was the Guǎnyì Shǐ 館驛使 [Director of Posthouses],
and above him the Jiānchá Shǐ 監察使 [Director of Investigations],
who was called Chácháng 察長 [Chief Censor].
Xiāyǎn Zǎixiàng 瞎眼宰相 [Blind Prime Minister]
Péi Guāngdé 裴光德 was in the Zhōngshū 中書 [Secretariat].
An old friend sought a position as a judicial officer in the capital prefecture.
The Duke said:
"This office is not suitable for you,
and I dare not, out of private friendship, undermine the court's regulations.
Perhaps someday a Xiāyǎn Zǎixiàng 瞎眼宰相 [blind prime minister] who pities you
might allow you to get it;
I certainly cannot."
Yè Fǎshàn 葉法善
The Daoist Yè Jìngnéng 葉靜能,
in the reign of Zhōngzōng 中宗, was executed for sorcery and delusion.
In the time of Xuánzōng 玄宗, there was a Daoist master,
who was Fǎshàn 法善.
Someone wrote a record stating,
Xuánzōng 玄宗 ordered the Daoist Yè Jìngnéng 葉靜能,
which is a mistake.
Réndào Shàngyòu 人道尚右 [Human Custom Prefers the Right]
The right is esteemed.
In rites, guests are given precedence.
Therefore, the west is yielded to guests,
and the host is in the east,
out of humility.
Nowadays, some yield the east to guests,
which is contrary to propriety.
Shíshìzhuāng 時世粧 [Fashionable Attire]
Cuī Shū’s 崔樞夫人 wife managed her household with strictness,
not allowing any of her wives or concubines to wear fashionable attire.
Géxià Zúxià Zhī Chēng 閣下足下之稱 [Terms of Address: Géxià and Zúxià]
In ancient times, the Sāngōng 三公 [Three Dukes] had their pavilions (gé 閣),
and regional governors, comparable to ancient feudal lords,
also had their own pavilions,
hence the term "Géxià 閣下" [Your Excellency].
Our predecessors, when writing to high officials,
often used "Zhíshì 執事" or "Zúxià 足下".
Liú Zǐyún 劉子雲 wrote to a prime minister using "Zúxià 足下",
and Hán Tuìzhī 韓退之 wrote to Zhāng Púyè 張僕射 using "Zhíshì 執事",
which are examples of this.
Jìshì 記室 [Secretary] was originally a title for a prince's or marquis's assistant,
and others should not use it universally.
However, "Zhíshì 執事" [Your Attendants]
refers to those around the person.
It can be used universally for both high and low ranks.
Furthermore,
to address a superior from a humble position
by saying "Zuòqián 座前" [before your seat] is especially inappropriate.
Géxià 閣下 is one rank lower than Diànxià 殿下 [Your Highness];
Zuòqián 座前 is one rank lower than Jǐqián 几前 [before your desk].
How can one usurp these terms?
Cuìhè Qǐ Shén Tóngrǔ Zhī Chòu 毳褐豈甚銅乳之臭 [How could the smell of coarse wool be worse than that of bronze nipples?]
A court official visited a friend.
He saw a Daoist wearing a patched robe sitting there.
Another day, he said to his friend:
"You are fond of men in coarse wool robes.
Why is that?
I don't know if they are virtuous or foolish,
but I just smell them."
His friend replied:
"How could the smell of coarse wool be worse than that of bronze nipples (bronze coins)?
You live among them,
never feeling ashamed or repelled,
yet you mock a man of the Dao.
In the Southern Dynasties, the croaking of frogs was preferred over drum music.
To me, coarse wool robes
are far superior to the vermilion and purple of today!"
Tóudié Biànhuàn 投牒便換 [Deposit Slip Exchange]
A scholar sold his property in another region,
obtaining tens of thousands of coins.
Fearing the difficulty of carrying it on river journeys,
he entrusted it to a public treasury through an acquaintance,
and received a deposit slip to take home.
This is what the world called a "convenient exchange" (biànhuàn 便換).
He placed it in his clothes bag.
One day,
being drunk, he patted the bag and said:
"Don't take this lightly;
there's something very good in here."
A thief, nearby, heard this.
That night, he killed him and took his bag,
thinking it contained gold.
When he opened it, he found nothing,
and threw the deposit slip into the water.
Mèng Liǔ Púdì 夢柳仆地 [Dream of a Willow Falling to the Ground]
Liǔ Yuánzōng 柳元宗, having been recalled from his post as Sīmǎ 司馬 of Yǒngzhōu 永州 to the capital,
went to a fortuneteller to inquire about his fate. He said:
"My surname is Liǔ 柳 [willow].
Yesterday, I dreamt of a willow tree falling to the ground.
Is this not ominous?"
The fortuneteller replied:
"When it lives, it is a willow tree (liǔshù 柳樹);
when it falls, it is willow wood (liǔmù 柳木).
Mù 木 [wood] sounds like Mù 牧 [to govern].
Will you not govern Liǔzhōu 柳州?"
It eventually came true as he said.
Mèng Yì Guān Rù Táng 夢羿棺入堂 [Dream of Carrying a Coffin into the Hall]
Lǐ Féngjí 李逢吉 had a maidservant
who dreamt that someone was carrying a coffin to the back of the hall and said:
"Place it on the ground for now;
it will be moved into the hall soon."
Soon after, he was appointed Zhōngshū Shèrén 中書舍人 [Secretariat Drafter].
Later, he was in charge of the imperial examinations (gòngjǔ 貢舉),
and before he finished, he became a prime minister.
Dōngxī Tái 東西臺 [Eastern and Western Bureaus]
Gāozōng 高宗 changed the Ménxià 門下 and Zhōngshū Shěng 中書省 to Dōngxī Tái 東西臺 [Eastern and Western Bureaus],
the Shàngshū Shěng 尚書省 to Wénchāng Tái 文昌臺,
and changed the Yùshǐ Tái 御史臺 to Nántái 南臺 [Southern Bureau].
Zhāng Qiān Chá 張騫槎
The *Hàn Shū* records Zhāng Qiān's exploration of the source of the Yellow River,
speaking of the great distance of his diplomatic mission,
but there is no mention of a "River of Heaven."
Only the *Bó Wù Zhì* says that a guest star violated the Dǒu Niú constellation,
and later people said he obtained Zhī Nǚ's loom-shuttle stone to ask Jūn Píng,
all of which are mere fabrications.
In the Bǎo Lì reign,
couriers in Jīng Luò carried Zhāng Qiān's raft,
but no one knew what it was.
Earlier poets often used the phrase "Zhāng Qiān's raft,"
perpetuating such errors.
A high official's son residing in the mountains
Lǐ Dé Yù recommended the recluse Wáng Guī as suitable for a Censor-in-Chief position.
Wǔ Zōng asked, "Whose son is he?"
He replied,
"He is Wáng Chāo's son."
The Emperor said,
"Recluses should be people of the mountains and wilds.
Guī is a high official's son;
how can he reside in the mountains?"
Dé Yù had no reply.
Buddhist monks' music school
During the Yuán Hé reign,
there was a monk, Wén Shú, who gathered people to discuss Buddhist scriptures,
under the pretext of teaching vulgar arts.
Unruly individuals eagerly imitated his melodies as songs,
calling it the "Buddhist monks' music school."
The "Household Lǐ Yì"
Lǐ Yì was talented in literature.
There was a son of a noble family with the same name.
People referred to Yì as "Literary Lǐ Yì"
and the noble's son as "Household Lǐ Yì."
Buying a concubine is not a prostitute
Liǔ Gōng Chuò once took a concubine.
Those in the same office knew of it,
and repeatedly demanded she be presented as a courtesan.
Gōng Chuò said,
"A gentleman has one wife and one concubine,
to manage the household chores
and prepare for guests.
Gōng Chuò bought a concubine,
not a prostitute."
End of Volume Fourteen.
Hairy Radish
FÉNG Xiān Zhèn, a commander in the Táng army,
entered the Jí Xián Yuàn to collate the *Wén Xuǎn*.
In his commentary on *zūn chī*, he wrote:
"What is now taro,
is precisely the hairy radish."
A knife in a smile
Lǐ Yì Fǔ had a gentle and respectful appearance,
but was narrow-minded, quick-tempered, and treacherous.
He would invariably undermine anyone who displeased him.
People said he had "a knife in his smile."
KAI YUÁN TŌNG BǍO coins
During the Wǔ Dé reign,
Wǔ Zhū coins were abolished,
and KAI YUÁN TŌNG BǍO coins were put into circulation.
The name of the coin and its calligraphy
were all done by Ōu Yáng Xún.
When the design was first submitted,
Empress Wén Dé pressed a fingernail mark into it,
and it was subsequently cast with that mark.
Yán Lì Běn's painting
When the King of Dōng Mán came to court,
Yán Shī Gǔ memorialized:
"In the time of King Wǔ,
distant states pledged allegiance,
and the Zhōu historian compiled the chapter 'Wáng Huì.'
Now, those in grass garments and bird-emblazoned robes
are all assembled at the imperial palace.
It is fitting to illustrate this event to pass down to future generations."
An imperial edict commanded Yán Lì Běn to paint it.
Not a single detail was missed,
and the spirit of the subjects was fully captured.
Three Patriarchs of Painting
From the Jìn dynasty onwards,
Gù Cháng Kāng, Zhāng Sēng Yáo, and Lù Tàn Wēi
were considered the three patriarchs of painting.
Guarding the danger of the Yālǜ River
Yuán Wàn Qǐng, serving as a clerk in Liáo Dōng,
wrote a proclamation mocking Gāo Lí, saying:
"They do not know how to guard the danger of the Yālǜ River."
Mò Lí Zhī replied:
"We respectfully acknowledge your command."
He then moved troops to guard it.
Wàn Qǐng was consequently punished for this offense.
Earth Mound Head
Those who became department heads (láng zhōng) without having served as supernumerary officials (yuán wài)
were called "earth mound heads."
Zhào Qiān first served as a Dà Lǐ Zhèng Qīng before becoming a Hù Bù Láng Zhōng.
The Yuán Wài Láng Zhào Hào mocked him, saying:
"Being a Yuán Wài has always been noble,
a Láng Zhōng's reputation is not as excellent.
Who would have thought that within the ornate palace,
one would become an 'earth mound head'?"
Qiān Guāng replied:
"Silk curtains are set up as one pleases,
and golden incense is burned at will.
My only worry is being placed as a Yuán Wài,
not fit to be ranked among the stars."
Medicine is intention
Xǔ Yì Zōng
was a famous physician.
When people asked why he did not write books,
he said:
"Medicine is intention.
The profound subtleties of the pulse
cannot be conveyed in words."
Failed Examination Poem
Luó Yǐn's poem after failing the examination says:
"My name is ashamed of a green branch in the Guì Yuàn,
I remember the red slices filling my chopsticks by the Sōng Jiāng.
Only Bào Shú deeply understands me,
another day, a hundred feet of wind in my canvas sail."
Huáng Zhōng Jūn and Guǐ Gǔ Zǐ
Dòu Tíng Zhī was good friends with the diviner Hú Lú Shēng.
One day, Hú Lú Shēng said to him:
"Calamity is about to befall your family.
Only by encountering Huáng Zhōng Jūn and Guǐ Gǔ Zǐ can you be saved."
He instructed Tíng Zhī to seek them out,
and he found Lǐ Bì,
and wholeheartedly befriended him.
Not long after,
he encountered Zhū Cǐ's rebellion,
and Tíng Zhī was trapped by the rebels.
When the trouble subsided,
Dé Zōng ordered his execution.
Bì reported the earlier prediction to the emperor,
and his death was specially commuted.
The Emperor said:
"Huáng Zhōng Jūn surely refers to Me.
Why did he call you Guǐ Gǔ Zǐ?"
Gold basin soaking white dragon skin
Lǐ Dé Yù, when hosting guests in the height of summer,
placed a gold basin soaking white dragon skin beside the seats.
In a moment,
a cool breeze and refreshing air,
brought a crisp feeling as if it were late autumn.
Jade Blossom
There were abundant jade blossoms at the Táng Chāng Guàn Daoist temple.
One day,
a woman of exquisite beauty
walked around the flowers,
with onlookers gathered like a wall.
Suddenly, she broke off several branches of flowers,
saying:
"Long ago, there was a promise at Yù Fēng;
from here, I can now depart."
She drifted into the sky and left.
Liú Yǔ Xī's poem says:
"A jade maiden comes to see the jade tree flowers,
a strange fragrance first envelops her seven-fragrance carriage.
Breaking branches, playing in the snow, she occasionally turns her head,
surprised that it is not yet dusk in the human world."
Rice cooked with refined charcoal
Wealthy young men in Luò Xià enjoyed exquisite food.
There was a Magistrate Lǐ, who also favored luxury.
He lavishly prepared a meal and invited them,
but they did not even pick up their chopsticks.
Magistrate Lǐ said:
"Please try it;
this was cooked with charcoal."
The wealthy young men reluctantly ate one or two bites,
saying:
"For all rice cooked with charcoal,
the charcoal is first burned thoroughly,
which is called 'refining the fire.'
This charcoal for cooking
has not yet been refined."
Later, during a period of warfare,
the wealthy young men begged for food in mountain temples and died.
Bái Chuán boating to Xiāng Shān
Lú Jiǎn Cí was visiting a villa in Yī Chuān,
when suddenly two young boys steered a small boat,
with a white-robed man and a monk sitting together in the stern,
cooking with a paulownia steamer,
reciting poems and laughing as if they were immortals.
When asked,
it was Bái Chuán boating to Xiāng Shān.
Mandarin ducks on the shoals
In the waters in front of Yīquē County
in Hénán, whenever a county official was to enter the Imperial Court,
a sandbank would first appear.
It was composed of pebbles and golden sand,
clear and lovely.
Niú Sēngrú was a county magistrate.
One day, the appearance of the sandbank was reported.
The county officials went to observe it.
An old clerk said:
"This must be for a Censor of the Branch Palace.
If it were for the Western Bureau,
there would be a pair of mandarin ducks."
Sēngrú prayed:
"Since there can be a sandbank,
why begrudge mandarin ducks?"
No sooner had he spoken
than a pair flew down.
Within ten days,
Sēngrú was indeed appointed Censor of the Investigation Bureau.
He saw me old and tottering, and so he made a joke of it.
Before Péi Jìnggōng attained his jinshi degree,
he was a sojourner in Luòzhōng.
One day, he rode his donkey onto Tiānjīn Qiáo.
At that time, Huáixī had been in rebellion for several years.
Two old men leaned against a pillar, conversing:
"When will Càizhōu be pacified?"
Seeing Jìnggōng,
they were astonished and said:
"We were just worried that Càizhōu was not yet pacified.
We must wait for this man to become prime minister."
I heard their words
and immediately told Gōng.
Gōng said:
"They saw me old and tottering,
and so they made a joke of it."
Afterwards, it turned out exactly as they had said.
"Ode of the Banished Immortal's Resentment"
When Mínghuáng fled to Shǔ,
one day he ascended a high mountain and looked towards Qínzhōu.
He said to Gāo Lìshì:
"Had I listened to Zhāng Jiǔlíng,
I would not have come to this."
He played a flute on horseback, creating a tune
called "Ode of the Banished Immortal's Resentment."
"A Mingjing graduate, why come to see me?"
During the Yuánhé era,
Lǐ Hè was famous for his songs and poems.
Yuán Zhěn was already old
and had passed the Mingjing examination.
He was also skilled in poetry
and wished to befriend Hè.
He presented his calling card to see him.
Hè saw the card and said:
"A Mingjing graduate,
why come to see Lǐ Hè?"
Zhěn withdrew in shame.
Not long after,
he passed the 制策 examination
and became a Lángguān in the Ministry of Rites.
He then argued that Hè's father's name, Jìn,
conflicted with the character for "jinshi,"
thus disqualifying him from the jinshi examination.
His contemporaries then slandered him.
This is why Hè did not pass the examination.
"The character Dào is carved on the stone"
Zànhuáng Gōng's Píngquán Villa
had over a hundred pavilions and terraces,
rare flowers and exotic plants,
precious pines and strange stones.
Thus, Gōng personally composed "Record of Píngquán Flowers and Trees."
Now all are gone.
Only the wild goose wing cypress, pearl-seed cypress, and clustered jade pistil remain.
The strange stones
were taken by a powerful person from Luòyáng.
On all the stones were carved the two characters "Yǒudào" (有道).
Dragon Tail Path
The Dragon Tail Path in front of Hányuán Diàn
had seven turns.
Looking north from Dānfèng Mén,
it resembled a dragon's tail hanging down.
Imperial Examination Notice
The stone decree and the characters for Gòngyuàn
were written with light ink and felt.
When Lǐ Shēn, the Shìláng, was about to release the list of successful candidates,
he ordered a clerk to write the notice.
Before he could fill in the characters for "right decree, Gòngyuàn,"
the clerk suddenly died.
The secretary Wáng Chǎng, who was skilled in calligraphy,
dipped his brush while drunk.
He could not add more ink,
so within one notice,
the shades of ink varied.
This instead made it beautiful
and became a customary practice.
"Brocade and Silk Youngster"
When Niú Qízhāng first drank with Lǐ Wèigōng,
Sēngrú said:
"How can a brocade and silk youngster participate in this hall?"
Wèigōng restrained him.
It is popularly believed that "Journey to Zhōu and Qín"
was not written by Sēngrú,
but by Zhāng Guàn, a disciple of Wèigōng.
Wénzōng said:
"This must be falsely attributed to Sēngrú.
If he were a Zhengyuan jinshi,
how could he dare to call Dézōng 'Old Woman's Son'?"
Six Classics
Liú Fén, in "Reading Wénzhōngzǐ," said:
"His talent is inherently mediocre,
attempting to imitate the works of the ancients."
Someone asked:
"How does it compare to the Six Classics?"
He replied:
"Like a slave to his immediate master."
Afterwards, Wénzhōngzǐ was thus referred to as the slave of the Six Classics.
Court Style
Most of the letters written by scholars in the Central Plains were in the Court Style.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Wú Tōngwēi, an Academician of the Hànlín Academy,
was skilled in the running-cursive Court Style.
Because he was close to the officials,
the clerks and scribes imitated his calligraphy,
making it widely popular in the world,
and its methods persist to this day.
"Ode to the Sea Gull"
Gù Kuàng studied under Lǐ Bì,
obtaining his method of qi cultivation,
enabling him to go without food for an entire day.
When Bì died,
he composed "Ode to the Sea Gull,"
which greatly incurred the jealousy of the powerful and influential,
leading to his demotion to Síhù of Ráozhōu.
He wrote a poem:
"Flying thousands of miles, becoming a seabird,
once allowed by the Vermilion Phoenix to borrow a branch.
One morning the phoenix departed, the wútóng died,
what can be done about the owls filling the eyes?"
Bái Chuán's Tomb
Bái Chuán was buried on Lóngmén Shān.
Travelers from all directions who passed by would invariably offer a cup of wine.
The square foot of earth in front of the tomb was always muddy.
Fápàn Tíng
When Lǐ Zànhuáng pacified Shàngdǎng and the Huíhú,
he boasted of his achievements.
At Píngquán Villa, he built the Gòusī Tíng and Fápàn Tíng.
Bái Chuán Not Granted a Posthumous Title
At the end of Dàzhōng, Bái Chuán submitted a memorial
requesting a posthumous title.
The Emperor said:
"Why not look at the epitaph of Mr. Zuìyín's tomb?"
In the end, no posthumous title was granted.
His younger brother Mǐnzhōng memorialized for the erection of a spirit way stele,
with an inscription by Lǐ Yìshān.
Eight-Cornered Well
To the north of Huátái city,
there was often a threat of flooding and sinking.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Chancellor Jiǎ dug an eight-cornered well at the city corner to suppress it.
Wénzhōngzǐ
In the late Suí dynasty, he lived in seclusion in Báiniú Xī
and wrote the Wáng Shì Liùjīng.
In the early days of the dynasty, many northern scholars who revered him held positions assisting in governance.
Liú Yǔxī greatly praised Wáng Tōng for his ability to elucidate the Kingly Way,
stating that his words established the Dàzhōng era,
and those who followed his school
were all outstanding talents in the empire.
Since then, when scholars and officials discuss history and historical writings,
none have mentioned Wénzhōngzǐ.
Hundred-Patch Guqin
Lǐ Yígōng's hundred-patch guqin
had an ancient design.
Its sound was incomparably clear and resonant.
Huàyuè Palm,
its stone resembled human flesh in color.
It appeared whenever the sun shone directly on it.
At dusk, it gradually became invisible.
Chéngní Inkstone
People from Jiàng County were skilled at making chéngní.
They sewed silk bags,
placed them in the Fén River,
and retrieved them after a year.
They fired them into inkstones,
and the water would not dry up.
Also, the old tiles from the two terraces of Yèjùn had the shape of the Wéijī constellation.
When broken and made into inkstones,
they were superior to chéngní.
Yú Měirén
The Yú Měirén plant in the Bāoxié Valley,
resembles a cockscomb,
large but without flowers,
and its leaves are all opposite.
If someone sings "Yú Měirén",
then the two leaves appear like hands clapping,
quite in rhythm.
Fēngshuǐ Xìng
The wind in Shǎnshàng Hóngfáng is cold,
and many people suffer from colds.
East of the Héluò region, the land is saline,
and the water is cold,
thus, even though the people eat millet and wheat flour, they do not suffer from热疾 (rèjí, heat-related illnesses).
The wind and water in Huátái are cold,
especially so, and the local officials and common people eat Fùzǐ,
like taro or chestnuts.
È zài Báimǎ
Lǐ Déyù,
a diviner once told him:
"You will one day reach the highest position among officials,
but your misfortune will be related to a white horse."
When he became chancellor,
even his relatives were not allowed to keep white horses.
Later, he was overthrown by Bái Mǐnzōng,
who ordered Mǎ Zhí to specifically oversee the Huáinán prisons.
Lǐ Déyù was exiled to Nánhǎi because of this.
Wǔxīng zài Kuí
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
the Five Planets were in Kuí,
located in the territory of Yǎnzhōu.
Tàizōng was Jìn Wáng,
and governed Yǎn Hǎi.
Kuí is the celestial servant's palace,
so those who served as attendants all quickly achieved wealth and high status.
Cháoyī Bùkě Líndiào
When Wáng Shūmì's father, Tàishī, passed away,
court officials came to mourn,
with purple and crimson robes filling the gate.
Only Xú Xuàn carried a hemp robe and a horn belt,
changed into them at the guest's quarters,
and only then entered to mourn.
Someone asked him,
and he replied:
"Court attire should not be worn when mourning."
Mò Cǎn Yī
Ài Zhòngrú, a Junior Mentor, said:
"When my grandmother first married,
there was a 'mourning black garment' in her trousseau.
Her sisters-in-law asked about it,
and she said that her parents had instructed her to wear it to comfort the elders on the private mourning day of her husband's family."
Now this custom has also disappeared.
Mù Yǎn Fáng
At the beginning of Jìn Gōng's banishment,
his dwelling was covered with wood for three days.
When Féng Zhěng died,
fire guarded his room.
When Wáng Qīnruò died,
fire swept his room.
Zhào Pǔ Wèi Gù Xiàng Shàng
When Zhào Pǔ was first appointed chancellor,
Tàizǔ said:
"Although you are chancellor,
you must yield your sitting and standing place in the ranks to former chancellors."
Pǔ replied:
"Your Majesty founded this dynasty,
and made me chancellor precisely to suppress all directions.
When I see former chancellors,
I must stand above them."
Tàizǔ was pleased with this.
Once, when he submitted a memorial,
it went against the emperor's wishes,
and the emperor, enraged,
tore the memorial by hand, crumpled it, and threw it away.
Pǔ calmly picked it up,
unfolded it, and presented it again.
The emperor grew even angrier,
flung his sleeves, and rose,
but Pǔ still submitted, saying:
"This matter should be handled thus;
allow your servant to enter and receive your decree."
Yù Yàn Zhí Yǔ
During Tàizǔ's grand banquet,
a sudden downpour began,
and the emperor was displeased.
Zhào Pǔ submitted, saying:
"The common people outside are eagerly hoping for rain,
so what harm is a grand banquet to the royal family?
It will only damage some furnishings
and dampen some official clothes.
If we perform various acts in the rain,
it will be even more amusing.
Rain is hard to come by at this time,
and when the people are happy,
it's a perfect time to drink wine."
Tàizǔ was greatly pleased,
issued an order for music to be played in the rain,
encouraged everyone to drink to the full,
and ended the banquet in high spirits.
Shìhuàn Jì Tàisù
My late father was often ill when young,
and his skin was almost entirely covered in moxibustion burns.
Therefore, my granduncle, Prime Minister Zhào, said to him:
"Generally, in one's prime, entering officialdom
should not be too rapid.
Bodily ailments lie in great abundance.
Looking at your vigorous energy and profound spirit,
though you have many illnesses in your body,
there is no need to worry."
Zhàodài
Every time the weather was mild and warm, Wáng Tàibǎo
would ride a small horse,
accompanied by three or four old servants,
carrying a zhàodài,
containing brushes, inkstones, a Rùnlǜe, knives, paper, and small musical instruments, etc.
The zhàodài was made of horsehide,
with a lid and buckles on all four sides,
and was commonly used by scholars during the Five Dynasties.
Qǐfù Pèi Yú
My late father,
was a Hanlin Academician at the end of the Xiǎndé era of Zhōu.
When he resumed office after mourning,
he wore a plain gauze wrap,
a soft-footed fútóu,
and a mournful purple official robe.
Every day when he went to court, he still wore a fish-pouch.
Someone said:
"The fish-pouch
symbolizes serving the ruler diligently day and night.
However, being adorned with gold
also shows its splendor.
During mourning, when emotions are suppressed,
one should not have gold or precious adornments."
My father immediately apologized for his oversight.
Shēngtáng Bài Zǎixiàng Fùmǔ Gùshì
If a chancellor had both parents or one parent still living,
when officials visited his private residence to request an audience,
they first had to send in their greetings before seeing the chancellor.
Those with deep relationships would all ascend the hall and bow,
and if they did not ascend the hall,
they still had to bow from afar facing north.
Recently, this ritual has rarely been practiced.
Cūguān
During the Táng dynasty, literati valued internal positions and slighted external ones,
referring to those who held regional posts as "crude talents."
Zhāng Yàngōng felt ashamed of not having comprehensive talent, and served as a "crude official" for the state.
Xuē Xǔchāng's poem "Thanking Someone for Tea" says:
"A crude official begging for it is truly forsaken,
but fortunately, poetic sentiment makes it worth tasting."
Wáng Yànwēi, who served as Tàicháng Bóshì during the Yuánhé era,
rose through various ranks to become a high official.
His poem says:
"Ten myriad brave soldiers of píxiū guard the mighty army,
this is precisely the time to repay kindness and serve the nation.
The waves of the Biàn River roar with drums and horns,
the willows on the Suí embankment brush against banners and flags.
In the vanguard are the scarlet-bannered generals from Guānxī,
seated in rows are the beautiful maids, the princesses of Zhào.
