Report to the cap-and-gowns of Cháng'ān that
a crude official is, after all, a man!"
Yànwēi was then the Xuānwǔ Jiédùshǐ.
Dòu Shì Wǔ Lóng
Dòu Yǔjūn, Censor-in-Chief,
had five sons,
all of whom passed the imperial examination.
Féng Dào's poem says:
"Dòu Shíláng of Yānshān,
taught his sons with righteous methods.
The one ancient divine tree stands old,
the five fragrant branches of the cinnamon blossom."
At the time, they were called "The Five Dragons of the Dòu Clan."
Jiàn Kè Wèn Sān Shì
When Lǐ Fǎng was chancellor,
every time he met a guest, he would ask three things:
What are the people's hardships?
What administrative skills or methods are there?
What are the shortcomings in current governance?
Shàngshū Lǐxíng
Old sayings:
“The Tàicháng is not a Qīng,
the Mìshū is not a Jiān.”
This is because their official positions and instruments are pure and important,
not comparable to other Qīng and Jiān.
My late father served as Hánzhǎng,
and due to illness, sought to be a Dàpéng.
Also,
the Tàicháng Qīng ranks below the six Shàngshū,
sharing an office with the Chéngláng,
and is called Shàngshū Lǐxíng.
Among the outstanding members of the imperial clan,
Táng Yuánzhěn,
travels were easy for him.
Zōngchéng’s memorial read:
“In the past, the descendants of the Liú clan who were on the imperial register numbered over 100,000 people.”
It was once observed that during Wáng Măng’s regency,
he wrote the "Dàgào" which stated:
“There are four hundred outstanding members of the imperial clan.”
Mèng Kāng’s commentary states:
“This refers to the living members of the various Liú families.”
Why is there such a discrepancy in numbers?
Could it be that these four hundred people were
survivors of Măng’s cruel predation,
all of whom supported Măng in stealing the Hàn,
and were sycophants who clung to life and coveted gain?
Otherwise, how could they have survived and
even been called outstanding by Măng?
Population figures of the realm
Population figures of the realm:
Former Hàn: 12,330,000;
Later Hàn: 16,070,000;
Later Wèi: 3,270,000;
Northern Qí: 3,030,000;
Later Zhōu: 3,500,000;
In our dynasty:
Zhēnzōng: 8,060,000;
Yīngzōng: 12,480,000;
Shénzōng: 17,300,000.
Féng Yánzì’s lyrics from Jiangnan
A scholar’s family collected a lyric poem from Lǐ Hòuzhǔ of Jiangnan,
said to be composed by Féng Yánzì.
The lyrics are:
“The copper clepsydra has just finished dripping,
the rooster crows halfway to the high pavilion.
Urging the opening of the five gates with golden locks,
the pearl curtains of the three halls still hang low.
The imperial willows before the steps sway green,
the palace flowers scatter red beneath the guards.
Several rows of mandarin duck tiles reflect the morning sun,
phoenix banners flutter a hundred turns in the spring breeze.
Attendant ministers step and dance, one after another,
may Your Majesty’s long life be eternally as the southern mountains.”
Model Calligraphy
The ten volumes of model calligraphy in the pavilion
were collected during the Chúnhuà era.
Many of them are about condolence and inquiring about illness.
Lǐ Fú, Libationer of the Guózǐ during the Táng dynasty, in his "Kānwù" said:
“Short letters originated during the military conflicts of the Jìn and Sòng dynasties.
At that time, the state forbade private correspondence;
unless for condolence or inquiring about illness,
no letters were allowed.
Therefore, Xīzhī’s letters begin with ‘death penalty,’
which indicates a violation of the regulations.”
Poem on Jífāng Tíng
When Ōu Yǒngshū was living in leisure in Rǔyīn,
a courtesan could perfectly memorize all the lyrics he composed.
He playfully told her that one day he would return as governor.
Later, he moved from Wéiyáng to Rǔzhōu,
but she was no longer to be seen.
He inscribed on Jífāng Tíng:
“Willow catkins have already carried spring far away,
crabapple blossoms must regret my late arrival.”
Thirty years later,
Dōngpō came to serve as governor.
Upon seeing it, he said:
“Isn’t this Dù Mùzhī’s line ‘green leaves forming shade’?”
Exchanged for ten acres of autumn on West Lake
When Ōu Gōng moved from Yángzhōu to Rǔzhōu,
he wrote a poem about West Lake:
“Green water chestnuts and red lotuses float on painted boats,
how could the prefect again recall Yángzhōu?
He has traded all the moon of the twenty-four bridges
for ten acres of autumn on West Lake.”
Dōngpō, moving from Rǔ to Yáng,
wrote a poem:
“What is there of the twenty-four bridges?
I exchange them for these ten acres of glassy wind.”
This was to use Ōu Gōng’s poem.
Jade Pavilion and Silver Sea
Dōngpō wrote a snow poem:
“The jade pavilion freezes, making one shiver with cold;
the silver sea glitters, making flowers appear before one’s eyes.”
Later, he saw Jīng Gōng, who said:
“Daoists refer to the two shoulders as the jade pavilion,
and the eyes as the silver sea.
Is this what you meant?”
Pō retreated and said:
“Only Jīng Gōng knows the origin of this.”
Sheep-Exchanging Letters
Huáng Lúzhí playfully said to Dōngpō:
“In the past, the Right General’s calligraphy was called ‘Goose-Exchanging Letters.’
Hán Zōngrú, being a glutton,
whenever he received one of your letters,
would exchange it with the palace marshal Yáo Lín for several catties of mutton.
Your letters could be called ‘Sheep-Exchanging Letters’!”
When Gōng was in the Hányuàn,
one day, on his birthday,
he was busy with memorials and compositions.
Zōngrú, following him, managed to draft a short letter in return for the calligraphy.
The messenger was pressing urgently for it.
Gōng smiled and said:
“Tell the official,
today is a day of no slaughter.”
Zhāng Gōngxiáng’s Poem
Zhāng Gōngxiáng was skilled at poetry in his youth.
One of his quatrains reads:
“Another year’s spring events have come to naught,
humming faintly with nose held, half-drunk.
Peach blossoms lining the road have just passed the rain,
the horse’s hooves have nowhere to avoid the fallen red.”
Skilled Flattery
In Jīngzhōu, there was Féng Xīlè,
who was skilled at flattery.
He once visited the magistrate of Chánglín County
and said:
“Yesterday, upon first entering the border,
I saw tigers and wolves with tails intertwined heading west.
This must be due to the influence of your benevolent governance.”
A moment later,
villagers reported that a tiger had eaten a person last night.
The magistrate playfully questioned him.
Féng immediately said:
“It must have merely eaten and passed through.”
Dù Zǐměi’s Tomb
is in Lèiyáng.
The Táng History says:
“Upon reaching Lèiyáng, he died after getting drunk on beef, roasted meat, and white wine one night.”
However, Yuán Wēizhī’s epitaph for Zǐměi states:
“He went down to Jīngchǔ in a small boat,
and eventually died there.
His temporary burial was in Yuèyáng,
until his successor, Yè,
finally buried him at Shǒuyángshān in Yǎnshī.”
The epitaph should be considered correct.
Zǐměi himself claimed to be a descendant of Dù Yuánkǎi, Marquis of Dāngyáng in Jìn,
hence his family was traditionally buried at Shǒuyángshān.
Zǐměi’s father, Xián,
once served as magistrate of Gǒng County,
so Zǐměi was considered a native of Gǒng County.
Shǒuyángshān is north of the official road,
with numerous ancient tombs.
Yuánkǎi’s tomb is still recorded in topographical records and can be verified.
Dozens of descendants were buried alongside him,
but it is not known which is Zǐměi’s tomb.
Kāiyuán Musical Airs
Shěn Kuò, as a Hàlín Scholar,
had four musical airs from the Kāiyuán period,
which Yùlíng loved.
They say:
“The sun is warm at the top of Guànquèlóu,
flowers fragrant in Pénglái Diàn.
Green grass and misty smoke accompany the imperial carriage,
the sky is high, the sun close to the imperial couch.”
“The pavilion looks directly upon the empty palace,
no human dwellings seen amidst the clouds.
Hánshí light mist softly envelops,
the city full of bright moonlight and pear blossoms.”
“Dancing amidst the shadows of Líshān,
returning phoenixes within the gleam of Wèishuǐ.
Jade flutes play under a sky of bright moon,
imperial banners fill the road with spring breeze.”
“Behind the palace, spring banners cluster the honor guard,
before the pavilion, imperial ranks pass through flowers.
Where a piece of red cloud opens,
outsiders distantly recognize the imperial family.”
Cǎoshū Qiánwén (Cursive Script Coin Inscriptions)
In previous generations, there were no coin inscriptions in cursive script.
During the Chúnhuà reign,
Tàizōng himself wrote them.
Once completed,
he bestowed them upon his close ministers.
Wáng Yuánzhī wrote a poem saying:
“Demoted official without stipend, chimney without smoke,
only embracing zithers and books, sleeping the whole day.
Still, there is one thing better than Zhào Yī,
in my purse I still keep imperial inscribed coins.”
Wáng Zhòngzhì Zhàoshì Shī (Wáng Zhòngzhì's Poem on Being Summoned for Examination)
Wáng Zhòngzhì
was a renowned scholar during Rénzōng's time.
His poem “Summoned for Examination at the Hanlin Academy” says:
“Lush trees cast deep shadows on the white jade hall,
only in old age do I test my literary skill here.
With the palace eaves long in the sun, my brushwork done,
I idly brush off dust to gaze at the painted walls.”
His poem “Staying at Huàyuè Guàn (Mount Huà Temple)” says:
“Ancient trees pierce the sky, clouds hang like leaves,
pear blossoms pressing on the roof, white as snow, illuminating people.
Deeply strange that the earthly immortal should teach a vulgar guest,
earnestly keeping me to see the spring of Huà Shān.”
Later, he inscribed again, saying:
“Stone platform, flowing water, coexisting with green moss,
a path opens amidst the bamboo grove.
Pity the pear blossoms have all flown away,
only now, a year later, do travelers return.”
Yuántōng Bùchūshì (Yuántōng Does Not Leave Seclusion)
Chán Master Yuántōng Fǎxiù
maintained a pure and strict life,
unwilling to leave seclusion.
He wrote a verse, saying:
“Who can comb their hair three times a day,
better to gather the roots firmly and then stop.
Essentially, her skin and bones are good,
without rouge and powder, she is still graceful.”
Téng Dádào Wǔyán (Téng Dádào's Five-Character Poems)
Téng Dádào excelled in five-character verse.
His poem “Introspection” says:
“At Hánshí, border sounds cease,
spring winds, the chill lingers.”
His poem “Befriending” says:
“Befriend heroes and mighty ones,
who would associate with children?
Gold adorns swords and pendants,
fierce beasts are painted on banners and staffs.
The Wolf Star of the North Pole falls,
the royal aura of the Central Plains rises high.
Eventually, the bandits of Hèlán
will not wear ochre-yellow robes.”
Èr Sòng Shī (Poems by the Two Sòngs)
Sòng Jǔgōng and his brother both had high reputations.
Summoned to compose “Falling Flowers,” the poem says:
“Overnight, the east wind swept the garden walls,
returning, where does the desolation remain?
Hàn Gāo's pendant is cold and wet beside the river,
Jīngǔ's wind is perilous, fragrance reaches the ground.
Tear-stained faces needing otter marrow to mend traces,
stage shadows receding, costing phoenix goblets.
Southern Dynasties' yuefǔ, stop composing songs,
Táoyè, Táoliáng, all are sorrowful.”
Jǐngwén's poem says:
“Falling white, flying red, each lamenting,
in the green tower's misty rain, enduring the sight.
Wishing to fly, it dances like a swirling wind,
already fallen, it still forms a half-face makeup.
The Cānghǎi traveler returns, pearls bursting as tears,
the Zhāngtái person leaves, bones retaining fragrance.
Perhaps unintentionally it sends a pair of butterflies,
and entrusts its fragrant heart to the honeycombs.”
His poem “Lake Exhibition, River Pavilion” says:
“Carving open a place where fish and birds forget their forms,
unfolding the vastness of rivers and lakes to the horizon.”
Yīngtáo Jiànlào (Cherries Offered with Curds)
Dù Mùzhī's “Cherry Poem” says:
“Thinking of using them to cook a red ox or camel,
following the joy of a jade plate.”
Tang people already used cherries with curds.
Liǔ Sānmián (Willow Three Sleeps)
Lǐ Shāngyǐn's rhapsody says:
“How can it be like the Cowherd Star by the river,
whose visit is heard only once a year?
Not like the human-willow in the imperial park,
who always gets three sleeps the whole day.”
It means outside the Hàn Yuàn there was a human-shaped willow,
which "slept" and "fell" three times a day.
Bìjiān Tíshī (Poems Inscribed on Green Paper)
South of Cháng'ān, at the foot of the mountain,
a scholar made a small garden, planting flowers and trees.
One day,
a golden calf chariot with several maidservants,
all beautiful,
descended and drank in his courtyard.
They invited the scholar to sit with them,
and were very cordial.
As they were about to leave,
one brought out a small green paper and inscribed a poem saying:
“No path to longing, do not long,
willow catkins in the wind are but for a moment.
Melancholy returning alone to deep chambers,
the dawn oriole's song breaks the green willow branch.”
Mèng Pāoqíu Shī (Dream of Throwing Balls Poem)
Lǐ Shènyán,
courtesy name Xīgǔ.
He dreamed he went to a palace,
where hundreds of courtesans were throwing balls,
each singing a poem.
He woke up remembering three poems:
“Feasting at dusk, unwilling to stop,
moonlight on jade steps flows like night.
In the morning, feeling most favored,
smiling, asking bystanders to recognize the embroidered ball.”
“Suí dynasty palaces locked in clear autumn,
once saw beauties tossing embroidered balls.
Golden keys and jade flutes, all silent,
a day's bright moon shines on the west tower.”
“How hateful, the several emperors of the Suí dynasty,
their dance skirts wore out the embroidered mandarin ducks.
Now returning to the place of ball-throwing,
it is not the old scent of the incense burner.”
Yīngwǔ Hū Pípá (Parrot Calls Pípá)
Cài Chízhèng was banished to Xīnzhōu.
His maidservant was named Pípá.
He once kept a parrot.
Whenever Chízhèng called Pípá,
he would strike a clapper,
and the parrot would echo the call.
After Pípá died,
he accidentally touched the clapper,
and the parrot still echoed the call.
Chízhèng was so saddened he fell ill
and did not recover.
He once composed a poem saying:
“The parrot's words remain,
Pípá's existence is no more.
Heartbroken by the miasma-filled river water,
we crossed together, but will not return together.”
Xuānshè Shī (Proclaiming Amnesty Poem)
Zhāng Shùnmín,
during the Shàoshèng reign, was implicated in the Yuányòu faction,
and demoted to Chángshā.
The amnesty decree still did not pardon party members.
He wrote a poem on proclaiming amnesty, saying:
“Drums beating fill the streets,
voices carried across the riverside.
The nation solemn with three years' rites,
grace sprinkled like spring across all lands.
Boats and oars approach the Southern Dipper,
officials bow towards the Northern Star.
South of the mountains and north of the mountains,
how many await their return home?”
Huíxiāng Shī (Returning Home Poem)
Hè Zhīzhāng's “Returning Home Poem” says:
“Many years since I left my hometown,
recently, half of the world's affairs have vanished.
Only the green lake water before the gate,
the spring breeze does not diminish its old waves.”
He also says:
“Left home young, returned old,
hometown accent hard to change, hair thinning.
Children see me, but do not recognize me,
instead asking, ‘Where does this guest come from?’”
Yuánxī Yùlóu Shī (Poem on the Lantern Festival at the Imperial Tower)
During the Yuányòu reign,
on the Yuánxī night, watching lanterns from the tower,
there was an imperial poem.
At the time, Wáng Yǔyù and Cài Chízheng were the left and right chancellors.
Cài Chízheng asked Wáng Yǔyù,
"How should one incorporate historical allusions
when composing a poem for the Yuánxī festival in response to the Emperor's command?"
Wáng Yǔyù replied,
"One should not use allusions outside of 'Áo Shān' (Mount Áo) and 'Fèng Niǎn' (Phoenix Carriage)."
Zhāng Zǐhòu laughed and said,
"Who doesn't know that?"
Two days later,
climbing Mount Cǎi,
he alone appreciated Wáng Yǔyù's poem,
which read:
"Snow has melted, the bright moon fills the immortal terrace,
Ten thousand candles light the hall, precious screens unfold.
Twin phoenixes descend in the clouds, supporting the carriage,
Six áos emerge from the sea, bearing mountains.
Hàojīng's spring wine moistens the Zhōu banquet,
Fénshuǐ's autumn wind makes Hàn talent seem inadequate.
A song of peace makes everyone joyful,
The monarch again sips the purple elixir cup."
That evening,
with music presented by Gāolì,
another cup was added.
Liú Gòngfù's Poem
Liú Gòngfù, having left his post as 校書郎 (xiàoshūláng), served as the deputy in Hǎilíng.
His poem read:
"The palace gate and golden palace gates open to the sky,
Five times I've seen palace flowers fall on the well-side sophoras.
Tomorrow, in a small boat, I'll depart for the vast sea,
Then from the clouds, I'll gaze towards Pénglái."
Poem on a Grotesque Stone
Huáng Yàfū
was the father of Lúzhí.
He had a quatrain titled "Grotesque Stone," which read:
"Mountain sprites and water monsters cling to lianas,
Heavenly green bìxié sleep on moss.
Drawing the curtain to sit opposite, heart speaking to mouth,
I once saw it come from Hàn and Táng's garden pavilions."
Lǐ Táibái's Poem on the Peak-Top Temple
Zēng Fù served as the magistrate of Qízhōu's Huángméi County.
There was a Peak-Top Temple,
over a hundred lǐ from the city.
It was amidst jumbled mountains,
where human footprints did not reach.
Zēng Fù, while surveying fields,
chanced upon a small plaque between the beams.
Covered in ancient dust, it was dim,
but it turned out to be a poem inscribed by Lǐ Bái.
The poem read:
"Staying overnight at the peak-top temple,
I raise my hand to touch the stars.
I dare not speak in a loud voice,
Fearing to startle the people in heaven."
Poem Thanking for a Foreign Silk Robe
During the Xīníng reign,
Huáng Lúzhí served as a palace instructor for five high-ranking officials.
After drinking,
one official took off a light-colored foreign silk robe and dressed him in it.
Lúzhí, while drunk, composed a poem that read:
"Layers of fragrant silk, a light-colored robe sent,
Wearing it, spring's qi enters the study.
At home, my kind mother asks in surprise,
I tell her it was the young noble who took it off and gifted it."
Yáo Sìzōng's Poem
Dōngpō saw a poem in a post-station in Guānzhōng,
liked it, and copied it down.
At first, he didn't know the author's name,
but later heard it was Yáo Sìzōng.
The poem read:
"Wishing to hang up cap and gown at Xuánwǔ Mén,
First, I'll seek waters and bamboos in Wèinán village.
Then, taking the Lóulán-slaying sword I once wielded,
I'll buy a plowing ox and teach my descendants."
Sīmǎ Gōng's Poem
Sīmǎ Chí, a Daìzhì,
and the father of Wēngōng,
had a poem that read:
"Colder than pond water, plainer than autumn,
The distant path ends, revealing the ferry crossing.
Luckily, there's no place for painting in this scene,
If painted, it would surely bring a lifetime of sorrow."
A Courtesan Asks Cānháo for a Poem
Cānháo came to Xúzhōu to visit Dōngpō.
At Dōngpō's banquet, he playfully ordered a courtesan to ask for a poem,
which read:
"Many thanks to the graceful lady before the cup,
How well you trouble King Xiāng with your secluded dreams.
My Zen heart is already set, buying mud-like catkins,
Not chasing the east wind, wildly up and down."
Poem Inscribed on a Small Stream
Cānháo inscribed a poem on a small stream in Qiántáng, which read:
"Beneath the city wall, wild waters winding green,
Graceful light boats skim the banks.
Wishing to gather orchids, but finding no place,
Wild flowers and riverside grasses dominate spring."
Dōngpō's Inscribed Poem
Hán Kānggōng, during the Yuánxī festival, invited several officials
and brought out household courtesans to serve drinks.
His favorite was named Lǔ Shēng,
who happened to be stung by a bee.
A moment later,
holding a fan, she approached Dōngpō to ask for a poem.
The poem contained the lines: "Fish blow fine ripples, songs shake the sun,
After the dance, flowers and branches, a bee enters the bosom."
The upper line records the surname,
the lower line records the event.
A Drunken Monk's Eulogy
Dōngpō said:
"There was a monk in Sūzhōu who loved to drink,
and died from drunkenness.
Before dying,
he wrote his own eulogy, which read:
'O spirit, born in Jambudvīpa,
Not greedy,
not jealous,
fond of drinking wine,
Falling down stairs, lying on roads.
I imagine you'll have to wait until you're born into the Tuṣita Heaven,
Only then can you break this habit.
Why?
Because in the Pure Land, there's no wine to buy.'"
Those with Many Beards Align with Physiognomy
Huáng Lúzhí said:
"Those with many beards that are sparse and elegant will surely be noble;
those dense and generally short indicate insufficient spiritual vitality."
Commander Wáng Jìnqīng and Marshal Cáo Guànzào both had no beards. Whenever beards were mentioned,
those with many were considered to align with physiognomy.
Wáng Jìnqīng often mentioned that between Gǒng and Luò,
there was a temple to Zhuāngzōng of Later Táng.
The divine statue had a beard all around its eyes.
He wrote a poem and sent it to Cáo Guànzào, which read:
"Slaying Liáng and succeeding Lǐ was a good plan,
Yet he was swayed by singing girls and lost his body.
Wiping away dust to examine the preserved image,
It turns out his face was covered in beard and mustache."
Yàn Shūyuán's Poem
During the Xīníng reign,
Zhéng Xiá submitted a memorial, which caused an incident,
and he was imprisoned.
All those who had been close friends with him during peaceful times were investigated.
A poem by Yàn Shūyuán to Zhéng Xiá was found at Zhéng Xiá's house;
it read:
"Small whites and long reds again fill the branches,
Outside the football field, I alone rest my chin on my hand.
The spring breeze is truly a guest of the human world,
How long can it preside over the flourishing splendor?"
Yùlíng praised it,
and immediately ordered Zhéng Xiá's release.
Spring Moon
When Dōngpō was in Rǔyīn,
in early spring, the garden plums bloomed,
their vibrant colors fresh and bright.
His wife said:
"The spring moon is better than the autumn moon.
The autumn moon makes people feel melancholy,
the spring moon makes people feel joyful and harmonious."
Dōngpō smiled and said:
"Indeed, what you say is true."
He immediately invited guests to drink
and composed "Jiǎnzì Mùlán Huā," which read:
"In the spring courtyard at midday,
The swaying spring wine glows as if dancing.
Turning along the winding corridor,
Half-fallen plum blossoms exhale a gentle fragrance.
Light breezes and thin mists,
All are places where youths enjoy themselves.
Unlike the autumn light,
Which only shines upon departing people, breaking their hearts."
Secret-Color Porcelain
Regarding today's secret-color porcelain,
people say that when the Qián family ruled the state,
Yuèzhōu fired and presented it,
and it was not allowed for use by officials and subjects.
Hence it was called "secret-color."
However, I recently saw Lù Guīmēng's collection, where the "Yuè Ware" poem reads:
"In the ninth autumn's wind and dew, Yuè kilns open,
Capturing the verdant color of a thousand peaks.
How well it holds the night dew in mid-autumn,
Competing with Jī Zhòngsàn over the remaining cups."
Thus, I learned that the Táng dynasty already had secret-color,
and it did not originate with the Qián family.
A bolt of silk for a horse
The *Hán Shī Wàichuán* says:
"Yán Huí looked at the horse at Wú Mén,
and saw a bolt of silk."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is a horse." Then the horse's gleam and shadow
were only a bolt long.
Therefore, later generations called it "a bolt."
Yìng Shào's *Fēngsú Tōng* also says:
"A bolt of silk for a horse.
Some say that when a horse travels at night,
its eyes illuminate four *zhàng* ahead,
hence it is called 'a bolt.'
Some say that a horse's length and width just measure a bolt."
Some say that a dead horse was sold for a bolt of silk.
Some say that according to the *Chūnqiū Zuǒ Shì* tradition,
when feudal lords presented each other with riding horses and bundles of silk,
the silk was measured in bolts,
and it just matched the horse,
Cháisāng
Today, many scholars commonly refer to Cháisāng Wēng as Yuānmíng,
unaware that Liú Yímín once served as the magistrate of Cháisāng.
Lètiān's poem "Staying at Xīlín Temple" says:
"Trees shed, sky clears, mountain greenness opens,
loving the mountains, I ride my horse into them.
Knowing in my heart I'm not equal to the Cháisāng magistrate,
after one night at Xīlín, I simply return."
Note:
Cháisāng Magistrate
was Liú Yímín.
Zhuàngyuán Xú Shì's Poem
In the early Chóngníng era,
the specifically selected *zhuàngyuán*, Xú Shì, had a poem that said:
"With white hair and a green robe, I received office late,
at Qiónglín, I suddenly felt my wine capacity widen.
Passing Píngkāng at night, no one asked after me,
keeping the official flower to gaze upon after waking."
Tǎn transforms into a snake
Zhāng Tǎn, the Yúhóu of Líndì County,
was cruel, violent, and greedy for profit.
He died of illness
and was buried outside the city.
More than a month later,
there were nightly shouts and calls.
People reported to his family,
saying he had revived.
His wife and others dug him up to look,
his body had already transformed into a giant snake,
but his head and face were still human.
They took him and placed him in a wicker basket.
Feeling cold, he asked for thick blankets,
eating two *jīn* of meat daily
and drinking a *dǒu* of wine.
He regained human speech.
Several months later,
his head also became a snake,
and gradually he could no longer speak human language.
His family sent him to live in the mountains.
Chén Zhīmò's Poem
Ougōng in his later years admired Chén Zhīmò's poetry
and regretted its scarcity.
He only mentioned two couplets of his.
One said, "Wind and smoke horizontally cross white birds on flat ground,
clouds and trees on the mountainside roll up dark vines."
The other said, "Clouds bury mountain foothills, hiding autumn rain,
leaves fall from treetops, carrying the evening breeze."
Three-level two-full prose
Chuán Líng zhī served as the Censor-in-Chief
and impeached Liú Zhòngféng.
One day,
Gòngfù saw him and said:
"What fault has my young nephew committed to trouble your esteemed judgment?"
Líng zhī said shamefacedly:
"It was merely 'three-level two-full' prose."
Gòngfù laughed and said:
"'Seven-up eight-down' talent!"
Zhāng Āndào's previous life
Zhāng Āndào was appointed to govern Chúzhōu.
On his way, he encountered a monk's dwelling.
Entering, he felt a sudden pang of recognition,
and then realized he had been a monk there in a previous life,
and had personally transcribed four scrolls of the *Léngjiā Jīng*.
He asked the disciples,
who fully explained that an old monk had recited this sutra his entire life,
and the ones he personally wrote were still kept in a box in the roof chamber.
He took them out to examine,
and the handwriting was exactly the same as in his current life.
He then entrusted Dōngpō to transcribe this sutra
and have it printed and distributed at Jīnshān Temple.
When Dōngpō became Assistant Prefect of Hángzhōu,
he visited Shòuxīng Academy.
Upon entering, he immediately realized he had been there before,
and could describe the hall behind the academy and the rocky area,
and wrote a poem to record it.
Lǐ Bái's Tomb
Lǐ Táibái's tomb is in Cǎishí Zhèn, Tàipíng Zhōu,
but the main tomb is on Qīngshān, south of the prefecture.
Perhaps, when he passed Cǎishí, he was drunk and tried to grasp the moon.
I secretly suspect that he was provisionally buried here at that time,
and later moved and interred on Qīngshān.
Capital City
The imperial city of Dōngjīng in the Táng Dynasty
was four *lǐ* east-west,
two *lǐ* north-south,
thirteen *lǐ* in circumference,
and forty-eight *chǐ* high.
The palace city of Xījīng was four *lǐ* east-west,
two *lǐ* north-south,
thirteen *lǐ* in circumference,
and thirty-three *chǐ* high.
The imperial city of Běncháo Dōngjīng was five *lǐ* in circumference.
The old city was twenty *lǐ* in circumference,
which is the city of Biànliáng.
In the second year of Jiànzhōng of the Táng Dynasty,
Jìdùshǐ Lǐ Miǎn rebuilt it.
In the early years of the dynasty, it was called Quē Chéng,
also known as Lǐ Chéng.
The new city was decreed to be separately built by Zhōu Shìzōng in the second year of Xiǎndé.
It was forty-eight *lǐ* in circumference,
and called Wài Chéng,
also called Luó Chéng,
and also Xīn Chéng.
Yù Líng ordered the internal official Sòng Yòngchén to rebuild it.
Jiāngyáo Zhù
*Hǎiwù Yìmíng* says:
"Jiāngyáo Zhù's shell is as beautiful as jade,
its bony pillar is an inch thick."
Guō Jǐngchún's *Jiāngyáo Fù* says:
"Jade *yáo* sea moon,
flesh spits out stone flowers."
People today do not use this character *yáo*,
because they are unaware of this.
Inner Treasury Wine and Běiyuàn Tea
Dōngpō said:
"Zhūgě's brush is like Inner Treasury wine and Běiyuàn tea."
Shāngǔ said:
"Office incense, official candles, and the way women in the capital comb their hair
are also unsurpassed in the world."
Paired Couplet
Dōngpō said:
"To associate with me, better to be me;
to be haggard for you, yet ashamed of you,
can be considered a good couplet."
Monk Huánxiāng
During Qián Shì's time,
there was a monk named Huánxiāng.
He would often sing:
"Returning home, silent and trackless,
no sails hoisted, water and land connected.
Stepping firmly on the land of my hometown,
there are no north, south, east, or west."
Someone asked for an explanation.
He said:
"Everyone will go next year."
Indeed, there was a fulfillment regarding the surrender of territory.
King Qián's Poem
King Qián had a poem that said:
"Scholars lament autumn colors, women harbor spring feelings;
this saying has always been true.
If there were indeed feelings of attachment and longing,
the weather of all four seasons would always cause sorrow."
Poem by the Recluse Chuán
Chuán Yìrén Yán
was a person of the Zhēnzōng era.
He presented Zhāng Zhōngdìng with a poem that said:
"Thinking of exchanging fleeting fame for leisure,
before my gate, flowing water faces green mountains.
Green mountains are silent, people are without affairs,
outside the gate, wind and flowers naturally come and go."
Zhāng replied:
"Sparse reeds rustle, reflecting on the gate and wall,
it is said that the flavor of sashimi is long in early autumn.
Why did you lightly abandon it and come to the imperial city?
Until now, your soul still circles the cold pond."
He also wrote "On the Wall":
"Cold crickets busily urge weaving as night falls,
hoopoes earnestly encourage plowing in deep spring.
If a person has no heart to aid the world,
how are they different from insects and birds?"
Volume Fifteen
End.
Āmàn respectfully serves as the honored guest.
Mínghuáng went to the residence of Níngwáng.
They drank very happily.
He said,
"Big brother makes a good host,
and Āmán humbly acts as a honored guest."
The next day,
Níngwáng and others submitted a memorial, saying,
"Although the emperor's words and deeds
are recorded by the left and right historians,
we fear they cannot fully capture the beauty within the inner court.
We humbly request that I, along with my brothers,
take turns daily to record them,
and send them to the historians."
By the end of Tiānbǎo,
three hundred scrolls were completed.
The emperor cherished this history,
and had a pavilion built to store it.
When Lù Shān captured Cháng'ān,
he first burned this pavilion.
Therefore, of the emperor's true records,
not even three or four out of a hundred are recounted.
Mínghuáng went to the Eastern Capital.
He ascended a pavilion with Yīxíng Shī to gaze out.
The emperor sighed, saying,
"Can I, Jiǎ, not remain completely unharmed?"
Yīxíng said,
"Your Majesty will travel ten thousand *lǐ*,
and your sacred reign will be boundless."
When he later went to Shǔ,
and reached Wànlǐ Qiáo,
he then understood Yīxíng's words.
Understanding Horse Lore
Mínghuáng asked Huáng Fānchuò,
"Who understands horse lore?"
He replied,
"All three Chéngxiàng understand it."
The emperor asked how he knew this.
He said,
"Every day on the sand embankment, I see that the horses ridden by the Chéngxiàngs are all fine steeds,
and from this, I know they understand horse lore."
The emperor laughed heartily.
Grand-Emperor and Bare-Emperor
When Mínghuáng was in the palace residence,
he requested leave to return to the capital.
It was late spring,
and several young men from wealthy families were amusing themselves at Kūnmíng Chí,
choosing a scenic spot for a feast.
The emperor, in military attire with a hawk on his arm,
rode directly in front of them.
The young men showed some displeasure.
One young man called out, saying,
"Let each state their family background and official rank."
The emperor loudly said,
"A former emperor, a bare-emperor!
My father is a prime minister-king,
and I am the Prince of Línzī Commandery!"
The young men were startled and fled.
The emperor drank a full cup of wine,
slowly stood up,
mounted his horse, and departed.
Birthday Noodles
When Empress Wáng's favor declined,
she wept and said,
"Sānláng,
do you not remember Āzhōng taking off his purple sleeveless jacket for your birthday noodles?"
The emperor was saddened by this.
Āzhōng
was the Empress's father's nickname.
Sū Huán Has a Son, Lǐ Qiáo Has No Son
Zhōngzōng once summoned the sons of Prime Ministers Sū Huán and Lǐ Qiáo to an audience.
The emperor said,
"You should recite the books you have studied."
Pǒ Zòu (Su Huan's son) said,
"Wood that follows the string becomes straight;
a queen who accepts remonstrance becomes sagely."
Lǐ Qiáo's son also advanced and said,
"He cut off the shins of those who waded across the ford in the morning,
and carved out the heart of a virtuous man."
The emperor said,
"Sū Huán has a son,
but Lǐ Qiáo has no son."
Peony Poems
Mínghuáng was admiring peonies in the palace hall
and asked his attendant ministers,
"Whose peony poem is the best?"
They replied,
"Lǐ Zhèngfēng's."
The poem read:
"Her national beauty, at dawn, is like wine,
her heavenly fragrance, at night, dyes the clothes."
The emperor said to his concubine,
"If you drink a purple gold cup in front of your dressing table mirror,
then Lǐ Zhèngfēng's poem can be seen."
Painting of the Kāiyuán Eastern Investiture
Wénzōng visited the eastern pavilion of the Three Halls
and saw a huge scroll hanging on the transverse corridor.
He ordered an inner servant to hang it under the eaves;
it was indeed the "Painting of the Kāiyuán Eastern Investiture."
The emperor picked up a white jade *rúyì*
and pointed to several people, including Zhāng Yuè, sighing,
"If only I could have one of them come,
then I could see Kāiyuán again."
He ordered several cups of fine wine
and quickly returned to his sleeping quarters in his palanquin.
He once said to Lǐ Shí,
"When I find the affairs of the world difficult to manage,
I drink strong wine
to resolve it through intoxication."
One Son Does Not Serve the Empress
When Dí Liánggōng was prime minister,
he had an aunt, Lú Shì,
who lived in a villa south of Wǔqiáo.
The aunt had only one son,
who had never come to the capital city.
During a leave of absence, the Duke went to inquire about his aunt's well-being.
He happened to see his cousin hunting,
returning with pheasants and rabbits.
The Duke said to his aunt,
"I am now prime minister.
What pleasure does my cousin enjoy following?
I am willing to do my utmost to fulfill his desires."
The aunt said,
"You are noble enough.
I only have one son,
and I do not wish him to serve the Empress."
The Duke left in great shame.
The Night-Luminous Screen Saves Zhāng Yuè from Trouble
When Yáo Chóng was prime minister,
one day, during an audience in the informal palace,
his left foot was not very agile.
The emperor said,
"Do you have a foot ailment, my lord?"
Yáo Chóng said,
"Your servant has an ailment of the heart and abdomen,
not of the foot."
Then he proceeded to memorialize about Zhāng Yuè.
Yáo Chóng urgently called the Censor-in-Chief Lǐ Línfǔ to hand him the previous imperial edict.
Before Zhāng Yuè was subject to Yáo Chóng's memorial,
a scholar-teacher had an affair with Zhāng Yuè's maidservant.
Zhāng Yuè was furious,
captured him, and sent him to the Jingzhao Prefect.
The scholar sternly said,
"Being unable to resist beauty
is also a common human emotion.
You, sir, are noble as a prime minister.
How could you not have occasions to employ people urgently?
Why are you so stingy over a mere maidservant?"
Zhāng Yuè was struck by his words,
released him,
and even gave him the maidservant.
One day,
the scholar suddenly said,
"You are being slandered by Prime Minister Yáo.
The external judgment is already prepared.
Please use the 'Chicken Forest Night-Luminous Screen' which you treasure, with a scheme involving the Ninth Princess,
and you will certainly be able to resolve your difficulties."
The princess spoke to the emperor, saying,
"Do you not remember that when you were in the Eastern Palace,
you wished to show continuous favor to Prime Minister Zhāng?"
The emperor urgently ordered Gāo Lìshì to go to the Censorate to demand the previous case file,
and dismissed it.
Hermit Wáng Zhēn's Divination
When Grand Commandant Wèi Gōng was a Registrar in Bìngzhōu,
upon taking office,
a hermit named Wáng requested an audience, saying,
"I am skilled at divination."
He wrote eight characters on paper,
saying,
"Reach the highest official position,
live sixty-four years."
Later, it indeed proved true.
Ancient Mirror
A fisherman in Qínhuái cast his net and caught an ancient mirror.
When one looked into it, it reflected the five *zàng* and six *fǔ* organs.
White Parrot
The kingdom of Línyì presented a white parrot.
Wèi Zhēng remonstrated, saying,
"Though a parrot can speak,
it is still a bird.
Your servant wishes Your Majesty to take this as a profound warning."
On Mínghuáng
Dézōng discussed Lǐ Bì becoming prime minister.
The Emperor once spoke of Mínghuáng,
sighing,
"The calamity of the Central Plains
began with Lín Fǔ.
With his brilliant and extraordinary talent,
why did Mínghuáng not discern this?"
Bì replied,
"Mínghuáng in his youth
experienced many difficulties.
Even if Jiāng Chōng intended to trap Lìyuán,
or Empress Jiǎ wished to scheme against Mǐnhuái,
the troubles that came to Ruìzōng
could not have been worse.
Demoted to Prince of Línzī,
then soon restored to the royal court,
he had the numerous unusual traits of Hàn Gāo,
and relied on Xiāo Wáng's utter sincerity.
His formidable power once roused,
treacherous villains were instantly destroyed.
And he had long esteemed Confucian scholarship,
deeply understanding governance and economics.
He disdained Hàn Gāo's 'words on horseback,'
and excelled at Wǔ Dì's 'questioning of replacements.'
Since ascending the throne,
he delighted in being close to upright people.
He was both diligent in state affairs
and had good ministers.
But as his desires grew deeper,
his governance also became lax.
Lín Fǔ had not yet become tiresome when
Xiānkè succeeded him.
In the past, Qí Huán survived and
achieved hegemony because of Guǎn Zhòng;
after Guǎn Zhòng died, numerous difficulties arose."
The Emperor listened with pleasure and acceptance,
then said,
"A prime minister who is also learned in books!
I can rest easy."
Exotic Objects
Yuán Xiānshēng presented Wéi Dān, the Minister, with a shark-gauze silk-floss white jade perfumed sachet,
along with a jade chain over two feet long, and an exotic bamboo mat over two hundred feet long.
Wéi Mǐn in a dream acquired a soft silk Shu brocade turban,
a Jìbīn Kingdom golden robe,
a West Shu woven Lántíng scroll,
a kingfisher pipe engraved with Lú Sīdào's "Yàngē Xíng",
and a white jade sword over two feet long.
Jade Dragon Statuette
When the Emperor was a royal grandson,
Empress Tiānhòu, marveling at him, said,
"This child will surely be a Heavenly Son of Great Peace."
She took a jade dragon statuette and bestowed it upon him.
The jade dragon was only a few inches long,
exquisitely crafted and extraordinary,
originally an item from Tàizōng's Jìnyáng period.
The Emperor treasured it greatly;
later, during droughts, prayers for rain with it always brought a response.
Merely a False Appearance
The Emperor appointed Sū Tíng as prime minister,
and ordered Xiāo Sōng to draft the edict,
but it was not skillfully done.
The edict read:
"The nation's precious treasure."
The Emperor said,
"Merely a false appearance."
Guards Discarding Food
The Emperor, peering from a covered walkway, saw guards finish eating
and discard leftover food into a drain.
The Emperor was enraged
and ordered them beaten to death.
Níng Wáng said,
"If one spies on the faults of guards from a covered walkway,
I fear people will not feel secure."
The Emperor said,
"My elder brother, with me,
truly helps in times of difficulty."
White Camel
During the Tiānbǎo era,
peace had reigned for many years.
From Kaiyuǎn Gate to the barbarian frontier, a distance of twelve thousand *lǐ*,
people filled the fields,
and mulberry and hemp were like woven cloth.
Gēshū Hàn, stationed in Qīnghǎi,
had a long journey.
He sent envoys who always rode white camels to present reports,
traveling five hundred *lǐ* a day.
Jade Flower Dapple-Grey
Among the horses the Emperor rode,
there were the Yùhuācōng and Zhàoyèbái.
Dancing Horses
The Emperor trained four hundred dancing horses,
dividing them into left and right divisions,
each with its own name,
such as "Such-and-such Family's Black-Muzzled Horse,"
and their music was called "Qīngpén Yuè."
Dozens of horses were all clothed in splendid brocade,
and bridled with golden bells.
Whenever the music began,
they raised their heads and wagged their tails,
moving freely in time with the rhythm.
Lù Shān took ten horses back to Fányáng,
which were later acquired by Tián Chéngsì,
who did not know their skill.
One day during a grand feast,
when the music played,
the horses heard the music and began to dance.
The stablemen thought it an omen
and beat them to death.
Among all characters, only 'péng' is not yet rectified – Dai Gan's Poem
The Emperor ascended the tower,
and the musicians from the Imperial Music Bureau were bitterly toiling with the pole-climbing act.
On a hundred-foot pole, they constructed a "water mountain,"
resembling Yíngzhōu and Fāngzhàng.
They commanded a small child, holding a crimson staff, to enter and exit
its midst.
Liú Yàn, as a child prodigy, was appointed rectification officer in the Secretariat.
The Imperial Concubine placed him on her lap, powdered and painted his face,
and gave him a kerchief and comb.
The Emperor asked,
"You are a rectification officer;
how many characters have you rectified?"
Yàn replied,
"All characters in the world are rectified,
only the character 'péng' is not yet rectified."
The Concubine bade him recite a poem about pole-climbing.
Yàn recited:
"In front of the tower, a hundred acts compete anew;
only the long pole is wondrously divine.
Who says the silken robes fluttering have strength?
Still, he dislikes being too light and adds more people."
The Emperor ordered him bestowed with an ivory tablet and a yellow patterned robe.
Niú Xiānkè Not Fit to Be Prime Minister
The Emperor appointed Niú Xiānkè as prime minister
and asked Gāo Lìshì for his opinion on how it was received externally.
Lìshì replied,
"He is a clerk,
not fit to be prime minister."
The Emperor was angered and said,
"Then I will immediately appoint Kāng Biàn."
This was an angry retort at the moment,
naming someone utterly unsuitable.
Someone reported that Biàn was indeed about to become prime minister,
and Biàn quite believed it.
Enjoying Wealth and Rank
Yáng Guózhōng said to a guest,
"My family rose from humble origins,
and through the empress's kin reached this position.
Unsure where I will retire,
I will ultimately not achieve a good reputation,
so I should rather enjoy the wealth and rank I have."
Jade Leaf Crown, Night-Glow Pillow, Chain Canopy
Princess Tèyíng's jade leaf crown,
Guóguó Fūrén's night-glow pillow,
and Yáng Guózhōng's chain canopy
were all rare treasures of the world.
Golden Basin Filled with Two *Dòu* of Serpentine
Guóguó Fūrén's favor was immense for a time.
Her residence was originally Wéi Sìlì's house.
While the Wéi family's sons and younger brothers were resting during the day,
they suddenly saw a woman in a yellow dress,
descending from a palanquin,
with dozens of maids.
She said,
"I heard this house is for sale;
what is its price?"
The Wéi family replied,
"It is our ancestors' old home,
which we cannot bear to part with."
Before her words were finished,
hundreds of workmen ascended the east wing
and tore down its tiles and wood.
The Wéi family immediately took their zithers and books
and abandoned them on the road.
They lamented that their lack of talent caused them to be robbed by a powerful family,
and the ancients' warnings were evident today.
When the hall was completed,
it was awarded to the artisans with a golden basin filled with two *dòu* of serpentine.
Later, during a great wind,
wood broke and stones fell,
but the hall suffered almost no damage.
When the tiles were removed for inspection,
they were all supported by wooden tiles.
Wáng Wéi Pardoned through Poetry
Lù Shān (祿山) attacked the capital.
Several hundred disciples of the Líyuán (梨園) were captured
and gathered at the Níngbì Chí (凝碧池).
The musician Léi Hǎiqīng (雷海青) threw his musical instrument to the ground,
faced west, and wept bitterly,
and was killed.
Wáng Wéi (王維) was implicated,
and detained in a Buddhist monastery.
He composed a poem which said:
“Ten thousand households grieve, smoke rises from the wilds;
When will officials once more attend the heavenly court?
Autumn locust leaves fall deep within the palace;
At Níngbì Chí (凝碧池) head, pipes and strings are played.”
He wrote it on the wall.
The rebels saw it.
Wéi (維) was spared punishment because of the poem.
Sable skin hats and *bùyáo chāi* (步搖釵)
In the early Tiānbǎo (天寶) era,
it was fashionable for men and women of all social classes to wear "Hu" (胡) style clothing.
Men wore sable skin hats;
women wore *bùyáo chāi* (步搖釵)
and narrow, small-sleeved garments.
Discerning people secretly sighed.
Dancing the *Língbō Qǔ* (凌波曲)
The female entertainer Xiè Āmán (謝阿蠻) was skilled at dancing the *Língbō Qǔ* (凌波曲).
Guìfēi (貴妃) bestowed upon her a gold-millet-decorated armlet.
Gāo Lìshì (高力士) eats shepherd's purse poem
Gāo Lìshì (高力士) was exiled to Wūzhōu (巫州).
Shepherd's purse grew abundantly in the mountains and valleys,
but people did not eat it.
Lìshì (力士) composed a poem to express his feelings, saying:
“In the two capitals it is sold by the catty;
In Wǔxī (五溪) no one gathers it.
Though Chinese and barbarian lands differ,
Its taste remains unchanged.”
Huái Shèn (懷慎) was frugal
Lú Huái Shèn (盧懷慎) was frugal.
For his personal needs, he had only one cloth bag.
His door had no blinds or screens;
during wind and rain, he would lift a mat to block them.
Sòng Jǐng (宋璟) visited him,
and ordered food to be served.
On the tray were two bowls of boiled beans
and a few platters of vegetables, that was all.
After his death,
only one old servant
came forward to sell himself to cover the funeral expenses.
The Four Excellences
Wéi Sìlì (韋嗣立) was appointed Zhōngshū Lìng (中書令).
Sū Huán (蘇環) drafted the official proclamations,
which were quite eloquent.
Xuē Jì (薛稷) wrote them in calligraphy.
At the time, they were called "The Four Excellences."
Reciting the character "Yǐn" (尹)
Sū Tǐng (蘇頲) could speak when very young.
A Jīngzhào Yǐn (京兆尹) visited.
After he left,
Tǐng (頲) was told to recite the character "Yǐn" (尹).
He said:
“Chǒu (丑) has feet,
but Jiǎ (甲) is not whole.
Seeing you, there is no mouth,
Knowing him, there are few people.”
The deceased Yáo Chóng (姚崇) outwitted the living Zhāng Yuè (張說)
Yáo Chóng (姚崇) and Zhāng Yuè (張說) served together as chief ministers.
When Chóng (崇) was ill,
he warned his sons:
“Prime Minister Zhāng (張) and I have a deep grudge,
but he is somewhat extravagant.
After my death,
colleagues will come to offer condolences.
You should display lavish clothing, ornaments, and precious artifacts in front of the curtain.
If he disregards them,
your entire clan will be in danger.
If he looks at them with interest,
you should present these artifacts to him
and ask him to compose the epitaph (*shéndào bēi*) (神道碑).
As soon as you get his composition,
record and submit it immediately,
and also prepare the stone beforehand to ensure quick carving.
Zhāng (張) often procrastinates;
if several days pass, he will certainly regret it.”
After Yáo (姚) died,
Zhāng (張) indeed came,
and looked at the clothing and artifacts several times.
The sons followed the instructions exactly.
The epitaph was then considered a masterpiece,
saying:
“Eight pillars support heaven,
placing him in a position of high brilliance;
Four seasons complete the year,
his nurturing功 (*gōng*) (功) endures.”
A few days later,
Zhāng (張) indeed took the original text, wishing to revise it.
The sons led the messenger to see it,
and the carving of the epitaph was already complete.
Yuè (說) regretted and said:
“The deceased Yáo Chóng (姚崇) still outwits the living Zhāng Yuè (張說).”
Jiǔlíng (九齡) composes "Returning Swallows" poem
When Zhāng Jiǔlíng (張九齡) was in the position of prime minister,
Lǐ Línfǔ (李林甫) secretly plotted against him.
Jiǔlíng (九齡) composed the poem "Returning Swallows" (*Guīyàn*) (歸燕) and presented it, saying:
“How tiny are the sea swallows,
They too come briefly in spring.
How can they know the mud is shallow,
They only see the jade hall opening.
Through vermilion doors they enter in pairs,
How many times a day in the splendid mansion.
With no desire to contend with others,
Let not the hawk suspect them.”
Línfǔ (林甫) knew he would surely retire,
and his anger gradually subsided.
One eagle seizing two rabbits
On the day Zhāng Jiǔlíng (張九齡) and Péi Huán (裴環) were dismissed from office,
the two bowed humbly and deferentially.
Línfǔ (林甫) was pleased with his own success.
Onlookers said:
“One eagle seizing two rabbits.”
Fáng Guǎn (房琯) as the reincarnation of Yǒng Gōng (永公)
During the Kāiyuán (開元) era,
Fáng Guǎn (房琯) was prime minister.
He lodged with the Daoist priest Xíng Hépú (邢和璞).
One leisure day, they went out of the city together,
to a ruined temple among the bamboos.
Hépú (和璞) struck the ground with his staff
and told them to dig.
They found a bottle.
Inside the bottle were letters from Lóu Shīdé (婁師德) to Yǒng Gōng (永公).
Hépú (和璞) said to Guǎn (琯):
“Do you remember this?”
Guǎn (琯) immediately realized with a start that he was the reincarnation of Yǒng Gōng (永公).
Many of Hépú’s (和璞) predictions regarding Guǎn’s (琯) life proved true.
Sweet dew soup
Lǐ Línfǔ’s (李林甫) son-in-law, Zhèng Píng (鄭平),
was a provincial official.
Línfǔ (林甫) saw his graying temples
and said:
“Tomorrow, the emperor will bestow sweet dew soup.
If Zhèng (鄭) eats it,
it can blacken his hair.”
The next day, he ate it,
but his hair turned even whiter, like floss.
Yīxíng (一行) seeks computational methods
Monk Yīxíng (一行) was skilled in the Dàyǎn (大衍) computational methods.
He heard that a certain monk at Guóqīng Sì (國清寺) on Tiāntái (天台) Mountain was expert in the art,
and went to seek him.
He did not dare to enter the temple immediately,
but secretly peeked through the gate.
He saw the monk calculating in the courtyard
and saying:
“A disciple will come to seek my art.
The water in front of the gate must flow west,
only then will the disciple arrive.”
Yīxíng (一行) then hurried out to ask for instruction.
The monk looked at the stream in front of the gate,
which had previously flowed east,
but suddenly flowed west.
So he imparted his art.
Watching a sword dance and painting on a wall
Wú Dàoxuán (吳道玄) was skilled at painting Buddhas,
and especially adept at depicting ghosts and spirits.
General Péi Mín (裴旻) asked him to paint a wall at Tiāngōng Sì (天宮寺) in Dōngdū (東都).
Dàoxuán (道玄) said:
“I hear the general is skilled at sword dancing.
Watching his mighty spirit
could aid my brushwork.”
Mín (旻) gladly performed the dance.
Dàoxuán (道玄) wielded his brush and completed the painting instantly,
as if divinely aided.
Dismissed from office and composing a poem
Lǐ Shìzhī (李適之) and Lǐ Línfǔ (李林甫) were prime ministers together.
Línfǔ (林甫) slandered Shìzhī (適之), who was then dismissed.
He composed a poem saying:
“To avoid the worthy, I am first dismissed from premiership;
To enjoy the wise, I shall raise my cup.
May I ask the visitors at my gate,
How many have come this morning?”
Several days before his dismissal,
several cauldrons in the kitchen leaped out and clashed,
breaking both their legs and ears.
He was subsequently demoted to Yíchūn (宜春) and died there.
Book bag mice become big
Lǐ Línfǔ one day, early in the morning,
took his book satchel.
Doubting its weight,
he opened it to look,
and a large rat leaped out.
It transformed into a dark-colored giant,
its eyes glaring and teeth bared,
looking up at Línfǔ.
He struck it with an object,
and it died instantly.
Línfǔ was disgusted by it.
A month later, he died.
Presuming upon talent and being frivolous
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Liú Xīyí, Wáng Chānglíng, Zǔ Yǒng, Zhāng Ruòxū, Mèng Hàorán, Cháng Jiàn, Lǐ Bái, Dù Fǔ,
though possessing literary renown,
all led wandering lives and were not fortunate.
This was due to presuming upon their talent and being frivolous.
Poem on the Bright Hall's Fire Pearl
Cuī Shǔ composed the poem "Bright Hall's Fire Pearl" saying:
"At night, the twin moons are full;
at dawn, a single star is solitary."
Not long after, Shǔ died,
having no sons,
only one daughter,
named Xīng (Star).
This was indeed a poetic omen.
Lǐ Qiáo, a true talent
The Emperor hosted a feast at Xīngqìng Palace.
Someone presented a "Shuǐdiào Gētóu" (Water Tune Prelude),
saying:
"Mountains and rivers fill my eyes, tears wet my clothes;
how long can wealth and glory last?
Do you not see that on the Fén River today,
only autumn geese fly year after year?"
The Emperor asked who composed this lyric.
It was said to be Lǐ Qiáo.
The Emperor said:
"A true talent!"
Thirty years without hempen mourning clothes
Cuī Lín's family members often rose to high official positions.
Whenever they gathered for a banquet,
their official sashes shone brightly.
A couch was set up for ivory tablets of office,
yet they were still piled on top of it.
For thirty years,
there was no mourning for relatives, whether near or distant.
Jade flute and pipa
The disciples of the Liyuan (Pear Garden) all resided in the North Ward of Yīchūn.
At that time, Mǎ Xiānqī, Lǐ Guīnián, and Hè Huáizhì were thoroughly conversant with musical theory and rhythm.
Ān Lùshān presented several hundred white jade flutes.
A palace eunuch returned from Shǔ,
bringing a pipa as a gift.
Its body was made of luómù wood,
lustrous like jade,
with golden threads and red patterns forming twin phoenixes.
Lǐ Guīnián builds a mansion
The musician Lǐ Guīnián built a residence in Tōngyuán Ward of the Eastern Capital.
The design of its central hall was exquisite and unparalleled.
Today, Pèi Jìngōng's Dìngdǐng Nánmén Villa Hall is it.
Later, Guīnián wandered to Jiāngnán.
Whenever he encountered a beautiful scene, he would sing a few tunes for people,
and none of the guests could help but weep.
Dù Fǔ dedicated a poem to him,
the fragmented line of which says:
"In the season of falling blossoms, I meet you again."
Four walls painted with dragons
During the Kāiyuán era, there was a great drought.
The Emperor built a hall by the Xīn Pond,
and summoned Féng Zhào to paint a dragon on each of the four walls.
On the west wall, a plain dragon writhed as if about to soar.
Wind and clouds arose on the wall with the brushstrokes,
its scales and armor glowed hot,
and white vapor issued from the eaves and corridors.
The waves in the pond surged,
and soon a white dragon rose on the clouds,
bringing a great storm.
Beef stew and white wine
Dù Fǔ was a guest in Léiyáng,
and was disliked by the magistrate.
Fǔ consequently presented a poem.
The magistrate sent him beef stew and white wine,
and he died from overeating and drinking.
Holding the reins in the shade of trees
The Emperor visited Xiùlǐng Palace.
The palace was cramped and very hot.
The Emperor sent someone to observe Yáo Chóng,
who reported:
"He is riding a small horse,
holding the reins in the shade of trees."
The Emperor followed his example,
and immediately forgot the oppressive heat.
Using an iron ruyi as collateral for wine
Emperor Míng used Yè Fǎshàn's magic.
On the night of the Lantern Festival, he traveled from Shàngyáng Palace to Xīliáng Prefecture to view the lanterns,
using an iron rúyì as collateral for wine before returning.
He sent an envoy to retrieve it,
and it was indeed there.
Emperor's music
If instruments are hung on four sides,
it is the music for the Emperor;
if hung on three sides,
it is the music for feudal lords;
if hung on two sides,
it is the music for high officials;
if hung on one side,
it is the music for scholars.
Civil and military dances
Civil dancers stood to the east,
holding pheasant feathers;
military dancers stood to the west,
holding battle-axes.
The Grand Minister of Ceremonies (Dà Cháng Qīng) supervised the music,
standing north of the instrument display;
the Deputy Director of Music (Xiélǜ Láng) held a decorated pole,
wearing green,
with wide sleeves,
and a crown.
Two drummers (Jǐnggǔ)
held vermilion banners to lead the music.
Nuo exorcism
Four Fangxiàng (exorcist figures) were used,
wearing crowns and masks,
with four golden eyes,
dressed in bear skins,
holding spears and shields,
making "nuónuó" sounds,
as if to expel evil.
Five hundred Zhuòzǐ (youth exorcists),
played by young boys,
wore red pleated jackets and green tunics,
and masks.
On the last day of the month, the Nuo exorcism was performed in front of the Zǐchén Hall with palace-hung music.
Left and Right Jiàofāng
During the Kāiyuán era, the Left and Right Jiàofāng (Imperial Music Bureaus) were established,
managed by palace officials.
A Music Official Academy was also established.
Eight-fold Plays
There was a drum called "dāgǔ,"
which is a waist drum.
Once, a man's father was wounded by a tiger.
He went up the mountain to search for the body.
The mountain had eight folds (bāzhé),
hence the tune "bā dié" (eight folds).
The performers wore disheveled hair,
mourning clothes,
and made faces of sorrowful weeping,
representing the state of mourning.
Sū Zhōngláng Pā,
was fond of wine and unconventional.
Whenever there was a singing performance,
he would enter and dance alone.
Today, the performers wear crimson,
and hats,
depicting his drunken state.
There were also "Tàyáoniáng" (Stepping Yao Lady),
"Yángtóu Húntuō" (Sheep's Head Full Detachment),
"Jiǔtóu Shīzi" (Nine-Headed Lion), "Tiàofán" (Jumping Ordinary), "Tǔhuǒ" (Spitting Fire), "Tūnlì" (Swallowing Strength), "Xuánpán Jīndǒu" (Spinning Plate Somersaults).
All these belonged to this department.
Three Dynasties establish proclamations, one person can sing
Singing is the sound of music.
Strings are not as good as bamboo,
bamboo is not as good as the human voice.
Ancient masters were Hán É, Lǐ Yánnián, Mò Chóu.
A good singer must first regulate their breath,
allowing it to rise warmly from the navel to the throat,
then utter the words,
distinguishing between high and low notes,
which can achieve the marvel of stopping clouds and echoing valleys.
There was Wéi Yīn,
who could sing.
He was originally a scholar,
and once wrote a poem himself saying:
"Three dynasties establish proclamations,
one person can sing."
He rose to the rank of general.
Yǒngxīn Song
During the Kāiyuán era,
the palace attendant Xǔ Zǐhé
was a girl from a musician's family in Yǒngxīn County, Jízhōu.
Upon entering the palace, she was known as Yǒngxīn.
She was skilled at creating new melodies.
Under a clear autumn moon,
one turn of her throat,
and the sound resonated across the nine thoroughfares.
One day,
a grand feast was held at Qínzhèng Lóu,
and the clamor of the myriad people
made it impossible to hear the music of the 'Fish and Dragon Hundred Acts'.
Yǒngxīn then swept back her hair and raised her sleeves,
and directly performed a flowing, extended melody.
The square became utterly silent,
as if no one was present.
During the chaos of Fúyáng,
the Six Armies scattered,
and Yǒngxīn was taken by a scholar.
Wéi Qīng, avoiding the troubles, took refuge in Guǎnglíng.
One moonlit night, leaning on a railing,
he heard someone singing a shuǐdiào tune from a boat,
and said:
"This is Yǒngxīn's song."
He boarded the boat to verify,
and they wept together.
Later, the scholar died,
and she fell into a life of hardship.
Before her death,
she said to her mother:
"Mother,
the money tree has fallen!"
Zhāng Hónghóng
During the Dàlì era,
the talented palace woman Zhāng Hónghóng, who originally sang and begged with her father on the streets,
was taken by Wéi Qīng as a concubine.
There was once a musician who composed a new melody.
Before presenting it,
he first sought Wéi Qīng's approval.
Wéi Qīng secretly had Hónghóng listen from behind a screen,
using a few handfuls of small beans to mark the beats.
When the song finished,
Wéi Qīng entered and asked the musician,
who said he had finished singing it.
Wéi Qīng went out and deceived him, saying:
"I have a female disciple
who sang this long ago;
it is not a new tune."
Then, he had Hónghóng sing it from behind the screen,
and everyone present was astonished.
Emperor Jìngzōng summoned her into the palace,
where she was known as 'Jìqǔ Niángzǐ' (Lady Who Remembers Tunes).
When Wéi Qīng died,
Hónghóng reported:
"I was originally a street beggar
who achieved a position within the palace,
and I cannot bear to forget his kindness."
With that, she let out a cry of grief and died.
Mǐ Jiāróng
During the Zhēnyuán era, there was Tián Shùnláng.
During the Chángqìng era, there were Mǐ Jiāróng
and Chén Yìnú.
Dancers
A dancer
is the form of music.
There are 'Great Drooping Hands' (Dà Chuíshǒu)
and 'Small Drooping Hands' (Xiǎo Chuíshǒu).
Some resemble startled swans,
others flying swallows.
'Pósuō'
is a dancing posture;
'Mányán'
is a dance formation.
There are vigorous dances (Jiànwǔ), soft dances (Ruǎnwǔ), character dances (Zìwǔ), flower dances (Huāwǔ), and horse dances (Mǎwǔ).
Dance tunes include Lǜyāo, Sūgǔxiāng, Juézhàhú, Wèizhōu, Tuánrǔxuán, and Gānzhōu, etc.
In character dances, the dancers lean their bodies to the ground
to form characters.
In flower dances, wearing green robes,
they bend their bodies to form flowers.
In horse dances,
the horse-handlers wear green robes,
hold whips, and perform a trotting dance on a raised platform,
all in time with the rhythm.
Sword Dance
During the Kāiyuán era,
Gōngsūn Dàniáng performed the sword dance.
The monk Huáisù's cursive calligraphy greatly improved,
as he based it on the pauses and movements of her dance.
Húxuán Dance
Dances include the Gǔchén Dance and Húxuán Dance.
with both feet remaining on the ball.
Straight-necked and Bent-necked Pípá
Pípá have straight necks
Both involve leaping and treading vertically and horizontally on small spherical balls,
Ancient tunes include "Mòshàng Sāng".
Fàn Yè, Shí Chóng, and Xiè Yì
were all skilled at this music.
Hè Huáizhì used stone for the soundbox,
kun chicken tendons for strings,
and iron for the plectrum.
Painted sash.
Recording Rhythm
The musician Yáng Zhì was skilled at playing the pípá.
His aunt particularly loved it;
she was originally a disciple of Xuānhuī,
later released from the palace,
and resided in Qiúmù Guàn.
Cherishing her art,
she always feared being heard by others,
only playing after midnight.
Yáng Zhì pleaded earnestly but was refused.
She said:
"I swear I will die rather than pass it on to anyone."
Mǎ Zhì lodged in the temple and secretly listened,
greasing his leather belt
and using his hand to mark the ornaments and rhythms on the belt.
The next day, he went to his aunt and played it.
His aunt was greatly astonished.
Mǎ Zhì told her the truth,
and thus the art was passed on through the markings.
During the Xiántōng era,
there was an unknown young man (Wèizhī Láng),
the son of Jiāróng,
who was exceptionally skillful.
Later, there was Wáng Lián'ér.
The stories of Kāng Kūnlún, Cáo Bǎo, and Zhèng Zhōngchéng
are already found in the 'Pípá Lù'.
Zhēng and Kōnghóu
The zhēng
was invented by Méng Tián.
The kōnghóu was the origin of the music of Zhèng and Wèi.
Because its sound was associated with fallen states,
it was called 'Kōngguó zhī Hóu' (Marquis of the Empty State),
or also Kǎnhóu.
There is an ancient yuefǔ tune called "Gōng Wú Dù Hé".
In the past, there was a white-haired madman
who drowned in the river.
His wife, Lì Yù,
composed this tune.
The shēng
was invented by Nǚ Wā,
resembling a phoenix's wing;
it is also called Cēncī.
Lǐ Móu Playing the Flute
This is Qiāng music.
The ancient tune "Luò Méihuā".
During the Kāiyuán era,
Lǐ Móu was unrivaled at the time.
Huángfǔ Zhèng, the prefect of Yuèzhōu, was boating on Jìnghú Lake on a moonlit night,
and ordered Lǐ Móu to play the flute.
An old man came in a small boat
and said:
"I was skilled at this in my youth."
Huángfǔ Zhèng handed Lǐ Móu's flute to him.
The old man played one note,
and the waves stirred.
After several repetitions,
the flute split in the middle.
He then took out a flute from his bosom to finish the tune.
Below the boat, two dragons guarded the boat and listened.
In a moment,
the old man entered his small boat
and disappeared.
Silver-Character Bìlì
The bìlì originally came from the country of Qiūcí,
also called Bēilì.
During Emperor Dézōng's reign,
there was Wèichí Qīng,
who rose to the rank of general
and was skilled in this art.
In Yōuzhōu, there was Wáng Mánú,
who was considered the best player in Hébèi.
Someone said:
"You do not know that in the capital there is General Wèichí,
whose skill is unparalleled, surpassing ancient and modern times."
Mánú immediately went to determine their superiority.
Wèichí Qīng invited him to sit on the floor,
took a silver-character bìlì, and played the Píng Bānshè tune himself.
Mánú wept and bowed, saying:
"Today, I have been fortunate to hear heavenly music,
and only now do I realize my former errors."
He then shattered his instrument
and never played again.
Five-String Lute Player
During the Zhēnguān era,
Zhào Bì was excellent at the five-string lute.
Bái Chuán's satirical admonitions mention a five-string lute player,
playing the Cānjūn.
It began with Shí Dān, the magistrate of Guǎntáo in the Hàn dynasty.
He was accused of embezzlement,
but Emperor Hé, valuing his talent, pardoned him.
At every banquet,
he was made to wear a white lined shirt,
and the jesters were ordered to mock and humiliate him.
He was only released after a year.
Later he became a Cānjūn.
Since the Dàzhōng era, there have been performances with fake women,
and also performances of Brahmins,
striking odes
originated from striking fous.
Guō Dàoyuán used twelve pairs of Yuè odes,
adjusting the water level,
and striking them with chopsticks.
Broken Qin
Léi Shēng of Chéngdū was skilled at breaking qín,
unrivaled in the world.
Clappers
originally had no musical scores.
Huáng Fānchuò created scores,
drawing two ears on paper,
and presented it, saying:
"With ear canals,
there will be no loss of rhythm."
Gōng tone goes and does not return
When Emperor Suí Yángdì toured Jiāngdū,
the musicians played "Ān Gōngzǐ" on the flute.
His father said:
"How did you get this tune?"
They replied:
"It's newly arranged in the palace."
His father said:
"Gōng represents the sovereign,
shāng represents the minister.
This gōng tune goes and does not return;
the imperial tour to the east will surely not come back."
Dàláng Shén
During Empress Tiānhòu's reign,
a scholar was wrongly imprisoned,
and his wife was assigned to the Yètíng.
She then composed the tune "Líbié Nán" to express her sorrow,
naming it "Dàláng Shén,"
which was taken from her husband's family rank.
Fearing discovery,
she changed its name three times,
calling it "Fēi Qiè Zǐ,"
and finally "Yuàn Huíhú."
Yèbàn Yuèqǔ
When Emperor Mínghuáng entered from Lùzhōu to quell the internal strife,
he cut down the gate of Chánglè Mén in the middle of the night,
leading his troops into the palace.
Afterward, he composed "Yèbàn Yuèqǔ."
Water Silkworm Woven Brocade
Old Kāng was originally a wealthy young man from Cháng'ān,
but squandered all his wealth.
He met an old woman holding old, cool, silkworm-woven cotton,
and immediately paid a thousand pieces of gold for it.
Kāng obtained it,
but soon spent it all again.
When Kāng died,
musicians lamented him
and composed a tune,
also named "Débǎozǐ."
Wàng Jiāngnán
Lǐ Wèigōng composed "Wàng Jiāngnán" for his deceased courtesan Xiè Qiūniáng,
also named "Mèng Jiāngnán."
Bái Chuán composed "Yángliǔ Zhī."
Playing the Reed Pipe
Emperor Xuānzōng played the reed pipe
and composed "Qīng Bēi" himself.
When he first took up the pipe,
he ordered Pái'ér Xīn Gǔchú to beat time.
He failed,
and the Emperor glared at him angrily.
Gǔchú, anxious and fearful,
died overnight.
Huáng Cōng
Emperor Tàizōng's warhorse was named "Xiānyáo."
When the horse died,
the Emperor sighed with regret
and ordered musicians to compose this tune.
Puppets
It originated from the siege of Píngchéng by Emperor Hàn Zǔ.
One side of the city faced Mòdú's wife, Èshì,
whose army was stronger than those on the other three sides.
Chén Píng found out that Èshì was jealous,
so he made wooden puppets,
operated by mechanisms,
and made them dance between the ramparts.
Èshì saw them
and thought they were real people.
Fearing that Mòdú would take them as concubines if he captured the city,
she withdrew her troops.
Historians only called it a secret strategy,
disdaining the lowliness of the plan.
Later, it was adapted into a play.
Among those who introduced the singing and dancing was a Guō Láng,
who had shaven hair
and was good at joking and amusing.
He was always at the head of the performers in any play.
Zhēng tone without a fixed pitch
Shùn harmonized the eight sounds,
using metal, stone, silk, bamboo, gourd, earth, leather, and wood,
totaling eight hundred types of musical instruments.
By the Zhōu dynasty, it was changed to gōng, shāng, jué, zhēng, and yǔ,
reducing the instruments to over five hundred types.
The Táng dynasty further reduced them by three hundred types.
Emperor Tàizōng selected string and wind instruments for the Hú music,
and gōng, shāng, jué, zhēng, yǔ were all divided into the four tones: píng, shàng, qù, rù.
The zhēng tone had sound but no fixed pitch.
Fāngxiǎng
Hú music did not have fāngxiǎng,
because its straight板 sound
did not correspond to the other pitches.
Emperor Tàizōng separately kept a piece of iron in the imperial treasury,
named Fāngxiǎng.
The zhēng, which corresponds to twenty-eight pitches,
only has gōng, shāng, jué, and zhēng pitches.
The bridges are temporarily moved to correspond to the twenty-eight pitches.
Luán Gū Fèngzhí
Zhāng Xiàntú failed repeatedly in examinations.
Due to his old age and imperial grace,
he was finally appointed to a minor official position.
He wrote to his family, saying:
"You act as a lonely phoenix,
and I serve as a humble official."
Dreaming of a female crane giving birth to a daughter
When Ōu Yǒngshū was in Yílíng,
he visited Jiāng Shī's temple
and secretly prayed for an heir.
His family dreamed of a crane flying in,
knowing it to be a female crane,
and indeed, a daughter was born,
who was very beautiful.
At eight years old,
she was startled in a nightmare, saying:
"I dreamed a crane flew away."
Not many days later,
she died suddenly.
Dreaming of a lamp
Several governors of Guǎng died consecutively,
most of them having first dreamed of a lamp.
Jiǎ Yè became governor,
dreamed of lamps throughout the commandery city,
and not long after, fell ill and died.
Profound in Xīqīng
Sòng Jǐngshào, a Palace Attendant,
dreamed of being a scholar in the Yúqīng Palace.
Not long after,
he was appointed Scholar of the Bǎowén Pavilion.
His official appointment announcement included the phrase "in Xīqīng."
Lǐ Chángshǐ of Chízhōu
Zhāng Dòng was the Transport Commissioner of Huáinán.
He dreamed someone announced, "Lǐ Chángshǐ of Chízhōu."
Later, a large carp was found in the pond,
which was the one from his dream.
Sìwèi Táng
Wáng Wénmù's wife was fierce and jealous.
Though he was a first-rank official,
he kept no concubines.
He built a hall in the garden behind his residence,
naming it Sānwèi.
Yáng Wéngōng joked with him, saying:
"It could be changed to Sìwèi."
Wáng asked for the explanation,
to which Yáng replied:
"Also fearing your wife."
Sòng Gōng's Dying Instructions
Sòng Jǐngwén Gōng's遗戒 (last instructions) said:
"After my death,
declare the family to be impoverished to manage the funeral.
Use washed and worn clothes,
a hèlàiqiú (a robe made of crane and turtle feathers),
a gauze cap, and hempen shoes.
Three days for the coffin,
three months for the burial.
The tomb should not be restricted by vulgar geomantic superstitions.
The coffin should be made of miscellaneous wood,
reinforced at its four joints,
and sealed with three coats of lacquer, and that is all.
It should be sufficient for several decades to inter my bones, rotten clothes, and cap.
My scholarship did not establish a school,
my writings merely reached the level of ordinary people,
not enough to be handed down to posterity.
As an official, I was below excellent Ěrqiānshí (two thousand piculs) officials,
not among the prominent few.
I had no achievements for the state,
no favors for the people,
so I cannot request a posthumous title,
cannot accept gifts,
cannot seek prominent officials to write a stele inscription,
and no Buddhist or Daoist rituals may be performed.
You must not disobey these instructions and perform them,
for that would mean treating my death as if I were ignorant."
Candle Burns Fútóu
Wáng Xiāng of Héyáng and Chén Xiāng of Zhèngzhōu were reading texts in a leaky house,
and the candle flame burned a hole in Chén Xiāng's fútóu (headwear).
At that time, Wáng Xiāng was excused from court attendance due to illness,
so Chén then exchanged his cap for Wáng's to enter.
After he left,
Wáng Xiāng regretted it and said:
"It was a blossom on his head,
yet he took my fútóu away."
Soon after,
both officials were dismissed from their premierships.
Moreover, Kòu Láigōng, Lǐ Cānzhèng Chānglíng, Zhāng Cānzhèng Bó, and Páng Xiāng Jiè all fell from their horses,
and several months later, they were all dismissed from their positions.
Bamboo Thrives Without Roots
Kòu Láigōng died in Hǎikāng,
and an imperial edict permitted his return for burial.
The route passed through Gōng'ān County in Jīngnán,
and the local people welcomed and sacrificed to him by the roadside,
cutting bamboo and sticking it into the ground
to hang paper money.
The bamboo then thrived without roots.
The local people regarded it as miraculous,
built a temple beside it,
and offered sacrifices with great reverence.
Black Gauze Screen
Generally, looking at
all five colors harms the eyes;
only black does not.
When the Lǐ family ruled Jiāngnán,
the Zhōngshū (Secretariat) all used black gauze screens,
to protect their eyesight.
Wáng Chéngxiāng, when in government,
also used black gauze screens.
From Humble Origins
When Zhāng Gǎoqīng was giving an audience,
Rénzōng said:
"You too come from humble origins."
Gǎo said:
"Your servant was originally a scholar.
Your Majesty promoted your servant,
and now I am a Zhōngchéng (Censor-in-Chief).
My three sons all wear official robes.
Your Majesty's age is advancing,
and the position of heir apparent is vacant.
Your servant is not from humble origins,
Your Majesty is the one from humble origins!"
The Emperor praised and accepted this.
Meeting Again, Unchanged Green as Before
Fàn Fèng was demoted from his position as Gěishìzhōng (Counselor) and
returned to Jìnán several years later.
At Zhāng Shì's garden pavilion west of the city,
he composed a poem during a banquet, saying:
"Reaching the garden again, my body is still robust;
all official duties cast aside, my dream has just awakened.
Only Nánshān and your eyes,
meet again, unchanged green as before."
Zhōnglí's Two Poems
On the wall of the Kāiyuán Temple in Xíngzhōu,
there are two poems by the Five Dynasties recluse Zhōnglí Quán,
saying:
"Enlightened high monks are not easy to encounter,
when shall I return and wish to accompany them?
Knowing my dwelling place connects to the azure sea,
it is distinctively the first peak of Pénglái."
"Do not dislike frequent pursuit of joy and laughter;
scattered thoughts can harm the spirit.
When idle, I count on my fingers from the beginning,
how many people have seen an era of peace?"
Treacherous Clerk of the Three Judicial Offices
Chén Guàn was the Vice-Minister of the Province.
A chief clerk of the Three Judicial Offices was cunning and treacherous,
secretly colluding with powerful favorites.
Whenever he greeted the Vice-Minister,
he would feign a yawn and stretch,
not daring to fully observe the ritual.
Chén was quite displeased
and wanted to dismiss him.
The clerk knew his intention
and served him with even greater diligence.
Chén also treated him well.
One day,
Chén said:
"My residence wants to invite female guests,
who can manage it?"
The clerk said:
"I can supervise."
What was needed for the banquet,
not even one-tenth was prepared.
The clerk took his young daughter
and went to Dōnghuámén Street to insert a paper sign,
saying:
"For Chén Shěngfù's invitation of female guests,
the kitchen manager has no money to prepare.
Now I am selling this daughter,
asking for so much money."
He secretly conspired with the patrolmen to report this,
and Chén was eventually dismissed from his post.
The Matchless Inn has the Bālóu
Zhào Cānzhèng retired from office,
returning to his old residence at Sòngmén in Suīyáng,
which was converted into a guesthouse,
then called the Matchless Inn.
Lǐ Zhōngshī was the administrator of Xīqīng.
The people of Jīngshī
built a new wine tower.
Lǐ admired its grandeur,
and someone grandly said:
"It has the Bà."
People at the time said:
"In Liángyuàn, Shúpíng has the Matchless Inn;
in Luòshī, Jūnxī has the Bālóu."
Ten Years Riding a Horse, Listening to the Court Cocks
Ōu Yǒngshú, while in government,
sent a poem to the recluse Cháng Zhì in Yǐngyīn, saying:
"Laugh at the recluse Cháng in Rǔyīn,
ten years riding a horse, listening to the court cocks."
Later, Wáng Jièfǔ took power,
and summoned Zhì to be Yòuzhèngzì (right corrector) and serve in the Shǐguǎn (Historiography Academy),
so Zhì started his official career.
An unnamed person revised the previous poem, saying:
"Formerly the recluse Cháng in Rǔyīn,
now comes riding a horse, listening to the court cocks."
Zhì previously studied the Chūnqiū,
writing dozens of volumes of commentaries,
considering that the meaning of the sages was all contained therein.
Jièfǔ did not like the Chūnqiū,
so Zhì then completely concealed what he had learned.
In the sixth year of Xīníng,
both Hé (Yellow River regions) suffered famine.
An order was issued that the capital for the Qīngmiáo (Green Shoots) loan program in various places
should temporarily be suspended.
Wáng Píngfǔ jokingly asked Zhì:
"Is your Chūnqiū
also temporarily suspended?"
Diǎnjiàngchún Lyrics
Wáng Píngfǔ, during the Xīníng era,
was the Judge of the Court of Appeals.
Suddenly he composed the court lyrics "Diǎnjiàngchún."
Wèi Tài said:
"The broken stanza has a sense of separation and wandering,
why is that?"
The next year,
he indeed fell into disfavor.
His lyrics said:
"A slight chill on an autumn night,
dreams return as the bright moon pierces the curtains.
A single Wútóng tree, desolate,
just circling the southern branch, a magpie.
The precious zither gathers dust,
the golden wild geese scatter in vain.
Feelings without a place to rest,
temple hair too lazy to comb,
not unlike the Emperor's fickle grace."
Excess from Measurement
Liú Chuò
served as an assistant official dispatched by the Supervisor of the Jingxī Circuit during the Tiānshèng era.
He inspected and measured the grain in various granaries.
He collected over 100,000 shí.
Upon returning to court, he submitted a memorial
requesting that it be handed over to the Three Departments for collection and safekeeping.
At that time, Empress Zhāngxiàn was presiding behind a screen.
She asked:
