"After the measurement, there was still some left. Should it be measured again?"
Liú Chuò said:
"Officials who previously measured often yielded to personal connections
and were unwilling to fully record all receipts."
She then said:
"Do you know Wáng Zēng, Zhāng Zhībái, Lǚ Yíjiǎn, and Lǔ Zōngdào?
These four men
did not attain their positions by collecting surplus grain through measurements."
Liú Chuò was greatly ashamed,
and said to others:
"At that time,
even if there were cracks in the floor tiles of the palace, I would have wanted to hide in them."
Poem on Concealment and Manipulation
Xiàhóu Gōng wrote a poem on various sleight-of-hand tricks, titled "Poem on Concealment and Manipulation," which says:
"Wielding ropes, throwing pearls, then spitting pills,
Concealing and manipulating in a thousand ingenious ways.
The lord sits upright, unable to perceive,
Yet passersby observe with cold eyes."
Zōngshū's Poem
Zhāng Zōngshū had a poem that said:
"Write characters large to guard against old age,
Buy extra gardens to prepare for leisure."
Had Long Waited to Weep for This Person
Zhèng Xiàng was the Prefect of Hángzhōu,
and Wáng Gěng was the Supervisor of Zhèxī.
They often debated each other.
When Gěng died,
Zhèng went to weep for him,
expressing full sorrow.
Someone asked:
"Lord Lóngtú always disliked Dūangōng,
why such profound grief now?"
Fàn Jí said:
"Lord Lóngtú had long waited to weep for this person."
Devious Plot to Kill a Courtesan
Yáng Zī, a scholar, came to the capital to take the imperial examination,
and had a very close relationship with a courtesan.
The courtesan spent all her possessions to support him.
After passing the examination, he had no way to thank her,
so he summoned her to be his wife
and they traveled together to Xiāngyáng.
One post-station away from the prefecture,
he said to her:
"I have had a wife and family for a long time,
and she is fierce and ill-tempered.
She will surely cause you trouble.
How about I give you medicine to die?"
The courtesan said:
"If you can die for me,
why should I hesitate?"
So they drank heavily together,
took poison mixed with wine,
and drank it all at once.
Yáng Zī held his cup and said:
"If we die together now,
my family will have to bury my body,
but your remains
will be immediately thrown into a ditch.
Why don't I bury you and then die?
It would not be too late."
The courtesan said:
"You tricked and lured me here,
and now you deviously poison me!"
Then she cried out loudly and died.
Yáng Zī later ended his career as an Aide in the Bureau of Sacrifices.
Elder Jīn Jiàn
Ǒuyáng Jǐng, a Grand Master of Remonstrance,
was always frivolous.
Elder Jīn Jiàn, lacking provisions for his fast,
was going to borrow rice from Elder Yùquán,
and asked Ǒuyáng Jǐng for a letter of recommendation.
Ǒuyáng Jǐng smiled and said:
"Yes."
When Elder Jīn Jiàn arrived,
Yùquán opened the seal
and found it was a poem,
which read:
"The gourd goes on its own to entangle the gourd."
Lion in the Imperial Garden
Shí Zhōnglì, an Administrator,
was humorous by nature.
During the Tiānxī era, when he was a supernumerary official,
the Xīchéng (Western City) presented a lion,
which was kept in the imperial garden
and given fifteen catties of mutton daily.
He led his colleagues to observe it.
Someone said:
"We are honored to serve as lang officials,
yet we are inferior to a beast."
Shí Zhōnglì said:
"Why do you not know your place?
That is a lion in the imperial garden;
we are merely supernumerary officials.
How can we be compared?"
Temporarily Resting a Fútoú
Zhāng Yì, a Secret Scholar, was the Prefect of Chéngdū.
The monk Wénjiàn sought an audience.
At that time, Zhāng Tángfǔ, the Registrar of Huáyáng, was also in the guest hall.
Tángfǔ wanted to scratch his hair,
so he removed his bird-cap,
glanced at Wénjiàn,
and placed it on the monk's head.
Wénjiàn was furious
and complained to Zhāng Gōng.
Zhāng Gōng asked for the reason.
Tángfǔ said:
"My head was itchy,
and I had nowhere to put down my fútoú.
Seeing that the Master's head was free,
I temporarily rested it there for a short while,
not expecting his anger."
The Crawling Picture
Chén Liè revered ancient rites.
When Cài Jūnmó was in mourning,
Chén Liè said:
"When common people are in mourning,
they crawl to assist.
I shall now do this."
So, wearing black gold-brocaded leather shoes,
he and over twenty students
crawled on their hands and knees,
wailing as they entered the mourning hall.
The women who saw them all laughed.
Cài Jūnmó smiled covertly as he received them.
Immediately,
Lǐ Gòu painted "The Crawling Picture."
Painting with Jī and Flowing Tassels
Ancient poets often sang of "jī-painted flowing tassels,"
but their appearance was unknown.
A craftsman in Nán'ēnzhōu was skilled at "xīxiāo,"
but he also did not understand the matter.
He said:
"What is called 'silver mud' in the capital is this."
He also said:
"To be able to 'jī-paint'"
is what is now called "shēngsè."
I often saw rental shops for funerary items in the capital
that mentioned "broken tassels."
These were woven balls tied to the four corners,
hanging down with five concentric colors.
Flowing tassel curtains were
used by ancient people to adorn the four corners of their curtains.
The Department of State Affairs Has Birth, Old Age, Sickness, and Suffering
In the Xīníng era,
Chancellor Fù suffered from a foot ailment,
and often did not attend court;
Chancellor Zēng was about to retire due to age.
Wáng Jièfǔ, Zhào Yuèdào, and Táng Zǐfāng served as Administrators.
Wáng Jièfǔ daily presented proposals to reform various government affairs;
Zhào Yuèdào found it rather difficult,
but could not oppose him,
only sitting back in his chamber, snapping his fingers and lamenting his suffering;
Táng Zǐfāng repeatedly argued before the Emperor,
and soon after, developed a carbuncle and died.
People in the capital said that
there was a saying in the Department of State Affairs about "birth, old age, sickness, and suffering,"
referring to Wáng Jièfǔ as "birth,"
Chancellor Zēng as "old age,"
Chancellor Fù as "sickness,"
Zhào Yuèdào as "suffering,"
and Táng Zǐfāng as "death."
Dreaming of Holding Up the Sky
Hán Wèigōng, when Prefect of Tàizhōu,
was ill for several days,
and suddenly said:
"I just dreamed twice that I was holding up the sky with my hands."
Afterwards, he supported Emperor Yīngzōng at his princely residence,
and assisted Emperor Shénzōng as Crown Prince.
Always Spoke for the New Policies
Wáng Jīnggōng once said:
"Since the discussion of the New Policies,
Zēng Bù was the one who consistently said they were viable,
and Sīmǎ Guāng was the one who consistently said they were not viable.
The rest all defected and then rejoined,
or were in and out."
When Will My Eyes Turn Red?
In our dynasty,
Hanlin Academicians wear golden belts.
A single scarlet-robed clerk leads the way.
For officials of the Two Bureaus, there are two clerks.
Their hu (tablet) is adorned with a jade fish,
called "heavy gold."
Those who have served long in the Two Administrations
would say:
"When will my eyes be red (from exhaustion),
and when will my waist be yellow (from the golden belt)?"
Those who have patrolled the inner court for a long time
would also say:
"When will my eyes be red and I be in the Two Administrations,
and when will my waist be yellow and heavy (with rank)?"
Gāolí Seeks a Poem from Wáng Píngfǔ
During the Xīníng reign,
an envoy from Gāolí requested a poem by Academian Wáng Píngfǔ (Wáng Ānshí's courtesy name) on the capital.
An imperial decree ordered Yuán Hòuzhī to transcribe it and present it.
Hòuzhī was then acting as the Administrator of Jīngzhōu.
He went to Píngfǔ to request a new work.
Píngfǔ jokingly composed a poem saying:
"Who sent the poetic immortal to the Phoenix Pool,
intending to send a merchant past Chicken Forest?"
Teasing Chén Yà
Cài Jūnmó teased Chén Yà saying:
"Chén Yà with a heart (心) is always evil (惡)."
Chén replied:
"Cài Xiāng without a mouth (口) becomes frail (衰)."
Later, Chén Yà was appointed Prefect of Nán'ēnzhōu.
He wrote a letter to his relatives and old friends saying:
"The prefect's five horses and twin banners
are merely a title;
crabs for one coin, two of them,
that is the plain truth."
The Aide's Face is the Color of His Robe
Hú Dàn Bái, who was the Compiler of Imperial Edicts, was dismissed from his post
and made Tōngpàn of Xiāngzhōu.
Xiè Mì, the Prefect, often came to his courtyard to drink wine,
his face flushed.
Xiè jokingly said:
"The Aide's face is the color of his robe."
Hú replied:
"The Scholar's heart is like his fú tóu (hat)."
Hú at that time wore scarlet.
Yánluó Sees a Vacancy, Please Hurry to Take Up Your Post
Wáng Jiè was bright and straightforward,
and his speech was often unconventional,
people called it "mind wind."
During the Xīníng reign,
he was transferred from Provincial Judge to Prefect of Húzhōu.
Wáng Jīnggōng sent him a poem saying:
"How beautiful is the Prefect of Wúxīng,
Liǔ Yùn's poetic talent is not much more.
I imagine the local people welcoming him as he alights from his palanquin,
on the isle of white duckweed, stirring up blue waves."
Because 'wind' (風, Fēng) can stir up waves.
Jiè understood his meaning
and wrote ten poems in response to the opening line.
One of them said:
"How beautiful is the Prefect of Wúxīng,
the Prefect has always detested Zhù Tuó.
If I do not become a Pillar of the State in life,
then in death I should replace Yánluó."
The Duke (Wáng Jīnggōng) laughed and said:
"Yánluó sees a vacancy,
please hurry to take up your post."
My Traces Are Increasingly Obscured
Zhāng Zhù, as Circuit Fiscal Commissioner of Jīngdōng,
was demoted to Tōngpàn of Tàipíngzhōu due to an official matter.
Gě Yuán was appointed Director of Mines and Metallurgy.
He requested Zhù's credentials,
intending to recommend him.
Zhù composed a poem saying:
"The Supervising Director of Mines and Metallurgy is a new appointment,
a rank one step higher than mine.
If you issue a recommendation and request my credentials,
my traces will become increasingly obscured."
Court Music Bureau Variety Show
During the Xīníng reign,
at a variety show of the Court Music Bureau,
Hóu Shūxiàn, who was then Acting Director of the Directorate of Waterways, had recently died.
A performer played a Daoist priest good at out-of-body travel,
and a monk good at entering meditation.
Someone asked the spirit what it had seen,
and it said:
"Recently I went to the Grand Heaven,
and saw someone in golden and purple robes in the Jade Emperor's hall.
Looking closely, it was actually Han Shìzhōng.
He held an object in his hands,
saying it was a 'Myriad Years Golden Branches and Jade Leaves Map' to present to the state."
The monk said:
"Recently I entered meditation,
and sat until I reached hell.
I saw someone in scarlet robes with a fish ornament by Yánluó's hall.
It was Hóu Gōngbù, Acting Director of the Directorate of Waterways.
He also held an object in his hands,
saying it was a 'Map of Shallow River of Nàihé (Styx)',
saying he wanted to dig a separate river channel."
At that time, Shūxiàn was promoting water conservancy,
this was meant to satirize the emperor.
Gǒng Dàqīng Presents Life Release
During the Xīníng reign,
Gǒng Dàqīng Shēn,
was skilled at ingratiating himself with powerful officials.
On the Prime Minister's birthday,
he would prepare a feast for monks and present a petition,
and offer caged magpies and pigeons.
When the Prime Minister was holding a family banquet,
he would open the cages in the guest chamber, insert his hu (tablet) into his belt,
and personally take out the magpies and pigeons.
He would kneel and release them.
With each bird released,
he would pray:
"May the Prime Minister live for one hundred and twenty years."
Caught in One Net
Sū Shùnqīn was Supervisor of the Imperial Bureau of Memorials.
Because he held a ceremony to worship the gods in the tenth month with his colleagues in the bureau,
Censor Liú Yuányú impeached him and he was imprisoned.
He was charged with embezzlement as supervisor and stripped of his rank.
All who attended the gathering were also banished.
Liú said to the then Prime Minister:
"Together, we caught them all in one net."
Eating Male Placenta
In Guìzhōu, when a woman gave birth to a son,
they would finely chop the placenta,
cook it with five flavors,
and invite close relatives to a banquet to eat it.
Those not invited would surely become angry and quarrel.
Marrying Off a Wife During Life, Divorcing a Wife After Death
Wáng Pāng,
the Prime Minister's second son,
had a mental illness.
He married Páng Shì,
but they were not harmonious and separated,
and he married her off (to someone else).
At that time, Hóu Shūxiàn died,
and his wife did not maintain her mourning curtains.
The Prime Minister reported the matter and had her sent away.
At the time, people said:
"Assistant Minister Wáng married off his wife during his life,
Director Hóu divorced his wife after death."
Lizards Pray for Rain
During the Xīníng reign,
the capital suffered a long drought.
Following ancient custom,
people in the alleys stored water in jars,
inserted willow branches,
and floated lizards in them.
Children would shout:
"Lizard,
lizard,
stir up clouds and spit mist.
Send down rain and muddy the ground,
then you may go home."
At that time, lizards could not always be found,
so geckos were often used instead,
but they would die immediately in water.
The children would then say:
"Woe is me,
woe is me,
I am a gecko.
So dim-witted,
how can I bring sweet rain?"
Dùyuán Jiǎ Yì
Chén Héshū, when he was a candidate for examination,
was generally unconstrained.
Later, when he took the special examination,
he suddenly became very simple and honest.
At the time, he was called "the readily ripe Yán Huí."
At that time, Kǒng Wénzhòng, in his policy recommendations,
spoke of things in the world that caused lamentation and profound sorrow.
Soon after, he was dismissed.
Chén said:
"Kǒngzǐ is truly Dùyuán Jiǎ Yì."
Wáng Píngfǔ said:
"Dùyuán Jiǎ Yì is a good match for the readily ripe Yán Huí."
Containing All Living Beings Under Heaven
Scholar Cáo Kuí made a large-sleeved robe,
intending it to contain all living beings under Heaven.
Yáng Wèi replied:
"This can only hold one person."
Revised Biography of Duke Péi
Zhāng Shòu 貌甚美。
He often painted his likeness and sent it to his elder brother, Huán,
who adapted Péi Jìngōng's encomium for a true portrait, saying:
"Your figure is very tall,
your face is very prominent.
You are not a general,
nor a chancellor.
A piece of spiritual platform,
which painting cannot depict."
The following year, strong and healthy, I came again
to the capital to offer sacrifices at the Sheji altar.
Many close officials were dispatched.
Wáng Yǔyù, who had been in the Two Prohibited Areas for twenty years,
wrote a poem in the斋宮, saying:
"Neighboring cocks haven't stirred, but the morning carriage urges me on,
again to the spiritual temple to drink a cup of wine."
He laughed at himself, "Knowing my deafness is not enough,
next year, strong and healthy, I will come again."
Heavenly Dog coming down to handle official business
Zēng Gǒng was the prefect of Xiāngzhōu.
The imperial court sent envoys to inspect water conservancy,
each selecting two or three suitable persons to handle official business.
One day, Gǒng hosted a banquet for these envoys.
A guest said:
"Yesterday, a heavenly star fell in the southwest,
with a very fierce sound,
and there was also a small star following it."
Gǒng said:
"The small star must be the Heavenly Dog coming down to handle official business."
Yam
Its original name was Shǔyù.
During the Táng Dynasty, Emperor Dàizōng's given name was Yù,
so it was changed to Shānyào.
Emperor Yīngzōng avoided the first character of his given name,
so it was called Yùyào.
Zhōng Shènsī's Memorial
Zhōng Shènsī's family was poor, but he studied diligently.
Chú Mǐnzhī, pitying him,
recommended him in a letter to a wealthy scholar.
But there was no sign of pity for the "royal grandson."
Zhōng took the letter and returned home,
then wrote another memorial, saying:
"The Lǔ arrow flies high,
signifying the inevitable fall of Liáochéng;
Qín cannot cut off the territory,
hoping to return with the Zhào bi."
Tea Table Riddle
Chén Gōnggōng was the prefect of Yángzhōu.
Chén Shàocháng said:
"I recently made a riddle:
four feet straight up,
four feet straight down.
It never descends throughout the year and seasons.
If it descends,
it's either the wind rising or the rain falling."
The Duke did not understand.
Shàocháng said:
"It is the tea table in the Vice Minister's hall.
If there is a banquet,
it means saving for the wind,
and it is difficult to deal with the rain."
Poem on Losing a Tooth
Cáo Yǎn, a Langzhong,
suddenly lost a tooth.
He wrote a poem saying:
"Yesterday, there was coarse sand in my rice,
secretly knocking out an old man's tooth.
Tell my wife and children not to be sad,
with my tongue intact, it's enough to support the whole family."
Disliking singing and dancing
Féng Dāngshì, in his later years, was fond of Buddhism.
When he was the prefect of Bìngzhōu,
he sent a letter to Wáng Píngfǔ, saying:
"The singing and dancing in Bìngzhōu are exquisite and beautiful,
but I close my eyes and dislike them.
I spend my days discussing Zen."
Píngfǔ replied:
"If it is as you have instructed,
you have not yet reached the principle.
Closing your eyes and disliking them,
that is already a difficult case."
Flying Fish renamed Chīwěn
The Hàn dynasty, due to frequent disasters in palaces and temples,
skilled persons said there was a fish in the sky called the Weixing star,
and it was fitting to make its image and crown it on the roof to ward off evil.
Since the Táng dynasty,
temples and palaces still had fish-shaped ornaments,
with tails pointing upwards.
It is unknown when they were renamed Chīwěn,
and their form no longer resembles a fish tail.
Dignified Bearing of Ministers
During the Zhìpíng era,
the National Academy's examination essay topic was "Dignified Bearing of Ministers."
A candidate's essay replied:
"Ministers like Wén Xiànggōng and Fù Xiànggōng
are ministers with dignified bearing;
ministers like Shěn Dāngshì and Shěn Wéntōng
are ministers with handsome appearances."
This meant that Wén and Fù were corpulent,
while Féng and Shěn were handsome youths.
Endowment for Honoring the Aged and Loving Relatives
Ōu Yǒngshū presided over the examination for the "Endowment for Honoring the Aged for their Relatives" essay.
A candidate wrote:
"Observing the appearance of these elders,
it resembles the countenance of my stern father."
Two tunes in plain style
When Emperor Zhāolíng's coffin was led out,
Wáng Yǔyù composed two tunes in plain style, saying:
"The Jade Emperor, morning and evening,
suddenly covered in ochre-yellow robes.
Sorrowful mist enshrouds the golden gate,
Pénglái awaits the arrival of immortal elixir,
but in the human world, things have already become past.
The dragon carriage of imperial guards turns towards the western capital,
banners and pennants fly into the clouds.
The palace maids, gazing at the mausoleum, shed red tears,
not seeing the return of the emerald carriage."
He also said:
"In the late spring of Shànglín Park,
once there was an imperial excursion.
In the water palace, dragon boats played,
the jade flute played till broken, urging the immortal chariot,
once gone, separated by a thousand autumns.
Travelers return to the bend of the Qǔjiāng River,
the past is gone, tears are hard to stop.
Only the imperial tent for passing wine remains,
the water still flows eastward."
Lù Gōng obtains a replacement
Lù Tǎn, a Senior Compiler of the Dali Temple,
once governed a county in the Prime Minister's jurisdiction,
which had a divine record.
It took four years to be relieved of duty.
Tǎn presented a poem, saying:
"Within a hundred li, he is called Lù Gōng,
after three years, getting a replacement is common throughout the world.
Only you have exceeded the norm by four years,
who else will follow this trend?"
His poem was heard at court,
and Tǎn was stripped of an official post and suspended.
Fig
The wooden bun is the fig.
Its taste is sweet and sour;
eating it can induce miasma.
It is especially abundant in Língnán.
Prefectures and counties often take it to arrange high on tea tables,
hence the saying, "Official banquets often feature stacked wooden buns."
Some say that outside Língnán, wooden buns are carved,
with the characters "Dàzhōng Xiángfú" carved on the bottom,
fifty pairs made in the same way.
This is a mistake by those who speak of it.
Who today is not Zhèng Jiàorén?
When Wáng Jièfǔ was prime minister,
he promoted officials without proper order.
When he was dismissed from his post again,
many slandered him.
When the Duke arrived in Jīnlíng,
whenever he obtained fresh fish,
he often released them into the pond.
A disciple wrote a poem saying:
"You must go to the pondside yourself and see,
who today is not Zhèng Jiàorén?"
Impeaching the imperial meal for having hair
Generally, if a Censor did not speak of official matters for a hundred days, he would be dismissed as an outside official.
侍御史 Wáng Píngyuan reached one hundred days without speaking of official matters.
Some said:
"The Censor is waiting for an opportune moment to act;
if he speaks,
it must be an important matter."
One day, he submitted a memorial,
impeaching the imperial meal for having hair.
The wording was:
"What kind of dignified countenance is this,
suddenly to see a curly strand?"
Fàn Wénzhèng's mosquito poem
Fàn Xīwén supervised the Xīxī salt field in Tàizhōu.
The area had many mosquitoes.
He wrote a poem saying:
"When full, they are heavy like cherries,
when hungry, light as willow catkins.
Just know to leave from here,
no need to ask about the future."
Three Obstinacies
During the Huángyòu reign,
Chángshā had "three stubbornnesses" (sān ǎo):
The elder of Kāifú Monastery shaved his head every season,
while Fán Zhùzuò Zhìshèn shaved his head every three days—
this was the first stubbornness.
Officer Sū, whose father had died, happily drank,
while Inspector Lín, whose wife had died, lived by her tomb—
this was the second stubbornness.
At that time, a frontier minister was a prefect;
he would not act without bribes.
Accountant Lù Jìng
never accepted bribes in his life—
this was the third stubbornness.
Shànxuè Courier Station
South of Xiāngzhōu there was a courier station
named Shànquè,
which was the Shànxuè Courier Station of the Táng dynasty.
It was the place where Chúnyú Kūn released a swan.
Liǔ Zǐhòu and Liú Mèngdé offered sacrifices to Mr. Chúnyú at Shànxuè Courier Station.
This is that very place.
Do not return to a place of triumph
Zhēnzōng summoned Chén Tuán to the capital.
Many literati and officials sought his words.
Chén Tuán said:
“Do not linger in places of ease,
and do not return to places of triumph.”
Zháo yě mǎ liú
Performers in the capital would spread various objects on the ground,
and send a macaque to identify them,
then say "Zháo yě mǎ liú."
During the Shàoxī reign,
the *zhuàngyuán* Yè Zǔqià attended a banquet.
A *jìnshì* who had failed the examination composed a poem, saying:
“For what reason do you come to enjoy spring?
You must have intentions to cherish the fragrant season.
Let not horse hooves trample scattered flowers into fragments,
but leave them for the sorrowful to get drunk upon as a mat.”
Sòng Luójiāng
During the Qìnglì reign,
a palace guard entered the palace gate without permission.
Censor Sòng Xī requested that a Luójiāng dog be kept in the inner court.
At the time, it was called Sòng Luójiāng,
or also Sòng Shéngǒu.
Volume Sixteen
End.
Drawing gourds from a template
Táo Gǔ had been in the Hanlin Academy for a long time
and hoped for a major appointment.
His partisans therefore spoke of his extensive contributions to the emperor,
subtly probing the emperor's will.
Tàizǔ said:
“Hanlin academicians draft decrees
by consulting old precedents from their predecessors.
It's what people call 'drawing gourds from a template.'
What contributions are there?”
Táo Gǔ wrote a poem, saying:
“Official positions must come from where one is born,
talent matters not if one has none when needed.
Laughable is Academician Táo of the Hanlin,
who every year draws gourds from a template.”
Questions about ghosts and spirits at Xuānshì, and books on the Fengshàn sacrifice at Màolín
Wáng Yǔchēng, when exiled to become prefect of Huángzhōu, stated in his memorial:
“Regarding questions about ghosts and spirits at Xuānshì,
how can I hope to return alive?
Regarding books on the Fengshàn sacrifice at Màolín,
I can only expect them after death.”
Zhēnzōng found his words resentful.
At that time, in his prefecture, two tigers fought and one ate the other.
The diviner said:
“The calamity lies with the prefect.”
So he was transferred to become prefect of Qízhōu.
The fighting ceased, but Wáng Yǔchēng had already died.
The Battle of Chányuān
Only Kòu Zhǔn requested the emperor to lead the campaign personally.
Lǐ Hàng and Sòng Shí supported him.
Chén Yáosǒu requested the emperor to take refuge in Shǔ.
Wáng Qīnruò requested the emperor to take refuge in Jiāngnán.
The emperor mentioned this to Duke Lái.
The Duke said:
“Who proposed these two schemes?
They should be executed and their blood used to anoint the drums,
then we can march north.”
The emperor then decided to proceed.
A general with good fortune is better than a general with wisdom
Zhēnzōng, at Chányuān,
said:
“The barbarian cavalry has not yet retreated.
If the Tiānxíong Army cuts off their rear,
and by some chance is trapped and annihilated,
then all of Héshuò will become barbarian territory.
Who can guard Wèi for me?”
The Duke said:
“A general with good fortune is better than a general with wisdom.
Wáng Qīnruò's good fortune and prosperity are not yet exhausted;
he should be made to guard it.”
When Duke Wáng heard the command,
he was at a loss.
Duke Lái poured a large cup of wine and made him drink it,
calling it "the mounting cup,"
and said:
“Counselor, strive hard.
Upon your return, you will be among my colleagues.”
Wáng Qīnruò entered Wèi.
Barbarian soldiers were everywhere,
blocking the four gates.
He sat precariously all day.
Seven days later, the barbarians retreated.
He was summoned and made a Píngzhāngshì.
The low status of the three-rank palace guards is evident
Tàizōng wished to know all matters under heaven,
so even minor officials could present their views.
Wáng Yǔchēng submitted a memorial, saying:
“The three-rank palace guards (sān bān fèng zhí),
their lowly status is evident.
Recently, upon their return from missions,
they too were allowed to ascend the hall.”
Not long after,
Wáng Yǔchēng was demoted to Vice Military Commissioner of Shāngzhōu for some matter.
One day,
during a national day of mourning where incense was offered,
a man in a purple robe holding a tablet stood by the side of the hall.
Wáng Yǔchēng thought his rank was high
and wished to arrange their positions in order of seniority.
The man said:
“My rank is indeed 'knowable'.”
Wáng Yǔchēng asked for the reason.
He said:
“You once said: 'The three-rank palace guards (sān bān fèng zhí),
their lowly status is evident (bēi jiàn kě zhī)'.
My official position is 'borrowed rank' (jiè zhí),
which is indeed 'knowable' (kě zhī).”
Dīng Jìngōng, the Crane Chancellor
When Dīng Jìngōng was Commissioner of the Yùqīng Zhāoyìng Palace,
whenever there was a *jiào* ritual or sacrifice,
he would report that immortal cranes were circling and dancing.
And when recording the Eastern Fengshàn sacrifice,
he also said immortal cranes led the way.
When Kòu Lái Gōng was acting prefect of Shǎnfǔ,
he sat in a mountain pavilion.
Dozens of crows flew by, cawing.
The Duke smiled and said:
“If Dīng Wèi saw this,
he would surely call them 'black cranes'.”
Moreover, because Dīng Wèi claimed descent from Lìngwēi,
he was fond of speaking of immortal cranes,
and both were called the Crane Chancellor.
The house slave stole silver utensils
When Zhāng Wéndìng Gōng Qíxián was Surveillance Commissioner of Jiāngnán,
during a family banquet,
a slave stole several silver utensils and hid them in his bosom.
The Duke watched him closely but said nothing.
Later, when he became prime minister,
many of his servants obtained official ranks,
but this slave never received any emolument.
He found an opportunity to weep and confess.
The Duke said:
“Do you remember stealing my silver in Jiāngnán?
I kept it in my heart for thirty years and told no one,
and you also did not know.
I promote and demote a hundred officials,
cleansing the foul and exalting the pure.
How could I recommend a thief?
Considering that you have served me for a long time,
I will now give you three hundred thousand coins.
You cannot stay here any longer.”
The slave bowed in gratitude and left.
It's hard to be a retired Bodhisattva
Sū Yìjiǎn had received the favor of Tàizōng
and was particularly ambitious and impetuous by nature.
When he was dismissed from his post as Counselor and became Prefect of Dèngzhōu,
he was just past his prime,
and sighed at his inability to bear the idleness and coolness of his new position.
He wrote a poem for a monk, saying:
“The two emaciated ministers are thirty-six,
their temperament not much different from yours, master.”
He also wrote to his relatives and old friends, saying:
“It's hard to be a retired Bodhisattva.”
He ultimately did not return to official service and died.
People say that the ambitious and impetuous Xiàhóu Jiāzhèng,
whose official position was humble,
was fond of alchemy (burning silver) all his life.
He often said:
“If I could see one coin's worth of mercury-silver,
I would have no regrets even if I only served as an official for one day.”
Both failed in their ambitions and died.
Qián Xīgōng Wéiyǎn, from Grand Councilor, became a Commissioner-Chancellor,
and sighed, saying:
“If only I could put my mark on the very last yellow document, it would be enough.”
Poetry of Xià Zhènggōng
Xià Zhènggōng Sǒng,
because his father died in the service of the state, was granted a three-rank official position.
He took his compositions and presented them to Lǐ Wénjìnggōng Hàng.
There were lines like, "The mountain range breaks like a wasp's waist,
The stream parts like a swallow's tail."
The next day,
he brought a poem in his sleeve to present,
begging to be exchanged for a civilian post.
Later, he passed the Imperial Examination (Zhìkē),
and while answering policy questions in the court,
an old eunuch said,
"I have seen many people,
this virtuous and talented man will certainly become noble in the future."
He asked for a poem on a Wú-patterned silk handkerchief.
The Duke inscribed,
"Inside the curtain, the imperial robes shine with embroidery,
Before the palace, banners and pennants wave like dragons and snakes.
With sweeping strokes, he writes three thousand characters,
Alone facing the Vermilion Terrace, the sun has not yet set."
Later, he was dismissed from the Privy Council (Shūfǔ) and guarded Nánjīng.
He wrote a poem saying,
"How grand is the balance of creation,
Personally wearing a jade Qílín at my waist.
Planting peach and plum trees on a moonlit night by the southern lake,
I intend to spend ten springs in Suīyáng."
He also said,
"By the Hǎiyàn Bridge, the spring water runs deep,
Hardly any dust reaches the shade of the flowers.
Unconcerned whether others know my inner thoughts,
The sand gulls naturally trust this heart of mine."
Establishing the Empress
Zhēnzōng wanted to establish an empress,
and asked Grand Councillor (Cānzhèng) Zhào Ānrén,
"I wish to make the worthy imperial concubine, Lady Liú, empress,
what do you think?"
He replied,
"She comes from a humble background,
and cannot be the mother of the realm."
The Emperor informed Wáng Qīnruò,
who said,
"Your Majesty might as well ask Ānrén whom he wishes to establish?"
The Emperor indeed asked him,
and Zhào replied,
"Consort Dé, Lady Shěn, is from the family of the former court's prime minister, Shěn Lún,
and is suitable to be the empress of the sagely ruler."
Jìgōng said,
"I know why this is;
Ānrén was once a retainer of Shěn Lún."
Zhào was dismissed from his post as Grand Councillor not long after,
and Consort Liú was eventually established,
who became Empress Regent Míngsù.
Guān Láigōng's Posthumous Title Zhōngmǐn
At the end of Tiānxī era,
Zhēnzōng fell ill,
and Empress Regent Zhāngxiàn Míngsù gradually became involved in governance.
Guān Láigōng then wished to depose the Empress,
establish Rénzōng,
honor Zhēnzōng as the Retired Emperor,
and execute Dīng Wèi, Cáo Lìyòng, and others.
All imperial edicts,
he had Yáng Yì compose,
and was about to act.
It happened that Láigōng's words were leaked to someone.
Jìngōng rode a calf-cart by night to Lìyòng's house to plan,
and upon entering, informed the Empress Regent,
accusing Láigōng of rebellion,
and having him exiled to the sea.
This incident was similar to that of Shàngguān Yí.
When Zhāngxiàn passed away,
Rénzōng issued an edict to clear his冤 grievance,
and gave him the posthumous title "Zhōngmǐn."
Yì was given the posthumous title "Wén." The edict read:
"At the end of Tiānxī,
the government gradually declined,
he was able to cooperate with a chief minister,
and vigorously resisted all extremes."
Why Were the Four Villains Not Transferred Far Away?
After Dīng Jìngōng was exiled to Zhūyá,
he submitted a memorial vehemently stating his merits in establishing the emperor,
and defending himself against false accusations.
When Shénzōng was in the Crown Prince's Palace,
Sūn Sīgōng served as his lecturer.
One day, while lecturing on the Mèngzǐ,
he reached the passage, "When one is helped to the utmost,
the world will follow him;
When one is helped the least,
his relatives will abandon him."
Sīgōng generally cited instances of being helped and followed,
but did not mention "his relatives will abandon him."
The Emperor said,
"Wēizǐ,
an uncle of Zhòu,
carried the sacrificial vessels and entered Zhōu;
was this not relatives abandoning him?"
Sīgōng was astonished and convinced.
Investigating the Ever-Normal Granary Law
After the Ever-Normal Granary Law (Chángpíngfǎ) was implemented,
the Assistant Director of the Imperial Censorate (Tóngzhī Jiànyuàn), Sūn Jué, memorialized,
"In the various counties within the prefectural jurisdiction,
suppression and encroachment are common."
The Emperor ordered Jué to jointly investigate with the Prefectural Circuit Inspector.
Jué memorialized,
"In ancient times, officials were established,
some were speakers,
some were doers.
The speaker was not expected to necessarily act,
and the doer was not expected to be able to speak.
I am an official of words,
how can I also carry out every single action?"
He begged to be relieved of the joint investigation command.
The Emperor was angered by his inconsistency,
and demoted him to Prefect of Guǎngdé Commandery.
Sabotaging the New Laws
Zēng Bù was the Commissioner of Finance (Sānsīshǐ).
He argued that the Market Trade Bureau (Shìyì) in the capital was inconvenient.
Now, Lǚ Jiāwèn is in charge of the Market Trade Bureau,
dispatching officials to various places to buy goods,
prohibiting merchants from lodging in inns,
and thus engaging in monopolization himself,
which is not the original intention of establishing the Market Trade Bureau.
Lǚ Huìqīng considered this an act of sabotaging the New Laws,
and Bù was demoted to Prefect of Ráozhōu.
Huìqīng then became a Grand Councillor.
Banishing Zheng Music Is Not as Good as Keeping Flatterers Away Wáng Jīnggōng, when first serving as Grand Councillor,
once read a short lyric poem by Yàn Yuánxiàn.
He said,
"Is it permissible for a prime minister to write such things?"
Píngfǔ said,
"He merely wrote it on a whim, indulging himself;
his accomplishments are far more than just this."
Lǚ Jífǔ, who held a position in the Academy (Guǎnzhí),
was also present and said,
"To govern, one must first banish Zheng music;
how much more so if one writes it oneself?"
Píngfǔ, with a stern expression, said,
"Banishing Zheng music is not as good as keeping flatterers away."
From then on, Lǚ and Píngfǔ fell out.
Painting the Refugee Map
At the end of Xīníng era,
there was a great famine in the northeast,
and the common people became refugees.
Zhèng Xiá, an imperial appointee who oversaw the Ānshàng Gate,
painted a map of the refugees and submitted a memorial detailing the failings of the current administration.
Xiá was exiled.
Vice Censor-in-chief (Zhōngchéng) Dèng Wǎn and Director of the Imperial Censorate (Zhī Jiànyuàn) Dèng Rùnfǔ stated that
Wáng Ānguó, a collator in the Secretarial Academy (Mìgé Jiàolǐ), encouraged his words,
with the intention of slandering his elder brother.
Because of this, he was dismissed and returned to his hometown, where he died.
He was an extraordinary talent of the realm,
and everyone in the world lamented his loss.
Begging to Cook Lǚ Jiāwèn
In the tenth year of Xīníng,
there was a drought in the capital.
Privy Councilor (Shūmìshǐ) Wáng Sháo said,
"Bǔ Shì begged to cook Sāng Hóngyáng to bring rain.
Now, the Market Trade Bureau (Shìyì) exploits the people's profits,
ten times more than Hóngyáng.
I beg to cook Lǚ Jiāwèn to apologize to the world,
and then the sweet rain can be brought."
Dream of Lingzhī Palace
Wáng Ānguó was on duty overnight at the Chóngwén Academy.
He dreamt that he was invited to the seashore,
where the palaces were magnificent,
and flutes and pipes played loudly.
It was titled "Lingzhī Palace."
Someone across the water stopped him and said,
"The time has not yet come;
for now, you must leave."
He suddenly awoke from the dream,
and the palace bells had already rung.
Píngfǔ wrote a poem saying,
"Ten thousand acres of surging waves, leaves fly,
Flutes and pipes play in the palace named Lingzhī.
Wielding the brush, it is unlike the human world,
The Chánglè bell rings as the dream awakens."
Wáng Jīnggōng in Power
Guō Xiángzhèng (郭祥正) was the Prefect of Xúnzhōu (潯州) and Wǔgāng (武岡) County.
He presented a memorial to the throne, requesting that the policies of the empire
be entirely subject to Wáng Ānshí's (王安石) discretion,
and that anyone holding a differing opinion, even a high minister, should be dismissed.
The Emperor asked Jīnggōng (荊公) (Wáng Ānshí),
"Do you know Guō Xiángzhèng?
His talent seems usable."
Jīnggōng said,
"He is manipulative and unprincipled."
When the Emperor produced Guō's memorial,
Jīnggōng was ashamed to be recommended by such a person,
and strongly argued that he was unusable.
Guō Xiángzhèng subsequently retired.
Constructing the Chuányán Pavilion (傳嵓亭)
Lǐ Shīzhōng (李師中) frequently disagreed with Jīnggōng's views.
Wishing to reconcile, Lǐ
built the Chuányán Pavilion in Shūzhōu (舒州),
because Jīnggōng had once served as an assistant official there.
Wú Xiàozōng (吳孝宗), in his policy recommendations, strongly denounced the New Policies.
Afterwards, he wrote "Aleyi" (巷議) (Street Debates) in ten chapters,
stating that everyone in the streets and alleys discussed the excellence of the New Policies.
Jīnggōng particularly disdained his character.
Who Remembers the Old Man at Jade Gate?
Cài Tǐng (蔡挺),
after the Bàoyuán (寶元) reign, served multiple border assignments.
In the early Xīníng (熙寧) era, he was still the commander of Píngliáng (平涼).
He composed a song
that contained the line, "Who remembers the old man at Jade Gate?"
This became widely circulated in the capital.
Not long after,
he was summoned to serve as the Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs.
Dèng Wǎn (鄧綰) Loses His Post
When Wáng Jīnggōng (王荊公) resumed political power,
after having expelled Lǚ Huìqīng (呂惠卿),
his subordinates again resorted to flattery to secure their positions.
A man named Liàn Hēngfǔ (練亨甫)
said to Dèng Wǎn (鄧綰), the Censor-in-Chief:
"Why don't you suggest to the Emperor
that the Chancellor be treated with special deference,
that his son Zǐpáng (子雱) be made Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs,
that all his brothers be appointed to the Hànlín Academy and Secretariat,
that his sons-in-law and nephews all hold palace library posts,
and that he be granted residences in the capital?"
Dèng Wǎn repeated all these suggestions as advised,
and the Emperor merely nodded.
He also recommended his associates for Censorate posts,
and consequently lost his position and was appointed Prefect of Hào Zhōu (號州).
The imperial decree stated:
"His thoughts are quite perverse,
his nature treacherous and deceitful.
When discussing matters and recommending people,
he does not adhere to his duties."
It also stated:
"My treatment of you
was clearly sincere.
Your service to me
was motivated by evil."
Lost Horse, Severed Snake
Zēng Lǔgōng (曾魯公) was particularly skilled in parallel prose.
When Zēng Bù (曾布) was Commissioner of Finance,
he was dismissed for criticizing the Market Exchange Law.
Lǔgōng sent him a letter saying:
"The old man at the frontier lost his horse;
there is no need to be sad yet.
The Chu (楚) Prime Minister severed the snake;
blessings will surely follow."
Lavish Burial for an Intact Body, Simple Burial for Crushed Bones
Zhāng Shìzhōng (張侍中) and Yàn Chéngxiàng (晏丞相) were both buried in Yángzhái (陽翟).
Thieves broke into Zhāng's tomb
and found many gold treasures.
They then repaired his coffin
and covered the entrance.
Next, they opened Yàn's tomb.
They heard what sounded like wild beasts roaring.
Frightened, the thieves
called one person to enter with them.
They then heard the sound of weapons and drums.
The thieves called another person to enter,
and then it became silent.
The three thieves said,
"The spirit of the Prime Minister must be here."
When they broke through the inner coffin,
there was nothing at all.
The thieves were enraged,
and crushed his bones with an axe before leaving.
Zhāng's lavish burial resulted in an intact body,
while Yàn's simple burial led to crushed bones.
Such things are truly unpredictable.
A Thirty-Year-Old Mother Turning Her Child Upside Down
Miáo Zhèn (苖振) came in fourth in the imperial examinations.
He was summoned for a test for a palace library post.
Prime Minister Yàn (晏) said,
"You should review a bit."
Miáo Zhèn replied,
"How can a thirty-year-old mother
turn her child upside down?"
After the test,
he indeed was not selected.
The Duke (Yàn) laughed and said,
"Mr. Miáo did indeed turn his child upside down."
Punishing a Courtesan with a Large Cup
Wáng Sháo (王韶) was dismissed from his post as Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs and became Prefect of Èzhōu (鄂州).
During a banquet with guests,
he brought out his household courtesans.
A guest named Zhāng Xù (張續), drunk, tugged at a courtesan's clothing,
stepping forward to embrace her.
The courtesan wept and complained to Wáng Sháo.
All the guests turned pale.
Wáng Sháo said,
"I brought you out to entertain the guests,
but instead you made a guest displeased."
He ordered a large cup to be brought and punished the courtesan.
Everyone admired his broad-mindedness.
Presenting a Painting of Fàn Lǐ (范蠡) Traveling the Five Lakes
Chén Gōnggōng (陳恭公) was the Prefect of Bózhōu (亳州).
On his birthday,
many relatives presented paintings of the God of Longevity.
His nephew, Shìxiū (世修), alone presented a painting of Fàn Lǐ traveling the Five Lakes,
and praised it, saying:
"How worthy was Táo Zhū (陶朱)!
He established the hegemony of Yuè (越) and pacified Wú (吳).
His fame achieved, he retired,
in a small boat on the Five Lakes."
Chén Gōnggōng immediately accepted his resignation that day,
and retired the following year.
If He is Called Ma Mo (Horse Silent), How Can He Bray Like a Donkey?
Liú Bān (劉攽) was witty and jocular by nature.
In the Xīníng (熙寧) era, he served as an examiner.
He set the examination topic as "On the Boundlessness of Thought through Teaching."
A candidate requested,
"What is the great image of this hexagram?"
Liú Bān replied,
"If you want to see an elephant,
you should go to the Southern Imperial Park."
Ma Mo (馬默) was a Censor
and impeached Liú Bān for being frivolous,
arguing that he should not be placed in the scholarly institutions.
Liú Bān said,
"Since he is called Ma Mo (Horse Silent),
how can he bray like a donkey?"
Lǚ Jiāwèn (呂嘉問) was in charge of the Market Exchange Bureau.
Zēng Bù (曾布) impeached him for illegal conduct,
but instead was punished himself,
and Lǚ Jiāwèn continued his work as before.
Liú Bān said,
"How could I have expected Zēngzǐ (曾子) to move aside
and look so stern?"
Lǚ Jiāwèn's courtesy name was Wàngzhī (望之).
Liú Bān's Memorial of Thanks
Liú Bān (劉攽) and Wáng Jiè (王介) served as examiners together.
A candidate used the character "xù" (畜) (animal, domesticate).
Wáng Jiè considered this a violation of the Emperor's taboo name (Xù - 緒),
but Liú Bān argued it should not be avoided,
leading to a dispute.
Wáng Jiè insulted Liú Bān with harsh words,
and was subsequently fined.
Censor-in-Chief Lǚ Gōngzhù (呂公著) was displeased with Liú Bān,
believing the punishment was too light,
and strongly insisted on a harsher judgment.
Liú Bān's memorial of thanks stated:
"The crossbow shoots at the target,
and my unfortunate fate is unavoidable;
a falling tile is before me,
but I bear no resentment in my heart."
He also said:
"In the art of the fletcher,
one only fears not causing harm;
but the field owner's ox,
has been taken away excessively."
While Wielding the Brush, the Lingering Hangover Remained
Zēng Bù was demoted to govern Ráo Zhōu due to a market affair.
Shèrén Xǔ Jiāng was drafting the imperial decree
and included quite a few disparaging remarks.
He went to see Zēng and said:
"Initially I wanted to withhold the wording,
but out of righteous indignation, I wished to provoke such a conflict,
making it inevitable that I would be similarly demoted,
which would be of no benefit to Your Excellency.
However, the language within it has been significantly altered,
and Your Excellency will know this in due course."
Zēng said:
"In the past, when Yàn Yuánxiàn was in power,
Sòng Zǐjīng was a Hàlín scholar,
and they were intimately close day and night.
At a Mid-Autumn banquet,
the Duke brought out courtesans to compose poetry.
The next day, he was dismissed from the premiership,
and Sòng drafted the imperial decree,
which contained extremely harsh denunciations.
At the moment of wielding his brush,
the lingering hangover was still present.
Such incidents have a long history;
why bother contesting it?"
Xǔ departed dejectedly.
Spirit as when Bèi Zhōu was breached
In the Jiāyòu era,
Wén Lùgōng and Fù Zhènggōng served as prime ministers,
while Liú Hàng and Wáng Yáochén served as councilors.
The matter of establishing the heir apparent was kept secret.
In the Yǒngfēng era,
the three dukes had already passed away.
Lùgōng went to the west as the retaining minister.
His courtesies and favors were abundant.
Upon his return,
the Emperor composed a poem to see him off,
which included the line "His reward lies in not speaking of his merits."
Wáng Yǔyù's poem states:
"His accomplishments were at their peak in the late Jiāyòu,
his spirit as when Bèi Zhōu was breached."
Mocking a stutterer
Wáng Fén had a stutter.
Liú Bīn mocked him, saying:
"Perhaps he is from the Chāng family,
yet again, I doubt he is of that kind.
His heroic name is unseen,
only a feeling of 'Ài' is heard."
Zhōu Chāng, Hán Fēi, Yáng Xióng, and Dèng Ài
all stuttered.
Another time, they went to court together,
and upon hearing the call of the roll,
Fén said:
"Below the Zǐchén Palace, they frequently call for you."
Bīn replied:
"At the Hánshí hilltop, I have repeatedly seen you."
A pedant's narrow view
Tài Zǔ once disagreed with Zhào Pǔ during a discussion.
The Emperor said:
"How can I find a prime minister like Sāng Wéihàn to strategize with?"
Pǔ said:
"Even if Wéihàn were alive,
Your Majesty would not use him."
This was because Hàn loved money.
The Emperor said:
"If one employs a worthy person,
one should protect them from their shortcomings.
A pedant has a narrow view;
if granted one hundred thousand strings of cash,
it would fill his broken house."
Recommending a spanking to take his place
Bīn and Wáng Jiè
were discussing the matter of using animals in examinations.
At the same time,
Yōng Zǐfāng was an open-palace official.
Playfully, he said:
"Each offense warrants thirteen spankings."
Bīn said:
"I have already written in my submission:
'I humbly observe that Yōng Zǐfāng
is tall and large in stature,
with ample and robust buttocks and thighs.
Your servant is truly inferior
and recommends him to take my place.'"
The Empress Dowager overlooks the white jade railing, admiring peonies
After Císhèng Yuánxiàn Empress passed away,
the Emperor was deeply saddened and yearned for her.
There was a man surnamed Jiāng who claimed to possess divine techniques that could revive the dead.
The Emperor tested his methods,
but after several tens of days, they proved ineffective.
Then he said:
"Your servant saw the Grand Empress Dowager feasting with Rén Zōng,
overlooking the white jade railing and admiring peonies.
She has no intention of returning to the human world."
The Emperor knew he was a charlatan,
but merely banished him to Chēn Zhōu.
Cài Chéngxǐ presented a witty verse:
"The jade railing flowers in heaven have already withered;
what use are the earthly sorcerer's arts?"
Hán Yù never made such a fuss
In the Qìnglì era,
the western frontier troubles were unresolved,
and Yàn Yuánxiàn was the Commissioner of Military Affairs.
During a heavy snowfall,
he hosted a banquet in the western garden.
Ōuyáng Yǒngshú composed a poem that read:
"One must pity the iron armor chilled to the bone,
over four hundred thousand border troops encamped."
Yàn said:
"In the past, Hán Yù could also compose words;
at Péi Dù's gathering,
he merely said, 'Gardens and forests offer ultimate delight,
bells and drums celebrate peaceful times.'
He never made such a fuss."
Fèi Xiàoxiān's divinatory shadow
Since the Jiāyòu era,
Fèi Xiàoxiān was renowned throughout the land for his divinatory shadows,
and many sought his predictions.
Wáng Píngfǔ said:
"Divination is originally intended for foreknowledge,
but 'divinatory shadows' are only proven true after the event.
Of what use is that?"
Heaven created me dark
Lǚ Huìqīng said to Wáng Jīnggōng:
"You have freckles on your face;
if you wash them with coriander, they will disappear."
The Duke said:
"My face is simply dark;
they are not freckles."
Lǚ said:
"Coriander can also remove darkness."
The Duke laughed and said:
"Heaven created me dark;
what can coriander do to me?"
Presenting oneself to Censorate, discussing face with Grand Councilors
Sūn Wèizhōng recommended two people for censor.
Someone asked:
"Your Excellency has never met these two people;
why did you recommend them so quickly?"
Sūn said:
"In the past, people were ashamed to present themselves to the censorate;
why would I now seek to discuss face with the Grand Councilors?"
Zuǒ Shì's falsehoods
In his early years, Ōuyáng Wénzhōnggōng failed the provincial examination in Suí Zhōu
because the rhyme for 'dismissed official' was not included.
At that time, his "Zuǒ Shì's Falsehoods"
was a very detailed discussion,
containing arguments such as: "The stone spoke in Sòng,
a deity descended in Xīn.
Outer snakes fought while inner snakes were wounded;
new ghosts were great while old ghosts were small."
Sweat-drenched Scholar
Scholar Wáng Píngfǔ was of a large and robust physique.
In midsummer, he entered the academy;
dismounting his horse, his clothes were soaked with sweat.
Liú Gòngfù said:
"You are truly what is called a 'sweat-drenched scholar.'"
When hungry, ask for food; when full, do not bow
Zhāng Dùn was skilled at nurturing his health in his youth.
He once said:
"When hungry,
one must ask for food even in unfamiliar places;
but when satiated,
one would not even bow to one's father."
Lǚ Gōng's peace proposal
Lǚ Huìqīng's mourning period ended.
Wáng Jīnggōng, residing in the mountains,
sent a letter to initiate reconciliation, saying:
"Coming together is to follow each other,
any doubt differing from a celestial bond;
separation, though perhaps ordained,
does not originate from human will."
He also said:
"Within the gates and walls, seeking good,
many times I sent letters of two reconciliations;
before the殿陛 (diànbì), I openly offered
the imperial edict of renewed harmony.
This was indeed my wish,
and I was about to pursue it,
when I was again afflicted with the sorrow of mourning,
thus delaying the presentation of my written appeal."
He further stated:
"Reflecting internally, though I am of shallow virtue,
I have no suspicion of minor grievances;
looking up to your lofty wisdom,
why would there be any thought of old animosities?
Humbly I consider Your Excellency,
who knows the profound depths of virtue,
and comprehends the essence of destiny.
Closeness and estrangement are suited to what is shared,
hatred and love dissolve into non-existence.
May the differences of ice and coal
be suddenly shown through your utmost grace;
may the harvesting of mulberries and elms
then lead to my plea for a change of service."
The Duke replied:
"My heart was once in accord with yours,
until differences arose;
these were all matters of state,
how could there be anything else?
Many in court were in disarray,
you alone supported them,
so what do I owe you?
Some spoke ill of you,
but I had no part in it,
so how can you blame me?
To adapt to the times and facilitate affairs,
I do not know how that is to be done.
Considering the facts and discussing sentiments,
you too should understand this.
Your opening words and detailed message,
I read with a sense of melancholy.
In the past, on my part,
there was truly no suspicion of minor grievances;
now, regarding you,
what old animosities are there left to remember?
However, I await the end of my days in the mountains and forests,
our paths of pursuit and abandonment are different;
to understand each other with feeling
is not as good as to forget each other entirely."
A Lifetime of Inexhaustible Food and Clothing
Wáng Yígōng once passed the provincial examination with distinction,
always achieving first place.
Hànlín Liú Zǐyí said:
"The zhuàngyuán (狀元) who passes all three examinations
will have inexhaustible food and clothing for a lifetime."
Yígōng replied with a serious expression:
"My lifelong ambition
is not in warmth and satiety."
Yán Lǔgōng's Calligraphy is like a Rustic with Clasped Hands and Joined Feet
In the early Táng (唐) dynasty, calligraphy was vigorous and strong,
inheriting the style of Jìn (晉) and Sòng (宋).
After the Kāiyuán (開元) era, it became thick and plump.
After the Yuánhé (元和) era,
followers of Liǔ (柳) and Shěn (沈) again valued clarity and vigor.
Yáng Níngshì (楊凝式) of the Five Dynasties,
and in the early dynasty, Xué Jiànzhōng (學建中),
were exceptionally brilliant for their time;
their brushwork was also thick and substantial.
Lǐ Chāngwǔ (李昌武) could not avoid being heavy and murky.
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ (李後主) of Jiāngnán (江南) was skilled in calligraphy.
There were those who said Yán Lǔgōng's (顏魯公) writing was firm, strong, and methodical.
Hòuzhǔ (後主) said:
"Zhēnqīng's (真卿) calligraphy has the proper kāifǎ (楷法) but lacks a 'stopping place,'
it's just like a rustic with clasped hands and joined feet."
Poem on Visiting the Latrine
Chéng Shīmèng (程師孟), when he was Prefect of Hóngzhōu (洪州),
built a 'Quiet Hall,'
and loved it so much that
he visited it every day.
He wrote a poem saying:
"Every day, however busy, I must visit once,
late at night I always come with a lamp."
Lǐ Yuánguī (李元規) laughed and said:
"This is a poem on visiting the latrine!"
Mercury Is Not Very Effective
Duàn Shǎolián (叚少連) in his later years, met and drank with village elders.
Shǎolián (少連) was skilled in music,
and when tipsy, he played the flute.
An old scholar said:
"My fate lacks the help of Venus,
which is why I cannot enjoy the arts."
Duàn (叚) laughed and said:
"Not only Venus,
but Mercury is also not very effective!"
Rhapsody on the Vast Earth Bearing All Things
Zhāng Hàng (張沆) was a humorist.
A guest in his retinue composed "Rhapsody on the Vast Earth Bearing All Things":
"There is a great virtue,
its name is Kūn (坤)."
Zhāng Hàng (張沆) said:
"If not a lecturer of sutras,
then a Buddhist monk imparting dharma."
Each Maid Brought a Half-Sleeve
Sòng Zǐjīng (宋子京), in his later years, was Prefect of Chéngdū (成都).
He brought the "History of Táng (唐)" (唐書) to his post for revision and editing.
After every banquet,
he would open his bedroom door,
lower the screen,
light two large candles,
with maids attending on either side,
grinding ink and spreading paper.
Onlookers near and far all knew that Shàngshū (尚書) was revising the "History of Táng (唐),"
and regarded him as an immortal.
He had many concubines.
Once, at a banquet in Qújiāng (曲江),
it happened to be slightly cold.
He ordered a half-sleeve garment to be brought.
Each maid brought one,
totaling more than ten.
Zǐjīng (子京) feared accusations of favoritism,
and ultimately dared not wear any,
enduring the cold as he returned home.
A Gentleman Likes Sour Food
Wáng Pāng (王雱) said:
"A gentleman mostly likes sour food,
while a petty person mostly likes salty food.
Sour obtains the nature of wood and rises,
while salty obtains the nature of water and descends."
Female Jiǎchén (甲辰), Small Wǔzǐ (戊子)
Táng Yìshǐ (唐逸史) records that
Jìngōng (晉公) and Lángzhōng (郎中) Yú Wēi (庾威) were born in the same Jiǎchén (甲辰) year.
Jìngōng (晉公) joked:
"Lángzhōng (郎中) is the female Jiǎchén (甲辰)."
Chéng Wénhuìgōng (程文惠公) and Páng Yǐnggōng (龐穎公) were born in the same Wǔzǐ (戊子) year.
Chéng (程) was already noble,
while Páng (龐) was still a minor official.
Chéng (程) once joked to Páng (龐):
"You are merely the small Wǔzǐ (戊子)."
Later, Yǐnggōng (穎公) was greatly promoted,
and Wénhuì (文惠) sent a letter to congratulate him, saying:
"Today the great Wǔzǐ (戊子) has become the small Wǔzǐ (戊子)."
Húi (回) Guest Offers Sacrifices
Téng Zōngliàng (滕宗諒) was the Administrator of Bālíng (巴陵).
A Huázhōu (華州) Húi (回) Daoist priest came to visit.
Téng (滕) knew him to be an extraordinary person
and impromptu composed a poem:
"A Huázhōu (華州) Húi (回) Daoist priest,
has arrived at Yuèyáng (岳陽) city.
Where will you travel after leaving me?
A single sword sweeps across the autumn sky."
The Húi (回) Daoist laughed loudly and departed.
A scholar, Xià Jūn (夏鈞), passed through Yǒngzhōu (永州),
and asked Hé Xiāngū (何仙姑):
"Where is Mr. Lǚ (呂) now?"
She replied:
"Today he is holding a vegetarian feast at Xīnghuàsì (興化寺) in Tánzhōu (潭州)."
Xià Jūn (夏鈞) went to the temple in Tánzhōu (潭州),
took out the feast calendar and looked at it.
Indeed, on that day, there was a Húi (回) guest from Huázhōu (華州) offering sacrifices.
Féng Dào is like All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas
Wáng Jīnggōng (王荊公) once argued before the emperor that Féng Dào (馮道) was able to humble himself to bring peace to the people,
like the actions of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Táng Jiè (唐介) said:
"As a prime minister, Féng Dào (馮道) caused the empire to change four surnames,
and served ten rulers in his life.
Can he be considered a pure official?"
Ānshí (安石) said:
"Yī Yǐn (伊尹) went to Tāng (湯) five times,
and to Jié (桀) five times;
he was precisely trying to bring peace to the people,
how could he not be a pure official?"
Sù (肅) said:
"If he had the aspirations of Yī Yǐn (伊尹), then yes."
Wáng Jīnggōng (王荊公)'s expression changed.
The Prime Minister Bestows Tea
Under the old system,
the prime minister, upon arriving at court in the morning,
was invited to sit.
If there were major military or state affairs, they would be discussed.
After a relaxed tea, they would withdraw.
As for all other decrees, appointments, dismissals, punishments, rewards, abolition, or establishment,
regardless of the matter's importance,
all were presented in written memorials.
The emperor would personally review them in the Forbidden Palace,
annotate the papers,
and at the end, use the imperial seal to approve the memorial.
This was called "seal painting" (yìnhuà),
and then it would be issued for implementation.
From the Táng dynasty to the Five Dynasties,
this system remained unchanged.
This is what the ancients referred to as "sitting and discussing the Way."
At the beginning of the dynasty,
Fàn Zhì, Wáng Tuán, and others, having served as prime ministers in the previous dynasty,
felt uneasy in their positions.
They jointly petitioned that for major matters of the Secretariat (Zhōngshū),
memorials (zházǐ) should be presented directly to the emperor for instructions,
and after court, each would proceed with their duties.
From then on, the emperor personally reviewed memorials,
sometimes until late in the day.
The ritual of being granted a seat and sipping tea was consequently abolished,
and indeed, there was no time for "discussing the Way."
This then became the established practice.
Seasonal Attire
On the emperor's birthday (Shèngjié), Duānwǔ Festival, and the beginning of winter,
seasonal attire was bestowed upon all officials;
this was an old custom.
However, for the winter solstice (Dōngzhì), people had always worn their old clothes,
and nothing was bestowed.
River Market Music (Héshìyuè)
During Emperor Tàizǔ's reign,
Duwèi Gāo Huáidé was first granted a staff of authority (jiéyuè)
and given jurisdiction over Suīyáng.
He was rather extravagant by nature,
and his singers and courtesans
were the best of their time.
A few miles outside Suīyáng city, beside the Biàn River, there was a bridge
where numerous residents lived
and prostitutes and entertainers gathered.
Gāo often made his courtesans imitate vulgar and rustic behaviors
for amusement,
calling it "River Market Music" (Héshìyuè).
No Pardon for Corruption and Embezzlement
During the Tàipíng Xīngguó era,
the corruption and embezzlement of court official Zǔ Jí came to light.
The case had not yet been finalized,
and the suburban sacrifice (jiāolǐ) was approaching.
Emperor Tàizōng was angered by his greed,
and specifically ordered that the suburban pardon should not extend to him.
Zhào Pǔ memorialized, saying:
"Corrupt officials deserve punishment,
and the law should be justly applied.
However, when the state performs the suburban sacrifice and issues a great pardon,
it is to respond to Heaven and Earth
and announce to the gods.
What kind of person is Zǔ Jí,
that he should be enough to undermine Your Majesty's pardon?"
The emperor approved his words and desisted.
Purple-Black Pig-Born Person
Zhāng Yǒngdé, the Fùmǎ Dūwèi of the Zhōu dynasty,
was generous with his wealth and fond of giving.
He met an extraordinary person who said:
"The world is about to become peaceful,
and the true ruler has already been born.
If you encounter a purple-black pig-born person
who is adept at warfare,
you should treat him well."
Zhāng Yǒngdé secretly sought him out.
When Emperor Tàizǔ's reputation and status gradually rose,
he devoted himself entirely to befriending him.
At the beginning of the dynasty,
due to his old favors,
his stature and wealth were on par with those who helped establish the dynasty.
The Prime Minister Should Be a Confucian Scholar
Emperor Tàizǔ used his divine martial prowess to pacify the world,
and not many Confucian scholars were greatly employed.
When he performed the suburban sacrifice and rode in the grand carriage (dàlù),
the Hanlin Academician Lú Duōxùn held the reins and was prepared for consultation.
His responses were detailed and astute.
Another day,
the emperor said:
"To be a prime minister, one should employ a Confucian scholar."
Lú was indeed greatly employed.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Hàn Was Just a Villager
Dīng Wèi, while in the Secretariat (Zhōngshū),
said to his colleagues:
"What kind of ruler was Emperor Gāo of Hàn?"
They replied:
"He was a heroic ruler."
Dīng Wèi said:
"What heroism was there?
Zhāng Liáng guided him left, and he went left;
Chén Píng advised him right, and he went right.
When Xiàng Yǔ died,
and the world had no master,
the empire naturally gravitated to him.
He simply went with the flow, followed the current,
and did not compete with others.
He was just a village elder."
He also said:
"The so-called loyal ministers and filial sons of antiquity
are all untrustworthy;
these are merely literary embellishments by historians,
who wished to create beautiful tales for later generations."
Daoist Priest Curses Lǎozi
Xú Yànbó wrote "Record of Divine Miracles in the State" (Guóhuí Shénjì Jì).
Emperor Xuánzōng was a heroic and magnificent ruler,
and Xú Yànbó was a renowned minister of his time.
Monarch and minister mutually respected and honored each other,
and spoke of him in this manner.
To make ignorant people disbelieve and not be confused,
how could that be achieved?
It is popularly said that a Daoist priest cursed Lǎozi, saying:
"Buddhism uses supernatural wonders, calamities, and blessings
to frighten people,
making everyone believe and follow,
so monks and nuns can enjoy abundance.
But our Lǎozi speaks highly of purity and tranquility,
thus leaving us feeling desolate."
Although this is vulgar language,
there is something to be learned from it.
Yán Lǔgōng Was Moved by Immortals
Yán Zhēnqīng wrote "Record of the Magu Altar and Hall" (Má Gū Tán Bìng Táng Jì).
His integrity and heroic spirit were as bright as the sun and moon,
yet he could not escape being moved by tales of immortals.
Buddhism and Daoism have indeed been a deep affliction for these people.
Luó Chí Stele
The inscription on the Luó Chí Temple Stele says "bù yǒu xīn chuán" (步有新船),
but collected editions render "bù" (步) as "shè" (涉).
For "lìzǐ dān xī jiāozǐ huáng" (荔子丹兮蕉子黃),
the stele omits the character "zǐ" (子) after "jiāo" (蕉).
The stele should be taken as correct.
However, where the stele says "chūn yǔ yuán yín xī qiū hè yǔ fēi" (春與猿吟兮秋鶴與飛),
then the stele is suspected of being incorrect.
Jǐngyáng Well Inscription
Emperor Suí Yáng wrote "Jǐngyáng Well Inscription" (Jǐngyáng Jǐng Míng),
and yet he himself indulged in debauchery,
even surpassing it.
The inscription is faintly still legible,
and states:
"The carriage in front has already toppled,
the one riding behind will soon sink."
Shūsūn Áo's Given Name Was Ráo
The "Stele of Hàn Shūsūn Áo" (Hàn Shūsūn Áo Bēi) says:
"His given name was Ráo (饒),
his courtesy name was Shūsūn Áo (叔敖)."
Those who have not seen this stele
do not know that his given name was "Ráo."
Ghost in the Thunder Department
Xiè Xiānzhě
was a ghost in the Thunder Department (Léibù).
Both husband and wife were three feet tall,
their complexion was like jade,
and they were in charge of spreading fire among humans.
Píngquán Records of Plants and Trees
Lǐ Déyù wrote "Píngquán Records of Plants and Trees" (Píngquán Cǎomù Jì).
His dying injunctions included the words:
"One who damages a single blade of grass or a single tree
is not my descendant."
Lù Hóngjiàn wrote
quite a few books,
namely "The Covenant Between Monarch and Minister" (Jūn Chén Qì) in three volumes,
"Source Explanation" (Yuán Jiě) in three volumes,
"Genealogies of the Four Great Families of Jiāngbiǎo" (Jiāngbiǎo Sì Xìng Pǔ) in ten volumes,
"Records of Figures from North and South" (Nánběi Rénwù Zhì) in ten volumes,
"Records of Officials in Wúxīng" (Wúxīng Lìguān Jì) in three volumes,
"Records of the Prefects of Húzhōu" (Húzhōu Cìshǐ Jì) in three volumes,
"The Classic of Tea" (Chá Jīng) in three volumes,
"Dream Interpretation" (Zhàn Mèng) in three volumes.
Poem on Ruǎn Kè's Former Residence
Lǐ Yángbīng's "Poem on Ruǎn Kè's Former Residence" (Ruǎn Kè Jiù Jū Shī) says:
"Where is Ruǎn Kè now?
Immortal clouds hang over the cave entrance.
A place where mortals never reach,
today I journey through here."
Ruǎn Kè's name is not seen,
he was probably a recluse from Jìn Yún.
New Edict from the County Magistrate
Xuánzōng of Táng selected one hundred and sixty-three county magistrates,
and bestowed upon them solemn admonitions.
Thereafter, all who served as county magistrates throughout the realm
had these new admonitions engraved on stone.
Yuán Jié loved the unusual.
Yuán Jié composed the "Wùtái Míng" (Inscription for the Bureau of Errors),
and also an inscription for [unclear],
and also the "Yánghuá Yán Míng" (Inscription for Yanghua Cliff).
Jié
was a man who loved the unusual;
wherever he resided amidst mountains and waters,
he would certainly inscribe them himself,
fearing they would not be unusual enough.
His writings were also like this.
A jūnzi (noble person) who wishes to achieve immortality
must have that which is within him manifest outwardly,
and it must originate from nature.
Yán Zǐ, in his humble alley, serene and aloof,
attained renown for ten thousand generations,
and this he gained naturally.
Jié's eager pursuit of posthumous fame
was indeed laborious.
Liánsháo Gōng
The "Línhuá Gōng Xíngdēng Míng" (Inscription for the Lanterns of Linhua Palace) and "Liánsháo Gōng Tóng Bóshān Pán Míng" (Inscription for the Bronze Incense Burner Plate of Liánsháo Palace)
were both made during the Wǔfèng era of the Hàn dynasty.
Línhuá Gōng
is not recorded in the *Hàn Shū*.
The "Xuāndì Jì" (Annals of Emperor Xuān) states:
"Therefore, in Liánsháo Gōng."
The commentary says:
"It is a county,
and should not have a palace."
Indeed, the Qin and Han dynasties had countless detached palaces and separate residences.
Unless they were mentioned due to specific events,
historians could not record them all.
Liǔ Zōngyuán, a sinner of the Hán school
Liǔ Zōngyuán composed the "Míchí Héshang Bēi" (Stele for Monk Míchí).
Since the Táng dynasty,
those who discuss literature only mention Hán Yù and Liǔ Zōngyuán.
How could Liǔ be a follower of Hán?
He was a sinner of the Hán school.
People of the world do not know that what he learned was incorrect;
they merely speak of him as a peer of his time.
Lùhè Míng
The inscription is titled "Composed by Huáyáng Zhēnyì"
and is engraved at the foot of Jiāoshān.
According to the *Rùnzhōu Tújīng* (Illustrated Gazetteer of Runzhou), it is by Wáng Xīzhī,
but the brushwork does not resemble Xīzhī's,
but rather Yán Lǔgōng's.
Huáyáng Zhēnyì is the Daoist appellation of Gù Kuàng.
The stele has no date.
It is suspected that someone from an earlier generation
Spirit of Frost Month, Day of Imperial Apex
The "Kǒngzǐ Miào Qì Biǎo Bēi" (Stele Inscription for the Utensils of Confucius's Temple) by Hán Míngfǔ of Hàn states:
"In the second year of Yǒngshòu,
Guīntān,
the spirit of the frost month,
the day of the imperial apex."
Yǒngshòu
is the reign title of Emperor Huán.
The meaning of "spirit of the frost month,
the day of the imperial apex" is unclear.
It is suspected to be the fifth day of the ninth month.
Liǔ's calligraphy
The calligraphy of Liǔ Gōngquán is highly esteemed.
Even maidservants who particularly love to copy it
do not lose its essence, and all its sharp points remain.
Cài Jūnmó said:
"The 'Yīnfú Jīng Xù' is the most refined of Liǔ's calligraphy."
He said he was good at concealing his brush's tip,
which is exactly contrary to my view.
Zhāng Lónggōng
Zhào Gēng's "Zhāng Lónggōng Bēi" (Stele for Zhāng Lónggōng) states:
"His personal name was Lùsī.
He passed the imperial examination in early Suí and became the magistrate of Xuānchéng.
His wife, Lady Shí,
bore nine sons.
When the Duke completed his term as magistrate and returned home,
whenever he went out,
from *xù* hour to *chǒu* hour (7 PM to 3 AM),
he often returned cold and wet.
Lady Shí found this strange and questioned him.
The Duke said:
'I am a dragon,
and Zhèng Xiángyuǎn is also a dragon.
He rides a white ox
and occupies my pond.
I have repeatedly fought with him but have not won.
Tomorrow, the matter will be decided.
You can have my sons shoot at him with bows and arrows.
The one with a green silk ribbon tied to his mane is Zhèng,
and the one with a crimson silk ribbon is me.'
So his sons shot and hit the one with the green silk ribbon.
Zhèng became angry
and went northeast to Héféi's Xīshān (West Mountain) and died.
That is now Lóngxuéshān (Dragon's Lair Mountain).
From then on, the Duke and his nine sons all transformed back into dragons."
In the woods, who has ever seen one?
"When we meet, everyone says they will quit official life,
but in the woods, who has ever seen one?"
This saying is popularly held to be excellent.
During the Qìnglì era,
Xǔ Yuán, a Vice Minister of the Grand Council,
served as the Commissioner of Transportation and found this stone in the Jiāng River at Chíyáng.
Only then was it known to be a poem by Língchè.
Emperor Xuánzōng called himself a disciple of Shàngqīng
The "Tángyáng Sòng" (Eulogy for the Tang Sun)
was composed by imperial edict of Emperor Xuánzōng.
Emperor Xuánzōng referred to himself as a "disciple of Shàngqīng."
How strange!
Those who are followers of the Buddha
are called "those who have no birth,"
that is what this refers to.
Followers of Lǎozi do not die,
this is called greed for life.
Lìnghú Táo holds a vegetarian feast
Lìnghú Táo of Táng held a vegetarian feast.
He valued conciseness in his writings.
Once, when he hosted monks for a meal,
a monk presided over the feast.
He knelt before the Buddha, holding an incense burner, and listened intently.
The monk chanted, saying:
"Lìnghú Táo's feast.
Buddha knows."
This was to accommodate his brevity.
His father, Chǔ, composed the "Báilóu Fù" (Rhapsody on the White Tower),
which had no other meaning
but reached over sixteen hundred characters.
How verbose!
The natures of father and son were opposite to such an extent.
Dragon-casting text
The "Huìchāng Tóulóng Wén" (Dragon-casting Text of Huìchāng) of Táng.
Emperor Wǔ referred to himself as "a disciple who inherits the Dao, continues the Mystery, illuminates the Three Luminaries, and is the True Man of the Blazing South Peak."
Bái Mǐnzhōng's Stele
Bì Xián of Táng composed "Bái Mǐnzhōng Bēi" (Stele for Bái Mǐnzhōng).
Its contents are largely similar to his official biography.
However, the biography records:
"Mǐnzhōng
was promoted by Lǐ Déyù.
When Déyù was demoted,
Mǐnzhōng strongly denounced him,
which was considered a great evil."
Yet, in the biography it says:
"During the Huìchāng era,
Déyù initiated legal proceedings,
implicating five chancellors
and exiling them to the Lingnan region.
After this,
within one year,
the wronged were all restored to their positions,
and for this, he was considered capable."
Thus, it is difficult to trust such praise and criticism.
Among women calligraphers, Lady Gāo is the only one.
The "Ān Gōngměi Gù Sòng" (Eulogy for the Late Ān Gōngměi)
is by Lady Gāo, wife of Fáng.
Her brushwork is powerful and beautiful,
unlike a woman's.
My collected records have also been passed down.
Among women whose brushwork is engraved on metal and stone,
Lady Gāo is the only one.
Calligraphy was never more flourishing than in the Táng dynasty;
its decline is never more severe than it is now.
The servants of Lady Wǔ of Táng,
their regular script handwriting,
every character is lovely.
Those I have recorded include Yú Shùn,
Gāo Pián,
down to Chén Yóuhuái and others.
Among today's flourishing literary scholars,
those whose regular script
can be counted are no more than three or four people.
Yíjiào Jīng
The *Yíjiào Jīng* (Sutra of the Buddha's Last Testament)
is traditionally attributed to Wáng Xīzhī,
but this is a mistake.
It was merely written by a scripture scribe of the Táng era.
Volume Seventeen
End.
Xiānzhǔ
His given name was Shēng,
his courtesy name Zhèng-Lún.
When the Zhū-Liáng (Later Liáng dynasty) ruled all under Heaven,
Yáng Xíng-Mì independently occupied Huái-Nán.
His great general Xú Wēn led an army to Háo-Shàng,
where he met the Former Lord.
He took him back, adopting him as his own son.
Consequently, he assumed the surname Xú,
and the given name Zhī-Gào.
The Governor of Affairs (Pú-Shè),
the ruler of Wú entrusted governance to the Former Lord,
and he was promoted to Left Pú-Shè.
The collapsed order was revived and uplifted,
and people near and far gladly supported him.
They called him the Governor of Affairs (Zhèng-Shì Pú-Shè).
He then received the abdication from Wú,
honoring the Wú ruler as the Abdicated Emperor (Ràng-Huáng),
and his adoptive father Wēn as the Martial Emperor (Wǔ-Huáng).
He changed the reign title to Shēng-Wén,
and reverted to the Lǐ surname.
Moon Poem (Yuè-Shī)
At the time of the圜qiū (Altar of Heaven) ceremony,
the Grand Astrologer reported, "The moon has extended by two kè."
It was early in the month,
and the moon should have been at the third watch,
but at the altar,
it was as bright as day.
After the ritual was complete, it set.
Initially,
he had the ambition to usurp the throne.
Suddenly, in the middle of the night, a temple monk struck the bell,
startling the entire city.
At dawn, he was about to execute him,
when the monk said that last night he had composed the "Moon Poem," which went:
"Slowly from the north of the Eastern Sea,
it gradually emerges onto the celestial path.
Tonight, a full disk,
where can its clear light not reach?"
The Former Lord was pleased and released him.
Also,
during the Tiān-Yòu era,
a children's rhyme said:
"A carp from the Eastern Sea flies up to Heaven."
Eastern Sea (Dōng-Hǎi)
was the ancestral home of the Xú clan;
Carp (Lǐ)
was a surname.
Heavenly omens and human affairs coincided in this way.
Red Army Children (Chì-Jūn-Zǐ)
The Successor Lord Jǐng,
courtesy name Bó-Yù,
succeeded to the throne,
and changed the reign title to Bǎo-Dà.
In that year, demon rebels in Chǔ-Zhōu caused unrest.
They all wore crimson clothes,
and were called the Red Army Children (Chì-Jūn-Zǐ).
Monk Biān (Biān Luó-Hàn)
Liú Yán of the prefecture
rebelled and attacked Cháng-Shā.
Biān Hào abandoned the city and fled.
Hào was gentle and weak,
and particularly fond of Buddhism.
As a general, his only concern was to preserve lives,
and he was called Monk Biān (Biān Luó-Hàn).
Later, he captured Tán-Zhōu,
but by this time he was weak and indecisive,
only engaging in fasting and giving alms.
People called him Monk Biān (Biān Hé-Shàng).
Three Hundred Thousand Soldiers (Jiǎ-Bīng Sān-Shí Wàn)
When Emperor Shì-Zōng ascended the throne,
the Successor Lord sent Sūn Jì to present a memorial and declare vassalage.
Soon after, he broke the agreement.
Emperor Shì-Zōng asked Jì about the strengths and weaknesses of Jiāng-Nán.
Jì replied:
"Although our country is small,
we still have three hundred thousand soldiers (Jiǎ-Bīng Sān-Shí Wàn),
so it is not easy to conquer."
Emperor Shì-Zōng said:
"Jiāng-Nán is no more than ten-some prefectures,
why do you deceive me?"
Jì replied:
"Although the elite troops are only a little over a hundred thousand,
yet the Yangtze River,
with its swift currents for a thousand lí,
can withstand an army of a hundred thousand.
And the elder of the state, Sòng Qí-Qiū, is a man like Wáng Měng or Xiè Ān,
who can withstand a hundred thousand."
Yù-Zhāng Renamed Nán-Dū
After Sòng Qí-Qiū died,
a comet appeared in the Dǒu-Niú sector (of the sky).
The Successor Lord discussed moving the capital to Yù-Zhāng to avoid it,
renaming Yù-Zhāng to Nán-Dū (Southern Capital).
Once there,
he often felt uneasy.
During a banquet for all officials in the palace hall,
he suddenly saw Sòng Qí-Qiū ascend the steps and advance.
He then fell ill and died.
Those who understood said it was because he believed slander and harmed the virtuous.
There Is Someone There Who Cannot Yet Be Conquered (Bǐ Yǒu Rén Yān Wèi Kě Tú Yě)
The Later Lord's given name was Yù,
his courtesy name Chóng-Guāng.
Emperor Shì-Zōng of Zhōu was angered by the refusal to cede Huái-Nán,
and was about to march on Jiàn-Kāng.
He saw a white qi pierce the sky.
He sent someone to observe it,
and it was the Later Lord hunting.
He sighed, saying:
"There is someone there (Bǐ Yǒu Rén Yān),
who cannot yet be conquered (Wèi Kě Tú Yě)."
In the second year of Gē-Dé,
iron coins were first used,
with one iron coin equivalent to one-tenth of a copper coin.
In that year, the state fell.
Names of Armies (Zhū-Jūn Míng)
Initially,
during the time of the Former Lord,
the people's land was measured and standardized
to establish the tax system.
Each household provided one soldier,
called the Righteous Army (Yì-Shī).
Also, from tenant households with three adult males, one was conscripted,
called the Regiment Army (Tuán-Jūn).
By the time of the Successor Lord,
people in all prefectures were allowed to compete in boat races.
