Each Duān-Wǔ Festival, the last place finishers were selected.
The winners were awarded a silver cup,
and this was called "hitting the mark" (Dǎ-Biāo).
By this time, all were conscripted as soldiers,
called the Ling-Bo Army (Líng-Bō-Jūn).
Also, commoners' hired slaves and live-in sons-in-law were conscripted,
called the Righteous Men Army (Yì-Nán-Jūn).
Furthermore, wealthy commoners were recruited,
who provided their own money, silk, and military equipment,
and gathered unreliable individuals,
called the Free-and-Easy Army (Zì-Zài-Jūn).
When the imperial army besieged them urgently,
they recruited old and weak commoners from outside who could wear armor,
called the Door-Facing Army (Pái-Mén-Jūn).
Poem by the Later Lord Lǐ (Lǐ Hòu-Zhǔ Shī)
After the imperial army entered Jiàn-Yè,
the Later Lord had already submitted,
and boarded a boat to proceed to the capital.
Tears fell as he sat in the boat,
and he composed a poem that said:
"Jiāng-Nán and Jiāng-Běi, my old homeland,
Thirty years have passed like a dream.
The palace chambers of the Wú苑are now desolate,
The towers and halls of Guǎng-Líng are already overgrown.
Clouds cast over distant peaks, a thousand fragments of sorrow,
Rain strikes the lonely boat, ten thousand lines of tears.
Four brothers, three hundred mouths,
Cannot bear to sit idly and ponder carefully."
This Is the Talk of a Pedant (Cǐ Cuò-Dà-Ér Yǔ Ěr)
Initially,
when the Later Lord defied orders and rejected commands,
he once said:
"If one day the imperial army comes to conquer,
I shall personally don military attire,
and fight a battle outside the city walls.
If I do not succeed,
I will take treasures and immolate myself."
Emperor Tài-Zǔ heard this and said:
"This is the talk of a pedant (Cǐ Cuò-Dà-Ér Yǔ Ěr);
he only has the words,
but surely not the will."
By this time, it indeed proved true.
The Later Lord Was Fond of Buddhism (Hòu-Zhǔ Hào Fó)
Hòuzhǔ酷信浮圖. Hòuzhǔ ardently believed in Buddhism.
After court was dismissed,
he and his empress would wear僧伽帽s (saṅghāṭī hats),
don kasayas,
recite Buddhist scriptures,
and prostrate themselves, bowing their heads to the ground until calluses formed.
He personally whittled toilet paper for the monks,
testing it himself on his cheeks;
if there was any rough spot,
he would rework it.
His hands would not fold naturally;
he would walk holding them in a Buddhist mudra.
In Jiànkāng, the number of monks reached over ten thousand.
When a monk committed adultery,
the officials would prepare documents to have him defrocked.
Hòuzhǔ ordered that they be exempted from punishment after prostrating before the Buddha three hundred times.
The Northern Dynasties secretly selected young men who were learned in the classics and eloquent to go and convert him.
Hòuzhǔ revered them,
calling one of them "a Buddha manifested in the world."
Morning and evening, he would discuss the six roots, the four noble truths, heaven and hell, and the cycle of karma with him,
calling him "Little Elder."
He also persuaded Hòuzhǔ to give generously and build pagodas and statues,
wearing himself three items of red damask embroidered with gold.
Hòuzhǔ found this too extravagant.
Then he said:
"Does Your Majesty not read the Huáyán Sūtra?
How then do you know the wealth of the Buddha?"
From then on,
military strategy and defense were neglected,
and financial resources became increasingly depleted.
He also built a large monastery on Niútóu Shān,
gathering a thousand disciples.
At dusk, a vegetarian feast was prepared,
full of rare delicacies;
if not finished in one day,
it would be prepared again the next morning,
which was called "folding over" (折倒).
At the time, this was seen as an omen.
When Wáng Shī conquered Chízhōu,
he ordered monks, laypeople, and soldiers to chant "Guānshìyīn Púsà who saves from suffering."
One thousand earnest pleas and ten thousand difficulties, the two words "hunger and cold."
Sòng Qíqiū said that Xiānzhǔ treated scholars with an open mind,
and built the Yánbīn Tíng (Pavilion for Welcoming Guests) to attract talented individuals.
Sūn Jì, Hán Xīzài, and others were all employed by him.
The attendants around Sīzhǔ
were all fair-faced youths from the Eastern Palace.
Xīzài and others frequently slandered and criticized them.
They believed that the old officials of the former court
would ultimately not be used by the young ruler.
Qíqiū requested to return to his old residence in Jiǔhuá,
and was granted the title Jiǔhuá Xiānshēng.
Qíqiū's talent was unrestrained and free;
for all steles and tablets he erected,
he personally composed the text,
and ordered Hán Xīzài to write it in Bāfèn script.
Xīzài often plugged his nose with paper,
saying:
"His words are foul and stinky."
Qíqiū once wrote a memorial which said:
"As for a thousand earnest pleas and ten thousand difficulties,
they are only for the two words 'hunger and cold.'"
Poem on a Landscape Painting
When Xiānzhǔ moved his garrison to Jīnlíng,
Shěn Bīn, who was famous for his poetry,
knowing that Xiānzhǔ wanted to take Ms. Yáng,
獻presented a poem on a landscape painting he had personally drawn:
"One must know that the brush has arranged it,
and not fear the difficulty of organizing mountains and rivers."
The Work of a Country Fellow by the Fireplace
Sūn Fáng was famous for his poetry.
Lǐ Jiànxūn first hid Fáng in his study,
and when Shěn Bīn arrived,
asked him what he thought of Fáng's poetry.
Bīn said:
"It does not have the style of the Guófēng, Yǎ, or Sòng [sections of the Shījīng],
but truly captures the work of a country fellow by the fireplace."
Fáng then came out and said:
"Is 'country fellow' not going too far?"
Bīn said:
"Your lines from 'Night Sitting' say:
'The more you poke, the colder the ash gets;
the longer you sit, the more the mat leaves a mark.'
If this isn't a work composed by a country fellow by the fireplace, then what is it?"
Fáng's poem "On Jīnshān Sì" says:
"A temple in the heart of waves for ten thousand ages,
Jīnshān's fame is ever intimate.
So much sky, it gains extra moons;
so little land, no dust is born.
Passing oars disturb the monk's dream,
startling waves splash the Buddha's body.
The boastful lay scholar Zhāng,
after his inscription, there will be no one else."
Ascending the Terrace to Watch the Rain
Lǐ Jiāmíng was witty
and good at indirect remonstrance.
He accompanied Hòuzhǔ as he ascended a terrace to watch the rain over Zhōngshān,
and said:
"Its momentum is about to arrive."
Jiāmíng said:
"Although the rain will surely come,
it dares not enter the city,
fearing Your Majesty's heavy taxes."
Sīzhǔ then ordered the tax on monopolies to be reduced by half.
He also saw an ox lying in the shade of a tree.
Sīzhǔ said:
"The ox is already hot."
Jiāmíng presented a quatrain, saying:
"Once suffered Níng Qī's whip on its horns,
and again was scorched by Tián Dān's fire.
Idly chewing dry grass with the setting sun on its back,
lately no one even asks if it's panting."
Poem on a Paper Kite
Sòng Qíqiū had only one son,
who died,
and he grieved incessantly.
Lǐ Jiāmíng made a large paper kite,
on which he wrote:
"Wishing to restore the Táng fortunes and overthrow the powerful Wú,
all these were Xiānzhǔ's designs.
If you cannot even protect one child,
what will become of the Prince Who Yields throughout the ages?"
He let it drift with the wind to Qíqiū's residence,
then cut its string, letting it fall.
When Qíqiū saw it,
he was ashamed and moved, and stopped grieving.
How Beautiful and Steep are These Several Peaks
When Sīzhǔ visited Nándū,
as the river had already been divided,
most boats traveled along the south bank.
Looking north at Wǎngōng Shān,
he said:
"How beautiful and steep are these several peaks!"
Lǐ Jiāmíng said:
"The dragon boat lightly sways with the brocade sail's wind,
precisely at the time of the emperor's tour, gazing at the distant sky.
Turning one's head, the green hues of Wǎngōng Shān,
their slanting shadows do not extend beyond the ceremonial cup."
Sīzhǔ was ashamed,
bowed his head and passed by.
A Great Talent Cannot Be Forced
Chén Dù took the imperial examinations twice,
but neither time made the main list.
He once said:
"I will surely have my descendants rectify this."
When his son Jiǔsī took the jinshì examination,
he also passed on the "old men's list."
The gentleman said:
"A great talent cannot be achieved by force,
and a great reputation cannot be seized by strength."
Why So Many Dusty Scrolls
Hán Xīzài (韓熙載) first became in charge of the imperial examinations.
Everyone considered this a monumental task.
Xīzài himself composed five poems,
and showed them to the students in the morning.
All were worth appreciating.
When he wrote over fifty essays of aphorisms,
his contemporaries rarely equaled him.
He mentored junior scholars,
and was called Hán Fūzǐ (韓夫子).
He was fond of jesting and frivolousness.
If someone with a poor character came to present a gift,
he would have a courtesan burn moxa to fumigate them.
When they arrived,
he would chide,
"Why do your scrolls smell so strongly of moxa?"
In his later years, he was sent as a tribute to Liángjīng (梁京).
He broke off all his old acquaintances
and wrote on a wall:
"Before reaching my old home,
I imagined it would be wonderful.
But upon truly returning,
it's better to have never come.
Not a single acquaintance remains,
coming and going only grieves my heart.
Wind and rain soughing in the autumn inn,
I return and collapse on the bed by the window, still dressed.
In a dream, I suddenly arrive on a Jiāngnán (江南) road,
and find my old residence in the capital.
Peach-blossom faces and moth eyebrows laugh as they come out the door,
vying to embrace and carry me away from the entrance."
He also wrote:
"I am originally a person of Jiāngnán,
now a guest in Jiāngnán.
Going again to travel north of the Jiāng (江),
I see no acquaintances anywhere.
The golden autumn wind chills me,
for whom does the autumn moon shine white?
Better to return home,
someone in Jiāngnán remembers me."
Someone asked:
"Why does Jiāngnán not eat peeled lamb?"
Xīzài replied:
"Because Jiāngnán produces silk brocade."
At the time, no one understood.
Only after Xīzài left did they realize,
but it was too late to catch him.
Taking Atractylodes and avoiding peaches and plums.
Hán Xīzài was later promoted to Zhōngshū Shìláng (中書侍郎).
At a banquet,
he saw garden attendants with red headbands,
leading several tens of imperial concubines,
all beautiful.
He then sighed:
"This position (referring to the garden attendant) would also be good to hold concurrently with Zhōngshū Shìláng."
When Xīzài was young, he had taken medicinal Atractylodes and
was advised to avoid peaches and plums.
Later, during an internal banquet hosted by the Hòuzhǔ (後主),
all the attending officials were given them.
Xīzài had no choice but to eat several pieces.
By evening,
he discharged ten or so "Atractylodes men" over an inch long and died.
Dreaming of a woman in white.
Lú Jiàng (盧絳) fell ill.
He dreamt of a woman in white who said:
"You should eat [unclear character] and you will recover.
I am Gěng Yùzhēn (耿玉真)."
She sang:
"In the deep night of clear breeze and bright moon,
Lú Láng (盧郎) with broom and dustpan still regrets the delay.
Our rendezvous at Mèngjiāpō (孟家陂) another day,
to meet again will be an auspicious time."
Later, the Hòuzhǔ's army crossed the river,
and arrested and sent Jiàng to Mèngjiāpō at the Liáng (梁) gate.
Indeed, he saw a woman in white,
and then sighed:
"My former dream has come true;
what regret is there in death?"
Yùzhēn's surname was Gěng.
Her husband died,
and she had an affair with the son of a woman.
She was executed with Jiàng in the same marketplace.
Not daring to hinder his spirits.
From Gāomì (高密) he fled to Jiānghuái (江淮).
The Xiānzhǔ (先主) greatly promoted him.
When the Hòuzhǔ ascended the throne,
he was quite suspicious of northern people,
often sentencing them to death.
Xīzài, fearing disaster,
indulged his passions and acted wildly,
spending his wealth to buy hundreds of courtesans.
When his monthly salary arrived,
he distributed it all to the courtesans,
leaving nothing.
When he could no longer afford it,
he dressed in rags and pretended to be blind,
carrying a one-stringed zither,
and made his student Shū Yǎ (舒雅) hold the clappers.
He would go from room to room, singing and dancing to beg for money,
to supplement his daily meals.
Morning and evening, their comings and goings were not restricted.
He secretly mingled with the students.
When Xīzài passed by,
he would laugh and say:
"I dare not hinder your spirits," and nothing more.
At night, they would run to the guest's chamber.
One of his guests composed a poem:
"Most difficult to stop is the fifth watch,
dressing by someone's head."
At the time, it was said that even Xú Zhīcái (徐之才) of the Northern Qí (北齊) could not surpass him.
His monthly income was insufficient,
so he submitted a memorial to the Hòuzhǔ saying:
"My family has no savings for even a day,
and I lack the wealth of a hundred gold pieces in the wilds.
Even Zhòngní (仲尼) ate plain vegetables,
and Píngzhòng (平仲) had calloused shoulders;
they were not like this.
Now the autumn wind has arrived,
the cold is gradually increasing,
but I do not know how to obtain padded garments and clothes."
The Hòuzhǔ annotated:
"Xīzài, tut-tut!
He means he wants money,
to spend and waste,
and to attract more courtesans.
It's like saying a messenger from Línchuān (臨川),
whose silks are light and flimsy,
does not err as a poor scholar.
Moreover, with a daily salary of over fifty thousand,
to call it insufficient
would mean that exhausting the nation's wealth
would still only support a hundred-odd poor scholars!"
So he was bestowed cotton and silk from the imperial treasury for seasonal clothing.
From then on, he often failed to attend court,
and was impeached by those around him.
He was assigned to a division in Nándū (南都).
He submitted a memorial begging to stay, saying:
"All Buddhas are compassionate,
and always allow repentance.
Xuānní (宣尼) was sagacious and wise,
and also permitted self-renewal.
Your servant has no merit in making even a blade of grass stand,
but has monstrous crimes.
Though my frail body remains,
my valiant spirit has completely vanished.
My boat is full of young children and infants,
my whole household weeps sitting and cries walking.
With fierce winds and a lonely candle,
how can my sick body long endure?
Across ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains,
I cannot bear to look back at an eternal farewell."
The Hòuzhǔ again annotated:
"Since you have no intention to mend your ways,
you have brought about self-inflicted blame.
I read your memorial expressing repentance with sorrow.
You may be permitted to retain your original post at the capital."
Hú Dàn's (胡旦) Jueju (絕句).
Xià Yīnggōng Sǒng (夏英公竦) was garrisoned in Xiāngyáng (襄陽).
Hú Mìjiān Dàn (胡秘監旦) became blind
and was very irritable during his period of mourning.
Yīnggōng (英公) had once been his student,
and specifically went to see him.
One day he said to Yīnggōng:
"Are you studying?"
He replied:
"I am too busy with matters in the commandery to read,
but I occasionally compose jueju."
Hú Dàn said:
"Try reciting one."
Yīnggōng recited:
"Sparrows flutter like tangled hemp,
at the Hàn Jiāng (漢江) shoals, is the prefect's home.
In the empty hall, I regret having no golden pellets,
let them chirp and twitter until sunset."
Ten Treatises
Zhēnzōng (真宗) summoned Zhǒng Fàng (種放),
who, dressed in plain cloth, bowed with a long salutation to the prime ministers.
Yáng Dànián's (楊大年) poem states:
"Not offering a single word to aid the Emperor,
he clasped his hands and bowed to the Three Dukes."
The Emperor summoned Yáng Yì (楊億) and said:
"How do you know that he had no words to aid me?"
He produced ten scrolls from a black pouch,
which were Fàng's memorials.
The book was titled "Ten Treatises" (Shí Yì),

namely: Treatise on the Way, Treatise on Virtue, Treatise on Benevolence, Treatise on Righteousness, Treatise on Military Affairs, Treatise on Punishments, Treatise on Governance, Treatise on Taxation, Treatise on Stability, and Treatise on Danger.
Yáng Yì said:
"I shall go offer an apology with thorns on my back."
Poem of Joy at Court
Yáng Dànián, at eleven years old,
was recommended as a "Divine Child" and reached the imperial palace.
Counselor Lǐ Zhì ordered him to compose a poem "Joyfully Facing the Imperial Palace."
It contained the lines:
"The waves of Qīmǐn are vast and distant,
The twin palace towers majestically greet the dawn.
Ascending the outer ridges beyond the clouds,
At night, crossing the tides beneath the moon."
The concluding couplet read:
"I wish to uphold a pure and loyal integrity,
And forever stand in the holy court."
Early Plum Blossom Poem
Wáng Yígōng (Wáng Cēng),
while still a commoner, presented his literary works to Lǚ Wénmùgōng Méngzhèng.
He had an "Early Plum Blossom Poem" that said:
"In the snow, I haven't yet considered the matter of flavoring the soup,
But first I bloom at the head of all flowers."
Wénmùgōng said:
"This person is already destined to be a zhuàngyuán and a prime minister."
Later, it all came to pass.
Preserving One's Official Position
Chén Yà governed Rùnzhōu,
but had no accomplishments in administration.
Zhèxiàn Mǎ Qīng was seeking to impeach him.
When Mǎ arrived,
they had a banquet at the pavilion of Gānlù Sì.
When Mǎ Qīng was drunk,
the imperial censor said:
"Pour a full zùnzi for Langzhōng."
Chén was startled and replied with thanks:
"I dare not hope for a full position.
It would be a great fortune if I could just preserve my official position and depart."
Dīng Jìnggōng's Letter of Thanks
When Dīng Jìnggōng was demoted to Yázhōu,
powerful ministers indeed played a role.
Later, he was recalled to Guāngzhōu
and reinstated.
The powerful ministers were sent to govern Xǔtián.
Dīng sent a letter of thanks saying:
"For thirty years, we were companions in the academies and households,
not without common cause;
For ten thousand li, through wind and waves,
all was due to your kindness and support."
Written by Dù
Shí Zhōnglì was in the Central Secretariat.
Shèng Dù wrote "Zhāng Wén'gōng's Spirit Path Stele Inscription."
Shí hastily asked:
"Who wrote it?"
Shèng quickly replied:
"Dù wrote it."
The whole hall burst into laughter.
Pear: The Knives and Axes of the Five Zàng
Lǐ Jiànxūn, after being dismissed as prime minister in Jiāngnán,
was sent to govern Yùzhāng.
One day, he was traveling in Xīshān,
and happened to hear an old man in a thatched cottage teaching several village children.
He held a banquet in the old man's hut,
and ate several pears.
One of his subordinates said:
"Pears are called the 'knives and axes of the five zàng,'
and should not be eaten in excess."
The old man smiled and said:
"The 'knives and axes of the five zàng' in the Héguānzi refers to the 'lí' (離) of separation,
not 'lí' (梨) the pear.
Indeed, the pain of separation in one's heart
is much like knives and axes."
He then went to the shelf and took out a small booklet.
He dusted it off and presented it to the prime minister;
it was indeed the Héguānzi.
Yuán Ān Lying in Snow Painting
When Dīng Jìnggōng governed Jīnlíng,
he rebuilt the Shǎngxīn Tíng.
He took a painting from his family collection, "Yuán Ān Lying in Snow," and displayed it on the pavilion's screen.
It was a work by Zhōu Fǎng of the Táng dynasty.
It had been through fourteen governors,
and although they loved it dearly,
none dared to take it.
Coincidentally, one commander secretly took it away
and replaced it with a painting of reeds and wild geese.
Later, Wáng Qí Jūnyù left a poem that said:
"A thousand li of Qínhuái is in the jade pot,
The beautiful landscape strengthens Wú Dū.
The ancient man has already transformed into a crane in the distant sky,
The old painting of 'Lying in Snow' is hard to find.
The fleeting years rapidly pass by in the capital,
My sparse white hair grows old in the rivers and lakes.
The lingering cicadas do not understand the meaning of my ascent and gaze,
And again they chirp in the west wind, entering my sitting corner."
Dīng and Guàn, Two Lords' Inscriptions
At Gānlù Sì in Rùnzhōu, there was a well called Zhuó Quán.
Guàn Láigōng, during his southward exile, passed by it
and inscribed:
"Píngzhòng drank from this well,
looked back at the Northern Palace,
and departed sadly."
Not long after,
Dīng Jìnggōng also passed by
and inscribed:
"He is said to have drunk from the well,
worshipped the Buddha, and then left."
When Fàn Fěng was the commander of Húnán,
he left a poem that said:
"Píngzhòng drank from the well and looked north,
He is said to have worshipped the Buddha and headed south.
The misty mountains, emerald-locked, line the path outside the gate,
Making even the eminent monks weary of favor and glory."
Examining Sūtras
In Tánzhōu, during the examination for sūtra-reciting children,
the examiner recited the first line of a sūtra:
"Three thousand great thousands."
At that time, a child from Mǐn, unable to pronounce it correctly,
spoke in a southern accent and asked:
"Revered examiner,
I don't know if there is a world inside
or no world inside?"
The prefectural officials burst into laughter.
Explaining the Jié Guà
During the Huángyòu era,
Waiting Official Wáng Ānguó lectured on the Zhōuyì in the Èryīng Gé.
When he reached the Jié Guà, which contains "be cautious in speech,
be moderate in diet,"
Wáng spoke simply.
Rénzōng asked Jiǎ Wèigōng:
"Be cautious in what speech?
Be moderate in what diet?"
The duke replied:
"From the perspective of a gentleman,
then all words that leave his mouth are cautious,
and all food that enters his mouth is moderate.
From the perspective of a king,
then decrees are his speech,
and banquets are his diet.
He who governs the world must be cautious with decrees
and moderate with banquets."
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
Daoist Hùndùn
Tài-Zǔ and Tài-Zōng secretly shone forth, saying,
they once traveled with a Daoist priest.
He had no fixed name,
calling himself "Hùn-Dùn"
or "Zhēn-Wú."
After the Emperor ascended the throne, he was not seen again.
On the Shang-sì festival, while performing the lustration ritual by the western pond,
the Daoist priest bowed to Tài-Zǔ and said:
"How have you been since we last met?"
He immediately saw him,
just as he had always been.
They clapped their hands and drank heartily.
The Emperor said:
"How much longer will my life last?"
He replied:
"On the twentieth night of the tenth month this year,
if it is clear, you can extend it by twelve years.
Otherwise, you should make arrangements quickly."
The Emperor urgently detained him,
ordering him to stay in the rear garden.
Later, he was sometimes seen sleeping in a large bird's nest,
and then not seen for several days.
On the appointed day,
the Emperor ascended the Tài-Qīng Pavilion to observe the weather.
That night it was indeed clear,
the stars and constellations shining brightly.
The Emperor's heart was just beginning to rejoice.
Suddenly, dark clouds rose from all sides,
the heavens and earth dramatically changed,
and snow and hail abruptly fell.
He moved his imperial guard and descended the pavilion,
urgently sending for the palace key to open the Duān-Mén Gate,
summoning the Prefect of Kāi-Fēng,
who was Tài-Zōng.
He was led into the great bedchamber,
where they poured wine and drank together,
dismissing all palace officials.
Only the flickering candlelight was seen, and Tài-Zōng occasionally rose from his seat,
appearing overwhelmed.
After drinking,
the palace drum signaled the third watch,
and the snow had already fallen several inches.
The Emperor took his pillar-axe and stuck it
(pronounced chǒu-jiǎo-qiē)
into the snow,
looking at Tài-Zōng, he said:
"Do a good job, do a good job."
Then he untied his belt and lay down to sleep,
his snoring like thunder.
That night,
Tài-Zōng stayed in the forbidden palace.
Nearing the fifth watch,
those on duty in the palace heard nothing,
the Emperor had already died.
Tài-Zōng received the imperial edict,
and ascended the throne before the coffin.
Close officials surrounded the imperial screen to gaze upon the sacred body.
It was five-colored and warm-lustrous,
as if freshly bathed.
A disciple presented three strategies.
When Lái-Gōng was dismissed from his premiership,
he was transferred to govern Cháng-Ān.
His situation was bleak,
when suddenly a celestial decree descended in Gān-Yòu County.
Some suggested it was the Emperor's intention
to have Lái-Gōng endorse it,
to gain the trust of the world.
Lái-Gōng followed this.
Scholarly opinion was critical and regretful,
but soon after, he was reappointed as prime minister.
A disciple said:
"I have three strategies.
First, it would be best to feign illness
and seek an external prefecture to avoid disaster.
Second, on the day of the imperial audience, reveal the truth of the Gān-Yòu affair in a sincere memorial,
to somewhat salvage your reputation for fairness throughout your life.
Third, it's merely about being prime minister."
Lái-Gōng was displeased,
and eventually undertook the journey to Hǎi-Kāng.
Lǚ Shēn-Gōng recommended Chén Wén-Huì.
Lǚ Shēn-Gōng repeatedly sought to retire.
Rén-Zōng asked who could replace him.
Shēn-Gōng said:
"There is none like Chén Yáo-Zuǒ."
The Emperor agreed.
So he was appointed prime minister.
Later, Wén-Xiàn-Gōng greatly cherished the kindness of this recommendation,
and composed a lyric,
carrying a wine cup and singing it:
"On the auspicious day of the two Shè festivals,
in a thousand courtyards,
gracefully, we again see a pair of returning swallows.
The phoenix nest is stable, allowing them to be neighbors;
why do they come so late from the misty Xiāo-Xiāng?
Randomly entering the red pavilions,
flying low by the green banks,
lightly brushing the painted beams, scattering the dust of song.
For whom do they return, for whom do they come?
The host's affection is deep, the pearl screens are rolled up."
Shēn-Gōng laughed and said:
"I regret that the person who rolls up the screens is already old."
Wén-Huì replied:
"Do not say that the task of seasoning the broth is without merit."
Old in the imperial court,
his profound wisdom was undiminished.
Once, for Wú-Jiāng, he wrote a poem:
"The calm waves are vast, the cliffs are green,
the wild rice is just ripe, the willows are yellow.
My small boat is tied to the shore, unwilling to leave,
in the autumn wind, the slanting sun, the home of the perch."
And another poem, "Bì-Lán Hall in Hú-Zhōu":
"Tiáo Stream is clear and shallow, Zhà Stream slants,
the cold jade light illuminates ten thousand homes.
Who listens through the bright moon all night,
the fish flute from Dòng-Tíng across the reeds?"
The elder has already reported it to the Emperor.
The recluse Chōng-Huì Lǐ Tuì-Fū
was eccentric in his actions,
living in the northern suburbs of the capital.
One day he was planting coriander.
It was popularly believed that for it to flourish, the master of the household must recite vulgar words.
Tuì-Fū, scattering seeds,
quietly recited phrases about the way of husband and wife,
the nature of human relations,
and so on,
without ceasing.
Suddenly, a guest arrived.
He ordered his son to finish it. The son
held the remaining seeds and said:
"The elder has already reported it to the Emperor."
In the Huáng-Yòu era,
when officials in the academy sometimes conversed,
they would say it was appropriate to scatter coriander in one place.
Begging for a book to be bestowed.
Hú Dàn, a grand supervisor, had been blind for many years.
Suddenly, he memorialized, requesting an audience.
Zhēn-Zōng granted it.
Wáng Yí-Gōng said:
"This old man has a sharp tongue;
if he faces the emperor, he will surely slander current policies."
Therefore, he memorialized, saying:
"Hú Dàn has been blind and incapacitated for a long time.
He might lose his composure and make mistakes.
I request that he be sent to the Secretariat to inquire about the reason for his request for an audience."
Dàn was very moved by this.
When he arrived at the hall,
Yí-Gōng and the other prime ministers performed the student's ritual of bowing in array.
Dàn bowed with a long salute and sat down.
Yí-Gōng asked how his eye condition was lately.
Hú replied:
"Recently, it has somewhat improved.
I can see the prime minister and the grand councilor about three or two parts of the way."
When asked why he came,
he firmly requested an audience.
After the imperial decree was conveyed,
it merely stated that there was no book from Xiāng-Yáng,
and he requested a book be bestowed.
Yí-Gōng said:
"This can certainly be granted."
He urgently memorialized, and the imperial edict was received:
"Act according to the memorial."
The request for an audience should not be granted.
What good are "zhī," "hū," "zhě," and "yě"?
Tài-Zǔ was about to expand the outer city,
and visited the Zhū-Què Gate.
The Emperor pointed to the gate plaque and asked Zhào Pǔ:
"Why does it only say 'Zhū-Què Gate'?
What use is adding the character 'zhī'?"
Pǔ replied:
"It's a particle."
Tài-Zǔ said:
"Zhī, hū, yě, zhě, what good are they?"
Tuì-Chuán's Spring Outing
Tuì-Chuán Zhāng Dèng-Gōng Shì-Xùn,
in late spring, rode in an an-yú (sedan chair) out through the Nán-Xūn Gate.
Towards evening, he pointed towards Yí-Qiū and entered.
The gate guards, holding a gate plaque, asked for his official rank.
Shì-Xùn wrote a quatrain:
"Idly wandering by the Ling-Zhǎo, seeing spring return,
why must the border official suspect me so much?
An eighty-year-old old man with no rank,
I once came to the Fèng-Chí three times."
Record of Hénán Post Station
Qián Sīgōng (錢思公) was stationed in Luò (洛),
and his subordinates were all outstanding talents of the time.
At that time, Hé'nán (河南) was establishing a large post station,
and Xiè Xīshēn (謝希深), Yǐn Shīlǔ (尹師魯), and Ōu Yǒngshú (歐永叔) were each ordered to compose a record.
Xīshēn's (希深) essay was nearly seven hundred characters,
Ōugōng's (歐公) was five hundred characters,
and Shīlǔ's (師魯) was only a little over three hundred eighty characters.
Ōugōng (歐公) was not content to be beneath Shīlǔ (師魯),
so he composed another record,
reducing Shīlǔ's (師魯) text by twenty characters to complete it,
which was even more perfect and structured.
Shīlǔ (師魯) said:
"Ōu Jiǔ (歐九) truly travels a thousand *lǐ* (里) in a day!"
Yìyán (奕嵓) avoids the enticement of the six palaces
Tàizōng (太宗) favored Yìyán (奕嵓).
An admonishing minister requested that the待zhào (待詔) Jiǎ Xuán (賈玄) be banished to Nánzhōu (南州),
saying that Xuán (玄) frequently presented new and wonderful chess positions,
charming and enticing the enlightened sovereign,
fearing that he would hinder the myriad affairs of state.
The Emperor said:
"I am not unaware,
but merely avoiding the enticement of the six palaces."
What about the discussion of the "Lord of Skins"?
Zhēnzōng (真宗) wished to select a court official who was skilled in archery and had a fine appearance,
to accompany the Khitan (虜) envoy in an archery contest.
At that time, only Chén Kāngsù Yáozī (陳康肅堯咨) possessed both qualities.
The Emperor said to the Hànlín (翰林) academician Yàn Shū (晏殊):
"If Chén (陳) is willing to switch to a military role,
I shall bestow upon him a marshal's staff.
You may convey this to him."
Kāngsù's (康肅) mother was still living,
and Chén (陳) said:
"I must inform my old mother;
I dare not act on my own."
His mother angrily slapped him and said:
"You were ranked first in the imperial examinations,
and both father and son gained fame as eminent officials through literary achievements in court.
Do you wish to illicitly usurp a high salary,
bringing shame upon our family?"
The Emperor wrote on a small piece of paper in tiny script and asked Yàn (晏):
"What about the discussion of the 'Lord of Skins'?"
A junior eunuch mistakenly sent it to the Zhōngshū (中書),
and the ministers were bewildered and did not understand.
The next day, when they reported,
the Emperor smiled and accommodated them, saying:
"I did not understand this phrase from the classics,
so I asked you all."
The Emperor dismissed the eunuch to the front office.
There is no land to build a tower, Prime Minister
When Guān Láigōng (冠萊公) was first born,
both of his earlobes had fleshy rings,
which did not close until he was several years old.
He suspected that he had once been an extraordinary monk,
and enjoyed visiting Buddhist temples and conversing with monks.
He had enjoyed wealth and high position for forty years,
but had no fields, houses, or gardens.
In Dàmíng (大名),
he personally issued an imperial examination topic titled "Rhapsody on Gōngyí Xiū (公儀休) Uprooting Garden Mallows" and "Poem on General Huò (霍) Declining the Construction of a Mansion,"
which reflected his aspiration.
Wèi Yě (魏野) presented a poem saying:
"Holding office in the imperial court,
yet no land to build a tower."
Later, a Khitan (虜) envoy entered Dàmíng (大名)
and asked:
"Is that not the Prime Minister who has no land to build a tower?"
The thieves in Shǎnxī (陝西) have not yet been caught
In Kāng's (康) residence,
the Western Róng (戎) bordered the frontier,
and the imperial army suffered a defeat.
A prime minister in power,
due to old age, was permitted to retire.
His colleagues came to his residence to congratulate him.
As the drinking became merry,
he boasted:
"I am but a mountain dweller;
I encountered a time when I could retire at home due to old age,
at a time when there was no trouble in the world.
This can be called a fortunate citizen of peaceful times."
Shí Cānzhèng (石參政) stood up and said:
"Only that band of thieves in Shǎnxī (陝西) has not yet been caught."
The entire company burst into laughter.
The talent and capacity of the three servants to become prime ministers
Tàizōng (太宗) had eight sons;
Zhēnzōng (真宗) was the third,
enfeoffed as Shòuwáng (壽王).
An edict ordered an extraordinary monk to examine all the princes.
The monk had already seen seven princes,
but only Shòuwáng (壽王) had not yet risen.
The monk reported:
"I have visited all the princely residences.
None are comparable to Shòuwáng (壽王)."
The Emperor said:
"You have not seen him;
how do you know?"
The monk said:
"Just now I saw three servants standing at the gate;
all possess the talent and capacity to become prime ministers.
Since his servants are like that,
the master can be known."
The three servants were:
Zhāng Xiàngqí (張相耆), Yáng Xiàngchóngxūn (楊相崇勳), and Guō Dàwèi Chéngyòu (郭大尉承祐).
Why is the Son of Heaven called "Guānjiā"?
Lǐ Shìdú Zhòngróng (李侍讀仲容) was good at drinking,
known as Lǐ Wànhuí (李萬回).
Zhēnzōng (真宗) had no equal in drinking capacity,
and whenever he drank, he would summon Lǐ (公).
One evening,
the Emperor ordered a huge goblet.
Zhòngróng (仲容) said:
"I beg Your Majesty (官家),
spare the huge goblet."
The Emperor then asked, "Why is the Son of Heaven called 'Guānjiā' (官家)?"
Zhòngróng (仲容) replied:
"Jiǎng Jì's (蔣濟) 'Wànjī Lùn' (萬機論) states:
'The Three Sovereigns governed the world publicly (官天下),
the Five Emperors governed the world as a family (家天下).'
Combining the virtues of the Three and Five,
therefore he is called 'Guānjiā' (官家)."
The Emperor was greatly pleased and said:
"This truly is what is called a thousand-year encounter between sovereign and minister."
Lǐ (李) replied:
"Loyalty and filial piety are lifelong sentiments."
Chì Hóngyá (赤洪崖) strikes Bái Hóngyá (白洪崖)
Dīng Jìngōng (丁晉公) received his first official appointment as deputy magistrate of Ráo (饒).
His contemporary Bái Jī (白積) sent a note requesting a loan of five hundred *qián* (錢).
Jī (積), being a new son-in-law to a wealthy family,
feared that Dīng (公) would bother him,
hence he did this.
Dīng (公) replied:
"How can I obtain blessings by deceiving Heaven?
Your scheming is greatly misguided.
Five hundred green *fú* (蚨) are missing from both families,
Chì Hóngyá (赤洪崖) strikes Bái Hóngyá (白洪崖)."
Some say that at that time, there was already a prophecy of Zhū Yá (朱崖).
The Daoist of Hemp Robes
Qián Wénxǐgōng Ruòshuǐ (錢文禧公若水),
while young, visited Chén Xīyí (陳希夷) to have his fortune told.
Chén (陳) invited him into his mountain study, to a hearth on the ground,
where he saw an old monk, wrapped in a worn robe, with eyes closed, leaning by the fire.
Qián (錢) bowed to him,
and the monk merely opened his eyes slightly.
After a long while,
Chén (陳) asked:
"How is it?"
The monk shook his head and said:
"He does not have this kind of bone structure."
Later, Chén Xīyí (陳希夷) saw him and said:
"I first saw your pure and clear divine countenance,
and thought you could learn the ways of immortals.
But this monk says you have no immortal bones,
and will only become a noble high official."
Qián (錢) asked:
"Who was that monk?"
Chén (陳) replied:
"The Daoist of Hemp Robes (麻衣道者)."
To prepare money to pay for the "green shoots" tax
Fǔ Rén Ráosǒng,
in the Xīníng reign, failed the imperial examination.
He presented a poem to Wáng Jīnggōng, saying:
"Flying back, with drooping wings, descending from the azure heavens,
I turn towards Línchuān, the homeward path is distant.
My two acres of barren land are all sold off,
to obtain money to pay the green shoots tax."
Ráosǒng had a long-standing acquaintance with Liú Xiāngchōng,
who was then the Prefect of Héngzhōu.
Ráosǒng called upon him.
The Duke was displeased by his visit.
Ráosǒng quickly said:
"I am but a minor official,
I would not dare to pass by secretly.
I will see you once and then depart."
The Duke asked what he lacked.
He replied:
"Nothing at all,
except for good wine."
So, the Duke presented him with a load (of wine),
and Ráosǒng whipped his horse and left.
When Ráosǒng arrived at Lèiyáng,
he secretly observed that its magistrate was negligent.
He immediately paid him a visit and said:
"The Prefect sends his regards.
He presents you with a double jug from his military store;
please prepare a letter of thanks."
The magistrate did not suspect he was lying,
and immediately ordered a wooden seal to be carved,
and collected money to present to Ráosǒng.
A few days later, Liú received the letter and laughed in surprise.
He also once failed the imperial examination and left the capital.
He used a major merchant's name for a large loan,
to avoid taxes.
He himself drafted a sheet of appointment notices,
all for major appointments.
Whenever he passed a checkpoint or presented his calling card,
he would quickly say:
"Have you heard about the recent official appointments?
I recorded them a few days ago just before leaving the capital."
No official was unwilling to see him.
Afterwards, he would say:
"I am but a humble student who failed the examination.
Although my boat contains nothing,
I dare trouble your officials for an inspection."
The person would say:
"Why bother with such a thing?"
Having spoken, he would float away.
By this means, he gained a great deal.
The Meaning of Cìbó
Xià Yīnggōng was garrisoned in Xiāngyáng.
When a general amnesty was declared,
it coincided with a peaceful year, and everyone was bestowed with cìbó.
At that time, Hú Dàn was blind and infirm in the prefecture.
The Duke, following the amnesty decree,
sent ten bolts of silk.
Hú laughed and said:
"Tell the Shèrén,
why is he so unobservant?
I return five bolts;
please consult the 'Hánshī Wàizhuàn' and the explanations of various scholars like Fú Qián regarding the meaning of 'cìbó jiājiān,
bì yú qiūyuán' (a small gift of silk for a recluse in the garden)."
The Duke checked it,
and indeed found the regulations for cìbó and cìxiū from the Three Dynasties.
A lord receiving cìxiū would get ten bundles (tǐng),
which was a bundle of dried meat;
cìbó, on the other hand, was rolled into two pieces of five bolts (pǐ),
symbolizing that the king had humility and showed deference to the way of hermits.
Casting a Bell for Qīngliáng Temple
During the time of the Lǐ family in Jiāngnán,
a commoner died and then revived.
He said he had gone to the Underworld,
and saw the former ruler engaged in very severe construction work.
The commoner was greatly alarmed and said:
"Why has Your Majesty come to this?"
The ruler said:
"I was misled by Sòng Qíqiū,
and killed over a thousand surrendered people from Hézhōu.
When you return, tell the current ruler
that whenever a great bell rings in a monastery,
my suffering temporarily ceases.
It would be even better if he could cast a bell for me."
Later, the ruler cast a bell for Qīngliáng Temple,
and inscribed on it: "To respectfully intercede for Lièzǔ Xiàohuángdì to escape the underworld and be relieved of distress."
Sūn Sīmiǎo Invites a Monk to Preach the Fǎhuā Jīng
A monk in Chéngdū recited the 'Fǎhuā Jīng' (Lotus Sūtra) with great devotion.
Even amidst military chaos in Shǔ,
it could not harm him.
Suddenly, a mountain servant arrived
and said:
"Tomorrow morning, the Master invites you to recite the sūtra."
He led the attendant across several streams and mountain ridges.
Amidst mist and haze was a mountain dwelling.
The servant said:
"The Master is late to rise due to illness.
Please recite until the 'Bǎotǎ Pǐn' (Stūpa Chapter).
When you reach it, please let us know,
as he wishes to hear it."
At that time, he indeed emerged,
dressed in rustic clothes and leaning on a staff.
His two ears hung down to his shoulders.
After burning incense and listening to the sūtra,
he entered and did not come out again.
There was a rattan plate, bamboo chopsticks, a bowl of glutinous rice,
and several bowls of wolfberry and chrysanthemum tea.
There was no salt or dairy,
yet it tasted as sweet as dew.
He received one coin as payment.
The servant saw him off to the path entrance
and asked:
"What is the Master's surname?"
He replied:
"My surname is Sūn."
When asked his given name,
the servant wrote the two characters "Sīmiǎo" on the monk's palm.
The monk was greatly alarmed,
and the servant disappeared.
He searched the mountains for three days,
but eventually lost the old path.
Upon returning, he examined the payment
and found it was a hundred copper coins.
From that one meal,
his body became light and free from illness.
During the Tiānxī reign,
the monk was a hundred years old.
Later, he became a recluse and was not seen again.
Ode to Crabs
Púyè Yán Xù,
initially, was despised by the world for his high position and lack of scholarship.
Jiāng Wénwèi composed the 'Xiè Fù' (Ode to Crabs) to satirize him,
which contained the lines:
"Outwardly, many feet;
within, no inch of intestine.
With a mouth full of yellow (critical remarks),
often losing its way when looking at itself;
with armor in its chest,
constantly gathering crowds to move sideways."
Yán Xù, knowing Hán Xīzài had talent and fame,
asked him to compose his father's tomb inscription,
wishing to casually gain praise and trust from others.
He generously gifted him gold, jewels, and a singing girl.
After Hán Xīzài finished the text,
it contained no mention of Yán Xù's deeds.
Yán Xù requested revisions.
Hán Xīzài returned all the gifts,
and only wrote a quatrain on a pair of gold-embossed silk ribbons, saying:
"Wind-blown willow flowers have no fixed branches,
the clouds and rain of Yángtái return in a dream.
In future years, when sounds from Péngdǎo cease,
keep the old dancing dress from before the wine cup."
A Small Star in the Purple Palace Enclosure
When Zǔ and Zōng were living in obscurity,
they roamed the market of Cháng'ān with Zhào Pǔ.
Suddenly, they met Chén Xīyí, who said:
"Shall we go to the market for a drink?"
Tàizǔ said:
"Zhào Xuéjiū can share a seat with us."
Chén Xīyí squinted at Hán Wáng and said:
"That's fine too."
Upon entering the wine shop,
Hán Wáng's leg became numb,
and he contended for the left seat.
Chén Xīyí angrily said:
"A small star in the Purple Palace Enclosure,
daring to occupy my seat,
is that permissible?"
He ordered him to sit on the right side of the seat.
Satirizing Chén Liè's Poem
Cài Jūnmó was the Prefect of Fútáng.
He invited Lǐ Gòu and Chén Liè to dine in his back garden.
It was late spring,
and wine was served.
Local people were enjoying themselves,
and courtesans, by custom, passed by with greetings.
The Duke kept them to assist with the wine.
As they sang a tune,
Chén Liè was alarmed and terrified,
climbing over the wall and up a tree to escape.
Lǐ Gòu composed a poem, saying:
"Gazing at the mountains and waters of Qīmǐn in my palm,
I ascend with zest until twilight.
Who is at the painted pavilion where wine is sold?
How many oars click as they return with the tide?
When clear, the sea's color is vaguely seen;
after drinking, homesickness gradually wanes.
Mountain birds do not know the joy of red powder,
one beat of the clappers sends them startling away."
This was to satirize his excessive affectation.
Phosphorescent Lights
Sēnglù Zànníng 博物 (was knowledgeable),
Wáng Yǔchēng and Xú Xuàn once studied with him.
Liǔ Kāi was defending Wéiyáng.
In the rear garden, when it was cloudy and rainy, green flames would flicker and rise,
and dissipate upon close touch.
Níng said,
“This is phosphorescence.
Blood from soldiers in battle or from oxen and horses,
when it adheres to the earth, congeals into this gas.”
Liǔ dug there,
and found broken spears and shattered swords.
It was an ancient battlefield.
He then composed a poem saying,
“Today, in the empty gate, I see Zhāng Huá.”
Naturally worthy of tears, why add a setting sun?
During Zhēnzōng's national mourning,
all those whose sons and younger brothers were appointed to the positions of zhāiláng (chaplain) or wǎnláng (mourning assistant),
if a zhāiláng, merely attended the mourning rites;
if a wǎnláng, even had to hold the funeral ropes and fans.
When Wáng Yígōng was in the Zhōngshū,
Hànlín Chéngzhǐ Lǐ Jì continuously visited the Zhōngtáng, seeking to exempt his son from the duty of a wǎnláng.
Gōng playfully said,
“Yesterday and today,
a zhāiláng and then a wǎnláng.”
Jì replied,
“Naturally worthy of tears,
why add a setting sun?”
Not many days later,
Dīng (his son) was indeed removed from his post,
and Lǐ Jì was subsequently demoted to the south,
fulfilling the omen of tears.
Yètíng concubines becoming nuns
Shēnguó Zhǎngzhǔ became a nun,
and over thirty Yètíng concubines followed her in becoming nuns.
Tàizōng issued an edict for the two Jin (academies) to each compose a poem to send them off.
Chén Péngnián’s poem says:
“They cast off all their flower hairpins and scatter them in Bǎojīn,
their cloud hair newly shorn in late spring.
Startled that a candle in the wind is hard to keep in the world,
they become pond lotuses, unstained in body.
As the palm leaves are flipped, they seem like brocade scrolls;
the Buddhist chants just learned are mistaken for dust on the beams.
From now on, after their enchanting forms return to emptiness,
on the Xiāngpǔ, there should be no one to untie a jade pendant.”
Zǐwēi loses Zhāng Jūnfáng
During the Xiángfú era, imperial scholars were ordered to compile the 《Rìběnguó Xiángguāng Jì》 (Record of Auspicious Light from Japan).
Those on duty were not learned enough,
and often had Zhāng Jūnfáng substitute for them.
Once, when the imperial summons was very urgent,
Zhāng was drunk in Fánlóu,
and the Zǐwēi was in a great predicament.
Later, Qián and Yáng Ergōng composed a 《Xián Máng Lìng》 (Ode to Leisure and Busyness).
Dànián said,
“Who in the world is most called leisurely?
The Supervising Censor, shaking off his robes, returned to Huàshān.”
This referred to Zhǒng Fàng.
Xībái said,
“Who in the world is most called busy?
The Zǐwēi has lost Zhāng Jūnfáng.”
Little Yóujī
Chén Wénhuìgōng Yáozuǒ and his brother Yáosǒu both reached the position of prime minister.
His brother Yáozī was especially skilled with the bow and arrow,
and called himself Little Yóujī.
During the Xiángfú era, he returned from governing Jīngnán.
His mother, Lady Mǎ, said,
“You presided over a famous prefecture, what unusual policies did you implement?”
Yáozī replied,
“The road was a vital thoroughfare,
and receiving and sending off guests was a daily occurrence.
However, with my bow and arrow, none were disobedient.”
His mother said,
“Your father assisted the country with loyalty and filial piety,
not engaging in benevolent governance and good transformation,
but solely performing the daily tasks of a hundred men!”
She struck him with a staff,
and his gold fish ornament fell to the ground.
Method for refining mercury
Fàn Wénzhènggōng Zhòngyān was extremely poor and distressed in his youth.
He often associated with a certain alchemist.
When the alchemist was gravely ill,
he told Wénzhèng,
“I have a method for refining mercury.
My son is young and not capable of it.
Now I impart this formula to you.”
He also gave him one catty of silver,
placing it in Wénzhèng’s bosom.
Later, Fàn became a remonstrance official.
When the alchemist’s son had grown up,
Fàn summoned him and informed him.
He took out the formula and the silver and gave them to the son,
the seal and mark perfectly intact.
Luòyáng flowers and wine arrive all at once
Chén Wénhuìgōng retired to Zhèngxià.
At that time, Xiàngshì Xùn of Zhāng (Zhang Xun), was the Prefect of Xīyáng,
and often sent him Yáohuáng and Wèizǐ peonies and wine.
Gōng replied with a poem saying,
“With flowers but no wine, my head is lazy to lift;
with wine but no flowers, my eyes are tired to open.
Just as I felt desolate in the west garden,
Luòyáng flowers and wine arrived all at once.”
The river god also has worldly feelings
Féng Cānzhèng Jīng,
during the Qìnglì era, was recommended from Èzhōu for the provincial examination.
Upon reaching the great river,
the winds and waves were turbulent,
almost causing the boat to sink.
The following spring, he became the top scholar in Nánshěng,
and also placed first in the palace examination.
Having received imperial favor, he returned to È,
again crossing the great river.
The wind was gentle and the waves calm,
and the boat was safe.
Gōng inscribed a poem at the river pavilion saying,
“The river god also has worldly feelings,
making the wind favorable for me.”
Poem on encountering wind while crossing the Huái River
Táng Jiè was crossing the Huái River.
In the middle of the river, he encountered a storm,
and the boatmen were very frightened.
Gōng recited,
“The enlightened Sòng is not the mad Chǔ,
the clear Huái is different from Mìluó.
My whole life relies on loyalty and trustworthiness,
today I yield to the wind and waves.”
At dusk,
the boat reached the shore,
and everyone was delighted.
Gōng completed his poem saying,
“The boat was indeed perilous,
with many turtles and alligators appearing and disappearing.
Fortunately, all was well at sunset,
so I bought wine and listened to fishing songs.”
Wěigǎo
In the fifth year of Jǐngyòu,
Sòng Jiāo and Qí Qímíng were equally famous,
the world called them the "Two Sòngs,"
likening them to the "Two Lùs."
When Qí was in Shǔ,
he had three hundred poems,
titled 《Wěigǎo》.
He once had a poem saying,
“The verdant clouds idly hold a three-year promise,
the bright moon vainly causes sorrow in two places.”
Later, he ultimately did not enter the two prefectures (high offices) before he died.
Báizhù Yín
Wáng Yànzé, when young, recited the 《Báizhù Xíng》 (Ballad of White Ramie) saying,
“Your heart should not weary of too much joy,
please look at the sun setting among the clouds.”
Commentators said,
“Beautiful it is,
but the setting sun,
with not much time left,
its meaning is close to a prophecy.”
Indeed, his life was not long.
Volume 18
End.
Lamp in the sutra pillar
Yáng Zhēn was studying at Zhāoyìng Sì (temple).
He often saw a red-clad woman reciting a poem:
“The golden hall cannot bear the autumn,
the moon slants, the stone tower is cold.
Who is the one who looks upon me?
Drawing the curtain, I pity my lone shadow.”
He asked her surname.
She replied,
“My distant ancestor’s name was Wú Jì,
surname Sòng.
For ten generations in Hàn, through promoting Buddhism,
he was enfeoffed as Chángmínggōng.
During the Kāiyuán era,
Mínghuáng established a sutra pillar for Yáng Fēi,
and I was enfeoffed as Xīníng Fūrén,
then granted a coral canopy to reside under.
Since then, Xùnshēng and Éláng no longer committed violence.”
Upon verification,
it was a lamp inside the sutra pillar.
Concubine exchanges horses
Bào Shēng, a wine-loving fellow, kept many singing girls.
Wéi Shēng, who lived in an outer residence, was fond of riding swift horses.
They traveled in all directions,
each pursuing their own pleasure.
One day, they met at a mountain temple
and exchanged their favorite possessions.
Bào Shēng traded a female entertainer skilled at the four-stringed instrument
for Wéi Shēng’s purple "Zhìbō" horse.
Suddenly, two men approached their table.
Their clothes and hats were very ancient in style.
They were invited to drink together.
The two guests said,
“We just heard of the exchange of a concubine for a horse.
Might we compose a joint *fù* on this theme?”
They then plucked a banana leaf from the courtyard and wrote on it.
One recited:
“That beautiful person,
like an essence of jade.
That fine horse,
bears the name of swiftness.
Intending to pursue the sun,
how can one begrudge sacrificing a beauty?
Fragrant and warm in her deep boudoir,
she had not yet tired of the color of her tender peach blossom;
The wind clear on the wide road,
it had often heard the sound of its jade-like snorting.”
The other said:
“She turns her steps back from the courtyard steps,
stands before the hall.
Looking for new favor,
fearing she is not my match;
Lamenting the old master,
suspecting I am ridden by another.
The fragrance disperses from the green horse,
my mind has already forgotten the black hair;
Sweat flows on the red cheeks,
love is no different from congealed fat.”
The *fù* was lengthy,
and is not recorded here.
The two guests introduced themselves as Jiāng Yān and Xiè Zhuāng.
The White-Robed Elder Chants
During the Huìchāng period,
Xǔ Xiàolián Lù traveled by the Gāntáng Guǎn,
and encountered a white-robed old man riding a horse and chanting loudly:
“Spring grass lush, spring water green,
Wild crabapple blossoms all spent, scattering fragrant jade.
Before the Xiùlǐng Palace, a white-haired person,
still sings the songs of Kāiyuán’s peaceful times.”
Xǔ was surprised by this,
and pursued him into the forest but saw nothing.
Huán Yíng Tú
Chén Jìxiāng was
a native of Jiāngnán.
He passed the *jìnshì* examination and went to Cháng’ān,
not returning for ten years.
One day, while visiting a monk at Qīnglóng Sì, he found him absent,
and rested in the great pavilion.
An old man from Zhōngnán Shān was also waiting for the monk,
and they sat together for a long time.
On the wall was a map called *Huán Yíng Tú*.
Jìxiāng traced the route to Jiāngnán and sighed, saying,
“If I could return from here,
I would not regret having achieved nothing.”
The old man said,
“This is easy.”
He rose, broke off a bamboo leaf from the steps,
and placed it in the Wèishǔi River, saying,
“Fix your gaze on this,
and your wish will be granted.”
Jìxiāng looked intently,
and saw the Wèishǔi River with turbulent waves.
A very large boat appeared,
and he was suddenly on board.
It traveled extremely fast.
On the way, he stopped at Chánkū Sì,
and inscribed a poem:
“Frost bells chime at dusk, the north wind is fierce,
Scattered crows once more gather in the cold woods.
At this moment, I stop my oar, grieving and chanting,
Alone, I stand facing the one peak of Liánhuá.”
The next day, he reached Tóngguān,
and again composed a poem:
“Having already made plans to be ashamed to return,
it is still better than being ashamed not to return.”
After more than ten days, he arrived home.
His wife greeted him with great joy.
After a couple of nights, he said,
“The examination date is approaching,
I cannot stay long.”
He then re-embarked on the boat,
and composed a poem to bid farewell to his wife:
“Wine adds to sorrow as I drink,
Poems are composed as I wipe away tears and chant.”
He floated away.
His family was astonished,
thinking he was a ghost.
Suddenly, he was back at the Wèishǔi River,
and hurried to Qīnglóng Sì.
The temple monk had still not returned,
and the old man from the mountain was still sitting, wrapped in his coarse robe.
Jìxiāng asked,
“Was it not a dream?”
The old man said,
“You will know it yourself another day.”
A month later,
his family came to visit,
fully recounting what had happened,
and all his inscribed poems were verified.
Observing Fish at Zǐshítán
Xú Lìzhī was reading at night
when he saw hundreds of figures, like grains of millet,
all wearing armor,
escorting a red-capped, purple-robed figure
walking on the table.
They called out,
“The King of Ants wishes to observe fish at Zǐshítán.”
Looking right and left, they retrieved dozens of fishing tools
and all entered the inkstone,
catching thousands of small fish.
Lìzhī was greatly startled.
He covered them with a book scroll,
held a candle and lit it,
but saw nothing.
Lǐ Tián Zuǎn, Shàngshū Yúbù Yuánwàiláng
Revision of the Demotion Edict for a Meritorious Official
There was a meritorious official during the reign of Emperor Xiànzōng of Táng
who had served for a long time,
but whose family had committed ugly acts.
The Central Secretariat submitted a demotion edict which read:
“His beastly conduct
has long been known to be forgetful of human ethics;
His greed, like that of a jackal or wolf,
is increasingly evident in public opinion.”
The Emperor said,
“He has public wealth,
which he has frequently used.
His sordid private conduct,
its truth and falsehood are hard to distinguish.
I fear that the ministers might be holding private grudges and falsely accusing him.”
He personally revised it to read:
“Failing to cultivate family conduct,
he is suddenly heard to be scorned by the literati;
Deeply betraying the nation’s grace,
how can he still glory in his official position?”
Táng Sù’s Clear Discernment
Táng Sù, who was a Daìzhì,
had previously passed the *jìnshì* examination with Dīng Jìngōng,
and they were close friends.
Later, when Dīng Jìngōng resided in the Shuǐguì Jiē residence,
and was about to receive a high appointment to assist the emperor,
Táng Sù moved to the north of the prefecture to avoid him.
Someone asked him the reason,
and he said,
“It is said that he will soon receive a great appointment.
If I associate with him frequently,
it will be seen as dependence.
If I don’t see him for a long time,
his feelings will surely become suspicious.
Therefore, I avoid him.”
Later, when Dīng Jìngōng was demoted to the south,
Táng Sù said,
“Dīng’s talent and skill
are like those of Lǐ Zànhuáng.
He is more active than still,
more knowing than benevolent.
He can assist in three matters,
but he cannot lead all officials.”
Pí Rìxiū Discusses Buddhist Scriptures
Pí Rìxiū of Táng strongly believed in Buddhist scriptures,
considering equality, karmic retribution, and naturalness as the fruit of Buddhahood.
During the turmoil of Guǎngmíng,
he was falsely appointed as a Hàlín Xuéshì.
When he was harmed,
he faced it with serenity.
Son Unknown to Father
Duàn Wénchāng was garrisoned in Chéngdū.
His son, Chéngshì, was fond of hunting,
which the Chancellor was concerned about.
Chéngshì distributed the pheasants and rabbits he caught to the staff,
sending a letter with each,
which cited many historical precedents.
Most of the staff did not understand the meaning
and showed them to the Chancellor,
who then realized his son was well-learned.
Xiānyú Judges a Case
Wèi Shǔ's Xiān Yú Cāo (鮮于操) was the magistrate of Huáyáng (華陽) county.
There was a woman whose surname was Táng (唐).
Her husband died.
She went to the county office to state her case,
begging to guard her husband's grave.
Cāo (操) adjudicated her petition, saying:
"Though husband and wife are intimate,
it is important for males and females to maintain separation.
While alive, one adheres to propriety,
and during the day, there are no rules for residing and sleeping together;
when dead, one must avoid suspicion,
and weeping aloud at night is forbidden.
Dwelling alone in a hut,
how can one guard against strong and violent individuals?
Only by returning to the same tomb together
can one truly show constancy from beginning to end.
It is truly necessary to forbid this,
to put an end to superficiality."
Mèng Zhǔ (孟主) promoted Cāo (操) one rank,
rewarding him for his understanding of propriety.
Half a Year as a Bandit
Zhāng Guāiyá (張乖崖) governed Shǔ (蜀).
A bandit was captured.
The Duke questioned him.
The bandit said:
"I always operate as a bandit for half a year.
From the third to the eighth month,
the nights are short and there are many mosquitoes and gnats,
so people tend to sleep less,
thus I dare not act as a bandit.
From the ninth to the second month,
the nights are long and the weather is cold,
many fear the cold and are lazy to get up,
so it is possible to be a bandit."
The Duke asked:
"What work do you do in spring and summer?"
The bandit replied:
"I do a little selling and peddling,
going to the prefectures and counties to carefully investigate households, their resources, and the entrances and exits of people,
which is why for over ten years I haven't lost a single sale."
The Duke exclaimed:
"Even bandits have their ways,
how true!"
The Method of Governance
Rèn Zhōngzhèng (任中正) succeeded Duke Zhāng (張公) in governing Shǔ (蜀).
He sought his advice on the method of governance.
The Duke said:
"If your own insights are superior to the law,
then abandon the law and use your own.
If your own insights are not superior to the law,
then you should uphold the law,
and not follow your own views.
For the law sets out major principles,
it is up to individuals to apply them with discretion regarding severity."
The Magistrate's Birthday
During the Kāibǎo (開寶) era,
there was a magistrate of Shénquán (神泉) county whose surname was Zhāng (張).
Outwardly, he appeared honest and incorruptible,
but inwardly, he was extremely greedy and corrupt.
One day,
he posted a notice at the county gate saying, "On such-and-such a month and day is the magistrate's birthday.
It is hereby announced to all county residents that no gifts are to be presented."
A clerk said:
"His Lord explicitly mentioned his birthday,
wishing us to know."
Everyone said:
"Indeed."
On the day, each brought silk as a gift,
saying, "For longevity garments."
The magistrate refused nothing.
He then announced again:
"Next month, on such-and-such a day,
is the county lady's birthday.
Do not bring anything again."
Wáng Wéi (王維) satirized him with a "Little Egret Poem," saying:
"Flying, it seems like a crane,
but where it lands, it seeks fish."
Lín Bū (林逋) Granted Silk
Lín Bū (林逋), a recluse, lived in seclusion by West Lake (Xī Hú).
The imperial court ordered the prefect Wáng Jìxiū (王濟休) to visit him.
Bū (逋) heard of it,
and submitted a petition,
the text of which was all in rhyming couplets.
Thus, he was recommended for his literary talent.
An imperial edict was issued,
granting him silk, and that was all.
Jìxiū (濟休) said:
"A man of the mountains and swamps,
his writings should study antiquity, and not be involved with kings and nobles;
a man of letters,
should cultivate his rhetoric and establish sincerity,
awaiting the time to be put to use.
Now Lín Bū (林逋) has missed this."
Chess Pieces Occupy the Mind
Dīng Jìnggōng (丁晉公) was fond of Buddhism and Taoism,
and also passionately loved playing chess.
After dining in the main hall, he would continue playing chess from night to day.
One day he asked Lǐ Tián (李畋) about the method of emptying the mind.
Lǐ Tián (李畋) replied:
"Please, apart from assisting and harmonizing the Imperial Household,
do not let your mind be occupied by chess pieces,
and half of your mind will be empty."
The Duke said:
"According to your words,
why stop at chess?
Whatever one is attached to,
then the mind is not empty."
A Subordinate's Mouth and a Superior's Nose
Shí Zhōngzhī (石中之), a参政 (cānzhèng), was witty.
A superior official, Lángzhōng (郎中) Pì (佖), advised him to be careful with his words.
He replied:
"What business is my subordinate's mouth to a superior's nose?"
One day,
he was reassigned as Lǐbù Lángzhōng (禮部郎中, Minister of Rites).
The prime minister at the time urged him, saying:
"The Emperor considers you clear, intelligent, thorough, and refined,
which is why you have been given this position.
You should reduce your jesting and humor."
He replied:
"My appointment says,
'Specially appointed as Lǐbù Lángzhōng (禮部郎中),
all other matters remain as before.'
Therefore, I dare not reduce anything."
Listening to Horse Hoofbeats
The diviner Wáng Shēng (王生) was blind but exceptionally good at hearing sounds.
When Dīng Jìnggōng (丁晉公) was governor of Jīnlíng (金陵),
Wáng Shēng (王生) secretly listened to the sound of his horse's hooves and said:
"The Cānzhèng (參政) will certainly be appointed Prime Minister within this month."
It turned out exactly as he said.
Later, Emperor Zhēnzōng (真宗) passed away.
The Duke was appointed Shānlíng Shǐ (山陵使, imperial tomb commissioner).
Wáng Shēng (王生) came to the capital,
and was asked to listen to the sound of the horse's hooves.
He said:
"There is a sign of two journeys."
His sons reproached him, saying:
"You knew that the Prime Minister was appointed Shānlíng Shǐ (山陵使),
which is why you said that."
Someone secretly asked him,
and he said:
"The hooves went west but there was no sound of return."
Indeed, he was dismissed from his post as Prime Minister and assigned to Xī Jīng (西京),
and then demoted to Yá Zhōu (崖州).
Poem on Yellow Crane Tower
Táng (唐) dynasty's Cuī Hào's (崔顥) poem "On Yellow Crane Tower" (Huánghè Lóu 黃鶴樓) says:
"The person of old has long since ridden away on a white cloud,
this place is left with only Yellow Crane Tower.
Once the yellow crane is gone, it never returns,
for a thousand years, white clouds drift idly.
Clear river, distinct Hànyáng (漢陽) trees,
fragrant grasses lush on Parrot Islet (Yīngwǔ Zhōu 鸚鵡洲).
At dusk, where are my home mountains?
Mist and waves on the river fill one with sorrow."
Tàibái (太白) (Lǐ Bái 李白) said, despite his great fame,
"There is scenery before my eyes that I cannot describe,
Cuī Hào's (崔顥) poem is already at the top."
Wishing to emulate it and compete for superiority,
he then composed "Poem on Ascending Phoenix Terrace" (Dēng Fènghuáng Tái Shī 登鳳凰臺詩).
Composing a Poem of Reflection
Ōuyáng Bīn (歐陽彬),
during the reign of Wáng Shǔ (王蜀), was a Hànlín Xuéshì (翰林學士, Imperial Academician).
During Emperor Míngzōng's (明宗) reign of Táng (唐), he entered Luò (洛),
but was ordered to return to Shǔ (蜀).
When the Mèng (孟) clan founded their state,
he was again a Hànlín (翰林).
He composed a poem saying:
"In past years, reminiscing brought tears streaming down,
today, pondering it is merely sorrow.
Easily gained, easily lost;
casually accomplished, casually ended.
The imperial domain was originally thought to be established for sons and grandsons,
but sharp blades turned kinsmen into foes.
Liáng (梁), Hàn (漢), and Later Táng (後唐) — three generations of rulers,
meeting in the netherworld, how vast and distant."
Poem on the Vajra
In the last years of the Shǔ (蜀) ruler,
most of his officials valued power and influence.
Jiǎng Yígōng (蔣貽恭) wrote a poem on the Vajra (Jīngāng 金剛) to satirize them, saying:
"With raised eyebrows and glaring eyes, a malevolent spirit,
put together, it seems real.
Attached to the trends of the time, borrowing power and influence,
unaware that the body itself is but a clay figure."
Ten Ox-hide Kites
Zhāng Guāiyá said:
“Governing Shǔ is like sewing ten cowhides to make a large air balloon.
If one can kick it up,
one must also be able to roll it around.
That is what it means to be capable.”
Therefore, he governed the people of Shǔ twice,
and even now, they still miss him.
At the imperial examination, one by one,
Táng Xióng Zhíyì was proficient in the Nine Classics.
At that time, many topics were set for recruiting scholars,
and Zhíyì achieved top grades in all of them.
Emperor Zhāngwǔ ordered a palace examination with two essays:
one on “Knowing Dangers from Simplicity and Ease,”
and the other on “The Right and Wrong of the Five Phases Following Each Other.”
He was limited to completing them in three thousand characters.
For the first essay, “Simplicity and Ease,”
he wrote three thousand characters.
For the essay on “The Five Phases Following Each Other,” he wrote at the beginning of the scroll:
“This is not something known by your humble servant's superficial learning.
The Five Phases Following Each Other originated from the Shǐjì,
not from clear classical texts.
Furthermore,
the Táng dynasty is currently under the influence of the Earth element,
so it is not appropriate to discuss this.”
The court appreciated his talent
and appointed him as Jíetuī of Xīchuān,
serving under Wǔ Yuánhéng.
Zhíyì authored the Wū Tǒng in five hundred volumes on the Nine Classics.
The Jīngtǐ characters
Wěi Shǔ Jù Zhōngzhèng had literary talent
and was skilled in brushwork.
When Shǔ was pacified, he went to the capital.
His memorials and audiences with the Prime Minister
were all in Jīngtǐ characters.
The palace gatekeepers did not recognize them
and laughed, saying:
“Today, Jù Zhōngzhèng has come again to pay respects to the Prime Minister!”
They took Jù to mean the character for "chapter and verse,"
and Cān to mean the character for "Zēng Cān."
Pictorial Representations of Classical Events
When Lǐ Tián was eight or nine years old,
his grandfather said:
“This is a great scholar.”
Whenever he taught him to read,
he would always order a painter to illustrate the events in the classics,
explaining their meaning one by one.
Tián, therefore, developed a great fondness for painting.
He painted for high officials,
and there were praises for his work.
Watching a chess game made a young man's hair turn white.
Táng Míngzōng’s crown prince, Cóngróng,
enjoyed writing poetry.
Reckless individuals
would compose poems with him.
For example, in "Watching Chess," it says:
“Watching one game end,
makes a young man’s hair turn white.”
Cóngróng indeed conspired to rebel,
and when the plot failed,
all who participated in the poetic exchanges
and whose words were deemed suspicious
were executed.
Therefore, in letters and documents exchanged, it is advisable to state matters directly,
and not to say things like “how about that matter,” etc.
Poem on the Hoeing Drum
The Shǔ monk Kěpéng composed the "Poem on the Hoeing Drum," which says:
“The drum at the farmer’s field,
the drum at the prince’s banquet.
Drums, oh drums, all are drums,
one is so joyful, one is so bitter.
Above, the scorching sun,
below, the parched earth.
May the Heavenly Lord send down rain,
so mulberries and hemp ripen,
and granaries are full.
No hunger, no cold,
all beating the same drum.”
Military Officials Do Not Involve Themselves in Civil Affairs
Tàizǔ pacified Shǔ,
and Mèng Lord entered the imperial court.
The Emperor said:
“When you were in Shǔ,
were there any unruly people?”
He replied:
“Although there were disloyal individuals,
there was no cause for disturbance.”
Tàizǔ asked:
“Why is that?”
He said:
“Military officials, beyond commanding troops,
did not involve themselves in civil affairs.
Their border garrisons were entirely staffed by great scholars.”
Military Officials Do Not Oversee Finance and Grain
Tàizǔ pacified Jiāngnán,
and the Latter Lord came to court.
The Emperor said:
“When you were in your former state,
by what method did you manage finance and grain?”
The Latter Lord replied:
“Officials were appointed in prefectures and counties
to collectively manage county affairs; military officials did not involve themselves in financial and grain documents.”
Breaking the Silver River
Tàizǔ was brave and resolute by nature.
There was a palace attendant, Shí Bàoliè, who was solely responsible for the Yellow River.
One day, when the river burst its banks,
Bàoliè submitted a detailed memorial.
Tàizǔ wrote in reply on his memorial:
“Breaking the silver river, losing the gold;
what use is it to ask you to be beheaded?”
Both within and outside the court, everyone was greatly terrified.
Not Accepting Unlawful Gifts
Gōulóng Zàn served as the Shǔbù of Xǔzhōu.
The people came to him with complaints about fields,
and Zàn handled them with complete impartiality.
The people were moved by his fairness
and presented him with a gold bird hairpin.
Later, the Wǔdé Department reported the matter to the Emperor.
Tàizǔ summoned and asked:
“Are the people’s offerings acceptable?”
Zàn replied:
“Your servant does not accept unlawful items.”
Tàizǔ
said:
“Is it permissible
by law?”
He was sent to the Hengmén,
given twenty strokes directly,
and then ordered to return to his post.
Establishing County尉
In the late Five Dynasties,
military officials usurped the authority of prefectures and counties,
and consequently dismissed the county lieutenants (xiànwèi),
sending junior officers and soldiers to govern instead.
This became quite a problem for the communities.
Tàizǔ wished to restore the old system.
At the Jiǎngwǔ Palace, he called out names for selection:
those who were willing to be xiànwèi stood to the east;
otherwise, they stood to the west.
Many selected individuals were unwilling,
often standing to the west.
Tàizǔ said:
“Such pedantic scholars!”
He ordered them to be driven out with a staff.
After this, many became willing,
and thus the old system was restored.
Avoiding Becoming Prime Minister
Hán Xīzài was a native of Qīngběn.
During the chaos of the Five Dynasties,
he crossed the river and submitted to the Former Lord,
eventually rising to the rank of Zhōngshū Shìláng.
He kept many female attendants,
who sang and danced day and night,
and guests would sit among them.
Xīzài visited the monk Démíng
and said:
“I am doing this
precisely to avoid the imperial order for me to become Prime Minister.”
The monk asked:
“Why avoid it?”
He replied:
“The Central Plains constantly eye this place like a tiger.
Once the true ruler emerges,
there won’t even be time to abandon our armor.
I cannot become a laughingstock for all ages.”
Iron Man
Lǐ Zūnyì served in Wěi Shǔ.
His discussions were charming and flattering,
with the demeanor of a woman or girl.
When Shǔ was pacified,
Tàizǔ saw him and said:
“Does he have such a demeanor?”
He shot him with an arrow with a felt tip,
hitting him squarely in the abdomen.
Zūnyì remained perfectly still.
Tàizǔ said:
“Soft on the outside, strong on the inside.”
He was appointed Gòngfèngguān
and commanded troops in Jiānghuái,
capturing many bandits.
People called him "Iron Man."
Not Cultivating Hegemonic Enterprise
After the Southern Lǐ dynasty of Jiāngnán submitted to the court,
the officials falsely appointed by them were mostly close confidantes.
Tàizōng visited the Hàn Yuàn,
and reviewed the regional documents.
The Latter Lord was then Jīnwú Shàngjiāngjūn,
among the ranks of the palace guards.
Xú Xuàn and Tāng Yuè and their ilk were in attendance.
Tàizōng saw the Jiāngnán official positioned above,
while the former lord was below,
and said to his attendants:
"Unable to accomplish a hegemonic enterprise,
only jesting with the wind and chanting with the moon,
this is fitting today."
The barbarian lord was angered that Shí Jìn
had stayed in the capital for a long time.
He executed Zhāng Yànzé,
angered by his disloyalty.
He reproached the Young Lord,
for his lack of trustworthiness.
As summer gradually approached,
he wished to return north to the barbarians.
His subordinates' attempts to make him stay also angered him.
He wanted to execute the Jìn officials.
Féng Dào said:
"In summer, reside in Běijīng;
in autumn, live in Nánjīng."
The barbarian lord was greatly pleased,
and so departed north.
Beehives and Ant-hills
In the eighth year of Kāibǎo,
the imperial army besieged Jīnlíng.
The imperial court held palace examinations on "Ode to Bridges Crossing the Yangtze River" and "Poem on Practicing Water Warfare."
Jiāngnán also held examinations on "Ode to Kings Valuing Kinship" and "Poem on Repelling Qín with Laughter."
Tàizǔ laughed and said:
"Jiāngnán raises civil and military officials,
as if they were flying and running animals.
Do they not know there is a true lord in the Central Plains?"
Zhào Pǔ said:
"Beehives and ant-hills
are not worth the sage's worry."
Reading the Diamond Sūtra
In Tàizǔ's later years,
he sojourned at Báimǎ Sì from Xī Luò,
and thus developed faith.
Upon returning to the imperial palace,
he copied and read the Diamond Sūtra.
Zhào Pǔ saw him during an audience.
The Emperor said:
"I do not wish to reveal this to men in armor.
If anyone sees it,
they need only say I am reading military texts."
The Emperor's Armor
Dīng Chōng was in the imperial guard.
When Tàizōng conquered Yōují,
Chōng arrived at the tent to offer congratulations,
wearing armor.
The Emperor said:
"It is late, why do you not remove your armor?"
Chōng said:
"The Emperor's armor
must not be removed casually."
The Emperor was pleased by this,
and subsequently promoted and employed him.
Liáo'ànzǐ
In the Southern Lǐ dynasty,
whenever someone wished to have an audience,
their portrait was first drawn to observe their beauty or ugliness.
Liáo Kèshùn had a green face,
and the people of Jiāngnán called him Liáo'ànzǐ.
Because of this, they disliked him,
and he was not allowed to be admitted for an audience.
Willow Branches Produce Catkins, Geese Lay Double Eggs
Lǐ Xiānzhǔ, finding the state's resources insufficient,
observed that
among the people
some goose eggs produced twin goslings,
and willow flowers became catkins.
A jester's lyric said:
"May the whole world be filled with auspicious celebrations,
willow branches produce catkins, geese lay double eggs."
The Art of Nurturing Life
Tàizǔ summoned Chén Tuán of Huàshān,
and asked about the art of nurturing life.
Tuán said:
"Where you have gained advantage, do not go again."
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and personally drafted a proclamation.
Yáng Yì was slandered by treacherous officials,
and disgraced, he requested leave to return to Xǔzhōu.
He was demoted to Bìshū Jiàn,
and assigned to Xījīng with a divided commission.
The Emperor personally added phrases to the proclamation,
which read:
"Repudiating the views of the many that are unacceptable,
it is my own sole decision."
Two 背 (bèi)
Liáng Jǐng was not good at calligraphy,
and always used Shǔ paper for drafts.
Zhào Ānrén was good at calligraphy,
and always used old paper for drafts.
People called them "Two 背 (bèi)."
The Incarnation of Lǐ Wèigōng
A monk visited Dīng Jìnggōng and said:
"You are the incarnation of Lǐ Wèigōng,
and will one day reach the highest position among officials."
He left and no one knew where he went.
Lotus Emerging from an Ash Pot
In Wēnzhōu, a woman died and her ashes and bones were placed in a vessel.
A green lotus sprouted in the vessel.
Zhījué Chánshī composed a gāthā:
"The gate of nature and mind,
thousands of sages are unified within it.
The spirit returns to the Pure Land,
a lotus emerges from an ash pot."
Wéncuì
Yáo Xuàn was demoted to Liánzhōu.
He once copied his work "Wéncuì" in one hundred volumes.
Enthusiasts stored it in the county tower.
Many officials dispatched clerks to copy it.
The clerks found copying it arduous,
and sprayed it with saltwater
hoping it would quickly deteriorate.
Later, they set fire to the tower, burning it down.
Jiǎ Zànshàn, Prefect of Shèzhōu
Sū Shòu
was Yì Jiǎn's eldest son.
He was Prefect of Sìzhōu.
Public funds were insufficient,
which he frequently lamented.
Shòu composed a poem saying:
"Ten thousand troops wearing hats and straw cloaks,
three thousand guests, angry when hungry, joyful when full."
Later, he was transferred to Yuèzhōu.
He did not get along with the assistant prefect Jiǎ Zànshàn,
and was transferred to Shèzhōu.
He had a poem which said:
"It was because of Jiǎ Zànshàn
that I came to be Prefect of Shèzhōu."
Lìzhī
Tián Cóngyì sent lìzhī to Cānzhèng Shèng,
and the poem said:
"Cherries are truly little fellows,
longan are common forms.
Olives are of a lower rank,
loquats are like guest children."
Shèng asked for an explanation.
He said:
"Cherries taste sour,
they are little fellows.
Longan have no pattern,
they are common forms.
Olives are very astringent at first,
they are of a lower rank.
Loquats have large pits and little flesh,
they are like guest children."
Military Funds
A commoner surnamed Chén from Zǐzhōu
was immensely wealthy but stingy.
He diligently did not marry,
nor did he eat meat.
His relatives persuaded him,
