so he married and ate meat.
He dreamt that a divine being rebuked him:
"How dare you use military funds!"
Later, he died,
and his money entered the treasury to aid the army.
Four Worlds
In Rùnzhōu, there was a mad Daoist
who often spoke of matters in the four worlds.
People called him "Four Worlds."
Hasty Orders and Mistakes
One day, Tàizǔ dismissed court,
and bowed his head, remaining silent for a long time.
The eunuch Wáng Jìxī asked him why.
"One morning I came to the front hall,
and gave hasty orders.
A messenger made an accidental mistake.
The imperial historians will surely record this,
which is why I am unhappy."
Jeweled Chamber Pot
Tài Zǔ 平偽蜀 (pacified the false Shǔ kingdom).
He inspected the items in Mèng Chǎng's palace.
There was a chamber pot adorned with jewels.
He immediately ordered it to be smashed.
He said:
"To indulge oneself with this,
what else can be expected but downfall?"
Opening all the gates of the Grand Palace
Tài Zǔ renovated the Grand Palace.
When it was finished,
he ordered all its gates to be opened wide,
with nothing to obstruct them.
He said:
"This is like my heart;
if there is even a slight deviation or crookedness,
everyone will see it."
Internal and external troubles
Tài Zōng said:
"If the state has no internal troubles,
although it is said there will certainly be external worries,
these are merely border affairs,
for which precautions can be taken in advance.
Only if cunning and evil people become an internal threat,
is it deeply to be feared.
Emperors should focus their minds on this."
The matter of demoting Zhào Féng
Tài Zōng personally led an expedition to Zé Lù.
Upon reaching Mount Tài Háng,
Zhào Féng, a Scholar of the Central Secretariat, was afraid of climbing the perilous path
and falsely claimed it was impossible to ascend the mountain.
Now he again feigned illness and claimed he could not draft decrees.
How dare a subject behave in such a manner?
He was demoted to Sī Hù of Fáng Zhōu.
Avoiding a distant appointment
Mèng Luán was appointed Lù Shì Cān Jūn of Dòu Zhōu,
but he avoided the distant appointment and did not take office.
So he went to the imperial court to state his case.
Tài Zǔ pardoned him,
but gave him twenty strokes of the cane
and exiled him to a sea island.
Guō Zhì governing Tiān Xióng
Zhēn Zōng appointed Gōng Bù Shì Láng Guō Zhì to govern Tiān Xióng Commandery.
Zhì pleaded his unsuitability,
weeping and unwilling to go.
The Emperor summoned his assisting ministers and asked them about it.
They replied:
"There are recent precedents of those who have received an appointment and then been allowed to stay."
The Emperor said:
"When I first ascended the throne,
I appointed Zhì to govern a prefecture.
If he refuses to go after being appointed,
how can I command others?"
He was finally dispatched,
and all the ministers were awed and submitted.
Reluctance to bestow titles and offices
Tài Zǔ ordered Cáo Bīn to attack Jiāng Nán.
He said:
"Go with me to conquer Jiāng Nán,
and upon your return, I will make you Shǐ Xiàng."
When Jiāng Nán was pacified,
he was reluctant to bestow titles and offices,
and did not give him the promised title.
He merely bestowed five hundred thousand in cash.
Then he said:
"If you take Tài Yuán for me,
then I will make you Shǐ Xiàng."
Urgent matter requiring an audience
One day, Tài Zǔ was in the imperial garden, holding a bow and arrow to shoot sparrows.
A minister knocked on the palace gate,
claiming to have an urgent matter and requesting an audience.
The Emperor promptly came out to see him.
However, what he reported was merely a trivial matter.
Tài Zǔ said:
"What is so urgent about this matter?"
He replied:
"It is also urgent, like shooting sparrows."
The Emperor was enraged
and struck his mouth with an axe handle made of yuán wood,
knocking out two teeth.
He slowly prostrated himself, picked up the fallen teeth, and placed them in his bosom.
The Emperor was extremely angry
and said:
"Are you going to take these teeth to accuse me?"
He replied:
"How dare I accuse Your Majesty?
The court historians will record it themselves."
The Emperor's anger subsided.
He bestowed gold and silk
and sent him off with words of comfort.
Tián Xī's direct remonstrance
Tián Xī was outspoken and fond of remonstrating.
Tài Zōng sometimes could not tolerate him.
Xī submitted a memorial, saying:
"Your Majesty, day by day, month by month,
cultivate your sagely nature."
Tài Zōng knew his words were loyal
and never got angry.
He once said:
"Such a remonstrating official
is also very rare.
When there is a flaw in the court's governance,
and I am still pondering it,
Xī's memorial has already arrived.
Who else would disregard their own safety for the affairs of the state?
Who would be willing to do this?
Whenever I review his memorials,
I must specifically speak with him
to encourage him."
Entertainers should not be governors
During Tài Zǔ's time,
Jiào Fāng Shǐ Dé Rén, being old, requested an external official post,
and citing the example of Emperor Zhuāng Zōng of the Later Táng,
sought to govern a prefecture.
Tài Zǔ said:
"Using entertainers as governors
is a matter of chaotic times.
How can one imitate that?"
The prime minister proposed appointing him as Shàng Zhōu Sī Mǎ.
Tài Zǔ said:
"Such people are only suitable for promotions within the music department.
High assisting official positions should not be lightly granted."
So he was appointed Yuè Lìng of Tài Cháng Sì.
The title Zhāo Xuān Jǐng Dé Diàn Shǐ
When the inner official Wáng Jì Ēn returned after pacifying Shǔ,
court opinion was to appoint him as Pí Mì Shǐ.
Tài Zǔ said:
"Such people should not hold positions of power and importance.
Another distinguished title should be chosen for him."
Thus, the title Zhāo Xuān Jǐng Dé Diàn Shǐ was established.
Inquiring about the people's suffering
Tài Zōng visited Jīn Míng Chí.
He ordered several tens of old peasant women from the villages to be brought to the palace by carriage.
He spread mats for them to sit on,
and then inquired about the people's suffering.
The women spoke frankly and thoroughly about the hardships of farming families
and the troubles in their villages.
The Emperor adopted their suggestions
and gave them all gold before they departed.
Not seeing artificial mountains, only mountains of blood
Yǎn Wáng's Yì Shàn, Yáo Tǎn,
criticized the king's artificial mountains, which were exceedingly elaborate.
Tǎn said:
"I don't see artificial mountains,
I only see mountains of blood."
The king asked him in surprise,
"They are all made from the fat and blood of the common people."
At that time, Tài Zōng was still a prince,
and his palace also had just completed an artificial mountain.
Hearing Tǎn's words,
he destroyed it that very day.
Chú Shuō
Dòu Yù, a commoner from Cháng Shān, presented five chapters of "Chú Shuō."
Zhēn Zōng ordered the Secretariat Directorate to summon him for an examination,
and bestowed him with three kinds of ritual gifts before he left.
Zhāng Qù Huá personally presented "Yuán Lùn," over twenty thousand characters long.
Zhēn Zōng ordered it to be transcribed onto silk,
making eighteen scrolls,
which were displayed in the Lóng Tú Gé.
The imperial heir not yet established
Xú Shì, the Běi Hǎi Bù of Wéi Zhōu, was summoned for an audience to speak on affairs of state.
Zhēn Zōng asked:
"What about the imperial heir not yet being established?"
Shì replied:
"The state rules the world by the virtue of fire.
Fire produces earth, and earth produces life.
Earth represents sons.
Earth also governs trustworthiness.
Currently, Your Majesty's trustworthiness has not yet been cultivated,
which is why you have not yet gained an imperial son."
The Emperor said:
"I have never lost trustworthiness.
Why do you say this?"
He replied:
"What Your Majesty cultivates is petty trustworthiness.
The trustworthiness of an emperor
means that when a command is issued or an order given,
if it is trustworthy, then all the people will submit.
If it is not trustworthy, then the entire world will be confused.
Currently, Your Majesty issues decrees in the morning that are changed by evening;
trustworthiness has not yet been established."
Granting official positions to relatives
資廕子弟 (Granting official positions to sons and younger brothers of high-ranking officials.)
Tàizǔ said:
"How can pampered sons and younger brothers, who can only play the pípa
and string and wind instruments at home,
govern the people?"
Thereupon, he did not allow them to govern the people.
He recorded the names of the palace guards.
Tàizōng said:
"Generally, one must be diligent in one's duties.
I always see the soldiers and guards in the palace;
if one sweeps an extra patch of ground,
or draws an extra bottle of water,
I must record their names."
Gold is a scarce commodity
Tàizōng asked Dù Hào:
"In the Western Hàn dynasty, gifts were all made of gold.
In recent times, it has become a scarce commodity.
Why is this?"
He replied:
"At that time,
Buddhist affairs had not yet flourished,
and the price of gold was very cheap."
The Chancellor signs edicts
In the second year of Gǎidé,
Fàn Zhì and Wáng Tuán were both dismissed from chancellorship.
Zhào Jìn was appointed to office.
When the edict was issued,
there was no chancellor to sign the edict.
The scholar Dòu Yí said:
"The current Emperor, as the Kāifēng Yǐn concurrently Píngzhāng,
holds the responsibility of a chancellor.
He can sign the edict."
Tàizōng happily said:
"Yí's words are correct."
Sons of emperors do not need literary skill
Tàizǔ asked his lecturing attendant Wáng Gōng:
"How is Qín Wáng's scholarship?"
He replied:
"His recent literary compositions are very good."
The Emperor said:
"The sons of emperors
do not necessarily need to be skilled in literature.
They only need to be proficient in the meaning of the classics and the governance and disorder of ancient and modern times,
so that in the future they can avoid being deceived by officials who twist laws and manipulate writings."
Explaining the Tàiguà
Zhēnzōng ordered Féng Yuán, a Dali Píngshì, to explain the "Tài Guà" of the *Zhōuyì*.
Yuán expounded on the structure of the hexagram,
saying that earth and heaven form Tài.
He said that when the qi of heaven descends,
and the qi of earth ascends,
then there is interaction and harmony (Tài).
This is like a ruler connecting with his ministers from below,
and ministers receiving from their ruler from above,
only then can the way between ruler and minister be unobstructed.
If heaven, being high and lofty, remains above,
then earth has no means to interact with heaven.
If heaven and earth do not interact,
how can there be harmony (Tài)?
If a ruler relies on his own尊大 (dignity and greatness),
and ministers have no means to approach the ruler,
if ruler and minister do not interact,
how can there be harmony (Tài)?
Taking kindness and frugality as treasure
Tàizōng advocated diligence and frugality.
After court, he wore a Huáyáng turban and coarse hempen clothes of fine texture.
His inner garments were only of coarse silk.
He once took all the exquisite and ingenious gold and silver vessels and destroyed them.
The chief storekeeper said:
"These are exquisitely crafted; they should be kept for imperial use."
The Emperor said:
"You value exquisite craftsmanship,
but I value kindness and frugality as treasures."
Hemp slippers and cloth skirts
Tàizǔ personally practiced diligence and frugality,
often wearing washed clothes.
In his sleeping chamber, he had a mat of woven reeds edged with blue cloth.
He once bestowed hemp slippers and cloth skirts upon his attendants,
saying:
"These are what I used to wear."
Bestowing wine upon Dù Hào
When Dù Hào was a Rectifier in the Lóngtú Pavilion,
Zhēnzōng ordered an imperial envoy to bestow fine wine upon him.
Hào was not good at drinking;
drinking it triggered an old illness,
almost to the point of being beyond help.
The Emperor personally came to the pavilion to inquire,
personally mixed medicines,
and called his son to attend to his illness.
When Hào revived,
he saw the Emperor and wished to rise.
The Emperor comforted him and told him to lie down.
The Emperor blamed himself,
believing that his gift of wine had caused the illness.
His treatment of his ministers was like this.
Sacrificing at Fén Yīn
When Zhēnzōng sacrificed at Fén Yīn,
he saw people operating boats to fish
and holding plows to farm.
He said:
"Are the common people happy with their work?
If county and prefecture officials do not harass them,
then their daily resources will be inexhaustible."
Modern laws are strict
Tàizǔ, while reading, sighed and said:
"In the era of Yáo and Shùn,
the Four Fiends' crimes were merely punished with banishment.
Why are modern penal laws so strict?"
Kòu Zhǔn pulls the ochre robe
Kòu Zhǔn, as Yuánwàiláng, submitted a memorial,
speaking directly and offending the Emperor.
Tàizōng rose in anger,
but Zhǔn thereupon pulled his ochre robe,
asking the Emperor to resume his seat,
and only withdrew after the matter was decided by the Emperor himself.
The Emperor appreciated and accepted it.
Tàizōng said:
"My obtaining Kòu Zhǔn
is like Táng Tàizōng obtaining Wèi Zhènggōng."
Requesting the execution of Zhū Néng
Seeking to speak to him Zhū Néng obtained a heavenly book.
Zhēnzōng welcomed him and bowed to him in the inner palace.
Sūn Shì, the Zhī Héyáng, submitted a memorial, saying:
"What does Heaven say?
How can there be a book?
Everyone says this book was forged by Zhū Néng,
only Your Majesty does not know.
It came only from Zhū Néng,
and the belief in it is heard only from Your Majesty.
I beg to execute Néng to dispel the confusion of the empire."
The Emperor, because of his outspokenness and directness,
did not punish him.
Later, Néng indeed failed.
Requesting the execution of Dīng Wèi
Zhēnzōng built the Yùqīng Zhāoyìng Palace.
Zhāng Yǒng submitted a memorial,
saying: "Exhausting the wealth of the empire
and harming the lives of the people
are all due to the treacherous minister Dīng Wèi deceiving and misleading Your Majesty.
I beg to execute Wèi at the gate of the capital to apologize to the empire,
and to execute Yǒng and place him at the door of Dīng's family to apologize to Wèi."
The eldest princess seeks an assassin
Qín Guó Zhǎng Gōngzhǔ sought a nearby prefecture's刺史 (cìshǐ) for her son, Liùzhái Shǐ Shìlóng.
Tàizōng said:
"The appointment of a Grand Administrator depends on the public deliberation of the court."
He did not permit it.
The Emperor's son commits an offense against a censor
Xǔ Wáng was impeached by a censor,
and Tàizōng investigated him.
Xǔ Wáng memorialized:
"I am the son of the Son of Heaven,
and now I am being investigated for offending a censor."
The Emperor said:
"Who dares to violate the regulations of the court?
If I make a mistake,
my ministers still point it out.
As Kāifēng Yǐn, how can you not be impeached?"
He was ultimately punished.
Wèi Tíngshì requests an audience
During Tàizōng's time,
Wèi Tíngshì, the transport commissioner of Yìzhōu circuit, came to court.
The Emperor said:
"If you have matters, you should report them to the Central Secretariat."
Tíngshì said:
"I have traveled three thousand seven hundred *lǐ* by post relay to arrive.
I have urgent matters to report to Your Majesty
to be decided by your imperial heart.
I did not come for the sake of the chancellor."
The Emperor immediately summoned him for an audience.
Sealed memorials
Zhēnzōng decreed that officials from the capital and court from Nèidiàn Chóngbān and above
could speak about the sufferings and benefits of the people,
and also about the places experienced by various circuit transport commissioners,
submitting sealed memorials to the cabinet gate.
Literary selections for nourishing life
Rèn Huìgōng was hale and strong in his later years.
Someone asked about the art of nourishing life.
The Duke said:
"I gained enlightenment from reading the *Wénxuǎn*.
What is meant by 'a mountain shines when it holds jade,
a river is charming when it contains pearls' is this."
Pressing the corners
When a Shèrén Yüàn (Court of Imperial Remonstrance) official, who knows the imperial edicts, submits a memorial,
a purple mat must be laid out in the courtyard.
He bows facing north in the hall.
The head of the secretariat stands to the east of the mat,
which is called Yājiǎo (pressing the corner).
Nángōng Shèrén Ruìjǐn Kē
In the Táng (Tang) dynasty, a Lǐbù Lángzhōng (Director in the Ministry of Rites) who managed the central literary affairs of the province
was called a "Nángōng Shèrén" (Southern Palace Remonstrance Official).
After a hundred days, he had to be familiar with drafting imperial edicts.
A Yuánwàiláng (Assistant Director) was also called a Ruìjǐn Kē (Auspicious Brocade Pit).
In front of the hall was a large stone.
All discarded seals sent from various prefectures
were broken on this stone.
Also, auspicious drawings and paintings
were all under the charge of the Yuánwàiláng.
Lìnghú Chǔ's poem says:
"How many times has the stone been moved to break old seals?
From where are new paintings sent after opening the box?"
Gōngrén Xié
Táng (Tang) dynasty court ladies' tombs were called "Gōngrén Xié" (Court Lady Slope).
Envoys were sent to offer sacrifices in the four seasonal months.
Shàngyuán Dēng (Lanterns of Shàngyuán)
The lighting of lanterns on Shàngyuán
is sometimes said to follow the Hàn (Han) dynasty custom of sacrificing to Tàiyī (Grand Unity) from dusk till dawn.
Liáng Jiǎnwén Dì (Emperor Jianwen of Liang) had a "Lièdēng" (Array of Lanterns),
and Chén Hòuzhǔ (Last Emperor of Chen) had a "Guāngbì Diàn Yányǒng Shāndēng Shī" (Poem on Mountain Lanterns in the Guangbi Hall Banquet).
During Táng Mínghuáng's (Emperor Xuanzong of Tang) Guāngtiān (Guangtian) era,
lanterns were displayed in Dōngdū (Eastern Capital);
during Wénzōng's (Emperor Wenzong of Tang) Kāichéng (Kaicheng) era,
lanterns were used to welcome the Empress Dowager.
Thus, before the Táng (Tang) dynasty, they were not regularly set up every year.
Yuányè Yùmén (Imperial Gate on the Shàngyuán Night)
During Tàizōng's (Emperor Taizong's) time,
the three Yuán (festivals) had no night curfew.
On Shàngyuán, the imperial carriage passed through Yuán Mén (Yuan Gate).
On Zhōngyuán and Xiàyuán, it was the Dōnghuá Mén (Donghua Gate).
However, the sightseeing on Shàngyuán was uniquely grand.
Xiǎogū Shān Shī (Poem on Mount Xiaogu)
Chén Jiǎnfū (Chen Jianfu) wrote the "Xiǎogū Shān Shī" (Poem on Mount Xiaogu) saying:
"The mountain is called by the lonely character,
the temple sculpts the form of a young woman.
Though passers-by know the error,
travelers only beg for blessings."
Cǎojiǎn (Draft and Document)
Regarding official documents,
the Zhōngshū (Central Secretariat) called them "cǎo" (drafts),
the Shūmìyuàn (Bureau of Military Affairs) called them "dǐ" (bases),
and the Sānsī (Three Departments) called them "jiǎn" (documents).
The Imperial Library has three rolls of Liáng Cháo Xuándǐ (Liang Dynasty Proclamations and Bases),
which are the writings of the Chóngzhèng Yuàn (Chongzheng Academy) during the Zhèngmíng (Zhengming) era.
Guòmǎ Tīng (Horse-Passing Hall)
The former residence of the Běidū Shǐ (Prefect of the Northern Capital) had a Guòmǎ Tīng.
According to Hán Wò's (Han Wo's) poem:
"When a foreign envoy presents a hawk, it is first tested;
When a eunuch passes a horse, it is not allowed to neigh."
The note says:
"The emperor rides a horse,
which eunuchs lead forward to present;
this is called Guòmǎ (passing the horse).
The Táng (Tang) dynasty regional governors usurped this practice,
and named their halls after it."
Chóngdài (Double Headwear)
In our dynasty, officials of the two provinces and department directors,
both wore Chóngdài when entering and leaving.
In the early days of the dynasty, the two drafting officials also did so.
Wáng Nèihàn's (Wang Neihan's) memorial of thanks when he became Zhī Chúzhōu (Prefect of Chuzhou) stated: "His head wears Chóngdài,
his body bears the court attire," which refers to this.
Since the Xiángfú (Xiangfu) era,
the two drafting officials have both removed them,
which is not the old custom.
Mèng Gě Jiāngjūn (Dream of General Ge)
Rénzōng (Emperor Renzong) dreamed he went to a great marsh,
lost his way,
and all his attendants and guards disappeared.
Suddenly, from the horizon, a procession with banners, streamers, chariots, and riders descended on clouds.
One person offered a carriage to the Emperor,
introducing himself as Gě Jiāngjūn (General Ge),
and sent the Emperor back.
He then ordered a search for his name.
The "Dàozàng" (Daoist Canon) says:
"There are three guardians at the Gate of Heaven;
one is named Gě Jiāngjūn,
who is in charge of banners."
An imperial edict ordered his image to be painted,
and officials to offer services to it in the viewing hall.
Dàshè Qǔshè Déyīn (Grand Amnesty, Partial Amnesty, Benevolent Edict)
According to the system of our dynasty,
there are three types of pardons:
namely Dàshè (Grand Amnesty),
Qǔshè (Partial Amnesty),
and Déyīn (Benevolent Edict).
These are not names for imperial edicts themselves,
but rather names for the imperial edicts as carried out by subordinates.
It is incorrect for the Son of Heaven to call them Déyīn himself.
It is incorrect.
Táng Cháng Gǔn (Chang Gun of Tang) compiled a chapter on pardons and edicts,
which he generally called a "submission by a minister."
Later Táng Zhuāngzōng (Emperor Zhuangzong of Later Tang) desired
to combine Zhèngshēng (Zheng music) with Húbù (foreign music) to play.
He called this Guōzhàng (cacophonous curtain),
and it would not stop from dusk till dawn.
He formed ten sworn brothers with entertainers.
Whenever he discussed matters with close ministers,
he would send messages to the actors,
explaining the reasons for the delay in meeting.
Huángzhǐ Shūchì (Imperial Edicts Written on Yellow Paper)
Táng (Tang) calendar.
An imperial edict from the third month of the third year of Shàngyuán (Shangyuan) stated:
"Since imperial edicts and commands are to be implemented as eternal regulations,
they were all written on white paper,
and many were damaged by insects.
From now on, the Shàngshū Shěng (Department of State Affairs) shall issue them to various prefectures and counties,
all written on yellow paper."
Qǔ Yōuzhōu Tú (Acquiring the Map of Yōuzhōu)
One day, Tàizǔ (Emperor Taizu) summoned Zhào Zhōnglìng (Zhao Zhongling)
and showed him a map of Yōuzhōu.
Zhōnglìng said:
"This must be the work of Cáo Hàn (Cao Han)."
The Emperor asked how he knew.
He replied:
"Among current generals and strategists,
none surpasses Hàn.
If Hàn goes,
he will surely take Yōuzhōu.
But after it is taken,
whom will you send to replace him?"
The Emperor remained silent.
Cháodiàn (Court Hall)
In our dynasty, the Wéndé Diàn (Wende Hall) was called the "Wàicháo" (Outer Court).
All court officials not handling specific duties
attended daily,
which was called "Chángcháo" (Regular Court).
The Chuígǒng Diàn (Chuigong Hall) was called the "Nèidiàn" (Inner Hall).
Chancellors and below, along with military officials, attended daily,
which was called "Guān Qǐjū" (Official Daily Attendance).
Every five days,
all civil and military court officials attended the Nèicháo (Inner Court),
which was called "Bǎiguān Dàqǐjū" (Grand Attendance of All Officials).
These were the three levels.
When the Son of Heaven holds court,
nothing is more important than the main imperial court.
According to etiquette,
ministers must not fail to attend court for a single day.
Therefore, even if the main imperial court is not held,
regularly attending officials still stand in their ranks
and withdraw only after the court is dismissed.
Èrfǔ Yìgōng Xiè (Two Bureaus Go to the Palace to Express Thanks)
When Wáng Jǐgōng (Wang Jigong) was reappointed as chancellor in the early Tiānshèng (Tiansheng) era,
he requested to go to Jǐngměi Gōng Fèngzhēndiàn (Fengzhen Hall of Jingmei Palace) to thank Zhēnzōng (Emperor Zhenzong).
He then established a Buddhist ritual space with five hundred thousand coins.
Thereafter, when officials of the Èrfǔ (Two Bureaus) were first appointed,
it became customary for them to go to the palace to express their thanks.
Chūxuè Jì (Records for Elementary Learning)
Xú Jiān (Xu Jian) of the Táng (Tang) dynasty compiled the "Chūxuè Jì."
Liú Zǐyí (Liu Ziyi) of Zhōngshān (Zhongshan) loved the book
and said:
"It is not only for elementary learning,
it can be a record for a lifetime."
Láihé Tiānzūn (Coming and Harmonizing Heavenly Venerable)
When Yáng Lì (Yang Li) had not yet passed the examinations,
he dreamed of someone leading him up to a hall,
where a young man sat facing south.
The guide said:
"This is Láihé Tiānzūn."
Later, when Zhēnzōng (Emperor Zhenzong) was Xiāngwáng (Prince of Xiang),
Lì was appointed Jìshì (Secretary),
and saw the Emperor exactly as he had seen him in his dream.
Sūn Gòngfèng (Attendant Sun)
When Táng Zhāozōng (Emperor Zhaozong of Tang) was exiled,
the only entertainer who followed his carriage was a monkey trainer.
The monkey was quite tame
and could follow the court ranks in daily attendance.
Zhāozōng (Zhaozong) bestowed upon it a scarlet robe and the title Sūn Gòngfèng.
Luó Yǐn's (Luo Yin's) "Xiàdì Shī" (Poem After Failing the Examination) says:
"How is it not better to learn from Sūn Gòngfèng?
With one smile, the monarch grants a scarlet robe."
When Zhū Liáng (Zhu Liang) usurped the throne,
he brought the monkey to perform daily attendance before the hall.
The monkey looked down the steps and saw Quánzhōng (Quanzhong).
It rushed towards the hall
and then jumped and attacked fiercely.
Quánzhōng immediately ordered it killed.
Many Táng (Tang) officials should be ashamed compared to this monkey!
Shàngdì Shàn Tí Dù Shī (Emperor's Fan Inscribed with Dù (Du) Poetry)
Shèng Wénsù dreamt he was in the imperial palace hall,
where a fan had a poem written on it, saying:
"In the deep night, I still hold a candle,
Facing each other as if in a dream."
He thought it was a poem by a celestial being,
but upon waking,
he remembered it was a poem by Dù Shī.
Wànbìngwán
In legal theory, there are things that should not be done,
which legalists easily latch onto,
calling them "Wànbìngwán" (Cure-all Pills).
The Yùshǐ Tái (Censorate) provisionally appointed an official,
ordering him to judge a case,
which he did unlawfully.
He then said:
"Things that should not be done
must be treated severely."
When asked about it,
he replied:
"If the Zhōngchéng (Vice Censor-in-Chief) wants severity,
then add to the main text;
if the Zádūan (miscellaneous official) wants leniency,
then note it on the side."
Shǐhuáng's Mountain-Driving Bell
A fisherman by the sea found a bell,
and when he struck it,
its sound was like thunder.
He asked a knowledgeable person,
who said:
"This is Shǐhuáng's mountain-driving bell."
A Chinese Scholartree Grew in the Room
When Lǚ Méngzhèng was about to take the imperial examination,
he rented a house near Dálóngguān.
He passed the preliminary exam and went to Luòyáng,
locking his room before he left.
He returned from winter to spring,
opened the door and saw
a clump of huái (Chinese scholartree) branches growing in front of the bed,
two or three feet high.
Méngzhèng passed the imperial examination that year.
Ten years later, it was thick enough for two arms to embrace,
and he became a chancellor.
The Chancellor's Power Diminishes Daily
Féng Dào said:
"I have served as chancellor three times,
and each time my power was less than before.
This can be seen from the promotion of relatives and old acquaintances.
The first time I was in office,
I could promote up to Chéngláng (Vice Minister);
the second time,
I could promote up to Yíbǔ (Rectifier of Omissions);
the third time,
it was no more than provincial and county officials.
This shows that the power of the prime minister is diminishing daily."
Marrying Off a Golden Silkworm
People in the south kept golden silkworms;
the silkworms were golden in color
and fed on Shǔ brocade.
They would take its droppings and put them in food and drink to poison people,
causing death.
The silkworm was good at attracting wealth,
making people suddenly rich.
But it was extremely difficult to get rid of,
as it could not be harmed by water, fire, weapons, or blades.
One had to use a lot of gold and silver,
place the silkworm in it,
and throw it by the roadside.
If someone picked it up,
the silkworm would follow them,
which was called "marrying off a golden silkworm."
Coalescing Gold Stone
Someone obtained a green stone,
as large as a basin.
On its back was a knob,
through which several zhang of iron chain passed,
forming a continuous loop with no join.
One day,
a sea merchant saw it
and exchanged tens of thousands of coins for it.
He said:
"This is a 'coalescing gold stone.'
Hang it in the sea,
pull it out after a night,
and there will certainly be gold on it."
Dragon Listening to Sutra Lecture
There was a monk lecturing sutras in a mountain temple.
An old man often came to listen.
When asked his name,
he said:
"I am the dragon from the deep pool below the mountain.
Fortunately, during this dry year, I have leisure
to come here to listen to the Dharma."
The monk said:
"Can you relieve the drought?"
He replied:
"The Heavenly Emperor sealed the rivers and lakes,
so I cannot use the water at will."
The monk said:
"Can the water in this inkstone be used?"
Thereupon, he drank the water from the inkstone and left directly.
That evening,
there was a great thunderstorm.
When they looked at dawn,
all the rain was black water.
Miswritten Characters
In the 《Táng Yùn》, in the Qián section, there is the character "懽";
in the Jīng section, there is the character "蟫".
The character "懽" originally took Gān
干
as its sound,
but was mistakenly written as 乾,
with the sound Qián.
Thus it entered the Qián section.
In 《Ěryǎ》:
means "báiyú" (silverfish).
It originally took Tán
談
as its sound,
but was mistakenly written as 蕈,
with the sound Xún.
Thus it entered the Jīng section.
Many similar rhymes exist in various sections.
Lǚ Shēngōng's Poem
Zhāng Dēnggōng retired from office
and resided in the capital.
Lǚ Shēngōng requested to lead the two ministries to congratulate him.
The Duke immediately composed a poem at the gathering,
which included the lines: "There should be no equal to this gathering in the human world;
Why must we visit Xiè Ān on Dongshan?"
A Poem Presented to Wèi Gōng
When Hán Wèigōng first served as chancellor,
he was sent to govern Cháng'ān.
Someone presented a poem:
"Don't ask the guests at the door about right and wrong;
Gains and losses must be judged by the old man beyond the frontier.
Take the green oil umbrellas and red banners and depart,
Get drunk on the spring breeze by the Yèwáng Tái."
The Duke considered it to be true,
and requested to guard Xiāngzhōu.
Yuán Chángshǐ
When Wéi Dān had not yet passed the imperial examination,
he saw a fisherman catch a very large soft-shelled turtle (yuán) at Luòyáng Bridge.
It was very large.
Dān found it extraordinary,
bought it, and released it into the river.
Later, a Chángshǐ (Chief Clerk) named Jùnzhī came to express his gratitude,
who was in fact that very soft-shelled turtle.
Empress Wǔ's Prison in Tang
After Huáng Jìngguó died,
he saw several prison guards in the underworld pointing to a place and saying:
"This is Empress Wǔ of Tang's prison.
Her wickedness was immense.
She is being kept in a large jar filled with scorpions and centipedes that sting her.
All cruel officials and treacherous ministers have their own prisons."
Volume 19
End.
Learning Non-Non-Thought
Śākyàfó was born into a Kṣatriya royal family,
emitting great wisdom light
that illuminated the worlds of the ten directions.
Golden lotuses welled up,
naturally supporting his two feet.
He pointed one finger to the sky and another to the earth,
making a lion's roar.
This was in the 24th year of King Zhāo of Zhōu.
At nineteen years old,
he wished to leave home.
At night, a celestial being named Jìngjū
respectfully addressed the Prince through the window, with clasped hands,
saying that the time for him to leave home had come.
So he cultivated the Way in Dántèshān,
studying "neither thought nor non-thought" with Yùtóulánfú.
On the eighth day of the second month, when the morning star appeared, he attained Buddhahood,
known as the Teacher of Gods and Humans.
He was then thirty years old.
In Lùyěyuàn,
he turned the wheel of the Four Noble Truths for Qiáomén Chénrú and others,
discussing the fruit of the Way and expounding the Dharma.
He lived in the world for forty-nine years,
and, taking his gold-threaded Saṅghāṭī robe,
transmitted the Dharma to Móhējiāyè,
speaking this verse on impermanence:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.
This is the arising and ceasing; when ceasing is ceased, stillness is bliss."
His disciples cremated him with fragrant firewood.
After the cremation,
the golden coffin remained as before,
seven Tāluó trees high.
It moved back and forth in the sky,
transforming into the Samādhi of Fire,
yielding eighty-four thousand Śarīra.
One thousand seventeen years after the World-Honored One's Nirvāṇa,
during the Yǒngpíng era,
the teaching reached Central Xià.
The golden coffin, seven Tāluó trees high,
is mentioned above.
Upon reaching the twin trees, he wept with sorrow. The First Patriarch, Jiāyè,
entered Parinirvāṇa.
Jiāyè came to the twin Sālá trees and cried out in sorrow and longing.
The Buddha manifested his twin feet from within the golden coffin,
and the handle of the jeweled canopy broke.
The Second Patriarch, Ānán,
Sanskrit Ānánda,
means here:
"Joyful Tathāgata."
He was widely learned and knowledgeable,
with unhindered wisdom.
The World-Honored One considered him foremost in comprehensive attainment
and upholding the Dharma treasury,
like water poured from one vessel to another.
Ānán, reflecting on his body's fragility, like a cluster of foam,
bade farewell to King Āhē.
The gatekeeper said:
"The King is asleep;
he cannot be disturbed."
The King dreamed of a jeweled canopy
adorned with delicacies;
wind and rain broke its handle, and it fell to the ground.
Upon waking,
he immediately went to Vísālí Domain,
where he saw Ānán emerging from the middle of the Cháng River,
about to enter Nirvāṇa in Xuěshān.
Five hundred immortals flew through the air to arrive,
and Ānán expounded the Dharma to them.
In an instant,
five hundred Arhats arranged for these immortals to leave home and receive full ordination.
Ānán leapt into the void,
performed eighteen transformations,
and divided his body into four parts:
one offered to the Sājié Dragon Palace,
one offered to the Vísālí Dragon King,
one part to Āàn.
Three stupas were built by each for veneration.
Body seventeen, nature seventeen.
The Third Patriarch, Shāngnàhéxiū,
having spread the Dharma for a long time,
obtained Yōupōjúduō as an attendant.
He then asked:
"How old are you?"
He replied:
"Seventeen."
The master said:
"Is your body seventeen,
or your nature seventeen?"
Héxiū knew he was a vessel for the Dharma,
so he shaved his head,
saying: "White hair is not a white mind."
Júduō said:
"My body is seventeen,
not my nature."
He uttered a verse:
"Neither Dharma nor non-Dharma,
neither mind nor non-mind.
When this mind-Dharma is spoken,
this Dharma is not mind-Dharma."
Three corpses transformed into a flower garland.
The Fourth Patriarch, Yōupōjúduō,
traveled in all directions to convert beings.
The demon palace shook,
and Bōxún exerted all his strength to harm the Right Dharma.
Secretly holding a garland,
he waited for the Venerable One to enter Samādhi,
and tied it around his neck.
The Venerable One took three corpses — human, dog, and snake —
and transformed them into a flower garland to return.
Bōxún was greatly pleased,
extended his neck to receive it,
but it immediately transformed into three types of foul-smelling corpses.
Bōxún exhausted all his demonic power but could not remove them.
So he ascended to the Six Desire Heavens
and asked all the Deva Kings and Brahmā King for a solution.
The King said:
"If you fell because of another,
you must rise because of that same other;
there is no other way."
Bōxún then paid homage to the Venerable One,
sorrowfully confessing his repentance.
Júduō said:
"You may proclaim your refuge in the Three Jewels."
The demon king clasped his hands and proclaimed three times,
and all the flower garlands were removed.
The Fourth Patriarch converted the most beings.
For each person he delivered, he placed a tally in a stone chamber.
It was eighteen xún in length
and twenty xún in width,
and it became full. Finally, he obtained Tíduōjiā,
and then transmitted the great Dharma eye treasury.
Precious mountain is the body.
The Fifth Patriarch, Tíduōjiā,
at birth, dreamed of a precious mountain,
from which springs welled up,
and the sun emerged from a cave,
illuminating heaven and earth.
The Fourth Patriarch said:
"The precious mountain is the body;
the gushing springs mean the Dharma is inexhaustible;
the sun emerging from the cave is the sign of entering the Way;
the illumination means wisdom surpasses all."
Coming from one's own mind.
The Sixth Patriarch, Mízhējiā,
arrived in this Tiānzhú kingdom.
A person holding wine asked:
"Master, from where do you come?
Where do you wish to go?"
The Master said:
"I come from my own mind,
and wish to go nowhere."
"Do you recognize yourself?"
"Totally untouched by a vessel."
He said:
"Master, do you recognize me?"
The Master said:
"My Master does not recognize;
if I recognize, it is not I."
Discussion of victory.
The Seventh Patriarch, Póshēnmì,
suddenly a wise man named Nántí Rì proclaimed himself,
wishing to debate with the Master.
The Master said:
"Benevolent one,
to debate is not to discuss,
to discuss is not to debate.
If one doubts the discussion,
it is ultimately not a discussion."
Nántí knew that the discussion would not be victorious,
and immediately said:
"I wish to seek the Way,
to be moistened by the taste of sweet dew."
Words align with the mind, actions align with the Way.
The Eighth Patriarch, Nántí,
had a son named Fútuómìduō from the Vísāluó family.
He bowed and said:
"Parents are not my true kin;
who is the one who sees true kin?
All Buddhas are not my Way;
who is the supreme one of the Way?"
The Venerable One said:
"Your words align with the mind,
parents cannot compare.
Your actions align with the Way,
which is the very mind of the Buddhas.
Seeking outwardly has form,
and the Buddha is not in accord with you.
As if desiring to know you,
the original mind is neither united nor separated."
Sixty Years in the Womb
The Ninth Patriarch, Fútuómìduō,
had an elder bring a child to him,
saying:
"This child was in the womb for sixty years,
and is thus called Nánshēng.
Now I wish for him to leave home and become a monk."
The Master recited a gāthā:
"True principle is originally nameless;
through names, true principle is manifested.
Having received the true and real Dharma,
it is neither true nor false."
Xié Zūnzhě
The Tenth Patriarch first served Fúgěng Zūnzhě,
and never slept.
It was said that his side never touched the mat,
and thus he was called Xié Zūnzhě.
Saw Meaning, Wood Meaning
The Eleventh Patriarch, Fùnàyèzhě,
was asked by Mǎmíng Dàshì:
"I wish to know the Buddha."
The Master said:
"That which you do not know is called the Buddha."
"Since I do not know,
how can I know that it is so?"
The Master said:
"Since you do not know the Buddha,
how can you know that it is not so?"
"The Master is the saw's meaning."
"That is the wood's meaning."
He then asked what the saw's meaning was.
He replied:
"It comes forth directly from the Master."
He then asked what the wood's meaning was.
He replied:
"You are dissected by me."
Mǎmíng thereupon became enlightened.
Can You Transform the Nature Sea?
The Twelfth Patriarch, Mǎmíng Dàshì,
suddenly saw a woman recite a gāthā:
"I bow to the venerable elder,
who shall receive the Tathāgata's prophecy.
As it is so,
you should attain the ultimate truth."
The Master said:
"There will be a māra coming."
Immediately, a golden dragon
shook the mountains and peaks.
The Master sat calmly,
and the māra vanished.
It reverted to its original form and said:
"My name is Jiāpímóluó.
I can transform a vast sea into a small container."
The Master said:
"Can you transform the nature sea?"
He replied:
"I have never known how."
The Master said:
"Mountains, rivers, and the great earth all conform to the Dharma.
The three veins and six spiritual powers manifest from this Dharma."
Jiāpímóluó then developed faith,
and, together with three thousand disciples, came to shave his head and receive ordination.
The Master then transmitted the Dharma.
Python Dwelling in a Stone Cave
The Thirteenth Patriarch, Jiāpímóluó,
entered the mountains and encountered a large python
coiling around the Master's body.
The Master administered the three refuges,
and the python transformed into an old man in plain clothes,
saying:
"I was formerly a bhikṣu.
Some novices would often come to ask for instruction,
and I was vexed by having to answer them,
giving rise to thoughts of anger and resentment.
Upon death, I fell into a python body.
I have lived in a cave for ten years.
Just now I heard the precepts and Dharma,
and so I came to express my gratitude."
He also said:
"To the north, there is a great tree,
shading an area of five hundred *zhang*.
The king of trees is named Lóngshù."
Remove My Curtain
The Fourteenth Patriarch, Lóngshù Zūnzhě,
arrived in Southern India.
Many people there believed in meritorious karma,
saying:
"Human beings have meritorious karma,
which is supreme in the world.
To merely speak of Buddha-nature,
who can perceive it?"
The Venerable One said:
"If you wish to see Buddha-nature,
you must first remove the curtain of 'self'."
Someone asked:
"What is the size of Buddha-nature?"
He replied:
"It is neither small nor large,
neither broad nor narrow.
It has no merit and no retribution,
neither dies nor is born."
A Needle Dropped into Water
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Jiānàtízī,
visited Lóngshù Dàshì.
When Lóngshù sent someone to show him a bowl full of water,
the Patriarch dropped a needle into the water,
joyfully understanding and agreeing.
Both Body and Mind Are Settled
The Sixteenth Patriarch, Luóhòuhànduō,
saw Sēngqié nándí emerge from samādhi.
The Venerable One asked:
"Is your body settled,
or your mind settled?"
He replied:
"Both body and mind are settled."
The Venerable One said:
"What is the difference between coming in and going out?"
He replied:
"Although there is coming in and going out,
the state of samādhi is not lost.
Like gold in a well,
the gold's substance remains constantly still."
Bells Ring, Wind Rings
The Seventeenth Patriarch, Sēngqié nándí,
saw a boy named Shānshè hold a round mirror and say:
"The great round mirror of all Buddhas,
without flaw inside or out.
Two people equally see it,
their hearts and eyes are alike."
He then left home and received the precepts,
named Gāyéshètà.
As the wind blew the bronze bells of the temple,
the Venerable One asked:
"Are the bells ringing,
or is the wind ringing?"
The Master replied:
"Neither the wind nor the bells,
my mind is ringing."
He asked:
"And who is the mind?"
He replied:
"Both are still and quiet."
Who is the one who answers 'None'?
The Eighteenth Patriarch, Gāyéshètà,
arrived at the house of a Brahmin in the Yuèzhī Kingdom,
and knocked on its door himself.
The householder, Luóduō, said:
"There is no one in this house."
The Venerable One said:
"Who is the one who answers 'None'?"
Luóduō opened the door, welcomed him,
sincerely committed to him, and left home.
Retribution for Good and Evil
The Nineteenth Patriarch, Jiūmóluódà, said:
"The retribution for good and evil
occurs in three times.
Ordinary people only see the benevolent die young and the violent live long,
thus deeming good inauspicious and evil auspicious,
and then conclude that cause and effect are nonexistent.
They do not realize that shadow follows form,
not deviating by a hair's breadth;
even after hundreds of millions of kalpas,
it will not be erased."
Having No Expectations in Mind is Called the Way
The Twentieth Patriarch, Shéyéduō, said:
"I do not seek the Way,
nor do I defile the Way.
I do not prostrate to the Buddha,
nor do I disrespect him.
I do not sit long,
nor am I idle.
I do not refuse food,
nor do I eat indiscriminately.
I am not content,
nor do I crave desires.
Having no expectations in mind,
this is called the Way."
Dream of Swallowing Two Pearls
The twenty-first patriarch, Pōxiūpántóu,
whose mother initially dreamt of swallowing two pearls, one bright and one dark, and became pregnant.
A Luóhàn said:
"You will give birth to two sons.
One will be the patriarch,
and one will be Chūní."
Previously, when Rúlái cultivated the Way on Snow Mountain,
Chūní nested on his neck.
After Fó achieved enlightenment,
Chūní was reborn as Nàtí Guówáng.
The Fójì states:
"Later, you will be a sibling to a sheng (saint).
Now you have no husband."
Chūní,
is Shūquèzǐ.
"In the forest, nine hundred [years] have already passed."
The twenty-second patriarch, Mónáluó, said:
"I have been in the forest for nine hundred [years]."
In India, one year is considered one yin.
The gài says:
"The mind follows myriad states and turns;
the turning place is truly profound.
If one can recognize the nature,
there is no joy and no sorrow."
"Shengzǐ"
The twenty-third patriarch, Hèlè,
at seven years old, traveled through villages.
He witnessed the people's licentious sacrifices.
Entering a temple, he reprimanded:
"You falsely bring forth calamity and fortune,
deluding people with illusions.
Yearly expenses for sacrifices and offerings,
the harm is truly great."
As soon as he finished speaking,
the temple's appearance suddenly deteriorated.
The villagers called him Shengzǐ.
"Opening his hand to offer the pearl."
The twenty-fourth patriarch, Shīzǐ Bīqiū,
had an elder bring his son to see the Master.
He said:
"When this child was born,
he clenched his left hand.
Now that he has grown,
he still cannot open it.
I wish to hear the karmic cause from a past life."
The Master immediately took his hand and said:
"Return my pearl."
The boy quickly opened his hand and offered the pearl.
The Master said:
"Previously, I was a monk,
and there was a boy, Pōshè.
I went to the Western Sea for a fast,
received a pearl as an offering, and entrusted it to him.
Now it has been returned."
Thus, he became his Dharma heir.
"Should perform Fóshì"
The twenty-fifth patriarch, Pōshèsīduō,
had the crown prince of the Central Indian kingdom seek to renounce worldly life.
The patriarch asked:
"If you wish to renounce worldly life,
what will you do?"
He replied:
"I will not do that."
The patriarch asked:
"Not do what?"
He replied:
"Not do worldly affairs."
The patriarch asked:
"Then what will you do?"
He replied:
"I will perform Fóshì."
"Yīngluò Tóngzǐ"
The twenty-sixth patriarch, Bùwèimìduō.
There was a Brahmín boy,
whose name was unknown.
Some called him Yīngluò,
and people called him Yīngluò Tóngzǐ.
The Zūnzhě said:
"This boy is Dàshìzhì Púsà."
"Priceless Gem"
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Bānruòduōluó.
The king of Southern India bestowed a priceless gem.
The prince said:
"This is a worldly treasure.
Among all treasures, the Dharma treasure is supreme.
This is worldly light.
Among all lights, the light of wisdom is supreme.
This is worldly brightness.
Among all brightnesses, the brightness of the mind is supreme."
"Established six schools"
The twenty-eighth patriarch, Dámó.
In Tiānzhúguó, there were many great Sages of the Buddha,
who established six patriarchs:
the first was the Patriarch of Form (Yǒuxiàngzǔ),
the second, the Patriarch of Formlessness (Wúxiàngzǔ),
the third, the Patriarch of Samādhi and Wisdom (Dìnghuìzǔ),
the fourth, the Patriarch of Precepts and Conduct (Jièxíngzǔ),
the fifth, the Patriarch of No Virtue (Wúdézǔ),
and the sixth, the Patriarch of Stillness (Jìjìngzǔ).
The Master lamented their divisions,
and one by one converted and subdued them.
The people of the six sects all returned to his teachings.
He also recited a gāthā, saying:
"In the womb, there is no body,
but in the world, one becomes human.
In the eye, it is called seeing;
in the ear, it is called hearing.
In the nose, it discerns fragrance;
in the mouth, it discusses.
In the hand, it grasps;
in the foot, it walks and runs.
Running and appearing encompass the Dharma Realm;
the Dharma is contained in a single speck of dust.
Those who recognize it know it is Buddha-nature;
those who do not recognize it call it a spirit."
The Master sailed across the sea to Guǎngzhōu.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng welcomed and invited him to Jīnlíng.
The Emperor said:
"I have built temples, offered sūtras, and ordained monks,
an immeasurable number of deeds.
What merit is there in this?"
The Master said:
"There is no merit at all.
These are merely small results for humans and devas,
causes with outflows.
Like a shadow following the form,
though present,
it is not real."
The Emperor asked:
"What is the supreme meaning of the Holy Truths?"
He replied:
"Vast and empty, there is no Sage."
The Emperor said:
"Who is it that stands before me?"
The Master said:
"I do not know."
The Emperor did not comprehend,
so the Master secretly returned to Luòyáng
and resided at Sōngshān Shàolín Temple.
He spent the whole day facing a wall, contemplating the Brāhmaṇa.
There was a monk, Shénguāng,
who reflected:
"This person seeks the Way,
would knock bones to extract marrow,
pierce veins to feed the hungry,
spread hair to cover muddy paths,
and throw oneself off cliffs to feed tigers.
If the ancients were like this,
who am I?"
That night, there was heavy snow,
and he stood upright without moving.
The Master said:
"What do you seek?"
Guāng said:
"I wish for the Venerable Master to open the gate of sweet dew
and widely save all sentient beings."
He then cut off his left arm and placed it before him.
The Master renamed him Huìkě.
Guāng said:
"My mind is not yet at peace;
I beg the Master to pacify it."
The Master said:
"Bring your mind, and I will pacify it for you."
Guāng said:
"I search for my mind, but cannot find it."
The Master said:
"I have pacified your mind already."
As the Master was about to return west,
he commanded his disciples to each state what they had attained.
Dàofù said:
"As I see it,
one does not cling to words,
nor depart from words,
but uses them for the Way."
The Master said:
"You have obtained my skin and fur."
Zǒngchí said:
"Once I have seen,
I will not see again."
The Master said:
"You have obtained my flesh."
Dàoyù said:
"The four great elements are fundamentally empty;
the five skandhas are nonexistent.
Yet in my perception,
there is one dharma that can be attained."
The Master said:
"You have obtained my bones."
Finally, Huìkě bowed,
and then stood in his place.
The Master said:
"You have obtained my marrow."
He also said:
"Many understand the Way,
but few practice the Way.
Many speak of principles,
but few comprehend principles.
You must propagate these principles,
so that one can awaken with a single turning of the mind,
and thus be the same as the original attainment."
He recited a gāthā:
"I originally came to this land,
to transmit the Dharma and narrate its essence.
One flower opens into five petals,
and the fruit naturally ripens."
Yáng Xuànzhī, the Governor of Qíchéng, said:
"The Master's name is unspoken,
how can it manifest transformation?"
The Master gave a prophecy, saying:
"The river divides at Wánglàng,
Guǎnjù opens the golden lock.
I
will be your guide,
and you shall go;
for ninety years there will be no self or other."
Later, these were all fulfilled.
At that time, Zen masters in the Wèi dynasty were as numerous as hemp,
and the Vinaya master Liúzhī Sānzàng
was a phoenix among monks.
He debated with the Master,
and right and wrong arose like sharp blades,
vying to administer poison.
The Master passed away peacefully while sitting.
Three years later,
someone met the Master in Cōnglíng,
carrying a single sandal in his hand,
drifting away alone.
When asked where he was going,
he said:
"To the Western Heaven."
Emperor Míng ordered his tomb opened;
it was only an empty coffin,
with one sandal remaining.
His skull resembled five peaks rising majestically.
The twenty-ninth patriarch, Great Master Huìkě,
sat in meditation on Mount Xiāng for eight years.
He saw a spirit who said:
"Are you about to receive the fruit?
Why do you tarry here?"
The next day,
he had a headache like being stabbed.
His teacher wanted to treat it,
but a voice from the sky said:
"This is merely a change of bones,
not ordinary pain."
The Master observed his head,
and his skull resembled five peaks rising majestically.
After taking his proper place,
there was a lay devotee who said:
"My body is afflicted by a severe wind disease;
please, Venerable Master, confess my sins."
The Master said:
"Bring your sins, and I will confess them for you."
The lay devotee said:
"I search for my sins, but cannot find them."
The Master said:
"I have confessed your sins already;
you should abide in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha."
He said:
"The Venerable Master is the Saṅgha,
but what are the Buddha and Dharma?"
The Master said:
"This mind is the Buddha;
this mind is the Dharma.
The Buddha and Dharma are not two,
and the jewel of the Saṅgha is also thus."
He said:
"Only today do I realize that sin,
surprisingly, is not within,
not without,
and not in between,
just as the mind is;
the Buddha and Dharma are not two."
The Dharma Gate of Liberation
The thirtieth patriarch, Great Master Sēngcàn,
had a śrāmaṇa who begged for the Dharma gate of liberation.
The Master said:
"Who binds you?"
He said:
"No one binds me."
The Master said:
"Then why do you seek liberation?"
The Nature of Emptiness
The thirty-first patriarch, Dàoxìn Dàshī,
met a small child.
The master said,
"What is your family name?"
He replied,
"My family name is Fó (Buddha)."
The master said,
"Do you have no family name?"
He replied,
"My family name is Kōng (emptiness)."
Originally there is not a single thing.
The thirty-second patriarch, Hóngrěn Dàshī.
Layman Lú Huìnéng came to visit.
The master said,
"Where do you come from?"
He replied,
"Lǐngnán."
The master said,
"What do you want?"
He replied,
"I seek to become a Buddha."
The master said,
"People from Lǐngnán have no Buddha-nature.
How can you attain Buddhahood?"
He replied,
"People have north and south,
but how can Buddha-nature be so?"
A monk, Shénxiù, wrote a gāthā on the corridor wall, saying:
"The body is the Bodhi tree,
The mind is like a bright mirror stand.
Diligently wipe it constantly,
Let no dust or grime settle."
Huìnéng secretly wrote next to the gāthā:
"Bodhi is fundamentally not a tree,
The bright mirror is also not a stand.
Originally there is not a single thing,
What need is there to wipe away dust?"
The Grand Master then transmitted the robe and dharma to Huìnéng.
Form is the root of the shadow, sound is the root of the echo.
Xiàng Jūshì wrote a letter to the Second Patriarch saying:
"Shadows arise from forms,
Echoes follow sounds.
Chasing shadows exhausts the body,
Not knowing that form is the root of the shadow;
Raising one's voice to stop an echo,
Not knowing that sound is the root of the echo."
Lǎnrǒng
The Chan master Fǎróng of Niútóu Mountain in Jīnlíng,
was well-versed in classics and history from a young age.
He sighed, saying,
"Confucianism and Daoism are worldly and not the ultimate dharma;
Prajñā (wisdom) and right view are the boat for transcending the world."
So he took refuge with a master and shaved his head,
entering Niútóu Mountain,
where there was the marvel of hundreds of birds carrying flowers in their beaks.
During his right view practice,
the Fourth Patriarch asked a monk,
"Is there a Daoist here?"
He replied,
"Which renunciant is not a Daoist?"
The patriarch said,
"Which one is the Daoist?"
The monk said,
"There is Lǎnrǒng in the mountains,
he is a Daoist."
So he entered the mountain to see the master.
There were several circuits of tigers and wolves around the hermitage.
He raised both hands in an upward gesture.
The master said,
"Why are these still here?"
The master then bowed his head and requested the true essence.
The patriarch said,
"A hundred thousand Dharma gates
all return to the ten directions.
The virtues like sands of the Ganges
are all in the source of the mind.
All karmic obstructions and afflictions
are fundamentally empty and tranquil.
All causes and effects
are like dreams and illusions.
There are no three realms to leave,
no Bodhisattvas to eternally strive for.
You just let your mind be free,
encounter circumstances with every glance,
be joyful and without worry,
hence it is called 'no Buddha'."
Pacifying the mind, revealing wisdom
Chan master Huìzhōng had a gāthā for pacifying the mind,
which said:
"Both people and phenomena are pure,
Good and evil are forgotten.
The true mind is truly real,
That is the Bodhi practice ground."
Form, sound, and a deadly poison
Chan master Bái Yúncuǐ of Zhōngshān,
first visited Niútóu Róng.
The master said,
"Form and sound are the deadly poison of non-birth;
sensation and perception, and even consciousness, are the pitfalls of humanity."
Stop upon encountering a path
Chan master Dàoqīn of Jìngshān,
was a disciple of Chan master Xuánsù.
The master said,
"You should follow the stream,
and stop when you encounter a path."
The master then traveled south,
and settled at Jìngshān.
A monk asked,
"What is the Dao?"
The master said,
"There are carp on the mountain,
and duckweed dust at the bottom of the water."
The Magpie Nest Monk and the Fabric Fluff Attendant
Chan master Dàolín of Hángzhōu,
first arrived at Qínwàng Mountain,
and saw a tall pine tree with branches and leaves coiled like a canopy.
He then settled there,
and was at that time called the Niǎokē Chánshī (Bird's Nest Chan Master).
There was also a magpie nest beside him,
so people called him the Quècháo Héshang (Magpie Nest Monk).
An attendant, Huìtōng, came to bid farewell and leave.
The master said,
"Where are you going?"
He replied,
"To various places to study the Buddha-dharma."
The master said,
"If it is the Buddha-dharma,
there is also a little bit of it here."
He picked up some fabric fluff from his body and blew it,
whereupon Huìtōng was enlightened.
He was then called the Bùmáo Shìzhě (Fabric Fluff Attendant).
During the Yuánhé era,
the governor Bái Jūyì entered the mountain,
saying,
"Your dwelling place is very dangerous."
The master said,
"Your danger, Governor, is even greater."
Bái Jūyì said,
"My position controls rivers and mountains,
what danger is there?"
The master said,
"Firewood and fire intermingle,
the discriminating mind never stops;
is this not dangerous?"
He also asked about the profound meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
The master said,
"Do no evil,
diligently practice all good."
Bái Jūyì said,
"Even a three-year-old child knows how to say that."
The master said,
"Though a three-year-old child can say it,
an eighty-year-old person cannot practice it."
Seeing nature and becoming Buddha
Chan master Zhī of Tiāntái Yúnjū,
was asked by a monk,
"What is the meaning of 'seeing nature and becoming Buddha'?"
The master said,
"The nature of purity
is originally clear and tranquil.
To see it clearly in this way
is to clearly see one's nature.
Nature is Buddha,
Buddha is nature.
Therefore it is called 'seeing nature, seeing Buddha'."
Abandoning one's father and fleeing
Chan master Shénxiù of Běijīng,
had a gāthā that said:
"All Buddha-dharma
is inherently within one's own mind.
To seek it externally with the mind
is like abandoning one's father and fleeing."
Like a person drinking water
Chan master Dàomíng of Méngshān said:
"Entering (the truth) is like a person drinking water,
only they themselves know whether it is cold or warm."
The Song of Understanding the Origin
Chan master Rénjiǎn of Luòjīng,
was summoned to the palace by Empress Tiānhòu of Tang.
Looking up at the Empress, he said,
"Do you understand?"
The Empress said,
"I do not understand."
The master said,
"This old monk observes the vow of silence."
The next day,
he presented nineteen short songs,
all in the Yínzhí style,
but only "The Song of Understanding the Origin" became widely popular.
Pòzàoduò
Héshàng was living in seclusion on Sōngshān.
There was a very efficacious temple.
One stove continuously cooked and slaughtered living beings.
The master tapped it three times with his staff and said:
"Hmph!
This stove is merely made of mud and tiles.
How can a 'saint' come from it?
How can 'efficacy' arise from it to so slaughter living beings?"
The stove then tilted, broke, and fell apart.
Presently, a person,
dressed in green robes and wearing a tall crown,
bowed and said:
"I am the stove god,
who has long endured karmic retribution.
Today, thanks to the master's dharma teaching,
I have been reborn in the heavens,
and have specially come to offer thanks."
Ān Guóshī then gave him the title Pòzàoduò,
and once sighed, saying:
"This fellow has thoroughly understood the unity of self and other,
just like the bright moon in the sky,
seen by all."
The Mountain God Receives the Precepts
Xiōng Guī Chánshī
had an unusual person, wearing a tall crown, arrive.
He said:
"I am the Mountain God,
capable of giving life and death to people."
The master said:
"I am fundamentally unborn;
how can you cause my death?
I regard life as equal to emptiness,
and I regard myself as equal to you.
Can you destroy emptiness or yourself?
If you could destroy me,
then I would be neither born nor perish.
Since you cannot,
how then can you cause my life or death?"
The god bowed his head and begged for the precepts.
The master said:
"I bestow upon you the five precepts.
Can you refrain from sexual misconduct?"
He replied:
"It is also assembly."
The master said:
"It means no obsessive desire."
He replied:
"I can, Master."
The master said:
"Can you refrain from stealing?"
He replied:
"What is 'me' to be taken?"
The master said:
"It means enjoying and benefiting from vice,
and bringing disaster upon the good by not offering to them."
He replied:
"I can."
The master said:
"Can you refrain from killing?"
He replied:
"I am indeed in charge of this power."
The master said:
"It means arbitrary, mistaken, suspicious, or confused actions."
He replied:
"I can."
The master said:
"Can you refrain from false speech?"
He replied:
"I am upright."
The master said:
"It means that your actions, whether prior or subsequent, do not accord with the will of heaven."
He replied:
"I can."
The master said:
"Will you not suffer from being sprinkled with wine and defeated?"
He replied:
"I can."
The master said:
"The above constitutes the Buddhist precepts."
Wind Moves, Banner Moves
Huìnéng Dàshī was residing at Fǎxìng Sì.
At dusk, the wind flapped the temple banner.
Two monks debated whether it was the banner moving,
or the wind moving.
The master said:
"Neither the wind nor the banner is moving;
it is your mind that moves."
Reciting the Fǎhuá Jīng Three Thousand Times
Hóngzhōu Fǎdá Chánshī,
at the age of seven, left home and recited the Fǎhuá Jīng.
When bowing to the Patriarch, his head did not reach the ground.
The Patriarch reprimanded him, saying:
"If your bow doesn't touch the ground,
why bother bowing at all!"
The master replied:
"I have already recited the Fǎhuá Jīng three thousand times."
The Patriarch said:
"You are burdened by this achievement,
and are completely unaware of your fault.
Listen to my verse:
'Bowing fundamentally involves lowering the canopy,
why does your head not reach the ground?
If there is ego, sin immediately arises;
seven accomplishments bring immeasurable blessings.' " He further said:
"Your name is Fǎdá,
you diligently recite without rest.
Empty recitation merely follows sound;
an enlightened mind is called a Bodhisattva.
Because you have affinity now,
I will speak to you now.
Just believe that the Buddha has no words,
and lotuses will issue from your mouth."
He further said:
"When the mind is deluded, the Fǎhuá Jīng turns;
when the mind is enlightened, it turns the Fǎhuá Jīng.
Long recitation without understanding the meaning
makes you a dual household with the meaning.
No thoughts means uprightness;
having thoughts turns into evil.
Neither existence nor non-existence is considered;
long drive the white ox cart."
The master said:
"The sūtra speaks of three carts;
what is the difference between the great ox cart and the white ox cart?"
The Patriarch said:
"The Buddha explains this principle for ordinary people.
Little do they know that having already mounted the white ox cart,
they still search for the three carts outside the gate."
The master rejoiced and said:
"Having recited three thousand volumes,
not a single word is lost to Lǔ.
Not yet understanding the purpose of liberation,
my efforts have been years of foolishness.
The sheep, deer, and ox are expedient means,
the good teachings of the beginning, middle, and end.
Who knew that within the burning house,
I was originally a king of the dharma?"
How Can Sitting Meditation Lead to Becoming a Buddha?
Nányuè Huáiràng Chánshī
saw a śramaṇa, Dàoyī, sitting in meditation.
The master asked:
"Virtuous one, what are you aiming for by sitting in meditation?"
He replied:
"To become a Buddha."
The master picked up a tile and rubbed it on a stone.
Dàoyī asked:
"What are you doing?"
The master said:
"I'm grinding it to make a mirror."
Dàoyī asked:
"How can grinding a tile turn it into a mirror?"
The master said:
"How can sitting meditation lead to becoming a Buddha?"
The master entered his chamber.
He had six disciples,
and the master affirmed each of them, saying:
"One has obtained my nose,
and is good at discerning 'qi';
one has obtained my tongue,
and is good at speaking;
one has obtained my mind,
and is good at ancient and modern wisdom."
Enlightened in One Night
Yǒngjiā Xuánjué Chánshī,
when he first visited the Sixth Patriarch,
lost the exchange of questions and answers,
and intended to leave.
The Patriarch kept him for one night,
and he was then called Yīsùjué (Enlightened in One Night).
The Mind Itself Is Buddha
Sīkōngshān Yī Jìng Chánshī,
Yáng Guāngtíng asked about the meaning of Buddha-dharma.
The master said:
"If you wish to seek Buddha,
the mind itself is Buddha.
If you wish to understand the Way,
no-mind is the Way."
Two Schools
In the fourth year of Tiānbǎo of the Táng dynasty, two schools were established:
The Southern Sudden School,
which is the Sixth Patriarch Huìnéng,
Lú Xíngzhě residing in Huìxī.
The Northern Gradual Teaching,
which is Shénxiù,
who was also a disciple of the Fifth Patriarch.
His understanding was unsurpassed,
and his dharma lineage branched out.
Wòlún's Verse
Wòlún Chánshī's gāthā says:
“Wòlún has skills,
Able to cut off a hundred thoughts.
Facing objects, the mind does not stir;
Bodhi is long like the sun and moon.”
Liùzǔ said:
“This gāthā has not yet illuminated the mind-ground.”
Then he composed a gāthā, saying:
“Huìnéng has no skills,
Does not cut off a hundred thoughts.”
Facing objects, the mind constantly stirs;
How can Bodhi grow long?”
When hungry, eat; when tired, sleep.
Dàzhū Huìhǎi Chánshī,
Someone asked: “How does the Heshang cultivate the Dao and apply effort?”
The Master said:
“When hungry, eat;
When tired, sleep.”
He asked:
“Do all people apply effort the same way as the Master?”
He said:
“Not the same.
When they eat, they refuse to eat properly,
Thinking of a hundred kinds of food;
When it's time to sleep, they refuse to sleep,
Making a thousand calculations and schemes.
Therefore, it is not the same.”
What does a tiger resemble?
Bīnshān Zhìjiān Chánshī,
Was traveling with Guīzōng and Nánquán,
And they passed by a tiger.
He asked Guīzōng:
“What does a tiger resemble?”
Zōng said:
“It resembles a kitten.”
The Master said:
“It resembles a puppy.”
Quán said:
“I see it as a great insect.”
Gāthā of the withered tree
Dàhǎishān Fǎ Chánshī had a gāthā that said:
“A withered tree, broken and battered, leans in the cold forest,
Through many springs, its heart remains unchanged.
Even a woodcutter, upon encountering it, pays it no heed,
How could a person from Yǐng bother to search for it?”
Dàkōng and Xiǎokōng, two tigers
Tánzhōu Huálín Shànjué Chánshī.
One day,
Inspector Pèi Xiū visited him,
And asked if he had attendants.
The Master said:
“I have one or two.”
He called out “Dàkōng! Xiǎokōng!”
And two tigers emerged from behind the alley.
The Master said:
“There are guests, please leave for now.”
The two tigers roared and departed.
Pèi Xiū asked what kind of practice he performed,
To invoke such a phenomenon.
The Master said:
“This mountain monk often recites Guānyīn.”
Ling Xíngpó
Fúyíng Heshang,
Was visited by Ling Xíngpó, who prostrated and asked questions.
A monk recounted this to Nánquán,
Quán said:
“Alas!
Fúyíng was crushed by that old woman.”
A single gulp to drain the Xījiāng River
Xiāngzhōu recluse Páng Yùn,
First visited Shítóu Heshang,
And later became friends with Dānxiá Chánshī.
Shítóu asked:
“What about daily affairs?”
He replied:
“Daily affairs are nothing special,
Only that I spontaneously harmonize.
Each thing is neither taken nor rejected,
Everywhere there is no conflict.
Who labels vermilion and purple?
The Five Mountains are utterly free of dust.
Divine penetration and wondrous function,
Carrying water and chopping firewood.”
Later, he visited Mǎzǔ and said:
“What is ‘not associating with myriad dharmas’?”
Mǎzǔ said:
“Wait until you can drain the Xījiāng River in one gulp,
Then I will tell you.”
The recluse was suddenly enlightened,
And said:
“With a son, not married;
With a daughter, not wed.
All gathered in joyful reunion,
Together speaking of the unborn.”
His daughter, named Língzhào,
Would take bamboo strainers and sell them,
To provide for their daily needs.
One step further at the top of a hundred-foot pole
Zhāoxián Dàshī's gāthā says:
“One who stands still at the top of a hundred-foot pole,
Though having entered, has not yet reached the true.
At the top of a hundred-foot pole, one must take a step further,
Then the ten-direction world is the whole body.”
He also said:
“People who study the Dao,
Do not recognize the true.
Merely because they have always recognized the discriminating consciousness.
The root of birth and death since beginningless eons,
Fools call it the original body.”
So poor there's no place to stick an awl
Yǎngshān Huìjí Chánshī asked Xiāngyán:
“What is your insight?”
Yán said:
“Last year's poverty,
Was not true poverty.
Today's poverty,
Is true poverty.
Last year there was no place to stick an awl,
This year, no awl either.”
The Master said:
“You have only attained Tathāgata Chan,
You have not yet attained Patriarchal Chan.”
Striking bamboo to make a sound
Xiāngyán Zhìxián Chánshī,
While clearing grass in the mountains,
Was struck by a tile chip on a bamboo, making a sound.
He was suddenly enlightened.
One thought of cultivating the unconditioned path
Chǔnán Chánshī said:
“Even if you, my sons, understand the Buddhist teachings of the three times as water poured from a bottle,
And absorb hundreds and thousands of samādhis;
It is not as good as one thought of cultivating the unconditioned path,
To avoid being bound by the karma of humans and gods.”
Whose song does the master sing?
Shǒushān Shěngniàn Chánshī,
A monk asked:
“Whose song does the Master sing?
Whose lineage does your style follow?”
The Master said:
“I personally observed it before the rocks of Shǎoshì.”
The monk said:
“Please sing another resounding note in harmony.”
The Master said:
“Now I also want everyone to know.”
Who gave you birth and death?
Shítóu Xīqiān Chánshī,
A monk asked:
“What is liberation?”
The Master said:
“Who binds you?”
Again asked:
“What is the Pure Land?”
The Master said:
“Who defiles you?”
Asked:
“What is Nirvāṇa?”
He said:
“Who gave you birth and death?”
Five kinds of Chan
There are five kinds of Chan:
There is ordinary Chan,
There is externalist Chan,
There is Hīnayāna Chan,
There is Mahāyāna Chan,
There is Supreme Vehicle Chan.
One-finger Chan
Jùzhī Heshang, when he first lived in his hermitage,
Encountered Tiānlóng Heshang, who raised one finger to him.
The Master was greatly enlightened.
Before his passing, he instructed:
“I received Tiānlóng's one-finger Chan,
And have not exhausted its use in my entire life.”
The field for selecting Buddhas
Dānxiá Tiānrán Chánshī initially studied Confucianism.
As he was about to take the imperial examination,
he met a Chan master on the road.
The traveler asked:
"Where are you going, benevolent one?"
He replied:
"I am going to seek an official post."
The traveler said:
"How does seeking an official post compare to seeking Buddhahood?"
He asked:
"Where should one go to seek Buddhahood?"
The traveler said:
"Jiāngxī Mǎ Tàishī has appeared in the world;
this is the place to seek Buddhahood."
The master went to see him.
Mǎzǔ then instructed him to visit Nányuè Shítou.
Clouds in the blue sky, water in the bottle.
Yàoshān Wéiyǎn Chánshī.
The prefect, Xué’áo, asked:
"What is the Dao?"
The master replied:
"Clouds in the sky, water in the bottle."
Áo composed a verse, saying:
"Having trained my body to be like a crane's form,
beneath a thousand pines are two cases of scriptures.
I came to ask about the Dao, with no other words,
clouds in the blue sky, water in the bottle."
Áo asked what are precepts,
samadhi, and wisdom. The master said:
"If the prefect wishes to preserve this matter,
you must sit on the highest mountain peak,
and walk in the deepest part of the sea.
If you cannot give up the things in your private chambers,
that inability will become a flaw."
One night, the master ascended the mountain and laughed heartily.
Áo presented a poem, saying:
"Returning to my secluded dwelling, content with nature's mood,
all year long, neither sending off nor welcoming.
Sometimes I ascend directly to the solitary peak's summit,
beneath the moon, parting the clouds, I laugh once."
Daily offering ten cakes.
Lóngtán Chóngxìn Chánshī
was the son of a cake seller.
Wù Héshàng lived in Huángtiān Sì.
The master would daily offer him ten cakes.
Wù once kept one cake,
saying:
"I bestow it upon you to shelter your descendants."
The master pondered, saying to himself:
"The cakes are what I brought;
why does he return one to me?"
Then he heard Wù say:
"Since it was you who brought them,
what fault is there in returning it to you?"
The master understood the profound meaning,
and subsequently requested to become a monk.
One day he asked about the essence of mind.
Wù said:
"Act freely according to your nature,
and let go widely according to circumstances.
Only exhaust the ordinary mind;
there is no other superior understanding."
Strictly avoid speaking.
Dàowúshān Yuánzhì Chánshī.
Yàoshān asked where he came from.
He replied:
"I came from wandering in the mountains."
Yàoshān said:
"Quickly bring the Dao here."
He replied:
"The birds on the mountain are white like snow,
the fish swimming in the stream are busy like a wheel."
Yàoshān said:
"Where wisdom does not reach,
strictly avoid speaking of it."
The master saw Yúnyán was unwell and said:
"Leaving this leaky shell,
where shall we meet?"
Yán replied:
"We shall meet in the place of neither birth nor death."
The master said:
"Why not say: 'Unless it is the place of neither birth nor death,
I do not seek to meet'?"
Boatman monk.
Huátíng Chuánzǐ Héshàng,
in Huátíng, Wújiāng, was rowing a small boat.
At the time, he was called Boatman Monk.
With a thatched roof over his head.
Déshān Xuānjiàn Chánshī.
Hóngshān asked the assembly:
"Do you recognize this master?"
The assembly said:
"No."
Hóng said:
"He will eventually have a thatched roof over his head.
He scolds Buddhas and curses patriarchs."
To discern the 'ignorant feast of one bowl'.
Liángjiè Chánshī, after passing away in meditation,
his disciples wailed in sorrow.
The master reopened his eyes and said:
"To toil in life and cease in death,
what is there to grieve about?"
He summoned the monastic in charge and ordered an 'ignorant feast of one bowl' to be prepared,
reprimanding them for their attachment.
After seven days,
when the meal was finally finished,
he sat upright and passed away.
The student's fundamental task.
Báimǎ Dùnrú Chánshī.
Someone asked: "What is the student's fundamental task?"
The master said:
"Last night, at the third watch, the sun shone brightly."
He was asked: "What is the matter beyond the Dharma-body?"
The master said:
"The toad at the bottom of the well swallowed the moon."
Dead wood dragon's roar.
A monk asked Xiāngyán: "What is the Dao?"
Yán replied:
"Dead wood dragon's roar."
The monk said:
"The student does not understand."
Yán replied:
"An eye in a skull."
Meeting a fierce tiger on the road.
Yúnjū Chánshī Dàojiǎn.
A monk asked:
"What about when one meets a fierce tiger on the road?"
The master said:
"Thousands of people do not meet one;
why do you alone meet one?"
He asked:
"What about sleeping alone on a solitary peak?"
He replied:
There is a ten-room monks' hall for the idle;
who told you to sleep alone on a solitary peak?"
Thirty years of staff-wielding power.
Dàoxī Chánshī, holding his staff, said:
"Thirty years in the mountains,
I gained this strength."
A monk asked:
"What strength did you gain from it?"
The master said:
"Crossing streams and crossing ridges,
propping east and propping west."
The final phrase.
Shǒuqīng Chánshī.
A monk asked about the final phrase.
The master said:
"Amidst the dust, I grew old on my own,
in the sky, the moon is ever bright."
He was asked: "What is the master's family style?"
He replied:
"One bottle and one alms bowl,
everywhere is a livelihood."
He was asked about the great meaning of the Dharma.
He replied:
"Busy and bustling,
morning rooster, evening bell."
Bamboo chopsticks and clay bowls.
Xīmíng Shēn Chánshī.
A monk asked: "What is the master's family style?"
The master replied:
"Bamboo chopsticks, clay bowls."
What is the ancient Buddha's mind?
Huáyán Huìdá Chánshī.
A monk asked:
"What is the ancient Buddha's
mind?"
The master replied:
"Beyond
the river, the great earth."
He was asked: "What is the Huáyán realm?"
The master replied:
"The entire view is without form or shadow."
When the East family's person dies, the West family helps in mourning.
Tiāntái Shíde was (a monk).
Fēnggān Chánshī, while traveling in the mountains,
arrived at Chìchéng
and saw a person.
He brought him to the temple
and named him Shíde.
One day, as he was sweeping the ground,
the temple abbot asked,
“What is your surname, ultimately?
Where do you live?”
Shíde put down his broom,
stood with clasped hands,
and the abbot was at a loss to understand.
Hánshān pounded his chest and said,
Oh Heaven,
oh Heaven!”
Shíde asked,
“What are you doing?”
He replied,
“Have you not heard the saying,
‘When a neighbor to the east dies,
the neighbor to the west helps with the funeral’?”
The two danced,
laughed loudly, and left.
What is the matter concerning Bùdài?
Bùdài Héshàng was
short and stout in build,
with a furrowed brow and a protruding belly.
He carried a cloth sack on a staff,
storing all his provisions in the sack.
Entering the market,
he would beg for anything he saw,
whether it was vinegar, sauces, fish, or pickled vegetables.
He would not put them to his mouth,
but put a small portion into his sack.
Báilù Héshàng asked,
“What is the cloth sack?”
The Master then put down the cloth sack.
He then asked,
“What is the matter concerning the cloth sack?”
The Master shouldered it and left.
Verse Before Execution
Sēngzhào Fǎshī,
having encountered calamity from the Qín ruler,
recited a verse before his execution:
“The Great Primal is originally without a master;
the Five Aggregates are fundamentally empty.
To hold my head to a white blade
is still like severing the spring breeze.”
No Going, No Coming
Lǐ Áo saw an old master sitting alone
and asked,
“While dwelling in the master’s room, what do you occupy yourself with?”
He replied,
“The Dharma-body is still and silent,
without going and without coming.”
How many people can know this mind?
Chányuè’s poem says:
“Zen practitioners meet and merely snap their fingers;
how many people can know this mind?”
Scroll Twenty
End.
This person will surely become a bandit.
During Jǐngdì’s reign,
