when Prime Minister Zhōu Yàfū had an audience for a banquet,
the Emperor, as the crown prince, attended at his side
and said,
“This person is formidable;
he will surely become a bandit.”
Star Trembling
In the first year of Yuánguāng,
the stars moved,
their brilliance illuminating the sky,
and only stopped after several nights.
Dǒng Zhòngshū said,
“This is called a star trembling;
the common people are in distress.”
At this time, there were plans to attack the Xiōngnú,
and the empire was indeed uneasy.
The Emperor called it wild talk
and intended to execute him.
Zhòngshū was afraid
and begged to be appointed as a harsh official to prove himself.
He was then appointed as a jūn hòu.
King Héjiān Laughed at the Emperor’s Capriciousness
King Héjiān came to court
and discussed ghosts and spirits with the Emperor.
The King laughed at the Emperor’s capriciousness,
and also, he did not participate in the Emperor’s campaigns,
often scorning the Emperor’s actions.
The Emperor sent a physician with medicine to poison him.
The King was virtuous and wise,
and the people of the empire mourned him.
The Emperor kept the matter secret
and gave him a lavish funeral.
Huáinán Wáng Ān
Huáinán Wáng Ān collected all the remaining books in the empire
and invited Daoist adepts.
The Emperor sent someone to spy on him,
learning that the King could summon immortals to travel with him,
changing forms without regularity,
sometimes appearing as a child,
sometimes as an old man.
He could also hide his form and fly,
subsisting on vital energy without eating.
The Emperor wanted to receive his Dao,
but the King refused.
Tradition says that there was no such event.
The Emperor was enraged
and intended to execute him.
Huáinán learned of this,
went out with his ministers and left,
and their whereabouts were unknown.
Bǎigǔ Seeks Juice
The Emperor traveled incognito
and arrived at Bǎigǔ at night,
asking the innkeeper for juice.
The innkeeper said,
“There is no juice,
only urine!”
He also suspected the Emperor of being a bandit
and gathered young men to attack him.
The innkeeper’s wife saw the Emperor’s appearance
and was astonished,
saying,
“This guest is no ordinary person.”
The husband did not listen.
The wife gave the husband wine to drink,
bound him when he was drunk,
and all the young men scattered.
The wife then killed a chicken for food
to apologize to the guest.
The next day, the Emperor returned,
summoned the wife and bestowed upon her a thousand catties of gold,
and appointed her husband as a Yǔlín Láng.
Fāngshuò Steals Peaches
Guìjī Jùn sent a dwarf,
seven inches tall,
fully dressed in official attire.
Upon seeing the Emperor,
the Emperor ordered him to walk on the table.
Dōngfāng Shuò said,
“Jùlíng,
why did you suddenly betray and come here?
Has Āmǔ returned yet?”
The dwarf did not reply
but said to the Emperor,
“The Queen Mother grows peaches,
which bear fruit once every three thousand years.
This little child has stolen them three times already
and has been banished here.”
Xiāngrú Composes a Rhapsody
The Emperor composed rhapsodies instantly.
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú took a long time to complete them.
The Emperor said,
“Would it be permissible for my speed to exchange for your slowness?”
Xiāngrú replied,
“For your servant, it would be permissible,
but I do not know how it would be for Your Majesty.”
Divine Palace
The Emperor appointed the Daoist adept Luán Dà as Wǔlì Jiāngjūn,
and built a nine-room divine palace,
intending to summon spirits.
The columns were painted with gold,
the rafter ends were made into dragon shapes,
white stone powder mixed with clear pepper juice was used for the walls,
white glazed tiles for the doors and screens,
pearls for the curtains,
reinforced with tortoiseshell,
and ivory was used for the roof ridges.
Miscellaneous precious treasures were used for the first (jiǎ) tent,
and the second (yǐ) tent was next to it.
The first was for the spirits to reside,
and he himself resided in the second.
The Queen Mother of the West Descends
On the seventh day of the seventh month, at the fasting ceremony in Chénghuá Diàn,
a green bird came from the west.
Dōngfāng Shuò said:
"Xīwángmǔ is descending
to visit Your Majesty."
So, screens and curtains were set up,
and powdered incense was burned.
The incense was an offering from Dōuguó.
It was smeared on the palace gates,
and its fragrance was perceptible a hundred *lǐ* away.
After a short while,
Xīwángmǔ arrived,
riding in a purple cloud chariot,
driven by a jade maiden.
The Mother wore seven victory adornments,
and a green aura like clouds surrounded her.
The Emperor bowed and requested the elixir of immortality.
The Mother said:
"The Emperor's desires are not fully extinguished,
and his covetous heart is still abundant;
the elixir of immortality cannot be granted yet."
Dōngfāng Shuò secretly peered through the Zhūquè window.
The Mother said:
"This child is fond of committing transgressions;
he has long been banished.
However, his original heart is not evil,
and he will soon be able to return."
The Mother took out seven peaches,
ate two herself,
and gave five to the Emperor.
The Emperor kept the pits, intending to plant them.
The Mother said:
"These peaches bear fruit only once every three thousand years;
they are not things that can be planted in the lower world."
Fāng Shuò, as the year star,
also went to the seaside
and investigated and executed over a hundred *dàoshì* who were particularly deceitful and boastful.
Xīwángmǔ sent an envoy, saying:
"To wish to see a divine person yet first engage in slaughter—
I am severed from the Emperor!"
On the day the envoy arrived,
Dōngfāng Shuò died.
The Emperor questioned the envoy in doubt.
The envoy replied:
"Shuò was the essence of the Wood Emperor,
serving as the year star.
He came down to wander among humans to observe the world;
he was not Your Majesty's subject."
Gōuyì Fūren
said to the Emperor:
"This concubine will die here this year."
Shortly after,
she passed away.
Thus, a Tōnglíng Tái was erected for her at Gānquán.
Green birds often flew back and forth on the terrace.
When the Emperor passed away, it ceased.
Dismissing the *fāngshì*
The Emperor said:
"Since I ascended the throne,
the world has suffered.
My actions have been reckless and perverse,
and cannot be regretted."
Tián Qiānqiū said:
"The Three Mountains are spiritual but difficult to verify;
the lake is distant and without proof.
Your servant requests that all *fāngshì* be dismissed
and sent away."
The Emperor said:
"The Grand Minister of Ceremonies' memorial is correct."
Whenever the Emperor met his officials,
he would lament his own foolishness and bewilderment:
"How can there be immortals in the world?
It's all deception and delusion. Fasting and taking medicine
might slightly reduce illness."
For two or three years, he was miserable and unhappy.
He said to Huò Guāng:
"When I depart, you will die,
Gōuyì's son—
you must assist him well."
Guāng wept and said:
"Your Majesty is still healthy and content;
how can such a thing be?"
The Emperor said:
"My illness is severe;
you just don't know it."
After one week, he died.
Maoling Palace Women
When the Emperor lay down during the day,
his complexion was unchanged,
but his body was cold and without breath.
The next day, his complexion gradually changed,
and his eyes closed.
Morning and evening offerings were made to the Emperor in the Wèiyáng Front Hall,
as if someone were eating them.
All those he had favored
were sent out to the Màolíng Park,
from *jiéhǎo* and below, over two hundred people.
The Emperor would visit them as if alive,
though bystanders could not see him.
Huò Guāng then released more palace women,
increasing the number to five hundred.
Then it ceased.
Màolíng Burial Objects
In the second year of Shǐyuán,
officials reported that commoners were stealing and using imperial carriage items.
The labels indicated they were burial objects from Màolíng.
Another person was selling a jade cup in the market,
whose form resembled the Emperor.
The county sent the artifact for investigation.
It was also an object from Màolíng.
The Emperor also appeared near the mausoleum and said:
"Although I have lost power as a ruler,
how can I allow officials and soldiers to sharpen their swords on my family's tomb?"
Upon investigation,
there was a square stone near the mausoleum that could be used for sharpening,
and officials and soldiers often secretly sharpened their swords on it.
At that time, bells and drums often naturally sounded at Gānquán,
and an imperial retinue like that of the Son of Heaven was seen.
It ceased during the reign of Xuāndì.
A Foot-long Scroll and a Gold Reward
On the day Xuāndì performed the ceremonial music for Wǔdì's temple,
a voice from the sky chanted "Excellent!"
Also, on the day a temple was established and sacrifices offered in Hédōng,
a tiger carried meat and placed it before the hall.
And another person rode a horse, holding a foot-long scroll, and gave it to the Minister of Works,
saying:
"If you continue and complete the work,
you will be rewarded with one *jīn* of gold."
Some did not see it,
but the scroll transformed into gold.
When Xuāndì personally made offerings at Gānquán,
purple *qì* and yellow clouds came from the northwest,
and music was heard in the sky.
The Emperor then suspected that the former emperor had become a spirit,
and again summoned various *fāngshì*,
hoping to attain immortality.
Summoning Scholars by Sedan Chair
On the day of Zhōngyuán,
a heavy rain would not stop.
He ordered his attendants to carry a sedan chair
to summon the scholar Yáo Chóng to discuss current affairs.
Both the court and the common people honored him.
He was bestowed with chopsticks to show his integrity.
Sòng Jǐng became Chancellor,
and the court and country gave their allegiance to him.
The Emperor bestowed golden chopsticks, saying:
"I bestow these chopsticks upon you
to symbolize your integrity."
Jǐng then descended from the hall, bowed, and thanked him.
Cutting Stirrups and Keeping Whips
Yáo Yuánchóng served as Governor of Jīngzhōu.
On the day he was to be relieved of his post,
the people and officials of the entire region wept, embracing his horse's head,
cutting the stirrups and keeping the whips
to express their admiration and reluctance to part.
Shameless as Iron Armor
The *jìnshì* Yáng Guāngyuǎn was endlessly greedy for power and wealth.
Even when subjected to flogging and humiliation,
he showed no remorse.
People at the time said:
"Yáng Guāngyuǎn's shameless face is as thick as ten layers of iron armor."
Seven-Jewel Seat
The Emperor, in Qínzhèng Lóu, constructed a mountain-shaped seat adorned with seven jewels,
seven *chǐ* high.
He summoned various scholars to discuss ancient and modern times.
The victor would be allowed to ascend.
Only Zhāng Jiǔlíng's eloquent debate was vibrant,
and he was the first to ascend this seat.
Others could not reach its level.
Bees and Butterflies Admiring Fragrance
The capital's famous courtesan, Chǔ Liánxiāng,
was of unparalleled beauty.
Whenever she went out, bees and butterflies would follow,
attracted by her fragrance.
Warmth in Cold Gathering
The wealthy magnate Wáng Yuánbǎo,
whenever there was heavy snow,
would clear a path from his residence to the entrance of the *fāngxiàng* (residential block)
to welcome and invite guests for drinking and feasting.
This was called a "Warmth in Cold Gathering."
Record-Keeping Pearl
Zhāng Yuè possessed a precious pearl,
of dark blue color with a luster,
named "Record-Keeping Pearl."
Whenever he had forgotten something, he would play with it,
and his mind would suddenly clear and understand.
Self-warming Cup
Within the imperial treasury, there was a green wine cup,
its patterns like tangled threads,
and it was as thin as paper.
When wine was poured into it,
a gentle warmth arose,
then it would bubble like boiling water.
It was named the Self-warming Cup.
Traveling Immortal Pillow
The kingdom of Qiūcí presented a pillow,
its color like carnelian.
When one slept on it, the Ten Continents and Three Isles,
the Four Seas and Five Lakes,
all appeared in dreams.
The Emperor named it the Traveling Immortal Pillow.
Cold-repelling Rhinoceros Horn
The kingdom of Jiāozhǐ presented a rhinoceros horn.
Placed on a golden tray in the palace hall,
its warm aura permeated the air.
The envoy said:
"This is a cold-repelling rhinoceros horn."
Letter-carrying Pigeons
Zhāng Jiǔlíng's family raised a flock of pigeons.
Whenever he wrote letters to relatives and friends,
he would tie them to the pigeons' legs,
and they would fly to deliver them.
He called them "flying slaves."
Record of Evils Stele
Lú Huàn served successively as a high minister.
Whenever he dealt with treachery and evil,
after pronouncing judgment,
he would also engrave the offenses on a stone and erect it at their gate.
If they offended again, they would surely be put to death.
At the time, it was called the "Record of Evils Stele."
Obtaining a Daughter by Pulling a Thread
Guō Yuánzhèn was handsome and refined in his youth.
Chancellor Zhāng Jiāzhēn wished to take him as a son-in-law.
He said:
"I have five daughters, each with her own beauty.
I will have one of them hold a thread behind a curtain,
and you may choose to pull any one you wish.
Whoever you get will be your match."
Yuánzhèn pulled a red silk thread,
and obtained the third daughter.
Calling Iron
The recluse Guō Xiū of Tàibái Shān
had the art of circulating qi and abstaining from grain.
When he struck an iron piece with a hammer,
birds and beasts hearing it
would immediately gather in the courtyard.
It was called "Calling Iron."
Green-robed Envoy
In Cháng'ān, a wealthy man named Yáng Chóngyì
had a wife, née Liú, who had an affair with a neighbor's son, Lǐ Yǎn.
They conspired to kill Chóngyì
and buried him in a dry well.
His servants and concubines were unaware,
only a parrot was on its perch.
Née Liú went to the yamen to make a statement,
claiming her husband had not returned
and she feared he had been harmed.
Day and night, thieves were apprehended,
hundreds of people were interrogated and beaten,
but the truth could not be found.
The county official returned to inspect again.
The parrot on the perch suddenly cried out:
"The one who wrongly killed the master
is née Liú and Lǐ Yǎn!"
Thus, the truth was apprehended.
Míng Huáng conferred upon the parrot the title of Green-robed Envoy.
Auspicious Charcoal
The kingdom of Xīliáng presented a hundred pieces of charcoal,
named "Auspicious Charcoal."
When burned, it produced no flame but gave light.
Each piece could burn for ten days,
and its heat was unbearable to approach.
Chopping Ice to Brew Tea
The hermit Wáng Xiū,
residing at the foot of Tàibái Shān,
would, in winter, take ice from the stream,
chop the clear and pristine pieces to brew tea,
and drink it with his guests.
Demonic Flowers and Trees
In front of the Chénxiāng Tíng, the tree peony flowers
had one stem with two heads.
In the morning, they were deep red;
at noon, deep green;
in the evening, deep yellow;
and at night, powdery white.
Throughout day and night,
their fragrance and beauty varied.
The Emperor said:
"These are demonic flowers and trees,
inauspicious."
Níng Wáng's Torches
Níng Wáng had a hundred torches.
Whenever guests and courtesans sat among them,
and in their drunkenness became wild,
the torches would dim
as if covered by something.
When they stopped, they would become bright again.
Dreaming of a Jade Swallow Entering the Bosom
Zhāng Yuè's mother dreamt a jade swallow flew into her bosom,
then she conceived and gave birth to Yuè.
Niànnú
Niànnú
was beautiful
and skilled in singing.
Whenever she held the clapper at a banquet,
her voice soared above the morning clouds.
Candle Slaves
Shēn Wáng carved a single-bunned boy from lónghuán wood,
dressed in a green robe with a fastened belt,
and had him hold painted candles in a row.
He called them "candle slaves."
Fish in a Basin Pond
Míng Huáng appointed Lǐ Línfǔ as chancellor.
One day, during a casual banquet with close ministers,
the Emperor said:
"I recently put several fish in the basin pond;
they are fresh, lively, and lovely."
Línfǔ replied:
"It is by Your Majesty's gracious favor that they are nourished."
Zhāng Jiǔlíng said:
"The fish in the basin pond
are like Your Majesty's appointment of people;
they can only be used for decoration and children's games."
The Emperor was displeased.
Golden-robed Young Master
Míng Huáng saw a yellow parrot in the imperial garden,
and called it the "Golden-robed Young Master."
Hate-dispelling Flower
When a thousand-petal peach blossom bloomed,
Míng Huáng said:
"Not only the daylily dispels sorrow,
this flower can also dispel hate."
Drunken Palanquin
Whenever Shēn Wáng was drunk,
he would have palace courtesans tie together a pouch of brocade,
carry him back to his bedchamber,
and call it the "drunken palanquin."
Courtesan Screen
Whenever Shēn Wáng suffered from the cold,
he would have palace courtesans closely encircle him by his seat
to ward off the cold air.
He called it the "courtesan screen."
Flowery Mire
The Píngkāng Fāng in Cháng'ān was a "flowery mire" (a place of pleasure and debauchery).
Ice Mountain
The jinshì Zhāng Tuàn
was diligent in study and widely renowned.
When Yáng Guózhōng was in power,
scholars flocked to his gate,
but Tuàn alone did not go.
He said:
"Do you all think Yáng Gōng's influence can be relied upon like Mount Tài?
In my view, it is an ice mountain!
Once the bright sun shines,
it will surely mislead people."
Later, he passed the imperial examination and became the Hūayīn registrar.
He sighed, saying:
"A man with the ambition to reach the clouds and surpass the world,
constrained in a low position,
is like standing in a low-roofed house,
unable to raise one's head."
So he shook out his robes and left forever.
Flower Mat
The academician Xǔ Shèn hosted a banquet with relatives and friends in a flower garden.
He gathered flowers to spread as seats,
saying:
"Since I have a flower mat, why do I need seating cushions?"
Moving Spring Enclosure
Yáng Guózhōng's relatives planted flowers in an enclosure,
which had wooden wheels on the bottom.
Wherever they went,
they would pull the enclosure ahead of them.
They called it the "Moving Spring Enclosure."
Flour Seal
In the capital, on the Yuánwán Day, flour seals were made,
with official position slips placed inside.
People competed based on rank as a game.
Clanging of Swords and Spears
Weapons in the imperial armory, dāo and qiāng, spontaneously rang.
Indeed, there was Lùshān's rebellion.
Carving Ice into Mountains
During the hot month, the Yáng family's sons carved a large block of ice into a mountain.
Banquet tables were set up all around it.
The Wáng Clan's Wealth Den
Wáng Yuánbǎo stacked gold and silver to form a house.
He also used copper wire to thread coins, paving the flower path with them.
Even when it rained, the mud was not slippery, making it precious.
At the time, it was called the "Wealth Den."
Flowers Growing on the Brush Tip
When Lǐ Táibái was young, he dreamt of flowers growing on the tip of his brush.
Later, his talent was abundant and unrestrained,
and his fame spread throughout the world.
Gold-Mud Good News
When new jinshì passed the imperial examination,
they would write a notice with gold mud to inform their families.
This was called "good news."
By the time of Emperor Wénzōng,
this custom was discontinued.
Half-Immortal Play
Palace women competed in swinging on qīuqiān for fun during the Cold Food Festival.
The Emperor called it "the play of half-immortals."
Brush Rest Predicting Rain
Sū Qīng had a brush rest made of variegated stone.
When it was about to rain, the stone rest would exude moisture.
He used this to predict rain,
and it was never wrong.
Beggars Warming Themselves by the Fire
Zhāng Jiǔlíng saw the court officials flocking to Yáng Guózhōng.
He said:
"They are all beggars warming themselves by the fire.
Once the fire is out and the ashes are cold,
where will the warmth be?
It won't be long before their frozen bodies are torn apart and their bones discarded in ditches and ravines."
Indeed, due to Lùshān's rebellion,
many clans were annihilated.
"Warming themselves by the fire"
means clinging to power and influence.
Ice Tendons
After a snowfall, the eaves' drippings all turned into ice strips.
The imperial consort knocked down two strips to examine and play with.
She said:
"These are ice tendons."
Wind-Predicting Chimes
In Qí Wáng's traveling palace,
small jade pieces were hung.
At night, when the sound of them touching each other was heard,
it indicated that there was wind.
They were called "wind-predicting chimes."
Time-Telling Ape
The hermit Gāo Tàisù of Shāngshān,
at every hour, had an ape that would come before his pavilion, bow, and cry out.
It was called the "time-telling ape."
Zhāng Gōng's Oral Judgments
Whenever Zhāng Jiǔlíng handled public affairs,
he would bring the prisoners before him,
distinguish right from wrong by face,
and compose the case documents orally.
All submitted to their guilt.
At the time, it was called "Zhāng Gōng's Oral Judgments."
Soul-Shattering Bridge
There was a bridge at Bālíng, east of Cháng'ān.
Those arriving and departing all crossed this bridge.
People called it the "Soul-Shattering Bridge."
Imperial Edict Prohibiting Alcohol
Ān Lùshān received imperial favor and affection.
The Emperor feared outsiders would poison him with alcohol.
So he bestowed upon him a golden tablet to wear on his back.
Whenever princes and dukes invited him to a banquet,
intending to offer a large goblet,
Lùshān would show the tablet,
saying:
"By imperial edict, alcohol is prohibited."
A Mighty Army in the Literary Field
Zhāng Jiǔlíng read Sū Tǐng's writings
and said:
"Truly a mighty army in the literary field."
Tear Make-up
Concubines in the palace applied white powder to their cheeks.
This was called "tear make-up."
Those who recognized it considered it inauspicious.
Leashed Fighting Cock
Lǐ Línfǔ failed to win the hearts of scholars.
All said his spirit was stubborn and tyrannical,
always like a leashed fighting cock.
Flesh Formation
In winter, Yáng Guózhōng selected fat and large maidservants
and arranged them in front to block the wind.
This was called the "flesh formation."
Flower That Understands Speech
A thousand-petaled white lotus bloomed magnificently in Lake Tàiyè.
The Emperor pointed to the Imperial Consort and said:
"How can it compare to my flower that understands speech?"
Oil Canopy
Wealthy families in Cháng'ān, when banqueting in spring,
traveled in carriages with oil canopies.
If they encountered cloudy or rainy weather, they would cover themselves with the canopy.
Phoenix Charcoal
Yáng Guózhōng molded charcoal dust into a pair of phoenixes.
Hundred-Treasure Railing
The Emperor bestowed a wooden tree peony upon Guózhōng.
Guózhōng made a railing for it with a hundred treasures.
Sucking Flower Dew
Whenever the Imperial Consort's hangover began to fade,
she often suffered from lung heat.
At dawn, she would stand by the flower branches
and suck the flower dew to moisten her lungs.
Holding a Jade Fish in the Mouth for Saliva
The Imperial Consort was naturally plump,
suffering from body heat
and lung thirst.
Every day, she held a jade fish in her mouth,
using its cool saliva to moisten her lungs.
Striking Mirrors to Save the Moon
During a lunar eclipse in Cháng'ān city,
men and women would take mirrors and strike them towards the sky,
saying it was to save the moon from the eclipse.
Song Behind the Screen
Níng Wáng had a beloved concubine who was a musician and singer,
beautiful and skilled in song.
Guests were not allowed to see her.
Lǐ Táibái said:
"Why does the Prince begrudge this woman so much
that he doesn't show her to the public?"
So, a seven-treasure flower screen was set up,
and the beloved concubine was summoned to sing behind the screen.
Bái said:
"Although I am not allowed to see her face,
hearing her voice is fortunate enough."
Night-Shining Pillow
Guóguó Fūrén had a night-shining pillow,
which illuminated the entire room,
without need for lamps or candles.
Spring with Feet
Sòng Jǐng loved the people and sympathized with all beings.
People at the time called him "spring with feet."
Meaning wherever he went,
it was like spring reaching all things.
Discourse of Scattered Flowers
When Lǐ Bái conversed with others,
all his words formed sentences and phrases,
like beautiful spring blossoms and elegant prose,
scattering from his teeth and tongue.
At the time, it was called Lǐ Bái's "discourse of scattered flowers."
Drunken Sage
Lǐ Bái was addicted to alcohol,
yet the articles he composed while deeply intoxicated
never contained errors.
He was called the "Drunken Sage."
Exploring Spring
City dwellers, men and women,
after the Lantern Festival, would ride in carriages and on horseback
to the countryside for a spring-exploring banquet.
Drunken Man's Annoying Words
Whenever Lǐ Línfǔ discussed public affairs with his colleagues,
he was like a drunkard,
never answering questions.
But when private matters of flattery were discussed,
he would respond instantly like flowing water.
Zhāng Jiǔlíng said:
"Línfǔ's discussion of affairs
is like a drunkard's annoying words."
Warm Jade Saddle
Qí Wáng had a saddle
which, when sat upon in winter,
felt as if there were warm fire.
Snow Thorns Filling the Chin
Sòng Jǐng requested to retire.
His memorial stated:
"Your servant's beard is like frost flowers,
and snow thorns fill my chin.
I request to retire and return to farming,
to nurture my indolence amidst the rocks."
Elegant Formation
Mínghuáng and his imperial concubine would get drunk every time.
The imperial concubine would lead over a hundred palace courtesans,
and the Emperor would lead over a hundred young palace eunuchs,
forming two formations.
They called it the "Romantic Formations."
They would attack and clash,
and the losers would be punished with a huge goblet.
At the time, this was considered an inauspicious omen.
Palace maids breathed on the brush.
Lǐ Bái was in the side hall drafting an imperial edict.
It was very cold and the brush was frozen.
The Emperor ordered ten palace maids, each holding an ivory brush, to breathe on it.
Lǐ Bái took it and wrote.
Chī Gēng Què.
Péi Yàoqīng kept a bird
that would surely sing at each watch.
It was called "Chī Gēng Què" (Watch-Knowing Sparrow).
Yìng Zhì Shī (Poem by Imperial Command).
Cháng'ān in spring was rife with banquets and outings.
Sū Tǐng's poem written by imperial command said:
"Flying dust forms red mist,
touring canopies drift like green clouds."
Jǐn Yàn (Brocade Geese).
In the imperial bath at the Hot Springs, there was the Jade Lotus Bath.
From the lotuses, sea valleys emerged.
Ducks and geese made of brocade were floated on it.
Kuài Yún'ér (Fast Cloud Child).
Shēn Wáng had a red Goryeo falcon.
Qí Wáng had a yellow North Mountain goshawk.
Every time they went hunting,
they would be perched on the arm at the front of the carriage.
They were given the name "Kuài Yún'ér."
Jiǔ Kǒng Zhēn (Nine-Holed Needle).
On the Qīxī Festival,
palace maids would face the moon and thread five-colored silk through a nine-holed needle.
Ròu Yāodāo (Flesh Scimitar).
Lǐ Línfǔ was jealous of the virtuous and envious of the capable.
He secretly slandered and denounced them.
People called him a "Ròu Yāodāo."
Yì Zhú (Righteous Bamboo).
The Emperor was touring the imperial garden
where there was a dense clump of bamboo.
The bamboo shoots did not grow outwards.
The Emperor looked at his princes and said:
"Fathers and sons, brothers and brothers, should be as intimate as this bamboo."
Thus, it was called "Yì Zhú."
Bǎi Zhī Dēng (Hundred-Branch Lamp).
Hán Guó Fūrén made a hundred-branch lamp,
eighty feet tall,
its light illuminating for tens of miles.
Guǐ Shén Pò Dǎn (Ghosts and Spirits Scared out of their Wits).
Lǐ Gǎo was the Magistrate of Luòyáng.
He was fair and just,
and the common people feared him.
There was a certain Liú Jiān who lodged at a village inn.
At night, he heard outside the door:
"The upright man of all ages, Magistrate Lǐ,
seeing his actions,
scares people out of their wits.
We should go to other counties for our blood offerings."
Jiān opened the door to look,
but there was no one.
They were ghosts and spirits.
Chán Dēng (Greedy Lamp).
In the south, there is a fish rich in fat,
which is refined into oil.
When lit for spinning and weaving, it is dim;
when used to illuminate feasts and entertainment, it is bright.
It is called "Chán Dēng."
Hù Huā Jīn Líng (Flower-Protecting Golden Bells).
Níng Wáng, during flower season, would hang golden bells beneath the flowers,
pulling them to startle birds.
They were called "Hù Huā Jīn Líng."
Qún Wò (Skirt Canopy).
When the ladies of Cháng'ān walked in the spring countryside,
upon encountering famous flowers, they would sit on the grass,
untie their skirts and spread them out like a canopy.
It was called "Qún Wò."
Shè Tuán (Shooting Dumplings).
On Duānwǔ, palace maids would make powdered dumplings and horn-shaped zòngzi.
They would store them on a golden tray,
and shoot them with small horn bows.
Those who hit the powdered dumplings got to eat them.
Lǐ Qiáo Zhēn Cáizǐ (Lǐ Qiáo, a True Talent).
The Emperor was about to move his residence
and ascended the Huá'è Lóu.
A young man sang Lǐ Qiáo's lyrics:
"Mountains and rivers fill the eyes, tears moisten clothes;
how long can wealth and glory last?
Do you not see that on the Fénshuǐ today,
only the autumn geese fly year after year?"
The Emperor tearfully said:
"He is truly a man of talent."
He left without waiting for the song to end.
Sìshí Nián Bù Dé Jiǔ Wèi (Forty Years Without Tasting Wine).
When the Emperor entered Xié Gǔ,
Cháng Tì obtained new wine
and presented it before the imperial horse.
The Emperor did not drink it.
Tì, fearing, drank it himself.
The Emperor said:
"When I was a princely official,
I once drank wine and harmed a person.
Therefore, I abstained.
For forty years, I have not known the taste of wine."
Yù Huán Pípá (Jade Ring Pipa).
Used by Ruìzōng.
The Emperor wished to travel west to Shǔ.
He ordered Hè Huáizhì to play it.
Yǐ Bǐng Shì Dāo (Using Cake to Wipe the Knife).
When Sùzōng was the Crown Prince,
the Emperor made him cut a sheep's shoulder.
He used a cake to wipe the blade
and slowly ate it.
The Emperor happily said:
"Fortune and prosperity should be cherished in this way."
Jīn Ōu Mìng Xiàng (Appointing a Chancellor with a Golden Bowl).
When the Emperor appointed a chancellor,
he would first write the name in Bāfēn script,
and cover it with a golden bowl.
Xīngqìng Xiǎo Lóng (Little Dragon of Xīngqìng).
It often appeared wandering in the Western Imperial Garden.
Later, when the Emperor wished to travel west,
one evening it rode the clouds southwest.
Later, it reached the Jiālíng Jiāng.
When the Emperor wished to board a boat,
there was a dragon beside the boat.
The Emperor tearfully said:
"This is the dragon from my pond."
He poured wine as a libation to it.
Āmán.
Lǐ Fǔguó falsely relocated the Retired Emperor to the Western Palace.
Midway, they saw soldiers glittering in the sun.
The Retired Emperor looked around in alarm.
Gāo Fāngshì was at his side.
Upon reaching the palace,
he reported safety.
The Retired Emperor wept and said:
"Without the general,
Āmán would have already become a ghost killed by soldiers."
Jiǎn Cǎi (Cut Brocade).
Yán Zhēnqīng's young maid in green attire
was named Jiǎn Cǎi.
Yán Zhēnqīng Dì Xiān (Yán Zhēnqīng, Earth Immortal).
Yán Zhēnqīng once obtained a divine elixir and consumed it.
Later, he was killed by Lǐ Xīliè.
After Xīliè was pacified,
they wished to rebury him.
When his coffin was opened,
his eyes were closed as if alive.
The hermit Cáo Yōngshān said:
"After thirty years, he will surely ascend and depart.
Clad in feathered robes, he travels among mountains and marshes,
this is what is called an earth immortal."
Yán Láng Shān Sè Rúcǐ (Yán Láng's Robe Color is Like This).
Yán Zhēnqīng asked the nun of the Fàn clan:
"Can I attain the fifth rank?"
The nun pointed to the purple silk cloth on the seat and said:
"Yán Láng's robe color is like this."
Kè Tǔ Wú Qì (Imported Soil Lacks Qi).
Hóng Shī and Zhāng Yuè were examining a residence.
Hóng Shī warned against disturbing the soil in the northwest,
as it would harm the prosperous qì.
Later, when he saw the qì diminish,
they indeed found three pits dug.
Zhāng Yuè wanted to fill them.
Hóng Shī said:
"Imported soil lacks qì,
and is not connected to the earth's脉."
Zhāng Guǒ Lǎo.
Xíng Hépú could calculate a person's lifespan.
When asked to calculate Zhāng Guǒ Lǎo's,
no one knew his birth cycle.
Shī Yèguāng could see ghosts.
He was ordered to look at Guǒ,
but ultimately could not see him.
Praying for Rain
Mínghuáng ordered Wúwèi to pray for rain,
who said, "The drought is certainly destined.
Summoning dragons will only lead to a downpour."
So he removed all the equipment for praying for rain,
and with a bowl of water,
he stirred it with a small knife.
In a moment,
a dragon as large as a finger
entered the bowl.
He stirred the bowl again,
and white mist emerged from the bowl.
A short while later, there was a great wind and rain.
Leaves of Paulownia and Bamboo Rubbed into Coins
Xuānyuán Xiānshēng lived on Mount Luófú.
Xuānzōng summoned him into the palace.
He was able to rub leaves of paulownia and bamboo into coins in his hands.
Attacking Hair with Qì
Xiānshēng could also loosen his hair and sit cross-legged,
using his qì to attack his hair,
making each strand stand straight.
Consulting the Pulse
In the palace, diagnosing the pulse was called "consulting the pulse."
Old Doctor
Péi Yùn presented a poem
that mentioned "Tàikāng."
Xuānzōng said,
"Tàikāng lost his kingdom,
how can he be compared to me?"
The chief ministers reported,
"It's a Jìn reign title,
the era name was changed to Tàikāng."
The Emperor said,
"The Son of Heaven must be well-read,
otherwise, I would have wrongly punished Yùn.
From then on, I indulged in studying classics and history,
reading books without rest.
The palace called me 'Old Doctor.'"
Spreading Imperial Virtue
The Emperor was brilliant in music theory,
and once composed a piece called "Spreading Imperial Virtue."
All wore square shoes and tall hats,
dancing in linked sleeves.
There was one called "Cōngxī Tàgē Duì" (Tap-dancing Troupe from West of the Onion Range).
Its lyrics mostly spoke of the joy of the people of the Cōnglǐng region,
and Héhoáng, hence it was said:
"Returning to be people of Táng."
There were also those holding banners and pennants,
like the transformation of soaring clouds and flying cranes.
Fragrant Liquor
When the Emperor was a prince,
he once fell from his horse while hunting,
and, distressed and thirsty, sought water.
When he was about to drink,
it had already turned into fragrant liquor.
Guǎnzǐwén
A scholar visited Lǐ Línfǔ,
claiming to be Guǎnzǐwén.
Later, he transformed into a brush.
Soft-footed Bureau
When Guō Zǐyí returned from Tóngzhōu,
an imperial decree ordered the ministers to set up a "soft-footed bureau" at his residence.
Each person contributed three hundred thousand.
Angler of Giant Aos
Zhāng Yòu visited Lǐ Shēn,
calling himself "Angler of Giant Aos."
Lǐ Shēng asked,
"What do you use for a fishing rod?"
He replied,
"I use a rainbow for a fishing rod."
"What do you use for a hook?"
He said,
"I use the moon for a hook."
"What do you use for bait?" He replied,
"I use a 'short Lǐ Xiāng' for bait."
Shēn was silent,
and gave him a generous gift.
Seven Entries into the Imperial Library
Xú Jiān was knowledgeable in many allusions,
and entered the Imperial Library seven times.
Ode on Dividing the River
At the end of the Bàodà era,
the recluse Shǐ Xūbái wrote "Ode on Dividing the River" to satirize, saying:
"Boats and carts are limited,
yet islands along the river are all idle;
Fish and turtles, though ignorant,
still interact and never stop."
He also composed "Poem of the Recluse," saying:
"The wind and rain tore off the roof,
but the whole family was drunk and unaware."
Bringing Out Courtesans and Untying Belts to Outdo a Single Throw
Prime Minister Yán Xù's singing girls
and Grand Secretariat Táng Gǎo's rhinoceros horn belt
were all treasures of their generation.
Táng admired the beauty of the courtesan,
and Yán desired the belt.
So there was a dice game (hūlú) gathering,
bringing out courtesans and untying belts,
to see who would win in a single throw.
Everyone held their breath,
and after several rounds of dice,
Táng won by a large margin.
Táng then poured wine
and ordered the beauty to sing a song to bid farewell to the Prime Minister.
He sadly left her behind.
When the Time Comes, Heaven and Earth Work Together
After Liú Yànzhēn's defeat at Shòuyáng,
our army was repeatedly routed.
Yuánzōng, leaning on the railing, asked Zhū Kuāngyè about strategies for defense.
Kuāngyè replied,
"When the time comes, heaven and earth work together;
when fortune is gone, heroes cannot do as they please."
For offending the emperor, he was exiled to Fúzhōu.
Sir Harm-to-Meat
There was a Daoist priest on Mount Lúshān,
whose physique was robust and grand,
and who drank and sang while consuming meat.
Suddenly, a pair of cranes drifted with the wind and rested at the Daoist temple.
As if from heaven,
they both died.
Chén Hàng wrote a poem, saying:
"Sir Harm-to-Meat desires to ascend,
yellow clouds are trampled, purple clouds collapse.
Dragon's waist and crane's back have little strength,
tell Mágū to borrow a great Roc."
Startling the Snake by Beating the Grass
Wáng Lǔ, as the magistrate of Dāngtú,
was accustomed to profiting from corruption.
Coincidentally, a local resident filed a joint petition accusing the chief clerk of avarice and bribery.
Lǔ then ruled,
"Although you beat the grass,
I am already startled like a snake."
Beating the Drum to Eat, Attaching the Brush Behind the Head
Dèng Yàzhàng was appointed Prefect of Qīngyáng,
and considered himself distinguished.
He said to his sons,
"You should think about studying,
to achieve eminence.
I, as a prefect,
beat the drum to eat,
and attach the brush behind my head.
This is the result of my diligent study of antiquity."
Drawing the Curtain to Drink Heavily
Cháng Mèngxī served in the Hànlín Academy,
and was upright and did not associate with the powerful.
Someone asked,
"When you are off duty,
how do you enjoy yourself in private?"
Cháng replied,
"By drawing the curtain and drinking heavily, that's all."
Jealous and Fierce Wife
Dù Yè served in Fúmì.
His mountain wife, Lady Zhāng, was jealous and fierce,
and there were no maids or concubines in their home.
Lièzǔ ordered Empress Yuán to summon Lady Zhāng to the inner palace,
and admonished her, saying:
"Yè's position and reputation are prominent,
he can have concubines.
Why are you so jealous?
Is this proper for a wife?"
Lady Zhāng replied,
"Yè was originally a wild scholar,
and his good fortune began recently.
Your Majesty relies on his humble efforts which are not yet exhausted.
He is prematurely old and often ill;
indulging him will certainly lead to mistakes in his service."
Lièzǔ greatly praised and admired her.
Dreaming of Hair Growing on the Tongue
Féng Yánzǐ was stationed in Línchuān.
He heard that he was about to be replaced.
That night, he dreamt of hair growing on his tongue.
A monk interpreted it, saying:
"Hair growing on the tongue
cannot be shaved off.
Will the Prime Minister not be replaced?"
And indeed, it turned out that way.
Almanac Wrapped Around an Orange
Zhōng Chuán (鍾傳) was garrisoned in Jiāngxī (江西).
A guest sought an audience by means of *fù shè* (覆射).
Chuán (傳) wrapped an orange in a calendar and placed it in his sleeve.
The guest recited extemporaneously:
"The Grand Commander (Tàisuì - 太歲) stands at the head,
No gods dare oppose him.
Within it is a thing,
Always carrying the fragrance of Dòngtíng (洞庭)."
Feigning Illness to Avoid Reading Poetry
Wèi Míng (魏明) was fond of composing poetry and lyrics,
but though numerous, they lacked style.
He once brought his recent poems to Hán Xīzài (韓熙載).
Hán (韓) feigned an eye illness,
and asked him to place them on the table to be perused later.
Míng (明) said:
"Your Excellency (Shìláng - 侍郎) has poor eyesight,
please allow me to recite them myself."
Hán (韓) replied:
"My deafness has worsened,
I particularly fear hearing nothing."
Jīnlíng (金陵) Children's Rhyme
During the siege of Jīnlíng (金陵),
many people suffered from leg weakness and died.
A children's rhyme said:
"Bringing the girl (niáng - 孃) in destroys the home,
Peaches and plums in the back garden bear no flowers.
Pigs and dogs all die out,
The cat raised meets with *chì jiā* (赤瘕)."
A monk interpreted it, saying:
"Niáng (孃) refers to the remarriage of Empress Zhōu (周后),
'Bearing no flowers' means withered and decayed.
'Pigs and dogs die out' refers to those who died of leg weakness in the Xū (戌) and Hài (亥) years.
*Chì jiā* (赤瘕) refers to
the cat's eye disease preventing it from catching mice,
meaning not seeing the Bǐngzǐ (丙子) year."
Old Man of Zhōngshān (鍾山)
When Yuánzōng (元宗) succeeded to the throne,
Lǐ Jiànxūn (李建勳) led an army to Línchuān (臨川).
Before departing, he told his confidants:
"The emperor's nature and habits are not yet settled;
if it is as the soothsayers say, he may not be able to maintain his legacy."
Later, when Féng Yánlǔ (馮延魯) attacked Mǐnzhōng (閩中),
and pressed for grain supplies very urgently,
Jiànxūn (建勳) sent a poem saying:
"Much grain is not necessarily a complete plan,
An aging army must guard against ambushes."
Soon after, they were indeed defeated by the Yuè (越) people.
Upon his return,
he was appointed Sīkōng (司空).
He repeatedly begged to retire from official duties,
calling himself the Duke of Zhōngshān (鍾山公).
An imperial edict appointed him Sītú (司徒),
but he did not take up the post.
Scholar Tāng Yuè (湯說) wrote a letter congratulating him.
Xūn (勳) replied:
"I am unwilling to be Sīkōng (司空),
How could I dare to be Sītú (司徒)?
Fortunately, there is the title 'Old Man Who Has Retired',
Why is it not used to address me?"
Earlier, Sòng Qíqiū (宋齊丘) had retired,
calling himself Mister Jiǔhuá (九華先生).
Before long, he resumed office,
and public opinion at the time scorned him.
Some compared Jiànxūn (建勳) to Sòng (宋),
so Jiànxūn (建勳) composed a poem saying:
"The peach blossoms and flowing water must be trusted,
Not like Liú Láng (劉郎) who leaves and does not return."
Plundered with the Land
King Wèi Zhīxùn (魏王知訓) was the commander of Xuānzhōu (宣州).
When he entered the court for an audience and attended a banquet,
an actor playfully performed as a large-faced cloth giant resembling a ghost.
Someone asked what it was.
It replied:
"I am the local deity of Xuānzhōu (宣州).
When the King came for his audience,
I was plundered along with the land,
and thus arrived here."
This was because Zhīxùn (知訓)'s oppressive policies extorted from his subjects.
Jīaohú (焦湖) for a Hundred *Lǐ* (里), Permitted to Be Otters
Zhāng Chóng (張崇) was an unlawful commander of Lú (蘆).
He once entered the court for an audience.
The people of Lú (蘆) said:
"He will surely not come back."
Chóng (崇) returned and
levied "Qúyī (渠伊) tax" according to the number of households.
The next year, he again entered the court for an audience.
It was widely rumored that he would be dismissed,
but no one dared to speak openly.
When they met, everyone stroked their beards in celebration.
Chóng (崇) returned and
again levied "Stroking Beard Tax."
An actor feigned someone who had died and was condemned,
destined to become an aquatic creature.
The Underworld court ruled:
"Jīaohú (焦湖) for a hundred *lǐ* (里),
Permitted to be otters."
Rain Feared Taxation and Did Not Enter the City
In the early days of Jīnlíng (金陵)'s (金陵) establishment,
military stores were not yet substantial,
and taxes on markets were harsh,
affecting all farmers, sericulturists, merchants, and traders.
At that time, a severe drought had lasted for a long time.
The emperor said:
"Areas near the capital all report sufficient rain,
but the capital city alone has no rain.
Why is this?"
Shēn Jiàngāo (申漸高) replied:
"The rain fears taxation,
and dares not enter the city."
The emperor immediately issued an edict to abolish extra taxes.
Soon after,
sufficient rain fell.
Thus, one knows that Yōu Zhān (優旃) painting the city,
and Nà Lǜ (那律) wearing tile clothing,
were not in vain.
Dream of a Sheep Ascending the Hall
After the Latter Lord (Hòuzhǔ - 後主) ascended the throne,
he dreamed of a sheep ascending to the imperial bed in the Wǔdé (武德) Hall.
He felt very disturbed by this.
When the city fell,
Supervising Censor Yáng Kèràng (楊克讓) was the first to take charge of the prefectural affairs.
The Tangerine Peel List
Serving Censor Qiáo Shùn (喬舜) was in charge of the imperial examinations.
Five candidates passed the advanced scholar examination.
All of them were ranked according to the number of previous attempts.
An anonymous person (Jiǎ Wúmíngzǐ - 甲無名子) said that Qiáo (喬)'s list resembled tangerine peel,
with many half-white ones at the top.
Good Things Are Not Necessarily Numerous
Yuánzōng (元宗) held a private banquet,
and ordered his attendants to compose poems.
Scholar Zhū Gǒng (朱鞏) only presented a couplet,
unable to complete the whole poem,
and then said:
"Good things are not necessarily numerous."
Those around him covered their mouths and laughed.
From then on, when officials and commoners presented gifts,
if they were not lavish or good,
they all used Zhū (朱)'s words as an excuse.
Dream of Someone Decapitating
Lièzǔ (烈祖) assisted Wú (吳),
and was planning to usurp the throne.
One night, he dreamed of someone drawing a sword and severing his neck.
He felt very disturbed by this.
Zhōu Zōng (周宗) immediately descended the steps and bowed,
saying, "It must be that you are to be enthroned."
A few days later, he abdicated internally.
Divine Object in the Alchemical Furnace
Zhāng Yìfāng (張義方) ordered a Daoist priest to compound the elixir of immortality,
but it was not completed after several years.
When he fell ill and was about to die,
the nine-turn elixir was not achieved.
One day,
he ordered his sons and nephews to open the alchemical furnace.
Beneath the furnace was a giant *huǐ* (虺) (snake),
with fiery mouth and brocade scales,
coiling within,
as if protected by a divine craftsman.
He then took one pellet of the elixir and ate it.
He died mute.
Those who understood believed that the *yīn* (陰) energy was not yet exhausted,
and it should not have been taken.
Volume 21
End.
Wine Sacks and Rice Bags
The Mǎ (馬) clan was extravagant and pretentious.
The princes and their attendants in various mansions were illustrious,
but they never paid attention to the ways of civil and military affairs.
At the time, they were called "wine sacks and rice bags."
Loosely Folded Skirts
When Zhōu Xíngféng (周行逢) was Military Commissioner (Jiédù - 節度) of Wǔ'ān (武安),
the skirts worn by women were all unsewn,
and were called "loosely folded."
Someone said, regarding skirts on the body,
having many folds (fú - 幅) was considered superior,
encircling the body.
Now to make them open and loose (sǎn - 散),
is to be incomplete (bù zhōu - 不周).
If it is incomplete and unsewn,
then both the surname (xìng - 姓) and given name (míng - 名) are gone.
For *fú* (幅) is *fú* (福) (fortune).
If fortune is broken and scattered,
how can it last long?
Soon after,
Xíngféng (行逢) died.
An Old Woman Marrying into Poetry
Cáo Yǎn 撰《Mǎ Shì Yě Shǐ》,
投進年巳衰耄。
獻老婦嫁詩云：
「滿頭白髮為新婦，
笑殺年少豪家兒。」
又詠鷺鶿云：
「終日灘頭延頸望，
能消大海幾魚多。」
存孤恤寡
Zhōu Xíngféng命Hé Jǐngshān為益陽令，
強取人家婦人。
Jǐngshān曰：
「卑吏無它，
蓋存恤孤寡。」
Xíngféng曰：
「何不寬其賦稅，
免其徭役？
乃置之於家，
於理安乎？」
戲謂僚吏曰：
「不如令佐海龍王去。」
遂投於江中，
舜作蟒蛇
Lǚ Qióng遊Shùn Dòng，
見一古碑，
謂舜曾於此洞作蟒蛇，
身受諸苦惱，
不知其幾世。
至Suí Rénshòu 中，
遇一尼摩頂受記，
遂得託生。
Qióng曰：
「悠悠蒼天！
被何人斯，
妄為玷瀆，
如此之甚。
聖莫大於Yáo Shùn，
暴莫大於Jié Zhòu。
安得Jié Zhòu至暴寂然無聞，
至聖反為蟒蛇？
又，
尼者一髡跣婦人，
有何功行摩頂受記，
使之託生耶？」
由是著《Jiě Fēn Piān》千餘言，
大市裏賣平天冠
Liáo Róng詩云「遠山秋帶雨，
水館夜多風。」
Pān Ruòchōng《Yángshuò Xiàn Shī》云：
「門連百越水，
地管數千峰。
郭影雲連樹，
林聲月帶春。」
二人更唱迭和，
詩家之勁敵。
Tàizōng懲五代場屋之弊，
以詞賦策論取士，
Róng、Chōng之徒，
稍稍引去。
Róng曰：
「豈知今日之詩道，
一似大市裏賣平天冠，
並無人問耶！」
又素性重僧，
前後贈詩甚多或。
問其故，
Róng曰：
「僧是詩家奴，
一人贈一篇，
且圖帶往東西南北去耳。」
謁戍將致詞
Lín Chǔcái窮窘，
Yìyáng戍將Lǐ Zhù謂Lín曰：
「大凡秀才必能道言語，
何不向我身上道一兩句？」
Chǔcái觀其額上耳後皆雕火珠雲雁，
即致詞曰：
「伏以太保，
氣貌雲橫，
身材筆直。
兩行秋鴈，
於耳畔以斜飛；
一顆明珠，
當額頭而突起。」
Zhù太喜，
厚贈之，
詠柳
Dí Huàn詠柳云：
「翠色折不盡，
離情生更多。」
《Dēng Níngbì Tíng》詩：
「數點分秋霽，
不知何處來。」
鷺鶿詩
Zhāng Zhòngdá《Yǒng Lùcí》詩云：
「滄海獨深處，
鱸魚銜得時。」
Zhāng Wénbǎo曰：
「隹則甚佳，
爭奈鷺鶿觜大長也。」
安知獲麟之筆為騎馬之用
Sūn Guāngxiàn為Jīngnán幕府，
常慕史氏之作，
每曰：
「安知獲麟之筆，
盡為騎馬之用。」
因吟Liú Yǔxī詩云：
「一生不得文章力，
百口空為飽暖家。」
Dèng Gōng Chí Tíng
Sūn Féngjí遊Dèng Gōng Chí Tíng，
問創置之由。
云Mǎ Shì諸公子舊園。
Féngjí留詩曰：
「馬家公子鬭亭臺，
斬斷山根碧沼開。
啼鳥不知人事變，
數聲尤傍水邊來。」
傳語縣君謝到
Lǐ Dàirén性迂緩，
非禮勿動。
娶Yán Shì，
年少，
與之異室。
私約曰：
「有興則見。」
忽一夕聞扣戶聲，
小豎報云：
「縣君欲見大監。」
Dàirén遽取百忌曆燈下看之，
大驚曰：
「今夜河魁在房，
不宜行事。
傳與縣君，
謝到。」
Yán Shì慚怒而去，
白傳琵琶行
Lǐ Shǒuyú聞人誦Bái Chuán《Pípá Xíng》,
笑曰：
「此婦本Cháng'ān娼女，
嫁茶商在外，
而Jūyì輒於夜中移船就之，
聽其琵琶以佐歡，
得非姦狀顯然耶？」
五臟榖
Lǐ Shǒuyù取黑豆緊小而圓者，
侵晨以井花水吞二七粒，
謂之五臟榖。
到老視听不衰，
一縫毬
Xú Bóshì為皮匠，
能為一縫毬。
晚為道士，
能導引，
握拳置口中。
或反手抱柱，
身隨起而足直上。
Tàizǔ召見，
曰：
「臣能走。」
乃脫履，
於殿庭走二十匝，
而出入之息如故。
《Jīnpō Yí Shì》Qián Wéiyǎn
玉堂之署
Tàizōng謂宰臣曰：
「Sū Yìjiǎn告朕，
乞御飛白書『玉堂之署』四字。
今付宰臣Lǐ Zhù以下，
來於中書堂面宣賜。」
大雪賜詩
Tàipíng Xīngguó 七年季冬，
大雪。
上賜學士詩曰：
「輕輕相亞凝如酥，
宮樹花裝萬萬株。
今賜酒鄉詩一盞，
玉堂閑話道情無。」
御樓侍立
Táng 制，
玉樓賜赦，
學士得升丹陽樓侍立。
五代以後，
因循廢之。
Sū Yìjiǎn奏，
自今上御樓，
覃恩與樞密使侍立御榻之側，
Huáng pán diāo
Old regulations state:
On the first day of the tenth month, extra gifts of brocade long robes are bestowed.
Since the beginning of the dynasty, green feather brocade was granted.
Tàizōng changed this to huáng pán diāo.
Jiāngnán Túhuà
The paintings Tàizǔ obtained after pacifying Jiāngnán,
fifty-plus scrolls, were bestowed upon the Xuéshì Yuàn.
In the Jǐngdé reign,
there was only "Yǔcūn Mùniú Tú" [Rainy Village Herding Cattle Painting],
of unknown artist,
"Hánlú Yā" [Ducks in Cold Reeds],
by Xú Xī,
"Wǔwáng Yǐnlào Tú" [Five Kings Drinking Milk Painting],
by Zhōu Wénjǔ.
Tàizōng yāchì
Táo Gǔ and Dòu Yí were in the Hànlín.
In Gǎdé second year,
Fàn Zhì and others were all dismissed from their prime minister posts.
An edict was issued to appoint Hánwáng to the position.
When the edict was issued,
there was no prime minister to sign it.
Gǔ said:
"Since ancient times, no high minister has been without a post.
Only after the Gānlù Incident during the reign of Táng Wénzōng,
did the court lack officials for a time.
At that time, Púyè Línghú Chǔ and Zhèng Tán executed imperial decrees.
Now, officials of the Nánshěng can also sign the edict."
Yí said:
"What Gǔ has presented
is not an affair of peaceful times
and is not a sufficient precedent.
Now, the imperial brother, the Kāifēng Yǐn Píngzhāngshì,
holds the position of prime minister."
Tàizǔ said:
"Yí's words are correct."
He immediately ordered Tàizōng to sign the edict and bestowed it.
Pòsuǒ Jiǎn Jiùzhāng
Hán Pī was good at poetry,
but after entering the Forbidden Palace,
he was not often used.
One night,
an imperial edict was urgently needed.
Hán stopped writing
and asked an official for old documents.
The official said that the archivist had locked the door and gone out for the night,
so they could not be searched.
Pī then broke the lock to retrieve them,
revised them, and presented them.
Yī Huīduī
Zhāng Jì, a scholar with extensive knowledge,
was sent as an envoy to present tribute in Jiāngnán.
Upon his return,
he composed ten poems.
Many disparaged the sights and customs of the capital,
including the line "yī huīduī" [a pile of ash],
to please his lord.
Sū Yìjiǎn obtained his original manuscript.
Later, Jì and Yìjiǎn became fellow academicians,
but they did not get along,
and often disagreed before the emperor.
Yìjiǎn said:
"If Qīnghé Gōng continues to contradict me,
I shall present the 'huīduī' line."
Jì was very afraid when he heard this,
and gradually yielded.
Yùbǐ Jièjiǔ
Sū Yìjiǎn was fond of wine.
The emperor's brush wrote a warning, saying:
"If you overturn your cup,
what worries do I have?"
Yìjiǎn accepted the decree and stopped drinking.
He no longer drank,
and the emperor did not blame him.
When he participated in major political affairs,
he found that the emperor no longer treated him with familiarity,
but only sternly criticized his official duties.
Therefore, in Yìjiǎn's poems,
he often thought of the Jìnlín.
Ménfēi Xià Qièchū
Kòu Zhǔn, when in the Zhōngshū,
often invited the "Liǎngzhì" (two departments of officials) to his residence for drinks,
and would always close the gates and forcibly detain them.
Those who were cautious were very afraid.
Lǐ Zōng'è once secretly slipped out from under the gate leaf,
got a horse, and rode off.
Later, he became the Xiūgōng Shǐ,
and his favor gradually deepened.
One day,
he was summoned to the Yùchén Diàn and given wine.
Zōng'è firmly declined, citing drunkenness,
and also said it was late.
The emperor ordered a eunuch to whisper in his ear:
"Here, you don't need to exit from under the gate leaf."
Língquè
There was a pair of magpies in the courtyard,
nesting in the crabapple tree behind the Yùtáng.
When the scholars gathered for meals,
they would certainly hover and gather.
If they chirped loudly,
it indicated a major imperial edict was about to be issued,
so they were called Língquè [Spiritual Magpies].
Thus, Cháo Hànlín's poem has:
"Upon hearing the Língquè, my heart must be joyful,"
and my poem says, "Língquè first perch upon the jade tree,"
which refers to this.
Dì Bàixiàng Xiōng Cǎomá
Qián Xībái
was Wéi Yǎn's cousin.
When Wéi Yǎn was appointed prime minister,
Xībái was in charge of drafting the imperial decree.
The world called this "the younger brother becomes prime minister,
the elder brother drafts the imperial decree,"
something unprecedented in history.
However, it was recorded in previous dynasties
that a examiner became prime minister
while his student drafted the imperial decree.
Jiǎotù Sānxuè Shǒushǔ Liǎngduān
When Qián Ruòshuǐ was a scholar,
Tàizōng treated him with great respect.
He once drafted an edict bestowing honors on Zhào Bǎozhōng, saying:
"Not executing Jìqiān,
is to preserve the 'three burrows of the cunning rabbit';
secretly doubting Guāngsì,
is to hold the 'two ends of the hesitant rat'."
The emperor said:
"These four lines perfectly express my thoughts."
Also, in the edict to Zhào Bǎojí, there were lines: "having already removed those close like hands and feet,
the momentum of the 'cart and jaw' has been lost."
The emperor wrote a comment afterwards:
"Excellent."
Bùkě Lìng Zhōu Hàn Zhī
Liáng Zhōuhàn was renowned for his literary talent from a young age,
but when he entered the Forbidden Forest,
he was already seventy.
In the Jǐngdé reign,
his reply to the prime minister's memorial confessing guilt was not to the emperor's liking.
The emperor separately ordered Zhào Ānrén to draft it,
saying:
"Do not let Zhōu Hàn know,
lest he feel shame and regret."
The emperor's sagely virtue and forbearance were thus.
Xí Qǐngjià Bǎngzi
Yáng Dànián was of a strong character
and frequently displeased the emperor.
His mother was ill in Yángzhái,
so he left a leave request note for the clerk
and secretly rushed away in the middle of the night.
The emperor pitied his talent
and ultimately showed him leniency,
only removing him from a minor division,
and still allowing him to remain in Yángzhái.
Zhèn Yǒu Sāntiáo Dài
Qián Chǔ presented precious belts.
Tàizǔ said:
"I have three belts,
which are different from these."
Chǔ requested that they be displayed.
The emperor smiled and said:
"One is the Biànhé,
one is the Huìmínhé,
and one is the Wǔzhànghé."
Chǔ was greatly ashamed and convinced.
Shǎnghuā Diàoyú
Only the director (Zhíshū) of the Three Academies was permitted to sit,
while those below the rank of collator (Jiàolǐ) composed poems and then retired.
During Tàizōng's time,
Lǐ Zōng'è was a collator
and wrote a poem saying:
"Having worn the palace flowers and composed the poem,
I am not allowed to see the vermilion robe again.
Bored, I leave the palace gate,
just like returning after failing the exams in those years."
The emperor immediately ordered him to attend the banquet,
and from then on, all, from collators downwards, were invited to the gathering.
Fù Shānshuǐshígē
Composing poems while appreciating flowers and fishing,
often meant responding to imperial requests.
During the Tiānshèng era,
Yǒngxīngjūn presented landscape rocks.
Consequently, an imperial command was issued to compose a song about the landscape rocks.
As it was unexpected,
many compositions were crude and bad.
An actor performing in the midst of the assembly entered the scene,
each holding paper and brush as if吟詠 (yínyǒng) [reciting poems],
when one person suddenly tripped over a rock and said:
"I've been composing poems about appreciating flowers and fishing lately,
preparing to respond to the imperial command,
but was tripped by this rock instead."
The next day, the poems were released,
and the Zhōngshū [Central Secretariat] was ordered to evaluate them.
Those deemed crude and bad were assigned to external posts.
Dreams of being summoned for an audience
Cài Zǐzhí knew Yīngzōng when the latter was a prince at the藩邸 (fāndǐ) [princely residence].
Later, when he became a zhìzhōu [prefectural governor],
he dreamt he was summoned for an audience, and he was told:
"Just stay in the north,
you cannot go anywhere else."
When he awoke,
it was the day the emperor's funeral carriage was to depart.
He wept uncontrollably,
and soon after, he died.
Military officials not observing mourning
According to precedent,
military officials did not observe mourning.
Hán Yù submitted a memorial requesting they observe mourning.
The matter was sent down to the two Zhì [Secretariats] and Táijiàn [Censorate] for deliberation.
Táng Zifāng, as a jiànguān [censor],
did not wish for them to observe mourning,
saying:
"Today, we cannot engage in high-minded discussions."
Yǒngshū [Ōuyáng Xiū] flared up and said:
"If one's parents die and one is commanded to observe mourning,
how can that be considered a high-minded discussion?"
Mèngdé [Sūn Biàn] sighed and said:
"What a brilliant man!
A spontaneous remark,
yet it hits the mark of reason."
The two Zhì and Táijiàn eventually presented two separate proposals,
whereupon an edict was issued that officials of Chóngbān [Palace Guard] rank and above should observe mourning,
while officials of Gōngfèng [Court Gentleman] rank and below should not.
This meant that higher-ranking officials could mourn for their parents,
while lower-ranking officials could not.
How then would those without official rank be handled?
Disagreement on medicine
Sīmǎ Jūnshí and I were the closest of friends,
but we only disagreed on medicine.
Falling out of rhyme
During the Jǐngdé era,
Lǐ Dí and Jiǎ Biān, both famous candidates who had passed the civil service examination,
both failed the imperial examination.
Lǐ Dí because his賦 (fù) [rhapsody] fell out of rhyme,
and Jiǎ Biān because in his "Dāng Rén Bù Ràng Yú Shī Lùn" (Treatise on Not Yielding to One's Teacher in Matters of Benevolence), he interpreted "shī" as "multitude,"
which differed from the注释疏 (zhùshū) [commentaries and annotations].
They then memorialized to request their reinstatement.
Wáng Wénzhèng Gōng, as prime minister,
said:
"Although Lǐ Dí committed an error of not meeting the standard,
it was unexpected.
His fault is forgivable.
Jiǎ Biān, however, put forth a unique and dissenting theory,
which would encourage later generations to pursue far-fetched interpretations,
disrupting the imperial examination system,
and such a trend must not be initiated."
Thus, Lǐ Dí was reinstated while Jiǎ Biān was dismissed.
The rich paying with expensive silk, the poor eating cheap rice
When Zhāng Shàngshū Yǒng was in Shǔ,
rice cost thirty-six wén per dòu,
and a bolt of silk cost three hundred wén.
The duke calculated the military provisions and then
ordered all remaining rice to be surrendered.
The surplus silk,
he allowed the poor people to buy.
The poor people were quite displeased.
Now, rice costs three hundred wén per dòu,
and a bolt of silk costs three guàn.
The rich pay with expensive silk,
while the poor eat cheap rice.
All are at the current market prices,
causing no loss or gain to the government,
and benefiting both the rich and the poor.
The people of Shǔ remember him with endless affection.
Guāiyá expressing his virtue
When Zhāng Shàngshū governed Shǔ,
the people's hearts were greatly at peace.
When his term ended,
he left a sealed scroll for the Saṅghārāja,
saying:
"Open it after ten years."
Ten years later, he died in Chénzhōu.
When the time came,
the sealed document was opened.
It was a portrait of the duke:
wearing a coarse robe,
a sash,
and straw sandals.
He had written his own inscription:
"Guāi (deviant) means going against the common customs,
Yá (cliff) means not harming others.
The name Guāiyá,
is merely to express my virtue."
Consequently, his portrait was painted in the prefectural yamen and temples and monasteries.
If a thousand forests rejoice, the unified spirit is naturally impartial
When Xuē Jiǎn Sù sat for the imperial examination,
he presented his writings to Féng Wèigōng.
The first piece contained the lines: "My books in the bag I bear in vain,
when will they reach the enlightened ruler?"
Féng Gōng said:
"I wonder what the xiùcái [scholar] carries in vain?"
He read until the third piece, "Spring Poem," which said:
"If a thousand forests rejoice,
the unified spirit is naturally impartial."
Then he said:
"This is what the xiùcái carries."
Using imperial edicts as a presentation scroll
Dīng Wénjiǎn once said that when he sat for the imperial examination, he used imperial edicts as his presentation scroll.
He then laughed at himself, saying:
"That was presumptuous."
Later, he became a Zhī Zhìgào Xuéshì Cāncèng [Academician in charge of Imperial Edicts and Vice Grand Councillor],
which also showed his long-standing aspirations.
Originally,
candidates would present their literary compositions as offerings to senior officials.
After the anonymization of examination papers, this practice gradually declined.
When Jiǎ Xǔ Gōng was Zhōngchéng [Censor-in-Chief],
he memorialized to abolish the practice of public scrolls,
and the etiquette of scholars was completely forgotten.
Zhuàngyuán provided with attendants
In Xiángfú eighth year [1015 CE],
Cài Wénzhōng was the zhuàngyuán [top scholar] in the imperial examination.
The Emperor, seeing his outstanding and imposing appearance,
looked at the prime minister and said:
"We have found the right person."
Consequently, an edict was issued to the Jīnwǔ [Imperial Guard] to provide attendants for him to make way and announce his presence.
This was the beginning of the zhuàngyuán having such an escort.
Dreaming of drafting edicts under a bright window
Sūn Mèngdé's initial name was Guàn,
courtesy name Dàoqīng.
When he was young and sat for the imperial examination,
he dreamt he climbed a pagoda
and saw someone holding a large scroll,
which was said to be the spring examination results.
He asked if Sūn Guàn was there,
and was told no,
only the third-place winner was Sūn Biàn.
When he awoke,
he changed his name to Biàn.
Later, he went to Huàyīn [Mount Hua],
and visited the Jīntiān Wáng Temple to seek a dream.
That night, he dreamt of drafting imperial edicts under a bright window.
The next year,
he indeed came in third place in the examination,
and later became a Zhī Zhìgào.
He once said:
"I was very happy when I first had this dream,
but as soon as I became a Hànlín Xuéshì [Academician],
I rather disliked it.
Human desire is boundless."
At that time, Mèngdé was already a Cānzhèng [Grand Councillor],
whose salary was somewhat higher,
and his position was not much different from an Academician,
except that it was less refined and comfortable than an Academician's,
and the responsibilities were greater.
Liú Huī becoming zhuàngyuán
A yá lì [yamen clerk] dreamt that a man named Liú from Huǒshān Jūn [Huǒshān Army] would become the zhuàngyuán.
The next year, the zhuàngyuán was indeed Liú Huī.
Hundred-day prime minister
Péng Nián was deeply skilled in numerology.
One day, he reported that a shejì gōng [Duke of Sheji] was appointed prime minister.
Péng Nián said:
"A hundred-day prime minister."
Later, his prediction proved true.
Péng Nián's courtesy name was Shòu.
Cài Jūnmó as a snake spirit
When Cài Jūnmó was Zhī Fúzhōu [Prefect of Fúzhōu],
he was unwell and did not attend to affairs.
For several nights, he repeatedly dreamt of climbing the drum and horn tower and falling asleep there.
The tōngpàn [assistant prefect] was puzzled why the drum and horn craftsman was not striking the third watch,
whereupon the craftsman replied:
"For several nights, a large snake has been coiled on the drum,
and I dare not approach it."
People then considered Cài Jūnmó to be a snake spirit.
The Sītiān [Directorate of Astronomy] memorialized that there was an attendant who escaped from the ruler
During the Xiángfú reign,
Yáng Hào, an official of the Directorate of Astronomy, reported that one of the attending ministers was about to flee.
The next day,
Yáng Wéngōng, citing his mother's illness,
returned to Yángzhái without waiting for permission.
Initially,
the Emperor desired to make Zhāngxiàn empress,
but Gōng refused to draft the imperial edict.
Once Zhāngxiàn was established,
he felt uneasy,
and so he departed, feigning his mother's illness.
Huáng Quán's Paintings
Huáng Quán, Huáng Jūlái, and Jūbǎo
were renowned painters from Shǔ,
especially skilled at depicting birds with feathers.
They often raised hawks and falcons,
observing their spirited beauty to portray them.
Later, some of their descendants abandoned painting to pursue hunting.
Since they raised many hawks and falcons,
they bought rats to feed them,
and later, there were also people who made a living by catching rats.
If a family kept gambling implements,
their descendants would inevitably gamble;
if they stored books,
their descendants would all read.
How can one not be careful about what one establishes?
Xiěshēng Zhào Chāng
In Shǔ, there was Sūn Zhīwēi,
skilled in painting landscapes, immortal officials, constellations, and figures.
Xué Huái was also skilled in landscapes and birds with feathers.
Zhào Chāng was good at painting.
Every morning, when the dew fell,
he would walk around the railings, observing intently,
mixing colors in his hand.
He called himself Xiěshēng Zhào Chāng.
People said that if one could touch the painting with their hand
without being obstructed by the colors,
it was a true Chāng painting.
His depictions of living vegetables, broken branches, and fruits were especially exquisite.
Furthermore,
Wáng Yǒu
was a soldier from Hànzhōu.
The prefect often ordered Chāng to paint,
and dispatched Yǒu to assist,
which is why Yǒu's paintings eventually were second only to Chāng's.
Ten Eyebrow Picture
On the wall of Tiāncí Temple, there was a fresco titled "Emperor Mínghuáng Enjoying Music, Ten Eyebrow Picture,"
where auspicious grasses grew on the ground,
called "Brocade Ground."
Zhāng Guāiyá once ordered it to be scraped flat
and the entrance sealed.
Later, when it was opened,
it had regenerated as before.
Nà Fish Climbing Trees
In Shǔ, there were Nà fish,
skilled at climbing trees,
making sounds like crying infants.
Mèngzǐ said, "climbing trees to seek fish."
Surely he had not heard of this?
Two Hawks Throwing Eggs
On the Jiāng River, two hawks were seen throwing eggs,
flying up and down to catch them,
presumably practicing their flight.
Was this the meaning of prenatal education?
Moreover, when their wings and feathers were not yet fully formed,
they would leap out of the nest,
often falling off cliffs to their death.
Their natural sharpness
is also a form of impetuosity.
Perceiving the Wind
Fish swim against the current,
birds stand facing the wind,
taking advantage of the alignment of their scales and feathers.
If one can perceive the coming wind,
by observing the direction the birds face,
one can know it.
Courtyard Pine Poem
Shì Zhì's poem "Courtyard Pine," which Xuē Jiǎnsù had studied, said:
"Before Fàn, Mómǔ was ugly;
in the snow, Qū Yuán awoke."
Gōng greatly praised it.
Twin Temples
When Wáng Zhì governed Càizhōu,
he destroyed Wú Yuánjì's temple
and erected the twin temples of Dí Rénjié and Lǐ Suò.
Modeling Oneself on Zēng Lǔgōng in Court
Modeling oneself on Zēng Lǔgōng.
Wáng Jǐngyí
was once asked:
"Who should one model oneself on when serving at court?"
He replied:
"Zēng Míngzhòng.
However, he was close to being discreet and restrained,
but overly strict,
and his blessings and longevity were not sufficient."
I'd Love to Take a Long Whip and Crack It
Yáng Wéngōng's quatrain, "Hosting a Feast for Shí Zhōnglì Zīzhèng," says:
"I'd love to take a long whip and crack it."
Shí replied in harmony:
"Normally, even when not summoned, I seek you out,
how much more so today when I receive your command."
Their witty conversations were like this.
A Song of Hémǎn Zǐ
During the Yuányòu reign,
a frivolous person added twenty-eight characters to an ancient poem:
"Zhòngchāng's old country three thousand *lǐ*,
Zōngdào in the deep palace twenty years.
In the殿院 a sound of Hémǎn Zǐ,
Lóngtú's twin tears fall before the sovereign."
Lóngtú was
Wáng Bówén.
One day, while speaking to the Emperor about his long service,
he involuntarily shed tears.
The Diànyuàn was
Xiāo Dìngjī.
He and Hán Wèigōng and others passed the examinations together,
and the candidates composed "Hémǎn Zǐ" to mock him.
Wáng Zōngdào lectured books for the gentlemen for twenty years,
and complained to the Emperor, seeking advancement.
Zhòngchāng,
a cousin of Xún Gōng,
argued about the unfairness of the imperial examinations,
and was dispatched back to Jiànzhōu.
Fèi Tiězuǐ
Old folks could recount events from the Shǔ period,
saying that when the Heavenly Army attacked Shǔ,
the ruler of Shǔ was greatly alarmed.
He assembled his court officials to recruit those who could resist the Heavenly Army.
Fèi Tiězuǐ stepped out of line and came forward to speak.
Everyone thought Tiězuǐ not only had eloquence
but also courage.
Listening closely,
he said:
"This minister would certainly not dare."
At this, everyone laughed and withdrew.
Writing Like a Brocade Screen
Xià Yīnggōng said:
"Yáng Wéngōng is like a brocade screen,
but without a frame."
Commentators said that Yīnggōng's writing was like spring water,
swift and turbulent.
However, in terms of vastness and breadth,
it was not as good as Wéngōng's.
Imperial Neighbor
When Tàizǔ was reviewing prisoners before the palace, a prisoner said:

"Please consider that your servant is an imperial neighbor." Tàizǔ thought he was a neighbor from Yān Sū and sent someone to ask. The prisoner replied, "Your servant lives outside the Dōnghuá Gate." Tàizǔ laughed and pardoned him.
Making a Hàn Chūnqiū Inkstone
Hú Dàn made a large inkstone,
several feet long,
and engraved on its side: "Sòng Hú Dàn made the Hàn Chūnqiū Inkstone."
He ordered it to be buried in his tomb.
Xuānxiàn Never Spoke Plainly
Sòng Xuānxiàn Gōng never spoke plainly.
When reviewing prisoners in the main hall of Hénán,
Gōng said:
"What grievance do you have with whom?"
The prisoner could not answer.
The officials present then asked in vernacular,
and the prisoner finally could answer.
Sòng Yuánxiàn Gōng,
when approached,
exuded a gentle and harmonious aura;
Jǐngwén Gōng, on the other hand, was brilliant and distinguished.
These three,
when observed for a long time, had not a speck of dust,
they were like immortals.
Boasting from Deficiency
Ōu Yǒngshú always boasted about his governance, not his writing;
Cài Jūnmó did not boast about his calligraphy;
Lǚ Jìshú did not boast about his chess;
Hé Gōngnán did not boast about his drinking;
Sīmǎ Jūnshí did not boast about his absolute integrity.
Generally, one boasts about what one lacks.
Xuē Chūyóu
Xuē Jiǎn Sùgōng 薛簡肅公 governed Jīng 京,
and everything was managed with strictness.
People called him "Xuē Chūyóu 薛出油" (Xuē, the Oil Extractor).
Later, he became the administrator of Chéngdū 成都.
The local custom was to enjoy outings.
The Duke composed ten poems titled "Héchù Chūnyóu Hǎo 何處春遊好" (Where Are Good Places for Spring Outings),
and he called himself "Xuē Chūnyóu 薛春遊" (Xuē, the Spring Outing Enthusiast),
wishing to change his former appellation.
Jiāng Shūmì Zūn 姜樞密遵 and Lǔ Sù Jiǎn Gōng 魯肅簡公 were also known for their strictness.
At the time, Jiāng 姜 was called "Jiāng Cāzi 姜擦子" (Jiāng, the Scrubber),
and Lǔ 魯 was called "Yútóu Gōng 魚頭公" (Duke Fish Head).
Shuǐjīng Dēnglong
Liú Suí Dàizhì 劉隨待制 served as the Administrator of Chéngdū 成都,
and was strict, clear-minded, and perceptive.
People called him "Shuǐjīng Dēnglong 水晶燈籠" (Crystal Lantern).
Zhàotiān Làzhú
Yóu Yuánjūn 由元均 governed Chéngdū 成都 with distinction.
When people had lawsuits,
those who were timid and unable to present their own case
would certainly have their circumstances inquired into in detail by him.
The people of Shǔ 蜀 called him "Zhàotiān Làzhú 照天臘燭" (Sky-Illuminating Candle),
and also "Bùcuò Shì Shàngshū 不錯事尚書" (Minister Who Makes No Mistakes).
Fàngshēng
Zēng Lǔgōng 曾魯公 performed fàngshēng 放生 (release of living creatures) using clams, mussels, and similar types,
because of the great number of lives.
One day, he dreamed that hundreds of armored figures came forward to complain.
After waking,
he found someone with several baskets of clams and mussels.
He immediately released them.
That night, he again dreamed of armored figures coming to express their gratitude.
Lǐ Jǐngchū’s 李景初’s family bought a giant turtle,
but Jǐngchū 景初 did not know about it.
That night, he dreamed of an old woman in black clothing coming to beg for her life.
He immediately sent someone to release the turtle.
He also dreamed of the old woman coming to express gratitude.
Jìnshí Xiāhá
Shěn Wéntōng 沈文通 administered Hángzhōu 杭州,
and prohibited the eating of shrimp and frogs (xiāhá 蝦䗫).
For two years, people dared not eat them,
and shrimp and frogs also did not breed.
When Wéntōng 文通 was replaced,
the prohibition was lifted,
and they bred again as before.
This is an example of the principles of nature that cannot be fully fathomed.
Yù Mǎi Chóujuàn
During Tàizōng’s 太宗’s reign,
Mǎ Yuánfāng 馬元方 was a judicial officer of the Three Departments.
He proposed:
"In early spring, when the people are in dire need,
the treasury should advance funds to purchase their goods,
and they can deliver silk to the government in summer and autumn."
The practice of advance purchasing of fine silk probably began here.
Tǐ Bèi Zhōnghé Zhī Qì
In the summer months, Rénzōng 仁宗 did not wave a fan;
he merely used a fly-whisk to drive away mosquitoes and flies.
In winter months, he did not use a brazier.
Physicians said:
"This is because his body possessed the vital energy of harmony and balance (zhōnghé zhī qì 中和之氣)."
Jiè Yǒu Wǔ Dé
People say that scabies (jiè 疥) has five virtues:
it does not appear on the face –
benevolence (rén 仁);
it likes to spread to others –
righteousness (yì 義);
it causes one to rub with one’s hand –
propriety (lǐ 禮);
it grows in the crevices between finger joints –
wisdom (zhì 智);
the itching always occurs at specific times –
trustworthiness (xìn 信).
Tiě Zhē
An iron anvil (tiě zhē 鐵碪) used for forging gold and silver
will not be damaged even after a hundred years.
If a bamboo basket is hammered on the anvil,
it will shatter in a single night.
A whip used to flog a horse
becomes smoother, more pliable, and tougher with prolonged use.
If it is used to strike a cat,
it will break and crack section by section.
Lìzhī Shú
Before people pick litchis,
for one day, insects dare not approach.
Once people pick them, insects, birds, bats, and similar creatures will all cause damage.
Therefore, those who pick litchis
do so at midday.
Bǎo Xīn Rú Zhǐshuǐ
Zhāng Wénxiào Gōng 張文孝公 was of a calm and quiet nature;
he never wrote in cursive script.
He composed a poem that said:
"Maintain a heart like still water,
and your writing will reveal true (standard) script."
People considered this to be a fitting description.
Huī Niú Bái Mǎ
Before the Qìdān 契丹,
there was a man riding a white horse,
and a woman driving a grey ox.
They met and became husband and wife.
They had eight sons,
who, as recorded in earlier histories, successively became rulers.
When the Qìdān 契丹 offer sacrifices to Heaven,
they still use a grey ox and a white horse.
Quàn Jiǔ Dāng Yǐ Liàng
Among the Qìdān 契丹, there was a man named Féng Jiànshàn 馮見善.
I (the author) hosted him and urged him to drink.
Jiànshàn 見善 said:
"When urging someone to drink, one should do so according to their capacity.
If not according to capacity,
it's like imposing corvée labor without considering the varying household ranks."
From this, I know that Qìdān 契丹 corvée labor was also based on household rank.
Did Zhōngguó 中國 (China) impose labor without considering household ranks?
Qìdān Fēngsú
The Qìdān 契丹 envoy Xiāo Qìng 蕭慶
said that the Dádá 達怛 people do not eat grain.
Families raise cattle and horses,
drink their milk,
and do not eat their meat.
Their bellies are like sinews,
and even if shot by an arrow, they do not die.
He also said that Qìdān 契丹 cattle and horses have a 'ripe' season,
just like the Southern Dynasty's silkworm rearing.
When there is snow, and about an inch of grass is exposed,
at this time, the cattle and horses are 'very ripe'.
If there is no snow, or if the snow covers the grass, then they are not 'ripe'.
Gǎi Zuì Jǐ Cí
During Rénzōng’s 仁宗’s reign, imperial edicts were never altered.
In the seventh year of Qìnglì 慶曆 (1047), there was a spring drought.
Yáng Yìfǔ 楊億甫 drafted an edict.
After it was submitted,
the Emperor felt that the self-reproaching words were insufficient,
and changed it to say:
"Since last winter,
timely snow has not fallen.
This spring, the drought is severe,
leaving a thousand li of barren land.
Heaven sensed Our diligence,
and used this to warn Our person.
Therefore, We humble Ourself before the virtuous,
and sincerely appeal to Heaven above.
We hope that the lofty heavens will descend and observe,
pitying the innocent common people.
Rather than inflicting illness upon the people,
it is better to transfer the calamity to Ourself.
From now on, We will avoid the palace and reduce Our meals,
and permit officials both within and outside the capital to submit sealed memorials expressing their true opinions."
Zhào Jūnpíng
Among the ten counties of Chéngdū 成都,
only Xīnfán 新繁 had equitable taxation.
When the taxes were first set,
there was a man surnamed Zhào 趙,
who assessed the fertility of the land to determine the varying tax rates.
To this day, people call him "Zhào Jūnpíng 趙均平" (Zhào the Equitable).
Xiàoyuán Chuán
In Jízhōu 吉州, there was a monkey catcher.
He killed a mother monkey, sold her skin and her child to the Xiāo family.
Ten days later,
when shown the mother's skin, the child jumped around and cried out,
refused to eat, and died.
Xiāo Shēng 蕭生 wrote "Xiàoyuán Chuán 孝猿傳" (Biography of the Filial Ape) for it.
Shǔ Chá
Tea is produced in several places in Shǔ 蜀.
Yǎzhōu Xiàngdǐng 雅州象頂 is the best.
It sprouts latest,
at the transition between spring and summer.
That place is what the Shū 書 (Book of Documents) refers to as "Càiméng Lǚpíng 蔡蒙旅平".
When the tea leaves sprout,
clouds and mist cover them,
as if protected by divine beings.
Wùlǐ Xiānggǎn
It is said that thorns can ward off frost,
and tumbleweeds (péng 蓬) can ward off sand;
this is due to the mutual influence of natural principles.
Where tumbleweeds grow, flowers and fruits do not gather,
but if surrounded by thorns, they flourish.
Hàn Sì Hú'ér Hú Sì Hàn
Dí Qīng,
a native of Fēnhé.
His face had tattooed characters,
which he refused to remove.
He became a Grand Councilor (Shūmì Shǐ).
Someone came to me with a prophecy (yáochèn) saying:
"Hàn resembles Hú children, Hú resembles Hàn;
changing heads and altering faces, it's all the same,
just beside the streams of Fēnhé."
I said:
"This refers to the matter of Táng Tàizōng killing Lǐ Jūnxiàn.
How could His Majesty do such a thing?
In recent times, some have spoken of Wáng Déyòng's appearance resembling Yìzǔ and his residence being built on Qiángāng,
a memorial was submitted,
but it received no reply,
and in the end, nothing happened."
That person was silenced.
Alas!
