In previous generations, many were executed for similar reasons,
how lamentable!
Iron Forest Cavalry (Tiě lín qí)
People on the western frontier call the "Iron Falcons" (Tiě yàozǐ) the Iron Forest Cavalry.
End of scroll twenty-two.
Five-Colored Waters of Kūnlún Shān
The earth is three hundred million three hundred thousand five hundred lì from north to south.
Among the high and great terrains is Kūnlún Shān,
from which five-colored waters emerge,
flowing into China,
named the Hé.
Beneath the earth are four pillars,
and three thousand six hundred axles,
interlocked like dog's teeth.
The earth has stone for its bones,
rivers for its veins,
grass and trees for its hair,
and soil for its flesh.
Stone is the root of metal.
Monsters (wùguài)
Monsters of water and stone are called lóngwǎngxiàng;
monsters of wood are called kuíwǎngliǎng;
monsters of earth are called fén yáng;
monsters of fire are called Sòng Wújì.
Mountain and Marsh Qi (Shānzé qì)
Royal mountains have much cloud;
iron mountains have many stones.
Mountain qi produces more males;
marsh qi produces more females.
Born of Harmonious Qi (Héqì suǒ shēng)
When harmonious qi interacts and gives rise to cinnabar grass,
mountains produce elephant chariots,
marshes produce divine horses,
high mounds produce black elixirs,
low hills produce earth monsters,
rivers produce large clams,
and the sea produces bright pearls.
When the sovereign has a long and prosperous life,
the world is in great peace.
Pregnancy Prohibitions (Rènshēn bìjì)
When a woman is pregnant,
she should not see ugly or evil things,
and in eating, she should avoid unusual flavors.
She must not see rabbits,
lest the child have a cleft lip.
She must not eat ginger,
lest the child have many fingers.
Method for Giving Birth to a Boy (Shēng nán fǎ)
If a woman is pregnant for less than three months,
she should wear her husband's clothes and hat,
and at dawn, walk counter-clockwise around
a well three
times,
without looking back,
and without letting others know;
she will surely give birth to a boy.
Making Fire (Qǔ huǒ)
Shave wood into a round shape,
hold it up toward the sun,
and place moxa under its shadow to obtain fire.
Viviparous and Oviparous (Tāi shēng luǎn shēng)
Those with nine orifices are viviparous;
those with eight orifices are oviparous.
Gecko (Shǒugōng)
It is a lizard,
also called yǎntíng.
Keep it in a vessel,
feed it cinnabar,
until its body is entirely red.
When it has eaten ten catties,
pound it a myriad times,
and apply it to a woman's limbs.
It will not fade for life,
except when engaging in sexual intercourse, it will disappear.
Therefore, it is called "Shǒugōng."
Dōngfāng Shuò reported to Hàn Wǔdì that using it was effective.
A rat that eats Croton beans for three years
will weigh thirty catties.
String-Rejoining Glue (Xùxián jiāo)
During the reign of Hàn Wǔdì,
someone from the Western Sea presented a glue
that could mend broken strings.
It was called "String-Rejoining Glue."
The Snake of Chángshān
has two heads.
Touch one head, and the other head will come;
touch its middle, and both heads will come together.
Sūn Wǔ used this to illustrate those skilled in warfare.
Wú Yúkuài
When King Wú was traveling on the river,
he ate sliced fish but did not finish it.
He discarded the remainder into the middle of the stream,
where it transformed into a fish,
several inches long,
named Wú Yúkuài.
Refining Stones to Sever the Ao (Liàn shí duàn áo)
When heaven and earth were initially incomplete,
Nǚwā refined five-colored stones to mend their deficiencies
and severed the legs of the Ao to sever the earth's four pillars.
Therefore, the sky tilts toward the northwest,
and the earth is not full in the southeast.
Hòujì and Yī Yǐn
If a scholar thinks of a woman without marrying, he can be moved;
if a woman thinks of a man without a husband, she can conceive.
Hòujì was born from a giant footprint;
Yī Yǐn was born from an empty mulberry tree.
Thousand-Day Wine (Qiānrì jiǔ)
Liú Xuánshí bought wine from a wine merchant in Zhōngshān.
The wine merchant gave him "thousand-day wine,"
forgetting to tell him its duration.
He returned home drunk,
and his family thought he was dead
and buried him.
When the wine merchant calculated that a thousand days had passed,
he went to see him,
and was told he had been gone for three years.
Then, the coffin was opened, and he woke up.
The common saying goes:
"Xuánshí drank wine
and was drunk for a thousand days."
Method for Dyeing Beards (Rǎn zī fǎ)
Take white lead (Húfěn) and lime,
mix them with water,
and apply to beard and temples to keep them from turning white.
Accumulated Oil Spontaneously Catches Fire (Jī yóu shēng huǒ)
If ten thousand piculs of oil are accumulated,
fire will spontaneously ignite.
During the Qín dynasty, the arsenal caught fire;
this was caused by
accumulated oil.
Method for Nourishing Life (Yǎngshēng fǎ)
Huángfǔ Lóng met the Daoist Fēng Jūndá, the Green Ox Daoist,
who said:
"The body should always be slightly active,
without overexertion.
Avoid rich and fatty foods,
moderate sour and salty tastes,
cut off excessive thoughts,
reduce joy and anger,
and be cautious in sexual matters."
Wild Kudzu (Yěgě)
Eating it kills people.
If cultivated kudzu is planted for three years
and not harvested,
afterward, any wild growth of it is also inedible.
Guest Star Violates Dǒu Niú (Kèxīng fàn Dǒuniú)
There was a person living by the seashore
who, every eighth month, saw a large floating raft passing by.
It was very large.
He waited for it to return,
packed provisions, and boarded it.
After traveling for more than ten days,
he suddenly arrived at a place
with city walls and dwellings.
Many weaving women were inside,
and he saw a man leading an ox to drink water.
This man asked where this place was,
and was answered:
"When you return,
ask Yán Jūnpíng, and you will know."
Later, he asked Jūnpíng,
who said:
"On a certain month and year,
a guest star violated Dǒuniú."
Then he knew it was the Heavenly River.
Killing the Eldest Son
East of Yuè there is a country of jiàomù trees.
Its custom
is to kill the eldest son when he is born.
This is called Yídì.
Superior, Medium, and Inferior Medicines
Superior medicines preserve life;
this refers to refining the body with "five stones" [wǔshí]
and prolonging life with "six zhǐ" [liùzhǐ].
Medium medicines nurture temperament;
this refers to huán huān [合歡] dispelling anger
and xuāncǎo [萱草] banishing sorrow.
Inferior medicines cure illnesses;
this refers to dàhuáng [大黃] clearing blockages
and dāngguī [當歸] stopping pain.
Zhū Húangdì's [黃帝] Ministers
Zhùróng [祝融] created markets;
he was a minister of Gāoxīn [高辛].
Chīyóu [蚩尤] created weapons;
he was a minister of Yándì [炎帝].
Huī [楎] created bows,
Móu [牟] created arrows,
Cāngjié [倉頡] created writing,
Róngchéng [容成] created the calendar,
Línglún [伶倫] created musical temperament,
Lìshǒu [隸首] created numbers;
all were ministers of Huángdì [黃帝].
Yídí [儀狄] created wine;
he was a contemporary of Yǔ [禹].
Miánjū [綿駒] was skilled at singing;
he was a person from Qí [齊].
Precious Swords
The names Chún’gōu [純鉤],
Zhànlú [湛盧],
Háocáo [豪曹],
Yúcháng [魚腸],
Jùquē [巨闕].
All five were cast by Ōuyězǐ [歐冶子].
Finger-Sycophant Grass
In the time of Yáo [堯], there was Qūyìcǎo [屈軼草]
growing in the courtyard.
When a sycophantic person entered the court, it would bend and point at them.
It was also called Zhǐnìcǎo [指佞草].
Celestial Grandson
The spirit of Tài Shān [泰山] is called Tiānsūn [天孫],
the grandson of the Celestial Emperor.
He is in charge of summoning people's souls and spirits.
Hāogōng [蒿宮]
When the virtue of Zhōu [周] was flourishing,
mugwort grew so large it could be used as pillars.
It was called Hāogōng [蒿宮].
Mountain Pheasant
It loves its own colors so much
that it gazes into the water all day.
When its eyes become dizzy, it drowns.
Shi [蓍]
At one thousand years old, it has three hundred stalks,
thus it can foretell good and ill fortune.
Precious Artifacts
The bow of Fánruò [繁弱],
the spear of Qūlú [屈盧],
the crossbow of Jīzǐ [雞子],
the ge-halberd of Gūfù [孤父];
all were ancient precious artifacts.
Three People Braving the Fog
Once there were three people who together braved the fog.
One fell ill,
one was unharmed,
and one died.
The unharmed one drank wine,
the ill one ate rice,
the dead one had an empty stomach.
Eating Wax
In a year of famine, eating half a jīn [斤] of wax
can sustain one for ten days of hunger.
Camels Know Water Veins
West of Dūnhuáng [敦煌], crossing the shifting sands for a thousand lì [里],
there is no water.
Beneath the sand are hidden streams,
which only camels know.
Whenever they reach a water vein, they paw the ground with their feet,
and digging there will certainly yield water.
Hóujué [猴玃], also known as Mǎhuà [馬化]
In the mountains southwest of Shǔ [蜀] there is a creature resembling a monkey,
more than a chi [尺] long,
that can walk like a human.
It is called Hóujué [猴玃],
also known as Mǎhuà [馬化].
When it encounters women on the road,
it often steals them away to be its mate.
It never returns them until they have a child.
Once they have a child, it sends them back to their home,
but does not raise its child.
The mother often dies.
When its children grow up,
they are completely identical to humans,
and all take Yáng [楊] as their surname.
Therefore, many people in the western borders of Shǔ [蜀] are surnamed Yáng [楊],
often descendants of Mǎhuà [馬化].
Cloud River Painting
Liú Bāo [劉褒],
a person from the time of Emperor Huán of Hàn [漢桓帝].
He painted the "Cloud River Painting" [《雲漢圖》];
those who saw it all felt hot.
He also painted the "Northern Phoenix Painting" [《北鳳圖》];
those who saw it all felt cold.
Herb of the Great Sun
Tiānlǎo [天老] said the herb of the Great Sun,
if consumed, grants longevity;
it is actually huángjīng [黃精].
Tiger Pouncing Hair
People of the Yǔshì [羽氏] kingdom
have wings,
but cannot fly far.
There is a beast with green fur resembling a leopard.
Its fur can be made into brushes,
and is called Hǔpūmáo [虎撲毛].
River Spirit
When Xià Yǔ [夏禹] was travelling along the river,
he saw a tall person with a fish body
who said:
"I am the river spirit."
Various Similar Objects
Wèi Wéndì [魏文帝] recorded various objects that were so similar they could be mistaken for the real thing:
wǔfú [碔砆] strange stones resembled beautiful jade,
shéchuáng [蛇床] was confused with míwú [蘼蕪],
mángní [莽苨] was confused with rénshēn [人參],
cíhuáng [雌黃] resembled realgar,
dùhéng [杜衡] was confused with xìxīn [細辛],
bǎibù [百步] resembled méndōng [門冬],
fángkuí [防葵] resembled lángdú [狼毒].
Yuǎnzhì [遠志]
Its seedling is called xiǎocǎo [小草].
The seedling of qióngqióng [芎藭] is called jiānglí [江籬].
Sun Eclipses when Qílín [麒麟]
When Qílín [麒麟] fight, the sun and moon are eclipsed.
When whales die, comets appear.
When babies cry, their mothers' milk flows.
When silkworms spin silk, the merchant's string breaks.
Tianhe [天河] Leans on a Pestle
The Hétú Jì [《河圖記》] states:
"After a hundred generations,
the earth will be higher than the heavens.
After a thousand generations,
the heavens can be leaned on with a pestle."
Spring Clouds and Autumn Winds
Zhòngcháng Tǒng [仲長統] said:
"Spring clouds are chariots,
autumn winds are teams of four horses."
Yùyún [矞雲]
Jīng Fáng Yì Zhān [《京房易占》] states:
"Clouds of two colors
are called yù [矞],
they are auspicious clouds."
Xún Qīng [荀卿] said:
"Clouds are friends with wind and children of rain."
Ink Soldiers
Sūn Qiáo [孫樵] referred to history books as "ink soldiers" [mòbīng].
Golden Articles, Jade Clauses
Yáng Xióng [楊雄] referred to penal laws as "golden articles, jade clauses" [jīntiáo yùkē].
Rabbit Eyes
After five days, huái [槐] sprouts are called "rabbit eyes" [tùmù].
After ten days, they are called "rat ears" [shǔ'ěr].
Their leaves look like this.
Cuckoo and Oriole
In the Gāotáng Fù [《高堂賦》],
the cuckoo is also called Zǐguī [姊歸] or Tǎoliú [討流].
In the dialect of Yōuzhōu [幽州],
the oriole is called huángyīng [黃鶯].
Wool Mat, Felt Home
The commentary to the "Record of the Western Regions" in the Hòu Hànshū [《後漢·西域傳》] explains zhān [氈] as "wool mat" [máoxí].
Liú Xiàoyí [劉孝儀] referred to the Dís' [狄] felt homes.
Marquis of Róngchéng
Sīkōng Tú [司空圖] referred to mirrors as "Marquis of Róngchéng" [Róngchéng Hóu].
Jīn Jiǒng [金炯] also called them "Mr. Shòuguāng" [Shòuguāng Xiānshēng].
Grand Mansion, Tiger Enclosure
Méi Shú [枚叔] generally referred to the face as "grand mansion" [dàzhái],
and the area between the eyebrows and eyes as "green yang" [qīngyáng].
Wáng Yuáncháng [王元長] referred to the Guózǐxuě [國子學] (Imperial Academy) as "tiger enclosure" [hǔwéi].
Pigeon Cart, Bamboo Horse
《Xù Hàn Yí》:
Old people were bestowed with staffs,
the ends of which were carved with doves,
representing their freedom from choking.
Jiǔ Guǎ
in "Qī Fā" says:
"The orphaned child's fishing line serves as the bridge,
the nine widows' earrings serve as the soundpost."
Taking objects from orphans and widows to adorn a zither
is meant to produce mournful sounds.
Jiǔ Guǎ means
nine widows.
Yángmǎ
Hé Píngshū referred to the corner beams of a roof as "Yángmǎ".
Bājí
Zōu Zǐ said:
"Zhōngguó
is one eighty-first of all under heaven,
encircled by the sea.
There are nine such regions,
further encircled by a great boundless sea,
collectively called Bājí."
Huàyāo
Yuán Zhào of the Later Wèi dynasty was able to cure illnesses.
A soldier's daughter was possessed by a spirit.
Zhào said:
"In the world, there are extremely divine demons,
extremely spiritual demons,
land-dwelling spirits,
and water-dwelling sprites."
He treated her with his method,
and it turned out to be a ghost from a mural in Huánghuà Sì.
Língkuí
The Yellow Emperor made a drum from a Língkuí,
its sound reaching a hundred *lǐ*.
Fēngrén
The Lǐngnán region has many maples.
When struck by lightning, they develop galls,
three to five *chǐ* long,
resembling human figures.
These are called Fēngrén.
Jīn Chū Hán
All mountains and rocks
sweat profusely in midsummer.
If they exude a reddish-yellow sweat, it is gold sweat;
if white with purple, it is silver sweat.
Yīnyáng Shí
In Yílíng, there are Yīnyáng Shí.
The *yīn* stone is always moist,
and the *yáng* stone is always dry.
In drought, flogging the *yīn* stone will bring rain;
if rain persists, flogging the *yáng* stone will make it stop.
Xiānjiāng
In Jūlóu Guó, there is a water-immortal tree,
whose trunk contains water called *jiāng*.
Those who drink it are drunk for ten days.
Jiǔ Yùzhāng
In the East, there are nine *yùzhāng* trees.
One tree governs one province.
On each tree are nine strongmen holding axes to fell them,
to divine the fortune of the nine provinces.
They chop and regenerate.
If regeneration is slow, the provincial governor will fall ill;
if it does not regenerate, the province will perish.
Tóu Jiǔ Yú Chuān
When Yuè Gōujiàn was traveling,
someone offered him a pot of wine.
The King said:
"If I drink alone,
what about the three armies?"
So he poured it into the stream,
ordering one army to drink from it.
All were pleasantly drunk.
Shǔ Zhòng Wàn Jīn
In the North, there is a layered water,
a hundred *zhàng* thick.
There are rats in the soil
that eat ice
but no plants or trees,
weighing ten thousand *jīn*.
Jiàqié
When an eggplant tree blossoms,
take its leaves and spread them on a path,
encircling them with ash.
The tree will yield double the fruit.
This is called Jiàqié.
Guān Rì Yù
It is as large as an eight-inch mirror.
When held up to the sun,
one can see palaces within the sun.
It is called Rì Yù.
Yù Huǒ
was presented as tribute by the Eastern Yí during the Táng dynasty.
It is red in color
and about an inch long.
Piled up, it can ignite a cauldron.
Placed in a room, one no longer needs to wear padded clothes.
Xiāngyún Xiāngyǔ
If the rotten stones of Yuánqiáo
are burned,
the smoke becomes fragrant clouds,
filling the sky,
and then fragrant rain falls.
Shèzhěn
Placing musk in a pillow
can stop bad dreams.
Lóngxū Fú
Yuán Zài obtained a Lóngxū Fú.
When placed in his hall,
mosquitoes dared not enter.
Shù Huà Yuānyāng
Sòng Hán Péng's wife was beautiful,
and Kāng Wáng seized her.
The wife committed suicide,
and the King buried her.
Overnight, trees grew from the grave,
their branches intertwined.
The King wanted to cut them down,
but they transformed into mandarin ducks and flew away.
Juān Fèn Xī
Táng Gōng Wáng had a rhinoceros horn the size of a pellet.
Wearing it
could dispel anger.
Sèmù
Táng Yìzōng bestowed a Sèmù upon a princess.
Its pattern resembled green silk,
threaded with pearls.
Even in a heavy downpour, it would not get wet.
Zhǐ Gē Lóng
In the early Yuánshàng period,
Guān Tiānshī often spoke of the Zhǐ Gē Lóng,
referring to Empress Wǔ.
Qiānnián Xiānlù
Míng Huáng hunted in the suburbs
and shot a large deer.
Zhāng Guǒ said:
"This is a thousand-year-old immortal deer.
During the Hàn Wǔ Emperor's time,
someone captured this deer alive.
The Emperor spared its life
and ordered that its year and month be marked with a copper plaque."
Guǒ found two small plaques on its left antler.
Yùqīng Sānbǎo
Cháng Yǎn dreamt he journeyed to Yùqīng Gōng.
The goddess of Yùqīng gifted him three treasures.
The first was a *yáo* cup,
the second a red *fū* pillow,
and the third a purple jade casket.
Jiàn Háma
Before Lǐ Kuí became prime minister,
he suddenly saw a large toad.
Xiǎo Fèng divined it, saying:
"The toad is a heavenly messenger,
a propitious omen."
Shortly thereafter, he was appointed prime minister.
Liǔ Jiāngjūn
Someone encountered Liǔ Jiāngjūn in an old house.
Upon examination,
it was a withered willow tree.
Jǐn Bànbì
Bǎo Cān was a Censor-in-Chief.
He dreamt that Dèzōng bestowed upon him a brocade *bànbì*.
An interpreter said:
"A *bànbì*
is the garment of a trusted assistant (lit. arm and thigh).
Will you not occupy the position of a trusted assistant?"
A few days later, he was indeed appointed prime minister.
Zhǐ Yuè
Yáng Huì zhī謁 Wáng Xiānshēng,
Xiānshēng ordered his daughter to cut paper into the shape of tonight's moon,
and place it on the wall.
That evening,
light emanated from the eastern wall,
illuminating the entire room.
It was the twelfth night of the eighth month.
When Huì zhī was about to leave,
Xiānshēng drew on the ground with his staff.
Looking at his courtyard,
there were ten thousand-rèn towering cliffs,
with stacked ravines of accumulated water.
Xiānshēng said:
"Valleys transform into hills and hills into valleys;
where will you, my son, return to?"
Huì zhī cried and said:
"Indeed, I did not know that in a single day such a change of mulberry fields could occur.
Could it be that a mere instant in the immortal realm is a thousand years in the mundane world?"
Xiānshēng laughed and said:
"Do not fear,
I was merely amusing myself."
Thereupon he took a broom and swept his courtyard,
and in a moment it was as it had been.
Huì zhī then returned.
Scaling a Ladder to Fetch the Moon
During the Dàhé era,
Zhōu Shēng possessed magical arts.
One Mid-Autumn Festival,
the moonlight was clear in the hall,
and several guests arrived.
Zhōu said:
"I can carry the moon into my embrace."
He then took several hundred bamboo poles and set them up,
saying:
"I will use this ladder to fetch the moon."
Then he closed the door.
After a long while,
the guests walked in the courtyard, waiting,
when suddenly the sky became dark and hazy,
yet looking up there was not a single wisp of cloud.
Presently, they heard Shēng shout:
"I have arrived!"
He lifted his robe and produced the moon,
about an inch in size,
and the entire room became bright,
with cold penetrating to the bone.
After a meal's time, it was as before.
Moon Garden of the White Jade Palace
When Lǐ Hè passed away,
his mother dreamt that Hè said:
"The Supreme Emperor is the ruler of the gods and immortals.
He recently moved his capital to the Moon Garden,
and built the White Jade Palace.
Due to my skills in writing imperial decrees,
I was summoned with several other literati to jointly compose the 'Record of the New Palace.'
The Emperor also built the Níngxū Diàn,
and commissioned me to compile musical scores.
Now I am one of the immortals,
and am very happy.
I hope my lady will not worry."
Zhūgě's Reincarnation
One month after Wéi Gāo was born,
a Hu monk saw him
and said:
"It has been a long time since we parted. Are you well?"
The infant seemed to show a joyful expression.
The crowd asked for the reason,
and the monk said:
"This child is the reincarnation of Zhūgě Wǔhóu."
Destined to Eat Ten Thousand Sheep in His Lifetime
Once, a monk said to Lǐ Déyù:
"You are destined to travel ten thousand lǐ south,
and the time is within ten days."
The Duke said:
"And will I truly return after that?"
The monk said:
"You will return."
The Duke questioned him about the matter,
and he said:
"The Chancellor is destined to eat ten thousand sheep in his lifetime.
He has now eaten nine thousand five hundred.
The reason for your return
is that you have not yet finished the remaining five hundred sheep."
The Duke said:
"Recently, I dreamt of traveling to Jìn Shān,
and the mountain was full of sheep.
A shepherd said:
'These are the sheep that the censor has eaten in his lifetime.'
It truly matches what the master said."
A few days later,
Zhū Jì, the Jìedù of Zhènwǔ, sent a letter,
presenting four hundred sheep.
The Duke was greatly astonished,
and the monk sighed:
"The ten thousand sheep are almost complete.
Will he not return?"
Within ten days, he was demoted to Húzhōu,
then repeatedly demoted to Yázhōu,
and eventually died at the place of his exile.
Dreaming of Holding the Sun
When Yáng Yán was young, he dreamt of ascending a high mountain,
and looking up at the auspicious sun,
its red light blazing brilliantly.
He then raised both hands to hold it.
Later, he became a chancellor,
which indeed accorded with the auspicious sign of holding the sun.
Rainbow Angels
When Wéi Gāo was garrisoned in Shǔ,
he hosted guests in the west pavilion.
There was a sudden storm,
but in a moment it cleared.
A rainbow descended from the sky,
its head reaching the banquet table,
and it drank all the food and drink.
Its head resembled a donkey,
and its five colors were like a beautiful cloud.
The Duke was frightened and ended the banquet.
The minor official Dòulú Shǔ said:
"A rainbow
is an angel.
If it descends upon evil, it signifies misfortune;
if it descends upon righteousness, it signifies auspiciousness.
You, Duke,
are a righteous person.
I dare to congratulate you."
Within ten days, he was appointed Zhongshū Lìng.
Hán Tuìzhī Sees a Divine Being
In the winter of the fourth year of Qìng,
Hán Tuìzhī lay ill,
and saw a divine being,
clad in armor and bearing a sword,
over ten feet tall,
standing before his bed, saying:
"I have a military matter which I wish to discuss with you."
The Duke said:
"I wish to hear it."
The divine being said:
"Wēicuì Gǔ, a separate nation,
has been an enemy of Hán for generations.
Now I wish to subjugate them.
My strength is insufficient.
What do you think of this?"
He replied:
"Your servant wishes to follow the Great King to subjugate them."
The divine being assented and departed.
He then sighed:
"What kind of omen is this?"
For several days he pondered its meaning,
but could not fathom it.
By winter,
the Duke passed away.
The White-Clad Man's Chant
On a moonlit night on Huà Shān,
a white-clad man walked along the stream, chanting:
"The murmuring stream flows endlessly,
the vast valley slopes bloom with wild flowers.
He comes and goes, unknown to others,
returning always to face the moon over the empty mountain."
Moonlit Night Linked Verses
Liáng Jǐng resided in a guesthouse on Mount Shāngshān.
It was the Mid-Autumn Festival, and the moon shone brightly.
He saw three gentlemen, named Xiāo Zhōngláng, Wáng Bùbīng, and Zhūgě Chángshǐ,
sitting with Jǐng in the courtyard.
Zhōngláng called his servant, saying:
"Yùshān-rén,
bring wine for us to drink together and compose linked verses."
Bùbīng said:
"The autumn moon is round as a mirror."
Zhōngláng said:
"The autumn wind is sharp as a knife."
Jǐng said:
"The autumn clouds are light as floss."
Chángshǐ remained silent.
The two urged him, saying:
"Please, let us prioritize speed over skill."
Chángshǐ mused and then said:
"The autumn grass is fine as fur."
The two burst into laughter, saying:
"It's clumsy, it's clumsy indeed,
but why so slow?"
Chángshǐ replied:
"Zhōngláng chose an obscure rhyme, which hindered my quick wit."
Zhōngláng then ordered Yùshān to summon Huìniáng to serve wine.
Soon after,
a beautiful woman arrived.
Chángshǐ teased:
"The lady came willingly at Zhōngláng's summons."
The beauty replied:
"How do you know I didn't come for everyone?"
Then she sang a tune from Fènglóu.
Zhōngláng then said:
"The mountain trees cast tall shadows."
Bùbīng said:
"The mountain flowers emit a quiet fragrance."
Then he pointed and said:
"Regarding the obscure rhyme earlier,
Zhōngláng was indeed at fault.
Now I wish to continue this to observe your quick wit."
Chángshǐ immediately said:
"The mountain sky is vast and clear."
Everyone burst into laughter, saying:
"Slow and not clever,
fast and clumsy — is this what quick wit is like?"
Jǐng said:
"The mountain stream rushes torrentially."
Zhōngláng said:
"How does Xiàolián know how to compose poetry?"
Jǐng grew angry,
and shouted at him with a thundering voice.
The guests in the room were startled,
and quickly disappeared.
Cáo Táng's Poems
The scholar Cáo Táng was renowned for his poetry.
He once composed the lines:
"Beneath the water, there is a heaven, silent in spring;
On earth, there is no path, the moon is vast and indistinct."
Suddenly, he saw a woman in plain white clothes stroll by gracefully,
reciting and appreciating these lines.
A few days later, Táng died.
Black Dragon Emerging from a Fingernail
Xuān Lǜshī suddenly felt his hand burning as if scorched by fire.
The master was alarmed and said:
"You,
a creature of the waters,
why are you lurking here?"
He then stretched out his arm and chanted a mantra.
Soon, a clap of thunder struck his fingernail,
and a black dragon emerged from within it.
At first, it was very small,
but in a moment, it grew over ten feet long,
with fiery mane and electric eyes,
and it soared into the sky and departed.
Yellow-Clad Woman Begging for Life
Liǔ Zōngyuán served as Sīhù of Yǒngzhōu.
When he reached Jīngmén Post Station,
he dreamt of a yellow-clad woman who said:
"My life is like a broken thread hanging in the wind,
perilously close to snapping and being carried away.
If you can save it,
how great would your gratitude be!"
The next morning,
the Jīngshī invited him to eat.
He recounted his dream.
They summoned an official to inquire,
who said:
"The day before yesterday,
fishermen caught a large yellow-scaled fish in their net,
and were preparing it for a meal.
Its head has now been cut off."
So, he ordered it to be thrown into the river.
That evening,
he dreamt the same woman came,
but she was headless.
Pool of Dark Yin
Someone saw a group of monks bathing in the water.
He asked them,
and they replied:
"This is the Pool of Dark Yin."
They also said:
"Those who trespass may listen to the Buddhist chants of our disciples."
Then they chanted together, raising a clamor,
and it turned out to be a chorus of frogs.
Clear Water Pearl
Yán Shēng from Féngyì once acquired a stone
shaped like a pellet.
Later, a Hu-man wished to exchange three hundred thousand coins for it,
saying:
"This is a supreme treasure from our Western country,
named the Clear Wood Pearl.
Since it was lost,
all the wells and springs in our country have become turbid,
and our people have all fallen ill.
That is why I crossed the sea and scaled mountains to seek it in the Middle Kingdom."
He then threw the pearl into the turbid water,
and it became serenely clear.
Grub Worm
A grub worm once transformed into a handsome man in white clothes,
who identified himself as a Cáo scion from Qí.
Jade Dragon Ointment
In Ānnán, there was Jade Dragon Ointment.
People in the south used it
to transmute silver into liquid.
Some said:
"If this ointment is brought north,
it will bring calamity."
When Hán Yuē became the Protector-General of Ānnán,
he obtained the ointment and brought it back.
That year, there was chaos in the capital,
and Yuē was executed with his clan for his association with Zhèng Zhù.
The Recluse Jīn Jīng
Wéi Sīxuán sought the art of alchemy.
One day,
a recluse named Xīn Ruì arrived,
claiming to be suffering severely from a carbuncle oozing blood.
Wéi was at a dinner party,
and the recluse urinated on the banquet table.
The guests were enraged and all rose,
and Ruì also announced his departure.
Suddenly, he disappeared.
Looking back, his urine was purple-gold liquid,
shining brightly.
A guest who understood said:
"The recluse is a spirit of gold."
They verified his name and surname,
and it was indeed true.
Zhìchuān True Lord
The monk Qìxū traveled to Zhìchuān.
On the mountain peak, there were palaces and towers above the clouds,
and in the hall sat a person wearing a hair ornament and official's cap,
who was called the Zhìchuān True Lord.
The True Lord asked:
"Have you eliminated the enemies of the Three Corpses?"
Qìxū could not answer.
The True Lord said:
"You cannot remain here."
The Pacification of Cài in the Jǐyǒu Year
In the early Yuánhé era,
Péi Jìnggōng campaigned against Wú Yuánjì.
Upon reaching the border,
he unearthed a stone
on which was carved the phrase: "The chicken is not yet fat,
the wine is not yet ripe."
Someone explained:
"'The chicken is not yet fat' means there is no meat.
Remove the 'meat' (肉) from 'fat' (肥), and it becomes '巳' (sì).
'The wine is not yet ripe' means there is no water.
Remove the 'water' (水) from 'wine' (酒), and it becomes '酉' (yǒu).
Will the defeat of the rebels be in the Jǐyǒu year?"
Later, Cài was pacified,
and indeed, they entered the city on that very day.
Painting of the Seven Sages
At Yúnguāng Sì there was a Shènghuà Diàn,
which in Cháng'ān was called Qīshèng Huà.
When the hall was first built,
a young man came to the temple and said,
"My seven brothers and I are skilled painters.
We wish to offer our labor."
The monks agreed.
The seven men brought their paints and brushes,
and warned,
"For seven days, be sure not to open the door."
The monks followed their words.
For six days,
there was utter silence,
leading them to suspect something strange,
so they broke the seal.
Suddenly, seven pigeons flew off into the sky,
and the painting was perfectly present in the western corner,
only the northwest was unfinished.
Later, a painter saw it,
and exclaimed,
"These are the brushes of divine women!"
Xiè Áo's poem
says:
"The slanting moon illuminates people's dreams tonight,
falling flowers stir the spring of last year."
It also says:
"Sorrow's mien deepens the dark green of eyebrows,
tear stains on the face like falling red flowers."
The Steaming Pot and Pestle as Monsters
Towards the end of Jiànzhōng,
Dúhú Yàn moored his boat on the Huái and Sì Rivers,
and walked by moonlight to a Buddhist temple.
There were two men,
one tall and in black clothes,
who called himself Jiǎ Qīnjì,
the fifth;
the other short and in green clothes,
named Zēng Yuán.
The man in black said,
"My ancestors
were originally of the Lú clan,
known in their youth for their stern determination.
Whenever something was obstructed and wouldn't pass,
they would certainly 'invade and scheme against it' to defy it.
People at the time all called me Qīnjì.
Later, I encountered an enemy,
and changed my surname to Jiǎ to escape the danger.
I have always been skilled in medicine,
but for 'ascending and descending, moving up and down,' I rely on others.
I have an uncle
with whom I never fail to be in company."
Zēng Yuán said,
"I am a descendant of the Táo Táng clan.
My surname was bestowed by Yáo Zēng,
and his descendants took his given name as their clan name,
hence the Zēng clan.
I have always been temperamental and irritable,
arrogant and domineering towards superiors,
enduring the slander of 'boiling over from below.'
My nature is firm and upright,
I would go through fire and water
to help those in urgent need."
Before their conversation was finished,
the temple monk returned,
and the two men fled and disappeared.
Yàn then realized,
"Isn't Zēng Yuán a steaming pot (zèng 甑)?
The character 'wǎ' (瓦, tile) attached to 'zēng' (曾) forms the character 'zèng' (甑).
As for the name Yuán (元), it is because the image inside 'wǎ' (瓦) is placed on top of 'wǎ' (瓦) to form the character.
As for Jiǎ Qīnjì,
isn't he a pestle (chǔ 杵)?
'Wǔ' (午) attached to 'mù' (木) forms the character 'chǔ' (杵).
'Jiǎ' (甲) refers to the eastern 'jiǎ-yǐ' (甲乙) wood.
'Dì Wǔ' (第五, fifth) also borrows the character 'wǔ' (午).
'Qīnjì' (侵計) is a reversed pronunciation of 'jīn jié' (金截),
'jié' (截) attached to 'jīn' (金) forms the character 'tiě' (鐵, iron).
If we analyze them comprehensively,
are they not a steaming pot and a pestle?"
The next day, indeed, among the accumulated earth, he found a pestle,
and also a steaming pot.
Volume 23
ends.
Bóyì Zhì, compiled by Gǔshénzǐ.
Studying prophecies and discussing monsters, it has been so for a long time.
Seeking out past events,
one ventures to title them all.
Roughly revealing warnings and rules,
but only for amusement and laughter.
Just like seeking oneself,
why must one mark one's name?
Hence, it is called Gǔshénzǐ.
Shī Kuàng's Seventh Mirror
During the Tiānbǎo reign,
Chén Zhònggōng lived in Qīnghuà Lǐ, Luòyáng.
There was a large well that liked to drown people.
One day,
Jìng Yuányǐng came to visit,
adorned with lead powder and dressed in crimson-green clothes.
He said,
"This well has a poisonous dragon,
which has resided here since the Hàn Dynasty.
Because it gets along well with the attendant dragons of Tàiyǐ's left and right,
they often cover for each other,
and it enjoys eating human blood.
Since the Hàn Dynasty,
it has killed three thousand seven hundred people.
I was driven by the dragon
to be a demon, to tempt and induce people to be eaten.
Last night, it already went to court Tàiyǐ,
and was also investigated and reprimanded by Hénán,
so it will only return in a few days.
If you order artisans to dredge it,
you will escape this disaster.
I wish to serve you for the rest of your life,
and there is nothing I cannot achieve."
Zhònggōng ordered artisans to enter the well,
and they retrieved an ancient bronze mirror.
That night, Yuányǐng appeared and thanked him, saying,
"I am originally the seventh among the twelve mirrors cast by Shī Kuàng.
During the Zhēnguān reign, I was dropped by Xǔ Jìngzōng
and enslaved by the poisonous dragon.
Fortunately, I met a gentleman,
and can see the human world again.
Tomorrow, I hope you will move house.
After this, I will no longer be seen."
The next day, a real estate agent came
and asked him to move.
The price for a large or small property was exactly like the one in Qīnghuà.
And it was said that the price, contract, and handover were all completed.
Three days later,
the old well collapsed,
and the hall and courtyard caved in.
Afterwards, whatever Zhònggōng needed,
was fulfilled with the same effectiveness as the house move.
On the back of the mirror, in 'tadpole script,' it read:
"On the seventh day of the seventh month, at noon, in the second year of Wéi Jìn Xīngōng,
cast at Báilóng Tán on Shǒuyáng Shān."
At the nose, it was inscribed "Mirror of Yí Zé."
Getting a Knife from a Fish's Belly
During the Kāiyuán reign,
Wáng Chānglíng was traveling by boat to Mǎdāng Shān.
The wind prevented him from stopping,
so he ordered wine, dried meat, and paper horses to be offered to the Great King,
and straw sandals to the Lady.
The poem said:
"Kūnlún is pulled from one side in view,
offered to the Great King without demanding money.
Only because of the fierce winds and turbulent waves,
do not blame Chānglíng for not disembarking."
At that time, there was a gold-inlaid knife stored inside his shoe,
which he mistakenly offered.
Suddenly, a red-scaled fish entered the boat.
Chānglíng ordered it cooked,
and upon cutting its belly, obtained the knife.
He sighed,
"Gé Xiāngōng ordered fish to deliver letters;
ancient people cut open carp to find silk scrolls.
It's quite similar!"
A Daoist Attains Immortality
The Daoists of Gōushì Xiānhè Guàn
were all highly skilled in talismans and registers.
Annually, on the third day of the ninth month,
one Daoist would attain immortality.
On that night,
they would all leave their doors unlatched,
in pursuit of ascension.
Zhāng Jiézhōng, as the county magistrate,
sent brave men to observe them.
They saw a black tiger enter the temple,
carrying out a Daoist, and leaving.
By morning,
none of the Daoists had attained immortality.
Jiézhōng led a great hunt,
killing several tigers.
Some had golden tablets and jade registers,
or caps, cloaks, human hair, and many bones,
all belonging to the Daoists who were supposed to attain immortality each year.
Essences of All Flowers
Cuī Xuánhuī,
one moonlit night, saw a maiden in green leading her companions, namely Yáng-shì, Lǐ-shì, and Táo-shì.
There was also a little girl in crimson, called Shí Cùcù.
Then, it was announced that Fēng-jiā Shíbā Yí had arrived.
Her words were cool and distant,
possessing a reclusive, unworldly air.
Their complexions were all exceptionally beautiful,
and a fragrant aroma wafted from them.
Cùcù said:
"All the maidens live in the garden,
and are often disturbed by fierce winds.
We must rely on Shíbā Yí for protection.
Sir, if you would make a scarlet banner for us every New Year's Day,
illustrating the sun, moon, and five planets on it,
and place it in the east of the garden,
then we would be spared from calamity.
This year has already passed,
so please place it on the twenty-first day of this month."
Cuī agreed to this.
On that day, he erected the banner,
and an east wind swept across the ground,
breaking trees and swirling sand,
yet the luxuriant flowers in the garden remained undisturbed.
Xuánhuī then realized that these were the essences of various flowers,
Cùcù was a pomegranate,
and Fēng Yí was the spirit of the wind.
Later, Yáng-shì and her companions came to express their gratitude,
each wrapping several *dǒu* of peach and plum blossoms, saying:
"Consuming these can ward off old age,
and we too will achieve longevity."
By the beginning of Yuánhé reign, Xuánhuī was still alive,
probably around thirty years old.
In Tiānzhù Shān Tīxiān Guó,
in the house of Yīn Yǐnkè in Fángzhōu Zhúshān Xiàn,
a well was dug over a thousand *chǐ* deep but yielded no water.
A worker felt the wall,
and discovered another world with its own heaven, earth, sun, and moon.
A sign read "Tiānzhù Shān".
Inside the gate, two boys with white teeth and flowing hair,
their feet washed, wearing golden crowns,
asked:
"Why have you come here?"
The worker explained the whole story.
After a moment,
a crimson-clad figure delivered an imperial decree, saying:
"Send him away with proper courtesy."
He was led to a clear spring to bathe,
and drank from a white spring,
which was so sweet it felt like intoxication.
After traveling for half a day,
he came to a city of a kingdom,
whose palaces and buildings were all made of gold and jade.
The city gate tower was inscribed with "Tīxiān Guó".
The worker inquired:
"What kind of place is this kingdom?"
They replied:
"Newly immortalized sages are sent to this kingdom,
where they cultivate for seven hundred thousand days,
and then ascend to various heavens,
or to Yùjīng, Pénglái, Kūnlàng, or Gūyè."
The worker then climbed the mountain to look for a path,
but the gatekeepers said:
"You have been here for but a moment,
but in the human world, more than ten years have passed.
If you wish to exit through the old opening,
it will likely be impossible.
We shall petition for the key to the Heaven-Connecting Gate to send you home."
He was led up to the Heavenly Gate.
Soon, the clouds parted,
and he was already in Fángzhōu.
He inquired about the Yīn family,
and was told that three generations had passed.
After this, the worker no longer ate grains
and his whereabouts became unknown.
Shàngqīng Tóngzǐ.
Cén Wénběn was avoiding the summer heat at his mountain pavilion.
Someone knocked on the door, saying:
"Shàngqīng Tóngzǐ Yuánbǎo requests an audience."
He wore a round green cap with corners,
and light green clothes.
He said:
"I attained enlightenment since the Hàn dynasty.
I was originally born in Wú,
and obtained the Way of not being hindered."
Wénběn spoke of events from the Hàn dynasty,
and he understood them as if he had witnessed them firsthand.
When asked about the peculiarity of his cap and stole,
he replied:
"My outer garment is round, but my heart is upright.
This is the Shàngqīng Wǔzhū robe."
He added:
"The particularly fine ones of the six *zhū* are the five *zhū*."
He walked out a few steps,
and disappeared by the wall.
Wénběn dug there,
and found only two ancient coins in an old tomb.
Wénběn realized
that Shàngqīng Tóngzǐ
was a name for copper;
Yuánbǎo
was the inscription on a coin;
its outer roundness and inner squareness
were the shape of a coin;
the green clothes
were the color of copper;
and the Wǔzhū robe
was also a coin inscription.
It was cast during the Hàn dynasty.
After this, Wénběn's wealth in coins and silk grew daily,
and he became Minister of the Secretariat.
Suddenly, he lost the ancient coins,
and then passed away.
Dancing Sleeves, Bowed Arches.
Xíng Fèngwàn lived in the Píngkāng Lǐ of Cháng'ān,
which was the site of the winding rooms of a former wealthy and powerful family's mansion.
In a daytime dream, a beautiful woman appeared, saying:
"This is my home."
She took a colored paper and wrote the "Yángchūn Qǔ" (Spring Melody):
"A Cháng'ān maiden treads in spring's warmth,
but where is the spring warmth that doesn't break hearts?
Dancing sleeves, bowed arches, all completely forgotten,
the silken curtains now only changed for nine autumn frosts."
Bālíng Ghost Poem.
Liú Fāngxuán lodged one night in an ancient inn in Bālíng.
He heard the sounds of a household whistling and singing.
An old maid in green said:
"Years ago, when young master was demoted,
he ordered this old body to ride a skewbald horse,
holding young master Jīng.
My left arm was injured in a fall,
and to this day, it aches when the sky is overcast.
Tomorrow, there will surely be heavy rain.
Now young master Jīng holds a high official position,
I wonder if he remembers this old body?
In those days, young master Jīng loved to recite 'Green, green riverside grass,'
but today it is 'A绵绵思远道' (Endless thoughts of distant paths)."
The next morning,
it indeed rained heavily.
On the wall was a poem:
"Father and Mother sent me to the roots of green maples,
I don't remember how many times the green maples have shed their leaves.
The flowers on my clothes then, when I stood upright in the pavilion,
are now ashes, unfit to wear."
The ink color was very fresh,
so he knew it was written by someone who had been there last night.
Daughter of the Dragon King of the Sea.
Xǔ Hànyáng,
a Zhēnjūn (Daoist master), was traveling by boat between Hóngzhōu and Ráozhōu.
At dusk,
he sought a small inlet to enter.
After traveling several *lǐ*,
he unknowingly arrived at a lake.
The water was only three or two *chǐ* deep.
The lake cliffs and courtyard buildings were very grand.
He saw several young women,
whose food and drink were unlike anything seen in the human world.
There was a tree,
its trunk like a *wútóng* tree,
its leaves like a banana plant.
Red flowers, as yet unopened,
were as large as a *dǒu* or a *àng*.
A servant in blue brought a bird like a parrot
and placed it on the railing.
With one sound, all the tree's flowers burst open.
Their fragrance assailed people.
Within each flower was a beautiful woman over a *chǐ* tall.
Pipes and strings were all present.
The young women raised their wine cups,
and all the music began.
Late at night, the flowers fell,
and their location was lost.
One young woman recited a poem, saying:
"The sea gate connects to Dòngtíng,
each time departing three thousand *lǐ*.
Once in ten years I return,
to the toil of Xiāoxiāng's waters."
The other young women said:
"We are delighted by this chance encounter during your journey."
With regret, they parted.
The next morning, he inquired at the mouth of the inlet,
and was told:
"Last night, four people drowned.
When they were fished out,
one of them
seemed alive.
After a long time, he spoke, saying:
"The daughters of the Sea Dragon King were returning to Dòngtíng,
and lodged here.
They took four people to make wine.
Because there were few guests,
they didn't drink much,
so I managed to escape."
Hànyáng asked who the guest was.
They replied:
"Just a poor scholar."
Hànyáng remained silent,
but felt discomfort in his abdomen.
He vomited several *shēng* of fresh blood,
only then realizing that human blood had been made into wine.
It took three days for him to recover.
Hú Èrjiě.
When Mǎ Suì was poor and humble,
he resided in Běijīng.
He sought an audience with a commander but accidentally used his taboo name,
and was rebuked and driven out of the court.
Suì fled outside the city wall.
The commander sent iron cavalry to pursue him.
Suì hid in a ruined house of refugees.
He saw a woman,
who said:
"Hú Èrjiě knows you are here,
and so has come to comfort you."
She took several *dǒu* of ash,
spread them across the ground,
and said:
"At midnight, strange creatures will try to scare you.
You absolutely must not move.
After this peril,
your achievements will be unmatched."
Having spoken, she left.
Indeed, he saw a night-yakṣa,
with red hair and golden teeth,
fierce eyes spitting fire.
It dared not cross Hú Èrjiě's ash.
Suddenly, he heard chariots and horses approaching the door, saying:
"Sir Mǎ must be hiding here."
The yakṣa leapt up,
devouring the people and horses almost completely before leaving.
Suì thus escaped.
Later, he established great achievements,
and his official rank was exalted.
He never knew where Hú Èrjiě was,
and was unable to repay her.
In spring and autumn sacrifices,
she was listed to the left and right of the temple.
Discussing Ministers and Chancellors.
When Mínghuáng fled to Shǔ,
Péi Shìyān accompanied him.
On horseback, they discussed ministers and chancellors.
Shìyān asked:
"What about Yáo Chóng?"
The Emperor said:
"He was capable."
"What about Sòng Jǐng?"
He said:
"He was virtuous and profound."
They discussed more than ten people,
all of whom fit his descriptions.
Finally, he asked about Lǐ Línfǔ.
The Emperor said:
"His jealousy of the worthy and hatred of the capable
is unmatched in ancient and modern times."
Shìyān said:
"Why then did Your Majesty entrust him with such a deep appointment?"
The Emperor bowed his head and said nothing.
Merman.
Chá Dào, a *Shìzhì* (Attendant in the Imperial Secretariat), was dispatched on a mission to Gāolì.
In the evening, he moored by a mountain.
He saw a woman in the sand,
in a red skirt with both shoulders exposed,
her hair coiled in disarray.
Behind her elbows were faint red scales.
Chá ordered a boatman to gently push her back into the water with a pole,
ensuring she wasn't harmed.
When the woman reached the water,
she rose and fell, then turned to look at Chá, bowing with clasped hands,
filled with emotion before disappearing.
The boatman said:
"I have never seen such a thing on the sea.
What was that?"
Chá said:
"That was a merman.
It can have sexual relations with humans.
Living among aquatic creatures,
it possesses human nature."
Jade Towers and Pavilions in Heaven.
The wife of a woodcutter from Jiǔhuá Shān, née Zhūgě,
fell ill with a seasonal ailment.
A few days later, she arose and told her parents-in-law:
"Your daughter-in-law is not only free from illness,
but has also attained immortality."
Soon after, she went out the door
and ascended into the sky.
After a few more days, she returned again,
saying:
"The towers and pavilions in heaven are all fashioned from green jade,
and the windows and doors are intricately adorned with pearls.
Gossamer curtains and drapes
shimmer with five colors.
Immortal maidens walk in bright light,
burning undying incense.
I have come now for a brief visit."
Soon, a five-colored chariot,
pulled by two dragons,
was driven by a strongman,
with young maidens accompanying it.
The woman rode it, slowly ascending and departing.
The Barefoot Immortal of Nányuè.
Yuè Shǐ, as a *Xījīng Liútái Yùshǐ* (Censor of the Western Capital Branch Office),
once dreamt that the Heavenly Emperor summoned him.
Suddenly, he saw magnificent palaces and gates.
The Emperor said:
"Your ruler seeks an heir;
I will choose one for him."
After a short while,
a person arrived.
The Emperor said:
"Zhōngyuán seeks an heir;
you shall go, do not refuse."
He bowed his head repeatedly, pleading to be excused,
but the Emperor said:
"Go!"
So he assented and departed.
A figure standing respectfully nearby said:
"This is the Barefoot Immortal Lǐ of Nányuè,
who is always deeply intoxicated."
The next year, Rénzōng was indeed born.
Sight of Imperial Guards at Shènghuì Palace.
Shènghuì Palace was east of Luòyáng,
where the divine spirits of the ancestors resided.
On the twenty-ninth day of the third month, in the eighth year of Jiāyòu, at midday,
after the *lòu* (water clock) had run out,
people saw imperial guards arrayed along the road.
The last person wore a vermilion robe,
held a yellow umbrella,
and rode a horse to the palace gate before disappearing.
The next day,
the palace gate was wide open.
The doors of all the halls,
though locked, were open.
Shortly after, a report came that Rénmiào had ascended to immortality.
Zēng Mén Hǎo.
During the Tiānshèng (天聖) and Míngdào (明道) eras,
in the capital city's markets,
whenever a thing was fine and beautiful, it was called "Cáo Mén (曹門) good";
when a thing was tall and grand,
it was called "Cáo Mén (曹門) tall."
In the Jǐngyòu (景祐) era, Rénzōng's (仁宗) granddaughter by Prince Cáo (曹王) became empress.
Prince Wáng (王) assisted Tàizǔ (太祖) in establishing the empire,
subduing Shǔ (蜀) and pacifying Wú (吳),
leading an army of a million,
yet never wantonly killed a single person.
It is fitting that his descendants should flourish.
Lǐquán Guān (醴泉觀)
During the Xiángfú (祥符) era,
a sweet spring (醴泉) gushed forth in the southeastern corner of the capital,
and turtles and snakes appeared beside it.
Those who drank from it recovered from illnesses,
so Xiángyuán Guān (祥源觀) was built on that spot.
Later, it suffered damage,
was renovated again,
and its name changed to Lǐquán Guān (醴泉觀).
During the Xīníng (熙寧) era,
it was recommended for further repair and embellishment,
and the imperial music bureau's (教坊) performers were ordered to play music in its courtyard.
On that day,
the image of Zhēnwǔ (真武) appeared within a large pearl on the temple's roof ridge,
with his retinue, divine officials, and banners all clearly visible.
Púyè Tīng (僕射廳)
Chén Yīnggōng (陳英公) Zhízhōng (執中),
initially, as a Right Rectifier of Words (右正言), was demoted to supervise the wine excise of Yǒngzhōu (永州).
One day,
he saw a golden plaque between the eaves of the roof,
inscribed with the words "Púyè Tīng (僕射廳)."
Later, he indeed rose to the position of a grand councilor (台輔).
Golden-armored divine being reprimands the physician
Lǚ Gōngbì (呂公弼) was
Shēngōng's (申公) second son.
At first,
when Shēnguó (申國) was pregnant, she fell ill
and was about to abort the child.
The physician Chén Xùn (陳遜) was boiling the medicine; as it was about to be ready,
it was already the second watch of the night.
He sat down and dozed off.
Suddenly, the cauldron overturned.
He boiled it again, and it overturned again.
He boiled it once more and added more fire.
Extremely tired, he lay down on his couch.
He dreamed of a divine being wearing golden armor and holding a sword,
who shouted,
"The one in the womb is a prime minister of this dynasty!
Who are you,
to dare to inflict poison and harm?"
Xùn (遜) woke up in fear
and reported it to the prime minister.
Later, Gōngbì (公弼) was born,
and during the Xīníng (熙寧) era, he held the position of Privy Council Vice-Administrator (樞密使).
Sweat-soaked socks
Shèng Wénsùgōng (盛文肅公) Dù (度) suddenly fell ill and died.
The next evening, he revived,
saying he had been pursued into a government office.
He saw the presiding official who said they were of the same surname and had been mistakenly pursued,
and promptly ordered him to return.
On the way, he saw the late prime minister Shěn Yìlún (沈義倫),
who said,
"Knowing that you are returning,
please tell my family
that I am quite tormented by sweat-soaked socks."
Wénsù (文肅) returned and told his orphan son,
who did not understand the meaning of "sweat-soaked socks."
When the mourning period ended and the ancestral tablet was removed,
there was a worn-out sock beside the couch.
Investigating its origin,
it turned out to be a sock that an old guard, on vigil, had accidentally placed there one night
and forgotten when he woke up in the morning.
He thought it was lost
and did not bother to search for it again.
Slinging at owls
Zhāng Tàiníng (張太寧) Jí (戢) inherently disliked owls.
He always carried a sling to chase them away.
He once lived in a Buddhist temple.
There was an owl's nest on the fish-shaped ornament (魚尾) of the main hall,
where two chicks were being raised.
As their wings gradually matured, Zhāng (張) personally slung at them and killed them.
The parent owl circled in the sky, hooting sorrowfully without cease.
Tàiníng (太寧) was walking in the courtyard when
one owl swooped down and snatched his turban,
and another owl clawed and injured his temple.
After more than ten days, the wound festered, and he died.
Dragon Head Mountain Man
The former jinshì Yáng Tōng (楊通) was on good terms with the zhuangyuan Yáng Zhì (楊寘).
He dreamed that Zhì (寘) sent a calling card,
identifying himself as the Dragon Head Mountain Man (龍首山人).
He passed the imperial examination during the Qìnglì (慶曆) era and then died.
Later generations explained this by saying,
"Dragon Head (龍首)
refers to a zhuangyuan (狀元);
Mountain Man (山人)
is a term for someone without an official salary."
Ghost writes grass script
Mǎ Shàobǎo (馬少保) Gōngliàng (公亮),
when young, once sat alone by the window reading a book.
A large hand, like a fan,
stretched forth from the window.
The next night, it came again.
Gōng (公) dipped his brush in realgar water and wrote a large "草" (cǎo) character (grass script).
From outside the window, a loud voice shouted,
"Quickly wash it off for me,
otherwise disaster will befall you!"
Gōng (公) did not listen and went to sleep.
After a while,
the hand grew very angry and demanded to be washed off with greater urgency.
Gōng (公) did not respond.
As dawn approached,
it wailed mournfully, and the hand still could not retract.
It also said,
"You are destined for great nobility.
I was merely playing a trick on you.
How can you bear to put me in such an extreme predicament?
Have you not seen the story of Wēn Jiào (溫嶠) lighting a rhinoceros horn?"
Gōng (公) suddenly understood.
He used water to wash off the "草" (cǎo) character.
The hand apologized humbly and departed.
Mother dies and returns
Pān Jìzōng (潘繼宗), a Senior Clerk (郎中),
lost his mother ten years prior.
One day, she suddenly appeared in the hall,
her appearance and clothes exactly as they had been in life.
She said,
"You can set up a curtain in the west of the hall,
and place two couches inside.
My two female companions will rest there with me."
She also said,
"Though I died, I committed no great fault.
The officials of the underworld placed me in a room,
not allowing me to go elsewhere.
Since you have received imperial titles,
and I am now a great lord of a county (縣大君),
I am allowed free movement.
Now I am to be reborn as a daughter in a certain family at a mill in Jìzhōu (冀州),
and thus I was able to come here."
The family provided food and drink daily,
but only the sound of chopsticks could be heard.
After more than a month, she announced her departure.
The whole family escorted her to the outskirts of the city,
where a sound of weeping was heard in the air.
Upright nose of a Senior Clerk
When Xú Lángzhōng (徐郎中) was young, he dreamed that a divine being carried a bamboo basket,
which contained many human noses.
Upon closer inspection, Xú (徐) said,
"Your features are not bad,
but your nose is crooked and small.
I will exchange it for you."
He selected a nose from the basket,
cut off Xú's (徐) nose,
and placed the chosen one in its stead,
feeling considerable pain.
The divine being laughed and said,
"What a fine upright nose of a Senior Clerk!"
Xú's (徐) nose had never been prominent or straight,
but from then on, it became straight.
He held various official positions as a Senior Clerk (正郎).
Releasing a large turtle
Sòng Chuánqìng (宋傳慶), a Central Gentleman (中舍),
once obtained several turtles
and gave them to his kitchen maid to stew.
One of them was very large,
and the maid could not bear to kill it,
so she released it into a ditch.
Over a year later, the maid fell ill with a feverish plague
and was about to die,
so she was carried to an outer chamber.
The next day,
her chest and ribs were covered in blue mud.
When asked,
she said,
"I don't know where it came from,
but the fever has slightly decreased."
The family watched over her.
At night, a large turtle emerged from the ditch, covering itself with mud,
climbed directly onto the maid's chest and cooled her.
Her illness then healed.
Daoist submits a memorial
When Fàn Zhòngyān (范仲淹) was Assistant Administrator of Chénzhōu (陳州),
the Prefect's mother fell ill.
He summoned a Daoist priest to perform a petitioning ritual.
Fàn Zhòngyān (范仲淹) smiled and said,
"How can an ordinary person convey a petition to the Heavenly Emperor?"
The Daoist priest held his tablet, prostrated himself before the altar,
and remained motionless all night.
When they tried to touch his body, it was stiff.
Around the fifth watch,
his feet were slightly warm.
After a long while, he said to the Prefect,
"Your mother has six more years of life;
do not worry about her suffering."
The Prefect asked why the petitioning ritual took so long that night.
He replied,
"As I was just leaving the Heavenly Gate,
I encountered the release of next year's spring list of successful candidates for the Imperial Examination.
Spectators thronged the roads,
which caused the delay."
Fàn Zhòngyān (范仲淹) asked what was the surname of the *zhuàngyuán* (狀元).
He said,
"The surname is Wáng (王),
with a two-character given name.
The character after the given name was blacked out,
with another character noted beside it,
which was too distant to discern."
Soon after, the Prefect's mother recovered from her illness.
The following spring,
the *zhuàngyuán* (狀元) was indeed Wáng Gǒngshòu (王拱壽).
The emperor's brush changed it to Gǒngchén (拱辰).
Fàn Zhòngyān (范仲淹) then began to sigh, acknowledging that the Daoist priest had supernatural communication.
Lord of the Fúróng (芙蓉) Pavilion
During the Qìnglì (慶曆) era,
a court official, going to court at dawn,
saw more than thirty beautiful women.
They were exquisitely made up and splendidly dressed,
riding two by two on horseback.
Dīng Dù (丁度), the Guānwén (觀文), followed behind them on his saddle and bridle.
The court official was startled and exclaimed,
"Dīng (丁) is known for his simplicity and frugality,
how can he have so many concubines?"
One person was walking last.
The court official asked,
"Where is Guānwén (觀文) taking his family members?"
He replied,
"No,
these women are going to welcome the Lord of the Fúróng (芙蓉) Pavilion."
Soon after, they heard that Dīng (丁) had died.
Zhāng Jiǔjiǔ (張酒酒)
The Daoist priest Zhāng Jiǔjiǔ (張酒酒)
would buy wine as soon as he got money,
never being sober for a day.
One day, he flung his robes and entered Wángwū Shān (王屋山),
standing to perform *shījiě* (尸解).
Seeking an Heir at the City God Temple
In Jiànzhōu (建州), there was a certain Zhāng (張) who had no son.
He repeatedly prayed to the City God for an heir.
He dreamt that the deity told him,
"You and your wife are fated to be without children.
But I pity your devout prayers,
so I will give you the Temple's Judge as your son."
Indeed, a son was born,
named Bóyù (伯玉).
He passed the Imperial Examination,
served as a Zheng Láng (正郎),
governed several commanderies, and then died.
He was talented and resolute,
fond of wine and unconcerned with his appearance.
His face was dirty, his hair disheveled,
like an earthen statue of a judge.
Fèi Xiàoxiān's (費孝先) *Fànwéi* (範圍)
Fèi Xiàoxiān (費孝先)
was from Chéngdū (成都).
He would create hexagrams based on a person's birth year, month, day, and hour,
which he called *Fànwéi* (範圍).
He also had "hexagram shadows,"
all depicting Táng (唐) attire and caps.
Their official ranks were also according to Táng (唐) official order.
Could this not be the manifestation of the spirits of Táng (唐) times?
Execution for Bribery
Hán Yuánqīng (韓元卿) was the Investigative Official for Xiázhōu (峽州).
Suddenly, he drew his blade and cut his own throat.
Although his throat was cut, he was not dead.
Zǔ Zézhī (祖擇之), who was then the Judicial Commissioner for Húběi (湖北),
and his fellow *jìnshì* (進士) from the same year,
went to see him.
Hán (韓) could not speak,
but only raised his hand as if asking for paper and a brush.
So, it was given to him,
and he wrote,
"Bribery is clear,
the crime deserves execution."
Zǔ (祖) ordered that his wound be sewn with mulberry root thread.
Hán Yuánqīng (韓元卿) tore it off with his hand,
and then died.
The Alligator Monster
In the Lèpíng (樂平) Bridge port of Tánzhōu (潭州),
there was an alligator causing trouble.
It ate many people,
and every year there were people who drowned.
A citizen named Lǐ (李)
had a younger brother who drowned,
and his body could not be found.
So, he pricked his palm to draw blood and wrote a petition,
which he burned during a night ritual.
That night, he dreamt he arrived at a place,
like a grand yamen.
Several officials had an iron chain tied to a creature,
tens of feet long,
like a dragon but with one horn,
its eyes shining like lightning.
After a moment,
a person descended from the hall and shouted,
"The river alligator has committed atrocities,
wrongfully harming innocent people!
It is sentenced to one hundred blows with the iron staff,
and death.
As for Lǐ (李) so-and-so, he improperly defiled a high deity with the blood from his palm,
and should be handed over to Wáng Shuò (王碩) to have fifteen strikes on his arm."
Several years later, Wáng Shuò (王碩) became the Prefect of Tánzhōu (潭州).
Lǐ (李) was found guilty of causing a fire and confessed his crime.
The Butcher Slaughtering a Lamb
The military officer Mǎ Zhòngfāng (馬仲方)
was given a ewe that gave birth to a lamb.
Mǎ Zhòngfāng (馬仲方) sold it to a butcher's shop.
The next day, as the butcher was about to slaughter it, he lost his knife.
After a long search, he found the knife in a ditch.
He took it out and cleaned it,
but then it was lost again.
It was the lamb that had taken the knife in its mouth and thrown it into the ditch,
and then trampled it into the mud with its feet,
so that it wouldn't be seen.
The butcher saw this
and was greatly moved.
From then on, he no longer slaughtered sheep.
Xǔ Piāntóu (許偏頭)
A painter in Chéngdū (成都) named Xǔ (許)
was skilled at portraiture.
One day, a poor man,
dressed in ragged clothes and looking emaciated,
came to commission a portrait.
Xǔ (許) laughed and said,
"Your appearance is like this,
yet you seek a portrait.
Why?"
The man untied his cloth bag,
took out a yellow Daoist robe,
a deerskin cap,
and a white jade hairpin.
He put on the cap, changed his clothes, and sat upright.
He stroked his face,
and it became youthful.
He pulled his beard,
and it turned black at his touch,
making him a handsome man.
Xǔ (許) was startled and said,
"I did not know a divine immortal had descended."
The Daoist said,
"You may paint my image,
and place it in your shop.
If someone wishes to buy it,
only take a thousand coins."
Later, someone who recognized him said,
"This is the true immortal Zhū (朱) from Língquán (靈泉)."
Seekers came in crowds.
Xǔ (許) was greedy for the painting's price,
and took two thousand for each image.
He dreamt the Daoist said,
"Your fortune is limited,
you should not take excessively.
How can you disregard my words and shorten your lifespan?"
He struck his left cheek.
When he woke up,
his head was indeed crooked.
From then on, he was called Xǔ Piāntóu (許偏頭) (Crooked-headed Xǔ).
Zhū Zhēnrén (朱真人) was Zhū Jūshì (朱居士),
whose given name was Xióng (雄).
He is mentioned in the Táng (唐) history,
and also in Dù Guāngtíng's (杜光庭) *Xiānzhuàn* (仙傳).
Accidentally Eating a Charm
Zhāng Táo (張燾), a Dragoon Supervising Censor (龍圖),
passed the imperial examination with the highest rank in the first *jiǎkē* (甲科) of the Jǐngyòu (景祐) era.
He once mistakenly ate dog meat.
He dreamt that a yellow-clad messenger pursued him to a palace.
A Daoist priest said,
“Why did you eat such an unclean thing?”
Zhāng Táo said,
“I did not dare to eat it intentionally,
it was a mistake.”
The Daoist priest said,
“Wait here.
I will speak for you.”
A short while later, he came out and said,
“You may express your gratitude.”
He was led to the front of the hall and announced,
“Zhāng Táo (張燾) mistakenly ate an unclean thing,
and offers his apologies.”
He kowtowed twice and awoke.
Zhāng (張) possessed a clear and refined spirit,
and an open and magnanimous mind.
Could he not be one of the celestial officials who was banished?
Seeing Boats on the Lake
Xú Xǐ (徐禧), a Scholar of the Imperial Academy (學士), was once boating on Pēnglí Hú (彭蠡湖)
when a white mist rose all around on the water.
He saw two enormous vermilion-lacquered boats,
with splendid banners and flags.
The rowers were solemn and silent.
They passed by at a distance of over a hundred *zhàng* (丈) and vanished.
He then saw vermilion warships,
interspersed with gold and jade decorations,
following one after another.
He then saw two white warships,
carrying several thousand armored soldiers,
with a dense array of spears and halberds.
They followed the three boats from behind.
As the boats moved further away, they became smaller.
Obtaining a Father's Stone Inscription
Zǔ Wúzég (祖無擇), a Dragoon Supervising Censor (龍圖),
once served as the Vice Prefect of Qízhōu (齊州).
Passing by an ancient river shoal,
he found a stone slab in the sand,
on which were several tens of characters.
It was an inscription marking the burial of his ancestors.
He sent someone to inspect the graves.
Not a single mound was missing.
He ultimately could not fathom its origin.
Chǔshì Máo (處士茅) Reprimands a Ghost
Liú Yè (劉燁), a Vice Minister (侍郎), had a detached residence in Xiāngtāng (襄湯).
After Liú Yè (劉燁) died,
his eldest son, Kùbù (庫部), also died.
The residence was then sold
and acquired by Chǔshì Máo (處士茅).
At night, he heard a voice calling,
“Kùbù (庫部) is coming.”
Suddenly, a person wearing a hat,
followed by several ghosts,
reprimanded Máo (茅), saying,
“This is my residence!
How dare you occupy it?
Get out quickly,
lest you invite disaster!”
This happened for three consecutive nights,
and the voice grew fiercer.
Máo (茅) shouted back,
“You were once a human,
and now you are a ghost.
Do you still rely on your noble status to act like this?
If I had presumptuously occupied your residence,
it would be fitting for you to force me out.
But your son was unworthy,
unable to preserve his ancestor's old home,
and sold it to me.
How dare you still try to drive me away?”
After he finished speaking,
he in turn shouted for them to leave quickly.
The ghosts then fled.
Cutting Off One Ear of a Pig
Luó Shào (羅紹),
a Hányáng (漢陽) native,
lived near the Wǔtōng Shén (五通神) Temple.
A neighbor annually raised a pig to sacrifice to the deity,
and it often damaged Luó's (羅) fences.
Luó Shào's (羅紹) father was angry,
caught the pig, and cut off one of its ears.
The neighbor complained to the deity.
Later, Luó Shào (羅紹) and his grandson were born,
each missing one ear.
Also, a wealthy man from Gōng'ān (公安),
seeing two dogs copulating,
used a knife to sever their genitals.
Later, his two sons were born, both eunuchs.
Duàn Gǔ (叚谷)'s Mad Chanting
Duàn Gǔ (叚谷) repeatedly failed the *jìnshì* (進士) examination.
Later, he suddenly became like a madman,
chanting in the marketplace:
“A small thatched hut,
still maintaining itself.
Believing the wild wind blew,
the eaves were shattered.
The main beam tilted precariously,
watching the walls collapse,
becoming a pile of scattered earth.
The master will never return.”
Later he died of illness.
When he was buried,
they opened the coffin and found only the coffin itself.
End of Scroll 24.
Róngchéng Shì (容成氏)
In the time of Róngchéng Shì (容成氏),
people walked like geese in single file on the roads;
when seated,
they placed infants in nests above,
and left leftover food for the hungry;
tigers and leopards could be approached from behind,
venomous snakes could be stepped upon.
By the time of Yáo (堯),
Yì (羿) slew the凿齒獸 (záochǐshòu) beast,
killed the Jiǔyīng (九嬰),
cut down the Xiūshé (脩蛇),
Yǔ (禹) shot down the ten suns,
and lassoed Dàfēng (大風).
All the people rejoiced
and made Yáo (堯) the Son of Heaven.
In later generations,
Jié (桀) built the Xuánshì (璇室), Yáotái (瑤臺), Xiàngláng (象廊), and Yùchuáng (玉床);
Zhòu (紂) created the Ròupǔ (肉圃) and Jiǔchí (酒池).
Tāng (湯) banished Jié (桀),
and Wǔwáng (武王) attacked Zhòu (紂).
Divine Transformation
The highest form is divine transformation;
the next is to prevent wrongdoing;
the next is to reward the worthy and punish the violent.
Small Heart, Great Ambition
The heart desires to be small, but the ambition desires to be great.
Wisdom desires to be rounded, but conduct desires to be square.
Ability desires to be abundant, but affairs desire to be few.
Good Doctors Save Lives
Tiānxióng (天雄) and niǎohuì (鳥喙) are the most virulent of medicines,
yet good doctors use them to save lives.
Dwarfs and blind musicians
are considered distressed and weakened people,
yet rulers use them to complete their orchestras.
Shùn (舜) did not leave his mat and the world was well-governed.
Jié (桀) did not descend his steps and the world was in chaos.
Observing the Tongue, Viewing the Scenery
Lǎozǐ (老子) studied under Shāng Róng (商容),
and by observing the tongue, he knew to guard softness.
Lièzǐ (列子) studied under Húzǐ (壺子),
and by viewing the *jǐngzhù* (景柱) (sundial gnomon), he knew to maintain a position of reserve.
Magpie Nests, Otter Dens
Magpie nests know where the wind arises from.
Otter dens know the rise and fall of water levels.
A bright sun indicates fair weather.
A halo around the sun indicates rain.
The Gentleman Forbids the Subtle
Accumulated feathers sink a boat;
many light weights break a heavy burden.
Therefore, a gentleman forbids evil from its subtle beginnings.
Zhōugōng (周公) Governs Lǔ (魯), Tàigōng (太公) Governs Qí (齊)
Tàigōng (太公) asked Zhōugōng (周公) how he governed Lǔ (魯).
He replied,
“Respect the honorable,
and cherish your kin.”
Tàigōng (太公) said,
“Lǔ (魯) will henceforth be weak!”
Zhōugōng (周公) asked,
“How do you govern Qí (齊)?”
Tàigōng (太公) replied,
“Elevate the worthy and reward merit.”
Zhōugōng (周公) said,
“Later generations will surely have rulers who are robbed and assassinated.”
Thereafter,
Qí (齊) grew stronger day by day,
eventually becoming a hegemon.
After twenty-four generations, the Tián (田) clan replaced them.
Lǔ (魯) grew weaker day by day,
and perished after thirty-two generations.
A Bird at Its Wit's End
The proverb says:
“A bird at its wit's end will peck,
a beast at its wit's end will gore with its horns,
and a person at their wit's end will resort to deception.”
Jiǔyě (九野)
What are the Nine Wilds (Jiǔyě)?
The center is called Jūntiān,
the east is called Cāng
tiān,
the south
east is called Mántiān,
the north is called Xuántiān,
the northwest is called Yōutiān,
the west is called Hàotiān,
the southwest is called Zhūtiān,
the south is called Yántiān,
the southeast is called Yángtiān.
The bamboo arrows of Kuàijī (Kuàijī) and
rhinos and elephants of Liángshān (Liángshān),
gold and stones of Huàshān (Huàshān),
pearls and jades of Gùshān (Gùshān),
tendons and horns of Yōudū (Yōudū).
Cháng'é
Yì (Yì) requested the elixir of immortality from the Queen Mother of the West (Xīwángmǔ).
Cháng'é (Cháng'é) secretly stole it and fled to the moon.
Born in ten months.
The spirit is received from heaven,
the physical body is endowed by earth.
In one month, it is fat (gāo);
in two months, it shows signs (zhèn);
in three months, it is a fetus (tāi);
in four months, it has muscles (jī);
in five months, it has tendons (jīn);
in six months, it has bones (gǔ);
in seven months, it is formed (chéng);
in eight months, it moves (dòng);
in nine months, it is restless (zào);
in ten months, it is born.
Yellow Dragon (Huánglóng) carries the boat.
Yǔ (Yǔ) inspected the regions and crossed the river.
A yellow dragon (huánglóng) carried his boat.
The people in the boat were pale with fear.
Yǔ (Yǔ) laughed and said:
"I received my mandate from Heaven.
Life is a temporary stay;
death is a return home.
How can this disturb my peace?"
He regarded the dragon as a mere gecko.
The dragon then lowered its ears and wagged its tail and retreated.
Golden Casket (Jīnténg) and Leopard's Strategy (Bàotāo).
If the discussions of Xǔyóu (Xǔyóu) are adopted,
then the Jīnténg (Jīnténg) and Bàotāo (Bàotāo) become obsolete.
When Yánlíng Jìzǐ (Yánlíng Jìzǐ) refused the state of Wú (Wú),
those who squabbled over farmland were ashamed.
The Jīnténg (Jīnténg) and Bàotāo (Bàotāo)
are books of secret strategies for territorial acquisition by Duke of Zhōu (Zhōugōng) and Tài Gōng (Tàigōng).
Gāotáo (Gāotáo) mute.
Gāotáo (Gāotáo), though mute, served as Grand Judge (Dàlǐ),
and there were no wrongful punishments in the world.
Shī Kuàng (Shī Kuàng), though blind, served as Prime Minister (Tàizǎi),
and the state of Jìn (Jìn) had no chaotic government.
One pluck, one touch.
Róng Qǐqī (Róng Qǐqī) plucked once,
and Kǒngzǐ (Kǒngzǐ) was joyful for three days,
moved by the harmony.
Zōu Zhì (Zōu Zhì) touched once,
and King Wēi (Wēiwáng) was sad for the entire night,
moved by the sorrow.
To have more than enough.
If one asks for fire,
and everyone gives it,
it is because what one asks for is sufficient.
One does not sell firewood in the forest,
nor fish by the lake,
because one has more than enough.
Can one speak subtly?
Bái Gōng (Bái Gōng) asked Kǒngzǐ (Kǒngzǐ):
"Can one speak subtly?
What if a mountain is thrown into water?"
He replied:
"A good swimmer can retrieve it."
He asked:
"What if water is poured into water?"
He replied:
"When the waters of Zī (Zī) and Mín (Mín) mix,
Yì Yá (Yì Yá) tasted them and distinguished them."
East house, west house.
To abandon rituals and customs is
like living in a house.
If the east house calls itself the west house,
and the west house calls itself the east house,
even Gāotáo's (Gāotáo) rituals cannot manage it.
Boundless journey to the nine heavens (jiǔgāi).
Lú Áo (Lú Áo) traveled to the North Sea (Běihǎi)
and saw a scholar with deep-set eyes and dark hair,
tears flowing and eagle-like shoulders,
broad upper body and slender lower body.
He saw Áo (Áo),
lowered his arm,
and was sitting on a turtle shell eating clams.
Áo (Áo) said:
"Can you be friends with Áo (Áo)?"
The scholar smiled and said:
"I have an appointment with Hànmàn (Hànmàn) beyond the nine heavens (jiǔgāi)."
He raised his arm, straightened his body, and entered the clouds.
Two dragons (jiāo) grasp the boat.
There was a Cìfēi (Cìfēi) from Jīng (Jīng).
Crossing the river,
he reached the waves of Yáng Hóu (Yánghóu) in mid-stream,
where two dragons (jiāo) grasped his boat.
Cìfēi (Cìfēi) drew his sword and said:
"A warrior can be persuaded by benevolence and righteousness,
but cannot be robbed and plundered.
These are merely rotten bones and decaying flesh in the river!"
He held his sword and plunged into the river to stab the dragons (jiāo),
cutting off their heads,
and all the people in the boat were saved.
Orangutan (xīngxīng) and Magpie (gānhú).
Orangutans (xīngxīng) know the past but not the future.
Magpies (gānhú) know the future but not the past.
Orangutans (xīngxīng) know people's surnames and given names;
this is knowing the past.
They get drunk and are captured;
this is not knowing the future.
Magpies (gānhú)
are also called magpies (què).
When people approach, they chirp;
this is knowing the future.
They know when the year will be windy,
and build their nests in tree branches.
But people always take their eggs,
so it is said they do not know the past.
Encountering a storm while boating.
There was a person from Chǔ (Chǔ) who, while boating, encountered a great storm.
When the waves came,
he threw himself into the water.
It was not that he did not love life and feared death,
but that he was so confused by the fear of death that he forgot life.
Human desires and cravings are similar to this.
Wine clouds the spirit.
A drunken person bows to enter a city gate,
thinking a seven-foot-high gate can cross the Jiāng (Jiāng) and Huái (Huái) rivers,
and thinking an ordinary ditch. Wine clouds his spirit.
Fear clouds one's vital energy.
A timid person sees a marker stone at night and thinks it's a ghost;
sees a sleeping rock and thinks it's a tiger.
Fear clouds their vital energy.
Sacrificing to the gods of the well and stove.
People nowadays sacrifice to the gods of the well, stove, door, broom, mortar, and pestle,
not because they believe these gods can truly enjoy the offerings,
but for fear of their virtues being neglected, leading to endless trouble and suffering.
Receiving the autumn chariot.
Yǐn Rú (Yǐn Rú) studied charioteering for three years.
In the middle of the night, he dreamed of receiving the autumn chariot (qiūjià) from his master.
The next morning, he called on his master.
His master said:
"Today I will teach you the autumn chariot (qiūjià)."
Rú (Rú) said:
"I am very fortunate;
last night I dreamed of receiving it."
Value what one has, despise what one lacks.
Prince Qìngjì (Qìngjì) died by sword.
Yì (Yì) died by a peach club.
Zǐlù (Zǐlù) was pickled in Wèi (Wèi).
Sū Qín (Sū Qín) died at the hands of
the people of Qí (Qí).
No one fails to value what they possess
and despise what they lack.
Human nature.
Generally, human nature is such that:
in youth, one is wild and reckless;
in prime, one is violent and powerful;
in old age, one is fond of profit.
Three states, two powers.
There will be three *shì* (forces/potentials) and two *quán* (powers).
If a general is filled with courage and lightly regards the enemy,
and the soldiers are resolute and delight in battle,
this is called *qìshì* (momentum/spirit force).
If one person guards a pass,
a thousand men cannot get through,
this is called *dìshì* (terrain/geographical advantage).
To take advantage of their idleness and disorder,
and drive out their restless ones,
this is called *yīnshì* (situational advantage).
To be skilled in using spies,
appearing unexpectedly,
this is called *zhīquán* (power of knowledge).
To deploy troops directly in front,
and inflict many casualties on the enemy,
this is called *shìquán* (power of action).
Be Cautious Not to Do Good
A man marrying off his daughter
said:
"Go,
be cautious not to do good."
She asked:
"Am I then to do evil?"
He replied:
"If one refrains from doing good,
how much more so from doing evil?"
Treating the Disease of No Disease
A good physician
often treats the disease of no disease,
and therefore has no disease.
A sage often treats the calamity of no calamity,
and therefore has no calamity.
Actions Accord, Interests Agree
Marriage is made through a matchmaker,
but it is not because of a matchmaker that it succeeds.
Friendship is made through a third party,
but it is not because of a third party that it becomes intimate.
If actions accord and interests agree,
they will follow each other for a thousand *lǐ*.
If interests do not agree and actions differ,
even neighbors cannot communicate.
Lifting the Heavy and Holding the Light
Better a hundred pricks with a needle
than one prick with a knife.
Better one lift of a heavy load
than long holding a light one.
Better one month of hunger
than ten days of starvation.
Chicken Toes
There are no pure white foxes in the world,
yet there are pure white furs,
because they are gathered from many white parts.
