A good scholar is like the King of Qí eating chicken;
he must eat its toes.
Clarifying the Great with the Small, Discussing the Distant with the Near
Tasting one piece of meat
knows the flavor of the whole pot.
Hanging one feather of charcoal
knows the humidity and dryness of the air.
This is clarifying the great with the small.
Seeing one falling leaf
knows that the year is nearing its end.
Seeing ice in a jar
knows the coldness of the world.
This is discussing the distant with the near.
All Are Inappropriate to Say
On the day of sacrifice to talk about a dog giving birth;
on the day of taking a wife to talk about mourning clothes;
on the day of setting out wine to talk about visiting graves;
when crossing a river to talk about the waves of Yánghóu—
all are inappropriate.
Washing Hair
One who washes their hair continues even if hair falls out,
because what is lost is little,
and what is gained is much.
Posthumous Child
If one does not think of their father,
it is because there is no image in the heart.
If one does not dream of an image,
it is because there is no form in the eye.
Swallows Congratulate
When bathwater is ready, lice comfort each other.
When a grand mansion is completed, swallows and sparrows congratulate each other.
Fish Have No Ears, Cicadas Have No Mouth
Dodder has no roots but grows.
Snakes have no feet but move.
Fish have no ears but hear.
Cicadas have no mouth but sing.
Crying at a Crossroads, Weeping over Silk
Yángzǐ cried when he saw a crossroads,
because it could lead south or north.
Mòzǐ wept when he saw raw silk,
because it could be dyed yellow or black.
Spirits
Yándì died by fire and became the Kitchen God (*Zào*).
Yǔ toiled for the world, died
and became
the Earth God (*Shè*).
Hòujì created agriculture and died, becoming the Millet God (*Jì*).
Yì eliminated harms from the world and died, becoming *Zōngbù*.
This is how spirits are established.
Three Dangers
There are three dangers in the world:
little virtue yet great favor,
this is the first;
low talent yet high position,
this is the second;
no great achievement yet abundant emolument,
this is the third.
Digging Up Buried Treasures Brings Calamity
A tree that bears fruit twice
will surely have its roots harmed.
A family that digs up buried treasures
will surely suffer calamity.
Fortune and Misfortune
Those with hidden virtues will surely have open rewards.
Those with hidden conduct will surely have manifest fame.
A man from Sòng was fond of good deeds;
without cause, his black ox gave birth to a white calf,
and the father and son became blind without cause.
Afterward,
Chǔ attacked Sòng.
The able-bodied men died,
and the old and young all mounted the city wall.
When the city was breached, they were all slaughtered;
only the blind father and son were spared from mounting the wall.
When the siege was lifted,
the father and son both regained their sight.
On the frontier, there was a man skilled in divination.
His horse mysteriously ran away into the land of the Hú.
His father said:
"How can we know this isn't a blessing?"
Several months later, the horse returned.
The father said:
"How can we know this isn't a misfortune?"
His son loved riding and broke his thigh.
People offered condolences,
but the father said:
"How can we know this isn't a blessing?"
A year later,
the Hú people invaded the frontier.
The able-bodied men drew their bows and fought,
nine out of ten died.
Only because of his lameness,
the father and son protected each other.
Nine Sages Appear Once Every Thousand Years
Yáo had eight-colored eyebrows,
and nine apertures were clear and unobstructed,
with one word, all the people were in order.
Shùn had double pupils,
which is called "double brightness."
Yǔ had ears that penetrated and flowed,
which is called "great penetration."
King Wén had four nipples,
which is called "great benevolence."
Gāoyáo had a horse-like mouth,
which is called "utmost trustworthiness."
Yǔ was born from a stone.
Xiè was born from an egg.
Shǐhuáng was born able to write.
Yì had a long left arm and was good at archery.
These nine sages appear once every thousand years.
Biǎnquè
What is valued
is not his adjusting medicine according to the illness,
but his pressing the breath, pulse, and blood,
knowing where the illness originates.
What is valued in a sage
is not his meting out punishment according to the crime,
but his knowing where disorder arises.
Heroes and Outstanding Figures
Talent surpassing ten thousand people is called *yīng*.
A thousand people is called *jùn*.
A hundred people is called *háo*.
Ten people is called *jié*.
Yáng Yóujī's Divine Archery
The King of Chǔ hunted,
saw a white ape and shot at it.
The ape was good at dodging arrows;
no one could hit it.
So he ordered Yáng Yóujī to shoot.
As soon as he grasped the bow,
the ape hugged a tree and wailed,
then they knew Yáng Yóujī was a divine archer.
On Generals
There will be three teams, four virtues, five practices, and ten observances.
The three teams are:
understanding the Way of Heaven above,
familiarizing with the terrain below,
and discerning human sentiments in between.
The four virtues are:
benefiting the state without abandoning soldiers,
serving the ruler without regard for one's own life,
facing difficulty without fearing death,
and resolving doubts without evading punishment.
The five practices are:
gentleness that cannot be rolled up,
rigidity that cannot be broken,
benevolence that cannot be violated,
trustworthiness that cannot be confused,
and courage that cannot be infringed upon.
The ten observances are:

clear spirit, far-sighted planning, firm conduct, keen discernment, not being swayed by wealth, not being entangled by things, not being influenced by spirits, not being pushed by circumstances, being impervious to joy, and impervious to anger.
A state cannot be governed from outside,
and an army cannot be commanded from within.
Léng Děng Dēng Kē
story:
After the examination results were announced,
candidates gave their thanks to the Prime Minister.
The top scholar gave a speech.
There was a man named Dīng Léng who stammered.
He wanted to say "Léng děng dēng kē" (Léng and others passed the examinations),
but when he stepped forward, he repeatedly said "Léng děng dēng" and could not complete his sentence, so he retreated.
Wáng Lǎo
Wáng Yuánbǎo
was very rich.
Because his money notes were as numerous as his name (yuánbǎo means "gold ingot"),
people called money Wáng Lǎo.
Lǘ Míng Gǒu Fèi
Yǔ Xìn traveled from the Southern Dynasties to the North.
He only loved the "Hánshān Sì Bēi" (Stele of Hánshān Temple) composed by Wēn Zǐshēng.
Someone asked Yǔ Xìn:
"How is the North?"
He replied:
"Only that one stone tablet at Hánshān Temple is worthy of conversation;
the rest is like the braying of donkeys and the barking of dogs."
Diǎn Guǐ Bù Suàn Bóshì
Wáng, Yáng, Lú, and Luò had literary renown.
People discussed their flaws,
saying:
Yáng was fond of using ancient people's names,
which was called "diǎn guǐ bù" (counting ghosts on a register).
Luò was fond of using numerical couplets,
which was called "suàn bóshì" (the arithmetic doctor).
Yī Chāshǒu Yī Yùn Chéng
Wēn Tíngyún's literary thoughts were quick and marvelous.
Lǐ Yìshān once got a line of poetry:
"In the distant past, like Zhào Gōng,
thirty-six years as Prime Minister."
Wēn Tíngyún responded:
"In the recent past, like Guō Lìng,
twenty-four terms as Secretary."
Whenever Wēn Tíngyún composed a fu,
he would complete a rhyme with one clasp of his hands.
Línghú Táo often entrusted him with writing but
disliked his loose talk,
so he kept him at a distance.
Wēn Tíngyún slandered him, saying:
"How can a Secretary sit in a General's position?"
He was mocking his lack of learning.
Jiǔ Dīng Pán
The Táng imperial kitchen served dishes arranged on nine stacked plates,
called jiǔ dīng pán.
Bǎihé Cǎolǚ
During the Dàlì reign,
five-petal straw sandals were presented.
Later, bǎihé cǎolǚ (lily straw sandals) were presented.
Dà Màozi
Originally the attire of elderly commoners,
it was worn by the Later Wèi.
In early Táng, it was made of gauze and fine silk,
to block wind and dust.
Xímào
Originally a Qiāng garment,
it was made of sheep's wool.
During the Qín and Hàn, old mats were used to roll it up.
Women also wore it,
with a net hanging down from its four edges,
decorated with pearls and kingfisher feathers,
called xímào.
When Emperor Yáng went to Jiāngdū,
he ascended the Zǐyún Lóu (Purple Cloud Tower)
to view the market.
Wanting to see the women's figures,
he ordered them to remove the nets.
Jīn Yín Qìmǐn
The Xià and Shāng dynasties first used gold and silver vessels.
Jiǎo Nǔ
Yí Móu established the jiǎo nǔ (horn crossbow),
used on horseback.
For foot soldiers against enemies, wooden crossbows were used.
The Hàn army had an "eight-dòu crossbow,"
used to shoot at the Chǔ camp.
Its arrows could reach ten lǐ.
Jì Míng
Jì (hair bun) means "to join."
Women must have something joined to others.
Nǚwā Shì used sheep's wool to braid it,
tying it to the back.
She made hairpins from thorn wood and bamboo,
which pierced the hair.
Hèlián Shì created a comb
with twenty-four teeth,
deriving its meaning from "shū tōng" (to loosen and clear).
Yáo and Shùn used copper for hairpins.
Shùn added head ornaments for women;
hairpins and combs were mixed with ivory and tortoiseshell,
interspersed with jade.
On top of the bun, vermillion, kingfisher feathers, and ornate flowers were added,
and lead powder was applied.
The Shāng dynasty's bun was called Fèngjì (phoenix bun).
There was also the Yúnjì (cloud bun),
which swayed with every step,
hence called Bùyáo (step-sway).
In the Qín Shǐhuáng's palace, the Wàngxiānjì (gazing-at-immortals bun) was combed.
The Hàn palace had the Yíngchūnjì (welcoming-spring bun).
During Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's time, when various immortals descended with the Queen Mother,
they all wore Fēixiānjì (flying-immortal bun) and Pánlóngjì (coiling-dragon bun),
pierced with Fèngshǒuchāi (phoenix-head hairpins),
Kǒngquè Sāotóu (peacock scratching-head ornaments),
and Yúntóubì (cloud-head combs).
They swept their eyebrows into an "eight-character" shape.
Emperor Míng of Hàn's palace women combed the Bǎihé Fēnshāojì (lily-separated-ends bun)
and Tóngxīnjì (concentric bun).
They swept their eyebrows with qīngdài (dark blue pigment) in the èméi (moth-antenna) style.
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi's palace women swept their eyebrows into a liántóuméi (joined-head eyebrow) style.
Emperor Huì of Jìn's palace women combed Fúróngjì (lotus bun),
used multicolored flowers made of tongcao pith,
and swept their eyebrows with black ink.
One stroke connected to the heart,
long and slender,
called "Xiān'é Zhuāng" (immortal moth makeup).
During Emperor Wén of Suí's Huá Palace, the Jiǔzhēnjì (nine-chastities bun) was combed.
During the Wǔdé era of Táng, Píngfānjì (pacifying-barbarians bun) and Chánglèjì (eternal-joy bun) were combed.
During the Kāihuà era, the Shuānghuán Wàngxiānjì (double-loop gazing-at-immortals bun) was combed.
In the Zhēnyuán era, the Piānjìzi (asymmetrical bun) was made.
Nìfěn
Qín Mùgōng's daughter Nòng Yù
was skilled at playing the xiao.
Xiāo Shǐ
descended to the palace,
refined a spiritual scroll.
The first transformation was to apply it to Nòng Yù,
named fěn (powder).
Today's mercury
is nìfěn (greasy powder).
Yānzhī (rouge)
was originally made by the Yānzhī Fūrén from safflower.
Chinese people call safflower hónglán.
Shuǐzhī
Lotus is also called shuǐzhī (water iris)
and shuǐhuá (water flower).
Qiàn (gorgon fruit)
is also called jītóu (chicken head),
and also yàntóu (goose head).
Yàn Què Míng
Yàn (swallow)
is also called Tiānnǚ Zhéniǎo (Heavenly Maiden's Hibernating Bird),
also Xuánniǎo (Dark Bird),
and also Yǐ.
Formerly, Jiàn Dí obtained a swallow's egg and swallowed it,
giving birth to Shāng,
with the surname Zǐ.
Later, Yǐ was used for the character Kǒng.
Què (sparrow)
is also called Jiābīn (distinguished guest),
meaning it gathers in people's houses like guests.
Jī Wǔdé
Chicken is also called Dúyè (solitary night)
and Sīchén (dawn-announcer).
It has five virtues:
a comb on its head,
symbolizing civility (wén);
spurs on its feet,
symbolizing martial prowess (wǔ);
fighting when it encounters an enemy,
symbolizing courage (yǒng);
calling others when it finds food,
symbolizing righteousness (yì);
crowing at the proper time,
symbolizing trustworthiness (xìn).
Xiào Shíwǔ Zhāng
Sūn Kāng (孫康) wrote an essay, "The Essentials of Whistling" (《嘯旨》),
stating that whistling has fifteen chapters:
The first is "Granting Power" (權與),
the second is "Flowing Clouds" (流雲),
the third is "Deep Stream" (深溪),
the fourth is "High Cicadas" (高蟬),
the fifth is "Ghosts in Empty Woods" (空林鬼),
the sixth is "Apes of Wūxiá" (巫峽猿),
the seventh is "Descending Swans and Geese" (下鴻鵠),
the eighth is "Kites of Old Trees" (古木鳶),
the ninth is "Dragon's Roar" (龍吟),
the tenth is "Earthquake" (地動),
the eleventh is "Sūmén" (蘇門),
the twelfth is "Liú Gōng (劉公) Commands Ghosts" (劉公命鬼),
the thirteenth is "Ruan's (阮氏) Untrammeled Rhyme" (阮氏逸韻),
the fourteenth is "Main Chapter" (正章),
the fifteenth is "Concluding Chapter" (畢章).
The Imperial Examination Granted to This Eccentric Fellow.
Liú Huáng (劉黃)
was a protégé of Yáng Sìfù (楊嗣復).
According to the "Records of Tang Dynasty Examination Success" (《唐登科記》),
in the second year of Bǎolì (寶曆) (826 AD),
Yáng Sìfù (楊嗣復) passed thirty-five people,
including Péi Xiū (裴休).
At that time, Huáng (黃) ranked fifteenth.

He took the examinations with the "Rhapsody on Qí (齊) and Lǔ (魯) Meeting at Jiágǔ (夾谷)" (《齊魯會于夾谷賦》) and the "Poem on Boating with Comrades on Kūnmíng (昆明) Pond on the Last Day of the Month" (《晦日與同志昆明池泛舟詩》).
His policy essays, when he passed the examination, spoke directly,
which angered the palace eunuchs.
Chóu Shìliáng (仇士良) said to Sìfù (嗣復):
"How could you allow this eccentric fellow to pass the imperial examination of the state?"
Sìfù (嗣復) replied fearfully:
"When Huáng (黃) passed the examination with me in the past,
he was not yet eccentric."
The "Bringing Sū (蘇)" Dance Troupe.
Dù Bīn'gōng (杜邠公) was the governor of Yángzhōu (楊州)
and indulged in banquets.
Xuānzōng (宣宗) appointed Cuī Xuàn (崔鉉) to replace him,
and sent him off with a poem that said:
"The markets and prisons of one region have received a 'bringing Sū (蘇)'."
The Yángzhōu (楊州) army supervisor, Chuán Xī (傳希), heard the imperial poem
and immediately taught and practiced the "bringing Sū (蘇)" dance troupe
to welcome Cuī Gōng (崔公).
Dù (杜) was quite displeased by this.
When he retired and returned to Luòyáng (洛陽),
whenever he met someone from Wéiyáng (維楊), he would ask:
"Is 'bringing Sū' (來蘇) well?"
He was referring to Chuán Xī (傳希).
Smearing the Street Towers.
Lǐ JǐngRàng (李景讓) was the Grand Censor (御史大夫).
All high officials and noble relatives who had street-viewing towers had them smeared (with mud),
fearing his impeachments.
The Vice Prime Minister and Humiliation of the Censorate.
The Grand Censor (御史大夫) was called "Vice Prime Minister" (亞相).
An old saying goes,
within a hundred days of being appointed Vice Prime Minister,
if someone is promoted to a higher office,
it is called "humiliation of the Censorate" (辱臺).
The "Nodding Cuī (崔) Family."
All eight brothers of Cuī Yōng (崔雍) passed the Jinshì (進士) examination.
At the time, they were called the "Nodding Cuī (崔) Family."
Dù Mù (杜牧) Changes His Name.
Dù Mù (杜牧) dreamt that someone said to him:
"You have finished changing your name."
Not long after, he died.
Grandma Wǔ (武) and Grandma's Dance.
Zhèng Cān (鄭傪) brought out courtesans to entertain Zhào Shēn (趙紳),
but the dancer was already old.
A performer recited an impromptu verse:
"The Prime Minister (相公) is skilled in both civil and martial arts,
the Court Attendant (常侍) likes both the present and the past.
In the past, we heard of Grandma Wǔ (阿武婆),
now we see Grandma's dance (阿婆舞)."
Turtle Treasure.
Grand Marshal Xú Yànruò (徐彥若) traveled to Guǎngnán (廣南)
and crossed a small sea.
In shallow water, he found a glazed bottle,
inside which was a turtle about an inch long,
spinning incessantly.
The mouth of the bottle was extremely narrow,
and he did not know how it had entered.
At midnight,
he felt the boat listing heavily.
When he looked,
a multitude of turtles had piled up and boarded the boat, circling the bottle.
Xú (徐) was frightened and discarded it.
Later, he asked the ship's captain,
who said:
"This is called 'turtle treasure' (龜寶)."
Lǐ Yǐng's (李郢) poem says:
"The river wind kept me awake all night,
twenty-five sounds mark the long autumn watch."
Three Absences on the Face.
Lǐ Kuān (李寬), the Court Attendant (常侍), had a subordinate named Lú (盧),
who was good at physiognomy.
He said:
"There are three things absent from Lǐ Gōng's (李公) face:
no sons, no home, and no grave."
The Duke had several sons,
all of whom died before him.
He had a home in his native village,
but never got to return,
dying in another province.
When his body was being transported home by boat,
the boat capsized,
and his bones sank.
The Elixir for Lone Success.
Xǔ Táng (許棠) passed the imperial examination in his later years.
He once said:
"Since achieving this one success,
my bones and muscles feel light and strong,
better than when I was young."
Thus, he knew that one's name on the list was the elixir for lone success.
The Dragon King Executes Water Creatures.
Ài Zǐ (艾子) hid in the sea.
At night, he heard crying voices saying:
"Yesterday, the Dragon King (龍王) decreed
that all water creatures with tails should be executed.
I am a turtle,
so I fear execution and cry."
Then he heard another crying voice saying:
"You, a frog, have no tail,
why do you cry?"
It said:
"Fortunately, I have no tail now,
but I fear that the matter of my tadpole days will be brought up."
Péng Zǔ (彭祖) Dies.
Ài Zǐ (艾子) saw an old woman dressed in coarse mourning clothes,
weeping very sadly.
Ài Zǐ (艾子) asked:
"Who is your deceased husband?"
She said:
"Péng Zǔ (彭祖)."
Ài Zǐ (艾子) said:
"Péng Zǔ (彭祖) lived for eight hundred years before dying,
which is certainly not short;
you should have no regrets."
The old woman said:
"My husband living eight hundred years is indeed no regret,
but there are those who live nine hundred years and do not die.
How could I not regret that?"
The Course of Nature.
Two pieces of wood rub against each other and ignite fire;
metal and fire meet and flow;
round things always roll,
hollow things always float;
these are the courses of nature.
What One Likes Becomes a Calamity.
Those good at swimming drown,
those good at riding fall.
Each, by what they like,
turns it into their own calamity.
Gòng Gōng (共工) Strikes Mount Bùzhōuzhī (不周之山).
Gòng Gōng (共工), with his strength,
struck Mount Bùzhōuzhī (不周之山),
causing the earth to tilt to the southeast.
He competed with Gāo Xīn (高辛) for the emperorship,
and then submerged himself in a deep pool.
Yue King Yì (越王翳) hid in a deserted mountain.
The Yue people smoked him out.
If a weapon is strong, it is destroyed;
if wood is strong, it breaks;
if leather is tough, it cracks;
if teeth are hard, they wear out before the tongue.
The soft and weak
are the basis of life;
the hard and strong
are the companions of death.
Sickness Transforms into a Tiger.
Niú Āi (牛哀) fell ill
and in seven days transformed into a tiger.
His elder brother went in to observe him,
and the tiger pounced and killed him.
End of Volume Twenty-five.
Feeling in the Dark.
Xǔ Jìngzōng (許敬宗) was naturally forgetful.
When he met people, he often forgot them.
He then said:
"You are hard to remember.
If I met Liú (劉), Shěn (沈), Cáo (曹), or Xiè (謝),
I could recognize them even by feeling in the dark."
Yùshù
Yúnyáng Xiàn had many stories of Hàn imperial villas.
There was a tree resembling a locust tree but with finer leaves.
Scholars all called it the yùshù.
Yáng Xióng's “Gānquán Fù” says:
"Yùshù are verdant and lush."
However, Zuǒ Sī believed that it was a false name for something rare and wonderful,
not real,
merely similar.
Língyùn's beard
Xiè Língyùn had a beautiful beard.
Before his execution,
he donated it to the Qíyuán Sì temple in Nánhǎi to be offered to Vimalakīrti.
The temple treasured it.
During Emperor Zhōngzōng's reign,
Princess Ānlè played the "hundred herbs contest" on the fifth day,
and sent someone to take it.
Then she cut off and discarded the rest.
The Běidǒu transforms into seven monks
Lǐ Chúnfēng reported:
"The seven star officials of the Běidǒu will transform into humans
and arrive tomorrow to drink wine at the West Market."
He sent someone to watch for them.
There were seven people drinking two dàn together.
Tàizōng sent someone to summon them.
The seven people laughed and said:
"This must be that little fellow Lǐ Chúnfēng talking about us."
Suddenly they vanished.
Gazing at the Shěnglóu
Cuī Rìzhī regretted not holding one of the eight high positions.
As Tàicháng Qīng,
he built a tower facing the Shàngshū Shěng.
People called it "Master Cuī gazing at the Shěnglóu."
Wáng Wéi plagiarizes others' poems
Wáng Wéi liked Buddhism,
hence his courtesy name Mójí.
His nature was lofty and profound.
He acquired Sòng Zhīwèn's Wǎngchuān 別yè,
whose mountains and waters were exceptionally beautiful;
today it is the Qīngliáng Sì temple.
Wéi had a poetic reputation,
but he liked to plagiarize others' poem lines.
For example, "Walking to where the water ends,
sitting and watching the clouds rise."
This is a poem from the Yīnghuá Jí.
"Misty paddy fields where white dew flies,
shady summer woods where orioles sing."
This is a poem by Lǐ Jiāyòu.
Monopolizing the field
When Táng people gathered for banquets, they always composed poems,
and one person would be chosen to "monopolize the field."
Guō Ài married Princess Shēngpíng.
At a grand gathering,
Lǐ Duān "monopolized the field."
When escorting Minister Liú on his tour of the Jiānghuái,
Qián Qǐ "monopolized the field."
Dūlú Yuánzhuàng Gē
Yuán Zài had long monopolized power.
A guest composed the "Dūlú Yuánzhuàng Gē"
to allude to his perilous situation and satirize him.
Zài wept upon reading it.
Tigers and mice
Lù Chángyuán, for his old virtues, was made Xuānwǔ Xíngjūn Sīmǎ,
and Hán Yù was the Xún Guān.
They served together in the same bureau.
Someone scoffed at the great disparity in their ages.
Yù said:
"Tigers and mice
are both among the twelve zodiac animals.
What disparity is there?"
Ascending Huàshān's peak
Hán Tuìzhī was fond of novelty.
He ascended Huàshān's highest peak with a guest.
Unable to return,
he went mad and wailed loudly.
The Huàyīn magistrate used every means to retrieve him.
When he got down,
the Huái imperial edict on bad poetry
In his later years, Emperor Dézōng's
poetry was quite skillful.
Grand Tutor Dù was in Huáinán
and presented a hundred poems by Cuī Shúqīng.
The Emperor said:
"These are bad poems,
why present them?"
At the time, it was called the "Huái imperial edict on bad poetry."
The prime minister is without virtue
Xī Áng and Wéi Zhì were good friends.
One day they discussed the prime ministers of the current dynasty.
Zhì said:
"Who is the most without virtue?"
Áng said:
"It is Wéi Ānshí."
Soon after, he ran out in a fright
and encountered Jí Wēn.
Wēn asked:
"Why this panic?"
He replied:
"Just now I was discussing with Minister Wéi who the most virtueless prime minister was.
I wanted to say Jí Xù,
but I mistakenly said Wéi Ānshí."
Immediately after,
he spurred his horse and ran again,
reaching the residence of Minister Fáng.
Guǎn held his hand and comforted him,
and again he named Fáng Róng as the answer.
Áng offended three people in one day.
Only Wéi Zhì then broke off relations with him.
Wūzhīqí
There was a fisherman in Chǔzhōu
who, while fishing in the Huái River, caught an ancient lock
that did not break.
The Inspector Lǐ Tāng gathered a large number of people to pull it.
When the lock reached its end,
a macaque leaped out
and then disappeared again.
Later, verifying with the Shānhǎi Jīng, it said:
"A water beast that loves to cause harm.
Yǔ locked it up,
named Wūzhīqí."
Heaven and Hell
Lǐ Zhōu said:
"If Śākyamuni were born in China,
he would establish teachings like Zhōu and Kǒng.
If Zhōu and Kǒng were born in the West,
they would establish teachings like Śākyamuni.
If Heaven doesn't exist, so be it;
if it does, gentlemen ascend it.
If Hell doesn't exist, so be it;
if it does, villains enter it."
Mágū offers wine
Lǐ Bì presented himself as given to the fantastical.
Once he told a guest:
"Have the family sweep and clean,
for Master Hóngyá is coming tonight."
Someone gave him fine wine.
Coincidentally, a guest arrived,
and he said:
"Mágū has brought wine,
let us share it."
Before he finished,
the gatekeeper said:
"Such-and-such a Shìláng wants his wine flask back."
Bì ordered it returned,
showing no sign of shame.
Snake wine cures wind disease
Lǐ Zhōu's younger brother suffered from wind disease.
Someone said snake wine cures wind disease.
So he sought a black snake,
placed it alive in a jar,
and brewed it with yeast and malt.
For several days, the snake's sounds did not cease.
When it was ready,
the aroma was intensely potent.
He poured a full cup and drank it.
Immediately, it turned into water,
only hair remained.
Hot wind
Zhèng Yúnkuí and Wáng Yànbó were neighbors.
Once, a guest seeking medical treatment
mistakenly visited Yúnkuí.
Kuí diagnosed:
"The hot wind is quite severe."
The guest was puzzled.
Someone said that the prescriptions were not as good as those of Wáng Gòngfèng next door.
The guest fled in surprise.
From then on, whenever there was a disagreement or criticism,
he would say "hot wind."
Pen mound
The monk Huáisù from Chángshā
loved cursive script,
and claimed to have mastered the samādhi of cursive script.
He discarded his pens, piling them up,
and buried them at the foot of a mountain,
calling it the "pen mound."
Simple means easy, straightforward means same
Róufú Wáng Shēng,
when asked about the difficulty of governing,
Shēng replied:
"Simple means easy."
When again asked:
"Are Confucianism and Buddhism on the same path?"
He said:
"Straightforward means same."
Yuánhé Tǐ
After Yuánhé,
scholarship in prose became eccentric due to Hán Yù,
and became abstruse due to Fán Zōngshī.
In gēxíng, it became unrestrained due to Zhāng Jí.
In poetry, it became exaggerated and forceful due to Mèng Jiāo,
superficial due to Bái Jūyì,
and decadent due to Yuán Zhěn.
All were named Yuánhé Tǐ.
Generally, the style of Tiānbǎo emphasized substance,
the style of Dàlì emphasized frivolity,
the style of Zhēnyuán emphasized profligacy,
and the style of Yuánhé emphasized the grotesque.
Western Excursion and Tax Exemption
Emperor Mínghuáng desired to make a western excursion.
Péi Huīqīng and Zhāng Jiǔlíng advised him, saying:
"The people's threshing grounds are not yet finished."
Lǐ Línfǔ said:
"The two capitals,
Your Majesty, are your eastern and western palaces.
Why bother choosing a time?
If it obstructs harvesting,
we can simply exempt the taxes along the route."
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and that very day set off on his western excursion to Cháng'ān.
Within ten days,
Zhāng and Péi were both dismissed,
and Niú Xiānkè was promoted.
Father-in-law and Son-in-law
Zhāng Pò and Zhāng Shú were both in the Hànlín Academy.
Because Pò had married a princess,
he alone was bestowed with rare treasures.
Shú said:
"This is for the father-in-law and the son-in-law,
not a gift from the Son of Heaven to a scholar."
Péi Mín Encounters a Real Tiger
When Mín was garrisoned in Běipíng,
the area had many tigers.
Mín was skilled in archery.
One day he killed more than thirty tigers.
An old man said:
"These are leopards (biāo),
they resemble tigers but are not."
Mín said:
"Where is a real tiger?"
The old man said:
"Go north and you will find one."
Mín galloped on horseback and went there.
From a thicket, a tiger leaped out,
small but fiercely powerful.
With one roar,
the mountains and rocks trembled.
Mín and his horse recoiled,
his bow and arrows fell,
he narrowly escaped.
From then on, he never shot again.
Bìluò Bēi
In Jiàngzhōu there is a stele.
The seal script is different from ancient characters.
On it are the two characters "Bìluò,"
so people call it the Bìluò Bēi.
Ascending the Steps in Socks
Wéi Zhì was ill.
Minister Fáng sent his sons to inquire about him.
Inside the sleeping quarters, all was covered with mats and carpets.
He ascended the steps in socks.
The serving maids all laughed.
Lùshān Laments at Mǎwéi
When Ān Lùshān heard of Concubine Yáng's death at Mǎwéi,
he sighed and lamented for several days.
Línfǔ had nurtured him,
Guózhōng had incited his rage,
yet his inner sentiments had their own origin.
Lǐ Guāngbì Commands the Troops
Guō Fényáng entered from Hétāng.
Grand Commandant Lǐ replaced him in leading his troops.
It was the old encampment,
the old soldiers,
the old banners.
But with one command from Guāngbì,
their spirit and vigor completely transformed.
Renouncing the World is a Task for a Great Man
Cui Zhàogōng asked Jìngshān, saying:
"Should this disciple renounce the world?"
He replied:
"Renouncing the world is a task for a great man;
it is not something prime ministers and generals can do."
Lǒngxī Lǐ Zhēn
Once believed that his aristocratic lineage was superior to his official rank.
Though he rose to the position of Zhì Shǐ,
when writing to others,
he only referred to himself as Lǒngxī Lǐ Zhēn.
Official Pigs as a Nuisance
Lú Sì was appointed Administrator of Guózhōu.
He reported that Guózhōu had several thousand official pigs,
which were quite a nuisance to the people.
The Emperor said:
"What if they were moved to Shāyuàn?"
He replied:
"Are the people of Tóngzhōu not also Your Majesty's people?
The nuisance would be the same.
These useless animals would be better off given to people to eat."
Emperor Dézōng said:
"You govern Guózhōu,
yet you worry about the people elsewhere;
you have the talent of a prime minister."
From then on, he intended to use Qǐ.
Yú Gōng Changes the Report
Emperor Dézōng read the report announcing the recapture of the capital.
When he reached, "Your servant has cleansed the palace,
reverently visited the imperial tombs,
the bells and stands are undisturbed,
the temple appearance is as before,"
he was moved to tears and choked up.
The report
was the composition of Yú Gōngyì.
Gōngyì was later resented by Lù Zhì,
who slandered him for improper conduct at home.
He was bestowed with a scroll of the Xiàojīng,
and his career was unfortunate.
The court and populace lamented this.
Máihuái Cūn
Mǎ Suì was campaigning against Lǐ Huáiguāng.
He led his troops to set up camp
and asked for the name of the place, "Máihuái Cūn."
He happily said:
"We are sure to capture the bandit!"
And indeed, they did.
The Buddha's Sweat
At the Xiàngguó Sì in Biànzhōu,
it was said that the Buddha sweated.
Liú Xuánzuǒ personally brought gold and silk to donate,
and restored the fasting hall.
Scholars and commoners competed to gather,
donating as if fearing they would be too late.
Tens of thousands were collected,
which were used to support the army.
Painting an Eagle
Péi Yánlíng, presuming upon imperial favor, was frivolous and impetuous.
Gù Shàolián painted an eagle
with many birds screeching at it,
and presented it to the Emperor.
The Emperor understood the public's anger,
and consequently did not give him great responsibility.
Felling the Huai Trees of the Two Capitals' Roads
During Zhēnyuán,
Dù Ài wanted to fell the huai trees along the roads to the two capitals for firewood.
Wèinán Commandant Zhāng Zào replied:
"The trees where Shào Bó rested
were not to be cut down;
how could the old haunts of the former emperor
be suitable for felling?"
Thereupon, he stopped.
Envy the Western River
Lù Yǔ, as a youth, served Jìnglíng Chánshī.
When the master passed away,
he wrote a poem expressing his feelings, saying:
"I do not envy white jade cups,
I do not envy golden *léi* vessels.
Nor do I envy entering the ministries in the morning,
nor entering the Censorate in the evening.
A thousand, ten thousand times I envy the waters of the Western River,
for they once flowed beneath Jìnglíng city."
The Emperor Does Not Suspect Me
After Emperor Dézōng recovered the palace,
he constantly feared troubles arising
and appeased the regional governors.
Only General Hún, when his petitions were not granted,
would happily say:
"The Emperor does not suspect me."
Imperial Edicts Not Kept in Private Homes
Gāo Zhēngōng served as a Scholar of the Central Secretariat.
His home had no drafts of edicts.
He said:
"Imperial edicts cannot be kept in private homes."
Wǔfú Tàiyǐ
During the Yuánhé reign,
Yīnyáng masters said that the Wǔfú Tàiyī was in Shǔ.
Thus, Liú Pì built the Wǔfú Tower.
Fú Zài wrote an inscription for it,
saying:
"Hearing the voice of heaven,
seeing the backs of birds."
Liú Pì swallowed people.
When Liú Pì first suffered from a heart ailment,
whenever a person came from outside,
he would want to swallow them.
Cuī Zuǒshí, who was in the same prefecture, was corpulent,
and Pì squatted on the ground and swallowed him.
Heart Ailment.
Wéi Huǎn and Lǐ Pán both became incapacitated due to heart ailments.
Wéi often suspected being poisoned,
and drank water from a locked well.
Lǐ Yì was young and prone to suspicion of illness,
which was also a heart ailment.
The heart,
being the spiritual abode,
when afflicted by external things,
never fully recovers.
Excessive contemplation
and excessive doubt
are the root of the illness.
Táng Qú excelled at weeping.
Táng Qú was old and had achieved nothing.
He excelled at weeping,
with a mournful and poignant tone,
making listeners shed tears.
At a banquet in Tàiyuán,
he wept after drinking heavily,
making everyone unhappy.
The host ended the feast because of him.
Three Prefects of Jīngzhào.
Xiànzōng had long been personally involved in governing.
Suddenly, he asked:
"How many prefects does Jīngzhào have?"
Lǐ Jífǔ replied:
"Jīngzhào has three prefects:
one Grand Prefect (Dàyǐn),
and two Vice Prefects (Shàoyǐn)."
People considered it a good reply.
Scolding a Monk.
When Wéi Guànzhī was Right Chancellor (Yòuchéng),
the palace monk Guǎngxuān came to his gate and said:
"Your Excellency will soon be appointed Chancellor (Xiàng)."
Guànzhī scolded him, saying:
"How dare you speak such impertinent words!"
He ordered a memorial to be drafted.
The monk left in fright.
Grass growing on the polo field.
Xiànzōng asked Zhào Zōngrú:
"People say that when you were in Jīngzhōu,
grass grew on the polo field.
Why was that?"
He replied:
"Grass growing does not hinder the polo ball."
The Emperor laughed.
Three ways to release a cangue.
Wáng Yuè was the commander of Duòzhì.
When soldiers violated regulations,
he put them in a cangue,
which was only removed after a hundred days.
There were three ways to remove it before a hundred days:
I die, then it is removed;
you die, then it is removed;
the Son of Heaven's command, then it is removed.
Because of this, not a single offense was committed.
Wáng Yànbó's medical practice was about to flourish.
Wáng Yànbó's medical practice was about to become popular.
He boiled medicine in his courtyard,
and old and young crowded his gate.
Yànbó pointed and said:
"Those with heat drink this;
those with cold drink this;
those with qi disorders drink this."
The next day,
each brought gold and silk as payment.
Whoever took it, none was ineffective.
The medicine seller Sòng Qīng.
Sòng Qīng sold medicine in the Cháng'ān market.
Whenever court officials were transferred or demoted,
he would buy medicine and send it as a gift.
When poor scholars requested medicine,
he often tore up many of their vouchers;
when people faced urgent difficulties,
he would help them with everything he had.
His annual income,
was also a hundredfold.
Therefore, Cháng'ān referred to someone righteous as "the medicine seller Sòng Qīng."
White wheat flour.
During the Dòu clan's prime,
a servant amassed wealth from the relatives
to supply white wheat flour.
Doctors said:
"White wheat is neutral in nature."
Because of this, they ate as much as they wanted and never fell ill.
Later, someone reported that what the servant supplied was ordinary wheat.
All the relatives suddenly developed fevers at once.
Láohuáng and Jìnhuáng.
Old folks said:
"For fifty years, there were many who suffered from 'heat yellowing' (rèhuáng).
In the old wards and alleys, there were businesses that opened wide their doors
to offer 'branded yellowing' (láohuáng).
In the Bàmí water,
people often sat from day to dusk,
which was called 'immersed yellowing' (jìnhuáng).
In recent times, these are all gone,
but people suffer from waist and leg pain,
which is suspected to be caused by tea."
Sand Embankment and Fire City.
Whenever a chancellor was appointed,
the ceremony transcended the ranks.
From the east of the inner city to his residence,
sand was laid on the road,
called a "Sand Embankment" (Shādī).
Sometimes, when officials inquired about his health,
the authorities would set up tents and arrange the ranks.
On New Year's Day, Winter Solstice, and Beginning of Autumn,
all officials would prepare their elaborate umbrellas,
and arrange candles up to five or six hundred torches,
called a "Fire City" (Huǒchéng).
When the Chancellor was about to arrive at the Fire City,
all the lights would be extinguished to avoid him.
Hall Documents.
Chancellors handled matters with "Hall Documents" (Táng'àn).
Instructions to all bureaus were called "Hall Dispatches" (Tángtiē).
Signing names in sequence was called "Flower Signature" (Huāyā).
When imperial edicts (Huángchì) were issued,
minor discrepancies were called "Tabled in Hall" (Tiētáng).
Hall Elders.
Chancellors referred to each other as "Hall Elders" (Tánglǎo).
Officials in the two departments referred to each other as "Pavilion Elders" (Gélǎo).
Secretaries (Chéng) and Directors (Láng) referred to each other as "Chiefs of the Bureau" (Cáozhǎng).
Officials like Lángzhōng, Yuánwàiláng, Yùshǐ, and Yíbǔ referred to each other as "Chiefs of the Court" (Yuànzhǎng).
Censors (Yùshǐ) referred to each other as "Lord Duke" (Duāngōng).
The Minister of Personnel (Púshè) rode a horse into the department.
According to old customs of the Southern Department (Nánshěng),
the Right and Left Ministers (Púshè) would ascend,
the Chancellors would escort them,
the Censors would hold the documents,
the Associate Directors (Yuánwàiláng) would hold the brushes,
the Palace Censors (Diànzhōng Shìyùshǐ) would guard the gate,
and all, from Secretaries (Chéng) and Directors (Láng) to Vice Censors-in-Chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng), would bow.
Court opinion held that this was treating the sovereign as an equal,
and the ceremonial regulations were too elaborate.
After the Yuánhé reign,
all old rites were abolished,
except for riding a horse into the department gate, which remained as before.
The Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) was the "eye of the department."
The Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) was the "Director of the Southern Department" (Nánshěng Shèrén).
The Ministry of Merits (Kǎogōng) and Ministry of Finance (Dùzhī) were "ranked as officials" (Zhènháng).
The Ministry of Justice (Bǐbù) was called "eating under the corridor,"
referring to feeding its retainers,
and was nicknamed "comparison plates" (Bǐpán).
The twenty-four bureaus called the Left and Right Departments (Zuǒyòu Sī) the "Capital Officials" (Dūguān).
A saying in the department went:
"The Rear Rank, Ministry of Sacrifices (Hòuháng Cíbù),
is not worth the Middle Rank, Ministry of Capital Affairs (Zhōngháng Dūmén);
the Middle Rank, Ministry of Justice and Ministry of Revenue (Zhōngháng Xínghù),
is not worth the Front Rank, Ministry of the Imperial Stud (Qiánháng Jiàkù)."
Xiāo Zhāi (Xiao Studio).
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng built a temple,
and ordered Xiāo Zǐyún to write the character "蕭" (Xiāo) in flying-white script.
Even today, one character remains.
Lǐ Yuē exhausted his wealth to buy it from Jiānghuái and brought it back to Dōngluò.
He built a room to admire it,
calling it "Xiāo Zhāi."
Lotus-petal Clepsydra.
The Yuè monk Língchè made a device from copper leaves as a lotus-petal clepsydra (Liánhuā Lòu).
It was placed on the surface of water in a basin.
Water leaked from a hole in the bottom,
and it would sink when half full.
It sank twelve times every day and night,
serving as the correct measure for monastic practice.
Waiting Hall.
Formerly, all officials for early court assembly
would stand with their horses outside Wàngxiānmén.
The Chancellors would stay in the Guāngzhái carriage yard to avoid wind and rain.
In the early Yuánhé reign,
the Waiting Hall (Dàilòuyuàn) was established.
The Noblest of Women
Fūrén Miáo was of noble birth.
Her father was the Grand Mentor (Tàishī),
her maternal uncle was Zhāng Hédōng,
her husband was Yán Shǎng,
her son was Hóngjìng,
and her son-in-law was Wéi Gāo.
Among noble women of recent times,
none can compare to her.
Retirement Edict
When Gāo Zhēnggōng retired,
the edict stated:
“Retiring due to age
is a practice with precedents.
In recent times, those lacking integrity
rarely follow this path.”
At that time, Dù Sītú was over seventy,
but had no intention of requesting retirement.
Péi Jìnggōng, then a chamberlain (shèrén),
used this to criticize him.
Measuring Necks for Cangues
Lǐ Xiān,
Lǐ Qí’s younger cousin,
was the Prefect of Sòngzhōu.
Upon hearing of Lǐ Qí’s rebellion,
he wept bitterly,
drove out all his wives, children, servants, and maids, regardless of age,
measured their necks for cangues,
and surrendered himself to the Surveillance Commissioner (Guāncháshǐ).
The court pitied him
and merely demoted him slightly.
Competing for Inscriptions
During the Zhǎng’ān era, there was a scramble for tomb inscriptions,
like merchants in a market.
When a high official passed away,
his household would be like a marketplace,
with even clamorous competition
not initiated by the mourning family.
Péi Jūn’s son requested an inscription from Chancellor Wéi,
offering rolls of silk and bolts of patterned cloth.
Chancellor Wéi declined, saying:
“I would rather die
than casually compose one.”
Cuī Zhāo Bribes
Péi Jí said:
“When I was young,
my maternal uncle, a court official
with a distinguished reputation,
returned from court
and sighed:
‘What kind of person is Cuī Zhāo,
that everyone praises him?
This must be due to bribery.
How can things not be in chaos with such practices?’
Before he finished speaking,
the doorkeeper announced that Assistant Prefect (Lángzhōng) Cuī from Shòuzhōu was waiting to call.
My maternal uncle angrily shouted at the doorkeeper,
and was about to whip him.
After a long while,
he reluctantly went out.
Soon after,
he urgently requested tea,
then wine and fruits,
and also ordered fodder for the horses and food for the servants.
I asked:
‘Why were you so arrogant before and so respectful now?’
When he re-entered the house,
he had a look of satisfaction.
It turned out Cuī Zhāo had presented him with a thousand bolts of official silk.”
Numerous White-Robed Scholars
A visitor satirized Sòng Jì, saying:
“Recently, why are there so many white-robed scholars (báipáozi)?”
Sòng Jì replied:
“It is because the scarlet-robed (fēipáozi) and purple-robed (zǐpáozi) officials have multiplied and transformed them.”
Announcing Examination Topics in Advance
In the early Jiànzhōng era,
Péi Jì said:
“If the Ministry of Rites were to announce to the world in advance:
‘In a certain year, such-and-such topic will be tested,
and such-and-such historical texts will be required,’
and it turned out to be true on the day,
this would also be a method for diligent study.”
Ranking Fruits by Name
Lǐ Zhífāng often ranked fruits by name,
placing green plums (lǜlǐ) first,
ridged pears (lénglǐ) second,
cherries (yīngtáo) third,
tangerines (gānzi) fourth,
and grapes (pútáo) fifth.
Someone recommended lychees (lìzhī),
and he said:
“The foremost among those specially presented.”
Sòng Wǔ’s Frankness
Sòng Jì was old in the literary arena.
During an examination, he failed a rhyme in his rhapsody,
and beating his chest, he exclaimed:
“Sòng Wǔ has been frank again!”
Later, when the Ministry of Rites submitted the list of successful candidates,
Dézōng asked:
“Was Sòng Wǔ frank (tǎnshuài)?”
The Lú Shì Záshuō differs slightly.
The Dragon Playing a Flute
Lǐ Zhōu obtained smoke-stained bamboo from a forest dwelling,
cut it to make a flute,
which was as hard as iron and stone,
and gave it to Lǐ Móu.
Lǐ Móu was the best flutist in the world.
One moonlit night, he was playing it while boating.
Suddenly, a guest called out to the boat, asking for a ride.
Once aboard,
the guest asked him to play.
The sound was clear and powerful,
enough to split mountains and rocks.
When it entered the waves,
the water seemed to breathe and surge,
shattering in response to the sound.
The guest was sometimes invisible,
and was suspected to be a dragon (jiāolóng).
Playing Flute on an Autumn Night
Lǐ Móu played the flute on an autumn night at Guāzhōu.
At the first note,
all living creatures fell silent.
After several movements,
a gentle breeze came rustling.
Shortly after,
the merchants in the boat began to sigh in complaint and weep in sorrow.
Playing the Five-Stringed Lute
Zhào Bì played the five-stringed lute (wǔxián),
saying:
“At first, my heart guides it;
in the middle, my spirit encounters it;
in the end, heaven follows it.
With vastness,
my eyes become ears,
my ears become nose,
and I no longer know whether the five-stringed lute is Zhào Bì,
or Zhào Bì is the five-stringed lute.”
Chancellor’s Lotus
Yú Jié found that a musical piece titled “Xiāngfū Lián” (相夫怜, Pity the Husband)
had an inelegant name.
A guest said:
“There was once an auspicious lotus in a Chancellor’s residence in the Southern Dynasties,
hence it was named ‘Xiàngfǔ Lián’ (相府蓮, Chancellor’s Lotus).
Later, the pronunciation became corrupted.”
Silver Deer
Yán Xiàn’s houseboy,
named Yín Lù (Silver Deer),
later served Duke Lǔ (Lǔgōng) for life.
Xiàmǎlíng
At Dǒng Zhòngshū’s tomb,
his disciples would all dismount their horses upon arrival,
hence it was called Xiàmǎlíng (Dismounting Horse Mound).
The pronunciation was corrupted to “Háma Líng” (Frog Mound).
Known for Wit, etc.
Wit (Huīxié),
Hè Zhīzhāng;
Frivolity (Qīngbó),
Zǔ Yǒng;
Playful Language (Hènyǔ),
Hèlán Táng;
Poetry on Plums (Yǒng Lǐ),
Xiāo Xīn;
Fable (Yùyán),
Lǐ Shū;
Riddle (Yǐnyǔ),
Zhāng Zhuó;
Quick-wittedness (Jījíng),
Lǐ Zhōu;
Allegorical Puns (Xiēhòu),
Yáo Xiàn;
Corrupted Pronunciation (Yǔ’é),
Evocative Description (Yìngdài),
Lǐ Zhífāng;
Observing People (Mùrén),
Cáo Zhuó.
Assassins
When there were no soldiers or weapons under Heaven,
there were many assassins.
Lǐ Miǎn served as the Captain of Kāifēng.
Among the prisoners, there was one who was a man of spirit.
Lǐ Miǎn released him and let him escape.
Later, Lǐ Miǎn traveled in Héběi
and coincidentally met the former prisoner.
He welcomed him home and treated him generously.
He told his wife:
"This man saved my life.
How can I repay his kindness?"
His wife said:
"Would a thousand bolts of silk be enough?"
He said:
"Not yet."
"Would two thousand bolts be enough?"
He said:
"Not yet."
His wife said:
"Better to kill him."
His servant pitied Lǐ Miǎn
and secretly informed him,
so he escaped.
In the middle of the night,
he arrived at Jīn Diàn.
An old man said:
"There are many fierce beasts here.
How dare you travel at night?"
Lǐ Miǎn explained his situation,
and a person on the beam glanced down and said:
"I almost mistakenly killed an elder!"
Then he left.
Before dawn,
he brought the heads of the former prisoner and his wife to show Lǐ Miǎn.
Captive's Tent Tea
Dǎng Lǔ was an envoy to Xīfān,
and tea was brewed in his tent.
Dǎng Lǔ said:
"It dispels worries and quenches thirst;
this is what tea is."
The Fān people said:
"We also have it."
Then they brought out several varieties:
"This is from Shòuchūn,
this is from Gùzhǔ,
this is from Qíhūn."
Ship Pigeons
When a ship departs on a sea route,
it must raise pigeons.
If the ship sinks,
even from several thousand *lǐ*, they can still return home.
Wife Avenge Father's Wrong
During the Zhēnyuán era,
there was a man in Cháng'ān who took a wife.
After several years,
she suddenly disappeared.
One night,
she arrived carrying a human head,
and told her husband:
"I had a father's wrong to avenge,
thus I was here.
Now it is avenged.
Please let me return."
She wept and bid farewell,
exiting the door like the wind.
A moment later, she returned,
cut the throats of their two sons, and left.
Roaring Hall
Whenever one enters a hall and refrains from speaking or laughing,
if there is something unbearable,
and someone from the miscellaneous ranks laughs loudly,
then everyone seated also laughs.
This is called "hōng táng" (roaring hall).
Reading is not as good as writing.
Zhāng Cān personally copied the Nine Classics.
He often said that reading is not as good as writing.
Black Silk Lined Paper
Between Sòng and Bó,
there was paper woven with ruled lines,
called "wūsīlán zhǐ" (black silk lined paper).
Playing the Qin to Know the Sound
Yú Dí asked a guest to play the *qín*.
His sister-in-law, who was knowledgeable in music,
said:
"Of three parts,
one part is *zhēng* sound,
two parts are *pípá*,
there is no *qín* resonance at all."
Deep and Floating Sounds
Dǒng Tínglán was skilled at producing "chénshēng" (deep sounds) and "fànshēng" (floating sounds),
both of which are *qín* sounds.
Bójīng
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Sòng Qīng presented one volume of *Bójīng*.
Forceful competition for victory
is called "liáolíng."
Borrowing money and silk
is called "nángjiā."
Taking one-tenth
is called "qǐtóu."
Exhausting Soldiers for a Solo Dance
Yú Dí heard that Wéi Gāo had presented the "Shèngyuè" (Sacred Music) to the emperor,
and he also composed the "Shùnshèngyuè" (Obedient Sacred Music) to present.
Mid-way through the piece,
all rows of performers prostrated themselves,
and one person danced alone in the center.
His staff member Wéi Shòu said:
"Why exhaust the soldiers for a solo dance?"
This was to satirize Yú Dí.
Yú Dí was the Commissioner of Xiāng Prefecture,
and he was tyrannical.
People called him the "Xiāng-style Jìdù" (Xiāng-style Military Commissioner).
Gōngdé Shān
Hán Jìnggōng visited Jìng Shān,
and had his wife bow before it,
requesting a title.
Jìng Shān said:
"Gōngdé Shān."
Chisel-Carved Wáng Family
The Four Surnames:
Róngyáng Zhèng, Gāngtóu Lú, Zédǐ Lǐ, Shìmén Cuī,
all achieved the *Dǐngjiǎ* (highest degree).
The Tàiyuán Wáng also rivaled the Four Surnames,
and were called the "Chisel-Carved Wáng Family,"
likening them to silver adorned with gold.
Four Army Purple
During the Zhēnyuán era,
there were four marching armies,
who bestowed purple robes upon themselves
and ascended to the Langshǔ (Secretariat).
They were called "Sìjūnzǐ" (Four Army Purple).
Thunder Like Pigs
Léizhōu has much thunder in spring and summer.
In autumn and winter, it lies hidden in the ground,
its shape like a pig.
People catch and eat them.
There are also "léifǔ" (thunder axes) and "léimò" (thunder ink),
which can be used in medicine.
Mosquito Mother Bird
In Jiāngnán, there is a "wénmǔ niǎo" (mosquito mother bird).
It cries at night in summer,
spitting mosquitoes into the reed thickets.
There is also a "wénshù" (mosquito tree),
resembling a loquat.
When ripe, mosquitoes emerge from it.
Flowing Cassia Spring
In the south, there are many cassia springs.
Later, a house was built as a temple for Hànzǔ.
There is also a Zǐxū Temple,
whose statue has its beard divided into five parts,
and both have spiritual efficacy.
Damaged Lotus Root
When Sūzhōu presented lotus roots,
the best were called "shānghé" (damaged lotus).
To make its root grow long,
its leaves are intentionally damaged.
Sāngluò Wine
In Hélùn, there is a Sāngluò Fáng (Mulberry Fall Ward).
It has a well.
Every time at mulberry fall,
when the temperature is just right,
wine is brewed with the well water,
which is excellent.
Lètiān's poem says:
"The mulberry fall's aroma warms the pearls and kingfisher feathers,
the Zhèzhī music lifts the winds and strings high."
It was named "Sāngluò Jiǔ."
People in the old capital called it "Sāng Láng,"
which was merely a mispronunciation.
Judging Miscellaneous Officials
Lǐ Zìchéng was the Magistrate of Chánggē.
A miscellaneous official committed a fault.
Lǐ Zìchéng jokingly judged him, saying:
"How can one hold something all day and not know its taste?"
Poem Cellar
Wáng Rénsú wrote ten thousand poems,
called "Shī Jiàozǐ" (Poem Cellar),
also known as "Qiānpiān Jí" (Collection of a Thousand Pieces).
Huáng Jūnán
There was a jǔzǐ who wrote disorderly poems and essays.
Each time he sent his calling card, it said:
"Xiānggòng Jìnshì Huáng Jūnán, courtesy name Lèdì,"
intending to emulate Bái Jūyì, courtesy name Lètiān.
There was also Zhāng Bì,
who specialized in songs and poems,
claiming to be a match for Lǐ Bái.
Dù Xúnyā.
In Liángyuán, there was a wealthy young master, Dù Sìláng,
who enjoyed hosting literati
and loved composing poetry.
He was then called "Dù Xúnyā"
to compare him to Xún Hè.
Whenever he had a poem,
he would inscribe it on a wall.
If relatives or guests defaced it,
he would say:
"For thirty years, dust has covered my face;
now I finally get some mud."
Tattooed Face.
Strongmen having tattooed faces
began with Liáng Tàizǔ.
Yáng Fēngzi.
Yáng Shè delivered the Imperial Seal to Tàizǔ.
His son, Níngshì, advised against it, but was not listened to.
Fearing the matter would be leaked,
he feigned madness,
and was called Fēngzi.
No End in Sight.
Qián Liú was enfeoffed as the King of Wúyuè.
Construction projects greatly increased,
and soldiers grumbled with resentment.
Some would write on the gates of the government office at night:
"No end in sight,
no end in sight,
as soon as the city walls are done, they dig a pond."
Liú came out and saw it,
and ordered an official to write:
"No end in sight,
no end in sight,
as soon as spring clothes are done, it's winter clothes."
The grumbling immediately ceased.
Ten Virtues Memorial.
Zhōng Fù rose from a merchant background
and particularly valued scholars.
Wàn Hào then selected ten outstanding deeds of his
and presented them in a memorial,
calling it the "Ten Virtues Memorial."
It is said that each character was rewarded with one thousand,
totaling five thousand mín.
Peony Poem.
Cáo Kāng and Luó Yǐn both had poetic fame.
Yǐn inscribed a poem on peonies, saying:
"If they could speak, they would overthrow a state;
even being emotionless, they move people."
Kāng said:
"This merely describes a maiden's screen."
Yǐn replied:
"Still better than your 'ghost poems'."
Then he recited Táng's "Poem on Emperor Hàn Wǔ Dì Feasting the Queen Mother of the West," saying:
"Beneath the trees, heaven is still and silent in spring;
in the human world, the moon is vast and pathless.
Is this not a ghost poem?"
Táng had no reply.
Floating Rock Becoming an Immortal.
Master Ěrzhū's spiritual practice was profound.
He met an extraordinary person who gave him a pill.
If he took it after seeing a floating rock,
he would achieve immortality.
Following the master's instruction,
whenever he encountered a rock,
he would throw it into the water.
Later, crossing the river at a gorge,
an old man moored his boat, waiting for him.
He asked his surname,
and the old man replied, "Shí."
He asked where he was from,
and the old man replied, "Fúzhōu."
The master suddenly realized his mistake
and took the pill,
immediately ascending lightly.
Dédē Monk.
The monk Guànhxiū entered Shǔ.
He presented a poem to Jiàn, saying:
"With one flask, one bowl, growing old;
from a thousand waters, a thousand mountains, I came 'dédē'."
Jiàn was greatly pleased,
and bestowed the title "Chányuè."
Thus, he was named Dédē Heshang.
Zhuāngzōng Composes Lyrics.
Zhuāngzōng had a refined taste for music.
For all military formations, front and rear,
he personally composed lyrics,
and had them sung aloud.
Upon entering battle,
regardless of victory or defeat,
as soon as the horse's head turned,
all instruments played in unison.
Thus, people forgot their fear of death,
which was also a unique military tactic.
Sparrow and Rat Waste.
Míngzōng visited a granary.
Two dòu were added to every shí as a loss
to account for damage by sparrows and rats,
called "Sparrow and Rat Waste."
The practice of adding loss at granaries began from this.
Autumn Evening View Poem.
Hé Zhòngjǔ was skilled in poetry.
Lǐ Gāo recited Zhòngjǔ's "Autumn Evening View" poem to him, saying:
"Trees welcome high birds returning to deep wilderness,
clouds follow the setting sun over several mountains."
Then he tapped the ground with his foot, saying:
"Zhòngjǔ is an eminent and unrestrained poet;
the rest are mere servants and soldiers, producing inferior works."
One-Eyed Barbarian Slave.
Xú Yín presented "Ode on Tàizǔ's Eastern Tour to Dàliáng."
At that time, Tàizǔ was an enemy of Tài Yuán Wǔ Huáng,
and Wǔ Huáng was blind in one eye
and came from the Shātuó tribe.
Wishing to flatter Liáng Zǔ,
his words were:
"The one-eyed barbarian slave
sees your heroic might and loses courage."
Zhuāngzōng destroyed Liáng,
and Yín was in Mǐnzhōng.
Wáng Shěnzhī instructed his attendants not to receive him.
Because of this, Yín was limited to the position of Zhèngzì in the Bìshūshěng.
Thanking for Fish Memorial.
Huáng Tāo served as a tuīguān for Wáng Shěnzhī.
Shěnzhī sent him fish.
Xú Yín wrote a thank-you memorial on his behalf, saying:
"They snap their broken ropes,
having just been hung by Yáng Xù;
arranged on a carved plate,
they arrive at Fèng Huān's dining place."
At the time, this was highly praised.
Unable to Shed Tears Even with a Well-Sweep.
Jìng Xīnmó was
a performer from Hédōng.
Zhuāngzōng originated from Shātuó Jùn.
After gaining the empire,
many of his guards and attendants were young men from barbarian tribes,
with many having high noses and deep-set eyes.
Xīnmó often mocked them,
and they all gnashed their teeth
and complained to Zhuāngzōng,
weeping.
Zhuāngzōng admonished Xīnmó,
who replied:
"The tears of these fellows cannot be shed even if struck with a well-sweep."
Zhuāngzōng laughed heartily.
Submitting to Fate with the Memorial.
Lǐ Tāo once angrily denounced Zhāng Yànzé,
submitting a memorial requesting Yànzé's execution.
Later, the Qìdān invaded from the south,
reaching Zhōngdùqiáo.
Yànzé was the first to surrender,
and entered the capital first.
He then, harboring old resentment, killed Sāng Wéihàn, the Yǐn of Kāifēng.
Tāo heard of this,
and personally wrote a memorial seeking an audience with Yànzé, saying:
"Lǐ Tāo, who memorialized to kill Taìwèi,
humbly submits to his fate with this memorial."
Yànzé was pleased,
and ultimately treated him well.
Dice for Dividing Children.
Zài Yǎn was skilled in poetry,
calling himself Xuánhuángzǐ.
The Mǎ family ruled a state,
and by Wénzhāo's time, luxury and extravagance were particularly favored.
Yǎn wrote "Fisherman" (《Yúfù》) in a hundred chapters to satirize this,
and consequently was not appreciated.
Suffering from increasing cold and hunger,
he said to his wife:
"We were wed,
and had one son and one daughter.
Now I fear we will fall into a ditch or ravine.
We should divide the children and flee."
Thereupon, he took up dice and made a pact with his wife, saying:
"Whoever rolls the higher score gets the son."
Yǎn rolled a lower score,
and thus tearfully parted, taking his daughter.
Moon Sinks in Xiāngpǔ
Shí Wéndé was skilled at poetry.
Mǎ Wénzhāo, because his son was sleeping,
never received him.
Wáng Zǐyán of the Southern Residence had him as a retainer.
Before long,
Madame Péng passed away.
Wénzhāo was grief-stricken,
and Wéndé presented him with a dirge,
which contained the lines:
"The moon sinks, the Xiāng Pǔ is cold;
flowers wither, the Hàn palace is autumn."
Wénzhāo exclaimed in surprise:
"Wéndé has such talent!
Am I, on the contrary, less discerning than the boy in the Southern Residence?"
So he received him.
Silver Leaves Protecting the Well
Gāo Yù was a strategist for Wǔmù Wáng,
greedy and presumptuous.
He often complained that the three wells at his residence were not clear enough,
so he used silver leaves to protect the wells,
covering all four sides, inside and out.
His excessive expenditures
were all of this kind.
Song of the Nine Provinces
Ōuyáng Bīn visited the Mǎ family in Húnán,
but could not gain entry.
There was a courtesan, Ruìqīng,
who admired his talent,
and invited him to her home.
At that time, Húnán originally administered seven prefectures,
but later Wǔlíng and Yuèyáng were added, making nine prefectures.
Ruìqīng sang a song about this,
but Wǔmù did not question it.
Bīn then went to Shǔ.
Nail-Pulling Money
Zhào Zàilǐ was in Sòngzhōu,
and his actions were unlawful.
The people suffered greatly from him.
One day, an imperial decree came down,
transferring him to Yǒngxīng.
The people congratulated each other, saying:
"A nail has been pulled from our eyes!
How joyful it is!"
When Zàilǐ heard this,
he submitted a memorial begging to be returned to his post,
and the court granted it.
Zàilǐ then collected a thousand coins per person,
calling it "nail-pulling money,"
and thus amassed millions.
Bamboo Branch Drawing on Ox Back
The monk Qí Sì,
a native of Chángshā,
was intelligent and perceptive at the age of seven.
He served as the administrator of Dàwéishān Temple,
often expressing his thoughts
by drawing poems on the backs of oxen with bamboo branches.
The other monks found this remarkable,
and thus allowed him to become a monk.
One-Character Teacher
Zhèng Gǔ was in Yuánzhōufǔ.
Qí Sì brought his poems to him.
His poem "Early Plum" read:
"In the deep snow of the front village,
a few branches bloomed last night."
Gǔ said:
"A few branches are not early;
it's not as good as 'one branch.'"
Qí Sì involuntarily prostrated himself in homage.
From then on,
the literati referred to Gǔ as the "One-Character Teacher."
Wǔ Yīgǔ
Wǔ Xíngdé made his living by gathering firewood,
and was very strong.
He claimed that he could carry an entire valley's worth of firewood,
so the villagers called him "Wǔ Yīgǔ."
Grave Robber
Liáo Níng read Péi Shuō's "Poem on Dù Gōngbù's Tomb" and said:
"You plan to chisel open the solitary tomb,
and bring the great master back to life."
He laughed, saying:
"Péi Shuō
is merely a grave robber."
Whirlwind and Reclining Moon
Lǐ Gāo and his younger brother Jié were both serving under the Mǎ family in Húnán.
They were composing a poem of thanks for warhorses for the Mǎ family.
Lǐ Gāo said:
"A horse has a whirlwind formation;
how can we get a pair?"
Jié said:
"The army has a reclining moon encampment."
Gāo then said:
"Swiftly seek the reclining moon encampment,
and array it into a whirlwind formation."
Water Grass King
Lǐ Yǎn was the Jìedù of Fèngxiáng.
He imprisoned Shēng Chén.
The envoy from Qínfèng was ugly and had a long beard,
while the envoy from Wèibó was young and resembled a beautiful woman.
The Wèibó envoy joked:
"Today I am sitting beside the 'Water Grass King.'"
The Qínfèng envoy said:
"Madam, don't say too much."
Everyone present laughed.
Bandit Chief
Wáng Rényù,
in the first year of Gānyòu, 214 people passed the examination.
He wrote a poem saying:
"Two hundred fourteen disciples,
their feathers just grown in the spring breeze.
They toss gold to gain high status in heaven,
and chisel walls to steal their names on the list."
Minister Táo saw the poem and said:
"I didn't expect Wáng Rényù to be a bandit chief today."
Mistaken for Liángshān
Lǐ Tāo's younger brother Huàn married a wife.
The wife bowed to Tāo.
Tāo said:
"I am ashamed to have no Zǐjiàn,
and am mistakenly called Liángshān."
Those who heard it burst out laughing.
Without an Inch of the Way
Féng Dào was in the Central Secretariat.
The aspiring scholar Lǐ Dǎo presented a formal greeting to him.
Dào reproached Dǎo for not avoiding his name.
Dǎo said:
"Your Excellency is 'without an inch of the Way.'"
Dào was not angry at all.
Thunder Circling the Hall
Féng Dào's son could play the pípa,
using leather strings.
Shìzōng ordered him to play,
and greatly admired it.
He then named the pípa "Thunder Circling the Hall."
Geese with Four Legs, Turtles with Two Skirts
The monk Qiānguāng,
talented and articulate, also drank wine and ate meat.
He once said:
"This old monk has no other wish, but to wish
that geese grow four legs and turtles grow two skirts, and that would be enough."
Twice a Tide in Twelve Hours
The Mǐn monk Qìyíng accompanied the King of Wúyuè to ascend Lùbō Tíng.
The King happily said:
"Three thousand li away, a single river."
Qìyíng said:
"Twice a tide in twelve hours."
People considered this a fitting couplet.
At that time, the tribute from the two Zhè provinces was shipped by sea to Qīngzhōu,
hence the mention of "three thousand li."
Good Ointment
Wáng Jiàn was a lawless man in Xǔxià.
He had once been punished for a crime and sentenced to penal servitude,
but without any marks from the rod.
When he occupied Shǔ,
he bared his back to his official Féng Juān,
wishing to justify himself.
Juān patted his back and said:
"How extraordinary!
How extraordinary!
Where did you get this good ointment?"
End of scroll twenty-six.
Finished.
Judgment Form, Pardon from Death
Sāng Dàomào (桑道茂) was initially a Gōngfèng (供奉).
Lǐ Shèng (李晟) was a minor general in the Shéncè (神策) army.
Dàomào (道茂) said:
"Once you become noble,
in three to five years, my life will be in your hands.
Will you be able to spare it?"
Shèng (晟) smiled and said:
"The Gōngfèng (供奉) mocks me."
Dàomào (道茂) took a written document from his bosom,
with his official title and name,
stating that the crime he had committed was under duress,
and humbly begging for mercy,
for which his life would be spared.
Shèng (晟) smiled and said:
"What would you have me write?"
Dàomào (道茂) said:
"I beg you to approve the petition and grant a special release."
Shèng (晟) wrote it for him.
Later, Zhū Cǐ (朱泚) rebelled,
and Dàomào (道茂) returned to his former post.
Shèng (晟) rescued the capital city,
capturing hundreds of rebels,
and had them executed under his banner.
Dàomào (道茂) shouted loudly:
"I have a petition!"
It was taken and examined,
and it was the one written years ago.
Shèng (晟) was astonished and enlightened,
released him, and treated him as an honored guest.
Yùchí Jìngdé's (尉遲敬德) Money
At the end of the Suí (隋) dynasty,
a scholar in Tàiyuán (太原) was extremely poor.
His dwelling was next to a government-confiscated treasury.
He secretly dug an underground tunnel into the treasury,
where there were tens of thousands of strings of coins.
Presently, he saw a golden-armored man holding a spear, who said:
"If you want money,
just bring a note from Yùchí Jìngdé (尉遲敬德);
this is his money."
The scholar searched and found him at an iron smithy.
There was Yùchí Jìngdé (尉遲敬德),
bare-chested and disheveled,
in the midst of forging.
The scholar bowed and said:
"I am poor,
while you are wealthy and noble;
I beg for five hundred strings of cash."
Yùchí (尉遲) angrily said:
"I am an iron-beater;
how can I be wealthy and noble?"
The scholar said:
"Just grant me a note;
you will know its meaning another day."
Yùchí (尉遲) had no choice
but to write:
"Give so-and-so five hundred strings of cash."
The scholar bowed, thanked him, and left,
returning to the treasury.
The golden-armored man smiled and said:
"This is it."
He ordered it to be tied high on a beam,
and allowed the scholar to take the money.
Later, Jìngdé (敬德) assisted Shényáo (神堯) in achieving extraordinary merits,
and was granted a treasury of goods in his hometown by imperial decree,
thus acquiring this money.
According to the original ledger,
five hundred strings of cash were missing,
and the responsible official
suddenly found the note on the beam,
which was what he had written when he was striking iron.
Five Kinds of Wontons
Lǐ Zōnghuí (李宗回) traveled with a guest into the pass.
He said:
"I can tell what people will eat and drink."
So, on New Year's Day,
they were going to visit the magistrate of Huáyīn (華陰) County.
The guest said:
"Tomorrow, you and I will each drink a cup of pepper and scallion wine,
and eat five kinds of wontons,
without eating rice."
The next day, when they saw the magistrate, he said:
"You two have endured the cold;
quickly bring two cups of warm wine."
It also contained scallions and pepper.
After a while,
a maid whispered to the magistrate,
and the magistrate said:
"Boil them all."
He said to the two guests:
"My young daughter often says
that she won't let me manage household affairs.
I was annoyed,
and had her oversee the food and drink for festivals.
Just now, she said:
'There are five kinds of wontons;
which ones should be boiled?'
I told her to boil them all."
The two guests finished their meal.
Suddenly, a messenger from an imperial envoy was reported to have arrived.
The county magistrate was startled,
hurriedly bade the guests farewell,
and they ultimately did not get to eat rice.
Two Plates of Gruel
During Emperor Mínghuáng's (明皇) time,
there was a diviner who predicted people's food,
determining everything in advance.
Lǐ Qīyún (李栖筠) asked:
"What will I eat tomorrow?"
He replied:
"Your Excellency is destined to eat two plates of gruel and twenty bowls of orange peel soup."
At dawn,
there was an imperial decree for an audience.
The Emperor bestowed upon him newly made glutinous rice gruel served in a golden plate.
Qīyún (栖筠), facing the Emperor,
dared not leave any unfinished.
The Emperor was greatly pleased and said:
"You eat very well."
He was given another plate,
which he also finished.
Upon his return,
he became ill with cholera,
abstained from all food,
and drank orange peel soup.
Only after twenty bowls did he recover.
Fifty-Year Emperor
When Emperor Mínghuáng (明皇) was still a hidden dragon (i.e., a prince not yet emperor),
he saw the monk Wànhuí (萬迴) who said:
"Fifty-year Emperor,
please take care of yourself."
Indeed, fifty years after he became Emperor,
the disaster of Lùshān (祿山) occurred.
Giant Snake Eats Wisteria Flowers
When Emperor Mínghuáng (明皇) was in his humble days,
he arrived in Luòyáng (洛陽),
and visited the residence of Cuī Rìzhī (崔日知).
Cuī (崔) had prepared a meal that was not yet ready,
so Mínghuáng (明皇) slept in the courtyard,
where a trellis of wisteria flowers had just begun to bloom.
Rìzhī (日知) saw a giant snake eating the wisteria flowers,
and then it vanished shortly after.
Mínghuáng (明皇) awoke and said:
"I am very hungry.
In my dream, I ate wisteria flowers and was quite full."
Rìzhī (日知) then realized this was a sign of his future ascension to sainthood (i.e., emperorship).
Two Blue-Clad Maids Carrying an Incense Burner
Ān Lùshān (安祿山) said to a sorcerer:
"I am not afraid even when facing the Emperor,
but I feel dread whenever I see Grand Councilor Lǐ (李)."
The sorcerer said:
"You have several hundred ghost soldiers,
with bronze heads and iron foreheads,
always by your side.
Why fear Grand Councilor Lǐ (李)?"
Lùshān (祿山) then hosted a banquet for the Grand Councilor,
and ordered the sorcerer to observe.
He was astonished and said:
"When I first saw the Grand Councilor arriving,
there were two blue-clad maids with double hair knots,
carrying an incense burner, who entered first.
Your attendants, the several hundred bronze-headed, iron-foreheaded guards, ran away by penetrating roofs and climbing walls.
I do not know the reason,
but they must be immortal officials banished to the human world."
Zǐsù Yuánjūn (紫素元君)
There was a man named Rèn Shēng,
who lived in reclusion on Sōngshān.
One night, a beautiful woman arrived,
and left a poem saying:
"My name is registered in the Upper Clarity realm,
I wander the Five Peaks as an exiled immortal.
Seeing that you are free from worldly attachments,
I come to encourage you to study the way of the immortals."
Rèn Shēng firmly refused to accept her.
Three days later, she returned and said:
"I am not a malevolent spirit;
my name is listed among the high immortals,
and by冥數 (ming su) fate, I am destined to be your partner."
She also presented a poem saying:
"Gě Hóng also had a wife,
the Queen Mother of the West also had a husband.
All immortals have their spiritual partners;
what about a gentleman like you, Rèn Shēng?"
He still did not respond.
The woman again said:
"If Ruan Lang remains unenlightened,
how can I express my sincere feelings?
The bright moon shines upon the spring sea,
but my ornate boat must return."
Several months later,
Rèn Shēng fell ill and died,
and was pursued by an officer.
On the way, he encountered a procession of banners and standards escorting a jade palanquin,
from which a woman laughed and said:
"Is this the ill-fated scholar of Sōngshān?"
She took the documents held by the officer and looked at them, saying:
"Since we have met now,
I cannot be heartless."
She asked for a brush and wrote a judgment:
"Grant him three more years."
Rèn Shēng bowed deeply again.
The officer said to him:
"This is Zǐsù Yuánjūn,
the most noble of the immortal officials."
The officer sent him back,
and he revived.
Three years later, he died.
Mínghuáng Journeys to the Moon Palace
Luó Gōngyuǎn attended Mínghuáng in the palace during the Mid-Autumn Festival to admire the moon.
He said:
"Does Your Majesty wish to go to the Moon Palace?"
He threw his staff into the air,
and it transformed into a silver bridge.
He ascended the bridge with the Emperor.
A chill penetrated their bodies,
and they arrived at a great city,
saying:
"This is the Moon Palace."
They saw hundreds of female immortals,
dressed in white silk and electric-like garments,
dancing in a spacious courtyard.
The Emperor asked the name of the tune,
and they replied:
"It is 'Nícháng Yǔyī'."
The Emperor noted down its melody,
and upon returning, composed the "Nícháng Yǔyī Qǔ".
Shooting Luó Gōngyuǎn
Mínghuáng wanted to learn the art of invisibility,
but Luó Gōngyuǎn kept it secret,
fearing the Emperor would abuse it for his pleasure.
The Emperor grew angry,
and selected skilled archers to lie in ambush by a wall.
He summoned Luó Gōngyuǎn to converse with him,
and all the arrows were fired at once.
The Emperor ordered him to be buried within the palace.
Over a month later,
a palace envoy returned from Shǔ,
saying:
"Your servant reached Luògǔ today,
and saw Luó Gōngyuǎn.
He asked me to convey his regards,
and is specifically watching for the imperial carriage in Chéngdū."
The Emperor was astonished,
and ordered the coffin to be opened.
Only a straw sandal was found,
with dozens of arrow holes.
Later, when the Emperor journeyed to Shǔ,
a man claiming to be Wéi Gōngyán came to pay respects,
but when summoned, he was nowhere to be seen.
Wéi Gōngyán was none other than Luó Gōngyuǎn.
The Emperor regretted this for a long time.
Huíxiàng Yuàn (The Reversion Monastery)
Mínghuáng dreamed that someone was carrying five hundred handkerchiefs
and five hundred kāṣāya robes
to donate to Huíxiàng Yuàn on Zhōngnánshān.
He then issued an edict to search for it.
A mad monk claimed to know its location,
though he actually did not.
He then took the items to be donated in the dream into Zhōngnánshān.
Among the clouds, there were vermilion pillars and white walls,
exquisitely beautiful like a painting.
He saw a monastery with a plaque,
which was indeed Huíxiàng Yuàn.
The mad monk entered the monastery,
heard the sound of bells and chimes for Buddha worship,
and saw an old monk.
He then said:
"The Emperor has sent me to donate handkerchiefs and kāṣāya robes."
Among them was a Hu (foreign) monk,
whose appearance was awe-inspiring.
The old monk said:
"This Hu monk temporarily acts as your master.
China will experience great chaos,
and countless people will die.
This one is called the Demonic King.
His empty room is your master's room.
When your master was in this monastery in the past,
he loved to play the chǐbā.
He was exiled to the human world,
but his term is now complete, and he should return.
You may give him the chǐbā."
The mad monk left the gate,
and clouds and mist enveloped everything.
He saw the Emperor
and fully recounted the story.
The Emperor took the chǐbā and played it,
recognizing it as something he had practiced before.
Ten years later,
the An Lùshān Rebellion occurred.
Lú Qǐ Becomes a Mortal Prime Minister
In the first year of Huìchāng, Lú Qǐ was a traveler.
He was caught in a storm and drifted to a great mountain.
He saw a Daoist priest who said:
"This is Pénglái Shān,
each person here occupies one peak."
Suddenly, wind and clouds arose,
soaring up into the blue sky.
He asked Mápó:
"How far is Luòyáng from here?"
She replied:
"Eighty thousand lǐ."
After a long while,
from atop a gourd,
he saw pavilions and palaces,
with crystal walls.
Women resided in the halls,
attended by hundreds of female servants.
Mápó stood among the guards.
The woman ordered Lú Qǐ to sit,
and served wine and dishes, saying:
"Young master, you may now choose one of three things:
the first is to stay in this palace,
with a lifespan as long as heaven itself;
the second is to become an Earth Immortal,
occasionally able to visit this place;
the lowest is to become a prime minister in the human world."
Lú Qǐ said:
"To reside here is my highest wish."
The woman happily said:
"This is the Crystal Palace.
I am Dàyīn Fūrén.
My immortal rank is already high,
and if the young master ascends in broad daylight,
I will surely present a memorial to the Jade Emperor."
A moment later,
a red-robed messenger announced the Emperor's command:
"Does Lú Qǐ wish to live in the Crystal Palace?
Or does he wish to be a prime minister in the human world?"
Lú Qǐ cried out loudly:
"A prime minister in the human world!"
The red-robed messenger presented the reply and left.
Dàyīn Fūrén's face lost color.
She ordered Mápó to quickly return,
pushed him into the gourd,
and he returned to his old dwelling.
The dusty bed was still there,
but the gourd and Mápó were nowhere to be seen again.
Jīntiān Wáng Detains Lǐ Zhǔbù's Wife
Zhǔbù Lǐ
was newly married.
Passing by the temple of Jīntiānwáng,
he took his wife to pay respects.
His wife collapsed, breathless.
Just then, Xiānshī Yè passed by,
and someone went to inform him.
The Immortal Master wrote a talisman with ink and spat on her,
and a sound like a whirlwind ensued.
For a long time, there was no change.
He made another talisman;
its sound was like thunder,
but again, no change.
The Master, angered,
took vermillion to make a talisman,
yelled loudly, and sprayed water,
with a sound like a thunderclap.
A moment later,
Lǐ's wife revived,
saying:
"When I first bowed to Jīntiānwáng,
the statue said:
'What a beautiful lady!
Keep her.'
Attendants led me back to the courtyard.
After three days of meeting guests,
I heard a knocking sound at the door.
The King said:
'Chase them away.'
After a moment,
it was very noisy outside the door.
Someone whispered into his ear,
and the King said:
'Let them go for now.'
Suddenly, a red dragon flew in
and struck the King directly on the throat.
The King repeatedly cried:
'Let her go!'
That was the third talisman."
From this, one knows that women should not enter temples of spirits.
Lǐ Xiànghù
Cānjūn Lǐ was skilled at appraising hu (tablets of office),
so people called him Lǐ Xiànghù.
He appraised Lù Zūn's hu, saying:
"You will see a Píngshìlángjūn."
Liú Zūn said:
"I have no children yet."
In a certain month, he became pregnant.
Zūn already had a singing girl living outside,
who indeed gave birth to a son.
Jīntiānwáng Leads the Imperial Carriage
Mínghuáng personally offered sacrifices at Xīyuè.
After the rites, he traveled east.
Upon exiting the temple gate,
the shaman reported:
"Jīndàwáng, armed and carrying a spear, is walking to lead the imperial carriage."
An edict ordered the selection of swift horses and strong men for the escort.
The shaman acclaimed:
"Jīndàwáng bows in gratitude."
After traveling several li,
the horses were sweating so much they could not proceed.
In all, ten horses were changed,
until they reached the palace and stopped.
The shaman said:
"Jīndàwáng bids farewell and returns."
A Sick Crane Requests Human Blood
Xiànggōng Lǐ was traveling Mount Sōng.
He heard groaning among the wild grass.
Looking,
it was a sick crane,
which said:
"I am an immortal,
but I met with misfortune.
I was injured by a woodcutter,
my leg is damaged.
I need a few measures of human blood to heal.
You have immortal bones,
which is why I can make this request.
