There are few true humans in the world,
and you are certainly not an ordinary person."
Thereupon, it plucked out an eyelash and said:
"Hold this and look through it,
and you will know."
On the way, Gōng Lǐ looked through it himself,
and saw only horse heads.
Upon reaching Luòyáng,
everyone he met was not fully human,
but rather like dogs, pigs, donkeys, or horses.
He saw an old man through it,
who was human.
Gōng Lǐ fully explained the situation,
and the old man bared his arm and bled.
Gōng Lǐ returned to the crane's location
and moistened the wound.
The crane thanked him, saying:
"You will become a prime minister,
and later ascend.
Our next meeting is not far off."
The crane soared into the sky and departed.
Gōng Lǐ later indeed became a prime minister.
Beidǒu Liánzhēn Jiāngjūn
When Lìnggōng Péi was young,
a diviner said:
"Your fate belongs to Beidǒu Liánzhēn Jiāngjūn.
You should offer sacrifices to him with clear wine,
and he will assist you."
From then on, Péi did not slacken.
When he became prime minister,
due to many affairs, he forgot.
Later, a shamaness said:
"Liánzhēn Jiāngjūn sent me to convey a message:
'You are too heartless,
you no longer acknowledge me!'
The General is very angry.
Why does Xiànggōng not apologize to him?"
Thereupon, Gōng Péi bathed and offered sacrifices.
He saw a man in golden armor,
holding a vermillion spear,
over three zhàng tall,
standing facing north.
Gōng Péi was startled and terrified.
From then on, he resumed his veneration.
Throwing a Scarf to Form a Crimson Bridge
There was a student, Cuī,
who traveled to Mount Qīngchéng.
He descended into a cave
and saw golden cities and crimson palaces.
An immortal elder in feathered robes and rosy stoles
offered the student wine and food,
and gave his daughter to him in marriage.
He took two pills from a green pouch and made him take them.
On the first and fifteenth day of each lunar month,
he would ride a crane to court at Ruǐgōng.
After more than a year,
the student requested to return.
He obtained a talisman for invisibility,
and then secretly roamed the imperial palace.
His clothes were of brocade and silk.
The emperor ordered Gōng Luóyuǎn to use magic to illuminate behind the hall,
and indeed, Cuī was found.
The emperor ordered him to be flogged to death.
Gōng Luóyuǎn said:
"This person has already resided in the upper realm.
Killing him would not be a blessing for the state."
The emperor dispatched armed guards to escort him to the entrance of the Qīngchéng cave,
where indeed, golden cities and crimson palaces were seen.
The student's wife threw a scarf,
which transformed into a five-colored crimson bridge,
allowing the student to cross.
It vanished with each step.
In a moment,
clouds and mist gathered from all directions,
and only the sounds of cranes, phoenixes, and sheng music were heard.
Kōnghóu with Vermillion Characters
There was a student, Lǐ,
whose maternal uncle, whose surname was Lú,
possessed magical arts.
He invited Lǐ to his residence
and said:
"I have found a courtesan
who is skilled at the kōnghóu."
He ordered her to attend them at their drink.
On the kōnghóu were vermillion characters that read: "In the clouds, discern the river trees;
at the edge of the sky, recognize the returning boat."
Later, Lǐ married Lù Chángyuán's daughter,
who was the one he had seen at Lú's house.
She was indeed skilled at the kōnghóu, and the vermillion characters were distinctly there.
Student Lǐ fully recounted the old story.
The woman said:
"I once dreamed that I was pursued by an immortal official."
It was exactly as Lǐ had said.
Xǔ Chán Enters Yaótái
Xǔ Chán
died suddenly for three days.
He revived, and someone asked him where he had gone.
Thereupon, he recited a poem:
"At dawn, I entered Yaótái, where the dew was fresh and clear;
among those present, only Xǔ Fēiqióng.
My worldly heart's attachments were not yet exhausted,
ten li down the mountain, only the bright moon remained."
Golden Lotus Candle
Xuānzōng was about to appoint Línghú Táo as prime minister.
A few days prior,
he summoned him into the palace at night,
and sent him back with a golden lotus candle from before the emperor.
The palace guards, seeing this,
thought it was the emperor's carriage.
This was considered a great honor at the time.
Able to Compose Poetry at Seven
Fàn Jù, a recluse from Wú,
had a son who could compose poetry at seven years old.
He presented a poem to a hermit, saying:
“Sweeping leaves is easy with the wind,
watering flowers is best in the shade.”
The recluse Fāng Gān said:
“This one will surely achieve fame.”
He also composed a “Summer Day Poem,” saying:
“Leisurely clouds rise but bring no rain,
ailing leaves fall but it is not autumn.”
Gān said:
“Alas,
he will not live long!”
Not long after, he indeed passed away.
Nán Chǔcái’s wife’s poem
The *jìnshì* Nán Chǔcái
initially married a woman from the Xuē family.
Later, he traveled to Yǐngchuān
and wished to marry into a noble family.
He sent a servant to fetch his zither and books,
showing no intention of returning.
Lady Xuē was skilled in painting and poetry.
Knowing that Chǔcái intended to abandon her,
she painted her own likeness
and inscribed a poem to send him, saying:
“Before taking up the vermilion brush,
I first pick up my precious mirror to gaze.
Already startled by my desolate face,
I gradually notice my temples thinning.
Tearful eyes are easy to depict,
but a sorrowful heart is difficult to portray.
Fearing that you will completely forget me,
I often unroll this painting to observe.”
Upon receiving the poem, Chǔcái was greatly ashamed.
Handprint on a screen
Emperor Mínghuáng’s favored concubine, Lady Wáng,
repeatedly dreamed of people inviting her to a secret rendezvous for drinks.
She reported it fully to the Emperor.
The Emperor said:
“This must be the work of a sorcerer.
If you go again,
mark it with something.”
That night,
she dreamed she went again.
She then dipped her hand in the inkstone and pressed it onto the screen.
When she awoke,
she told the Emperor.
They secretly searched outside
and indeed found her handprint in the Dōngmíng Temple,
but the Daoist priest had already fled.
Composing a poem to gain a courtesan
When Wéi Yìngwù was the Prefect of Sūzhōu,
he once attended a banquet hosted by Dù Hóngjiàn.
After getting drunk, he stayed overnight at a relay station.
When he sobered up,
he saw two courtesans by his side.
They said:
“The *Lángzhōng* (referring to Dù Hóngjiàn, or perhaps a higher-ranking official) on the banquet seat gave a poem to the *Sīkōng* (referring to Wéi Yìngwù),
and thus sent us to you.”
The poem read:
“High coiled hair, cloud-like chignons in palace style,
a spring breeze tune from Dù Wéiniáng.
The *Sīkōng* is accustomed to such ordinary things,
but it breaks the heart of the Prefect of Sūzhōu.”
A poem for bidding farewell to a brother
During Rúyì’s reign (Empress Wǔ Zétiān’s era name),
there was a girl of seven years old who could compose poetry.
Zétiān summoned her
and ordered her to compose a poem for bidding farewell to a brother, saying:
“On the parting road, clouds begin to rise,
at the farewell pavilion, leaves are falling.
What a pity that humans are unlike wild geese,
they do not return in a single line.”
The promise of Yùxiāo
When Wéi Gāo had not yet entered officialdom,
he resided at the residence of Commander Jiāng.
Jiāng treated him very well
and gifted him a young maidservant named Yùxiāo,
who was beautiful and alluring.
After several years,
Gāo returned home to visit his parents
and made a promise with Yùxiāo to return in seven years,
giving her a jade finger ring as a token.
Gāo was late and did not return.
Yùxiāo sighed, saying:
“Master Wéi is not coming back!”
She stopped eating and died.
Later, Gāo was stationed in Shǔ.
On his birthday,
Minister Lú of Dōngchuān presented a singing girl as a birthday gift,
also named Yùxiāo.
He quickly called her over to look at her;
she was indeed the old acquaintance,
and there was a jade ring distinctly raised on her middle finger.
The noble gate is deep like the sea
Cuī Jiāo’s aunt
had a very beautiful maidservant.
Jiāo once had a secret affair with her.
Not long after,
the maidservant left
and later entered Yú Dí’s household.
Jiāo, during the Cold Food Festival, went out for an excursion
and saw her from inside his carriage.
He stopped his horse, lingered, and they looked at each other.
He secretly presented her with a poem, saying:
“Young masters and noble sons follow in the dust,
Lǜzhū sheds tears, drenching her silk kerchief.
Once entered into the noble gate, it is deep as the sea,
from then on, Xiāo Láng is a stranger.”
Upon seeing the poem, Dí
gave the maidservant to Jiāo.
The Qúyī tax
Zhāng Chóng was appointed governor of Lúzhōu,
and committed many unlawful acts,
causing suffering to the gentry and common people.
One day he went to the capital for an audience.
The local people hoped for his reassignment
and said to each other that “Qúyī (he)” would surely not return.
When Chóng returned and heard their words,
he then levied a “Qúyī (he)” tax on each household.
The following year, he again went for an audience,
and it was widely rumored that he would be dismissed again.
The people of the prefecture dared not speak openly,
but because Chóng had many whiskers,
they all stroked their whiskers in celebration.
When Chóng returned,
he again levied a “stroking whiskers” tax.
Monk knocks on a moonlit door
Jiǎ Dǎo, while intensely composing poetry
and traveling to the capital for the imperial examination,
came up with a line:
“Birds roost on trees by the pond,
a monk knocks on a moonlit door.”
He also wanted to change “knocks” to “pushes.”
Riding on a donkey, he raised his hand, reciting,
making gestures of pushing and knocking.
Unconsciously, he collided with the retinue of the Mayor of the Capital, Hán Tuìzhī.
His attendants surrounded him and brought him forward.
He fully explained the situation.
Tuìzhī smiled and said:
“The word ‘knocks’ is better.”
He then ordered Jiǎ Dǎo to ride his donkey alongside him, reciting poetry.
After a long time, they parted ways.
The Brocade-Clad General
Qián Liú,
in his hometown of Ānrénlǐ, had a large tree
under which Liú played as a child.
Later, when he became King of Wúyuè,
he hosted a banquet for the elders,
and all the hills and forests were covered with brocade.
He named the tree “Brocade-Clad General.”
The Hemp-Robed Monk
During the reign of Zhōu Tàizǔ,
there was a Hemp-Robed Monk who could observe *qì* (auras).
Lǐ Shǒuzhèng was administering Hézhōng,
and Emperor Zhōu Tàizǔ personally led an expedition.
The Hemp-Robed Monk said to King Zhào and King Hán:
“How can Minister Lǐ long reside here?
Beneath the city are the *qì* of three emperors.”
Not long after, the city fell.
At that time, Zhōu Shìzōng was traveling with Tàizǔ and Tàizōng.
Dragon in the Cauldron
During the Southern Táng dynasty,
a servant held a painting of “Dragon Water” for sale.
Someone acquired it
and was preparing to boil it to make a decoction.
Suddenly, steam rose from the cauldron,
and two dragons were seen leaping and soaring,
then piercing through the wall and departing.
Lóngxīng Temple
In the old capital of Biàn, there was a Lóngxīng Temple.
Zhōu Shìzōng abolished it and converted it into a granary.
At the beginning of the (Sòng) dynasty,
the temple monks repeatedly appealed for its restoration as a temple.
Tàizōng was angered by their annoyance
and sent an envoy with a sword to execute them,
saying:
“If they are afraid, execute them immediately.
If not afraid, report back.”
The monks were not afraid at the execution.
Tàizōng was very pleased
and that day restored it as a temple.
Fèngxiáng Tàipíng Palace
During the Kāibǎo era,
a deity descended upon the Zhāng clan in Fèngxiáng Fǔ.
Its voice was like an infant's,
and prayers were always answered.
It declared itself to be acting on a decree from the Heavenly Venerable (Shàngtiān Zūnzhào),
and ordered that its abode be designated as the Tàipíng Gōng.
It was to be solemnly worshipped,
and the Zhāng clan was to serve as Dàoshi (Yǔshì),
managing the palace.
Previously, the Zhāng clan had a reputation for misconduct in the village.
When some people spoke of this,
the deity said:
"From Shǎnxī westward,
the only person whose family has produced sons for three generations
is this Zhāng.
His rural indiscretions
are not worth worrying about."
Carrying a Zither and Leaping over a Wall
When Zhēnzōng performed sacrifices at Fén Yīn,
he ascended a mountain and saw a pavilion amidst the forests and foothills.
It was the thatched cottage of the recluse Wèi Yě.
An envoy was sent to summon him.
Wèi Yě was just playing his zither and teaching cranes to dance.
Hearing of the envoy's arrival,
he picked up his zither, leapt over a wall, and fled.
The Emperor sighed in admiration.
Poem of Returning to Seclusion
Wáng Yìjiǎn was appointed Zǔo Shíyí.
He resigned from office and returned to seclusion,
writing a poem that said:
"Lost in the imperial court, I am ashamed of my lack of talent;
Who can humble themselves in the dust?
If green mountains can be reached, then go and return;
Official positions, if they come, will come naturally again."
Poem on Whiteness
Liáo Níng, at ten years old,
composed a "Poem on Whiteness" saying:
"The gulls on the sandbar do not disperse,
In one game, black loses completely."
Poem on a Lone Goose
Dí Zǐyán's poem on a lone goose said:
"No sound follows anymore."
People regarded it as a prophecy,
and indeed, he lost his children and remained childless his entire life.
Two Sons Died Young
Fàn Jù had a son who, at seven years old,
composed a poem for a recluse saying:
"Sweeping leaves goes with the wind,
Watering flowers takes advantage of the shade."
His summer poem said:
"Idle clouds gather but bring no rain,
Sick leaves fall but it is not autumn."
Fāng Gàn said:
"He will certainly not live long."
He died before he was ten years old.
Ōuyáng Bīn's son composed a poem for a farmer saying:
"Mulberry and thorn trees in the setting sun,
Sons and grandsons amidst falling leaves."
He also died young soon after.
The Master of One Character
When Zhāng Jiǒng was young, he dreamt of five-colored clouds descending from the sky.
He took a ball of it and swallowed it,
after which he became skilled in poetry.
He had a "Poem Sent Far Away" that said:
"To whom can this brocade letter be entrusted?
In the quiet courtyard, the grass has withered again.
The long night, the lamp's shadow extinguished,
The distant sky, the goose's cry lonely.
Her cicada-like hair is almost gone,
Are his dragon-beard whiskers still black?
How many times have I been too sad to speak,
Because I look at a map of the northern regions?"
The monk Qí Sī changed "qiú zī bái yě wú" (虯髭白也無 - are his dragon-beard whiskers also white?) to "qiú zī hēi zài wú" (虯髭黑在無 - are his dragon-beard whiskers still black?).
Zhāng Jiǒng then bowed to him as his "master of one character."
Linked Verse
Mǎ Xīzhèn and the monk Yōng Guàn often composed linked verses.
Mǎ Xīzhèn said:
"Ant-children carrying insect-children."
Yōng Guàn said:
"Cat-kittens catching sparrow-chicks."
Xú Zhòngyǎ's Poems
When Wénzhāo Wáng welcomed the Four Lady-Confidantes (Sì Yí Fūrén),
Xú Zhòngyǎ composed a poem saying:
"The cloud-path half-opens, a thousand miles of sun,
The cave gate obliquely closed, a day of spring."
He also wrote a palace poem saying:
"Palace maids rise at dawn, fearing the spring chill,
Lightly lift the silk curtain to gaze at peonies.
A handful of willow threads cannot be gathered,
The gentle breeze obliquely drapes them over the jade balustrade."
The Rhapsody on White and The Rhapsody on Red
Guàn Bào and Xiè Guàn both entered the tutelage of Prime Minister Cuī Yì.
Xiè Guàn once composed a "Rhapsody on White,"
which contained the lines:
"In the evening, entering the park of King Liáng,
Snow covers all the mountains;
At night, ascending Yǔ Liàng's tower,
The moon shines bright for a thousand miles."
Guàn Bào composed a "Rhapsody on Red," saying:
"On the day Tián Dān defeated Yān,
Fire scorched the plains;
At the time Wǔ Wáng attacked Zhòu,
Blood flowed, enough to float pestles."
Guàn Bào soon resigned and left,
while Xiè Guàn still relied on his patronage.
At a banquet, there were many flies.
Xiè Guàn said:
"Green flies are fanned by fans away from the table."
Guàn Bào looked up and saw a painting of a Báizé on the door,
and replied:
"A Báizé is nailed by nails to the door."
Wú Náor
Wú Hélíng was a Dàoshi,
residing on Nányuè,
and was commonly called Wú Náor.
He loved to sleep,
going for ten days without food or drink.
He often said:
"If a person wants to be at leisure,
they will be lazy;
if diligent,
they will not be at leisure."
Poem on Butterflies
Wáng Zhù's poem on butterflies said:
"If tonight you rest amidst fragrant grasses,
Please convey my message to the young lord (wáng sūn)."
Dòngtíng Hú
Mǎ Xīfàn of Húnán entered the court for an audience.
Zhuāngzōng said:
"In Húnán Province, the waves of Dòngtíng Hú are boundless,
is that so?"
Mǎ Xīfàn replied:
"Should Your Majesty tour the south,
this lake is not even enough to water your horses."
Poem on a Moonless Mid-Autumn
The former Jìnshì, Gāo Ruònè,
brought his literary works in his sleeve to see Gāo Cónghuì in Jīng (Jīngzhōu).
He had a "Poem on a Moonless Mid-Autumn" which said:
"Though not seen by humans,
Beyond the heavens, it is perfectly clear."
Gāo Cónghuì said:
"Though this poem is good,
I fear that in the future you will lose your sight."
Later, it happened as he said.
There was also a monk Kělóng, whose poem said:
"After much thought, one acts;
One mistake ruins all previous efforts."
Gāo Cónghuì said:
"This poem must have been inspired by an event."
Kělóng said:
"My original surname was Mùróng,
and I was a fellow student with Sāng Wéihàn.
When young, I was arrogant
and often dismissed him.
When Sāng Wéihàn became prime minister,
I was still a student taking exams,
and I failed repeatedly for years,
all due to Sāng Wéihàn's obstruction.
Thus, I shaved my head and became a monk,
and these lines truly reflect that past event."
Rhapsody on Crabs
Yán Xù was in the Zhōngshū (Chancellery),
merely filling a position,
without academic learning,
and was despised by his peers.
Jiāng Wénwèi's "Rhapsody on Crabs" satirized him, saying:
"From its mouth comes 'yes' and 'no' (cí huáng),
ever crossing paths when lost;
In its chest, military armor,
often gathering crowds to scuttle sideways."
It also said:
"Outwardly, many legs,
Within, no inch of gut."
Hán Xīzài's Letter
When Hán Xīzài passed the Jìnshì examination,
he sent a letter to Lǐ Dǐng saying:
"He who fishes for a great turtle (ào)
does not cast bait meant for small fish;
He who slays a long whale
why would he use a knife for butchering a chicken?"
He also said:
"A sword at the waist and a hammer in the sleeve,
A tongue in the mouth and a brush in the hand."
Paper Window
Guō Xīshēng's
poem "Paper Window" says: "It suits the mossy wall, fit for quiet recitation,
white like stream clouds, thin like ice.
It's not that a wild man dislikes the moonlight,
but to prevent the wind from disturbing the lamp for study."
His poem "Hearing the Cricket" says:
"It saddens those who have left home and not yet achieved their ambitions,
a sound by sound reaching the pillow, heard.
Do not groan bitterly towards the vermilion gates,
for with ears full of music and singing, they will not listen to you."
The Young Noble's Song
When the King of Shǔ, Jiàn, usurped the throne,
he visited the Lónghuá Chan Monastery,
and summoned the monk Guànhyū to recite recent poems.
At that time, all the kings, relatives, and retainers were in attendance,
and Hū wanted to admonish them.
He then recited "The Young Noble's Song," saying:
"Dressed in splendid, fresh robes, holding a falcon,
strolling leisurely with a frivolous demeanor.
Totally ignorant of the hardships of farming,
what are the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns?"
Divine Arrow
Yuányīng, son of Shǔ King Jiàn,
once shot and hit a target made of coins.
Hànlín Academian Máa Wénxī composed a rhapsody praising him.
Yuányīng said:
"Is this a divine arrow, or is the poor scholar afraid?"
Common people rejoice at small gains
Wáng Zōngchēng was the Prefect of Jìnzhōu.
A sea merchant was selling expensive Borneo camphor,
asking for double the usual price.
Zōngchēng ordered a brocade quilt to be brought and shown to the merchant,
then signaled his attendants to carry off the camphor bottle.
He also ordered a broker to buy two courtesans,
each sixteen years old,
for a price of thirty-two strings of cash.
Zōngchēng took them,
and called an old maidservant, saying to the broker:
"This one is already fifty,
worth fifty thousand strings of cash.
After paying for the two courtesans,
there are still eighteen thousand strings of cash remaining.
Buy a piece of plain cloth bedding,
weighing ten catties."
He then ordered fifteen catties of old hemp rope to be taken from the wine room to pay for it.
The common people looked at each other and laughed.
Zōngchēng said:
"The common people rejoice at a gain of five catties."
The officials and people filed complaints,
and he was demoted to the Judicial Officer of Wéizhōu.
Grand Pivot and Minor Pivot
Pān Kàng and his brother Qiào jointly managed the affairs of state,
and were known as the Grand Pivot and Minor Pivot.
Kàng favored his beautiful concubine Jiěchóu,
whose surname was Zhào.
Her mother dreamed of a crabapple blossom pistil when she conceived her.
She was skilled at imitating monks' voices and good at writing short poems.
When Shǔ King Jiàn visited his residence,
he saw her and said:
"There is no one like this in my palace."
He intended to take her.
Kàng said:
"She is my humble servant,
I dare not recommend her to Your Majesty."
In fact, he cherished her like a younger brother.
Qiào said:
"Shouldn't we beware of the disaster of Lǜzhū!"
Kàng said:
"Life is about doing what one desires,
how can one love death and not satisfy one's own heart?"
Holding a Wúzhē Assembly
Jìn Huī, the King of Hóngnóng Commandery,
was initially a bandit with Jiàn.
One night, they docked their boat in an ancient tomb in Wǔyáng,
and heard someone calling out to a ghost in the tomb, saying:
"Yǐngchuān is holding a Wúzhē Assembly,
will you come along?"
The ghost in the tomb replied:
"The King of Shǔ is here,
I cannot accompany you."
Prison's Grievances
In Tóngzhōu, when digging the ground, an object was found,
weighing over eighty catties.
Liú Yuán said:
"This is a place of imprisonment,
where grievances have accumulated."
Shuǐdiào Yínhàn Qǔ
Pǐzǐ Yǎn ascended the throne.
He cruised by boat to inspect Lángzhōng,
and all the boatmen were dressed in splendid brocade.
He personally composed the Shuǐdiào "Yínhàn Qǔ."
Hè Kāng, a local of the commandery, had a beautiful daughter.
When she was about to marry,
Yǎn took her,
and bestowed a hundred bolts of silk on her husband's family.
Her husband cried out in grief and died.
Ancient Mirror
Zōng Shòudìng's kinsman
obtained an ancient iron mirror.
Below it were eleven seal characters.
Suddenly, it reflected a small boy in green clothes sitting in a wine shop.
He sent someone to find him.
The boy in green clothes came along,
and said:
"I lost this a hundred years ago.
This is a divine object,
and will eventually transform and depart.
It is better to return it to me."
Zōng Shòu went out and gave it to him.
The boy in green clothes cut open his abdomen, put the mirror inside, and left.
The small boy transmitted the art of *bìgǔ tǔnà* (abstinence from grains and breathing exercises).
Wáng Yī Lái Qù
Yǎn forbade the common people from wearing small hats.
Yǎn liked to travel incognito,
often staying at courtesans' houses
and drinking in wine shops.
He would ask for a brush and write:
"Wáng Yī Lái Qù" (Wang comes and goes).
Fearing people would recognize him,
he therefore ordered the common people to all wear large hats.
Chicken Knife to Decapitate Dogs
Zhāng Yún served as a Remonstrance Official,
and was upright and outspoken in court,
comparing himself to Zhū Yún.
Someone said:
"In the past, Zhū Yún requested the 'Horse-Beheading Sword' to execute Zhāng Yǔ.
Now, the Imperial Arsenal only has chicken-slaughtering knives.
Do you want to use them?"
Yún said:
"Although a chicken knife is small,
it can still decapitate a pack of dogs."
Unfortunate to Have Three Sons
Zhāng Yún was prone to boasting.
He often said:
"It is my misfortune to have three sons.
One studies Sun and Wu's military tactics,
one studies Hán Yù's minor essays,
and one studies Dù Fǔ's minor poems.
This is truly a misfortune for my family."
Red Gardenia Flower
When Mèng Xiáng of Shǔ usurped the throne,
he summoned all officials to a banquet in Fānglín Garden,
to admire gardenia flowers.
Their shape was six-petaled.
Sleeping Prime Minister
Xú Guāngtuán became Prime Minister.
He enjoyed discussing matters,
which was greatly resented by Lǐ Mín and others.
Later, Guāngtuán ceased speaking.
Whenever there was a group discussion,
he would merely feign sleep.
At the time, he was called "Sleeping Prime Minister."
Zhèng Yì's Song
says:
"Do not say you have read five cartloads of books,
do not say your writing is like Máa Xiāngrú.
It is better to have one *yì* of gold and a bag of pearls at home,
which can bribe the prime minister's sons and younger brothers,
and befriend the prime minister's servants.
Then you can be a butcher or peddler in the morning,
and ride in a grand carriage in the evening."
The lyrics are numerous,
so they are not fully recorded.
Imitating Shěn Xiè to Mock the Wind and Chant the Moon
Zhèng Yì once taught his son using the *Wénxuǎn*.
His elder brother said:
"Why don't you teach him to read the *Xiàojīng* and *Lúnyǔ*,
to prevent him from learning from Shěn and Xiè to mock the wind and chant the moon,
which would stain his conduct?"
A Drum-and-Pipe Band of Flesh
Lǐ Kuāngyuǎn was harsh and impatient.
If he did not inflict punishment for a day,
he would be somber and unhappy.
He once heard the sound of flogging
and said:
"This is my drum-and-pipe band of flesh."
Before his death, he said:
"I killed all monks and Daoist priests in my life,
and thus enjoyed a lifespan of eighty-two years."
When he was buried,
robbers unearthed his tomb
and severed his four limbs,
which was the retribution for his cruel punishments.
Dreaming of Standing under the Northern Dipper
When Yuán Kuò first took the imperial examination,
he dreamt he stood under the Northern Dipper.
Indeed, he passed as the seventh person.
Recalling a Previous Life's Events
Wén Dàn was four years old
when he told his mother:
“I have a silver gourd, a lacquered ball, and a five-colored sachet on an apricot tree.”
They went to retrieve them,
and indeed found them.
It turned out that when Dàn was five years old, he had fallen into a well,
and this was his rebirth.
Yùlěi Jí
The monk-poet Kě Péng
had a collection of poems titled *Yùlěi Jí*.
His poem about Dòngtíng reads:
“Water contains the vastness of the sky's reflection,
Mountains rise, making the land high.”
Another poem about an old residence reads:
“Heartbroken, all day there are crying birds,
Walking alone in late spring, only fallen flowers.”
He styled himself "Zuì Kūn" (Drunken Shaved Head).
Pántáo Kernel Cup
Liú Guāngzuò, a Zhongshū Shèrén, presented a wine cup made from a pántáo kernel,
claiming he obtained it from Chén Tuán on Huà Shān.
Poor and Frugal Beggar
Lǐ Mín served in office for fifty years,
accumulating vast wealth.
He once read the *Wáng Kǎi Shí Chóng Zhuàn* and said:
“A poor and frugal beggar,
to consider this wealth,
ridiculous!
Ridiculous!”
Cold Words Freezing People
Pān Zhùyíng,
during the Mèng Shǔ era, used his wealth to curry favor with powerful officials.
Someone warned him,
but he replied:
“It is not to seek favors;
I simply do not wish to freeze people with cold words.”
Monk Shaving Hair
Hán Zhāo did everything like a monk shaving his hair,
leaving not an inch (of hair, i.e., no personal gain or trace).
Lost Ox
Gāo Yǒu was a Cāngmù (granary official).
Someone lost a black ox
with white hair on its back.
Yǒu then falsely pretended to buy ox hides from the prefecture and county,
paying double their value,
and made the owner identify his ox,
thus catching the thief.
Cuī Yīng
was nine years old.
Qín Wáng Fú Jiān asked:
“What books are you reading, my lord?”
He replied:
“The *Xiàojīng*.”
Fú Jiān asked:
“What is its meaning?”
He replied:
“Those above should not be arrogant.”
He was asked again what other meanings it had.
He replied:
“Superiors love inferiors,
and inferiors respect superiors.”
Fú Jiān said:
“You may go, and when you are seventeen, I will employ you as a Dàfū.”
Yīng said:
“The sun and moon can be seen again,
but Your Majesty, the most honored, cannot be seen a second time.
A scholar may be useful now;
why wait for a later date?”
Fú Jiān said:
“Study diligently,
and at seventeen I will surely summon you.”
When the time came,
he was appointed Jiànyì Dàfū.
Fàn Zhì
Wáng Fànzhì
was from Líyáng.
In Wáng Dézǔ's family, there was a crabapple tree that grew a burl,
as large as a peck measure.
When the burl rotted,
Dézǔ peeled off its skin,
and saw a child emerging from the sac.
At seven years old, he could speak and asked who raised him.
He was told the truth,
and so he was named Fàntiān,
later changed to Fànzhì,
indicating a manifestation of a Bodhisattva.
Zōu Luòtuó
Zōu Fèngchì had high eyebrows and a crooked back,
and was nicknamed "Luòtuó" (Camel).
He was very wealthy.
He bought timber from Nán Shān,
estimating one bolt of silk per tree.
He said:
“The mountain timber may be exhausted,
but I will have silk to spare.”
Fèngchéng Yuán
Mǎ Sītú's son, Chàng,
presented large apricots from his residence to Dòu Wénchǎng,
who then presented them to Dèzōng.
As Dèzōng had never seen such,
he was quite surprised and ordered a palace eunuch to seal the tree where they grew.
Chàng, in fear, presented his residence,
which was then converted into Fèngchéng Yuán.
Good at Crying
Táng Qú had literary talent,
but achieved nothing in his old age.
He was good at crying,
his voice mournful and poignant,
moving listeners to tears.
Song of the Orphan
Cuī Yīng grew up with his maternal relatives when he was young,
and was not well-regarded.
When he grew up,
he wrote the "Song of the Orphan by the Roadside" to satirize his maternal clan.
Taking a Concubine as a Wife
Dù Yòu, Jìedùshǐ of Huáinán,
had first married into the Liáng clan,
and had seven children.
When the Liáng wife died,
he made his favored concubine, Lady Lǐ, his principal wife,
and she was enfeoffed as a Guófūrén.
Cuī Yīng advised him to posthumously ennoble his deceased wife.
Dù Yòu asked Yīng to write a memorial, which read:
“Taking a concubine as a wife is forbidden by the *Lǔ Shǐ* (Annals of Lu).”
It also said:
“Was it because when one was of humble status,
the wife shared in the hardships;
but after attaining high office,
the concubine enjoys the honorable enfeoffment?”
Consequently, the Liáng wife was posthumously enfeoffed,
and Lady Lǐ also received her title,
but she resented Cuī Yīng for it in the end.
One day,
the Duke ordered pork to be eaten.
As Lǐ was carving it, she collapsed and died.
Earlier, Yīng had favored a minor general from the Taishǒu of Wǎnlíng.
This person, grateful, entrusted his daughter to Yīng.
Seeing Yīng's wild nature,
and later fearing he would abandon her,
he requested a written promise saying:
“The woman sought cannot be made a concubine.”
Later, Yīng indeed abandoned her,
and the man presented the document to argue his case,
and Yīng was at a loss for words.
Wet Nurse Breaking the Law
Hán Jìngōng was the Zhéxī Guāncháshǐ.
His wet nurse sought external favors.
The Duke intended to execute her.
She secretly sought Gu Yīn to intercede.
Gu Yīn went to the Duke and asked about it.
The Duke said:
“Everyone knows I uphold the law,
and my wet nurse was the first to violate it.”
Gu Yīn said:
“When you were young,
whether rising early or sleeping late, you needed your wet nurse.
Now that you are a Hóubó,
what use is a wet nurse?
Indeed, she should be killed!”
The Duke immediately spared her.
Volume 27
ends.
Shéngào Lù
During the Kaihuáng reign of the
Suí dynasty, Táng Shényáo met an old man who said:
“You do not possess the countenance of a subject;
rather, you are a successor to Dānqiūzǐ.”
The Emperor asked:
“Who is Dānqiū?”
The old man replied:
“He is closely related to you,
but you are unaware.
He lives as a recluse between Hù and Shè,
his emotions detached from worldly affairs.
If perchance he condescends to join you,
he will assist you in the Central Plains later on;
he shall be your aide.”
The Emperor, with sword in hand, requested to meet him,
intending to sketch his portrait.
Upon seeing his demeanor and appearance,
his heart was struck with awe and his spirit surged.
The master said:
“I have long grown weary of this defiled world;
happily, I have no concerns about being feared.”
The Emperor was astonished and apologized,
asking about his way of aiding the world,
but he did not reply.
The Emperor returned disheartened.
In the early Wǔdé period,
he visited again,
but his dwelling was already empty.
From the Shàngqīng Zhuàn:
Dòu Cān was walking in the central courtyard on a moonlit night
when Qīngyī Shàngqīng said:
“There is someone in the courtyard tree;
please be careful to avoid him.”
Cān said:
“Lù Zhì has long wanted to usurp my power and position;
now disaster is imminent!”
He shouted loudly:
“The gentleman in the tree must have been sent by Lù Zhì!
If you can spare this old man’s life,
how dare I not repay you handsomely!”
The person in the tree responded and came down,
and it was a man in mourning clothes.
He said:
“My family has suffered a great loss,
and I cannot afford the funeral rites.”
Cān gave him a thousand bolts of silk.
The mourner asked to throw the silk outside the wall,
and Cān agreed.
The next day,
Dézōng angrily said:
“You consort with jīngjiāng (military governors),
harboring assassins.
Your position is as lofty as the grand ministers;
what more do you seek?”
Cān replied:
“It is the work of my enemies.”
The following month,
he was demoted to Chēnzhōu,
and subsequently exiled to Huānzhōu.
His family property was confiscated,
and an imperial edict ordered him to commit suicide.
Shàngqīng was registered in the Yètíng (palace women’s quarters)
and, being skilled in repartee
and able to brew tea,
gained favor.
The Emperor asked:
“How did you come to be here?”
Shàngqīng replied:
“I was originally Dòu Cān’s maidservant.”
The Emperor said:
“Cān was very corrupt;
the imperial silver vessels collected previously were truly his.”
Shàngqīng said:
“All the silver objects were bestowed by Your Majesty.
On the day they were to be cataloged,
I saw that the prefectural and county officials, trying to please Lù Zhì,
scraped off the characters on the silver vessels
and engraved the names of the fānzhèn (military governors) instead.”
The Emperor took the vessels and re-examined the scraped areas,
finding them to be as she said.
The Emperor also asked about Cān harboring assassins.
She replied:
“All of it was Lù Zhì’s malicious plot.”
The Emperor angrily said:
“This savage slave!
I removed his green robe and gave him a purple one,
and even called him ‘Lù Jiǔ’.
I was pleased when I appointed Dòu Cān.
He had me unjustly kill others,
and yet when power fell into his hands,
he was as soft and weak as a lump of mud!”
Thereupon, an imperial edict was issued to clear Cān’s name.
From the Shényì Jì:
The jinshi Bāo Jìngbó,
dreamed one night of two men in yellow robes who came with a talisman to summon him.
They walked along the roadside
and entered a dilapidated wall amidst weeds.
He saw an old woman who said:
“My surname is Yú,
and I am your maternal aunt.
My son, Cuī Xuān,
is now a Langzhōng (Secretary).
Unfortunately, he is disobedient and rebellious,
leaving me unburied for thirty years,
my bones exposed.
Now you are destined to be sent back,
and he should be made to re-bury me.
If he treats your words as false,
then I will complain to the Heavenly Emperor,
and a severe punishment will be inflicted.
I also pray that you will write a copy of the *Jīnguāngmíng Jīng* for me,
so that I may receive its blessings.”
They then walked to a government office,
where a judge said:
“Jìngbó’s allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted;
this summons was a mistake in the records.”
Jìngbó then asked about longevity, premature death, nobility, and lowliness.
The judge replied:
“The affairs of the underworld are secret;
the law forbids their disclosure.”
He held up a register and covered the paper with his hand,
revealing two lines which read:
“Bāo Shú, thirty-five years old,
shall be appointed county尉 of Fènghuà county, Míngzhōu, upon passing the imperial examination.”
Jìngbó said:
“I have never been called Shú.”
The judge said:
“It is not a mistake.”
When he awoke,
he saw Yú Shì’s son and
fully recounted the previous events,
but the son did not believe him.
The next year,
the man accepted a spurious appointment from Zhū Cǐ.
When the rebellion was quelled,
his entire family was condemned to death.
After the execution, Jìngbó submitted a sealed memorial.
When Xià Shú, a scribe of the Jīnwú (Bureau of the Palace Guard), was copying the dates and names at the end,
Shú mistakenly wrote his own name.
The Emperor praised the document
and instructed the prime minister, saying:
“The memorialist Bāo Shú
should be given an official position.”
Thus, he was appointed county尉 of Fènghuà county, Míngzhōu.
He then wrote the *Jīnguāngmíng Jīng*
and fed monks to make offerings for Yú Shì.
From the Jìnglóng Jì:
During the Dàbǎo period,
Yángzhōu presented a Water-Heart Mirror,
clear and shimmering, dazzling to the eye,
with a coiled dragon on its back.
Earlier, there was an old man,
who called himself Lóng Hù,
with a young boy named Xuánmíng.
They came to the casting workshop and said:
“This old man can cast a true dragon mirror.”
He ordered Xuánmíng to enter the furnace area,
locked the doors and windows,
and after three days, when the doors were opened,
Lóng Hù and Xuánmíng were nowhere to be found.
The mirror craftsman moved the furnace onto a boat
and cast it in the middle of the Yángzǐ Jiāng on the fifth day of the fifth month.
Later, there was a great drought with no rain.
Yè Fǎshàn worshipped the mirror dragon in the Níngyīn Diàn.
Shortly after,
clouds filled the hall,
and heavy rain began to fall.
From the Gǔjìng Jì:
Wáng Dù, a Yùshǐ (Imperial Censor) of the Suí dynasty,
possessed a precious mirror in his home.
During the Dàyè period,
a Hu (Western Region monk) said:
“There is always a continuous green light above your residence for days,
and a continuous crimson aura for months.
This is the aura of a precious mirror.
If it is simply fumigated with golden smoke,
washed with jade water,
then smeared with golden ointment,
and polished with pearl powder,
even if hidden in mud,
it will not grow dim.”
There was a severe plague between Pú and Shǎn.
Wáng Dù ordered his servant Zhāng Jū to hold the mirror and shine it on them.
All the sick people rose in surprise,
saying:
“We saw a moon coming to shine upon us.”
And they all recovered.
Zhāng Jū dreamt of a person
with a pearl crown and purple robes,
who said:
“I am the spirit of the mirror,
named Zǐzhēn.”
Wéi Xiānwēng
During the reign of Dài Zōng,
Wéi Shìyù was dispatched as an envoy to Huà Shān to pay respects at the altar of Huáng Dì.
Upon reaching the inn at the foot of the mountain,
he saw an old man,
and asked him the location of the altar.
The old man knew it,
and moreover said his surname was Wéi,
and his family also held official positions.
He described his lineage,
and it turned out he was the great-great-grandfather of Shìyù.
They went into the mountain together,
the old man leaning on his staff and walking ahead.
Wéi whipped his horse but could not catch up.
When he reached a stone chamber, he saw
two old women who said,
"These are your grandmother and great-aunt."
Both had double coiled hair,
and wore clothes adorned with leaves.
They joyfully said,
"Ages have changed,
and in one day we have seen our great-great-grandson!"
Soon after, he went up the mountain with the old man,
paid his respects at the altar,
and then took his leave to return.
Later, when he tried to find them again,
he had forgotten the old path.
People at the foot of the mountain said,
"That old woman comes once every two or three years,
but we don't know where she lives."
The Story in the Pillow
During the Kāiyuán era,
the Daoist old man Lǚ Gōng,
passing through Hándān, stopped at an inn along the road.
There was a young scholar, Lú Shēng,
staying at the same inn.
The host was steaming yellow millet,
and they were all waiting for it to be cooked.
Lú unexpectedly sighed deeply,
and Gōng asked him why.
Lú fully explained his life's difficulties and misfortunes.
Gōng took a pillow from his bag and gave it to Lú, saying,
"If you rest on this, you will achieve glory and success as you wish."
Lú bowed his head,
and only remembered his body entering the pillow's aperture,
and then he arrived at his home.
Before long,
he rose through the ranks of officialdom,
serving as a general and prime minister for fifty or sixty years.
His children and grandchildren all held prominent positions,
and his glory and prosperity were unequaled.
He submitted a memorial saying,
"Your humble servant is over eighty years old,
has held positions in the Three Ducal Ministries,
and has only failed to repay your profound benevolence;
I permanently resign from this sacred dynasty."
On the night of his death,
Lú Shēng yawned and awoke.
Lǚ Wēng was beside him,
and the yellow millet was not yet cooked.
Lú thanked him, saying,
"This is how you, master, blocked my desires.
How dare I not accept your instruction?"
He bowed again and departed.
Pú Pú Xiānsheng
He called himself Pú Pú.
For over thirty years, he was at Huángtǔ Shān in the former Zhōu Lè'ān county,
meditating intently and consuming apricot elixir.
During the Kāiyuán era, he ascended to heaven on a cloud.
Míng Huáng changed the name of Lè'ān to Xiānjū County.
Recorded by Liǔ Shì.
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Hán Hóng was renowned for his poetry.
He was good friends with the rich man Lǐ Shēng,
who gave him his favorite concubine, Liǔ Shì.
The following year,
Hóng passed the highest imperial examination
and set up his household in Qīngchí.
More than a year later,
rebels overran the two capitals,
and officials fled in terror.
Liǔ Shì, fearing that her beauty would not spare her,
cut her hair at Fáyún Sì.
At that time, Hóu Xīyì was the Jìdū of Zībíng and Qīng.
He invited Hóng to be his secretary.
Hóng sent an envoy to secretly seek Liǔ Shì,
carrying a silk pouch containing gold dust,
and inscribed it with the words:
"The willows of Zhāngtái,
the willows of Zhāngtái,
are the once verdant branches still there today?
Even if the long branches still droop as before,
they must have been broken by other hands."
Liǔ Shì replied:
"Willow branches,
in the season of fragrance,
what a pity to be gifted for parting year after year.
A single leaf carried by the wind suddenly heralds autumn;
even if you were to come, how could you break them?"
Not long after,
the barbarian general Shāzhìlì, having just achieved distinction,
learned of her beauty,
and forcibly took her to his residence,
favoring her exclusively.
Hóng accompanied Xīyì to an audience in the capital.
When he reached Lóngshǒu Gāng,
he saw Liǔ Shì in a carriage,
and was almost overwhelmed with emotion.
A patrol officer, Xǔ Jùn, said,
"I will surely bring her to you."
So, he dressed in a barbarian robe,
wore a double quiver,
and with one rider,
went directly to Shāzhìlì's residence.
Waiting for Shāzhìlì to leave,
he pushed open the gate and shouted loudly,
"The general has fallen ill,
and sent me to summon the lady!"
The servants scattered,
and he ascended the hall,
pulled Liǔ Shì onto his saddle,
and galloped away, raising dust,
arriving suddenly.
At that time, Shāzhìlì was exceptionally favored,
and Hóng feared disaster,
so he appealed to Xīyì,
who reported the matter to the imperial court.
An edict was issued for Liǔ Shì to return to Hóng.
Biography of Qí Guó Fūrén
Lǐ Wá,
a courtesan in Cháng'ān.
During the Tiānbǎo reign,
a son of the Lord of Róngyáng went to Cháng'ān to take the imperial examination.
He once roamed the East Market,
and arrived at Míngkē Qǔ,
where he saw a mansion.
Its gate was imposing and deep.
A woman, leaning on a maid in green, stood there,
her beauty unrivaled for generations.
The young man stopped his horse
and lingered, unable to leave.
He pretended to drop his whip on the ground,
waited for his attendant to arrive,
and ordered him to retrieve it.
He gazed repeatedly,
and their eyes met with great affection.
The young man inquired of his friend,
who said:
"This is the residence of Lǐ Wá, a courtesan of the alley.
Her family is quite wealthy;
unless you have millions, you cannot sway her heart."
The young man said:
"I only fear it won't succeed;
why regret a million?"
Slowly, he went to knock on the door.
A maid recognized him,
and rushed inside, shouting:
"The gentleman who dropped his whip earlier has come!"
Wá adjusted her makeup and came out.
She saw an old woman,
who was Wá's mother,
and addressed the young man as "gentleman."
The next morning,
the young man moved all his belongings
and settled into the Lǐ family's residence.
After more than a year,
his wealth, bribes, servants, and horses were all spent.
The old woman said:
"My daughter and the gentleman have known each other for a year,
but there is no pregnancy or heir.
The divine response from the Bamboo Grove temple is as quick as an echo.
Would it be acceptable to offer sacrifices and pray for a son?"
The young man was overjoyed,
and went with Wá to the temple.
They returned after two nights.
Their path led through Xuānyáng Lǐ,
where Wá said:
"From this small alley,
that is my aunt's residence."
She led the young man to pay respects.
The pond and garden were exquisitely secluded,
with bamboo and trees shading the windows.
The young man said:
"Is this your aunt's private residence?"
Wá smiled and did not answer.
After a short while,
a person riding a large Dàwǎn sweat-blood horse galloped up and said:
"The old woman has suddenly fallen ill;
you should return quickly."
Wá said to her aunt:
"My mind is in a turmoil.
I will ride ahead.
You should arrange for a returning carriage to bring the gentleman."
It was late in the day,
but the carriage did not arrive.
The aunt said:
"Perhaps the gentleman should go and check on them."
The young man went to his former residence,
but it was securely locked.
A neighbor said:
"The old woman moved two nights ago."
The young man rushed to Xuānyáng,
questioned his aunt,
but knocked on the door to no avail.
An official slowly came out and said:
"This is Cūi Shàngshū's residence.
Yesterday, a woman rented its courtyard,
saying she was waiting for a distant relative to arrive,
but she left before dusk."
The young man was bewildered.
He then sought out his former lodging,
and became very ill.
The innkeeper sent him to a funeral parlor,
where he gradually recovered.
He was made to hold the funeral canopy,
earning his keep this way.
His elegiac songs
were sung with utmost skill.
When he sang the verses of "Xiè Lù,"
listeners covered their ears.
It so happened that the young man's father came to the capital.
An old servant saw him
and told his father:
"The singer's appearance
is remarkably similar to the young master's."
The father said:
"My son was harmed by robbers because of his great wealth.
How could he have come to this?"
The servant then rushed over,
grabbed his sleeve, and said:
"Is this not young master so-and-so?"
He was brought back by cart.
The father said:
"Such conduct
disgraces my family."
He then took him to the Xìngyuán in Qǔjiāng,
flogged him several hundred times, and left him for dead.
His father abandoned him and left.
The funeral workers told their comrades to bury him,
but finding him slightly warm,
he revived after a night.
After ten days, he could get up.
Dressed in a patched cloth robe,
he held a broken bowl and begged for food in the alleys.
One day, during a heavy snow,
his begging cries were particularly mournful.
One door opened its left half,
which was Wá's residence.
Wá heard his voice,
stepped out quickly,
embraced his neck, and pulled him in with her embroidered robe,
weeping loudly:
"That you have come to this,
is my fault!"
The old woman angrily said:
"He should be driven out!
How can he be allowed to come here?"
Wá said:
"This is a young man from a respectable family.
In the past, he drove splendid carriages,
and spent all his gold.
Mother and daughter conspired to drive him away,
causing him to lose his ambition
and disregard human morality.
Deceiving Heaven and betraying others,
neither gods nor ghosts will bless us.
Now, Mother is sixty years old.
I wish to calculate twenty years' worth of expenses for your food and clothing,
to buy my freedom.
I will then find another suitable match for this young man."
The old woman was moved
and agreed.
With the remaining few hundred gold pieces,
they rented a small dwelling,
and bathed the young man.
First, they used hot gruel to clear his bowels,
then butter and milk to nourish his internal organs,
gradually offering various delicacies.
By the end of the year,
he was fully recovered as before.
Wá said:
"Your body is now well,
and your spirit is strong.
You can review your studies
and devote yourself to learning."
She made him study at night,
and Wá always sat beside him.
After two years,
his studies had greatly progressed.
Wá said:
"Not yet."
After another year,
she said:
"You may proceed now."
He then passed the highest imperial examination,
and also the "Straight Talk and Bold Admonition" examination,
ranking first.
He was appointed Cānjūn of Chéngdū Prefecture.
Wá said:
"Today's events
have restored you to your original state.
I have not let you down.
I wish to return and care for my mother.
You should marry into a prominent family,
and not defile yourself.
I will see you to Jiànmén and then return."
When they reached Jiànmén,
the young man's father had been appointed Prefect of Chéngdū.
After a week,
his father arrived.
The young man presented his calling card to his father.
His father, seeing his ancestral official carriage,
was greatly surprised,
and cried out:
"My son, let us be as before, father and son!"
The young man fully explained the whole story.
His father asked:
"Where is Wá?"
He replied:
"She saw me to this point;
she should be returning now."
His father said:
"No!"
He built a separate mansion to house her,
and prepared the Six Rites to welcome her.
Wá's conduct as a wife was exceptionally virtuous.
Later, when the young man's parents died,
she observed mourning with extreme devotion.
A spirit ganoderma grew by the mourning hut.
A single stalk produced three ears,
and there were white swallows nesting on her roof.
Shēng was repeatedly promoted and became very prominent.
His daughter was enfeoffed as Qīinguó Fūrén.
Her old name was Yīzhīhuā.
This story is based on the self-performance of Yīzhīhuā.
The Tale of the Spirit Matrimony of Dòngtíng
During the Yífèng reign,
Liǔ Yì failed the imperial examination.
He was returning to the banks of the Xiāng River.
At a place on the road to Jīngyáng,
he saw a woman herding sheep.
She said:
"I am the youngest daughter of the Dragon Lord of Dòngtíng.
I was married to the second son of Jīngchuān,
but he was infatuated by another woman,
and day by day grew cold towards me.
Moreover, I offended my parents-in-law,
and was demoted to this place.
Dòngtíng is far away,
and no news can be exchanged.
Hearing that you are returning,
I entrust this short letter to you.
To the north of Dòngtíng there is a large orange tree,
called 'Júshè' (Orange Altar).
Strike the tree three times,
and someone will respond."
Yì agreed,
and then asked:
"What do you herd these sheep for?"
The woman said:
"They are not sheep.
They are rainworkers,
of the thunder and lightning kind."
Yì looked at them;
their eating and chewing were very strange,
but their size, fur, and horns were indistinguishable from sheep.
Yì said:
"Another day, may Dòngtíng not avoid me."
Later, he reached Dòngtíng.
Indeed, there was an orange tree.
He struck it three times and stopped.
An old man came,
parted the water, and led Yì to be introduced.
There were a thousand gates and ten thousand households,
exotic flowers and rare trees.
The old man said:
"This is the Língxū Diàn."
There were white jade pillars, green jade beds, coral curtains, and amber beams.
The king was currently at Xuánzhū Gé,
discussing the Huǒ Jīng with Tàiyáng Dàoshì.
A moment later,
he saw a person dressed in purple holding a ceremonial tablet.
Yì said:
"Yesterday I went to Jīngchuān,
and saw your beloved daughter herding sheep.
Her hair was disheveled by wind and rain,
a sight I could not bear to see."
He took out the letter and presented it.
The Dòngtíng Lord wept, saying:
"It is my old fault that caused this tender child to suffer misfortune.
You, Sir, are but a stranger on the road,
yet you are able to help her."
Soon,
everyone in the palace wept bitterly.
The Lord hurriedly said:
"Let no sound be made in the palace,
lest Qiántáng learn of it."
Yì asked:
"Who is he?"
He replied:
"He is my younger brother.
In the past, he was the chief of Qiántáng,
surpassing others in bravery.
When Yáo suffered the great flood for nine years,
it was due to this son's rage.
Recently, he incurred the displeasure of the Heavenly Generals,
shaking their five mountains.
The Emperor ordered him to be restrained here."
Before his words were finished,
a red dragon, over ten thousand *zhàng* long,
with a thousand thunders and ten thousand lightnings entwining its body,
tore through the sky and flew away.
Suddenly,
auspicious winds and propitious clouds,
warm and gentle,
streamers and bells jingling,
accompanied by the sound of flutes,
thousands of red-dressed women,
laughing and talking joyfully.
Among them was a person,
with naturally delicate eyebrows,
adorned with bright pendants all over her body,
her silk gauze garments layered.
She was the one who had entrusted the letter earlier.
The Lord smiled and said:
"The marriage from Jīngshuǐ has arrived."
The person dressed in purple holding a ceremonial tablet
was Qiántáng.
He reported to his elder brother:
"Just now,
I departed Língxū at Chén (7-9 AM),
reached Jīngyáng at Sì (9-11 AM),
fought there at Wǔ (11 AM-1 PM),
and returned here at Wèi (1-3 PM)."
The Lord asked:
"How many were injured?"
He replied:
"Six hundred thousand."
"Did you harm the crops?"
He replied:
"Eight hundred *lǐ*."
"Where is the heartless man?"
He replied:
"I ate him!"
Then, Yì was entertained in the Bìyún Gōng,
with a guest banquet,
and grand music was played.
Yì was presented with pearls and jade,
which were buried next to his seat.
Qiántáng's expression changed, and he said:
"A fierce gentleman can be torn apart but not coiled,
a righteous warrior can be killed but not shamed.
I have a heartfelt desire
to present to you, Sir.
If it is acceptable, we shall both escape to the clouds and sky;
otherwise, we shall both be leveled into dust and dirt.
My disgraced sister from Jīngyáng wishes to entrust herself to your noble righteousness,
and for us to be relatives for generations."
Yì said:
"First, I heard that you stride across the nine provinces,
embrace the five sacred mountains,
and vent your anger.
Then I saw you break golden locks,
snap jade pillars,
and rush to rescue her from dire straits.
This is truly a man of valor.
How can you disregard your principles
and impose your will on others?
My humble self is not strong enough to withstand even one scale of the King's power,
yet I dare to use my unyielding heart
to overcome the King's unrighteous spirit!"
Qiántáng retreated and offered an apology,
forming a bosom friendship with Yì.
After the banquet,
he took his leave and departed.
Yì's next two marriages both ended in the deaths of his wives.
He lived as a widower in Jīnlíng,
and married a woman named Lú,
whose appearance resembled the dragon maiden.
After more than a year,
she bore a son.
His wife said:
"I am indeed the daughter of the Dòngtíng Lord.
At Jīngshàng, when I was humiliated,
you were able to save me.
At that time, I vowed in my heart
to repay you forever.
After my uncle's discussion and advice,
I longed for you and became ill.
My parents wished to marry me to a young man from Zhuójǐn,
but I shut myself in, cut my hair,
to show my disinterest.
It happened that you had successively lost your wives,
and I was able to serve you in your inner chambers.
Do not think that because I am of a different kind, I am insincere.
I can live for ten thousand years,
and now I will share this with you."
Later, they moved to Nánhǎi,
their appearance showing no decline.
Together they returned to Dòngtíng,
and their whereabouts became unknown.
The Tale of Huò Xiǎoyù
During the Dàlì period,
Lǐ Yì, having passed the *jìnshì* examination,
was selected through the *bácuì* examination,
awaiting an appointment in Cháng'ān.
When he first married the Zhèng氏,
he swore he would not marry again.
One day, Zhèng氏 passed away.
He saw her in a dream,
and she said:
"Between the visible and the invisible,
how can one not feel sorrow?
I wish you to strive and carefully preserve your radiance."
He went to her tomb, expressed his profound grief, and returned.
Later, he married the Lú氏.
After the wedding,
he suddenly heard Zhèng氏's angry voice,
and saw a handsome man
repeatedly beckoning the Lú氏.
Another person appeared,
throwing a striped rhinocerous-horn flower box
tied with a lovers' knot,
which fell into Lú氏's embrace.
Lǐ Yì was furious,
and Lú氏 could not explain herself.
He brought a lawsuit and sent her away.
His concubines and maids,
who briefly shared his bed,
immediately became jealous.
By the time of his third marriage,
all were like the first,
as Zhèng氏 had vowed.
Spiritual Marriage on Huáyuè
Wéi Zǐqīng was recommended as *xiàolián*.
He went to the Huáyīn Temple
and, having drunk deeply, strolled through the courtyards.
When he reached the Third Daughter's Courtyard,
seeing her beauty,
he said:
"When I return after passing the examination,
I will marry the Third Maiden."
That spring, he passed the examination.
On his way home, he stopped north of the Wèi River.
He saw two men in yellow clothing who said:
"The Great King sends a command for Young Master Wéi."
Zǐqīng was astonished.
They added:
"It is the Great King Jīntiān of Huáyuè."
Soon, he saw a bustling procession of carriages and horses,
and a magnificent and solemn palace.
He saw a man
with a golden seal and purple ribbon.
After the meeting,
a day was chosen for the wedding ceremony.
The woman was exceptionally beautiful,
truly an immortal.
Seven days later,
the deity said:
"You may return now."
His wife said:
"I am a divine maiden,
certainly not your match.
It is unacceptable that you should have no descendants your whole life.
It cannot be.
When you arrive at Sòngzhōu,
the prefect will surely give his daughter to you in marriage.
Just marry her.
I will also break off with you,
but do not reveal my affairs.
If the matter is exposed, it will benefit neither of us."
Zǐqīng arrived at Sòngzhōu,
and the prefect indeed discussed a marriage alliance with him,
so he married her.
The divine maiden once visited Zǐqīng and said:
"You have just acquired a beautiful new bride,
and she must be very much to your liking."
Zǐqīng hesitated, feeling uneasy.
The maiden said:
"It was just a joke.
I have already agreed to your marriage,
how could I resent you?
However, you must not forget the old in favor of the new."
Later, the prefect's daughter fell ill for two years,
and treatment was ineffective.
There was a Daoist master skilled in talismans and incantations,
who said:
"Your son-in-law, Wéi Láng, has an aura of evil.
Your beloved daughter's illness
comes from Wéi."
He used a talisman to capture Zǐqīng and interrogate him.
Zǐqīng recounted the whole story.
The Daoist flew a black talisman to summon the divine maiden.
The maiden said:
"As a woman,
I dwell deep in my chambers.
Matters of marriage
are arranged by my parents."
The Daoist then flew a red talisman to summon the Mountain Deity and reproached him:
"You, with the尊(dignity) of a mountain guardian,
why did you marry your daughter to a mortal,
and furthermore cause the prefect's daughter to fall ill?"
The deity said:
"Zǐqīng wished to marry my daughter,
and he knew she was not a mortal match.
I instructed him to marry another尊(worthy woman).
Master, consider this point;
how could there be any intention to harm?"
He flicked his robes and departed.
The Daoist told the divine maiden:
"Although the fault is not yours,
as a deity or spirit,
daring to communicate with mortals
without any punishment or reprimand
is unacceptable." He then struck her three times with a staff and banished her.
More than a month later,
the prefect's daughter died.
Zǐqīng suddenly saw the divine maiden, who said:
"I told you not to reveal it,
fearing calamity would befall you.
Now you have not heeded my words."
She bared herself and said:
"How have I wronged you
to bring this upon me!"
Zǐqīng looked,
and three marks were faintly visible.
The divine maiden then shouted at her attendants:
"Are you not going to kill him?
How much longer will you wait?"
The attendants dragged Zǐqīng and beat him,
and that night he died.
Records of Strange Encounters
Shěn Jǐng was dispatched on a mission to Qínlǒng.
Passing by the temple of Zhāng Nǚláng,
he offered water and flowers.
That evening,
he gazed at the moon and played the *qín*,
composing "Phoenix Nurturing its Young," saying:
"A cry is called but no one cries,
where is the coyness contained?
Lingering moon over the flowers,
a pitiful night passes in vain."
He also said:
"The gentle spring breeze arrives,
the faint spring dew is light.
Alas for the moon over the passes and mountains,
it again becomes a useless brightness."
Suddenly, two maidens arrived.
The elder maiden said:
"I am married to the eldest son of the Fūrén of Lúshān."
She pointed to the younger maiden and said:
"She is married to the youngest son of the Fǔjūn of Héngshān.
We are visiting our elder aunt together,
with many feelings after a long separation."
They then prepared wine and food,
singing and making merry.
Shěn Jǐng slept with the younger maiden.
A beautiful maidservant
came forward and said:
"Héng'é is jealous of people,
it is not good to let her light remain.
Zhīnǚ is mischievous,
and has already crossed the river diagonally."
As dawn approached,
they parted with sobs.
Records of the Wandering Soul
Zhāng Yì's family lived in Hēngyáng Jùn.
His daughter, Qiànniáng,
was of unparalleled beauty.
Yì's maternal nephew, Wáng Zhòu,
was handsome and elegant.
Yì once joked:
"Later, I shall give my youngest daughter to you as wife."
Coincidentally, Yì had a guest official whom
he wished to marry her to.
The daughter heard this and became depressed.
Zhòu also felt resentful and dejected,
and set off by boat for the capital.
After sailing for several *lǐ*,
in the middle of the night,
a person came slowly from the shore.
It was Qiànniáng.
Zhòu was extremely happy.
That night, they fled,
doubling their pace to enter Shǔ.
They lived there for several years,
and had two sons.
Qiànniáng thought of her father and
said:
"In the past, I could not betray myself,
and abandoned great righteousness to run away with you.
What now?"
Zhòu said:
"Do not worry."
So he ordered a boat
and they all returned to Hēngyáng.
When they reached the city outskirts,
Zhòu alone went to see Yì,
bowing and apologizing for his daughter's ungrateful desertion.
Yì said in astonishment:
"Which daughter?"
Zhòu said:
"Qiànniáng."
Yì said:
"She has been ill in her boudoir for several years."
Zhòu said:
"She is currently in the boat."
Yì sent someone to verify it.
They saw Qiànniáng in the boat
and hurried back to report to Yì.
The family members told the girl in the room about the situation.
The girl happily rose
and smiled without speaking.
Qiànniáng alighted from the carriage,
and the girl in the house came out to meet her.
Instantly, the two forms merged into one body.
Yì said:
"Since Zhòu left,
my daughter has not spoken,
always appearing as if drunk.
I truly knew her spirit had left."
The daughter said:
"I honestly did not know my body was at home.
When I first saw Zhòu leave with resentment,
I, in my sleep, urgently rushed to catch up with Zhòu's boat.
I also don't know if the one who left was myself,
or if the one who stayed was myself."
Chuánqí
Zhāng Jūn was staying at the Pǔjiù Temple in Púzhōu.
Madam Cuī, a widow, also resided at this temple.
The madam
was a daughter of the Zhèng clan,
and Zhāng hailed from the Zhèng clan.
Tracing their kinship,
she was a cousin on his mother's side from a different branch.
Previously, after Grand Master Hún passed away,
the soldiers caused disturbance due to the funeral,
plundering the people of Púzhōu extensively.
Zhāng was on good terms with the generals' faction,
and he had officials protect them,
so they were not affected by the calamity.
His aunt invited Zhāng for a meal,
ordering her young daughter to come out and bow,
saying:
"Your elder cousin saved you."
The girl's dangling hair and lightly penciled eyebrows
were radiant and captivating.
Zhāng was enchanted by her.
Cuī's maid, named Hóngniáng,
privately conveyed his feelings.
Hóngniáng said:
"Why don't you seek to marry her on account of your kindness?"
Zhāng said:
"If we wait for the betrothal gifts and exchange of names,
then in a matter of three or five months,
you'll find me at a dried fish market!"
The maid said:
"Cuī enjoys writing.
Why don't you try to compose a love poem to disarm her?"
Zhāng immediately penned two spring verses and gave them to her.
That evening,
Hóngniáng brought a decorated letter, saying:
"This is from Cuī."
The piece was titled "The Fifteenth Night of the Bright Moon" (《月明三五夜》),
and the verses read:
"Waiting for the moon outside the western chamber,
the door half-open to the wind.
Flower shadows move beyond the wall,
I suspect my beloved is coming."
There was an apricot tree in Cuī's eastern garden.
On the evening he had hoped for,
Zhāng used the tree to climb over the wall to the western corridor,
and indeed, the door was half-open.
Zhāng thought a tryst was certain.
But when he arrived, she maintained a stern expression
and reprimanded Zhāng severely, saying:
"Your kindness in saving my family is profound.
Because of this,
my kind mother entrusted her weak son and young daughter to you.
How could you, influenced by an unprincipled maid,
send such licentious and defiling words?
To replace disorder with disorder,
how much difference is there?
I wish to maintain myself even unto death,
without falling into impropriety."
Zhāng Jūn departed in shame.
A few evenings later,
Hóngniáng suddenly gathered the quilt and carried a pillow, saying:
"She has arrived!
Why are you sleeping?"
And with pillows side-by-side and sharing a quilt, they departed.
At first, when Cuī arrived,
the slanting moon shone bright,
and she floated like a celestial being,
not appearing to be from the human world.
Later, Zhāng Shēng went to Cháng'ān,
and after several months,
he again visited the temple.
Cuī, at a different time, played the qín alone at night,
her sad music sounding mournful and pathetic.
Zhāng secretly listened,
but when he sought her out,
she no longer played.
The Shēng was scheduled to take the literary examination and
was again about to go west.
Cuī said to Zhāng:
"To begin with disorder
and end with abandonment
is indeed appropriate.
But if you are the one who initiated the disorder,
and you are the one who concludes it,
that would also be your favor!"
The following year,
Zhāng failed the literary examination,
and so he remained in Jīng.
He sent her a gift to convey his intentions.
Cuī replied:
"I respectfully received your inquiry
and am deeply touched by your concern.
The flowers are more beautiful than lip rouge;
seeing these objects deepens my thoughts.
In the past, as cousins,
we sometimes dined together.
Enticed by a maid,
we then pledged our private sincerity.
A child's heart
could not maintain its resolve.
While the gentleman offered his qín as a challenge,
this humble person did not reject the thrown shuttle.
Having seen the gentleman,
I could not establish our feelings with propriety.
My heart was as steadfast as the pine and cypress,
leading to the shame of offering myself.
If, perchance, an enlightened gentleman disregards affection,
forsaking the minor for the major,
considering an earlier match a disgrace,
and believing a solemn oath can be deceived,
then I shall turn to bone and dissipate in form,
but my sincere heart will not perish.
I send one jade bracelet
to be worn as an ornament for your lower body.
Jade is chosen for its firmness and purity, not to be stolen,
and the ring for its endlessness, without beginning or end.
One tassel of colorful silk and a bamboo tea grinder
convey my sincerity through these objects,
to be cherished forever."
Zhāng showed her letter to his friends.
Yáng Jùyuán composed the "Poem for Cuī and Zhāng" (《崔張詩》), saying:
"The pure and gentle Pān Láng is not as good as jade,
in the central courtyard, the huì grass just begins to emerge from the melting snow.
The romantic scholar has many spring thoughts,
but it is Xiāo Niáng's single letter that breaks his heart."
I also composed "The Poem of Meeting the True" (《會真詩》) in thirty rhymes, saying:
"Faint light penetrates the window lattice,
crystal clear it passes through the azure sky.
Traversing the heavens, at first ethereal,
the writing gradually becomes distinct.
Dragon's breath passes through courtyard bamboos,
phoenix's song brushes against moonlit parasol trees.
Silk gauze hangs like thin mist,
jades and pendants chime with the light breeze.
Crimson banners follow the Queen Mother of the West (Jīn Mǔ),
cloudy hearts hold the jade youth.
Deep into the night, people are quiet,
the morning tryst is misty with rain.
Pearls gleam on embroidered shoes,
flowers bright, their charm subtly veiled.
Jade hairpins adorned with colorful phoenixes,
silk shawls cover crimson rainbows.
Eyes illuminate the jasper river bank,
brows hold the deep blue sky.
Wandering north of Lǐchéng,
by chance, east of Mǐ Jiā.
Playful teasing at first met with slight resistance,
soft affections already secretly communicated.
Lowered hair-knot, cicada-like shadows stir,
turning steps, jade dust gathers.
Turning her face, flowers and snow flow,
mounting the bed, embracing the brocade.
Mandarin ducks sleep with intertwined necks,
kingfishers nestle in joyous union.
Eyebrows shyly gather,
crimson lips warm and melt.
Breath fragrant with orchid essence,
skin moist, jade flesh plump.
Weak, she lets her wrist be moved,
full of charm, she loves to draw in her body.
Drops of sweat glisten white,
hair disheveled, green and lush.
Just rejoicing in a ten-year reunion,
suddenly hearing the fifth watch concludes.
Both lingering with regret,
their intimate feelings hard to end.
Her slow face held a sorrowful expression,
her parting words vowed sincerity.
Gifting rings that turn together,
leaving knots that unite two hearts.
Teardrops stain the clear mirror,
residual incense wafts around dark crickets.
The brilliant light still lingers softly,
the rising sun gradually brightens.
The swift horse returns to Luòyáng,
the flute player also ascends Sōngshān.
Her clothes' fragrance still carries musk,
the poem yet retains a hint of crimson.
Rows upon rows of pond grass,
drifting and enraged like tangled weeds.
Plain strings sound like resentful magpies,
looking to the Milky Way for a startled swan.
The vast sea is truly hard to cross,
the high heaven is not easy
to reach.
Floating clouds have no fixed abode,
Xiāo Shǐ remains in the tower."
Zhāng Jūn was resolute in his decision, bearing it with indifference,
regretting that he did not let feelings sprout.
After more than a year,
Cuī married someone else,
and Zhāng also took a wife.
When he happened to pass through that area,
he asked her husband to let him see Cuī as an "elder cousin" from her mother's side.
Cuī ultimately did not come out.
Instead, she composed a poem, saying:
"Since my face grew thin and lost its glow,
countless turns and twists, too weary to rise from bed.
It's not for others' shame I don't get up,
but for my lord I've pined, yet I'm ashamed before my lord."
She then composed another chapter to sever ties, saying:
"Why speak of abandonment now?
Back then, you were close to him.
Still, with your old feelings,
Pity the person before your eyes."
My intimate friend composed "The Song of Yīngyīng" to transmit it.
Cuī,
whose pet name was Yīngyīng,
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú's lute provocation.
Sīmǎ Xiàngrú travelled to Línqióng.
Zhuó Wángsūn had a daughter, Wénjūn, who was newly widowed.
Xiàngrú played the lute and sang:
"O phoenix, O phoenix, return to your old home,
Roaming the four seas, seeking your mate.
The time has not yet come, nowhere to lead,
Why this evening do I ascend this hall?
There is a beautiful and virtuous lady in this room,
The room is near, but the person is distant, only I am sorrowful,
By what缘 are we entwined as mandarin ducks?"
The Governor of Nánkē's Tale.
Chúnyú Fén lived in Guǎnglíng.
South of his residence was an ancient locust tree.
He was fond of drinking heavily beneath it,
and became ill from drunkenness.
Two friends helped him back to his bed in the east wing.
He dreamt of two purple-clad envoys who said:
"The King of Huái'ān invites you."
Chúnyú Fén followed the two envoys into a carriage.
They pointed to the ancient locust tree,
and entered a hole in it.
There was a grand city with vermilion gates,
inscribed "The Great Huái'ān Kingdom."
A horseman shouted:
"The Royal Son-in-Law has arrived from afar!"
He led Chúnyú Fén to a grand hall,
where he saw a person dressed in white silk,
with a hairpin of red flowers,
who ordered Chúnyú Fén to bow.
The King said:
"I previously received an order from the Supreme One,
permitting my daughter Yáofāng to serve Your Excellency."
Several immortal maidens,
playing music and holding candles, led the way.
Golden and emerald screens,
continuously intricate.
They arrived at a gate,
called Xiūyí Palace.
A woman, named Princess Jīnzhī,
appeared like a goddess.
They exchanged vows and completed the rites;
their affection grew daily.
The King said:
"The government affairs of my Nánkē Commandery are not in order;
I ask you, my lord, to be its governor."
He commanded the officials to bring forth gold, jade, brocade,
servants, concubines, carriages, and horses,
and to decorate the wide thoroughfares
to send off the princess.
The Queen admonished the princess:
"Chúnyú Láng is stubborn and fond of wine;
the way of a wife lies in gentleness and obedience.
You must serve him well."
Chúnyú Fén arrived at the commandery after several days.
Officials, monks, Daoists, and musicians came to welcome him.
He dismounted to observe the local customs
and examine the sufferings of the people.
The commandery was well-governed.
For twenty years,
the common people erected living shrines to him.
The King bestowed titles and land,
and his position was among the highest ministers.
He had five sons and two daughters,
and his glory and prosperity were incomparable.
The princess fell ill and died.
Chúnyú Fén requested to escort the coffin back to the capital.
The King and Queen, dressed in plain clothes, wept bitterly in the suburbs,
with full ceremonial guard, feathered banners, drums, and wind instruments,
and buried the princess on Pánlóng Gāng.
As a royal relative,
Chúnyú Fén's power and influence grew daily.
Someone submitted a memorial saying:
"A celestial omen of disaster has appeared,
causing great fear.
The capital city will be moved,
and the ancestral temples will collapse.
The trouble is within the household."
At that time, it was discussed that this was a consequence of Chúnyú Fén's extravagance and presumption.
The King then ordered Chúnyú Fén, saying:
"You may temporarily return to your native village
to see your relatives.
Leave your grandsons here;
do not worry about them."
He then commanded the two envoys to send him out of a hole,
and he awoke.
He saw his household servants surrounding him in the courtyard,
and his two guests washing their feet on the couch.
The setting sun had not yet hidden behind the western wall,
and its lingering light shone on the east window.
He then went with his two guests to search,
and saw the hole below, brightly illuminated,
large enough for a couch.
On it was a ring of earth,
forming the shape of a city wall, outer city, and palaces.
There were several pecks of ants.
Two large ants with white wings and red crowns
were the King and Queen of Huái'ān.
They then explored another hole,
which went straight up to a southern branch.
A colony of ants gathered there;
this was Nánkē Commandery.
Yet another hole meandered like a dragon or snake,
with a small mound over a foot high;
this was Pánlóng Gāng.
Chúnyú Fén recalled and sighed with emotion,
and ordered everything to be covered up.
That night,
a storm broke out.
In the morning, when they looked at the hole,
the ants were all gone,
no one knew where.
What was said about "the kingdom having great fear,
and the capital city being moved"—
this was its verification.
The Essences of the Three Stars.
Yáo Yùshǐ had three sons,
who were dull-witted and pathetic.
He ordered them to study at Tiáoshān.
Suddenly, they saw a woman,
who called herself 'Madame',
bringing three daughters to be their spouses.
Their jade-like faces and dark hair,
and their demeanor were extraordinary.
Madame said:
"As long as you do not reveal this to others,
you will live long and transcend the world,
and attain the highest positions among men."
The three sons said:
"We are foolish and dull-witted, finding it difficult to succeed.
How can we achieve such nobility?"
Madame commanded the earthly ruler to summon Kǒng Xuānfù.
Soon, he arrived, wearing his cap and sword.
Xuānfù bowed and rose very respectfully.
Madame gently greeted him and asked,
saying:
"My three sons-in-law are new to learning;
you must guide them."
Xuānfù pointed to the titles and sections of the Six Classics to show them,
and they instantly comprehended.
She then ordered Zhōu Shàngfù to show them Xuánnǚ's military talismans and Yùtóng's secret formulas.
Their father was surprised by their outstanding spiritual vigor
and their refined and elegant replies.
He suspected they were possessed by ghosts or demons.
He whipped them and questioned them,
and they fully recounted the whole story.
A scholar said:
"I saw the stars Zhīnǚ, Wùnǚ, and Xūnǚ all without light.
These are the essences of the three female stars descended to the human world,
bringing good fortune to the three sons.
Now that the heavenly secret has been leaked,
it is fortunate to avoid disaster."
Yáo immediately sent the three sons back to the mountain.
The three daughters seemed as if they no longer recognized them.
Madame said:
"Since you did not heed my words,
and have leaked the heavenly secret,
I must bid you farewell."
She then forcibly gave the three sons a drink,
and they became as dull and foolish as before.
The Tale of Xiè Xiǎo'é.
Xiè Xiǎo'é married Jiǎ Jūzhèng.
Her father and husband were trading goods together on a boat on the rivers and lakes
when they were killed by bandits,
who plundered their gold and silk.
Xiǎo'é drifted about, begging for food,
until she reached Shàngyuán County,
where she resided in the chamber of Jìngwù at Miàoyào Temple.
She dreamt her father said:
"Those who killed me are
'monkey in a cart'
and 'grass east of the gate'."
Then she dreamt her husband said:
"Those who killed me are
'running in the grain'
and 'husband with one day'."
Xiǎo'é did not understand,
and widely sought wise people to interpret it.
In the eighth year of Yuánhé,
Lǐ Gōngzuǒ told her:
"Remove the upper and lower strokes from '車' (chē, cart),
