and it becomes '申' (shēn),
which is also the monkey zodiac sign,
hence 'monkey in a cart'.
Below '草' (cǎo, grass) is '門' (mén, gate),
and inside '門' is '東' (dōng, east),
which makes the character '蘭' (lán).
'Running in the grain' (禾中走) means 'crossing the fields' (穿田過),
which is also the character '申' (shēn).
Adding one stroke above '夫' (fū, husband)
and having '日' (rì, day) below it
forms the character '春' (chūn).
So, the one who killed your father is Shēn Lán,
and the one who killed your husband is Shēn Chūn."
Xiǎo'é then changed into men's clothing,
and worked as a servant among the rivers and lakes.
After more than a year,
she arrived in Xúnyáng.
There was someone hiring a monthly servant,
and Xiǎo'é answered the call.
The master was indeed Shēn Lán.
Later, Shēn Chūn came to Lán's house.
É remained in Lán's house for two years,
and he never knew she was a woman.
Lán and Chūn would go out for a whole month at a time,
often returning with much wealth and silk.
One day, they gathered with other bandits for a night banquet and became deeply intoxicated.
É drew a knife and chopped off Lán's head,
then called out to the neighbors and captured Chūn as well,
recovering goods worth tens of thousands.
Having completed her revenge,
É vowed never to marry,
cut her hair, donned coarse robes,
and became a disciple of the Niútóu school's Níjiāng Vinaya master.
She even used Xiǎo'é as her dharma name,
not forgetting her origins.
The account in the Yōuguài Lù differs slightly,
so both are preserved.
Míngyīn Lù
In Kāichéng,
Lǐ Yǎn's concubine, Lady Cuī,
dreamt her deceased aunt wept and said:
"In the underworld, I am registered with the Jiàofāng,
serving in the palace of Emperor Mùzōng."
The lady then took her zither, sat down,
closed her eyes, and played it herself,
gaining proficiency with each stroke.
One day, she learned ten tunes:
the ten tunes of Yíngjūn Yuè, Húlíntàn, Shǎngjīn Gē, Guǎnglíng Sàn, Xínglù Nán, Shànghóng, Jìnchéng Xiàn, Sīzhú Gē, and Hóngchuāng Yǐng were completed.
She said to the lady:
"These are all newly composed tunes from the palace.
Emperor Mùzōng summoned the Shèrén Yuán Zhěn to compose them,
and during banquets, he ordered the palace women to sing them in turn.
The emperor himself held a jade rúyì,
beating time in harmony.
Among the various Táng emperors, palace musicians and entertainers were mutually selected to be presented to the palaces of Shényáo and Tàizōng.
Recently, Princess Xiāngwáng took me as her daughter,
and secretly permitted me to return
to fulfill your wish."
Bìyù Húyè
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ had a secret affair with Lady Wáng.
After his death,
Lǐ Jīng, who was his heir,
saw Lady Wáng come to sleep with him.
As dawn approached,
she took out an object,
dark blue,
like jade but cold,
shaped like a small leaf,
and gave it to him, saying:
"This was given by the Jade Lady of the Western Peak,
it is not something found in the human world.
It is a treasure from the jié,
originating from the Xuánpǔ of Kūnlún."
It was carved into the shape of an oak leaf.
Zhōu Qín Xíngjì
Niú Sēngrú failed the imperial examination in the first year of Zhēnyuán.
He arrived at the southern road of Yīquè.
He came to a large residence,
and entered through more than ten gates.
The great hall had pearl curtains.
From behind the curtains a voice said:
"I am the Han Emperor Wén's mother, Empress Dà Bó (Bó Tàihòu).
This is a temple.
Sir, you should not be here."
Sēngrú said:
"My home is in Wǎnxia.
I lost my way on my journey back,
and beg for shelter for the night."
The Empress summoned him to the main hall:
"Are you not weary from your journey?"
After a long while,
two women emerged.
The Empress said:
"These are Emperor Gāozǔ's Concubine Qī,
and Emperor Yuán's Wáng Qiáng."
Once they were seated,
the Empress sent her chamberlains to welcome members of the Yáng family and Pān family.
Suddenly, two women descended from the clouds.
The Empress said:
"These are Concubine Tàizhēn of the Tang Dynasty, and Concubine Pān Shú of Emperor Qí."
Soon, food arrived,
and wine was served.
The utensils were made of precious jade.
The Empress said to Tàizhēn:
"Why have you not visited for so long?"
She replied:
"Sānláng often favored Huáqīng,
and I was too busy accompanying him."
She then said to Pān:
"You also haven't come.
Why?"
The concubine hid a smile and did not reply.
The Empress asked:
"Who is the current Son of Heaven?"
Sēngrú said:
"Emperor Dàizōng's eldest son."
Tàizhēn laughed and said:
"Old woman Shěn's son is the Son of Heaven?
How very strange."
The Empress composed a poem:
"Sleeping in the moonlit flower palace, I served my lord,
Even now I still feel shame before Lady Guǎn.
The Han household was once a place of pipes and songs,
How many autumns and springs have passed over the misty grasses?"
Wáng Qiáng said:
"In a cold hut amid the snow, I see no spring,
Though Han clothes are old, my tears are ever new.
Even now I resent Máo Yánshòu,
Who loved to wrongly paint people with his pigments."
Concubine Qī said:
"Since parting from the Han palace, I ceased the Chu dance,
Unable to adorn myself with powder, I resent the emperor.
Without gold, how could one welcome the Old Man of Shang?
The Lǚ clan was so rude and stubbornly strong."
Tàizhēn said:
"My golden hairpin fell to the ground as I parted from the emperor,
Red tears flowed like pearls, filling the jade bed.
After our separation at Mǎwéi amidst clouds and rain,
Lí Palace no longer saw me try the 'Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Robe Dance'."
Concubine Pān said:
"How many times have autumn moon and spring wind returned,
The mountains and rivers are still there, but the Yè Palace is gone.
The sunset's gathering once formed a lotus land,
But now only the empty golden-threaded robe drags."
Sēngrú said:
"A fragrant breeze led me to the Great Heaven,
On moonlit ground and cloudy steps, I bowed to cave immortals.
Together we spoke of the melancholy affairs of the human world,
Unaware of what year this evening might be."
Another beautiful woman played the flute,
She was Shí Chóng's Lǜzhū.
The Empress said:
"Who will accompany Scholar Niú tonight?"
Concubine Qī said:
"Rúyì is already grown,
She certainly cannot."
Concubine Pān said:
"Emperor Dōnghūn died and his state was abolished as a royal child,
It is not right to let him down."
Lǜzhū declined, saying that Shí Wèiwèi was strict,
And she could not be disorderly.
The Empress said:
"Tàizhēn was the Emperor's noble consort this morning,
Certainly do not speak of her for that."
Then she said to Zhāojūn:
"You first married Hūhán Chányú,
and then became the wife of his younger brother, Sāncān Chányú.
This is appropriate.
Moreover, in such a cold land,
what could the barbarian ghosts do?"
Zhāojūn was ashamed and resentful, but did not reply.
Soon, Sēngrú was escorted into Zhāojūn's courtyard.
At dawn,
an attendant announced it was time to leave.
The Empress sent a person in a red robe to escort him to the western road of Dà'ān.
The sky was just beginning to brighten.
He asked the person,
who said:
"About ten *lǐ* from here is Empress Bó's temple."
Lament of Xiāngzhōng
During the Chuígǒng era,
the *jìnshì* Zhèng Shēng set off early from Tóngtuórǐ.
As he crossed Luòqiáo,
there was a very mournful crying sound below.
He saw a beautiful woman with her face veiled, who said:
"I, alone,
was raised by my elder brother and his wife.
My sister-in-law was always cruel to me,
and now I intend to throw myself into the water."
Zhèng Shēng said:
"Can you come with me?"
She replied:
"As your maid, I have no regrets."
So he took her with him,
calling her "Sì Rén".
She could recite the *Songs of Chu*, compose mournful songs, and compiled *Fēngguāng Cí*.
Zhèng Shēng was poor.
Sì Rén produced some light silk.
A Hu-person paid a thousand pieces of gold for it.
As Zhèng Shēng was about to proceed to Cháng'ān,
that evening she said:
"I am the younger sister of the dragon in Xiāngzhōng.
I was banished and followed you.
Now my year is complete,
and I cannot stay much longer."
She bid farewell and departed.
More than ten years later,
Zhèng Shēng's elder brother became the governor (*cìshǐ*) of Yuèzhōu.
On the third day of the third month,
he ascended Yuèyáng Lóu.
A painted boat floated towards them,
with string instruments and wind instruments playing.
All the musicians were ethereal beauties,
their robes like mist and clouds.
One person in the middle rose to dance,
with a shy and resentful look,
her appearance was like Sì Rén.
Soon after,
the wind and waves raged furiously,
and they lost sight of where she went.
The Story of Rèn (Rèn Shì Zhuàn)
Rèn Shì
was a female demon.
Wéi Cén, the Prefect,
was travelling with his paternal younger sister's husband, named Zhèng Liù.
As they walked along the streets of Cháng'ān,
they saw a woman in white clothing,
whose face was exceedingly beautiful.
Zhèng jokingly said:
"So beautiful and charming,
why are you walking alone on the road?"
The woman in white smiled and said:
"I have a carriage but cannot spare it,
what else can I do but walk?"
They looked at each other and laughed heartily.
They followed her to Lèyóu Yuán,
where the dwelling was very beautiful.
They drank heartily and slept happily.
When morning came,
they agreed to meet again later and departed.
They asked the villagers:
"To the east of north,
whose residence is that?"
"It's an old abandoned ruin.
Inside there's a fox,
which often seduces men.
We've seen it three times already."
Later, they met her again.
She said to Zhèng:
"There are many like me in the human world;
you just don't recognize them.
Most of my kind
are feared by people
because they harm others.
I am not like that.
You have seen no evil from me.
I am willing to serve you.
If I should ever be slightly negligent,
I will withdraw myself,
without waiting to be expelled."
So, she rented a small house and lived there.
Cén saw her and became frantic,
embracing her and trying to force himself on her.
She resisted him several times,
then sighed deeply and said:
"Alas!
How pitiable Zhèng Liù is!
He has a six-foot body yet cannot protect one woman."
From then on, Cén spent his days with her,
privately caressing her,
but never going so far as to commit impropriety.
Cén loved and cherished her.
After more than a year,
Zhèng Zǐ was appointed an official in Jīnchéng,
and invited her to go with him.
Rèn Shì said:
"A sorcerer told me that
this year it is not auspicious for me to travel west."
Zhèng insisted,
so, having no choice,
she went.
She rode on horseback in front of Zhèng,
while Zhèng urged his donkey behind.
At that time, hunters from Xīzhōu had surrounded the area to hunt in Luòchuān,
and happened to be on the road.
A grey dog suddenly sprang out,
and Rèn Shì instantly fell to the ground,
reverting to her original form while still running,
and was caught by the dog.
All her clothes were on the saddle,
her shoes and stockings still hung from the stirrups,
like a cicada's蛻.
Zhèng redeemed her and buried her,
then returned, weeping bitterly.
Volume 28
End.
Yānzhōng Xiān
Yáng Fù, a fisherman from Yuè,
had a daughter of exceptional beauty,
who could only compose two lines of poetry.
Someone asked:
"Why do you not finish the poem?"
She replied:
"My emotions are too entangled,
and after two lines, my thoughts become confused and I cannot continue."
There was a Xiè Shēng who sought to marry her.
Her father said:
"My daughter should be matched with a Duke or Minister."
Xiè replied:
"The proverb says:
'A young girl and a young man
find joy together and never forget it;
a young girl and an old man
experience different joys and sorrows.'
Moreover, where are there young Dukes or Ministers?"
The old man said:
"My daughter's poems are only two lines.
If you can continue them
to match her meaning,
then she will be your wife."
He showed him her lines:
"Pearl curtains cover half the bed's moon,
green bamboos fill the forest with wind."
Xiè continued:
"What is this evening's scene about,
that no one can share it?"
The daughter said:
"Heaven-born is my husband!"
And so, they became a couple.
Seven years later, one spring day,
Yáng suddenly wrote:
"When spring ends, flowers follow suit,
but what if one is oneself a flower?"
Xiè said:
"Why do you make such an inauspicious line?"
Yáng said:
"I will not be long in the human world!"
Xiè continued:
"It has always been said of flowers,
they are merely this fleeting beauty."
Yáng then closed her eyes and passed away.
One year later,
the mist on the river shimmered and wavered,
and Yáng was seen standing in the middle of the river, saying:
"I was originally an immortal,
exiled to live in the human world.
If you should miss me later,
I will be exiled again,
and will not attain immortality."
Cuī Huī
Cuī Huī, a woman from Pú,
of the same prefecture, Péi Jìngzhōng, served as the envoy for Liáng in Pú.
Upon seeing her, he was moved,
and they consorted for several months.
When Jìngzhōng announced his return,
Huī could not leave,
and was so distressed that she could not bear it.
Several months later,
Jìngzhōng's close friend, Zhī Tuì, arrived in Pú.
There was a Qiū Xià who was skilled at painting portraits.
Zhī Tuì conveyed Huī's message to Xià,
and indeed obtained a superb portrait.
Huī held the painting and said to Zhī Tuì:
"Please tell Jìngzhōng for me,
that Cuī Huī is suddenly no better than a woman in the street,
and Huī will die for you, my lord!"
The next day, she went mad,
and from then on, claimed illness,
no longer saw visitors, and died.
Zhuózhuó
was an official courtesan in Jǐnchéng,
skilled in dance and acrobatics,
and sang "Shuǐdiào".
At a banquet in the Prime Minister's residence,
she sat with a man from Hédōng.
Her spiritual power was spontaneously transmitted,
as if they were old acquaintances,
and from then on, they never met again.
Zhuózhuó gathered many red tears on soft silk,
and secretly sent them to the man from Hédōng.
Yànzǐ Lóu
Zhāng Jiànfēng, the Púshè, controlled Wǔníng.
His dancing girl, Pànpàn,
was housed by the duke in the Yànzǐlóu.
Bái Lètiān once passed through Xú,
and gave her a poem that said:
"Drunk and charming, without strength,
swaying like a peony in the wind."
After the duke passed away,
Pànpàn vowed not to marry again,
often using poetry for communication.
There are nearly three hundred poems by her,
titled *Yànzǐlóu Jí*.
She once wrote three poems saying:
"The lingering lamp in the tower accompanies the morning frost,
a lonely sleeper rises from the lovebird bed.
How deep is the yearning through the night?
The ends of the earth and sky are not so long."
"Pine and cypress on Běimáng lock in the sorrowful mist,
thoughts are silent in the Yànzǐlóu.
Since managing the sword and shoes, the singing dust has scattered,
the red and soft beauty vanished for ten years."
"Just saw the migrating geese return from Yuèyáng,
then the dark birds of smoke passed through after the spring festival.
The jade zither and jade flute hold no interest,
let them be covered in spiderwebs, let them turn to ash."
Lètiān replied with a poem saying:
"The window full of bright moonlight, the curtain full of frost,
the quilt cold, fragrance vanished, lying alone in bed.
Before the Yànzǐlóu on a clear moonlit night,
autumn lingers only for one person."
"Repeatedly comforting the silk gown, its color like smoke,
each time I see it, I shed a tear.
Since no longer dancing the 'Níshang Qǔ',
how many years has it been folded in an empty chest?"
"This year a visitor returns from Luòyáng,
coming to the tomb of the Rú Dào Shàngshū.
They say the poplars are fit to be pillars,
how then can red powder not turn to ash?"
Another quatrain said:
"Not hesitating to sell golden eyebrows,
choosing five or four branches like flowers.
Teaching song and dance exhausted my heart and strength,
but when I died, they did not follow."
Pànpàn wept and said:
"It is not that your concubine cannot die,
but I fear that after a hundred years,
people will value me more for my beauty."
So she harmonized with Bái gōng's poem saying:
"Guarding an empty tower, I draw my brows in sorrow,
my form like a peony branch after spring.
The Shèrén does not understand my deep meaning,
just saying I should not follow to the underworld."
Wúshuāng Xiānkè
Wáng Xiānkè of the Táng dynasty,
was the nephew of Liú Zhèn.
Zhèn had a daughter named Wúshuāng,
who as a child often played with him intimately.
Zhèn's wife playfully called Xiānkè "Wáng Lángzi".
Later, when Wúshuāng grew up,
her maternal uncle, seeing his high position and prominent office,
wanted to annul their prior agreement.
Each time he secretly saw Wúshuāng,
she was bright and beautiful like a celestial being.
A maid told Xiānkè:
"The marriage arrangements may be falling through."
One day,
Zhèn hurried back from court,
suddenly riding his horse and saying:
"The soldiers from Jīngyuán,
Yáo Língyán leading troops, have entered the Hànyuándiàn.
The Son of Heaven has left through the northern gate of the palace grounds,
and all officials are fleeing to the temporary residence.
I have called Xiānkè to take charge of family affairs,
and will marry Wúshuāng to him.
I will pack gold and silk and lead them out,
through the Kāiyuǎnmén.
My relatives and I will leave through the Qǐxiàmén and follow along the city wall."
Xiānkè followed instructions and left the city,
waited a long time but they did not arrive,
so he went to the Qǐxiàmén.
The guards at the Qǐxiàmén were all holding white staffs.
Xiānkè asked:
"What happened in the city?
Who left this gate today?"
They replied:
"Zhū Tàiwèi has become the Son of Heaven.
In the afternoon, someone heavily laden,
bringing his family, wanted to leave,
it was Liú Shàngshū, the Commissioner of Taxation and Labor.
The gate guards dared not let him out,
and pursued him northwards."
Xiānkè was terrified and fled back to Xiāngyáng.
Later, knowing that the capital had been recovered,
he entered the capital to visit his maternal uncle.
He saw an old servant, the old servant Sàihóng.
Xiānkè said:
"How are my uncle and aunt?"
Hóng replied:
"The Shàngshū received a false command,
and both he and his wife were executed.
Wúshuāng has already entered the palace,
and among the family, only the maid Cǎipíng remains."
He found Cǎipíng and lived with her.
The Jīngzhàoyǐn appointed Xiānkè as Fùpíng Wèi.
Suddenly, a report came that a palace envoy was escorting thirty palace women to the imperial tombs.
Xiānkè ordered Sàihóng to pretend to be a postal courier.
Deep in the night,
from behind a curtain, he called Sàihóng and said:
"Is Láng healthy?
Tomorrow, retrieve a letter from under the purple cushion."
The next day, Hóng found a letter which said:
"I once saw an imperial edict that said,
'Fùpíng Gǔ Yáshù
is a kind-hearted man in the world,
can you find him?'"
So Xiānkè went to find him.
Old Gǔ,
lived in a village villa,
and was generously given gold and treasures.
After more than a year,
Old Gǔ said:
"I perceive your intention,
that you have something to ask of this old man.
I am willing to break my body into pieces to repay such deep kindness."
Xiānkè told him the truth.
Old Gǔ said:
"This matter is very easy."
Half a year later,
he said:
"Who recognizes Wúshuāng?"
Xiānkè replied, Cǎipíng.
Old Gǔ said:
"Let her stay for a few days."
Later, they suddenly heard that a high-ranking official had passed by,
dealing with the palace women at the imperial tombs.
Xiānkè ordered someone to investigate who had been killed,
and it was Wúshuāng.
That evening,
there was an urgent knock at the door.
Old Gǔ entered carrying a bundle
and said:
"This is Wúshuāng.
She is dead now,
but will be alive again the day after tomorrow."
Old Gǔ also said:
"Lend me Sàihóng for a moment."
Then he drew a knife and cut his neck.
Xiānkè was very angry.
Old Gǔ said:
"Today is enough to repay you, Lángjūn!
I heard that the Máo Shān Daoists have a medicine,
whoever takes it dies immediately,
and revives in three days.
I obtained one pill.
Yesterday I instructed Cǎipíng to pretend to be a palace envoy,
and citing Wúshuāng as a rebel,
bestowed the medicine for her to commit suicide.
At the imperial tombs,
I used a pretext of kinship
and redeemed her body with a hundred lengths of silk.
The guards and others were all killed to silence them,
and this old man will also commit suicide."
After speaking,
he raised the blade and died.
Xiānkè took Wúshuāng, changed their names, and returned to Xiāngyáng to live out their old age together.
Liánhuā Jì
Yán Zǐmù governed Yùzhāng.
Chén Táo lived in seclusion in Xīshān,
known for his pure conduct.
The governor wished to sway him,
and sent the little courtesan Liánhuā to serve him.
Táo did not acknowledge her at all.
The courtesan then presented a poem requesting to leave, saying:
"My name is Liánhuā, my cheeks are jade,
I thank the Shàngshū for sending me here.
The hermit does not dream of the Wūxiá,
needlessly wearying the goddess to descend to Yángtái."
Táo replied:
"Recently my poetic thoughts are clearer than water,
my aging romantic feelings are thinner than clouds.
I have already found the gateway to ascending to heaven,
and deeply shame the embroidered quilt of Zhuó Wénjūn."
Shǔ Courtesan Xuē Tāo
In the Yuánhuī period, during the Yuánhé era, when [Yuán Huī] was dispatched as an envoy to Shǔ,
there was a courtesan named Xuē Tāo,
who possessed both talent and beauty.
The prefect, Sīkōng Yán Zhīyuán, knowing Yuán's feelings,
sent Tāo to attend to him.
Later, upon entering the Hànlín Academy,
he sent a poem, saying:
"The Jǐn Jiāng is smooth and clear, Mount Éméi is fair,
Giving birth to Wénjūn and Xuē Tāo.
Their clever words steal the parrot's tongue,
Their writings snatch the phoenix's feathers.
Numerous poets all cease their pens,
Every duke and marquis dreams of swords.
Since parting, we yearn for each other across misty waters,
As irises bloom and five-colored clouds rise high."
Ài'ài,
whose surname was Yáng,
was a courtesan's daughter from Qiántáng.
On the Qīxī festival, she boated on Xī Hú, gathering lotus fragrance,
and was accosted by Zhāng Chéng, a youth from Jīnlíng.
They eloped together to the capital.
After two years,
Chéng was captured by his father and taken away.
Later, it was rumored that Chéng had died,
and Ài'ài died of grief.
Her young maid, Jǐn'ér, brought out her old embroidered hand-stitched perfume sachet and brocade shoes,
which were fragrant and fresh as new.
Sūxiāng.
Secretary Dù Mìshū was a man of great emotion and talent,
renowned for his short verses.
As Yuán Huī said, he "could speak what was in people's hearts,"
and indeed it was true.
Next door lived a wealthy old man,
whose surname was Zhāng.
He had an unmarried daughter with the pet name Sūxiāng,
who could recite all the songs composed by talented people.
One night,
she climbed over the wall and arrived.
Dù suspected a ghost.
The girl said:
"I am your neighbor's daughter;
I admire your verses
and beg you not to abandon me."
Dù had not expected this,
and at dawn, he moved to a remote place.
The wealthy old man, having lost his daughter,
dared not reveal it himself.
Ten years later,
Dù's servant made a mistake,
and Dù wrongly flogged him.
The servant reported it to the authorities.
Dù was arrested and the truth was investigated,
his name was removed from the register,
and he was exiled to Héshuò.
On the verge of departure,
he composed a lyric, "Chéngguò Lè," as a farewell.
The girl held the paper and sang it three times,
then cut her throat and died.
The Swallows' Tomb.
At the end of the Sòng dynasty,
a courtesan named Yáo Yùjīng
married Jìng Yú, a minor officer from Xiāngzhōu.
Jìng Yú drowned,
and Yùjīng remained chaste, caring for her parents-in-law.
There were always a pair of swallows nesting between the beams.
One day,
they were caught by a bird of prey,
and one flew alone, crying sadly,
hovering until autumn.
It landed on Yùjīng's arm,
as if saying farewell.
Yùjīng tied a red thread to its foot,
saying:
"You must return in spring to be my companion."
The next year, it indeed returned,
and she gifted it a poem, saying:
"Last year you hesitated as your mate departed,
This spring you have returned again.
Your old friend's kindness is profound,
You cannot bear to fly in pairs again."
From then on, it returned in spring and left in autumn for six or seven years.
That year,
Yùjīng died of illness.
The next year, it returned again,
flying around and crying sadly.
The family told it:
"Yùjīng is dead;
her tomb is in the southern suburb."
The swallow then flew to the burial place
and also died.
Whenever the wind was clear and the moon bright,
people of Xiāngzhōu saw Yùjīng and the swallow frolicking together above the Hànshuǐ River.
Qín Niáng.
Wéi Shàngshū's household had a skilled singer
who met with musicians and composed new melodies for the pípa.
When Shàngshū died,
she was acquired by Zhāng Xuán, the Cìshǐ of Qízhōu.
When Xuán died,
Qín Niáng had nowhere to go.
She embraced her musical instrument and wept,
her voice raw with sorrow.
Liú Yǔxī sang:
"Qín Niáng's home was originally west of Chāng Mén,
Green waters before her gate circled the golden dike.
Sometimes, when her makeup was done and the weather fair,
She would run onto Gāo Qiáo to pluck flowers and play.
The elegant prefect, Wéi Shàngshū,
Suddenly stopped his falcon banner by the roadside.
Pearls by the measure, a bird carrying words,
One day she was welcomed into his exclusive residence.
Following her lord west into the imperial city,
Noble guests and beautiful adornments filled the screens and windows.
With bowed head, she slowly gazed, embracing the bright moon,
Her slender fingers plucked and strummed, creating exotic tunes.
Once, prosperity vanished and ceased,
The sword at the waist lost its gleam, the sound of shoes ceased.
Master Zhāng, the Cìshǐ of Qízhōu,
Rode his white horse personally to Tóngchí Lǐ.
He claimed to buy laughter for a thousand pieces of gold,
From then on, the moon fell into the clouds.
How could he know the owl flew at the corner?
The lonely wandering soul could not be summoned.
Qín's family's mirror was broken, given long ago,
Hán Shòu's perfume faded from her old dancing dress.
Looking around, the wind and smoke were not as before,
Returning to seek the branching roads, many were uneven.
How can I take these two streams of tears,
And sprinkle them again on the bamboos of Xiāng Jiāng?"
Zhāng Hǎohǎo.
Dù Mù assisted Shěn Chuánshī in Jiāngxī.
Zhāng Hǎohǎo, thirteen years old,
first entered the courtesan registry because of her excellent singing.
When Duke Shěn moved his post to Xuānchéng,
he again registered Hǎohǎo in Xuānchéng.
Two years later,
she was taken in by Guò Shěn Shī Zuòzhù's Shuanghuán.
The Hair-bun Girl of Húzhōu.
At the end of the Tàihé era, Dù Mù traveled to Húzhōu.
Cūi Jūn, the Cìshǐ, whom Dù Mù held in high regard,
presented all the famous courtesans,
but none pleased him.
Dù Mù said:
"I wish to arrange a water spectacle,
so that all the people of the prefecture can watch,
and I will discreetly observe."
The Cìshǐ did as he said.
Spectators lined both banks like a solid wall.
Suddenly, an old village woman led a girl with a hair-bun,
about ten years old,
a true beauty of the land.
Dù Mù intended to bring her into his boat,
but both the old woman and the girl were frightened.
Dù Mù said:
"Do not bring her in immediately;
we shall make a later appointment.
I will surely become a prefect in ten years.
If I do not come,
then she may marry someone else."
He then sealed the promise with a large sum of money.
When he entered the court as a minister,
Dù Mù submitted a memorial requesting to govern Húzhōu.
By the time he arrived at the prefecture,
fourteen years had passed.
The girl he had betrothed
had already been married for three years
and had two children.
Dù Mù urgently summoned her,
and her parents, fearing she would be taken away,
brought their young children to him.
The mother said:
"You promised ten years,
and that she could marry after you didn't come.
She has been married for three years now."
Dù Mù bowed his head and said:
"Her words are truthful;
to force it would be inauspicious."
He then politely dismissed her
and composed a melancholic farewell poem, saying:
"It is I who sought spring too late,
No need to be sorrowful and blame the fragrant season.
The wild wind has blown away all the deep red,
Green leaves have formed a shade, and fruits fill the branches."
Three Officials' Inscriptions.
It says:
“My family originally resided east of Ruòyē Xī,
and with like-minded companions in the inner chambers, we wove orchid sashes and wore fragrant girdles.
We sought a leisurely life,
and did not follow others.
Unfortunately, my good husband is already lost,
and I am utterly without support.
I take up my brush and briefly write a quatrain:
My surname is 'two nines,'
followed by 'child under father.'
Jade without blemish,
a cap without a head.
Jīngshān stones
are frequently found.
As brush and ink are not a woman's affair,
my name is intentionally hidden and not written.”
The poem says:
“Once I followed my good husband west into Guān,
my good husband died, and I returned east.
Xiè Niáng and Wèi Nǚ no longer await me;
as rain and clouds, I return to my old mountain.”
Lǐ Shū explains:
“'Two nines'
is eighteen,
ten plus eight makes the character for 'wood' (木, mù).
'Child under father' (子為父後, zǐ wéi fù hòu) means 'child' (子, zǐ) under 'wood' (木, mù),
forming the character Lǐ (李).
'Jade without blemish'
means removing the dot (點, diǎn) from jade (玉, yù).
'A cap without a head'
means retaining its 'gōng' (廾) radical.
'Jade' (玉) under 'gōng' (廾)
forms the character Nòng (弄).
‘Jīngshān stones
are frequently found’ means
that Jīngshān stones often contain jade.
Therefore, her surname must be Lǐ (李) and her given name Nòngyù (弄玉).”
Poem at Huánglíng Temple
During the Kāibǎo period,
Jiǎ Zhīwēi met Madame Dù Lánxiāng of Lǔ Chéng and Shùn’s two concubines in Bālíng.
The two concubines recited Lǐ Qúnwáng’s “Poem at Huánglíng Temple” saying:
“Before Huánglíng Temple, spring grass is green,
the daughters of Huánglíng wear new crimson skirts.
In light boats with short oars, they sing and depart,
the water is distant, the sky is long, sorrow kills people.”
Jiǎ and the Madame then instructed a maid to cover fifty pills of cinnabar with an autumn cloud silk scarf, saying:
“This silk was woven by the Weaver Girl from spun jade silkworm threads.
When there is thunder and rain, it must be carefully put away.
As for these immortal pills, taking just one a year
will preserve you for a year.”
Later, during a great thunder and rainstorm,
they saw something in the casket like clouds and smoke,
soaring into the sky and departing.
Poem Gifted to a Courtesan
Ōuyáng Zhān gifted a poem to a courtesan from Tàiyuán, saying:
“The high city is already unknown,
how much more so the people within the city.”
Emperor Wénzōng’s Poem
Emperor Wénzōng conspired with his prime ministers to eliminate the eunuchs,
but the plot was exposed, and he was instead killed by the inner officials.
When the emperor went on outings or pleasure trips,
he was never happy;
he often stared blankly and spoke to himself,
then inscribed a poem on a palace pillar, saying:
“Spring grass grows on the imperial carriage road,
flowers fill the branches in Shànglín Park.
Standing high, what boundless thoughts,
no longer known to attendant officials.”
The next day, he viewed peonies in the side palace, saying:
“Those that droop are like sorrow,
those that look up are like joy.
Those that open are like laughter,
those that close are like sobbing.”
After chanting,
he then realized it was Shū Yuánwú’s lyrics,
sighed, shed tears,
and ordered music to soothe his mood.
Court lady Shěn Qiáoqiáo danced the “Hémǎnzǐ,”
its lyrics said:
“Floating clouds obscure the white sun.”
The emperor said:
“Do you know literature?
This is the first ancient poem in the ‘Wénxuǎn,’
it speaks of ruler and ministers being obscured by villains and evil,
which is exactly today’s situation.”
He then bestowed a golden armlet.
Qiáoqiáo was skilled at the jade fangxiang (stone chimes),
using rhinoceros horn as mallets and purple sandalwood as the stand.
Later, she left the palace,
returned to Qín Chéng,
and served on an embassy to Rìdōng.
Qiáoqiáo brought her jade fangxiang, ascended a tower, and composed a piece
named “Yì Qínláng.”
Fēiyān
Wǔ Gōngyè,
during the Xiántōng period, served as the Henan Recorder of Merits.
His beloved concubine was named Fēiyān,
skilled in Qín music
and fond of literature.
Zhào Xiàng, a northern neighbor,
spied her and was enamored.
He then sent a quatrain through a gate nurse.
Fēiyān replied with a poem on golden phoenix stationery.
Xiàng again composed a poem on jade leaf paper,
and Fēiyān again sent a poem with a double-cicada brocade sachet and green moss stationery.
One night, Xiàng climbed a ladder,
scaled the wall, and entered the hall,
expressing his deepest affection.
The next day,
Xiàng sent a poem saying:
“Though the ten caves and three pure realms are obstructed,
with a willing heart, one can still approach the jasper terrace.
The fragrant wind of ruìxiāng leads thoughts deep into the night,
knowing it is the arrival of an immortal chariot from the rǔi palace.”
Fēiyān again replied:
“I only fear we loved but did not truly know each other,
and meeting again, I worry about parting from you.
I wish to transform into a crane on a pine tree,
a pair flying together into the drifting clouds.”
Before long,
Fēiyān lightly beat a maidservant,
and the maidservant seized the opportunity to inform Wǔ Gōngyè.
Gōngyè bound her to a large pillar,
whipping her until blood flowed.
She only said:
“Living, we loved each other;
dying, what regrets can there be!”
Then she succumbed to the torture and died.
In Luòyáng, there were two scholars, Cuī and Lǐ,
who associated with Recorder Wǔ.
Cuī's poem said:
“Just like the person passing the flower has left,
the most abundant branches are beneath the empty forest pond.”
That night, Fēiyān appeared in a dream and thanked him, saying:
“My beauty did not equal that of peaches and plums,
but my demise surpassed theirs.”
Lǐ's poem said: “If her glamorous spirit and fragrant soul still exist,
she should be ashamed to see the one who fell from the building.”
In a dream, Fēiyān grabbed his hand and said:
“A scholar has a hundred virtues;
are you perfect in all of them?
Why slander me so bitterly?
I shall make you bow beneath the ground to testify.”
A few days later, the scholar died.
Xuē Qióngqióng
She was the foremost zither player in the Kāiyuán palace.
On the Qīngmíng Festival,
the emperor ordered court courtesans to go on a spring outing.
The unrestrained scholar Cuī Huáibǎo secretly spied on Qióngqióng,
was charmed by her,
and through the court musician Yáng Gāo,
managed to get acquainted with her within the ranks.
Gāo instructed Cuī to write a short lyric before he could see Xuē.
Cuī wrote lyrics saying:
“In my life, I have no other wish,
than to be a zither in music.
To be close to the jade person’s slender hand,
to make a charming sound on her rubbed silk skirt,
even to die then would be an honor.”
Gāo gave Huái the “fragrance-permeating wine” to drink,
saying:
“This is made from the ‘everlasting spring grass,’
also known as the ‘thousand-year vine grass.’
It can turn white hair black
and lead to the path of immortality.”
When Cuī became the Secretary of Records for Xíngnán,
Qióngqióng’s zither playing
led her to be taken by officials
to the capital.
Emperor Mínghuáng then bestowed her upon him.
Liǔzhī Niáng
She was a street courtesan in Luòyáng.
Hearing Lǐ Yìshān’s “Yàntái Poem” recited,
she broke a willow branch and tied it into a sash,
presenting it to Yìshān to ask for a poem.
Zhào Gǔjī
The *Jìnshì*, Zhào Gǔ, had a concubine who was slender and beautiful.
When he was about to set out for the examinations,
intending to take her with him on his journey west,
his mother prevented it.
So, he left her at Hèlín Sì.
During a vegetarian feast in the Central Plains,
the military governor of Zhè, spying her,
forcibly took her and made her his own.
The next year,
Zhào Gǔ passed the examinations,
and admonished the governor with a poem, saying:
"In the lonely hall, the sun once more sets,
The Wūshān clouds depart, never to return.
Then, it was said she belonged to Shāzhālì,
Now, this young beauty belongs to the *Shǐjūn*."
The governor felt very ashamed upon receiving it,
and sent her back.
Qín Kè was
Liǔ Yíchéng’s beloved concubine,
skilled at playing the *qín* and *sè*.
When Yíchéng requested retirement,
Qín Kè was married off to Gù Kuàng,
and sang:
"A beauty, slender as jade, born in the north,
Though her home is Hándān, she is no courtesan.
Her hair bun is soft, her fingernails long,
She plays the *qín* and *sè* with great artistry.
The railings of Nánshān are draped with a thousand *zhàng* of snow,
At seventy, no one can warm themselves without human heat.
That human affection fades is common since ancient times,
The *Xiànggōng*’s heart is especially outstanding.
Supreme goodness is like water, adapting to square and round,
Remembering yesterday’s fondness, today abandoned.
Taking medicine is not as good as sleeping alone,
Let him marry another youth."
Xiāng’ér
was Yuán Zài’s singing girl, Qióngyīng.
As a child, she was fed fragrant powders mixed with food and drink,
so when she grew up, her skin was fragrant,
and she was also called Xiāng’ér.
Yú Mèiniáng
was married to a man of the Zhōu clan.
After her husband died,
she maintained her integrity and chastity.
Lù Xīshēng sent a matchmaker to persuade her.
Mèiniáng said:
"If *Lù Lángzhōng* does not keep concubines or maidservants,
then I can be his wife."
Xīshēng agreed.
For two years after their marriage,
they would tear paper, dip ink, and alternately sing and respond to each other’s poems.
Mèiniáng was also skilled at preparing five-color minced fish,
a culinary art that was beyond compare.
Not long after,
Xīshēng took Shùnyīng as a concubine.
Mèiniáng assented,
and Xīshēng thought she was truly sincere.
Once they lived together,
Mèiniáng said nothing.
When Xīshēng went out,
she locked Shùnyīng in a room,
killed her with her own hands,
minced her body,
put it into two large boxes,
sealed and labeled them, saying:
"Sending items back to the villa."
The gatekeeper found it strange,
and sent it to the Jīngzhào prison.
Mèiniáng was then executed.
Pots and Kettles All Move — From *Língguài Jí*
When the *Shàngshū* Zhèng Yīn retired from his premiership,
all the pots and kettles in his residence’s kitchen started moving.
They only settled down at the end of the day.
A few days later,
Zhèng died.
Fire Carriage
Lǐ Lìng, during the Kāiyuán era, served as *Mìshūjiān*.
He was quite fond of exquisite dishes,
and used cruel methods to obtain flavors.
When he was gravely ill,
several squads of armored guards followed a fire carriage into his gate.
Hearing people in the hall chanting scriptures,
the armored guards turned back.
After a long while,
a ghost in a scarlet robe strode in and kicked open the door
with a sound like thunder.
From inside, it helped the *Lìng* out,
threw him into the fire carriage,
and carried him away.
Three Monsters in a Ruined House
Yáo Kāngchéng slept overnight in a ruined house.
He saw three people enter the corridor room and compose poetry.
One was black, thin, and tall.
He chanted:
"In former days, I burned fiercely, known only to myself,
Now, without a beacon or stove, what can I do?
Alas, what use is a long handle now?
Lǔ saw the time when Suì Rén created fire."
Another was thin and long,
his face full of scars.
He chanted:
"Then, I was full of pride and spirit,
A single tune before the lord was worth ten thousand gold.
Today, I am not as good as the bamboo in the courtyard,
When the wind comes, it can still mimic the dragon's roar."
Yet another was fat and short,
his beard and hair hanging loose.
He chanted:
"My head is scorched, my temples bald, but my heart remains,
My strength is spent in the dust, no more discussion.
Do not laugh at me now, like the reeds of Lǔ,
Throughout the day, I sweep the brushwood gate."
The next day, he searched,
and found a single iron cauldron,
a broken flute,
and a bald broom made of millet stalks.
Woman Leaning on a Tree Chanting
During the Dàhé era, the *Jìnshì* Cáo Táng,
at night, saw a woman,
with an elaborate headdress and yellow robes,
her clothes like mist and smoke,
leaning on a tree and chanting:
"Temporarily tuning the clear *sè* to play the *nícháng*,
How can worldly thoughts know the length of a crane’s dream?
Within the trees lies a realm of silent spring,
On earth, no path, the moon is vast.
Jade sand and magic herbs connect to the green stream,
Clouds, water, and peach blossoms fill the fragrant cave.
Mist, water, and wind lamps are easily scattered,
I wonder on what day I will see *Liú Láng* again."
Cáo Táng died the next day from illness.
*Wǔdài Shǐ Bǔ* records this poem as Cáo Táng’s work.
Tiger Sheds Skin to Become a Woman
Cuī Tāo stayed overnight at a posthouse in Chúzhōu.
At night, he saw a tiger enter the door.
Cuī Tāo was afraid.
He hid and watched,
and saw the tiger shed its skin.
It was a woman,
who went up to the main hall and slept.
Cuī Tāo came out and asked her.
She said:
"My family makes its living by hunting."
Cuī Tāo took the skin and threw it into a well,
and took the woman away with him.
Later, Cuī Tāo passed the examinations,
and was taking his wife and child to his official post in Xuānchéng.
When they again reached the Chú驿 station,
he looked into the well,
and the tiger skin was still there.
Cuī Tāo retrieved it.
As soon as his wife put it on,
she transformed back into a tiger,
roared as she went up to the hall,
ate Cuī Tāo and his son, and left.
—From *Jīzhí Jí*
Sun Three Poles High
In *Nán Qí Tiānwén Zhì*, it states:
In the fifth year of Yǒngmíng,
the sun rose three poles high,
scarlet, yellow, with a red halo.
Half-Ring Moon
Hán Wò’s poem:
"The moon like a half-ring, the frost like jade."
Star Prison
The nine stars of Guànsǔo [Constellation Corona Borealis]
are the prison for common people;
if all nine stars are bright,
the prisons throughout the land will be crowded.
—From *Liè Sù Tú*
Silver Bay
Refers to the Milky Way,
from Xǔ Dòng’s poem.
Mulberry Grove Rain
Yìng Qú’s letter says:
"Tāng prayed in the mulberry grove,
and was able to bring about rain."
Five *Chǐ* from Heaven
Wéiqū and Dùhù
are near Cháng’ān.
A proverb says:
"Wéiqū and Dùhù,
five *chǐ* from Heaven."
Lonely Cloud Rain Corner
The *Guǎngjì* mentions that south of Yuán,
there is a treacherous and dangerous road,
called "Lonely Cloud Rain Corner,
a mere grasp from Heaven."
Fēnxiāng
Lù Shìhéng's 《Diào Wèi Wǔ Xù》 (Elegy for Emperor Wǔ of Wèi) states:
"Emperor Wǔ's dying instruction said:
'The remaining incense can be divided among the various ladies.' "
Chúntú
Wéi Zǔ said:
"Water shield roots,
are exquisitely delicious in soup;
people in Jiāngdōng call them chúntú."
Bào Wèng
《Yǔ Lín》 (Forest of Sayings) states:
"Gān Yǎ Shū brewed wine in winter,
making people hold the urn,
to quickly achieve good flavor."
Shí Zhū
Emperor Míng of Sòng could eat roasted pork,
up to two hundred slices.
Qióngyán
Zhāng Yuè's poem says:
"Jade goblets fly with a thousand days,
jeweled banquets present eight delicacies."
Cháng Qiāng
Lǐ Hè's poem:
"Long spears of glutinous rice are ripe,
small trees of jujube flowers are fragrant."
Shǔ Mǐ Chèng Xīn
Jīn Zǎi said:
"Wéi Zhuāng was frugal and stingy,
counting rice grains before cooking,
weighing firewood before burning."
Chāi Zé
Féng Yǎn's wife, Rèn Shì, was fierce and jealous.
She had only one maidservant,
whose head had no hairpins or ornamentation,
and whose face had no powder or rouge.
Xiūxiūxiū
Sīkōng Tú's song says:
"Stop, stop, stop,
do not stop.
Though skills are many, nature is wicked;
laziness is where busy people always look to relax."
Bái Zú Chán Sēng
During the time of Emperor Wǔ of Wèi,
there was a monk with white feet,
named Sī Shǐ,
who possessed great supernatural powers.
He was called the "White-Footed Zen Master."
Tán Bǐng
Dà Láng Fǎshī of Qīxiá Temple in the Southern Dynasties,
always held
a pine branch while discussing,
using it as a "discourse handle."
Jiǎ Yǐ Yè
Emperor Wénzōng of Táng said:
"If one does not observe affairs in the first watch of the night,
and read books in the second watch of the night
how can one be a ruler?"
Chū Yú Xì Biǎo
Yǔ Xìn's 《Āi Jiāngnán Fù》 (Rhapsody on Mourning Jiāngnán) commentary states:
"Hé Xiū, upon seeing Zhèng Xuán's commentary on the 《Yì》, said:
'The Way of the Master
Xuē Tāo
In the early Yuánhé era,
Xuē Tāo enjoyed composing short poems.
Regretting that the paper sheets were too large,
she had them narrowed and made smaller.
Everyone found this convenient,
and all reduced paper sheets became small,
named Xuē Tāo Jiān.
Liǔ Sān Mián
Lǐ Yìshān's rhapsody states:
"How can it be like the Cowherd Star by the river,
heard of only once a year;
not equal to the human-shaped willow in the imperial garden,
which gets to 'sleep' three times throughout the day."
Commentary:
"In the Hàn imperial garden, there was a human-shaped willow,
which stood up and fell down three times a day."
Jí Tān Shàng Shuǐ Chuán
Péi Yányù of Táng, while in the inner court,
was quick with documents,
and was called "downstream boat."
When Emperor Tàizǔ of Liáng received the abdication,
Yáo Bó became a scholar,
and was called "upstream boat,"
and also "upstream boat on a rapid."
Tiān Rǔ Xīng
《Liè Xīng Tú》 (Atlas of Stars) states:
"When the Tiān Rǔ Xīng is bright, sweet dew descends."
Yín Pǔ
Lǐ Hè referred to the Milky Way as Yín Pǔ.
Lǜ Suō Tīng
Hézhōng Fǔ previously had a Lǜ Suō Tīng.
Wáng Yuánzhī's poem says:
"The Lǜ Suō Tīng Shì of old echoed with crickets."
Piǎo Wǎ
Glazed tiles are called Piǎo Wǎ.
Liú Táo's poem says:
"Azure-blue is used for tiles."
Jī Zhí
《Lǚ Shì Chūnqiū》:
"A good learner is like King Qí eating chicken,
he must eat its foot."
Cí Jiǎ Chén
Péi Jìnggōng was gifted a huái gall.
Lángzhōng Yǔ Wēi, who was present,
said:
"This grew from a female tree."
The Duke asked the Lángzhōng's age.
He replied:
"I am of the same Jiǎ Chén year as Your Excellency."
The Duke laughed and said:
"The Lángzhōng is indeed a female Jiǎ Chén."
Bù Bài Chányú
Hào Xūzhōu wrote 《Sū Wǔ Bù Bài Chányú Fù》 (Rhapsody on Sū Wǔ Not Bowing to the Chányú),
asserting that the one who upheld Hàn integrity was Zhèng Zhòng,
not Sū Wǔ.
Lǐ Hàn's 《Méng Qiú》 also clearly states:
Sū Wǔ held the imperial staff,
Zhèng Zhòng did not bow.
Chē Mǎ Xíng Sè
Those who send people off
often say the "carriages and horses have the look of travel."
Zhuāngzǐ mentions Liǔ Xiàjì encountering Fūzǐ returning from Dào Zhí's place,
not departing.
As the carriages and horses had dusty faces,
it implies they had come from a distant journey.
This usage should be carefully considered.
Why not rely on the text's meaning to correct the error?
Xínglǐ
The character Lǐ,
apart from being a surname,
has no other meaning.
In the 《Zuǒ Zhuàn》, the Lǐ of Xínglǐ,
Dù (Yù) did not investigate its meaning,
and commented:
"Xíng
means envoy."
Now, the order of packing for a distant journey
is called xínglǐ,
without realizing it means "traveling envoy."
According to older texts, the character "使" (shǐ, envoy) was written as "岑" (cén),
and was mistakenly copied as "李" (lǐ).
The ancient character for "使"
had "山" (shān, mountain) on top of "人" (rén, person),
or "人" on top of "子" (zǐ, child).
Lù Lǐ
Among the Four Greybeards of Hàn,
one was named Lù Lǐ.
The character "甪" is pronounced Lù;
today it is often called Jué.
Wèi Zǐyǒu, in his 《Kǒng Shì Mì Jì》 (Secret Records of the Kǒng Clan), anticipating future errors,
directly wrote Lù Lǐ.
Kè Sàn
Today, when guests leave a host's door,
one invariably says "kè sàn" (guests have dispersed).
They do not know that "kè sàn Mèng Cháng mén" (guests dispersed from Mèng Cháng's gate)
is Wáng Wéi lamenting the death of the prefect,
and thus says "autumn wind is desolate."
It mourns that after the master's death, all his colleagues dispersed.
How can it be used [in other contexts]?
Yào Lán
The yào lán in a garden
is in fact yào lán (藥闌),
meaning "enclosure" or "fence,"
not a railing for medicinal plants (藥欄).
Some do not understand this,
and mistakenly pair it with "vine trellis vegetable garden" for a perfectly matching couplet.
Emperor Xuān of Hàn's imperial garden's "medicine enclosure" was where those who received imperial favor
would lend their power to the poor.
The 《Hàn Shū》 (History of Hàn) says:
Lán (闌, enclosure) entered the palace forbidden area,
and the character was often written with the grass radical (蘭);
with "闌" at the bottom,
then "藥闌" (yào lán) is even clearer.
Qī Bù
Chén Sī Wáng's (曹植) seven-pace sprint,
if applied to the present-day imperial princes,
would be highly inappropriate.
Why?
To compose a poem in seven steps
is the twenty-character poem about burning beanstalks to cook beans.
If we consider the princes' swiftness,
and there might unexpectedly be similar ten-step affairs,
why not adopt the practice of the Later Wèi (北魏) dynasty?
Wèi Yáng (渭陽)
The matter of summoning a maternal uncle must use "Wèi Yáng".
How can it be taken lightly?
When Qí Yáng Yīn (楊愔) was young,
his maternal uncle asked if he had reached "Wèi Yáng".
Yīn (愔) immediately burst into tears.
Furthermore, there is the sentiment of yearning for the two palaces (father and mother);
its meaning should not be used lightly.
Similar to this,
wàn jī (萬幾)
"One or two days, myriad affairs."
Kǒng Ān Guó (孔安國) said:
"Jī (幾)
means subtle,
implying one should be mindful of the subtle beginnings of myriad affairs."
Jìn Tài Zōng (晉太宗) (Sī Mǎ Yǎn 司馬炎) acted as prime minister,
and for any matter, it would invariably take years.
Huán Wēn (桓溫) was puzzled by his slowness.
He replied:
"How can the myriad affairs (wàn jī 萬幾) be handled quickly?"
This reply truly grasps the meaning of the *Shū* (書) (Book of Documents).
The recent change to the *jī* (機) of "pivot" and "opportunity" (shū jī 樞機)
must be due to the Hàn (漢) dynasty's Wáng Jiā (王嘉)'s memorial to the throne, mistakenly using the character with the wood radical (木傍).
Yán Shì (顏氏) did not cite Kǒng (孔)'s commentary to prove it,
and later generations did not trace its origin,
instead saying:
"The *Hàn Shū* (漢書) (History of the Han Dynasty) is like this,
unaware that Bān (班) (Bān Gù 班固) and Yán (顏) (Yán Shī Gǔ 顏師古) themselves misled later scholars."
Zuó Hóu (酇侯)
When Xiāo Hé (蕭何) was enfeoffed as a marquis,
everyone in the world called it "Cuó" (醝).
If someone called it "Zàn" (贊),
they would cover their mouth and smile scornfully,
which is highly astonishing.
Zōu Shì (鄒氏) said:
"If it belongs to Pèi Jùn (沛郡),
the sound is cuó.
If it belongs to Nán Yáng (南陽),
the sound is zàn."
Moreover, *Mào Líng Shū* (茂陵書) states:
"Xiāo Hé's (蕭何) state was in Nán Yáng (南陽)."
Combining the explanations of the two families,
the pronunciation zàn is clear.
Gān Luó (甘羅)
The world says Gān Luó (甘羅) became prime minister of Qín (秦) at age twelve,
which is a great mistake.
The *Shǐ Jì* (史記) (Records of the Grand Historian) states:
"Luó (羅) served Lǚ Bù Wéi (呂不韋),
and due to his success in persuading Zhào (趙),
Shǐ Huáng (始皇) enfeoffed him as a high minister (shàng qīng 上卿)."
Lǚ Bù Wéi (呂不韋) was the prime minister.
The Qín (秦) prime minister,
was Luó's (羅) ancestor,
named Mào (茂).
Yā Yá (押牙)
Military officials have the title "yā yá" (押衙).
*Yá* (衙)
should be written as *yá* (牙),
not the "yā yá" (押衙) government office.
It refers to holding the "yá qí" (牙旗) (general's banner).
According to military texts:
The "yá qí" (牙旗)
is the general's standard,
thus it is erected at the gate.
Historical records mistakenly wrote it as "yá mén" (牙門) (gate of the general's residence).
Now that "yā yá" (押牙) is written as "yā yá" (押衙),
"yá mén" (牙門) (general's residence) is also referred to as "yá mén" (牙門).
Yáng Zhōu (揚州)
It is named for its light and frivolous customs (fēng sú qīng yáng 風俗輕揚).
To use the "yáng" (楊) of "willow" (yáng liǔ 楊柳) now
is a mistake.
Xīng Huǒ Pù (星火鋪)
Stalls that sell goods by displaying them in baskets, in hampers, leaning, or hanging in rows,
are called:
Xīng Huò Pù (星貨鋪).
It means that
the displayed goods are clustered and numerous, like stars.
The common pronunciation of it as Xīng Huǒ Pù (星火鋪)
is a mistake.
Bào Zhí (豹直)
When new officials stay overnight at their own department,
it is called bào zhí (爆直).
It should be the character bào (豹).
Leopards are clean by nature,
and skilled at regulating their breath.
During rain, snow, frost, or fog, they lie low and do not emerge,
fearing to dirty their bodies.
*Liè Hù Zhuàn* (列戶傳) (Biographies of Notable Households) quotes Táo Dá Zǐ (陶答子)'s wife as saying:
"There is a spotted leopard (wén bào 文豹) in the southern mountains,
which does not eat for seven days during fog and rain,
wishing to moisten its fur and make its patterns complete."
Xiǎo Xiè (小謝) (Xiè Líng Yùn 謝靈運)'s poem says:
"Although I lack the posture of a black leopard (xuán bào 玄豹),
I will ultimately hide in the mists of the southern mountains," which is this.
*Nán Huá* (南華) (Zhuāng Zǐ 莊子) also says:
"Leopards dwell in mountain forests,
and in mountain caves."
Thus, staying overnight at the public office
truly embodies the meaning of a leopard lying low.
Jí Jí Rú Lǜ Lìng (急急如律令)
The final phrase "Jí jí rú lǜ lìng" (急急如律令) in talismans and prayers
is commonly understood to mean "like the regulations for drinking wine,"
that is, to leave quickly and not linger.
Another theory states that during the Hàn (漢) dynasty, every official document issued
would say "rú lǜ lìng" (如律令).
It meant that even documents that were not laws or edicts
should be executed as swiftly as laws and edicts.
Hence, talismans and prayers contain the phrase "rú lǜ lìng" (如律令).
However,
the *lìng* (令) in *lǜ lìng* (律令)
should be in the flat tone (píng shēng 平聲),
pronounced as *líng* (零).
*Lǜ Líng* (律令) are swift spirits associated with thunder;
these spirits are good at running,
and move as quickly as thunder.
Therefore, it means "as swift as these spirits."
Cù Róng (蹙戎)
In contemporary chess (yì qí 奕棊), when one occupies a path
and moves five pieces,
it is called "cù róng" (蹙融).
*Róng* (融)
should be *róng* (戎).
This game originated from Huáng Dì's (黃帝) *cù jū* (蹙鞠) (kickball),
and its meaning is related to military affairs (jūn róng 軍戎).
It is certainly not the meaning of "fusion" or "harmony" (yuán róng 圓融).
What Yú Yuán Guī (庾元規) wrote in *Zuò Shí* (坐石) as "cù róng" (蹙戎)
is today's "cù róng" (蹙融).
Duān Wǔ (端午)
Zhōu Chǔ's (周處) *Fēng Tǔ Jì* (風土記) states:
"On Duān Wǔ (端午) of midsummer,
duck is cooked and horn-shaped glutinous rice dumplings (jiǎo shǔ 角黍) are eaten."
*Duān* (端) means "beginning";
it refers to the fifth day of the fifth lunar month.
The common writing "Duān Wǔ" (端午)
has no basis in meaning.
In my family's collection, the imperial edicts from the Yuán Hé (元和) era concerning Duān Wǔ (端午)
none use the character *wǔ* (午).
Yù Zhí (寓直)
These two characters originated when Pān Yuè (潘岳) was a Wǔ Bēn Láng Zhōng Jiāng (武賁郎中將) (Commander of the Valiant Guards).
During the Jìn (晉) dynasty, those who had not yet been formally assigned
would temporarily serve (jì zhí 寄直) in the Sàn Qí Shěng (散騎省) (Palace Secretariat).
Now, all officials serve (zhí 直) in their respective departments,
which is definitely "dāng zhí" (當直) (on duty).
How can it be called "yù" (寓) (to reside temporarily)?
Common Misconceptions
There are countless common misconceptions:
calling a prefectural governor (jùn cì shǐ 郡刺史) "cì shǐ" (刺使);
referring to *bān shè* (般涉) as *guān zhì* (官陟);
calling *qiàn* (茜) *qiàn* (塹);
when eating fish, calling *guì* (鱖) *guì* (桂);
using *zhǎ hóu* (鮓鱟) to insult people;
calling a "sniff" (zhèn bí 振鼻) "sneeze" (pēn tì 噴涕);
and calling "opening the mouth wide" (qù kǒu 呿口) "loving wealth" (ài fù 愛富).
They are utterly unaware that sneezing (pēn chè 噴嚔) is *yī* (噫),
pronounced *ài* (隘),
which is the gas from the internal organs being expelled.
They also call an iron (yù dòu 熨斗) *yùn* (醞);
scissors (jiǎn dāo 剪刀) *jiàn* (箭);
a veil (mì 羃) *mù* (幕);
*lǐ* (禮) (ritual) *lǐ* (理) (reason);
*bǎo* (保) (to protect) *bǔ* (補) (to mend);
*bāo* (褒) (to praise) *bǔ* (捕) (to catch);
*bào* (暴) (violent) *bǔ* (捕) (to catch).
Such examples are numerous,
and cannot all be enumerated.
Má Hú (麻胡)
The common people scare babies by saying "Má Hú."
The Suí general, Má Hù,
was cruel and severe by nature.
Young children would scare each other, saying:
"Má Hù is coming!"
Hù was changed to Hú,
just as during Emperor Xiànzōng's reign, Hǎo Pín, the general of Jīng,
was feared by all the barbarians.
When a baby cried,
they would scare it with Pín and it would stop.
During Emperor Wǔzōng's reign,
children threatening each other with "Xuē Yǐn is coming"
was similar to this.
Sāntái
Today's *sāntái* for urging drinks.
Some say:
"There are three terraces in Yè,
the place where Shí Chóng feasted,
and musicians used them to urge quick drinking."
It is also said:
"Cài Yōng traveled around the three terraces within three days,
and the Music Bureau, knowing Yōng's musical acumen, composed this piece,
hoping for a generous reward."
Cuòdà
Scholars are called *cùdà*,
meaning their sharp "vinegar" quality ranks first among the four classes of people.
One theory says their attire is so solemn that it cannot be offended,
and if offended, retribution is certain,
even more certain than vinegar.
Or it is said there was a scholar living in poverty in Xīnzhèng,
who carried vinegar on a donkey to sell around the city,
and the townspeople pointed to his vinegar-laden donkey and called him by that name.
It is also said that Zhèng has a Cùgōu (Vinegar Ditch),
and many scholars reside in that area,
especially east of the ditch.
The prominent families were ranked in order,
hence "cùdà."
All four explanations are incorrect.
*Cù* is written as *cuò*,
simply meaning they are capable of handling important matters, and that is all.
Tóuzǐzhě
Means "to throw or cast."
Today, some write it as "tóu" (head) character,
saying it is made of bone,
which is incorrect.
Some write it as "tóu" (dice) character.
According to:
the books of various scholars,
骰 (tóu) is the same as 股 (gǔ) character,
and not pronounced *tóu*.
In the *Shǐjì*, Cài Zé told Fàn Suī:
"As for gambling,
some wish to 'throw big'."
It refers to throwing jade.
Thus, it is known that it uses stone and jade for the meaning of "throwing,"
how can there be a principle of throwing dice?
Wūtóu
It is common to call the latrine *wūtóu*.
People from Bìngzhōu dug rooms into the earth,
with the latrine above their living quarters,
hence the name.
Another theory is that
Emperor Wénxuān of Northern Qí, angered at Cuī Shúbǎo,
poured excrement juice on his head.
Juǎnbáibō
The name for drinking alcohol, *juǎnbáibō*,
originated in the Eastern Hàn.
After the Báibō bandits were captured,
they were slaughtered as if rolling up a mat.
Thus, banquets imitated this,
to satisfy people's feelings and spirits.
Wúniú Wèiquè
In the "Moon" section of the *Chūxuéjì*,
Wúniú is juxtaposed with Wèiquè.
The Wú ox pants upon seeing the moon;
Emperor Wǔ of Wèi said:
"The moon is bright and the stars are sparse,
the magpies fly south."
This is the basis.
If so, why not say Wèi Wū (Wèi crows)?
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's *Qiūfēng Cí* states:
"The autumn wind rises and white clouds fly,
grass and trees yellow and fall, and geese return south."
If Wèiquè is used for the moon,
then Hàngyàn (Hàn geese) should also be used for wind matters.
Dù Dù
Those whose names were identical to *shìzhēng* were invariably called Dù Dù.
Hán Wén Gōng's *Huì Biàn* also cites this, doesn't it?
Dù Shù's *Dúlùn* says:
"Dù Cāo,
courtesy name Bódù.
During the Wèi dynasty, because his name was the same as Emperor Wǔ's, he concealed his given name and used his courtesy name.
Later generations removed the character 'Bó'.
Shù and Bódù are the same person.
How can one not believe the original truth of *Dúlùn*,
but rather follow Wén Gōng's later error!"
Volume 29
End.
Liǎngtóushé
Sūn Shū'áo, when he was a child, went out to play,
returned and cried.
His mother asked him the reason,
he replied:
"Whoever sees a two-headed snake is sure to die.
I saw one just now,
and so I am weeping with sorrow."
His mother said:
"Where is the snake now?"
He said:
"Fearing others might also see it,
I killed and buried it."
His mother said:
"One who performs a hidden virtue
will certainly receive an open reward.
You will not die now."
Yúqiūzǐ Xiánsì
King Zhuāng of Chǔ dismissed the court and held a banquet.
Fán Jī asked the reason,
the king said:
"I was conversing with the worthy minister Yúqiūzǐ,
and did not realize it was late."
Fán Jī smiled and said:
"Yúqiū has been minister for several decades,
yet has never advanced a single worthy person.
To know and not advance them is disloyalty;
to not know them is unintelligence;
how can he be considered worthy!"
Yúqiūzǐ then resigned his position and recommended Sūn Shū'áo,
and the king consequently achieved hegemony.
Shǐ Yú Shījiàn
Shǐ Qiú, courtesy name Zǐyú,
was ill and about to die.
He said to his son:
"I could not advance Qú Bóyù,
nor dismiss Mí Zǐxiá.
Alive, I could not rectify the ruler;
dead, I should not be accorded proper rites.
Place my corpse in the North Hall, that will suffice."
After Qiú died,
Duke Líng went to mourn him.
His son fully recounted what happened.
The Duke said:
"This master, while alive, advanced the worthy and dismissed the unworthy,
and in death, remonstrated with his corpse.
He can be called loyal!"
Then he summoned Qú Bóyù to be a minister,
dismissed Mí Zǐxiá,
moved the corpse to the main hall,
completed the rites, and then returned.
Wèi was thus well-governed.
Jūnrénzhě Chénzhí
Marquis Wén of Wèi asked his ministers and grandees:
"What kind of ruler am I?"
All said:
"A benevolent ruler."
Zhái Huáng said:
"Your Lordship attacked Zhōngshān,
but did not enfeoff your brother, instead enfeoffing your son.
From this, I know Your Lordship is not a benevolent ruler."
Marquis Wén was angry and expelled Huáng.
Rèn Zuò said:
"Your Lordship
is a benevolent ruler."
He asked:
"How do you say so?"
He replied:
"When the ruler is benevolent, his ministers are upright.
Huáng's words are upright,
this is how I know Your Lordship is a benevolent ruler."
Marquis Wén said:
"Excellent."
He appointed Huáng as Senior Minister.
Fùxià Cuì Bèishàng Máo
Jìn Pínggōng was floating on the Western River,
and sighed, saying:
"How can I find worthy scholars to share this joy with?"
The boatman, Gù Sāng, said:
"Swords are produced in Yuè,
pearls are produced in the Jiāng and Hàn rivers,
jade is produced in Kūnshān.
These three treasures all arrive without feet.
If you truly love scholars,
worthy scholars will come."
The Duke said:
"I have three thousand retainers.
In the morning, there isn't enough food, so
in the evening I collect market taxes;
in the evening, there isn't enough food, so
in the morning I collect market taxes.
How can I still not love scholars?"
Gù Sāng said:
"When a swan flies high,
what it relies on
are its six primary feathers.
The down under its belly,
the feathers on its back,
if you add a handful,
it doesn't make its flight higher or lower.
I wonder if your retainers are the six primary feathers,
or the down and feathers of the belly and back?"
There are Five Obscurities in the World
Jìn Pínggōng said to Shī Kuàng:
"How great
is your obscurity!"
He replied:
"There are five obscurities in the world,
about which I dare not speak.
Courtiers offer bribes to gain fame,
the common people are oppressed and wronged with nowhere to complain;
this is the first.
Loyal ministers are not employed,
employed ministers are not loyal;
inferior talents occupy high positions,
the unworthy preside over the worthy;
this is the second.
Treacherous ministers deceive and defraud,
the state coffers are empty;
this is the third.
The state is poor and the people resentful,
superiors and inferiors are not in harmony;
this is the fourth.
The highest đạo is not clear,
laws are not enforced;
this is the fifth.
If a state has these five obscurities and is not endangered,
such a thing has never existed.
My obscurity
is but a small obscurity;
what harm can it do to the state?"
The Zhōngháng Clan Will Perish First
Zhào Wénzǐ asked Shū Xiàng:
"Which of the six armies of Jìn will perish first?"
He replied:
"The Zhōngháng clan governs
by treating harshness as discernment,
deceit as sincerity,
severity as loyalty,
multiplying schemes as goodness,
and accumulating wealth as excellence.
It is like peeling off hide.
Great it is, indeed,
but it is the way of fragmentation;
they are bound to perish first."
Jǐnggōng Does Not Offer Humans as Sacrifices
During the time of Qí Jǐnggōng,
there was a great drought for three years.
Divination revealed:
"You must sacrifice a human."
The Duke said:
"All that I seek rain for
is for my people.
Now, if it must rain only by sacrificing a human,
I, the solitary one, will take it upon myself."
Before his words were finished,
the heavens rained.
There are Ominous Signs in the State
Wǔwáng defeated Yīn and captured two prisoners.
He asked:
"Are there ominous signs in your state?"
One prisoner said:
"Seeing stars during the day and snow in summer;
these are the ominous signs of our state."
The other prisoner said:
"In our state, sons do not listen to fathers,
younger brothers do not listen to elder brothers,
the ruler's commands are not enforced;
these are the greatest of ominous signs."
Wearing Fur Inside Out and Carrying Faggots
Wèi Wénhóu went out on a stroll
and saw a man on the road wearing a fur garment inside out and carrying faggots.
Wénhóu asked,
and the man replied:
"I cherish its fur."
Wénhóu said:
"Do you not know that when the lining wears out, the fur will have nothing to rely on?"
State Policy
Chǔ Zhuāngwáng asked Sūn Shū'áo:
"I have not yet decided upon a state policy."
'Áo replied:
"If a state has 'right' in abundance,
it will be hated by 'wrong';
I fear Your Majesty will not be able to stabilize it."
The King said:
"I wish to consult the entire state, along with the lords, scholars, and officials, to decide upon a state policy.
How dare I, with my small state, be arrogant towards my scholars and common people!"
A Dubious Case
In Liáng, there was a dubious legal case.
The ministers generally considered the accused innocent,
and even the King of Liáng had doubts.
He summoned Táo Zhūgōng and asked him about it.
The Duke said:
"My family has two white jade discs,
their color is similar,
their diameter is similar,
their luster is similar,
yet the price of one is a thousand gold pieces,
and the other five hundred gold pieces."
The King said:
"Why?"
He replied:
"If you look at it from the side,
one is twice as thick;
that is why it is a thousand gold pieces."
The King said:
"Excellent."
Therefore, in dubious legal cases, follow leniency;
in dubious rewards, follow generosity.
The state of Liáng was greatly pleased.
From this perspective,
a thin wall quickly crumbles,
thin silk quickly tears,
a thin vessel quickly breaks,
thin wine quickly sours.
Indeed, that which is thin and can last long
has almost never existed.
Therefore, those who govern a state, nurture its people, and implement policies and education
should make them substantial; only then can they endure.
Swallowing a Leech
Chǔ Huìwáng was eating cold leeks and found a leech.
He then swallowed it,
and had an illness in his abdomen, unable to eat.
The Prime Minister inquired about his illness.
The King said:
"I found a leech while eating leeks.
I considered condemning and executing [the responsible parties],
meaning the head cook and food supervisor would all be liable to death according to the law.
But my heart could not bear it,
fearing the leech would be seen [by others],
so I swallowed it."
The Prime Minister said:
"Your Majesty possesses benevolence and virtue,
which Heaven supports.
The illness will not cause harm."
That evening,
the leech emerged from Huìwáng's posterior,
and his long-standing abdominal illness was completely cured.
Do Not Forget Being in Jǔ
Huán Gōng was drinking with Guǎn Zhòng, Bào Shú, and Níng Qī.
Bào Shú said:
"I wish our ruler not to forget being in Jǔ, Guǎn Zhòng not to forget being bound and following from Lǔ, and Níngzǐ not to forget feeding cattle under the carriage."
The Duke said:
"If I and you two grand masters never forget your words,
the altars of the state of Qí will surely not fall into disuse."
Approving the Good and Hating the Evil
Qí Huán Gōng went out on an excursion.
He saw the ruins of the former Guō Shì family,
which belonged to a perished state, and asked a rustic:
"Why is the Guō Shì estate a ruin?"
The rustic replied:
"They appreciated good and detested evil."
The Duke said:
"Appreciating good and detesting evil
is a good human deed.
Why then did it become a ruin?"
The rustic said:
"They appreciated good but could not practice it;
they detested evil but could not eliminate it.
Therefore, it became a ruin."
The Duke returned and told Guǎn Zhòng,
who said:
"Your Highness is also like a Guō Shì."
Thereupon,
the Duke summoned the rustic and rewarded him.
Fond of learning and accepting admonition
Yè Gōng Zhū Liáng asked Yuè Wángfù:
"What kind of person is the Jin Grandee Zhào Wénzǐ?"
He replied:
"He is fond of learning and accepts admonition.
Being fond of learning
is wisdom;
accepting admonition
is benevolence.
The Jiāng (Yangtze River) flows out of Wèn Shān,
its source is like the mouth of a jar,
but when it reaches the state of Chǔ,
its width is ten *lǐ*.
There is no other reason
than its many downstream tributaries.
When a person is fond of learning and accepts admonition,
it is fitting that he should establish himself."
Hanlin veteran scholar
Wáng Yǔchēng,
a Hanlin veteran scholar,
was repeatedly exiled as a guest.
He requested to release the students who had passed the imperial examination from seeing him off in the suburbs,
and his memorial was approved.
Yǔchēng wrote a poem in thanks, saying:
"What an honor it is for them to send me off in a line;
an old crane riding a carriage, I am ashamed before the valley orioles.
Three times I entered Chéngmíng but did not know how to advance,
watching others release students from their gates."
At that time,
friends and relatives followed the prevailing likes and dislikes,
not daring to privately send him off.
Dòu Yuánbīn clasped his hand, weeping at the palace gate, saying:
"Alas!
Is this not fate?"
After the Duke departed,
he thanked him with a poem:
"Only Dòu Yuánwài of Nángōng,
shed tears for me before the palace gate."
Not long after arriving in the prefecture,
two tigers fought within its borders,
one died;
chickens crowed at night;
there was winter thunder and hail.
The Supervisor of Astronomy memorialized:
"The local administrator bears the blame."
Immediately, an order was given to move him to Qí.
His memorial of thanks said:
"The questions of ghosts and spirits in Xuān Shì
gave no hope of returning alive.
The interactions for the Fēng and Shàn sacrifices at Mào Líng
only caused troubles after death."
A month later, he died.
Tài Zōng once admonished him, saying:
"You are intelligent,
and your writing is no less than Hán's,
but you are too rigid to accommodate others.
Many people hinder you,
making it difficult for Us to protect you."
Lǐ and Hán's writings
Lǐ Gǔ and Hán Xīzài shared a desk early on.
When they parted, they made a pact:
"Each shall choose his lord based on his talent and destiny."
In the Guǎngshùn era, Lǐ Gǔ served the Zhōu dynasty,
becoming a Pingzhangshi.
Hán Xīzài served Lǐ Xiānzhǔ of Jiangnan,
becoming a Guangzhengdian Scholar.
Hán Xīzài sent a letter to Lǐ Gǔ, saying:
"If Jiangnan truly supports me as minister,
I will drive straight to pacify the Central Plains."
Lǐ Gǔ replied:
"If the Central Plains truly supports me as minister,
descending upon Jiangnan will be like taking something from a bag."
Later, Lǐ Gǔ became a minister,
and personally led a campaign against Jiangnan,
but Hán Xīzài had already died.
Great national calamity
Jìn Píng Gōng asked Shū Xiàng:
"What is the greatest national calamity?"
He replied:
"When high officials receive heavy salaries but do not admonish strongly,
when close ministers fear punishment and dare not speak,
and when the sentiments of the lower classes do not reach the top,
this is the greatest calamity."
The Duke issued an order saying:
"Whoever wishes to present good advice and is blocked by an usher shall die."
Sòng Zhāo returns to his state
Sòng Zhāo Gōng fled into exile,
and sighed:
"I now know why I perished:
A thousand court officials,
when issuing policies or promoting officials,
all said, 'Our lord is sagacious!'
Several hundred attendants,
dressed in fine attire,
all said, 'Our lord is beautiful!'
Neither internally nor externally did I hear of my faults until this point!"
Therefore, King Sòng Zhāo, being able to awaken to this,
was able to return to his state, it is said.
Sòng Yù meets King Xiāng
Sòng Yù, through his friend, met Chǔ Xiāng Wáng.
King Xiāng treated him no differently from others.
Sòng Yù blamed his friend,
who said:
"Ginger and cinnamon grow according to the land,
but are not pungent because of the land;
women marry because of a matchmaker,
but are not intimate because of the matchmaker.
Your service to the King has not yet begun,
why blame me?"
Sòng Yù said:
"Suppose there was a cunning rabbit in Qí called Dōngguō Jùn,
which once ran five hundred *lǐ*;
and a good dog called Hán Lú,
which also ran five hundred *lǐ*.
If one were to see the rabbit from afar and point it out,
then even Hán Lú would not catch up to the dust of the common rabbits.
But if one were to follow its tracks and unleash the leash,
then even Dōngguō would not be able to escape.
Now, your introduction of me to the King,
was it to follow my tracks and unleash the leash?
Or to see from afar and merely point me out?
His friend replied:
"I am at fault."
The chicken has five virtues
Tián Náoserved Lǔ 'Āi Gōng but was not recognized.
Tián Náo said:
"Does Your Highness not see the chicken?
A comb on its head,
is civility (*wén*);
spurs on its feet,
is martiality (*wǔ*);
daring to fight when an enemy is present,
is courage (*yǒng*);
calling to others when seeing food,
is benevolence (*rén*);
keeping watch at night without missing the time,
is trustworthiness (*xìn*).
Having these five,
Your Highness cooks and eats it,
because of how close it comes.
A swan flies a thousand *lǐ* in one go,
stops at Your Highness's distant pond,
eats Your Highness's fish and turtles,
pecks Your Highness's beans and grains.
It has none of these five,
yet Your Highness still values it,
because of how far it comes.
Please consider the swan as distant."
The Duke said:
"Stop.
I will record your words."
Tián Náo said:
"If a scholar is not used,
what is the point of recording his words!"
Then he left for Wú.
Yè Gōng loves dragons
Yè Gōng Bái Gāo loved dragons.
The dragon heard of this and descended,
peeking its head through the window,
and dragging its tail into the hall.
Yè Gōng abandoned his home and fled,
his soul and spirit
lost all color.
This shows that Yè Gōng did not truly love dragons,
but loved what merely resembled a dragon, not a true one.
Chǔ Qiū Xiānshēng
When Qū Qiū was seventy years old,
wearing a fur robe and a belt, he was summoned to an audience with Lord Méngcháng.
The Lord said:
"Sir, you are old!"
Qū Qiū said:
"Alas!
Are you going to make me chase chariots and spur horses?
Throw stones and leap great distances?
Pursue elk and grapple with leopards and tigers?
I am already dead,
how can I have time to be old!
Are you going to make me issue upright pronouncements and contend with the feudal lords?
Resolve doubts and settle hesitations?
I am just entering my prime,
how can I be old?"
Lǘqiū Áng Meets King Xuān
In Qí there was a man named Lǘqiū Áng,
eighteen years old.
He met Duke Xuān.
His family was poor and his parents were old,
so he wished to obtain a minor official post.
The King said:
"You are still young,
this is not yet possible."
Áng said:
"Zhuānxù was twelve years old when he governed the world.
Xiàng Tuó of Qín was a sage's teacher at seven years old."
The King said:
"There has never been a colt with small horns that could bear heavy loads and travel far.
A scholar is only usable when his hair is white and his head is bald."
Áng said:
"A foot has its shortcomings,
an inch has its strengths.
Huá Liú and Lù Jì [swift horses],
are the swiftest horses in the world,
but if tested in the kitchen,
they may not be able to surpass a weasel or a stoat.
Yellow swans and white cranes,
fly a thousand *lǐ* in one flight,
but if tested in the hall or corridor,
they cannot surpass a sparrow [whose wings are] folded."
King Xuān said:
"Excellent!"
And went home with him.
Duke Líng Digs a Pond
When Duke Líng of Wèi was digging a pond,
Wǎn Chūn said:
"The weather is cold, starting this project will likely harm the people."
The Duke said:
"Is it cold?"
Wǎn Chūn said:
"Your Majesty wears fox fur,
sits on a bear-skin mat,
and has a stove in the corner;
that is why you do not feel cold.
But now the common people's clothes are unpatched,
their shoes are broken and unstitched.
Your Majesty does not feel cold,
but the people are truly cold."
The Duke said:
"Good."
And ordered the project to be stopped.
Drinking for Five Days and Five Nights
Zhào Xiāngzǐ drank wine
for five days and five nights without stopping.
Yōu Mò said:
"Zhòu drank for seven days,
now Your Majesty drinks for five days."
Xiāngzǐ said:
"Then will my state perish?"
He [Yōu Mò] said:
"No, it will not perish."
Xiāngzǐ said:
"I am only two days short of Zhòu,
if it won't perish, what am I waiting for?"
Yōu Mò said:
"When Jié and Zhòu perished,
they met Tāng and Wǔ.
The whole world was like Jié,
and you, my lord, are like Zhòu.
When Jié and Zhòu exist in the same era,
how can they destroy each other!
However, it is still perilous!"
Ducks and Geese Eat Husks
Duke Mù of Zōu ordered that ducks and geese be fed husks,
not millet.
There were no husks in the granary,
so they sought to exchange with the people,
two *shí* of millet for one *shí* of husks.
An official requested to feed them millet.
The Duke said:
"The common people fill their cattle and plow,
expose their backs and weed.
Are they doing this for birds and beasts?
Millet,
is the best food for humans.
You know only petty calculations,
but do not understand great benevolence.
If birds eat the husks of Zōu,
it does not harm the millet of Zōu.
Whether millet is in the granary or with the people,
what difference does it make to me!"
When the people of Zōu heard this,
they all knew that their private savings and the public household were one entity.
Refusing Fish
Someone presented fish to the chancellor of Zhèng,
but the chancellor of Zhèng did not accept them.
Someone asked him:
"You love fish,
why do you not accept them?"
He replied:
"Because I love fish,
I do not accept fish.
If I accept fish, I will lose my salary,
and have nothing to eat fish with.
If I do not accept fish, I will keep my salary,
and eat fish for the rest of my life."
Bái Gōngshèng Offers a Sword
When Bái Gōngshèng was about to assassinate King Huì of Chǔ,
King Huì fled.
The Prime Minister (Lìngyǐn) and the Minister of War (Sīmǎ) both died.
He drew his sword and offered it to Qū Lú, saying:
"If you join me,
I will spare you;
if you do not join me,
I will surely kill you."
Lú said:
"You kill your paternal uncle and seek fortune from me, Lú,
is that acceptable?
A scholar who understands fate
is unmoved by profit
and unafraid when facing death.
As a minister,
one lives when it is time to live,
and dies when it is time to die.
One who understands the mandate of Heaven above
and the duty of a minister below,
how can he be coerced?"
Yuán Jīng Refuses Food from a Robber
In the East, there was a scholar named Yuán Jīng.
He was starving by the roadside.
A robber from Húfù, named Qiūrén,
saw him,
took down his flask and meal, and offered them to him.
Yuán Jīng took three mouthfuls and was able to see again.
He asked:
"Who are you?"
He [the robber] said:
"I am a robber."
Yuán Jīng said:
"Alas!
You are a robber,
and why did you feed me?
