Because I will not eat [food from a robber]."
He braced his hands on the ground and tried to vomit, but nothing came out.
He then collapsed, gasping, and died.
Benevolence Extends to Decayed Bones
King Wén of Zhōu built the Spirit Tower,
and while digging the ground, found a dead person's bone.
The King said:
"Rebury it."
An official said:
"This has no owner."
King Wén said:
"He who possesses the world
is the owner of the world.
He who possesses a state
is the owner of the state.
I am certainly the owner,
so where else should I seek an owner?"
So he reburied it.
Everyone in the world said:
"King Wén is truly wise!
His benevolence extends even to decayed bones,
how much more so to living people!"
Learning Can Secure the State and Protect the People
Lǔ Āigōng asked Zǐxià:
"Must one study before they can pacify the state and protect the people?"
Zǐxià replied:
"Huángdì studied with Tàizhēn;
Zhuānxù studied with Lǜtú;
Dìkù studied with Chìsōngzi;
Yáo studied with Jūnchóu;
Shùn studied with Wùchéngfū;
Yǔ studied with Xīwángguó;
Tāng studied with Wēizǐbó;
Wénwáng studied with Jiǎoshízīsī;
Wǔwáng studied with Guōshú;
Zhōugōng studied with Tàigōng;
Zhòngní studied with Dān.
These eleven sages,
if they had not encountered excellent teachers,
their achievements would not have been manifest,
and their names would not have been transmitted.
Indeed, those who do not study do not understand the ancient Way,
and yet are able to pacify the state and protect the people—
there has never been such a one."
Averting Disaster
Yànzǐ did not leave the space between the wine goblet and the meat platter,
yet knew what was a thousand *lǐ* away;
this can be called averting disaster!
The Ugly Woman Wúyán
In Qí there was a woman of extreme ugliness,
whose appellation was Wúyán Nǚ.
When she reached the age of thirty,
having nowhere to settle,
she went to Xuānwáng,
wishing to serve in the rear palace.
The King was then setting out wine on Jiàntái,
and his attendants burst into laughter, saying:
"This is the most brazen woman in the world!"
The King said:
"This woman is not tolerated in her village,
a commoner wishing to approach the lord of ten thousand chariots—
does she perhaps have some extraordinary ability?"
She replied:
"I have secretly enjoyed the art of invisibility."
The King said:
"Invisibility is
precisely what this寡人 wishes to see."
The King took an invisibility text and read it,
but still could not understand.
The next morning he asked her,
but she again did not reply with invisibility,
merely raising her hand to slap her elbow, saying:
"Danger!
Danger!
Your Majesty internally gathers treacherous ministers,
and the populace is not attached;
you honor what you like and neglect what you rely on—
this is the first danger.
Jiàntái has five stories,
and the myriad people are exhausted to the extreme—
this is the second danger.
Worthy individuals hide away in mountains and forests,
while sycophants firmly occupy positions by your side—
this is the third danger.
Wine flows freely,
continuing night into morning—
this is the fourth
danger."
Xuānwáng sighed, saying:
"How painful are the words of Wúyán Jūn!
My danger
was almost complete."
Thereupon, he stopped the construction of Jiàntái, dismissed the female musicians, removed the sycophants, discarded the carvings, selected soldiers and horses, filled the treasuries,
invited forth honest criticism,
extended invitations to those of humble origin,
chose an auspicious day to establish a crown prince,
promoted a kind mother,
honored the hidden woman,
and appointed Wúyán Jūn as queen.
The state became greatly peaceful—
this was the power of the ugly woman.
Bad Dreams
If a feudal lord has a bad dream, he should cultivate his virtue;
if a grand master has a bad dream, he should cultivate his office;
if a scholar has a bad dream, he should cultivate his person.
If this is done, disaster will not come.
Three Fears
An enlightened ruler has three fears:
Firstly, occupying a high position and fearing not hearing of one's faults.
Secondly, being successful and fearing arrogance.
Thirdly, hearing the most profound words in the world and fearing being unable to act upon them.
Three Inauspicious Things
Qí Jǐnggōng asked Yànzǐ:
"Today I went hunting,
saw a tiger on the mountain,
and a snake in the marsh below.
Is this not inauspicious?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"A state has three inauspicious things:
Having worthy individuals but not knowing them—
this is the first inauspicious thing.
Knowing them but not employing them—
this is the second inauspicious thing.
Employing them but not trusting them—
this is the third inauspicious thing.
Now, seeing a tiger on the mountain,
that is the tiger's home.
Seeing a snake in the marsh below,
that is the snake's home.
How can this be inauspicious?"
No Calamities, Pray to Mountains and Rivers
Chǔ Zhuāngwáng said:
"When heaven does not show calamities and earth does not produce misfortunes,
then pray to the mountains and rivers, saying:
'Has Heaven forgotten me?'
One who can seek fault in Heaven
will surely not go astray."
Chéngtāng's Six Matters
In Tāng's time,
there was a great drought for six years.
He sent a person carrying a three-legged vessel
to pray to the mountains and rivers, saying:
"Is the government not temperate?
Are the people sick?
Are bribes rampant?
Are slanderers thriving?
Are palaces being built?
Are female attendants powerful?"
Before he finished speaking,
Heaven rained.
Zǐgòng Did Not Know How to Be Subordinate
Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ:
"I am a subordinate person,
but I do not know the Way of being a subordinate person."
The Master said:
"One who is a subordinate person,
is he not like the earth?
Plant in it, and the five grains grow.
Dig it,
and sweet springs emerge.
Grass and trees are planted in it.
Birds and beasts are nurtured by it.
Living people stand upon it.
Deceased people enter it.
It performs many merits but does not speak.
One who is a subordinate person,
is he not like the earth!"
The Young Serving the Old, the Humble Serving the Noble
Sūnqīng said:
"The young serving the old,
the humble serving the noble,
the unworthy serving the worthy—
this is a universal principle of the world.
If there is a benevolent Way,
but one cannot be superior
and is ashamed to be subordinate—
this is the heart of a villain.
If one's person is not free from a villainous heart,
and one's actions are not free from a villainous Way,
and yet one seeks public praise,
is this not difficult?"
Carrying Rice for Parents
Zǐlù said:
"One who carries heavy burdens and travels far
does not choose the ground to rest.
One whose family is poor and parents are old
does not choose his salary when serving.
In the past, when I served my two parents,
I carried rice for a hundred *lǐ*.
After my parents passed away,
I would sit on layers of cushions,
and eat from rows of dishes.
I wished to eat wild greens and carry rice for my parents again,
but I could not do so again."
Seventy Years Old and Desiring to Learn
Jìn Pínggōng said:
"I am seventy years old,
and I wish to learn,
but I fear it is already too late."
Shīkuàng said:
"Why not light a torch?"
The Duke said:
"How can a minister joke with his lord?"
He replied:
"This blind minister would not dare to joke with his lord.
I have heard:
To be fond of learning when young
is like the rising sun;
to be fond of learning when in one's prime
is like the light of the setting sun;
to be fond of learning when old
is like the brightness of a lit torch."
Yúgōng's Valley
Qí Huán Gōng went out hunting.
He pursued a deer into a mountain valley.
He asked an old man,
"What valley is this?"
The man replied,
"This is Yú Gōng's Valley,
named after me, your servant."
The Duke said,
"Looking at your appearance,
you are no fool."
The man replied,
"I once raised a free-roaming cow.
When it gave birth to a calf that grew large,
I sold it and bought a colt.
A young man said,
'A cow cannot give birth to a horse!'
So he took the colt away.
When the neighbors heard of this,
they considered me foolish,
hence this valley is called Yú Gōng."
The Duke said,
"You are truly foolish!
Why did you give it to him?"
Huán Gōng returned
and told Guǎn Zhòng.
Guǎn Zhòng said,
"This is my, Yí Wú's, foolishness.
If Yáo were on the throne,
and Gāo Yáo were the judge,
how could anyone take another's colt?
If there were such an old man subjected to such violence,
he certainly would not give in.
You know the injustice of the legal system,
that is why he gave it.
Please let us withdraw and reform our governance!"
Upper Overflow, Lower Leakage
Wén Wáng asked Lǚ Wàng,
"What is the state of the world?"
He replied,
"A Royal State enriches its people.
A Hegemonic State enriches its scholars and officials.
A barely surviving state enriches its high officials.
A state on the verge of collapse enriches its granaries and treasuries.
This is what is meant by 'upper overflow and lower leakage'."
Wén Wáng said,
"Good."
That month,
he opened the granaries and treasuries to relieve the poor.
The Way of Governing a State is to Love the People
Wǔ Wáng asked Tàigōng,
"What is the way to govern a state?"
He replied,
"Only to love the people.
Benefit them, do not harm them.
Help them succeed, do not cause their failure.
Let them live, do not kill them.
Give to them, do not seize from them.
Bring them joy, do not make them suffer.
Make them happy, do not anger them.
This is the way to govern a state.
If the people neglect their duties,
it is harming them;
if farmers miss their season,
it is causing their failure;
if punishments and penalties are severe,
it is killing them;
if taxes and levies are heavy,
it is seizing from them;
if corvée labor is excessive,
it is making them suffer;
if these things exist to disturb them,
it is angering them."
Changing Laws
Tàigōng said,
"For a state to frequently change its laws and decrees
is not to have law.
Law
is what one considers good as law.
Therefore, if decrees are issued and create chaos,
when there is chaos, the laws are changed."
Closing the Heart
Gōngyí Xiū was the prime minister of Lǔ.
When the ruler of Lǔ died,
his attendants asked to close the gates.
Xiū said,
"Stop.
I did not tax the ponds and depths,
nor did I levy from Mount Méng.
I could have prevented the ruler from dying.
My heart is already closed;
why close the gates?"
Zǐ Lù Governs Pú
Kǒngzǐ said,
"Pú has many valiant men,
and it is difficult to govern.
I tell you:
be respectful and reverent,
and you can control the brave;
be just and upright,
and you can accommodate the multitude;
be honest and pure,
and you can win the trust of your superiors."
Governing the World is Like Turning Things in One's Palm
Yáng Zhū saw King Liáng,
and spoke of governing the world as being like turning things in one's palm.
The King said,
"Sir, you cannot even manage one wife and one concubine,
nor weed a three-mǔ garden.
Yet you speak of governing the world as being like turning things in one's palm.
How can this be?"
Yáng Zhū said,
"Have you not seen a flock of sheep?
A hundred sheep in a flock,
if a five-chi boy
carries a staff and follows them,
they will go east if he wants them to go east,
and west if he wants them to go west.
If Yáo were to lead one sheep,
and Shùn carried a staff and followed it,
that would be the beginning of change."
A Man from Zhèng Crosses the Water
Jǐng Chā was the prime minister of Zhèng.
There was a man from Zhèng who crossed the water in winter,
and came out with cold shins.
Jǐng Chā passed by,
alighted from his carriage's side seat and gave the man a ride.
Shū Xiàng said,
"Jǐngzǐ, as a state's prime minister,
is this not troubling?
I have heard that a good official, in three months, repairs the canals;
in ten months, the dams and bridges are completed;
even the six domestic animals do not get their feet wet,
how much less people!"
Women Dressed as Men
Jǐng Gōng liked women who dressed as men,
and all the people in the state adopted this fashion.
The Duke sent officials to prohibit it,
saying,
"For women who dress as men,
tear their clothes
and cut their sashes."
Clothes were torn and sashes cut,
but they looked at each other and did not stop.
Yànzǐ said,
"Your Highness merely prohibits it externally,
it is like hanging a cow's head at your gate
and seeking to buy horse meat.
Why does Your Highness not have those in the palace refrain from wearing it,
then those outside will not dare to do so?"
The Duke said,
"Good."
He had those in the palace refrain from wearing it,
and within a month, no one in the state wore it anymore.
Love Extends to the Crows on the Roof
Wǔ Wáng conquered Yīn
and asked Tàigōng,
"What should be done with their officers and multitude?"
Tàigōng said,
"Those who love a person
love even the crows on their roof;
those who hate a person
loathe even their stored provisions.
Completely exterminate their enemies,
leaving no survivors.
How about that?"
The King said,
"No."
Zhào Gōng said,
"Kill the guilty,
govern the innocent.
How about that?"
The King said,
"No."
Zhōu Gōng said,
"Let each reside in their dwelling,
till their fields.
Do not change the old and the new,
only cherish benevolence.
If the common people have faults,
the responsibility lies with me alone."
The King said,
"How grand!
This will pacify the world!"
Quarrels are a Lifelong Calamity
Xún Qīng曰：
「A fighter
forgets his own body,
and forgets his lord.
Indulging in a momentary rage
brings lifelong misfortune;
this is forgetting one's body.
One's family scattered,
and relatives massacred;
this is forgetting one's kin.
Violating the great prohibitions of the law;
this is forgetting one's lord.
All fighters
believe themselves to be in the right,
and others to be in the wrong.
If one is truly in the right,
and others are truly in the wrong,
then one is a jūnzi and they are xiǎorén.
For a jūnzi to harm a xiǎorén,
is that not excessively much! 」
Zǐlù held a sword.
Kǒngzǐ said:
「Why use this? 」
Zǐlù said:
「The good,
I help with goodness;
the bad,
I use it to defend myself. 」
The Master said:
「A jūnzi takes loyalty as his substance,
and benevolence as his defense.
He moves the bad with loyalty,
and transforms violent bandits with benevolence.
Why must he hold a sword? 」
Making a beautiful chamber
Xiāngzǐ made a beautiful chamber.
Zhì Bó said:
「The chamber is beautiful! 」
Shì Zhuó said:
「Your servant also has fears.
High mountains and steep ravines
do not grow grass and trees.
Where there are pines and cypresses,
the ground beneath is not fertile.
Now, if earth and wood overpower man,
your servant fears it will not settle man. 」
When the chamber was completed,
three years later, the Zhì clan perished.
Old and self-sustaining
Huán Gōng campaigned against Pínglíng.
He saw a household with an old man sustaining himself.
The Duke asked the reason,
and he replied:
「I have nine sons.
My family is poor and has no means to marry them off.
They were sent out as laborers and have not yet returned. 」
The Duke took five of his outriders and married them to the man's sons.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
「Your Grace's beneficence is also too small.
If you wait for what you see to bestow favors,
then few in the state of Qí will have wives. 」
The Duke said:
「What then? 」
Guǎn Zhòng said:
「Order the people of the state that men should marry at twenty,
and women should marry at fifteen. 」
Two ways of fishing
Fú Zǐjiàn was the magistrate of Dānfù.
Yáng Zhòu said:
「There are two ways of fishing,
please let me present them to you.
If you cast your line with bait,
and they rush to swallow it,
these are the yángjiǎo fish,
they are lean and not tasty.
If they seem absent, yet present,
eating, yet not eating,
these are the fáng fish,
they are broad and richly flavored. 」
Zǐjiàn said:
「Excellent. 」
Before reaching Dānfù,
officials' carriages and caps were constantly meeting on the road.
Zǐjiàn said:
「Drive the carriages on!
The yángjiǎo fish have arrived! 」
Thereupon,
upon arriving in Dānfù,
he visited the elders,
honored the worthy,
and governed with them.
Dividing land
Jìn Wén Hóu asked Jiù Fàn about governance.
He replied:
「Dividing cooked food is not as good as dividing raw meat;
dividing raw meat is not as good as dividing land.
If the ruler acquires land, the people know wealth.
If the ruler loses land, the people know poverty. 」
Thrice expelled, five times dismissed
Yáng Sì saw Zhào Jiǎnzǐ and said:
「Your servant has been expelled from his village thrice,
and dismissed from serving his lord five times.
I heard that Your Lord favors worthy men,
so I came to meet you. 」
Jiǎnzǐ stopped eating and sighed.
His attendants remonstrated, saying:
「Expelled from his village thrice,
this means he is not tolerated by the multitude.
Dismissed from serving his lord five times,
this means he is not loyal to his superior. 」
Jiǎnzǐ said:
「Beautiful women
are the enemies of the ugly.
Men of great virtue
are alienated by troubled times.
Upright conduct
is hated by the crooked and perverse. 」
Consequently, he appointed him as prime minister,
and the state became greatly well-governed.
Máo Jiāo remonstrates Qín Huáng
Qín Shǐ Huáng's empress dowager was not discreet,
and was moved to Bèiyáng Gōng.
Twenty-seven people had died for remonstrating her.
The Qí guest Máo Jiāo came to remonstrate.
The Emperor said:
「Have you not seen the piled corpses beneath the palace gate? 」
Máo Jiāo said:
「Heaven has twenty-eight constellations.
Now twenty-seven people have already died.
Your servant wishes only to complete that number. 」
Shǐ Huáng appointed Máo Jiāo as Zhòngfù,
raised his rank,
and the minister welcomed the empress dowager back to Xiányáng.
Píng Gōng dismantles his terrace
Jìn Píng Gōng sent Shū Xiàng to make an envoy to Wú.
Wú polished their boats to welcome him,
with five hundred people on each side,
some in embroidered robes and leopard furs,
some in brocade robes and fox furs.
Píng Gōng said:
「Wú will surely perish!
Why do they revere boats?
Why do they revere their people? 」
Shū Xiàng said:
「Your Grace built the Chídǐ Terrace,
from which above you can deploy soldiers,
and below you can array bells and drums.
When the feudal lords hear of Your Grace,
they also say:
『Why does he revere the terrace?
Why does he revere his people? 』
What is revered differs for each. 」
Thereupon, Píng Gōng dismantled the terrace.
Your servant laughed at his emptiness
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ raised an army to attack Qí.
Anyone who dared to remonstrate would die.
The armored warrior Gōng Lú laughed loudly.
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ said:
「Why do you laugh, sir? 」
He replied:
「Your servant has a long-standing laugh.
At mulberry harvest time,
my neighbor, husband and wife, went to the fields together.
He saw a woman among the mulberries,
and immediately went to pursue her.
He could not catch her,
so he returned.
His wife was angry and left him.
Your servant laughed at his emptiness. 」
Jiǎnzǐ said:
「Now, I am attacking a state and will lose my own state.
This is my emptiness. 」
Thereupon, he recalled the army.
Blunt and prosperous
Wǔ Wáng was blunt and prospered;
Zhòu Lī Lī perished.
If a lord has no blunt ministers,
a father no blunt sons,
an elder brother no blunt younger brothers,
a husband no blunt wives,
a scholar no blunt friends,
their demise can be awaited.
Tilting vessel
Kǒngzǐ observed the lopsided vessel in the Zhōu temple,
and asked the temple guardian,
“What kind of vessel is this?”
He replied,
“It is the vessel for the seat-side.”
The Master said,
“Fetch water and test it.
When full, it overturns;
when empty, it is lopsided;
when half-full, it is upright.
How can there be one that is full and does not overturn!”
Zǐlù said,
“Is there a way to hold fullness?”
Kǒngzǐ said,
“Diminish it by ladling out;
to be high and yet able to descend;
to be full and yet able to empty;
to be rich and yet able to be frugal;
to be noble and yet able to be humble;
to be wise and yet able to appear foolish;
to be brave and yet able to appear timid;
to be eloquent and yet able to appear reticent;
to be learned and yet able to appear superficial;
to be clear-sighted and yet able to appear dim.
This is called diminishing without being inadequate.
Only those of supreme virtue
can practice this Way.”
Five Kinds of Cold
A state experiences five kinds of cold,
and ice and frost are not among them.
First is external governance;
second is the oppression by women;
third is the divulging of plans;
fourth is disrespecting the ministers and thus the state perishes;
fifth is being unable to govern internally while focusing on external affairs.
Sudden Perishing in the Spring and Autumn Period
Shí Chóu said,
“In the Spring and Autumn period, there were those who perished suddenly and completely.
Rulers of states must not be careless.
If wives and concubines are not singular in purpose,
it is enough to cause ruin;
if the ducal clan is not intimate,
it is enough to cause ruin;
if chief ministers are not entrusted,
it is enough to cause ruin;
if state titles are not utilized,
it is enough to cause ruin;
if one is close to flatterers and listens to slander,
it is enough to cause ruin;
if all affairs are undertaken at improper times,
it is enough to cause ruin;
if officials and commoners are not restrained,
it is enough to cause ruin;
if punishments and laws are not just,
it is enough to cause ruin;
if one loses the people's hearts internally,
and disrespects great states externally,
it is enough to cause ruin.”
Water Can Ruin a State
During the time of the Six Jìn,
the Zhì clan was the strongest.
They destroyed the Zhōngháng clan,
and then diverted the Jìn River to flood the city of Jìnyáng,
but it was not full by three planks.
Zhì Bó traveled on the water,
Wèi Xuānzǐ drove the chariot,
and Hán Kāngzǐ rode as outrider.
Zhì Bó said,
“I never knew that water could be used to ruin a state.”
Xuānzǐ elbowed Kāngzǐ,
and Kāngzǐ trod on Xuānzǐ’s foot.
The elbow and foot connected in the chariot,
and Zhì Mǐn was dismembered, his state perished,
becoming a great laughingstock for the world.
Wine Goes In, Tongue Comes Out
Qí Huán Gōng prepared wine,
Guǎn Zhòng arrived late,
and after drinking half, poured out the wine.
The Duke said,
“Arriving after the appointed time,
and then drinking and pouring out wine,
is this permissible by ritual?”
He replied,
“Your minister has heard that 'wine goes in, tongue comes out.'
When wine goes in and the tongue comes out,
it means losing one's words.
When one loses one's words,
one's person is abandoned.
Your minister calculates
that abandoning one's person is worse than abandoning wine.”
Three Regrets in Weeping
Kǒngzǐ heard someone weeping with great sorrow.
He went to see,
and it was Qiū Wú Zǐ.
Kǒngzǐ said,
“Why do you weep so sorrowfully?”
He said,
“I have three regrets:
When young, I loved learning,
and traveled all over the world.
Upon returning, my parents had passed away –
this is the first regret.
I served my ruler with extravagance and arrogance,
and my admonitions were not followed –
this is the second regret.
I formed deep friendships but later severed them –
this is the third regret.
The tree wishes to be still, but the wind does not cease.
The child wishes to care for their parents, but the parents do not wait.
That which goes and does not return
is one's years;
those who cannot be seen again
are one's parents.
I beg to take my leave from this point.”
He then slit his own throat and died.
Prince È’s Embroidered Quilt
Xiāngchéng Jūn wore a kingfisher-feather robe,
carried a jade sword,
and wore white silk sandals,
standing by the flowing water.
A Chǔ grandee named Zhuāng Xīn
wished to hold the prince's hand,
but the prince was angry and said nothing.
Xīn said,
“Prince È Zǐzhé was boating on the fresh waves,
riding in a green-painted boat,
with a kingfisher-feather canopy unfurled,
accompanied by the sound of bells and drums.
A Yuè boatman, grasping an oar, sang:
‘What evening is this, pulling amidst the current?
What day is this, to be able to share a boat with the prince?
On the mountain there are trees, on the trees there are branches;
my heart delights in you, sir, but you do not know.’
Prince È then extended his long sleeve to embrace him,
and raised his embroidered quilt to cover him.
How is your Highness superior to Prince È?
How is your servant alone inferior to the boatman?
I wish to hold your hand, but it is not allowed!”
Things Cannot Prosper Simultaneously
Intentions cannot be equally sharp;
things cannot prosper simultaneously.
That which flourishes in one aspect
must decline in another.
That which is long on the left
must be short on the right.
One who enjoys sleeping late
will certainly not rise early.
Five Kinds of Death for People
The sage can eliminate three of them,
but cannot remove two.
Death from hunger and thirst
can be removed;
death from freezing cold
can be removed;
death from suffering the five weapons
can be removed.
Death from old age
cannot be removed;
death from carbuncles and boils
cannot be removed.
Death from hunger and thirst is
due to internal emptiness;
death from freezing cold is
due to external elements overcoming the interior;
death from suffering the five weapons is
due to a lack of virtue.
Death from old age is
when one's years are complete;
death from carbuncles and boils is
due to imbalance in blood and qi.
Lifelong Worries
The noble person has lifelong worries,
but no troubles of a single day.
They follow the Way and act according to it,
follow reason and speak accordingly.
Joy does not make them lax,
anger does not make them harsh.
Píngshí
When Chǔ Zhāowáng crossed the Jiāng,
there was a thing as large as a dou
that struck directly against the king's boat.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"This is called a píngshí.
Command for it to be cut open and eaten.
Only a hegemon can obtain it."
In Qí, there was a one-legged flying bird
that landed in front of the palace.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"This is called a Shāngyáng.
Heaven will soon have a great rain."
Indeed,
Losing One's Wife and Losing One's Self
Lǔ Āigōng said:
"I have heard of no greater loss
than moving and losing one's wife.
Is there such a thing?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"This is not a loss;
a greater loss is losing oneself."
The Sound of the Se Is Mournful
Yìnghóu sat with Jiǎ Yúzǐ,
and heard the sound of him playing the qín.
Yìnghóu said:
"Why is the qín so mournful?"
He replied:
"The strings are taut and the tuning is low,
hence it makes it mournful.
One who has taut strings
is a person of excellent talent,
and one whose tuning is low
is of low official rank.
To employ excellent talent in a low rank,
how can it not be mournful?"
Jiè Zǐtuī Becomes Prime Minister of Jīng
Jiè Zǐtuī was fifteen years old when he became Prime Minister of Jīng.
Zhòngní sent someone to observe,
who returned and said:
"In the corridor there are twenty-five brilliant gentlemen,
and in the hall there are twenty-five old men."
Zhòngní said:
"Combine the wisdom of twenty-five people,
and it is wiser than Tāng and Wǔ;
combine the strength of twenty-five people,
and it is stronger than Péngzǔ.
To govern the world with this,
it would surely be successful,
let alone Jīng!"
Gentlemen from All Under Heaven Arrive
Zhōugōng descended to the thatched huts of one hundred seventy gentlemen,
and gentlemen from all under Heaven all arrived.
Yànzǐ shared clothes and food with one hundred people,
and gentlemen from all under Heaven also arrived.
Zhòngní cultivated the Way and his conduct,
and put his writings in order,
and gentlemen from all under Heaven also arrived.
Kǒngzǐ sighed
and said:
"If Tóngdī Bóhuá had not died,
the world would surely have been settled."
Advancing the Worthy as Worthy
Zǐgòng asked Kǒngzǐ:
"Among the ministers of today,
who is worthy?"
The Master said:
"In the past, Qí had Bào Shú,
and Zhèng had Zǐpí,
they were worthy."
Zǐgòng said:
"Did Qí not have Guǎn Zhòng,
and Zhèng not have Zǐchǎn?"
The Master said:
"Advancing the worthy is to be worthy.
I heard of Bào Shú advancing Guǎn Zhòng,
and Zǐpí advancing Zǐchǎn,
but I have not heard of Guǎn Zhòng or Zǐchǎn advancing anyone."
Expelling Gāo Liáo
Yànzǐ expelled Gāo Liáo.
His attendants remonstrated, saying:
"Liáo has served you for three years,
yet you have never given him a noble title,
and now you expel him.
Is this righteous?"
Yànzǐ said:
"This man has served me for three years,
but has never helped me correct my mistakes.
Therefore, I have expelled him."
King of Chǔ Forgets His Bow
Chǔ Gòngwáng went hunting and forgot his bow.
His attendants requested to search for it.
The King said:
"A man of Chǔ lost it,
a man of Chǔ will find it.
Why seek it again?"
Zhòngní heard of this and said:
"Alas!
It is not great enough.
He also said:
"A man lost a bow,
a man found it, that is all.
Why must it be Chǔ?"
Five Shames
A gentleman has five shames:
not sitting at court,
not debating at banquets –
a gentleman is ashamed of this;
holding a position
but having no relevant words –
a gentleman is ashamed of this;
having words
but no corresponding actions –
a gentleman is ashamed of this;
having obtained something
and then losing it again –
a gentleman is ashamed of this;
having abundant land
but insufficient people –
a gentleman is ashamed of this.
Though a gentleman may be impoverished,
he does not remain in a position for a doomed state;
though he may be poor,
he does not accept emoluments from a chaotic ruler.
Fond of Speaking Ill of Others
Others will also reveal their faults.
Those who are fond of hating others
are also hated by others.
King Huì Listens to Slander
Suǒshèzǐ met Qín Huìwáng,
and the King was pleased with him.
Tánggū slandered him.
When he met the King again,
Huìwáng harbored anger and waited for him.
It was not that his words were different,
but that the listener was confused.
Therefore, taking zhǐ for yǔ [musical notes]
is not the fault of the string;
taking sweetness for bitterness
is not the fault of the taste.
Shāng Progresses Daily, Cì Declines Daily
Kǒngzǐ said:
"After Qiū's death,
Shāng will progress daily,
and Cì will decline daily.
Shāng likes to associate with those who are more virtuous than himself,
while Cì likes to speak to those who are not his equal."
Serving One's Ruler in Order to Serve One's Parents
Qí Xuānwáng said to Tián Guò:
"A Ruist mourns his parents for three years.
Which is heavier, ruler or father?"
Guò said:
"Father is heavier."
The King was angry and said:
"Why then do you leave your parents and serve your ruler?"
Guò said:
"Without the ruler's land,
there is no place for my parents;
without the ruler's grain and emoluments,
there is no means to support my parents;
without the ruler's rank and position,
there is no way to honor and make my parents prominent.
Receiving from the ruler
and conveying it to one's parents –
all service to the ruler is for the sake of one's parents."
Xuān became silent.
Marquis of Lǔ Flees to Qí
Lǔ Āihóu abandoned his state and fled to Qí.
The Marquis of Qí said:
"Why are you so young and abandon your state so early?"
He replied:
"When I first became crown prince,
many ministers admonished me,
but I received their advice and did not use it.
Many people loved me,
but I distanced myself and did not approach them,
like autumn mugwort that dislikes its roots
but flourishes in its branches and leaves.
When the autumn wind rises,
its roots will soon be pulled out."
Lǎozǐ Asks Cháng Chuāng
Cháng Chuāng had an illness.
Lǎozi asked,
"Sir, your illness is severe.
Do you have any final teachings to instruct your disciples with?"
Chuāng said,
"Passing by one's hometown and dismounting from the carriage,
do you understand this?"
Lǎozi said,
"Is it not to signify one does not forget one's origins?"
Chuāng said,
"Indeed!
That's right!
Passing by a tall tree and quickening one's pace,
do you understand this?"
Lǎozi said,
"Is it not to signify respect for the elderly?"
Chuāng said,
"Indeed!
That's right!"
He opened his mouth and said,
"Is my tongue still there?"
He replied,
"Yes."
"Are my teeth still there?"
He replied,
"No.
The tongue remains because it is soft,
the teeth are gone because they are hard."
Chuāng said,
"That's right!
All the affairs of the world are now clear."
Governing a State: Honoring the Worthy and Disdaining the Unworthy
Zǐlù asked Kǒngzǐ,
"How should one govern a state?"
The Master said,
"Honor the worthy and disdain the unworthy."
Zǐlù said,
"The Fàn and Zhōngháng clans honored the worthy and disdained the unworthy,
yet why did they perish?"
He said,
"The Zhōngháng clan honored the worthy but could not employ them,
and disdained the unworthy but could not remove them.
The worthy, knowing they would not be employed, resented them;
the unworthy, knowing they were disdained, hated them.
Even if the Zhōngháng clan wished not to perish,
how could they succeed?"
Your servant requests to help Your Lord
Wèi Wénhóu hosted a banquet for his grandees in Qǔyáng.
He sighed and said,
"I alone have no Yù Ràng as a minister."
Jiǎn Chóng raised his cup and said,
"Your servant requests to help Your Lord.
Your servant has heard that renowned parents do not know filial sons,
and a lord of the Way does not know loyal ministers.
What kind of lord was Yù Ràng's lord?"
Wénhóu said,
"Excellent."
He accepted and drank the cup, saying,
"It is because there were no Guǎn Zhòng and Bào Shú as ministers
that there was the accomplishment of Yù Ràng."
Unhappy in a Corner
The sage's relation to the world
is like being in a single hall.
Now if there is a hall full of drinkers,
and one person weeps alone in a corner,
then all the people in the hall are unhappy.
Eating Horse Meat and Getting Wine
Qín Mùgōng lost his fine horse,
and went himself to search for it.
He saw people had already killed his horse
and were sharing its meat.
The Duke said,
"Those who eat the meat of a fine horse and do not drink wine are murderers."
He immediately supplied them with wine to drink.
The horse killers were ashamed and left.
Three years later,
Jìn attacked Qín.
Those who had eaten the horse meat at that time said to each other,
"We can now repay the kindness of eating horse meat and getting wine with our lives."
Mùgōng was ultimately relieved from the difficulty.
Kǒngzǐ is like the Rivers and Seas
Zhào Jiǎnzǐ asked Zǐgòng,
"What kind of person is Kǒngzǐ?"
He replied,
"Cì cannot comprehend him.
It is like a thirsty person drinking from the rivers and seas;
that is all.
Kǒngzǐ is like the rivers and seas;
how can one sufficiently comprehend him!"
Volume Thirty
End.
Tàiqiū Bears a Heavy Reputation in the World
A guest asked Chén Jìfāng,
"What merits or virtues does Tàiqiū possess
to bear such a heavy reputation in the world?"
Jìfāng said,
"My esteemed father is like a cassia tree growing in the bend of Tàishān.
Above, it reaches a height of ten thousand ren;
below, it has an unfathomable depth.
Above, it is moistened by rain and dew;
below, it is nourished by deep springs.
At such a time,
how can the cassia tree know the height of Tàishān,
or the depth of the deep springs?
It does not know whether it has merits or virtues."
Rent Money to Aid the Poor
King Liáng and King Zhào,
close relatives of the state,
were highly esteemed at the time.
Péi Lìnggōng annually requested several million in rent money from the two states,
to aid his poor maternal and paternal relatives.
Some criticized him for begging for goods to bestow favors,
Péi said,
"To give away what is superfluous,
and supplement what is insufficient,
is the Way of Heaven."
Virtue Eclipsing His Words
Wáng Róng said,
"During the Tiānbǎo and Zhèngshǐ eras,
there were those who could not speak.
But when one conversed with them,
their profound principles were clear and far-reaching.
Could it be that their virtue eclipsed their words?"
Having the Look of Wanting Roasted Meat
Gù Róng was in Luòyáng.
Once, responding to an invitation,
he noticed that the person serving the roasted meat had a look of wanting some.
He then stopped eating and gave his portion to him.
Those sitting with him mocked him.
Róng said,
"How could someone hold it all day long and not know its taste?"
Later, during a time of chaos,
a certain small person often stayed by his side.
When asked why,
it was the person who had wanted the roasted meat.
Grand Tutor Teaching His Son
Xiè Gōng's wife was teaching her son.
She asked the Grand Tutor,
"How is it that I have never seen you teach your son?"
When she was free,
she took her son and went to him,
just as Lǐ was combing her hair.
Her hair hung to the ground,
her complexion glowed like jade,
yet he remained unmoved.
He slowly said,
"The state is broken, the family destroyed; I have no desire to live until today.
If I could be killed,
that would be my original wish."
The hostess was ashamed and withdrew.
Pardoning the Whole Yùtái Household
Sōu Xī was executed,
and his younger brother Yùtái was about to be killed.
Yùtái's daughter-in-law,
who was Xuānwǔ's younger sister,
rushed in,
crying loudly,
"If Yùtái is always dependent on others,
with legs only three inches long,
could he still commit crimes?"
Xuānwǔ laughed and said,
"Jìn itself is too harsh."
Thus, he pardoned the entire Yùtái household.
Fearing to Harm His Great Virtue
Xiè Gōng's wife drew a curtain around all the concubines,
and made them sit in front.
The Grand Tutor saw them for a moment,
then withdrew.
The Grand Tutor requested to see them again,
but his wife said,
"I fear it would harm your great virtue."
Curved-handle Hat
Only Língyùn liked to wear a curved-handle hat.
You Lot are Just Ordinary
Wáng Yòujūn's wife Xī Fūrén,
said to her two younger brothers, Sīkōng and Zhōngláng,
"When the Wáng family sees the two Xiè gentlemen,
they empty their baskets and tumble their shoes [in eagerness];
but when you lot come,
it's just ordinary.
You needn't bother going again."
The Demeanor of the Forest, the Elegance of the Boudoir
Xiè Ài [謝遏] always highly regarded his older sister.
Zhāng Xuán [張玄] often praised his younger sister.
There was a nun, Jìní [濟尼],
who visited both families.
When asked about their relative merits,
she replied:
"Lady Wáng [王夫人] is clear-spirited and expansive,
thus possessing the air of one who lives among forests.
The Gù family's wife [顧家婦] has a pure heart and shines like jade,
truly a beauty of the boudoir."
The Qīngzhōu [青州] Assistant [從事],
Huán Gōng [桓公], had a Registrar [主簿] who was skilled at discerning wine.
Good wine he called "Qīngzhōu Assistant",
bad wine he called "Píngyuán [平原] Inspector [督郵]".
Qīngzhōu has Qí Jùn [齊郡],
Píngyuán has Géliáo Xiàn [鬲縣].
The Assistant said it reached the navel (qí 臍),
the Inspector said it stopped above the diaphragm (gé 膈).
Excessive Diligence [精進大過]
Xī Yīn [郗愔] was very diligent in practicing the Dao [道].
He often suffered from an internal ailment in his abdomen.
Yú Fǎkāi [于法開] was a good physician.
After feeling his pulse, he said:
"The ailment Your Excellency suffers from
is precisely due to excessive diligence."
He prescribed a decoction. After taking it,
Xī Yīn [郗愔] had a major bowel movement,
expelling several pieces of paper, each the size of a fist.
When cut open and examined,
they were found to be talismans he had previously ingested.
Fǎkāi [法開] once traveled and sought lodging in the evening.
The host's wife was in labor and in critical condition for many days, unable to deliver.
Fǎkāi [法開] ordered her to eat ten portions of fatty mutton
and then performed acupuncture.
In a moment, the baby was delivered,
and the mutton fat also came out.
Painting of the Nándū Fù [南都賦圖]
Dài Āndào [戴安道] lectured Fàn Xuān [范宣] on studying.
When Fàn [范] read, Dài [戴] also read;
when Fàn [范] copied books, Dài [戴] also copied books.
Only Dài [戴] was fond of painting.
Fàn [范] considered it useless
and not worthy of mental effort.
Dài [戴] then painted a picture of the "Nándū Fù" [南都賦圖].
Fàn [范] looked at it and sighed with admiration,
deeming it beneficial,
and only then began to value painting.
《Shìshuō》[世說]
Gù Chángkāng's Paintings [顧長康畫]
Xiè Dàfù [謝大傅] said:
"Gù Chángkāng's [顧長康] paintings
are unprecedented since the dawn of humanity."
Gù Chángkāng [顧長康] once sent a cabinet of his paintings to Huán Xuán [桓玄],
all of them his masterpieces.
Later, when the cabinet was opened to retrieve them,
the seals and labels were as before,
but the paintings were all gone.
He simply said that his marvelous paintings were spiritual
and had transformed
and departed.
Sitting in Seclusion, Talking with Hands [坐隱手談]
Wáng Zhōngláng [王中郎] considered Go to be "sitting in seclusion" (zuòyǐn 坐隱).
Zhī Gōng [支公] considered Go to be "talking with hands" (shǒután 手談).
《Yǔlín》[語林] says:
"Wáng [王] considered Go to be 'talking with hands,'
when he was in a period of mourning.
After the funeral rites, guests came.
He set up the board for a game."
Why Do You Enter My Trousers? [何為入我裩中]
Xiè Lìng [謝令] indulged in wine,
sometimes stripping off his clothes and remaining naked in his house.
People saw him and mocked him.
Lìng [令] said:
"I consider the world to be my house,
and the house to be my trousers.
Why do you gentlemen enter my trousers?!"
Is Ritual Made for Our Kind? [禮豈為我輩設]
Ruan Jí's [阮籍] sister-in-law once returned to her family home.
Jí [籍] went to see her off.
Someone criticized him for this.
Jí [籍] said:
"Is ritual made for our kind?"
A Ten-Thousand Li River with a Thousand Li Bend [萬里長江千里一曲]
Someone criticized Zhōu Púyè [周僕射] for engaging in vulgar and mixed jesting with relatives and friends.
Zhōu [周] said:
"If I am like the Yangtze River, stretching ten thousand li,
how can there not be a bend in a thousand li?"
Corpses Piled Under the House [屋下陳屍]
Zhāng Zhàn [張湛] liked to plant pine trees in front of his study.
Yuán Sōng [袁崧], when he went out,
always liked to have his attendants sing dirges.
At the time, people referred to Zhāng [張] as "corpses piled under the house" (wūxià chénshī 屋下陳屍),
and Yuán [袁] as "a funeral procession on the road" (dàoshàng xíngbìn 道上行殯).
Never Tasted White Mutton in My Life [一生未得白羊肉]
Luó Yǒu [羅友] served as the Qīngzhōu [荊州] Assistant [從事].
Huán Wǔ [桓武], as Wáng Chējì [王車騎], hosted a farewell gathering for him.
Yǒu [友] sat for a long time,
then excused himself to leave.
Xuānwǔ [宣武] said:
"I intended to consult you on some matters;
why are you leaving so soon?"
He replied:
"I, Yǒu [友], heard about white mutton
and lamented that I had never had the chance to eat it in my life,
so I presumptuously came forward just for that.
There is nothing to consult me about.
Now that I am full to the brim,
I must go."
He showed no sign of shame.
A Place of Beauty [勝地]
Wáng Wèijūn [王衛軍] said:
"Good wine naturally leads people to a place of beauty."
Lumps in the Chest [胸中壘塊]
Wáng Xiàobó [王孝伯] asked Wáng Dà [王大]:
"How was Ruǎn Jí [阮籍]?"
He replied:
"Jí [籍] had 'lumps in his chest' (xiōngzhōng lěikuài 胸中壘塊),
so he needed wine to wash them away."
A Son Like This Is Enough to Comfort One's Heart [生兒如此足慰人意]
Wáng Hún [王渾] was sitting with his wife, Madame Zhōng [鍾氏].
Seeing Wǔzǐ [武子] pass through the courtyard,
Hún [渾] said:
"A son like this
is enough to comfort one's heart."
His wife laughed and said:
"If your wife had been married to Cānjūn [參軍],
the children born would certainly not have been merely like this."
The Nose Is the Mountain of the Face [鼻者面之山]
Kāng Sēngyuān [康僧淵] had deep-set eyes and a high nose.
Wáng Chéngxiàng [王丞相] often teased him about it.
Sēngyuān [僧淵] said:
"The nose
is the mountain of the face;
the eyes
are the abyss of the face.
If the mountain is not high, it is not spiritual;
if the abyss is not deep, it is not clear."
Is Your Ambition to Become a Buddha Not Too Grand? [卿圖作佛不亦大乎]
Hé Cìdào [何次道] visited Wǎguān Sì [瓦官寺] and prayed very diligently.
Ruǎn Sīkuàng [阮思曠] said:
"Your ambition encompasses the universe,
and your courage surpasses all ages."
Hé [何] said:
"Why do you suddenly praise me today?"
Ruǎn [阮] said:
"I aspire to govern a prefecture of several thousand households,
and I still cannot achieve it.
You, however, aspire to become a Buddha.
Is that not too grand?"
Sending a Rhinoceros Horn Rúyì [送角如意]
Yǔ Zhēngxī [庾征西] launched a major campaign against the Hú [胡].
After setting out,
he stopped and garrisoned Xiāngyáng [襄陽].
Yīn Yùzhāng [殷豫章] sent a rhinoceros horn rúyì [如意] to tease him.
Yǔ [庾] replied:
"Having received what you sent,
though it is a broken thing,
I still wish to mend and use it."
Buying a Mountain to Live in Seclusion [買山而隱]
Jiāo Dàolín [交道林] wanted to buy Máng Shān [邙山] from Shēn Gōng [深公].
Shēn Gōng [深公] replied:
"I have never heard of Cháo [巢] or Yóu [由] buying a mountain to live in seclusion."
Why Is There a Dog Hole? [何為開狗竇]
Zhāng Wúxīng [張吳興] was missing eight teeth.
An elder statesman jokingly asked:
"Why is there a dog hole in your mouth, sir?"
Xuánzhī [玄之] immediately replied:
"It's precisely for people like you to enter and exit through it!"
Flattering the Buddha and Fawning on the Dao [諂佛佞道]
The two Xī [郗] families were devoted to Daoism,
and the two Hé [何] families were devoted to Buddhism,
all with bribes.
Xiè Zhōngláng [謝中郎] said:
"The two Xī [郗] families fawned on the Dao,
and the two Hé [何] families flattered the Buddha."
Wearing Tattered Rags Among Thorns [著敝絮在荊棘中]
Wáng Wéndù [王文度] lectured with Dharma Master Lín [林法師].
Many people were present.
When Master Lín's [林公] argument was slightly defeated,
Sūn Xīng [孫興] said:
"Today, the Dharma Master is like one wearing tattered rags among thorns,
catching and snagging everywhere."
Came Down from the Leaky Roof
Zǔ Guǎng (祖廣) habitually hunched his head.
When he visited Huán Nánjùn (桓南郡),
as soon as he stepped out of his carriage,
Huán Gōng (桓公) said:
"The sky is very clear,
but Zǔ Cānjūn (祖參軍) looks as if he has just emerged from a leaky roof."
Huán Xuán (桓玄) Asks for Peaches
Huán Yá (桓崖) had excellent peaches in the capital.
Huán Xuán (桓玄) requested some,
but did not receive the best ones.
Xuán (玄) said:
"If one obtains them in an age of peace and enlightenment,
then the Sùshèn (肅慎) will contribute their poor arrows;
if it is not so,
even things from between the fences and walls cannot be obtained."
Famous Scholars' Idle Talk
Wáng Dàwèi (王大尉) asked Méizi (眉子):
"Your uncle is a famous scholar,
why do you not hold him in high esteem?"
Méizi (眉子) replied:
"What famous scholar?
He talks idly all day long."
Drawing Wúyán (無鹽) and Insulting Xīzǐ (西子)
Yǔ Yuánguī (庾元規) said to Zhōu Bórén (周伯仁):
"Everyone compares you to Yuè Lìng (樂令)."
Zhōu (周) replied:
"How can you draw Wúyán (無鹽)
and insult Xīzǐ (西子)?"
Three Dou (斗) of Thorny Thickets in the Chest
Shēn Gōng (深公) said:
"People call Yuánguī (元規) a famous scholar,
but he has three dou (斗) of thorny thickets in his chest."
A Flock of White-Necked Birds
Zhī Dàolín (支道林) went east,
and saw Wáng Zǐyóu (王子猷) and his brothers returning.
When asked how he found the Wáng (王) brothers,
he replied:
"I saw a flock of white-necked birds,
idly making 'a-a' sounds."
Losing the Falconer
Wáng Xīngdào (王興道) compared Xiè Wàng (謝旺) and Cài Huò (蔡霍) to having lost a falconer.
Aijiali (哀家梨)
Whenever Huán Nánjùn (桓南郡) saw someone displeased,
he would scold them:
"If you get an aijiali (哀家梨) [sorrow-home pear],
will you still not steam and eat it?"
Resembling His Maternal Uncle
Huán Bàonú (桓豹奴),
maternal nephew of Wáng Dānyáng (王丹陽),
resembled his maternal uncle,
which Huán (桓) greatly disliked.
Xuānwǔ (宣武) said:
"Don't be afraid.
Sometimes he resembles his form,
sometimes he resembles his spirit."
This made him even more displeased.
I Am Not As Good As You For Having a Good Son
Zhāng Cāngwú (張蒼梧) was the grandfather of Zhāng Píng (張憑).
He once said to Píng's (憑) father:
"I am not as good as you for having a good son."
Píng (憑), then a few years old,
clasped his hands and said:
"Grandfather, how can you joke with a son about his father!"
The Southern Barbarian Adjutant Speaking Barbarian Language
Hǎo Lóng (郝隆) was the Southern Barbarian Adjutant for Huán Gōng (桓公).
At a gathering on the third day of the third month,
he composed a poem which said:
"Jūyú (娵隅) leaps in the green pond."
Huán (桓) asked what jūyú (娵隅) was,
and he replied:
"The barbarians call fish 'jūyú' (娵隅)."
Huán Gōng (桓公) said:
"Why do you use barbarian language when writing poetry?"
Lóng (隆) replied:
"Having traveled a thousand li to serve you,
and only just become a Southern Barbarian Adjutant,
how can I not speak barbarian language?"
Let Me Just Play One Tune
Yīn Hóngyuǎn (殷洪遠)'s poem:
"Let me just play one tune."
Liú Zhēncháng (劉真長) laughed at his clumsy words,
and asked:
"Where do you want to play it?"
Yīn (殷) replied:
"A clumsy one can also play,
why must it be a master of the qing (鎗) and ling (鈴)?"
Yuǎnzhì (遠志) and Xiǎocǎo (小草)
When Xiè Gōng (謝公) first had the aspiration for Dōngshān (東山),
he then went to Huán Sīmǎ (桓司馬).
Among Bào Huán's (鮑桓) medicinal herbs was yuǎnzhì (遠志).
Gōng (公) said:
"This medicine is also called xiǎocǎo (小草),
why does one thing have two names?"
Xiè (謝) did not answer.
Hǎo Lóng (郝隆) said:
"This is very easy to explain:
when staying, it is yuǎnzhì (遠志) [far-reaching ambition],
when going out, it is xiǎocǎo (小草) [small grass]."
Xiè (謝) was very ashamed.
How Dare These Rats!
Wáng Zǐjìng (王子敬) and his brothers visited Xī Gōng (郗公) to inquire after him.
They wore their shoes,
and diligently observed the etiquette of maternal nephews.
When Jiābīn (嘉賓) died,
they all wore tall clogs,
and their demeanor was disrespectful.
Xī Gōng (郗公) sighed and said:
"If Jiābīn (嘉賓) had not died,
how dare these rats behave like this!"
Yīn Zǐ Qǐ (愔子起),
who gained favor with Huán Wēn (桓溫),
was therefore treated with respect by Wēn (溫), surpassing others.
How Did Ā Qǐ (阿乞) Get This Item?
Wáng Zǐyóu (王子猷) visited Xī Yōngzhōu (郗雍州).
Seeing a rug,
he said:
"How did Ā Qǐ (阿乞) get this item?"
He ordered his attendants to send it back home.
When Xī (郗) came out and noticed,
Wáng (王) said:
"Just now, a strong man carried it away quickly."
Xī (郗) showed no offense.
Ā Qǐ (阿乞)
was the childhood name of Jí (忣).
Heart Troubled by Mundane Affairs, Limited Innate Talent
Wáng Jiāngzhōu (王江州)'s wife said to Xiè È (謝遏):
"Why have you made no progress at all?
Is it because your heart is troubled by mundane affairs,
or is your innate talent limited?"
All Troubling Things Are Exhausted
Although Xiè Qìngxù (謝慶緒)'s insight was not exceptional,
all the things that could trouble his mind were exhausted.
Brothers' Ambitions and Endeavors Greatly Differ
Dài Āndào (戴安道) having secluded himself in Dōngshān (東山),
his elder brother wished to establish achievements in warding off invaders.
Xiè Ān (謝安) said:
"How greatly do your brothers' ambitions and endeavors differ?"
He replied:
"Your humble servant cannot bear its sorrow,
while my younger brother does not change his joy."
Climbing a Hundred-Foot Tower and Taking Away the Ladder
After Yīn Zhōngjūn (殷中軍) was deposed,
he resented Jiǎnwén (簡文) and said:
"He put me on top of a hundred-foot tower,
and then carried away the ladder."
Terrain and Landscape
Yīn Zhōngwén (殷中文) believed he was destined for court politics,
but was suddenly made Governor of Dōngyáng (東陽),
which greatly displeased him.
Upon arriving at Fùyáng (富陽), he sighed and said:
"Looking at this terrain and landscape,
another Sūn Bófú (孫伯符) is sure to emerge."
Wáng Bùliúxíng (王不留行)
When Wèi Zhǎn (衛展) was in Xúnyáng (潯陽),
an old acquaintance came to him,
but he did not attend to him at all,
only sending him a copy of Wáng Bùliúxíng (王不留行).
When this person received the gift,
he immediately ordered his carriage.
Lǐ Hóngfàn (李弘範) said:
"My uncle is so harsh,
he even makes plants work for him."
Wáng Bùliúxíng (王不留行)
treats metal wounds,
and dispels wind.
Cannot Let the Eldest Son Know
Wáng Chéngxiàng (王丞相) was frugal.
The fruits under his tent piled up and were not distributed,
rotting by spring.
The Dūdū (都督) reported this,
and Gōng (公) ordered them to be discarded,
saying:
"Be careful not to let the eldest son know."
Does Not Recognize Paddy Fields
Xuē Fēng 與 Liú Zhuó 相善，
Zhuó 詞藝不逮 Fēng，
Fēng 每侮之。
後 Zhuó 作相，
Fēng 為郎官。
有薦 Fēng 知制誥者，
Zhuó 以故事給舍須歷郡縣，
出 Fēng 為 Bāzhōu Cìshǐ。
Yáng Shōu 作相，
Fēng 詩云：
「須知金印朝天客，
同是沙堤避路人。」
Shōu 啣之。
Wáng Duó 作相，
Fēng 又作相逢詩曰：
「昨日鴻毛萬鈞重，
今朝山岳一毫輕。」
Duó 亦怨。
恃才褊忿，
終於祕書監。
嘲短身而傴
Cuī Shànwéi 為 Zuǒchéng，
令史惡其聰察，
以其身短而傴，
嘲之曰：
「崔子曲如鉤，
隨到得封侯。
膊上全無項，
胸中別有頭。」
輸忠不效
Tài Zōngquán 為其將所執，
Zhāozōng 御樓受俘，
Jīngzhǎo Yǐn Sūn Kuí 以組練繫之，
狥於市。
Zōngquán 檻中引頸曰：
「尚書明鑒，
Zōngquán 豈反者耶？
但輸忠不效爾。」
霖雨閉坊門
Shénlóng 中，
每霖雨，
必閉坊門禳災。
Sòng Wùxiān 上疏云：
「雨陽或愆，
貌言為咎，
豈有一坊一市遂能感格星靈？
暫閉暫開，
寧便發揚神造。
巷議街言呼坊門為宰相，
謂能節宜風雨，
燮調陰陽。
赫赫師尹，
便為虛設。
悠悠蒼生，
復何所望。
Jǐnglóng 中，
東都霖雨百餘日，
閉坊市北門，
駕車者各遷遠街，
謂宰相不能調陰陽，
致茲常雨，
令我遷行。」
Yáng Zàisī 曰：
「於理則然，
亦卿牛劣耳。」
懷寶詐降
Táng Zhuāngzōng 趨 Dàliáng，
Liáng Wáng 召宰相謀之。
Zhèng Jué 請懷傳國寶詐降以舒難。
Liáng Wáng 曰：
「今日固不敢愛寶，
但如卿此策果可了否？」
Jué 俛首久之：
「但恐未了。」
左右皆笑。
四鄰那得不畏
Zhōu Hángféng 廉總 Húxiāng，
兵將積功檢校官至王公者以千數。
Hángféng 生日，
諸道各遣使致賀。
Hángféng 有矜色，
謂 Xú Zhòngyǎ 曰：
「四鄰亦畏我乎？」
對曰：
「侍中境內，
彌天太保，
徧地司空，
四鄰那得不畏？」
大朝小朝
Jiāngnán Hàlín Xuéshì Cháng Mèngxī，
屢言 Féng Yánsí 等虛誕，
Táng Wáng 不聽。
及臣服於 Zhōu，
Yánsí 之黨謂 Zhōu 為大朝。
Mèngxī 曰：
「諸君常欲致君堯舜，
何意今日自為小朝耶？」
問山中所須
Pān Shīzhèng 居 Sōngshān，
服松葉飲水而已。
Gāozōng 問山中所須，
對曰：
「松樹清泉，
山中不乏。」
州攝衙推
Yuánhé 初，
Zhāng Zhíyì 貶 Yázhōu Sīhù。
Cìshǐ Lǐ Jiǎ 舉牒云：
「前件官久在朝廷，
頗諳公事，
幸其佐理，
勿憚摩賢，
事須州攝，
軍以衙推。」
江總題棺
Chén Lǔ Guǎngdá 為將，
Chén Rén 被執，
憤慨而卒。
Jiāng Zǒng 題其棺曰：
「黃泉雖抱恨，
白日自留名。
悲君感義死，
不作負恩生。」
末帝誌文
Zhū Liáng 末帝，
Táng Zhuāngzōng 納其妃 Guō Shì，
許收葬 末帝。
Duàn Péng 作誌文云：
「七月有期，
不見望陵之妾。
九疑無色，
空餘泣竹之妃。」
能鱗渠十六院
Suí Yángdì 作西苑，
苑內為海，
有龍鄰渠，
作十六院，
前皆臨渠，
彩為芰荷，
隋主奢盛
Táng Tàizōng 與 Xiāo Hòu 宮中觀燈曰：
「孰與隋主？」
Hòu 曰：
「彼亡國之君，
陛下開基之主，
奢儉固不同爾。」
Dì 曰：
「隋主何如？」
Hòu 曰：
「每除夜，
殿前諸位設火山數十，
每一山焚沉香數車，
沃以甲煎，
焰起數丈，
香數十里，
一夜用沉香三百餘車，
甲煎二百餘石。
房中不燃膏火，
懸寶珠一百二十照之。
陛下殿前所焚柴木，
所爇膏油，
但覺烟氣薰人。」
Tàizōng 口刺其奢，
心伏其盛。
楊后埋銘
Mínghuáng Yáng Hòu，
Sùzōng 母也，
命 Zhāng Yuè 作《埋銘》云：
「石獸澀兮綠苔粘，
宿屮殘兮白露沾。
園寢闒兮脂粉膩，
不知何年開鏡奩。」
恨樓下無井
Jiāngnán Jǐng Gōng 中作高樓，
眾皆歎美。
Xiāo Yǎn 曰：
「恨樓下無井，
以此不及 Jǐngyánglóu。」
Request to Revive the Eight Academies
During the time of Táng Mínghuáng,
Zhāng Pǔ (張溥), the sìyè (司業) of the Guózǐ (國子), memorialized the emperor to revive the Eight Academies,
in order to expand the number of students.
According to the Lìudiǎn (六典):
“The Guózǐ Jiàn (國子監) has six schools: the Guózǐ Xué (國子學),
Tàixué (太學),
Sìmén Xué (四門學), Lǜxué (律學), Shūxué (書學), and Suànxué (算學).”
The tradition that speaks of eight academies
is mistaken.
Asked about the characters "Gūxī"
Féng Yù (馮玉), the chancellor of the Shí Jìn (石晉),
once asked someone about the characters “gūxī” (姑息).
The person taught him the character “gūfù” (辜負).
Yù (玉) assented to it.
Not Paying Debts for Chess
Chén Bǎobǎo (陳寶保) of the Shí Jìn (石晉)
was extremely mean and stingy by nature.
Whenever he lost a game of chess to someone,
he would mess up the board with his hand,
fearing that he would have to pay the money he had gambled.
When he died,
he had no wife or children in his home.
He only had a thousand ingots of white gold,
which became the property of others.
Hunting for Wine
Wéi Sī (韋思) of the Wǔdài Hàn (五代漢)
was in Shàngdǎng (上黨) for five years.
He was solely occupied with accumulating wealth,
and never entertained guests or associates.
If an envoy came to request an audience,
Sī (思) would angrily say:
“He must be here to hunt for wine!”
He would order the Dǐankè (典客) to give him a drink and send him away.
Keys Tied Beneath His Robe
Zhāng Yǔn (張允), the Lìbù Shìláng (吏部侍郎) of the Hàn (漢),
had property worth ten thousands, but was stingy by nature.
He did not entrust anything to his wife or children,
but personally tied all the keys beneath his robe,
making a sound like jade pendants.
When Guō Wēi (郭威) entered the capital,
Yǔn (允) hid above the painted ceiling of a Buddhist temple.
The board broke, and he fell,
dying of cold and hunger.
Hóngyá Xiānshēng's Pūtóu
Lǐ Huán (李寰) governed Jìnzhōu (晉州).
His maternal cousin, Wǔ Gōng (武恭), was fond of Daoism but was fantastical and untrustworthy.
On Huán’s (寰) birthday,
Gōng (恭) sent an old black jacket,
saying:
“This is what Lǐ Xīpíng (李西平) wore when he recovered the capital.”
On Gōng’s (恭) birthday,
Huán (寰) gave him a broken pūtóu (撲頭) and said:
“This is the pūtóu (撲頭) Hóngyá Xiānshēng (洪崖先生) wore when he first attained the Dao.”
Memorializing during a "Zhuǎnduì" to Burn Incense in Pagodas and Temples
Wáng Liáng (王梁) of the Hòutáng (後唐) served as a Jǐshìláng (給事郎).
During a zhuǎnduì (轉對), he memorialized,
stating that since the celestial constellations were in harmony,
and the wind and rain were timely,
he requested one box of imperial incense.
The emperor was to personally light one stick,
and the rest were to be burned in pagodas and temples.
Kowtowing, Facing North, and Calling Out for the Enlightened Ruler
Hé Zé (何澤) served as Lìbù Lángzhōng (吏部郎中)
and Xiu Zhuan (脩撰) at the academy.
He would often stay behind alone after the court audience,
knock his forehead with his hu (笏),
face north, and call out, “Míngzhǔ (明主)!”
Míngzōng (明宗) knew of his flattery,
but did not blame him.
Yěgé
Zhūgě Yǐng (諸葛穎) had access to Yángdì’s (煬帝) private chambers,
sharing mats and couches with the empresses, concubines, and palace women.
Yǐng (穎) often slandered and disparaged others.
People called him “Yěgé” (冶葛).
Presenting a Goblet to Wish Quánzhōng Long Life
Cuī Yìn (崔胤) summoned Zhū Quánzhōng (朱全忠) to assist himself.
He welcomed and met him at Wèiqiáo (渭橋),
presenting a goblet to wish him long life,
and holding a tablet to sing for Quánzhōng (全忠).
He even composed the song himself,
praising his achievements.
Begging for the Jiédùshǐ of Wèibó
The Lǐ (李) Lord of Jiāngnán (江南) captured Húnán (湖南),
and then believed that other states could be easily subdued by his command.
Wèi Cén (魏岑) spoke at a banquet, saying:
“When I was young, I traveled to Yuánchéng (元城)
and enjoyed its customs.
When Your Majesty pacifies the Central Plains,
I beg for the Jiédùshǐ (節度使) of Wèibó (魏博).”
The Táng (唐) Lord granted his request.
Cén (岑) hurried down to bow.
The lord's arrogance and the minister's flattery were like this.
Feigning Loss in Chess
Lǐ Dàogǔ (李道古) was obsequious and adept at official maneuvering.
He often visited the homes of high officials with wine, food, and chess.
During gambling contests,
he would feign defeat and then pay his stakes,
thus gaining temporary false fame,
and those who loved profit all befriended him.
Indulging in Pleasure During Mourning
Yáng Yá (楊涯) of Huáinán (淮南) indulged in pleasure day and night during mourning.
He burned
candles ten arm-spans in circumference to play polo,
each candle costing tens of thousands of coins.
Storing Horses in Brocade Tents
Zhū Jǐn (朱瑾) of Zhū Liáng (朱梁) had a horse he rode.
In winter, he stored it in a brocade tent,
and in summer, he protected it with a silk canopy.
Meat Platters
Sūn Shèng (孫晟) was in Jiāngnán (江南),
and had many courtesans.
Whenever he ate, he did not set up dining tables,
but had the courtesans each hold a dish,
calling them “ròu táipán” (肉臺盤).
The Shǔ (蜀) Lord’s Extravagance
Wáng Yǎn (王衍), the Shǔ (蜀) Lord,
was excessively extravagant.
He erected brocade screens and played polo within them,
often traveling far away without outsiders knowing.
He burned various incenses day and night without interruption.
After a long time, he grew tired of them,
and instead burned soap pods,
to alter the scent.
He constructed mountains from silk,
and palaces and towers upon them.
Sometimes he would feast and drink on the silk mountains,
not descending for days.
Before the mountains, he dug canals connecting to the forbidden palace.
He would return by boat at night,
ordering thousands of official courtesans to hold candles in the front boats,
standing backward to illuminate,
making the water surface as bright as day.
Nine Dragon Hall
Mǎ Xīfàn (馬希範) of Húnán (湖南) built the Nine Dragon Hall,
carving eight dragons from agarwood,
decorating them with gold and jewels,
embracing pillars and facing each other.
Xīfàn (希範) sat in the middle,
considering himself one of the dragons.
His pūtóu (撲頭) had appendages over a丈 (zhàng) long,
to resemble dragon horns.
Silver Troughs for Feeding Horses
Bái Chéngfú (白承福), the chieftain of the Tǔyùhún (吐谷渾) in Shí Jìn (石晉), was very wealthy.
He used silver troughs to feed his horses.
Zhōu Xuánbào Discussing Physiognomy
Zhōu Xuánbào (周玄豹) of the Hòutáng (後唐) possessed the skills of Yuán Xu (袁許).
He described people's appearances
by comparing them to tortoises, fish, birds, and beasts.
By visual observation and intuitive judgment,
he always grasped the underlying principles.
Upon seeing Wáng Dū (王都), he said:
“His form is like a carp,
unable to escape the chopping board.”
Dū (都) was indeed killed.
Lú Chéng (盧程), dressed as a Daoist priest, and two companions visited him.
Xuánbào (玄豹) said:
“The two gentlemen will both be gone by the time the flowers bloom next year.
Only the Daoist priest will achieve great honor.”
The following year, the two men indeed died,
and Chéng (程) later became a chancellor.
Thick on the Outside, Thin on the Inside
Zhái Guāngyè (翟光業) of the Hòuzhōu (後周) had plump and fair skin,
and was skilled at the Pivotal Secretariat and the Directorate of Astronomy.
Zhào Yányì (趙延義) said:
“Master Zhái (翟) is thick on the outside but thin on the inside.
Although noble, he will not live long.”
He died at the age of forty-six.
Few High Officials Possessed Virtue
Zhào Yányì (趙延義).
During the Qīngtài (清泰) period,
Lǚ Qí (呂琦), a Direct Academician of the Privy Council, secretly asked about the nation's destiny.
Yányì (延義) said:
“To preserve the state lies in its penal administration,
and to preserve the body lies in virtue.
As for penal administration,
soothsayers dare not speak;
but alas, few of the high officials in power possess virtue.
I have a deep concern for the threads of destiny.”
Request to Read the Zhēngguān Zhèngyào
During the reign of Hàn Yǐndì,
there were often strange occurrences in the palace.
The Emperor asked Zhào Yányì about rituals to ward off misfortune.
He replied:
"Your servant's profession is astronomy and divination by date and time;
rituals for warding off misfortune are not what I am practiced in.
However, if a ruler cultivates virtue, calamities and anomalies can be mitigated."
The Emperor asked how to cultivate virtue.
Yányì replied:
"Please read and emulate the Zhèngguān Zhèngyào."
Gāo Pián was fond of immortals.
The Daoist practitioner Lǚ Yòngzhī, together with Zhāng Shǒuyī and Zhūgě Yīn, deceived and deluded him.
They said:
"The Jade Emperor considers your official duties bothersome and heavy,
and has now commanded a venerable deity to assist you."
The next day, they paid their respects,
and their deceptive arguments flowed freely,
which Pián
believed to be true.
Yīn suffered from wind-dampness,
and Pián's dogs, sensing Yīn's smell,
came close to him in great numbers.
Yīn laughed and said:
"I used to see them before the Jade Emperor;
after several hundred years apart, they still recognize me."
Yòngzhī said:
"The Jade Emperor sees your meritorious efforts in burning incense and cultivating oneself as significant,
and is about to appoint you a true immortal official.
Luan-phoenixes and cranes are expected to descend any day now.
My term of banishment is also complete,
and I shall certainly accompany your banner and pennant to return to the Upper Clarity realm."
Whenever Yòngzhī faced Pián, he would utter incantations and exhale qi,
and bow upwards into the air,
claiming an immortal was passing by.
Pián would invariably follow and bow to them.
Later, Yòngzhī was executed by Yáng Xíng,
and when his central hall was excavated,
a figurine was found,
with Pián's name written on it,
shackled and nailed.
End of Chapter Thirty-One.
Luòpǔ Shénnǚ Gǎnzhen Fù
Xiāo Kuàng played the qin by the Luòshǔi River.
There was a woman who was the Luòpǔ Shénnǚ.
Kuàng said:
"I have heard that the Luò Shén is Zhēn Hòu.
After the Empress passed away,
Chén Sīwáng encountered her spirit by the Luò River,
composed the Gǎnzhen Fù,
which was later changed to Luòshén Fù,
attributing it to Mì Fēi.
Is this true?"
The woman said:
"It is true.
I am Zhēn Hòu.
I enjoyed playing the qin.
Whenever I played Bēifēng or Biéhè Cāo,
my tears would always dry up like jade chopsticks,
the oil in the golden lamp would be exhausted,
the moonlight in the courtyard would seem bitter,
and the crickets on the wall would chirp mournfully."
Kuàng said:
"Where is Sīwáng now?"
The woman said:
"He is currently the king of Zhēxū Guó."
Suddenly, another woman appeared,
named Zhīxiāo Niángzi,
the beloved daughter of the Luòpǔ Lóngjūn.
Kuàng asked:
"Do dragons, for their power, fear iron?
Is this so?"
The woman said:
"The 'arrogant dragon' is the Lǎodān of this world.
Those who fear iron
are the jiāo and chí types."
She also said:
"Dragons love to sleep,
for a thousand years if large,
or several hundred years if small."
The woman ordered her attendants to pour sweet wine and pass the cups,
their beauty was captivating.
On her left were Qióngzhī and on her right Yùshù,
and they enjoyed themselves for the entire evening.
Xuē Zhāo
Xuē Zhāo served as the commandant of Pínglù,
and was demoted to a commoner in Hǎikāng.
An old man from the mountains gave him a pill,
saying:
"Going east will not only allow you to escape calamity,
but also to acquire a beautiful woman."
Indeed, he encountered the Lánchāng Gōng,
where three women poured sweet wine and sacrificed, saying:
"Good fortune and auspiciousness!
Good people meet,
bad people avoid each other."
Zhāo eagerly stepped out and said:
"I wish to be counted among the good people."
He inquired about their names.
The eldest said her name was Zhāng Róngyún,
the second Xiāo Fèngtái,
and the third Liú Lánqiáo.
Lánqiáo threw dice,
and whoever had the highest score would be chosen as a bedmate.
Róngyún won several times.
Zhāo said:
"Where are you from, madam?"
Róngyún said:
"I
was a maidservant of Yáng Guìfēi,
and once performed the Nísháng dance alone.
The Consort gave me a poem, saying:
'Her silk sleeves moved, fragrance ceaseless,
Red lotuses swayed gracefully in autumn mist.
Light clouds on mountain ridges, suddenly stirred by wind,
Tender willows by the dike, first brushing the water.'
At that time, the Emperor was discussing the Dao with Shēn Tiānshī,
and gave me a pill of Jiàngxuě Dān,
saying:
'If you take this,
even if you die for a hundred years,
when you encounter a living person
and obtain their vital essence,
you will become an Earth Immortal.'
It has now been a hundred years."
Zhāo then asked about the appearance of the Tiānshī.
She said:
"He was the burly mountain old man."
He also asked about the two younger ones, Lán and Fèng.
She said:
"They were palace women at that time,
who were envied by the Jiǔxiān Yuán,
poisoned to death,
and buried next to my tomb."
Fèngtái sang a poem:
"Sleeping flowers, not yet bloomed, holding much seclusion,
Today, spring's warmth uniquely changes to autumn.
I guard lonely smoke without daylight,
Cold clouds on the mound add to sorrow."
Lánqiáo said:
"In the secluded valley, warbling orioles preen their wings,
Jade chilled in sunken mud, sighing to itself.
Moonlight cannot bear to close the spring's gate,
Dew drips on pine branches, a night of cold."
Róngyún said:
"Glorious light, unregarded, turning into dust,
Once encountered a golden elixir, perhaps with divine power.
Unexpectedly, Scholar Xuē brings old melodies,
Opening a unique branch of spring in the secluded valley."
Zhāo said:
"Mistakenly entering the palace walls, a person who slipped through the net,
Moonlight cleanses the dust on jade steps.
I suspect I flew to the peak of Péngshān,
Three branches of jade trees, spring at midnight."
Lán and Fèng took their leave.
Zhāo and Róng shared a bed for several nights,
unaware of day or night.
Róng said:
"I have revived,
but my clothes are torn.
If I get new ones, I can rise.
I have a golden bracelet;
you can sell it to buy clothes."
That night, Zhāo went to the cave,
opened the burial shroud.
Her original body had indeed come to life.
They returned together to a secluded dwelling in Jīnlíng,
and are still alive today.
Could it be that they all took the Tiānshī's medicine?
Táo Tàibái Yǐn Zǐxū
Táo Tàibái and Yǐn Zǐxū traveled together to Chónghuá.
Beneath a pine tree, they saw an ancient man and a woman.
The two gentlemen said:
"How did immortals come to be here?"
The ancient man said:
"I was a laborer for Qín,
and this Maonǚ was also a palace woman of Qín.
Ordered to be buried alive with the emperor,
we escaped the disaster at Líshān
and hid here.
I don't know how many *jiǎzǐ* cycles have passed since then."
The two gentlemen said:
"Fortunate to meet a great immortal,
we wish to ask for the elixir of immortality."
The ancient man said:
"I was originally a mortal.
Initially, I ate pine nuts,
and later consumed pine resin.
With the passage of years,
I could float in the air,
and my hair turned a deep blue-green.
I do not know what the elixir of immortality is."
The Maonǚ recited a poem:
"Who knows that ancient ways were right and modern ways are wrong?
Idly treading on pure mists, I wander around the emerald peaks.
The pipes and flutes of Qínlóu must be silent now,
as colorful clouds idly cling to my ivy robe."
The man said:
"I have ten-thousand-year-old pine branches
and thousand-year-old pine nuts.
You may consume them
and also attain transcendence."
The two gentlemen now make their abode on Liánhuāfēng.
Zhèng Délín, a native of Chángshā,
went to Jiāngxià to visit his relatives.
On his return,
he shared a boat with a salt merchant and stayed overnight on Dòngtíng Hú.
A girl named Wéi was fishing from the water window.
Délín wrote a poem on a red silk scarf, saying:
"A delicate hand casts a hook from the water window,
red lotus in autumn's splendor illuminates the long river.
If you can unfasten your jade pendant and cast it into the dragon's abode,
might I beg a pair of bright pearls?"
He used the red silk scarf to lure the hook,
and the girl retrieved it.
At dawn,
he set sail with the favorable wind and departed.
As dusk approached,
a fisherman said:
"The merchant's huge boat
has sunk in Dòngtíng."
Délín was grieved and penned a poem mourning Wéi Shū:
"Dòngtíng's wind is strong, the reed flowers bloom in autumn,
the freshly drowned young maiden sorrows with the small waves.
Tears fall on white duckweed, but you do not see,
under the bright moon, light gulls are on the river."
He poured a libation and cast it into the water.
The water spirit brought it to the Water Palace.
The Lord of the Palace said:
"Délín will one day be a wise magistrate in our district."
He summoned his attendant to send the Wéi girl to Zhèng Shēng.
The girl looked at the Lord of the Palace,
who was an old man.
In the middle of the night, Délín felt something bumping his boat.
He rescued it,
and it was the Wéi girl.
He then took her as his wife.
Several years later,
he indeed became the magistrate of Bālíng.
When he arrived at Dòngtíng,
an old man said:
"The Water Palace saved your life that day."
Wéi Shì thanked him and said:
"Are my parents in the Water Palace? Can I visit them?"
The old man said:
"You may."
In a moment,
the boat sank,
but they suffered no discomfort.
Her parents' dwelling was no different from that of mortals,
and they said:
"All things that drown come here,
but there is no fire to burn them,
and we eat only water caltrops and foxnuts."
Soon,
the boat emerged by the lake.
Wén Xiāo
Wén Xiāo arrived at Zhōnglíng.
On Xīshān, there was the ascension residence of Xǔ Zhēnjūn.
Every year on the Mid-Autumn Festival,
men and women gathered closely,
many famous courtesans were invited,
and at night they stood side by side with men,
holding arms, walking in step, and singing.
Wén Shēng saw a courtesan sing:
"If you can accompany me to ascend the immortal altar,
you should attain Wén Xiāo riding a colorful luan.
With embroidered robes and bejeweled tents ready,
the Jade Terrace fears no frost or cold."
After singing,
she held a candle, passed through a large pine grove,
ascended the mountain, and felt along the rocks.
Shēng also secretly followed her tracks.
The courtesan looked back and said:
"Is this not Wén Xiāo?"
She led him to the summit,
where the guard was very strict.
Two immortal maids held ledgers,
requesting detailed judgments,
mostly concerning people drowned in rivers and lakes.
One maid said that the wind and waves accidentally killed a child.
The courtesan angrily said:
"How could it be accidental and easy?!"
The immortal maids took the books and left.
Suddenly, heaven and earth grew dim,
wind and thunder roared in fury.
An immortal boy held a celestial decree, saying:
"Wú Cǎiluán, for revealing heavenly secrets out of private desire,
is demoted to be a mortal wife for twelve years."
The courtesan and Shēng walked hand in hand down the mountain.
He then questioned her about her origins.
The courtesan said:
"My father was Wú Xiānjūn,
courtesy name Měng,
from Yùzhāng.
I became an immortal,
in charge of the underworld records,
six hundred years ago.
Seeing your form aroused my heart,
and I incurred punishment.
You, too, because of me, may transcend the mortal world."
Shēng could not support himself.
His wife daily copied a volume of Sūn Mǐn's *Tángyùn*,
selling each for five *mín*,
for almost ten years.
In the early years of Huìchāng,
she and Shēng fled to Yuèwáng Shān,
and she wrote a poem:
"One shift, then two shifts,
leading us into Yuèwáng Shān.
The allotted time has now completely passed,
among misty vines, we may return again."
That night there was wind and rain,
and by dawn,
woodcutters saw the two each riding a tiger,
ascending the peaks and departing.
Péi Háng
Péi Háng rented a boat on the Xiāng-Hàn river.
On the same boat was Fán Fūrén,
a woman of peerless beauty.
Háng bribed the maid Xiāo Yān to deliver a poem, which said:
"Even strangers from Hú and Yuè sharing a boat inspire longing,
how much more so when I meet a celestial maiden separated by a brocade screen.
If ever you go to the Jùjīng for an assembly,
I wish to follow the luán and hè into the azure sky."
The lady replied:
"Your humble servant has a husband in Hànnán;
please do not take my words as a jest.
Because you have a minor karmic affinity,
in the future, you are destined to become a spouse."
Her reply poem said:
"Drinking one cup of jade nectar, a hundred emotions arise;
after pounding out the profound frost, one sees Yún Yīng.
Lánqiáo is itself an immortal's grotto,
why bother with the arduous climb to Jùjīng?"
Later, passing by Lánqiáo Yì,
he was extremely thirsty.
In a thatched hut, an old woman was spinning hemp.
Háng bowed to her and asked for water.
The old woman said:
"Yún Yīng,
bring a bowl of water."
Háng drank it,
and it was truly jade liquid.
Háng said to the old woman:
"The young lady's beauty is astonishing;
what do you say to a marriage proposal?"
The old woman said:
"Though old and ailing, I have this granddaughter.
An immortal left a medicinal powder, a single *dāoguī*,
which must be pounded for a hundred days with a jade mortar and pestle to be ready.
If you wish to marry this girl,
you only need to bring the jade mortar and pestle;
I have no use for gold or silk."
Háng departed dejectedly.
More than a month later,
he indeed obtained a mortar and pestle,
and brought them to Lánqiáo.
The old woman untied the medicine from her sash,
and Háng immediately began pounding it.
At night, the old woman took the medicine into an inner room.
Háng peeked in,
and saw a jade rabbit holding the pestle,
its snowy light illuminating the room.
When a hundred days were complete,
the old woman swallowed the medicine
and said:
"I will enter the grotto to prepare the bed hangings for Péi Láng."
Suddenly, a grand mansion appeared,
and immortal attendants led Háng into the bed-chamber.
Many of the relatives were immortals.
There was a woman
who said she was his wife's elder sister,
and she said:
"Do you not remember sharing a boat at Èzhǔ on the way to Xiāng-Hàn?"
Those around them said she was Yúnqiáo Fūrén,
the wife of Tiānshī Liú Gāng,
and an imperial historian for the Yùhuáng.
Háng brought his wife into Yùfēng Dòng,
took the elixirs of Jiàngxuě and Yáoyīng,
and ascended to become a High Immortal.
Cuī Wěi
Cuī Wěi, at the Kāiyuán Sì in Nánhǎi,
saw a begging old woman stumble and knock over someone's wine jar.
The shopkeeper at the counter beat her.
Wěi took off his clothes to pay for the damage.
The old woman said:
"I am skilled at cauterizing warts.
I offer you a small amount of moxa from Yuèjǐng Gāng."
Later, he lost his footing and fell into the Wútóng Jǐng,
which was over a hundred *zhàng* deep,
and contained a large snake.
The snake had a wart on its lip.
Suddenly, a burning ember floated into the hole.
Wěi took out the moxa and cauterized the snake's wart,
which immediately fell to the ground.
He then followed the snake for about ten *lǐ*,
when it suddenly bumped against a stone,
and a door opened. Wěi entered the doorway
and saw embroidered curtains and jade jewelry,
unable to tell what kind of grotto-mansion it was.
A green-clad attendant said:
"Yùjīngzǐ has brought the young master from the Cuī family."
In a moment, four women in shimmering rainbow dresses said:
"Young Master Cuī has presumptuously entered the Emperor's Profound Palace."
Wěi asked:
"Where is the Emperor?"
They replied:
"He has briefly gone to the Zhùróng feast.
The messenger from Yángchéng will arrive shortly.
The Emperor has already married Tián Fūrén to be his wife,
and she, Fūrén,
is the daughter of Qí Wáng Tián Héng."
Suddenly, a white sheep
flew down from the sky.
The women said:
"If Master Cuī wishes to return to Fānyú,
we are willing to take him there."
They said to Wěi:
"The Emperor has commanded us to give you a yángsuì pearl.
On Zhōngyuán Day, prepare wine and food,
and we will escort Tián Fūrén there.
We know you have Bào Gū's moxa,
could you leave us a little?"
Wěi did not know who Bào Gū was,
but left the moxa for them and
rode away on the sheep's back.
His former residence
had already passed three years, they said.
He then went to the Fan market to sell the pearl.
An old Hu said:
"Young master, you have come from the tomb of Nányuè Wáng Zhào Tuó!
Tuó was buried with pearls.
Our Dàshí kingdom's yángsuì pearl
was stolen by an extraordinary person for Tuó
and has been there for a thousand years."
Cuī then realized that the Emperor was Zhào Tuó.
At the city's Cónghuáng Gate temple, he saw that its deity resembled the messenger,
thus he knew that Yángchéng was Guǎngzhōu Chéng,
and the temple contained five sheep.
Later, on Zhōngyuán Day,
the four women indeed accompanied the Fūrén.
Wěi asked:
"Fūrén, you are the daughter of the Qí King,
how did you come to be married to Nányuè?"
She replied:
"My state was shattered and my family destroyed.
The King of Yuè captured me as a concubine.
When the King died,
I was buried with him as a sacrifice.
Watching Lì Shēng being boiled
feels like yesterday.
The four women were all sacrificed with me."
He then asked the four women:
"Who is Bào Gū?"
They replied:
"She is Bào Jìng's daughter,
and Gě Hóng's wife,
who performed many cauterizations in Nánhǎi."
He also asked:
"And the snake that was Yùjīngzǐ,
what was that?"
They replied:
"That was Ānqí Shēng, who rode that dragon to the Yùjīng."
Wěi later took his family to visit Bào Gū,
but did not know where she had gone.
Yuán Chè
Yuán Chè and Liǔ Shí sailed from Hépǔ,
met a storm, and landed on an isolated island.
Two young maidens with braided hair said:
"The Revered Master Yùxū and Fūrén Nánmíng are scheduled to meet here."
No sooner had they spoken than they arrived.
The Fūrén said:
"In the past, there were Liú and Ruǎn;
now there are Yuán and Liǔ."
The Revered Master said:
"Meeting by chance,
you should be given divine medicine,
but your innate destiny has its own master."
The Fūrén gave them a jade pot,
and ordered a maid to escort the two guests away,
with a poem that said:
"You came in a single-leaf boat,
you go across the bridge of a hundred flowers.
If you knock on the jade pot in the human world,
mandarin ducks will clearly speak for themselves."
Suddenly, there was a long bridge,
whose railings were all made of exotic flowers,
thousands upon thousands,
wound around to form the pillars.
The two men then reached Hépǔ.
Looking back,
the bridge was gone.
They asked for directions to return to Héngshān.
Upon knocking on the jade pot,
a mandarin duck spoke, saying:
"Go forward, you will meet him yourself."
