Later, they met the Nányuè Tàijí Xiānshēng,
who said:
"This pot is where I kept my jade liquid,
it has been missing for several hundred years."
The two then followed him to Zhùróng Fēng
and did not emerge.
Fēng Zhì
Fēng Zhì (封陟) resided on Shàoshì Shān (少室山).
An immortal maiden wished to serve him as a domestic.
Zhì (陟) said:
"I am steadfast in my poverty,
and will never contemplate impropriety.
Immortal, please return quickly."
The maiden left a poem saying:
"Exiled from the Jade Pond to Pénɡdǎo (蓬島),
in the lovely spring mist and flowers, I have a thought.
For I cherish your pure and white heart,
I wish to hold a broom and serve behind your screen."
Seven days later,
she returned,
and said in a poem:
"Nònɡ Yù (弄玉) had a husband who both attained the Dao,
Liú Gānɡ (劉綱) and his wife both ascended to immortality.
If you can carefully observe the morning dew,
you must follow the cloud chariot to pay respects at the grotto-heaven."
Seven days later, she arrived again,
saying:
"I can make your lifespan reverse that of the three pines and cypresses,
and your pupils fill both eyes.
You may freely wander in the immortal mountains and spiritual abodes.
Do not plant hibiscus flowers,
and cease striking sparks from stones."
Zhì (陟) angrily said:
"I do not deceive in the dark room;
what kind of demon are you,
so relentlessly pressing me!"
The maiden sighed and said:
"The reason for my earnest entreaties
is that I am a descendant of the Qīnɡníu (青牛) Daoist.
If I miss this opportunity now,
it will be another six hundred years.
This man is truly stubborn."
She left another poem saying:
"Lord Xiāo (蕭) disregarded the woman in the phoenix pavilion,
the clouds were heavy as her chariot turned, tears fresh on her face.
How sorrowful is the path back to Pénɡyínɡ (蓬瀛),
difficult to glimpse the green peaches of the old garden in spring."
Then she said:
"Farewell, farewell. Do not regret this later."
Three years later,
Zhì (陟) fell ill and died,
pursued by Tàishān (太山).
On the way, he encountered an immortal retinue,
clearing the path with great strictness.
It was announced:
"Shànɡyuán Fūrén (上元夫人) is touring Tàiyuè (太嶽)."
Zhì (陟) looked up into the golden chariot,
and it was indeed the maiden who had formerly sought his hand.
The lady requested his arrest warrant,
and said:
"He cannot be without feeling."
With a large brush, she rendered a judgment, saying:
"Although Fēng Zhì (封陟)'s nature was deluded,
his conduct was exceedingly firm and pure.
It was truly due to his simplicity and dullness,
and he cannot be blamed for his lack of romantic inclination.
He should be granted an extension of twelve years."
After a long while, he revived.
Wéi Zìdōnɡ (韋自東)
Wéi Zìdōnɡ (韋自東) met a Daoist,
who said:
"I am compounding the Dragon-Tiger Elixir.
It will be completed in two nights,
but there are many demons and monsters.
I need brave men and heroes to draw their swords and intercept them.
When the elixir is ready, I will share it with you."
Zìdōnɡ (自東) followed the Daoist to the chamber for burning elixirs in a high peak's stone cave.
The Daoist said:
"Please stand at the cave entrance with your sword,
and strike any strange creatures you see without fear."
Soon, a giant python appeared,
and Zìdōnɡ (自東) struck it with his sword, and it vanished.
Then a beautiful woman arrived;
he struck her, and she also disappeared.
A Daoist rode a crane,
with a jade boy holding a banner,
and praised Zìdōnɡ (自東), saying:
"My disciple's elixir is about to be completed!"
A poem was recited:
"Three autumns of prostrating and knocking before the true spirits,
when dragon and tiger meet, the elixir liquid forms.
Once the crimson snow solidifies, the body can transcend,
and auspicious clouds arise atop Pénɡhú (蓬壺)."
Zìdōnɡ (自東), thinking it was the Daoist's master,
set aside his sword and was about to pay respects,
when he suddenly entered the cave and
heard the sound of the elixir cauldron exploding.
The Daoist wept bitterly.
The two then cleaned the cauldron and drank [its remnants].
Though Zìdōnɡ (自東) later grew old,
his appearance retained a youthful look.
Cuī Shēnɡ (崔生)
Cuī Shēnɡ (崔生) was a man
whose father was close to a first-rank meritorious official.
His father ordered Shēnɡ (生) to visit the official who was ill.
The official admired his refined elegance
and ordered the courtesan Hónɡxiāo (紅綃) to see him out.
The courtesan held up three fingers,
then turned her palm over three times,
pointed to a small mirror on her chest,
and said:
"Remember!
Remember!"
Shēnɡ (生) returned,
pondering but unable to understand her meaning.
His household had a Kūnlúnnú (崑崙奴) named Mòlè (磨勒),
who said:
"Three fingers
mean that among the official's ten courtesan courtyards,
this is the third courtyard.
Turning the palm over three times and pointing to the mirror
means the fifteenth night,
when the moon is full like a mirror;
she wants you, young master, to come."
Shēnɡ (生) happily said:
"But how?"
Mòlè (磨勒) said:
"This is a minor matter.
The official's household has fierce dogs like tigers
guarding the courtesan courtyard;
I will go and kill them."
That night,
he carried a chain hammer and went.
He returned after the time it takes for a meal,
saying:
"The dogs are dead."
He carried Shēnɡ (生) there,
and the concubine was greatly delighted.
At dawn,
he carried Shēnɡ (生) and the concubine, flying over the steep wall,
and then returned to the academy to hide her.
Later, while strolling by Qǔjiānɡ (曲江),
the official's family secretly recognized Hónɡxiāo (紅綃)
and summoned Cuī Shēnɡ (崔生) to question him.
Shēnɡ (生) dared not conceal the truth.
The official ordered armed guards to capture Mòlè (磨勒).
Three people tried to seize him,
but in an instant, he was nowhere to be found.
Later, someone saw him selling medicine in the barbarian market.
Xǔ Qīyán (許栖岩)
Xǔ Qīyán, having failed the imperial examination in Cháng'ān,
wished to buy a horse.
There was a Daoist master skilled in the *Yì*,
whom he asked to divine for him.
He drew the fifth line of Qián:
"The flying dragon is in the sky;
it is favorable to see a great person."
The Daoist said:
"This horse
is a dragon's offspring."
Qīyán traveled to Shǔ.
When he reached Jiàngé,
the horse was startled and plunged down a ten-thousand-foot cliff.
He walked out of a cave mouth
and saw over ten thousand jade peach trees.
Two jade maidens said:
"Who are you?
How did you suddenly come to the chamber of Tàiyī Yuánjūn?"
Yuánjūn summoned him and said:
"What do you like in the human world?"
He replied:
"I love the Dao and
have read much of the *Lǎo*, *Zhuāng*, and *Huángtíng Jīng*."
Yuánjūn said:
"What lines from the three books did you each get?"
Qīyán replied:
"The *Zhuāngzi* says:
'The breath of the true person issues from the heels.'
The *Lǎozi* says:
'Its essence is truly real.'
The *Huángtíng* says:
'Just contemplating one part grants endless longevity.'" Yuánjūn said:
"You are close to the Dao."
She commanded him to drink stone marrow
and said:
"Jī Kāng could not obtain it,
yet you have obtained it;
it is your destiny."
Suddenly a Daoist master arrived.
Yuánjūn said:
"Please calculate three things:
What spirit split Mount Huá?
What ghost built the sea bridge?"
(Missing character in original)
(Missing character in original)
The Daoist master calculated for a long time
and said:
"Though the one who split Mount Huá is said to be Jùlíng,
it is actually the spirit of Kuāfù.
Though the one who built the sea bridge is said to be ugly and monstrous,
it is actually the ghost of Wǔdīng."
(Missing character in original)
Yuánjūn said:
"Calculate what I will do tonight."
He replied:
"Tonight you will travel thirty thousand *lǐ* eastward."
Qīyán looked at the Daoist master
and realized he was the one who had divined about the horse before.
The Daoist master said:
"The Qián hexagram is fulfilled today."
Presently,
an immortal youth said:
"Dōnghuáng Jūn invites you to enjoy the moon on Qǔlóng Shān Bridge tonight."
Yuánjūn invited Qīyán, saying:
"You can come along to Qǔlóng."
Together they mounted a deer and a dragon and departed.
In an instant they arrived
and saw a perilous bridge,
like a long rainbow stretching across the sky,
its momentum connecting to the Milky Way,
and deeply plunging into the dark ocean.
Dōnghuáng commanded wine to be served.
Phoenixes sang and dancing luan birds
resounded to beyond the heavens.
As the sun began to rise,
they commanded their chariots and all returned.
Yuánjūn said:
"You have drunk the stone marrow
and have already gained a thousand years of life."
She commanded Qīyán's horse to be led forward
and said:
"This was originally a dragon child from my grotto.
Because it became angry and damaged crops,
it was punished to carry burdens.
It was fated to meet you.
When you return to the human world,
release it by the Wèi River."
The jade maiden said:
"When the dragon child returns,
please bring a small quantity of needles from old lady Tián in Guóxiàn."
He mounted the horse
and arrived at the old estate in Guóxiàn in the space of a meal.
He inquired about old lady Tián,
who said:
"Tàiyī's sisters, Zǐxiāo,
once sent a message asking to buy needles."
So he took the needles and tied them to the horse's mane.
He released it by the Wèi River,
where it transformed into a dragon and departed.
Gāo Yù
Gāo Yù moored his boat at Zhāotán.
That night, he secretly watched three large lotus flowers on the潭,
with three beautiful women each sitting on one.
One said:
"Tonight is suitable for questioning the netherworld."
Another said:
"Should the small boat not listen to our words?"
Yet another said:
"Even if there is a person,
if they are not a scholar of high integrity,
there is no need to fear them."
They said to each other:
"Zhāotán is bottomless, and Júzhōu floats.
This saying is truly not false.
Let each of us state what we like."
One said:
"I study Buddhism."
The next said:
"I study Daoism."
The last one said:
"I study Confucianism."
Then they said:
"Let each calculate what we will obtain tomorrow."
They replied:
"Each according to our preference."
The next morning,
a monk indeed crossed to the middle of the current and drowned.
There was also one Daoist master and one Confucian scholar,
all of whom drowned within a short time,
just as divined.
Presently, a boat carried an old man,
who said he was an old man from Qíyáng Shān.
Yù then recounted the events.
The old man angrily said:
"How dare they be like this!"
He took a vermillion brush and inscribed characters,
commanding his disciple to send them to the bottom of the潭.
The disciple walked as if on flat ground.
He saw a large coiling rock,
with three women lying on it.
Upon seeing the talisman arrive,
they transformed into three fish.
The eldest woman said:
"We beg the Heavenly Master to allow us three days to move away."
The old man angrily said:
"You must leave here tomorrow,
otherwise,
I will send the Six Dīng to wield swords and slay you!"
The next day,
with black clouds and wind and rain,
three large fish flowed away along the current.
Zhōu Hán
Zhōu Hán had a slave skilled in diving into water,
whom Hán named Shuǐjīng.
Hán's boat passed through Qútáng,
and he ordered Shuǐjīng to dive down
to explore for gold and treasures and bring them out.
Again, passing Niúzhǔ Jī,
Shuǐjīng disappeared for a while
and returned with jade.
He said:
"There were many water monsters,
all with angry eyes and menacing hands.
I barely escaped harm."
Later, they reached Xiāngzhōu.
North of the prefecture, there was a well
said to contain a yellow dragon.
He ordered Shuǐjīng to dive down.
After the time it takes to eat a meal, he came out
and said:
"There is a large yellow dragon,
holding a bright moon pearl, sleeping soundly.
I just wanted to seize it,
but regretted not having a sharp blade."
Hán gave him a precious sword,
and he re-entered.
After a short while,
he leapt out.
There was a golden hand
that snatched Shuǐjīng from the air and pulled him in.
Presently,
an old man said:
"This Kàngjīn Lóng is an envoy from the High Heavens,
bestowing benevolence upon this region.
How can one wield a small sword to seize it!
If the dragon were to suddenly become enraged,
shaking the heavenly gate
and swaying the earthly axis,
a hundred *lǐ* would become a river, sea, fish, and turtle.
How could you escape?
You should quickly apologize to the dragon
and prevent its anger."
Hán then prepared sacrificial animals and offerings.
Níng Yīn
Níng Yīn 寓居山庄,
夜聞叩關,
云桃林 Bān Tè 處士相訪.
曰:
"某少時,
兄弟競生頭角,
每讀《春秋》至 Yǐng Kǎoshū 挾輈以走,
恨不佐助其間.
讀《史記》至 Tián Dān 破燕,
恨不奮擊其間.
讀《東漢》至 Guāngwǔ 新野之戰,
恨不騰擲其間.
今無嗣子,
空懷舐犢之悲."
俄有南山 Bān Yín 將軍奉謁,
目 Tè 為兄,
因共奕棋,
未分勝.
負 Yīn 教一著,
曰:
"管中窺豹,
特見一班."
兩 Bān Yín 曰:
"大有微譏,
亦一發雨藐耳."
Yīn 傾壺請飲,
言詞紛拏.
Tè 曰:
"弟誇猛毅,
若值下莊,
當為虀粉."
Yín 曰:
"兄誇壯勇,
若值 Páo Dīng,
不存其皮."
Yīn 曰:
"無多言,
各賦一詩."
Yīn 詩曰:
"晚讀雲水淨,
夜吟山月高.
焉能履虎尾,
豈用學牛刀."
Yín 曰:
"但得空林嘯,
焉能當路蹲.
渡河何所適,
終是怯 Liú Kūn."
Tè 曰:
"無非怜 Níng Qī,
終是怯 Páo Dīng.
若遇 Gōng 為守,
蹄涔向北溟."
Yīn 稱 Tè 詩曰奇才,
Yín 怒曰:
"古有班馬,
豈有班牛?"
乃長揖而去.
Tè 亦怒曰:
"古所重者,
白眉耳,
今白額,
何相怒也?"
遂亦告辭.
及明,
門外惟牛跡虎跡而已.
Yán Jùn
Yán Jùn, with the servant Zhào Yòufāng, traveled by boat to Jiànyè.
Upon reaching Báishā,
Yòufāng said,
"On the Zhongyuan Festival, a divine being will gather at Wǎguān Temple."
On that day,
a beautiful woman was indeed seen.
Jùn gazed intently, unable to turn away.
The twin hair rings laughed, saying,
"You foolish bumpkin, put your eyes away!"
The beauty said,
"My home has a clear stream,
and many pines and moonlight.
Young master, please visit tonight."
Jùn walked several li,
and was led into an inner chamber.
A short while later,
Lady Kǒng arrived,
speaking much about events during the Chén and Suí dynasties.
Jùn asked the lady's name,
and she replied,
"I am Consort Zhāng of the Chén dynasty;
she is Consort Kǒng.
Unfortunately, the state perished,
and we were executed by Yáng Guǎng.
In the past, Liú Shàn also had empresses and consorts,
but the Wèi ruler did not punish them;
Sūn Hào certainly had imperial concubines,
but the Jìn emperor did not execute them.
This bandit was inhumane,
and only this injustice was brutal!
He built a Great Wall in Guǎngxī,
campaigned eastward to Liáohǎi,
met his end in Guǎnglíng,
and died at the hands of a common man."
Yòufāng said,
"I was also a maidservant to the Consort.
When the state fell, I entered Suí,
became an imperial concubine of Emperor Yáng,
and later was buried with him beneath Wúgōng Terrace.
I just came here to pay respects to the Consort."
The Consort inscribed a poem:
"Autumn grasses on the desolate terrace face the night cricket,
withered poplars diminish the mournful wind.
Decorated stationery was once folded to surpass Jiāng Zǒng,
the dust in the brocade pavilion settles, 'Jade Trees' are empty."
The Consort said:
"Precious pavilions reach the sky, called 'Wangxian',
five-colored clouds rise beautifully, embracing the heavens.
The clear stream still holds the moon of that time,
once shone on qiónghuā blooming at brocade banquets."
Yòufāng said:
"The bright orb first full, regretting the blue moth eyebrows,
how much more the flourishing splendor?
In the Southern Dynasties, only empty flowing water,
still becomes a passing wave in the human world."
Jùn said:
"Flutes and pipes play clear laments for Lìhuá,
autumn sky, cold moon, slanted by the brocade window.
Ashamed not to be a guest writing poems for the empress,
from time to time seeing flowers on the Línchūn Pavilion."
Jùn and the Consort went to bed,
the others all took their leave.
The next morning, upon inquiry in Jiànyè,
they were found to be tombs of Chén palace women.
Jiǎng Wǔ
Jiǎng Wǔ was skilled at drawing a strong bow;
meeting tigers and leopards, they would die at the twang of his string.
Suddenly, he saw an orangutan riding a white elephant, saying,
"In the mountain village to the south, there is a snake several hundred zhang long.
Whenever an elephant passes by,
it is devoured.
Knowing that I can speak,
the elephants have entrusted me to appeal to you."
Wǔ was moved by its words,
sharpened his arrow, and went.
With one shot, he killed it.
Subsequently, ten elephants,
each holding a hollow tusk with its long trunk, knelt and offered them.
Suddenly, another orangutan appeared, riding a tiger,
holding dozens of golden hairpins and bracelets, and announced,
"This tiger has one male and three cubs in a single den.
They encountered a yellow beast,
which seized their ears
and mashed their brains.
Yesterday, they saw the mountain guest relieve the elephants' suffering,
so they came to appeal to you."
Wǔ grasped his arrow, ready to go,
when the former orangutan riding the elephant arrived,
saying,
"Yesterday, five tigers together devoured several hundred people.
Heaven sent that beast,
which has eaten four of them.
Now the mountain guest accepts bribes
and wants to shoot the beast;
this is 'raising a tiger to devour people'.
Looking at these hairpins and bracelets,
you can tell how many women they have eaten.
The orangutan riding the tiger
is aiding evil."
Wǔ said, ashamed,
"I should be careful."
He turned his arrow to kill the tiger,
and knocked down its orangutan,
hanging the hairpins and bracelets at his door.
Many villagers came to recognize them,
saying they had been eaten by the tiger.
Wǔ took nothing at all.
Jiāng Sǒu
There was an old man by the river, a Sǒu, who was skilled at playing the long flute,
able to produce the cry of a dragon.
Later, he traveled to Mǐnxiāng.
At the Yùpándòuguǎn inn, beneath a large locust tree by the roadside, he fell asleep drunk.
That night, he saw a man several zhàng tall,
who said:
"I thought it was Níchú by the locust tree,
but it is Bìzhuó by the jar."
Then he knocked on the locust tree and said:
"The second son from Jīngshānguǎn has come to see Big Brother."
Immediately, he heard someone descend from the locust tree and speak.
The next day, he went to Jīngshānguǎn
and saw a locust tree in the courtyard ten spans in circumference.
Suspecting a divine being was attached to it,
he said:
"I am fond of the Way [Dào],
but have not met a master.
If the tree spirit has power,
I beg for guidance."
The spirit said:
"Just enter Jīngshān,
seek the immortal master Bào Xiānshī,
and you will surely achieve transcendence."
The old man entered the mountain
and indeed met the immortal master.
The master bade the old man play the flute.
With a single breath, it was pure and ethereal;
the five notes were stirring and resonant,
driving springs to gush forth from mountains,
leading geese to fly low,
causing withered leaves to abandon their branches,
and light clouds to emerge from the peaks.
The immortal master said:
"Your art has reached its pinnacle,
but what you play is a bamboo flute.
Today I bestow upon you a beautiful jade flute.
After playing it for three years,
the dragons in the cave will surely bring you a water elixir [shuǐdān].
Swallow it, and you will become a water immortal [shuǐxiān],
without the need for my medicine.
Indeed, you possess the visage of Qín Gāo."
Three years later, the old man
was playing his flute on the tower of Yuèyángsì temple,
when a dragon, transformed into a human,
came bearing the elixir.
The old man consumed it,
and immediately his face became youthful.
He could enter water without getting wet.
Zhāng Wúpǒ
Zhāng Wúpǒ encountered Yuán Dàniáng, who bestowed upon him a jade dragon ointment [yùlónggāo],
contained in a warm golden casket.
She said:
"It can recall the soul and revive the dead,
and also win a renowned beauty."
A few days later,
a yellow-robed man indeed knocked on his door,
saying that Guǎnglìwáng had summoned him.
So he boarded a painted boat [huàgě]
and entered layers of gates to the east.
He saw a mighty man
dressed in kingly robes,
who said:
"My beloved daughter is ill;
I wish to request your divine ointment."
Two eunuchs led him to the princess's [guìzhǔ] courtyard.
Inside a pearl-embroidered curtain was a girl.
He took out the dragon ointment and she swallowed it,
and the princess's illness was immediately cured.
Wúpǒ gazed at her, enchanted, for a long time.
The king presented him with a rhinoceros horn bowl that startled chickens [hàijīxīfěicuìwǎn] and beautiful jade and bright jewels [lìyùmíngguī].
After traveling for more than a month,
a man in green suddenly brought a poem from the divine maiden, saying:
"Ashamed to remove my bright pendants to seek the Han shore,
I can only rely on spring dreams to visit the ends of the earth.
Day after day passes in the red tower, and orioles fly away;
sorrow fills the deep palace as flowers fall upon the steps."
Soon after, another envoy arrived, saying:
"The princess's illness has returned to its former state,
and the king commands your recall."
Wúpǒ went joyfully,
saying:
"If she takes the medicine again,
the illness will depart,
root and branch."
The king discerned his daughter's intentions
and thus married her to Wúpǒ,
providing boats and ships, treasures, gold, and jade,
and they resided in Sháoyáng.
Suddenly, Yuán Dàniáng came and said:
"Today, Zhāng Láng offers a sacrifice for good fortune, and the young lady is to reward the matchmaker."
So she thanked her with precious treasures.
The divine maiden said:
"This is Yuán Tiānwǎng's daughter,
the wife of Mr. Chéng."
Thereafter, every three years,
Guǎnglìwáng would arrive at night,
wearing golden bells and ringing jade,
with a throng of attendants filling the streets,
startling the villagers.
Wúpǒ gradually feared that people would suspect and execute him,
so he took her to another dwelling.
Zēng Jìhéng
Zēng Jìhéng served his grandfather, who was appointed to Wǔyuán.
A servant reported:
"Once, the daughter of Administrator Wáng died suddenly here;
she was a beauty of the nation."
Jìhéng lit incense and pondered deeply,
not distinguishing between humans and ghosts.
Suddenly, a young woman,
ethereal with the demeanor of an immortal,
who was indeed the daughter of the Wáng family, appeared.
From then on, she would arrive every evening.
Jìhéng accidentally divulged this to his subordinate officers,
and the woman said:
"Because of this, we can no longer enjoy our time together."
She left a poem:
"Without destiny, we part and are scattered like Hú and Yuè,
like swallows separated and orioles departed, when fragrant grasses wither.
Youth and fleeting beauty find spring everywhere;
at Běimáng, I only regret the clear autumn moon."
Jìhéng said:
"The river grass is green, and geese are about to return;
jade cheeks and pearl tears fall at the parting road.
Cloudy hair drifts away, fragrant winds gone;
sorrowfully, I see orioles singing on red plum branches."
Héng said:
"When shall we meet again?"
The woman said:
"Unless sixty years pass,
there is no date for us to meet."
Having spoken, she vanished.
Lú Hán
Lú Hán's family lived in Luòxià.
As he was going to his mountain villa,
on the way he saw a new house in a cypress grove.
A woman in green, very charming,
invited Hán to drink with her,
singing:
"Alone, I hold my kerchief and comb, covering the dark gate,
no one in the mountain tent, the candle flame dim.
My silken robes of yesteryear have all turned to dust;
the wind through the white poplars brings cold to the grave mound."
When the wine was finished, she wanted to refill it.
She took a candle and an ancient bronze zūn and went inside.
Hán peered in
and saw a black snake hanging,
its blood dripping into the zūn.
Hán was greatly frightened,
left the house, untied his horse, and fled.
The woman in green repeatedly called out:
"Tonight, you must stay, young sir, for one night."
She then called out to Fāng Dà, the neighbor to the east,
"And help me catch him!"
Presently, a person with a very deep voice responded.
Then, from a white area in the forest, someone said:
"You must capture this person,
otherwise,
you will surely suffer misfortune."
Hán was even more terrified.
By the time he reached the villa, it was the third watch.
He tied his horse beneath
the carriage box.
A man
from Hàn, carrying a halberd,
stabbed a small child inside the villa with the tip of the halberd.
Presently, a cry of lamentation was heard, saying:
"The child has died!"
The next day, Hán led his household servants to investigate the forest.
They found a clay burial figurine [míngqì] of a woman,
and beside it, a black snake that was already dead.
They also found a large Fāng Xiàng figure.
So they burned them all.
They then searched for the white object,
which was a skeleton.
They threw it into a deep trench.
Hán suffered from a wind ailment [fēngjí],
which was cured by drinking the snake wine.
Presenting Cherries to Xī Gōng
Tàizōng was about to send cherries to Xī Gōng,
who was enfeoffed as Xī Gōng after the Suí dynasty.
To call it "offering" [fèng] seemed too respectful;
to call it "bestowing" [cì] seemed too humble.
Yú Jiān said:
"In the past, Emperor Liáng sent them to King Bālíng and called it 'presenting' [xiǎng]."
So they followed this.
Three Jīngzhàoyǐn Officials
Xuānzōng suddenly asked:
"How many Jīngzhàoyǐn officials are there?"
Lǐ Guīfǔ replied:
"There are three Jīngzhào officials:
one Grand Administrator [Dàyǐn] and
two Lesser Administrators [Shàoyǐn]."
People considered it a good answer.
Female Daoist of Zhìdéguàn
Xuānzōng, in disguise, visited Déguān.
He saw female Daoist priests dressed in elaborate clothing and heavy makeup,
and, greatly enraged, returned to the palace.
He immediately summoned the Left Street Commissioner of Merit and Virtue,
ordering him to expel all of them,
and to select fourteen men to reside there as abbots.
Entertainers Interfere with Court Affairs
The entertainer Zhù Hànzhēn had served in successive courts,
and was witty and skilled at discerning the emperor's intentions.
When Xuānzōng summoned him,
he clapped his hands and laughed,
and spoke quite a bit about matters outside the court.
The Emperor said with a stern expression:
"I support you all to entertain me,
how dare you interfere with court affairs?"
Thereupon, he distanced himself from him.
This House Has No Water Outlet
Lù Yuánfāng of Dōngjùn was selling a small house.
His family was about to receive the payment,
when Yuánfāng said:
"This house is very good,
but it has no water outlet."
The buyer immediately declined to purchase it.
Hán Yù Dies of Leprosy
Hán Yù was gravely ill and about to die.
He summoned a local monk and said:
"I am not well,
and am now about to die of this illness.
Look closely at the patterns on my hands and feet,
so that no one will falsely claim that Hán Yù died of leprosy."
The Youngster is Rude
Cuī Jǐng was very beautiful.
Lǐ Yōng had often wished to meet him.
When Cuī Jǐng presented his composition,
its opening line was "At fifteen, I married Wáng Chāng."
Lǐ Yōng shouted for him to leave, saying:
"The youngster is rude."
He thereupon refused to meet him.
Conferring the Title of Fūrén upon a Concubine
Xuānzōng's maternal uncle, Zhèng Púshè, had previously been stationed in Hézhōng.
He conferred the title of Fūrén upon his concubine,
but she refused it.
Her memorial stated:
"In a humble dwelling, we share sorrow, having lost our companion who sang like a phoenix;
within vermilion gates, we find our own joy, it is difficult to accommodate a motley person."
The Emperor said with delight:
"Who taught my maternal uncle to do such a good thing?"
He replied:
"The judicial official, Tián Xùn, serves as secretary."
The Emperor wished to summon him to the Hànlín Academy,
but critics argued that he had not entered through the jinshi examination,
so the matter was dropped.
Chóu Is Not As Good As Xiū
The three brothers of the Péi family, all prime ministers, were renowned.
The world said that Qiú was not as good as Chóu,
and Chóu was not as good as Xiū.
Xiū was fond of Buddhism,
and was skilled in clerical script.
Many of the plaques and signboards in various places were written by him.
A Pine and a Scholar Tree Correctly Faced
Jiǎ Jiāyǐn, at seven years old,
was summoned for an audience as a child prodigy.
Lǐ Jì playfully asked in the imperial court:
"What tree am I leaning against?"
Jiāyǐn replied:
"A pine tree."
Lǐ Jì said:
"This is a scholar tree,
why do you say pine?"
Jiāyǐn said:
"With a duke (gōng) paired with wood (mù),
how can it not be a pine (sōng)?"
Zhǎngsūn Wújí then asked:
"What tree am I leaning against?"
He replied:
"A scholar tree."
Zhǎngsūn Wújí said:
"Can you not make another clever retort?"
Jiāyǐn replied:
"Why must I make a clever retort?
I'm just taking the 'ghost wood' (guǐ mù, referring to huái, 'scholar tree')."
Lǐ Jì said:
"How can a small child with a barbarian (liáo) face
be so intelligent?"
Jiāyǐn replied:
"If a barbarian (hú) head can still be a prime minister,
why should a barbarian (liáo) face impede intelligence?"
Lǐ Jì had a barbarian-like appearance.
Consort Xú's Poem
Tàizōng summoned Consort Xú Xiánfēi,
but she was late,
which angered him.
Thereupon, she presented a poem saying:
"This morning I stood before my dressing table,
after makeup, I lingered.
A thousand gold pieces for a single smile,
how can I come at a mere summons?"
An Eight-Cash Scholar
Lǐ Shū, a minister, was fond of joking.
Once, returning from court,
a hawker, called to, did not make way.
Lǐ Shū cursed him, saying:
"You one-cash soldier-slave,
how dare you obstruct a high official!"
The hawker replied:
"You eight-cash scholar,
don't put on such airs!"
A Prefecture Map as a Skirt
A poor scholar in Xìnzhōu
was asked by someone for a prefecture map.
He dyed and washed it, turning it into a skirt.
The ink marks did not fade.
It happened that a neighbor invited him out.
Several courtesans served wine.
After a long while,
a maid reported in surprise, saying:
"Sir, you've accidentally burned your skirt."
The man quickly asked where it was damaged.
The maid said:
"It burned right through the gate tower of Dàyún Temple."
Could Not Gain Even a Bit of Power
Lǐ Chéng became prime minister in the ninth year of Dàhé.
He once discussed elixirs with Lǐ Shí,
saying:
"Do you take stalactite powder?
I've recently been taking it,
and I feel it's very effective."
Sītú (Lǐ Shí) replied:
"I could not gain even a bit of power (rǔ lì, also meaning 'milk power')."
This was a satire on Lǐ Chéng's inability to provide urgent relief as prime minister.
Thousand-Character Poem
Xuē Tāo, a courtesan from Shǔ, was intelligent and skilled in poetry.
A Prefect of Lízhōu composed a thousand-character poem,
including "bird (qín)," "fish (yú)," "bird (niǎo)," and "beast (shòu)."
She then said:
"Yǒu Yú Táo Táng (referring to the legendary sage emperors Yáo and Shùn)."
Tāo said:
"Zuǒ Shí Ā Héng (referring to the capable minister Yī Yǐn)."
The man thought her phrases lacked "fish" and "bird,"
and asked for a penalty.
Xuē Tāo said:
"The character Héng (衡) still contains a small 'fish' (魚) character.
As for your Excellency's 'Yǒu Yú Táo',
there is not a single fish in Táng (唐)."
The guests present laughed greatly.
Abdominal Pain Summons Female Slave
Lǐ Fú's wife, Péi, was very jealous.
When Fú was stationed in Huátái,
someone offered him a female slave.
Fú said:
"My official position is that of a military commissioner,
and envoys are no more than slaves.
Won't Madam be very displeased?"
Péi replied:
"I don't know what you desire, my lord."
Fú pointed to the offered slave.
Péi assented.
Fú bribed his attendants: "Tell me when Madam washes her hair."
When they informed him,
Fú feigned abdominal pain,
and urgently summoned the female slave.
When she went,
the attendants also informed Péi.
Péi quickly came out, leaving her hair in the basin,
barefoot, and asked about his suffering.
Fú had already spoken of his illness,
and seemed as if he could not bear it.
Péi then offered him medicine in his urine.
The next day,
the Supervisor of the Army's aide came to inquire about his health.
Fú recounted the whole story to him,
and he laughed heartily.
Tea-Brewing Doctor
Yùshǐ Dàfū Lǐ Jìqīng was sent to comfort the Jiangnán region.
When he arrived at Línhuái,
someone mentioned Cháng Bóxióng was skilled in tea.
Master Lǐ invited him.
Bóxióng wore a yellow tunic and a black gauze cap,
held tea implements in his hands,
recited tea names from his mouth,
and distinguished and pointed them out.
Those around him watched in awe.
When the tea was ready,
Master Lǐ drank two cups.
When he arrived outside the Jiāng region,
he again summoned Lù Hóngjiàn.
Hóngjiàn, dressed in plain clothes,
entered with his tea set.
Once seated,
he laid out the items as Bóxióng had done previously.
Master Lǐ secretly despised him.
After the tea,
he ordered a servant to fetch thirty coins
to pay the previous "tea master."
Hóngjiàn had long roamed the Jiāngjiè region,
familiar with and intimate with eminent scholars.
At this, he felt ashamed and embarrassed.
He then wrote the “Discourse on Destroying Tea.”
Silver Buddha
Shèngshàn Sì had a silver Buddha,
whose ear was cut off by thieves.
Bái Jūyì, being a devout Buddhist,
used three silver ingots to repair it,
but it was still not as good as the original.
During the Huìchāng persecution, temples were demolished,
and a powerful court eunuch was ordered to destroy the statues
and collect them for the imperial treasury.
People said that the silver Bái Gōng added
was several tens of liǎng less than the original casting.
They then went to Jūyì to retrieve the remaining silver.
Gourd for storing ashes
When Lǐ Wèigōng was in Zhūyá Jùn,
there was a Wàngquè Tíng to the north.
Gōng wrote a poem:
“Alone I ascend the river pavilion to gaze at the imperial capital,
Birds flying still take half a year to reach it.
Even the emerald mountains fear people will return home,
Circling the commandery city a hundred times, a thousand times.”
In a small southern Chan monastery,
he went for a walk and saw
an old monk with more than ten gourds hanging on his wall.
Gōng pointed and said:
“Are there medicines inside?”
The monk said:
“No,
they are all human ashes.
Grand marshal, you are a key figure in the court;
those who were dismissed here due to private grudges,
this poor monk pities them.
So I collect their remains and burn them,
store their ashes,
awaiting their descendants to visit.”
Gōng was deeply saddened as if he had lost something,
and returned with a heavy heart.
That night, he passed away.
Xú family's lungs, Shěn family's spleen
Xú Huì loved wine,
Shěn Fùshī was good at eating.
Yáng Sìfù said:
“Xú family's lungs,
Shěn family's spleen—
is that truly peaceful and stable?”
Political decisions determined by son
Prime Minister Línghú Táo
would, for every major court matter,
always have his son Hào make the final decision,
just like Yuán Zài's Bóhé,
and Lǐ Jífǔ's Déyù.
Burning the tail scholar
When a scholar first attains prominence,
gets promoted,
or is appointed as a尉 (magistrate),
the celebratory banquet is called a “burning the tail banquet.”
Once, a tiger transformed into a human,
but only its tail did not change.
It had to be burned away before it could become a full human.
It is used to describe a person newly appointed to office,
like a tiger becoming human,
with its original tail still present.
Another explanation says that when a new sheep enters a flock,
it is butted by the other sheep
and not accepted.
Burning its tail makes it settle down.
Gōngyá
In recent times, the court of a prefecture was commonly called Gōngyá,
which is the ancient Gōngcháo.
The character originally was 牙 (yá),
mistakenly written as 衙 (yá).
The Shī Jīng says:
“Qífù, the king's fangs and claws.”
The Grand Marshal was in charge of military preparedness,
symbolizing fierce beasts using their claws and fangs for defense.
Hence, the great military banner
had the act of “erecting the yá” when setting out on an expedition.
The army, to receive orders,
must assemble beneath the yá banner.
The name of the official title
In recent times, when the Selection Bureau appoints officials,
the previous office is listed first,
then the proposed office is written afterwards.
The old and new are linked together,
hence it is called “guānxián” (official link),
also called “tóuxián” (head link).
Like a person or animal holding something in its mouth,
it implies continuity.
Also like a horse having a bit (xián),
to control its head.
The ancients called it “xiánwěi xiāngxù” (head and tail continuously linked),
which is its meaning.
Qièchóng
Some families have tiny insects,
that make a very faint sound.
If you search for them,
you ultimately cannot see them.
They are called qièchóng,
and it is said that having them is inauspicious.
These insects are as large as sesame seeds,
and resemble a mouse carrying something.
They have two heads,
are white,
and shaking their heads produces a sound.
They are often found in dark places on windows and walls.
Shíyí Mèng Chāngcháo was demoted to Hèzhōu
and wrote a “Qièchóng Fù,”
comparing it to a ghost,
which seems to misunderstand its meaning.
Yìngbìng
Someone suffered from yìngbìng
and consulted the medical official Sū Chéng.
Chéng said:
“There is no ancient prescription for this.
I will select from the Běncǎo,
all the medicines under heaven,
and try reading them.”
Every time he uttered a name,
the patient's abdomen would respond.
Only for one particular medicine,
there was no sound after repeating it multiple times.
Chéng then prescribed a remedy,
with this medicine as the main ingredient,
and the illness was cured.
Zhōngshū Jiěwǎ
Zhèng Tián and Lú Xíe were both in the Zhōngshū.
During a debate on politics, they fiercely argued and smashed an inkstone.
Wáng Yì sighed and said:
“I did not expect the Zhōngshū to actually have an incident of ‘disintegration like tiles.’”
Jiàngtáo and Liǔzhī
Hán Tuìzhī had two concubines,
one named Jiàngtáo,
the other Liǔzhī,
both skilled in song and dance.
When first sent to Wáng Tíngcòu,
upon arriving at the Shòuyáng post station,
he wrote a quatrain:
“The scenery is about to stir, leaving Cháng'ān,
Mid-spring in the border town is exceptionally cold.
Neither garden flowers nor alley willows are seen,
Only the full moon hangs above the horse's head.”
Liǔzhī later climbed over a wall and ran away.
His household servants pursued and caught her.
When he first returned to Zhènzhōu,
he wrote a poem:
“The willows on the street since we parted,
Sway in the spring breeze, seemingly wanting to fly.
Only the small garden's peaches and plums remain,
Holding their blossoms, not letting them fall, awaiting their lord's return.”
From then on, he favored Jiàngtáo exclusively.
Wǔ Shì Sāntóu
Wǔ Yìhuáng,
when chosen as the top scholar in the prefectural examination, was called jiětóu (解頭);
when he passed the imperial examination, he was called zhuàngtóu (狀頭);
and when he excelled in the hóngcí examination, he was called chìtóu (敕頭).
This is what is known as “Wǔ Shì Sāntóu.”
Requesting salary to write books
Dù Hénán accumulated tens of thousands of scrolls.
On the back of each scroll, he wrote:
“Requested salary to write and personally proofread,
May you, my children, read this and know the sacred Way.
To discard or sell it would be unfilial.”
Obsessed with green-headed ducks
Lǐ Yuǎn (李遠) was the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Hángzhōu (杭州),
and was fond of eating green-headed ducks.
When distinguished guests passed through,
he offered no other gifts;
those he was close to received only a pair of green-headed ducks.
Jade Bowl and Golden Goblet
Lǐ Wèigōng’s (李衛公) residence was in Ānyì (安邑),
Sāng Dàomào (桑道茂) called it the Jade Bowl.
Móu Xiàng’s (牟相) residence was in Xīnchāng Běijiē (新昌北街),
and was called the Golden Goblet.
Ménzhuàng (門狀)
Before Wénzōng (文宗), there were no ménzhuàng.
Since Lǐ Wèigōng (李衛公) became distinguished and prosperous,
officials had no way to gauge his intentions.
They would use an old *cì*
(which is today’s calling card)
to leave their official title,
and await an audience.
This was called *ménzhuàng*.
Juǎn (卷) 32
ends.
Gold and Jade armlets
È Lǜhuá (萼綠華) was a mountain person from Yúnnán (雲南),
a woman,
about twenty years old.
She wore a blue garment from top to bottom.
In Shēngpíng (升平) 1st year, she descended to Yáng Quán’s (羊權) house.
In one month, she visited six times.
Finally, she presented Quán (權) with a poem which said:
“What I seek is not the morning glory,
but to be with my son in the twilight years.”
She also gave him a fire-resistant cloth hand-towel and one each of gold and jade armlets, saying:
“You must not reveal this.
I am Luó Yù (羅郁), a woman who attained the Dao in the Jiǔyí Shān (九疑山).”
Combing Hair
Qīnglíng Zhēnrén (清靈真人) said:
“When combing hair,
one should comb it excessively.”
Qīngxū Gōng (清虛宮)
The Lady of Nányuè (南嶽夫人) said:
“Tomorrow I shall go to Qīngxū Gōng (清虛宮) in Wángwū Shān (王屋山).”
Xiāngyīng (香嬰)
Zǐwēi Wángfūrén (紫微王夫人) came with a divine maiden,
wearing a cloud-brocade robe, a green embroidered belt, her hair in a bun on the crown of her head,
the rest of her hair reaching her waist.
She wore a gold ring on her finger,
and white pearls encircled her arm.
Her countenance was like jade,
and the five fragrances were as rich and fragrant as the scent of burning *xiāngyīng* (香嬰).
*Xiāngyīng* (香嬰)
is *yīngxiāng* (嬰香),
which comes from foreign lands.
She composed a poem which said:
“Cloud-gate stands vertically in the sky,
Jade terrace soars among dense clouds.
Bending down, I rinse from the cloud-vase's stream,
Looking up, I pluck the green *nài* flowers.
I wash my feet in the Jade Heavenly Pool,
And ply the oar in the Cowherd’s River.”
Fúróng Guān (芙蓉冠)
Wáng Zǐqiáo (王子喬), the Zhēnrén (真人) of Tóngbó Shān (桐柏山),
wore a *fúróng guān* (芙蓉冠),
a scarlet robe,
adorned with pearls sewn on,
and carried a sword.
Burying a Dog in a Golden Coffin
Qīngxū Zhēnrén (清虛真人) said:
“The Dao of *huángchì* (黃赤) and the method of mixing *qì* (氣)
are but one technique of the methods taught and propagated by Zhāng Dàolíng (張道陵) for generating offspring,
not the business of a true immortal.
I have often seen those who practice this path become childless,
and never seen offspring generated who attain true life.
This is like embracing jade and rushing into fire,
or burying a dog in a golden coffin.”
This Dao lies in nourishing and dividing life
Zǐwēi Fūrén (紫微夫人) said:
“The yellow books and red realms,
though secret essentials for longevity,
are actually inferior techniques for attaining life.
They are not for the celestial true immortals of the upper palace, nor for those who traverse in carriages of clouds and enjoy the evening scenery, to speak of.
This Dao lies only in nourishing and dividing life.
Those who harbor lustful thoughts,
and also practice the hidden scriptures,
are merely grasping the brush of the water official,
and beating the drum of the three officials.”
Four Difficulties
The Lady of Nányuè (南嶽夫人) said:
“Falsehood
is the ailment of virtue;
ostentation
is the disaster of the body;
lust
is the beginning of loss;
shame
is the key to the body.
Sending away these four difficulties
allows one to inquire about the Dao.”
Consuming the Sun and Eating the Clouds
Jiǔhuá Zhēnfēi (九華真妃) said:
“The sun
is the essence of the clouds;
the clouds
are the essence of the sun.
I have only heard of the method of consuming the sun's essence,
but have not seen knowledge of nourishing with the clouds' essence.
The scripture for consuming clouds is very secret,
but the Dao for attaining clouds is very easy.
This is the method of causing the body to produce jade light,
and the clouds to reflect in the Pure Heavens.”
She also said:
“The eyes
are the mirror of the body;
the ears
are the windows of the body.
Too much looking dulls the mirror,
too much listening closes the windows.
I have a stone for polishing mirrors,
and a technique for opening windows.
The face
is the courtyard of a person;
the hair
is the flower of the brain.
A sad heart withers the face,
a diminished brain grays the hair.
Thus, internal loss of vital essence,
depletes the cinnabar elixir.
I have a scripture for keeping the face youthful,
and a method for restoring black hair.
Essence
is the spirit of the body;
clarity
is the treasure of the body.
Too much toil scatters essence,
too much ambition dissipates clarity.
I have a Dao for benefiting essence,
and a scripture for extending clarity.”
Zhāng Liáng’s (張良) Three Terms
The Lady of Nányuè (南嶽夫人) said:
“Words
are the complete success or failure of one's nature and destiny;
trust
is the key to gain and loss.
Zhāng Liáng’s (張良) three terms
can be called deeply practicing the Dao and clarifying the mind.”
Guarding the Oneness
Diligently practice for one year,
and the head will not turn white,
and bald hair will regrow.
Internally connecting with children and grandchildren, constrained by one's profession;
externally managing royal affairs and friendships.
Widely using eyes and ears,
with mixed sounds and influences,
this Dao is not exclusive,
and actions are fruitless.
If one does not lose their talent,
most examples are recluses,
dwelling among forests and mountains,
far from human society and embracing tranquility,
then one will surely have a youthful face and black temples.
Jade Sweet Wine, Golden Elixir, Intertwined Pears, and Fire Jujubes
These are medicines for soaring and flying,
not comparable to golden elixirs.
If the body is not true, and impure thoughts fill the heart,
I fear these things
will not come.
The roots of fire jujubes and intertwined pears,
for those in whose hearts they should first grow,
if their hearts still contain thorns mixed in,
then these two trees will not be seen.
One can cut away the thorns,
allowing these trees to regrow,
and bear their fruits,
which will not be long.
Daoist Xu in the Mountains and Grand Scribe Xu in the Human World
Yúnlín Wángfūrén (雲林王夫人) said to Grand Scribe Xǔ (許長史):
“Jade sweet wine, golden elixir,
intertwining divine pears,
Fangzhang fire jujubes,
profound immortal ganoderma –
I will give these to Daoist Xǔ (許道士) in the mountains,
not to Grand Scribe Xǔ (許長史) in the human world.”
Daoist Xǔ’s (許道士) given name was Yùfǔ (玉斧),
and he was the son of the Grand Scribe.
Seven Brothers Attained the Dao
Wáng Zǐjìn’s father was Zhōu Líng Wáng.
He had thirty-eight sons.
Zǐjìn
was the crown prince,
and was known as Zǐqiáo.
Seven of his siblings attained the Dao,
five males and two females.
His younger sister’s name was Guānxiāng.
She received the Dao of flying liberation from Zǐqiáo,
and entered the Gōushì Mountains.
His elder brother, Méishòu,
also attained the Dao.
Qīngtóng Shī
Qīngtóng Dàjūn said:
"If you wish to eradicate the root of oblivion,
you must uproot the plant of birth and death.
Hesitating, you fall into the Nine Springs,
merely because you cling to your form and bones."
Shénxíng Rú Chēmǎ
Dàxū Zhēnrén said:
"When observing the spirit carrying the form,
it is also like a carriage following a horse.
When the carriage breaks and the horse flees,
their connection is temporarily severed.
Alas, the world does not recognize this;
they merely cherish their qi.
They sow sins upon the heavenly net,
and suffer torment in the depths of hell."
Dùxíng Zhōu
Xīchéng Zhēnrén said:
"The form is the boat that carries the spirit;
once it docks, it must depart.
Lingering in the wheel of birth and death
is merely the agony of an indecisive mind."
Zǐwēi Gē
Zǐwēi Fūrén sang:
"I lifted my skirt to cross the green river,
and there I saw Fúsāng Gōng.
A grand gathering at Dàlín Xū,
feasting and reclining in Xuánhuá Gōng.
If one truly trusts the Dao with pure sincerity,
why not dwell on the eastern peak?"
Cǎi Wǔzhī
Shíyīng chanted:
"One with a heart promised to Fǔzǐ
spoke of gathering the five zhǐ.
The zhǐ grass may not be obtained,
and you may not be able to come either."
Jīnjiāng Yùruí
Shíyīng referred to the Qióngdān,
one dose of which enables the Nine Glories to fly thrice.
In the morning, the cloud liquid is deeply imbibed,
and the flowing yellow lingers.
One swallows the golden plasma,
and chews the jade essence.
One’s appearance changes in the mansion of the three yin,
and one’s corpse undergoes nine transformations to regain a youthful face.
Nánzhēn Fūrén
Nán Rén,
who is Nánzhēn Fūrén,
is said to have attained the Dao and departed the world,
sometimes appearing, sometimes hidden.
Sometimes she would re-imbibe the essence of jade and knock on her coffin,
while one dose of dāoguī would cause the corpse to decay.
Lùpí Wēng swallowed the jade essence, and worms emerged from his pores.
Qiú Jìzǐ swallowed golden fluid, and the stench was perceptible for a hundred li.
Huángdì forged the Nine Cauldrons at Jīngshān,
yet there remained the tomb of Qiáolǐng.
Jìzhǔ took the cloud powder to ascend in concealment,
yet his head and feet were in different places.
Mòqiū swallowed the rainbow elixir and threw himself into water.
Níngshēng took rock marrow and plunged into fire.
Wùguāng cut leeks and entered the abyss of Qīnglíng.
Bǎichéng absorbed qi, and his intestines and stomach decayed thrice.
The traces of those who attained the Dao, whether they departed or remained, were truly unpredictable.
Shījiě
After a person's death,
if their form appears as if alive,
it is all shījiě.
The feet are not green,
the skin is not wrinkled,
the eyes are not damaged,
no different from a living person.
Those whose hair falls out completely and whose bones lose their form
are all shījiě.
Ascending to heaven in broad daylight is truly becoming an immortal,
not an instance of shījiě.
Rén Sǐ Shì Tàiyīn
If a person temporarily dies,
they enter the Great Yin.
Those who temporarily pass through the Three Officials,
whose flesh decays and blood sinks,
will have their five zàng organs regenerate.
Their white bones become like jade,
their seven pō souls constantly attend,
and their three hún souls guard within.
The three yuán qi temporarily cease,
and the Great Spirit is enclosed within.
After twenty or thirty years, they emerge at will,
collecting blood and nourishing flesh,
generating essence and refining fluids,
restoring their substance and forming a body,
which is superior to their appearance before death.
This is what is meant by a zhēnrén refining their form in the Great Yin
and changing their appearance at the Three Officials.
Dé Dào Zhī Shì
For scholars who have attained the Dao and temporarily sojourn in the Great Yin,
Tàiyī guards the corpse,
the three hún souls protect the bones,
the seven pō souls guard the flesh,
and the fetal spirit records the qi.
Yùchén Dàdào Jūn
The Tàishàng
is the descendant of the Dao,
and is the Shàngqīng Zhēnrén,
namely the son of Yùchén Dàdào Jūn.
Sì Zhēnrén
Lǎojūn
is a disciple of the Tàishàng.
At the age of seven, he knew the essentials of longevity,
and thus became Tàijí Zhēnrén.
There are four zhēnrén.
Lǎojūn is on their left,
wearing the talisman of the divine tiger,
carrying bells of flowing gold, a staff with purple fur, and a headdress of golden essence.
Báifà Xuánshí Zhòng Shíwàn Jīn
Liú Wěidào of Zhōngshān
studied immortality for twelve years.
An immortal tested him with a stone,
weighing one hundred thousand jin.
It was suspended by a single white hair,
and the immortal made Wěidào lie beneath it.
Wěidào felt at peace in mind and body,
and lay beneath it for twelve years.
The immortal then bestowed upon him a divine elixir, and he ascended to heaven in broad daylight.
Dōngwáng Gōng Xīwáng Mǔ
In the early Hán dynasty,
there were four or five children playing.
One child sang:
"Wearing a green skirt,
entering the heavenly gate.
Bowing to Jīnmǔ,
saluting Mùgōng."
At that time, no one understood,
only Zhāng Zǐfáng went and paid homage to them.
This was the jade boy of Dōngwáng Gōng.
Jīnmǔ
is Xīwáng Mǔ.
Mùgōng
is Dōngwáng Gōng.
Immortals bow to Wáng Gōng,
and salute Wáng Mǔ.
Shí Táopí Yǐn Shí Zhōng Huángshuǐ
Huáng Zǐyáng,
a man from Wèi,
was in the Bólùo Mountains.
He ate peach skin
and drank yellow water from rocks.
Sīmǎ Jìzhǔ offered him respect as an immortal in all directions,
and thus he passed into the next world.
Sānguān
For practicing the Dao, one must keep the three passes constantly in harmony.
The three passes are:
the mouth as the heart pass,
the feet as the earth pass,
and the hands as the human pass.
If the three passes are in harmony,
the five zàng organs are at peace,
and then the entire body will be without illness.
Xīn Bùzhèng
To make the heart upright,
one should always, when the sun is three zhàng high,
cross one's hands and place them on both shoulders,
with the sun directly over the heart.
When warmth is felt in the heart,
the heart will be upright.
There was Jiāng Bózhēn who practiced the Dao.
While gathering herbs, he encountered an immortal.
The immortal made him stand upright in the sun, but his posture was crooked.
The immortal said:
"You are earnestly dedicated to learning immortality,
but you do not know that an unrighteous heart is a flaw."
Thereupon, he taught him this method,
and he subsequently attained the Dao.
Firm Grasp
Constantly at midnight,
remove the pillow and lie flat.
Maintain a firm grasp and relax the body.
When the qi is regulated and subtle,
the body and spirit are complete.
Hidden Shell Worm
Those who attain the Dao possess the method of the hidden shell worm,
and thus perceive the technique of the three corpses (sān shī).
When the shell worm dies, the three corpses wither.
When the three corpses wither, they naturally fall away.
Nine Difficulties
Students of the Dao have nine difficulties:
having aspiration but no time,
having time but no friends,
having friends but not meeting their teacher,
meeting the teacher but not understanding,
understanding the teacher but not being diligent,
being diligent but not adhering to the Dao,
or adhering but not firmly,
firmly but not enduring.
These are the nine difficulties for a person.
Great Taboos for Studying the Dao
Joy and anger damage aspiration.
Sorrow and grief damage nature.
Glory and splendor affect virtue.
Yīn and Yáng exhaust essence.
These are the great taboos for studying the Dao.
Do Not Eat Too Much, Do Not Lie Down When Full
Be careful not to eat too much;
eating too much causes illness.
Lying down immediately after being very full,
lying down causes the mind to wander.
A wandering mind often leads to loss of nature.
If eating too much causes illness,
then medicine will not be effective.
Shìguī Method
The Shìguī method makes one's eyes clear.
Always at the Jiǎzǐ (甲子) cycle, take eastward flowing clear water,
mix it with real cinnabar (zhēndān) and wash the eyes with it.
Exhale Stale Qi, Inhale Fresh Qi
Those who wish to cultivate the Dao
should constantly exhale stale qi from the mouth
and inhale fresh qi.
Be cautious with laughter and measured with words,
constantly contemplate its form.
Yángtái
Wángwū Shān (王屋山)
is a celestial realm separate from the earthly,
known as Yángtái (陽臺).
Those who initially attain the Dao
all proceed to Yángtái,
which is the abode of pure emptiness.
Tàidòng Zhēnjīng
Tàidòng (太洞)
is Shénzhōu (神州).
Shénzhōu has two other mountains,
each mountain has seven palaces,
and each palace has seven transformations.
In the morning, they transform into gold;
at midday, they become copper;
at night, they transform into light;
or they become mountains, or water, or stones.
These are called the seven transformations.
The seven transformations have seven scriptures,
and the seven scriptures have thirty-one jade youths (yùtóng) who accompany this book.
Therefore, it is called the Tàidòng Zhēnjīng (太洞真經).
Read it ten thousand times and you will become an immortal.
Tàijí Yǐnzhī
Làngyě (閬野)
is the residence of Làngfēng (閬風).
On Kūnlún (崑崙) there are nine residences,
which are the nine palaces (jiǔgōng).
Tàijí (太極) is the Great Palace.
All immortals are officials of the nine palaces.
Those who understand the Great Cavern (Dàdòng) are immortal ministers (xiānqīng).
Those who consume golden elixir (jīndān) are grand masters (dàfū).
All varieties of Ganoderma (zhī) are imperial censors (yùshǐ).
By consuming the Tàijí Yǐnzhī (太極隱芝),
one becomes a left or right immortal duke (xiāngōng) and a True Person (zhēnrén).
Corpse Release Immortal
Corpse Release Immortals (shījiě zhī xiān)
cannot ride the phoenix canopy (huágài),
mount flying dragons,
ascend to Tàijí,
or wander the nine palaces.
Yángdān
Yángdān (陽丹) in nine transmutations.
People of the world all possess this art,
referring to matters of the bedchamber (fángzhōng zhī shì).
Yángdān can also be made into Yīndān (陰丹).
A Treatise on Taking Zhú
Madame Zǐwēi's (紫微夫人) "A Treatise on Taking Zhú (Fúzhú Xù)" says:
"Observing how quickly various herbs benefit oneself,
none compare to Zhú (朮).
The qi of Zhú suppresses malevolent qi,
lightens the body and prolongs life,
clears bodily fluids,
enriches blood,
nourishes the brain,
expels evil,
attracts the True,
preserves essence,
and guards life.
Ancient people called it the 'Essence of the Mountain's Herbs'
and 'Essence of Mountain Ginger.'"
The Tàishàng Zūnxiān Míng (太上遵仙銘) says:
"If you desire longevity,
you should take the essence of the mountain.
If you desire to soar lightly,
you should take mountain ginger."
Five Difficulties
Lord Xīchéng Wáng Jūn (西城王君) said:
"For a person to depart from the three evil paths and be reborn as a human is
difficult;
to leave the female form and become male is
difficult;
to have complete six senses and four limbs is
difficult;
to be born in the Central Kingdom (Zhōngguó) is
difficult;
to meet virtuous parents and a benevolent ruler is
difficult."
Uprooting the Root of Love and Desire
Lord Qīngtóng Jūn (青童君) said:
"For a person to cultivate the Dao,
being able to uproot the root of love and desire
is like picking hanging pearls,
picking them one by one,
there will be a time when they are all gone;
eliminating external evils
will also have an end.
When they are gone, then it is the Dao."
The Dao is in the Interval of Breath
Tàishàng (太上) said:
"A person's life is but a few days."
Someone said, "It is but a single day."
Someone else said, "It is but the interval of a meal."
Tàishàng said these were not yet the Dao.
Someone then said, "It is in the interval of breath."
Tàishàng said:
"Excellent!
This can be called the Dao."
Feeding Dao Students
Tàixū Zhēnrén (太虛真人) said:
"Feeding a hundred ordinary people
is not as good as feeding one virtuous person;
feeding a thousand virtuous people
is not as good as feeding one Dao student."
There Are Five Difficulties in the World
Madame Zǐyuán (紫元夫人) said:
"There are five difficulties in the world:
giving charity when poor is difficult;
studying the Dao when rich and powerful is difficult;
controlling one's destiny and not dying is difficult;
gaining access to the Dòngjīng (洞經) is difficult;
being born in the sagely age after Rénchén (壬辰) is difficult."
Practicing the Dao is Like Polishing a Mirror
Tàishàng said:
"Practicing the Dao is like polishing a mirror.
When the dirt is removed, clarity remains,
and one will see one's true form.
Cut off the six emotions,
maintain emptiness,
and see the truth of the Dao,
and you will also know your past lives.
Furthermore,
to contemplate the Dao, practice the Dao, and believe in the Dao,
thereby attaining the root of faith,
its blessings are immeasurable."
Children Craving Honey on a Blade
Madame Zǐwēi (紫微夫人) said:
"For those who cultivate the Dao,
it is like carrying a fire into a dark room;
the darkness immediately vanishes,
and only light remains.
Wealth and sensuality to oneself
are like a child craving honey on a blade;
its sweetness is not enough to please the mouth,
but there is the danger of cutting off the tongue."
Without love, there is no worry.
Nánjí Fūrén said:
“From love, people give rise to sorrow;
when sorrow arises, then there is fear.
Without love, there is no sorrow;
without sorrow, there is no fear.”
Practicing the Dào is like playing the qín
Tàishàng Zhēnrén asked someone:
“Have you ever played the qín?
What is it like when the strings are slack?”
They replied:
“It makes no sound, nor is it sorrowful.”
He asked again:
“What is it like when the strings are taut?”
They said:
“The sound is cut off and it is sorrowful.”
He asked again:
“What is it like when the slackness and tautness are just right?”
They replied:
“All sounds are in harmony,
and the eight tones play wonderfully.”
Zhēnrén said:
“When practicing the Dào, holding the mind in proper adjustment
is also like playing the qín;
then the Dào can be attained.”
Cherishing Qì
The heart of practicing the Dào is like remembering the morning meal;
there is no one who does not attain it.
Cherishing qì is like cherishing one's face and eyes;
there is no one whose integrity is not preserved.
Seeking fame is like burning incense
People, following custom, seek fame,
like burning incense.
Everyone smells its fragrance,
not knowing that it is consumed by its own burning.
When it is completely burned, its qì perishes.
When fame is established, the body perishes.
Digging a well
Practicing the Dào is like digging a well:
the deeper the shape, the harder it is to transport the excavated soil.
One must open one's heart
and rectify one's conduct,
then the spring source will be seen.
Rubbing the face
The Tàisù Jīng says:
“On the face,
the two hands should constantly rub and wipe it to make it warm,
which makes people radiant
and prevents wrinkles and spots from appearing.
Lightly rub the two palms together to make them warm,
then wipe the two eyes with them,
and then smoothly stroke the hair as if combing it.
Alternately rub the two arms with the hands.
The hair will not turn white,
and the pulse will not float externally.”
Managing the city walls and irrigating the central peak
The Xiāomó Jīng says:
“If the body is not at ease,
one should curl the tongue back to block the throat, gargle fully,
and swallow the fluid countless times.
The body will naturally become relaxed and soft.
Pressing and suppressing frequently
makes one intelligent and clear-sighted;
this is called ‘managing the city walls’
and having one's name recorded in the imperial register.
One should also press the left and right sides of the nose
to make the qì balanced;
this is called ‘irrigating the central peak’
and having one's name recorded in the emperor's register.”
Closing the eyes and looking inward
The Jīng says:
“When sitting, one should always close the eyes and look inward,
visualizing the five zàng organs and intestines and stomach.
If practiced for a long time,
one will naturally see them clearly and distinctly.”
Clacking the teeth and swallowing fluid
Zǐwēi Fūrén said:
“When waking up at night,
clack the teeth nine times,
swallow fluid nine times,
and press the nose up, down, left, and right with the hands several tens of times.”
Hair-combing incantation
The Jiéfà Zhòu says:
“Níwán Xuánhuá,
preserve essence and long endure.
The left is the hidden moon,
the right is the root of the sun.
The six harmonies are refined and purified,
and all spirits receive grace.”
After the incantation, swallow fluid five times.
If one can consistently practice this,
the hair will not fall out and will grow daily.”
The Jīng says:
“When grooming hair, one should face the royal direction.”
Burning incense
Nányuè Fūrén said:
“When burning incense, do not look back,
lest you offend the true qì and invite evil responses.
When entering a quiet chamber,
first place the right foot forward,
so that one's message can reach higher realms.
When eating, do not speak of death,
fearing it might bring evil qì to the food.
When bathing, always visualize the six Dīng,
which allows one to attain whatever one wishes.”
Holding breath and bowing in stillness
The Zhèngyī Píng Jīng says:
“Hold your breath and bow in stillness,
making all ghosts fear and dread.
Then the Gōngcáo envoys and Lónghǔ Jūn
can be seen and spoken to daily.”
Good and bad dreams
Frequently encountering bad dreams
may be due to: first, soul monsters;
second, mental trials;
third, corpse thieves.
Upon waking from a dream,
pinch the philtrum fourteen times with the left hand,
and clack the teeth fourteen times.
This will turn ill luck into good fortune.
If you have a good or bad dream at night,
upon waking,
you should rub your eyes fourteen times
and clack your teeth fourteen times.
Ingesting the sun and moon
Dōnghuá Zhēnrén ingests the images of the sun and moon.
Men ingest the image of the sun,
women ingest the image of the moon.
If not abandoned for a single day,
it makes people intelligent
and the five zàng organs flourish.
Tàixū Zhēnrén said:
“On the fifth day of the month, at midnight,
visualize the image of the sun in your heart.
The sun enters through the mouth,
shining within the entire heart.”
Archery
To practice the Dào should be like shooting an arrow:
go straight forward without looking back,
then one can reach the target.
Reading the Dàodé Jīng
Tàijí Zhēnrén said:
“Read the Dàodé [Jīng]'s five thousand words ten thousand times,
and then a cloud chariot will come to welcome you.”
Impetuous nature
Zhōng Jūn said:
“An impetuous and violent nature
is the thief-disease of one's body,
and a stubborn obstacle to seeking the Dào.
Those who pursue it, the truth departs;
those who change it, the Dào comes.”
Compounding elixir
Xiǎo Máojūn said:
“Cinnabar, realgar, and orpiment
are found in every household,
yet no one ever compounds them.”
He also said:
“One can compound several furnaces,
bathe frequently,
soak in the qì of its waters to cure ailments,
and eliminate the stupidity of accumulated filth;
this is also a step towards true attainment.”
Beds should be high
When people sleep, their beds should be high.
If high, the earthly qì does not reach,
and ghosts cannot affect one.
Ghost qì, when it invades people,
does so by rising from the ground upwards.
Method for slaying ghosts
The method for the emperor to slay ghosts:
first clack the teeth thirty-six times,
and then recite the Tiānpéng Zhòu.
Wind disease
Wind disease originates in mounds, graves, and damp, shaded places,
where the three springs are obstructed and stagnant.
Therefore, the earth officials, by stirring up water qì,
often cause wind paralysis.
Eight seasonal nodes
On the days of the eight seasonal nodes,
one should plan good deeds.
One must not be angry or quarrelsome, happy or sad,
or inflict punishments.
True people and the six fluids
A student's method
should not involve weeping, shedding tears, or excessive spitting.
Therefore, the Perfected Person (Zhēnrén) regularly practices exhalation and inhalation, swallowing saliva,
to harmonize the six fluids.
On the days of the Five Maǒ (Wǔ Maǒ),
Jiǎyín and Gēngshēn,
which are days when corpse-demons (shīguǐ) compete and cause chaos, and the spirit is restless and defiled,
husband and wife should not share a mat.
One should fast purely and not sleep.
On all days of the Five Maǒ,
one should purify the heart and preserve the spirit,
keeping the vital energy (qì) ever-present.
If this is done,
Jade Maidens (Yùnǚ) will descend.
Do not eat garlic.
Huáng Xiānjūn’s oral instructions:
When taking medicine, one should not eat garlic, pomegranate seeds, or pig and dog head meat.
At dusk, visualize the sun and moon.
Qīngniú Dàoshì’s oral instructions:
At dusk, when lying down, visualize the sun on the forehead and the moon on the navel.
This wards off a thousand ghosts and ten thousand evils,
and causes Jade Maidens (Yùnǚ) to descend.
Treasure Gold and White Jade of the Earth's Lungs (Dìfèi Bǎojīn Báiyù).
Jīnlíng has the richness of the Gōudū.
The Earth's Lungs (Dìfèi) of Jùqǔ
have been trodden by tens of thousands,
but none truly know them.
Máoshān, the foremost altar in the world,
has treasure gold and white jade on all four sides,
each weighing nine thousand jīn,
buried only nine chǐ deep.
Bowing to a tree to beg for longevity.
There was a person who loved the Way (Dào),
but did not know its methods.
Morning and evening, he would bow to a withered tree,
always saying, "I beg for longevity."
He did this for twenty-eight years without growing weary.
One day, the tree sprouted purple blossoms (huá),
and their sweet sap was like honey.
After eating them, he immediately became an immortal (xiān).
This was due to his utmost sincerity.
There was a person who frequently bowed and paid respects towards Tàihuàshān.
One morning, the Elder of the Western Marchmount (Xīyuè Zhàngrén) bestowed upon him the path of immortality.
Another person bowed to the river for ten years,
and consequently saw the River Lord (Héhóu) and the River God (Hébó),
who taught him the method of traveling on water without drowning.
Three grades of addressing the earth.
There are three grades of those who address the earth's masters.
There are also three grades of addressing ghosts and spirits.
Ingesting mist energy (wùqì).
Zhāng Wēizǐ of Hàn often ingested mist energy.
He said that mist energy is the essence (huájīng) of mountains, marshes, water, and fire,
and the abundant energy (yíngqì) of metal and stone.
Long-term ingestion allows one to scatter one's form and enter the void,
merging with cloud energy.
Wēizǐ received the method from Dōnghuá Yùfēi.
What is true for the great is also true for the small.
Wáng Yǎn's daughter of Jìn,
courtesy name Jìnxián,
was the consort of Mǐnhuái Tàizǐ.
When Luòyáng was in chaos,
Liú Yào abducted Jìnxián,
intending to make her his wife.
Jìnxián cursed, saying:
"I am the wife of the Crown Prince (Huáng Tàizǐ) and the daughter of the Minister of Works (Sītú Gōng)!
How dare you, a barbarian boy (húqiāng xiǎozǐ),
interfere with me?"
She then threw herself into Mèngjīn.
Her maidservant Liùchū said:
"What is true for the great,
is also true for the small."
She too threw herself into the river.
Perfected Woman of Sōnggāo (Sōnggāo Nǚzhēn).
Hán Xīhuá went out traveling,
met and befriended two people,
and took them into the cave within Huáyáng Guān.
Five-colored hidden zhǐ (wǔsè yǐnzhī).
In Dàhuò of Luójiāng, there is a cave.
Within the platform, there are five-colored hidden zhǐ.
In Huáyángdòng, there are excellent five-night种光芝.
In Chángshān, there are fluorescent zhǐ.
If one eats one piece,
one aperture in the heart becomes clear.
If one eats seven pieces, seven apertures become clear.
If one eats forty-nine pieces,
one's lifespan is ten thousand years.
Planting five fruits.
Jiāng Shēngmào, Marquis of Bālíng,
lived at the foot of Jùqǔshān.
He planted five fruits and five pungent vegetables,
and often bought vegetables to trade for cinnabar (dānshā).
Shēngmào was enfeoffed as a marquis during the Qín Dynasty.
Today, this place is named Jiāngdì.
There was also Guō Sìcháo, who planted apples (nài),
known as the apples of Fúxiāng.
Ingesting fetal energy (tāiqì).
Lóng Bógāo of the Later Hàn Dynasty
received the method of ingesting fetal energy from the immortal Dāo Dàolín.
Prisons of the Three Officials (Sānguān Yù).
The Three Officials (Sānguān) have a prison official (yùguān)
named Dàlǐ.
Lǐ Fēng was appointed as Dàlǐdū.
Another position remained vacant,
intended for Wáng Fùzǐ,
but it was not given to Xǔ Hǔ.
Buddhist Way (Fódào) and Immortal Way (Xiāndào).
Perfected Person (Zhēnrén) Péi had thirty-four disciples.
Eighteen of them studied the Buddhist Way,
and the rest studied the Immortal Way,
receiving the method of concealing the form and transforming the body (cángjǐng huàxíngfǎ).
Sīmǎ Jìzhǔ entered Wěiyǔshān
and received the method of "Stone Essence Gold Light Concealing Form and Transforming Body" (Shíjīng Jīnguāng Cángjǐng Huàxíngfǎ) from Tàixuán Xiānnǚ.
Traveling three thousand lǐ in a day.
Sòng Déxuán,
a contemporary of Zhōu Xuān,
attained the Way (Dào)
and could travel three thousand lǐ in a single day.
Dragon's Music in Ling'e, Phoenix Drums in Yunzhí (Lóng Zòu Líng'ē, Fèng Gǔ Yúnchí).
Sipping nine-turn elixirs and transforming into a corpse,
swallowing knife-blade elixirs and flowing like worms –
Sīmǎ Jìzhǔ, Yān Zhāowáng, and Wángzǐ Jìn are examples of this.
Zhōu Mùwáng traveled north to the foot of Kūnlún,
drank the stone marrow of Jiàngshān,
and ate the fruits of the jade trees,
yet was ultimately buried in Jí Jùn.
Xià Yǔ went to Zhōngshān,
ate purple apples (zǐnài), got drunk on golden wine (jīnjiǔ), ingested spiritual fruits (língshí), and practiced the Nine Truths (Jiǔzhēn),
yet was still buried in Kuàijī.
Dàwáng of Běiróng Chánghú presented Emperor Shùn with white wolf jade frost (báiláng zhī yùshuāng).
Shùn transformed into purple splendor (zǐhuá) and then died,
buried in the wilderness of Cāngwú.
All these sages, though performing dragon's music in Líng'ē and phoenix drums in Yúnchí,
how can they be compared to decaying skeletons in the Great Yin (Tàiyīn),
who feed their flesh to worms and ants?
Péngzǔ's name was Kēng.
Mr. Qīngjīng, Péngzǔ,
whose name was Kēng,
the Four Hoary Elders of Nánshān and the Eight Dukes of Huáinán,
all chose to retreat to mountains and forests in luxury,
finding joy in wandering as immortals,
and sorrow in ascending to the void.
It was not that they could not ascend to heaven,
but that they chose not to.
The Perfected Being (Zhìrén).
The Perfected Being (Zhìrén) in the Primal Qi (Yuánqì) is the Primal Lord (Yuánjūn);
in the Dark Palace (Xuángōng) is the Dark Master (Xuánshī);
in the Southern Star (Nánchén) is the Old Man of the South Pole (Nánjí Lǎorén);
in the Great Void (Tàixū) is the Perfected Person of the Great Void (Tàixū Zhēnrén);
in the South is Chìsōngzǐ.
Tóngbáishān is
eighteen thousand zhàng high.
The mountain has eight circling layers,
extending over eight hundred lǐ.
The trees are sparse, fine jade, and jasper.
The springs are stone nectar and gold essence.
The entire mountain is made of five-colored gold.
Fēngdū Palace names.
If people know the names of the six heavenly palace gates of Fēngdū,
then a hundred ghosts will not dare to cause harm.
Rice named Chóngsī.
The rice of Fēngdū
is named Chóngsī.
Its grains are like pomegranate seeds,
and are also offered to immortal officials (xiānguān).
Ghost Official of the Northern Dipper (Guǐguān Běidǒu).
The Lord of the Ghost Official of the Northern Dipper (Guǐguān Běidǒu Jūn)
is the examining official of the seven stars (qīchén) and the Northern Dipper (Běidǒu) in Daoism.
This ghost official (guǐ yīguān)
is also subordinate to the essences of the Nine Stars (Jiǔxīng Jīng),
and reports to the Jade Lord of the Northern Dipper (Běichén Yù Jūn) in heaven.
Since the Northern Dipper in heaven has overseeing duties,
the ghost officials also establish this position.
Wǔwáng Fā is now the Lord of the Northern Dipper (Běidǒu Jūn);
Xià Qǐ is the Duke of Eastern Illumination (Dōngmíng Gōng),
leading the Dipper Lord masters;
Wénwáng is the Duke of Western Illumination (Xīmíng Gōng),
leading the Northern Dipper masters;
Shào Gōng Shì is the Duke of Southern Illumination (Nánmíng Gōng);
Wú Jìzhā is the Duke of Northern Illumination (Běimíng Gōng).
The Four Dukes of Illumination (Sìmíng Gōng) have four guests and friends,
and these four dukes will also ascend to the immortal ranks later.
The Four Dukes of Illumination lead the ghosts of the four directions.
Pavilion Head of the Heavenly Gate (Tiānmén Tíngzhǎng).
Běidǒu Jūn is the Pavilion Chief of the Heavenly Gate.
Currently, Zàng Hóng, Jì Zhān, and Yú Tán
are taking turns for one day to guard the Heavenly Gate.
Yīn Hào attends the Imperial Morning Court,
facing Hé Yàn.
Wēn Tàizhēn is the Earl who oversees the Sea Countries.
He appointed Dù Yù as his Chief Clerk.
A clean and flourishing abode.
One's bedroom should be kept clean.
If it is flourishing, it receives spiritual energy.
If it is not flourishing, it receives old energy.
When old energy disturbs a person's abode,
what they do will not succeed,
and what they create will not be established.
The same is true for their own person.
One should wash and bathe to be clean.
Old energy
is the turbid, impure energy of ghosts and spirits.
Ghosts and spirits and teeth-gnashing.
When walking at night, one should constantly gnash their teeth.
Ghosts and spirits fear the sound of teeth-gnashing,
thus they cannot harm people.
In addition, rinsing the mouth with saliva is also good.
Attending the Imperial Morning Court.
There are eight people attending the Imperial Morning Court:
Lǐ Guǎng, Wáng Jiā, Hé Yàn, etc.
They are like the Palace Attendants of this world.
Four Luminaries' guests and friends.
Wèi Wǔdì is the Grand Preceptor of the Northern Palace.
Sūn Cè, Hàn Gāozǔ, Jìn Xuāndì, and Xún Yù
are the guests and friends of the Four Luminous Lords.
Southern Palace Immortals.
Those with hidden virtue
are directly appointed to immortal official positions.
Or they enter the Southern Palace to be transformed,
unrestricted by rank.
In this world, their family's portion is weighed by the amount of good and bad deeds.
Generally, those who practice hidden virtue
and show much compassion for the poor and distressed
all proceed to the Southern Palace to become immortals.
Yuánguī leads ghost soldiers.
Gēng Yuánguī is the Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Emperor's Central Guard.
He appointed Huà Xīn as his Chief Clerk,
who is called Jūn Gōng.
He leads several thousand ghost soldiers.
Wénjǔ seeks a substitute.
Kǒng Wénjǔ is the Grand Master of the Rear Central Guard.
General Táo Kǎn is the Marquis of Xīhé.
He requested Téng Hán to substitute for himself.
It was not granted yet.
Yìshǎo imprisoned.
Yìshǎo was imprisoned for a matter.
It has been five years.
It is said that the matter has been resolved.
Loyal and filial people as rulers of the underworld.
Loyal and filial people,
upon their death,
all become rulers of the underworld.
After 140 years, they receive the teachings of the lower immortals,
are granted the Great Dao,
and gradually become immortal officials.
Bǐ Gān is now in Róngshān.
Xuè Shàn is in Shàoshì.
Many have achieved this transformation.
These two are merely cited as examples.
Utmost Truth.
Those of utmost truth
cannot have their righteous energy scattered by worldly splendor.
Speaking of men,
it is the conduct of Wù Guāng.
Speaking of women,
it is the daughter of Sòng Jīntán.
Heroes do not become immortals.
The talents of various heroes
are to punish the violent, rectify chaos, and establish imperial reigns.
Upon their death,
they receive documents from the Three Officials and Four Assistants,
or become the Prime Ministers of the Five Emperors,
or become the guests and friends of the Four Luminaries.
They assist in governing the hundred ghosts
and manage life and death in the villages.
These individuals are subject to the Three Officials,
and have no hope of advancing to immortality
because of their killing, cruelty, and harm.
Qín Shǐhuáng is now the Prime Minister of the Northern Emperor.
Liú Jì is a guest and friend of Nánmíng.
This is the case.
Colleagues of the Three Officials.
Qí Huángōng is the Chief Prohibitor of the Three Officials,
who presides over the registers of life and death.
Jìn Wéngōng is the Director of Destinies for the Water Official.
These positions are colleagues of the Three Officials.
They are not involved in the affairs of true immortals.
Yùchí Xuángōng.
Bāchúnshān is fifty *lǐ* high.
It is connected to Cānglàng Fāngshān.
Below it is the Azure Sea.
Above it is Sānglín Zhēnrén Yùchí Xuángōng,
the place where Dōngwáng is stationed.
Dì Kù's Nine Transformations and Ten Metamorphoses Classic.
The Jade Son
is Dì Kù.
He went to Zhōngshān,
obtained the Nine Transformations and Ten Metamorphoses Classic,
to conceal himself from the sun and moon
and travel among the stars.
One day he collapsed and died quickly.
Later, those who unearthed his tomb
only found a sword
that made sounds like a dragon roaring and a tiger howling.
Yùxiāo Língfáng.
Dàdào Yùchén Jūn,
ascending to Yùxiāo Língfáng,
looks out over the world for those with ambition and a desire for distant travels.
Learning the Dao by first curing illness.
Those who learn the Dao
must first cure illnesses,
so that the body does not have deficiency or evil, or lack blood and brain reduction.
There was a Daoist, Wáng Zhòngfǔ,
who absorbed the two luminaries and consumed *xiá* (aurora) for over forty years,
but felt no benefit.
His son also practiced it,
and ascended to heaven in broad daylight after eighteen years.
The Nányuè Zhēnrén descended and taught Zhòngfǔ, saying:
"Your body has a great illness.
Your brain palace is diminished,
and your tendons and fluids do not flow.
Although you perform the methods of the luminaries and consume *xiá*,
it is not beneficial for your body."
Zhòngfǔ then took medicine to treat his illness
and continued his practice.
