Later, he also ascended to heaven.
Preserving spiritual light.
When preserving spiritual light and performing immortal practices,
one must not lend clothes to others
nor wear objects that are not one's own.
Headwear, robes, shoes, and clogs
should all be kept fresh and clean.
The three *hún* and seven *pò* spirits may reside within them,
and they are also the *qì* of the five spirits.
Therefore, dampness and defilement are avoided.
Pondering the Dao and expounding on scriptures.
Whenever contemplating the profound Dao,
while reading ten or twenty words of sacred scripture,
one should lick their lips and swallow saliva once or twice.
For one hundred or fifty words,
one should gnash their teeth three or two times
to harmonize the spirits and regulate blood and *qì*.
Divine medicine.
When taking divine medicine,
do not face north, as it is a heavenly taboo.
On *hài* and *zǐ* days, one should not sleep,
as it causes loss of essence, loss of *qì*,
and reduces one's lifespan.
Lǎozǐ's days for pulling out white hair.

The 4th day of the 1st month, the 8th day of the 2nd month, the 11th day of the 3rd month, the 16th day of the 4th month, the 20th day of the 5th month, the 24th day of the 6th month, the 28th day of the 7th month, the 19th day of the 8th month, the 16th day of the 9th month, the 13th day of the 10th month, the 12th day of the 11th month, the 7th day of the 12th month
are Lǎozǐ's days for pulling out white hair.
The Heavenly Emperor's days of killing.

The *gēngshēn* day of the 1st month, *xīnyǒu* of the 2nd month, *gēngxū* of the 3rd month, *guǐhài* of the 4th month, *rénzǐ* of the 5th month, *guǐchǒu* of the 6th month, *jiǎyín* of the 7th month, *yǐmǎo* of the 8th month, *jiǎchén* of the 9th month, *dīngsì* of the 10th month, *bǐngwǔ* of the 11th month, *dīngwèi* of the 12th month
are the Heavenly Emperor's days of killing.
All matters are unsuitable on these days.
Yúnlín Fūrén.
Wáng Mèilán,
the thirteenth daughter of Āmǔ's younger brother,
is named Yúnlín Fūrén.
Jade pendant and gold *dāng*.
Immortals have jade pendants and gold *dāng*
to ascend to the Great Ultimate.
Method of consuming the sun and moon's rays.
The sun has nine rays,
and the moon has ten rays.
At Fāngzhūgōng, there is a method for consuming the sun and moon's rays.
Patrolling the Grotto Heavens.
The Dōnghǎi Jūn rides a solo *piāo* flying-wheel chariot
to patrol all the Grotto Heavens.
Hánzhēntái.
Recluses who attain the Dao
reside at Hánzhēntái.
Maiden immortals who attain the Dao
reside in Xiāotáng.
Hair not turning white.
Concentrate your mind, empty your form, embrace the Xuan, contemplate the spirit, and steadfastly guard the True One.
Then your hair will not turn white,
and baldness will instead become thick and black.

There has never been anyone who, with a hundred thoughts entangled in their chest, with cold and heat breaking their spirit, whose mouth spoke of the convergence of auspicious and inauspicious, whose body arranged the gates of gain and loss, who embraced the Dao but did not practice it, who held treasure but did not use it,
yet hoped their head would not turn white.
Such a thing is rarely heard of.
The Ford of Death, the Way of Life.
Xiǎo Yǒu Zhēnrén said:
"Those who lose the Dao follow the Ford of Death.
The three souls are bewildered on the Way of Life.
The day of life is already distant,
the day of death is already early."
Taking huánglián brings immortality.
Liú Fènglín,
a man of the Zhōu dynasty,
studied the Dao on Sōngshān for four hundred years.
He thrice successfully concocted divine elixirs,
but was thwarted by evil entities.
So he entered Wěiyǔ Shān.
He could hold his breath for three days without exhaling.
Now, over a thousand years later, he has still not ascended to immortality,
but merely by taking huánglián, he achieved immortality,
though he cannot command or direct anything.
Báishí Shēng breaks from grain.
One who often boiled white pebbles in the mountains,
using stones as food,
was known by the world as Báishí Shēng.
End of Scroll 33.
Dēngkē Jì (Records of Successful Candidates)
Before Yǒnghuī,
the two examinations of Jùn and Xiù were still ranked alongside the Jìnshì;
after Xiánhēng,
all those who were recommended by the authorities through literary studies
competed in the Jìnshì examination.
From then on, Zhào Cǎn and others subsequently discarded the Jùn and Xiù categories.
Therefore, it was designated as "Jìnshì Dēngkē Jì".
Heroes enter my snare.
Táng Tàizōng privately visited Duānmén,
and upon seeing the newly successful Jìnshì candidates walking out in procession,
he joyfully exclaimed:
"The heroes of the realm have entered my snare!"
Jìnshì titles.
Lǐ Zhào's 《Guóshǐ Bǔ》 (Supplement to the History of the State) says:
"The Jìnshì examination has long been esteemed by the times.
Those who emerge from it
remain literati for life.
The main examination hall where they gather
is commonly referred to as Xiùcai;
submitting their name card is called Xiānggòng;
passing the examination is called Jìnshì;
mutual admiration and respect are called Xiānbèi;
passing together is called Tóngnián;
the official in charge is called Zuòzhǔ;
those who passed the examination in the capital, Jīngzhào, and were promoted, are called Děngdì.
Those recommended by external prefectures without examination are called Bájiě;
those who vouch for each other before the examination are called Hébǎo;
grouping together for practice examinations is called Sīshì;
soliciting requests from powerful figures is called Guānjié;
promoting one's reputation and prestige is called Huánwǎng.
After passing, listing one's name on the Cí'ēn Sì pagoda
is called
Tímíng;
the grand banquet at Qǔjiāng is for those
registered and selected,
and is called Chūn Guān.
Being drunk and satiated without passing is called Dǎ Màosào;
anonymously slandering is called Wúmíngzǐ;
retreating to continue studies is called Guòxià;
bringing one's previous work is called Xiàkè;
bringing a statement to the examination is called Shūcè."
Commoner Grandees.
The Jìnshì examination began in the Dàyè era of the Suí dynasty,
and flourished during Zhēnguān.
Although high-ranking officials attained the highest positions as subjects,
those who did not pass the Jìnshì examination
were ultimately not considered distinguished.
Annually, eight or nine hundred people were recommended,
and they were called "Báiyī Gōngqīng" (Commoner Grandees),
or "Yīpǐn Báishān" (First-Rank White-Robed Scholars).
Their difficulty was described as: "A thirty-year-old passing the Míngjīng is old;
a fifty-year-old passing the Jìnshì is young."
At the time, there was a poem that said:
"Emperor Tàizōng's truly long-term strategy
tricked all the heroes until their hair turned white."
Xījiān (Western Directorate).
According to Suí regulations:
The Xījiān was established during the Lóngxiáng period.
Before Kāiyuán,
it was considered shameful for Jìnshì candidates not to pass through the two directorates.
Jìnshì candidates return to the Board of Rites.
The Jùn, Xiù, and other categories
were initially managed by the Bureau of Merits.
During the Kāiyuán era,
the junior official Lǐ Áng, who was strong-willed and impetuous,
gathered the tribute scholars and said:
"The merits and flaws of your writings are all known.
If there are any solicitations or requests,
I shall be the first to reject them."
Soon after, Áng's maternal uncle, who was close to Chancellor Lǐ Quán,
recommended Quán to Áng.
Áng became enraged,
summoned Quán, and publicly rebuked him in the courtyard,
further humiliating Quán by pointing out flaws in his verses and sentences.
Quán bowed and stepped forward, saying:
"My humble writing is indeed not good;
I have already heard your command.
However, you, sir, once wrote a poem that said:
'My ears I wash by the clear Wèi River,
my heart is at leisure towards the white clouds.'
Emperor Táng Yáo, in his old age,
weary of the world,
intended to abdicate to Xǔ Yóu.
Yóu, disliking what he heard,
therefore washed his ears.
Today, His Majesty is in the prime of his life,
and does not offer abdication to you,
yet you wash your ears.
Why is this?"
Áng was shocked and terrified,
and reported to the high officials, claiming Quán was mad and disrespectful.
Consequently, Quán was handed over to the authorities.
Thereafter, if there were any requests or connections,
none were refused.
The imperial court, considering the power of the bureau officials too light,
from then on changed to using the Minister of the Board of Rites.
Shénzhōu Děngdì Lù (Records of Ranked Candidates from Shénzhōu).
The recommendations from Shénzhōu,
from the time of Tiānbǎo and Kāiyuán,
usually included more than ten people,
who were called "Děngdì" (ranked).
They always sought those whose reputation matched their actual ability.
The Junior Minister of Rites would select them,
sometimes to the point of complete transformation;
otherwise,
seven or eight out of ten would be chosen.
If there was any deviation from this,
a formal request would be sent to the examination office to have them dropped.
Hence, there was the "Shénzhōu Děngdì Lù" (Records of Ranked Candidates from Shénzhōu),
to commemorate the abundance of talented individuals.
Zhāng Yòu and Xú Níng's Poems.
When Bái Lètiān was governor of Hángzhōu,
many Jìnshì candidates from Jiāngdōng hurried to Hángzhōu to take the recommendation examination.
At that time, Zhāng Yòu and Xú Níng both arrived.
Yòu said:
"I should be the first-place candidate (Jiěyuán),
it is fitting."
Níng asked:
"What excellent lines do you have?"
Yòu replied:
"In 《Gānlù Sì》, there are 'The light of sun and moon arrives first,
the might of rivers and mountains all comes forth.'
In 《Jīnshān Sì》, there are 'Tree shadows seen amidst the flowing current,
the sound of bells heard on both banks.'" Níng said:
"Good, indeed good,
but how do they compare to the commoner's lines:
'For a thousand ages, it flies like white silk,
a single strip breaking the green mountains' hue'?" Yòu was astonished.
Níng indeed was selected.
The giant 鳌 (áo) crowns Pēngshān.
Lú Zhào,
during Kāichéng, took the Jiāngxī recommendation examination,
and ultimately did not pass.
Zhào thanked him, saying:
"The giant áo carries the bìxì,
crowning Pēngshān."
The examiner said:
"Yesterday, because the candidates were ranked together,
I am deeply ashamed to accept your request regarding the ranking.
How can there be talk of 'crowning'?"
Zhào replied:
"A stubborn rock sits on top,
a giant áo carries it.
Is this not 'crowning' itself?"
Báiyī Qīngxiàng (Commoner Grandee).
Lú Huī, a Jìnshì,
styled himself "Báiyī Qīngxiàng."
He sought to gather at the college.
After the results of the *jìnshì* examination were released,
Xiè Hòu (謝後) went again to the Periodical Assembly Institute (*Qījí Yuàn* 期集院).
On that day,
the *zhuàngyuán* (狀元) met with his *tóngnián* (同年) (fellow graduates),
and one person was invited to serve as the recorder (*lùshì* 錄事).
Others were appointed to host the banquet, preside over the wine, manage the music, act as the *tànhuā* (探花), or serve the tea, and so on;
all were assigned on that very day.
There were two music managers (*zhǔyuè* 主樂),
one of whom oversaw the courtesan singers (*yǐnjì* 飲妓).
After the榜 *bǎng* (list) was released,
the two *dàkētóu* (大科頭) were
of the first section.
The one *xiǎokētóu* (小科頭) was
of the second section.
An ordinary banquet was managed by the *xiǎokētóu*;
a grand banquet
was managed by the *dàkētóu*.
Even if there was no banquet,
they were given tea money on the day of gathering.
For the Grand Assembly at Qújiāng (曲江),
a dispatch was first sent to the Imperial Music Bureau (*Jiàofāng* 教坊) to request a performance.
The Emperor would ascend the Zǐyún Tái (紫雲臺),
lower the curtain, and observe.
Families of dukes and ministers often chose sons-in-law on this day.
Carriages and horses filled the roads.
Those invited as *yīpō* (衣鉢) (spiritual heirs),
from the *zhuàngyuán* downward,
would dismount at the residence of the chief examiner (*zhǔsī* 主司),
stand in a line,
present their folded name cards,
and formally bow to the chief examiner.
The chief examiner would say:
"Please state your *míngdì* (名第) (rank in the exam),
which number,
and your *yīpō* (衣鉢)."
Banquet Names
There were nine banquet names:
First was *Dà Xiāngshí* (大相識), when the chief examiner had both parents living.
Second was *Cì Xiāngshí* (次相識), when the chief examiner had one parent living.
Third was *Xiǎo Xiāngshí* (小相識), when the chief examiner had brothers.
Fourth was *Wénxǐ* (聞喜), the banquet given after the imperial decree.
Fifth was *Yīngtáo* (櫻桃).
Sixth was *Yuèdēng* (月燈).
Seventh was *Mǔdān* (牡丹).
Eighth was *Kàn Fóyá* (看佛牙) (Viewing the Buddha's Tooth Relic).
Ninth was *Guān Yàn* (關宴).
This was to mark the difficult banquet for the eldest son (*dàláng nán yán* 大郎難筵).
Presumptuous Due to Talent
Xiāo Yǐngshì (蕭穎士) was presumptuous due to his talent.
He once carried wine to the countryside.
A sudden storm of wind and rain arrived,
and an old man in purple robes sought shelter from the rain.
Yǐngshì was quite rude and insulting.
After a short while, the rain cleared.
Carriages and horses suddenly arrived.
The old man mounted his horse
and departed with attendants clearing the way.
It was said that he was Minister Wáng (王尚書) of the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù* 吏部).
The next day, Yǐngshì prepared a long letter and went to his gate to apologize.
The minister reprimanded him, saying:
"I regret that I am not your relative;
otherwise, I would give you a stern family lesson!
You bear the name of a literary scholar,
yet you are so arrogant and negligent.
Will you stop at merely passing one examination?"
Yǐngshì indeed ended his career as a Judicial Assistant (*gōngcáo* 功曹) in Yángzhōu (揚州).
The Bureau (*Tuánsī* 團司) Catches Lú Tuán (盧彖)
Cuī Hàng (崔沆) was the chief recorder for penalties.
His *tóngnián*, Lú Tuán,
skipped the *Guān Yàn* nearby
and requested leave to go to Luòyáng (洛).
When the *tóngnián* were feasting at the Qújiāng Tíngzi Tuán (曲江亭子彖),
Lú Tuán,
with an ornate carriage carrying courtesans,
dressed in plain clothes, loosely holding the reins, looked on,
and was caught by the Bureau.
Hàng ruled, saying:
"Deeply tucked his pointed hat,
tightly held the reins of his felt carriage.
Seeking spring on the purple streets,
he was thus separated from the faces of his *tóngnián*;
having found a path to high office,
it is known what his future intentions will be."
Surpassing Yuán (元) and Bái (白)
In the *Yùlì* (玉曆),
Chancellor Yáng Sīfù (楊嗣復), with both parents still living,
was subsequently appointed to two other positions.
At that time, the former Executive Assistant (*púyè* 僕射) entered the court from eastern Luòyáng.
Sīfù led his students to welcome him at Tóngguān (潼關).
Upon his return,
a grand banquet was held at his residence in Xīnchāng Lǐ (新昌里).
The students sat respectfully,
Yuán Zhèn (元稹) and Bái Jūyì (白居易) were both present.
Poems were composed.
Only Yáng Rǔshì's (楊汝士) poem was finished later,
and it was the best.
Yuán and Bái admired and submitted to it.
Rǔshì, drunk, returned home and said:
"Today, I have surpassed Yuán and Bái."
His poem's striking lines were:
"The old value of literature remains in the imperial antechamber,
new shade of peach and plum is in the carp court."
Hú Qí's (胡錡) Congratulatory Letter
Minister Cáo Fén (曹汾) was stationed in Xǔxià (許下).
His son, Xīhàn (希幹), passed the examination,
using twenty *wàn* (萬) (200,000) *qián* (錢) (copper coins).
When the list arrived at the garrison,
on the day the congratulatory banquet was held,
it was displayed on the side.
The *jìnshì* Hú Qí presented a letter, saying:
"Where the cassia branch is broken,
it wears the colorful robe of rapeseed;
when the willow leaf is pierced,
it uses Lǔ Lián's (魯連) old arrow."
He also said:
"From a thousand *lǐ* (里) away,
one observes the scenery of the capital;
before ten thousand troops,
one displays the spring beauty of Cháng'ān (長安)."
The 'Two-Headed Lady' Bows to the Madam
Minister Yáng Rǔshì (楊汝士) was stationed in Dōngchuān (東川).
His son, Zhīwēn (知溫), passed the examination.
At the banquet,
Rǔshì ordered an official courtesan to be given a bolt of red silk.
A poem said:
"The young master is proud in his youth,
and the general of Shǔ (蜀) is not poor.
One high song, one bolt of silk,
the 'two-headed lady' bows to the madam."
Cherry Blossom Banquet (*Yīngtáo Yàn* 櫻桃宴)
New *jìnshì* particularly valued the Cherry Blossom Banquet.
During the Qiánfú (乾符) reign,
Chancellor Liú (劉相) was stationed in Huáinán (淮南).
His son, Tán (覃), passed the examination.
He instructed his household manager, saying:
"Collect contributions for the expenses,
just enough will suffice."
At that time, cherries were just in season.
They were mixed with sugar and cream,
each served in a small jar,
no less than several *shēng* (升).
Reporting Luó (報羅)
Luó Jiè (羅玠),
passed the examination in the Zhēnyuán (真元) period and held a banquet.
While boating on Qújiāng,
Jiè drowned.
Later, those who died before the final imperial examination were
called "reporting Luó".
Red Name Cards
Péi Sīqiān (裴思謙) passed the examination as *zhuàngyuán*.
He made more than ten red name cards
and went to Píngkāng Lǐ (平康里),
where he stayed overnight.
He composed a poem, saying:
"The silver lamp leans back, unfastening ringing pendants,
soft whispers congratulate the jade lord in hushed tones.
From this day forth, I know not the value of orchid and musk,
for last night I caught a new scent of cassia branches."
Chǔ Rùn (楚閏) Has Feelings
Zhèng Héjìng (鄭合敬) stayed in Píngkāng Lǐ after passing the examination.
His poem said:
"In spring, there's nowhere one doesn't stroll idly,
Chǔ and Rùn look at each other with special feelings.
How delightful it is, waking from residual wine at the fifth watch,
to repeatedly hear calls for the *zhuàngtóu* (狀頭) (top scholar)."
Chǔ Niáng (楚娘) and Rùn Niáng (閏娘)
were among the most prominent courtesans.
Indeed Returned with the Brocade Pennant
Lú Zhào (盧肇),
a native of Yíchūn (宜春),
went to take the imperial examination with Huáng Pō (黃頗) from the same prefecture.
Pō was wealthy, Zhào was poor.
The prefect of the commandery gave Pō a grand farewell,
while Zhào passed by on his limping donkey.
The next year,
Zhào returned after passing the examination as *zhuàngyuán*,
and was welcomed by officials from the prefect downward.
While watching a dragon boat race,
Zhào composed a poem at the banquet, saying:
"They said it was a dragon, but I wouldn't believe it;
indeed it returned holding the brocade pennant."
Granny Three to Five Years Younger
Xuē Jiān (薛監) in his later years suffered setbacks in his official career.
Once, he rode his emaciated horse to court.
He happened to encounter newly successful jinshì (進士) candidates filing out.
The servants of the metropolitan secretariat (團司) seeing them approached, shouted at him, and ordered him to make way.
Xuē Jiān dispatched a messenger saying:
"Report to them, don't ask for a prime minister (xiàng 乞相)!
When this old woman (ā pó 阿婆) was three or five years younger,
she also scribbled around a bit."
Cùjū Huì (蹙鞠會)
During the Xiántōng (咸通) era,
new jinshì gathered at Yuèdēng Gé (月燈閣) for a cùjū (蹙鞠) gathering.
Viewing stands were densely arrayed on all four sides,
and fellow graduates (tóngnián 同年) looked on from every direction.
Zōu Huí (鄒希回), over seventy years old,
had passed the examination at the very end of the list.
When his fellow graduates were about to take their seats,
Zōu Huí insisted on taking one more tour around.
Someone joked about him saying:
"How could he even hope for a 'return' (huí 回)!?"
Tǎ Xià Tímíng (塔下題名)
Since the Shénlóng (神龍) era,
after the Apricot Garden (Xìngyuán 杏園) banquet,
it became customary to inscribe names beneath the pagoda of Cí'ēn Sì (慈恩寺).
Among the fellow graduates, a calligrapher was chosen to record the names.
Later, if one became a general or prime minister,
their name would be written in red ink.
After passing the examination, if one learned of
or encountered a name inscribed from a time before passing,
the character "qián" (前, "former") would be added.
Someone composed a poem saying:
"At the place where names were once inscribed, a 'qián' character is added,
sending off the city-goer, begging for an old poem."
Yī Shuāng Qián Jìnshì Liǎng Gè Ā Háir (一雙前進士兩箇阿孩兒)
Miáo Táifú (苗台符) was sixteen years old,
Zhāng Dú (張讀) was seventeen.
They both passed the jinshì examination in the same year,
and together served as aides in the staff of Zhèng Shàoshí (鄭少時) in Xuānzhōu (宣州).
They once jointly inscribed their names in Xīmíng Sì (西明寺),
where someone secretly added a note saying:
"A pair of 'former' jinshì,
two little children."
Wéi Chán Tí Shī (韋蟾題詩)
Lǐ Yáng (李陽) inscribed his name on the tower of Zhāoyìng Xiàn (昭應縣).
Wéi Chán (韋蟾) playfully inscribed a poem:
"The Wèi (渭) River and Qín Chuān (秦川) flash brightly before my eyes,
but why is Xīrén (希仁) so lacking in poetic sentiment?
He must have only learned from the husband of Yú Jī (虞姬),
only able to write his name."
Yī Jǔ Jídì (一舉及第)
Bái Lètiān (白樂天) passed the examination on his first attempt,
and wrote a poem saying:
"At the place of inscription beneath Cí'ēn Pagoda,
the youngest among seventeen people."
At that time, he was twenty-seven years old.
He carried his provincial examination essays, "Xìng Xí Xiāng Jìn Yuǎn Fù" (性習相近遠賦) and "Yù Chuān Jì Fāng Liú Shī" (玉川記方流詩),
to pay a visit to Lǐ Féngjí (李逢吉).
Initially, Lǐ Féngjí paid him no mind,
but upon seeing the beginning of the fu (賦) which read:
"Alas!
It descends to man,
and ascends to reach the lord;
virtue is established by compliance,
and nature is divided by habit,"
Féngjí was greatly astonished by him.
Jìnggōng Yīndé (晉公陰德)
Péi Jìnggōng (裴晉公) had a small and insignificant physique.
A physiognomist said:
"Sir, your form and spirit do not match the physiognomic texts.
If you do not achieve great nobility,
you will surely starve to death.
I truly do not see any noble traits in you now."
One day, he visited Xiāngshān Sì (香山寺).
A woman placed a piece of fine patterned silk upon the railings of the sanghā (僧伽) hall, praying and wishing.
She cast divining blocks, bowed, and left.
Péi Jìnggōng saw what she had left,
and picked it up.
By evening,
the woman had not returned.
The next morning, he carried it back again.
The woman from before rushed forward, clutching her chest, and said:
"My father was unjustly imprisoned.
Yesterday, I asked someone
to borrow two jade belts and
one rhinoceros-horn belt
to give to an influential person.
Unfortunately, they were lost,
and my old father's calamity cannot be escaped!"
Péi Jìnggōng then returned them to her.
The woman bowed and wept,
asking to keep one of them.
Péi Jìnggōng did not answer and left.
Later, he saw the physiognomist who said:
"You must have performed some hidden virtuous deeds that benefited others.
Your future is boundless,
not something I can comprehend."
Péi Jìnggōng indeed reached the highest position among officials.
Yóu Zhù Máyī Dài Zhìgōng (猶著麻衣待至公)
Liú Xūbái (劉虛白) and Péi Gōng (裴公) of Tàipíng (太平) had studied together early on.
By the time Péi Gōng became a chancellor,
Liú Xūbái was still a jinshì candidate.
He presented a poem before the screen saying:
"Twenty years ago on this very night,
the same lamps, the same wind.
Who knows how many years have passed,
still clad in plain cloth, waiting for the illustrious Duke."
Cǎo Lǐ Lùn (草裡論)
Fāng Gàn (方干) was a student of Xú Níng (徐凝).
Fāng Gàn once satirized Xú Níng saying "debating new poems in the weeds,"
which was a pun for "village elder (cūn lǐ lǎo 村裡老)."
Lǐ Pín (李頻) was a student of Fāng Gàn.
Later, Lǐ Pín passed the examination,
and the monk Qīngyuè (清越) presented Fāng Gàn with a poem:
"The disciple has already obtained the cassia (guì 桂),
the master still tends the garden."
Hán Tuìzhī Gǔ Zhī Wén Gǔ Zhī Rén (韓退之古之文古之人)
Lǐ Áo (李翱) said:
"The writings of Hán Tuìzhī (韓退之)
are the writings of the ancients;
the man himself
is a man of the ancients."
Huáng Pǒ (黃頗) of Yíchūn (宜春), a student of Hán Yù (愈),
also achieved renown.
Huáng Pǒ, seeing Lú Zhào (盧肇) climbing a stele,
spat scornfully and walked away.
Hán Yù, in his interactions with people,
if someone died, he would assist their orphans,
and arrange humble marriages for them.
Mèng Jiāo (孟郊), Zhāng Jiè (張藉), and others were examples of this.
Téngwáng Gé (滕王閣)
Wáng Bó (王勃) wrote "Téngwáng Gé Xù" (滕王閣敘)
when he was fourteen years old.
Governor Yán Gōng (閻公) did not believe it,
and ordered someone to observe him as he wrote.
The initial report said:
"Old Nánchāng (南昌) Prefecture,
new Hóngdū (洪都) Commandery."
The Duke said:
"An old scholar's common talk."
Then it continued:
"Stars divide Wěi (翼) and Zhěn (軫),
the land connects Héng (衡) and Lú (廬)."
The Duke remained silent.
Upon reaching "Fallen clouds and a lonely wild goose fly together,
autumn waters and the vast sky are of one color,"
the Duke, startled, said:
"This is true genius!
It will endure eternally!"
Pāibǎn Yuē Yuè Jù (拍板曰樂句)
Hán Yù (韓愈) and Huángfǔ Shí (黃甫湜)
were the 'dragon gate' of their generation.
Niú Sēngrú (牛僧孺) brought his works to visit them.
The first piece, "Shuō Yuè" (說樂),
Hán Yù, upon seeing the title,
immediately closed the scroll and asked:
"And what is a pāibǎn (拍板)?"
Niú Sēngrú replied:
"It is a musical phrase (yuè jù 樂句)."
The two dukes greatly praised him.
Waiting for an opportune moment,
they visited him,
and wrote in large characters on his gate:
"Hán Yù and Huángfǔ Shí visited together."
The next day,
from the passes downward,
everyone came to present their calling cards.
Consequently, his fame soared.
Fànhòu Zhōng (飯後鐘)
Wáng Bō (王播) was poor and an orphan in his youth.
He once stayed at the Mùlán Yuàn (木蘭院) in Yángzhōu (楊州),
eating meals with the monks.
The monks grew tired of him,
so by the time Wáng Bō arrived,
they had already eaten.
Two decads later,
he came to govern this region.
The inscription he had written earlier was already covered with a green gauze curtain.
Wáng Bō wrote a poem:
"Twenty years ago, I visited this temple,
Mùlán flowers bloomed, the courtyard newly repaired.
Now I revisit the path I walked,
trees are old and flowerless, monks are white-haired."
He also wrote:
"After the morning meal, everyone scattered east and west;
I am ashamed, Venerable Śramaṇa, for the bell after the meal.
For twenty years, dust has covered my face;
only now do I get a green gauze cage."
Fùguì Zài Lǐ (富貴在裡)
Zhèng Lǎng xiànggōng met a monk who said:
"Lángjūn's position is as high as a minister to the emperor,
but he has no share in passing the imperial examination.
If he passes,
his entire life will be fraught with difficulties."
Later,
he became a *zhuàngyuán* and passed the examination.
Congratulatory guests filled his gate,
but this monk did not come.
When he was re-examined,
and subsequently retired,
many people offered condolences,
but this monk alone offered congratulations,
saying:
"Wealth and honor are within."
It turned out exactly as predicted.
**Washing Bowls with a Monk**
Shāng Xiànggōng studied at Zhōngtiáo Shān Sì,
washing bowls with a monk.
**Robes like Tarnished Silver, Writings like Brocade**
During the Yuánhé reign,
Lǐ Liánggōng's thirty-three candidates were all from humble backgrounds.
At the time, there was a poem that said:
"In the *bǐngshēn* year of Emperor Yuánhé,
thirty-three people became immortals together.
Their robes were like tarnished silver, their writings like brocade,
together they ascended to the azure heavens in broad daylight."
**Lonely and Cold Shed Tears**
Lǐ Déyù greatly opened the path for those from humble backgrounds.
When he was demoted and exiled to the south,
someone composed a poem:
"Eight hundred lonely and cold people all shed tears,
at once looking south towards Lǐ Yázhōu."
**Zhào Yǐlóu**
Dù Zǐwēi, upon reading Zhào Wèinán's poem, recited:
"A few scattered stars, wild geese cross the frontier,
a long flute's sound, a person leans against the tower."
Therefore, he referred to Jiǎ as "Zhào Yǐlóu."
He further presented a poem saying:
"Among the generals of literature in this era,
who can ascend the altars of Lǐ and Dù?
Bālíng's whale sea stirs,
the Hányuàn's crane sky is cold."
**Spirit of the Great White Star**
Lǐ Táibái paid a visit to Hè Zhīzhāng.
Hè Zhīzhāng said:
"You are not a person of the human world,
could you not be the spirit of the Great White Star?"
**Above All Talents**
Sūn Wò once dreamed of hundreds of stacked logs,
and Wò walked back and forth upon them.
Lǐ Yuán said:
"Next year you will certainly be the *zhuàngyuán*.
Why?
You are already above all talents."
It turned out exactly as he said.
**The Latter Will Surely Get It**
In the year Bì Xián xiànggōng passed the examination,
at night he listened to a divination.
For a long time, he heard nothing.
Suddenly, someone threw a bone to the ground,
and a pack of dogs rushed to contend for it.
One said:
"The latter will surely get it."
**Mistook Yán Biāo for Duke Lǔ**
Zhèng Xūn shìláng, presiding over the literary examination,
mistakenly believed Yán Biāo was a descendant of Duke Lǔ.
At that time, Xú Fāng was not yet pacified,
and his intention was to inspire loyalty and bravery.
So he made Biāo the *zhuàngyuán*.
On the day of gratitude,
when asked about his ancestral temple.
Biāo said:
"Being from a humble background,
I have never had one."
Only then did he realize his mistake.
Someone mocked him, saying:
"The examiner's mind is utterly muddled,
mistakenly taking Yán Biāo for Duke Lǔ."
**Caught the Clothes Thief**
On the night Lǐ Tíngbì was taking the examination,
he unexpectedly found a half-sleeve in his cubicle.
Tíngbì rose and put it on.
His roommate said:
"This is not given by the gods."
Soon after,
someone was captured,
shouting loudly:
"The clothes thief has been caught!"
**Sweet Osmanthus Close to Cháng'é**
Péi Yún married Xiāo Chǔgōng's daughter,
and immediately passed the *jìnshì* examination.
Luó Yǐn's poem said:
"Upon closer look, the moon still holds meaning,
truly knowing the sweet osmanthus is close to Cháng'é."
**Wearing Straw Cloaks Over Brocade Robes**
Xǔ Mèngróng passed the *jìnshì* examination.
As a scholar who passed the imperial examination,
he was then known as "wearing straw cloaks over brocade robes."
**The *Jìnshì* Are Prone to Frivolity**
Huángfǔ Shí wrote to Lǐ Shēng, saying:
"Recently, there has been a tendency towards frivolity,
especially among the *jìnshì*,
to the extent of a saying 'one modesty for twenty years.'
Before a poem has a single line from Liú Chángqīng,
they already call Ruǎn Jí an old soldier;
before a brush-speech has a single character from Luò Bīnwáng,
they already curse Sòng Yù as a criminal.
Before they know how to write characters,
they talk loftily of Jì and Qì;
before they know the punctuation of their books,
they look down on Fú and Zhèng."
**Ten Sages of Fānglín**
Shěn Yúnxiáng and ten others,
having connections with powerful eunuchs,
were called the "Ten Sages of Fānglín."
Fānglín
was the name of a gate,
through which one entered the palace.
**Acquaintance of the Emperor**
Liú Yè was specially granted the *jìnshì* degree.
Wéi Xiù's congratulation said:
"Thirty years of superficial fame,
happens every year.
An acquaintance of the emperor,
is something unheard of for ages."
**Four Kinds of Affinity**
Lǐ Zhì and Lǐ Mǐn shared the same surname,
were of the same age,
entered the same school,
and passed the examination in the same year.
Zhì's poem said:
"Though our destinies differ across three eras,
our affinities are the same in four ways."
**Song of the Noble Young Master**
Qín Tāowáng's *Song of the Noble Young Master* says:
"Before the steps, the clover balls roll not,
the turtle's eye sprays fragrance, impossible to pluck.
Scattered flowers weave brocade, willow twists thread,
adorning the pond pavilion, painting screens unfold.
They laugh at the scholar holding his book scroll,
having learned Yán Huí's hunger-enduring face."
**Five Elders' List**
Dù Déxiáng passed Zēng Sōng and five others,
all over seventy years old.
At that time, it was called the "Five Elders' List."
**Sutra of a Thousand Buddhas' Names**
Zhāng Zhào failed the examination.
He held the list of successful candidates on his head, saying:
"This is the Sutra of a Thousand Buddhas' Names!"
**Visiting Prime Minister Lǐ and Not Meeting Him**
Píng Zēng visited Prime Minister Lǐ in Huázhōu but did not meet him.
He chanted:
"This old man stood before the gate for three days,
the pearl curtain and silver screen remained closed all day.
My poetry scroll is cast back into my bookbag,
just like idly watching Huàshān come into view."
**Name Card Growing Hair**
Liú Lǔfēng went to visit an acquaintance,
but was blocked by the gatekeeper.
He chanted:
"Liú Lǔfēng, a scholar of ten thousand volumes,
travels a myriad *lǐ* through mist and waves to visit Wénwēng.
Having no money to bribe the usher Hán,
my name card grows hair, he will not announce me."
**Song of the Wine Barbarian**
Lú Wāng, whose clan was foremost in the realm, failed the *jìnshì* examination.
His poem said:
"Sorrowful that rise and fall depend on silk and finery,
the world still chooses fair ladies.
Yuèwáng conquered the state of Fūchā,
one Xīshī was already too many."
In his later years, disheartened,
he wrote the
*Song of the Wine Barbarian*, saying:
"The barbarian's appearance resembles a man,
tipping from side to side without stability.
Haste and slowness are decided by man,
not by the wine barbarian.
Not a single drop enters the gut,
idly letting the wine barbarian be called wine barbarian."
**Ice Soul, Snow Spirit**
Liú Dé-rén,
son of Guì,
frequently participated in the imperial examinations,
but ultimately achieved nothing.
He said:
"Although my maternal relatives are emperors,
I have no close kin in power."
After his death,
the monk Qī-Bái wrote a poem:
"Having endured hardship for poetry until now,
his icy soul and snowy spirit are already difficult to recall.
Only when osmanthus blossoms fall upon his tomb,
and a branch sprouts, will his grievance truly dissipate."
Flower ornaments covering the face, Xú Fēi's half-makeup
When Jiǎng Níng took the Hongcí examination,
the fu he composed only reached four rhymes,
yet it was instantly widely circulated.
Someone remarked:
"A white-haired person with flower ornaments covering the face
is not as good as Xú Fēi's half-makeup."
Fu on Slaying the White Serpent
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Bái Lè-tiān took the Hongcí examination.
He was tested on "The Fu on Hàn Gāo-zǔ Slaying the White Serpent,"
but failed.
The fu contained the lines: "Those who know me
slay the White Emperor;
those who do not know me
slay the white serpent."
While the fu of those who passed the examination were unheard of,
Bái Gōng's fu
was circulated throughout the realm.
Embroidering with folded gold
Zhào Mù emulated Lǐ Cháng-jí in writing short songs,
which could be described as "embroidering with folded gold,"
leaving no trace on the surface.
Plum Blossom Poems
Cuī Lǔ's "Plum Blossom Poems" say:
"More than half are thin due to last night's snow,
a few branches are sorrowful because of the evening sky."
And also:
"Just opened, already painted on carved beams;
not yet fallen, already fearing the jade flute's blow."
His "Lotus Flower Poem" says:
"Without cause, I untie my dust-free sleeve,
to hold the lingering fragrance, cherishing it all day long."
Lǐ Tāo's Poems
Lǐ Tāo had a reputation for poetry,
such as "The sound of water is always in my ears,
the mountain colors never leave my door,"
"When sweeping the ground, flowers leave shadows;
when dusting the bed, the zither has a sound,"
"The sun sets on Cháng'ān Road,
autumn locust trees are covered with blossoms on the ground."
Exempted from village duty for poetry
Rèn Tāo's poem contains the lines: "Dew gathers, sand gulls rise;
people lie, fishing boats drift."
He failed the examination several times.
Lǐ Zhì, as Inspector of Jiāngxī,
specially exempted him from village duty.
When some criticized this,
Zhì ruled:
"Within Jiāngxī province,
anyone whose poetry is as good as Tāo's
will also be exempted from village duty,
not just Tāo."
Fu on Wrestling
Zhōu Jiān's "Fu on Wrestling" says:
"Those in front are powerful, those behind are adversaries,
all are strong individuals;
grasping with the left, seizing with the right,
all are hands skilled in boxing."
Poem on the Osmanthus in the Moon
Zhāng Qiáo tested with his "Poem on the Osmanthus in the Moon":
"With the moon, it is perpetually vast and indistinct,
its sparse branches forever unchanged.
Its roots are not born of the low earth,
its leaves do not fall in autumn wind.
Each time it is round, it is full;
it becomes empty when the moon wanes.
Its shadow is high above other trees,
its fragrance fills the entire orb.
Before it was planted in the azure sky,
it must have filled the white jade palace.
When will I, through feather-transformation,
get to subtly question its divine power?"
Pile of Brocade
Xiè Tíng-hào was famous for his ci and fu,
and was called "Pile of Brocade."
Lǐ Dòng's Poems
Lǐ Dòng's poem says:
"In the sound of the mortar, I pound a remnant dream;
in the shadow of the tea pot, I boil a solitary lamp."
His "Poem for Sending Someone Back East" says:
"Islands divide many nations,
the Milky Way shares a single sky."
Wú Zǐ-huá's Poems
Wú Zǐ-huá's poem says:
"In the warm ripples, fish leave their young;
in sunny rambles, deer lead their fawns."
Apology for violating a taboo
The jinshì Chǔ Zài presented his credentials to Assistant Minister Sū Wēi,
and some characters inadvertently violated the taboo name.
Zài submitted an apology,
which roughly said:
"Although Cáo Xīng's paintings are exquisite,
he ultimately regretted his mistaken brushstroke;
Yīn Hào's careful conduct had a great flaw,
leading to the delivery of an empty letter."
Young Master of the Eastern Pavilion
On the Double Ninth Festival, Lǐ Yì-shān visited Chancellor Líng-hú,
but did not see him.
He inscribed a poem on a screen and left.
The poem says:
"Once with Shān Gōng, I held a wine cup,
in frosty heavens, white chrysanthemums were scattered.
Ten years beneath the springs, no news;
on the Double Ninth before the wine-jar, I have thoughts.
Do not learn from Han officials who planted lucerne,
but rather be like the Chu guest singing of river orchids.
The young master is ashamed to be a running horse,
and has no reason to peer again into the Eastern Pavilion."
Vajra Pestle
Xuē Bǎo-xùn was fond of distributing his voluminous works,
and called himself "Vajra Pestle."
During the Tàihé era, the homes of high officials and gentry were filled with scrolls,
often becoming fuel for the gatekeepers' and maids' lamps.
Upon seeing those who took it lightly, he would say:
"If it is a scroll by Xuē Bǎo-xùn,
the compensation received is double the usual."
Nine-ribbed Turtle of Yuán-jiāng
When Lú Zhào first
took the imperial examination, someone asked where he came from.
Zhào said:
"I am a citizen of Yuán."
Someone replied:
"Does Yuán-zhōu produce successful candidates?"
Zhào said:
"Yuán-zhōu produces successful candidates,
just as Yuán-jiāng produces turtle shells;
those with nine ribs are truly rare."
Great Skinny Fellow
Lǐ Bái jokingly presented Dù Fǔ with a poem:
"By Chánglè Slope, I met Dù Fǔ,
wearing a bamboo hat at midday.
May I ask, why is your figure so skinny?
It is simply because you have always toiled hard at poetry."
White Paper Table
Successful candidates often covered their tables with white paper.
Zhèng Chāng-tú's poem says:
"A newly covered table,
its whiteness like silver.
Entering examinations, exiting examinations,
for a thousand springs, ten thousand springs."
Sea of Bitterness
Zhèng Guāng-yè had a large leather trunk.
Whenever he received a submission that was laughable,
he would throw it into it,
calling it the "Sea of Bitterness."
Mortal eyes, poor bones
When Zhèng Guāng-yè was taking an examination,
a colleague burst in at night,
and in the Wú dialect said:
"Absolutely, absolutely,
may I share your space?"
Guāng-yè cleared half a bed space for him.
The person said:
"I beg to take a scoop of water,
and further ask for a bowl of tea to be brewed."
Guāng-yè happily fetched water
and brewed tea for him.
Two days later,
Guāng-yè passed the examination as zhuàngyuán.
The person offered an apology, saying:
"You were troubled to fetch water,
and even to brew tea.
At that time, I did not recognize a noble person, having but mortal eyes;
today, suddenly, you are advanced,
and I am left with my poor bones."
Those of the common sort begging for a couplet
Jiǎ Dǎo (賈島) was not good at the imperial examinations.
Every time he folded his own examination papers,
he would walk around the cubicles and tell people:
"Those of you who started writing, please give me a couplet!"
When *jìnshì* (進士) rode donkeys
at the end of the Xiántōng (咸通) era,
the officiating officials were displeased that the examination candidates' (jǔrén, 舉人) servants and horses were too numerous,
and petitioned for all *jìnshì* to ride donkeys.
Zhèng Guāngyè (鄭光業) was of large build,
and someone mocked him, saying:
"This year an edict has been issued for all to ride donkeys;
short reins and long saddle-flaps fill the nine avenues.
Lean lads might still be alright,
but among them, Zhèng Chāngtú (鄭昌圖) is troubled to death."
A pair of poor-looking eyes
Cuī Lǔ (崔櫓) offended Lù Gōng (陸肱) Langzhong (郎中) after drinking.
He apologized with a poem, saying:
"When drunk I stumble and fall, when sober I cease;
yeast and grains urge a man and give no freedom.
How unbearable is this pair of poor-looking eyes,
that do not see the flowers and plants before them."
Imprisoning the wine star, burning the drunken eyes
Wèi Yuánguī (衛元規) offended Dīng (丁) Púshè (僕射) after drinking.
He apologized with a letter, saying:
"From now on, I will imprison the wine star in the celestial prison,
and burn my drunken eyes in the pit of Qín (秦)."
Ten Poems of Separation
When Yuán (元) Xiànggōng (相公) was in Zhèdōng (浙東),
there was Secretary Xuē (薛) in his retinue.
After drinking, they quarreled over commands,
and Xuē wounded the young master with a wine vessel,
and was consequently dismissed from the retinue.
After he left,
he composed the "Ten Poems of Separation" to present:

"Dog Separated from Master," "Brush Separated from Hand," "Horse Separated from Stable," "Parrot Separated from Cage," "Swallow Separated from Nest," "Pearl Separated from Palm," "Fish Separated from Pond," "Hawk Separated from Master," "Bamboo Separated from Pavilion," "Mirror Separated from Stand."
The dog poem said:
"Tamed and obedient in the vermilion gate for four or five years,
fragrant fur and clean paws, cherished by the master.
Unexpectedly bit a kinsman's foot,
can no longer sleep on the red silk carpet."
The brush poem:
"Yuè (越) tubes and Xuān (宣) bristles first met my liking,
scattering jade-like flowers on red paper.
All because long use wore out its tip,
it can no longer be held in Xīzhī's (羲之) hand."
The parrot poem:
"In Lǒngxī (隴西), it still entrusts its solitary body,
flying to and fro upon the brocade cushion.
All because its words lacked tact,
it can no longer call out to people in its cage."
The swallow poem:
"Entering and exiting the vermilion gate, unwilling to leave,
the master always loved its chirping calls.
Carrying mud, it soiled the coral mat,
it can no longer build a nest among the beams."
Wēn's Eight Chants
Wēn Tíngyún (溫庭筠) never drafted poems under candlelight;
with sleeves draped and leaning on a table,
he would compose only a single chant.
In the examination hall, he was known as "Wēn Bāyín" (溫八吟, Wēn the Eight-Chanter).
Spring Snow Poem
When Duǎn Lǐ (短李) governed Yángzhōu (揚州),
Zhāng Xiàobiāo (章孝標) composed "Spring Snow Poem," saying:
"Six-petaled flying flowers drift everywhere,
sticking to windows, brushing steps, landing on cold branches.
By evening, the vermilion gates are hardly a foot deep,
all because the joy of the three armies has vanished."
Dù Mù (杜牧) asks for dice to gamble for wine
Zhāng Yòu (張祐) was a guest in Huáinán (淮南).
At a banquet in the retinue,
Dù Mù sat with him.
Having a particular intention,
Dù Mù asked for dice to gamble for wine.
Mù (牧) recited:
"The dice are quickly clasped in the hand,
there's no way to see the slender jade fingers."
Yòu (祐) replied:
"Just report that the golden hairpin has fallen,
and perhaps the fingertips will be revealed."
Secretly Killing Eight People
Wēn Fēiqīng (溫飛卿) liked to write on behalf of others.
When Shěn (沈) Shìláng (侍郎) was in charge of literary selection,
he specially summoned Fēiqīng (飛卿) to test him before the screen.
Some said he secretly killed eight people.
Water splashes on silk robes
Péi Qìngyú (裴慶餘) assisted Lǐ Gōng (李公) in the Huáinán (淮南) retinue.
Once, while traveling on the river,
the boatman's punt pole splashed water, wetting those seated nearby.
Lǐ Gōng's expression changed.
Qìngyú (慶餘) composed a poem, saying:
"A face full of goose-yellow, clothes of gold thread,
emerald kingfisher pins gently sway, jade hairpins dangle.
Let the water splash and wet the silk robes,
knowing that the rain-making goddess of Wūshān (巫山) has returned."
Downstream Boat
Péi Tíngyòu (裴廷祐) was in the inner court during the Qiánníng (乾寧) era.
His documentation was swift,
and he was called "Xiàshuǐ Chuán" (下水舡, Downstream Boat).
Yáo Pō (姚泊) was called "Jítān Chuán" (急灘舡, Rapid Shoal Boat) and "Shàngshuǐ Chuán" (上水舡, Upstream Boat).
Upstream Boat Order
Lìnghú Táo (令狐綯) served as minister in Wéiyáng (維楊).
He was intimate with Zhāng Yòu (張祐).
Lìnghú Táo made a game order, saying:
"Upstream boat,
the wind is fierce.
People below the sail,
must stand firm."
Zhāng Yòu replied:
"Upstream boat,
the boat bottom is broken.
Good guests,
do not lean on the rudder."
Often recall parting from home when seeing others off
In Cháng'ān (長安), there was a monk who was good at criticizing others' writings,
especially adept at correcting where meaning and intention matched.
Zhāng Jiè (張藉) was quite annoyed by this.
He searched even more diligently,
and thus obtained the couplet:
"Often when seeing others off,
I recall the time I parted from home."
The monk said:
"Someone has already said this."
Then he recited:
"Seeing the peach and plum trees blossom,
I remember the spring in the backyard."
Mùlián (目蓮) visits his mother
Zhāng Yòu's (張祐) poem mourning a deceased courtesan said:
"Where were the mandarin duck inlaid belts discarded?
To whom do the peacock silk robes belong?"
Bái Lètiān (白樂天) called this a "questioning head."
Zhāng Yòu replied:
"Your Excellency also has 'Mùlián (目蓮) visits his mother.'
The 'Chánghèn Cí' (長恨詞, Song of Everlasting Sorrow) says:
'Up to the azure sky, down to the yellow springs,
both places are vast and nothing is seen.'
Is this not 'Mùlián (目蓮) visits his mother'?"
Zhāng Xiàobiǎo's (章孝表) Examination Success Poem
After Zhāng Xiàobiǎo (章孝表) passed the imperial examination,
he sent a message to Bái Lètiān (白樂天), saying:
"Passing the examination completely surpasses ten government officials,
gilded with gold, emerging from Cháng'ān (長安).
My horse's head gradually enters the road to Yángzhōu (揚州),
I announce to the people of the time: open your eyes and see!"
Bái Lètiān replied:
"False gold needs true gold to be gilded,
if it were true gold, it would not be gilded.
After ten years in Cháng'ān (長安), you finally passed;
why must you empty your stomach and have such high aspirations?"
Eyes afflicted by an obstruction, lips that open trousers
Fāng Gān (方干) was thin and lacking,
and had a habit of insulting people.
Once, he drank with Lóngqiū (龍丘) Lǐ (李) Zhǔbù (主簿).
Lǐ (李) had a cataract in his eye.
Fāng Gān (方干) changed the game order to mock him, saying:
"A *cuòdà* (措大, pedant) eats wine with salt,
a military general eats wine with medicine.
One only sees fences outside the door,
but never an obstruction in the eye."
Lǐ (李) replied:
"A *cuòdà* (措大) eats wine with salt,
a lower-class person eats wine with pickled fish.
One only sees an orchid on an arm,
but never lips that open trousers."
Cold and bland life
When Péi Lìnggōng (裴令公) resided in Dōngluò (東洛),
he hosted a night banquet with linked verses.
Yuán (元) and Bái (白) showed their delight.
When it came to Yáng Rǔshì (楊汝士), he said:
"In bygone days, Lántíng (蘭亭) had no beauties,
but at this time, Jīngǔ (金谷) has noble men."
Bái (白) said:
"With pipes and songs so vibrant,
do not lead such a cold and bland life."
Yuán (元) said:
"Lètiān (樂天) can preserve his reputation in full."
Péi Sān (裴三), Sòng Wǔ (宋五), Lù Jiǔ (陸九)
Gāozǔ (高祖) called Péi Jì (裴寂) "Péi Sān" (Péi the Third).
Mínghuáng (明皇) called Sòng Jì (宋濟) "Sòng Wǔ" (Sòng the Fifth).
Dézōng (德宗) called Lù Zhì (陸贄) "Lù Jiǔ" (Lù the Ninth).
Silver Cake Filling
Wéi Ào (韋澳) and Sūn Hóng (孫宏) were together in the Hàn Yuàn (翰苑).
Xuānzōng (宣宗) bestowed silver cakes with filling.
They tasted exceedingly delicious,
all made from cream, cheese, and rich ingredients.
Zhào Gǔ's (趙嘏) poetry
Zhào Gǔ’s poems say:
“When I have roughly repaid my debts,
I will be a free man by the water and beneath the woods.”
He ended up as Wèi Nán Wèi.
The old saying:
One says, hearing much and seeing little,
traces still but heart stirring,
eyes at the scroll’s head,
no anger in the belly.
The second says, appearance cautious and aura harmonious,
seen little,
heard of much.
Strictly avoid six things:
First, seeking success through disciples;
Second, seeking recommendation from monks and Daoists;
Third, speaking before others of one’s cousins holding important positions;
Fourth, boasting of being a guest;
Fifth, enjoying lavish benefits;
Sixth, being useless.
Dung beetle pushing dung balls.
Gāo Huàn repeatedly failed the examinations,
someone joked,
“One hundred and twenty dung beetles
cannot push one dung ball up.”
Concubine named Zhēnzhū.
Huángfǔ Sōng,
Níu Zhānggōng’s nephew,
resented not being recommended,
and wrote a defamatory poem saying:
“At night entering Zhēnzhū’s chamber,
in the morning wandering in Dàimào palace.”
Zhēnzhū was the name of his concubine.
Elegy for Bái Fù.
Xuānzōng’s elegy for Bái Lètiān’s poem said:
“Threading jade and stringing pearls for thirty years,
who taught you to be a poetic immortal on the path to the underworld?”
Abdomen’s treasury.
Wú Zǐhuá was writing a rhapsody,
and one night it was completed in his abdomen’s treasury.
Moon poem.
Wú Bīn’s “Moon Poem” says:
“How can there be earth at the root of the cassia?
Beyond the light, there is no more void.”
Letter to the Prime Minister.
Wáng Língrán wrote a letter to the Prime Minister saying:
“Sir, when you have literary talent, do you not wish for those with literary talent to see it?
When you were not rich and noble,
did you not wish for the rich and noble to see it?
Now you are honored and renowned in court,
and your writing is praised in this era.
When you see those with literary talent yet not rich and noble in the world,
what should you do?”
Wēn Xiàn’s prolonged frustration.
Wēn Xiàn,
passed the examination during the Tiānshèng era,
and served as a staff member in Shānnán.
Lǐ Jùchuān expressed his prolonged frustration saying:
“Beautiful brows are envied first,
so Míngfēi left her country;
Ape arms lament themselves,
so Lǐ Guǎng was a general who was not enfeoffed.”
Iron footstool.
Hú Zhēng and Péi Qìng met,
if anyone transgressed,
he would be seized with an iron footstool, which was a lampstand.
Gù Yún seeking a letter.
Gù Yún,
during the Dàshùn era, he compiled history with Yáng Zhāoyè.
At that time, Liú Zǐcháng Púyè enjoyed a clean reputation.
Yún sought a letter from Gāo Fēngxiū Jiànyì for an introduction.
Yún secretly opened and read it.
It was one whole sheet,
saying nothing at all,
but
merely,
“Yún and Zhāoyè and others intend to stain their feet one foot three inches,
by stepping on his burnt remnants of the Dragon’s Tail path, that is all.”
Shūsūn Chuò.
When Lǐ Xiàng was reading the Chun Qiu,
he mistakenly pronounced Shūsūn Chuò,
read as ‘chì lüè fǎn’ (sound of chì and lüè reversed).
He called him Nì.
Read as ‘nǚ lì fǎn’ (sound of nǚ and lì reversed).
A junior official said:
“I, because of my teacher’s instruction,
mispronounced characters;
now I hear you, Xiànggōng, pronounce Chuò as Nì,
only now do I understand.”
The Duke said:
“That is not so.”
He then checked the annotations,
and indeed it was ‘chì lüè fǎn’.
The Duke was greatly ashamed,
and called the junior official “Teacher of One Character.”
Pine three feet in circumference, then passed examination.
Zhōng Fú built a mountain studio,
and personally planted a pine tree.
He dreamed that a crimson-clad official said:
“When the pine reaches three feet in circumference,
you will pass the examination.”
Thirty years later,
he was enrolled,
and the pine’s circumference was indeed three feet.
Yáng Sān Xǐ.
Yáng Jìngzhī was appointed Guózǐ Sīyè.
His second son, Dài,
passed the jinshi examination.
His eldest son, Sān Lì, passed the imperial examination.
At that time, they were called “Yáng Sān Xǐ” (Yang’s Three Joys).
High chariot passing.
Lǐ Hè, at seven years old,
his name moved the capital.
Hán Tuìzhī and Huángfǔ Shí read his writings and said:
“If he were an ancient,
we would never have known;
if he were a contemporary,
how could we not know of him?”
The two Dukes then visited his door.
Hè, with his hair in two knots, came out in simple clothes.
The two Dukes asked him to compose a rhapsody on the spot,
naming it “High Chariot Passing.”
Elegy for Lù Guīméng.
Lù Guīméng,
Yán Yáozhì inscribed his tomb.
Wú Zǐhuá composed an elegy for him saying:
“Touch it and it shatters,
the moon beneath the deep pool.
Wipe it and it vanishes,
dust on jade.”
Feasting with Xǔ Dàbǐ.
Yán Méng wrote essays,
admiring Xǔ Dàbǐ’s grand writing.
Writing in light ink.
The jinshi list at the examination hall.
Four sheets of yellow paper were affixed.
The four characters “Lǐbù Gòngyuàn” were written in light ink with a felt brush.
Concealing intent.
Liú Guāngyuǎn composed poetry,
especially skilled at concealing intent.
Flying Spring Pavilion poem.
On the road to Shǔ, there was a Flying Spring Pavilion,
with over a hundred poem plaques.
Xuē Néng passed by and removed them,
leaving only Lǐ Duān’s “Wū Shān Gāo” poem.
Presenting purple robe and gold fish to the examination chief.
Yǔ Chéngxuān’s essay.
It took six or seven years for him to be granted purple and gold attire.
His disciple Lǐ Shí had already received the imperial favor.
Shí presented the purple robe and gold fish to his examination chief.
Xiāoxiāng Rhapsody.
Hé Juān composed the “Xiāoxiāng Rhapsody,”
which was transmitted throughout the world.
At the same time, Pān Wěi
was famous for his “Ancient Mirror Poem.”
Someone said:
“Pān Wěi spent ten years contemplating the ancient mirror,
Hé Juān composed the Xiāoxiāng Rhapsody in one night.”
Fondness for jianbing.
Jiǎ Wéi was fond of jianbing.
When one jianbing was cooked,
he would compose a rhyming poem.
Eight-inch empty throat.
Táo Yánjié and Lú Zhào met at the Jiang Pavilion.
Zhào changed the command saying:
“Looking into the distance at a fishing boat,
it’s not even eight inches wide.”
Yáo Jù drank and vomited,
then returned the command saying:
“Leaning on the railing and spitting once,
I already feel an empty throat.”
Hóng’ér.
Luó Qiú was equally famous with his clansmen Yǐn and Yè.
At that time, they were called “The Three Luó.”
After the Guǎngmíng rebellion,
he followed Lǐ Xiàogōng in Fūzhōu.
Among his household registers was Hóng’ér,
skilled in singing.
Luó Qiú composed a hundred quatrains,
called “Poems comparing to Hóng’ér,”
which were widely circulated at the time.
My servant is Dù Shěnyán’s son.
Dù Fǔ, after getting drunk,
loudly asked Yán Wǔ:
"Are you the son of Yán Tǐngzhī?"
Wǔ's expression changed.
Fǔ said:
"I am the son of Dù Shěnyán."
Ān Lùshān
Táng Mínghuáng summoned Ān Lùshān,
and bestowed upon him a low, gold-lined stool to sit on.
Sùzōng offered remonstrance from the green mat (an allusion to a court position).
The Emperor said:
"This barbarian has an unusual appearance;
I use him to suppress (evil omens/rebellions)."
Sùzōng said:
"Why not kill him?"
The Emperor said:
"Killing a fake might give rise to a real one."
Sùzōng then invited Lùshān to drink,
and instructed palace maids to offer him a cup of poisoned wine.
As Lùshān was about to drink,
a swallow happened to drop mud into the cup.
Lùshān became suspicious,
and thus did not drink.
Lǐ Bái Travels to Huàshān
Lǐ Bái, disheartened, traveled to Huàshān.
He encountered a county magistrate who was opening his gates to administer justice.
Bái, riding a donkey while drunk, passed through the gate.
The magistrate was enraged,
unaware that it was Tàibái,
and led him to the courtyard, saying:
"Who are you?
How dare you be so disrespectful!"
Bái requested to submit a statement.
The statement had no name,
but said:
"I once had dragon towels wipe my vomit,
and imperial hands prepare my soup.
The noble consort presented me with an inkstone,
and the strongman wiped my boots.
Before the Son of Heaven's gates, I was allowed to ride a horse,
but within Huàyīn County, I am not allowed to ride a donkey!"
The magistrate rose in surprise,
and bowed, saying:
"I did not know the Hanlin (academician) had come here."
Tàibái mounted his limping donkey and departed.
The Country of the Black Garments
Wáng Xiè of the Táng dynasty,
residing in Jīnlíng,
made his living by seafaring.
Caught in a storm, his boat broke.
Xiè clung to a plank and reached a certain state (or island).
He saw old men and women all dressed in black,
who said:
"This is our master's young lord."
They led him to a palace,
where he saw a king sitting in a grand hall,
surrounded by women.
The king wore a black robe and a black crown,
with glittering gold flowers.
The old man gave his daughter to Xiè in marriage.
Xiè asked his wife:
"What is the name of this country?"
She replied:
"It is the Country of the Black Garments (Wūyī Guó)."
The king summoned a banquet in the Precious Ink Hall.
All the utensils were black.
He ordered a black jade cup to toast Xiè, saying:
"Among those who have entered our country,
Hàn (dynasty) had Méi Chéng,
and today we have you."
The king ordered him to compose a poem.
The final stanza said:
"I regret not being born with wings on this body."
The king said:
"Although I cannot give you wings,
I can enable you to ride on smoke and mist."
After the banquet,
his wife said:
"Why did the last line of your poem mock (us)?"
The king sent a messenger saying:
"You shall return on a certain day."
His wife took a spiritual elixir,
and placed it in a Kūnlún jade box,
giving it to Xiè, saying:
"This elixir can summon people's souls.
If a person has died less than a month ago,
it can bring them back to life."
The king ordered the Flying Cloud Chariot.
When it arrived,
it was merely a black sandalwood basket.
He instructed Xiè to enter it,
close his eyes,
and after a short while, he had already arrived home.
Twin swallows on the beam twittered and looked down.
Xiè then realized that the place he had stayed was the Country of Swallows.
By autumn,
the two swallows were about to leave,
crying mournfully at the courtyard door.
Xiè wrote a note,
and tied it to a swallow's tail, saying:
"Mistakenly came to the land of Huāxū,
where the jade maiden day and night pities my talent.
The Cloud Chariot drifted away without news,
shedding tears in the spring breeze hundreds of times."
The following spring, the swallows arrived,
with a small note on their tails,
which contained a poem that said:
"Our past encounter was destined,
now this distant separation is like death while living.
Next spring, there will still be words of longing,
but in the third month, no swallows fly to the south of heaven."
The next year,
the swallows indeed did not come.
Liú Yǔxī's 'Three Odes to Jīnlíng' contains the poem 'Wūyī Xiàng' (Black Garment Lane),
from which we know that Wáng Xiè's story is not false.
Preface to the Pavilion of Prince Téng
Wáng Bó, on his boat, was at Mǎ (River, likely a branch of the Gàn Jiāng),
by the water's edge.
He saw an old man who said:
"Tomorrow, the Preface to the Pavilion of Prince Téng will be composed.
You can construct it,
and your name will be remembered for generations."
Bó said:
"Hóngshǔi is six or seven hundred *lǐ* from here.
How can I reach it tonight?"
The old man said:
"I will assist you with a clear wind for a journey.
The Water Mansion of Zhōngyuán,
I am the master of this shrine."
Bó boarded the boat and hoisted the sail.
Before dawn, he reached Hóng (likely Hóngzhōu).
He paid his respects to the governor, Yán Gōng.
Gōng asked him to compose the preface,
and presented him with a hundred bolts of silk.
Returning to the boat and landing,
the old man was sitting on the stone reef ahead.
He said:
"Since the spirit lent you a favorable wind,
and also taught you (that you are) not dull-witted,
can you know about your lifespan, poverty, or success?"
The old man said:
"Your spirit is strong, but your bones are weak;
your *qì* is clear, but your body is frail;
your brain bone is deficient,
your eyeballs are incomplete.
You are showy but without substance,
and ultimately will not be noble.
When you pass by the shrine at Chánglú,
burn ten thousand *yīnqián* (ghost money) there.
I have a gambling debt yet to be paid."
The old man slowly disappeared into the water.
Later, when he passed Chánglú,
a flock of crows gathered on his mast and rigging.
The boat would not move.
Bó took out paper and burned it.
The boat then proceeded.
Monk Màn Dìng
Chén Jué 陳覺, feeling dejected after failing the imperial examinations,
traveled to Yàndàng Shān 雁蕩山.
From afar, he saw a tree that resembled a green canopy,
so he climbed vines and groped stones to reach the tree.
Trailing weeds entwined around it,
where a monk sat in meditation.
When he touched the monk's clothing,
it turned to dust in the wind.
Jué 覺 built a hermitage beside it,
when the monk suddenly stretched, opened his eyes, and said:
"I have clothes stored in a mountain cave,
guarded by a tiger.
Take my tin staff and retrieve the clothes;
the tiger will not harm you."
Jué 覺 entered the cave and retrieved the clothes,
and the tiger wagged its tail and left.
The monk put on the new clothes and expounded the Dharma,
stating:
"To attain wonder within wonder is the Dharma-nature;
to attain samādhi within emptiness is true emptiness.
Accumulating good or evil,
all comes from your intention.
Becoming a Buddha or a ghost,
all originates from your own mind.
All Dharma gates
are fundamentally gateless.
All wondrous functions
are fundamentally functionless.
What does one's body possess?
The myriad dharmas ultimately return to emptiness.
You may shave your head to follow my teaching."
Jué 覺 replied:
"My hair and skin are received from my parents;
I dare not damage them."
The monk said:
"The sun, moon, and stars are the three luminaries,
but their brightness is one.
Heaven, Earth, and man are the three powers,
but their Way is one.
Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism are the three teachings,
but their Way is also one.
Daoism nourishes nature,
Buddhism adapts to nature,
and Confucianism cultivates nature."
Thereupon, he imparted to Jué 覺 the method for saving the world.
Later generations called that cave Shuōfǎ Yán 說法岩 (Dharma-Expounding Cave).
The elder Wù Biàn 悞卞,
a monk named Wù Biàn 悞卞,
resided as abbot of Láng Shān 琅山 in Tōngzhōu 通州.
He entered Kāiyuán Sì 開元寺 in the city to expound the Dharma.
A monk asked:
"Since you are called an elder,
why are you so young?"
The master mused and said:
"A thousand-year-old crimson-crested crane
is a phoenix chick for a day."
The monk asked:
"Why was your answer so slow?"
The master replied:
"Clouds emerge late from deep caves,
and water flows slowly in wide ravines."
Someone else asked:
"Why did the elder of Láng Shān 琅山 come to Kāiyuán Sì 開元寺 to expound the Dharma?"
The master said:
"Every household has Guānshìyīn 觀世音."
Someone else asked:
"What is the meaning of the wooden fish?"
He replied:
"Fish do not close their eyes day or night;
those who wish to cultivate the Way should forget sleep day and night to contemplate the Way."
The Old Monk Moves Again Today
Chǔ Lángzhōng 楚郎中 traveled to Máoshān 茅山 with his sons and nephews,
gazing at the forest ravines from afar.
When they arrived at a small hermitage,
the monk was eighty or ninety years old.
He said:
"Why have you come here, gentlemen?
Three li from here,
there is a temple where you can stay."
So the gentlemen left.
As dusk approached, they reached the temple
and recounted what had happened.
The temple monks exclaimed in surprise:
"We know him!
This monk has been hidden in the Northern Mountains for thirty years,
and we have never seen him.
We wish to pay him homage together."
At dawn, they arrived at the hermitage,
but it was already empty.
A poem was left with the title:
"A few pines and cypresses are not enough to eat,
a pond of water caltrops and lotus provides more than enough clothes.
Just as I was questioned by passers-by,
the old monk moves again today."
Red Plum Blossoms
In Shǔzhōu 蜀州, there were several red plum trees.
The Prefectural Marquis built a pavilion and locked it,
so travelers could not see them.
One day, two women,
with high topknots and wide sleeves,
leaned on the railing, talking and laughing.
When the Prefectural Marquis unlocked the pavilion, no one was there,
only a poem on the east wall that read:
"Southern branches face the warmth, northern branches feel the cold;
the same spring breeze produces two different effects.
Please do not blow the flute from the high pavilion,
let everyone enjoy leaning on the railing."
Wáng Kuí Zhuàn 王魁傳
Wáng Kuí, having failed the imperial examination and feeling dejected,
went to Láizhōu, Shāndōng.
A friend invited him to visit the North Market.
In a deep lane, in a small house,
there was a woman of exceptional beauty.
She poured wine and said:
"My name is Guìyīng.
Wine is the finest nectar from heaven.
If you acquire Guìyīng and drink heavenly nectar,
it is an omen of passing the examination next spring."
She then took a silk scarf (擁頂羅) and requested a poem.
The student (Wáng Kuí) wrote:
"At Lady Xiè's banquet, I heard a refined song,
who plays jade behind the curtain?
A single note pierces the azure autumn sky,
several passing clouds dare not fly."
Guìyīng said:
"You just focus on your studies;
all your needs for the four seasons,
I will provide for them."
From then on, Kuí came and went morning and evening.
After more than a year,
an imperial edict sought talented individuals.
Guìyīng prepared the necessities for his journey west (to the capital).
When they reached the north of the prefecture,
they swore an oath at the Temple of the Sea God:
"Guìyīng and I swear never to betray each other.
If we are separated,
the gods shall strike us down."
When Kuí arrived at the imperial examination hall in the capital,
he sent a letter saying:
"Polishing the moon and grinding the clouds falls to our lot,
occupying flowers and seizing willows is for men.
If I succeed next spring,
I will ensure a good upbringing for our mandarin ducks in one pond."
Later, he was proclaimed the top scholar in the realm.
Kuí privately thought that since his scholarly reputation was such,
to be disgraced by a courtesan,
moreover, his strict father at home would not tolerate it,
so he no longer corresponded with her.
Guìyīng sent a letter saying:
"A husband's nobility, a wife's glory, is a matter for all ages,
your talent and appearance are well-matched with mine."
She also wrote:
"In the capital, I adorn myself according to the times,
expecting my beloved to think of me upon seeing me.
When you return to my secluded chamber,
you must paint my new eyebrows, like Zhāng Chǎng did."
She also wrote:
"On the road, pipes and songs, a land of brocade,
the immortal lord is full of得意 and quite wild.
Little does he know the haggard one in the secluded chamber,
whose spring dress sash feels longer day by day."
Kuí's father arranged a marriage with the Cuī clan,
and he was appointed as Assistant Prefect of Xúzhōu.
Guìyīng rejoiced, saying:
"Xúzhōu is not far from here;
he will surely send someone to welcome me."
She dispatched a servant with a letter.
Kuí was then sitting in the hall adjudicating matters.
He was furious,
and angrily refused the letter.
Guìyīng said:
"Kuí has betrayed me to this extent;
I must repay him with death."
She wielded a blade and slit her own throat.
Kuí was in the examination hall in the southern prefecture,
when someone emerged from beneath a candle.
It was Guìyīng.
Kuí said:
"Are you truly unharmed?"
Guìyīng said:
"You lightened your affections and thinned your loyalty,
betraying your oath and forsaking your pledge,
causing me to reach this state."
Kuí said:
"It is my fault.
Shall I offer food to monks and recite Buddhist scriptures for you,
burn much paper money,
and then you leave me be?"
Guìyīng said:
"I will stop when I take your life;
I know nothing else."
Kuí wanted to stab himself,
but his mother said:
"Why are you so rebellious and disordered?"
Kuí said:
"I meet my enemy every day,
who forces me to die."
His mother summoned the Daoist priest Gāo Shǒusù for repeated rituals.
One night, Shǒusù arrived at the official residence.
Kuí and Guìyīng stood with their hair intertwined.
Someone warned:
"If you know this, then do not pull it out again."
A few days later, Kuí indeed died.
Dreams of the Jade Stream (Yùxī Mèng)
Jīn Yú traveled through Guānzhōng,
passing Dàhuí Mountain.
Looking towards the western peak,
the rock face shone like blood in the sunlight.
An elder said:
"Qín buried scholars alive here."
Yú inscribed a poem:
"The scholars' blood not yet dry, the Qín deer fled,
The smoke of burnt books ceased, Hàn soldiers called out.
Returning to benevolence, abandoning tyranny, is the will of the common people,
The black-haired people have never been truly foolish."
That night, he dreamt of two officials chasing him to a place
resembling a king's residence.
They said:
"This is Qín Huáng's Jade Stream Palace (Yùxī Gōng)."
Soon, Qín Huáng appeared and said:
"Times are different for you, and dynasties have changed.
Why is the present right and the past wrong?
Slandering the ancients is forbidden by law,
insulting superiors is a crime not to be pardoned."
He ordered his attendants to behead him.
Yú said:
"Had Your Majesty listened to the upright words of honest scholars,
and rejected the wicked theories of sycophants,
from where would the empire have rebelled?
Yet you still apply the tyrannical spirit of yesteryear
to a blameless person of today."
Qín Huáng's anger subsided slightly.
He ordered Yú to write an apology.
Then he ordered food to be bestowed in the eastern wing,
and also ordered him to write about why Qín failed
and Hàn succeeded.
Qín Huáng read the memorial
and wept, saying:
"Your words hit precisely my mistakes.
I regret not living in the same era as you."
Yú said:
"Even if your subject had lived in Your Majesty's time,
he might not have been used. Were there no righteous people at that time?"
Qín Huáng said:
"I have been secluded in this palace,
not knowing how many years and months have passed.
Your words have made me blame myself incessantly.
You may return."
He ordered an official to escort him back.
Palace Poems of the Southern Lǐ Dynasty (Jiāngnán Lǐ Shì Gōngzhōng Shī)
Ōu Yǒngshū said:
"Poetry originates from the heart.
Wealth, poverty, sorrow, and resentment are tied to one's circumstances."
A palace poem from the Southern Lǐ Dynasty states:
"The sun through the curtain is already high, fifteen feet shining through,
In the golden censer, incense-burning beasts are successively replenished.
Red brocade floor covering follows the infant's steps,
The beautiful woman finished her dance, her golden hairpins sliding.
When sick of wine, she occasionally plucks and sniffs a flower bud,
From other palaces, sounds of flute and drum are occasionally heard."
This is quite different from the lines: "Occasionally picking wild vegetables and boiling them with their roots,
Immediately chopping fresh firewood and burning it with its leaves."
How Many "Weak Crowns"? (Ruòguàn Yǒu Jǐ)
Wáng Wénzhèng Gōng said:
"When juniors interact with elders,
or attend to teachers and paternal friends,
they should answer truthfully when asked.
Recently, there was a son of a prominent family.
I asked him his age.
He replied, 'Ruòguàn' (twenty years old).
When asked if he rode horses,
he said, 'A thousand chariots' (meaning he commanded many).
A donkey,
he said, 'There is a guard.'
I also asked if he had ever visited a certain official.
He said, 'I obtained a calling card,
and was deemed suitable for appointment.'"
On the Zither (Lùn Qín)
Shùn made a five-stringed zither,
sang the 'Southern Wind' (Nánfēng),
reflecting on the virtue of nurturing growth.
Later, Wén and Wǔ added two strings.
When Shī Kuàng had not finished a single piece,
a great storm followed,
and for three years the country suffered a great drought.
How profound!
The playing of true music
should not be heard by those of thin virtue.
Its pieces are no more than "Guǎnglímgsǎn," "Fēng Rù Sōng," and "Bié Hè Yuàn," a mere dozen movements.
Today, zither enthusiasts mix them with new tunes.
Alas!
Lǐ Jīhuà Becomes a Tiger
Táng Yǎn 唐儼 served as an Imperial Censor.
He was dispatched on an imperial mission to the Lingbiǎo 嶺表 region,
and his route passed through Jīngnán 荊南.
The post official said:
“There is a tiger in the winding stream.
You can take the road behind the mountain instead.”
Yǎn 儼 said:
“I bear the king's mandate.
Why should I avoid a tiger?”
He whipped his horse and departed.
A tiger leaped out,
then returned into a large patch of grass, saying:
“I almost hurt my old friend.”
Yǎn 儼 recognized its voice.
It was his friend, Lǐ Jī 李積.
He asked:
“How did you come to be here, sir?”
The tiger said:
“Yesterday, I had an attack of madness,
and ran into the valleys,
transforming into a tiger.
Since then,
I have pounced upon and eaten
those wearing caps and hurrying,
those with wings soaring,
and those with fur holding things.
Just now, there was a woman with a silver bracelet.
I carried her to the water,
a hundred paces from here.
If you pass by and take it,
you can give it to my family.
Alas, to eat a person and take their belongings to give to one's wife and children
is not what a human would do.
Today, I am acting against the natural order and doing things in reverse.”
Yǎn 儼 said:
“Do you have any regrets about what you have gained in your life, sir?”
The tiger said:
“I once had a private affair with a widow.
Her family always harbored intentions to harm me.
In a drunken rage,
I killed their entire family and left.
This is my only regret.”
Yǎn 儼 had not yet settled down on the mountain
when he saw a giant tiger roar loudly,
its sound shaking the trees, and then depart.
The Merman
Zhāng Shǒuxìn 張守信 anchored his boat on Xīnkāi Hú 新開湖.
A fisherman cast his net and caught a fish weighing nearly a hundred catties.
From the waist down, it was a fish,
but above the waist, it was a beautiful woman.
Shǒuxìn 守信 poured wine and offered it to her,
and her face became even redder and more beautiful.
Someone took a ladle of hot soup and offered it to her,
but she quickly spat it out,
as if injured by the heat.
The boatmen said:
“Killing it would be inauspicious.”
They returned it to the deep water.
The fish pressed its palms together and said:
“Before the Kalpa fire destroys everything,
I, a human-headed fish-bodied being,
was formerly a Grand Historian of Dōnglǔ 東魯,
and now I am the Little Lord of Pōshuǐ 泊水.
You offered me wine,
for which I am truly grateful.
But to offer me hot soup,
that too is inhumane.”
The Jinshì 進士 Lǚ Kǒu 呂口
Yáng Yuàn 楊愿 was supervising the granaries in the capital.
Someone presented a calling card, saying:
“Lǚ Kǒu 呂口, a Jinshì 進士 from Jiāngzhōu 江州.”
After they met,
he handed over a short letter, saying:
“Faint light in a dark room,
a frozen drop from a cold spring.
Yáng Yízhī’s 楊宜之 kitchen is often empty,
where has Kǒng Xù’s 孔緒 carriage gone?”
Yuàn 愿 asked:
“What is the story of Kǒng Xù’s 孔緒 carriage?”
The person said:
“Yáng Sān 楊三,
Yáng Sān 楊三!
You are the grandson of Yáng Fǎn 楊返,
and the son of Yáng Zhōng 楊中.
Why do you need to ask about Kǒng Xù’s 孔緒 matter?”
Yuàn 愿 was enraged
and wanted to strike him.
The person suddenly fell to the ground,
only a wrapped headscarf visible.
Yuàn 愿 quickly dug at it with a hoe,
and it transformed into a large rat that scurried into the granary.
Sleeping Alone in a Solitary Lodge
Cuī Qìngchéng 崔慶成, an Officer in the Prefectural Administration of Tángzhōu 唐州,
was escorting a convoy of spices and medicinal herbs to the imperial treasury.
Upon reaching the Huánghuá Yìshè 皇華驛舍 (Imperial Splendor Post Station),
he saw a beautiful woman at night who said:
“Today I see you,
and you must have doubts.
If I leave you today,
will I not regret it?
Wait until you return,
and we can plan another meeting.”
She threw down a paper with words that said:
“Dog in Sichuan (Chuānzhōng gǒu 川中狗),
eyes of the common people (bǎixìng yǎn 百姓眼),
mother pounces on son (māmū'ér 媽撲兒),
imperial kitchen meal (yùchú fàn 御廚飯).”
When he returned,
he dared not stay at the Huánghuá Yì 皇華驛,
but lodged in an inn.
The previous woman came and said:
“Can today's matter be accomplished?
Can you decipher the twelve characters?”
Qìngchéng 慶成 did not respond.
She then ordered a maidservant in green to bring wine.
He still did not raise his cup.
So, she composed a poem, saying:
“Demonic souls and fragrant spirits have been numerous and potent since ancient times,
my heart and courage are like those in life.
Knowing you are not a romantic type,
I return to the secluded plains to resent the bright moon.”
The maidservant in green said:
“Our young mistress raised a parrot for over ten years,
but it never spoke.
Is this its verification?”
The woman sighed and said:
“Yes, it is!”
Then she composed the ‘Poem of the Mute Parrot,’ saying:
“Tamed and kept in a carved cage for so long,
never a single word throughout the year.
I deeply resent the great blunder of the Creator's sentiment,
why did he especially grant it beautiful plumage?”
She threw the paper to the ground,
and all the lamps and fires went out.
Dīng Jìnggōng 丁晉公 once saw these twelve characters
and said:
“Chuānzhōng gǒu 川中狗 (dog in Sichuan) is a Shǔquǎn 蜀犬 (Sichuan dog),
which combines into the character dú 獨 (alone).
Bǎixìng yǎn 百姓眼 (eyes of the common people) is mínmù 民目 (people's eyes),
which combines into the character mián 眠 (sleep).
Māmū'ér 媽撲兒 (mother pounces on son) is guāzǐ 瓜子 (melon seed),
which combines into the character gū 孤 (solitary).
Yùchú fàn 御廚飯 (imperial kitchen meal) is guānshí 官食 (official food),
which combines into the character guǎn 館 (lodge).
These are the four characters ‘dú mián gū guǎn 獨眠孤館’ (sleeping alone in a solitary lodge).”
Dài Sōng’s 戴嵩 Oxen
Táng Dài Sōng 唐戴嵩 was skilled at painting water buffaloes.
If his brush fell,
it would become a black ox.
When he painted an ox drinking water,
its shadow would appear in the water.
When he painted a cowherd leading an ox,
the cowherd would be visible in the ox's pupils.
Hú Dàpó 胡大婆
Niú Shìjī (牛世基) studied at Dōnglínshān Temple (東林山寺).
One night, someone knocked on the door,
saying,
"Hú Sānpó (胡三婆) is here to wait upon you."
Once seated,
she said,
"I am the paternal aunt of the Dragon King of Dōnghǎi (東海).
The Dragon King's merits are lofty,
and Heaven has permitted a stele to be erected for him.
Thus, I have come to entrust this task to you."
Shìjī (世基) did not agree.
Then she said,
"My words are light.
Let the wives of our two families convey the message."
Soon, Hú Èrpó (胡二婆) arrived,
saying,
"Why won't you put pen to paper?
I shall have the eldest wife convey the message;
she is very temperamental."
Immediately, a cold wind touched his face,
and the eldest wife's eyes were like lightning.
She sternly said,
"I just asked my second sister to entrust you with making the stele.
The white *chī* (螭) stone has already been ground,
and Lord Zǐyáng (紫陽) has been invited to inscribe the title.
If you enter this karmic connection,
you will be immortal for ten thousand kalpas."
