Shìjī (世基) hastily took paper and wrote,
"The vast cause of the sacred fruit has already been achieved."
A servant named Gōulóng Xìn (勾龍信)
then held a staff and said,
"In the dead of night on an empty mountain,
what gods or ghosts dare to disturb people!"
He struck the eldest wife behind her shin.
The eldest wife brandished her hands and said,
"This matter shall be resolved by General Sūn (孫) of the Cavalry."
Then a voice was heard saying,
"Fortunately, under the earth there are Hán Wéngōng (韓文公) and Lǐ Bái (李白) and their like,
who can express words according to their share.
Which enemy instructed this person to be entrusted with it!
Inciting someone to strike and injure the eldest wife,
this official matter cannot be settled."
Suddenly, armored cavalry stopped east of the hall,
and summoned Shìjī (世基), saying,
"I am General Sūn (孫) of the Cavalry.
Gōulóng Xìn (勾龍信) will be dealt with in due course,
and you, scholar, must also receive a slight reprimand."
An officer tattooed Shìjī's (世基) face, saying,
"You are banished to Běishān (北山) to herd sheep."
General Sūn (孫) led his troops out of the temple,
and saw that Gōulóng Xìn (勾龍信) had already died by the stove.
Shìjī (世基), with his face inscribed by the monster,
wanted to commit suicide.
The old monk said,
"Why not fly a memorial to the Emperor to complain?"
As Shìjī (世基) picked up his pen,
the characters on his face had already disappeared.
His servant, however, never came back to life.
Poetic Prophecies
Liáo Róng (廖融), a reclusive scholar, wrote a couplet:
"Clouds pierce the herb-pounding hut,
snow presses down the fishing boat."
Róng (融) himself interpreted it, saying,
"The hut is broken and clouds pierce through it,
meaning there is no one.
The boat is pressed down by snow,
meaning it is useless."
Not long after, he indeed passed away.
Buddhist Homeland
Yú Āndào (余安道), while traveling to a mountain temple, wrote in a poem:
"Temporarily leaving the human world,
and arriving at the Buddhist homeland."
Commentators considered this inauspicious,
and he indeed passed away.
Cānglángtíng Poem
Sū Zǐměi's (蘇子美) Cānglángtíng (滄浪亭) poem says:
"I sigh that I am not as joyful as the swimming fish,
vainly living half a lifetime as a human."
Also, "Mountain cicadas with sound pierce pine windows,
wild vines coil greenly into broken windows."
The window is broken,
vines coil within it,
as if no one resides there,
which was a pity for the world.
Yáng Xuān's (楊軒) lamp poem:
"It can illuminate places where the sun and moon do not shine,
and uniquely brightens times when heaven and earth are not yet bright."
However, if the sun and moon do not shine there,
what is the use of light?
If heaven and earth are not yet bright,
what is the use of being able to illuminate?
Xuān (軒) eventually died as a commoner.
My Fate is Known
Táo Hóngjǐng (陶弘景) wrote to his older cousin:
"My official career was expected to be as Shàngshūláng (尚書郎) around forty years old,
then I would retire and live a lofty life.
Now I am thirty-six and only a Fèngcháoqǐng (奉朝請).
My fate is known,
it is better to leave early."

End.

Nánrú
means angry words.
Gòuhuī
is a name for someone who does not understand affairs.
Yìyuè
means a lock button.
Nuòliú
Nuòliú
is the Punica granatum (pomegranate).
Hán'è
is a type of pastry.
Jùyǐn
Drinking by pooling funds is called jùyǐn.
Gǒuqǐ
In spring it is called tiānjīngzǐ,
in summer it is called gǒuqǐyè,
in autumn it is called quèlǎozhī,
and in winter it is called dìgǔpí.
Jīrǎng
The Fēngsújì says:
"Jīrǎng.
In the time of Yáo,
an old man was playing jīrǎng at Kāngqú."
Suōlǐ
The Chǔ people call suōlǐ chú.
Tǔjīng
Tǔjīng resembles a human hand
and is found underground.
It is also called Báizé;
eating it grants freedom from illness and great strength.
Qiǎofùniǎo
is also called gōngquè,
and also nǚ'ōu.
Zǎojǐng
The carved lotus and water chestnut designs in the zǎojǐng of palaces and halls
use water elements to ward off fire.
Lùjiēlǐ
Guōpú's commentary on the Éryǎ says:
"Egrets have fine threads on their heads and wings.
South of the Yangtze River, they are called lùjiēlǐ."
Dǒuzhàng
is a small curtain,
shaped like an inverted dipper.
Xuèdàn
Sòng Wéndì liked to eat xuèdàn,
pronounced kān.
A cook mistakenly put peeled lotus root in it,
and the blood turned into water.
The Běncǎo says:
"Lotus root peel turns blood into water,"
this knowledge came from a cook.
Yǔbì
The Jìnián says:
"In the seventh year of Huìchéngwáng,
jade rained in Yǐng."
Jūnchénzuǒshǐ
Medicine has jūnchénzuǒshǐ [sovereign, minister, assistant, envoy]
to harmonize and assist each other.
It combines one sovereign, two ministers, and three assistants.
It is also said to be one sovereign, three ministers, nine assistants, and three envoys.
Yīnyáng Pèihé
Medicines have yīnyáng pèihé,
zǐmǔ xiōngdì, gēnjīng huāshí, chēshí gǔròu.
Some act alone,
some treat each other,
some assist each other,
some fear each other,
some dislike each other,
some are contrary to each other,
and some kill each other.
Shīyào
All wet medicines,
when dried,
lose a lot of their weight.
One should first increase the amount to get the desired powder,
then weigh it to be considered the main ingredient.
Fúlónggān
refers to the yellow earth beneath an old stove.
Zhú
is also called shānjīang.
Bàntiānhé
is the water collected on bamboo fences.
Chūnxuě
contains insects,
and the water also quickly spoils,
making it unsuitable for collection.
Shānyù
Shǔyù
is also called shānyù.
In Qín and Chǔ, it is called yùyán;
in Zhèng and Yuè, it is called tǔzhū.
Shǒutián
Bànxià
is also called shǒutián.
Júhuā
is also called rìjīng,
also zhōuyíng,
and also fùyánnián.
Gāncǎo
is also called guólǎo.
Dàhuáng is called jiāngjūn.
Rénshēncàn
Ginseng is an essential medicine.
It has the same efficacy as gāncǎo but is easily infested by worms.
Only when sealed in a container
can it last for years without spoiling.
The Gāolì people wrote a tribute to ginseng, saying:
"Three branches, five leaves,
facing shade, shunning sun.
If you wish to find me,
seek me by the jiǎ
tree."
The jiǎ tree's leaves resemble those of ginseng,
and ginseng often grows beneath it.
Zhòngsīzǎo
is named after the immortal Zhòngsī, who ate it.
Yuányī
is moss on a wall in the shade.
It is also called wūjiǔ,
and also tiānjǐu.
Shuǐzhīdān
Lotus seeds
are also called shuǐzhīdān.
絲蓴 (Sīchún)
becomes 豬蓴 (Zhūchún) in winter,
also named 龜蓴 (Guīchún).
It is also said:
before July or August, it is called 絲蓴 (Sīchún);
in late autumn and early winter, it is called 瑰蓴 (Guīchún).
木筆 (Mùbǐ)
辛夷 (Xīnyí) is also called 木筆 (Mùbǐ).
桃奴 (Táonú)
Peaches that dry on the tree without falling are called 桃奴 (Táonú).
There are two kinds of swallows.
The 胡燕 (Húyàn) has black spots on its chest,
and likes to build long nests,
some of which can hold a bolt of silk.
The 越燕 (Yuèyàn) has a purple chest,
commonly called 紫燕 (Zǐyàn),
and builds extremely shallow nests.
崖蜜 (Yámì)
also named 石蜜 (Shímì).
There are also 土蜜 (Tǔmì) and 木蜜 (Mùmì).
蛇符 (Shéfú)
A snake's slough,
also named 蛇符 (Shéfú).
馬通 (Mǎtōng)
Horse dung,
also named 馬通 (Mǎtōng).
二蔗 (Èrzhè)
There are two kinds of sugarcane.
The red one is called 崑崙蔗 (Kūnlúnzhè),
the white one is called 荻蔗 (Dízhè).
屋松 (Wūsōng)
Also named 屋遊 (Wūyóu).
雞頭 (Jītóu)
Made into flour and eaten,
it is a medicine for longevity.
If children eat it, they cannot grow tall.
Also named 鴻頭 (Hóngtóu),
also named 雁喙 (Yànhuì).
八穀 (Bāgǔ)
Yellow millet (黃梁米),
also named 竹根 (Zhúgēn).
Yellow millet (黃黍), panicled millet (稷), rice (稻), great millet (梁), grain (禾), hemp (麻), beans (菽), and wheat (麥)
are called the eight grains (八穀).
神護草 (Shénhùcǎo)
Placed above the door,
when people approach, it makes a sound like a reprimand.
五木之耳 (Wǔmùzhī'ěr)
Paper mulberry (楮), pagoda tree (槐), elm (榆), willow (柳), mulberry (桑)
are the "ears of the five trees" (五木之耳).
They can be eaten and used in medicine.
艾作餛飩 (Àizuòhúntún)
Mugwort leaves (艾葉),
also named 冰臺 (Bīngtái),
cure all kinds of ghostly afflictions.
It is excellent when made into wontons (餛飩).
Swallow three to five pieces,
and press them down with rice;
it is effective.
使君子 (Shǐjūnzǐ)
Guō Shǐjūn (郭使君) of Èzhōu (鄂州)
often used this substance to treat children.
Physicians therefore called it 使君子 (Shǐjūnzǐ).
佩萱 (Pèixuān)
Pregnant women
who wear daylilies (萱草) will give birth to boys.
絡婦 (Luòfù)
Spider,
also named 絡新婦 (Luòxīnfù).
餘甘 (Yúgān)
Amla (菴摩勒).
Extract its juice and mix with oil
to turn white hair black and prevent aging.
Its fruit is first bitter, then sweet,
hence called 餘甘 (Yúgān, "aftertaste sweetness").
頭垢 (Tóugòu)
Treats strangury with obstructed urination.
Also treats dysphagia (噎).
Also cures relapsing illness (勞復).
菱實 (Língshí)
Immortals steam it to make flour, mix it with honey, and eat it.
It allows one to abstain from grains.
Among aquatic plants,
this is the least effective in treating illness.
胡桃 (Hútáo)
Zhāng Qiān (張騫) brought it from the Western Regions.
As for its tree,
in spring, its bark can be cut and its sap extracted to wash hair until it turns black.
In autumn, its kernel is harvested.
嘗百草 (Chángbǎicǎo)
《世本》 (Shìběn) says:
"Shénnóng (神農) tasted a hundred herbs to blend medicines
and benefit people."
煮鹽 (Zhǔyán)
Sùshā Shì (夙沙氏) boiled seawater to make salt.
He was a minister of Shénnóng (神農).
棄市 (Qìshì)
In the second year of Zhōngyuán (中元) of the Hàn (漢) dynasty (148 BCE),
crucifixion (磔) was changed to public execution (棄市).
疫鬼 (Yìguǐ)
《祀紀》 (Sìjì) says:
"Zhuānxū Shì (顓頊氏) had two sons.
Those who died young became plague demons (疫鬼).
One resided in the middle of the Jiāngshǔi (江水),
causing malaria;
the other resided in people's houses and corners,
and was good at startling children.
Therefore, in the first month of the year, Fāngxiàng Shì (方相氏) was ordered to lead the exorcism (儺) to drive away the plague demons."
都水使者 (Dūshuǐshǐzhě)
In the fifth year of Tàikāng (太康) of the Jìn (晉) dynasty (284 CE),
the position of 都水使者 (Dūshuǐshǐzhě) was established.
弓矢 (Gōngshǐ)
Chuí (倕) made bows,
Yízé (夷則) made arrows.
The spirit of the bow is named Qūzhāng (曲張),
the spirit of the arrow is named Xùcháng (續長).
That which kills people from a hundred paces away
is the arrow.
童子郎 (Tóngzǐláng)
《續漢書》 (Xùhànshū) says:
"The Qín (秦) dynasty summoned sons of high officials to be scholars (諸生).
Those with ambition and integrity were recorded
and called 童子郎 (Tóngzǐláng)."
六丁 (Liùdīng)
《春秋成分圖》 (Chūnqiūchéngfēntú) says:
"The Yellow Emperor (黃帝) asked Tàiyǐ (太乙) about the path to immortality.
Tàiyǐ (太乙) said:
'By fasting and observing the Six Dīng (六丁), success can be achieved.'
Dīng (丁)
takes the meaning of carefulness and caution."
武帝傷足 (Wǔdìshāngzú)
Jìqiū Jūn (稷丘君)
was a Daoist from the foot of Tàishān (太山).
When Emperor Wǔ (武帝) made an eastern tour,
Jìqiū Jūn (稷丘君) welcomed and bowed, saying:
"Your Majesty will surely injure your foot."
Several *li* up,
his left big toe was indeed severed.
神魚子英祠 (Shényúzǐyīngcí)
Zǐyīng (子英)
was a person from Shūxiāng (舒鄉).
He caught a red carp while fishing,
and raised it for several years.
It grew over a *zhàng* in length,
and had both horns and wings.
Zǐyīng (子英) rode it and ascended to heaven.
He returned to see his wife and children,
and the fish came again to greet him.
In Wú (吳), people built a shrine for the divine woman Zǐyīng (子英) at their doors.
幞頭 (Fútóu)
In ancient times, a three-foot black silk gauze was used as a head covering.
Later, in the Zhōu (周) dynasty, it became a four-footed headwear.
靴 (Xuē)
Originally a foreign attire,
created by Zhào Wǔlíng Wáng (趙武靈王).
雲幕 (Yúnmù)
Nǚwā (女媧) made cloud curtains (雲幕).
The Marquis of Wèi (衛侯) made tiger tents (虎幄),
which were also a type of curtain.
集賢學士 (Jíxiánxuéshì)
In the fifth year of Kāiyuán (開元) (717 CE), the Lìzhèng Xiūshūyuàn (麗正修書院) was established.
Mǎ Huáisù (馬懷素) and Chǔ Yuánliàng (褚元量) were appointed as envoys.
In the thirteenth year (725 CE),
eighteen scholars (學士) were appointed.
Zhāng Yuè (張說), the Minister of the Central Secretariat (中書令), concurrently served as Grand Academician of the Jíxiándiàn (集賢殿大學士).
Zhāng Yuè (張說) declined the position of Grand Academician,
and supervised the academy's affairs.
Xú Jiān (徐堅) was his deputy.
弘文館 (Hóngwénguǎn)
In the early Wǔdé (武德) era (618-626 CE), the Xiūshǐguǎn (修史館) was established.
Emperor Tàizōng (太宗) gathered books from the four divisions at the Hóngwénguǎn (弘文館),
and established the Hóngwénguǎn (弘文館).
He selected Yú Shìnán (虞世南) and others to concurrently serve as academicians (學士) in their original official capacities,
and brought them into the palace to discuss literature and meanings.
Chǔ Suìliáng (褚遂良) was appointed as inspector.
崇文館學士 (Chóngwénguǎnxuéshì)
Emperor Míng of Wèi (魏明帝) selected those skilled in writing to fill this position.
Emperor Gāozōng of Táng (唐高宗) also established it.
崇賢館學士 (Chóngxiánwénguǎnxuéshì)
In the Zhèngguān period, it was established
under the Left Spring Palace,
along with the Rectifier Scholars,
to instruct the various princes.
Scholars of the Chóngxuán Hall
In the twenty-ninth year of Kāiyuán,
students were ordered to be placed at the Xuányuán Emperor's Temple to study Daoist scriptures.
Later, Chén Xīliè concurrently held the post of Scholar of the Chóngxuán Hall
and was the Supervisor-General of palaces and temples in both capitals.
Compiler of the Imperial Library
In the Later Hàn, there was the title of Compiler of the Eastern Gallery,
but not an official post.
Emperor Wèi first established the posts of Compiler and Assistant Compiler.
Generals and Prime Ministers of the Huángdì
The Xuānyuán Běnjì says:
The Huángdì appointed Fēng Hòu as his prime minister
and Lì Mù as his general.
Appointed Prime Minister
Sùzōng appointed the Jiedushi Guō Yuánzhèn, Lǐ Guāngbì, and others as Pingzhangshi of the Zhongshu and Menxia departments,
known as appointed prime ministers.
Waiting Hall
During the Yuánhé period,
the Waiting Hall was established at the court gate.
Imperial Examinations
In the Former Hàn, only policy questions were tested.
The Suí and early Táng also only tested miscellaneous essays.
At the beginning of the Shénlóng period,
the Six Classics were tested.
During the Tiānbǎo period, candidates of the First Class
were tested with poetry and rhapsodies in addition to policy questions, making three rounds.
Military Examinations
Military examinations were established in Cháng'ān.
The tests included the Five Strengths, target shooting, mounted archery, spear fighting from horseback, foot archery, and responsiveness,
similar to the Jìnshì exam.
Daoist Examinations
Mínghuáng established Daoist examinations,
recruiting students for the Chóngxuán Hall,
which was called the Daoist examination.
Yielding White
At the beginning of the Tiānbǎo period,
sixty-four people were selected and judged as passing.
Zhāng Shì, the son of the Vice Imperial Censor Zhāng Yǐ, was judged as passing with a high grade.
He was impeached by those who failed.
Mínghuáng observed the examination from below the Qínzhèng Tower.
Only twelve people were moderately superior;
the rest all failed.
Zhāng Shì did not utter a single word.
This was then called "yielding white."
Shàowēi Star
The Classic says:
The four stars of Shàowēi are southwest of Tàiwēi.
The first in the northern row is the recluse.
Executive of the Central Secretariat
The Wèi established the Tongshi Lang,
who managed imperial edicts.
The Jìn established the Zhongtongshi Sheren.
The Qí changed it to Zhongshu Sheren.
During the Lóngxiáng period of Táng, it was changed to Xītái Sheren.
During the Guāngzhái period, it was changed to Fènggé Sheren.
During the Kāiyuán period, it was changed to Zǐwēi Sheren,
and later restored to Zhongshu Sheren.
Gate Card
In ancient times, there was no paper.
Bamboo or wood was shaved to write names,
hence it was called cì.
Later, when paper was used,
it was called míngzhǐ.
During the Táng, Lǐ Déyù was a powerful prime minister.
This custom was changed to a formal presentation,
a document for inquiring about daily life,
called a gate card.
Men's Bow
The Later Zhōu system
ordered palace women in the palace halls to perform a men's bow.
Temporary Resident
Pān Yuè of the Jìn was a Huben Zhonglangjiang.
At that time, there were no official residences.
Yuè lodged and slept at the province of the Sanqi,
hence Yuè said "temporary resident."
Today, all officials and Hanlin scholars are on duty in their own departments and academies,
hence they are on duty.
How can it be called a temporary resident?
Imperial Music Bureau
At the beginning of the Kāiyuán period,
the Imperial Music Bureau was established next to the Pénglái Palace.
Consequently, an envoy was appointed to manage its instruction.
Edicts Written on Yellow Paper
In the Zhèngguān period,
Tàizōng ordered imperial edicts to be written on hemp paper.
Gāozōng, because white paper was often worm-eaten,
ordered the Ministry of Personnel to distribute
only yellow paper to the prefectures and counties.
Phoenix Edict
Shí Jìlóng of the Later Zhào established the Xìmǎ Observation Tower.
Imperial edicts were placed on the tower,
using five-colored paper held in the mouth of a wooden phoenix and then promulgated.
Hence Luó Yǐn said:
"A thousand layers of palace gates,
no one reaches.
Five-colored silk threads,
only the phoenix holds."
Bēitián Monastery
During the Kāiyuán period,
official beggars in the capital
were provided with sick wards
and rations.
In recent times, it was changed to Bēitián Monastery,
or Yǎngbìng Monastery.
Clay Figures for Praying for Clear Weather
During the Tiānbǎo period,
after more than two months of autumn rain,
an imperial edict ordered people to make three-foot-tall clay figures in front of their doors,
with the left hand pointing to the sky
and the right hand pointing to the ground,
to pray for clear weather.
Bhikkhu
A monk said:
"Bìchú (Bhikkhu)
was originally the name of a plant
with five meanings:
First,
it grows without turning its back to the sun;
Second,
it is evergreen in winter and summer;
Third,
its nature is soft and pliable;
Fourth,
its fragrance spreads far;
Fifth,
its tendrils spread widely.
As a disciple of the Buddha,
it should naturally be so.
Those who are perfected are called Shāmén,
which in Hàn means 'to cease the mind.'
In Sanskrit, it is called 'śramaṇa,'
translated into Chinese as 'Shāmén.' "
Huógúo Sanzàng
Dàizōng ordered the monk Chónghuì from Hángzhōu
to be bestowed a purple kāṣāya by the court.
He was titled "Huógúo Sanzàng."
Great Virtue
Yáo Xīng of the Later Qín said to Móluóshí:
"Great Master's wisdom and enlightenment are unparalleled in the world."
Shí Hǔ called Fótúchéng "Heavenly."
The Jìnshū says:
"Preaching scriptures at Cǎotáng Temple,
there were over a thousand court officials and great virtuous shāmén."
Thus, the term "Great Virtue" came into being.
Dàzhào Chánshī
Wèi Tàizǔ considered Shāmén Fǎguǒ to be deeply accomplished.
Later, he was appointed auxiliary official and Viscount of Yíchéng.
He was successively promoted to Marquis of Zhōngxìn and Duke of Ānchéng.
Upon his death,
he was posthumously granted the titles General Lǎoshòu and Duke Húlíng.
Suí Wén considered Shāmén Yànzōng to be a scholar of the Fānyī Jīngguǎn (Sūtra Translation Institute).
During the Kāiyuán period,
monk Pǔjì died
and was posthumously named Dàzhào Chánshī.
Shāmén Using the Surname Shì
Jìn Dào'ān received instruction from Fótúchéng.
Chéng's surname was Bó.
As no teacher surpasses the Buddha,
he adopted Shì as his surname.
The practice of Shāmén in central China using Shì
began with Dào'ān.
Caltrops
Iron water caltrops.
Suí Yángdì placed them in crucial areas during his campaigns against Liáo,
to pierce horses.
Daoists Bestowed Purple
During the Zhōngzōng period,
the Daoist Yè Jìngnéng was granted golden purple.
During Dàizōng's reign,
Lǐ Bì requested to travel to Mount Héng.
An edict granted him official salary
and bestowed a purple Daoist robe.
Thereafter, the bestowal of purple upon Daoists began with Bì.
Sweat-shirt
In ancient times,
within the court ceremonial robes (gǔnfú) there was a white gauze undershirt (zhōngdān),
and among the hundred officials’ suburban sacrificial robes there was a bright garment (míngyī).
All were in the style of undershirts.
During the war between Hàn Gāozǔ and Xiàng Yǔ,
sweat soaked through the zhōngdān,
which was then called a "sweat shirt" (hànshān).
Bànchú
During the Dàyè reign of the Suí dynasty,
palace officials often wore bànchú,
which are the long sleeves of today.
Táng Gāozǔ shortened their sleeves,
calling them "bànbì" (half-sleeves).
Lǚxì
Single-soled shoes are called lǚ,
while double-soled shoes are called xì.
During the Yǒngjiā era, pigeon-head (jiūtóu) and phoenix-head (fèngtóu) lǚ were made.
Qí Gāozǔ ordered officials to wear purple leather lǚ.
Liáng Wǔdì made them of silk,
calling them "jiětuōlǚ" (liberation shoes).
Xiāngyīng
In ancient times,
when a wife first met her parents-in-law,
she would hold a xiāngyīng (fragrant sash) to bow.
It was made of five-colored silk.
Suí Niú Hóng proposed
to use an eight-foot length of plain silk, folded in the middle,
named "bóbài" (silk bow),
to replace the xiāngyīng.
Jiǔlìng
In ancient times,
the jiǔlìng (drinking game) was called "juǎnbáibō".
It originated in the Eastern Hàn dynasty when the Báibō bandits were swept away "like rolling up a mat".
Therefore, it was spoken of at drinking banquets,
to please people.
Piāntí
In the early Yuánhé era,
wine was poured using zūnsháo (wine vessels and ladles).
Before long,
zhùzǐ (wine pitchers) were used instead.
Later, Chóu Shìliáng disliked its name being similar to Zhèng Zhù [commentaries],
so he removed the handle and attached a strap,
naming it piāntí.
Tóuzi Sìsīfēi
The Shēngpǔ says:
Bólù [game]
is the name of a dice roll.
Chén Sī Wáng invented the shuānglù board [game],
and placed two dice.
By the late Táng dynasty, there was the sāizǐ game
— no one knows who invented it —
so the number of dice was increased to six.
The character tóu (骰),
should properly be tú (投),
meaning to cast or throw.
Those who made the tóu [dice]
did not decorate the fours with red.
When Míng Huáng and Guìfēi were playing a dice game and were about to lose,
only a double four could turn defeat into victory.
The Emperor threw,
and repeatedly shouted to it,
and the dice spun to form a double four.
The Emperor was greatly pleased,
and ordered Gāo Lìshì to award the double four with red [silk].
Xióngbáishēng
During the Zhēnyuán era,
Mù Níng was the cǐshǐ.
While he was eating,
his sons stood in attendance.
Seeing bear fat (xióngbái) and dried venison (lùxiū),
one said:
"The white is fatty, the dried meat lean;
they complement each other well."
He then wrapped the dried meat in the fat and presented it.
They ate the bear fat as a raw dish (shēng).
Yúdài
In the Three Dynasties, leather was used to make suàndài (counting bags),
containing counting sticks, small knives, whetstones, etc.
The Wèi dynasty changed them to guīdài (turtle bags).
During the Yǒnghuī era of the Táng dynasty,
officials of the fourth rank and above were all given personal yúdài (fish bags).
Tiānhòu changed the fish to turtles.
In the early Táng dynasty,
when qīngdàfū died,
their yúdài were reclaimed.
During the Yǒnghuī era,
an imperial edict stated that for those who used it as an honor during their lifetime in office,
it was unbearable to reclaim it upon their death.
Thus, when officials of the fifth rank and above died,
their yúdài were not reclaimed.
Guójì Zòujūnlè
In the first year of Shéngōng, when they returned victorious from defeating the Qìdān,
the palace envoy Qín jiāngjūn entered the city,
and military music (jūnlè) was played as was customary.
Now, during the imperial mourning month (guójì yuè),
it is prepared but not played.
Wáng Fāngqìng presented a memorial:
"When Jìn Mùdì married his Empress,
it was in the ninth month,
which was Kāngdì's mourning month.
The matter was sent to the Tàicháng [Court of Imperial Sacrifices],
and ritual officials such as Xún Nà deliberated, saying:
'There are only mourning days, but no mourning months.
If there were mourning months, there would have to be mourning years.'
So Nà's proposal was followed.
Moreover, military music is for military display,
different from ordinary music,
and there is no impropriety in the matter."
So it was followed.
Bù Huì Xiánmíng
When holding office, one does not avoid taboo names that are merely similar.
The records state:
Fàn Yè,
son of Tàimì,
was appointed Prince's Grand Tutor (tàizǐ zhānjì),
but firmly declined.
The court deliberated that according to ritual, merely similar names (xiánmíng) are not taboo,
so he accepted the position.
Táng Jiǎ Zēng was appointed Zhongshū Shèrén (Secretariat Drafter),
but because his father's name was Zhōng,
he resigned and did not accept.
It was deliberated that Zhongshū (中書) is the name of an office,
and although its sound is similar to Zēng's father's name, the characters are different,
so there is no taboo according to ritual.
Zēng then took up the post.
Mùzhì
When Qí Tàizǐ Mùfēi was to be buried,
there was a discussion about erecting a stone stele (shízhì).
Wáng Jiǎn said:
"The shízhì is not found in the Lǐjīng (Book of Rites).
It began with Yán Yánzhī making a mùzhì (epitaph) for Wáng Zhēn,
because the latter was of common stock and had no mǐngyú (eulogistic inscription).
Thus, it became a common practice.
Wèi Shìzhōng Miù Xí buried a document [epitaph]
beneath his parents' tomb,
intending that after a thousand years,
when hills and valleys change,
later generations might know,
only recording names, official posts held, ancestors, and in-laws.
If there were virtues and accomplishments,
then a mǐng (inscription) would be made.
King Dàwáng's tomb edict had several hundred characters.
Therefore, since the Wèi and Jìn dynasties,
there have been mùzhì.
Hàn Dù Zǐxià, nearing his end, made a mǐng and carved it on stone to be buried in front of his tomb.
Subsequently, mùzhì [epitaphs]
probably began from this."
Wǔsèqún
Liáng Wǔdì created five-colored embroidered skirts,
and added twisted pearls strung with rice to adorn them.
Suí Yángdì made long skirts with twelve pleats,
calling them "xiānqún" (immortal skirts).
Yāodài
In ancient times, there were leather belts with the hanging end inserted downwards.
Qín Èrshì created and named them yāodài (waist belts).
Táng Gāozǔ issued an edict ordering the hanging end to be inserted downwards,
taking the meaning of submission.
Xiàtiáo Dōngbīng
The Tàigōng Jīnguì Shū says:
Summer branches can be tied,
winter ice can be broken.
Biǎnquè Xiōngdì
The Hégūanzǐ says:
Biǎnquè and his two brothers were all physicians.
Wèi Wénhóu asked who was the best.
Biǎnquè said:
"My eldest brother's divine insight [prevents illness],
so his name does not leave the household.
My second brother's divine diagnosis [detects illness at its onset],
missing not a single hair,
so his name does not leave the neighborhood.
I, your humble servant, puncture people's blood vessels and administer strong medicines,
so my name is known among the feudal lords."
Xīxiào
Huán Tán's Xīnlùn says:
"A common saying in Guāndōng is:
'When people live in peace and happiness in Cháng'ān,
they go out and smile towards the west.'"
Qǐjiǎng Déjiǔ
Yuán Wéizhèng's writings say:
In the year of shēn-yǒu,
one asks for gruel and gets wine.
In the year of chén-sì,
one marries off one's wife and sells one's children.
Zhàoshū Guàbì
Cuī Yuánshǐ’s 《Zhènglùn》 says:
The prefectural and commandery systems are like sudden thunderbolts.
When imperial edicts arrive, they are merely hung on the wall.
Useless writings
I was six years old,
when my father and elder brothers taught me to write;
after another seven years,
I gradually heard of the Sages’ Way;
now, twenty-seven years later,
I occasionally gain something,
and write it down to show others.
Those who judge highly say:
“Your writings are commonplace and lack originality,
something everyone knows.”
Those who judge lowly say:
Your writings are circuitous and impractical,
yielding no benefit to the world.”
Therefore, I named my writings “Commonplace Writings” [Yōngshū],
also called “Circuitous Writings” [Yūshū].
Admonishing
a circuitous man [Yūfū] says:
“Words must not be taken lightly.
Have you not seen bells and drums?
They ring only when struck,
emitting a resonant sound,
which people do not find strange.
But if they were to ring on their own without being struck,
who would not call it an omen of evil?
To be able to speak but not to speak,
is like striking a bell or drum and having it not ring,
which is also to have a废 [fèi] bell or drum.”
Knowing wrong
Someone said:
“Does Qú Bóyù [Qu Boyu] truly know forty-nine wrongs by the age of fifty?”
Is this true?
I say:
“Among the gentlemen of old,
some knew what they had done before their death was wrong even as they were on their deathbeds,
let alone at fifty!
The Way is like a mountain;
the further one ascends, the higher it gets.
It is like a road;
the further one walks, the farther it extends.
Scholars merely exert their utmost effort and then stop.”
Heaven and man
What is beyond human power
is human,
hence there is ploughing, weeding, harvesting, and storing;
what is beyond human power
is Heaven,
hence there are floods, droughts, locusts, and other plagues.
No wonder.
For every event, there is a reason;
for every reason, there is an event.
What common people find strange
is merely what they rarely see.
To an enlightened person,
there is nothing strange in the world.
Serving parents
The circuitous old man [Yūsǒu] serves his parents,
not surpassing others,
but merely being able to not deceive them.
His service to his lord is also like this.
No benefit
Words that bring no benefit
are better left unsaid.
Deeds that bring no benefit
are better left undone.
I have long known this,
but lament my inability to act on it.
The essence of learning
Learning is for the purpose of cultivating one’s mind.
If one’s learning is extensive but one’s mind is not cultivated,
how can it be considered learning?
Cultivating the mind
Petty people cultivate their actions;
gentlemen cultivate their minds.
Harm of literature
Someone said to the circuitous old man [Yūsǒu]:
“You have grasped one or two aspects of the Way,
but alas, you lack literature to express it.”
The circuitous old man [Yūsǒu] said:
“Gentlemen use literature to clarify the Way;
petty people use literature to advance themselves.
Indeed, to turn white into black,
to turn south into north,
if not for those petty people with literary skill,
who could accomplish such things?”
The Way of man
The Way of the Sages is like Heaven and Earth;
there is nothing between Heaven and Earth that it does not encompass.
The way of ordinary people is like mountains and rivers,
like hills and valleys,
like birds and beasts,
like plants and trees,
like insects and sand —
each fulfilling its own part,
unaware of what lies beyond.
Heaven and Earth, however, encompass everything,
and pervade everywhere.
Forgetting kindness
One who receives kindness from others and cannot bear to forget it
will surely be filial as a son
and loyal as a minister.
Envy and satiety
Human nature is such that people are sated with what they have
and envy what they cannot obtain.
Before obtaining, they envy;
once obtained, they are sated.
When sated, they seek something new,
and then there is no evil they will not commit.
Buddhism and Daoism
Someone asked:
“Is there anything to be gained from Buddhism [Shì] and Daoism [Lǎo]?”
The circuitous old man [Yūsǒu] said:
“Yes, there is something to be gained.
From Buddhism, one takes its emptiness [kōng];
from Daoism, one takes its non-action [wúwéi] and naturalness [zìrán].
Other than these,
there is nothing to be gained.”
Eulogy of Non-action
Those who study Huáng-Lǎo [Huang-Lao] say that
the mind is like dead ashes,
and the body like withered wood.
The circuitous old man [Yūsǒu] considers this not to be so,
and composed the 《Wúwéi Zàn》, saying:
“Cultivate the mind with uprightness,
preserve the body with stillness.
Advance and retreat with righteousness,
gain and loss are by destiny.
Upholding the Way lies with oneself,
success is from Heaven.
What more is there to do?
Nothing is not natural.”
Taboo on having
Human nature
taboos having but not not having.
Though Lílóu [Lilu] had keen sight,
people called him blind,
and he was not resentful.
Though Liǔxià Huì [Liuxia Hui] was pure,
people called him defiled,
and he was not ashamed.
Denouncing Zhuāngzǐ
Someone said:
“Zhuāngzǐ’s [Zhuangzi] arguments
cannot be refuted even by the most learned scholars of his time.”
The circuitous man [Yūfū] said:
“He is a glib person!
What Yáo [Yao] punished,
what Shùn [Shun] found difficult,
what Kǒngzǐ [Confucius] worried about,
these are the 'green flies' that turn white into black.
Do you alone delight in them?”
Someone else said:
“No one can emulate Zhuāngzǐ’s [Zhuangzi] writings.”
The circuitous man [Yūfū] said:
“Does a gentleman’s learning
aim for the Way
or for literature?
If literature excels but the Way is not attained,
a gentleman abhors it.”
Distinguishing Yángzǐ
Someone said:
“Yángzǐ [Yangzi] was a flatterer,
considering Wáng Mǎng [Wang Mang] capable of succeeding Zhōu Gōng [Duke of Zhou] and transcending Āhéng [Aheng].”
The circuitous man [Yūfū] said:
“How could he do otherwise!
When Yángzǐ [Yangzi] wrote his books,
he evaluated the people of his time,
from the Shuāngzǐ [Shuangzi] of Shǔ [Shu] to Zhēn Zhòngyuán [Zhen Zhongyuan],
none were missed.
When Mǎng [Mang] ruled the world and likened himself to Yī [Yi] and Zhōu [Zhou],
Yángzǐ [Yangzi] agreed with him;
but if he likened himself to Huáng [Huang] and Yú [Yu],
he would not have agreed.
His intention was to say that to be an Yī [Yi] or a Zhōu [Zhou] would suffice;
this would be acceptable;
but not stopping there and proceeding to usurpation,
would Yī [Yi] and Zhōu [Zhou] have done that?”
No factions
Someone asked:
“You reject Zhuāng and cite Yáng,
are you forming a faction?”
I replied:
“I have no faction.
If Zhuāng speaks on behalf of Yáng,
I will agree with him.
If Yáng speaks on behalf of Zhuāng,
I will reject him.
Who is forming a faction?”
Sān Qī
the pedant said:
“Bowing and acting obsequiously
are not enough to be considered respectful.
Lamenting loudly and shedding tears
are not enough to be considered sorrowful.
Wearing coarse clothes and eating simple food
are not enough to be considered frugal.
These three can deceive people,
but they cannot move them.
As for the gentleman who moves people,
is it not sincerity alone?
As for one who deceives others,
people will know it before long.
As for one who moves others, the longer it lasts,
the more people will trust him.”
Heaven and Man
That which Heaven cannot do, but man can,
is man.
That which man cannot do, but Heaven can,
is Heaven.
Sowing and reaping,
is man.
Abundance and scarcity,
is Heaven.
Volume 35
ends.
The Nine Dǐng
Qín raised an army and approached Zhōu to demand the Nine Dǐng.
Zhōu was troubled.
Yán Shuài said:
“Your Majesty has no need to worry.”
Shuài went to Qí and said:
“Qín has raised an army to demand the dǐng.
The lord and ministers of Zhōu have planned,
and it is better to return them to your great state.”
The King of Qí was greatly pleased,
and dispatched an army to rescue Zhōu and demand the dǐng.
Zhōu was again troubled.
Shuài went to Qí and said:
“Zhōu relies on the righteousness of your great state,
and thus its lord, ministers, fathers, and sons can protect each other.
We wish to offer the Nine Dǐng,
but are not sure which route to take?”
The King said:
“Send them via Liáng.”
Shuài said:
“If the dǐng enter Liáng,
they will certainly not leave for Your Majesty.”
The King said:
“Send them via Chǔ.”
Shuài said:
“If they enter Chǔ,
they will certainly not leave for Your Majesty.
When Zhōu conquered Yīn and obtained the Nine Dǐng,
nine myriad men pulled each dǐng,
a total of eight hundred and ten thousand men,
and the implements were commensurate with this.
Now, even if we have all these men,
which route shall we take?”
The King of Qí then stopped.
Xī Zhōu Stops Water
Dōng Zhōu wanted to plant rice.
Xī Zhōu would not release water.
Sū Zǐ saw the lord of Xī Zhōu and said:
“Your plan is mistaken!
Not releasing water now
is how you oppose Dōng Zhōu.
But now their people can all plant wheat,
and you receive no virtue.
If you were to release water,
to harm what they have planted,
Dōng Zhōu would certainly revert to planting rice,
and then you could take it away again.
The people of Dōng Zhōu could then be made to obey your command.”
Xī Zhōu then released the water.
Ministers Praised is Not a Virtue of the State
The Lord of Sòng took time from his people to build a terrace,
and the people criticized him.
There were no loyal ministers to cover up for him.
Zǐ Hǎn resigned as prime minister to become Sīkōng,
and the people criticized Zǐ Hǎn but praised his lord.
Qí Huán Gōng had seven markets in his palace,
and seven hundred courtesans.
The people of the state criticized him.
Guǎn Zhòng deliberately built a family of Sān Guī [three large mansions],
to cover up for Huán Gōng,
not to harm himself among the people.
The Chūnqiū records cases of ministers assassinating their lords,
all of whom were ministers who received praise.
Ministers receiving praise is not a virtue of the state.
Sacrificing to the Earth for Calamity
Zhào took the sacrificial land of Zhōu.
Zhōu was troubled.
Zhèng Cháo said:
“Your servant requests to retrieve it with thirty jīn of gold.”
Zhèng offered the gold to Zhào's Grand Diviner,
and then informed him about the sacrificial land.
When the king fell ill,
he ordered a divination.
The Grand Diviner said:
“Zhōu's sacrificial land is causing a calamity.”
Zhào then returned it.
Spreading the Net
Dù Hè wanted to increase Jǐng Cuì's influence in Zhōu.
He said to the lord of Zhōu:
“Your state is small.
Using all your precious treasures and jewels to serve the feudal lords
must be carefully considered.
It is like one who spreads a net:
if he spreads it where there are no birds,
he will catch nothing.
If he spreads it where there are many birds,
he will certainly frighten the birds.
If he spreads it between where there are birds and where there are no birds,
then he will catch many birds.
Now, if you bestow favors upon important figures,
important figures will slight you.
If you bestow favors upon commoners,
commoners have nothing to offer in return,
and you will only waste wealth.
You must bestow favors upon the struggling scholars of today,
who will soon become important figures,
and thus you will achieve your desires.”
Counter-espionage
Chāng Huà fled Xī Zhōu
to Dōng Zhōu,
and revealed all the secrets of Xī Zhōu.
Xī Zhōu was furious.
Féng Dàn said:
“Your servant can kill him.”
The lord gave him thirty jīn of gold.
Féng Dàn sent a man with gold and a letter,
covertly delivering it to Chāng Huà, saying:
“If the matter can be accomplished,
strive to accomplish it.
If it cannot be accomplished,
flee quickly,
lest the matter be revealed over time,
and you bring about your own death.”
Dōng Zhōu immediately killed Chāng Huà.
Yáng Yóujī's Archery Skill
Sū Lì said to the lord of Zhōu:
“Bái Qǐ is skilled in military tactics.
Now he is attacking Liáng.
If Liáng falls, Zhōu will be in danger.
Your Majesty had better stop him.
Say to Bái Qǐ:
‘Chǔ had Yáng Yóujī who was skilled in archery.
He could hit a willow leaf from a hundred paces,
hitting it every time.
A passerby once said:
“Shooting a hundred times and hitting every time is not enough.
Soon, your strength will be exhausted,
your bow will be strained, and your string will be loose.
If you miss one shot,
all your previous achievements will be lost.”
Since your achievements are many,
and now you are again attacking Liáng,
if you do not achieve this one feat,
all your previous achievements will be wiped out.
It is better to feign illness and not go out.’”
Attacking Shǔ
Sīmǎ Cuò and Zhāng Yí debated before King Huì.
Cuò wanted to attack Shǔ.
Yí said:
"Attack Hán,
to oversee the Two Zhōus,
and hold the Son of Heaven to command the world.
I have heard that those who compete for fame do so in the court,
and those who compete for profit do so in the market.
Sānchuān and the Zhōu royal house
are the world's market and court;
if Your Majesty does not compete for them,
you will be far from the kingly enterprise."
Cuò said:
"To enrich a state,
one must expand its territory.
To strengthen an army,
one must enrich its people.
To become a true king,
one must broaden one's virtue.
Shǔ
is a remote western state.
If Qín attacks it,
it will be like a wolf chasing a flock of sheep.
In one move, both fame and tangible gains will be acquired.
Now, attacking Hán and coercing the Son of Heaven
is a bad reputation,
and may not be profitable,
and furthermore, it bears the name of injustice."
The King said:
"Good."
And so, Shǔ was attacked.
Zhōngxiào (Loyalty and Filial Piety)
If Xiào Yǐ loves his parents,
the world wishes to have him as a son.
If Zǐxū is loyal to his lord,
the world wishes to have him as a minister.
Servants and maids sold in the alleyways
are good servants and maids.
Divorced women who remarry in the countryside are good
women.
Cì Hǔ (Stabbing the Tigers)
There were two tigers fighting over a man.
Biàn Zhuāngzǐ was about to stab them.
Guǎn Yǔ said:
"Tigers
are fierce creatures.
Humans
are sweet bait.
Now they are fighting,
the smaller one will surely die,
and the larger one will surely be injured.
If you wait until they are injured and then stab them,
this is one action that will get you both tigers."
Zhāng Yí Chóu (Zhāng Yí's Enemies)
When King Huì died,
Gōngsūn wanted to corner Zhāng Yí.
Lǐ Chóu said:
"It would be better to summon Gān Mào from Wèi,
Gōngsūn Xiǎn from Hán Qǐ,
and Chūlǐzǐ from within the state.
These three are all Zhāng Yí's enemies.
If Your Lordship uses them,
then the feudal lords will see that Zhāng Yí has no Qín backing."
Bìng Zài Ěr Qián Mù Xià (Illness before the ear and below the eye)
Biǎn Què met King Wǔ of Qín.
King Wǔ showed him his illness.
Biǎn Què said:
"Your Majesty's illness is before the ear
and below the eye.
Removing it may not cure it,
and it will cause your ears to be deaf
and your eyes to be blind."
Chǔ Shǐ Duō Jiàn (Chu envoys are often assertive)
King Qín said to Gān Mào:
"The envoys from Chǔ are often assertive;
they argue with me,
and I am repeatedly cornered.
What should be done?"
Mào said:
"Your Majesty need not worry.
If the assertive ones come as envoys,
then Your Majesty should not listen to their matters.
If the soft and weak ones come as envoys,
then you must listen to them.
In this way, the assertive ones will not be employed."
Wèi Chǒufu
Queen Dowager Xuān of Qín loved Wèi Chǒufu.
When the Queen Dowager was about to die,
she wanted him buried with her as a sacrifice.
Wèi Zǐ was worried about this.
Yōng Ruì said:
"Do you believe the dead have consciousness?"
She replied:
"They have no consciousness."
Yōng Ruì said:
"Since you clearly know that the dead have no consciousness,
why would you bury one whom you loved in life
with the unconscious dead?
If the dead had consciousness,
the former king's accumulated anger would have been long-standing.
The Queen Dowager would have no time to atone for her mistakes;
how would she have time to favor Wèi Chǒufu privately?"
The Queen Dowager then stopped.
Sì Bǎo (Four Treasures)
Zhōu had the Dǐ Shí,
Sòng had the Jié Lǜ,
Liáng had the Xuán Lí,
and Chǔ had the Hé Pú.
These four treasures
were famous artifacts throughout the world.
Jiāo Shū Yán Shēn (Distant relationship, profound words)
Lǚ Shàng met King Wén.
His identity as a fisherman
indicated a distant relationship.
Yet, with a single conversation, he was appointed Grand Mentor
and taken back together with the king;
this shows the profundity of his words.
If King Wén had treated Lǚ Wàng distantly and not spoken profoundly with him,
Zhōu would not have possessed the virtue of a Son of Heaven,
and King Wén and King Wǔ would have had no one to help them achieve their kingship.
Shàn Guó Zhī Wèi Wáng (One who monopolizes the state is called a king)
Fàn Suī said:
"Qí has Tián Dān,
but I have not heard of a king;
Qín has the Queen Dowager, Ráng Hóu, Jīngyáng, and Huáyáng,
but I have not heard of a king.
Indeed, he who monopolizes the state is called a king;
he who can determine benefits and harms is called a king;
he who controls life and death is called a king.
One who is good at governing a state
solidifies his authority internally
and strengthens his power externally.
The Odes say:
'When a tree's fruit is too abundant, its branches break;
when its branches break, its heart is wounded.
He who enlarges his capital endangers his state;
he who honors his ministers debases his lord.'"
King Qín then deposed the Queen Dowager, banished Ráng Hóu, expelled Gāolíng, and drove away Jīngyáng.
Shǔ Pǔ (Rat Pǔ)
The people of Zhèng called an unworked jade a "pú."
The people of Zhōu called an unsmoked rat a "pú."
A man from Zhōu, carrying an unsmoked rat, passed a merchant from Zhèng and said:
"Do you want to buy a pú?"
The merchant took it out to look,
and said:
"It's a rat!"
Consequently, he declined and did not take it.
Dōngmén Wú
Dōngmén Wú's
son died, but he did not grieve.
His chamberlain said:
"Your Lord's love for your son
is unmatched in the world.
Now that your son is dead, you do not grieve.
Why is this?"
Wú said:
"I did not grieve when I had no son.
Now that my son is dead,
it is the same as having none."
Zhì Shèng Bù Jí Dàolǐ (Extreme prosperity does not reach reason)
Duke Huán gathered the feudal lords nine times
and unified the world.
At the assembly of Kuíqiū,
he showed signs of arrogance,
and nine states defected.
King Fūchā of Wú was unrivaled in the world,
disregarded the feudal lords,
and encroached upon Qí and Jìn.
Eventually, he brought about his own death and the ruin of his state.
Xià Yù and Tàishǐ Qǐ terrified three armies with their shouts,
but died at the hands of common men.
These all reached the height of prosperity,
but failed to adhere to reason.
Xíng Bǎi Lǐ Bàn Jiǔ Shí Lǐ (Walking a hundred li, ninety li is half)
"Of a hundred li journey,
ninety li is half."
This refers to the difficulty of the final stretch.
Hàn Rén
The King of Qín and Zhōngqī debated,
but the King could not win.
The King was angry.
Zhōngqī slowly walked away.
Someone spoke to the King of Qín on Zhōngqī's behalf, saying:
"He is a fierce person.
He merely met an enlightened ruler, that is why.
Had he met Jié or Zhòu,
they would surely have killed him."
The King of Qín consequently did not punish him.
Winning a victory in the royal court.
Zōu Jì of Qí, who was over eight chì tall,
dressed in his cap and robes, looked in the mirror,
and asked his wife:
"Who is more handsome, I or Duke Xú of the city's north?"
His wife said:
"My lord is very handsome;
how could Duke Xú compare?"
He asked his concubine again.
His concubine said:
"How could Xú compare?"
He then asked his guest.
The guest said:
"Duke Xú is not as handsome as you, my lord."
The next day, he carefully observed Duke Xú,
and knew for himself that he was far inferior.
He said:
"My wife calls me handsome
because she loves me.
My concubine calls me handsome
because she fears me.
My guest calls me handsome
because he has something to ask of me."
He entered the court and saw King Wēi, saying:
"I am not as handsome as Duke Xú.
My wife loves me,
my concubine fears me,
and my guest has something to ask of me,
and all of them called me more handsome than Duke Xú.
Now, within the thousand-lí territory of Qí,
among the palace women and attendants,
none do not love Your Majesty.
Among the ministers in the court,
none do not fear Your Majesty.
Within the four borders,
none do not have something to ask of Your Majesty.
Your Majesty is greatly misled!"
The King said:
"Excellent!"
Thereupon he issued an order that any official or commoner who could openly criticize his faults
would receive a high reward.
Those who submitted written remonstrances
would receive a medium reward.
Those who could criticize in the markets and courts
would receive a low reward.
Initially,
remonstrances were as numerous as in a marketplace.
After several months,
remonstrances were offered from time to time.
After a year,
even if one wished to speak,
there was no fault to offer.
Yān, Zhào, Hán, and Wèi all paid tribute to Qí.
This is what is meant by "winning a victory in the royal court."
Seven Hairpins
The Queen of Qí died.
There were seven concubines (rúzǐ) all close to the King.
Xuē Gōng wanted to know whom the King wished to establish,
so he presented seven hairpins,
making one particularly beautiful.
The next day,
he observed where the beautiful hairpin was placed,
and advised the King to establish that concubine as the Queen.
An ivory bed worth a thousand jīn
Mèngcháng Jūn arrived in Chǔ,
and presented an ivory bed.
Dēngtú of Yǐng,
a direct official ordered to deliver it,
did not want to go.
He saw Gōngsūn Shù and said:
"An ivory bed is worth a thousand jīn;
if it is damaged even as much as a hair,
selling my wife and children would not be enough to repay it.
If Your Excellency can make it so I don't have to go,
I will gladly offer you my precious sword."
Shù went in and saw Mèngcháng Jūn, saying:
"The small states all praise your righteousness.
Now that you have just arrived in Chǔ
and accepted an ivory bed,
how will the states you have not yet reached treat you?"
The Jūn said:
"Understood."
Shù hurried away from the Jūn.
The Jūn summoned him, saying:
"You advised Wén not to accept the ivory bed,
which was very good.
But why is your step so high and your ambition so lofty now?"
Shù said:
"Dēngtú promised me a precious sword."
The Jūn said:
"Accept it quickly!"
He then wrote on a door panel, saying:
"Anyone who praises Wén's name,
or stops Wén's errors,
yet privately gains treasure from outside,
must immediately come and see him."
Seeing seven scholars in one day
Chúnyú Kūn saw seven scholars in one day before King Xuān.
The King said:
"Isn't that too many?"
Kūn said:
"Birds with the same wings gather together;
beasts with the same feet travel together.
If you seek chái hú and jié gěng herbs in the Jǔtán marshes,
you will not find even one in generations.
But if you go to the shady side of Gāoyī and Liángfù,
you will fill carts to overflowing.
All things have their kind.
Kūn
is of the kind of worthy men.
When Your Majesty seeks scholars from Kūn,
it is like drawing water from a river,
or taking fire from a fire-starter.
How could it be limited to just seven scholars?"
Attacking Wèi
Qí wanted to attack Wèi.
Chúnyú Kūn said:
"Hán Lú
is the fastest dog in the world.
Dōngguō Jùn
is the cleverest rabbit within the seas.
Lú chased Jùn,
circling the mountain three times,
and leaping over mountains five times.
The rabbit was exhausted in front,
and the dog was tired behind.
Both dog and rabbit were spent,
and each died in its place.
A farmer saw them and claimed their spoils.
Now Qí and Wèi are locked in conflict.
Your servant fears that powerful Qín and great Chǔ will follow behind them,
gaining the farmer's spoils."
The King of Qí was afraid,
and excused his generals and rested his troops.
Are you well?
The King of Qí sent an envoy to inquire after Queen Wēi of Zhào.
He asked:
"Are the harvests well?
Are the people well?
Is the King well?"
The envoy said:
"How can one first ask about the lowly and then about the noble?"
Queen Wēi said:
"If there are no harvests,
how can there be people?
If there are no people,
how can there be a ruler?
Qí has the recluse Zhōnglízǐ,
is he well?
He feeds those who have grain,
and he feeds those who have no grain.
He clothes those who have clothes,
and he clothes those who have no clothes.
He helps the King nourish the people,
why has he not yet been employed?
Yèyángzǐ, is he well?
He pities the widowed and childless, and cares for the orphaned and solitary.
He helps the King bring peace to the people,
why has he not yet been employed?
The daughter of Běigōng, Yīng'érzǐ, is she well?
She broke her jade bracelets and ear ornaments,
and remained unmarried until old age,
to support her parents.
Why has she not yet been received in court?
Two scholars not employed,
and one woman not received in court.
How can one rule the state of Qí and treat the myriad people as one's children?
Yúlíng Zhòngzǐ above does not serve the King as a minister,
and below does not manage his household,
and leads the people in performing useless tasks.
Why has he not yet been executed?"
Tián Pián does not serve as an official.
A man from Qí
and
said:
“I heard that your honor has lofty principles,
and though you refuse official posts,
you wish to serve.”
Tián Pián
said:
“What did you hear?”
He
replied:
“My neighbor’s daughter,
resolved not to marry,
was thirty-seven years old.
Not marrying is one thing,
but she had already married excessively.
Now, your honor’s words about not seeking office,
while nurturing a thousand different disciples—not holding office is one thing,
but you have already become excessively rich.”
Tián Zǐ
saw Tián Pián
declined.
Wángsūn Jiǎ
leaned on the gate and waited for
King Mǐn
The King fled,
and his whereabouts were unknown.
His mother
said:
“If you go out in the morning and return late,
I lean on the gate and wait.
If you go out in the evening and do not return,
I lean on the village gate and wait.
Now you serve the King,
and when the King flees, you don’t know his whereabouts.
Where will you go now?”
Jiǎ
went to the eight marketplaces
and
said:
“Nào Chǐ
has thrown Qí guó
into chaos and
killed King Mǐn.
Whoever wishes to punish him with me,
bare your right arm!”
Four hundred people from the marketplace followed him,
and they
then executed Nào Chǐ.
Tián Dān
removed his clothes.
There was an old man crossing the Zī
River who was cold.
Tián Dān
took off his fur robe and gave it to him.
King Xiāng
said:
“Is Tián Dān
going to seize my country?
Are there no people around me?”
A man threading pearls beneath the hall
said:
“It would be better for Your Majesty to issue an order
saying:
‘I am worried about the people’s hunger,
so Dān
collects food and feeds them.
I am worried about the people’s cold,
so Dān
clothes them.
I am worried about the toil of the common people,
and Dān
also worries about it.’”
The villagers
said to each
other:
“Tián Dān’s
love for the people
is the benevolent influence of the King.”
Eating jade and burning cassia.
Sū Qín
went to Chǔ,
and only after three days was he granted an audience with the King.
When he
bade farewell to depart,
the King
said:
“Won’t you stay a little longer?”
He
replied:
“In Chǔ guó,
food is more expensive than jade,
and firewood is more expensive than cassia.
It is as difficult to see the usher as it is to see a ghost,
and it is as difficult to see the King as it is to see the Lord of Heaven.
Now your minister has eaten jade and burned cassia,
and through a ghost has seen the Lord.”
The King
said:
“I understand your point.”
Nán Zhèng.
Zhāng Yí
went to Chǔ,
was poor,
and wished to return.
Nán Zhèng
said:
“Your minister will go north to see
the King of Jìn.
Does Your Majesty have no requests for Jìn?”
Catching a tiger with a leg-trap.
Wèi Jiè
said to Jiànxìn Jūn:
“A man set a leg-trap and caught a tiger.
The tiger was enraged,
broke its paw,
and escaped.
It was not that the tiger did not love its paw,
but that it chose not to harm its seven-foot body
for the sake of a mere inch of paw—that is weighing options.
Now, possessing a state is not just a seven-foot body.
And your person,
vis-à-vis the King,
is not a mere inch of paw.
I hope you will consider this carefully.”
Setting a hunting appointment with the gamekeeper.
Wèi Wénhóu
set a hunting appointment with his gamekeeper.
Even though it rained,
how could he fail to keep the appointment?
So he went,
and personally dismissed it.
It was then that Wèi
began to become strong.
An old concubine serving her mistress.
Zhāng Yí
went to Wèi,
and the King of Wèi
was about to welcome him.
Zhāng Chǒu
admonished him
saying:
“Has Your Majesty heard of an old concubine serving her mistress?
When she is old and her beauty fades,
she is remarried, and that is all.
Now, my service to the King
is like an old concubine serving her mistress.”
So, Zhāng Yí
was not received.
There is a tiger in the market.
Páng Niàn,
who was held as a hostage with the Crown Prince in Hándān,
asked the King of Wèi:
“If one person says there is a tiger in the market,
does Your Majesty believe it?”
The King
said:
“No.”
“If two people say there is a tiger,
do you believe it?”
The King
said:
“I would doubt it.”
“If three people say there is a tiger,
do you believe it?”
The King
said:
“I would believe it.”
Páng Niàn
said:
“It is clear there is no tiger in the market,
yet three people’s words create a tiger.
Now, Hándān
is further from Dàliáng
than the market,
and those who speak ill of your minister
Xìnlíng Jūn
instructed Jìn Bǐ to rescue Hándān,
defeated the Qín people,
and preserved the State of Zhào.
The King of Zhào met him in the suburbs.
Táng Qíe said to Xìnlíng Jūn:
"There are things that one cannot but know;
there are things that one cannot know;
there are things that one cannot forget;
there are things that one cannot but forget."
Xìnlíng said:
"What are they?"
He replied:
"When others hate me,
I cannot but know it;
when I hate others,
it cannot be known.
When others have done me a kindness,
I cannot forget it;
when I have done kindness to others,
I cannot but forget it.
Now, you have killed Jìn Bǐ, rescued Hándān, defeated the Qín people, and preserved the State of Zhào;
this is a great kindness.
Now, the King of Zhào is meeting you in the suburbs,
and you will suddenly see the King of Zhào.
I hope you will forget it."
Wú Jì said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
Gōngzhòng Did Not See Yán Shuài
Yán Shuài sought an audience with Gōngzhòng,
but Gōngzhòng did not see him.
Shuài said:
"You must think that I will criticize you,
that is why you do not see me.
Gōngzhòng loves pleasure,
but I say he loves scholars;
Gōngzhòng is stingy with
his wealth, but I say he is generous;
Gōngzhòng is immoral,
but I say he loves righteousness.
From now on, I will speak plainly and truthfully."
Gōngzhòng immediately rose and met him.
Underestimating the Waves of Yánghóu
Bì Cháng said to Gōngshú:
"If you ride in a boat,
and the boat leaks and you do not plug it,
then the boat will sink.
If you plug the leaking boat,
but underestimate the waves of Yánghóu,
then the boat will capsize.
Now you think yourself cleverer than Xuē Gōng and underestimate Qín,
this is like plugging a leaking boat and underestimating the waves of Yánghóu."
Scolding a Dog
A high official of Qí, Zhūzǐ, had a dog,
which was fierce and could not be scolded;
if scolded, it would certainly bite people.
A guest asked to scold it.
He stared fiercely at it and then scolded it,
and the dog immediately lost the will to bite people.
Bólè Appraising a Horse
Sū Dài, acting for Yān, persuaded Qí.
He first spoke to Chúnyú Kūn, saying:
"There was a man selling a fine horse,
and it stood in the market for three mornings,
but no one recognized its worth.
He went to see Bólè and had him appraise it,
and the horse's price increased tenfold.
Now I wish to present a fine horse to the King,
but there is no one to introduce me.
Are you willing to be my Bólè?"
Kūn went in and spoke of it,
and the King of Qí was greatly pleased with Sūzǐ.
The Snipe and the Clam
Zhào Dàn attacked Yān.
Sū Dài, on behalf of Yān, said to King Huì:
"As I crossed the Yì Shuǐ,
a clam was basking itself,
and a snipe pecked at its flesh.
The clam closed, clamping its beak.
The snipe said:
'If it doesn't rain today,
and it doesn't rain tomorrow,
there will be a dead clam.'
The clam likewise said to the snipe:
'If you don't get out today,
and you don't get out tomorrow,
there will be a dead snipe.'
Neither would let go of the other,
and a fisherman came and caught them both."
Redeeming an Ex-Convict with a Hundred Gold Pieces
During the time of Wèi Sì Jūn,
an ex-convict who had committed a crime, and was a worthy official, fled to Wèi.
Wèi offered a hundred gold pieces to redeem him,
but Wèi did not agree.
Then Wèi asked to exchange him for the territory of Zuǒshì.
The officials of the Wèi town said:
"To redeem an ex-convict
with a territory of a hundred chariots,
is this not inappropriate?"
The ruler said:
"In good governance, nothing is trivial;
in disorder, nothing is too great.
If the people are instructed and enlightened,
a city of three hundred [li in circumference]
is enough for good governance.
If the people lack integrity and shame,
even with ten Zuǒshìs,
how can they be used?"
The New Wife's Misspoken Words
A man from Wèi was receiving his new wife.
The wife got into the carriage
and asked:
"The side horses [cān mǎ],
whose horses are they?"
The charioteer replied:
"They are borrowed."
She said to the attendant:
"Attach the side horses (fù cān),
do not whip the shaft horses (fú)."
Fù
means to tie.
The horses on the two sides are called cān,
those in the shafts are called fú.
If their cān are tied,
then the two fú horses in the middle will not be overworked.
When the carriage arrived at the gate,
she again instructed her escorts:
"Reduce the stoves to prevent fire."
Entering the room and seeing a mortar,
she said:
"Move it under the window,
it obstructs passers-by."
The host laughed at her.
These three statements were all important,
yet she could not avoid being laughed at
because of the untimely nature of their delivery.
Mutton Broth Leading to National Ruin, a Pot of Food Gaining Warriors
The Ruler of Zhōngshān hosted a banquet for his capital's scholars.
The Grandee Sīmǎ Zǐqī was present.
The mutton broth was not distributed evenly,
and Zǐqī angrily went to Chǔ,
and persuaded Chǔ to attack Zhōngshān.
The Ruler of Zhōngshān fled.
There were two men carrying halberds who followed him.
The ruler looked back and said:
"Who are you?"
They replied:
"Our father was once starving and near death.
You gave him a pot of food to eat.
When our father was near death,
he said:
'If Zhōngshān has trouble,
you must die for it.'
Therefore, we have come to die for you."
The ruler sighed and said:
"In giving, do not measure by quantity,
but by necessity in a predicament;
in resentment, do not measure by depth or shallowness,
but by hurt feelings.
I lost my state over a cup of mutton broth,
and gained two warriors with a pot of food."

Lǎncán
There was a monk at Héngyuè Temple who performed duties.
He was by nature lazy and ate leftovers (cán),
Lǐ Bì found this unusual.
One day, Lǐ Bì went to see him,
and found him poking a fire, roasting taro and eating it.
He took half of it and offered it to Bì, saying:
“Don’t speak much.
You will be prime minister for ten years.”
Yuánzé as a Pregnant Woman’s Child
Lǐ Yuán and the monk Yuánzé were close friends.
They traveled together to the Sānxiá gorges.
When they reached Nánpǔ,
they saw a pregnant woman.
Yuánzé said:
“This is where I am destined to reside.”
He then hastily bid farewell to Yuán:
“Twelve years from now, we shall meet in Hángzhōu.”
That very evening, he indeed passed away.
The woman gave birth to a son.
Yuán arrived at Tiānzhú Temple in Hángzhōu as promised,
and heard a shepherd boy with a knot of hair singing a bamboo-branch song.
It was Yuánzé.
He called out from across the stream:
“Our paths are different;
you must not come near.”
The boy sang:
“The old spirit on the Three-Lives Stone,
discuss not appreciating the moon or chanting of the wind.
I am ashamed, my dear friend, that you have come so far to visit;
though this body is different, my nature remains ever present.”
The Courtesan Hóngxiàn
Xūe Sōng, the military governor (lù shī) of Táng, had a courtesan named Hóngxiàn.
After the Zhìdé era,
the two rivers (Héxī and Hénán) were not yet peaceful.
Tián Chéngsì harbored rebellious ambitions,
and recruited three thousand brave warriors,
calling them "outer house men."
Sōng was worried about this,
and often muttered to himself.
Hóngxiàn said:
“It’s easy!
I am willing to go and observe his situation.
I will set off at first watch,
and be back by the third watch.”
She went out the door and suddenly disappeared.
Before dawn, she returned,
bringing with her a golden casket from Chéngsì’s bedchamber.
Sōng sent an envoy with the casket and a letter, saying:
“A visitor came from over there,
and said he obtained this golden casket from near the Marshal’s head.”
Chéngsì was greatly dismayed,
and disbanded his "outer house men."
Héběi was pacified.
Lǐ Móu’s Flute
The musician Xǔ Yúnfēng was skilled at playing the flute,
and claimed to have learned from his maternal grandfather, Lǐ Móu.
Wéi Yìngwù showed him an ancient flute,
saying:
“During the Tiānbǎo era,
I obtained it from Lǐ Gōngfèng.”
Yúnfēng looked at it,
and said it was not the flute his maternal grandfather had played.
The Duke (Wéi Yìngwù) asked:
“How do you know?”
Yúnfēng said:
“The method for selecting bamboo
is to cut it before the full moon of the seventh month of the current year.
If it’s past the date, the sound will be heavy (shí);
if it’s before the date, the sound will be hollow (fú).
A hollow bamboo
is externally moist but internally dry,
not having fully received qi,
and thus that bamboo is flawed (yāo).
This flute is one of the flawed ones;
when it encounters a perfect note, it will surely crack.
Let me try playing it now.”
Yúnfēng raised the flute and played “Liù Zhōu Biàn,”
and before one repetition was finished,
the flute suddenly split in the middle.
The South-Pointing Chariot
The Yuèshāng clan came to pay tribute,
but forgot their way home.
Zhōu Gōng gave them a South-Pointing Chariot,
and when they reached their country, the iron axle-pins of the chariot were all worn away.
Peach Bow and Reed Arrows
The Qín dynasty made "evil-repelling chariots,"
and hung them on gates.
With peach bows and reed arrows,
to ward off misfortune.
Leopard Chariot
Zhōu Gōng made leopard-tail chariots,
symbolizing the grandees’ ambition for a "leopard transformation."
Ancient military commanders used to erect them.
Now only the emperor's carriage is permitted to have them.
Jīnwú (Golden Crow/Vanguard)
A Jīnwú
is a chariot spoke,
a staff.
The Hàn Dynasty’s Zhí Jīnwú (Director of the Golden Crow) also carried a staff,
made of bronze,
gilded at both ends,
and called Jīnwú.
The Yùshǐ Dàfū (Grandee Secretary) and Sīlì Xiàowèi (Colonel Director of Retainers)
were also permitted to wield it.
Commandery governors and county magistrates
ordinarily used wooden wú.
It was used to flank chariots,
shaped like a chariot spoke.
Huágài (Ornamental Canopy)
When Huángdì fought Chīyóu at Zhuōlù,
there was always a five-colored cloud of qi,
with golden branches and jade leaves resting above the Emperor.
Because of this, the huágài was made.
Qūgài (Bent Canopy)
When Wǔ Wáng attacked Zhòu,
a strong wind broke his canopy.
Tài Gōng then bent it,
and it became a qūgài.
Cricket
Also called jiōng.
People of Jǐnán call it lǎnfù (lazy wife).
Pheasant-Tail Fan
Originated in the Yīn dynasty.
Gāozōng had an auspicious omen of the mynah’s tail.
White Pen
A remnant of the ancient practice of wearing a pen tucked into one’s hair.
Wearing a pen at the sword hilt
shows that a gentleman possesses both civil and military accomplishments.
Yínghǔ (Fly Tiger)
Also yínghú (fly fox),
or yíngbào (fly leopard).
Wǔmíng Shàn (Five-Light Fan)
Shùn broadly expanded his sight and hearing,
seeking worthy men as assistants.
Therefore, he made the wǔmíng shàn.
Earthworm
People of Jiāngdōng call them "singing girls."
Also called "míngqì" (singing on steps).
Six Swords
Wú Dàdì had six precious swords:
one named Báidì,
two named Zǐdiàn,
three named Pìxié,
four named Liúxīng,
five named Qīngmíng,
and six named Bǎilǐ.
Three precious swords (another set?):
one named Bǎiliàn,
two named Qīngdú,
three named Lòuyǐng.
Zǐsài (Purple Frontier)
The Qín dynasty built the Great Wall, all of it purple,
and called it Zǐsài.
The earth color of the southern frontier was vermillion,
so it was called Dānjìao.
These were to block the Yōngsài and Yídí.
Jiào
means "to surround."
Its purpose was to prevent encroachment on the Central Plains.
Gōulán (Hooked Railing)
At the Hàn dynasty's Gù Chéng Temple,
gōulán for supporting the elderly were installed.
Tūqiū (Bald Autumn)
Resembles a crane,
the large ones are eight feet tall.
Good at fighting people,
and fond of eating snakes.
Wild Goose
Crossing the Jiāngnán from Héběi,
they are thin and able to fly,
not fearing silk nets.
Jiāngnán is fertile and rich,
so upon returning to Héběi,
they are fat and cannot fly high,
fearing capture by people.
They often peck at reeds to defend against nets and arrows.
Donkey and Mule
When a female donkey (lǘ pìn) and a male horse (mǎ mǔ) mate,
they produce a mule (luó).
When a female horse (mǎ pìn) and a male donkey (lǘ mǔ) mate,
they produce a màimǎ (hinny).
Seven Horses
Qín Shǐhuáng had seven horses,
named:
Zhuīfēng, Báitù, Nièjǐng, Zhuīdiàn, Fēihé, Tóngjué, Chángfú.
Magpies, swallows, sparrows, and mynas.
A magpie is called Shénnǚ.
A sparrow is called Xǐbīn,
like a guest in a human household.
A swallow is named Tiānnǚ,
also named Zhìniǎo.
A myna
is also named Shījiū.
A swallow is also named Xuánniǎo.
Chickens, dogs, pigs, and sheep.
A chicken
is also named Zhúyè,
and also Hàn'yīn.
A dog is called Huángyáng.
A pig is called Cānjūn.
A sheep is called Ránzhǔbù.
Fireflies
are also named Yàoyè,
also named Dānniǎo,
also named Yèguāng,
also named Xiāozhú.
A rat has five abilities,
but cannot master any skill.
First, it flies but cannot clear a roof.
Second, it climbs but cannot reach the top of a tree.
Third, it swims but cannot cross a valley.
Fourth, it burrows but cannot conceal its body.
Fifth, it runs but cannot escape people.
Bats
are also named Xiānsǔ.
At five hundred years old, their color is white and their brain is heavy.
When they alight on something, their head hangs down,
which is called 'upside-down birth'.
Whales and females whales.
Whales,
the large ones are a thousand *lǐ* long,
the small ones are several thousand *zhàng* long.
In the fifth and sixth months, they come to the shore to give birth.
In the seventh and eighth months, they lead their young back to the vast sea.
They beat the waves into thunder,
and spray water into rain.
Water creatures are startled and flee,
none dare to face them.
The female is called ní.
Her eyes are like pearl flowers.
The Water Lord
looks like a person riding a horse,
with many fish escorting him.
He is also named Yúbó.
Someone saw him;
the person and horse both had scales and armor,
like a large carp.
His hands, feet, ears, and nose were no different from a human's.
He looked at the person for a long time,
then entered the water.
Turtles and softshell turtles.
A turtle
is also named Xuánshuǐdūyóu.
A softshell turtle
is also named Hébócóngshì,
and also Hébóshǐ.
Cuttlefish
are also named Hébódùshǐxiǎolì.
Butterflies are called Fèng.
Brush-footed butterflies
are also called Yě'é.
Wind butterflies,
the large ones are called Fèngzǐchē,
or black ones
are named Guǐchē.
Dragonflies
are sometimes called húdié,
which are qīngtíng.
The small ones are called Húlí,
also named Chìyīshǐzhě,
and also Chìbiànzhàngrén.
The Yaoming
During the time of Yáo,
there was a *míng* tree in front of the palace.
From the first to the fifteenth of the month,
it opened one leaf each day.
From the sixteenth to the end of the month,
one leaf withered each day.
Water flowers
Hibiscus,
also named Hēhuā,
also named Shuǐzhī,
also named Shuǐhuā.
Chénniàng
The Wūsūn kingdom has an azure-field nut fruit.
If one measures its tree,
the root is as large as a five or six *dǒu* gourd.
If water is stored in it, it becomes wine.
Liú Zhāng obtained three nuts;
twenty people drank from them without exhausting them.
They were called Qīngtiánhújiǔ.
A Han *sèfū*,
stayed overnight at a ford.
It was called Chénniàng.
Water poured into it
made one deeply drunk all night.
Thus it was named Chénniàng.
Zhíchú
If sheep eat it,
they stagger and die.
This is also how it got its name.
Running boats and startled-sail horses
Sūn Quán made running boats,
which moved as fast as horses galloping.
Zēng Zhēn had a swift horse named Jīngfān,
its speed was like a fierce wind raising a sail.
Sháoyào
In ancient times, when parting ways,
they would give *sháoyào* as a gift.
Sháoyào
is also named Kělí, hence.
When inviting someone, they would give *wúwén* as a gift.
Wúwén
is also named Dāngguī.
To make one forget worries,
they would give Dānjí as a gift,
which is also named Wàngyōu.
To dispel one's anger,
they would give Héhuān.
Héhuān
means to forget anger.
Fěibàngmù
Yáo set up Fěibàngmù,
which is today's huábiǎo,
with horizontal beams crossing the pillar tops,
also called Jiāowǔmù.
Innate awareness
There are living things without awareness;
plants are an example.
There are non-living things with awareness;
ghosts and spirits are an example.
There are non-living things without awareness;
water is an example.
Mosquitoes and millet people
People in Hénèi saw thousands of people and horses,
like millet grains,
moving about.
When burned,
they were mosquitoes.
The horses all turned into large ants.
Thus, mosquitoes are called Shǔmín,
and ants are called Xuánjū.
The Qi woman
The Queen of Qí, full of resentment, died
and transformed into a cicada.
She climbed a tree and chirped loudly.
The king felt regret.
Thus, cicadas are called Qínǚ.
Needle god
Wèi Wéndì's beautiful concubine, Xuē Língzhī,
entered the palace after a short selection.
Zhī bid farewell to her parents and ascended the carriage,
catching her tears in a jade spittoon.
The spittoon turned entirely red.
The emperor sent a light carriage to welcome her.
He looked at her and sighed:
"In former years, morning was wandering clouds,
evening was wandering rain.
Now it is neither cloud nor rain,
neither morning nor evening."
He then named her Yèlāi.
She was exquisite in needlework skill;
if not for Yèlāi's tailoring, the emperor would not wear the clothes.
She was called Zhēnshén.
Huánkuì
Huán means
the wall of a market.
Kuì means
the gate of a market.
Sì
is where goods for sale are displayed.
Diàn
is where goods for sale are stored.
Pánjì
Hairstyles of women in Cháng'ān:
Some styled the "horse-following bun,"
also called the "toppling horse bun."
There was also the "coiled dragon bun."
Dùyǔ
The first king of Shǔ was called Cáncóng,
the next Bóyōng,
and the next Yúfú.
He was also known as Dùyǔ, King of Shǔ,
who styled himself Wàngdì.
Liùzhào
The six tribes of the Southern Mán were not unified.
Each time the Son of Heaven issued an edict,
a copy was given to each,
hence the name Liùzhào.
Furthermore, in their dialect,
"zhào" meant "king."
At the end of the Kāiyuán era of the Táng dynasty,
Jìdùshǐ Wáng Yù accepted bribes
and petitioned for them to be united.
The great chieftain Méng Guīyì was enfeoffed as the King of Yúnnán.
Only then did they exclusively call themselves Nánzhào.
Once they grew powerful,
they became a border menace.
Jǐnlǐ
Jǐnzhōu is south of the city,
with the Luòqiáo bridge.
In the time of Eastern Shǔ, there was a Brocade Palace,
also known as Jǐnlǐ.
Cánnǚ
Her tomb is in Miánzhú County.
A statue of a girl is fashioned
and draped with horsehide.
It is popularly known as the Mǎtóuniáng Temple.
Qīngpíngguān
When Nánzhào was pacified,
those who served as literary officials were called "Qīngpíngguān."
Zhíshòuzi
The Hàn Shìzhōng was in charge of imperial carriage items.
Among the personal effects was an item called a "shòuzi."
Hence, the Shìzhōng was called Zhíshòuzi.
Lángzhōnglìng
The Qín dynasty first established the system.
The Lángzhōnglìng's subordinates included three bureaus:
one was the Wǔguān Zhōnglángjiāng,
the second was the Zuǒ Zhōnglángjiāng,
and the third was the Yòu Zhōnglángjiāng.
Each bureau also had Lángzhōng
and Shìláng.
The Western Hàn continued this system.
Only Tián Fén served as Zhūcáoláng in his youth,
which was a Shàngshū Láng.
Others, like Féng Táng, served as Lángzhōng,
and an elder was appointed.
Zhí Bùyí, Yán Sì, and similar individuals
all belonged to the three bureaus.
End of Volume Thirty-six.
Huángdì and Qíbó's Discussion
Huángdì, having ascended the throne,
sat in the Míngtáng,
surveying the eight directions,
and establishing the Five Constants.
He believed that human life carries yin and embraces yang,
eats flavors and is adorned with colors;
cold and heat contend,
joy and anger alternate.
So he and Qíbó thoroughly investigated the celestial principles above
and profoundly explored geographical principles below;
they drew extensively from external things
and intimately from the human body;
they questioned each other back and forth.
Léigōng and others received and transmitted their teachings,
and thus the Nèijīng was composed.
When the Cāngzhōu flourished,
Qín Hé elaborated on the theory of the Six Qì,
which was fully recorded by the Left Scribe.
Subsequently, Yuèrén grasped one or two of its principles,
and elaborated on them in the Nánjīng.
In the Western Hàn, Cānggōng transmitted the old teachings.
In the Eastern Hàn, Zhòngjǐng compiled his remaining treatises.
In the Jìn, Huángfǔ Mì arranged them into Jiǎyǐ.
In the Suí, Yáng Shàngshàn compiled the Tàisù.
In the Táng, Wáng Bīng was devoted to it
and greatly expanded its annotations.
Suwèn has only eight scrolls
Bān Gù said:
The Nèijīng has eighteen scrolls.
The Suwèn comprises nine scrolls of that classic,
and combined with the nine scrolls of the Língshū,
that makes up its number.
Although eras changed,
the transmission of knowledge still exists.
Fearing it might fall into the wrong hands,
it was sometimes kept hidden.
Therefore, Volume Seven,
a single scroll, was hidden by the Master's family,
and only "Juǎněr" was circulated.
In the Zhōu dynasty, there were Hé and Huǎn.
In the Hàn, there was Chúnyú.
In the Wèi, there were Zhānggōng and Huágōng.
All these individuals attained this profound path.
Decline at fifty
The Emperor asked the Celestial Master:
"Ancient people at a hundred years old did not decline in activity,
but modern people at fifty all decline in activity."
He replied:
"Ancient people who understood the Way
followed the principles of yin and yang,
understood methods and calculations,
had moderation in eating and drinking,
regularity in daily life,
did not engage in reckless labor,
and thus completed their natural lifespan.
Modern people use wine as beverage,
take recklessness as normalcy,
enter the bedchamber while drunk,
and exhaust their essence.
Therefore, they decline at fifty."
Tiānguǐ
For women, at fourteen years, the tiānguǐ arrives.
The Rènmài opens,
the Tàichōng flourishes,
and menstruation occurs on time.
Thus, they can bear children.
For men, at sixteen (two eights), kidney qi flourishes,
tiānguǐ arrives,
seminal essence overflows,
and yin and yang are in harmony.
Thus, they can bear children.
Those who bear children in old age
have continuously open qi channels
and abundant kidney qi.
For bearing children,
men do not exceed sixty-four (eight eights),
and women do not exceed forty-nine (seven sevens),
for then the vital essence of heaven and earth is exhausted.
The lifespan of children does not exceed the number of tiānguǐ.
The Way of the Four Seasons
Spring is called "developing and spreading";
heaven and earth are born together,
and all things flourish.
One sleeps at night and rises early,
takes wide steps in the courtyard,
lets hair loose and relaxes the body,
to allow the spirit to grow.
Give life and do not kill,
give and do not take away,
reward and do not punish;
this responds to the Way of birth and nurturing.
Summer is "luxuriant growth";
the qi of heaven and earth intermingle,
and all things blossom and bear fruit.
One sleeps at night and rises early,
avoids the midday sun,
keeps the spirit free from anger,
so that qi can be discharged;
this responds to the Way of growth and development.
Autumn is called "containing and balancing";
the qi of heaven becomes urgent,
and the qi of earth becomes clear.
One sleeps early and rises early,
rising with the chickens,
to allow the spirit to be at peace and the body to be collected;
this responds to the Way of harvesting and storing.
