Winter is called "closing and concealing";
water freezes and the earth cracks.
One sleeps early and rises late,
must await daylight,
moves away from cold and seeks warmth,
does not expose the skin,
to allow the spirit to be tranquil;
this responds to the Way of concealment and storage.
Nèigé
The Way
is followed by the sages
and turned against by the foolish.
Following yin and yang leads to life;
going against them leads to death.
Following them leads to order;
going against them leads to chaos.
To reverse conformity and embrace opposition
is called Nèigé.
Internal nature resisting and opposing
is not the Way of Heaven.
Sages do not treat an already existing illness,
but prevent illness;
they do not manage existing chaos,
but prevent chaos.
Ácuō Fèi
Whenever a person experiences great anger,
their qi in form and spirit becomes obstructed, and blood stagnates upwards,
causing them to faint and injure their sinews.
If the turbid qi does not exit,
it causes hemiplegia.
When sweat exits and meets dampness,
áčuō fèi then arise.
Fēng, the beginning of a hundred diseases
Fēng is
the beginning of a hundred diseases.
When one is clear and quiet, the internal and external are securely guarded.
Though a hundred afflictions come,
they cannot cause harm.
Therefore, if a disease persists, it transforms and spreads;
if the upper and lower are not harmonious,
even a good physician cannot treat it.
Qi at dawn
At dawn,
human qi begins to rise;
at midday,
yang qi flourishes;
at sunset,
yang becomes deficient,
and the gates close.
Therefore, one should gather and guard in the evening,
not disturb the sinews and bones,
and avoid mist and dew.
Acting contrary to these two times
will cause the body to become weak and frail.
The qi of the four seasons alternately harms the five zàng
If one is harmed by fēng in spring,
the evil qi remains in summer,
then causing incessant diarrhea;
this is because wood overcomes spleen earth.
If one is harmed by shǔ in summer,
it becomes malaria in autumn.
If one is harmed by shī in autumn,
there is adverse qi and coughing in winter,
leading to flaccidity and cold extremities.
If one is harmed by hán in winter,
they will definitely have a warm disease in spring.
The qi of the four seasons
alternately harms the five zàng.
Not pressing and stretching in winter
In spring, the qi disease is in the head;
in summer, the qi disease is in the zàng;
in autumn, the qi disease is in the shoulders;
in winter, the qi disease is in the four limbs.
Not pressing and stretching in winter
refers to not massaging and stretching vigorously,
nor disturbing the sinews and bones.
Then yang qi can be hidden and stored.
If one does not suffer from nosebleed in spring —
“gǔ” means water coming out of the nose;
“nǜ” means blood coming out of the nose —
it is because water does not exhaust wood.
Furthermore, if one does not have diseases of the head and neck in spring,
does not have diseases of the chest and hypochondrium in midsummer,
does not have incessant diarrhea in late summer,
does not have fēng-malaria in autumn,
and does not have bì-pain in winter,
all these are due to not pressing and stretching in winter.
Yīn and Yáng, Hán and Rè
Yīn is still, Yáng is restless;
Yáng generates, Yīn grows;
Yáng emerges, Yīn stores.
Yáng transforms qi,
Yīn forms shape.
Extreme hán generates rè,
extreme rè generates hán.
Hán qi generates turbidity,
rè qi generates clarity.
Swelling
Pain first, then swelling,
means qi injures the form.
If fēng prevails, there is pain;
if rè prevails, there is swelling;
if zào prevails, there is dryness;
if hán prevails, there is floating;
if shī prevails, there is dampness.
Four seasons, five phases, five zàng, five qi
Heaven has four seasons and five phases,
generating, growing, gathering, and storing,
thereby producing hán, shǔ, zào, shī, and fēng.
Humans have five zàng,
transforming five qi,
thereby producing joy, anger, sorrow, worry, and fear.
Thus, joy and anger injure qi;
hán and shǔ injure the form;
sudden anger injures Yīn;
sudden joy injures Yáng.
If one can understand the seven harms and eight bursts,
then Yīn and Yáng can be harmonized.
For women, at seven sevens (49 years),
tiān guǐ ends.
For men, at eight eights (64 years),
tiān guǐ reaches its peak.
If one understands this, they will be strong;
if not, they will grow old and sick.
Ears, Eyes, Hands, Feet
Heaven is deficient in the northwest,
thus a person's right ear and eye are not as clear as the left.
Earth is not full in the southeast,
thus
a person's left
hand and foot are not as strong as the right.
The East is Yáng;
its essence converges above, thus the upper
is abundant and the lower is deficient;
therefore, the ears and eyes are keen,
but the hands and feet are not agile.
The West is Yīn;
its essence converges below,
thus the lower is abundant and the upper is deficient;
therefore, the ears and eyes are not keen,
but the hands and feet are agile.
Evil Fēng
When evil fēng arrives,
it is as swift as wind and rain.
A skilled healer first treats the skin and hair,
then the muscles and flesh,
then the sinews and vessels,
then the six fǔ,
then the five zàng.
Treating the five zàng
is a matter of half life, half death.
Pulse Diagnosis
One skilled in using needles
draws Yáng from Yīn,
and draws Yīn from Yáng;
treats the left with the right,
and treats the right with the left;
knows the other through oneself,
and knows the interior through the exterior.
One skilled in pulse diagnosis
observes the complexion and presses the pulse,
first distinguishing Yīn and Yáng.
They discern clarity and turbidity to understand the different parts,
observe breathing and listen to sounds to know the suffering,
and examine the balance, compass, and square to know where the disease arises.
They press the cùn and chǐ, observe floating, sunken, slippery, and choppy pulses to know where the disease is located.
Four Channels and Twelve Courses
Humans have four channels and twelve courses.
The four channels correspond to the four seasons,
and the twelve courses correspond to the twelve months,
which correspond to the twelve pulses.
Spring is wiry, summer is surging, autumn is floating, winter is sunken—
these are the seasonal channels.
The courses refer to the harmonious flow of heavenly qi,
divided into the twelve earthly branches.
The twelve pulses
refer to the three Yīn and three Yáng of the hand,
and the three Yīn and three Yáng of the foot.
Twelve Officials
The heart (xīn) is the official of the sovereign;
spiritual intelligence (shénmíng) emanates from it.
The lung (fèi) is
the official of the minister and傳 (chuán, though it means transmission here, it is usually part of a title with xiàng),
regulation and rhythm (zhìjié) emanate from it.
The liver (gān) is
the official of the general;
strategy and deliberation (móulǜ) emanate from it.
The gallbladder (dǎn) is
the official of impartiality and rectitude;
judgment and decision (juédàn) emanate from it.
The pericardium/chest (tánzhōng) is
the official of the臣使 (chénshǐ, minister-envoy);
joy and happiness (xǐlè) emanate from it.
It is located between the two breasts,
and is the sea of qi (qì).
The spleen (pí) and stomach (wèi) are
the officials of the granaries;
the five flavors (wǔwèi) emanate from them.
The large intestine (dàcháng) is
the official of transmission;
transformation and change (biànhuà) emanate from it.
The small intestine (xiǎocháng) is
the official that receives and stores;
the transformation of substances (huàwù) emanates from it.
The kidney (shèn) is
the official that undertakes strength;
skill and dexterity (jìqiǎo) emanate from it.
The triple burner (sānjiāo) is
the official that determines and dredges;
water passages (shuǐdào) emanate from it.
The bladder (pángguāng) is
the official of the prefecture and capital;
bodily fluids (jīnyè) are stored there.
All twelve officials
must not lose their proper functions.
The spleen (pí) and stomach (wèi) are two organs that function as one official.
Climate (qìhòu)
Three days is called a hòu (候);
five hòu are called a qì (氣);
six qì are called a shí (時);
four shí are called a suì (歲).
Six pulses (liùmài)
In all people, the various vessels (mài) belong to the eyes (mù),
the marrow (suǐ) belongs to the brain (nǎo),
the sinews (jīn) belong to the joints (jié),
the blood (xuè) belongs to the heart (xīn),
and the qi (qì) belongs to the lung (fèi).
The six pulses (liùmài)
are the tides of qi (qì).
When a person sleeps, blood returns to the liver (gān).
When a person sleeps,
blood returns to the liver (gān).
The eyes (yǎn) receive blood and can see;
the feet (zú) receive blood and can walk;
the palms (zhǎng) receive blood and can grasp;
the fingers (zhǐ) receive blood and can pick up.
Corresponding to Heaven, emulating Earth
The True Person (zhēnrén)
corresponds above to Heaven (tiān) to nourish the head (tóu),
emulates below Earth (dì) to nourish the feet (zú),
and imitates human affairs in the middle to nourish the five zàng (wǔzàng).
Six qi (liùqì)
The qi of Heaven (tiānqì) communicates with the lung (fèi);
the qi of Earth (dìqì) communicates with the throat (ài);
the qi of wind (fēngqì) communicates with the liver (gān);
the qi of thunder (léiqì) communicates with the heart (xīn);
the qi of valleys (gǔqì) communicates with the spleen (pí);
the qi of rain (yǔqì) communicates with the kidney (shèn).
The intestines (cháng) and stomach (wèi) are the sea (hǎi);
the nine orifices (jiǔqiào) are the water (shuǐ).
Five zàng (wǔzàng) and six fǔ (liùfǔ)
The five zàng (wǔzàng)
store essence-qi (jīngqì) and do not discharge it,
therefore they are full but cannot be solid.
The six fǔ (liùfǔ)
transmit substances and transform them without storing them,
therefore they are solid but cannot be full.
When water and grain enter the mouth,
the stomach (wèi) becomes solid and the intestines (cháng) become empty.
After food descends,
the abdomen (fù) becomes solid and the stomach (wèi) becomes empty.
Stomach (wèi) as the sea of water and grain
The stomach (wèi)
is the sea of water and grain,
and the source of the six fǔ (liùfǔ).
The five flavors (wǔwèi) enter the mouth,
are stored in the stomach (wèi),
to nourish the five zàng (wǔzàng).
The qi口 (qìkǒu) is also the Great Yin (Tàiyīn).
The qi (qì) of the five zàng (wǔzàng) and six fǔ (liùfǔ) all emanates from the stomach (wèi) and transforms,
appearing at the qi口 (qìkǒu).
The five qi (wǔqì) enter the nose (bí),
and are stored in the lung (fèi).
If the lung (fèi) has a disease,
the nose (bí) will be obstructed.
Diagnostic method (zhěnfǎ)
The diagnostic method (zhěnfǎ) is usually performed at dawn (píngdàn),
when yin qi (yīnqì) has not yet moved,
yang qi (yángqì) has not yet dispersed,
food and drink have not yet been consumed,
the main meridians (jīngmài) are not yet replete,
the collateral meridians (luòmài) are regulated and even,
and blood (xuè) and qi (qì) are not yet disturbed.
Therefore, diagnosis can be performed.
By palpating the pulse's movement and stillness,
internally observing the essence and brightness,
examining the five colors (wǔsè),
observing the excess or deficiency of the five zàng (wǔzàng),
the strength or weakness of the six fǔ (liùfǔ),
and the prosperity or decline of the form (xíng) and qi (qì),
one can thereby determine the distinction between life and death.
Blood vessels (xuèmài)
The vessels (mài)
are the abode of blood (xuè).
If blood (xuè) is full, the vessels (mài) are full;
if blood (xuè) is empty, the vessels (mài) are empty.
Five colors (wǔsè)
Colors (sè)
are the efflorescence of qi (qì).
Red (chì) should be like white silk wrapped in vermillion (zhū),
not like a reddish-brown (zhě) or off-white (bái).
White (bái) should be like goose feathers,
not like salt.
Blue-green (qīng) should be like the luster of a dark jade disk,
not like indigo (lán).
Yellow (huáng) should be like a silk sash wrapped around realgar (xiónghuáng),
not like earth (tǔ).
Black (hēi) should be like multiple layers of lacquer,
not like roof dust.
If the subtle essence of the five colors (wǔsè)
shows signs of decay,
longevity will not be long.
Gaining strength means life, losing strength means death.
The five zàng (wǔzàng)
are the strength (qiáng) of the body.
The head (tóu)
is the abode of spirit (jīngshén);
if the head (tóu) is tilted and the gaze is deep,
the spirit (jīngshén) is about to be taken away.
The back (bèi)
is the abode of the chest (xiōng);
if the back (bèi) is bent and the shoulders (jiān) droop,
the chest (xiōng) is about to fail.
The waist (yāo)
is the abode of the kidney (shèn);
if one cannot turn the waist
diligently,
the kidney (shèn)
is about to fail.
The knees (xī)
are the abode of the sinews (jīn);
if one cannot flex and extend to walk,
the sinews (jīn) are about to be exhausted.
The bones (gǔ)
are the abode of the marrow (suǐ);
if one cannot stand for long,
and trembles when walking,
the marrow (suǐ) is about to be exhausted.
Gaining strength means life,
losing strength means death.
Movements of the four transformations
The warmth of spring (chūn)
becomes the heat of summer (xià);
the anger of autumn (qiū)
becomes the fury of winter (dōng);
the movements of the four transformations
and the pulse (mài) ascend and descend.
Spring (chūn) should correspond to the carpenter's square (jǔ),
summer (xià) should correspond to the compass (guī),
autumn (qiū) should correspond to the steelyard beam (héng),
winter (dōng) should correspond to the steelyard weight (quán).
A healthy person is not ill.
When a person exhales once,
the pulse (mài) moves twice;
when a person inhales once,
the pulse (mài) also moves twice.
During a regulated breath (hūxī),
the pulse (mài) moves five times,
supplemented by a deep breath.
This is a healthy person who is not ill.
If the pulse (mài)
is deficient, it is slow;
if it is excessive, it is rapid.
The stomach (wèi) is the normal qi of a healthy person.
The normal *qì* of a healthy person
is received from the *wèi*.
The *wèi*
is the normal *qì* of a healthy person.
When a person has no *wèi qì*,
it is called "reversal" (*nì*).
Those with reversal (*nì*) die.
Loss of blood (*tuō xuè*):
If the arms have many bluish veins,
it is called "loss of blood" (*tuō xuè*).
If the *chǐ* pulse is slow and hesitant (*huǎn sè*),
it is called "dissolution and merging" (*jiě bìng*).
If the pulse is strong while lying still,
it is called "loss of blood" (*tuō xuè*);
lying down for a long time injures *qì*.
Wèi jaundice (*wèi dǎn*):
If after eating, it feels like muscle,
it is *wèi dǎn*.
If the *wèi* is hot, food is digested quickly.
Facial swelling is called "wind" (*fēng*).
Swelling of the feet and nape is called "water" (*shuǐ*).
Spontaneous yellowness is called "jaundice" (*huáng dǎn*).
Pregnant women (*rèn zǐ fù rén*):
If the *shào yīn* pulse moves intensely,
it is pregnancy (*rèn zǐ*).
The *shào yīn* pulse
is found in the depression behind the palm, where the little finger moves and responds to the hand.
Water and grain (*shuǐ gǔ*):
Humans take water and grain as their foundation,
so deprivation of water and grain leads to death.
A pulse without *wèi qì* also leads to death.
Normal heart pulse (*píng xīn mài*):
If the normal heart pulse comes
intermittently, like a string of pearls,
like tracing *láng yú*,
it is called "normal heart" (*píng xīn*).
In summer, *wèi qì* is taken as the root.
If the diseased heart pulse comes
gasping and continuous,
with slight undulations,
it is called "heart disease" (*xīn bìng*).
If the dying heart pulse comes
bent in front and stiff behind,
like holding a belt hook,
it is called "heart death" (*xīn sǐ*).
Normal lung pulse (*píng fèi mài*):
If the normal lung pulse comes
faintly, like falling elm pods,
it is called "normal lung" (*fèi píng*).
In autumn, *wèi qì* is taken as the root.
If the diseased lung pulse comes like tracing chicken feathers,
it is called "lung disease" (*fèi bìng*).
If the dying lung pulse comes
like something floating,
like wind blowing hair,
it is called "lung death" (*fèi sǐ*).
Normal liver pulse (*píng gān mài*):
If the normal liver pulse comes
harmonious, soft, and separate,
like the tip of a pole,
it is called "normal liver" (*gān píng*).
In spring, *wèi qì* is taken as the root.
If the diseased liver pulse comes
like tracing a long pole,
it is called "liver disease" (*gān bìng*).
If the dying liver pulse comes
tight, like a newly strung bowstring,
it is called "liver death" (*gān sǐ*).
Normal spleen pulse (*píng pí mài*):
If the normal spleen pulse comes
harmonious, soft, and separate,
like a chicken treading on the ground,
it is called "normal spleen" (*pí píng*).
In late summer, *wèi qì* is taken as the root.
If the diseased spleen pulse comes
like a chicken lifting its foot,
it is called "spleen disease" (*pí bìng*).
If the dying spleen pulse comes
sharp and hard,
like a bird's beak,
like a bird's spur,
like a leaking roof,
like flowing water,
it is called "spleen death" (*pí sǐ*).
Normal kidney pulse (*píng shèn mài*):
If the normal kidney pulse comes
gasping and intermittent,
and feels like a hook when pressed,
it is called "normal kidney" (*shèn píng*).
In winter, *wèi qì* is taken as the root.
If the diseased kidney pulse comes
like pulling kudzu,
and becomes harder when pressed,
it is called "kidney disease" (*shèn bìng*).
If the dying kidney pulse comes
snapping like a cut rope,
and crackles like a slingshot hitting a stone,
it is called
kidney death (*shèn sǐ*).
Diseases of the five *zàng* (*wǔ zàng bìng*):
The five *zàng* are interconnected,
and their transference always follows a sequence.
If the five *zàng* have disease,
they each transmit it to the one they overcome.
If untreated for three months,
or six months,
or three days,
or six days,
when transmitted through all five *zàng*, it will certainly lead to death.
The *wèi* as the root of the five *zàng* (*wèi wǔ zàng zhī běn*):
All five *zàng* receive their *qì* from the *mào*.
Sweating (*hàn chū*):
When eating and drinking are excessive,
sweat comes from the *wèi*.
When startled and essence is lost,
sweat comes from the heart (*xīn*).
When carrying heavy loads and traveling far,
sweat comes from the kidneys (*shèn*).
When running swiftly and feeling fear,
sweat comes from the liver (*gān*).
When shaking the body and toiling,
sweat comes from the spleen (*pí*).
The Five Intrusions (*wǔ rù*):
Sour enters the liver (*gān*).
Pungent enters the lungs (*fèi*).
Bitter enters the heart (*xīn*).
Salty enters the kidneys (*shèn*).
Sweet enters the spleen (*pí*).
These are called "the Five Intrusions" (*wǔ rù*).
The Five Aversions (*wǔ è*):
The heart (*xīn*) dislikes heat.
The lungs (*fèi*) dislike cold.
The liver (*gān*) dislikes wind.
The spleen (*pí*) dislikes dampness.
The kidneys (*shèn*) dislike dryness.
These are called "the Five Aversions" (*wǔ è*).
The Five Fluids (*wǔ yè*):
The five *zàng* transform into fluids:
The heart (*xīn*) into sweat.
The lungs (*fèi*) into nasal discharge.
The liver (*gān*) into tears.
The spleen (*pí*) into saliva.
The kidneys (*shèn*) into spittle.
These are called "the Five Fluids" (*wǔ yè*).
What the five *zàng* store (*wǔ zàng suǒ cáng*):
The heart (*xīn*) stores the *shén*.
The lungs (*fèi*) store the *pò*.
The liver (*gān*) stores the *hún*.
The spleen (*pí*) stores the *yì*.
The kidneys (*shèn*) store the *zhì*.
These are called "what the five *zàng* store" (*wǔ zàng suǒ cáng*).
The Five Dominances (*wǔ zhǔ*):
The heart (*xīn*) dominates the vessels.
The lungs (*fèi*) dominate the skin.
The liver (*gān*) dominates the sinews.
The spleen (*pí*) dominates the flesh.
The kidneys (*shèn*) dominate the bones.
These are called "the Five Dominances" (*wǔ zhǔ*).
What injures the five *zàng* (*wǔ zàng suǒ shāng*):
Prolonged looking injures blood.
Prolonged lying injures *qì*.
Prolonged sitting injures flesh.
Prolonged standing injures bones.
Prolonged walking injures sinews.
These are called "what injures the five *zàng*" (*wǔ zàng suǒ shāng*).
The pulses of the five *zàng* (*wǔ zàng zhī mài*):
The liver (*gān*) pulse is wiry.
The heart (*xīn*) pulse is hooked.
The spleen (*pí*) pulse is intermittent.
The lungs (*fèi*) pulse is superficial.
The kidneys (*shèn*) pulse is stone-like.
These are called "the pulses of the five *zàng*" (*wǔ zàng zhī mài*).
Double Vacuity (*chóng xū*):
If the *qì* pulse is vacuous above and the *chǐ* pulse is vacuous,
this is called "Double Vacuity" (*chóng xū*).
Wind Fainting (*fēng jué*):
Sweating with body heat is wind (*fēng*).
Sweating with vexation and fullness that does not resolve is fainting (*jué*).
All diseases arise from *qì*.
When angry, *qì* ascends;
when joyful, *qì* slackens;
when sorrowful, *qì* disperses;
when afraid, *qì* descends;
when cold, *qì* contracts;
when hot, *qì* leaks;
when startled, *qì* becomes chaotic;
when fatigued, *qì* is consumed;
when pensive, *qì* stagnates.
If the nine *qì* do not move,
what illness can arise?
Cold and Heat *Jué*
If the *yángqì* declines in the lower body,
it is called cold *jué*;
if the *yīnqì* declines in the lower body,
it is called hot *jué*.
Lung *Qì*
The Lungs
are the cover of the *zàng* organs.
If Lung *qì* is abundant,
then the pulse is large;
if the pulse is large,
then one cannot lie supine.
Spleen Itch
If someone has a sweet taste in the mouth due to illness,
it is an overflow of the five *qì*,
and is named “*Pí Dàn*”;
if someone has a bitter taste in the mouth due to illness,
it is named “*Dǎn Dàn*.”
Deficiency and Excess
If *qì* is in excess, the form is in excess;
if *qì* is deficient, the form is deficient.
If grains are abundant, *qì* is abundant;
if grains are deficient, *qì* is deficient.
If the pulse is in excess, blood is in excess;
if the pulse is deficient, blood is deficient.
This is the normal state;
the opposite of this is illness.
The Nine Needles
Corresponding to Heaven, Earth, *Yīn*, and *Yáng*:
one is Heaven,
two is Earth,
three is Man,
four is the seasons,
five is the musical notes,
six is the *lǜ* pipes,
seven is the stars,
eight is the winds,
nine is the wildernesses.
One needle for the skin,
two needles for the flesh,
three needles for the blood vessels,
four needles for the sinews,
five needles for the bones,
six needles regulate *yīn* and *yáng*,
seven needles augment *jīng*,
eight needles expel wind,
nine needles open the nine orifices,
and eliminate the three hundred and sixty-five *jiéqì*.
One *chánzhēn*,
two *yuánzhēn*,
three *tízhēn*,
four *fēngzhēn*,
five *jìzhēn*,
six *yuánlìzhēn*,
seven *háozhēn*,
eight *chángzhēn*,
nine *dàzhēn*.
All Illnesses Originate in the Skin and Hair
All illnesses, when they first arise,
must begin in the skin and hair.
When evil [*qì*] invades it,
the *còulǐ* open;
when open, it enters and lodges in the *màiluò*.
If it stays in the *màiluò* and does not leave,
it transmits into the *jīng* channels;
if it stays in the *jīng* channels and does not leave,
it transmits into the intestines and stomach.
Excess and Deficiency
Spirit can have excess and deficiency;
*qì* can have excess and deficiency;
blood can have excess and deficiency;
form can have excess and deficiency;
will can have excess and deficiency.
All these ten aspects,
their *qì* is not equal.
The Five Flavors Each Return to Their Preferred Organ
When the five flavors enter the stomach,
each returns to its preferred organ.
Thus, sour first enters the Liver;
bitter first enters the Heart;
sweet first enters the Spleen;
pungent first enters the Lungs;
salty first enters the Kidneys.
Flesh Divisions and Ravines
Large areas of flesh
gather to form *gǔ* (ravines).
Small areas of flesh
gather to form *xī* (crevices).
Between the divisions of flesh,
where *xī* and *gǔ* meet,
the *róngwèi* circulate,
and the greater *qì* converges.
If evil [*qì*] overflows and *qì* is blocked,
the vessels become hot and the flesh decays.
If *róngwèi* do not circulate,
it will surely turn into pus.
Internally, it consumes the bone marrow;
externally, it breaks open large sores.
If it remains in the joints and *còulǐ*,
it will surely lead to decay.
If accumulated cold remains and settles,
*róngwèi* do not reside there.
The flesh retracts and the sinews contract,
the elbow cannot extend.
Internally, it becomes bone *bì* syndrome;
externally, it becomes numbness,
named deficiency.
This is when great cold remains in the *xī* and *gǔ*.
Deficient *Qì* and Rebellious *Qì*
If evil *qì* is abundant,
it is excess;
if essential *qì* is depleted,
it is deficiency.
One with deficient *qì*
has deficient Lungs.
One with rebellious *qì*
has cold feet.
If it occurs at an inappropriate time, life occurs;
if it occurs at the appropriate time, death occurs.
The other *zàng* organs are also like this.
Three Regions and Nine Positions
The pulse has three regions;
each region has nine positions.
With these, life and death are determined,
and all illnesses are diagnosed.
Spleen Governs and Resides in the Four Seasons
The Spleen governs and secures the middle,
always through the four seasons,
nurturing the four *zàng* organs,
for eighteen days each.
If its governance is not achieved,
it solely presides over the season.
Hot-Middle, Consuming-Middle, Wealthy People
Frequent drinking and urination is called “*xiāozhōng*” (consuming-middle);
excessive joy is called “*diān*” (epilepsy);
excessive anger is called “*kuáng*” (mania).
Hot-middle and consuming-middle
are both conditions of wealthy people.
Moving Vessels
All twelve *jīng* channels have moving vessels,
but only the *cùnkǒu* is examined
to determine the *wǔzàng*, *liùfǔ*, life, death, auspiciousness, and misfortune.
The *cùnkǒu*
is the great convergence of the vessels,
the moving vessel of the Hand *Tàiyīn*.
In one exhalation,
the pulse travels three *cùn*;
in one inhalation,
the pulse travels three *cùn*.
In one complete breath,
the pulse travels six *cùn*.
In one day and night, a person takes twelve thousand five hundred breaths in total.
The pulse travels fifty circuits around the body.
The water clock drops one hundred *kè*,
*róngwèi* circulates through *yīn* and *yáng*,
each twenty-five circuits forming one cycle.
Thus, after fifty circuits, they converge again at the Hand *Tàiyīn*.
The *cùnkǒu*
is where the *wǔzàng* and *liùfǔ* begin and end.
Pulse Excess and Deficiency
Pulses can be in excess
or in deficiency.
There is *yīn* and *yáng* mutual dominance,
there is latent and overflowing,
there is constrained and blocked.
*Yīn* and *Yáng* Deficiency and Excess
The pulse can have *yáng* excess and *yīn* deficiency,
or *yīn* excess and *yáng* deficiency.
If it is small when palpated superficially,
and large and full when palpated deeply,
it is therefore called *yīn* excess and *yáng* deficiency.
If it is small when palpated deeply,
and large and full when palpated superficially,
it is therefore called *yáng* excess and *yīn* deficiency.
This is the meaning of *yīn* and *yáng* deficiency and excess.
Regarding diseases of the zàngfǔ [organs]:
If they are rapid,
it is of the fǔ [organs];
if slow,
it is of the zàng [organs].
Rapid implies heat,
slow implies cold.
All yáng implies heat,
all yīn implies cold.
Thus, these are used to distinguish diseases of the zàngfǔ.
Dead Pulse:
When the pulse beats
twice per exhalation, it is called "normal" (píng);
three times, "deviating from the channels" (líjīng);
four times, "depletion of essence" (duójīng);
five times, "death";
six times, "life pulse extinguished."
These are pulses of death.
Pulses of the Four Seasons:
The spring pulse is xián [string-like];
the summer pulse is gōu [hooked];
the autumn pulse is máo [hairy];
the winter pulse is shí [stony].
These are the pulses of the four seasons.
It is said, "He who suffers seven transmissions dies,
he who has intervening zàng lives."
Why is this?
Transmission (chuán)
means transmission to that which it overcomes.
Intervening zàng (jiānzàng)
means transmission to its child.
For example, if a heart disease transmits to the lungs,
the lungs transmit to the liver,
the liver transmits to the stomach,
the stomach transmits to the kidneys,
the kidneys transmit to the heart—
if one zàng does not transmit twice,
then he who suffers seven transmissions dies.
He who has intervening zàng obtains what generates it, and thus lives.
For example, if a heart disease transmits to the spleen,
the spleen transmits to the lungs,
the lungs transmit to the kidneys,
the kidneys transmit to the liver,
the liver transmits to the heart—
this is a mother-child self-transmission,
ending and then beginning anew,
like a ring without end;
therefore, it is said to lead to life.
Zàng Diseases are Difficult to Treat, Fǔ Diseases are Easy to Treat:
Zàng diseases are difficult to treat,
fǔ diseases are easy to treat.
Why?
Zàng diseases transmit to that which they overcome,
whereas fǔ diseases transmit to their child.
Treating Undiseased States:
The Classics say:
"The superior-superior physician treats undiseased states;
the middle-superior physician treats already diseased states."
Why is this?
Upon seeing a liver disease,
one knows that the liver will transmit to the spleen.
Therefore, one first strengthens the qì of the spleen,
preventing the spleen from being affected by the liver's evil qì.
This is called "treating undiseased states."
Upon seeing a liver disease,
if one does not understand the transmission,
and focuses solely on treating the liver,
this is called "treating already diseased states."
Five Kinds of Shānghán [Cold Damage]:
There are five kinds of shānghán:
zhòngfēng [wind-strike],
shānghán [cold-damage],
shīwēn [damp-warmth],
rèbìng [heat disease],
wēnbìng [warm disease].
From the Frost's Descent (Shuāngjiàng) to the Spring Equinox (Chūnfēn),
if one catches a cold wind and becomes ill,
it is called shānghán.
If one receives cold qì in winter,
and then catches wind in spring and becomes ill,
it is called wēnbìng.
If it manifests in summer,
it is called rèbìng.
If the illness involves profuse sweating,
it is called shīwēn.
If one is harmed by vacuous evil at the eight seasonal nodes,
it is called zhòngfēng.
True Heart Pain:
For diseases of the head and heart,
there is juétòng [rebellious pain]
and zhēntòng [true pain].
If the three yáng channels are affected by wind-cold,
it is juétóutòng [rebellious headache].
If it enters and connects with the brain,
it is zhēntóutòng [true headache].
If the qì of the five zàng interfere with each other, it is juéxīntòng [rebellious heart pain].
If the pain is severe,
and confined to the heart,
with bluish hands and feet,
it is called zhēnxīntòng [true heart pain].
For true head and heart pain,
if it occurs in the morning, one dies in the evening;
if it occurs in the evening, one dies in the morning.
Chapter on the Upper:
Purple smoke rises and falls, three primeval clouds.
The Upper Dāntián (shàng Dāntián), Middle Dāntián (zhōng Dāntián), and Lower Dāntián (xià Dāntián)
all possess the qì of sunlight.
Chapter on the Ultimate Dào:
The spirit of the hair is Cānghuá,
courtesy name Tàiyuán.
The spirit of the brain is Jīnggēn,
courtesy name Níwán.
The spirit of the eyes is Mínggōng,
courtesy name Yīngxuán.
The spirit of the nose is Yùlǒng,
courtesy name Língjiān.
The spirit of the ears is Kōngxián,
courtesy name Yōutián.
The spirit of the tongue is Tōngmìng,
courtesy name Zhènglún.
The spirit of the teeth is Èfēng,
courtesy name Luógān.
All within the face have spirits.
Chapter on the Heart Spirit:
The heart spirit is Dānyuán,
courtesy name Shǒulíng.
The lung spirit is Yuánbái,
courtesy name Xūchéng.
The liver spirit is Lóngyān,
courtesy name Hánmíng.
The kidney spirit is Xuánmíng,
courtesy name Yùyīng.
The spleen spirit is Chángzài,
courtesy name Húntíng.
The gallbladder spirit is Lóngyào,
courtesy name Wēimíng.
The official of the lung region resembles a canopy (huágài);
urgently preserve the white primeval qì (báiyuán) and the six qì.
Báiyuán Jūnjǔ is the spirit of the lung palace.
The heart region contains splendid scarlet brocade (huádānjǐnfēi);
it is often draped in jade gauze within the deep inner chambers (zhòngwéi).
The heart is red,
with qì above it like jade light.
The palace of the liver region is verdant and layered within;
it wears a blue brocade robe and jade bells.
The palace of the kidney region is a dark, round palace gate (xuánquè);
blue brocade cloud-garments dance like coiling dragons.
The palace of the spleen region belongs to Wùjǐ;
externally it responds to the chǐzhái with fragrant radiance.
Chǐzhái
is the face.
The palace of the gallbladder region is the essence of the six fǔ [organs];
thunder and lightning, eight tremors, raising the king's banner.
Chapter on Spleen Longevity:
Gargle and swallow golden nectar (jīnlǐ) and jade essence (yùyīng),
preserve and irrigate the jade dwelling (yùlú) to delight oneself.
Yùlú
is the nose.
The numinous platform (língtái) is lush and abundant, gazing upon the yellow wild (huángyě).
The spleen is called huángyě.
Chapter on the Three Gates:
The mouth is the Heavenly Gate (tiānguān),
the hands are the Human Gate (rénguān),
the feet are the Earth Gate (dìguān).
Chapter on If One Obtains:
If one obtains and preserves the two officials of the profound elixir (xuándān),
the tears of Tàiyǐ will rest on Kūnlún.
The twelve rings of the heavy tower (zhònglóu) are the central gate;
from top to bottom, all are true people (zhēnrén).
The Jade Hall (yùtáng) and the Scarlet Character (jiàngzì) are all profound palaces;
the Xuánjī and Yùhéng are a riot of colors.
Chapter on the Jade Chamber:
Within the Jade Chamber (qióngshì), the eight primeval qì gather;
Madame Níwán stands in the center.
The inch-field (cùntián) and foot-dwelling (chǐzhái) can govern life,
external objects are not excessive but tranquil.
Each of the three Dāntián is one cùn [inch].
Chángniàn Zhāng
Storing the five sprouts, one does not hunger or thirst,
Shénhuá holds the towel, the Liùdīng attend.
The five sprouts [wǔyá] are
the vital energy of the Five Phases,
distributed among the five organs.
Lǎojūn Liùjiǎ Jiàng says:
"The god Dīngmǎo is
Sīmǎ Qīng.
The god Dīngchǒu is
Zhào Zǐyù.
The god Dīnghài is
Zhāng Wéntōng.
The god Dīngchǒu is
Zāng Wéngōng.
The god Dīngwèi is
Shí Shūtōng.
The god Dīngsì is
Cuī Yuēqīng."
Wǔxíng Zhāng
Fúniú's secluded palace is arrayed with various items.
Fúniú is
the image of the kidney;
the kidney is the secluded palace [yōujué].
The father is Níwán, the mother is Cíyī.
The mouth commands the spiritual radiance, the five stars.
The mouth emits five-colored cloud qi.
Yǐncáng Zhāng
Zǐdān offers food and drink, dark and yellow.
These are called "wolf's fat" and "jade frost."
Kǒu Wéi Zhāng
The mouth is the Jade Pool, the Grand Harmony Palace.
Rinsing and swallowing the spiritual fluid prevents calamity.
The body emits radiance, and qi fragrant as orchids.
It repels all evils, refining the face with jade.
Yínpán
In a strange country in the northern wilderness, there is a silver plate [yínpán],
fifty zhàng long,
with a bright pearl inside,
several zhàng in size,
illuminating a thousand lǐ.
Huāliǔ Jiǔ
In Hélíng Guó,
willow blossoms are used to make wine.
Tiāndì Chángnán Gōng
On Dōngmíng Shān there is a palace,
with a silver plaque and green carved characters that read "Palace of the Eldest Son of Heaven and Earth" [Tiāndì Chángnán zhī Gōng].
Zhīnǚ Jiàng
Guō Hàn encountered Zhīnǚ descending to his room,
wearing a robe of dark gauze,
and a shawl of frosted silk.
She wore a phoenix crown with projecting ornaments,
and trod in jade-black shoes.
She spread a canopy of vermilion hubs,
and laid out a mat of nine-crystal jade blossoms.
She turned a fan that created a swirling wind,
and had a pillow with concentric dragons.
Hàn asked:
"Where is Niúláng?"
She replied:
"The Heavenly River obstructs us;
we no longer hear from each other."
The next day,
she sent Hàn a piece of green silk with writing in red and black ink.
Chìguō
People of the South are seven chǐ tall,
with a waist circumference likewise.
They wear vermilion robes and white sashes,
with red snakes entwined around their necks.
They only eat evil spirits,
devouring three thousand in the morning,
and three hundred in the evening.
They are called "Chìguō,"
also "Shíxié,"
and also "Huángfù."
It is also said:
They take ghosts as food,
and mist as drink.
Dānsù
Jǔ Shān has much cinnabar millet [dānsù].
Mìdū
Qīngyào Shān is called "The Emperor's Honey Capital" [Dì zhī Mìdū].
Jiǔ'ěr Zhōng
Fēng Shān has a nine-eared bell [jiǔ'ěr zhōng].
It rings by itself every time frost descends.
Qīngniǎo
Xīwángmǔ of Guī Shān has three blue birds [qīngniǎo],
who are responsible for fetching food for the Mother.
Wǔqú
Shàoshì Shān has a tree
whose flowers have five pathways [wǔqú].
The flowers have five petals,
like cross-roads.
Jiǔdài Wǔ
Xià Hòu created the Nine Generations Dance [Jiǔdài Wǔ].
Jiǔdài is
the name of a horse.
Chángshān Shé
Chángshān has a giant snake,
nine zhàng long.
If something strikes its head,
its tail reaches;
if something strikes its tail, its head reaches;
if something strikes its middle, both head and tail reach.
It is called "Shuàirán."
Sūnzǐ Bīngfǎ says:
"When generals lead the three armies,
their momentum is like the Shuàirán,"
this is what it refers to.
Huā Sìzhào
Above Zhāoyáo,
its flowers illuminate in four directions [sìzhào].
Bólè Xiàngmǎ
Wáng Liáng asked Bólè:
"May I ask about judging horses?"
He replied:
"The horse's head should be correct,
and preferably square.
The eyes are the support,
they should be bright.
The neck is the general,
it should be strong.
The belly is the city wall,
it should be broad.
The four lower limbs are the commanders,
they should be long.
The sweat groove should be deep.
The ears should be small,
like cut bamboo.
If the color inside the mouth is like sunlight or moonlight,
it can travel a thousand lǐ.
If there is black inside the mouth, it is called Yùwū,
and is short-lived.
A white forehead reaching into the mouth
is called Gǒuyàn,
also Lúlú."
Tāishēng
The Yang Crow [yángwū] is
born from the qi of metal and fire.
After three years, its neck turns red;
after seven years, it flies well;
after another seven years, it crows at all twelve hours.
After sixty years, thick feathers grow,
and mud cannot stain it.
After one hundred and sixty years,
male and female conceive by looking at each other.
After one thousand six hundred years,
it is born viviparously without eating;
it is an immortal Qíjì.
Its characteristics are: a long neck and slender toes make it crow well;
a tortoise back and soft-shelled turtle belly enable it to dance.
Lánzhū
The Lánzhū wants to be large;
it is the tail of the forest.
The Fēngyuè wants to be high;
it is the bone of the thigh.
The Chuíxīng wants to be high;
it is the hoof.
The Shàngzhù wants to be large;
it is the cart bone.
Volume 37
End.
Kǒngzǐ Wéi Zhōngdū Zǎi
When Kǒngzǐ first served as the Magistrate of Zhōngdū,
he established regulations for nurturing life and conducting funerals:
the old and young ate separately,
the strong and weak had different duties,
men and women walked on separate paths,
nothing was picked up from the road,
and utensils were not carved.
He used hills and mounds for graves,
without raising a tumulus or planting a tree.
Dìnggōng said:
"How would your laws, Master,
fare in governing the state of Lǔ?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"They would be suitable even for all under Heaven,
let alone just the state of Lǔ!"
Lǔ Yǐ Jūnzǐ Dào Fǔ Qí Jūn
Dìng Gōng met Qí Hóu at Jiágǔ.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"For civil affairs, there must be military preparations;
for military affairs, there must be civil preparations.
Please provide the Sīmǎ."
The Duke agreed to this.
Qí envoys, disguised as performers, with weapons and drums, began to shout,
attempting to intimidate Dìng Gōng.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When two rulers are forming a friendly alliance,
for captive barbarians to dare to disrupt it with weapons
is not the way to command the feudal lords.
Barbarians do not plot against the Zhōngxià,
Yi tribes do not disturb the Huá,
captives do not interfere with covenants,
and weapons do not threaten friendship."
Qí Hóu felt ashamed in his heart,
waved his hand, and made them withdraw.
A moment later,
actors and dwarfs performed in front.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Commoners who insult feudal lords
deserve execution!"
Thereupon, the dwarf was beheaded,
his hands and feet severed from his body.
When Qí Hóu returned,
he reproached his ministers, saying:
"The Lord of Lǔ guided his ruler with the Way,
while you only taught me with the ways of Yi and Di!"
The Three Families Exceeded the Regulations
Kǒngzǐ spoke to Dìng Gōng, saying:
"Families do not keep armored troops,
and cities do not have walls of a hundred zhì –
this is the ancient regulation.
The Three Families have exceeded these regulations;
I request that they be reduced."
Kǒngzǐ Governed
Among those who sold sheep in Lǔ was Shěn Yóu Shì,
who always gave his sheep water in the morning
to deceive market-goers.
There was Gōng Shèn Shì,
whose wife was promiscuous and he did not control her.
There was Shèn Kuì Shì,
who was extravagant beyond the law.
Those who sold livestock in Lǔ
decorated them to inflate their price.
When Kǒngzǐ governed,
Shěn Yóu Shì dared not give his sheep water in the morning,
Gōng Shèn Shì expelled his wife,
Shèn Kuì Shì crossed the border and migrated,
those who sold cattle and horses did not inflate prices,
and those who sold lambs and piglets did not embellish them.
Executed Alike in Different Eras
Zhòng Yóu said:
"Shào Zhèng Mǎo
is a renowned person in Lǔ.
That the Master executed him,
might it not be a mistake?"
The Master said:
"This man is indeed a treacherous hero.
Yīn Tāng executed Yǐn Xié,
Wén Wáng executed Pān Zhèng,
Zhōu Gōng executed Guǎn and Cài,
Tài Gōng executed Huá Shì,
Guǎn Zhòng executed Fù Yǐ,
Zǐchǎn executed Yú Hé.
All these seven rulers
executed people alike in different eras.
Because these seven individuals were evil alike in different eras,
they could not be pardoned."
Seven Teachings and Three Ultimates
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Enlightened kings cultivate seven teachings internally
and implement three ultimates externally.
When the seven teachings are cultivated, the state can be defended.
When the three ultimates are implemented, it can conquer.
For its defense,
it checks the enemy a thousand *lǐ* away.
For its conquest,
the army returns even before leaving the sleeping mat.
Emperor Shùn had Yǔ on his left and Gāo Táo on his right,
and without leaving his mat, the empire was well-governed."
Zēngzǐ said:
"What are the seven teachings?"
The Master said:
"When superiors respect the aged,
inferiors become more filial.
When superiors honor seniority,
inferiors become more fraternal.
When superiors delight in generosity,
inferiors become more magnanimous.
When superiors befriend the worthy,
inferiors choose friends carefully.
When superiors love virtue,
inferiors do not conceal it.
When superiors detest greed,
inferiors are ashamed of contention.
When superiors are humble and yielding,
inferiors have self-restraint.
These are called the seven teachings."
"What are the three ultimates?"
The Master said:
"Ultimate propriety requires no yielding, yet the empire is well-governed.
Ultimate reward requires no expenditure, yet scholars throughout the empire are pleased.
Ultimate music has no sound, yet the people of the empire are harmonious.
These are called the three ultimates."
A Principle Not Far Off
Extending a finger, one knows an inch;
extending a hand, one knows a foot;
extending an arm, one knows a fathom.
These are principles not far off.
Great Marriage
Kǒngzǐ said:
"If Heaven and Earth do not unite,
the myriad creatures will not be born.
The great marriage
is the succession for ten thousand generations."
Five Types of Character
Kǒngzǐ said:
"There are five types of character:
the mediocre person (*yōngrén*),
the scholar (*shìrén*),
the noble person (*jūnzǐ*),
the worthy person (*xiánrén*),
and the sage (*shèngrén*).
The mediocre person
does not harbor a cautious plan for the end
and does not utter instructive and upright words.
Seeing little, they obscure the great,
not knowing what to focus on.
They follow things like flowing water,
not knowing what to hold firm to.
The scholar
does not seek much knowledge,
but must examine what they do know;
does not seek many words,
but must examine what they clarify.
The noble person's
words are always loyal and trustworthy,
benevolence and righteousness are embodied,
thoughts are clear and discerning,
and they earnestly practice and believe in the Way.
The worthy person's
virtue does not transgress boundaries,
and their conduct aligns with rules and standards.
The sage's
virtue is in harmony with Heaven and Earth,
transforming and adapting without fixed limitations."
Āi Gōng said:
"I, the lonely one, was born in the depths of the palace,
raised by the hands of women.
I have never known sorrow,
never known worry,
never known toil,
never known fear,
never known danger.
I fear I am insufficient to practice the teachings of the five types of character."
Method of Selecting People
Āi Gōng asked about the method of selecting people.
The Master said:
"When assigning duties to officials,
do not choose the quick-tongued (*jiéjié*),
do not choose the glib-tongued (*qiánqián*),
and do not choose the verbose (*tūntūn*)."
Disasters and Omens Cannot Overcome Good Governance
Āi Gōng said:
"The survival or destruction, misfortune or fortune of a state
surely depends on Heaven's mandate,
not solely on human effort."
The Master said:
"Survival, destruction, misfortune, and fortune
all depend on oneself, and that is all.
Heavenly disasters and earthly omens
cannot affect them.
Heavenly disasters and earthly omens
are sent to warn rulers;
startling dreams and strange occurrences
are sent to warn ministers.
Disasters and omens cannot overcome good governance,
and waking and sleeping cannot overcome good conduct."
There Are Three Deaths for a Person
Āi Gōng said:
“Do the wise live long?
Do the benevolent live long?”
The Master said:
“People have three kinds of death,
which are not their destiny,
but brought upon themselves by their conduct.
Those who sleep and rest irregularly,
eat and drink immoderately,
or labor and rest excessively,
are killed by illness.
Those who occupy a lowly position yet seek to usurp their lord,
and whose desires are insatiable,
are killed by punishment.
Those who, being few, offend the many;
being weak, insult the strong;
whose anger is not measured;
and whose actions are disproportionate to their strength,
are killed by weapons.
As for the wise and benevolent,
they follow the proper course with moderation,
act and rest with righteousness,
and feel joy and anger at the appropriate times,
without harming their nature;
is it not proper for them to attain longevity?”
Different Origins
Fragrant and foul cannot be stored in the same vessel,
Yáo and Jié cannot rule the same state;
this is because their origins are different.
Receiving a Gift from a Benevolent Person
A fisherman offered fish,
saying:
“It is very hot,
the market is far,
and there is no place to sell them.
Rather than discarding them in the dung heap,
it is better to present them to a virtuous man.”
The Master instructed his disciples to sweep the ground,
intending to offer a sacrifice.
His disciples said:
“He was going to discard them;
why does the Master use them for sacrifice?”
The Master replied:
“How can one receive a gift from a benevolent person and not offer a sacrifice?”
One Action Sets the World Right
Wén Wáng took Wáng Jì as his father,
Dà Rèn as his mother,
and Dà Sì as his wife;
he had Wǔ Wáng and Zhōu Gōng as sons,
and Dà Yuán and Hóng Yāo as ministers;
his foundations were indeed excellent!
Wǔ Wáng rectified himself,
thereby rectifying his state;
he rectified his state,
thereby rectifying all under Heaven.
He punished the unprincipled
and executed the guilty;
with one action, all under Heaven was set right.
Presenting Silk to Chéng Zǐ
Kǒng Zǐ met Chéng Zǐ on the road,
and they tilted their carriage covers to speak all day,
so deeply fond of each other,
he took some tied silk to present to him.
Zǐ Lù said:
“If a scholar is not known by reputation,
like a woman marrying without a matchmaker,
a junzǐ does not associate with him;
this is propriety.”
The Master said:
“Chéng Zǐ
is a worthy scholar of all under Heaven.
If I do not present him now,
I may never see him again in my life.”
Loyalty and Trustfulness Approach Water
Kǒng Zǐ rested his carriage by a river bridge.
There was a waterfall thirty rén high,
and the circular current extended ninety lǐ.
A man, by swimming against it, came out.
Kǒng Zǐ asked:
“Do you have a special technique?”
He replied:
“I enter it with loyalty and trustfulness.”
Kǒng Zǐ said:
“If water can be approached by a loyal and trustworthy person,
how much more so can people be?”
Shāng Is Short on Wealth
Kǒng Zǐ was about to leave,
and it rained, but he had no carriage cover.
A disciple said:
“Shāng has one.”
“Shāng, as a person,
The Master said:
I have heard that when interacting with people,
one should promote their strengths
and overlook their weaknesses,
thus relationships can last.”
Duckweed Fruit
The King of Chǔ crossed the Jiāng River
and found a duckweed fruit.
It was as large as a dou,
and red like the sun.
He cut it open and ate it;
it was as sweet as honey.
Do the Dead Have Knowledge?
Zǐ Gòng asked:
“Do the dead have knowledge,
or no knowledge?”
The Master said:
“If I were to say they have knowledge,
I fear that dutiful sons and compliant grandsons would harm their lives to send off the dead;
if I were to say they have no knowledge,
I fear that undutiful sons would abandon their parents and not bury them.
Whether they have knowledge or no knowledge,
is not an urgent matter now;
you will know it yourself later.”
Lǔ's Law on Redeeming People
According to Lǔ's law:
those who redeemed subjects or concubines from the feudal lords
would all receive gold from the treasury.
Zǐ Gòng redeemed someone,
but declined to take the gold.
The Master said:
“Cì has erred!
The actions of a sage
are not solely for his personal conduct.
Now in the state of Lǔ,
the wealthy are few and the poor are many.
If redeeming people and accepting gold
is considered unprincipled,
then how can people redeem each other?”
From then on,
the people of Lǔ no longer redeemed people from the feudal lords.
Three Forbearances
A junzǐ has three forbearances.
If he has a lord he cannot serve,
yet expects to be served by his subjects,
this is not forbearance.
If he has parents he cannot be filial to,
yet expects a return from his children,
this is not forbearance.
If he has an elder brother he cannot respect,
yet expects his younger brother to be compliant,
this is not forbearance.
One who can understand these three forbearances
can rectify himself.
Clad in Coarse Cloth, Embracing Jade
Zǐ Lù said:
“What about a man here
who is clad in coarse cloth, yet embraces jade?”
The Master said:
“If the state is without the Way,
a recluse is acceptable;
if the state has the Way,
then one should wear a ceremonial robe and hold jade.”
Asking About Shùn's Crown
Āi Gōng said:
“What crown did Shùn wear?”
Kǒng Fūzǐ did not reply.
The Duke said:
“Why not?”
He said:
“Shùn's
governance loved life and detested killing;
he appointed the worthy and dismissed the unworthy.
His virtue was like Heaven and Earth,
his transforming influence like the four seasons.
Your Highness neglects these matters and asks about crowns,
which is why I am slow to reply.”
Valuing the Trust of a Single Word
Kǒng Fūzǐ read history up to Chǔ restoring Chén,
and sighed, saying:
“How worthy!
The King of Chǔ valued the trust of a single word
over a state of a thousand chariots.”
Who Says Cān Does Not Know Propriety?
Zēng Zǐ said:
“Excessive familiarity leads to disrespect,
excessive solemnity prevents intimacy;
therefore, a junzǐ's familiarity is enough to foster joy,
and his solemnity is enough to maintain propriety.”
The Master said:
“Who says Cān does not know propriety?”
Yú and Ruì Contend for Land
The two states of Yú and Ruì contended for land and brought their dispute to court.
They said:
"The Xībó
is benevolent;
why not go and submit to his judgment?"
Upon entering his territory,
farmers yielded boundaries,
and travelers yielded roads.
Upon entering the court,
scholars yielded to dàfū,
and dàfū yielded to qīng.
Yú and Ruì said:
"We are petty people,
unfit to enter the court of a jūnzi."
They treated the disputed land as unused wasteland [and withdrew their claim].
Three Troubles
A jūnzi has three troubles:
the trouble of not hearing [the Way];
having heard it,
the trouble of not learning it;
having learned it,
the trouble of not being able to practice it.
The Widow
There was a man from Lǔ who lived alone in his house.
His neighbor, a lífù,
a widow,
also lived alone.
One night,
a violent storm struck.
The lífù's house collapsed,
and she rushed to seek shelter with him.
The Lǔ man closed his door,
saying:
"Males and females under sixty years of age do not live together.
Now you are young and I am also young,
therefore I dare not let you in."
The woman said:
"Why don't you learn from Liǔ Xiàhuì?
Moreover, I am an old woman, not a young girl who has not yet left home."
The Lǔ man said:
"Liǔ Xiàhuì could do it,
but I certainly cannot.
I intend, by means of my inability,
to learn from Liǔ Xiàhuì's ability."
Overbearing Temperament
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A jūnzi with an overbearing temperament
will not die a natural death.
A petty person with an overbearing temperament
will be subjected to repeated punishments and executions."
Asking about Ritual and Visiting Music
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Lǎo Dān is learned in ancient and modern times,
knows the origins of ritual and music,
and comprehends the return of the Dào and virtue;
thus he is my teacher.
Now I shall go to him."
So he went to Zhōu,
asked Lǎo Dān about ritual,
and visited Cháng Hóng to learn about music.
Lǎozǐ said:
"The rich and noble give people wealth;
the benevolent give people words.
The scholars of today,
those who are intelligent, deeply discerning, and thus close to death,
are those who love to mock and criticize others.
Those who are broadly eloquent, greatly accomplished, and thereby endanger their own lives,
are those who love to expose others' wickedness."
Kǒngzǐ returned to Lǔ from Zhōu,
and his Dào became even more revered.
The disciples who came from distant lands
numbered some three thousand.
Three Seals
Kǒngzǐ observed Zhōu,
and entered the temple hall of Tàizǔ and Hòujì.
Before the right steps, there was a golden figure
with its mouth sealed three times,
and an inscription on its back read:
"This is an ancient person who spoke cautiously.
Beware!
Speak not too much;
much talk leads to many failures.
Do not meddle in too many affairs;
many affairs lead to many troubles.
In joy and peace, always be cautious!
If a small flame is not extinguished,
what will the raging fire be like?
If a trickle is not blocked,
it will eventually become a river.
What harm is the mouth?
It is the gate of disaster.
The arrogant and overbearing will not die a natural death;
those who love to win will surely meet their match."
Duchess Dāng of Wèi Línggōng's Unseemly Household
Áigōng asked:
"Who among today's rulers is worthy?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Wèi Línggōng?"
The Duke said:
"Within his private chambers, there is no distinction [of propriety];
why do you rank him as worthy?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"I speak of his court,
not of his private family affairs."
Government Lies in Frugality
Qí Jǐnggōng asked about governance.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Government lies in frugality."
He also said:
"Qín Mùgōng's state was small,
and located in a remote area,
yet he became a hegemon.
Why was this?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Though his state was small,
his ambition was great.
Though its location was remote,
his governance was central [to the Way].
He first promoted Wǔ Gǔ,
granting him the rank of dàfū.
He spoke with him for three days,
and then entrusted him with governance.
Even becoming a king would have been possible for him;
his hegemony was a minor achievement."
Asking about Governance
Áigōng asked about governance.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Among urgent matters of governance,
none is greater than making the people wealthy and long-lived.
Reduce corvée labor,
and lighten taxes;
then the people will be wealthy.
Cultivate ritual and education,
and keep them far from crime and transgression;
then the people will be long-lived."
The Duke said:
"If I wish to follow your words,
I fear my state will become poor."
Kǒngzǐ said:
"An amiable and benevolent jūnzi
is the father and mother of the people.
There has never been a case where the children are wealthy but the parents are poor."
How Profound was Zǐxī's Admonition!
The King of Chǔ was about to visit Jīngtái.
Sīmǎ Zǐqí admonished him.
The King was enraged.
Lìngyǐn Zǐxī said:
"The sights of Jīngtái are not to be missed."
The King was pleased,
saying:
"I will enjoy them with you."
Zǐxī rode his horse ten lǐ,
then pulled the reins and stopped, saying:
"Zǐqí is a loyal minister,
while I am a flattering minister;
I wish Your Majesty would reward the loyal and punish the flattering."
The King said:
"He alone can restrain me!
What about later generations?"
Zǐxī said:
"Restraining later generations is easy!
After Your Majesty's ten thousand years [death],
erect your mausoleum on Jīngtái;
your descendants will surely not bear to visit their parents' tomb
for enjoyment and pleasure."
The King then returned.
Kǒngzǐ said:
"How profound,
Zǐxī's admonition!
He drew him in by ten lǐ,
and restrained him for a hundred generations thereafter."
When the State Possesses the Dào
Kǒngzǐ said:
"When the state possesses the Dào,
then worthy persons thrive,
and ordinary people are employed."
Zǐlù Governs Pú
Three years.
When Kǒngzǐ entered its territory,
he thrice praised its excellence,
saying:
"Upon entering its territory,
the fields are completely cultivated,
the weeds and wild grasses are all cleared,
and the irrigation ditches are very well-managed;
this is because of their reverence and trustworthiness,
thus their people exert their full strength.
Upon entering its city,
the walls and houses are intact and solid,
and the trees are very lush;
this is because of their loyalty and trustworthiness with leniency,
thus their people are not lax.
Upon reaching the court,
the court is very clear and tranquil,
and those below obey orders;
this is because their words are clear, discerning, and decisive,
thus their governance is not disturbed."
Six Fundamentals
A person has six fundamentals,
only then can they be a jūnzi.
To establish oneself, there is righteousness,
but filial piety is the fundamental.
For mourning rituals, there are rites,
but sorrow is the fundamental.
For battle formations, there are ranks,
but courage is the fundamental.
For governing, there are rites,
but agriculture is the fundamental.
For residing in a state, there is a way,
but heir is the fundamental of life.
For wealth, there is a time,
but effort is the fundamental.
Good Medicine and Loyal Words
Good medicine tastes bitter but benefits illness;
loyal words grate on the ear but benefit conduct.
Tāng and Wǔ prospered through honest remonstrance,
while Jié and Zhòu perished through obsequious flattery.
A Jūnzi Is Cautious About Whom They Follow
Kǒngzǐ saw that all the sparrows caught by a bird-catcher were small, chirping sparrows.
He said:
"Large sparrows are easily startled and difficult to catch,
while small sparrows are greedy for food and easy to catch."
The Master said:
"Those easily startled keep away from harm;
those eager for food forget about danger,
and this is inevitable.
One's fortune or misfortune depends solely on whom one follows,
therefore, a jūnzi is cautious about whom they follow."
Not Being Careful at the Beginning and Regretting It Later – How Can It Be Helped?
Zǐlù explained the ancient ways
and the meaning of following them.
The Master said:
"No.
In the past, a daughter of the eastern Yí barbarians admired the rites of the various Huá states.
She was a woman who became a widow,
and became a private son-in-law in the inner quarters,
never marrying again throughout her life.
Although she did not marry again,
it was not true integrity.
Cāngwú Ráo married a beautiful wife
and yielded her to his elder brother.
Although he yielded,
it was not a yielding according to ritual.
Not being careful at the beginning,
and regretting it later,
alas, how can it be helped!"
Zēngshēn's Unfilial Conduct
Zēngzǐ was weeding melons
and accidentally cut their roots.
Zēng Xī became enraged,
struck his back with a large staff,
and Zēngzǐ fell to the ground unconscious.
After a long time, he revived.
He said:
"Just now, Shēn offended you,
and you, Father, used your strength to teach Shēn.
Are you not ill?"
He then withdrew to his room,
took up his qín and sang,
wishing to let Xī know that his body was well.
Kǒngzǐ angrily said:
"Shēn, in serving his father,
yielded his body to await violent anger.
If he had died, he would have implicated his father in unrighteousness.
What unfilial conduct is greater than this?"
Visiting the Common Scholar
The Dūke of Zhōu, holding the esteemed position of Prime Minister,
and formulating the policies for all under heaven,
still visited common scholars.
He met 170 people daily,
desiring to acquire talented individuals.
Discussing the Four Disciples
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Huí's trustworthiness is superior to mine,
Cì's quickness is superior to mine,
Yóu's courage is superior to mine,
Shī's solemnity is superior to mine."
Zǐxià said:
"Why then do these four serve the Master?"
The Master said:
"Huí can be trustworthy but cannot adapt,
Cì can be quick but cannot yield,
Yóu can be courageous but cannot be timid,
Shī can be solemn but cannot be accommodating."
Three Joys
Róngshēng Qī, wearing a deerskin robe tied with ropes,
played his qín and sang:
"Heaven gives birth to all things,
but none are as noble as humans.
I was fortunate
to be born human;
this is my first joy.
Men are honored, women are lowly.
I was fortunate to be born a man;
this is my second joy.
Among those born into life, some never see the sun and moon, or escape swaddling clothes.
I am now ninety-five years old;
this is my third joy.
Poverty is common for a scholar,
and death is the end for everyone.
To live commonly and achieve one's end,
what is there to worry about?"
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Excellent!
He is one who can console himself!"
Huí Has Four Ways of a Jūnzi
The Master said:
"Huí possesses four ways of a jūnzi:
he is strong in acting righteously,
weak in accepting remonstrance,
relaxed in receiving emolument,
and cautious in cultivating himself."
Seeing One Good, Forgetting a Hundred Faults
The Master sees one good and forgets a hundred faults,
thus the Master is easy to serve.
To see another's good as if it were one's own,
this is to be without contention.
Upon hearing good, to invariably practice it oneself,
this is to be capable of diligence.
Shāng Improves Daily, Cì Declines Daily
Kǒngzǐ said:
"After my death,
Shāng will improve daily,
while Cì will decline daily.
Shāng likes to associate with those superior to himself,
while Cì likes to associate with those inferior to himself.
To know not a son, observe his father;
to know not a person, observe their friends;
to know not a ruler, observe those whom he employs;
to know not a land, observe its plants and water.
To dwell with good people
is like entering a room filled with fragrant orchids;
after a long time, one no longer smells their fragrance,
having assimilated with them.
To dwell with bad people
is like entering a shop selling salted fish;
after a long time, one no longer smells their stench,
having also assimilated with them.
Therefore, a jūnzi must be cautious about those with whom he associates."
Human Nature Has Excesses and Deficiencies
Kǒngzǐ said:
"The nature of ordinary people:
if they have excess, they become extravagant;
if they have deficiency, they become frugal.
Without prohibition, they become frivolous;
without measure, they become unrestrained;
if they follow their desires, they fail.
Thus, children who are whipped and beaten do not follow their father's teachings,
and people who are punished by law do not follow their ruler's commands."
When People Are Desperate, They Resort to Deceit
When birds are desperate, they peck;
when beasts are desperate, they seize;
when people are desperate, they resort to deceit;
when horses are desperate, they bolt.
From ancient times to the present,
there has never been one who pushed their inferiors to desperation and could still maintain good relations.
Parting While Alive
Kǒngzǐ heard a very sorrowful crying sound.
Yán Huí said:
"It is not only for the dead,
but also for those experiencing parting while alive.
The birds of Huánshān give birth to four chicks,
and when they are about to scatter to the four seas,
their mother sends them off with sad cries,
the mournful sound is like this;
it means they will go and not return."
Kǒngzǐ asked about it,
and indeed it was said that the father had died, the family was poor,
and a child was sold to pay for the burial.
The Master said:
"Huí,
you are skilled at discerning sounds."
Encounter or Not
Kǒngzǐ said:
"Whether one encounters opportunity or not
is a matter of time.
Whether one is worthy or unworthy
is a matter of talent.
Many a noble person, broadly learned and deeply thoughtful,
does not encounter their time.
Orchids grow in deep forests,
yet do not cease to be fragrant because no one is there;
a noble person cultivates the Way and establishes virtue,
and does not change their integrity because of poverty or hardship."
A Slight Compromise
Zǐgòng said:
"The Master's Way is too grand,
the world cannot accommodate it;
why not make a slight compromise?"
Asking About Entering Office
Zǐzhāng asked about entering office.
The Master said:
"To secure one's person and earn a good reputation is difficult.
If you have goodness, do not monopolize it;
if you teach and are able, do not be lax with others;
if you have faults, do not reveal them;
if you make a slip of the tongue, do not cling to it;
if you have something bad, do not pursue it;
when acting, do not procrastinate."
Zhào Kills Míngdú
Kǒngzǐ heard that Zhào Jiǎnzǐ had killed Dòu Chōu Míngdú and Wǔ Huá,
and sighed, saying:
"How beautiful the vast waters are!
That Qīu cannot cross this
is fate.
If one cuts open fetuses and kills infants,
then the Qílín will not reach one's suburbs;
if one drains the marsh to fish,
then the Jiāolóng will not dwell in its abyss;
if one overturns nests and breaks eggs,
then the Fènghuáng will not soar over one's city;
each has its own kind."
Thereupon, he composed 《Pánqín》 to lament it.
Eight Orifices, Nine Orifices
At the beginning of winter, swallows and sparrows enter the water and transform into clams.
Silkworms eat but do not drink;
cicadas drink but do not eat;
mayflies neither drink nor eat.
Those that bite and swallow have eight orifices and are oviparous;
those that chew have nine orifices and are viviparous.
Five Things Not to Marry
There are five types of women one should not marry:
daughters from rebellious families,
daughters from disorderly families,
daughters whose families have been subject to punishments for generations,
daughters with serious diseases,
and eldest daughters who have lost their fathers.
Eating Soil
People from hard soil are solid;
people from loose soil are weak;
people from sandy soil are
beautiful; people from fine breathing soil are beautiful;
people from depleted soil are ugly.
Those who eat water are good swimmers and resistant to cold;
those who eat earth are mindless and do not rest;
those who eat mulberry leaves are coherent and harmonious;
those who eat meat are brave and fierce;
those who eat air are divine and long-lived;
those who eat grain are wise and skillful;
those who eat nothing do not die and are divine.
Kǒngzǐ Learns the Zither
Kǒngzǐ learned the zither from Shī Xiāngzǐ,
and said:
"Qīu has now grasped the person it represents.
Dark and black,
tall and long,
vast and gazing like a sheep,
encompassing the four directions.
Who but King Wén could have created this?"
His teacher said it was the 《Wénwáng Cāo》.
Five-String Zither
Shùn played the five-string zither,
and composed the poem 《Nánfēng》, saying:
"The warmth of the south wind
can soothe the grievances of our people.
The timeliness of the south wind
can enrich the wealth of the people."
Practicing the Music of a Doomed State
Ordinary people,
who have no regard for the institutions of the former kings,
but practice the music of a doomed state,
how can they preserve their six-foot bodies?
Music Symbolizes Accomplishment
Music symbolizes accomplishment.
Holding shields and standing like a mountain
was the work of King Wǔ.
Leaping and brandishing weapons
was the system of Tài Gōng.
Harsh Government Is Fiercer Than Tigers
There was a woman crying in the wilderness,
saying:
"My father-in-law died from a tiger,
my husband also died from it,
and my son also died from it!"
Zǐgòng said:
"Why do you not leave?"
She said:
"There is no harsh government here."
The Master said:
"Youngsters, remember this:
harsh government is fiercer than tigers!"
Valuing Age
The Yǒuyú clan valued virtue and respected age;
the Xiàhòu clan valued rank and respected age;
the Zhōu people valued kinship and respected age.
From Yú, Xià, Shāng, to Zhōu,
the most flourishing kings of the world,
none neglected the elderly.
Gained Three Bings of Grain
Zēngzǐ was born in the state of Lǔ,
and wished to obtain three bǐng of grain.
At that time, Zēngzǐ valued his salary heavily and his person lightly.
After his parents' death,
Qí invited him as chancellor,
Chǔ invited him as Prime Minister,
and Jìn invited him as a minister.
At that time, Zēngzǐ valued his person heavily and his salary lightly.
Unbenevolent, Disloyal, Untrustworthy
The Commentary says:
"The ultimate lack of benevolence is to neglect one's parents;
the ultimate lack of loyalty is to betray one's ruler;
the ultimate lack of trustworthiness is to deceive one's friends.
These three,
the sage kills without pardon."
Sacrifice One's Life
Wángzǐ Bǐgān sacrificed his life to achieve his loyalty;
Liǔxià Huì sacrificed his life to achieve his trustworthiness;
Bóyí and Shúqí sacrificed their lives to achieve their integrity.
These three individuals
were exemplary gentlemen of the world.
Appearance of Fatted Animals
Zǐgòng asked Mǐn Zǐqiān:
"When you first saw the Master,
you had a famished look;
now you have the appearance of someone fed on fatted animals.
Why is this?"
Mǐn Zǐ said:
"I came out from among the reeds,
and entered the Master's gate,
my heart secretly delighted in it.
Then I went out and saw feathered carriages and dragon banners,
with furs and blankets following,
and my heart also delighted in it.
These two conflicted in my chest and I could not proceed,
hence I had a famished look.
Now, immersed deeply in the Master's teachings,
internally I understand the meaning of choosing to advance or withdraw,
and when I go out and see feathered carriages and dragon banners, they are like mere lumps of earth.
Hence I have the appearance of someone fed on fatted animals."
Three Sayings of the Noble Person
Zēngzǐ said:
"A noble person has three sayings
that can be strung together and worn:
first, do not be distant within and intimate without;
second, do not blame others when you yourself are not good;
third, do not call upon Heaven only after disaster has arrived."
Entrusting to People, Entrusting to Strength
Zǐjiàn governed Dānfù.
He played the zither,
never leaving his hall,
yet Dānfù was well-governed.
Wūmǎ Qī said: “Those who rely on people are at ease;
those who rely on strength toil;
those who accumulate wealth perish.”
Chéng Hóu and Sì Gōng
were rulers who accumulated wealth and calculated [their gains];
they had not yet reached the stage of winning the people.
Zǐchǎn
was one who won the people,
but had not yet reached the stage of governing.
Guǎn Zhòng
was one who governed,
but had not yet reached the stage of cultivating rites.
Therefore, those who cultivate rites become kings;
those who govern become strong;
those who win the people are secure;
those who accumulate wealth perish.
Great Loyalty, Secondary Loyalty, Lesser Loyalty
There are those of great loyalty,
there are those of secondary loyalty,
there are those of lesser loyalty,
and there are traitors to the state.
To assist the ruler with the Dao and transform him—
this is great loyalty;
the Duke of Zhōu to King Chéng is an example of this.
To advise against the ruler's wrongdoing and incur his resentment—
this is lesser loyalty;
Wú Zǐxū to Fūchā is an example of this.
To illicitly conform and complacently tolerate,
to cling to one's salary and cultivate connections—
this is a traitor to the state;
Chu Long to Zhào is an example of this.
A King Regards the People as Heaven
Qí Huán Gōng asked Guǎn Zhòng:
“What does a king value?”
He replied:
“He values Heaven.”
The Duke looked up at the sky.
Guǎn Zhòng said:
“The Heaven I speak of
is not the vast and boundless sky.
A king regards the people as Heaven.”
Three Seedlings, One Sprout
In the time of King Chéng,
three seedlings grew through a mulberry tree,
forming a single sprout.
The Duke of Zhōu said:
“The world will likely become unified.”
Indeed, people from Yuècháng came, having made nine translations,
and presented a white pheasant.
The interpreter said:
“Our country's elders with yellow hair commanded us, saying:
‘For a long time, Heaven has not had swift winds or fierce rains,
nor has the sea surged.
It has been three years now.
It seems there must be a sage in the Middle Kingdom.
Why not go and pay him homage?’
Therefore, we have come.”
The Altar Rat
Qí Jǐng Gōng asked Yàn Zǐ:
“What is one to worry about as a ruler?”
He replied:
“One worries about the altar rat that steals outside
and takes refuge in the altar.
To pour water would destroy the wall;
to smoke it would burn the wood.
Now, your attendants,
when they go out, they betray you for profit; when they come in, they take refuge in you.
These are the worries of the altar rat.”
The Duke said:
“Alas,
how could this be true?”
“There was a man who sold wine that was very fine.
He set up a very tall sign,
yet his wine turned sour and remained unsold.
He asked the villagers the reason.
The villagers said:
‘Your dog is very fierce.
When people carry vessels intending to go,
the dog invariably bites them.
This is why the wine turned sour and was not sold.’
If a scholar wishes to see a king of ten thousand chariots,
and those in power greet and bite him,
they are also the state's vicious dogs.”
Three Benefits, Three Harms
Shū'áo met the elder of Húqiū,
who said:
“Where there are three benefits, there must be three harms.
High rank makes people jealous;
a great office makes the lord dislike one;
a generous salary brings resentment upon one.”
Sūn Shū'áo said:
“The higher my rank,
the humbler my ambition.
The greater my office,
the smaller my heart.
The more generous my salary,
the broader my generosity.
Can I thus be free from harm?”
Húqiū said:
“Excellent words!”
Loyalty and Filial Piety
Bó Qí was filial yet abandoned by his parents;
Yǐn Gōng was benevolent yet murdered by his brother;
Shū Wǔ was virtuous yet murdered by his elder brother;
Bǐ Gān was loyal yet executed by his ruler.
Wrapping Rough Cloth to Avoid Thorns
Dōngguō Xiānshēng knew that Sòng was about to perish,
so he pulled up his coarse clothes and passed through its court,
saying:
“Sòng is about to suffer the calamity of thorns that will entangle my rough clothes,
so I am pulling them up to avoid it.”
The King of Sòng considered this ominous talk
and had him killed.
Three years later,
Sòng indeed perished.
Praising Kǒngzǐ
Qí Jǐng Gōng asked Zǐgòng:
“Whom do you follow as your teacher?”
He replied:
“Zhòngní.”
“Is Zhòngní worthy?”
He replied:
“He is a sage!
How could he merely be worthy?
One lives one's whole life beneath Heaven,
yet does not know how high Heaven is;
one treads on the earth one's whole life,
yet does not know how thick the earth is.
My service to Zhòngní
is like drinking from the Jiang or the Sea;
I leave with a full belly,
but how could I know the depth of the Jiang or the Sea?”
The Duke said:
“Your praise, sir,
is it not excessive?”
He replied:
“My praise of Zhòngní
is like carrying two handfuls of earth and adding them to Mount Tài;
its uselessness is clear.
If I do not praise Zhòngní,
it is like grasping Mount Tài with both hands;
its lack of harm is also clear.”
Rites for a Great Invasion (Famine)
One grain not harvested is called qiàn (poor harvest);
two grains not harvested is called jī (famine);
three grains not harvested is called jǐn (severe famine);
four grains not harvested is called huāng (desolation);
five grains not harvested is called dàqīn (great invasion/famine).
The rites for a dàqīn are:
the ruler does not eat dishes of more than one flavor;
terraces and pavilions are not decorated;
roads are not swept;
all officials are appointed but not adorned;
prayers are offered to spirits and deities, but no sacrifices are made.
These are the rites for a dàqīn.
Dismemberment
There was someone in Qí who had offended Jǐng Gōng.
The Duke was greatly enraged
and summoned his attendants to dismember him.
Yàn Zǐ held the head in his left hand,
sharpened his knife in his right,
looked up, and asked:
“In ancient times, when enlightened kings and sage rulers
dismembered people,
from which limb, I wonder, did they begin the dismemberment?”
Jǐng Gōng said:
“Let him go!
The fault lies with me.”
Those who wait for others will not see them; those who rely on others will not last.
Wèi Wénhóu asked Hújuànzǐ,
"Is a virtuous father dependable?"
He replied,
"No."
"Is a virtuous son dependable?"
He replied,
"No."
"Is a virtuous elder brother dependable?"
He replied,
"No."
"Is a virtuous younger brother dependable?"
He replied,
"No."
"Are virtuous ministers dependable?"
He replied,
"No."
"A father's virtue did not surpass that of Yáo,
yet Dānzhū was banished.
A son's virtue did not surpass that of Shùn,
yet Gǔsǒu remained stubborn.
An elder brother's virtue did not surpass that of Shùn,
yet Xiàng was arrogant.
A younger brother's virtue did not surpass that of Zhōu Gōng,
yet Guǎnshū was executed.
Ministers' virtue did not surpass that of Tāng and Wǔ,
yet Jié and Zhòu were overthrown.
Those who look to others will not attain their goal;
those who rely on others will not last long.
If a ruler wishes to govern well,
it must begin with himself.
How can one rely on others?"
The Way of the Yì
There is a way in the Yì:
great enough to govern all under heaven,
moderate enough to bring peace to the state,
and close enough to protect oneself.
Is it not humility in virtue?
The Old Horse
Tián Zǐfāng was out
when he saw an old horse on the road.
His charioteer said,
"This is a public horse;
it is worn out and no longer useful,
so it was released."
Fāng said,
"It exhausted its strength in its youth,
and now in its old age it is cast out.
A benevolent person would not do this."
He tied silk to it and redeemed it.
When poor scholars heard of this,
they knew where their loyalty should lie.
The Mantis Striking the Wheel
Qí Zhuānggōng was out hunting,
and there was a mantis raising its forelegs to strike the wheel.
The charioteer said,
"This insect knows how to advance but not how to retreat;
it overestimates its strength and lightly confronts an enemy."
Zhuānggōng said,
"If it were a man,
it would surely be a great brave warrior."
Thereupon, he turned his chariot to avoid it,
and brave warriors came to him.
Is There Hatred Among Men?
Wèi Wénhóu asked Lǐ Kè,
"Is there hatred among men?"
Kè replied,
"The noble are hated by the lowly;
the wealthy are hated by the poor;
the wise are hated by the foolish."
Wénhóu said,
"Excellent.
If one acts in these three ways
to prevent people from hating,
is it possible?"
He replied,
"If the noble humble themselves before the lowly,
the common people will not hate them.
If the wealthy share with the poor,
then the impoverished scholars will not hate them.
If the wise teach the foolish,
then the ignorant will not hate them."
Wénhóu said,
"What excellent words!"
What Is Relied Upon
There was a bird here
