that built its nest on the tip of a reed.
When a great wind came,
the reed broke and the nest was destroyed,
because what it relied upon was weak.
The millet bee is not attacked;
the temple rat is not smoked out;
this is because of what they rely upon.
Therefore, the Sage seeks the virtuous to assist himself.
Indeed, a fish that can swallow a boat is large;
but if it is large and loses its water, it will be controlled by ants and maggots,
because it has lost its support.
The Eastern Neighbor Kills a Pig
When Mèngzǐ was young,
his eastern neighbor killed a pig.
He asked his mother,
"The eastern neighbor is killing a pig,
what for?"
His mother said,
"To feed you."
His mother regretted it,
and said,
"When I was pregnant with this child,
I would not sit if the mat was not straight,
and I would not eat if the cut of meat was not proper.
This was prenatal education.
Now, he is just beginning to understand things, and I have deceived him.
This is teaching him not to be trustworthy."
So she bought pork from the eastern neighbor to feed him,
to show that she had not deceived him.
Appointing the Governor of Xīhé
Wèi Wénhóu asked Jiě Hú,
"I am about to appoint a governor for Xīhé,
who is suitable for the post?"
He replied,
"Jīng Bóliǔ is a virtuous man;
he is certainly suitable."
Wénhóu appointed him governor of Xīhé.
Jīng Bóliǔ met Jiě Hú,
and thanked him, saying,
"You have indeed excused my faults."
Jiě Hú said,
"My recommendation of you was for the public good;
my resentment towards you is personal.
The public matter has been carried out;
my resentment towards you remains as before."
Zhāng Gōng shot it;
it ran ten steps and then fell dead.
This can be called courageous.
Cutting Divination Reeds and Losing the Hairpin
Kǒngzǐ was traveling
when he saw a woman crying very sadly.
Kǒngzǐ sent his disciple to ask her.
The woman said,
"Just now, when cutting divination reeds,
I lost my divination hairpin,
which is why I am sad."
The disciple said,
"Cutting divination reeds and losing a divination hairpin,
why be sad about that?"
She replied,
"I am not sad about losing the hairpin,
but rather that I did not lose it before."
The Wife's Lack of Propriety
Mèngzǐ's wife was alone at home,
sitting with her legs apart.
Mèngzǐ entered the door and saw her,
then reported to his mother, saying,
"My wife is ill-mannered;
please let me divorce her."
His mother said,
"It is not your wife who is ill-mannered,
but you who are ill-mannered."
Does not the Lǐ say:
'When about to ascend the hall,
one must make one's voice heard.
When about to enter a door,
one must cast one's gaze downwards.'
This is to avoid catching people unprepared.
Now you entered a private place
without making a sound at the door,
and then saw her sitting with her legs apart.
This is your lack of propriety,
not your wife's lack of propriety."
Thereupon, Mèngzǐ blamed himself
and dared not divorce his wife.
Three Expenses
Zǐxià 過 Guǎng Zēngzǐ.
Zēngzǐ 曰:
"Enter and eat."
Zǐxià 曰:
"Will this not be a public expense?"
Zēngzǐ 曰:
"A junzǐ has three expenses,
eating and drinking are not among them.
A junzǐ has three joys,
bells, chimes, qín, and sè are not among them.
Having parents one can rely on,
having a wife one can return to,
having children one can leave behind –
this is the first joy.
Having parents one can admonish,
having a wife one can divorce,
having children one can be angry with –
this is the second joy.
Having a ruler one can counsel,
having friends one can help –
this is the third joy.
To learn in youth,
and forget in old age –
this is the first expense.
To serve one's ruler with merit yet be lightly regarded for one's poverty –
this is the second expense.
To have a long friendship and then break it off midway –
this is the third expense."
A good judge of character
In Chǔ, there was a good judge of character.
King Zhuāng summoned him and asked.
He said:
"I am not able to judge people,
but I can judge people's friends.
When observing a commoner,
if all his friends are filial, fraternal, earnest, and prudent,
his family will surely prosper daily,
and his person will surely improve daily.
This is what is called an auspicious person (jírén).
When observing one who serves a ruler,
if all his friends are sincere, trustworthy, and fond of goodness,
his affairs will prosper daily,
and his official position will advance daily.
This is what is called an auspicious minister (jí chén).
When observing a ruler,
if his court officials are mostly virtuous,
and those on his left and right are mostly loyal,
his state will be at peace daily,
and his ruler will be revered daily.
This is what is called an auspicious king (jí wáng)."
The King said:
"Excellent."
Two Peaches
Qí Huángōng went out on a journey
and met a man
wearing a broad robe and walking with an even pace,
carrying a "peach staff" (táo shū).
The Duke was surprised and asked him about it.
He said:
"This is called 'two peaches' (èrtáo).
The word 'peach' (táo) here means 'perish' (wáng).
If one is careful with peaches day by day,
what troubles can there be?
The altars of perished states serve as a warning to the feudal lords.
The warning of benevolence lies in the 'peach staff'."
The Duke was pleased by his words
and took him into his carriage.
The following year, in the first month,
all commoners wore them.
The Three Disciples' Wishes
Kǒngzǐ was touring Jǐngshān
and said:
"When ascending a height, one must compose a fu.
What wishes do you, my young disciples, hold?
I will guide you."
Zǐlù said:
"Yóu wishes to wield a long halberd,
to sweep through three armies.
With a nursing tiger behind me
and enemies before me,
I would advance to resolve the troubles of two states."
The Master said:
"A courageous warrior!"
Zǐgòng said:
"When valiant warriors array their ranks,
and dust fills the heavens,
without holding a foot of weapon
or a peck of grain,
I would resolve the difficulties of two states."
The Master said:
"An eloquent debater!"
Yán Yuān said:
"I wish to be the minister of a small state.
The ruler would govern by the Way,
the ministers would transform by virtue.
Ruler and ministers would share loyalty,
and internal and external affairs would respond in harmony.
Actions would be in accordance with the Way,
and demeanor would be in accordance with ritual.
Those who speak of benevolence and righteousness would be rewarded,
and those who speak of war and conflict would be put to death."
The Master said:
"A sage scholar!
When great men emerge,
the young disciples hide.
When sages arise,
the worthy retreat.
If Huí were to hold power,
then would Yóu and Cì still display their abilities?"
Kǒngzǐ's zither music has the ambition of greed
Kǒngzǐ was playing the sè.
Zēngzǐ listened from the side door
and said:
"The Master's sè music has the ambition of greed (tānláng zhī zhì)
and the conduct of depravity (xiépì zhī xíng).
Why is it so unbenevolent and excessively driven by profit?"
Zǐgòng entered
and reported Zēngzǐ's words.
The Master said:
"Shēn
is a worthy man of the world;
he is indeed skilled in music.
A moment ago, as I played the sè,
a mouse came out to play.
A cat saw it from the roof,
creeping along the beam with subtle steps.
It approached stealthily,
narrowing its eyes,
arching its back,
and showing a hostile expression,
but failed to pounce on it.
I played the sè to match its sound.
Shēn took me for greedy and depraved.
Is it not appropriate!"
Mother leaves, three sons are cold
Mǐn Zǐqiān's mother died,
and his father remarried.
Zǐqiān was driving the carriage for his father
and dropped the reins.
His father held his hand;
his clothes were very thin.
When his father returned home,
he called his stepmother's son
and felt his clothes;
they were very thick.
He immediately said to his wife:
"The reason I married you
was for my sons.
Now you deceive me.
Leave!
Do not stay!"
Zǐqiān said:
"When mother is here, one son is thinly clad.
When mother leaves, three sons will be cold."
His father said:
"What filial piety!"
One 'pǐ' of a horse
Yán Huí gazed at the Wú Gate
and saw a 'pǐ' of white silk (liàn).
Kǒngzǐ said:
"It is a horse."
Thus, the appearance of a horse is 'one pǐ long,'
hence from ancient times, a horse has been called a 'pǐ'.
Three worries
Kǒngzǐ said:
"A junzǐ has three worries:
If one is not known,
can one be without worry?
If one knows but does not learn,
can one be without worry?
If one learns but does not act,
can one be without worry?"
Yī Yǐn (伊尹) went to Tāng (湯).
Jié (桀) created a pond of wine and a dike of dregs,
indulged in extravagant music,
and three thousand people drank like oxen.
The ministers, holding each other, sang:
"The river's waters surge!
The boats and oars are broken!
Our king is ruined!
Let us hasten back to Háο (毫),
for Háο (毫) is also great!"
Again they sang:
"Joy!
Joy!
Our four steeds are proud,
our six reins are fine.
Cast away the bad and follow the good,
why should we not be joyful?"
Yī Yǐn (伊尹) knew that a great calamity was approaching,
so he raised his cup and approached Jié (桀),
saying:
"If Your Majesty does not listen to your minister's words,
your ruin is but days away."
Jié (桀) said:
"You speak ill omens again!
My possession of the world
is like Heaven's possession of the sun.
Can the sun perish?
When the sun perishes,
then I too shall perish!"
Thereupon, Yī Yǐn (伊尹) picked up his sandals and hurried away,
then went to Tāng (湯).
Tāng (湯) made him prime minister.
This can be called reaching the land of joy.
A gentleman's demeanor and appearance
are what a superior person encounters.
Demeanor and appearance come first,
voice second,
actions last.
Therefore, one who is looked up to as a ruler
is judged by their demeanor.
One who is trusted up close
is judged by their appearance.
One whose words bring peace
is judged by their speech.
One who is admired over time
is judged by their actions.
Thus, a gentleman's demeanor and appearance
are observed by all under Heaven as a model,
making them fit to be a ruler without needing words.
The *Shī* (詩) says:
"A countenance like ruddy ochre"—
surely that is a ruler!
Zǐ Xià (子夏) reads the *Shī* (詩)
Zǐ Xià (子夏) had finished reading the *Shī* (詩).
The Master said:
"What do you make of the *Shī* (詩)?"
He replied:
"The *Shī* (詩), in its treatment of affairs,
is as clear as the light of the sun and moon,
and as brilliant as the arrayed stars.
Above, it contains the Way of Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜);
below, it contains the righteousness of the Three Kings.
Even if a disciple lives in a humble dwelling,
they can play the qín and chant the master's style.
If there are others, they too enjoy it;
if there are no others, they still enjoy it.
It can inspire one to forget food in their zeal."
The Master said:
"You have seen its surface,
but not its interior."
Yán Yuān (顏淵) said:
"Its surface has been seen,
what more could there be in its interior?"
The Master said:
"If you peek into its gate but do not enter,
how can you know where its hidden treasures lie?
However, to hide it is not difficult.
Qíu (丘) once devoted his whole heart and mind
and entered it.
Before me were towering peaks,
behind me deep valleys,
and such was the serene and established sight.
Unable to see its interior
probably refers to the subtle essence."
Punishing Jié (桀) and the breaking of the shield
King Wǔ (武王) attacked Jié (桀).
Upon reaching Xíngqīu (刑丘),
a shield broke into three pieces,
and it rained for three days without ceasing.
The King was afraid
and asked Tàigōng (太公):
"Is Zhòu (紂) not yet to be attacked?"
He replied:
"No.
The shield breaking into three pieces
means the army should be divided into three.
The three days of rain
are meant to wash our weapons."
The King said:
"Indeed,
what then?"
He replied:
"Love the person,
even to the crows on their roof;
hate the person,
even to the remnants of their bones.
Exterminate all their enemies,
leaving none behind."
The King said:
"Alas,
the world is not yet settled!"
Zhōu Gōng (周公) said:
"No.
Let each measure their dwelling,
and cultivate their fields,
without distinction of old or new.
If the common people have faults,
the blame is mine alone."
The King said:
"The world is now settled!"
Jì Sūn (季孫) governs Lǔ (魯)
Jì Sūn Zǐ (季孫子) governed Lǔ (魯).
When many people committed murder, they were surely punished according to their crime;
when many people were fined, they were surely punished according to their fault.
Zǐ Gòng (子貢) said:
"How tyrannical
is this governance!"
Jì Sūn (季孫) said:
"Why?"
Zǐ Gòng (子貢) said: [136)"Zǐ Chǎn (子產) governed Zhèng (鄭).
After one year, the faults leading to fines decreased;
after two years, the crimes leading to corporal punishment and execution ceased;
after three years, there were no prisoners in the jail.
When Zǐ Chǎn (子產) fell ill and died,
scholars and officials wept in the court,
merchants and travelers wept in the marketplace,
farmers wept in the fields,
all as if they had lost their parents.
Now, when you, Master, are ill,
the people of the state rejoice;
when you recover,
the people of the state are startled.
To congratulate one another on your death,
and to dread one another at your life,
if this is not tyranny, what is?
To govern by relying on laws is called tyranny;
to impose a deadline without prior warning is called cruelty;
to execute without prior instruction is called villainy;
to overpower others with one's own person is called blame.
One who blames loses their person;
one who is villainous loses their ministers;
one who is cruel loses their government;
one who is tyrannical loses their people.
One who holds a high position and commits these four
has never failed to be ruined."
Jì Sūn (季孫) said:
"I respectfully accept your instruction."
The wise delight in water
Someone asked:
"Why do the wise delight in water?"
He replied:
"Water flows according to principle,
not abandoning small streams,
seeming to possess wisdom.
It moves downwards,
seeming to possess propriety.
It falls into depths without hesitation,
seeming to possess courage.
It clarifies when obstructed,
seeming to understand destiny.
It traverses dangers to reach far-off places,
ultimately achieving its goal without being destroyed,
seeming to possess virtue.
This is why the wise delight in water."
The benevolent delight in mountains
Someone asked:
"Why do the benevolent delight in mountains?"
He replied:
"Mountains
are gazed upon and admired by all people.
Grasses and trees grow there,
all things are planted there,
birds gather there,
beasts rest there.
They give forth clouds and guide winds,
sighing between Heaven and Earth.
This is why the benevolent delight in mountains."
On Shùn (舜) being incorrect
The performance of *Sháo* with shields and axes
is not supreme music.
Shùn marrying two daughters
is not upholding ritual.
Enfeoffing ninety sons of the Emperor
is not righteous by law.
Going to the fields and weeping bitterly
is not fully obeying fate.
When viewed by people,
this is right;
when measured by law,
this is not yet right.
A good leader does not forget those beneath them.
A good charioteer does not forget their horses.
A good archer does not forget their bow.
A good leader does not forget those beneath them.
If there is genuine love and benefit,
within the four seas,
all will be as one family.
If there is no love but only benefit,
a son may kill his father,
how much more so the world?
The conduct of a petty person
causes trouble for their clan when they go out,
and worry for their village when they stay in.
This is the conduct of a petty person.
The three types of assistants:
Those whose knowledge is like a spring,
who can serve as models,
are human teachers.
Those whose knowledge can temper conduct,
and who can serve as advisors,
are human friends.
Those who uphold the law and guard their duties,
and do not commit wrongdoing,
are human officials.
Those who seek immediate gratification,
and respond with "yes" to every command,
are human servants.
A supreme ruler takes teachers as assistants.
A middle ruler takes friends as assistants.
A lesser ruler takes officials as assistants.
A ruler facing peril and ruin takes servants as assistants.
Bending a bow to shoot a sleeping stone:
A brave warrior's shout makes three armies retreat;
this is the sincerity of a warrior.
When Chǔ Xióngzǐ was traveling at night,
he mistook a sleeping stone for a crouching tiger.
He bent his bow and shot it,
burying the shaft and feather.
Looking down,
he realized it was a stone.
The stone was split open because of this;
how much more so would a person be affected?
A *Jūnzǐ* avoids three points:
Birds with beautiful feathers, hooked beaks,
other birds fear them.
Fish with wide mouths, drooping eyes,
other fish fear them.
People with sharp tongues and eloquent words,
other people fear them.
Therefore, a *Jūnzǐ* avoids three points:
They avoid the pen-point of a scholar,
the blade-point of a warrior,
and the tongue-point of a debater.
What was born yesterday?
What was accomplished today?
One must contemplate returning to sincerity,
one must contemplate managing life's days.
Be cautious for one day,
and it will be as complete as a golden fortress.
Beware of these four things:
Laziness in office follows success in career.
Illness worsens after a slight recovery.
Calamity arises from懈怠 (laxity).
Filial piety declines because of one's wife and children.
If one examines these four,
they will be as cautious at the end as at the beginning.
How can one be arrogant towards others?
When Tián Zǐfāng went to Wèi,
the Wèi Crown Prince led a hundred chariots to welcome him outside the city.
The Crown Prince bowed twice,
but Zǐfāng did not descend from his chariot.
The Crown Prince asked,
"May I ask, how can one be arrogant towards others?"
Zǐfāng said,
"There are those who were arrogant towards others with the world and perished.
Poverty and low status can make one arrogant towards others.
If one's aspirations are not met, one can go to Qín or Chǔ;
where can one go without finding poverty and low status?"
Master Běiguō
King Zhuāng of Chǔ invited Master Běiguō.
The Master said,
"I have a wife who sweeps the floor;
I wish to go in and consult her."
He then said to his wife,
"Chǔ wants me to be its Prime Minister,
what do you think?"
His wife said,
"Even with carriages yoked four abreast and a retinue of riders,
the comfort is no more than a space for the knees.
Even with food spread out a square *zhàng*,
the sweetness is no more than the taste of one piece of meat.
To then sacrifice oneself to the worries of the state of Chǔ,
how could that be acceptable?"
Thereupon, he did not accept the invitation.
The Phoenix
When the phoenix first rose,
the ordinary sparrows chirped and laughed at it.
When it ascended to the lesser sun,
now crouching, now stretching,
soaring and turning among the clouds,
the sparrows by the fence then realized they were far inferior.
A scholar in coarse cloth and worn garments
has never been complete.
Eating coarse mixed grains,
has never been full.
Common people of the world
consider this a shame.
But when such a scholar emerges,
they can bring peace through a hundred plans.
When employed,
they extend the lives of the people.
The common people of the world then realize they are far inferior.
Scroll 38
End.
Temple Calculations
Warfare is
the way of deception.
If temple calculations show victory before battle,
it is because many calculations were made.
If temple calculations show no victory before battle,
it is because few calculations were made.
Many calculations lead to victory;
few calculations lead to no victory.
How much more so with no calculations at all?
Blunting the Army
Blunting the army, eroding its keenness,
exhausting its strength and depleting its wealth,
the feudal lords will take advantage of its weakened state and rise.
Even if there are wise people,
they cannot manage the aftermath well.
Clumsy Speed
We have heard of clumsy speed in warfare,
but have not seen clever protraction.
Skilled in Warfare
Those skilled in warfare
do not enlist twice,
and do not transport provisions thrice.
They draw their resources from their own country,
and forage for food from the enemy.
Thus, the army's provisions can be sufficient.
General, Commander of the People's Fate
Warfare values victory,
not prolonged duration.
Therefore, a general who understands warfare
is the commander of the people's fate,
and the master of the nation's peace and peril.
Using the Art of War
The art of employing troops:
To preserve the enemy's whole country is best;
to destroy it is second best.
To preserve the enemy's whole army is best;
to destroy it is second best.
To preserve the enemy's whole brigade is best;
to destroy it is second best.
To preserve the enemy's whole company is best;
to destroy it is second best.
To preserve the enemy's whole squad is best;
to destroy it is second best.
Subduing the Enemy without Battle
To win a hundred battles in a hundred engagements
is not the height of excellence.
To subdue the enemy's army without fighting
is the height of excellence.
Superior Warfare
The highest form of warfare is to attack the enemy's plans.
Next is to attack their alliances.
Next is to attack their army.
The lowest is to attack walled cities.
The method of attacking walled cities
is only to be used when there is no other option.
If ten times stronger, encircle.
The principles of warfare:
If ten times the enemy's strength, surround them.
If five times, attack them.
If double, divide them.
If equal, engage them.
If fewer, evade them.
If not as strong, avoid them.
A strong enemy,
a weak enemy's firmness,
is the capture of a strong enemy.
The general is the state's assistant.
The general is the state's assistant.
If the assistance is complete,
the state will surely be strong.
If the assistance is flawed,
the state will surely be weak.
To bind the army
is to be unaware that the army cannot advance or retreat.
This is called "binding the army."
Victory and defeat.
Know the enemy and know yourself,
and you will not be imperiled in a hundred battles.
If you do not know the enemy but know yourself,
you will win one battle and lose one.
If you do not know the enemy and do not know yourself,
you will be defeated in every battle.
A skilled warrior.
A skilled warrior
first makes himself unconquerable,
and then waits for the enemy to become conquerable.
Inconquerability lies with oneself;
conquerability lies with the enemy.
A skilled warrior stands in an invincible position.
Therefore, victorious armies win first and then fight;
defeated armies fight first and then seek victory.
Engagement.
When two armies face each other,
it is called "engagement."
Victorious army.
A victorious army is like weighing an *yǐ* against a *zhū*;
a defeated army is like weighing a *zhū* against an *yǐ*.
The battle of a victorious army
is like releasing accumulated water from a ravine a thousand *rèn* deep.
This is the form.
Orthodox for engagement, unorthodox for victory.
Generally, in war,
use the orthodox for engagement,
and the unorthodox for victory.
The strategy of war is nothing more than orthodox and unorthodox,
giving birth to each other like a cycle.
Selecting people and employing momentum.
A skilled warrior
seeks it in momentum,
not in people.
Thus, they can select people and employ momentum.
The army of a skilled warrior
is like rolling a round stone down a mountain a thousand *lǐ* high.
This is momentum.
Compel others, but be not compelled by others.
One who occupies the battlefield first and awaits the enemy is at ease;
one who occupies the battlefield later and rushes into battle is weary.
Therefore, a skilled warrior compels others,
but is not compelled by others.
If you know the place of battle
and the day of battle,
you can fight a battle a thousand *lǐ* away.
If you do not know the place of battle
and do not know the day of battle,
then your left, right, front, and rear cannot come to your aid.
How much less those who are several thousand *lǐ* away,
or even several *lǐ* away?
Military formation is like water.
The form of water avoids heights and rushes downwards;
the form of an army avoids the strong and strikes the weak.
Water flows according to the terrain;
an army achieves victory according to the enemy.
Double march.
Roll up armor and rush,
day and night without stopping,
double march,
a hundred *lǐ* can be leveled.
Warfare is established by deception,
moved by profit,
and varied by division and concentration.
Seizing spirit and morale.
The spirit of the three armies can be seized;
the morale of the general can be seized.
Night battles and day battles.
Night battles use many fires and drums;
day battles use many banners and flags.
This is to alter the enemy's ears and eyes.
Avoiding the sharp edge.
In the morning, the spirit is keen;
at noon, it is sluggish;
in the evening, it is exhausted.
A skilled commander
avoids their keen spirit,
and strikes when they are sluggish or exhausted.
Managing the mind and managing strength.
To wait for disorder with order,
to wait for clamor with calm,
this is managing the mind.
To wait for the distant with the near,
to wait for the weary with the rested,
to wait for the hungry with the full,
this is managing strength.
Do not intercept an army with perfectly arrayed banners.
Do not attack an army in a grand and imposing formation.
Do not block an army returning home.
The principles of warfare:
Do not ascend high hills.
Do not oppose an army with its back to a position.
Do not pursue feigned retreats.
Do not attack elite troops.
Do not eat sweet bait.
Do not block an army returning home.
Do not seal off a surrounded army.
Do not pursue a desperate army.
These are the principles of warfare.
The general receives orders from the sovereign.
Having received orders from the sovereign:
Do not encamp on broken ground.
On intersecting ground, seek alliance.
On barren ground, do not linger.
On surrounded ground, strategize.
On deadly ground, fight.
Do not rely on them not coming.
The principles of warfare:
Do not rely on them not coming;
rely on having the means to await them.
Do not rely on them not attacking;
rely on having something that cannot be attacked.
Five dangers.
A general has five dangers:
If resolute to die, they can be killed.
If determined to live, they can be captured.
If quick to anger, they can be insulted.
If fond of integrity, they can be shamed.
If loving the people, they can be troubled.
Certain victory.
Generally, an army
prefers high ground and dislikes low ground,
values the sunny side and disdains the shady side.
Come to life in solid ground.
If the army has no hundred ailments,
this is called certain victory.
Impassable ravines.
Generally, all terrains with impassable ravines (*juéjiàn*), sky wells (*tiānjǐng*), sky prisons (*tiānláo*), sky nets (*tiānluó*), sky traps (*tiānxiàn*), and sky gaps (*tiānxì*),
must be quickly abandoned,
and not approached.
Mountains and waters that are deep and large are called *juéjiàn*.
Ground that is high on four sides and low in the center is called *tiānjǐng*.
Deep mountains that resemble a dense cage are called *tiānláo*.
Those that can net and cut off people are called *tiānluó*.
Terrain that is sunken is called *tiānxiàn*.
Ravines that are narrow and deep are called *tiānxì*.
Discussing military momentum.
Dust that is high and sharp
indicates chariots approaching.
Dust that is low and wide
indicates infantry approaching.
Dust that is scattered and long-reaching
indicates woodcutters and foragers.
Little dust, but coming and going,
indicates an army establishing camp.
Advancing halfway and retreating halfway
is a feint.
Standing in formation
means they are hungry.
Drawing water but drinking first
means they are thirsty.
Seeing an advantage but not advancing
means they are weary.
Birds gathering
means the place is empty.
Cries at night
mean they are afraid.
An army in disorder
means the general is agitated.
Waving of banners and flags
means confusion.
Slaughtering horses for meat
means the army is without provisions.
Hanging up water jars but not returning
means they are desperate bandits.
Frequent rewards
mean they are in distress.
Frequent punishments
mean they are in difficulty.
Coming to make apologies
means they want to rest.
Advancing without seeking fame,
retreating without avoiding blame,
only safeguarding the people,
and benefiting the lord—
this is a treasure of the state.
Cherishing infants and beloved sons
Treat the soldiers as infants,
and you can lead them into deep ravines.
Treat the soldiers as beloved sons,
and you can lead them to die together.
Shuàirán
One who is skilled in employing troops
is like the "Shuàirán."
The Shuàirán
is a snake from Chángshān.
Strike its head, and its tail responds;
strike its tail, and its head responds;
strike its middle, and both head and tail respond.
Death ground and desperate ground
Plunge them into death ground, and they will survive;
plunge them into desperate ground, and they will live.
Escaping rabbit
At first, be like a virgin,
so the enemy opens his door.
Afterward, be like an escaping rabbit,
so the enemy cannot resist in time.
Five types of fire attack
Generally, there are five types of fire attack:
one is burning people,
two is burning stores,
three is burning chariots,
four is burning arsenals,
five is burning formations.
Raising an army of one hundred thousand costs a thousand gold pieces a day
Raising an army of one hundred thousand
and campaigning a thousand *lǐ*,
the expense to the populace
and the tribute to the public treasury
amount to a thousand gold pieces a day,
causing turmoil within and without.
Five types of spies
There are local spies,
internal spies,
doubled agents,
doomed spies,
and living spies.
Inaugurating Wú Qǐ at the temple
Wèi Wénhóu personally spread out a mat,
his consort held the goblet,
and inaugurated Wú Qǐ at the temple,
appointing him as Grand General,
to guard Xīhé.
He fought seventy-six great battles with the feudal lords,
won sixty-four complete victories,
expanded territory on all four sides,
and extended land for a thousand *lǐ*,
all due to Qǐ's achievements.
Four discords
One who plans for the state
must first educate the people and be close to all citizens.
There are four discords:
If there is discord in the state, one cannot deploy the army.
If there is discord in the army, one cannot array the formation.
If there is discord in the formation, one cannot advance to battle.
If there is discord in battle, one cannot achieve victory.
Winning a battle and holding the victory
Winning a battle is easy;
holding the victory is difficult.
Therefore it is said:
"Among the warring states, one who wins five times brings disaster;
one who wins four times is exhausted;
one who wins three times becomes a hegemon;
one who wins twice becomes a king;
one who wins once becomes an emperor."
Causes of war
There are five:
one is contending for fame,
two is contending for profit,
three is accumulated evil,
four is internal strife,
five is due to famine.
The army's destiny
Within an army,
there must be tiger-swift officers
whose strength can lift a tripod,
whose feet are swift as warhorses,
who can seize banners and capture generals;
there must be capable individuals.
Such individuals,
select and set them apart,
cherish them and assign them responsibilities;
this is called the army's destiny.
Ways to attack
Wǔhóu asked about the ways to attack the enemy.
Qǐ said:
"If the enemy has come from afar and their formation is not yet settled, you can attack.
If they have eaten but are not yet prepared, you can attack.
If they are fleeing, you can attack.
If they are toiling, you can attack.
If they have not secured favorable terrain, you can attack.
If they have missed their opportunity, you can attack.
If they are marching without rest, you can attack.
If they are crossing water halfway, you can attack.
If they are in a narrow pass, you can attack.
If their banners and flags are in disarray, you can attack.
If they are frequently moving, you can attack.
If the general is separated from his soldiers, you can attack.
If their hearts are fearful, you can attack.
In all such cases,
attack swiftly without hesitation."
Four lightnings
The art of employing troops
first clarifies the 'four lightnings':
terrain makes the horse light,
the horse makes the man light,
the man makes the battle light,
the battle makes the enemy light.
For advancing, there are heavy rewards;
for retreating, there are heavy punishments.
Good generalship
In any battlefield,
a place of certain death:
one who is resolved to die will live;
one who hopes to escape will face change.
A good general
is like one sitting in a leaking boat,
or beneath a burning house,
causing the knowing not to have time to plan,
and the brave not to have time to consider.
Heaven's furnace
Wǔhóu said:
"The advance and halt of the three armies have their ways:
Do not confront Heaven's furnace,
do not confront Dragon's head.
Heaven's furnace
is the mouth of a great valley.
Dragon's head
is the peak of a great mountain.
When about to do battle,
carefully observe the direction from which the wind comes.
If the wind is favorable,
lure the enemy and follow the wind.
If the wind is adverse,
strengthen your formation and await them."
Comet's tail
Chǔ general Gōngzǐ Xīn with Qí people fought.
At that time, there was a comet appearing,
its tail pointing towards Qí.
Where the tail points,
victory
is not to be attacked.
Gōngzǐ Xīn said:
"What does a comet know?
Those who fight based on comets
will surely turn their backs and yet win."
The next day, he fought with the Qí people,
and utterly defeated them.
Aiding the battle
All states under Heaven aid my battle,
like swift steeds Jùnjì and Lù'ěr running.
If those slow and clumsy steeds compete,
how can they dampen my spirits?
Three victories
In warfare, there are victories through the Way,
victories through prestige,
and victories through force.
Executions
If killing one person makes the three armies tremble,
kill him.
If killing one person makes ten thousand rejoice,
kill him.
Stepping drum
The stepping drum urges the battle,
one drum for each step.
Controlling the enemy
For conventional forces, priority is given to the vanguard;
for unconventional forces, priority is given to the rear.
Whether vanguard or rear,
it is about controlling the enemy.
Utmost without fault
Rewards like mountains,
punishments like streams.
The utmost is without fault,
the next is to amend faults.
Fond of war, forgetting war
Though a state may be great,
if it is fond of war, it will surely perish.
Though the world may be peaceful,
if it forgets war, it will surely be in peril.
Pursuing the fleeing, relaxing the pursuit
In ancient times, pursuing the fleeing did not exceed one hundred paces;
relaxing the pursuit did not exceed three stages.
Rewards and punishments
Rewards are not delayed beyond their time,
wanting the people to quickly gain the benefits of doing good.
Punishments are not postponed,
wanting the people to quickly see the harm of doing evil.
State etiquette
In ancient times,
state etiquette did not enter the army;
army etiquette did not enter the state.
Garrisoned army
In ancient times,
a garrisoned army was not called upon for three years,
out of concern for the people's toil.
Superiors and subordinates reciprocate,
which is the ultimate understanding.
When successful, they sing songs of triumph,
showing a single joy.
They lay down the pole and the spirit banner,
responding to the people's toil,
showing submission.
Seven Policies:
First, humanity (rén);
second, rectitude (zhèng);
third, speech (cí);
fourth, skill (qiǎo);
fifth, disaster (zāi);
sixth, water (shuǐ);
seventh, military (bīng).
These are called the Seven Policies.
A basket of wine poured into the river
Commanders must share the same flavors and dangers with their soldiers;
only then can the enemy be overcome,
and a complete victory achieved.
In the past, a good general was offered a basket of wine;
he had it poured into the river,
so that he and his soldiers could drink of the flowing water together.
That one basket of wine
could not flavor an entire river's water,
yet the three armies were willing to die for him,
because they felt the flavor reached them.
General's etiquette
If the army's well has not reached water,
the general does not speak of thirst.
If the army's tents have not been pitched,
the general does not speak of weariness.
If the army's stoves have not cooked,
the general does not speak of hunger.
In winter, he does not wear fur;
in summer, he does not wield a fan;
in rain, he does not raise an umbrella.
This is called the general's etiquette.
Financial rewards
If the army has no money,
soldiers will not come.
If the army has no rewards,
soldiers will not go.
Heavy rewards for brave soldiers
Beneath fragrant bait,
there must be hanging fish.
Under heavy rewards,
there must be brave soldiers willing to die.
Profound grace
For a state raising an army,
the priority is to first extend profound grace.
For a state seeking to conquer,
the priority is to first nurture the people.
Self-reliance
When deploying troops and marching an army,
the general must be self-reliant.
If advancement and retreat are controlled internally,
then success is hard to achieve.
Employ the intelligent, employ the brave,
employ the greedy, employ the foolish.
The intelligent rejoice in establishing their achievements;
the brave love to act on their ambitions;
the greedy seek their profits;
the foolish do not regret their deaths.
Good bow stored away
When high-flying birds are dead,
good bows are stored away.
When enemy states are eliminated,
plotting ministers perish.
Soldiers disperse
Once a crowd of people gathers,
it cannot be easily dispersed.
Once authority and power are given,
they cannot be easily shifted.
Ruler honored, people at peace
King Wén said:
"How can one make the ruler honored and the people at peace?"
Tàigōng said:
"By loving the people, and that's all.
Benefit them and do not harm them,
complete them and do not ruin them,
give them life and do not kill them,
give to them and do not take from them,
make them happy and do not make them suffer,
let them rejoice and do not make them angry."
Six Safeguards
A ruler has six safeguards:
First, benevolence (rén);
second, righteousness (yì);
third, loyalty (zhōng);
fourth, trustworthiness (xìn);
fifth, courage (yǒng);
sixth, strategy (móu).
Three Treasures
A ruler must not lend the three treasures to others;
if he lends them to others, the ruler loses his authority.
Grand Agriculturist, Grand Artisan, Grand Merchant
are called the three treasures.
Losing the opportune moment
At noon, it must be bright;
wielding a knife, one must cut;
grasping an axe, one must chop.
If it is not bright at noon,
this is called losing the opportune moment.
If wielding a knife, one does not cut,
the time for profit is lost.
If grasping an axe, one does not chop,
then people will deceive.
If trickles are not dammed,
they will become rivers.
If tiny flames are not extinguished,
how can one deal with blazing fires?
Six Thieves
For a monarch, there are six "thieves" (dangers):
First, when ministers grandly construct palaces,
it harms the monarch's virtue.
Second, when the common people are impulsive and act as wandering vigilantes,
it harms the monarch's transformative influence.
Third, when ministers form cliques and obscure the worthy,
it harms the monarch's authority.
Fourth, when scholars have unyielding aspirations and lofty principles,
it harms the monarch's prestige.
Fifth, when ministers lightly regard their ranks and emoluments, and readily court danger,
it harms the people's labor.
Sixth, when powerful clans encroach and plunder,
it harms the joy of the common people.
Seven Harms
There are also seven harms:
Those without wisdom, strategy, or cunning,
a monarch must not appoint as a general.
Those with reputation but no substance,
must not be consulted for advice.
Those who appear humble and dress poorly,
are hypocrites;
do not draw near to them.
Those with extensive knowledge and grand pronouncements,
are treacherous individuals;
do not favor them.
Those who are opportunistic, lightly regard death,
and crave ranks and emoluments,
must not be employed.
Those skilled in elaborate ornamentation,
who harm agricultural affairs,
must be prohibited.
Witchcraft, sorcery, and heterodox ways,
that mislead good people,
must be stopped.
Rewards and Punishments
Reward one to encourage a hundred;
punish one to warn the multitude.
In applying rewards, value trustworthiness;
in applying punishments, value certainty.
The Sage Preparing to Act
When a fierce bird is about to strike,
it flies low and folds its wings.
When a ferocious beast is about to pounce,
it flattens its ears and lies prostrate.
When a sage is about to act,
they must appear foolish.
Three Admonitions
There are three admonitions:
In winter, do not wear a fur coat.
In summer, do not carry a fan.
In rain, do not open an umbrella.
Command from Within
The people cannot be governed from outside.
The army cannot be commanded from within.
The General as the Giver of Life to Men
If a general is not benevolent,
the three armies will not be close.
If a general is not courageous,
the three armies will not be sharp.
If a general is not discerning,
the three armies will be doubtful.
If a general is not clear-sighted,
the three armies will be overturned.
If a general is not meticulous,
the three armies will lose their opportunities.
If a general is not constantly vigilant,
the three armies will lose their preparedness.
If a general is not strong and resolute,
the three armies will fail in their duties.
Therefore, the general
is the giver of life and death for men.
Three Formations
The sun, moon, and stars,
one to the left, one to the right,
one facing, one backing –
this is called the Heavenly Formation (Tiānzhèn).
Hills and springs,
also distinguished by left, right, front, and back –
this is called the Earthly Formation (Dìzhèn).
Using chariots, using cavalry, using civil methods, using military methods –
this is called the Human Formation (Rénzhèn).
Enemy Encampment: Strengths and Weaknesses
King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng) asked:
"How does one discern the strengths and weaknesses of an enemy's encampment?"
Grand Duke Tài Gōng (Tài Gōng) replied:
"A general must understand the ways of Heaven above,
understand the geography below,
and understand human affairs in between.
Ascend to a height and look down,
observing the enemy's movements and changes.
Observe their encampment,
to know its strengths and weaknesses.
Observe their officers and soldiers,
to know their intentions to leave or stay."
The Weak Overcoming the Strong, the Few Striking the Many
King Wǔ (Wǔ Wáng) asked:
"To overcome the strong with the weak,
and strike the many with the few,
how is this done?"
Grand Duke Tài Gōng (Tài Gōng) replied:
"To strike the many with the few,
one must do so at dusk,
lie in ambush in deep grass,
and intercept them in a narrow pass.
To overcome the strong with the weak,
one must gain the assistance of a large state and neighboring states."
Chariots and Cavalry
Chariots
are the wings of the army,
used to penetrate strong formations, intercept powerful enemies, and block retreating foes.
Cavalry
are the scouts and vanguard of the army,
used to pursue defeated armies, cut off supply routes, and strike invading raiders.
Orthodox and Deceptive Tactics
Emperor Tàizōng (Tàizōng) was about to attack Gāolì (Gāolì),
and asked:
"With few troops and distant land,
by what method should we approach it?"
Lǐ Jìng (Lǐ Jìng) replied:
"Your servant recommends using orthodox tactics (zhèngbīng)."
Emperor Tàizōng (Tàizōng) said:
"We pacified the Tūjué (Tūjué) using deceptive tactics (qíbīng);
why do you now speak of orthodox tactics?"
Lǐ Jìng (Lǐ Jìng) replied:
"Zhūgě Liàng (Zhūgě Liàng) captured Mèng Huò (Mèng Huò) seven times,
and it was purely orthodox tactics.
Since the time of the Yellow Emperor (Huángdì),
orthodox precedes deceptive,
benevolence and righteousness precede expediency and cunning.
In the Battle of Huòyì (Huòyì),
the army's righteous cause
was orthodox.
When Jiànchéng (Jiànchéng) fell from his horse,
and the Right Army retreated slightly,
that was deceptive."
Eight Formations
Emperor Tàizōng (Tàizōng) asked:
"Heaven, Earth, Wind, Cloud, Dragon, Tiger, Bird, Snake –
these eight formations,
what do they mean?"
Lǐ Jìng (Lǐ Jìng) replied:
"Those who transmitted this are mistaken.
The ancients kept this method secret,
inventively giving it eight names.
It is fundamentally one,
but divided into eight.
Heaven and Earth refer to flag signals;
Wind and Cloud refer to banner names;
Dragon, Tiger, Bird, and Snake refer to distinctions between troop formations.
Later generations imaginatively devised these symbols;
why stop at just eight?"
The Well-Field System Method
The Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) first established the well-field system (jǐngtián zhīfǎ),
and thereby regulated military formations.
A well-field (jǐng) is divided into four paths,
with eight families dwelling in it.
Its shape is the character '井' (jǐng),
opening into nine squares.
Five are for arraying troops,
four are for idle land;
the count starts from five.
The center is empty,
where the commander-in-chief resides.
Surrounding its four sides,
all divisions are linked and encircle it.
This is what is meant by "ending in eight."
Cyclic Interplay of Orthodox and Deceptive
Emperor Tàizōng (Tàizōng) said:
"You captured Hán Qínhǔ (Hán Qínhǔ),
who said you could discuss Sūn Wú (Sūn Wú) with him.
Was he referring to the orthodox and deceptive (qízhèng)?"
Lǐ Jìng (Lǐ Jìng) replied:
"Hán Qínhǔ (Hán Qínhǔ) didn't truly understand orthodox and deceptive.
He merely took the deceptive as deceptive,
and the orthodox as orthodox.
He had no idea of the endless cyclic interplay of orthodox and deceptive."
Four Kinds
What Zhāng Liáng learned
was the Liù Tāo and Sān Lüè.
What Hán Xìn learned
was Ráng Jū and Sūn Wǔ.
Generally, it does not go beyond these three categories and four types.
Tài Gōng’s eighty-one chapters of strategies
cannot be exhausted by words.
Gōng’s seventy-one chapters
cannot be exhausted by military means.
The Tàigōng Bīngfǎ’s eighty-five chapters
cannot be exhausted by talent.
These are the three categories.
Generally, in military strategy,
power and stratagem constitute one type,
form and disposition another type,
and Yīn and Yáng techniques constitute two types;
these are the four types.
Fan soldiers are skilled with horses, Han soldiers are skilled with crossbows.
Tài Zōng said:
"Fān soldiers are only known for reining in their horses and charging;
is this an irregular force?
Hàn soldiers excel at strong crossbows and flanking maneuvers;
is this a regular force?"
Jìng replied:
"Fān soldiers are skilled with horses;
horses are advantageous in quick battles.
Hàn soldiers are skilled with crossbows;
crossbows are advantageous in protracted battles."
Generals understanding the real and the void.
Sūn Wǔ Shísān Piān
is entirely about the real and the void.
When employing troops, if one understands the dynamics of the real and the void,
then there will be no defeat.
Presently, generals can only talk about avoiding the strong and attacking the weak,
but when facing the enemy,
they rarely recognize the real and the void.
This is because they cannot manipulate the enemy,
but are instead manipulated by the enemy.
Methods of military governance to be widely announced to generals.
Tài Zōng said:
"What Sūnzǐ said,
how is it for governing troops?"
Jìng replied:
"To await the distant with the near,
to await the weary with the rested,
to await the hungry with the full —
these are merely general outlines.
Extending these three principles,
there are six more:
to await the coming with defense,
to await the agitated with tranquility,
to await the light with the heavy,
to await the lax with strictness,
to await chaos with order,
to await attack with defense."
Tài Zōng said:
"Those who study Sūnzǐ nowadays
only recite empty words.
His methods for governing troops
should be widely announced to all generals."
Old generals dying off.
Tài Zōng said:
"The old generals have died first,
almost entirely withered away.
The newly appointed armies
have not experienced facing the enemy."
Squad formations.
Tài Zōng said:
"Among the various squad formation methods,
which is the most crucial?"
Jìng replied:
"The Zuǒ Shì says:
'First, organize into squads.'
The Sīmǎ says:
'Five men constitute a squad.'
Wèi Liáo Zǐ has 'Orders for Squad Formations.'
The Hàn system had 'Chǐ jí Wǔ fú' (wooden tallies and squad insignia).
Later generations made these tallies and registers from paper.
I have adapted their methods,
changing from five men to twenty-five men,
and from twenty-five men to seventy-five men.
Among all military strategies, the squad formation method is the most crucial.
What Ráng Jū called five men making a squad
and fifteen a company
is still followed today.
This is its essence."
The Six-Flower Formation.
Tài Zōng said:
"Lǐ Jì's discourse on warfare
often aligns with yours.
However, Jì doesn't thoroughly investigate the origins.
From what technique did your 'Six-Flower Formation' originate?"
He replied:
"It is Zhūgě Liàng's 'Eight-Array Formation.'
Large formations enclose small formations,
large camps enclose small camps,
corners interlock,
and turns face each other.
This was the ancient system;
I followed it in my diagrams.
Therefore, the square within
and the circle without
are formed.
The 'Six Tuō' (Six Drags)
is merely a popular name."
Cáo Gōng's Xīn Shū.
Cáo Gōng was arrogant and loved victory.
At that time, his generals presented the Xīn Shū,
but none dared to point out its flaws.
Setting up markers when facing the enemy,
is it not too late?
The meaning of the three covers.
Tài Zōng said:
"Cáo Gōng had battle cavalry and skirmishing cavalry.
Which do these correspond to today?"
Jìng replied:
"The Xīn Shū places six battle cavalry in front,
charging cavalry in the middle,
and skirmishing cavalry in the rear.
Their names are divided into three categories.
Cáo Gōng divided the front, rear, and middle
into three covers,
not merely mentioning two flanks as one instance.
Later generations did not understand the meaning of the three covers.
I am skilled in using this method:
skirmishing cavalry in front,
battle cavalry in the rear,
and charging cavalry dividing as the situation changes;
all are Cáo Gōng's techniques."
Tài Zōng sighed:
"How many people have been misled by Cáo Gōng!"
Not confiscating the homes of false officials.
Tài Zōng said:
"When you pacified Xiāo Ruì,
the generals wanted to confiscate the homes of the false officials
to reward the soldiers.
Only you disagreed.
You argued that Kuǎi Tōng was not executed by Hàn,
and afterwards, the Jiāng and Hàn regions submitted.
'One who can rally the populace through culture,
and awe the enemy through military might,'
this must refer to you."
Sincerity.
Lǐ Jìng said:
"When I campaigned against the Tújué,
commanding both Fān and Hàn troops,
I traveled a thousand li beyond the frontier,
and never killed a single Yáng Gān
or executed a single Zhuāng Jiǎ;
it was also by showing utmost sincerity."
Turning the guest into the host.
Foraging from the enemy
is turning the guest into the host.
Making the full hungry,
and the rested weary
is turning the host into the guest.
Iron caltrops.
Tài Zōng said:
"Were iron caltrops and chevaux de frise
invented by Tài Gōng?"
Jìng replied:
"Yes,
but they are only for resisting the enemy.
The art of war values manipulating the enemy,
not merely resisting them.
Tài Gōng's Liù Tāo speaks only of defensive equipment,
not what is used in offensive warfare."
Dividing and being able to combine.
Fú Jiān commanded a million troops
but was defeated at Féi Shuǐ;
this is an army that combines but cannot divide.
Wú Hàn attacked Gōngsūn Shù,
and he and his deputy general Liú Xiàng divided their camps,
twenty li apart.
When Shù attacked Hàn,
Xiàng came out to join the attack,
and thoroughly defeated him;
this is an army that divides and can combine.
Lǐ Jì is trustworthy to hold office.
Tàizōng said:
“If Lǐ Jì and Zhǎngsūn Wújí
were to jointly manage state affairs,
what would be the outcome in the future?”
Jìng replied:
“Jì
is a loyal and righteous minister;
he can be trusted.
Wújí
is a minister who supported the founding of the dynasty,
a close relative,
yet his outward appearance is not benevolent,
and inwardly he is also jealous of the capable.
Therefore, Yùchí Jìngdé openly criticized his flaws,
and he consequently withdrew.
Hóu Jūnjí resented his forgetfulness of old friends,
and for this reason committed treason;
Wújí caused that to happen.”
The Emperor said:
“Do not reveal this;
I will consider its arrangement slowly.”
Volume 39
End.
The Divine Maidens of Kāngwáng Temple
The Lùcháo Lù says:
“Liú Zǐqīng resided on Lúshān.
There were five-colored twin butterflies that came to play among the flowers,
as large as swallows.
At night, he saw two women,
who said:
“We are moved by your affection for the creatures among the flowers,
and so we have come to visit you.
Does the gentleman perhaps have any intentions?”
Zǐqīng said:
“I wish to extend an intimate relationship.”
One woman said:
“We are moved that you yielded to your elder sister tonight;
the remaining nights can be known.”
The next night,
the elder sister said:
“Tonight’s joy
I leave to you.”
From then on, they came once every ten days for several months.
On Lúshān there was Kāngwáng Temple,
with two mud-sculpted divine maidens,
whose countenances resembled the two women.
Clouds and Rain Come from Wūshān
The Zhēngtú Jì says:
“Xiāo Zǒng met the Luòshén Nǚ,
and later encountered rain.
Recognizing the fragrance,
he said:
“These clouds and rain come from Wūshān.”
The Sea Goddess of Dōnghǎi
The Lùcháo Lù says:
“The scholar Xiāo Yuè arrived in Yánlíng,
and moored his boat in front of Jìzǐ Temple.
There was a woman,
accompanied by three or four maidservants,
who threw an autumn orange at Yuè.
Consequently, wine was ordered in the boat,
and she departed as evening approached.
Yuè entered the temple
and saw the woman depicted in the second painting on the eastern wall.
Looking closely at her,
he smiled,
for it was the woman he had seen.
The inscription next to the painting read “Dōnghǎi Nǚgū.”
Lady Lǐ's Leftover Hēngwú Fragrance
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn, longing for Lady Lǐ,
lay in Yánliáng Hall
and dreamed that Lady Lǐ left him the fragrance of hēngwú.
Upon waking, his clothes and hat bore an unusual scent,
which did not dissipate for three months.
The Emperor then composed a melody named “Yífāng Mèng,”
and also wrote the “Luòyè Āichán Qǔ.”
Boat Made of Shātáng Wood
The Jiāngbiǎo Jì says:
Emperor Chéng built a boat on Tàiyè using shātáng wood,
taking advantage of its unsinkable quality.
He adorned its prow with precious and exotic objects,
naming it “Yúnzhōu.”
Linked-Pillow Trees
The Sānwú Jì says:
Pān Zhāng and his wife died and were buried,
and the trees on their tombs intertwined branches,
known as “Bìngzhěn Shù.”
Horse Skin Transforms into Silkworm
The Sōushén Jì says:
“There was a man who traveled far away,
and his family had only one horse
and one daughter.
The daughter missed her father,
and jokingly said to the horse:
“If you bring my father back,
I will marry you.”
The horse then dragged its bridle to the father’s location
and carried him home.
Whenever the horse saw the daughter, it would be angry with her.
She told her father about her previous words,
and her father was greatly enraged.
He killed the horse
and skinned it.
The daughter saw the skin and kicked it,
saying:
“Dead horse, you wanted a human for a wife!”
The skin suddenly rose,
rolled up the daughter, and carried her away.
Among large trees, she was seen transforming into a silkworm,
spinning silk onto the tree and forming a large cocoon.
Liúhuán
The Jiāngbiǎo Jì says:
Wú Wáng's Lady Pān,
while spitting into a pot,
poured it out
and found a fire-red finger ring.
She hung it on a pomegranate branch,
and a terrace was built and named “Huánliú.”
Someone said:
“Now that we are vying for supremacy with Shǔ,
the name ‘Huánliú’ is inauspicious.
It should be changed to ‘Liúhuán’.”
Rainbow Transforms into a Woman
The Jiāngbiǎo Lù says:
On Shǒuyángshān, there was a twilight rainbow
that descended to drink from the stream,
and transformed into a woman.
Emperor Míng summoned her into the palace.
She said:
“I am a celestial maiden,
temporarily descended to the human world.”
The Emperor wanted to force himself upon her,
but found her appearance difficult.
Suddenly there was a sound like thunder,
and she transformed back into a rainbow and departed.
Báiyú Jiāngláng
The Sānwú Jì says:
“Wáng Sù, a commoner from Yúyáo,
had a daughter
of extraordinary beauty.
A young man, calling himself Jiāngláng,
sought her hand in marriage.
After a year,
the daughter gave birth to something
resembling a silk pouch.
Her mother cut it with a knife,
and it was all fish roe.
So, she waited for Jiāngláng to go to sleep,
and carefully examined the clothes he wore;
they were all in the shape of scales and armor.
She then crushed him with a stone pestle.
At dawn, a fish,
six or seven feet long, was seen under the bed.
Sù took a knife and cut it,
ordering his family to cook and eat it.
Later, his daughter married another man.
Book-Belt Grass
The Sānqí Jì says:
“Beneath Zhèng Kāngchéng’s mountain, grass grew like large chives,
with leaves over a foot long.
The locals named it ‘Kāngchéng Shūdàicǎo’.”
Looking into a Well to Bear a Son
The Bówù Zhì says:
“If a woman is pregnant,
before three months are full,
she should wear her husband's clothes and hat,
and at dawn, walk three times around a well.
Looking at her reflection in the water,
without looking back,
she will surely bear a son.
Once, someone had nine daughters.
His wife walked three times around the well,
and cursed, saying:
“Daughters are Yin,
sons are Yang.
Many daughters bring disaster,
many sons bring auspiciousness.”
The well was locked for three days and no water was drawn.
At the appointed time, she indeed bore a son.
Dù Lánxiāng at the Place of Báidì Jūn
《Zhēngtú Jì》 says:
"Zhāng Shuò of Jìn parted from Dù Lánxiāng.
Later, in Bāxiàn, he saw a green-clad servant who said:
'Lánxiāng is at the residence of the White Emperor.
If you hear the bell of the White Emperor's wild temple carried on the wind,
then Lánxiāng will also arrive with the wind.' "
At night,
indeed, he heard the bell,
and Lánxiāng also arrived.
Dragon Resides
《Jiǔjiāng Jì》 says:
"Lù Shè'ér of Jiāngxià,
returning home at night,
met a woman who asked for lodging,
whose looks were very beautiful.
Shè'ér had no choice
but to return home with her and sleep together.
Suddenly, he heard a violent storm and thunder,
and saw a hairy hand
snatch the woman away.
By morning,
villagers said:
'Seven or eight *lǐ* from here,
there is a *jiāo* (dragon)
over a hundred *zhàng* long,
with blood on the ground,
and thousands of birds
gathered around it, crying out.'
From then on, Shè'ér was frightened and agitated,
often like one deranged.
Tuó Lǐ
During the Later Wèi dynasty, four surnames were designated.
The Lǐ family,
being a great surname,
feared they would not be included.
They rode a clear *tuó* (camel/mule) by night into Luò,
but the matter had already been decided.
People called them 'Tuó Lǐ'.
Lǜzhū Yuàn
Qiáo Zhīzhī had a maid named Bìyù.
Wǔ Chéngsì borrowed her to teach a singing girl,
took her in, and did not return her.
Zhīzhī composed "Lǜzhū Yuàn" and sent it to him,
saying:
"Shí Jiā's Jīngǔ has a new sound,
ten *hú* of bright pearls bought a beauty.
On this day, how pitiful that you allowed yourself,
at this time, song and dance win people's hearts.
Your family's inner chambers have never been at peace,
you delight in using song and dance for others to see.
Your high spirits are unreasonable,
your arrogant power intervenes.
To leave you, to abandon you, I finally cannot bear it,
in vain I cover my face, injuring my lead powder.
A hundred years of parting sorrow in the high tower,
one day my appearance will be wasted for you."
Bìyù, upon receiving the poem,
shed tears and threw herself into a well to die.
Chéngsì found the poem on her skirt sash,
and killed Zhīzhī.
Immortal Presents Fruit
Lǐ Quán,
during the reign of Empress Wǔ, served as an imperial censor,
and his interrogation of prisoners was extremely cruel.
His torture methods all had names,

such as "Immortal Presents Fruit," "Jade Maiden Ascends Ladder," "A Thread Suspends a Colt," "Donkey Pulls Stake," "Phoenix Sunning Wings," "Monkey Locks Fire," "Climbing the Wheat Rope," and "Descending the Single Rail," and so on.
Person in Black Robe and White Collar Delivers Amnesty
During the Zhēngguān era,
Lí Jǐngyì lived on Kōngqīng Shān,
feeding a magpie,
and loved it very much.
Later, Jǐngyì was falsely accused and imprisoned.
A magpie looked down at Jǐngyì from the vent of the prison cell,
joyfully chattering as if to say "There is an amnesty."
The official questioned him about the day,
and he said that he had met a person in a black robe and white collar on the road who said
an amnesty would arrive in three days.
It was the magpie that conveyed it.
Chènshé Guànquè
Wèi Guāngchéng was fond of judging people.
Yáo Yuánzhī was tall and large,
and walked quickly,
so he was called "Chènshé Guànquè" (Stork Chasing Snake).
Wáng Xù was tall, dark, and ugly,
so he was called "Yānxūn Mùchēng" (Smoke-Smoked Wooden Post).
Yáng Zhòngsì was restless and irritable,
so he was called "Rè'áo Shàng Húsūn" (Monkey on a Hot Griddle).
Learning Archery but Not Taught the Arrow-Biting Method
Zǎn Jūnmó was skilled in archery.
He shot with closed eyes,
and hit the target as soon as his eyes perceived it.
There was a Wáng Língzhī
who learned his method,
mastering its every subtlety.
He wanted to shoot Jūnmó and kill him.
Jūnmó at that time had no bow and arrow,
so he held a short knife,
and whenever an arrow came, he struck it and broke it.
The last arrow,
he caught with his mouth,
and then bit off its arrowhead.
He said to Língzhī:
"You've studied archery for three years,
but I just haven't taught you the method of biting off arrowheads yet."
Nothing Moves Without Money
Zhèng Yīn served as an Assistant Minister of the Ministry of Personnel,
in charge of selections.
He was corrupt and acted unlawfully.
On the day of official selection,
a candidate tied more than a hundred coins to his shoelaces,
making noise as he walked.
Yīn asked him about it,
and he replied:
"In today's selections,
nothing moves without money."
Golden Ox Censor
During the reign of Empress Wǔ,
Yán Shēngqī was an imperial censor.
While inspecting Jiāngnán,
he indulged in beef and accepted much gold,
so he was called "Jīnniú Yùshǐ" (Golden Ox Censor).
Crane Cries in Chicken Tree
Dù Jǐngjiǎn, the Fenghé Attendant Minister,
was lofty and profound in both literature and knowledge.
At the time, he was called "Hè Míng Jī Shù" (Crane Cries in Chicken Tree).
Pigeon Gathers in Phoenix Pond
Wáng Jíshàn's talent and conduct were mediocre.
As Nei Shi,
he was called "Jiū Jí Fèng Chí" (Pigeon Gathers in Phoenix Pond).
Frost Hawk in September
Sū Wèidào and Wáng Qìngfāng both served as Fenghé Attendant Ministers.
Someone asked Zhāng Yuán:
"Which of the two is more virtuous?"
He replied:
"Sū is like a frost hawk in September,
Wáng is like a frozen fly in October."
Granted Several Carts of Hemp
Táng Téngwáng Yīng and Jiǎngwáng Yùn
were both fond of corruption.
The Emperor often bestowed precious objects upon the princes,
but these two princes alone received several carts of hemp,
to be made into money ropes.
Eight-Slap General
Téngwáng served as the Prefect of Lóngzhōu,
and committed many unlawful acts.
The Aide, Péi Yù, remonstrated with him.
The King was angry
and ordered his attendants to slap him.
Another day,
Yù entered to report
and fully recounted the matter to the Emperor.
The Emperor asked Yù how many slaps he had received,
and Yù replied:
"Eight slaps in total."
So, he was ordered to be promoted eight ranks.
Yù returned and sighed:
"How thin is my fortune!
If I had said nine slaps,
I would have entered the fifth rank!"
Those who heard him chuckled,
and called him "Bātā Jiāngjūn" (Eight-Slap General).
Mèngqīng
Hóu Sīzhǐ referred to the large cudgel for executing prisoners as "Mèngqīng."
Vajra Dance and Night *Yì* Song
During the Suí dynasty, Zhūgě Áng and Gāo Zàn
competed in extravagance.
Áng outdid Zàn by
stringing together eight-foot-long cakes,
over a *zhàng* wide,
with coarsely ground wheat as thick as pillars.
As wine flowed,
he performed the "Jīngāng Wǔ" (Vajra Dance) to entertain.
Zàn, in turn, outdid Áng
by having wine transported by cart,
meat by horse,
minced fish prepared by mortar,
and crushed garlic by mill.
He sang the "Yè *Yì* Gē" (Night *Yì* Song) to entertain.
He also cooked a small slave boy as a dish,
and after eating,
presented the skull.
Áng then steamed another slave.
The Prefect is Not a Shoe-Guard
Guō Rénkǎi
was vile and cunning. He once served as the Cìshǐ of Mìzhōu.
One of his household servants complained that his shoes were worn out.
Rénkǎi immediately called a government clerk who had new shoes
and ordered him to climb a tree to pick fruit,
allowing the servant to steal his shoes and leave.
When the clerk came down and complained,
Rénkǎi said,
"The Cìshǐ is not a shoe-keeper."
Sè Tǐ
Tú Yànbó, when composing literary works,
often sought novelty through extensive changes.
He rendered "Fènggé" as "ōu yán",
"Lóngmén" as "shī hù",
"Jīngǔ" as "xiǎn xī",
"Yùshān" as "qióng yuè",
"chúgǒu" (straw dog) as "huì quǎn",
"zhúmǎ" (bamboo horse) as "xiǎo cān",
"yuètù" (moon rabbit) as "pò tù",
and "chìniú" (red ox) as "yán dú".
Later generations imitated him,
calling it "Sè Tǐ".
Báilà Míngjīng
Zhāng Yuè, a Míngjīng, was called "Qīngqián Xuéshì"
because he succeeded in every examination he took.
At that time, there was a Míngjīng named Dǒng Wàn,
who failed nine successive examinations,
and was called "Báilà Míngjīng".
He was Zhāng Yuè's counterpart.
Pábō Tuī Wǎn Tuō
During Wǔ Hòu's reign,
official positions were excessive.
A popular ballad went:
"Bǔquē are loaded by the cart,
Shíyí are measured by the peck.
Censors are scraped off with a hoe,
collators are thrown off with a bowl."
Báibǎn Hóu
During Wǔ Hòu's reign,
many people were ennobled as marquises.
There were not enough seals to cast,
to the extent that some were "Báibǎn Hóu" (blank-tablet marquises).
Zhū Hào Wūjīn
In Táng □zhōu,
there was a man who became rich by raising pigs,
and he called his pigs "Wūjīn" (black gold).
Jī Sì
The wealthy commoner Luó Huì became rich by picking up dung,
and people called him "Jī Sì" (chicken market).
It meant he gained something by digging in dung.
Quèwěi Sháo
Chén Sīwáng had a "quèwěi sháo" (magpie-tail ladle),
with a long, straight handle.
When placed in a wine jar,
whenever the king wanted to encourage someone,
he would call out, and its tail would point to that person.
Dòujiǔ Zhuózú
When Mǎ Zhōu first arrived in the capital,
at Bàshàng,
several young masters were drinking at an inn,
disregarding Mǎ Zhōu.
Mǎ Zhōu bought a dòu of wine and washed his feet with it.
Everyone found it strange.
Tónghè Zūn
Hán Wáng Yuánjiā
had a bronze crane-shaped wine vessel.
When wine was poured into its back,
one foot would lean.
When full, it stood upright;
when not full, it tilted.
Xìng Fāng Guìrén Rèn Wèi Qīnqī
During the Táng dynasty, there was a scholar surnamed Fāng
who was fond of boasting about his lineage.
Any prominent person also surnamed Fāng
he would claim as a relative.
Someone once joked to him,
"How is Fēngyì Gōng related to you?"
He replied,
"He's my second cousin (from my paternal side)."
The jester laughed and said,
"Since he's Fāng Xiāng's nephew,
he's only good for scaring ghosts."
Fēngyì Fāng
was where cruel instruments were made and sold.
Lóu Shīdé Hào Wèilíng Gōng
Lóu Shīdé was tall
and had an unusual appearance,
and also suffered from a foot ailment.
Zhāng Yuányī called him "Shīzhé Fāngxiāng"
and also "Wèilíng Gōng,"
meaning he guarded the coffin,
also a Fāngxiāng.
Qílín Xuàn
Táng Yáng Jiǒng often referred to court officials as "Qílín Xuàn" (stuffed qílín).
Someone asked him about it,
and he said,
"Nowadays, those who pretend to be a Qílín
must repair and adorn its form,
cover a donkey with it,
and it truly looks like a strange creature.
But when its skin is removed,
it's still just a donkey.
Those who wear purple and crimson without virtue,
how are they different from this?"
Qiáo Mén Fù Mǐ
Cuī Shí was the Lìbù Shìláng,
in charge of selections.
A candidate seeking appointment saw Cuī Shí
and said,
"I can lift a gate and carry rice."
Cuī Shí asked,
"If you are so strong,
why don't you seek selection in the Bīngbù?"
The candidate replied,
"External opinion says that under Assistant Minister Cuī,
those with strength are selected."
Zhù Āo
Zhù Qīnmíng was stubborn and suspicious,
so people called him "Āo."
Āo
is a lump of flesh,
without the seven orifices,
which a countryman found during Qín Mùgōng's time.
Suōcōng Shìláng
Hóu Sīzhǐ, when eating lóngbǐng,
would always order less scallion
and more meat,
hence he was called "Suōcōng Shìláng" (less-scallion assistant minister).
Lóngbǐng
is mànitóu.
Huì Zhǎng Sānchǐ
Lù Yúqìng was the Luòzhōu Zhǎngshǐ.
He was good at discussing matters but erred in making judgments.
At the time, people mocked him, saying:
"When discussing matters, his beak is three chǐ long;
when judging matters, his hands weigh five jīn."
His son said,
"His brush-tip is weak, but his mouth is hard."
Húzūn Zhìfú
Zhèng Yīn would crouch like a fox before the noble
and hide like a pheasant before the humble gate.
Qí Zhū Zhèng Nán Huán
Wǔ Yìzōng encountered an enemy,
abandoned his weapons, and fled.
Zhāng Yuányī mocked him, saying:
"Long bows pass short arrows,
Shǔ horses leap over steps.
Seven hundred lǐ from the enemy,
he fought alone leaning against a wall.
All armor and weapons were abandoned,
riding a pig, he returned straight south."
The Empress asked,
"Why didn't he ride a horse?"
He replied,
"Riding a pig
is 'jiā shǐ' (夾豕), which sounds like 'jiǎshǐ' (甲士 - armed warrior)."
Shénxiān Tóngzǐ
Táng Yuánjiā was intelligent
and young,
and was called "Shénxiān Tóngzǐ" (Immortal Youth).
Bù Fú Zhìshì
During Wǔ Hòu's reign,
Hóu Zhīyī, the Xiàguān Shìláng,
was ordered to retire
due to old age.
Hóu Zhīyī then went to the imperial court,
jumping and running,
to demonstrate his agility.
At the time, people called Hóu Zhīyī "Bù Fú Zhìshì" (unwilling to retire).
Zhǐ Guī Dé Zhānshì
Zhāng Yuè's daughter married into the Lú family,
and once sought an official position for her maternal uncle.
Zhāng Yuè did not speak,
but only pointed to the tortoise supporting the bed.
His daughter happily returned and told her husband,
"Maternal uncle will get the position of Zhānshì!"
And indeed, he did.
Sān Zhěn
The sister of a commoner in the capital
used a leopard-head pillow to ward off evil spirits,
a Báizé pillow to ward off demons,
and a bear pillow to ensure male offspring.
Wèi Chéng Wū
Wèi Lìng served as the Cchéng of the Western Dì.
He raised a red-beaked crow
which would often beg for money among the crowds and bring it home.
It was called "Wèi Chéng Wū."
Hǔ Shì
There was a divine shaman
who could build an altar and summon tigers.
When a person was suspected of a crime,
they would be ordered to ascend the altar.
Those who were guilty would be injured by the tiger;
those who were innocent would be ignored by it.
This was called "Hǔ Shì."
Yín Tù Fú
In the early Táng dynasty, it was called "Yín Tù Fú,"
with the rabbit as an auspicious omen.
Later, it became "Tóng Yú Fú,"
with the carp as an auspicious omen.
Wǔ Hòu took Xuánwǔ as an auspicious family name,
and thus made copper tortoise tallies (guīfú).
Jiǎzǐ Yǔ
A folk proverb says:
"If it rains on a Jiǎzǐ day in spring,
the land will be barren for a thousand *lǐ*.
If it rains on a Jiǎzǐ day in summer,
one can travel to the market by boat.
If it rains on a Jiǎzǐ day in autumn,
ears will grow on the grain heads.
If it rains on a Jiǎzǐ day in winter,
snow will fly for a thousand *lǐ*."
Ěr Lěng Bù Zhī Yǒu Qīng
Mèng Hóngwēi said to Xuān Zōng:
"Why does Your Majesty not know of me,
and not summon me to service through writings?"
The Emperor angrily replied:
"My ears are cold,
and I do not know of you!"
The next day,
he instructed his輔臣 (fǔchén) saying:
"This minister is impetuous and presumptuous,
desiring to become an inner minister."
So he demoted him.
Xián Shèng Bù Guò Wǔ Rén
Yīn Ān once said:
"Among the sages of a hundred generations,
there are no more than five.
Fúxī, who exhausted the principles of heaven and earth with the Eight Trigrams,
is one."
Then he bent one finger.
"Shénnóng, who planted the five grains to aid the myriad people,
is two."
Then he bent two fingers.
"Zhōu Gōng, who established rites and created music,
which has been practiced for a hundred generations,
is three."
Then he bent three fingers.
"Kǒngzǐ, who knew the past without limit
and the future without end,
excelling among his peers,
is four."
Then he bent four fingers.
"After this,
there is no one worthy of Ān's bent finger."
After a long pause, he said:
"And Ān is five."
His irreverence was thus.
Yī Guān Sǒu Zé
Jiānglíng was called "Yī Guān Sǒu Zé."
People said there were more *pípá* than rice steamers,
and more scholars than crucian carp.
Zhī Dǐng Shí
East of Chénzhōu there are three mountains,
thousands of *zhàng* high.
Ancient sayings tell:
Kuāfù, when contending with the sun,
cooked his food here;
this is the Zhī Dǐng Shí.
Qīng Lóng Wò Qiáo Shàng
The Zhàozhōu Stone Bridge,
when viewed, resembles a new moon emerging from clouds,
or a long rainbow drinking from a gorge.
During the reign of Tiānhòu,
Mòchuò wanted to pass south.
Upon reaching the bridge,
his horse suddenly stopped moving.
He saw a green dragon lying on the bridge,
and so he departed.
Bì Lóng
Chái Shào was strong,
able to leap over a hundred-foot building,
and was called "Bì Lóng."
Fēi Pō
During the Yǒngchāng era,
a western slope south of the Fūshuǐ Inn in Qínzhōu
flew four or five *lǐ* in broad daylight,
directly blocking Chìshuǐ.
The mulberry beds and wheat ridges on the slope
remained undisturbed.
Ōuyáng Tōng Shū
Ōuyáng Tōng valued his calligraphy highly.
He used rhinoceros horn for the brush handle,
covered with badger hair at the core and autumn down,
pine soot for ink,
and musk at the end.
Bǎi Bǎo Xiāng Lú
Ānlè Gōngzhǔ had a "Bǎi Bǎo Xiāng Lú"
three *zhàng* high.
Shēn Dài Mǔ Bìng
Cuī Hún was extremely filial.
When his mother fell ill,
he prayed to the gods,
asking to substitute himself for her illness.
He felt the illness enter through his ten fingers,
and soon it spread throughout his body,
while his mother recovered.
Zàng Yā Lóng Jiǎo
Hǎo Chǔjùn served as a Shìzhōng.
After his burial,
a diviner passed by his tomb
and said:
"The burial presses on a dragon's horn;
its coffin will surely break."
Sān Lì
Zhōngshū Lì Lǐ Qiáo had three perversities:
he liked glory and promotion but resented others' advancement;
he liked literary works but resented others' literary talent;
he liked corruption and greed but resented others' taking and receiving.
Hǎo wénzhāng,
zēng rén wénbǐ;
xìng hǎo tānzhuó,
zēng rén qǔshòu.
Diǎn Guǐ Bù Suàn Bóshì
Lú Zhàolín,
at a young age, was appointed Diǎnqiān of the Dèng Wáng's residence.
The Wang's secretariat was entirely entrusted to him.
The Wang had twelve carts of books.
Lín perused them
and could roughly memorize them.
Yáng Jiǒng, when writing,
liked to use ancient people's names in succession,
such as "Zhāng Píngzǐ's discussions,
Lù Shìhéng's records,"
and "Pān Ānrén is indeed crude,
Zhòngcháng Tǒng is not worth knowing."
This was called "Diǎn Guǐ Bù."
Luò Bīn's prose favored numerical couplets,
such as "The Qín land has a hundred and two important passes,
the Hàn imperial family has thirty-six detached palaces."
At the time, this was called "Suàn Bóshì."
As for Lú Shēng's writings,
no one could evaluate their merits or flaws.
Unfortunately, he suffered from the illness of Rǎn Gēng,
and wrote *Yōu Yōu Zǐ* to vent his frustrations.
Wǔ Hú Zǐ
Lánlíng Wáng of Northern Qí had ingenious ideas.
He created "Wǔ Hú Zǐ."
If the king wished to persuade someone,
the *hú zǐ* would then present a goblet and bow to him.
Xīn Hóngzhì Shī
It is said:
"You are like the grass by the sand,
its heart abundantly grows in spring.
I am like a mirror on a stand,
only clear when it begins to reflect."
Cháng Dìngzōng changed "始" (shǐ) to "轉" (zhuǎn),
and they argued over this poem.
Bóshì Luó Dàozōng ruled:
"'Shǐ' returns to Hóngzhì,
and 'zhuǎn' returns to Dìngzōng."
Zhàn Shè
If magpies gather on branches at night,
or a halo surrounds the moon,
both indicate an amnesty.
If ants gather to form a market,
it will surely rain.
Yǔ Hòu
At midnight,
if black qi pursues each other in the Milky Way,
the common saying is "black pigs crossing the river,"
which is a sign of rain.
Sān Bái
"Three whites in the first month,
the field elder laughs gleefully."
Má Hú Kǒng Xiǎo Ér
Hòu Zhào's Shí Lè's general, Má Qiū,
was cruel and treacherous.
He was a Hú (barbarian) from Tàiyuán.
When children cried,
their mothers would scare them, saying,
"Má Hú is coming!"
The crying would immediately stop.
This is still told as a story today.
Galloping horses delivered news to
Zhāng Yìzhī's brothers,
who competed in extravagance.
Later, they were executed,
and the common people cut their flesh into pieces.
At that time, this was called "galloping horse reports."
New Makeup Poem
Yáng Yíngchuān's niece, named Róng Huá,
composed "New Makeup Poem," which said:
"Sleeping birds startled awake,
windows open with the dawn.
Phoenix hairpins woven with gold thread,
luan mirrors on jade stands.
Adorned, she emerges by the pond,
people suspect she descends from the moon.
Pitying herself, she never truly sees,
wishing to leave, yet lingers still."
Ancient Tomb Inscription
Gāo Liúzhī was the Cìshǐ of Xúzhōu.
The river burst its banks,
water encircled the city,
and an ancient tomb was breached.
An inscription was found, saying:
"Three hundred years after death,
spring water flowed from my back.
Fortunate to meet Gāo Liúzhī,
who moved me to higher ground."
Liúzhī had a coffin and outer coffin made
and reburied him.
Bestowing Wine on a Jealous Wife
The Bīngbù Shàngshū Rèn Huán
was bestowed two palace maids by Tàizōng,
both of national beauty.
His wife, Liǔ Shì, was jealous
and ruined the two maids' hair, causing it to fall out completely.
The emperor ordered a Hú (foreign) bottle of wine to be brought and bestowed, saying,
"Drink this, and you will die instantly.
If you are no longer jealous, you need not drink it;
if you are still jealous, then drink it."
Liǔ Shì bowed and accepted the imperial decree, saying,
"Your concubine and Huán became husband and wife,
both originating from humble backgrounds,
and rose to honored positions.
Now Huán has many favorites within his household,
it is truly better to die."
She drank it all, pulled the covers over herself,
and when she woke up,
nothing at all had happened.
The emperor said to Huán,
"If a person does not fear death,
they cannot be intimidated by death.
Even We cannot restrain her,
what can you do?
As for the two maids,
have them placed in a separate residence."
The Imperial Censor Who Didn't Return Cartage Fees
The Yùshǐ Lǐ Shěn requested his salary rice.
When it was delivered to his residence,
his mother sent someone to measure it,
and three shí were left over.
When she asked the attendant why, he said,
"It is customary for imperial censors not to level the measure."
She then asked how much the cartage fee was,
and he again said,
"It is customary for imperial censors not to return cartage fees."
His mother was angry,
sent the leftover rice and cartage fees back,
and reprimanded Shěn.
All the imperial censors looked ashamed.
The Donkey-Driving Chancellor
Wáng Fāngqìng was promoted to Zuǒ Chéng.
He had no other significant administrative achievements.
However, he forbade the attendants' donkeys from entering the palace gate,
chasing them away all day long.
At the time, he was called "The Donkey-Driving Chancellor."
Dipper City
