The old city of Cháng'ān:
the southern part of the city was shaped like the Southern Dipper,
the northern part of the city was shaped like the Northern Dipper.
Therefore, it was called "Dipper City."
Bronze Sparrow
On the twin towers west of Cháng'ān city,
there was a bronze sparrow.
When it sang, the five grains would ripen.
Stone Father and Stone Mother Shrines
In Kūnmíng Chí, there were two stone figures,
representing the Cowherd and the Weaving Maid, standing in the lake.
To the east and west, there are still Stone Father and Stone Mother Shrines.
Rafters Transform into Dragons and Phoenixes
At Tōngtiān Tái,
the Yuánfèng Mén spontaneously collapsed,
and its rafters and purlins transformed into dragons and phoenixes and flew away.
Ice Tower
North of Jiànzhāng Gōng,
ice was piled up to form a tower.
Nine Markets
Cháng'ān had nine markets.
Golden Thresholds and Jade Steps
Míngguāng Diàn
had curtains and blinds made of gold, jade, pearls, and precious stones,
with golden thresholds and jade steps.
It glowed brightly day and night,
located within Guì Gōng.
Wall Gate
The main gate of Wèiyāng Gōng was called the Wall Gate.
It had thirty-two platforms and halls.
Jade Trees and Verdant Greenery
Gānquán Gōng had huái trees,
whose roots and trunks were intertwined.
At the time, they were called "Jade Trees and Verdant Greenery."
Crane Isle and Duck Islet
In the Rabbit Garden of Héjiān Wáng Rìhuá's palace,
there were Crane Isle and Duck Islet.
Stone Whale
In Kūnmíng Chí, a stone whale was carved,
three zhàng long.
When it rained, its throat would move.
Cosmic Kalpa Fire
When Wǔdì excavated Kūnmíng,
it was all ash.
A Fangshì (alchemist/magician) said,
"This is the remnant of the cosmic kalpa fire."
Fish Repays with Bright Pearls
Someone was fishing in Kūnmíng Chí,
but the line broke, and the fish got away.
Wǔdì dreamt that the fish begged him to remove its hook.
Three days later,
he saw a large fish gasping for air.
He immediately took out the hook and released it.
Later, by the waterside, he found a pair of bright pearls.
These were repaid by the fish.
Huái Market
The Imperial Academy had a hundred rows of huái trees.
Scholars would gather here on the first and fifteenth of each month,
each selling goods from their native prefectures and commanderies.
It was called "Huái Market."
Volume 40
ends.
Huái Flowers Yellow, Scholars Busy
Cháng'ān examinees
who failed the examinations after June would not leave the capital.
This was called "passing the summer."
Many would borrow quiet monastic temples to compose essays,
calling their chapters "summer lessons."
At the time, the saying went:
"Huái flowers yellow,
scholars busy."
Long Name List
It was the custom of the Lìbù
to post a "Long Name List."
An old saying went:
Before the Long Name List,
the selected candidates belonged to the Shìláng.
After the Long Name List,
the Shìláng belonged to the selected candidates.
First Rank Tomb
According to old regulations:
A first-rank official's tomb
was one zhàng and eight chǐ high.
Only when Guō Zǐyí died,
ten chǐ were added to his.
Three Uniques
Lǐ Bái was uniquely talented,
Bái Jūyì was uniquely humane,
Lǐ Hè was uniquely ghostly.
Gave Birth to Sixteen Sons
Chéng Wěi of Huáinán was originally from a wealthy family,
but in three years, everything was burned and lost.
His wife, Máo Shì,
gave birth to sixteen sons consecutively.
Father and sons walked together, begging in the market.
List Flower
Since the Dàzhōng period,
the Ministry of Rites, when announcing exam results,
annually selected two individuals whose surnames were rare or unusual,
calling them "Sèmù Rén" (People of Special Categories)
or "Bǎnghuā" (Exam List Flowers).
The Chancellor wearing scarlet:
Zhāng Jiāzhēn was Chancellor during the Kāiyuán era
and wore scarlet.
Fù Yóuyì,
who held the chancellorship during the reign of Empress Wǔ,
wore green.
Painting of a serene night stroll in the Western Garden:
Gù Chángkāng painted it.
There is a colophon by a prince of the Liáng dynasty saying:
"Among the thousands of people in the painting,
all enjoy imperial emoluments."
During the Zhēngguān era,
Chǔ Hénán remounted it.
Jade-leaf crown:
Princess Yùzhēn had a jade-leaf crown,
the value of which no one could calculate.
Orange trees bearing fruit:
During the Tiānbǎo era,
orange trees planted in the palace bore fruit,
totaling one hundred and fifty oranges.
Master Luófú:
Xuānyuán Jí was known as Master Luófú.
He was several hundred years old,
standing on his bed,
with hair reaching the ground.
Granting the four seas as kings:
In the tenth year of the Tiānbǎo era,
the four seas were first granted as kings.
Casting Zhāng Yuè's ill-gotten wealth:
Lú Huáishèn died suddenly and revived,
saying:
"In the underworld, there are thirty furnaces,
day and night casting ill-gotten wealth for Zhāng Yuè,
but I have none."
Strange people speaking of transfers:
Lǐ Déyù's three transfers to different garrisons
were all spoken of by strange people beforehand.
Only his exile to the southern wilderness
was not foreknown.
Lǐ Xiàng Hù (Lǐ who reads scepters):
Lǐ Cānjūn was skilled at interpreting ceremonial tablets (hù),
foretelling good or ill fortune.
He was called "Lǐ Xiàng Hù."
There was also Lóng Fùběn,
who was blind.
Whenever he encountered an ivory tablet or bamboo hù,
he would touch it with his hand
and unfailingly know one's official rank, salary, and lifespan.
Writing:
Lǐ Hàn said that writing should be like a thousand soldiers and ten thousand horses,
yet without human sound.
His calligraphy surpassed his father's:
Lǐ Héguāng was skilled in calligraphy.
Someone said:
"His brushwork surpasses his father's."
Upon hearing this,
he never wrote again for the rest of his life.
Tiger entering a private temple:
In the eighth year of the Dàlì era, a tiger
entered Yuán Zài's private temple.
Stumbling and falling:
During the Xiāntiān era,
Wáng Xiānkè was a Supervising Censor.
Suddenly, he was appointed to the junior position of Yúanwài of the Bureau of Provisions,
which greatly disappointed him.
Jìng Zhōng said:
"He intended to avoid the Ministry of War,
and focused his hopes on the Ministry of Personnel.
Who knew he would stumble and fall,
ending up east of the provincial wall?"
The Bureau of Provisions was in the northeast corner of the provincial administration.
Edict for the demotion of Grand Commandant Lǐ:
During the Dàzhōng era,
Grand Commandant Lǐ was demoted three times, eventually to Zhūyá.
At that time, both drafters of imperial edicts were tasked with composing the edict;
it was the work of Línghú Táo.
Lǐ Yúzhòng's collection contains this edict, which is especially superior,
but it is unknown which is correct.
There is a popularly circulated edict that says:
"The snake uses two heads,
the fox wags nine tails.
If the nose is crooked, the body is crooked;
if the eyes are slanted, the heart is also slanted."
This is slander from an enemy.
Clash of cold and heat among clerks of the Ministry of Works:
The Bureaus of Gates, Penalties, Military Farms, Forestry and Waterways, and Guests
were all simple and without much work.
There was a wrestling performance
where actors pretended to be a clerk from the Ministry of Personnel and a clerk from the Bureau of Forestry and Waterways meeting each other.
Suddenly, both fell down,
unconscious for a long time,
saying:
"A clash of cold and heat."
Tribute of soil and water:
Of all the tributes from the empire,
only Cháng'ān County offered soil,
and Wànnián County offered water.
Three twists of the fruit stem:
Huáng Cháo ordered Pí Rìxiū to compose a prophecy that said:
"If you want to know the sage's surname,
it is 'Tián Bā Èrshíyī' (Field, Eight, Twenty-one - implying Wáng, a common surname).
If you want to know the sage's given name,
it is 'guǒ tóu sān qū lǜ' (three twists of the fruit stem)."
Cháo's head was ugly,
and his hair did not cover it completely.
He suspected the phrase "three twists" was a mockery,
and thus calamity ensued.
Lady Liú's poem:
Dù Gāo's wife, Lady Liú,
was skilled in poetry.
Gāo failed the imperial examinations repeatedly.
As he was about to return home,
his wife first sent a poem that said:
"My husband truly possesses extraordinary talent;
why is he sent back year after year?
Now I would be ashamed to see your face;
if you come, come late at night."
Upon seeing the poem, Gāo immediately turned back.
Soon after, he passed the examination.
His wife again sent a poem that said:
"From Cháng'ān, there's not much distance;
a vibrant, flourishing auspicious aura floats.
My husband is triumphant and still young;
on what tower will he sleep drunk tonight?"
Monk of Cuìwēi Temple:
Cuī Shènyóu was governor of Xīchuān.
There was an extraordinary old man, Zhāng Sǒu, who said:
"You will have no son at forty;
I will seek one for you.
There is a monk at Cuìwēi Temple on Mount Zhōngnán
who has abstained from food for fifty years.
You should send him clothes and ornaments to play with.
If he loves them and accepts them,
then he will be your heir."
Indeed, he accepted them.
The monk soon died,
and a son was then born.
Zhāng Sǒu again prophesied:
"He will be more noble than you,
but will not die a natural death."
His childhood name was "Nàsēng" (monk's robe),
and also "Zīláng" (dark-robed young man).
Recalling three past lives:
Liú Sānfù could recall events from three past lives,
saying he had once been a horse.
The horse was constantly thirsty,
neighing when it saw an inn,
and if its hoof was injured, the pain went to its heart.
Later, when Sānfù rode a horse over rough terrain,
he would always loosen the reins.
If there were rocks,
he would always remove them.
For whom do they wither, for whom do they bloom?:
Yán Dàn,
courtesy name Zǐzhòng,
was skilled in poetry
and good friends with Dù Mù.
He had a poem that said:
"Where does the spring light gently return?
Again, before the flowers, I raise a cup.
All day I question the flowers, but they do not speak;
for whom do they wither, for whom do they bloom?"
Regretting not being able to compile history:
Yú Zhìníng, as Grandee Secretary,
compiled history,
and regretted not having scholars come.
Jì, as a scholar,
regretted not being able to compile history.
The princess habitually broke seven chopsticks:
During the Dàzhōng era,
Yú Cóng was chosen to marry Princess Yǒngfú.
Suddenly, the selection was put on hold.
The emperor said:
"This daughter of mine, when dining with me,
habitually broke seven chopsticks in front of me.
Her temperament is such
that I fear she cannot be the wife of a scholar-official."
Soon, he was changed to marry Princess Guǎngdé.
Liǔ Gōngquán Fáfèng
In the 11th year of Dàzhōng,
during the New Year's greetings,
Lú Jūn, as Grand Tutor to the Crown Prince, led the hundreds of officials.
He was over eighty years old,
with a clear voice and dignified appearance,
and the entire court praised and admired him.
The following year,
Liǔ Gōngquán, also as Grand Tutor, led the ranks,
also eighty years old.
His energy was weak and weary,
and he mistakenly omitted one character from the emperor's honorific title.
He was fined one season's salary.
Many people were ashamed for him.
Gùzhǔ Gòngbèi
According to Táng regulations:
Húzhōu produced the most tea,
known as "Gùzhǔ Gòngbèi".
Annually, eighteen thousand four hundred and eight catties were produced.
Shì Pánchóng Zhǎojiǎ
Lín Shūmíng was fond of insects,
Quán Chángrú was fond of human nails.
These are also like scabs and sores.
Dàláng Bàxiàng
Wéi Chéngqìng was dismissed from his premiership,
and appointed Minister of Rites.
Sì Lì entered and was appointed Píngzhāngshì of Luántái.
At the time, there was a saying:
"The eldest son (Dàláng) is dismissed from premiership,
the youngest son (Xiǎoláng) is appointed premier."
Niànzhū Hùcáo
The Director of the Household Department in Jīngzhào
received a monthly salary of one hundred and eight (strings of cash),
so it was called "Niànzhū Hùcáo" (Prayer Bead Director of Household Department).
Chú Déyù Rénqíng Pàfǒu
Grand Commandant Lǐ, in the seventh year of Dàhé, returned from Xīchuān and was appointed premier.
The Emperor asked Wáng Yá:
"Today Déyù is appointed.
Are people afraid or not?"
He replied:
"The loyal and good are very happy;
among the common people, there are also those who are afraid."
The Emperor said again:
"They ought to be afraid of him!"
Yá was then the Salt and Iron Commissioner.
Dàwù Sān Rì
When Lǐ Qí was executed,
a great fog did not lift for three days.
Some heard ghosts crying,
and the emperor inwardly suspected injustice.
An edict was issued permitting his burial.
Jiāng Róng Shī Qǐzuò
Jiāng Róng, as Left Historian,
was framed and executed.
His corpse rose and sat down again three times.
Even when his head was cut off,
he seemed to remain furiously unappeased.
Not long after,
Zhōu Xìng was defeated.
Tiānhuāng Què
The Prefect of Xīnzhōu was called "Tiānhuāng Què" (Heavenly Desolate Gap),
probably because many who served there died.
Yùnyīng
During the Tiānbǎo era,
Hanlin Academicians Chén Yǒu and Yuán Tíngjiān compiled ten scrolls of "Yùnyīng".
It had not yet been put into practice
when Xījīng fell.
Púsàmán
In the early Dàzhōng era,
the women of the Mán Kingdom came to pay tribute.
They wore towering topknots, golden crowns,
and necklaces covering their bodies.
Thus, they were called "Púsàmán" (Bodhisattva Barbarians).
Consequently, this tune was composed.
Zuòzhǔ Ménshēng Hàngxiè Yīqì
Dù Shěnquán,
in the 12th year of Dàzhōng, presided over the imperial examination,
and passed Lú Chǔquán.
Someone joked about it, saying:
"The examiner (Zuòzhǔ) is Shěnquán (judges power),
the student (Ménshēng) is Chǔquán (manages power).
One could say power does not lose power."
In the second year of Qiánfú,
Cuī Hàng passed Cuī Xiè.
Commentators said:
"The examiner and the student,
Hàng (clear dew) and Xiè (heavy dew), are of the same ilk."
Lǐwéi Tíshī
In the first year of Dàzhōng,
Wèi Fú presided over the examination in the Ministry of Rites.
He composed a poem that read:
"Wútóng leaves fall, filling the courtyard with shade,
the vermilion gates are locked, the examination hall is deep.
This was once the place of bitter toil in past years,
I will not fail the former vow today."
When the results were posted,
an unknown person shortened it into a five-character poem
to mock him.
Wúgōng Ròu
In the fourth year of Tiānbǎo,
in Guǎngfǔ, a centipede was washed ashore by the tide.
It died,
and one of its claws was cut off,
yielding one hundred and twenty catties of meat.
Huà Hútóu
The Zīshuǐ Post Station
was east of the Cháng'ān Post Station.
Emperor Ruìzōng, when he was a prince,
passed by the north hall.
On the west wall of the hall was painted a barbarian's head.
He thereupon inscribed:
"Why hide your eyes so deeply,
call them out!
Why retract your nose,
fearing not to smell the fragrance?"
Fù Cuīzhuāng Shī
Chén Jiào, courtesy name Jǐngshān,
was solitary and without support.
He failed the examinations numerous times.
In his later years, he finally achieved a famous position in a distant village,
already at the age of sixty.
The virtuous villagers married him to a scholarly family's daughter.
By the time of the wedding,
he was nearly eighty.
On the night of the wedding feast, literati gathered competitively,
all composing "poems to urge the bride's makeup",
which became a witty satire of his old age.
Jiào himself composed one verse:
"Péngzǔ is still said to have lived eight hundred years,
Chen-láng is still a young child."
All the guests roared with laughter.
Jiào once had a "Poem on Leisurely Living" that said:
"The small bridge and moonlight are yearly affairs,
what can be done when Pān Ān grows old?"
Jílímàng
When Wéi Dān served in Hóngzhōu,
he encountered Máo Hè's rebellion.
He manufactured one thousand caltrop-maces.
Quánchén Suǒjū Fāng
It was a recent custom
to refer to powerful officials by the residential ward where they lived:
Ānyì,
Lǐ Jífǔ.
Jìng'ān,
Lǐ Zōngmǐn.
Yìfāng,
Wéi Ào.
Lèhé,
Lǐ Jǐngràng, too.
Hòuxíng Cítún
A saying within the Secretariat was:
The Back Row's Ancestral Temple Granary
is not as good as the Middle Row's Capital Gate.
The Middle Row's Criminal Households
are not as good as the Front Row's Carriage Depot.
Fǎlán Yán Jíxiōng
In the early Kāiyuán era,
there was a monk named Fǎlán from Lùyuàn Temple.
He often spoke with subtle meaning.
Liú Chāngyuán, the magistrate of Shèxiàn, visited him.
Fǎlán said:
"Magistrate, leave your belt and hemp sandals for me to see."
Not long after,
Liú suffered an internal family bereavement.
Chuánzuò
According to the customs of Cháng'ān,
on New Year's Day, people successively invited each other to eat and drink,
calling it "Chuánzuò" (passing the seat).
Hú Jiē Liǎng Tóu Sū Lián Sān Wěi
At the end of the Xiántōng era,
Zhèng Hún was the Supervisor of Sūzhōu,
Tán Zhū was an official in the Salt Bureau,
Zhōng Fú was the Circuit Inspector,
all from the Guǎngwén Academy.
At that time, the Prefects of Húzhōu, Lǐ Chāo and Zhào Méng,
were successively top scholars in the imperial examination.
The two prefectures were adjacent.
At the time, there was a saying:
"Hú (Húzhōu) connects two heads (top scholars),
Sū (Sūzhōu) links three tails (inferior officials)."
Fú Fùzǐ Liúhuáng
Hán Fán 端gōng, after retiring from Xuānzhōu, resided in Zhōngshān.
Due to an overdose of Fùzǐ and Líuhuáng,
blood flowed from all nine orifices and all hundred hairs,
leaving only skin and bones.
No small shroud could contain him;
they simply used a blood-soaked cloth to lift his bones into the coffin.
Páng Jūshì’s passing
Páng Jūshì of Xiāngyáng,
was about to pass away.
The provincial governor, Yú Gōng, visited him to inquire about his illness.
Páng Jūshì said:
“I only wish to empty all that exists,
and be careful not to solidify all that does not exist.
All good things in the world,
are like echoes and shadows.”
After saying this,
he rested his head on Yú Gōng’s lap and died.
Owl’s cry
At the end of the Tiānbǎo era,
Wéi Bīn was banished to Qíchūn.
At that time, Lǐ Bì was also exiled as a recluse.
They had a midnight banquet together,
and repeatedly heard an owl’s cry.
Wéi Bīn wept.
Lǐ Bì said:
“This sound,
people consider an ill omen,
but listen to it,
and there’s nothing to be sad about.
Please drink wine.
Whoever doesn’t hear the owl’s cry,
shall be fined a full cup (with táibái).”
Everyone present strained to hear the sound,
and were not tired of it the whole night.
Fragrant Isle contributes Dùruò
During the Zhēngguān era,
the Imperial Pharmacy requested Dùruò,
and an imperial edict was sent to the Ministry of Revenue.
A department official, recalling Xiè Tiào’s poem which says “Dùruò grows on fragrant isles,”
then assigned Fāngzhōu to contribute it.
The local official of that prefecture ruled:
“Fāngzhōu does not produce Dùruò.
This must be due to a misreading of Xiè Tiào’s poem.
How can a department official make such a ruling
without fearing the twenty-eight constellations judging people?”
Tàizōng heard of this,
and demoted the official to Judicial Supervisor of Yōngzhōu.
Lǐ Kuí enters officialdom
He did not serve as a county magistrate or clerk,
but became a separate prefectural administrator.
He did not serve in the Two Capital regions,
but became the Administrator of Jīngzhào.
He did not serve as a Censor-in-chief,
but became a Grand Master.
He did not serve in the Secretariat or Chancellery.
but became a chancellor.
He did not serve as an Inspector,
but became a Military Commissioner.
However, he did not die a natural death.
Jiǔchénggōng Envoy
In the seventh year of Tiānbǎo,
Yáng Zhāo, then a Grand Master of Remonstrance, was appointed Jiǔchénggōng Envoy.
The title of “Gōngshǐ” (Palace Envoy),
began from this time.
Seeing a toad enter the premiership
When Lǐ Kuí was Minister of Rites,
he saw a toad several feet tall
in front of his hall,
and covered it with a jar.
The next day, when he opened it,
it was gone.
A few days later, he became a chancellor.
Obtaining lines in a dream
Zhèng Hào obtained lines in a dream, saying:
“The mist and dew on the stone gate are white,
the moss on the jade palace is green.”
He then continued it into a long poem.
This couplet,
is from Dù Shī.
A cloth sack of rice, laid down, empties slowly.
Dù Bīn Gōng ate and drank heartily;
as soon as he was full, he would sleep.
Someone admonished him that this was not a principle of health preservation.
He said:
“Have you not seen a cloth sack filled with rice,
when laid down, empties slowly?”
Fond of eating sheep’s heads
At the end of the Kāiyuán era,
there was a man who was fond of eating sheep’s heads.
One morning, as he went out,
there was a monster there:
a sheep’s head on a human body,
magnificently dressed.
It said:
“I am
the god of the wèi [未] hour.
My domain is over sheep.
Because you are fond of eating sheep’s heads,
I seek you out.
If you stop eating them, that’s that.
If you don’t stop,
I will kill you.”
The man was greatly frightened,
and thereafter never ate them again.
Begging your official title
Fáng Guāngtíng,
once attended a funeral and left through Dìngdǐngmén.
It was late and he was hungry.
He happened upon a seller of steamed buns,
and entered with several companions.
He had no money with him,
and the seller pressed him for payment.
Fáng said:
“Begging your official title (or: ‘I beg your forgiveness’ for my lack of money),
I am a Right Censor.
You can collect it whenever you wish.”
His unconstrained and informal manner was admired.
Zǐyánghuā
There are many cassia trees on Línyǐnshān in Hángzhōu.
The temple monks said:
“They were planted from the moon.”
Even today, on Mid-Autumn nights,
their seeds often fall.
The temple monks have also picked them up.
The monks of Zhāoxiánsì planted cassia,
which was fragrant and lovely.
The prefect, Bái Gōng, named it “Zǐyánghuā.”
Crow pulls the bell
Wēn Zhāng was the Administrator of Jīngzhào.
One day, he heard a bell being pulled three times,
it was a crow.
He said:
“Someone must have taken its young,
and it has come to complain.”
He ordered his clerk to follow it,
and indeed found the person who had taken the young.
All Hú in the world now bear the surname Lìng
Lìng Hútáo’s
surname was rare.
When relatives of his clan arrived,
he was not stingy.
Because of this, people from near and far flocked to him.
There was even a nephew named Hú Wèi Lìng.
Wēn Tíngyún jokingly said:
“Since Yuán Lǎo assumed high office,
all Hú in the world now bear the surname Lìng.”
Not building a private ancestral temple
During the Zhēngguān era,
Wáng Guī, having served in office for a considerable time,
did not build a private ancestral temple.
He still offered sacrifices in his bedchamber during the four seasons,
for which he was impeached by the relevant authorities.
Emperor Wénhuáng indulged him,
and specially established an ancestral temple for him in Yǒnglè Fāng.
Wǔyángchéng
Wú Xiū was the Inspector of Guǎngzhōu.
Before he arrived at the prefecture,
five immortals rode five-colored sheep,
carrying five grains.
Today, paintings of five immortals riding five-colored sheep are depicted on the beams of the provincial hall as an auspicious omen.
Therefore, Guǎngnán is called “Wǔyángchéng.”
The Sū family buried together
Wèi Zhīgǔ died at the age of seventy.
His wife, Sū Shì, did not weep.
After the shrouding was complete,
she burst into a single wail of grief,
and they were buried together on the same day.
Reciting the Jīngāng Jīng
Bái Rénzhé was the commandant of Zhūyáng during the Lóngshuò era.
He was dispatched to transport rice to Liáodōng.
Entering the sea, he encountered a storm,
and all around was dark and dim.
Bái Rénzhé urgently recited the *Jīngāng Jīng* three hundred times.
Suddenly, as if in a dream,
he saw a Sanskrit monk,
who said:
“You have recited the true sutra,
therefore I have come to save you.”
Léigōng Mò
To the west of Léizhōu, there is a Léigōng Temple.
The common people annually contribute and offer a雷鼓車 (thunder drum cart).
If anyone eats yellow fish and pork together,
they are immediately struck by lightning.
After every major thunderstorm,
people often pick up dark stones in the wilderness,
called "Léigōng Mò" (Thunder God Ink).
When struck, they ring鏘然 (qiāngrán),
and their luster is like lacquer.
Also, at places struck by lightning, objects shaped like wedges or axes are collected,
called "Pīlì Xiē" (Thunderbolt Wedge).
Worn by children,
they ward off fright and evil.
When ground and taken by pregnant women,
they induce childbirth.
All are effective.
Bàozhí (爆直)
According to historical precedent:
When first entering the office,
one serves as an auxiliary official for twenty-five days.
During festivals and holidays,
one serves for five days.
This is called "Fúbào Zhí" (伏豹直, Crouching Leopard Duty).
In all government departments, prefectures, and counties,
those first appointed as auxiliary officials
all have this designation.
Dù Yìjiǎn explained the meaning of "Fúbào" saying:
Those on duty,
staying away from home to sleep alone,
are valued by human sentiment.
When such a person is first bestowed with honor and appointment,
this is how they are treated.
When all other officials leave,
this person remains alone,
like a crouching leopard;
waiting to pounce.
Thus it is called "Fúbào".
Hán Wǎn interpreted it as "Bàozhí" (爆直, Bursting Duty),
likening it to burning bamboo,
which bursts at the joints.
Fēng Yǎn believed that an old saying mentioned the red leopards of Nánshān,
which cherished their fur and bodies.
Whenever there was snow, frost, rain, or fog,
all other birds and beasts would come out,
but only the leopard would hide deeply.
Therefore, ancient people used this to metaphorically refer to wise men living in seclusion to avoid the world.
Bāo Míngyuǎn's rhapsody says:
"How could it compare to the red leopards of Nánshān,
hiding deeply when rain and fog appear?"
"Bào Zhí" (豹直) likely takes the meaning of "not going out".
For the first official serving as an auxiliary,
there was already the name "Fúbào".
Why must it be compared to the dryness of burning bamboo joints when encountering a festival?
Who Died Sitting and Who Died Standing?
Monk Zhìxián,
in the second year of Qiánníng, suddenly asked his attendant:
"Who
died
sitting?"
He replied:
"Sēngjiā."
"Who died standing?"
He replied:
"Sēnghuì."
Then he walked seven steps,
lowered his hands, and passed away.
The Name of an Official Title
It must be that for selection, appointment, and promotion, one's qualifications must be preserved.
When a memorial is submitted to the emperor,
the former official's rank and name are first stated,
written at the beginning,
followed by the proposed official's name at the end,
so that the old and new titles are continuously linked.
Hence, it is called "Tóu Xián" (頭衘, Head-bit).
Just as a person holds something in their mouth,
it signifies continuity.
Like a horse having a bit to control its head,
the front horse advances,
and the rear horse follows,
in an unbroken sequence.
Ancient people called it "xiánwěi xiāngshǔ" (衘尾相屬, holding tails in connection),
which is precisely this meaning.
Human Flesh Cures Emaciation
During the Kāiyuán era,
Chén Zàngqì, a man from Míngzhōu, compiled the 《Běncǎo Shíyí》 (本草拾遺), stating:
Human flesh cures emaciation.
From then on,
people in the villages emulated each other by cutting their thighs.
Changing the Shàngshū
In the fourth year of Tiānbǎo,
the character "pǒ" (頗) in 《Shàngshū》 was changed to "pó" (陂).
Three Unsatisfactory Things in Life
Lín Bīn Gōng, who held an extremely high position among officials,
once said that there are three unsatisfactory things in life:
The first was becoming the Cìshǐ (刺史) of Lǐzhōu.
The second was being demoted to Sīnóng Qīng (司農卿).
The third was moving the garrison from Xīzhōu to Guǎnglíng,
when the boat was at Qútáng,
he was startled by violent waves.
His attendants could not be summoned,
and being very thirsty, he poured tea for himself to drink.
Building a Temple for a Concubine
Wáng Jìn, when serving as prime minister,
built the Gǎnyìng Temple for his concubine.
Its grandeur and beauty were unparalleled,
drawing ridicule from those who knew.
Zhèng Tán Enters the Premiership
Zhèng Tán served over thirty official posts,
never leaving the capital gate,
before ascending to the prime minister's position.
Inscribing the Xīshī Stone
Wáng Xuān moored his boat at Zhùluó Shān
and inscribed the Xīshī Stone, saying:
"A thousand peaks on the ridge are beautiful,
fine grasses by the river are spring green.
Today I encounter the washing-silk stone,
but see no washing-silk maiden."
Suddenly, a young woman,
shaking her jade ornaments,
leaning on a stone笋 (shǔn, stalagmite-like stone),
said:
"I returned from the Wú Palace to the Yuè Kingdom,
in plain clothes for a thousand years, unrecognized.
At that time, my heart was harder than gold and stone,
but today for you, it cannot be so firm."
Then they had a rendezvous like mandarin ducks,
and she recited verses of sorrowful parting.
Later, a man named Guō Níngsù,
hearing of Wáng Xuān's encounter,
often recited poems by Huànxī,
but met no one.
Zhū Zé mocked him, saying:
"The peach and plum of three springs are originally silent,
but are vexed by the clamor of birds in the setting sun.
May I ask the eastern neighbor who imitates Xīzǐ,
how is Guō Sù to be compared to Wáng Xuān?"
Xuē Yuàn's Poem
Nán Chǔcái,
a guest in Chén Yǐng,
was offered the governor's daughter in marriage.
Chǔcái already had a wife at home,
but was reluctant to refuse the governor's wishes,
so he agreed.
His wife, Xuē Yuàn, sketched her own image in a mirror,
and sent a poem with it, saying:
"Wishing to apply the vermilion brush,
I first gaze into the precious mirror.
Already startled by my faded complexion,
I gradually feel my hair withering.
Tear-filled eyes are easy to portray,
but a sorrowful heart is difficult to depict.
Fearing you might completely forget,
sometimes unfold this painting to see."
Cutting Water into Flowers
Lù Chàng's poem on "Snow" says:
"How ingeniously do heavenly beings
cut water to make flowers fly?"
Shèn Shì's Poem
Yán Guànfū married Shèn Shì,
but after more than ten years, they had no son.
So he found a fault in her and divorced her.
Shèn Shì wrote a poem to bid farewell, saying:
"At that time, our hearts were already entwined,
like scattering rain and flying clouds, in a moment.
Even if a solitary sail departs from here,
I cannot bear to pass by Wàngfū Shān (Husband-Gazing Mountain) again."
Guànfū, reading the poem, was deeply moved,
and thus they became husband and wife as before.
Shèng Xiǎocóng
Lǐ Nà, Shàngshū,
ascended the Yuèchéng Lóu at night,
and heard a song that said:
"Above Yànmén,
wild geese first fly."
Delighted by its intensity,
he summoned the singer.
She said:
"I am Shèng Xiǎocóng, a courtesan removed from the register."
He asked:
"How is it that your singing is so excellent?"
She replied:
"This is sung by the niece of Nán Bùxián, a Liyuán供奉 (Court Musician),
who taught it to me."
At that time, Cuī Yuánfàn, an Yùshǐ (Censor), was proceeding to the capital,
and Nà held a farewell banquet for him at Jìng Hú.
He ordered Xiǎocóng to sing,
and everyone present composed a quatrain.
Nà said:
"The embroidered official departs with much affection,
a beautiful woman from the southern lands lowers her emerald brows.
Once I listened to court music in the Jiàofāng (Imperial Music Bureau),
now for you, I sing Shèng Cóng's song again."
Poems Inscribed in Courtesan Quarters
Cuī Yá and Zhāng Yòu were equally famous.
Whenever they inscribed poems in courtesan quarters,
if they praised a woman,
carriages and horses would follow one after another.
If they disparaged her,
her cups and dishes would be neglected.
Cuī Yá mocked one woman, saying:
"You only have the face of Sū Zǐ,
yet still covet tortoiseshell skin.
Ten months pregnant,
you give birth to a Kūnlún child."
Another poem: "A cloth robe over a padded jacket, a burnt felt blanket,
a paper quilt, a kōnghóu with hemp strings joined.
Moreover, wearing a pair of leather slippers,
she clops and clacks out the door."
He also mocked Lǐ Duānduān, saying:
"At dusk, silent and not knowing how to walk,
her nose like a smoke stack, her ears like a pot.
Alone she uses an ivory comb to pin her hair,
the new moon rises on Kūnlún Mountain."
Duānduān saw the two men by the roadside,
and bowed twice, saying:
"Duānduān humbly greets Sān Láng and Liù Láng,
I earnestly hope for your pity."
So they presented a new poem to her, saying:
"A yellow stallion found, its saddle embroidered,
from Shànhé Fāng we fetch Duānduān.
Yángzhōu has recently become quite unusual,
a walking white peony."
Thereupon, guests flocked to her door.
Someone remarked:
"Lǐ family maiden,
no sooner out of the ink-pool,
than she ascends the snowy peaks,
how is it that in one day, black and white are so unevenly distributed?"
Yōng Nǚ Shaves Her Head to Become a Nun
Cuī Yá's wife, Madame Yōng,
was the daughter of the Yángzhōu 总教 (Chief Instructor).
The Yōng clan, knowing Cuī had poetic fame,
provided a very generous dowry.
He showed absolutely no respect,
merely calling his father-in-law "Yōng Lǎo" and nothing more.
Yōng, brandishing a sword, called his daughter and said to Cuī:
a man from Héshuò,
am only skilled in archery and horsemanship.
My daughter should have married into a military household.
Merely admiring the virtues of scholars,
you are so heartless!
My little daughter cannot be remarried,
she shall immediately become a nun!"
He immediately ordered her to shave her head and become a nun.
Yá wept sadly, repented,
and in anguish, left a farewell poem that said:
"The spring on the ridge divides below the ridge,
heartbroken sobs, unbearable to hear.
Cháng'é once entered the Moon Palace and departed,
Wūxiá's white clouds remain for a thousand autumns in vain."
The 'Throwing and Playing' Game
When Dù Cōng left Lǐyáng,
Lǐ Xuāngǔ,
who often accompanied him on outings and banquets,
showed such deep disrespect that
Cōng could not endure it.
He made him lie in the mud to humiliate him.
Princess Chánglín said:
"To treat a scholar like this,
how can you gain the reputation of Píngyuán?"
She sent someone to help him up and gave him new clothes.
Xuāngǔ composed a poem, saying:
"Red lanterns first rise, the moon disk is high,
illuminating ten thousand peach blossoms before the hall.
The bǐlì's tune is clear in its silver-lettered pipe,
the pípá's sound is bright from its purple sandalwood trough.
The singing beautiful woman's face is like jade,
Xiāo Láng, who enjoys drinking, has eyes like knives.
But how can we endure the late night 'throwing and playing' game,
dancing and caressing, making people tired."
At the time, among those at the banquet, was a woman named Cuī Yúnniáng,
whose appearance was gaunt and thin.
Xuāngǔ presented her with a poem, saying:
"What is most lamentable?
Yúnniáng is simply extraordinary.
Her thin fist throws the game swiftly,
her long beak utters songs slowly.
Only fearing her shoulders encroach on her temples,
only worrying her bones show through her skin.
There is no need for her to stand by the door,
there is Zhōngkuí above her head."
Poem for the Fat Lùshì
When Dù Mù passed through Shǎnqí,
there was a Lùshì (Record-keeper)'s daughter who was fat and large.
Mù presented her with a poem, saying:
"Pángǔ then had a distant descendant,
still allowing his family to show off today.
A cartload of white earth to plaster her neck,
ten red banners to mend her torn trousers.
Footprints met in Wǎguān Sì,
palm prints seen before Huàyuè Shān.
No need to cry and worry about being hard to marry,
I will take a letter to report to Luò Shén for you."
Poem for the Hú Maiden
Lù Yánmèng's poem "Presented to a Hú Maiden at a Guìzhōu Banquet" says:
"Her eyes are deeper than the Xiāng Jiāng's water,
her nostrils higher than Huàyuè Shān."
Sending off Wēn Tíngyún
Jǐ Tángfū's poem "Sending off Wēn Tíngyún" says:
"Why do you often weep jade in this enlightened age,
Cháng'ān sees no spring in Xìngyuán.
Though a phoenix decree has descended and touched your fate,
your high parrot-like talent instead burdens your person.
For now, drink lùlíng to dispel your accumulated resentment,
speak not of a yellow ribbon brushing off worldly dust.
If Fāngchéng is compared to the distant Chángshā,
it is still separated by a thousand mountains and ten thousand ferries."
Let us contend before the wine-cup, keeping our present selves
Niú Sēngrú's poem "Presented to Liú Zhōngchéng of Rǔzhōu" says:
"Discuss not the rise and fall of worldly affairs,
let us contend before the wine-cup, keeping our present selves."
Yǔ Xī harmonized, saying:
"The old cap and sword from that time are there,
waiting for you, Lord, to brush off the dust in three days."
Lord Niú said:
"The matter of three days,
how dare I accept it!"
This referred to the Chancellor taking charge of the seal three days later,
which could lead to promotion in all departments.
Hú Dīngjiǎo
Liè Yùkòu's tomb was in the suburbs of Zhèng.
There was a poor scholar named Hú,
who as a youth engaged in the craft of cleaning mirrors and mending joints,
and was called "Hú Dīngjiǎo."
Whenever he had good wine, tea, or fruit,
he would sacrifice them at Yùkòu's shrine,
seeking intelligence.
Suddenly he dreamt of a person
who cut open his abdomen with a knife
and placed a scroll of books in his heart and guts.
When he awoke,
he was able to compose poetry.
He once presented a poem to Hán Shǎofǔ, saying:
"Suddenly I hear Méi Fú has come to visit,
laughing, I see his lotus-leaf clothes emerge from the thatched hut.
Children unaccustomed to seeing carriages and horses,
rush to hide deep within the reeds."
Guō's Cangtóu
A servant (cāngtóu) of the Guō family in Xiányáng,
named Pěngjiàn,
was often flogged.
One day,
he suddenly inscribed a poem, saying:
"A blue bird carries grapes in its beak,
flying onto the golden well railing.
The beauty fears it might be startled and fly away,
not daring to roll up the curtain to look."
His master then gradually tolerated him.
Not Handsome at Playing the Qín
During the time of Míng Huáng,
Zhāng Yěhú played the bǐlì,
Léi Hǎiqīng played the pípa,
Lǐ Guīnián sang,
and Gōngsūn Dàniáng performed sword dances.
The emperor himself beat drums,
but did not like playing the qín,
saying it was not elegant.
Also,
Níng Wáng played the pípa,
and was extremely skillful.
The emperor went to Mín Shān,
and all the officials were scattered and humiliated.
Only Guīnián fled to Jiāngtán,
fell ill and died,
then revived,
and said:
"I met the two consorts,
who ordered me to teach their two daughters, Lánsháo, to sing.
After the xì purification ritual,
I was released. "
He also said that Cháng'ān would have a restoring sovereign.
Yú Shùn, Pìyáng Hóu
Lǐ Qúnyù, after serving as a collator, returned to Xiāngzhōng,
and while inscribing a poem at the temple of the two consorts,
saw two young women,
who said:
"We are Éhuáng and Nǚyīng.
In two years,
we shall have a 'cloud and rain' tryst with you, sir. "
Soon after, their shadows vanished.
Jiǎ Chéngshì joked about him, saying:
"I didn't realize you were the Pìyáng Hóu of Yú Shùn! "
Qúnyù died two years later.
Jiǎ wrote a poem to mourn him, saying:
"Once spoke of Huánglíng's affairs,
now hurried by the white sun.
Old, with no male descendants to burden,
who will weep for him at the springs below? "
Poem on the Xiāng Spirits Playing the Sè
Qián Qǐ's poem "Xiāng Líng Gǔ Sè" says:
"Skilled at playing the cloud-harmonized sè,
often heard is the spirit of the emperor's daughter.
Féng Yí dances in vain,
the Chǔ guest cannot bear to listen.
Sublime melodies harmonize with metal and stone,
pure sounds issue from the deep abyss.
From Cāngwú comes longing and admiration,
white zhǐ flowers emit their fragrance.
The flowing water carries it along the Xiāng River banks,
a mournful wind passes over Dòngtíng Lake.
The music ends, the person unseen,
on the river, several peaks remain green. "
Failing to Recognize Wèi Gāo as a Noble Person
Zhāng Yánshǎng was choosing a son-in-law,
and Wèi Gāo was lofty in character,
not constrained by minor details.
The Duke insulted him,
and treated him disrespectfully,
so Gāo resigned and left.
Later, from Jīnwú, he held the imperial credentials and went to Xīzhōu,
to replace Yánshǎng.
Gāo changed his name to "Hán Āo".
Thirty lǐ from the city,
someone reported:
"The one replacing the Prime Minister
is Wèi Gāo,
not Hán Āo. "
Madam Miáo said:
"It must be Wèi Láng. "
Yánshǎng said:
"How many people in the world share the same name?
That Wèi Shēng has already filled a ditch and gully,
how could he possibly take my position? "
The next day, when Gāo entered the prefecture,
he then knew there was no mistake.
The Duke said:
"I misjudged people! "
And exited through the west gate.
In earlier days,
servants and maids who were disrespectful,
Gāo killed them all and threw them into the Shǔ Jiāng.
Later, Guō Yuán wrote a poem saying:
"Confucius departed Zhōu ritual for Qín,
which worthy of old was not troubled by worldly dust?
At that time, Zhāng Yánshǎng was greatly surprised,
not recognizing Wèi Gāo as a noble person. "
Poem Inscribed on a Leaf
During the time of Míng Huáng,
a palace woman in the Yètíng wrote on a fallen leaf,
and let it flow with the imperial stream,
saying:
"Former favor, I grieve like an autumn fan;
new grace, I send like spring grass.
Casually I inscribe a leaf,
to send to one who finds it flowing. "
Gù Kuàng harmonized with a poem, saying:
"Sorrowfully I see orioles sing and willow catkins fly,
it is a time of heartbreak for the palace women of Shàngyáng.
The emperor's grace cannot restrain the eastward-flowing water,
to whom can the poem inscribed on the leaf be sent? "
Inscribing Red Leaves
Lú Wò, by the imperial ditch,
saw a red leaf,
on which was a quatrain that read:
"Why is the flowing water so swift?
In the deep palace, I am idle all day long.
Earnestly I thank this red leaf,
may it go well to the human world. "
Later, Xuānzōng dismissed palace women,
and Wò acquired one,
who was the very person who had inscribed the red leaf that year.
Corpse Flesh Wrapped in Cakes
At Xīnghuà, there was an abbot monk,
who one day made large cakes,
gathered his disciples,
went into the charnel ground,
wrapped corpse flesh in the cakes and ate it.
The other monks covered their noses and fled.
The abbot said:
"Only if you can eat this flesh,
can you then eat pork. "
From then on, the Buddhist disciples became diligent.
Leftover Fish for Kuài
Master Bǎozhì ate kuài in front of Liáng Wǔdì.
The Emperor said:
"I haven't known the taste for over twenty years,
why must the Master do so? "
Zhì Gōng then spat out small fish,
all with scales and tails.
Today at Mòlíng there are "kuài remnant fish".
Judgment on Monks Drinking Wine
Lù Chángyuán Lángzhōng,
passed judgment on monks Chángmǎn, Zhīzhēn, and others for drinking at a brothel, cooking, slaughtering, and other offenses, saying:
"Their mouths speak the teachings of the Tathāgata,
but everywhere they are greedy for wealth;
their bodies wear the robes of a Buddhist monk,
but they eat meat all day long.
Their ascetic practice is not like Kāśyapa's,
yet they call themselves dhūta;
what divine powers do they have like Vimalakīrti's,
entering various brothels?
You violate your strict precepts,
and defile my clear laws.
Moreover, gathered are monks from near and far,
who shall be severely flogged thirty times to death. "
Monks Banned from Gambling
Hán Huàng Xiànggōng of Zhè Xī,
banned monks Yúnyàn and others from gambling and quarreling,
saying:
"When has the True Dharma ever held gambling tools?
The empty gate does not accumulate surplus wealth.
If by day you can gamble,
then through the night you must be drunk with wine.
They strongly claim heaven is hard to reach,
and also say hell is always open.
Let them all be handed over to the river god for custody,
the waves shall be their springs below. "
Wáng Fànzhì's Poem
Wáng Fànzhì 王梵志 was born in the Western Regions upon a tree,
hence his name Fànzhì 梵志.
There is a poem that says:
“Do not envy those who get money through deceit,
for what they gain, they soon lose.
Coming and going, the recompense is clear,
it's just a change of head, but the face remains unrecognized.”
He also said:
“Before the Lord of Heaven gave birth to me,
I was in the dark, knowing nothing.
Then the Lord of Heaven suddenly gave birth to me,
but what for did he give birth to me?
No clothes to keep me warm,
no food to stave off my hunger.
Give me back, Lord of Heaven,
give me back the time before I was born.”
He also said:
“My flesh is the flesh of sentient beings,
the forms differ, but the nature is not different.
Originally, we share the same life,
it's just a different body.
It suffers pain and dies,
and then is taken for one's own needs.
Do not let Yánlǎo 閻老 judge,
think for yourself what your intention is.”
He also said:
“Acquiring many estates and building grand residences,
buying up all the neighbors' land, still feeling cramped.
Carved beams and towering structures, without rest;
for how many days can one be a guest among guests?
Still busy acquiring estates,
while the sound of weeping fills the hall, for the body is already dead.
All those who weep are the ones dividing the money,
their mouths weep, but their hearts are secretly joyful.”
He also said:
“A coarse monk,
whose heart is not yet sincere.
At a poor feast, he acts slow,
at a rich feast, he acts fast.
He covets others' oil-fried pastries,
and loves your sweet treats.
He eats his fill without shame,
suffering punishment without end.”
He also said:
“I do not wish for great wealth,
nor do I wish for great poverty.
Yesterday's matters are settled today,
today's matters are settled by tomorrow morning.
This is the great vow,
this is the great cause.
If one's wishes are only like this,
one truly becomes a supreme person.”
He also said:
“Originally a bag of feces and urine,
forcibly painted with rouge and powder.
Ordinary people know nothing,
and call it a cluster of flowers.
Leading each other into hell,
this is the greatest enemy.”
He also said:
“Sentient beings wish for nothing,
constantly dwelling in the cave of ignorance.
Their hearts are full of deceit,
their mouths feign chanting Buddha's name.
There are no centenarians in the world,
yet they plan for a thousand years.
Making iron door sills,
ghosts see it and clap their hands, laughing.
If there are Fànzhì's 梵志 poems at home,
one avoids entering hell in life and death.
Never mind useful things,
just let the ear be familiar.
Paint a screen on white paper,
and when guests come, read it to them.
Eating plain rice with a pinch of salt,
is also better than offering wine and meat.
I advise you not to kill living things,
lest you incur wrath behind your back.
You eat them, they eat you,
a continuous cycle of being the master.”
He also said:
“To see your face, no mirror is needed,
to give alms, no wealth is required.
Sitting upright, contemplating true reality,
this is the Tathāgata.
Large bark covers large trees,
small bark covers small trees.
One doesn't need many children,
one is enough to manage affairs.
Saving the trouble of dividing fields and residences,
no one will oppress you.
Just act with an impartial heart,
Heaven will also remember the solitary.
Before death, one is already worried.
If there are five sons at home,
where will they mourn me?
If they mourn me, I will not hear,
if they don't mourn me, I will still depart.
When impermanence suddenly arrives,
who knows where the body will be?”
Ode to Crabs
Pí Rìxiū's 皮日休 poem "Ode to Crabs, presented to the Commissioner of Xīzhè 西浙" says:
“Before journeying the azure sea, its fame was known,
it has bones that grow from its flesh.
Do not say it has no heart to fear thunder and lightning,
it still moves sideways in the court of the Dragon King of the Sea.”
Also, "On Gold Money Flower" says:
“Yīn and Yáng 陰陽 have no charcoal, the earth has no furnace,
yet gold coins are cast without a mold.
Don't boast of your beauty before people,
without knowing if you can help the poor or not.”
A Maiden's Thoughts
Zhū Qìngyú 朱慶餘 wrote the poem "A Maiden's Thoughts" which says:
“In the bridal chamber last night, the red candles burned till late,
waiting for dawn to bow before my parents-in-law in the hall.
After finishing my makeup, I softly asked my husband,
‘Are my eyebrows drawn too deep or too shallow for the fashion?’”
Zhāng Jiè 張籍 replied:
“The Yuè 越 maiden, newly made up, emerges from the heart of the mirror,
knowing her own brilliance, yet still ponders.
Qí wán 齊紈 silk is not valued enough by the world,
one tune of a water caltrop song is worth ten thousand gold.”
Dreaming of a Man in Black Robes
Lǐ Quán 李筌 annotated the Yīnfú Jīng 陰符經,
reaching "The control of the five qi by birds and beasts,"
he could not understand it for a year.
He dreamed of a man in black robes who taught him,
and he then understood its meaning.
Jade Flute and Ring
Wéi Gāo 韋皋 traveled to Jiāngxià 江夏,
and had a romance with Jiāng Jīngshì's 姜荊室 maid, Yùxiāo 玉簫.
Upon parting,
he promised to meet her again in seven years,
leaving a jade ring as a token.
Over eight years passed,
but he did not arrive.
Yùxiāo 玉簫 starved herself to death.
Later, Wéi Gāo 韋皋 became the military governor of Shǔ 蜀,
and a fortune-teller from Xiāngshān 相山 who had the art of summoning the dead
made her appear.
Yùxiāo 玉簫 said:
“In three more years, I will serve you again as a concubine.”
Later,
Hū Bāzuò 虛八坐 of Dōngchuān 東川 sent a singing girl,
who was truly Yùxiāo 玉簫.
And on her middle finger, a piece of jade protruded,
exactly like the jade ring.

End.
Gifts to Attendants
On the third day of the third month,
attendants were bestowed with delicate willow rings,
which when worn, prevented scorpion stings.
During Hánshí 寒食 Festival,
attendants were bestowed with embroidered silk balls,
and embroidered grass on the Xuan Platform.
On the start of spring,
flowering silk trees were bestowed.
On Làyì 臘日,
scholars of the Northern Gate were bestowed with lip rouge and lard,
contained in green silk-tasseled ivory tubes.
Snail Tracks Form the Character "Son of Heaven"
When Ruìzōng 睿宗 was Prince Jì 冀,
snail tracks on a wall formed the character "Tiānzǐ 天子" (Son of Heaven).
After he ascended the throne,
he carved jade and cast gold into snail shapes,
and placed them before Buddhist and Taoist statues.
Nǚwā's Tomb
Sùzōng 肅宗 arrived at Língwǔ 靈武.
At dusk,
a woman carrying a carp,
with scales on her arms,
approached the army gate,
and asked:
“Where is the Emperor?”
The guards shouted at her,
and she instantly disappeared.
Later, Guózhōu 虢州 reported:
At Nǚwā's 女媧 tomb, the sound of wind and rain was heard at night,
and in the morning, two willow trees were seen sprouting from her tomb.
People suspected that the woman who appeared
was her spirit.
Fetal Hair Brushes
In the Southern Dynasties, there was an old woman
who was skilled at making brushes,
using fetal hair for the brush tips.
During the Kāiyuán 開元 era, a brush craftsman named "Tiětóu 鐵頭"
could make brush handles as hard as iron.
Right Foot Sūtra Copying
During the Dàlì reign,
there was a beggar at Tiānyáng Qiáo in Dōngdū.
He had no hands.
He used his right foot to hold a brush and copy sūtras,
begging for money.
Evil-Repelling Powder and Evil-Dispelling Pills
Every New Year's Day, Liáng Wǔdì would bestow upon his officials three things: "New Year's Day Wine," "Evil-Repelling Powder," and "Evil-Dispelling Pills."
Wedding Rites
In recent times for wedding rites:
When fetching the bride,
millet is used to fill a mortar,
a mat is used to cover a well,
and hemp is used to block windows.
When the bride gets into the carriage,
the groom rides his horse around it in a circle.
When the bride enters the gate,
she first bows to the stove.
The day after the ceremony,
millet is offered.
These customs have been passed down through generations,
but their meaning is not fully understood.
Only the nine items for the betrothal gifts
have discernible meanings:
Glue and lacquer
are for their firmness.
Cotton floss
is for its softness and pliability.
Reeds and rushes
are for their ability to bend and straighten.
Auspicious grain
is for sharing blessings.
Paired stones
symbolize mutual steadfastness.
Titles from Qín and Hàn Dynasties Onwards
From the Qín and Hàn Dynasties onwards:
For the emperor,
one would say "Bìxià."
For the crown prince,
one would say "Diànxià."
For generals,
one would say "Huīxià."
For envoys,
one would say "Jiéxià" or "Gǔxià."
For officials with a salary of two thousand bushels,
one would say "Géxià."
For parents,
one would say "Xīxià."
For peers or general address,
one would say "Zúxià."
Wú Gāng Chopping the Tree
The cassia tree on the moon is five hundred zhàng tall.
Beneath it, there is a man who constantly chops it,
but the tree's wounds heal immediately.
The man's surname is Wú and his given name is Gāng.
He committed a fault while studying immortality,
and was thus ordered to chop the tree.
Shadow in the Moon
Buddhist scriptures state:
To the south of Mount Xūmí there is a Yánfú tree.
When the moon passes over,
the tree's shadow enters the moon.
Some say the toad and cassia in the moon
are the shadow of the earth;
the empty spaces
are the shadow of water.
This statement is somewhat closer to the truth.
Grand Astrologer Reports the Disappearance of the Big Dipper
Monk Yīxíng was skilled in calculations.
His good friend, Old Woman Wáng,
had a son imprisoned for murder,
and sought Yīxíng's help.
Yīxíng said:
"I have divined it through calculation;
there will be an amnesty."
The next day,
he sent his disciple,
giving him a cloth bag,
and instructed him:
"Wait in a certain abandoned garden.
When something comes,
seven in number,
capture them all.
Bring them here in the bag;
do not let them escape."
The disciple went as instructed,
and indeed seven pigs entered the garden,
and he caught them all.
Yīxíng placed them in a large urn,
covered it secretly,
sealed it with "Six-One mud,"
and wrote Sanskrit characters in cinnabar.
The next morning,
Míng Huáng urgently summoned him and asked:
"The Grand Astrologer reported that
the Big Dipper was not seen last night.
What omen is this?"
Yīxíng reported:
"This is unprecedented in ancient times.
Only in the Later Wèi period was Huò Xīng (Mars) lost,
which is comparable.
Only by showing benevolence can this be responded to.
Buddhists say:
'An angry mind destroys all good,
a compassionate mind subdues all demons.'
It would be best to grant a great amnesty to the world."
The emperor agreed.
That evening,
the Grand Astrologer reported:
"One star of the Big Dipper has appeared."
After a total of seven days, it was restored.
Golden-Backed Toad
During the Chángqìng reign,
someone on the Mid-Autumn night saw moonlight shining in the woods,
like a bolt of cloth.
Upon looking,
it was a golden-backed toad,
the one from the moon.
The Moon is Made of Seven Treasures
During the Dàhé reign,
two men were traveling Mount Sōng,
and got lost.
They heard snoring in a thicket
and saw a commoner,
resting his head on a bundle.
The two men asked him.
He replied:
"Do you know that the moon is made of seven treasures?
The moon is spherical,
and its shadow
is the sun shining on its convex parts.
There are always eighty-two thousand households repairing it,
and I am one of them."
He then opened his cloth bundle,
which contained several axes and chisels,
and two packets of jade-dust rice.
He shared it with the two men,
saying:
"Although this is not enough for immortality,
it can ensure a lifetime without illness."
Having spoken, he vanished.
Lord of the Yánbīn Palace
Buddha was the Lord of the Yánbīn Palace for the Thirty-three Heavens Immortals.
Kǒngzǐ was the Immortal of the Yuán Palace.
Zhuāng Zhōu was the Wéibiān Láng, True Immortal of the Tàijí.
Guarding Gēngshēn
The hún (ethereal soul) takes essence as its root,
the pò (corporeal soul) takes the eyes as its gate.
On the Gēngshēn day, the Fúshī reports people's transgressions.
On one's Běnmìng day, the Tiāncáo records people's conduct.
The Sānshī (Three Corpses) make three reports a day.
The Upper Shī, Qīng Gū, damages people's eyes.
The Middle Shī, Bái Gū, damages people's five viscera.
The Lower Shī, Xuè Gū, damages people's stomach and life-force.
It is also said:
"One resides in a person's head,
making them prone to excessive thought and desire,
and fond of chariots and horses.
One resides in a person's abdomen,
making them fond of food and drink, and prone to anger.
One resides in a person's feet,
making them fond of sensuality and killing.
If one guards Gēngshēn seven times,
the Sānshī are eliminated.
If one guards Gēngshēn three times,
the Sānshī are subdued."
Lǎo Jūn
His mother was called Xuánmiào Yùnǚ.
Heaven sent down a dark yellow qi,
which entered her mouth and caused pregnancy,
the spirit condensing in the Qióngtāi Palace.
After three thousand seven hundred years,
he was born on the slopes of Yùshān.
It is also said:
Lǎo Jūn was in the womb for eighty-one years,
and was born by cleaving his left armpit,
with white hair at birth.
It is also said:
The essence of the sun entered her mouth and caused pregnancy,
and after seventy-two years, he was born under a plum tree west of the Nine Wells, south of the Guō River in the state of Chén,
nine chǐ tall.
Some say twenty-nine chǐ.
Dragon Palace Immortal Prescriptions
Sūn Sīmiǎo (孫思邈) lived as a recluse on Mt. Zhōngnán (終南山),
and was acquainted with Xuān Lǜshī (宣律師).
At that time, there was a great drought.
A Buddhist monk from the Western Regions requested to set up an altar at Kūnmíng Chí (昆明池) to pray for rain.
After seven days,
the water level had shrunk by several feet.
One night, an old man came to Xuān Lǜshī (宣律師) to beg for help,
saying:
"Your disciple is the dragon of Kūnmíng Chí (昆明池).
The Hu (胡) monk covets my brain,
deceiving the Son of Heaven by claiming to pray for rain;
my life hangs in the balance."
Xuān Lǜshī (宣律師) said:
"This humble monk merely upholds the monastic precepts;
you should seek Mr. Sūn (孫)."
The old man went to Sīmiǎo's (思邈) chamber,
and Sūn (孫) said:
"In the dragon palace of Kūnmíng Chí (昆明池) there are thirty immortal prescriptions.
If you transmit them to me,
I will save you."
The old man said:
"The Heavenly Emperor does not permit these prescriptions to be transmitted carelessly.
But now it is an urgent matter,
so I certainly will not be stingy."
Soon, he brought the prescriptions.
Sūn (孫) said:
"You may return now;
have no fear of the Hu (胡) monk."
From then on, the pond water overflowed.
The Hu (胡) monk died of shame and resentment.
Sūn (孫) authored the thirty-volume *Qiānjīn Fāng* (千金方),
with one prescription per volume,
which people could not comprehend.
When Míng Huáng (明皇) journeyed to Shǔ (蜀),
he dreamt that Sīmiǎo (思邈) begged for realgar.
So he commanded an imperial envoy to bring ten *ge* (個) and send them to the summit of Éméi (峨嵋).
The imperial envoy ascended the mountain
and saw an old man wearing a simple cloth headscarf and a coarse robe,
attended by two youths in green clothes,
who said:
"There is a memorial to be presented to the Emperor."
The imperial envoy looked at the stone
and saw more than a hundred characters written in red.
He then transcribed them,
and as he wrote, they disappeared.
In an instant,
a white mist rose up,
and he vanished suddenly.
Applying the blood of a three-generation human to a crane's sore
Péi Hàng (裴沆) was traveling to Zhèngzhōu (鄭州) with a hundred generals.
By the roadside, someone was moaning,
which turned out to be a sick crane
whose wing joint was ulcerated and featherless.
Suddenly, an old man said:
"Is the young master pitying this crane?
If it can be smeared with human blood,
it will fly immediately.
However, the person must be of three generations of humans
for their blood to be effective.
Only Hú Lúshēng (胡盧生) from Luòyáng (洛陽) is of three generations of humans."
Péi (裴) then visited Hú Lúshēng (胡盧生).
Hú (胡) extended his arm for a needle prick
and returned to where the crane was.
The old man ordered him to apply all the blood.
Then he invited Péi (裴) to a manor.
Péi (裴) was very thirsty and
asked for tea.
The old man pointed to a niche in the earth,
where there was an apricot pit as large as a bamboo hat,
full of liquid.
Péi (裴) used all his strength to lift and drink it.
It tasted like apricot juice.
He also said:
"You who drink apricot juice
will weep for nine generations of relatives;
moreover, you should abstain from wine and women."
Péi (裴) lived to be ninety-seven.
The *Shàngqīng Wùshēn Lù* (上清戊申錄)
Zhào Guāng (趙光), a *míngjīng* (明經) scholar,
in the Zhēnyuán (貞元) period,
dreamt that a person in red clothes with a flat headdress led him to the underworld.
He saw his brother-in-law Jiǎ Yì (賈奕) and himself arguing about a牛(cow) killing incident,
debating with each other.
Jiǎ Yì (賈奕) remained stubborn.
Suddenly, a giant mirror, ten feet in diameter,
hung suspended in mid-air,
clearly showing Jiǎ Yì (賈奕) wielding a knife.
Zhào (趙) showed a look of unbearable pity,
and Jiǎ Yì (賈奕) finally admitted his guilt.
The person in red clothes led him out and said:
"Can you visit Shàngqīng (上清)?"
They ascended a mountain together.
In the southern courtyard, there was a man in a crimson cap
sitting in the main hall with the man in red clothes.
He ordered Zhào Guāng (趙光) to review the *Wùshēn Lù* (戊申錄),
which was like human official documents.
At the beginning, the birth year of the person wearing the cap
was linked to their name and age,
with their birth month and day noted below.
A separate line laid out the sixty-day cycle of the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子).
All merits and demerits
were recorded under the respective days.
If there were none,
the character '無' (*wú*) was written.
The man in red clothes said:
Every sixty years,
people in the world are reviewed,
their good and bad deeds examined and corrected,
and their lifespans adjusted accordingly.
A skull one inch and eight *fen* thick
Wáng Jiǎo (王皎) was skilled in divination.
In the Tiānbǎo (天寶) period,
he pointed to the stars at night and said:
"Soon, the world will be in chaos!"
At that time, the Emperor was old
and quite superstitious.
His words were reported by someone,
and the Emperor ordered him killed.
The executioner broke open his skull,
and his skull bone was one inch and eight *fen* thick.
When the Ān-Shǐ (安史) Rebellion was pacified,
Wáng Jiǎo (王皎) suddenly appeared with a staff and sandals to see Attendant Minister Dáxī (達奚 Shìláng),
only then realizing he was an extraordinary person.
Eight people make the character for fire
The Celestial Master Zhái Gānkū (翟乾枯) often foretold events.
One day, he shouted loudly in Kuízhōu Shì (夔州市):
"Tonight, eight people will pass by;
you should treat them well."
That evening,
an accidental fire burned down several hundred homes.
Only then did people realize that "eight people" (八人) forms the character for "fire" (火).
Jade pavilions and golden palaces
Celestial Master Zhái (翟) once gazed at the moon over the river.
Someone asked:
"What is truly within this?"
Zhái (翟) smiled and said:
"You can observe it by following my指(finger)."
Suddenly, the moon appeared to cover half the sky,
filled with jade pavilions and golden palaces.
In an instant, it was no longer seen.
Paper moon
In the early Chángqìng (長慶) period,
Yáng Yǐnzhī (楊隱之) visited Layman Táng (唐),
and was invited to stay overnight.
Táng (唐) called his daughter and said:
"Please bring the waning moon."
His daughter took a piece of paper, made it into the shape of a moon,
pasted it on the wall,
and said:
"Tonight we have a guest;
we wish for some light."
Soon,
the entire room became bright.
Wooden drill penetrates bedrock
Mr. Fù (傅) was cultivating himself in the mountains.
He encountered an extraordinary person who gave him a wooden drill
and instructed him to drill through a stone,
which was about five *cun* thick.
He said:
"When this stone is penetrated,
you will attain the Dao."
After forty-nine years,
the stone was penetrated.
He found divine elixirs beneath,
took them,
and indeed ascended to immortality.
Late mirror, cold crows gather
Wéi Biǎowēi's (韋表微) elder cousin, Shàowēi (少微),
was fond of tattooing.
His youngest uncle told him to undress and examine him.
On his chest, a tree was tattooed,
with dozens of crows gathered at its tip.
Below it hung a mirror,
with a rope tied to its knob,
and a person stood beside it, pulling the rope.
His uncle asked the reason.
Shàowēi (少微) said:
"Uncle, have you never read Zhāng Yàn Gōng's (張燕公) poem: 'Late mirror, cold crows gather'?"
Secretary Bái's (白舍人) Illustrated Poems
Gě Qīng (葛清), a street vendor from Jīngzhōu (荊州),
had Bái Jūyì's (白居易) poems tattooed all over his body, from the neck down.
"It is not that this person particularly loves chrysanthemums"
was depicted by
a person holding a cup beside a chrysanthemum bush.
And "yellow tie-dyed forest, cold with leaves"
was depicted by a tree with tie-dyed cloth hanging on it.
In total, more than thirty places were engraved,
and people called him "Secretary Bái's (白舍人) Illustrated Poems."
Húntún
is now a famous dish among gentry families.
There is "Xiāo Jiā Húntún"
from which the fatty broth has been skimmed,
which can be used for steeping tea.
Yīngtáo Bìluó
Hán Yuē was skilled at making cherry pastries (yīngtáo bìluó),
whose color would not change.
Tiānlán
Sweet pomegranates
are called "Tiānlán."
Wǔyuè Shàngwū
It is a popular taboo to go up to the roof in the fifth month,
as it is said that people shed their souls in the fifth month.
If one goes up to the roof and sees a shadow,
the soul will depart.
Rǔjīn
Gold that has been in burial mounds or used for bracelets and chamber pots
is called "Rǔjīn" by Táo Yǐnjū.
It should not be smelted together.
Yǐnjiǔ Miànqīngchì
For drinkers,
if their liver *qì* is weak, their face will be sallow (qīng);
if their heart *qì* is weak, their face will be red.
Yǒngnù
A brave pulse
and anger make the face sallow (qīng).
Brave bones
and anger make the face pale.
Brave blood
and anger make the face red.
Shānzé Děng Qì
Mountain *qì* produces many males;
marsh *qì* produces many females.
Water *qì* produces many mutes;
wind *qì* produces many deaf people.
Wood *qì* produces many hunchbacks;
stone *qì* produces great strength.
Hazardous *qì* produces many goiters;
summer heat *qì* produces many disabilities.
Cloud *qì* produces longevity;
valley *qì* produces many paralysis.
Hill *qì* produces many emaciated people;
plain *qì* produces much benevolence;
hillock *qì* produces much greed.
The god of the brain is called Juéyuán;
the god of the hair is called Xuánhuá;
the god of the eyes is called Xūjiān;
the god of the nose is called Chōnglóngyù;
the god of the tongue is called Shǐliáng.
Míng Tiāngǔ
Those who study the Dao must "strike the celestial drum"
to summon all the gods.
Striking the left side is the celestial bell;
striking the right side is the celestial chime.
Striking the center up and down
is striking the celestial drum.
Běixiàng Lǐfà
Ordinary people should not cut their hair, undress, spit, or relieve themselves facing north.
Jīn Huī Fù Gān
A filial son applies collar ash
to a scab.
Rénfà Guà Guǒshù
If human hair is hung on a fruit tree,
birds will not dare to eat its fruit.
A fruit with two tips (claws) on its nose or two navels (peduncles),
if eaten, will kill a person.
Xiǎo'ér Yètí
Grass from the edge of a well
is effective for children who cry at night.
Place it under the mother's mat,
without letting her know.
Xiàng Rén Yǐng
During the Bǎolì reign,
there was a Mr. Wáng Shānrén who, on a person's birth day,
would light lamps at the fifth watch to observe their shadow
and predict their fortune.
He said that a person's shadow should be deep;
a deep shadow signifies nobility and longevity.
The shadow should not be cast on water, wells, or bathtubs.
Ancient people avoided casting shadows for this reason.
Recently, there have been those skilled at cauterizing human shadows to cure diseases.
Tiānzàng Dìzàng
In Buddhist paintings, there are "Tiānzàng Púsà" and "Dìzàng Púsà."
When viewed closely and carefully,
the painted gold and wood seem to emit light.
Xījīng Zájì
Yú Xìn, when writing poetry,
used a story from the *Xījīng Zájì*,
then promptly revised it,
saying:
"This is Wú Jūn's wording;
I'm afraid it's not suitable for use."
Tú Mǎ Bì Huǒ
Xú Jìngyè, at over ten years old,
was skilled in horsemanship and archery.
Yīnggōng often sighed, saying:
"This child has an ill-omened appearance;
he will ruin my clan."
The Duke often hunted,
ordering Jìngyè to enter the forest to drive out beasts.
Then, taking advantage of the wind, he started a fire,
intending to kill him.
Jìngyè, seeing the fire approaching,
slaughtered the belly of the horse he was riding
and curled up inside.
When the fire had passed,
he stood up, bathed in blood.
Yīnggōng was greatly astonished by this.
Níngwáng Dú Yuèpǔ
Xuánzōng once secretly observed his imperial brothers.
Níngwáng, in mid-summer, would wipe away sweat while beating a drum,
and the book he was reading was the *Qiūcí Yuèpǔ*.
The emperor was pleased,
saying:
"Imperial brothers should enjoy themselves to the fullest."
Zéisēng Jié Mò Shì Suǒ Guì Zhōng
Níngwáng was hunting in Hùxiàn territory.
In the forest, there was a cabinet,
very securely locked.
When it was opened,
it contained a young woman.
The woman said her surname was Mò,
and she lived in a village.
Last night she encountered bandits;
in the firelight, she recognized two monks
who had kidnapped her and brought her here.
Her seductive charm was abundant,
and the prince was pleased by her,
so he placed her in his carriage.
At that time, they had just captured a bear,
so he placed it in the cabinet,
locking it as before.
He was seeking extraordinary beauty,
so he presented Lady Mò to the emperor,
to become a Cairen.
After three days,
the Jingzhao Prefecture reported:
In Hùxiàn, two monks carried a cabinet into an inn.
Late at night, there was a thumping sound.
When the sun came up, the door was not opened.
When they removed the door to look,
a bear burst out, attacking people.
One monk was already dead,
his bones completely exposed.
The emperor greatly praised, saying:
"My brother Níng handled these monks very well."
Mù Zhōng Duì Qí
There were robbers who opened the tomb of the Former Lord of Shǔ.
They saw two people playing chess by lamplight.
The robbers were frightened.
One person looked up and said:
"Will you drink?"
Then each drank a cup,
and they also gave several jade belts,
ordering the robbers to leave quickly.
When the robbers reached the outside,
their mouths were already covered in lacquer.
The belts were actually giant snakes.
Dùfù Jīn
Línjì has a Dùfù Jīn.
Tradition has it that during the Tàishǐ era of the Jìn dynasty,
Liú Bóyù's wife, Duàn Míngguāng, was extremely jealous.
Bóyù once read the "Luòshén Fù" and said:
"If one were to take a wife like this,
I would have no regrets."
Míngguāng drowned herself that night
and appeared to Bóyù in a dream, saying:
"I have now become a deity."
Bóyù never crossed water again in his life.
When women crossed,
they would all ruin their clothes and makeup
before daring to cross.
Otherwise,
storms and waves would violently erupt.
Even if an ugly woman adorned herself,
the deity would still not tolerate her adornment.
Ugly women, fearing this,
would all disfigure themselves
to avoid ridicule.
The Qí people have a saying:
"If you want to find a beautiful wife,
stand at the ford's mouth.
When women stand by the ford,
their beauty and ugliness will reveal themselves."
Chángxū Guó
In the early Tàihé era,
a scholar accompanying an envoy from Xīnlüo
was blown by the wind to a certain place,
which people called the "Chángxū Guó."
They appointed the scholar as a fùmǎ.
Its ruler was very beautiful,
with dozens of whiskers.
On the night of the full moon, the King held a grand assembly.
The scholar saw that all the concubines had whiskers,
and so he composed a poem:
"Flowers without stamens are not lovely,
women without whiskers are also ugly.
My lord, try to remove them all,
they may not be as good as before."
The King laughed and said:
"Has the fùmǎ not yet been able to forget the area around my little daughter's chin?"
After more than ten years,
the scholar had one son and two daughters.
Suddenly, they wept and said:
"Our country is in peril,
and only the fùmǎ can save us!"
They then prepared elixirs
and sent two envoys with the scholar,
saying:
"Please trouble yourself to visit the Sea Dragon King,
just say that the Chángxū Guó on the seventh island of the third stream of the Eastern Sea is in peril and seeks help!"
They boarded a boat,
and in an instant reached the shore.
The sand on the shore was all made of seven treasures,
and the Dragon Palace resembled a Buddhist temple.
The Dragon King inquired about their purpose,
and the scholar explained everything.
The Dragon King immediately ordered a quick investigation.
After a long while,
one person reported:
"There is no such country within our territory."
The King angrily ordered a meticulous search and investigation.
Soon after, a report came:
"This island of shrimp serves as food for His Majesty this very day."
The King said:
"The guest has certainly been deluded by shrimp."
So he ordered the shrimp to be gathered
and sent two envoys to escort the guest back to the Central Plains.
One night they arrived at Dēngzhōu.
Looking back at the two envoys,
they were giant dragons.
Long-stationed men grow old easily, long-campaigning horses are not fat.
Guō Lìnggōng was living in the mountains.
At night, a person with a face like a plate
blinked under the lamp.
The Duke was not afraid at all,
and inscribed on its cheek:
"Long-stationed men grow old easily,
long-campaigning horses are not fat."
These were the Duke's insightful lines.
A few days later,
he saw a giant tree with white fungus,
as large as several dòu,
and the inscribed lines were there.
Yěyòu Steals a Village Girl
A villager in Rǔzhōu
lost his daughter at night.
In an ancient pagoda,
she saw a handsome man
who said:
"I am a Celestial Being,
it is destined for you to be my wife."
He returned twice a day
to fetch food.
After a year,
the girl secretly watched him,
and saw him soaring like flight,
with fiery hair and a blue complexion,
and ears like a donkey's.
Upon reaching the ground,
he would transform back into a human.
When that creature returned,
it said:
"You have indeed spied on me.
I am actually a Yěyòu.
We have a destined connection,
and I will ultimately not harm you."
The pagoda was very close to human habitation.
The girl asked:
"Earlier, I saw people in the street who respected you,
and others who treated you with great contempt.
Why is that?"
It replied:
"There are people in the world who eat beef;
I can deceive them."
After a year,
it wept and said:
"Our connection is exhausted,
you may leave."
In a short while, she had arrived home.
Dancing Sleeves, Bowed Waist
In the early Yuánhé era,
a scholar, drunk and lying down,
saw a woman from a screen stepping and singing before his bed:
"Cháng'ān daughters tread on spring's warmth,
everywhere spring's warmth breaks the heart.
Dancing sleeves and bowed waist are utterly forgotten,
moth-like brows are merely tinged with the frost of late autumn."
The scholar asked:
"What is 'bowed waist'?"
The singer then pressed her topknot to the ground,
her waist shaped like a bow.
The scholar yelled at her,
and she returned to the screen.
Fox Wearing a Skull
An old saying goes,
a fox named Zǐhú,
at night, strikes its tail,
and fire comes out,
then it becomes a demon.
It must wear a skull
and bow to the Big Dipper,
then it transforms into a human.
Cicada Transforms into Qí Empress
Birds give birth to Dùyǔ.
Coconuts are the heads of the Yuè kings.
Gourds are the necks of Dù Yù.
Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Zhīcǎo
If zhīcǎo grows on a house pillar without cause:
white indicates a funeral,
red indicates blood,
black indicates thieves,
yellow indicates joy.
If it resembles a woman's face,
it means loss of wealth.
If it resembles an ox or horse,
it means distant service.
If it resembles a tortoise or snake,
it means depletion of fields and silkworms.
Qúyù
Take its eye essence,
grind it with human milk,
and drop it into the eyes.
One can then see things beyond the misty clouds.
Elephant Gallbladder
It is in the four legs according to the four seasons:
spring in the front left,
summer in the front right,
autumn in the back left,
winter in the back right.
Like a tortoise, it has no fixed location.
Tiger Whiskers Cure Toothache
Tigers mate under a lunar halo.
The immortal Zhèng Sīyuǎn often rode a tiger.
His old friend Xǔ Yǐn sought a cure for his toothache.
Zhèng said:
"Tiger whiskers generate heat.
Insert them between the teeth and it will heal immediately."
He then pulled out several strands and gave them to him.
Lángbèi
These are two creatures.
The bèi has extremely short front legs.
Whenever it travels, it always rides two láng.
If it loses the láng, it cannot move.
Thus, the world uses "lángbèi" to describe difficult situations.
Discussion on Cats
A cat's pupils are round at dawn and dusk,
but at noon, they contract vertically like a slit.
Its nose is usually cold,
only warm on the summer solstice.
Folk saying has it that if a cat washes its face past its ears,
a guest will arrive.
A cat,
is also called "Méngzé",
and also "Wūmò".
Those with patterns,
in Língwǔ, there are red chìbō and qīngcōng ones,
which are auspicious.
If a mouse gnaws on
one's upper garment, it signifies joy.
In general, if it gnaws, one desires it to obtain its cover;
without a cover, it's inauspicious.
Clams
predict wind and rain,
and can fly with their shells as wings.
Camphorwood Boats
Camphorwood:
people in Jiāngdōng often use it to make boats.
Some boats engage in battles with dragons and serpents.
Seven Qualities of Persimmons
Persimmons have seven excellent qualities:
first, longevity;
second, abundant shade;
third, no crow's nests;
fourth, no insects;
fifth, beautiful frosted leaves;
sixth, it welcomes good guests;
seventh, its fallen leaves are large and thick,
suitable for writing upon.
Yánbó Flower
Most flowers have five petals.
The gardenia has six petals,
which is the Yánbó flower of the Western Regions.
Peony
Previous histories have no mention of it,
only in the *Xiè Kānglè Jí* it says:
"Among bamboo, by the water's edge, peonies are abundant."
Towards the end of the Kāiyuán era,
Péi Shìyān was dispatched as an envoy to Zhòngxiāng Temple in Fénzhōu,
where he obtained a white peony stem,
which he planted in his private residence.
At that time, renowned officials composed poems saying:
"The young people of Cháng'ān lament the passing of spring,
vying to recognize the purple peony of Cí'ēn Temple.
There is another jade plate holding cold dew,
but no one rises to look at it in the moonlight."
In the early Yuánhé era,
they were still few,
but now, compared to the hollyhock, they are much more numerous.
Eggplant
Also named "Luòsū",
and "Kūnlúnzǐzhǎo".
Shěn Yuē's poem "Xíngyuán" says:
"Purple eggplants flourish luxuriantly,
green taros rise in charming disarray."
In Lǐngnán, eggplants are plentiful;
some perennial roots grow into trees.
During flowering season, leaves are picked and spread on the road;
when people tread on them, the fruits become more numerous,
hence it's called "Jiàqiézi".
Water Chestnut Turtle
Lǐ Wèigōng said:
"Water chestnut root,
when made into soup, is exceptionally delicious.
People in Jiāngdōng call it 'Chúntuī'."
Swallows Roost on Wùjǐ
Magpies nest with their backs to the Grand Commander of the Year (Tàisuì),
swallows roost on Wùjǐ,
tigers charge and break through.
Magpies know what is coming,
and orangutans know what has passed.
Treasure Sprout
If there is green onion on a mountain,
there must be silver beneath it.
If there is garlic,
there must be gold.
If there is ginger,
there must be copper and tin beneath it.
If there is jade on a mountain,
the branches of the trees beside it will hang low,
which is called "Bǎomiáo".
Kestrel Lays Two Chicks
It is traditionally said that a kestrel lays only two chicks.
If there are three chicks,
then one will be an owl.
Mantis Shrimp
Resembling a centipede,
it eats shrimp.
Tiger's Might
On both sides of a tiger's ribs, beneath the skin and fur,
