there is a bone called "Hǔwēi",
suitable for wearing when governing people.
Bright Camel
It is traditionally said that a bright camel has "thousand-li legs".
It is said that when a camel lies down and bends its legs,
its belly does not touch the ground, allowing light to pass through,
making it exceptionally capable of long journeys.
Water Chestnut
The *Wǔlíng Jì* states that water chestnuts with two horns are called "líng",
and those with four horns are called "jì".
Gorgon euryale,
is commonly called "Shuǐlì".
Selling a Donkey to Pay for a Funeral
During the Kāiyuán era,
a man in Cháng'ān whose father had died,
rode a donkey into the market,
intending to exchange it
to pay for the funeral.
The donkey suddenly spoke in human language, saying:
"My surname is Bái,
my given name Yuántōng.
I have already served your family sufficiently,
owing only four thousand five hundred cash.
You can exchange me at a certain place, at a certain family."
He followed its words and went, and indeed, it was the exact amount.
A few days later, he went to inquire,
and the donkey had already died.
Those who eat plants
are strong and foolish.
Those who eat meat
are brave and fierce.
Those who gnaw and swallow have eight orifices and are oviparous,
those who chew have nine orifices and are viviparous.
Those who eat leaves produce silk,
those who eat soil never rest.
Those who eat but do not drink are silkworms,
those who drink but do not eat are cicadas,
and those who neither drink nor eat are mayflies.
Louse Divination
When people in Lǐngnán are ill,
they use lice for divination:
if it faces the body, it is auspicious;
if it faces away from the body, it is inauspicious.
Teeth Are an Obstruction
Yuán Tuì, a reclusive scholar, was over seventy years old,
and ate without teeth,
yet his chewing was even stronger.
He often said:
"Now I realize that teeth are an obstruction."
Bamboo Well-being
Lǐ Wèigōng said:
"In Běidū, only Tóngzǐ Temple has a single bamboo stalk,
barely a few feet long.
The Duke ordered the temple's Vihāra guardian
to report daily on the bamboo's well-being."
Official Request for Huai Leaves
In Xīxià, there were no huai trees,
only one specimen in Xiàzhōu.
If other prefectures needed its leaves,
they would issue an official document to obtain them.
Crab Spines
In the eighth month,
crabs have genuine rice awns in their bellies,
about an inch long,
which they deliver eastward to the sea god.
Before the awns are delivered,
they should not be eaten.
Grapes Resemble Unripe Litchi
Yú Xìn said to Wèi envoy Wèi Jǐn:
"When I was in Yè,
I ate grapes which were exceptionally delicious."
Chén Zhāo asked:
"What did they look like?"
Xú Jūnfāng said:
"They resembled soft dates."
Yú Xìn replied:
"Sir, you truly do not appreciate things well.
Why not say they resembled unripe litchi?"
Oranges and Pomelos: Gold Skin, White Flesh
Chén Zhāo said:
“How do grapes compare to tangerines and pomelos?”
Xìn replied:
“Their juice is remarkably superior,
but their fragrance is inferior.”
Wèi Jǐn said:
“With a golden skin and a white interior,
they are presented as tribute when in bud.
They dissolve in the mouth,
which other fruits truly cannot match.”
Wáng Qīngběn
There was a man who was felling a withered tree.
He saw a large black snake coiled beneath it.
It raised its head and said:
“I am Wáng Qīngběn.”
The man was frightened and covered it up.
Later, a man named Wáng Qīng went to fell trees,
and found a jar full of money.
He consequently became rich.
Sores on the arm like a human face
There was a man who had a sore on his arm like a human face,
complete with mouth and nose.
When given alcohol to drink,
the face turned red.
When given food,
the arm swelled.
He then tried various medicines on it.
When it came to Fritillaria bulb (bèimǔ), the face wrinkled and the mouth closed, refusing it.
So he forced the mouth open and poured it in.
After several days, a scab formed and it healed.
Two Musicians of the Supreme Deity
Wáng Bù had a very beautiful daughter,
but each of her nostrils had a very large polyp,
which no treatment could cure.
A Brahmān monk came,
blew a little medicine into her nose,
and in a moment, removed them.
Soon after, a young man arrived at the door,
and asked:
“Did a Hu monk come just now?”
Bù recounted the whole affair,
and the young man sighed:
“The Supreme Deity has lost two music spirits,
and I was commanded to retrieve them.
Now, that person has preempted me,
and I will surely receive a heavy punishment.”
Hūléi Bó
The horse ridden by Qín Shúbǎo,
named “Hūléi Bó,”
was regularly given wine to drink,
and two felt blankets were laid out for it every night.
When a stream or gully was before it,
it would leap over it in one bound.
This is the method of gaining an advantage.
Yī Xíng Shī was originally not good at chess,
but after observing a game played by Wáng Jīxīn,
he became his equal.
He said:
“This is the method of gaining an advantage.
If you remember my four lines of addition and subtraction,
then everyone will become a national master.”
Scabies on the wall
During the Dàlì reign,
Lǎn Xuán Chánshī resided at Zhìqǐ Sì in Jīngzhōu.
Zhāng Zǎo often painted ancient pines on the walls,
Fú Zài wrote eulogies for them,
and Wèi Xiàng composed rhapsodies.
Scholars called it the “Three Perfections.”
The Master saw it and said:
“Why are you giving my wall scabies?”
He ordered it to be whitewashed.
Person who refined form with the Great Yin
There was a man digging in the ground,
who encountered a stone casket.
When he opened it,
a person lay reclining,
with white hair covering their body,
and a complexion like jade.
In a moment,
they shook their hair and rose,
then immediately disappeared.
A Daoist master said:
“This is a person who refined their form with the Great Yin.
When the day cycle is full, they emerge on their own.”
Flesh Stool
During Emperor Mínghuáng's reign,
there was a young eunuch named Huáng Wáng'ér,
who was quite clever and intelligent.
The Emperor often leaned on him when walking,
calling him his “Flesh Stool.”
Tàibái enters the Moon
Lǐ Bái, hearing of Ān Lùshān’s rebellion,
composed the poem “Hú Wúrén,” saying:
“When Tàibái enters the moon, the enemy can be destroyed.”
Later, on the day Lùshān died,
Tàibái was indeed seen eclipsing the moon.
Amber
Maple sap entering the earth transforms into amber.
A thousand years of accumulated ice solidifies into glass.
The blood of ghosts transforms into agate.
Extreme Cold
Liáng dispatched Míng Shǎoxiá to host a banquet for the Wèi envoy Cuī Jié.
Jié said:
“This year is exceptionally cold;
even the Jiāng and Huái rivers are frozen.”
Pounding three planks of chaff
People from Xīnlüo, floating on the sea,
drifted to the Land of Ghosts.
The ghosts seized them,
and said:
“Can you pound three planks of chaff for us?
Or do you want your nose to be a zhang long?”
The person asked to pound chaff,
but after a long time, could not succeed.
So the ghosts pulled his nose like an elephant's.
Mùyǐn Zhōu
Within the territory of Zhūyá, there is an island.
Its inhabitants are numerous,
but there are no wells.
The seawater is especially salty,
so they drink the juice of plants and trees.
It is called “Mùyǐn Zhōu.”
Locusts
It is traditionally said:
Locusts eating crops
are summoned by the greed and cruelty of officials and scribes.
Those with black bodies and red heads
are military official locusts.
Those with black heads and red bodies
are civil official locusts.
Cricket (Zàomǎ)
They resemble crickets
and burrow beside the stove.
It is a folk saying that if a stove has “horses,”
there will surely be plenty of food.
Jūnwáng Yán
At Bái Yányá,
there is salt like crystal,
named “Jūnwáng Yán.”
Olive
A single-rooted branch.
The branch pointing east is called “Mùwēi.”
The branch pointing south is called “Gǎnlǎn.”
Idle Pleasures (Xiánzhōng Hǎo) Lyrics
Chéng Wǔ and several literati composed “Idle Pleasures” lyrics, saying:
“Idle pleasures,
all day long with pines as companions.
This delight people do not know,
a light breeze passes through the monk's temple.
Idle pleasures,
worldly affairs do not entangle the heart.
Sitting facing the moon before the window,
watching its shadow shift three sides.”
Pickled Fish Memorial
Liáng Wáng Lín wrote a “Pickled Fish Memorial,” saying:
“Humbly I observe the imperial decree,
appointing Your Subject as General of Fermented Jars,
Captain of Oil Steaming,
and Governor of Pickled Meat Prefecture.”
Camel Hump Meat
General Qū Liánghàn
made camel hump meat,
which was very delicious.
Bōluó Wood
The Western Regions' “Memorial on Presenting Bōluó Wood” states:
“It neighbors the red osmanthus of the moon,
and faces the white elm of the heavens.”
Shèngfēng (Victorious Wind)
Emperor Mínghuáng commanded Gēshū Hàn to campaign in the west,
and he often encountered a victorious wind.
Wǎsōng (Houseleek)
Wǎsōng on a roof is called “Xīyē”;
on a wall, it is called “Yuányī.”
Bamboo Grove Painting
Níng Cǎihuà's《Zhúlín Tú》 (Bamboo Forest Painting) was very skillful.
A scholar named Liǔ Chéngxiù said:
"I wish to enter that painting with my humble skill,
to make its brilliance even more extraordinary,
how about that?"
Then he leaped into the painting,
groping but finding nothing.
After a meal's time,
he emerged,
and pointed at the statue of Ruǎn Jí, saying:
"The skill only extends this far."
The crowd looked at it,
and noticed that the statue alone was different.
Hán Gàn's Horses Attain Divinity
A divine entity led a horse to a horse doctor,
claiming it had a foot ailment.
The horse doctor said:
"It looks very much like one painted by Hán Gàn."
Suddenly, Hán Gàn appeared,
and Hán Gàn said:
"This is truly one that I colored!"
Even now,
when one looks at the painting,
there is a small black missing spot on the foot,
indicating that the painting had attained divinity.
The money the horse doctor received
turned into mud.
Strengths and Weaknesses of Birds and Beasts
Cuī Shào said:
Magpies building nests to avoid wind
is a strength of birds;
foxes being indecisive and hesitant
is a weakness of beasts.
Owls and Gìngs
Today, those who speak of xiāo jìng
often refer to the spider on the wall as a jìng,
seeing its round and flat shape,
and believing that when it lies on its young, the young will surely eat it.
In the Western Hàn dynasty, during the spring sacrifice to the Yellow Emperor (Huángdì),
one owl (xiāo) and a broken jìng were used.
Because owls eat their mothers,
owl soup was made on the fifth day of the fifth month.
The broken jìng eats its father,
like a chǔ,
with tiger eyes.
The Yellow Emperor (Huángdì) wished to eradicate their kind,
so he used them in all sorts of things.
Fù Xuán's ode says:
"Sacrificing a zhì and a broken jìng,
using an owl as well."
Fúxī
Among scholars, many mistakenly call the protective net for sparrows in the eaves of halls fúxī.
This is an error.
The《Jì》 (Record) says:
"Shū píng is the decoration of the Son of Heaven's (Tiānzǐ) ancestral temple."
Zhèng's commentary says:
"A píng is called a shù,
which is now a fúxī.
Carved with clouds, qi, insects, and beasts,
like today's quē (watchtowers)."
《Guǎng Yǎ》 says:
"Fùxī is called a píng."
Liú Xī's《Shìmíng》 says:
"A fúxī is outside the gate.
Fú,
means 'again' (fù).
When ministers are about to enter to request matters,
they should reconsider (fù sī) here."
When the fúxī of Emperor Wén of Hàn's (Hàn Wéndì) eastern quē caught fire,
it represented the vassal lords outside.
Indeed, seven years later, they raised troops.
Wáng Mǎng, fond of auspicious days and minor calculations,
sent envoys to destroy the fúxī of the Wèi Líng Park Gate,
saying:
"This will make the people no longer think of the Hàn (Hàn dynasty) again (fù sī)."
I have seen dozens of gentry members
all making erroneous statements about "xiāo jìng and fúxī."
Hù Rǎn
The《Rǎn Zhí Yí》 (Ritual of Dyeing Offices) states:
The eight-seat Shàngshū wrapped their hand tablets with purple gauze,
with white silk threads attached to the top like a brush.
The《Tōng Zhì》 says:
"The hand tablets of the Púyè and Shàngshū
were wrapped in purple cloth,
named 'hù rǎn' (dyed tablet).
Since the middle ages,
only the sovereign holding a tablet had a white brush attached to the top,
wrapped in a purple bag.
Other dukes and ministers merely held hand tablets.
Chén Xīliè found it inconvenient to carry a tablet,
so when riding a horse, he wrapped it in silk
and had his attendants carry it.
Lǐ Yòuzuò said this would become a future precedent.
Qīnglú
In the homes of scholars and officials, the outdoor tent for weddings
was called "entering the tent."
The bride riding a saddle
was a custom remaining from the Northern Dynasties.
Northern wedding ceremonies
used a house made of blue cloth curtains,
called "qīnglú" (blue hut).
There, they performed their bows,
and as a joke, beat the groom with bamboo branches,
some even becoming greatly exhausted.
Zāizhí Jīng
Volume three says:
Some trees suffer from "sour heart" disease.
Keeping a beard to show masculinity
On Mount Shíshì in Héngzhōu,
there was a monk
who did not shave his hair;
his hair hung down and brushed his shoes.
This was probably out of admiration for keeping hair to show masculinity.
Yōng Gōng's Method of Nurturing Life
Yōng Gōng said:
"When lying down, one should retract the feet;
one should not sleep on the left side.
I have washed my feet every evening
for over forty years.
This year I am sixty-nine,
and I have never been ill."
Zhēng Family Surname
In all undertakings,
one should avoid the day Hài.
Because fire is extinguished in Hài,
it is the day of extinguished energy for the Zhēng family.
One should also avoid Xū,
the tomb day for the Zhēng family.
The Night God's (Yèshén) incantation,
reciting it when traveling at night
or sleeping,
can ward off fear and nightmares.
The incantation is:
"Pó Sān Pó Yǎn Dǐ."
Téng Wáng's Butterfly Paintings
Téng Wáng's《Dié Tú》 (Butterfly Paintings)
include names like "Jiāngxià Bān," "Dàhǎiyǎn," "Xiǎohǎiyǎn," "Cūnlǐ Lái," and "Càihuāzi."
Bear Gallbladder and Mouse Gallbladder
A bear's gallbladder
is in its head in spring,
in its belly in summer,
in its left foot in autumn,
and in its right foot in winter.
A mouse's gallbladder is in its head;
it is present only if taken while alive.
Sealing the Five Sacred Mountains
In the early morning, people wished to "seal the Five Sacred Mountains (Wǔyuè)" seven times,
which meant bending the index finger and the other four fingers,
and sweeping with the thumb.
This was called "sealing the Five Sacred Mountains."
Monkeys (húsūn) have no spleen;
they eat with their jaws.
Chanting Dice
Sòng Jūshì said the incantation for throwing dice is:
"Yī Dì Mí Dì Mí Jiē Luó Dì."
After chanting it 100,000 times,
the numbers will appear as called.
Píngquán Flowers and Trees
Wèi Gōng's Píngquán Villa
had yellow magnolias (xīnyí) and purple lilacs (dīngxiāng),
as well as co-hearted calyxes (tóngxīn dì) and cotton roses (mùfuróng).
Liǔ Hún's Poem on Peonies
During the Zhēnyuán era,
peonies were already numerous.
Liǔ Hún famously said:
"Lately, what can be done about peonies?
Tens of thousands of cash buy one stalk.
Only this morning did I finally see clearly
how little they differ from common mallows (róngkuí)."
Suffering from Sores
Treading on and damaging hearth earth
causes people to suffer from sores.
Stepping on eggshells
causes people to get vitiligo.
Killing Snakes
One should not kill snakes in the Yǐ year.
Three-Legged Crow
During Empress Tiānhòu's time,
someone presented a three-legged crow.
Those around her sometimes said:
"One leg is fake."
The Empress laughed and said:
"As long as the historical records record it,
why bother investigating its authenticity?"
The dirge [wǎnɡē]
originated from Tián Héng’s [Tián Héng] death,
when his followers dared not weep aloud,
and so composed songs to express their sorrow.
The Xīnlǐ [Xīnlǐ] says:
“Dirges originated from Emperor Wǔdì [Wǔdì] of Hàn [Hàn].
Laborers were toiling hard,
and their singing was mournful and poignant.
Thus, these songs were used for funerals,
which was not an ancient custom.”
Yán Hòuběn [Yán Hòuběn] said:
“Dirges have been around for a long time.”
The Zuǒzhuàn [Zuǒzhuàn] says:
‘Gōng [Gōng] met with the Count of Wú [Wú] to attack Qí [Qí].
Before the battle,
Gōngsūn Xià [Gōngsūn Xià] ordered his followers to sing “Yúbīn” [Yúbīn],
to show their resolve to die.’”
Tí Fān Chuò [Tí Fān Chuò] Enters Water
Emperor Xuánzōng [Xuánzōng] often had his attendants carry Huáng Fān [Huáng Fān] into a pond,
and after he came out again,
said:
“I just saw Qū Yuán [Qū Yuán] smiling at me,
asking, ‘You met a sagacious and enlightened ruler,
how did you also come to this?’”
Exposed Tendons [Lùjīn]
Between Jiāng [Jiāng] and Huái [Huái] there is Lùjīn Yì [Lùjīn Yì].
A drunken person once stopped there.
One night,
a white bird picked at their exposed tendons, and they died.
The Běidàojì [Běidàojì] says:
“From Shàobó Dài [Shàobó Dài], it is thirty-six lǐ [lǐ] to Lùjīn Yì [Lùjīn Yì].
This place has many white birds.
One night, a deer was eaten by them,
and by dawn, only its tendons were visible.
Hence, it was named after this.”
Hàn [Hàn] Swallows
The Shìshuō [Shìshuō] says:
“Those that build nests with mud,
and whose calls are mostly soft and small, are called Hàn [Hàn] swallows.”
The Běncǎo Zhù [Běncǎo Zhù] says:
“Those with purple chests and small bodies are Yuè [Yuè] swallows.
Those with black spots and loud calls are Hú [Hú] swallows,
and they are good at building long nests.”
End of Scroll Forty-two
End.
Xiānggòng Jìnshì [Xiānggòng Jìnshì] Lǐ [Lǐ] So-and-so
Emperor Xuānzōng [Xuānzōng] of Táng [Táng] favored refined scholars.
He kept the list of successful candidates from the new imperial examinations [gòngjǔ],
and inscribed on a palace pillar: “Xiānggòng Jìnshì [Xiānggòng Jìnshì] Lǐ [Lǐ] So-and-so.”
Bùdá Jìnshì [Bùdá Jìnshì]
Emperor Xīzōng [Xīzōng] enjoyed cùjū [cùjū] and cockfighting.
Confident in his skill at bùdá [bùdá],
he said to the entertainer Shí Yězhū [Shí Yězhū]:
“If I were to become a bùdá [bùdá] jìnshì [jìnshì],
I would certainly achieve the chuàngyuán [chuàngyuán] rank.”
The reply was:
“If you were to meet Yáo [Yáo], Shùn [Shùn], Yǔ [Yǔ], and Tāng [Tāng] acting as Ministers of Rites [lǐbù shìláng],
Your Majesty would still fail the examinations.”
Qiūyù Júdú [Qiūyù Júdú] Cold and Warm Go Stones
A prince from Rìběn Guó [Rìběn Guó] presented tribute,
and was skilled at the game of Go.
The emperor ordered the Imperial Attendant Gù Shīyán [Gù Shīyán] to play against him.
The prince produced a board from his own country, made of qiūyù [qiūyù],
which was a dark green jade,
the color of qiū [qiū] leaves.
The Go stones were made of cold and warm jade [lěngnuǎnyù].
They were warm in winter and cool in summer.
Gù Shīyán [Gù Shīyán], fearing to disgrace the imperial command,
with sweaty hands and a determined heart,
finally dared to make a move.
The prince lost,
and asked the protocol official.
The official said:
“That was the third-best player.”
The prince wished to see the best player.
The official said:
“If you defeat the third,
you may see the second.
If you defeat the second,
you may see the first.”
The prince sighed and said:
“The best of a small country
is not equal to the third-best of a great country.”
Oil Merchant Playing Chess
Ān Chóngbà [Ān Chóngbà], an Inspector [cìshǐ] in Shǔ [Shǔ],
was insatiably greedy for bribes.
In the prefecture there was an oil merchant named Dèng [Dèng].
Ān [Ān] summoned him to play chess,
but only allowed him to stand and wait.
Each time a piece was played,
he was made to retreat and stand by the wall,
waiting for Ān [Ān] to calculate the moves before advancing.
The entire day,
only a few dozen pieces were played,
and Dèng [Dèng] grew tired of standing and
could barely endure the hunger.
Someone hinted:
“This marquis likes bribes;
he’s not really playing chess.”
Dèng [Dèng] understood,
and was able to escape by offering ten gold ingots.
Not Reading Bái’s [Bái] Writings
Liú Yǔxī [Liú Yǔxī] paid his respects to Lǐ Déyù [Lǐ Déyù] and said:
“Have you ever obtained Bái Jūyì’s [Bái Jūyì] collected works?”
Lǐ Déyù [Lǐ Déyù] said:
“I have been dissatisfied with this person
for a long time.
Why should I read his writings?”
Submitting a Memorial of Grievance
Lìnghú Táo [Lìnghú Táo] abused his power.
When sent to govern Wéiyáng [Wéiyáng],
he submitted a memorial of grievance, saying:
“If your servant does not have fine wine and delicious meat,
how can he satisfy the mouths of the multitude?”
Nánhuá [Nánhuá] is Not an Obscure Book
Lìnghú Táo [Lìnghú Táo] consulted Wēn Qí [Wēn Qí] about a historical matter.
Wēn Qí [Wēn Qí] replied that the matter came from the Nánhuá [Nánhuá] (Zhuāngzǐ [Zhuāngzǐ]),
and further said:
“It is not an obscure book;
when you, Your Excellency, have leisure from managing affairs,
you should occasionally read ancient texts.”
Lìnghú Táo [Lìnghú Táo] was enraged,
and memorialized that Wēn Qí [Wēn Qí] had talent but lacked moral conduct,
and had him appointed as Prefect of Fāngchéng [Fāngchéng].
Wēn Qí’s [Wēn Qí] poem says:
“From this, I know this regret is amassed by many,
regretting having read the second chapter of Nánhuá [Nánhuá].”
Dragon and Tiger Qi [qì] Intermingle in the Nose
Wáng Tíngcòu [Wáng Tíngcòu] was born in a villa.
There were dozens of doves [jiū] that
gathered in the courtyard trees in the morning,
and roosted under the eaves in the evening.
He often slept by the road.
Someone introduced himself as Lúo Shānrén [Lúo Shānrén] from Jìyuán [Jìyuán], saying:
“I see the qì [qì] from your nose on the left is like a dragon,
and on the right is like a tiger.
When dragon and tiger qì [qì] intermingle,
a king will appear this autumn.
His descendants will succeed him,
for a full hundred years.
When the great tree reaches the hall,
that will be the omen.”
That year, he was indeed established as the acting military governor [liúhòu] by the three armies of Zhènzhōu [Zhènzhōu].
By the appointed time,
the courtyard trees of the villa were indeed luxuriant.
Xǔ Dòngtíng [Xǔ Dòngtíng]
Xǔ Táng [Xǔ Táng] had a poem titled Dòngtíng [Dòngtíng],
which was particularly skillful,
and at the time he was known as “Xǔ Dòngtíng [Xǔ Dòngtíng].”
Farmer’s Poems
Niè Yízhōng’s [Niè Yízhōng] poem “Yǒng Tiánjiā” [Yǒng Tiánjiā] (Ode to a Farming Family) says:
“Fathers plow the fields on the plain,
sons clear the wasteland below the mountain.
In the sixth month, the grain has not yet bloomed,
but the officials have already repaired the granaries.”
“Hoeing the fields at midday,
sweat drips onto the soil below the grain.
Who remembers that the food in the bowl,
every grain, is hard-won?”
It also says:
“In the second month, they sell new silk;
in the fifth month, they sell new grain.
To cure the sore before their eyes,
they cut the flesh from their heart.
I wish the king’s heart
would transform into a bright candle.
Not illuminating the embroidered feasts,
but particularly illuminating the homes of fugitives.”
Post-meal Bell
Duàn Xiàng [Duàn Xiàng] Wénchāng [Wénchāng] was poor in his youth.
Each time he heard the meal bell from Céngkǒu Sì [Céngkǒu Sì],
he would go to visit.
The temple monks grew weary of him,
so they struck the bell after meals.
Later, when he became a chancellor [xiàng]
and was sent to govern Jīngnán [Jīngnán],
he inscribed at Céngkǒu Sì [Céngkǒu Sì]:
“Once met the dhuta [dhūtā]’s post-meal bell.”
Some say that Wáng Bò [Wáng Bò], the chancellor [xiànggōng], inscribed a poem at Yángzhōu Wòsì [Yángzhōu Wòsì],
and both versions exist.
Washing Feet in a Golden Lotus Basin
After Jiǎ Wénchāng became wealthy and noble,
he had a golden lotus basin made,
filled it with water, and washed his feet in it.
Someone peeked at him,
and he replied,
"How short is life?
I want to fulfill the dissatisfactions of my entire life!"
Lǐ Dìshī Selects a Son-in-Law
Lǐ Guāngyán's beloved daughter was not yet betrothed.
His guests and subordinates highly praised a scholar Zhèng Xiùcái for his literary scholarship and prominent family.
The Duke said,
"I
am a brave warrior
who by chance achieved some minor merit.
How can I presumptuously seek a son-in-law from an official family?
I have already chosen an excellent son-in-law."
Then he summoned a junior officer from the guest department and said,
"This is the match for my daughter."
He promoted him three to five ranks in military office
and generously gave him gold and silk.
Someone said,
"Lǐ Dìshī, in seeking a marriage with the Wáng and Xiè families for Hóu Jǐng,
how far off was that?"
Sleeping with Crossed Hands
Wáng Wéngōng Níng,
whenever he slept, would always cross his hands,
fearing that he might see the spirits of his ancestors in his dreams.
Bald Monks
Gāo Pián governed Shǔ.
One evening, a monk from Kāiyuán Sì performed a praise ceremony.
The Duke ordered him to be captured,
flogged on the back,
and all monks expelled.
He said to his generals and officers,
"Monks praying and chanting are not guilty.
However, ten years from now,
there will be bald monks causing rebellion,
and I detest them for that reason."
Later, indeed, local people with shaved heads bore arms,
called Dàkūn and Xiǎokūn,
and occupied this temple as their stronghold.
This Pig is Well-Proportioned
Lù Yán was handsome
and good at wearing headscarves.
If there was someone in the alleys who was well-dressed and groomed,
people would invariably mock,
"Are you not Lù Shìzhōng?"
Once, at a pork vendor's stall,
he saw a pork butcher
and said the pig on the chopping block was well-proportioned,
and Lù Shìzhōng was not as good.
Where Does the Departing Soul Break?
Lù Shìzhōng moved his post from Chéngdū to Zhǔguān.
At the Héjiāng Tíng farewell banquet,
Guān Qí Xíngyún and others performed the lyric "Gǎn'ēn Duō,"
which says, "Where does the departing soul break?
Misty rain on the southern bank of the river."
Brocade Sleeveless Jacket
Zhèng Yú wore a brocade sleeveless jacket.
Later, he presented his literary work to Què Xuán.
Xuán said,
"You truly deserve that brocade sleeveless jacket."
Old Man of Ample Grain
Wéi Zhòu was skilled in managing household affairs.
His estate in Jiānglíng accumulated seventy piles of grain.
Xuānzōng said,
"This is what is called the 'Old Man of Ample Grain'."
An Appointed Hero, an Auspicious Omen Among Men
Wú Xínglǔ served the eunuch Xīmén Jūnrong when young.
One day, while washing his feet,
the Middle Commandant showed him the lines on the sole of his foot,
saying,
"With such lines,
how could one not become a Jūnrong?"
Xínglǔ said,
"I also have them."
Then he took off his shoes and presented his feet.
The Middle Commandant sighed and said,
"I will make it happen for you."
Later, he was given a military position.
He achieved merits
and was appointed Jiedushi of Xīchuān.
The Imperial Edict said:
"He is an appointed hero of his generation,
an auspicious omen among men."
Three Transformations of an Undutiful Son
There are three transformations for undutiful sons:
The first transformation is into locusts,
meaning they sell their estates to live.
The second transformation is into bookworms,
selling books to live.
The third transformation is into great beasts,
meaning they sell their servants to live.
Which era is without such people?
Tablet Without Words
Zhào Chóng
was dignified and imposing in appearance,
but did not write articles,
and was called "Tablet Without Words."
Proper Official
Xuē Néng, a Grand Secretary, prided himself on his literary compositions.
Repeatedly posted to military garrisons,
he was always dispirited.
He had a poem thanking someone for sending tea from a pillar, saying:
"A coarse official position is truly thrown away,
but happily my poetic fame is worth tasting."
When he was garrisoned in Xǔchāng,
he ordered his son to wear armor and visit the staff,
saying,
"Let him dispel misfortune."
This was because he did not get a proper official position,
and he feigned this to show his ambition.
Since You Have Received Official Rank, Why Not Eat Meat?
Cuī Shènyóu was the Censor of Zhèxī.
A monk from Wǎguān Sì became his disciple.
A diviner said,
"The Grand Minister's complexion indicates a noble son."
Since his wife and concubines showed no signs,
he summoned an official courtesan who had previously served him in changing clothes.
The diviner said,
"Indeed, she is the one."
When the child was born,
there was a pattern under his armpit, just like that of the Wǎguān monk,
and he was named after it.
His courtesy name was Fān Láng.
At seven years old, he still did not eat meat.
A monk slapped his cheek
and said,
"Since you have received official rank,
why do you not eat meat?"
From then on, he began to taste meat and blood.
He was Guó Yìn.
Preferences
Cuī Xuán liked to eat freshly picked dates.
Dù Bīngōng ate dried meat with leftover rice every morning.
Cuī Shìzhōng Ānqián loved watching bullfights.
Eight Folded Lines of Paper
Lú Xiāng Guāngqǐ's ancestors were executed.
Thereafter, his brothers diligently cultivated themselves,
telling relatives and friends,
"This is like clearing barren land."
After being appointed to office,
he gained the recognition of Zūyōng Zhāng Jùn.
Whenever he sent letters or memorials,
each matter would be on a separate sheet,
with eight lines folded.
The practice of using separate sheets began with the Duke.
Breaking the Heavenly Barren
Every year, many candidates from Jīngzhōu took the examinations
but failed to achieve fame,
and thus it was called "Heavenly Barren Division."
Liú Tuì passed the examination from Jīngzhōu,
and thereafter it was called "Breaking the Heavenly Barren."
Hán in the North, Guō in the South
Chéng Lìnggōng Ruì was once encircled by a giant snake at night.
He said,
"If I owe something,
life and death are up to fate."
Soon,
the snake also departed.
Later, he governed Zhǔgōng,
and meticulously managed its affairs.
The imperial court called him "Hán in the North, Guō in the South."
Hán was Hán Jiàn of Huázhōu.
Chéng Lìnggōng's surname was Guō,
which he later reverted to.
Playing with a Tablet and Singing "Huànxīshā"
Xuē Zhāowěi relied on his talent and was arrogant.
Every time he entered the court or department,
he would play with his official tablet while walking.
He also liked to sing the lyric "Huànxīshā."
A student offered advice, saying,
"The Vice Minister values virtue;
hereafter, please do not play with your tablet or sing 'Huànxīshā'."
At the time, this was considered profound wisdom.
Liǔ's Maidservant and the Silk Broker
Liǔ Zhòngyǐng 僕shè
had a maid who, having fallen out of favor,
was sold in Chéngdū.
It happened that Jùyuán shǐjūn desired her,
and took her into his household.
One day,
a seller of patterned silks was in the main street,
and peeped through the window.
Gài Gōng was selecting and unrolling silks from a bundle,
negotiating their suitability.
The Liǔ maid cried out and collapsed,
as if struck by wind-stroke.
Gài Gōng ordered her to be helped out.
The next day, she said:
“Although I am a humble person,
I once served as a maid in the Liǔ family.
I would rather die
than serve a silk-selling broker! ”
Wēn Fēiqīng's Demotion
Wēn Tíngyún, courtesy name Fēiqīng,
sometimes written with “筠”
his old name was “Qí.”
Whenever he took an examination,
he would compose an essay following the official rhyme scheme,
completing eight rhymes in eight hand movements.
He often lent a hand to neighboring candidates,
and was known as “the savior of several men.”
Emperor Xuānzōng had a poetic line with “golden hairpins,”
which Wēn followed with “jade bracelets.”
When a medicinal name “old man with white hair” was given,
Wēn responded with “cocklebur seed.”
Emperor Xuānzōng enjoyed incognito travels,
and Wēn, not recognizing him,
questioned him, saying:
“Are you not of the rank of Sīmǎ or Zhǎngshǐ,
or perhaps a Wéncān or Bùwèi?”
The Emperor replied:
“No.”
He was demoted to the post of Fāngchéng County Lieutenant.
The imperial edict stated:
“He possesses unbridled talent,
but rarely puts it to practical use at the right time.”
He eventually wandered and died.
He once inscribed a poem on a village family's garden pavilion, saying:
“Golden-threaded willows before Zhuó Shì's tavern,
the wind of brocade sails by Suí's embankment.
Too eager to bring timely rain to two lands,
he missed the pond's duckweed glowing red in the sun.”
The Nun of Dōngshān Losing Her Resolve
The nun of Dōngshān was lecturing on the Dharma.
The Chan master Dèng Yǐnfēng,
a man of profound virtue,
tested her resolve.
In the middle of the night, he entered her meditation cell with a blade,
intending to commit violence.
The nun, fearing death, lost her resolve.
Yǐnfēng took her undergarments,
and gathered the assembly to expose her,
whereupon her disciples immediately dispersed.
White Phoenix
Shěn Xún shìláng
was pure, refined, and handsome.
When he was appointed the military commissioner of Shānběi,
everyone in the capital recited Cáo Táng's “Poem on Roaming with Immortals,” saying:
“The imperial decree newly appoints Shěn shìláng,
who is then granted territory to lead the East.
One wonders where he roams tonight,
attended by escorts all riding white phoenixes.”
His graceful appearance can thus be imagined.
Water-Moon Guānyīn
Jiǎng Níng shìláng
was also a man of remarkable presence,
and was at the time called “Water-Moon Guānyīn.”
Reading Ten Thousand Scrolls and Drinking A Hundred Cups
Gāo Cè's “Memorial to Zhāng Yàngōng” said:
“Reading ten thousand scrolls,
drinking a hundred cups.”
Gōng said:
“Ten thousand scrolls are not easily verified,
but a hundred cups of wine can be tested.”
So, he offered him wine,
and indeed, it was as he said.
Untwisting Sock Threads
Hán Zhāo, when serving in Shǔ,
had a rough literary style.
Lǐ Táigǔ said:
“Hán Bāzuò's literary skill is like untwisting sock threads –
not a single long strand.”
Good Donkeys and Horses Do Not Enter the Market
Lǐ Déyù was not keen on taking the imperial examinations.
His father encouraged him,
to which he replied:
“Good donkeys and horses do not enter the market.”
Because of this, he was appointed to official posts based on his family status.
Naturally Averse to Drinking
A scholar visited Prime Minister Lù Yǐ,
who offered him wine.
The scholar declined, saying:
“By nature, I do not drink wine.”
Gōng said:
“If that is truly the case,
you have already eliminated five-tenths [of regret].”
This implied that if one's lifetime regrets
amounted to ten-tenths,
not drinking wine
would naturally reduce them by half.
Prime Minister Zhū Is Not a Prime Minister
In the Guānghuà era,
Zhū Pú rose from a professor of seven poetic forms to a high position,
claiming he could bring about great peace immediately.
On the day of an inner court banquet,
the actor Mù Dāolíng,
acting as a sutra reciter,
approached the imperial presence and said:
“If you see Prime Minister Zhū,
he is not a Prime Minister.”
Not Even a Thread of Merit
When Zhū Pú was appointed prime minister,
people said:
“Zhū Gōng has not even presented a thread of merit, yet he is pardoned.
The court musician plays the pílí.”
Ms. Sūn's Poetry
Mèng Chāngqī, a jinshì, had a wife, Ms. Sūn,
who was skilled in poetry.
Upon hearing of this, he thought that such talent was not suitable for a woman.
She had a “Poem on a White Candle” that said:
“Its inherent pure fragrance surpasses orchids,
a strip of white jade brings a chill.
In a spring night in the forbidden palace someday,
I'll drunkenly write heavenly letters and gaze intently.”
Her “Poem on Hearing the Qín” said:
“Close by, like a flowing spring from green cliffs;
afar, like a dark crane descending from the azure sky.”
Her “Poem of Thanks for Wine” said:
“How delightful is a moonlit night by the green window,
a cup sways, filling the heart with spring.”
The Qín Fù Yín Xiùcái
Lǐ Yuǎn's poem said:
“Human affairs are a thousand cups of wine,
fleeting years are a game of chess.”
Emperor Xuānzōng did not consider him capable of governing people,
and did not appoint him as a prefect.
When Wéi Zhuāng, Prime Minister of Shǔ, was taking the imperial examinations,
Huáng Cháo attacked the capital.
He wrote “Qín Fù Yín,” saying:
“The inner treasury burned to ashes of brocade,
the imperial street was trampled with the bones of nobles.”
Many were surprised by this,
and he was called the “Qín Fù Yín Xiùcái.”
The Qu Zǐ Prime Minister
Hé Níng, Prime Minister of Jìn,
was fond of composing *qu zǐ* (songs),
and was known as “The Qu Zǐ Prime Minister.”
A Hundred Poems Like One
Xuē Néng's poem “Returning Liú Réndé's Scroll” said:
“A hundred poems are like one,
the beginning of the scroll is like the end of the scroll.”
This satirized his inability to vary his style.
Lǐ Chéng's Rhyme-prose Is Still Here
Lǐ Chéng was promoted for his “Rhyme-prose on the Five Colors of the Sun,”
and became the Administrator of Hénán.
A candidate, Hào Xūzhōu, included his “Rhyme-prose on the Five Colors of the Sun” in his portfolio.
Chéng read to the last rhyme,
“Its rays stir the late waters,
it gazes down on cold mountains and sends forth splendor.”
He laughed heartily, saying:
“Lǐ Chéng's rhyme-prose is still here!
How can the auspicious sun send forth splendor at night?”
A Piece of Guāngshāng
Shěn Guāng had a “Rhyme-prose on Dòngtíng Lè.”
Wéi Xiù described this rhyme-prose as “a piece of guāngshāng (melancholy music).”
Gaining Support from Cats and Dogs Lú Yánràng had lines that said:
“Foxes rush past the official road,
dogs bark to open the inn door.”
And again:
“A hungry cat approaches a mouse hole,
a greedy dog licks the fish chopping board.”
And again:
“Chestnuts burst, burning through the felt mat,
a cat jumps, knocking over the tripod.”
These were greatly appreciated by the nobles of the time.
Lú said:
“I spent my life submitting petitions to high officials,
never expecting to gain support from cats and dogs.”
Bàqiáo Wind and Snow
Someone asked Zhèng Qǐxīn,
who replied:
"Poetic inspiration is found amidst the wind and snow of Bàqiáo, on a donkey's back.
How can it be obtained here?"
Poem on Qín Huáng
Xuānzōng was reviewing Zhào Gǔ's poetry scroll.
It contained a poem titled "On Qín Huáng" which read:
"From this, we know the state followed the axe (power),
and there were no scholars to distinguish right from wrong."
The emperor was displeased.
Eunuchs first used lǎnhù
After the Ān Shǐ Rebellion,
the military authority of the Táng dynasty was entirely handed over to powerful eunuchs;
Yú Cháo'ēn and Dòu Wényáng were their leaders.
It was only from Yáng Fùgōng that lǎnhù were first used;
before that, only zǐquē (purple belts) were used.
Rhapsody on a Coiled Dragon Tortoise
Pí Rìxiū went to call on Minister Guī Róng,
but was not received.
Consequently, he composed the "Rhapsody on a Coiled Dragon Tortoise,"
mocking Guī Róng for not showing his head.
Guī Róng also composed the "Rhapsody on Leather Slippers,"
and they slandered each other back and forth.
Lǐ Yìshān's inscription on Double Ninth Festival
Lǐ Shāngyǐn,
an old subordinate of Lìnghú Táo's father, Chǔ,
was poorly treated and not promoted.
On the Double Ninth Festival,
Yìshān went to the main hall
and left an inscription that read:
"Ten years under the springs, no news;
On the ninth day, before the wine cup, thoughts arise.
Your Lordship's official position is high, requiring a carriage to proceed,
The east pavilion allows no reason for me to peek again."
The Chancellor then locked this hall,
never using it again for the rest of his life.
Out of anger towards Yìshān,
he was only given the post of a junior staff member.
When the sky is still, stars can be plucked
Gù Yún wrote a eulogy for Gāo Yàn Gōng's study which said:
"When the sky is still, stars can be plucked."
Such a wonderfully daring phrase,
when applied to something utterly respectful,
is it appropriate?
Record of Successive Emperors
Kǒng Wěi,
whenever a court official presented a memorial,
would not have time to read it thoroughly,
but would simply say:
"The rise and fall of ancient and modern times,
I know them.
I am not clear what the advantages and disadvantages of your submission are."
Qiān Huì's "Memorial to Chancellor Cuī" was several thousand words long,
ranging from Yáo and Shùn at the top,
down to the Suí and Táng dynasties;
each rise and fall,
it was merely a "Record of Successive Emperors."
Chóngwén's snow poem
Gāo Chóngwén was originally a military commander;
he was appointed Jìedù of Xīchuān due to his achievements.
He once wrote a "Snow Poem" that said:
"Chóngwén, skilled in military arts, not civil,
Raises his spear and exits the fortress, known as General.
That 'jiào'er' shoots down a wild goose,
White feathers fall scattered in the empty air."
The vulgar term for calling a person is
"jiào'er."
Poem on a Kite
Gāo Pián was pacifying Shǔ,
and built a circumvallation forty lǐ long.
The court suspected him.
One day, hearing music,
they knew there was a change of heart,
so he wrote on a kite:
"In the silent night, string music resonates in the azure sky,
Gōng and Shāng trust the coming and going winds.
Vaguely like a tune, barely audible,
I only fear the wind blows it to another key."
Soon after, a report came that he had moved to Zhǔgōng.
Dòngtíng Lake has no beard in winter
Dòngtíng Lake is several hundred lǐ wide.
In autumn, the water returns to the ravines,
leaving only a single Xiāngchuān river.
Monk Qí Sì wanted to compose a poem,
but hadn't succeeded.
A certain Cài Yāyá recited:
"How pitiful Dòngtíng Lake,
When winter arrives, it has no beard."
This refers to its not forming a lake.
Jiǎ Dǎo Buddha
The jinshì Lǐ Dòng admired Jiǎ Dǎo so much
that he wished to cast his image and wear it on his head,
often chanting "Jiǎ Dǎo Buddha."
Crude and vulgar lines
Bāo Zàn often composed crude and vulgar lines,
such as: "Bitter bamboo shoots sprout green stumps,
Pomegranate trees hang small jars."
Also:
"A tomb is a mountain bell's son,
A boat is a water slipper."
And:
"Oars shake, scraping the boat's temples,
Wind moves, pounding the water's chest."
Poem of Self-Falling Advantage
A folk-transmitted "Lost Poem" says:
"Under the window, a poem keeps guests overnight,
In the room, no business accompanies the monk to sleep."
It is called the "Poem of Self-Falling Advantage."
Reining the horse on mountains and rivers
Gù Kuàng, dressed as a Daoist priest, was on Máoshān.
A scholar passed by, reciting:
"Reining the horse on mountains and rivers."
Kuàng said:
"When the wind comes, there is much smell of shit."
The scholar said:
"Daoist priest, do not be rude."
Gù said:
"It is Kuàng."
The man retreated in shame.
Mussels are not refined objects
Sūn Guāngxiàn's poem says:
"In the morning kitchen, cooking mussels,
On the spring loom, weaving cotton flowers."
Niú Hànlín said:
"How does my son know that mussels are not refined objects?"
Golden lock, jade hook
Dù Xùnhè's poem says:
"Old clothes are full of ash and lint,
New wine is full of bamboo dregs."
Chancellor Wéi's poem says:
"Stamps are sealed with golden locks,
Curtains are hooked with jade hooks."
Their styles can thus be seen.
Those who leave home become shaven
Chancellor Cáo Xiúng dreamed of becoming a monk,
and hated the idea.
A scholar said:
"Your Excellency will certainly be promoted day and night.
Those who leave home
have their heads shaven."
At that time, Chancellor Dù was dispatched to govern Jiāngxī,
and Cáo Xiúng was indeed greatly appointed.
Becoming a chicken-blessing elder
Lǐ Déyù, upon arriving at Zhūyá,
wrote forty-nine treatises
to express his aspirations.
He once sent a letter to Duàn Chéngshì:
"Since arriving in Yázhōu,
I am fortunately still robust and healthy.
The residents here mostly raise chickens,
which often fly into the official residence.
For now, I shall be a chicken-blessing elder."
Hóu Yǒng's first offense
Dòulú Zhuó, after being dismissed as chancellor,
took advantage of his leisure to visit a monastery and sit alone,
looking very much like an old man.
The scholar Hóu Yǒng entered from the outer gate,
and paid him no heed.
He bowed and said to the old man:
"Are you a civil attendant to the prefect?"
He replied:
"No."
"An aide?"
He replied:
"No."
"A prefect of a distant prefecture?"
He replied:
"A bit higher."
Again, he asked:
"A junior minister or supervisor?"
He replied:
"Even higher than that."
The scholar was startled and uneasy,
suspecting it was a chancellor.
Upon leaving the gate, he realized it was Chancellor Lú.
Returning home,
he submitted a long memorial acknowledging his first offense,
and Lú also forgave him.
He kept him and ordered wine,
ten bowls in all;
it was a minor punishment.
Hearing his father's bitter chanting, he was reborn as a son
Gù Kuàng, courtesy name Būwēng,
had a son in his later years,
who was the previous incarnation of Fēixióng.
One day, the son died suddenly.
Kuàng grieved profoundly,
and thus recited:
“An old man loses his beloved son,
weeping blood as the sun sets.
The old man is seventy years old,
this parting will not be for long.”
Fēixióng heard this in the underworld,
and pleaded his case.
The underworld officials all pitied him,
and thus allowed him to be reborn into Kuàng’s family.
At the age of three,
he could speak of having heard his father’s bitter lament in the underworld.
“Used up a lifetime’s heart”
Lǐ Pō’s poem says:
“Just with five-character lines,
used up a lifetime’s heart.”
Ghostly Soldiers Seek Revenge
Yáng Shōu was demoted and died in the Lingnan region.
Zhèng Yú, the Shàngshū, was stationed in Nánhǎi,
when he suddenly saw Chancellor Yáng.
The Chancellor said:
“I was harmed by the Army Supervisor Yáng Xuánjià’s plotting.
I petitioned the Emperor [of Heaven],
who granted me ghostly soldiers to seek revenge.
I wish to borrow a hundred thousand *mín*.”
Zhèng promised him half.
Yáng said:
“These are not copper coins.
When you burn them, please do not let them touch the ground.”
He bowed deeply and vanished.
Zhèng immediately prepared paper money and offered sacrifices.
Later, he saw Chancellor Yáng riding a white horse,
with a scarlet bow on his back,
and holding a red arrow.
A celestial officer held the horse’s reins.
Yáng said:
“I have killed Yáng Xuánjià,
shooting him in the leg.”
Soon after, Xuánjià suffered from a leg ailment and died.
White Lotus Jade Bracelet
During the Yuánhé era,
Sū Chāngyuǎn resided in Wúzhōng.
A maiden from the water country,
in plain clothes with a red face,
was like one of the immortals.
They became intimate,
and he gave her a jade bracelet.
One day,
he saw a white lotus blooming in front of the balustrade.
Within the flower was an object,
which was the jade bracelet.
Because of this, he broke off the relationship,
and it ended.
Flamboyant with Flames
The courtesan Xú Yuèyīng sent someone a poem that said:
“Sorrowfully, ten thousand things go against one’s wishes in the human world;
two went together, but only one returns.
I utterly detest the water in front of Píngwàng Pavilion,
that cruelly reflects mandarin ducks flying apart.”
A singing girl in Jīnlíng died and was cremated.
Yuèyīng said:
“This lady was flamboyant in life,
and even in death, she carries flames.”
Zhōu Lǐ Treasury
Lǐ Fú, the Shàngshū, was known as the “Zhōu Lǐ Treasury,”
for he was proficient in ancient classics.
Does Not Love Purple-robed Monks
Dí Guīchāng, the Yòuchéng, loved to associate with monks.
But if they wore purple *jiāshā*,
he would distance himself from them.
He often recited the poem of a predecessor:
“Passing by a bamboo monastery, I chanced upon a monk to converse with,
and thus gained another half-day of leisure in this floating life.”
Monks Compared to Shǔ Tea
Zhèng Gǔ also loved monks,
comparing them to “Shǔ tea,” saying:
“Not all monks are good,
but I do not wish to abandon them.”
Never Kept an Oiled Raincoat
Kǒng Jí, the Shìláng, encountered rain on his way back from court.
He took shelter under a street elder’s curtain,
and was invited into the main hall.
The elder, in a black cap and gauze turban,
greeted him very respectfully,
then prepared wine and delicacies,
all exquisitely fine.
Kǒng Gōng asked to borrow an oiled raincoat.
The elder said:
cold or not,
hot or not,
windy or not,
rainy or not,
have never kept an oiled raincoat.”
Kǒng Gōng unwittingly forgot his official aspirations.
Internal Urgency, Just Ask Guāng for a Visit
A Chéngláng,
experiencing an internal urgency while on horseback,
hurried to an empty residence.
He went straight to the privy.
This was the empty house of the great actor Mù Diāolíng.
As he was about to remount his horse,
the actor Mù suddenly arrived and said:
“Shìláng, if you have an internal urgency another day,
just ask Guāng to visit.”
Buying Shoes
Before Xiē Shìláng passed the imperial examination,
he went to a shop to buy shoes.
The shoemaker said:
“Scholar, what number is your foot?”
He replied:
“It has served Zhāowěi,
but it has never been assigned a number.”
Ascending Mount Huà
The Daoist Chéng Zǐxiāo ascended Mount Huà,
and accidentally stumbled.
Yǔwén Hàn joked:
“I don’t know if he can ascend or not,
but it’s strange that he’s suspended again and again.”
Āhuī Composes a *Huànxīshā* Poem
Zhāng Huī, the Shìláng, lost his beloved concubine,
and his grief was unending.
His nephew (or son) Shǔ composed a *Huànxīshā* poem:
“Pillow screen, censor, separated by embroidered curtains,
for two years, day and night, we longed for each other.
Only the good wind and bright moon should know.
Where have you gone, between heaven and earth?
Old joys, new dreams, felt upon waking.
Dusk, light rain, painted curtains hanging low.”
When the Grand Court recessed,
Zhāng Huī saw the poem and cried mournfully:
“It must have been composed by Āhuī.
However,
in terms of moral teachings,
it is still unacceptable.”
Āhuī was the childhood name of the Zhongjiàn.
Failed Examination Poems
Gāo Chán’s failed examination poem says:
“Heavenly jade peaches planted with dew,
red apricots by the sun planted near the clouds.
Hibiscus blooms by the autumn river,
not complaining to the east wind that it has not yet opened.”
Hú Zēng’s failed examination poem says:
“When will the Hanlin Academy stop marrying off daughters,
when will writing cease bearing sons?
New osmanthus in the imperial park blooms every year,
but commoners are not allowed to break off a single branch.”
Altar Offering Poem
Lǐ Yǎn’s “Altar Offering Poem” says:
“A red sealed letter,
to present matters of the mortal world.”
Heavenly Emperor Summons Huá Néng to Play Chess
Huá Néng, a Daìzhào,
was very skilled at chess,
rarely encountering an opponent.
A young man named Zhāng asked for a handicap of one line,
and Huá Néng responded readily.
One day, Zhāng said:
“I am not a chess player;
the Heavenly Emperor has commanded me to fetch you to play chess with him.
Please give instructions for your family affairs.”
Huá Néng passed away suddenly.
Fond of Eating Bamboo Partridges
A wealthy merchant died suddenly.
The physician Liáng Xīn examined him and asked:
“What did he usually crave?”
The servant replied:
“He was fond of eating bamboo partridges.”
Xīn said:
“Bamboo partridges eat *bànxià* (pinellia ternate),
he was poisoned by *bànxià*.”
He ordered pounded ginger juice to be administered to him,
and only then did the merchant revive.
Eating Sliced Raw Fish Causes Blurred Vision
There was a young man,
who constantly saw a mirror in his eyes.
The medical artisan Zhào Qīng said:
“Young master has eaten too much fish salad,
and the soy sauce and vinegar were not pleasant.
There are also fish scales in his chest,
which is why his vision is blurry.”
So, a bowl of mustard vinegar was prepared,
and he drank it on an empty stomach,
whereupon he recovered.
Poem by a Maidservant or Butler
Lǐ Chāngfú wrote fifty poems titled 《Bì Pú》 (Maidservant or Butler),
in which he said:
“Regardless of autumn chrysanthemums or spring flowers,
each one can guzzle empty stomach tea.
Without reason, do not let them frequently enter the storehouse,
for they demand a little of every idle thing.”
Daoist Priest's Impious Ritual
Two Daoist priests from the Yùjú Guàn ascended the altar to perform a ritual.
Their servant suddenly saw four figures in scarlet descend from the heavens,
drag the two Daoist priests before the altar,
whip their backs twenty times,
and shortly thereafter, they both developed boils on their backs and died.
Stele of the Liaodong Expedition
Zhāng Jiànzhāng encountered a storm while sailing the sea.
Suddenly, a man in green robes said:
“By celestial command,
I invite the Grand Master.”
Soon he arrived at a large island,
where there was a very grand female immortal.
After eating, he requested leave.
The female immortal said:
“You do not deceive in the dark room;
you are a gentleman.”
When he returned,
the wind and waves were calm.
Then, a whirlwind returned to the west bank,
and Emperor Tàizōng’s stele commemorating the Liaodong expedition was in the water.
Jiànzhāng wrapped wheat flour in silk,
went into the water, felt for the stele, and read it,
not missing a single character.
Dream of Flying Banners on Fingers
When Liú Rén'gōng was of humble status,
he dreamt of Buddhist banners flying from his fingers.
Someone said:
“When you are forty-nine years old,
you will surely attain the nobility of banners.”
Indeed, it came true.
Jupiter Enters Nándǒu
During the Qiánfú era,
Jupiter entered Nándǒu.
Those who knew the stars all said,
if Venus, Mars, or Saturn offend Nándǒu,
it means disaster,
but only Jupiter brings blessings.
The diviner Biān Gāng said:
“Wood in Nándǒu
forms the character ‘Zhū’ (朱).”
Those who understood said there was a prophecy for the Táng dynasty concerning scarlet robes.
The character Péi (裴) is interpreted as “scarlet robes” (緋衣),
and the character “Níu” (牛) with “Rén” (人)
is “Zhū” (朱).
Péi Dù and Níu Sēngrú
always corresponded to this prophecy.
How could they have known it would culminate in the “Zhū” of Dàngshān?
Jade Ruler
Zhào Guāngféng had an exceptionally elegant and distinguished demeanor,
and was known as “Jade Ruler.”
Examiner Disgraces His Student
Fēng Shùnqīng and his student Zhèng Zhìyōng both entered the Hànlín Academy.
Zhèng had exceptional talent,
while Fēng was considered dull.
People at the time called this “the examiner disgraces his student.”
Poem of the Sick Crane
The Buddhist monk Guànhxiū,
besides his literary and poetic talents,
was skilled in calligraphy.
Chéng Zhōnglìng asked him about his brushwork.
Xiū said:
“This matter requires ascending an altar to transmit it;
how can it be spoken of casually?”
Chéng resented him
and demoted him to Qiánzhōng.
Guànhxiū then expressed his feelings with the 《Bìng Hè Shī》 (Poem of the Sick Crane),
which said:
“It is said that where the air is pure, evil does not enter;
from where, then, did your sickness come?”
Five Whiskers
There was a villager in Jiānglíng
who worshipped the god Wǔ Zǐxū,
but mistakenly called him “Wǔ Zīxū” (Five Whiskers).
So he drew five men,
all with full beards,
and invoked them.
He sacrificed to them saying:
“One whisker,
two whiskers,
five whiskers.”
Chāng Ghosts
By the rivers and lakes, there are many chāng ghosts.
They often call out people's names,
and whoever answers will surely drown.
Collecting Turtle Urine
People in the south collect turtle urine,
because of the turtle's jealous nature when mating with snakes.
When collecting, they take a male turtle
and shine a mirror on it.
Once it sees the turtle in the mirror,
it becomes sexually aroused and loses its urine,
which is then collected with an implement.
Sleeping Dragons
Among the reeds and rushes of Jiāngnán,
sleeping dragons are often set ablaze.
In Chénzhōu, people set one dragon ablaze,
and on all sides, strong winds, thunder, and heavy rain
could not extinguish it.
Soon it turned to ashes,
but its horns did not melt,
remaining bright white like jade.
Shooting a Deer
There was a hunter in Tángzhōu who hunted in the deep mountains.
He shot a deer,
and when he looked at it,
it was a human.
The human called out to the hunter, saying:
“I have been dwelling in seclusion on this mountain since the beginning of the Suí dynasty.
Today, it is fated for me to die by your hand.
Just place me in a stone chamber.”
The hunter agreed,
and after a moment, the human expired.
The hunter returned ten days later,
but the body was gone.
Liùjiǎ Walking Kitchen
Those who have deep cultivation in Daoist practices
enjoy the “Liùjiǎ Walking Kitchen.”
Whatever they need,
it arrives as soon as the thought arises.
Five-Colored Ladder
Féng Juān was disheartened and struggling,
and he wrote a poem saying:
“When will the water-fetching officer's task be done?
When will the firewood-splitting councilor's work cease?”
At eighty-five years old,
he wound a five-colored cloth around a ladder,
penetrated the roof,
directly wearing his official hat and belt,
stood on one rung of the ladder, and passed away.
Walk This Way, Walk That Way
The Latter Lord of Shǔ wore a small headscarf,
its tip like an awl.
Many palace courtesans wore Daoist robes,
and adorned their hair with lotus flower crowns.
They then applied rouge to their cheeks,
calling it “drunken makeup.”
He composed lyrics saying:
“Walk this way,
walk that way,
just seeking flowers and willows.
Walk that way,
walk this way,
do not be weary of the golden cup of wine.”
Ān Tiānlóng
A commoner's son in Cāngzhōu
met a white snake on the road.
He tied it with a rope
and shook its head off.
Soon after,
thunder and lightning seized this son and took him into the sky,
where he was burned to death by electric fire.
There was a red inscription saying:
“This person killed Ān Tiānlóng,
and was executed by heavenly decree.”
Deer Antler
There are many deer in the southern regions.
One male supervises a hundred or so females.
They become thin in spring,
but grow fat in summer by eating calamus.
Hunters first tie a rope around their antlers,
cut them off,
and then scatter the ends.
Purple Flower
A dragon gave birth to two eggs,
one of which was a *jíliǎo* (吉了).
It went ashore and mated with a deer,
or it left its semen on a withered tree stump,
which was called "Zǐshāohuā" (紫稍花).
It strengthens the *yáng* (陽) channel.
Diǎndiǎn Shī (點點師)
In Língjiù Shān (靈鷲山) in Shǔzhōu (蜀州),
there was a monk who slept in a room.
He constantly pointed at his chest with his hand.
At that time, he was called "Diǎndiǎn Shī" (點點師).
Frying cakes to attract ghosts
Making frying cakes at night
often attracted ghosts and spirits.
A scholar went out into the main thoroughfare,
and there was a ghost saying,
"Last night, the monks of Chóngfúyuàn (崇福院) made frying cakes and meat broth.
I overturned their cooking vessels.
Their meat broth was mixed with ash and buried in the flower bed."
Another ghost, unable to get frying cakes at a certain family's house,
pushed their small maidservant into the fire.
Another ghost arrived
and said,
"I can cure fire burns.
You just need to give me frying cakes."
So, it taught them.
There was a *jī* (姬) [concubine],
who was making frying cakes at night.
Suddenly, a green hand appeared in the window,
took a cake, and disappeared.
Fire burns:
there is nothing better than vinegar mud,
it is very effective.
Official-hatted owl
*Qǐjū Láng* (起居郎) Sū Jiē (蘇階)
was despicable and immoral.
People called him an "official-hatted owl" (*yīguān tǔxiāo* ∙ 衣冠土梟).
One step, one plan
Lǐ Kèyòng (李克用) entered Wèibó (魏博).
Scouts reported,
"There are flags moving back and forth on the city wall."
King Jìn (晉王) said,
"Liú Xún (劉鄩) makes one plan for every step."
He ordered a more thorough investigation.
Indeed, straw was tied into human figures,
flags were tied to them,
donkeys carried them,
and they walked along the battlements.
Xún's (鄩) army had already left two days prior.
Mugwort cakes
Guànhyū (貫休) was very frank.
Once, a monk promised him mugwort jerky,
but had not yet delivered it.
He clapped his hands and said,
"Where are your mugwort cakes?"
White Peony Old Woman
When it comes to the affairs of a family,
it is crucial to guard against improper conduct.
It is often the case that
improper couplings occur
between young widows and virgin servants.
There was an old woman called "Bái Mǔdān" (白牡丹) [White Peony],
who kept abortifacient drugs.
At her death, she saw countless infants gathering and devouring her brain.
Reciting the Tiānpéng Zhòu (天蓬咒)
Cáo Sù's (曹肅) western manor was often tormented by a scholar riding a white crane.
There was a recluse named Wèi (魏処士),
who, when pursued by someone riding a donkey at night,
recited the *Tiānpéng Zhòu* (天蓬咒)
and was unharmed.
He also dreamt that ghosts were chasing him very urgently.
Someone in the sky gave him a large axe.
With one swing,
both the man and the donkey died.
Donkey thief
When Wáng Xiānzhǔ (王先主) was obscure,
he stole a donkey and was punished.
When he attacked Dōngchuān (東川),
the soldiers guarding the battlements called him "donkey thief" day and night.
Xiānzhǔ (先主) said to the actor Wáng Shèchéng (王舍城),
"Scold them for me!"
The actor pointed a halberd at the people on the city wall,
and told them to listen quietly,
saying,
"Did I steal the donkey from your house?"
Everyone on the city wall laughed.
One day,
Xiānzhǔ (先主) bared his back to Shèchéng (舍城), showing no scars.
Shèchéng (舍城) said,
"Excellent!
Excellent!
Where did you get this ointment?"
Shǔ Zhǔ's (蜀主) poetry
The Later Lord of Shǔ (蜀後主) was indulgent in wine and women.
On moonlit nights, he would often say,
"Melancholy!
Melancholy!"
He also said,
"Indeed, how short is a human life?
Those with fate are merely puppets."
Upon entering Qín (秦),
he reached Jiànzhōu (劍州)
and admired the beauty of the river water.
He wrote a poem saying,
"It's not to attend the imperial court
that I'd like to build a thatched hut here."
Upon arriving in Xiányáng (咸陽),
he composed a song saying,
"It's all just a puppet show."
Avoiding a summer offering
Guànhyū's (貫休) monastic discipline was strict and pure;
he sought alms to support his community.
Xú Jiǎnfū (徐簡夫) said,
"The elders in various places
are like dung beetles.
When they see the dung burnt out,
they suddenly fly away."
The monks gathered and ate according to the elder.
When the monk died,
they dispersed immediately.
Xiū (休) was angry and
stormed out.
Jiǎnfū (簡夫) said,
"He has again avoided a summer offering."
Substitute
Lǐ Yù (李遇), the Dūtóu (都頭) of Jīngnán (荊南),
was gravely ill.
He was taken to the underworld
and met a person
who had died earlier.
He said,
"How did *Chángshì* (常侍) come here?"
Another person said,
"Lǐ Yù (李遇) has already been summoned."
Then he revived
and saw his wife weeping.
Under his body lay a painted figure,
called a "substitute" (*tìdài* ∙ 替代).
Literacy causes emotional disturbance
Lǐ Yìshān's (李義山) *Zázǎn* (雜纂) says:
"If a woman is literate, she will become emotionally disturbed.
It is especially not advisable for her to write poetry,
as poetic thoughts do not extend beyond two hundred *lǐ* (里)."
Dragon's nest overturned
In Yílíng (夷陵) River, large logs sometimes floated,
blocking the water surface.
People called this "dragon's nest overturned" (*lóngcháo fān* ∙ 龍巢翻).
Begging for food at a courtesan's house
Péi Xiū (裴休), wearing a coarse monastic robe,
held an alms bowl and begged for food at a courtesan's house.
He said,
"Not being tainted by worldly desires,
one can preach the Dharma to people."
Extraordinary commoner
Pí Rìxiū (皮日休) was arrogant and unrestrained.
He called himself an "extraordinary commoner" (*jiànqì bùyī* ∙ 間氣布衣).
Stealing from Jiāngdōng (江東)
Yè Wáng (鄴王) Luó Shàoxián (羅紹咸) admired the poetry of Luó Yǐn (羅隱) from Jiāngdōng (江東).
He called his collected works "stealing from Jiāngdōng" (*tōu Jiāngdōng* ∙ 偷江東).
Monk Luán's (鸞) poetry
Monk Luán (鸞) disdained Jiǎ Dǎo's (賈島) poetry.
He ironically recited his own lines, saying:
"The whale's eye burns, reddening half the sea;
the ao's (鰲) head, the waves crash, churning the sky white."
He also said,
"I cannot dwell on thoughts within fences and puddles."
Playing the *qín* (琴) and blowing the flute
Wēn Tíngyún (溫庭筠) was skilled at playing the *qín* (琴) and blowing the flute.
He said,
"If there are strings, I will pluck them;
if there are holes, I will blow them.
There is no need for Kētíng (柯亭) bamboo or Cuàntóng (爨桐) wood."
Consulting the manual for wrestling
When Yán Wáng Yún (顏王雲) discussed military tactics,
he would invariably roll up his sleeves and shout commands,
as if facing a great enemy.
People called him "consulting the manual for wrestling" (*jiǎnpǔ juézhī* ∙ 檢譜角觝).
No household tax in the realm of intoxication
Liú Xūbái (劉虛白) was fond of wine.
He had a poem saying:
"Knowing there is no household tax in the realm of intoxication,
let the lower *dāntián* (丹田) lie fallow."
Princess does not view the sick
Xuānzōng's Wànshòu Princess's consort, Zhèng Shàngshū's younger brother, Kǎi, had a critical illness.
The Emperor sent someone to inquire about it.
Upon his return,
he asked if the Princess had visited the sick man.
He replied:
"She's at Cí'ēnsì watching a play."
The Emperor said:
"I wonder why the scholar-officials are not close to me;
there is truly a reason for it."
He summoned the Princess and reprimanded her, saying:
"How can your younger brother-in-law be ill,
and you go watch a play elsewhere?"
He immediately sent her back to her residence.
Sending Dù Huángshāng money and a felt carriage
Lǐ Shīdào was tyrannical,
and feared Dù Huángshāng as prime minister.
He dared not be disrespectful,
so he ordered a diligent official to send several thousand strings of cash,
and also a felt carriage worth a thousand strings.
The envoy waited in front of the residence
for several days.
A green palanquin emerged,
followed by two tattered green-clad servants.
He asked:
"Who is that?"
They replied:
"The Prime Minister's wife."
The envoy then returned
and reported this to Shīdào.
This foiled his plan,
and he dared not act disrespectfully for the rest of his life.
The young man at the end of the seating was completely different.
Pān Yán,
a Hanlin Academician during Dézōng's reign,
had a wife
who was Liú Yàn's daughter.
The Jīngzhào Prefect had some business,
and waited for several days but could not get an audience.
He then gave the gatekeeper three hundred bolts of silk.
The wife said:
"How can a subject,
the Jīngzhào Prefect, wishing to meet someone,
give three hundred bolts of silk to a servant?
His danger is evident."
She advised Yán to relinquish his position.
Their son, Mèngyáng,
was initially a Vice Minister.
His mother said:
"With your talent,
to be a Vice Minister,
I fear disaster will strike.
Try gathering your colleagues;
I will observe them."
When the guests arrived,
the wife happily said:
"They are all your peers.
Who is the wretched green-clad young man at the end of the seating?"
He replied:
"It's the Remonstrance Official Dù Huángshāng."
The wife said:
"This person is completely different;
he must be a famous minister."
Truthfully admitting one's limitations is better than being able to compose poetry.
Yuán Zhěn was in Èzhōu,
and Zhōu Fù was his aide.
The Prime Minister composed a poem,
and ordered the officials in the office to compose matching verses.
Fù said:
"I merely obtained an official position through my association with Your Excellency;
in truth,
I am incapable of composing poetry or essays."
The Prime Minister said:
"To admit the truth so readily
is better than being able to compose poetry."
Gold and bronze tea caddies, covered with something
Cuī Zào retired for a year or two,
and felt restless in his leisure.
He said to his sons and nephews:
"We haven't received any gold and bronze tea caddies, covered with something, from other circuits!"
So, he resumed his official duties.
Money up to 100,000 can reach the gods.
Zhāng Yánshǎng was managing the Ministry of Finance.
There was a case that was quite unjust and excessive.
The Duke summoned his clerks and sternly warned them:
"This must be resolved within ten days!"
The next day,
there was a small note on his desk that read:
please do not investigate this case."
The Duke was angry and urged them on further.
The next day,
the note said:
"50,000 strings of cash."
The Duke was also angry.
The next day,
he again saw a note that read:
"100,000 strings of cash."
He then stopped investigating.
His close associates inquired about it.
The Duke said:
"When money reaches 100,000,
it can reach the gods.
There's nothing that cannot be done.
I fear that disaster will strike me,
so I cannot but stop."
Yuán Zài obtained a thousand bolts of silk with one letter.
When Yuán Zài was in the Secretariat,
an elderly man came to seek his patronage.
He judged that the man was not fit for office,
so he gave him a letter for Héběi.
The elderly man had no choice but to take it.
When he arrived at Yōuzhōu,
he opened and examined it,
but there was not a single word,
only a signature.
He was greatly remorseful and angry,
and wanted to return.
He tried to visit a yamen clerk.
A moment later,
a high-ranking officer holding a box
again requested the letter.
The letter entered,
and he was lodged in the best quarters.
He stayed for several days,
and was presented with a thousand bolts of silk.
Monk Duàn composed "Xīliángzhōu."
Yuán Zài's son, Bóhé,
wielded immense influence both inside and outside the court.
The Commissioner of Fúzhōu sent him musicians and performers.
Upon their arrival,
they could not be presented for half a year.
The envoy spied on the household staff,
and found that Pípá player Kāng Kūnlún was the closest.
So he lavishly bribed him to facilitate the introduction.
Once the performers were presented,
Bóhé tested them once,
and gave them all away.
There was a monk, Duàn, who was skilled at the pípa.
He had composed his own "Xīliángzhōu."
Kūnlún asked for it,
but he wouldn't give it.
After Kūnlún gave him half of his music,
he transmitted it.
Xuānzōng asked about the eunuch envoys.
Xuānzōng asked Wéi Ào:
"How do I compare to the eunuch envoys?"
Ào immediately recounted the Emperor's unparalleled power and control over previous dynasties.
The Emperor closed his eyes and waved his hand, saying:
"Not at all!
Not at all!
I'm still afraid of them.
What plan should we devise?"
Ào said:
"To scheme outside the court
might lead to incidents like those at the end of Tàihé.
It would be better to select talented and insightful individuals from among them
and entrust them with the plan."
The Emperor said:
"I have already done so.
From yellow to green,
from green to crimson,
they are all grateful.
But once they wear purple robes, they become a single faction."
The Duke was ashamed and withdrew.
Establishing the Heir Apparent
Péi Xiū once argued that "the Heir Apparent should be established."
Xuānzōng said:
"If the Heir Apparent is established,
then I will become an idle man."
Long days are only passed with a game of chess.
When Xuānzōng held court,
the officials waiting for an audience had to wait until their breathing was even
before he would ask about affairs.
Lìnghú Xiāng recommended Lǐ Yuǎn to govern Hángzhōu.
The Emperor said:
"Yuǎn's poem states, 'Long days are only passed with a game of chess.'
Can he govern a prefecture?"
Yuǎn's memorial of thanks from the prefecture.
Xuānzōng read Yuǎn's memorial of thanks from his prefecture.
His attendants said:
"This is not worth troubling Your Sacred Majesty."
The Emperor said:
"Apart from routine memorials and reports,
only these memorials
show genuine sincerity. How can I not know?
I dare not overlook them."
Zhāng Chángshǐ's calligraphy.
Zhāng Chángshǐ was the county magistrate of Chángshú.
An old man passed by and submitted a petition, which was judged and taken away.
A few days later, he returned,
saying,
"I didn't really come to discuss the matter;
I just saw that your handwriting was wonderfully skillful."
The price of rice is currently high, so living is not easy.
Bái Jūyì first presented his poetry to Gù Kuàng.
Gù Kuàng looked at his name closely and said,
"The price of rice is currently high,
so living (Jū) is not easy (Yì)."
He opened the scroll and the first lines read:
"On the plains of Xiányáng, the grass,
withers and flourishes once a year.
Wildfires cannot burn it completely,
and the spring breeze makes it grow again."
Gù Kuàng said,
"If you can express such words,
then living (Jū) will be easy (Yì)."
Because of this, he promoted him,
and his reputation greatly flourished.
Exceptionally towering.
Qiáo Yí,
for the prefectural examination of Jīngzhàofǔ, wrote an impressive line in his "Ouwā Mǎ Fù" (Ode to the Ouwā Horse):
"Four hooves like flowing silk,
traversing the frost blossoms of the boundless desert;
a single snort generating wind,
causing the leaves of the Hú mountains to fall."
They immediately wanted to rank him first,
but then said,
"He is exceptionally towering;
it is appropriate to recommend him as an assistant in the examination."
The Prefect of Yànmén.
Lǐ Hè came to present his songs and poems.
Hán Lìbù returned,
extremely exhausted,
and unfastened his belt to read them.
The first poem, "Yànmén Tàishǒu Xíng" (Song of the Prefect of Yànmén), said:
"Dark clouds press on the city, as if to crush it;
armor gleams in the sun, like golden scales opening."
He then re-fastened his belt,
and invited him in.
Seeking Lǐ Hè's lost writings.
Lǐ Fān often collected Lǐ Hè's songs and poems.
Knowing that Lǐ Hè's maternal cousin had been acquainted with Lǐ Hè's writing,
he entrusted him to seek out what was left.
That person said,
"I remember all the pieces he composed,
and many have been revised.
Please let me correct those you have collected."
Lǐ Fān gave them all to him.
After a full year, he disappeared.
Lǐ Fān was angry
and summoned him for questioning.
He replied,
"I resented his arrogance and neglect,
and always thought of retaliating.
His writings have already been thrown into the latrine."
Therefore, few of Lǐ Hè's poems and writings have been circulated.
Acting as Son of Heaven.
Miáo Dìshī failed the examination.
As he left the capital gate,
an old man said,
"Do you want to know about your future?"
Miáo Dìshī said,
"Do I have a chance at a degree?"
The old man said,
"You have something much greater."
Miáo Dìshī said,
"A prefecture?"
The old man said,
"Higher."
Miáo Dìshī said,
"An Imperial Censor?"
The old man said,
"Higher."
"A general or prime minister?"
The old man said,
"Higher."
Miáo Dìshī angrily said,
"Will I act as the Son of Heaven?"
The old man said,
"As for the Son of Heaven,
you won't get to be the true one,
but you will get to be a pseudo one."
Later, he indeed became a general and prime minister.
When Dézōng passed away,
he briefly acted as the chief minister for three days.
Niú Sēngrú visits Yú Dí.
Niú Sēngrú went to Xiāngyáng to visit Yú Dí,
seeking recognition.
Yú Dí treated him as a common traveler.
Niú Sēngrú became angry and left.
Later, Yú Dí summoned a guest officer and asked if Scholar Niú had left yet.
He replied,
"He has already left."
Yú Dí immediately ordered a junior officer to carry a letter and five hundred bolts of silk to chase after him.
Niú Sēngrú did not open the letter,
bowed, and turned back.
Taking a child to compensate for golden color.
Hóu Qìng, from Nányáng, Liáng,
had a bronze statue.
Hóu Qìng intended to gild his ox.
The statue said,
"You and your wife have long owed me my golden color and have not repaid it.
Now I will take your ugly daughter to fulfill the color."
By dawn,
the ugly daughter (Chǒuduō) had died.
The statue suddenly acquired a golden color by itself,
its light illuminating the four neighbors.
The neighbors all came to see it.
Curing eyes with a golden spatula.
Zhāng Yuán of the Later Zhōu dynasty.
His grandfather had lost his sight.
Zhāng Yuán lit a seven-tiered lamp for seven days and nights,
reading the "Yàoshī Jīng" (Sūtra of the Medicine Master).
Each day he walked and prayed,
saying,
"Today I universally offer this lamplight to the Dharma Realm,
begging for my grandfather's eyes to see,
and I, Yuán, ask to take his blindness."
That night he dreamt of an old man
curing his grandfather's eyes with a golden spatula.
Three days later,
his grandfather's eyes indeed recovered.
Dreaming of Pindola.
Shì Dào'ān of the Jìn dynasty
annotated the Prajñā Sūtras.
Fearing they might not be rational,
he vowed,
"If what I explain does not deviate from reason,
then a propitious sign shall appear."
Thereupon, he dreamt of a Western monk
with white hair and long eyebrows,
who said,
"The sūtras you have annotated are quite in accordance with reason.
I cannot enter Nirvāṇa,
but reside in this realm.
I shall assist in their propagation.
You may offer food from time to time."
Later, Yuǎn Gōng said,
"The monk your esteemed master dreamt of
was indeed Pindola."
Girl in a green robe and white cap transforms into a sheep.
In Cháng'ān's market in the Táng dynasty,
every year after New Year's Day,
people would invite each other to eat and drink,
calling it "Chuánzuò" (Passing the Seats).
Zhào Tàicì of the East Market was to host it.
A guest arrived early
and saw a young girl in a green robe and white cap on a pounding block,
tied by a rope around her neck to the pounding post.
She wept and said,
"I am the master's daughter.
I stole money from my parents,
intending to buy cosmetics,
but died before I could.
The money is now in the wall of the kitchen.
Because of this, I incurred this sin,
and now I must pay with my life."
After speaking, she transformed into a green sheep
with a white head.
The guest was startled and told the host.
The host asked about her appearance,
and realized it was his youngest daughter,
who had died two years ago.
They found the money in the kitchen wall.
Thereupon, they sent the sheep to a Buddhist temple,
closed their doors, and no longer ate meat.
Owing money and becoming an ox.
During the Yǒnghuī era,
Lù Bódá, a man from Fénzhōu, owed a thousand coins to a fellow villager.
Later, he swore before the Buddha with the moneylender, saying,
"If I have not repaid you,
I vow to die and become an ox for your family."
A year later, he died.
The moneylender's cow gave birth to a red calf
with three white characters on its forehead:
"Lù Bódá."
The Sūtra of Forty-two Chapters.
Hàn Míngdì dreamt of a golden man flying through the air.
Not long after,
the monk Móténg arrived from Tiānzhú.
Thereupon, a monastery was established for him to reside in.
This is the Bái Mǎ Sì west of Luòchéng today.
He translated the "Sìshí'èr Zhāng Jīng" (Sūtra of Forty-two Chapters),
which was transmitted to the world.
諸天 Yǔ
Dōushuàitiān Yǔ Mónízhū,
Hùshìchéng Yǔ Měishàn,
Āxiūluótiān Yǔ Bīngzhàng.
Yánfú Shìjiè is said to be hot.
晤言消戚戚 (Wùyán Xiāo Qīqī)
Xiè Ān wrote to Zhī Dùn, saying:
"Life is but a temporary stay.
To be constantly troubled
—I await your coming to converse and dispel it."
般若臺 (Bānruòtái)
Chén Wéndá recited the *Jīngāng Jīng*.
Someone entered the underworld
and saw a platform being built.
They asked,
"This is the Bānruòtái,
awaiting Chén Wéndá."
判夢四法 (Pànmèng Sìfǎ)
There are four methods for interpreting dreams:
First, the熏習 (xūnxí) of ignorance;
second, the wandering of old consciousness;
third, great excesses;
fourth, omens of good and evil.
鵲尾爐 (Quèwěilú)
An incense burner with a handle that can be held
is called a "Quèwěilú."
誦法華經 (Sòng Fǎhuá Jīng)
Shì Huìqìng recited the *Fǎhuá Jīng*.
At night, there were sounds of finger-snapping praise in the air.
Once, encountering a storm,
Qìng continued to recite, and the boat,
amidst the waves,
was as if pulled by someone,
suddenly arriving at the shore.
醉鄉所宜 (Zuìxiāng Suǒyí)
There are things suitable for drunkenness:
Drunkenness among flowers is best by day,
to absorb their light.
Drunkenness in snow is best at night,
to dispel its cold.
Drunkenness from triumph is best with singing,
to express its harmony.
Drunkenness when about to part is best with striking a bowl,
to strengthen its spirit.
Drunkenness with an elder is best with careful rhythm and strict rules,
fearing their contempt.
Drunkenness with a dashing person is best with more goblets and added banners,
to assist their fervor.
Drunkenness in a tower is best in summer,
to draw upon its coolness.
Drunkenness by water is best in autumn,
to let its freshness pervade.
These all involve discerning what is suitable
and engaging with the scene.
To do otherwise
is to miss the heaven of drinking.
君子中人小人 (Jūnzǐ Zhōngrén Xiǎorén)
As for wine:
that which is clear in color, heavy in taste, and sweet is called "sage" (shèng);
