that which is golden in color, mellow and bitter in taste is called "worthy" (xián);
that which is black in color, sour and thin is called "foolish" (yú).
One who makes others drunk with homemade glutinous rice wine (jiāláo nuòshāng) is a jūnzǐ;
one who makes others drunk with homemade millet wine (jiāláo shǔshāng) is a zhōngrén;
one who makes others drunk with common sorghum wine (xiàngláo shúshāng) is a xiǎorén.
不歡之候 (Bùhuān zhī Hòu)
There are nine occasions of displeasure:
The host is stingy,
first.
The guest slighting the host,
second.
The arrangements are shabby and not properly presented,
third.
Music plays, but the courtesans are arrogant,
fourth.
Frequently changing the drinking game rules,
fifth.
Engaging in bovine drinking (excessive),
sixth.
Alternating with strange jokes,
seventh.
Hands touching each other,
eighth.
Gambling with dice,
ninth.
害馬 (Hàimǎ)
One who is not suitable for drinking with is called a "Hàimǎ (harmful horse) in the pleasure arena."
歡候 (Huānhòu)
There are thirteen occasions for pleasure:
Getting the right time,
first.
Host and guest having been apart for a long time,
second.
Wine being mellow and the host strict,
third.
Not singing without a goblet,
fourth.
Being unable to make one feel ashamed,
fifth.
Not having a heavy meal while drinking,
sixth.
Not moving the mat,
seventh.
The recorder (lùshì) having a stern demeanor and strict rules,
eighth.
The prefect (míngfǔ) not accepting solicitations,
ninth.
Abolishing selling laws,
tenth.
Abolishing substitutions,
eleventh.
Not relying on wine,
twelfth.
Making sure there is no excessive joy or violence,
thirteenth.
明府 (Míngfǔ)
In all drinking,
one person acts as the Míngfǔ,
in charge of moderation.
A weak drinker is called a "vacant official" (kuàngguān),
meaning cold.
A strong drinker is called a "harsh government" (kēzhèng),
meaning hot.
飲餙 (Yǐnshì)
Yǐnshì refers to
things like placing cold mats and ice in summer.
三材 (Sāncái)
In all drinking,
one person acts as the recorder (lùshì),
to correct those seated.
One must choose those with drinking talents.
There are three talents:
being good at rules, knowledgeable in music, and a generous host.
犯觥令 (Fàngōnglìng)
Upon the first offense against the rules,
the recorder punishes them according to their household (status).
If they do not stop,
a goblet is placed.
The recorder throws a banner in front
and says:
"So-and-so has violated the goblet rule."
飲儲 (Yǐnchú)
Side dishes for drinks are called "Yǐnchú."
Drinking vessels:
large ones are called Wǔ,
small ones are called Wén.
六鶴齊飛 (Liùhè Qífēi)
In ancient times,
social gatherings often involved board games.
The *Lièzi* says:
"The Yú clan set up music and drank wine,
playing board games and hosting scholars.
Their pieces were made of ivory,
decorated with feathers,
five inches long,
six in number,
with one end carved
into the shape of a crane."
The *Xiānjīng* says:
"Six Cranes Flying Together" (Liùhè Qífēi)
is indeed its name.
From the Sòng and Qí dynasties onwards,
many used chúpú (a dice game) to decide drinking forfeits.
The design of dice
is also a variation of Liùhè and chúpú.
Holding the rules,
spinning the cup like a ram's horn,
and flicking the sleeves like a tiger's eye.
Only then can one 'hunt and fish' the wind and moon,
shoot arrows at sheng and yu,
to summon fellow drinkers.
狂花病葉 (Kuánghuā Bìngyè)
There are some who are brave in bovine drinking (excessive),
who are drenched with a giant goblet,
which both shakes 'mad flowers' and withers 'sick leaves'.
Drinking circles refer to those who glare as "mad flowers,"
and those whose eyes are sleepy as "sick leaves."
招手令 (Zhāoshǒulìng)
The Signal for Beckoning says:
Flatten its tiger's breast,
which means the palm.
Bend its pine roots,
which means the finger joints.
Place the squatting osprey beneath the tiger's breast.
The squatting osprey
is the thumb.
Place the hooked halberd beside the jade pillar.
The hooked halberd
is the index finger.
The jade pillar
is the middle finger.
The hidden hornless dragon
is three fen wider than the jade pillar.
The hidden hornless dragon
is the ring finger.
The strange soldier
is one cùn wider than the hidden hornless dragon.
The strange soldier
is the little finger.
Kill its three luò,
which means drooping the wrist.
Bring to life its five peaks,
a collective term for the five fingers.
Ten Sayings of the Signal
The Signal has ten sayings:
There is "eight heads,"
there is "lifting the tail,"
there is "throwing over,"
there is "turning the river,"
there is "picking the heart,"
there is "tapping the head,"
there is "five segments,"
there is "three parts,"
there is "turning open,"
there is "closing to the ground."
Collecting Names
Collecting human names from wind and clouds,
such as:
Zhū Yún, Húlǜ Míngyuè.
Collecting human names from birds and animals,
such as:
Wèi Bào, Biǎn Què.
Collecting human names from plants and trees,
such as:
Dèng Ài, Yuè Jiāo.
Collecting human names from cloth,
such as:
Jì Bù, Yuán Sī.
Collecting human names from colors,
such as:
Wèi Qīng, Lǐ Bái.
Collecting human names from physical forms,
such as:
Zhāng Ěr, Bó Yá.
Collecting human names from relatives,
such as:
Wáng Láng, Wèi Zǐfū.
Collecting human names from furniture,
such as:
Liú Pénzǐ, Gōngsūn Chǔjiù.
Collecting human names from provinces and commanderies,
such as:
Féng Táng, Kǒng Guānglǐ.
Method for Cold Feast Ice
To make ice for a cold feast:
In midsummer or early summer, place a wok beside a well.
Use a large piece of crystal,
the size of a fist,
without flaws or cracks.
Boil newly drawn water with a fierce fire until it boils a thousand times.
Take it out.
Use a bottle with a small mouth and a large belly.
Fill it with the hot water.
Seal its mouth with oilcloth,
preventing any air from leaking.
Then boil it again in a double boiler until it boils a thousand times.
Immediately sink it to the bottom of the well.
Take it out at dawn,
break the bottle,
and ice will have formed.
Thunderous Ferment
In summer months,
when there is a great thunderstorm,
collect rainwater.
Scoop rice and cook it into a meal.
Brew wine.
It is called "Thunderous Ferment."
Bamboo's Birthday
Bamboo has a birthday:
the thirteenth day of the fifth month.
When transplanting bamboo,
it is advisable to do so on this day.
If it is rainy and the soil is loose,
then the bamboo shoots will grow crisscrossing next year.
Stealing Bamboo Shoots
If commoners steal bamboo shoots,
bury beneath the wall across the fence.
Another version says bury cats and dogs.
The shoots will then burst forth on their own.
Volume 43
End.
Educating Children is Like Saving the Sick
Those who cannot educate their children
do not wish to lead them into evil,
but are heavy of speech,
fear harming their reputation,
and cannot bear to beat their skin and flesh.
One should use illness as an analogy:
How can one not use medicine, acupuncture, and moxibustion to save them?
The Solemnity of Father and Son
The solemnity between father and son cannot be treated with familiarity.
The love between kin cannot be treated with informality.
If informal, kindness and filial piety will not connect.
If familiar, laziness and disrespect will arise.
Not Personally Teaching Children
Someone asked:
"Why does a gentleman not personally teach his children?"
The reply was:
"The Shī Jīng has satirical verses,
the Lǐ Jīng has warnings against suspicion,
the Shū Jīng has tales of rebellion and chaos,
the Chūnqiū has criticisms of wickedness,
the Yì Jīng has images of myriad things.
None of these are suitable for father and son to speak of directly,
thus they are not personally taught."
Loving Children
A person's love for their children
lies in being impartial.
The wise and outstanding can naturally be cherished and loved.
The stubborn and dull should also be pitied and cared for.
Those with favoritism,
even if they wish to show them special favor,
are instead harming them.
Gòngshū's death
was truly caused by his mother.
The King of Zhào's execution
was truly caused by his father.
Liú Biǎo's family destruction and clan annihilation,
Yuán Shào's territorial loss and troop decimation,
can serve as warnings.
Teaching Xiānbēi Language and Playing Pípá
In the Qí Dynasty, there was a scholar-official who said:
"I have a son
who is quite knowledgeable in writing.
If I teach him Xiānbēi language and how to play the pípá,
and he serves high officials,
there will be no one who does not favor and love him.
This is also an important matter."
How strange!
This man's way of educating his son.
Even if through these skills you yourselves achieve the rank of minister or prime minister,
I would not wish you all to do so.
Servants as Sparrows and Rats, Wives and Children as Wind and Rain
After both parents have passed,
brothers looking out for each other
should be like body and shadow,
sound and echo.
Cherish the physical remains of ancestors,
and value one's own shared vital energy.
For example, when living in a house,
if there's a hole, plug it;
if there's a crack, seal it.
Thus, there will be no worries of collapse.
If one does not care for sparrows and rats,
and does not guard against wind and rain,
when walls collapse and pillars fall,
it cannot last long.
Servants being sparrows and rats,
wives and children being wind and rain—
how extreme!
Not Dressed in Hat and Robe, Not Responding
If brothers are not harmonious,
then sons and nephews will not be loved.
If sons and nephews are not loved,
then distant relatives will be estranged,
and children will become enemies.
Liú Jìn of Wú Pèiguó and his elder brother Liú Huán lived in connected houses, separated by a wall.
Huán called him several times, but he did not answer,
only responding after a long while.
Huán asked him, surprised,
and he said he hadn't put on his hat and robe yet.
Stepmother Abusing Child
Later husbands often dote on the orphans of their predecessors,
but stepmothers invariably abuse the children of their predecessors' wives.
This is the natural consequence of circumstances.
Luòsuǒ Āgū Cān
The nature of women
is often to dote on their sons-in-law and abuse their daughters-in-law.
Doting on sons-in-law causes resentment among brothers;
abusing daughters-in-law gives rise to calumny among sisters.
If a woman's conduct causes her to be offensive to her family,
her mother is truly responsible for it.
This even led to the proverb:
"Luòsuǒ Āgū Cān" (The worn-out aunt eats last),
which is its retribution.
How can one not be warned?
Cherishing Classics
All borrowed classics must be cherished.
If they are already damaged,
they should be mended and repaired.
This is also one of the hundred virtues of a scholar-official.
Jiāyáng Jiāng Lù,
when reading, even if he had not finished,
and though there was great urgency,
would always wait for the scrolls to be neatly rolled up
before getting up.
People did not tire of asking him for loans [of books].
Some leave books scattered on tables,
with ledgers and dossiers dispersed,
often stained by children, servants, or maids,
or damaged by wind, rain, insects, or rats.
This truly harms one's virtue.
Avoiding Taboos
During the Liáng dynasty, Xiè Jǔ had a great reputation.
He would scrupulously avoid any word that was a taboo (the name of an emperor or superior),
and this was ridiculed by the world.
A scholar in Yángdū had a personal name, Shěn (審),
and yet he socialized with someone whose surname was Shěn (沈).
When Shěn (沈) wrote to him,
he used the given name but omitted the surname.
This is not human nature.
As for those who avoid taboos,
they may use a homophone or synonym to replace it.
If a minister's personal name is Bái (白),
there is a saying of "Wǔ Hào" (Five Whitenesses) [instead of "Wǔ Bái"].
If King Lì's personal name is Cháng (長),
a qín might be described as "xiū duǎn" (long and short) [instead of "cháng duǎn"].
I have not heard of calling cloth "bù hào" (cloth whiteness) [instead of "bù bái"],
or calling kidneys and intestines "shèn xiū" (kidney length) [instead of "shèn cháng"].
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng's childhood name was Ā Liàn (阿練).
His descendants all called liàn (練, to refine) "juàn" (絹, silk),
so they called "xiāoliàn wù" (物品, refined objects) "xiāojuàn wù" (物品, silk objects).
Or some who had a taboo name Yún (雲),
called fēnyún (紛紜, confused) "fēnyīn" (紛絪, confused).
Some who had a taboo name Tóng (桐),
called a tóng tree "bái tiě shù" (白鐵樹, white iron tree).
These are merely jokes.
The Duke of Zhōu named his son Qín (禽),
and Confucius named his son Lǐ (鯉).
This was limited to their own persons,
so there was naturally no prohibition.
As for the prince of Wèi and the crown prince of Chǔ, both named Jīshī (蟣虱, lice and fleas);
Chángqīng (長卿) named "Quǎnzǐ" (犬子, dog cub);
Wáng Xiū (王修) named "Gǒuzǐ" (狗子, dog cub);
these only involve connections [to others],
and the principle is not well-understood.
What was practiced in antiquity
is laughed at today.
In the north, some names are Lǘ (驢, donkey), Gǒu (狗, dog), or Túnzǐ (豚子, piglet) for children.
To make them refer to themselves by such names, or for their brothers to use them,
how could one bear it?
In the Former Hàn, there was Yǐn Wēngguī (尹翁歸);
in the Later Hàn, there was Zhèng Wēngguī (鄭翁歸);
in Liáng, there was Kǒng Wēngguī (孔翁歸);
in Jìn, there were Xǔ Sībi (許思妣) and Mèng Shàogū (孟少孤).
Such names
should fortunately be avoided.
When naming a son,
one should consider the grandson's generation.
Among relatives and acquaintances, if there are taboos like Qín (秦), Zhōu (周), Qīng (清), Hé (和), Yǔ (禹),
then in casual encounters,
one might commit a hundred offenses in one sitting.
Jiāfù Jiāmǔ
Hóu Bà’s descendants referred to their grandfather as "jiāgōng" (家公).
Chén Sīwáng referred to his father as "jiāfù" (家父) [my father]
and his mother as "jiāmǔ" (家母) [my mother].
Pān Ní referred to his grandfather as "jiāzǔ" (家祖).
What was practiced by ancient people
is laughed at by people today.
Moreover, in the customs of the North and South,
when speaking of one's grandfather or father,
no one says "jiā" (家).
Only country bumpkins use such expressions.
Shedding Tears at Farewell
Parting is easy, meeting is hard;
this was valued by the ancients.
In Jiāngnán, at farewells,
people shed tears when saying goodbye.
In the northern customs,
this matter is not bothered with.
At crossroads, when parting,
they laugh and separate.
However, some people by nature shed few tears;
though their hearts may be breaking,
their eyes still sparkle.
Such people
should not be forced [to cry].
Testing the Child
In Jiāngnán customs,
when a child reaches its first birthday,
it is tested with treasures, toys, and food.
Ritual is born of human emotion, benevolence is decided by righteousness
Lù Xiāng of Wú Commandery,
whose father suffered a cruel punishment,
wore coarse clothes and ate plain food his entire life.
Even when ginger and vegetables were cut, he could not bear to eat them.
At home, he only supplied the kitchen by picking and plucking.
Yáo Zǐ of Jiānglíng, whose mother died by burning,
could not bear to eat roasted meat his entire life.
Xióng Kāng’s father was killed by a slave while drunk,
and he never tasted wine again in his life.
However, ritual is born of human emotion,
and benevolence is decided by righteousness.
If a parent died by choking,
one should also not be unable to eat.
Teaching the New Daughter-in-law
The proverb says:
"Teach the daughter-in-law when she first arrives,
teach the child when it is an infant."
How true these words are!
A Shop of Salted Fish
Living with good people
is like entering a room filled with fragrant orchids,
after a long time, one naturally becomes fragrant;
living with bad people
is like entering a shop of salted fish,
after a long time, one naturally becomes smelly.
If Not Falling from a Carriage, Then a Zùozuò
During the Liáng dynasty, the sons of noble families
often lacked scholarly knowledge.
A proverb said:
"If one doesn't fall from a carriage, then one becomes a Zùozuò (著作, Compiler),
if one asks 'How is your body?', then one becomes a Mìshū (秘書, Secretary)."
They all perfumed their clothes, shaved their faces,
applied powder and rouge,
rode in long-eaved carriages,
wore high-heeled clogs,
sat on checkered square mats,
leaned on silk pillow bags,
leisurely came and went,
looking like immortals.
When passing the civil service examination, they hired someone to answer the policy questions;
at major public banquets,
they borrowed someone's hand to compose poems.
Since the period of chaos,
we have seen these captives.
Even the humblest of people who, for a hundred generations,
knew how to read the Lúnyǔ and Xiàojīng,
were still regarded as teachers.
While those who wore the cap and robes of nobility for a thousand years,
but did not understand writing,
all ended up plowing fields and raising horses.
If one can always be satisfied with several hundred scrolls of books,
one will ultimately avoid becoming a humble person.
The proverb says:
"Accumulating ten million in wealth
is not as good as having a small skill oneself."
Among skills worth valuing,
none surpasses reading.
Learning is like Planting a Tree
Learning
is like planting a tree.
In spring, one enjoys its flowers;
in autumn, one harvests its fruit.
Discussing literature and writing
is the spring flower.
Cultivating oneself and acting righteously
is the autumn fruit.
Late Learning
When Yán Zhītuī was seven years old, he recited the "Fù on the Línɡɡuānɡ Palace".
Even today,
after ten years of reviewing it once,
he still has not forgotten it.
Beyond the age of twenty,
the sūtras and classics he recited,
if neglected for a single day,
would become completely forgotten.
If a person encounters misfortune
and misses their prime,
they should still study in later years,
and not give up on themselves.
Kǒnɡzǐ learned the Yì at fifty,
Zēnɡzǐ only began to learn at seventeen,
Xún Qīnɡ started learning at fifty,
Gōnɡsūn Hónɡ only began reading the Chūnqiū and Lúnyǔ at forty,
Huánɡfǔ Mì only started receiving instruction in the Xiàojīnɡ and Lúnyǔ at twenty,
Zhū Yún also began studying the Yì at forty;
all became great rú.
Followers of Lǎo and Zhuānɡ who indulged in freedom
The books of Lǎo and Zhuānɡ,
advocate preserving one's innate nature and nourishing one's vitality,
not wishing to be burdened by external things.
Lǎo Dān concealed his name as a "pillar historian" (archivist),
and ultimately trod the moving sands.
Zhuānɡ Zhōu hid his tracks in the lacquer garden,
and ultimately declined the position of Chǔ chancellor.
These were followers who indulged in freedom.
Misreading "dūnchī" as "yánɡ"
In Jiānɡnán, there was a powerful noble
who misread a commentary in a faulty edition of the "Shǔdū Fù":
"Dūnchī,
is a taro."
He wrote it as the character "yánɡ" (sheep).
When someone presented him with lamb,
his reply letter said:
"Thank you for the dūnchī."
Shallow learning
The "Wánɡ Mǎnɡ Zàn" says:
"Purple coloration and frog voice,
a remnant usurper."
This refers to one who corrupts the genuine with the fake.
There was a brilliant scholar,
whose reputation was very high,
who said:
"Wánɡ Mǎnɡ not only had owl eyes and tiger jaws,
but also purple coloration and a frog voice."
Furthermore, the "Lǐyuè Zhì" says:
"Supply the Great Official with tónɡmǎjiǔ."
Lǐ Qí's commentary says:
"It is wine made from mare's milk."
The characters "zhǒnɡ" and "tónɡ" have now become two characters;
both should be read with the "cái" radical and the "shǒu" radical,
pronounced "zhuànɡ" and "dǎo".
This means to pound and mash it,
to make it into curdled wine.
However, that same scholar also believed
that when the tónɡ trees were planted, the Great Official's mare's milk wine was ready.
His ignorance was such.
Villagers embellishing phrases
Among the officials and scholars in the villages of Jiānɡnán, those who heard things second-hand,
insisted on embellishing their words.
They called "zhēnɡzhì" (a note in the pentatonic scale) "Zhōu Zhènɡ" (two ancient states),
and referred to "huòluàn" (cholera)
as "Bólù" (a place name or title).
When going up to Jīnɡzhōu,
they must say "Xiáxī" (west of the gorges);
when going down to Yánɡdū,
they must say "Hǎijùn" (sea prefecture).
When speaking of "eating," they say "húkǒu" (to make a living);
when speaking of "money," they say "kǒnɡfānɡ" (square hole).
When asking about moving, it's "Chǔqiū" (a place name);
when discussing marriage, it's "Yàn'ěr" (newly wed).
When it came to Wánɡ, there was no one who wasn't Zhònɡxuān;
when speaking of Liú, there was no one who wasn't Gōnɡɡàn.
There are about one or two hundred such instances,
passed down from one to another.
If one traces them, the origin is unknown,
and when applied, they are often misplaced.
The fault of "ear-learning"
Zhuānɡshēnɡ had the saying "qúeshǐ" (to rise like a magpie, taking advantage of the moment),
hence Xiè Tiào's poem says:
"Like a magpie, I ascend the Wú terrace."
Someone wrote a Qīxì poem saying:
"Tonight, the magpies of Wú terrace,
also rise to fill the river."
The "Luófúshān Jì" says:
"Looking from the flat ground, the trees are like jǐ (shepherd's purse)."
Hence Dài Háo's poem says:
"The trees of Chánɡ'ān are like jǐ."
Someone writing a poem about trees said:
"Looking afar at the jǐ of Chánɡ'ān."
I also once saw "jīndàn" (arrogant and boastful) referred to
as "kuābǐ" (exaggerated and boastful),
and "ɡāonián" (old age) as "fùyǒu chūnqiū" (rich in springs and autumns).
These are all faults of "ear-learning."
Naming
In recent times, some people named their sons:
If brothers all had names with the "shān" (mountain) radical,
then there was one named "Shì".
If brothers all had names with the "shǒu" (hand) radical,
then there was one named "Jī".
If brothers all had names with the "shuǐ" (water) radical,
then there was one named "Rú".
There are many such examples.
Cōnɡcōnɡ
The world uses "cōnɡcōnɡ" (hastily),
but does not know its origin.
According to the "Shuōwén":
"Cōnɡ refers to
a flag erected in towns and villages,
depicting its pole and three streamers.
It was used to move people for affairs,
therefore, those who were hurried
were called cōnɡcōnɡ."
Dòubī
I was sitting with my teacher,
and saw a small light on the ground.
I asked those around what it was.
A Shǔ servant went to look,
and replied:
"It's dòubī."
It was a small bean.
In Shǔ, they call "lì" (grain) "bī".
At the time, no one understood.
According to the "Sāncānɡ" and "Shuōwén",
the character "lì" has the pronunciation "bī",
pronounced fānɡlì (方力) reversed.
One should not presume to make pronouncements
without having thoroughly read all the books under heaven.
Lùkuí
There was a Cài Lǎnɡ,
who observed a naming taboo on the character "chún" (pure),
and so called water shield (chún) "lùkuí" (dewy mallow).
Ignorant people
successively imitated this.
In the Chénɡshènɡ era,
a scholar was sent as an envoy to Qí.
The official in charge of guests, Lǐ Shù, asked:
"Does Jiānɡnán have lùkuí?"
He replied:
"Lùkuí is chún,
which grows in water regions.
What we eat today is just lǜkuí (green mallow)."
Talent and brilliance not tolerated by one's wife and children
An aristocratic family in Bìnɡzhōu
liked to compose ridiculous poems and fù.
Everyone mocked and ridiculed him,
but outwardly praised him.
He slaughtered oxen and poured wine,
inviting people to enhance his reputation.
His wife wept and remonstrated with him.
This person sighed and said:
"My talent and brilliance are not tolerated by my wife and children,
let alone by strangers!"
He never realized it until his death.
When learning to write essays,
first consult with relatives and friends.
Only after getting their comments
should one begin to put pen to paper.
Be careful not to rely solely on your own judgment,
and become a laughingstock to others.
Essays
In all essay writing,
it is like a person riding a qíjì (fine steed).
Although it has a spirited disposition,
it must be reined in with a bridle,
not allowed to stray from the path,
and plunge willfully into ditches and banks.
The reasoning and logic should be the heart and kidneys of an essay,
the tone and rhythm its sinews and bones,
the subject matter and meaning its skin,
and the splendor its crown.
The current generation,
following one another, tends to pursue the superficial and abandon the fundamental,
mostly being frivolous and ostentatious.
When words contend with reason,
words win and reason is suppressed;
when events contend with talent,
events are convoluted and talent is diminished.
Those who are unrestrained wander aimlessly and forget their way back;
those who are pedantic patch things together but are still inadequate.
Sānyì
Shěn Yǐnhóu said:
“When writing essays, one should aim for three ‘easy’ things.
Easy to see the subject,
is the first.
Easy to understand the subject,
is the second.
Easy to read aloud,
is the third.”
Xíng Zǐcái said:
“Shěn Hóu’s essays,
use allusions without making people realize it,
as if they were his own heartfelt words.”
Zǔ Xiàozhēng said:
“Shěn’s poem says:
‘Cliffs tilt, protecting stone marrow,’
how can this be considered an allusion?”
Xíng Zǐcái and Wèi Shōu both had great reputations.
Xíng admired Shěn Yuē but belittled Rèn Fǎng,
while Wèi loved Rèn Fǎng but disparaged Shěn Yuē.
In Yèxià, there was a great dispute,
each having their own faction.
Xiàozhēng said:
“The right or wrong of Rèn and Shěn,
is actually the superiority or inferiority of Xíng and Wèi.”
Discussing Poetry
Xiāo Què has an Autumn poem that says:
“Hibiscus fall as dew descends,
willows sparse beneath the moon.”
Its graceful ease is vivid before one’s eyes.
Hé Xùn’s poetry is
clear and clever, with many similes.
It is a pity that he was always afflicted by illness and died prematurely,
and was full of poverty and coldness,
not matching Liú Xiàochuò’s graceful composure.
Xiàochuò placed Xiè Tiǎo’s poems on his desk,
reciting and savoring them whether moving or still.
Jiǎnwén loved Táo Yuānmíng’s writings,
and was likewise.
Applying Croton Beans to the Face
Recently there was a person of high rank,
renowned for filial piety.
During mourning, he grieved deeply,
but while on his mat of straw, he applied croton beans to his face, causing sores,
to exaggerate his weeping.
With one falsity, he sacrificed a hundred sincerities.
This was due to insatiable craving for fame.
Serving in the Kitchen Gains a Taste
Wáng Zǐjìn said:
“Serving in the kitchen gains a taste,
joining a fight gains an injury.”
This means one should not side with people in unrighteous acts.
A cornered bird flying into one’s bosom
is pitied by a benevolent person.
If a loyal warrior pledges allegiance to me,
should I abandon him?
Wǔ Yuán entrusting himself to a fishing boat,
Jì Bù hiding in Guǎng,
Kǒng Róng concealing Zhāng Jiǎn,
Sūn Hāo sheltering Zhào Qí—
if one is thus implicated,
one would willingly accept death with eyes closed.
Taking Medicine
Yǔ Jiānwú often took sophora fruit,
and at over seventy, his beard and hair were still black.
There was a scholar who exclusively took杏仁 (apricot kernel), 枸杞 (goji berry), 黃精 (Siberian Solomon’s Seal rhizome), 朮 (Atractylodes rhizome), and 車前 (plantain),
and many benefited greatly.
I once suffered from a toothache,
my teeth were loose and about to fall out.
Eating hot or cold food
all caused painful aching.
I saw in the Bǎopǔzǐ a method for strengthening teeth:
in the early morning, tap the teeth three hundred times.
After practicing for several days,
it completely healed.
Chicken’s Beak, Ox’s Rear
Tàishǐ Gōng said:
“Better to be a chicken’s beak,
than an ox’s rear.”
This is simply an abridged version of the Zhànguó Cè.
Ān Yándǔ’s Yīnyì says:
“尸 (shī) is the master of the chicken,
從 (cóng) is the child of the ox.”
Thus, “口 (kǒu)” should be “尸 (shī),”
and “後 (hòu)” should be “從 (cóng).”
The popular writing is mistaken.
The String-tuning Has Not Yet Ceased
In ancient musical compositions,
first the three sons are mentioned,
then the three wives.
“Wife” is a term used when addressing one’s husband’s parents.
The last stanza says:
“Where is the old man now?
The string-tuning has not yet ceased.”
In ancient times,
sons and wives served their husband’s parents,
by their side morning and evening,
no different from one’s own sons and daughters,
hence this saying.
“丈人 (zhàngrén)” is probably “大人 (dàrén).”
Cooking with a Doorbolt
An ancient Yuèfǔ song for Bǎilǐ Xī says:
“Bǎilǐ Xī,
five sheepskins.
Recalling the time of parting,
cooked a broody hen,
and blew on a doorbolt.”
“吹 (chuī)” should be “炊 (chuī)” for cooking.
Cài Yōng’s Yuèlìng Zhāngjù says:
“鍵 (jiàn)
is a doorbolt (guānmǔ),
used to stop a door,
also called yǎnyí.”
At that time, due to poverty,
they even used the wooden doorbolt as fuel for cooking.
Do Not Disbelieve What Ear and Eye Cannot Reach
Buddhists warn people
not to dismiss something as illusory just because their ears and eyes cannot perceive it.
For example, mountain dwellers do not believe there are fish
as large as trees; sea dwellers do not believe there are trees as large as fish.
Emperor Wǔ of Hàn did not believe in lute-strings made of glue.
Emperor Wén of Wèi did not believe in fire-resistant cloth.
Foreigners, upon seeing brocade,
did not believe it was made of silk spun by insects eating trees.
Formerly, in Jiāngnán, people did not believe in felt tents for a thousand people;
after coming to Héběi,
they did not believe in ships carrying twenty thousand hú.
In the world, there are illusionists
who can walk on fire and tread on blades,
plant melons and move wells,
transforming in a flash,
with ten changes and five transformations.
How much more so for the supernatural powers and wondrous responses,
which are immeasurable?
A thousand-mile jeweled banner,
a hundred-yojana seat,
transforming into a pure land,
and a marvelous stupa emerging?
Five Gēng
Someone asked:
“Why are there five gēng in a night?”
The answer was:
“Since the Hàn and Wèi dynasties,
they were called jiǎyè, yǐyè, bǐngyè, dīngyè, wùyè.
Also called yīgǔ, èrgǔ, sāngǔ, sìgǔ, wǔgǔ.
Also called yīgēng, èrgēng, sāngēng, sìgēng, wǔgēng.
All use five as a division.
The Xīdū Fù also says:
‘Guarded by the office of strict gēng.’
The first month is jiànyín,
the Big Dipper points to yín in the evening,
and to wǔ in the morning,
covering five zī (hours).
Although winter and summer vary in length,
the interval between the zī is wide,
not reaching six when long,
and not shrinking to four when short,
always fluctuating between five.
Gēng
means to establish,
or to pass through;
hence it is called five gēng.”
Guō Tū
Among puppets there is Guō Tū.
The Fēngsú Tōng says:
“All of the Guō clan avoid the word ‘tū’ (bald).”
It must be that in a previous generation there was someone named Guō who suffered from baldness,
and it was made into a humorous jest,
so later generations made his effigy,
and called it Guō Tū.
Borrowing Fǔ for Fù
“Fǔ” is an honorific term for a man.
Ancient texts often borrow it for the character “fù” (father).
Northerners consequently no longer call anyone “fǔ.”
Only the appellations for Guǎn Zhòng and Fàn Zēng
must be read according to the character itself.
A Thousand-mile Countenance
The proverb says:
Even if you read sparsely,
you will have a thousand-mile countenance.
This skill does not need to be overly refined,
lest one be exploited.
Wáng Yìshǎo,
a refined and talented scholar,
a natural and famous person,
yet the whole world only knows his calligraphy.
Wéi Zhòngjiāng’s last injunctions
had deep meaning.
Corrupt Characters
Since the
Jìn and Sòng dynasties, many
were skilled in calligraphy, but a great change occurred in the Liáng dynasty.
Xiāo Ziyún altered the script,
and Shàolíng Wáng practiced corrupt characters.
Examples include writing "草" above "前" or "長" beside "能".
When writing the character "一",
only a few dots were seen.
Some would presumptuously make adjustments,
changing characters for convenience.
After the chaos of the Northern Dynasties,
calligraphy became crude and vulgar.
Arbitrary characters were even more prevalent than in Jiāngnán.
Thus, "百念" was used for "憂",
"言反" for "變",
"不用" for "罷",
"追來" for "歸",
"更生" for "蘇",
and "先又" for "老".
Such instances were numerous,
filling the classics and commentaries.
Divination
In recent times,
there are no longer any good masters of divination.
In ancient times, divination was used to resolve doubts;
today, people create doubts through divination.
Those who adhere to the Dao and trust their plans,
when intending to undertake something,
if they obtain an inauspicious hexagram through divination,
instead become irritable.
Furthermore, if six or seven out of ten predictions are correct,
it is considered expert;
if one merely grasps the general idea,
it is not precise.
When shooting for odd or even,
it is naturally fifty-fifty.
How can one rely on it?
Slight Understanding of Medicinal Properties
The matter of medical prescriptions
is extremely difficult to master.
To have a slight understanding of medicinal properties,
and be able to make minor concoctions,
allows one to provide emergency relief at home,
which is also an excellent skill.
Huángfǔ Mì and Yīn Zhòngkān
were such people.
Ignorance of the Qín is Considered a Deficiency
A gentleman does not remove his qín or sè without good reason.
Initially,
for descendants of aristocratic families who did not know the qín,
it was considered a deficiency.
This music, though seemingly confusing,
possesses profound elegance and taste!
However, one must not seek fame,
or be employed by the powerful and noble,
sitting in the lower seats,
and suffer the humiliation of leftover food and drink.
Games of Chance
The sages did not use games of chance for teaching.
But since scholars cannot always be diligent,
and sometimes become tired and play them,
it is still better than being full and drowsy, sitting idly.
Tóuhú (Pitch-Pot)
In ancient times,
the tóuhú was filled with small beans
to prevent the arrows from bouncing.
Today, bouncing is considered esteemed,
and called "jiāo" (arrogance/pride).
There are even names like "yǐ gān" (leaning pole), "dài jiàn" (wearing sword), "hú" (pot), "bào wěi" (leopard tail), and "shǒu lóng" (dragon head).
The most exquisite is the "liánhuā jiāo" (lotus bounce).
Some even place a small screen outside the pot,
and hit it without fail.
"Jiāo" is also written as "xiāo".
Xìngcài (Water Shield)
In Jiāngnán, it is called "zhūchún" or "kǔcài";
in Héběi, it is called "lóngkuí" or "mǎlán".
The Guǎngyǎ calls it "mǎxiè".
Chīwěi
The Chī
is a sea beast.
The Báiliáng Diàn of Emperor Wǔ of Hàn had Chīwěi,
which are the essence of water,
and can ward off fire disasters.
Hence, their images were placed on top.
Calling them "chīwěi" (owl tail)
is incorrect.
Lóuluó
Lóuluó refers to
being capable and effective in handling affairs.
The world says "Lóu Jìng" and "Gān Luó",
which is incorrect.
Gānmò
"Gānmò" has the same meaning as "lùchén".
The Hàn commentary is erroneous.
Lóngzhōng
Lóngzhōng describes
a state of not flourishing or not standing out.
Similar to "líu sān", "lā dā", or "jiě zòng".
Jiǔhuāqiú
During the reign of Dàizōng,
Fànyáng presented a horse,
nine chì tall at the forehead,
a true qíu dragon.
Its body was covered with five-color patterns,
and it was named "Jiǔhuāqiú".
Later, it was bestowed upon Guō Zǐyí.
Jīncán
During the Tiānbǎo period,
a foreign country presented a soft jade whip,
which could be bent so that its head and tail met,
but when straightened, it was as rigid as a rope.
The emperor ordered an embroidered pouch to be made for it,
and a scabbard of green jade silk.
The green jade silkworm silk
was a tribute from the Míluó Kingdom.
In that country, silkworms on mulberry trees
were golden in color,
and their silk was green,
also called "Jīncánsī" (Golden Silkworm Silk).
The silk,
when loosely measured at one chì,
could be stretched to one zhàng.
Shàngqīng Zhū
In the early Kaiyuán era,
the Jìbīn Kingdom presented a Shàngqīng Zhū,
whose light illuminated an entire room.
Within it, immortal beings, jade maidens, and auspicious cranes swayed.
In times of drought, flood, or military conflict,
if one prayed devoutly to it,
it would always prove effective.
Língguāng Dòu
During the Dàlì period,
the Rìlín Kingdom presented Língguāng Dòu,
which emitted a red light several chì long.
It was also called "Jiéduō Zhū".
When cooked with菖蒲 (calamus),
it would become as large as an egg,
weighing one jīn,
and its fragrant deliciousness would last for several days.
Lóngchāi
The Rìlín Kingdom presented a Lóngjiǎo Chāi (Dragon Horn Hairpin),
engraved with a coiled dragon.
The emperor bestowed it upon Concubine Dúgū.
As they toured Lóngdān together,
purple clouds transformed from the hairpin into two black dragons that ascended and flew away.
Wànfó Shān
The Xīnluó Kingdom presented a five-colored qújū rug,
within each square cùn of which
were musicians, mountains, and rivers,
as well as bees and butterflies moving,
and swallows and sparrows flying.
They also presented a Wànfó Shān (Mountain of Ten Thousand Buddhas),
about one zhàng tall,
carved from沉檀 (agarwood and sandalwood), pearls, and jade.
The largest Buddhas were over one cùn,
the smaller ones a few fēn.
The terraces, halls, banners, and canopies
seemed to be in flight.
Below was a purple-gold bell,
which, when struck, caused thousands of monks to perform prostrations,
touching their heads to the ground,
with a faint sound of Buddhist chanting.
Yù Pìxié
Sùzōng bestowed two fragrant Yù Pìxié (Jade Pixiu) upon Lǐ Fǔguó,
whose fragrance could be smelled hundreds of steps away.
One day,
one Pìxié suddenly burst into loud laughter,
while the other wailed mournfully.
Fǔguó crushed them to powder
and placed them in the latrine.
He often heard sounds of grievance and pain.
Not long after,
Fǔguó died.
A favored slave, knowing they were extraordinary objects,
secretly collected two hé (measures) of the powder.
Yú Cháo'ēn bought them for 300,000 cash.
When Cháo'ēn was about to be executed,
they transformed into white butterflies and flew away.
Yúnhuī Táng
Yuán Zài built the Yúnhuī Hall.
Yúnhuī
is a fragrant herb,
originating from the kingdom of Yútián.
Its white color is like jade,
and buried in soil, it does not decay.
It was ground into powder to paint the walls,
and a Xuánlí screen
and a purple xiāo curtain were also set up.
The screen
was a treasure of Yáng Guózhōng. On it
were carved beautiful women, dancers, and musicians,
with dàimào and shuǐxī for embellishments.
The curtain was so dense
that no wind could enter.
In the height of summer, it was naturally cool and refreshing.
Yáo Yīng consumed fragrance.
Yuán Zài’s favored concubine, Xuē Yáoyīng,
had consumed fragrance since childhood,
hence her skin was fragrant.
Zài housed her in a golden silk curtained bed
with a dust-repelling mattress.
She wore a lóngxiāo robe,
one set of which, when crumpled,
did not fill a hand.
Yáoyīng was light-bodied,
so she wore this garment.
Jiǎ Zhì presented a poem saying:
"Afraid to dance, for the gauze gown is heavy;
smiling, as if a peach blossom face opens.
Only now do I know that Emperor Hàn Chéngdì
built the Wind-Sheltering Terrace in vain."
Propitious Whip
During the reign of Dézōng,
a middle regular attendant presented a propitious whip.
When it was waved in the dark,
it shone like lightning.
When the emperor went on his western tour,
he had two horses:
one was named Shénzhìjùn,
and the other Rúyìliú.
The emperor recited:
"Mandarin duck-colored, dappled white, with freshly aligned teeth,
in the setting sun, between flowers, drop emerald hooves.
The jade bridle, just turning, first froths with foam,
the golden whip, about to descend, fails to make them neigh."
This was a poem by Hán Hóng, a Secretariat Drafter.
Lú Méiniáng
During the reign of Shùnzōng,
Nánhǎi presented the extraordinary girl Lú Méiniáng.
She could embroider the Fǎhuá Jīng on a single red xiāo silk,
with characters the size of millet grains.
She also made a flying immortal canopy,
using a single strand of silk for the canopy.
Within its five layers were the Ten Continents and Three Islands.
Daily she ate three hé of sesame seed rice.
Xiànzōng bestowed a golden phoenix bracelet to bind her wrist,
and sent her home.
People of Nánhǎi often saw her riding a purple cloud, roaming over the sea.
Fèngzhī Lóngzhú
In the Yuánhé period,
Gěishì Zhāng Wéizé returned from an embassy to Xīnluó.
At sea, he saw flowers, trees, terraces, and halls.
There were several young gentlemen dressed in purple mist robes,
who said, "We are the five friends
of the Tang emperor."
They presented a golden tortoise seal
to be given to the emperor.
The seal script read:
"Fèngzhī Lóngzhú,
destined for boundless longevity."
Wéizé reported the matter in full.
That month,
two auspicious ganoderma fungi grew on the conjoint trees in front of the imperial bedchamber,
resembling dragons and phoenixes.
The emperor said,
"Fèngzhī Lóngzhú,
this is its verification."
Spirit Herbs and Dragon-Tiger Jade
Xiànzōng was fond of immortals.
There was a recluse, Yīqí Xuánjiě.
The emperor always held him in high esteem,
saying,
"Sir, though your years are advanced,
your complexion does not age.
Why is this?"
Xuánjiě replied,
"I cultivate spirit herbs by the sea
and consume them."
He then planted them in front of the palace:
one was called "Double Ganoderma,"
another "Six Harmony Mallow,"
and a third "Myriad Root Vine."
The emperor took them,
and they were miraculously effective.
At that time, the Western Regions presented two beautiful jades, one round and one square.
Xuánjiě said,
"These are Dragon-Tiger Jades.
The round one is born of water,
treasured by dragons;
the square one is born of mountains,
treasured by tigers."
He had the envoy inquired,
and indeed, they were obtained by fishermen and swineherds.
Golden and Jade Butterflies
In Mùzōng's forbidden palace,
a thousand-petal peony bloomed at night.
There were tens of thousands of yellow and white butterflies
flying and gathering among the flowers.
Palace women tried to catch them with silk scarves,
but none succeeded.
The emperor ordered a net to be set in the air,
and several hundred were caught.
At dawn, upon inspection,
they were all made of gold and jade.
Inner palace women competed to tie their feet with crimson threads
to make head ornaments.
Tortoiseshell Basin
In the early Bǎolì period,
the Nánchāng Kingdom presented a tortoiseshell basin, a floating-light fur coat, and a night-shining rhinoceros horn.
Golden Snake
In the early Kāichéng period,
in the inner palace, there was a yellow snake
that emerged from the imperial treasury at night.
The emperor ordered a search of the treasury
and found a golden snake.
The emperor said,
"Emperor Suí Yángdì gave a golden snake to Lady Chén."
His attendants then noticed the character "阿" under its chin,
and "Ānuó"
was Suí Yángdì's childhood name.
The emperor ordered a glass ring to be tied to the forefoot of a jade pig to suppress it,
and it was not seen again.
This was because pigs could eat snakes.
Bodhisattva in a Clam
Emperor Wénzōng was fond of eating clams.
Among them, there was one that could not be pried open.
The emperor burned incense and prayed to it.
After a short while, it opened by itself.
Inside were two figures
with spiral topknots and璎珞 (yīngluò) necklaces,
their feet resting on lotus blossoms,
which were called Bodhisattvas.
The emperor placed them in a golden millet sandalwood incense box,
bestowed them upon a virtuous temple,
and ordered reverence to be paid to them.
Luán Honey
During the reign of Dézōng,
the Wúmíng Kingdom presented luán honey.
Its bees sounded like luánfèng,
their bodies covered in five colors,
and the large ones weighed over ten jīn.
Their honey was emerald green,
and when stored in a white jade bowl,
it appeared like emerald liúlí, both inside and out.
Eating it granted longevity.
Fire Jade and Pine Wind Stone
During the reign of Wǔzōng,
the Dàyú Kingdom presented fire jade.
When placed indoors,
one no longer needed to wear padded clothes.
They also presented a pine wind stone,
one zhàng square,
with a withered pine tree inside.
In the height of summer, a rustling sound
and a cool breeze emerged from its opening.
Cāngzhōu
The recluse Yuán Zàngjǐ
of the Suí dynasty,
while serving as an envoy to the sea, encountered a storm and his boat was wrecked.
He was carried on broken wood to an island.
The islanders said:
"This is Cāngzhōu,
tens of thousands of lí from your country."
The island was a thousand lí square,
with flowers and trees perpetually like the second or third month,
and many people did not die.
It produced melons with separate stems,
two chí long.
Green dates and red chestnuts
were all as large as pears.
In the ponds were four-legged fish and golden lotus flowers,
which women picked to wear as hair ornaments.
They said:
"If you don't wear golden lotus flowers,
you cannot be among the immortals."
Yuán Zàngjǐ suddenly thought of Zhōngguó,
so the islanders built him a "wind-riding boat" (Língfēng Gě) and sent him off.
It propelled through the water like an arrow,
reaching Dōnglái in ten days.
When he asked about the country,
it was the Táng dynasty.
From Dàyè to Zhēnyuán,
two hundred years had passed.
Divine Gold for a Remaining Physician
An empress of Xuānzōng's Hòugōng fell ill,
and a physician was summoned.
When she recovered,
the Emperor took several liǎng of gold from his sleeve and gave it to him,
saying:
"Do not let the inner officials know of this,
lest it get out,
and then the remonstrance officials submit a memorial."
Púsàmán
In the early Dàzhōng period,
the Nǚmán Guó presented a pair of twin-dragon rhinoceros horns and "rosy mist brocade" (Míngxiá Jǐn).
The people of that country wore towering hairpins and golden crowns,
with瓔珞 (yīngluò) covering their bodies.
They were called "Púsàmán" (Bodhisattva Barbarians),
and so this tune was composed.
Understanding the "Two-Front Chess Position"
A prince from Rìběn Guó came to court,
and played weiqi with Attendant Gù Shīyán.
At the thirty-third move,
it was called "Zhenshéntóu" (Suppressing the Spirit's Head),
which is to understand the "two-front position" (Liǎngzhēng Shì).
*Běimèng Suǒyán* also details this passage.
Xuānyuán Jí
Fúluó Xiānshēng Xuānyuán Jí was
several hundred years old,
yet his complexion showed no aging.
His hair hung to the ground,
and his gaze extended several zhàng.
Emperor Xuānzōng once spoke of the absence of bean flowers and litchis in the capital.
In a moment,
both flowers, with branches and leaves,
appeared, several hundred of each.
The Emperor asked:
"How many years will I be emperor?"
He immediately wrote "forty years."
But the character for "ten" (十) had a hooked stroke.
When the Emperor died,
it was indeed fourteen years.
The Marriage of Princess Tóngchāng
During the Xiántōng period,
Princess Tóngchāng was married off.
Well railings were made of gold and silver,
and scoops were carved from gold.
Beds of crystal and liúlí were made,
supported by golden turtles and silver *áo*.
There were also several hú of gold and silver grains of rice,
presented by the Tiáozhī Guó during the reign of Tàizōng.

In the hall were set up pearl-stringed curtains, cold-repelling screens, rhinoceros mats, ivory mats, dragon and phoenix quilts, partridge pillows, kingfisher boxes, divine silk embroidered blankets, and vexation-removing rhinoceros *rúyì*.
There was also patterned cloth,
which did not get wet when wiping water.
"Fire silkworm floss" (Huǒcán Mián)
came from Yánzhōu;
one liǎng was used for a padded garment,
more than that
would make it too hot to wear.
There was a hairpin of nine jades,
engraved with nine luán,
all of nine-colored jade,
bearing the characters "Yù'ér".
One day, she dreamt someone said:
"Pān Shūfēi of Southern Qí will take the nine-luán hairpin."
When the princess died,
the hairpin also vanished.
Red Honey and White Ape Fat
Princess Tóngchāng was gravely ill.
The physicians said:
"Red honey and white ape fat,
if eaten, can cure her."
The inner treasury obtained several shí of red honey,
originally supplied by the Dōulí Guó.
Several wèng of white ape fat
were originally presented by the Nánhǎi region.
Song of "Lamenting a Hundred Years" Dance Troupe
Emperor Xuānzōng grieved for Princess Tóngchāng.
Lǐ Kějí presented the "Song of Lamenting a Hundred Years" (Tàn Bǎinián Qǔ),
teaching several thousand people
to form the "Hundred Years Troupe" (Bǎinián Duì).
Eight hundred pí of official silk
were used to make floor coverings depicting fish, dragons, and waves.
With each dance,
pearls and kingfisher feathers scattered across the floor.
On the Emperor's birthday,
the palace decorated a temple with colored silks,
and bestowed brocade robes upon officials from those who attended court downwards.
Lǐ Kějí also created the "Púsàmán Troupe" (Púsàmán Duì).
Refining the Crown
When Emperor Xuānzōng decreed the welcoming of the Buddha's relics,
there was a monk who covered the top of his head with moxa,
which was called "refining the crown" (Liàn Dǐng).
When the fire ignited and pain began,
youths from the neighborhoods seized him,
not allowing him to move.
He cried out in the streets,
and those who saw him laughed loudly.
Buddha's Relics
The Buddha's relics entered the inner sanctuary,
where golden flower curtains were set up,
warm and clean beds, dragon-scale mats,
phoenix-tail quilts,
burning jade marrow incense,
and offerings of琼膏 (qiónggāo) liquid.
Monks and disciples gathered in the markets,
setting up Buddha statues,
blowing conches and striking bowls.
They also had young children in jade belts, gold-adorned foreheads, and white leggings,
chanting and singing among them,
all for amusement.
Overcoming Poverty and Calamity
An ancient saying goes:
"Strength can overcome poverty,
prudence can overcome calamity."
For diligence can prevent poverty,
and caution can avoid disaster.
What Hunger and Cold Urge
Chén Sīwáng said:
"One who is cold does not desire red jade but seeks coarse clothes;
one who is hungry does not long for a thousand pieces of gold but finds a single food delicious.
There are times when urgent needs arise."
Quick Riches
Yī Dùn,
a poor scholar from Lǔ,
heard that Táo Zhūgōng was rich,
and asked him for the method.
He said:
"If you want to get rich quickly,
raise five breeding cows."
Managing Fields
When any family manages fields,
they must assess their own strength.
It is better to have a few good ones
than many poor ones.
Three-Cun Deep Furrow
Hoeing and weeding must be done in season.
The proverb says:
"A hoe's three-cùn deep furrow," and this is it.
The ancients said:
"If one does not cease plowing and hoeing due to drought or flood,
one will surely be rewarded with a bountiful year."
If one lives near cities,
plant more melons, vegetables, eggplants, etc.,
for they can supply the household,
and any surplus can be sold.
The Yellow Emperor Asked
Huángdì asked Shī Kuàng,
“I wish to understand the full extent of joy and sorrow.
Is this possible?”
He replied,
“When the year desires sweetness,
sweet grasses sprout,
which are water caltrops.
When the year desires bitterness,
bitter grasses sprout,
which are peppergrass.
When the year desires rain,
rain grasses sprout,
which are lotus roots.
When the year desires drought,
drought grasses sprout,
which are caltrops.
When the year desires floods,
flood grasses sprout,
which are tumbleweeds.
When the year desires illness,
illness grasses sprout,
which are mugwort.”
Báibèiláo
When plowing high or low fields,
regardless of spring or autumn,
it is essential that the dryness and wetness are appropriate.
If water and drought are not balanced,
it is better to be dry than wet.
Spring plowing requires immediate "láo" (tilling with a hoe),
while autumn plowing awaits "báibèiláo."
Therefore, in antiquity it was called "fù,"
and today it is called "láo."
Since spring has much wind,
if "láo" is not performed immediately,
the soil will certainly become dry and loose.
Wet "láo" in autumn fields makes the soil hard.
The proverb says:
“Plowing without 'láo'
is worse than leaving it fallow.”
This means that timely moisture is hard to come by,
and one delights in favorable weather.
Early and Late Fields
Generally, fields should have a mix of early and late crops.
In a leap year,
the solar terms fall later,
so late fields are suitable.
Generally, early planting is preferred,
with early fields being twice as many as late fields.
When sprouts are like horse ears, hoe them,
and hoe and replant in sparse areas.
For all five grains, hoeing is beneficial.
Full Harvest, Medium Harvest, Low Harvest
For all five grains,
generally, those planted in the first ten days of the month yield a full harvest,
those in the middle ten days yield a medium harvest,
and those in the last ten days yield a low harvest.
Days for Planting Five Grains
When planting the five grains,
those planted on vigorous growth days bear much fruit;
those planted on ominous death days yield poorly;
those planted on forbidden days suffer damage.
It is also good to use days of achievement, fullness, peace, and stability.
Adzuki beans avoid Mǎo,
rice and hemp avoid Chén,
millet avoids Bǐng,
broomcorn millet avoids Chǒu,
glutinous millet avoids Yín and Wèi,
wheat avoids Xū,
barley avoids Wǔ,
soybeans avoid Shēn.
For all nine grains,
if planted without avoiding forbidden days,
there will be much damage.
Warding off Epidemic Dragons
The Yúhétú says:
“On the eve of the year, at the fifth watch,
take fourteen beans, some wheat, and a little hair from family members,
put them together into a well,
and chant a spell over the well.
This will prevent the family from suffering from typhoid fever throughout the year,
and ward off epidemic ghosts from the five directions.”
Planting Gourds
Gourds can be planted in the first month,
stored in the sixth month,
and cut in the eighth month.
The white flesh inside gourds can be used to feed pigs to fatten them,
and their segments can be made into candles for light.
When planting taro,
the roots should be deep,
Water early,
and hoe any weeds.
Treating taro in this way,
and the soil around them loosened by hoeing.
which can relieve famine,
and help survive lean years.
Planting Ginger
Ginger should be planted in white sandy soil,
mixed with a little manure.
Plow thoroughly as if for hemp,
the soil cannot be too well-worked,
seven times lengthwise and crosswise is especially good.
Pepper Wine
Cuī Shí’s Yuèlìng says:
“On the first day of the New Year, each person presents pepper wine to their family elder,
raising a cup to wish them longevity,
with great joy.”
Forecasting Grains
Shī Kuàng forecasted grains, saying:
“Millet establishes its price base in autumn,
and is expensive by next summer.
Rice establishes its price base
in winter,
and is expensive by next autumn.
This is the timeline for grain harvests, near and far.
The difference in price indicates whether it's early or late.
Millet,
when it is expensive in spring and summer, the price drops by seven-tenths in autumn and winter,
and becomes expensive again by summer.
When it is nine-tenths in autumn and winter,
this is the extreme of the yang way.
Sell it quickly,
do not hold it.”
Valuation of Cattle and Horses
Huángdì asked Shī Kuàng,
saying:
“If you wish to know the value of cattle and horses,
when small mallows grow beneath autumn mallows,
they will certainly be expensive.”
Silkworm Rearing Method:
When collecting silkworm eggs,
be sure to take those from cocoons located in the middle of the silkworm frame.
Those near the top produce thin silk,
and those near the bottom do not produce offspring.
Planting Trees
When planting trees,
note their orientation to yin and yang,
and do not allow it to be altered.
Trim large trees,
plant trees in deep pits,
and water the soil.
Make it like thin mud,
shake it east, west, north, and south for a long time,
then tamp it firmly.
Irrigate it from time to time,
and bury it deeply.
After planting,
do not touch it with hands or allow livestock to bump into it.
The Huáinánzǐ says:
“If the yin-yang nature of a transplanted tree is lost,
none will fail to wither.”
Difficulty in Achieving Success Out of Season
Wénzǐ said:
“With much water, one can wash rice;
in summer, wood can be tied.
Opportunity is hard to gain and easy to lose.
When wood is flourishing,
one can collect it all day and it will regenerate.
When autumn wind brings frost,
it withers in a single night.
When it is not the right time,
success is hard to achieve.”
New Year's Willow Branches
On the morning of the first month,
take willow branches and place them above the door,
and a hundred ghosts will not enter the house.
Sufficient Firewood
Táo Zhūgōng said:
“Planting a thousand willow trees will provide firewood for ten years.
Pruning one tree at a time yields one load.
Pruning two hundred trees annually,
completes a cycle in five years.”
Planting Bamboo
It is advisable to plant bamboo on high and level ground.
Yellow soil and soft soil are good.
In the first and second months, dig up shoots from the southwest,
taking a few root stalks.
Prune the leaves,
and plant them in the northeast corner of the garden.
Make the pit two chì deep,
cover with five cùn of soil,
and fertilize with wheat compost.
Do not water.
Do not allow livestock into the garden.
In the second and third months, eat light bamboo shoots;
in the fourth and fifth months, eat bitter bamboo shoots.
Steam, boil, roast, or pickle them,
according to one's preference.
For those who wish to make utensils,
it is suitable to cut them after frost.
Assess the strength of oxen and horses
When using oxen for plowing and horses for riding,
assess their capabilities,
and provide them with appropriate cold/warm water and fodder,
to suit their natural disposition.
If they do not become fat and reproduce,
such a case has never existed.
Method for assessing horses
The method for assessing horses
first eliminates the three weak and five sluggish types,
and then assesses the rest.
A large head and small neck
is one weakness.
A weak back and large belly
is the second weakness.
A small neck and large hooves
is the third weakness.
A large head and drooping ears
is one sluggishness.
A long head that does not curve
is the second sluggishness.
Short upper body and long lower body
is the third sluggishness.
Large qià
qià, jià sound.
and short flanks
is the fourth sluggishness.
Shallow hips and thin thighs
is the fifth sluggishness.
Raising sheep
When raising sheep, always keep the lambs born in the twelfth and first months for breeding,
those born in the eleventh and second months are secondary.
When pasturing sheep, it is best to keep them far from water.
Let them drink every two days,
drive them slowly,
and do not let them stop and rest.
In spring and summer, let them out early;
in autumn and winter, let them out late.
A method for raising sheep
is to place salt in an earthenware vessel inside the sheep pen.
Sheep like salt,
they will repeatedly eat it themselves,
without needing human herding.
A sheep with one horn,
if eaten, will kill a person.
Raising pigs
When raising sows,
those with short snouts and without soft hair are good.
For boars,
the offspring and mother should not be in the same pen.
For sows,
there is no concern if they are in the same pen.
The pen cannot be too small,
the living space cannot be too dirty.
Raising chickens
For breeding chickens,
those born after the mulberry leaves fall are good;
those born in spring and summer are not good.
Children should not eat chicken.
The "Yǎngshēng Lùn" (Treatise on Nurturing Life) says:
"Chicken meat should not be given to children to eat.
Eating it will cause them to develop parasitic worms,
and also make their bodies thin and emaciated."
Classic on Fish Rearing
Táo Zhūgōng's "Yǎngyú Jīng" (Classic on Fish Rearing) says:
"Wēigōng (Lord Wēi) invited Gōng (Lord) and asked:
'When you were in Hú (Lake), you were the fisherman;
when you were in Qí (Qi), you were Chīyí Zǐpí;
when you were in Xīróng (Western Rong), you were Chìsōngzǐ;
when you were in Yuè (Yue), you were Fàn Lǐ.
Is this true?'
He replied:
'It is true.'
He asked:
'Your family has accumulated billions in gold,
what is your method?'
He replied:
'There are five methods for managing livelihood;
aquatic livestock is the first,
which is a fish pond.
In the pond, create nine islets.
Seek carp,
and put them into the pond on the first Gēng day of the Chén month.
Keep the water silent,
and the fish will surely multiply.
By the fourth month,
place one 'spirit guardian' inside;
in the sixth month, two 'spirit guardians';
in the eighth month, three 'spirit guardians'.
'Spirit guardians'
are turtles (biē).
The reason for placing turtles inside
is that when the fish reach fifty thousand three hundred and sixty,
a jiaolóng (dragon-like creature) will become their leader,
and will fly away with the fish.
With turtles present, the fish will not leave,
but will circulate among the nine islets in the pond endlessly,
considering it their river and lake.
Rearing carp
they do not eat each other,
grow easily,
and are not costly.' "
Planting lotus
Method for planting lotus (liánhuā) from lotus roots (ǒugēn):
In early spring, dig up segments of lotus roots
and place them in a fish pond.
Once lotuses bloom,
they will surely produce lotus seeds.

End.
Protecting guests
Shàngshū (Minister) Zhāng Gōng (Lord Zhāng)
came from a prominent family with three prime ministers,
and was a respected figure across four dynasties.
His knowledge of things was comparable to Zhuāng Wǔ's,
and his extensive learning surpassed Xū Chén's.
Chuò (another name for Zhāng Gōng) avoided disaster in Pútián,
residing temporarily in a Buddhist temple.
His official position was like a mere seal,
and his reputation was even lower than a wine vendor's.
I presumptuously welcomed him as a guest,
and always allowed him to attend conversations.
His compilations were particularly unique,
interspersed with humor.
He wrote "Shàngshū Gùshí" (Old Stories of the Minister), so it is said.
Jade Casket Storing Lántíng
Tàizōng (Emperor Tàizōng) possessed three thousand six hundred sheets of the Great King's (Wáng Xīzhī's) original calligraphy,
each typically mounted on a scroll one zhàng and two chì long.
Among those he treasured, the "Lántíng" (Orchid Pavilion Preface) was the most prized.
He once whispered to Gāozōng (Emperor Gāozōng):
"After I die,
take my 'Lántíng' with me."
Later, it was stored in a jade casket within Zhāolíng (Zhaoling Mausoleum).
White Cloud Carriage
Sīmǎ Tiānshī Chéngzhēn (Celestial Master Sīmǎ Chéngzhēn)
resembled Táo Yǐnjū (Tao Hongjing) in appearance.
Míng Wáng (King Míng) said:
"Chéngzhēn
is Hóngjǐng's (Hongjing's) reincarnation."
A carriage descended from heaven,
with the characters:
"Bestowed upon Chéngzhēn."
He departed by 'corpse liberation,'
white clouds filled the courtyard,
and he was called "Báiyún Xiānshēng" (Mr. White Cloud).
Therefore, people made a carriage for him, called the White Cloud Carriage.
One-legged Crane
During the time of Hàn Wǔ (Emperor Wǔ of Han), someone presented a one-legged crane.
Dōngfāng Shuò (Dongfang Shuo) reported:
"This is what the 'Shānhǎi Jīng' (Classic of Mountains and Seas) calls a bìluán."
Upon verification,
it was indeed so.
Therefore, he ordered his court officials
to all read the "Shānhǎi Jīng."
Yellow-White Art
There was Wáng Gǔ (Wang Gu)
who obtained the Yellow-White Art (alchemy),
and could transform瓦礫 (tiles and rubble) and mud into gold instantly.
There was also Wáng Xiū (Wang Xiu)
who could transform bamboo leaves into gold.
Painting of a Clear Night Tour in the Western Garden
The "Qīngyè Yóu Xīyuán Tú" (Painting of a Clear Night Tour in the Western Garden)
was painted by Gù Chángkāng (Gu Changkang).
It has colophons by various princes of the Liáng (Liang) dynasty,
stating that the numerous people in the painting
would all receive heavenly blessings.
During the Zhēngguān (Zhenguan) era,
Chǔ Hénán (Chu Henan) mounted and preserved it.
Liáng Zhāomíng's Shin Bone
Gōng once saw the shin bone of Prince Liáng Zhāomíng at a noble family's home.
It was slightly red and unusually lustrous.
He also saw a preserved human specimen, about a foot long,
with eyebrows, eyes, hands, and feet all intact.
Some believed it to be a person of the Jiāojiǎo people.
Immortal Riding a Crane
Gōng's cousin, Lú Jūn,
one day saw the clear blue sky
and watched an immortal riding a crane pass by,
with several other cranes flying before and behind.
He observed one crane's back swaying
just like a person controlling a horse.
Holes in Steles
Ancient steles all have round holes.
The character 碑 (bēi, stele)
is derived from 悲 (bēi, sorrow).
Originally placed in burial grounds,
each tomb had four.
When first interring, ropes were threaded through the holes
to lower the coffin.
This was the ancient ritual of "suspension burial" (xuán biàn).
The Lǐjì (Book of Rites) says:
"The ducal household observes the fēngbēi (grand stele),
while the three noble families observe the huán yíng (pillar-like markers)."
Later, to record their virtues,
steles and markers came into being.
Subsequently, "steles of virtuous governance" (dézhèng bēi) appeared,
also featuring round holes,
without knowledge of their original purpose.
Prefect of Táizhōu
The Grand Counselor, Duke of Hédōng,
was in the prime minister's position during the Kāiyuán era.
There was a Zhāng Jǐngzàng who could foretell good and ill fortune.
He suddenly visited the Duke
and wrote a large character "台" (tái).
The Duke said:
"I am currently in the position of Grand Counselor (Táishī),
what does this mean?"
A few days later,
he was demoted to Prefect of Táizhōu.
Hermit Rearing Dragons
Chancellor Niú governed Xiāngyáng.
There was a prolonged drought.
There was a hermit whom
everyone called "the dragon-rearer."
The Duke asked him to bring rain.
The hermit said:
"There are no dragons in the Jiānghàn region,
only one black dragon in a small pool.
Forcing it out will surely cause disaster
and will be difficult to control."
The Duke insisted,
and indeed there was a great rain
that swept away ten thousand households.
Wáng Nèishǐ's Letters
Wáng Nèishǐ wrote letters.
In a letter to the Administrator of Shǔjùn,
he requested cherries and láiqín, saying "give me vine shoots."
Láiqín,
meaning "its sweet taste attracts many birds,"
is commonly written as línqín.
He also said that walnut seedlings had already matured.
He also asked if Sīmǎ Xiāngrú and Yáng Zǐyún had descendants.
Seeking the Supervisor of Xīntíng
Gù Kuàng was skilled in calligraphy.
With few strokes,
he once sought the position of Supervisor of Xīntíng.
Someone asked him,
"I want to write about the vast mountains and seas."
Peonies
It is commonly said that peonies are a recent phenomenon,
presumably because there are no peony poems in the collections of literati from the current dynasty.
Zhāng Gōng once said that Yáng Zǐhuá of Northern Qí painted peonies very distinctly.
Thus, we know that peonies already existed in Northern Qí.
Gù Kuàng's Poem
Gù Kuàng's aspirations were detached and unrestrained.
He was once invited by a prime minister,
who intended to offer him a good official position.
Kuàng replied with a poem:
"The four seas are now at peace;
why does the prime minister need to summon this mad scholar?
This body is still a crane in a cage;
I look east to the vast ocean and cry out once."
Sū Kángfó (Sū Who Carried a Buddha)
During the Huìchāng Persecution of Buddhism,
envoys were dispatched to record gold Buddhas and precious images.
There was an official named Sū who
secretly took a Buddha in his sleeve and brought it home.
At the time, he was called "Sū Kángfó."
Someone asked Wēn Tíngyún what his antithesis would be.
He said:
"Nothing surpasses Mìtuó Sēng (Monk Mitabha)."
Five Stars and Evil Buddhas
Images of the Five Stars and evil Buddhas
are now commonly painted in people's homes.
Mixing the Five Stars among Buddhas
is incorrect.
Five-Court Censors
According to the regulations of the Censorate,
from Grand Master to Investigating Censor,
they were collectively called "Five-Court Censors."
In our dynasty, three individuals held positions in all five courts:
Lǐ Shāngyǐn, Zhāng Yánshǎng, and Wēn Zào.
Assistant Director in the Bureau of Population
Dù Zǐwēi dreamed someone said:
"Resign in spring, but not in autumn; both 'kūn' (昆) and 'jiē' (皆) have 'tóu' (头) at the top and 'jiǎo' (脚) at the bottom."
Indeed, he was appointed Assistant Director in the Bureau of Population (Bǐbù Wàiláng).
Hermit Helping in Emergency
There was a fallen scion of an official family
whose late father's close friend was now a regional governor.
So he traveled far
hoping for generous relief.
When they met,
the governor's attitude was very ordinary.
The young man then walked idly along the long road,
sighing endlessly.
Suddenly, he met a man
whose clothes were dirty and tattered.
The man walked past him
and said:
"Do you have something unjust troubling you?
I wish to know."
So he told him the truth of his situation.
The man replied:
"A small matter!
I am a hermit,
currently serving as a prison guard,
but my main purpose is to help people in urgent need."
At midnight, he took a bowl,
lifted it to look,
and saw a grizzled old man in purple robes,
several inches tall.
This man reproached him, saying:
"You have a connection with this person,
yet you do not care for his orphan.
Is this acceptable?"
The purple-robed man humbly apologized for a long time.
Afterward, he covered the ground with the bowl,
and when he lifted it again,
there was nothing there.
The next morning,
he heard shouts asking,
"Where is Scholar So-and-so?"
He hurried there,
and found the regional commander (liánshuài) suddenly very warm in his feelings,
and bestowed upon him a hundred bolts of silk.
He did not mention the earlier incident.
Was this not an immortal?
Śarīra
There was a monk in Luòyáng who obtained several śarīra.
He kept them in a glass vessel,
and offered incense and donations day and night without fail.
There was a scholar, pressed by hunger and cold,
who said to the monk:
"I wish to have a śarīra
to hold and examine."
The monk then took it out and handed it over.
The scholar immediately swallowed it.
The monk was frightened as if mad.
The scholar said:
"Give me some money,
and I will take medicine to pass it out."
The monk bribed him with two hundred guàn of cash,
and also gave him "Wanbing Wan" (Ten Thousand Illnesses Pills) to take.
A short while later, he excreted the śarīra.
He washed it and retrieved it.
Hánjù
In the Jìnshū (Book of Jin), there is a food item called "hánjù"
without any annotations.
Later, I found it in the Shíjīng (Food Classic) section of the Qímín Yàoshù (Important Arts for the People's Welfare),
which is what is now called "huánbǐng" (ring cakes).
Jīngēn Chē (Golden Root Chariot)
Hán Chǎng,
Yú's son.
Although his teaching was righteous,
his nature was quite dull and inferior.
He served as a collator.
In the historical records, there was "jīngēn chē."
Chǎng thought it was a mistake
and changed all instances of "gēn" (根, root) to "yín" (银, silver).
Later, when appointed Remonstrance Official (shíyí),
he was dismissed due to this comment.
Migrating Orioles
Now, passing the imperial examination is called "qiān Yīng" (遷鶯, relocating orioles).
This is based on the *Máo Shī* (毛詩): "Fá mù dīng dīng,
niǎo míng yīng yīng.
Chū zì yōu gǔ,
qiān yú qiáo mù" (伐木丁丁，鳥鳴嚶嚶。出自幽谷，遷于喬木. Chopping wood, ding ding; birds cry ying ying. From the gloomy valley, they move to tall trees).
It also says:
"Yīng qí míng yǐ,
qiú qí yǒu shēng" (嚶其鳴矣，求其友聲. They cry ying, seeking the sound of their friends).
There is no character "yīng" (鸎) here.
A few years ago, the student examination featured a poem "Yīng Qiú Yǒu" (鶯求友, Oriole Seeks Friend),
and another poem "Yīng Chū Gǔ" (鶯出谷, Oriole Leaves Valley).
There is no evidence for this in other books.
Is this not a mistake?
*Qiān Zì Wén* (千字文)
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng (梁武帝) instructed his princes to practice calligraphy.
He ordered Yīn Tiěshí (殷鐵石) to select a thousand unique characters from the calligraphy of the Grand Kings,
each character on a small piece of paper,
disordered and fragmented.
The Emperor summoned Zhōu Xīngsì (周興嗣) and said:
"You have talent and ingenuity,
please arrange them into rhymes for me."
Zhōu Xīngsì compiled them in one day,
and when he presented them,
his hair and beard had all turned white.
Eighteen Vats of Worn-out Brushes
Zhiǒng (智永), a grandson of Yòujūn (右軍),
personally copied the *Qiān Zì Wén* (千字文) eight hundred times.
Later, he left one copy at each of the various temples in Jiāngnán (江南).
Master Yǒng (永公) lived at Yǒngxīn Temple (永欣寺) in Wúxīng (吳興).
He studied calligraphy for many years,
accumulating eighteen vats of worn-out brush heads.
People came to seek his calligraphy like a market.
The threshold of his residence became worn through,
so it was wrapped in iron sheets.
It was called "Tiě Ménxiàn" (鐵門限, Iron Threshold).
Buddhism Belongs to Guǐxiù
Buddhism astrologically belongs to the Guǐxiù (鬼宿) constellation.
When it is dark, Buddhism declines.
Regret Not Learning to Extract Silver
Zhāo Wěi (昭緯) experienced the chaos of the bandit Zhāo (巢賊),
wandering and lacking food.
Suddenly, he met an old acquaintance, a silversmith,
who invited him to a lavish meal.
Zhāo Wěi (昭緯) wrote a poem that said:
"A plate of dozens of felt roots,
and on the platter, even more red scales.
Had I known early that literature brings so much hardship,
I would regret not learning to extract silver at the start."
Intestine-Clearing Rice
During the chaos of Sūn Rú (孫儒) in Jīngnán (荊南),
a *dòu* (斗) of rice cost forty thousand *qián* (千).
One could exchange gold and jewels,
only to get a pinch or a *gě* (合).
This was called "tōngcháng mǐ" (通腸米, intestine-clearing rice).
It meant that starving people could not eat other things,
only boil and drink rice water,
which could slightly clear the intestines and stomach.
Knocking Down the Ten Sages
During the Wéndé (文德) era,
Zhào Tāo (趙滔) was the Yǐn (尹) of Pínglù (平陸).
A horse escaped into the Temple of Confucius,
knocking down the statues of the Ten Sages.
The commander Sūn Huī (孫揮) rushed to report, saying:
"A horse entered the Temple of Confucius,
knocking down two yámén (衙門) officials."
Embracing Lamb Broth
The people of Bǎiyuè (百越) considered frogs to be the finest delicacy.
First, a small lamb was placed in a pot.
When the water boiled,
all the frogs embraced the lamb and were cooked.
This was called "bào yáng gēng" (抱羊羹, embracing lamb broth).
It is also said:
The skin of a person with scabies is the best.
Therefore, people say,
it must not be removed.
This is a "jǐn ǎozi" (錦襖子, brocade jacket).
Lice Are Pín
Lǐ Pín (李蠙), the Sīkōng (司空), was initially named Qiú (虯).
As he was about to take the imperial examination,
he dreamt that a stroke was added to his name,
forming the character "shī" (虱, louse).
He awoke and said:
"Shī (虱) is Pín (蠙)."
He then changed to his current name,
and indeed passed the examination.
Lǐ Qúnyù's Poem
Though the partridge flies back and forth east and west,
at the beginning of opening its wings,
it must first fly south.
Its name it calls itself is "Bó Dùzhōu" (薄杜州).
Moreover, the *Běncǎo* (本草) says:
"It calls itself gōu zhōu gé dié" (鉤輈格碟).
Therefore, Lǐ Qúnyù's (李群玉) poem says:
"Just traversing a winding, rugged path,
again hearing the sound of gōu zhōu gé dié."
Ghost Chariot
The owl is also called xiūliú (鵂鶹).
It flies at night and rests during the day.
It can eat human nails and toenails,
to discern good or bad fortune.
If it's bad fortune, it cries on the roof of the house.
Therefore, people always hide their trimmed nails.
It is also called "Yèyóunǚ" (夜遊女, Night-roaming Woman),
fond of troubling with infant ghosts.
It is also called "Guǐchē Niǎo" (鬼車鳥, Ghost Chariot Bird),
able to enter people's houses
and collect their souls.
It has ten heads.
One head was bitten off by a dog,
and it constantly bleeds.
If the blood drips into a person's house, it is ominous.
Therefore, upon hearing its sound, people strike dogs,
making them bark to ward it off.
Heavenly Roasted Meat
Ark clams are called wǎwūzi (瓦屋子).
People in Guǎng (廣) value them.
They are also called "Tiān Luán Zhì" (天臠炙, Heavenly Roasted Meat).
Sea Mirror
People in Guǎng (廣) call it "gāoyè pán" (膏葉盤).
Two pieces join together to form its shape.
It is round on the outside and very clear and clean inside.
Its flesh is like a clam fetus.
Inside, there are small red crabs,
as tiny as beans,
complete with pincers and legs.
When the sea mirror drinks,
the crabs come out to eat.
When the crabs are full and return to its belly,
the sea mirror is also full.
Jellyfish
People in Mǐn (閩) call it "dì tuó" (地坨).
It is an amorphous mass,
as large as an overturned hat.
Its belly is like hanging fluff.
It has a mouth but no eyes.
Shrimp often follow it,
eating its saliva and foam,
floating on the water.
If one tries to catch it,
it suddenly disappears.
This is because the shrimp have seen something.
Dancing Elephant
The Barbarian King entertained the Han envoy.
He arranged a dancing elephant show in front of the Bǎihuā Tower (百花樓).
Every beat perfectly matched the rhythm.
The elephants trained by Emperor Míng (明皇),
during the chaos of Tiānbǎo (天寶),
Lù Shān (祿山) held a grand banquet for the Hú (胡) chieftains.
He brought out the elephants to deceive them,
saying:
"These ran here from the Southern Sea.
Because I have the Mandate of Heaven,
even these different creatures,
when they see me, must bow and dance."
Those around him instructed them,
but the elephants glared angrily and did not move,
refusing to bow in the end.
Lù Shān (祿山) grew angry
and killed them all.
Aphid Snail
It is called "zǐjù" (紫具).
Viewing the Moon from Tiānzhù Peak
Zhào Zhīwēi (趙知微) possessed Taoist arts.
During the Mid-Autumn Festival, the sky remained overcast,
and everyone regretted the passing of the good time.
Zhīwēi (知微) said:
"We can prepare wine and food
and ascend Tiānzhù Peak (天柱峰) to view the moon."
As soon as they left the house,
the sky cleared.
When they reached the peak,
the moonlight was as bright as day.
They stayed until the moon set before returning.
Below the mountain, there was a chilly wind and bitter rain,
as dark and gloomy as before.
Ancient Mirrors in a Fish's Belly
Yuán Zhěn (元稹) ascended Huánghè Tower (黃鶴樓).
He saw a light by the riverbank like a star.
He sent someone to investigate
and they found a carp.
When it was cut open,
there were two ancient mirrors in its belly,
the size of coins, with twin phoenixes and dragons on their backs.
Light emanated from their mouths.
Ascending Liánhuā Fēng
Wáng Xuánchōng wanted to ascend Liánhuā Fēng.
The temple monks laughed at him.
Xuánchōng said:
"When I reach the peak, I will make smoke as a signal."
The next day,
he carried fire and ascended.
The monks waited for him for several days,
and indeed, smoke rose.
He stayed for twenty days,
then descended again,
saying:
"On the peak there is a pond,
with lotus flowers in full bloom,
lovely.
In it, there is a broken iron boat."
Lúshān Jīng
Liú Bǐngrén was the Cìshǐ of Jiāngzhōu.
He brought a camel from the capital to the commandery,
and released it at the foot of Lúshān.
The wild people saw it and were greatly alarmed,
and together shot and killed it.
Then they reported to the prefecture, saying:
"We captured a Lúshān Jīng in a certain place."
Liú ordered it to be brought,
it was the camel he had released.
Xiànshān
Āndìng Jùn has Xiànyáng Fēng.
On the peak there is a pond.
If it rains, clouds rise,
and in the pond, it is like a carriage canopy.
Therefore, a local proverb says:
"When Xiànshān puts on its canopy, the rain pours."
Zhāng Suì
Yīxíng Chánshī,
his secular surname was Zhāng,
given name Suì.
Zhǔbù Chóng
Zhèzhōng formerly had no scorpions.
One person, when he was the Jīntán Bù of Rùnzhōu,
brought several tens in bamboo tubes to his official residence.
People called them "Zhǔbù Chóng".
Bò Míng Jiē Jiǎo
《Táng Huìyào》:
"In the fourth year of Zhēnyuán,
the Lìbù reported:
'Since the period of difficulty,
records have been lost or forgotten,
and many people falsely claim or deceive.
Those currently holding office,
are called 'bò míng' (splitting names).
Those succeeding the deceased,
are called 'jiē jiǎo' (joining heels)."
Dàoshì Chángchímǎn
The Rǔyáng Wáng drank with Yè Jìngnéng.
Yè said:
