"I have a disciple who can drink,
I should have him come to visit."
The next day,
one who announced himself said:
"Dàoshì Chángchímǎn."
They saw him,
he was a dwarf.
He spoke of the Dao of the primordial chaos.
They offered him wine.
When he reached about five dòu,
he suddenly fell over drunk.
He was a jar.
Chéngdéqì
Someone called himself "Chéngdéqì"
and asked people for wine.
Someone struck it,
and it was a broken wine jar.
Tiāocài Shī
Lù Guīméng's poem says:
"Where they rest, they always lean on the shadows of nephews and maternal uncles;
When picking frequently, one often sees the hearts of fathers-in-law and mothers-in-law."
Yújù
All are called "língxíng."
Fishing clothes are all called "jiàowū."
Bǎi Zhú Míng
Fán Zōng's poem "Yuán Jì":
Cypresses are called Cāngguān,
bamboos are called Qīngshì.
Yǎnquán
Bào Róng's poem refers to tears as "yǎnquán",
and to graves as "qīngsōng zhái".
Yǔ Jìn
Someone prayed for rain very devoutly.
He dreamt that a god said:
"The rain prohibition is extremely severe."
Bā Yú
Liǔ Zihòu named his stream, hill, spring, ditch, pond, pavilion, hall, and island
all with "yú" (foolish),
calling them "Bā Yú" (Eight Follies).
Guàqián Wǔ
When Wáng Tíngzhòu was obscure,
he once visited a Wǔmíng Dàoshì for divination.
He threw the divination coins,
and all the coins danced.
Shǔ Guài
Lǐ Zhīwēi lodged in the Dūshěng.
At night, he heard calls for the Chídào Dūwèi and Sīchéng Zhǔbù.
He saw several small people
enter a hole under an ancient huái tree.
The next day, he opened and examined it,
and they were rats.
Yù Qì
Cuī Shénqìng memorialized, saying:
"Summon the Crown Prince using a jade tally."
Zétiān followed this.
Shìjiǔ Shàncān
Xú Huì loved wine,
Fù Shī was good at eating.
Yáng Sìfù said:
"Xú family's lungs,
Shěn family's spleen,
Is that truly peaceful and secure?"
Ài Guānchásǐ Pà Dàchóng
During the Yuánhé era,
several junior officials were drinking in the imperial secretariat,
talking about their lifelong loves and dislikes, and what they feared.
Some said they loved paintings and board games,
others feared recklessness and flattery.
Zhōu Yuàn, a Yuánwàiláng from the two departments, alone said:
"I love the Xuānzōng Guānchásǐ,
and fear tigers."
《Shèngsòng Duōyí》
Shèngsòng refers to,
from the founding of the state to the current dynasty,
the virtues of rulers and fathers,
the deeds of ministers and sons,
the conduct of common people,
what can serve as a warning or be regulated,
what can transform or inspire,
that which is manifest to the people's ears,
gathered and compiled.
Preface dated Tiānshèng Jiǎzǐ.
Wáng Zhù Tòngkū
The Emperor once held an intimate banquet for the Hànlín Xuéshì.
Wáng Zhù, drunk,
returned to his residence weeping bitterly.
One of his subordinates said:
"Zhù wept bitterly yesterday,
recalling the special regard and trust of Zhōu Shìzōng."
The Emperor said:
"Truly a loyal subject."
He was bestowed thirty jars of superior wine.
Tián Xī Zhāngshū
The Emperor visited the Lóngtú Pavilion to read books.
He pointed to a lacquered box on a shelf in the northwest corner,
and said to Xuéshì Chén Yáozī:
"These are Tián Xī's memorials."
He was saddened for a long time.
Dí Yàn
One day, the Emperor was writing a book.
His brush was clogged,
and he wanted to remove the old ink.
He looked to his left and right,
but no one was there.
So he rose himself, took a copper basin, and washed it.
When he had finished,
his attendants arrived.
The Emperor slowly said:
"Where did you all come from?"
Tǎo Shǔ
Cáo Bīn campaigned against Shǔ.
Initially, he captured Chéngdū.
Those who captured women,
Bīn gathered them all in one residence, with a small opening to pass food.
He said:
"These are to be presented to the Emperor,
they must be secretly guarded."
When the matter was settled,
he inquired for their relatives to return them,
and those without relatives were married off.
Tàizǔ Yùlóu
Liú Wēnsǒu was the Censor-in-chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
One day, he passed by the Qiányuán Mén gate.
His attendants rushed to tell him:
"Táizǔ is currently on the imperial tower."
Wēnsǒu walked to the side of the tower,
dismounted, and entered to report:
"According to established custom,
Your Majesty does not ascend the tower unless bestowing a great pardon.
Now, Your Majesty is on the tower without cause,
and if the military and common people hear of it,
they will anticipate special grants.
Your servant dared not dismiss your escorts,
not wishing to startle them."
The Emperor immediately returned,
and gave 3,000 *mín* from the imperial treasury
to the county officials as self-punishment.
The Son of Heaven does not use the back gate
Wáng Sìzōng was the Censor-in-chief (Yùshǐ Zhōngchéng).
One day, Zhēnzōng visited Xiàngguó Sì temple
and returned through the north gate.
Sìzōng presented a memorial, saying:
"The Son of Heaven walks the 'Yellow Path' (Huáng Dào);
how can he use the back gate?"
The Emperor gave 3,000 *mín* from the imperial treasury as self-punishment.
From then on, the north gate was not frequently opened.
Inspecting the treasury money
Cáo Càn,
son of Bīn,
was a Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ).
One day, his mother inspected several thousand *mín* of accumulated money in the treasury,
summoned Càn, and pointed it out, saying:
"The late Vice-Chancellor (Xiān Shìzhōng) served in both the capital and the provinces,
but never had such an accumulation.
I know you are far from being as capable as your father."
Twenty years in the Secretariat
Wáng Dàn was in the Secretariat (Zhōngshū) for twenty years.
Every day after work,
he would rush to his study, close the door, and rest,
not receiving even close family members.
When his illness became critical,
he said to his family:
"Shave my head
and dress me in a black monastic robe
to fulfill my lifelong aspiration."
He died shortly after.
All were about to follow his instructions,
but his son-in-law, Sū Qí, strongly opposed and stopped them.
A stick of ice
Chén Péngnián was in the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín),
holding more than ten positions,
all relating to literary and confidential matters.
People called his list of titles "a stick of ice."
Court clerk purchasing pearls
Féng Zhěng had many concubines.
While in the Secretariat (Zhōngshū), he secretly sent a court clerk to buy pearls,
personally holding them to give as gifts.
If the purchased items were not satisfactory,
he would secretly carry them in and out,
sometimes up to three or four times.
Lǔ Zōngdào was a Censor (Zhèngguān).
Zhēnzōng was somewhat wary of him.
Zōngdào pleaded his case before the Emperor, saying:
"Your servant is in the remonstrance office;
remonstrating is my duty.
If Your Majesty is wary of me because of the frequency,
your servant humbly wishes to resign."
The Emperor comforted and encouraged him,
and personally inscribed "Lǔ Zhí" on the palace wall.
Praying for blessings with paper money
Wáng Sìzōng was a Military Governor (Jiédùshǐ),
with an upright and resolute character.
He was often ill,
and his family secretly burned paper money to pray for blessings.
Sìzōng loudly called out and stopped them,
saying:
"If the gods truly exist,
would they pervert justice and accept bribes?"
Two sons attending on him
Chén Shěnghuá was at home as a high-ranking official (Zhèngqīng).
His son Yáosǒu was a Vice-Director of the Bureau of Military Affairs (Cān Shūmì),
and Yáozī managed the Imperial Edicts (Zhìgào).
Each time they returned from court,
they would stand formally dressed, attending on him,
and when guests arrived, they would announce their names.
Zhāng Guāiyá memorialized
On his deathbed, Zhāng Yǒng
memorialized that Dīng Wèi was treacherous and wicked,
and using him would corrupt the national laws,
wishing that he be executed to apologize to the world.
Chóng Fàng lived in seclusion on Zhōngnán Shān mountain,
and remained unmarried until old age.
He supported his mother,
and would not feed her grain unless it was from his own strenuous farming.
Hundreds of people came from all directions to study with him.
Blessings should be cherished thus
Zhā Dào governed himself with diligence and frugality.
As a Drafter (Dàizhì),
he would always finish every dish he ate.
If he felt he could not finish it,
he would not pick up his chopsticks,
even for vegetables.
He often said:
"Blessings should be cherished thus."
Kòu Láigōng taking *dìhuáng*
Kòu Zhǔn was over thirty years old.
Tàizōng wished to promote him significantly,
but still considered him too young.
Zhǔn immediately took *dìhuáng* (rehmannia root)
and ate radishes
to counteract this.
Soon his hair became white.
Each generation worse than the last
Táo Gǔ was sent as an envoy to Wúyuè.
Zhōngyì Wáng hosted a banquet for him,
and during the meal, they ate swimming crabs.
When asked about their relatives,
Zhōngyì Wáng ordered more than ten kinds to be served, from swimming crabs to crabs with soft shells.
Gǔ said:
"This truly is what is called 'each generation worse than the last'."
Borrowing Xióngzhōu for hunting
Wáng Qīnruò re-entered the Secretariat (Zhōngshū).
In the early Tiānshèng era,
the Northern Dynasty sent an envoy with a letter,
stating that there was famine in their territory
and requesting to borrow the land of Wéizhōu for hunting.
At that time, Qīnruò was on leave,
and neither the court nor the provinces knew how to respond.
He was summoned back,
and the Emperor asked him about the matter.
He replied:
"I wish to grant it to them."
The Emperor said:
"What will be the reason?"
He said:
"During the Xiánpíng era, they invaded our borders;
did they send a letter first?"
So, it was answered accordingly.
Third-rank officials ascending the hall
Tàizōng ordered third-rank officials (Sānbān Fèngzhí) to ascend the hall
after returning from their missions
to inquire about the welfare and hardships of the people.
Tián Xī memorialized:
"Your Majesty has ordered third-rank officials to ascend the hall to speak on affairs;
then what use are Lǚ Méngzhèng and others?"
So, the practice was abolished.
Diagram of the Zen Assembly
Lǐ Zūnxù, Yáng Yì, and Liú Yún
gathered with two or three monks to discuss Zen nature (Zōngxìng),
and each painted their portraits,
calling it the "Diagram of the Zen Assembly" (Chánhuì Tú).
Elder Zhā
Zhā Dào was of pure and ancient character.
He resided at Lángshān Sì temple in Chángzhōu,
personally performed manual labor
to provide for the monks,
and everyone called him "Elder Zhā" (Zhā Zhǎnglǎo).
Cabinet food
Dù Hào was extensively learned
and served as a Scholar of the Longtuge (Lóngtúgé Xuéshì).
Zhēnzōng asked which family "cabinet food" (Dúshí) originated from.
Hào replied:
"When Emperor Jǐng of Hàn was
the Crown Prince,
Emperor Wén doted on him greatly.
After he resided in the Eastern Palace,
Emperor Wén said:
'The Crown Prince's food will surely be different from mine.' So he ordered the Grand Provisioner (Dàguān) to prepare two cabinet boxes for him each time.
This was its origin."
Old Fish Head
Lǔ Zōngdào was a Vice-Chancellor (Cānzhèng),
taking responsibility for his loyalty and integrity.
People at the time called him "Old Fish Head" (Yútóu Gōng).
This was to describe his unyielding uprightness.
Illustrious ministers of Tiānshèng
In the early Tiānshèng era,
the imperial court was clear and bright,
and rewards and punishments were always trustworthy.
At that time, Wáng Qīnruò, Wáng Zēng, Zhāng Zhíbái, and Lǔ Zōngdào all served the country with loyalty and righteousness.
Even Yáo and Sòng assisting Táng,
and Xiāo and Cáo aiding Hàn,
could not surpass these gentlemen.
Heavenly Scroll Bestows Appointment
Qī Lún (戚綸) was made a Provisional Official.
When the Heavenly Scroll (天書) first descended into the Pavilion of the Dragon Chart,
all the officials came to congratulate,
and their words were all excessively flattering.
Only Lún (綸) said:
"Such an event has never occurred in ancient times.
It should not be relied upon as an auspicious sign.
We should rather interpret it as an encouragement to be cautious and to examine ourselves."
Zhēn Zōng (真宗) marveled at him.
Admonishing Against the Construction of Zhāoyìng Palace
Shí Dàiwèn (石待問), who had passed the imperial examination, initially opposed the construction of Zhāoyìng Palace (昭應宮). He submitted an admonition, which roughly stated:
"All officials compare Your Majesty to Yáo (堯) and Shùn (舜),
but I say you are far inferior to Táng Tàizōng (唐太宗)."
Because of this, he was demoted to serve as the Prefect of Chúzhōu (滁州).
Late Opening of the Celestial Eye
Wáng Sìzōng (王嗣宗) was made Vice Grand Councilor,
but he declined the position due to old age.
Zhēn Zōng (真宗) abruptly stopped him.
Sìzōng (嗣宗) said:
"My strength is no longer sufficient.
I only regret that my celestial eye opened twenty years too late."
Retreat and Contemplation Rock
Lǔ Zōngdào (魯宗道), upon meeting the emperor through his grandson's directness, had a small studio built.
He decorated it with paintings of mountains and rivers,
and named it:
"Retreat and Contemplation Rock" (退思岩).
Every time he returned from the Central Secretariat,
he would spend the entire day there.
Zhāng Zhībái's Words
Zhāng Zhībái (張知白) said to his colleagues:
"We were originally scholars.
Having reached such high positions,
only by following public interest and suppressing private desires can we repay the nation."
Cutting a Cow's Tongue
When Zhāng Yǒng (張詠) was Prefect of Yǒngxīng (永興),
an old man complained that his cow's tongue had been cut off by someone.
Yǒng (詠) asked:
"Among your neighbors, who holds the deepest grudge against you?"
He replied:
"There is a certain Mr. Jiǎ (甲氏) who once borrowed millet from me,
but I refused,
and he harbors a deep resentment."
Yǒng (詠) sent him away, saying:
"Go home and immediately slaughter your cow and sell its meat."
The old man followed the instruction.
The next day, someone reported an unauthorized slaughter of a cow.
Yǒng (詠) bellowed:
"You cut off that man's cow's tongue
to avenge the denied millet loan,
and now you turn around and sue him?"
That person confessed his crime.
Cloth Robe and Gold Belt
When Kòu Zhǔn (寇準) was exiled to Yíngdào (營道),
he only wore a white cloth robe,
a gold official belt,
and an official cap.
Those who sought to criticize him ridiculed his transgression of etiquette.
Zhǔn (準) said:
"These were bestowed by the sovereign and my father.
I wear them to not forget them.
I do not see any breach of etiquette."
The satirists were greatly ashamed.
End of Scroll Forty-Five.
Chasing the Tiger Stele
In Yùnzhōu (鄆州), there was a "Chasing the Tiger Stele,"
which was broken and could not be examined.
The elders said:
Once, when Assistant Minister Zhāng (張侍郎) was Prefect of Yùn (鄆),
a tiger was harming creatures within the prefecture.
The Duke ordered an official to take an official talisman to chase the tiger,
threatening to execute him if he failed to go.
The official bid farewell to his family,
drank heavily, and set off.
Indeed, he saw a giant tiger.
He placed the talisman on the ground,
the tiger stared intently,
then carried the talisman and followed the official.
The entire city closed its doors,
climbing onto roofs and into trees to watch.
When the tiger arrived at the prefecture office,
it closed its eyes and crouched down,
as if awaiting punishment.
The Duke shouted:
"You are a creature of a different kind,
yet you dared to occupy the official road
and prey on travelers!"
Then he called an official to administer punishment,
ordering him to whip it according to the law.
The Duke admonished the tiger,
ordering it to leave the territory within three days.
Otherwise,
he would kill them all.
The tiger then departed,
and died in that place,
transforming into a stone.
It is now called "Tiger Stone."
Unequal Division of Property
When Duke Zhāng Yǒng (張公詠) was Prefect of Hángzhōu (杭州),
Shěn Zhāng (沈章) sued his elder brother Yànjūn (彥均) for an unfair division of family property.
The Duke had him whipped and sent away.
Half a year later,
the Duke happened to pass by their residence.
He dismounted and summoned Zhāng (章) and Yàn (彥),
saying:
"Your younger brother sued you, claiming you managed the household and finances,
and that he was young
and unaware of the amount of property,
and that you divided it unequally.
Is this true?"
Yàn (彥) said:
"It was equal and fair."
Zhāng (章) said:
"It was not equal."
The Duke ordered the elder brother's relatives to move into the younger brother's house,
and the younger brother's relatives to move into the elder brother's house.
They exchanged residences immediately.
No one dared to disobey.
The Emperor's Beloved Huái (檜)
The Tàiqīng Temple (太清宮) in Bózhōu (亳州) was constructing its front hall,
but an old huái (檜) tree's southern branch obstructed the eaves.
The officials wanted to cut it down with axes.
One night,
there was a great thunderstorm.
The next day, when they looked,
the branch had already turned north.
Zhēn Zōng (真宗) visited the temple,
loved its flourishing growth,
and named it "The Emperor's Beloved Huái" (御愛檜).
Shí Mànqīng (石曼卿)'s poem says:
"Human axes are not allowed near it,
heavenly winds and clouds turn its branches."
Xiè Hónglián (謝紅蓮)
During the Xīníng (熙寧) era,
Director Pí (皮郎中) was traveling through the Northern Capital,
and stayed at the Censorate.
A maidservant cried out, claiming to be possessed by a ghost.
She said:
"I am Xiè Hónglián (謝紅蓮).
I was once a concubine,
but unfortunately, the mistress murdered me.
My bones are buried here,
and I cannot attain rebirth."
The next day, Pí (皮) saw Duke Wèi (魏公)
and fully recounted the incident.
The Duke said:
"Buried corpses often become spirits."
He then ordered a search,
but nothing was found.
A laborer dreamed of a woman who said:
"My bones are between the kitchen and the bath."
Indeed, the bones were found
and buried on a high plain.
A clerk named Lǐ (李生) from the Duke's office
dreamed of the woman who said:
"Please thank Duke Wèi (魏公) very much for me!
The Duke is an upright man of his time,
currently noble and prominent,
with guards and soldiers protecting him,
so I dared not appear before him.
I hope you will sincerely convey my gratitude."
Kitchen God
Péng Jiè was the Cìshǐ of Jīngzhōu.
In the middle of the night, there were lights in the kitchen.
Jiè secretly peered in,
and saw a person in a black robe with a red cap,
sitting with legs spread,
scolding and beating someone.
Jiè pushed open the door and entered.
The others all scattered,
only the one in the black robe stood up and bowed.
His face was scorched black.
He said,
"I am the Zàoshén."
The Duke said,
"Who are those you were scolding?"
The deity said,
"They are hungry, ownerless ghosts,
stealing food.
If you can offer sacrifices to them by the water in spring and autumn,
and for the ownerless bones,
choose a spot to bury them,
that would be no small virtue.
Your seeing me
means you will have a slight illness.
Quickly take niúhuáng,
and insert shēngxī into your nose,
and you will have no trouble."
The Duke returned,
followed his words, and recovered.
Then he sacrificed to the hungry ghosts by the water,
and buried the遗骨 (yígǔ) on the plateau.
After the Duke died,
his coffin was returned to Chángshā.
Crying sounds were heard in the air.
Yùyuán Dàojūn
Liú Chéngxiàng, on his way to take the imperial examination in Jīngshī,
passed through Dúmù Zhèn.
An old man presented him with a poem, saying:
"This year you will cross on a poor mule,
another day you will return riding a precious horse."
He also said,
"You are indeed the Yùyuán Dàojūn of Luófú Shān."
From Qúnyù Gōng,
the jìnshì Niú Yì,
leaving the capital gate,
rested under a willow shade.
He dreamt he arrived at a grand mansion with high gates.
An official said,
"This is Qúnyù Gōng."
Soon, someone arrived on horseback,
and the official greeted him very respectfully.
Yì looked closely,
and it was his old acquaintance Lǚ Zhēn Nèihàn.
Lǚ said,
"I am in charge of this palace."
Yì saw a white jade stele in the hall,
with red characters,
covered with crimson gauze.
The large characters read "Zhōngzhōu Tiānxiān Jí."
Below it were thousands of names.
Among them, he only recognized a few people:
namely Lǚ Yíjiǎn, Lǐ Dí, and Yú Jìng.
Yì asked about the details of the Tiānxiān.
Lǚ said,
"There is a definite order.
Above the Zhēnrén,
is not something you can know.
Dàojūn ranks below Zhēnrén,
Tiānxiān below Dàojūn,
Dìxiān below Tiānxiān,
Shuǐxiān below Dìxiān,
and the earthly rulers below Shénxiān.
They generally progress from their initial practice
to ascend the immortal ranks."
Yì said,
"Are the high officials and prime ministers of this generation
mostly immortals?"
He replied,
"Seven or eight out of ten."
Yì said,
"Fù Gōngbì,
a venerable elder of the state,
is he an immortal?"
He replied,
"Fù Gōng is a Kūntái Zhēnrén,
and will only return to Kūnfǔ at ninety-three years old."
Yì said,
"What is your current position?"
He replied,
"I will be appointed an earthly ruler in another three hundred years."
Yì said,
"What kind of official is a ruler?"
He replied,
"One who governs the Wǔyuè, the Sī Dú, famous mountains, and great rivers."
Yì awoke from his dream,
and composed a poem, saying:
"One must believe that matters beyond the dust
are clearly before one's eyes.
How many transient worldly guests
are all entangled by fame and profit."
Entering the Jar
Cíyún Chánglǎo's surname was Yuán,
originally named Dào.
Waiting to take the imperial examination in Nángōng,
he fell ill but strongly ventured to Xīchí.
A monk invited him into a thatched hut.
There seemed to be no smoke from cooking,
only a huge jar,
covered with a broken hat.
He secretly thought it must contain stored grain.
He tried to lift the hat.
Inside the jar was bright,
with towers and terraces high and low,
people coming and going.
Someone called Dào by name,
and following the voice, he was already inside.
There was a prime minister, Lǐ Fǔguó,
who summoned Dào as a household guest,
and married his daughter to him.
That autumn, he passed the imperial examination,
and was subsequently appointed Yùshǐ.
At that time, the Son of Heaven personally led a campaign against the northern Di.
Dào submitted a memorial, saying:
"Attacking the Yi and Di is like shooting sparrows with bright pearls.
Even if you get the sparrow, you lose the pearl.
Acquiring their land is like stony fields,
unfit for cultivation.
The ancients said there was no supreme strategy for resisting barbarians,
which is not an accurate statement.
I believe forming alliances through loyalty and trust is the supreme strategy.
Selecting generals to guard the borders is the next best strategy.
Attacking them with troops is a middle strategy.
Marrying them off with daughters is a lower strategy.
Forming alliances with jade and silks is no strategy at all."
The Emperor was pleased with his memorial,
and decreed him as Zhōngchéng.
Soon after, he was appointed prime minister,
assisting and harmonizing in governance.
The Son of Heaven deposed Empress Wáng and established Consort Mǎ as empress.
Dào strongly remonstrated.
The Emperor was enraged,
and demoted him to Sīmǎ of Qióngzhōu.
Later, the remonstrating officials discussed his loyalty,
and he was again appointed prime minister.
At that time, a large army was raised to campaign against Liáo.
Dào's memorial was very blunt.
The Emperor was furious,
and had Dào executed in the eastern marketplace.
As the blade reached his neck,
he suddenly realized he was sitting beside the jar.
He bowed twice to the monk and said,
"Wealth and honor, success and failure,
are destiny,
these belong to Heaven.
Life, spirit, heart, and intellect,
are qi,
these belong to the body.
I shall follow Heaven and focus inward."
The monk said,
"That is right."
He saw Dào out the door,
and the monk and the temple both disappeared.
Then Dào shaved his head and put on monastic robes,
residing in Tàicí Sì,
both his Zen practice and age were advanced.
As he was about to pass away,
he composed a poem, saying:
"Coming from no coming and no going,
always going this way,
do not mistake the path."
Gāo Yán's Poem
Gāo Yán was fond of learning,
and had noble aspirations.
He wrote a poem, saying:
"Last night, the gloomy wind pierced to the bone with cold,
the earthen stove had no fire, the wine bottle was dry.
A man's generous spirit is his life's pursuit;
from time to time, he takes up his sword by the peach lamp to gaze upon it."
Poem on Lí Shān
Zhāng Yú of Xīshǔ wrote two *juéjù* poems titled "Leaving a Message on Lìshān" which said:
"Golden and verdant pavilions pierce the azure sky,
Sheng and xiao sounds weave into the heavenly wind.
At that time, the nation's beauty and the beauty of spring,
All lay within the emperor's gaze."
"The Jade Emperor's pavilions are locked in rosy mists,
Year-round, peony shoots are nurtured.
Unwary, a wild deer enters, leaping over the wall,
And carries out the palace's most prized flower."
Later, Yú stayed overnight at Wēntāng,
And dreamed of a green-clad boy who said:
"I am a servant of the sea immortal,
Commissioned to summon you."
Yú asked:
"Who is the immortal?"
The boy replied:
"She is Tàizhēnfēi of the First Palace of Pénglái."
He was led to a palace,
Where the immortal lady said:
"Your poems on Lìshān are excellent."
Yú rose from his mat and bowed in response.
The immortal entered the imperial bath,
The water's reflection was deep,
The tiles formed dragons and phoenixes.
She commanded Yú to undress and enter the bath,
Remaining a few steps apart.
After bathing,
They held hands and entered the rear courtyard.
Yú said:
"Seeing the immortal's splendor now,
How could one Lùshān stir her will?"
The immortal replied with shame:
"That matter was due to heavenly principles,
Please do not question it."
Yú asked:
"Where is Mínghuáng now?"
She replied:
"Mínghuáng is a High Celestial,
He now governs Yùyǔchuān,
Between Tán and Héng."
Then she ordered the cups and plates cleared away,
And they slept facing each other on couches.
Yú said:
"I wish to share a couch."
The immortal replied:
"Our predestined union is not yet fulfilled,
In two *jì* (twenty-four years),
I shall await you at Yīshuǐ."
She gave him a sachet of baihe (lily) fragrance.
The next day, Yú playfully composed a poem:
"Last night I encountered the hot spring,
And dreamed of bathing with Yángfēi.
I dared to present Yù Ràng's charcoal,
Presumptuously facing Biàn Hé's jade.
Sharing joy for one night,
Is enough for a thousand, ten thousand lives.
Thinking of Táng Mínghuáng,
How happy, how blessed!"
Chén Túnán's Poems
Chén Bó, styled Túnán,
Was enfeoffed by Táng Xīzōng as Qīngxū Chǔshì,
And also bestowed three palace women.
The Master composed a poem saying:
"Snow for flesh, jade for cheeks,
I deeply thank the monarch for sending them.
A recluse does not dream of Wūxiá,
Vainly tiring the clouds and rain to descend upon Yángtái."
During the Five Dynasties period, he traveled to Huàshān,
Often not emerging.
Zhēnzōng sent an imperial envoy to summon him,
The Master played a zither and declined, saying:
"My nature is like that of apes and birds,
My heart like earth and ashes.
I do not understand the depths of benevolence and righteousness,
How can I know the proper conduct of rituals and etiquette?
Withered lotus leaves for clothing,
Shed bamboo sheaths for a crown.
My body has green hair,
My feet lack straw sandals.
If I were to approach the imperial court,
I would bring laughter to the sagely dynasty."
He also said:
"A few lines of imperial edict,
Vainly tire the colorful phoenix to bring;
A piece of idle heart,
Has already been held by the white clouds."
He once wrote a poem saying:
"The highest point of Huàshān is my palace,
When I emerge, I soar through the sky, astride the morning wind.
The halls and pavilions are not closed with golden locks,
When I return, they are naturally sealed by white clouds."
Recluse Huí Grinds a Mirror
Jiǎ Shīxióngláng had an ancient iron mirror,
Which he treasured greatly,
And had long wished to polish.
There was a recluse named Huí,
Who offered to grind mirrors,
He had medicine in a basket which he piled on the mirror,
And said:
"The medicine is little, I must go back for more."
After he left,
He did not return for a long time.
Someone was sent to inquire about his lodging,
And he was found in a temple.
He had inscribed a poem on the temple gate which said:
"The green snake in my hand soars under the white sun,
The immortal medicine in the cave shines with eternal spring.
Know that I am a guest of mist and clouds beyond the material world,
Not a mirror-grinder amidst the dust."
The Duke looked at the mirror,
The medicine had already flown away.
A point of brilliant light,
Penetrated through like jade.
Lǚ Dòngbīn's "Qìnyuánchūn"
Cuī Zhōngjǔ, a *jìnshì*,
Traveled to Yuèyáng,
To visit his old friend Lǐ Lángzhōng,
And lodged in a city inn,
Singing "Qìnyuánchūn".
A shoe repairman said:
"What song is this?"
Cuī replied:
"It's a new tune from the capital."
The man said:
"I cannot write,
If you could write for me,
I would compose a lyric in this tune."
Cuī reluctantly wrote it down,
Its meaning was deeply spiritual,
So he asked for his name.
He replied:
"I was born at the mouth of the river (Jiāngkǒu),
Grew up at the mouth of the mountain (Shānkǒu).
Now I am a guest guarding the valley."
The next day, Cuī met the Grand Administrator,
And fully recounted the matter,
Who then ordered him to be summoned.
He knocked on the door,
The responding sound gradually faded.
He called again,
No answer.
He pushed open the door,
And found it empty, no one there.
On the wall was a poem which said:
"The infant within my belly has matured,
For now, I dwell in the city market to amuse myself temporarily.
Unexpectedly, an uncultivated scholar lightly wags his tongue,
So I return to wander in the deep places of white clouds."
The Grand Administrator said:
"Jiāngkǒu and Shānkǒu,
Are two 'mouths' (*kǒu*),
Which forms the character 'Lǚ'.
'Valley' (*gǔ*),
Is 'Dòng'.
'Guest' (*kè*),
Is 'Bīn'.
The immortal's name is clear.
They both sighed regretting that worldly ties hindered them,
And they did not encounter a true immortal."
The Cave of Divine Purity
Ōuyáng Yǒngshū and Méi Shèngyú were traveling at Sōngshān,
When drunk, they gazed at a giant cliff on the west peak,
Where four large characters written in red said "Shénqīng zhī Dòng".
Yǒngshū pointed it out to Shèngyú,
Who said he saw nothing.
The Duke then kept silent.
Later, when he sought to retire from the world,
He wrote a poem saying:
"Four red characters on a ten-thousand-ren cliff,
The Cave of Divine Purity locks the pavilions.
Mist and clouds fill the distant view, no one reaches it,
Luan and cranes must now be awaiting my arrival."
A few days later, he passed away.
The Duke, in his lifetime, never spoke of immortal matters,
Maintaining that his Dao should be thus.
Hán Xiāng's Poems
Hán Xiāng,
courtesy name Qīngfū,
was the nephew of Wéngōng.
He was unrestrained and unconventional,
always singing loudly when drunk.
The Duke said:
"You are a dignified seven-foot man,
yet I have never seen you read a single line of a book.
How will you establish yourself in the distant future?"
Xiāng smiled and said:
"I can slightly make poetry."
Then he immediately said:
"The cloud-water grotto in the green mountains,
this place is my home.
Throughout the night, precious liquid flows,
at dawn, I chew on rosy clouds.
My qín plays a melody of green jade,
my stove warms white cinnabar.
Precious smiles conceal golden tigers,
in the primal field, white ravens are nurtured.
A single gourd contains the world,
a five-foot blade slays demons and evil.
I can make wine in an instant,
and make flowers bloom in a moment.
If anyone can learn from me,
we can together watch immortal blossoms."
The Duke said:
"How can you command creation to make flowers bloom?"
Xiāng said:
"This matter is very easy."
He took some soil and gathered it in a pot,
and in a moment,
two green flowers appeared,
resembling peonies.
Their leaves had small golden inscriptions which read:
"Clouds hang over Qínlǐng, where is my home?
Snow engulfs Lánguān, my horse cannot advance."
The Duke did not understand the meaning of the lines.
Later, when he was demoted to Cháozhōu,
he met Xiāng on the way, who said:
"Do you remember the lines on the flowers?"
He inquired about the place name,
and it was indeed Lánguān.
The Duke said:
"I know you are an extraordinary person;
I will complete this poem for you."
They both reached Yuánxiāng,
and sang many poems in response to each other.
Xiāng bid farewell,
and the Duke composed a poem saying:
"Many talents have been used by the world since ancient times,
but whose grand writing surpasses this?
Wait until the day your achievements are complete,
then withdraw and lie among the misty vines."
Xiāng's poem said:
"The whole world is enslaved by fame and gain,
but I alone awaken to the Way.
One day, I am destined to ascend and fly,
breaking through the autumn sky, a tiny speck of green."
Sū Zǐměi's poem
The long bridge of Wújiāng spans Tài Hú,
a magnificent sight of the two Zhè regions.
Sū Zǐměi's poem says:
"On the cloud-tops, golden cakes brightly open,
on the water's surface, a colorful rainbow deeply rests."
Yáng Pán's poem says:
"A hundred-foot long rainbow rests its shadow in the clear sky,
a thousand qǐng of jade, flawless and pure."
Zhèng Yìfū says:
"The sky-piercing rainbow is wide as a jade waist,
the sea-spanning whale is high-backed with gold."
Jīnshān Sì's poem
At Jīnshān Sì in Rùnzhōu,
Zhāng Yòu's poem says:
"The temple's reflection is seen in the flowing stream,
the sound of bells is heard on both banks."
Luó Yǐn's poem says:
"The old monk finishes his fast and closes his door to sleep,
uncaring of the waves rising on all four sides."
Sūn Shān's poem says:
"Building his hermitage on a lonely peak,
practicing meditation amidst the giant waves."
Lù Zǐlǚ's poem says:
"Having a small farm, it's good to return;
having no official prospects, it's best not to come."
Wáng Āi's poem says:
"The moon hangs high in the sky, a thousand gates are closed,
on the great road, no one walks alone."
Staff poem
Wáng Āi's "Staff" poem says:
"Probing the water, it breaks the head of a golden áo,
parting the clouds, it snaps the leg of a tiger."
Hard-wrought line
Ōu Yǒngshū once spoke of a hard-wrought line, saying:
"A line obtained while sitting,
a fragment of heart from beyond the heavens."
Qīngwù's poem
Monk Qīngwù's poem says:
"Birds return, flower shadows move,
fish dive, water ripples circle."
Fàn Wénzhèng's tea poem
Cài Jūnmó said to Fàn Wénzhèng:
"Your 'Tea-Picking Song' says:
'By the golden stand, green dust flies,
in the jade bowl, emerald waves rise.'
Now, the finest tea
is very white in color,
emerald green is only inferior.
How about changing it to 'jade dust flies' and 'plain waves rise'?"
How about it?"
Xīwén said:
"Excellent!"
Six-character song
Shí Shǒudào was appointed lecturer at the Imperial Academy,
and Dù Diǎn of Púzhōu composed a "Six-character song" to send him off, saying:
"Galloping on the path of benevolence and righteousness,
at ease in the mansion of poetry and books.
His horns and teeth startle shrimp and crabs,
an old dragon in the ocean of learning.
His claws and spurs chase out foxes and rabbits,
a great tiger before the gate of the sages.
Overthrowing Yáng Zhū and Mò Dí,
upholding Zhòngní and Zhōugōng.
A single path out of the jar's mouth,
how many stages of life entrusted to the clouds.
Water immerses mountain shadows, inverted and green,
in spring, flower tips are half red."
Because of this song,
he was among the "Three Heroes" of that year.
Another poem, "To Ōuyáng Yǒngshū," says:
"A clear mind hangs a bright moon,
a myriad feet of literary flame fly like a long rainbow.
Begging for a ladle of water from the Phoenix Pool,
to revive a long-parched mud-coiled dragon."
His grand and unrefined style was all of this kind.
Daoist Shí's poem
Daoist Shí had a poem that said:
"Stones press, bamboo shoots emerge crookedly,
cliffs hang, flowers grow inverted."
Later, a prefect entered the temple,
and angered by the unkempt courtyard,
flogged him.
This insult
was foreseen by the previous poem's meaning.
Then he composed a poem to the prefect, saying: "It's not that people are lazy to sweep in spring,
but they cherish the green moss that covers the fallen flowers."
The prefect regretted it,
invited him for a drink,
and he again composed a poem saying:
"Breaking open the withered sheaths reveals new bamboo,
picking up fallen flowers adorns old branches."
A rough official is still a man
Prime Minister Lǐ said:
"At that time, a rough official was stationed in an outer region.
A scholar sent tea to this rough official,
and the official had a poem saying:
'A rough official begs for truly undeserved sincerity,
luckily, I have poetic sentiment to be worthy of tasting.'
Fú Yànqīng and Biàn had a poem saying:
'A whole army of one hundred thousand embraces a mighty force,
this is precisely the time to repay grace and serve the nation.
The waves of the Biàn River roar with drums and horns,
the willows on the Suí embankment brush against banners and flags.
In the vanguard are red banners of the generals from Guānxī,
around them sit fair maidens, courtesans of Zhàoguó.
Report to the officials of Cháng'ān,
a rough official is still a man!'"
Poem of expressing feelings
Zhāng Tuìwēng had a "Poem of Expressing Feelings" that said:
"Fate teaches me to enjoy life as it is,
heaven grants a lifetime of leisure."
Lǐ Qīngchén's poem
When Hán Wèigōng was in charge of Zhōngshān,
Lǐ Qīngchén came to visit him.
His attendant reported:
"The Grand Supplicant is currently sleeping."
Qīngchén composed a quatrain saying:
"The young master enjoys leisure, lying in a red kitchen,
the white-robed old clerk slighting the humble scholar.
Does he not dream of Zhōugōng,
who once spoke of spitting out food for guests?"
When Wèigōng saw his poem, he said:
"I have known this man for a long time."
Ultimately, he was chosen as his son-in-law.
Leisurely and unhurriedly, sealed inscriptions are definitely not read.
Jiǎng Táng, assistant minister, retired to Gūsū.
There was a monk about to travel to Qiántáng,
who requested a letter from Lǚ Jìshū.
The Duke wrote a poem that said:
"Retiring from you, I merely close my door;
For years I've had no business on the riverbank.
My master, do not be surprised that no letter goes,
For a leisurely and careless seal on a title will surely not be looked at."
Jìshū saw it,
treated the monk generously,
and expressed shame with a letter.
Crying children, empty rice basket
A scholar, Zhāng Qiú, presented a poem to Lǚ Shēngōng, saying:
"Recently the kitchen has lacked provisions,
Children cry and the rice basket is empty.
Mother then whispered to her child,
'Father has a new poem for the Grand Councilor.'"
The Grand Councilor saw the poem,
was very pleased,
and consequently gave him a generous gift.
Poem on Swallows Leaving the Nest
During the reign of Táng Xīzōng,
Qiānhuà Mào relied on Vice Minister Cài,
and was given a position in his household.
One day, he announced his departure.
He composed the poem "Swallows Leaving the Nest," which said:
"The old nest's crumbling clay is ruined,
This year, before the community rituals, I return.
The towering mansion reaching the clouds offers no resting place,
To whose household gate shall I fly next?"
The master saw the poem,
and retained him again.
Zhāng Tuìwēng's Poem
Chancellor Zhāng Shìxùn's poem "Sending off Hermit Wèi" said:
"A wisp of idle cloud comes to the imperial city,
But flying back, it refuses to wait for autumn wind."
Courtesan Cuī Lányīng
Chén Shūwén passed the imperial examination
and was appointed county clerk of Yíxīng.
The courtesan Cuī Lányīng had about a thousand strings of cash in her purse
and wished to marry.
Shūwén said:
"I am not yet married."
So they made an agreement.
Upon returning, he deceived his wife, saying:
"I am poor and have no travel expenses,
I will go to my official post alone for now."
Then he went downstream with Cuī on the Biàn River.
Three years later,
he returned from his post,
ascending the Biàn River.
He privately thought that Yīng did not know he had a wife,
and his wife did not know he had Yīng,
so upon returning, a lawsuit would surely arise.
Therefore, he drank heavily with Yīng,
pushed her into the water,
and pushed her maidservant in as well.
Later, while visiting the Xiàngguó Temple,
he saw two women.
He looked closely,
and it was Yīng.
She sent her maidservant to call Shūwén.
Shūwén said:
"Are you unharmed?"
Yīng said:
"I fell for your scheme!
We two fell into the water,
embraced and floated,
crying out for help.
Someone rescued us,
and we lived.
As for what happened today,
let's not speak of it again.
But since I am alive,
I bear you no grudge.
I live outside the city gate,
so come quickly tomorrow.
Otherwise,
I will sue you to the authorities!"
Shūwén had no choice
but to buy mutton and wine and go there.
When he arrived outside the city gate,
the maidservant had already come out to meet him.
Shūwén entered,
and did not come out by evening.
His servant then went in
and found Shūwén lying face down with his hands tied behind his back,
as if one who had suffered today's ultimate punishment was dead.
Lǐ Tàibǎo's Maidservant
Gōng Qiú was in the capital.
On the night of the Lantern Festival,
he idly followed a carriage with a green felt cover.
A woman alighted from the carriage,
carrying a green pouch,
and left very quickly.
Qiú then went to a dark place.
She said:
"I am a maidservant from Lǐ Tàibǎo's household.
I am past the allowed age,
and my suffering has increased.
Tonight I am running away.
If you can take me in,
I wish to serve you."
Qiú took her hand and walked with her,
then falsely pointed to an alley and said:
"This is where I live.
You wait at the alley mouth for now.
I will first inform my family,
and then call you."
Then he took the green pouch, entered the end of the alley,
and exited through another street.
The pouch contained only gold and pearls.
He sold them between Jiāng and Huái,
obtaining a thousand strings of cash,
and traveled as a merchant,
his money increasing even more.
One evening,
he moored his boat in Shānyáng.
On a neighboring boat was a woman,
who seemed familiar but he couldn't recall.
The woman said:
"I have searched the ends of the sky and the corners of the earth,
and descended into the Nine Springs,
but found you nowhere.
You were just here!
I
was the maidservant who ran from the carriage that time.
You took my green pouch and left me.
I waited until dawn,
was arrested by the street officials,
and sent to prison for a thorough investigation of the pouch's contents.
I had no one to appeal to.
Shackled and whipped,
my flesh was ruined,
my limbs fell off,
and I eventually died in prison.
I appealed to the netherworld,
and was granted to confront you."
Qiú said:
"Can you forgive me?"
She said:
"When I think of the suffering in prison,
I wish I could not just cut you into ten thousand pieces!"
The woman furiously boarded the boat.
His family cried out in alarm,
but saw nothing.
Qiú lay as if drunk,
dreaming he was seized by an officer and taken to the netherworld.
The King summoned an officer and said:
"Qiú's lifespan and fortune are exhausted.
But Wáng's kin suffered greatly,
and it is right that he repay it in the human world."
He ordered the officer to send him back.
Afterwards, Qiú's body broke out in sores,
so foul that no one could approach him.
He screamed day and night,
his limbs fell off, and he died.
Art Criticism
When painting landscapes,
it is important that the rocks are old yet lustrous,
and the water faint yet clear.
Springs and rocks are distinguished by their height and depth,
and mountains and rivers discerned by their distance.
Wild paths wind intricately,
and clouds and mist appear and disappear.
A thousand miles of rivers and mountains
are brought within sight.
When painting pines and bamboos,
it is important that their posture defies mists and clouds,
and their spirit scorns frost and snow.
Strange joints stand in dense rows,
straight trunks lean against the sky.
Twisted branches coil and bend,
reversing the entanglement of dragons and snakes.
Sprawling canopies droop low,
as if concealing wind and rain.
When painting pavilions and towers,
it is important that ten thousand trees embrace and gather,
and the many tiles glisten like scales,
so that a skilled craftsman, seeing it,
dares not lay a hand on it.
Sāng Wéihàn Summons an Old Friend
Sāng Wéihàn 拜相 (bàixiàng),
his old friend Hán Yú (Hán Yú) came to visit,
but the Duke remained silent.
Yú retreated and said:
"Duke Sāng (Sāng Gōng),
my old friend,
I see him now,
and he has an air of inviolability."
The next day,
Yú took his leave.
The Duke said:
"I will submit your name,
and grant you the position of scholar."
Soon, two officials arrived carrying a box,
which contained a yellow imperial edict and robes and tablets.
The Duke set out wine and pondered, saying:
"How is Zhū Bǐng (Zhū Bǐng) the scholar?
We were once very fond of each other;
send for him."
Bǐng arrived,
and was treated exactly like Yú.
From the box came an edict and official robes,
and he was appointed Military Inspector and Judge.
Another day, the Duke inquired of Yú again:
"Where is Qiāng Hù (Qiāng Hù) the scholar?
He once greatly disparaged me,
and insulted me severely.
Now I am in a position of power,
while he is still struggling in obscurity.
A gentleman does not dwell on past grievances;
write a letter for me to summon him,
and I shall grant him an official post."
When Hù arrived,
the Duke ordered that he be given an official position within the manor.
Several plain-clothed officials
seized Hù and brought him to the main thoroughfare.
One official declared:
"Qiāng Hù (Qiāng Hù) plotted rebellion;
his crime warrants execution!"
Hù cried out:
"Hán Yú (Hán Yú) summoned me to receive an official post;
what crime have I committed?"
Then he was executed.
Yú wailed loudly:
"Hù's death,
I summoned him to it!"
Thereupon, he feigned illness and returned to his hometown.
One day,
the Duke was sitting in a small pavilion,
when he saw Hù approach.
Hù said:
"Your life and death are in your own hands.
Hù and I were once colleagues in the examination hall,
and we often joked around;
it was merely playful banter.
How could Your Excellency retaliate so severely?
You caused my body to be cut by a sharp blade,
my corpse abandoned in the wilderness,
and my wife and children to starve.
Is Your heart at peace?
I appealed to the Celestial Emperor,
who pitied my innocence
and appointed me Judge in the Ministry of War."
The Duke said:
"I will feed a thousand monks for you,
and recite a thousand scrolls of Buddhist scriptures;
will that suffice?"
Hù replied:
"I only need your life;
nothing else is useful."
Soon after, the Duke died,
with wounds all over his hands and feet.
Fényáng Wáng (Fényáng Wáng)
was staying at a farmhouse in the suburbs when he was young,
and heard someone coughing under the candle,
but could not see their form.
Someone under the couch called out:
"We two each take one watch."
That night, someone stole the Duke's horse and led it out beyond the wall.
The two crawled out,
seized the thief, and said:
"Who are you,
daring to steal the horse of Fényáng Wáng (Fényáng Wáng)?"
They took back the horse and returned.
Hán Wèigōng (Hán Wèigōng) became a Zǐfǔ Zhēnrén (Zǐfǔ Zhēnrén).
Yòushì Jìn Sūn Miǎn (Yòushì Jìn Sūn Miǎn)
was managing the riverbank dikes in Yuánchéng (Yuánchéng),
where many dikes collapsed.
A soldier said:
"There is a giant turtle-dragon burrowed underneath,
which comes out whenever the weather is clear."
Miǎn waited for it to appear,
drew an arrow and shot it,
hitting it squarely in the neck.
Miǎn dreamt during the day that an official summoned him, saying:
"You killed the turtle-dragon;
you are now summoned as a witness."
He followed to an official palace,
and the official said:
"This is the palace of Zǐfǔ Zhēnrén (Zǐfǔ Zhēnrén)."
Miǎn asked:
"What is the Zhēnrén's surname and given name?"
He said:
"It is Hán Wèigōng (Hán Wèigōng)."
Miǎn privately thought,
"I once received his patronage;
I should seek his help now."
Upon entering,
he saw the Duke sitting on the main hall,
attended by green-robed child attendants.
Miǎn bowed twice,
begging the Zhēnrén for great protection.
The Duke looked around,
took a yellow imperial edict from a green pouch,
and read the edict, saying:
"A turtle-dragon takes five hundred generations to achieve the nobility of a human body.
The matter of burrowing and damaging the dikes
falls under Miǎn's responsibility."
The Duke ordered him to be sent away.
Líshān Jì (Líshān Jì)
Zhāng Yú 遊 Líshān,
saw an old man,
who said:
"I once heard my grandfather speak of events from the time of Táng Mínghuáng."
He then produced six illustrated maps of Líshān,
showing nine large and small palaces,
and sixty-two pavilions and terraces.
At that time, there was someone who presented peonies,
which were called "Yángjiā Hóng" (Yang Family Red),
as they were flowers from Yáng Miǎn's family.
The Imperial Consort applied face cream in the evening,
and with her lip rouge still on her hand,
she pressed it onto the flower.
An imperial edict ordered them to be planted in the Xiānchūn Guǎn (Hall of Early Spring).
The following year, when the flowers bloomed,
there were red traces of a finger impression on them.
The Emperor named it "Yī Niǎn Hóng" (A Pinch of Red).
The Emperor ordered the commanderies and states to cast Kāiyuán coins,
and the Consort accidentally touched the mold with her fingernail.
The foundry official dared not change it,
and to this day, the back of the coins bears the nail mark.
People offered yellow peony flowers,
whose faces were nearly a foot across,
and several inches tall.
Before the Emperor could appreciate them,
a deer carried them away in its mouth.
A sycophant played a memorial, saying:
"Buddhists have deer
that carry flowers to offer to golden immortals."
The Emperor privately said:
"Wild deer roaming in the palace
are not an auspicious sign!"
Little did he know that Lùshān's rebellion would deeply disturb the inner palace,
and this was its omen.
The Imperial Consort frolicked and played with Lùshān daily.
One day, in a drunken game,
he was especially disrespectful,
extending his hand and scratching the Consort's breast.
The Consort wept and said:
"This is my fault for secretly favoring you!"
Fearing the Emperor would see the mark,
she used a golden hēzi (bodice) to cover it.
Later, all in the palace followed suit.
Lùshān once lay drunk beneath the Míngxiá Gé (Pavilion of Luminous Clouds),
and a palace maid accidentally spilled water on his face.
Lùshān glared, exhaled sharply,
horns grew on his head,
and wings on his body;
he writhed as if about to fly.
The Emperor rushed to observe,
and said:
"There is nothing to fear;
this is but a pig-dragon."
A moment later,
Lùshān awoke and
said:
"Your servant dreamt that someone poured water on him,
and your servant transformed into a dragon."
The Consort asked the Emperor about it,
and the Emperor said:
"Lùshān is not a true dragon,
but a pig-dragon;
he will surely die by military weapon one day."
The Consort said:
"Will this not be a problem?"
He replied:
"Beyond this, it is not for you to know."
One day,
after the Consort bathed
and came out,
while evening her face before a mirror,
one breast was slightly exposed above her skirt-waist.
The Emperor caressed it and said:
"Soft and warm, freshly peeled chicken-head meat."
Lùshān responded:
"Moist and smooth, like fresh butter from beyond the frontier."
The Consort laughed heartily and said:
"Indeed, this Hu slave only knows butter."
When Lùshān departed to govern Yúyáng,
he said to the Consort:
"This journey is deeply unpleasant for me.
After this separation, will there be a time for us to meet again?"
The Consort smiled and did not answer.
Lùshān said:
"People only fear having no heart;
if one has a heart,
even if one's intestines are drawn out and blood splatters,
enduring ten thousand lives and ten thousand deaths,
one would still not hesitate.
Your servant must come to see Your Ladyship!"
He then embraced the Consort and wept,
for a long time without stopping.
Lùshān frequently behaved improperly towards the Consort;
in her later years, the Consort disliked it even more,
lamenting that she had no means to cut him off.
After he left,
she was very dejected.
She ordered her advance riders to play music.
Lùshān said:
"Music contains sounds of departure,
and people often feel the sorrow of separation;
this has been so from ancient times to the present."
Later, he raised an army in rebellion,
and privately said:
"I do not dare covet the great throne,
but merely wish to kill Yáng Guózhōng and a few others,
see the Imperial Consort once to narrate our estrangement,
enjoy three or five days of shared joy,
and then even dying would be happiness!"
Wáng Yòuyù's lines
Wáng Yòuyù
was a famous courtesan.
She once had lines saying:
"Only when spring silkworms die do their threads run out,
only when candles turn to ash do their tears dry."
Taking Sūn Shì's pulse
Zhōu Mò,
appointed registrar of Yíxīng,
was fond of medicine and prescriptions from youth.
A neighbor, Zhāng Fù,
had a wife, Sūn Shì.
Zhāng fell ill,
and requested him to take a pulse.
Mò saw his wife's beauty,
and thinking he had no way to obtain her,
he told his mother to invite her for a drink,
showing good neighborliness,
but his advances were not reciprocated.
Mò thought:
"I am still young,
and Sūn is also in her prime.
Her husband is very old."
So he folded a note and sent a poem,
saying:
"A fifty-year-old decrepit man with a twenty-year-old wife,
his eyes dim and hair white, his head already bowed.
In the depths of the crimson curtain, let there be no discussion,
beyond the heavens, a blue phoenix paired with a wooden rooster."
Sūn replied with a poem, saying:
"Rain collects in a dry pond, briefly turning green;
vines encircle an old tree, making it fresh again.
For now, I enjoy the present scenery,
decorating pavilions and terraces according to the spring."
Each time she received his note,
she would quickly read and then destroy it,
fearing his wickedness would be exposed.
She then said:
"Taking advantage of medical skill to invite and seize someone,
even common people in the marketplace would not do this,
let alone a scholar?"
When Mò was about to take up his official post,
he wrote a note saying:
"An ancient poem says:
'The later waves of the cold river push the former waves,
in this floating world, new people replace old ones.'
Thus the old one should pass away first.
I vow never to marry in my life to await you."
Sūn replied:
"Such unfounded words,
I dare not accept.
The length or shortness of a person's life
naturally has its appointed time.
Should misfortune occur,
I shall wait for another day."
Three years later,
Mò returned after his term,
and upon inquiring,
found that Fù had already died.
He then sent a matchmaker to form good relations with Sūn
and married her.
Nízǐ Jì
A guard, Qián Qiān,
walked along the riverbank.
He saw a clay figure lying on the ice,
its colors bright and clear.
Qiān took it home
and gave it to his wife.
His wife said,
"Are you giving me this because I have no son?"
She then made it a colorful garment,
held it in her arms during the day,
and slept with it in her bed at night.
One evening,
the clay figure urinated on the bedding.
Qiān then discarded it in a ditch.
In the middle of the night,
the clay figure came in through the gate
and tearfully begged for its mother's milk,
climbing onto the bed and into the quilt.
Qiān was afraid
and sought Kāng Shēng for a divination.
Kāng cast the hexagram and said,
"The matter involves the lives of three people."
Qiān became even more frightened
and asked for a magical solution.
Kāng said,
"When you return, strike it with a sharp blade;
that will put an end to its strangeness."
Qiān sharpened his sword
and waited for the strange creature to arrive.
He struck it,
and there was a clang.
He held a candle to look at it;
the strange creature was gone,
but his wife lay dead in a pool of blood.
The next day,
guards arrested Qiān and brought him before the authorities.
Qiān explained that Kāng Shēng had instructed him.
The officials pursued Kāng Shēng to be a witness.
Kāng, frightened,
hanged himself.
Qiān ultimately could not clear himself
and was executed in the eastern marketplace.
Liú Hóng Jì (Floating Red Leaf)
During the reign of Táng Xīzōng,
there was a Yú Yòu who was strolling in the forbidden thoroughfare in the evening.
A red leaf floated by,
on which were two lines:
"Sincerely I thank the red leaf,
farewell, go to the human world."
Yòu then added a poem:
"I once heard of red sentiments inscribed on a leaf,
on a leaf a poem is written, asking whom?"
A well-wisher gifted a poem, saying:
"The emperor's grace does not forbid the eastward flowing water,
the palace sentiments flowing out are from this channel."
Later, Yòu married a palace lady, Hán Shì.
She saw a red leaf in Yú Yòu's book cabinet
and exclaimed in surprise,
"This is what I wrote!
My stream also received a red leaf!"
It was exactly what Yòu had written.
When she first received the leaf,
she had once written a poem:
"Walking alone by the Heavenly Ditch,
by the stream I found a leaf.
Who could understand this feeling?
My heart breaks over this couplet."
Thereupon, they faced each other, deeply moved and weeping,
saying,
"How could this be accidental?
Is it not predetermined?"
Tán Yìgē Jì (Story of Tán Yìgē)
Tán Yìgē was a relative by marriage (uncle's daughter) who
drifted to Chángshā.
At the age of eight,
she was fostered in the home of the bamboo craftsman Zhāng Wén.
The official courtesan Dīng Wǎnqīng saw Yìgē's dazzling beauty
and casually thought that if she could acquire her,
her house would surely be overflowing.
So she generously rewarded Zhāng Wén
and sought to buy her.
Before she reached marriageable age (fifteen),
she was uniquely prominent for a time,
with carriages and horses like a market.
She was especially skilled in poetry and calligraphy.
When the prefectural governor was hosting guests,
a medical doctor came to the prefecture for a reason.
The governor said,
"When the medical doctor bows, he must glance at the ground."
Yìgē responded,
"When the prefectural lord feasts, the curtains cover the sky."
The Vice-Prefect Jiǎng Tián pointed to Yìgē's face and said,
"After winter melon frost, her frown adds powder."
Yìgē held the governor's robe sleeve and said,
"Even the wooden date in autumn also wears crimson."
At the gathering, Zhāng Zhèngzì of Rǔzhōu was an official in Tán and Chá.
They got along very well,
and Yìgē returned with him.
A person of sentiment gifted a poem, saying:
"Talent and beauty meet, then comes joy,
a graceful encounter, the matter is even better.
The peony moved to the immortal capital,
from now on, there will be no good flowers in Xiāngdōng."
Later, Zhāng was transferred to another official post.
Yìgē saw him off and said,
"You are from a renowned family,
while I am a prostitute.
This parting now
definitely has no future reunion.
I have been carrying your child for several months already,
you should remember this."
After the parting, she sent him a poem:
"By the Xiāoxiāng River, spring returns,
all the cold ice has melted, all the plum blossoms have fallen.
I wish my husband and son were like the colors of spring,
returning once a year."
Internally, Zhāng was pressured by his kind mother's instructions,
and externally by public criticism.
He arranged a marriage with Sūn Diànchéng's daughter
and dared not write to Yìgē.
Yìgē wrote a letter saying:
"My coarseness and humility,
I know very well.
Once I entered your inner chambers,
I diligently practiced the wifely virtues.
To be suddenly abandoned like this
has caused me to lose my way.
From the perspective of human feelings,
it seems cruelly unjust.
If there is righteousness, then we unite,
I uphold your former words.
To be separated without cause
hurts my humble and weak self.
My young son is three years old;
I hope for him to grow up.
I only shelter myself."
Three years later,
Zhāng's wife, Sūn Shì, passed away.
A guest came from Shā
and said that Yìgē had shut her door and did not go out,
bought a hundred *mǔ* of land to support herself,
and personally taught her son.
Zhāng then went to Chángshā.
Yìgē refused to see him,
saying,
"You already have a household;
you should leave,
do not trouble me."
Zhāng said,
"My wife has already died."
Yìgē said,
"Engage a matchmaker,
perform the six rites,
then I dare to heed your command."
Zhāng followed her request
and brought her back to the capital.
Yìgē managed the household with propriety and order,
and her son passed the imperial examination as a *jìnshì*.
Guī Xī Qì (Turtle Breath Technique)
Wáng Zhāosù
was able to practice the turtle breath technique.
He only died when he was over ninety years old;
his head had shrunk into his abdomen.
Xiǎo Lián (Little Lotus)
Lǐ Lángzhōng's bondmaid
greatly confused him.
One day, she wept and said,
"I am a fox from atop the city wall.
In a previous life, I was a concubine
and slandered my principal wife.
My husband listened to me,
and she died of grief and indignation,
complaining to the officials of the underworld.
I received this punishment.
The time has now elapsed,
and I am to die under the claws of eagles and dogs.
Or my body will fall into cauldrons and chopping boards,
and my fat will fill the mouths and stomachs of people.
I am also delayed
and cannot attain rebirth.
On a certain day, when you leave the capital gate,
there will be someone carrying a fox.
You should buy it with much money,
make clothes for it from paper,
make a coffin from cloth,
and bury it in high ground.
This would be your benevolence."
The next day, she bade farewell and left.
He went out the gate as scheduled,
and indeed found a fox.
He buried it.
Zhū Shé Jì (Red Snake Story)
Lǐ Yuán (李元) saw a small scarlet snake on the bank of Wújiāng (吳江),
less than a foot long,
being tormented by a shepherd boy.
Yuán (元) bought it for a hundred coins
and released it into dense grass.
The next year, passing by Chángqiáo (長橋) again,
a patrolman, Zhū Jùn (朱浚), came to greet him, saying:
"Jùn (浚) lives but a few hundred paces from the bridge-end.
My lord has sent me to summon you,
please pardon me for asking you to move."
He invited Yuán (元) into his boat,
and they arrived at a mountain.
The buildings and palaces were richly adorned,
and the guards were very strict.
Presently, a person in a tall cap and Daoist robes
led Yuán (元) to a seat,
saying:
"This humble one was unlucky,
almost dying at the hands of a mischievous boy.
Thanks to your kindness, this humble life was saved."
Zhū Jùn (朱浚) ordered him to bow again.
Then, a feast was prepared,
with dishes from land and sea.
He said:
"I am a scaly creature from Nánhǎi (南海),
having rendered service to the world.
The Heavenly Emperor decreed that I reside here,
and appointed me King Ānliú (安流王).
I have a female attendant,
nicknamed Yúnjiě (雲姐).
I now wish to bestow her upon you.
If you accept her,
you will receive her assistance."
Soon after, Yuán (元) departed.
Later, he went to the Imperial Examinations (lǐwéi, 禮闈),
and the next day was the test.
Yúnjiě (雲姐) secretly entered and stole the test questions.
Yuán (元) then reviewed his old compositions and entered the examination,
scoring very well,
and was recommended to pass the imperial examination.
Yúnjiě (雲姐) bid farewell,
saying:
"By the King's command,
I dare not stay long."
She wrote a poem to bid him farewell:
"For six years here, I've repaid deep kindness,
The aquatic realm, the fish's home, is my journey's path.
Do not mourn this separation after our new marriage,
Give all old loves to the new person."
Yuán (元)
had just recently married, hence the poem.
Zhōu Pó (周婆) Would Surely Not Write Such a Poem
Cáo Guī's (曹圭) wife, Zhū Shì (朱氏), was fierce and unyielding.
Someone advised her son to recite the chapter "Guān Jū" (關睢) to admonish her.
The mother said:
"Who wrote 'The Mao Odes'?"
The son replied:
"The Duke of Zhōu (周公) wrote it."
Zhū (朱) said:
"If it were Zhōu Pó (周婆), she would surely not write such a poem."
Later, Guī (圭) became a county magistrate.
Whenever men and women litigated in his court,
even if the woman was in the wrong,
Zhū (朱) would make her appear in the right.
Guī (圭) and his wife suddenly fell ill
and dreamt that two officers escorted them to the underworld.
The Prefect ordered a document written, declaring:
"The wife is strong, the husband weak;
firm within, gentle without.
If one wife cannot be controlled,
how can the common people be disciplined?
Whip the back X times!"
Zhū Shì's (朱氏) charge read:
"As a woman,
it is proper to manage the inner chambers.
But she usurped her husband's authority,
and twisted right and wrong to follow her own desires.
Whip the back X times!"
When they awoke,
each had whip marks on their backs.
Record of a Spring Outing to the Western Pond
Hóu Chéngshū (侯誠叔) lived in the capital for a long time
and once visited Xīchí (西池).
There was a woman,
whose appearance was exceedingly charming.
She sent a young maid (qīngyī, 青衣) with a poem, saying:
"Humanity's spring beauty is all in the third month,
The scenery by the pond is worth a myriad gold.
Fortunately, there's a path back to Peach Blossom Spring,
Why does the talented gentleman not seek it out?"
Another day, he received another poem:
"Spring light enters the water, utterly emerald,
Wild colors follow people, the same everywhere.
No need to ask too eagerly,
My home simply resides east of Apricot Garden."
The maid led Hóu (侯) to a grand mansion.
Cups and plates were numerous,
lamps burned as brightly as day.
Hóu (侯) returned home for several months,
then went back to that place,
but was completely lost, unable to find the old path.
An old man said:
"There are fox spirits here,
many of whom become human wives."
Hóu (侯) expressed a desire to see her again.
The maid again sent a poem, saying:
"Months of separation, no sound or letter,
You ask the old neighbor, and learn the whole story.
Secretly pondering ancient affairs with tears,
It was Zhèng Shēng (鄭生) who truly composed for his lover."
Then they met again.
The lady (Jī, 姬) bowed her head in shame and embarrassment.
Hóu (侯) said:
"A true man should sleep among mist and moonlight,
cherishing willows and pitying flowers,
then he will have no worries."
They went hand in hand into the bedchamber.
Her cosmetic pouch was extremely thick.
Hóu (侯) had relatives on his mother's side in Nányáng (南陽),
so he went to visit them.
His uncle arranged for him to marry Hǎo Shì (郝氏) as his wife.
Hóu (侯) then sent a letter to the lady (Jī, 姬), breaking off their relationship.
Ten years later,
Hǎo Shì (郝氏) died,
and Hóu (侯) also lost his official position.
Once, passing out of Sòngmén (宋門),
he saw a light carriage drawn by a flower-decorated ox.
The curtain was lifted, and someone called out to Hóu (侯), saying:
"Are you not such-and-such a gentleman?
I have already entrusted myself to another.
I dare not say much,
my co-resident is a relative of my good man."
Biography of Virtuous Gentleman Jī (雞)
Virtuous Gentleman Jī Lǔgǎn (雞魯敢),
met a maid (qīngyī, 青衣) on the Xīchéng (西城) road,
who said:
"The guest in the east chamber has been waiting for you for a long time."
He returned to the courtyard
and saw a woman plucking flowers and playing with petals,
her body shaded by flowers.
Jūn (君) suspected she was a fox spirit,
and with a stern expression, kept his distance.
The woman also slowly departed.
More than a month later,
she flew down from the sky,
saying:
"I am
a descendant of the Queen Mother of the West (Xīwángmǔ, 西王母),
and live in the Xīzhēngé (西真閣) of Yáochí (瑤池)."
As if in a dream,
she led Jūn (君) to mount a colorful qilin together.
In the cold light and azure void,
they overlooked a ten-thousand-foot-deep chasm,
ascended the Pántáo Lǐng (蟠桃嶺) (Peach Peak),
and looked west at the Qiónglín (瓊林) (Jade Grove),
shining like a world of gold and silver.
She said:
"This is Yáochí (瑤池)."
Blue waves and misty ripples
glistened for ten thousand acres.
Pearl towers and jade pavilions
were intricately layered a thousand-fold.
Amidst red glow and emerald haze,
it was as if rainbow light hung in the sky
and rain threads pierced the earth.
She invited Jūn (君) to ascend the Xīzhēngé (西真閣),
saying:
"I once saw Zǐyún Niáng (紫雲娘) reciting your excellent verses."
Before she finished speaking,
he saw thousands of beautifully dressed women,
with tinkling jade pendants,
starry eyes, and rosy cheeks.
A woman in a rosy dress
was exceptionally beautiful,
her charm radiating around her.
Xīzhēn (西真) said:
"This is my Xīwángmǔ (西王母)."
After a long time,
Zǐyún Niáng (紫雲娘) also arrived.
Xīzhēn (西真) said:
"This is Virtuous Gentleman Jī (雞)."
Soon,
goblets were passed around.
The rosy-clad official requested to perform the "Luánfèng Hémíng Qǔ" (鸞鳳和鳴曲) (Phoenixes Singing in Harmony Melody),
and then the "Yúnyǔ Qìng Xiānqī Qǔ" (雲雨慶先期曲) (Clouds and Rain Celebrating the Early Date Melody).
When the wine was flowing freely,
they entered another cave.
Green peaches and vibrant apricots
emitted fragrance as thick as mist.
Xīzhēn (西真) said:
"Someday, when you return to the human world,
we will live together here."
Jūn (君) then bid farewell and returned.
Zhāng Shìníng's (張世寧) Divine Descent
Zhāng Shìníng, an assistant instructor in Tàiyuán Prefecture,
suddenly fell ill.
As he was about to die,
he chanted:
"Green feather banners and parasols in the仙子xiānzǐ's chamber,
Purple cloud towers and palaces in the Jade Emperor's realm.
Mortal scenes and objects easily scatter,
Looking back, Wǔlíng is empty with fallen flowers."
After he died,
his spirit descended upon his daughter, saying:
"My registry belongs to the eighteenth grotto of the Jade Immortals in Heaven.
While attending a gathering at Yáochí,
and examining the 'Record of Earthly Immortals' Merits and Deeds' in the mortal world,
I smelled the fragrance of mortal wine
and lingered, failing to proceed,
thus incurring the penalty of tardiness.
Xīwángmǔ revealed this matter,
saying I had a share of mortal wine to consume,
and should be banished to repay it.
I dwelled as a fleeting existence,
and now return to my original registry."
Then he sang:
"Rest, rest, rest,
When you can steal a moment of rest, then it's good to rest,
Joyful enemies are endless."
The Three Furen of Táoyuán
Chén Chún arrived at Táoyuán.
Enchanted by its beautiful mountains and waters,
he packed provisions and walked along the stream.
After eighty-one days,
he reached the foot of a thousand-丈-high cliff.
At night, he heard human voices among the rock walls.
Chún, exhausted and out of food,
smelled a beautiful fragrance
and saw more than ten large flowers drifting by,
moving very quickly.
Chún quickly grabbed one flower,
which was one foot five inches across.
He ate it.
Feeling extremely thirsty,
he drank several dou of stream water,
and had diarrhea for three days.
His walking speed then increased greatly.
A boy in green clothes, picking duckweed by the bank,
said:
"This is the land of the Three Furen of Táoyuán.
The upper realm is Yùyuán,
the middle realm is Língyuán,
and the lower realm is Táoyuán.
On the night of the Mid-Autumn Festival,
the three immortals will meet here."
That evening,
ice-bound pavilions were visible in the distance.
A boy said:
"Furen Yùyuán summons you."
Chún went to see them.
The three Furen were seated in a crimson hall,
with all kinds of music playing.
Yùyuán asked Chún:
"Can you recite one or two lines of recent Mid-Autumn moon poetry?"
Chún replied:
"Do not decline to watch the entire night,
for often it means a wait of another year."
Táoyuán said:
"The sentiment is good,
but this could also apply to the moon on the fifteenth night of the seventh month."
Yùyuán then composed a poem, saying:
"The jade rabbit steps through the ethereal blue,
The ice wheel grinds the vast clear sky."
Língyuán responded:
"It's not that the moon's essence is different,
It's all because the autumn air is clear."
Táoyuán said:
"Now autumn is half gone again,
A single wheel hangs across ten thousand li."
Chún said:
"As autumn quietens, the night is truly still;
As the moon rounds, people become even more complete."
The Immortals smiled and said:
"This scholar is good!
Don't let him eat the immortal flower,
lest he turn into withered bones another day.
How dare he randomly express such thoughts?"
Chún replied:
"It was merely an accidental rhyme."
As dawn approached,
they descended in the same boat,
arriving shortly.
With latticed windows and vermilion pavilions,
it was unlike anything in the human world.
Yùyuán warned Chún:
"Be careful not to enter the South Pavilion,
as it will be detrimental to you."
Chún secretly went there.
In the pavilion was a jade flute.
Chún took it and played it.
Suddenly, he saw people and landscapes,
which were his hometown and family.
Others called his father 'father,' and his wife called another man 'husband.'
They were feasting, conversing, and laughing.
After a long time, they disappeared.
Chún vomited an egg onto the ground,
which transformed into a red crane and flew away.
The Immortal came and saw Chún,
rebuking him:
"You did not heed my warning;
now I cannot save you!
Is it not fate?
Thirty years from now,
you shall return here.
You should cultivate your true essence within,
and promote good deeds without."
She sent Chún back by boat.
The beggar from Lónghéqǔ,
Lǐ Wúyán, went to the capital to seek an official appointment.
Upon reaching Zhūtíng Zhèn,
two beggars were loudly quarreling in the street.
An old woman said:
"I have begged all my life,
accumulating several hundred gold coins.
This fellow borrowed them,
and hasn't repaid them for half a year."
Wúyán took out paper money equal to the owed amount and gave it to her.
The beggar thanked him, saying:
"I did indeed owe her the money.
You are a passerby,
yet you are able to repay it to resolve our dispute.
My home is in Lónghéqǔ;
the bamboo fence and green curtain
mark my dwelling.
If you can visit me,
I shall offer a generous reward."
Wúyán found his words strange.
Later, he entered Lónghé,
and indeed found the curtain and fence.
Upon entering the gate,
he saw several beggars sharing a fire in an earthen stove.
Entering the inner room,
a person in official attire stood in the hall—
it was the beggar he had met earlier.
After the beggar sat down,
he said:
"You can have a small drink to ward off the cold."
Wúyán felt bewildered and very suspicious.
The man earnestly urged him,
but Wúyán politely declined,
ultimately not drinking,
only wetting his lips.
It was then extremely cold,
but the plates contained summer fruits.
He took three small imperial peaches and carried them home.
The beggar composed a poem, saying:
"A gentleman with too much doubt makes too many mistakes;
People without faith achieve nothing.
The path to my home is flat as a whetstone,
Why, sir, are you unwilling to walk it?"
When Wúyán arrived at his lodging and took out the peaches,
they were three pieces of purple gold.
He then felt great regret.
The next day, he visited again,
but they were already gone.
When he inquired,
no one knew anything.
Wúyán carved the gold into drinking vessels.
He lived to be over seventy years old,
with a rosy complexion.
Could this be the power of merely wetting his lips with wine?
Biography of Rú Kuí
Rú Kuí
was from Hédōng.
His full name is not recorded,
as it was taboo.
In the capital, he associated with the famous courtesan Hú Wényuán.
After some time,
Yuán gladly served him.
When Kuí went out, she would close her door,
so even a son of ten thousand gold coins could not see her.
Yuán once composed a poem on 'Hibiscus' (Shǔkuí Huā), saying:
"There is one aspect that invites regret:
the flowers turn their backs and do not lean towards the sun."
Courtesan's Poem to Chén Xīyí
The courtesan Shàn of Chéngdū presented a poem to Mr. Chén Tuán, saying:
"An emperor's teacher cannot be attained,
The sun and moon grow old, this must be difficult."
Wine Like a Thread
Yáng Yì, at Dīng Jìnggōng's banquet, proposed a riddle, saying:
"There is wine like a thread,
When poured, it becomes visible."
The answer was:
"There is a cake like the moon,
When eaten, it diminishes."
Fire Tongs and Iron
Dīng Jìngōng was in the Mìgé,
fond of being near the fire,
often using iron tongs to draw and write among the ashes.
His colleagues would wait for the duke to temporarily rise,
then heat the fire tongs.
When the duke returned, he was branded by the tongs,
and said:
"Last night I heard the drum sounds,
and couldn't sleep all night."
When asked the reason,
he said:
"I was enjoying the ancestral brands."
樂 (lè)
is 烙 (lào).
Volume 46
ends.
A Thief Enters Wèi Gōng's Chambers
When Hán Wèi Gōng was stationed in Xiāngzhōu,
he was offering sacrifices to Xuánní,
and stayed overnight in the province for purification.
At night,
a thief entered his chamber,
holding a blade, and said:
"I cannot save myself,
I seek salvation from Your Excellency!"
The duke said:
"The implements on the table,
worth hundreds of thousands,
I give them all to you."
The thief said:
"I wish to obtain your head,
to offer to the Westerners."
The duke immediately bared his neck.
The thief kowtowed and said:
"Because your virtue and magnanimity surpass others,
I came to test you.
The items on the table,
I have already received your generous gift,
I wish for nothing else."
The duke said:
"Very well."
He never told anyone about it.
Later, the thief was sentenced for another crime,
and was to die.
In the marketplace, he fully recounted the incident,
saying:
"I fear that after my death,
Your Excellency's enduring virtue will not be passed down to the world."
Drunken Monk
Sūn Yuánguī governed Hángzhōu,
and was known for his sagacity.
There was a monk who, during the Yuánxī festival, roasted meat in the marketplace,
begging for donations,
amassing a mountain of profit.
The duke ordered the arrest of several of his wives and daughters,
and had them executed according to the law.
There was also a monk who lay drunk on the road,
and was apprehended by the patrols.
Guī asked:
"As a monk, why do you drink?"
He replied:
"It is a wilderness habit I crave,
I cannot restrain myself."
Thereupon, he offered the monk a pot of wine,
which the monk drained in one gulp.
The duke ordered him to be helped home,
and not to be insulted or harmed.
The next day, the monk sounded the drum and ascended the seat,
saying:
"I am a person from the Western Regions,
my tracks have been mingled here,
unfortunately I have been recognized by this gentleman,
I cannot remain any longer."
He sat cross-legged and passed away.
Jīnggōng Contemplates the Xián and Héng Hexagrams
Wáng Jīnggōng governed Chángzhōu,
and never smiled when facing guests.
One day during a gathering of guests,
with courtesans and actors in the courtyard,
the duke suddenly burst into laughter,
which greatly surprised people.
A guest took the opportunity to ask the duke,
who said:
"Last night, sitting down, I happened to think of the *Xián* and *Héng* hexagrams,
and was delighted with my insight,
so I couldn't help but laugh."
Snow Poem
Luó Kě once composed a hundred-rhyme poem on "Snow,"
which contained the lines:
"Slanting onto Pān Yuè's temples,
horizontally upon Mǎ Liáng's eyebrows."
Military Adjutants and Secretaries Receive Flogging
Dù Fǔ's poem says:
"Escaping from the humble posts of secretaries,
then for the first time bidding farewell to flogging."
Hán Yù said:
"Low-ranking officials like judicial assistants dare not speak out,
and cannot escape flogging amidst the dust."
Dù Mù said:
"Military adjutants and secretaries,
are in a flurry of dust and alarm.
One wrong word,
and whips lash the body, covering it with sores."
From this, we know that in the Táng dynasty, military adjutants and secretaries,
if they made a mistake, would receive the punishment of flogging,
just like today's clerks.
Luó Shàowēi's Poetry
Luó Shàowēi, during the late Táng, was the military commissioner of Wèibó,
and enjoyed writing poetry.
At that time, Luó Yǐn of Jiāngdōng had a reputation for poetry,
so Shàowēi treated him with great courtesy,
