and thus titled his own poems *Tōu Jiāngdōng Jí* (Collected Poems Stolen from Jiāngdōng).
Lines such as: "Before the tower, the faint sun in the cloud tops,
outside the curtain, the rustling wind with streaks of rain,"
were not inferior to Yǐn's.
Jīnshān Poetry
Guō Xiángzhèng's *Jīnshān Shī* (Poem on Jīnshān),
Wáng Jīnggōng greatly loved it.
It says:
"Birds fly endlessly into the green evening sky,
fish songs suddenly cease in the reedy wind."
His *Shān Jū* (Mountain Dwelling) also says:
"There are not many scenes in the Xiè family village,
only two or three sounds of orioles."
Xīshānsì Poetry
A Táng poem inscription at Xīshānsì says:
"Forever obstructing the new moon,
half the river has no evening sun."
Jīnggōng's Jīnshān Poem
His *Jīnshānsì Liú Tí Shī* (Poem Inscribed at Jīnshānsì) says:
"Tree shadows are seen midstream,
bell sounds are heard on both banks."
Also:
"The sky is vast, yielding extra moon,
the land is small, not producing dust."
What would be wrong with using this for Luòxīngsì?
Wáng Jīnggōng said:
"At the edge of the sky, sea clouds lie horizontally over Běigù,
amidst the mist, the sandy shore resembles Xīxīng."
This is particularly accurate.
Xú Yín's Poetry
Púyáng's Xú Yín's poem says:
"Leisurely, I don't tire of frequent guests,
old, I particularly cherish my youngest child."
Luòyáng's Lǐ Dù's poem says:
"Drunk, I make light of worldly affairs,
old, I value my hometown people."
Little Spring Color is Needed to be Moving
A Táng dynasty poem says:
"A single red dot on a tender green branch,
little spring color is needed to be moving."
The author's name is not recorded.
Wáng Jīnggōng personally wrote these two lines in a book.
Some thought they were Jīnggōng's own work,
but this is not so.
Poets Consider Abandoning Office as Noble
Poets generally consider abandoning official posts to return to reclusion as noble.
Zhào Gǔ said:
"Sooner or later, when my personal affairs are roughly settled,
I will return by the water as a leisurely person."
If personal affairs are settled,
then the mind will also be fervent,
and there will be no date for return.
Wáng Yìjiǎn Gōng:
"If you can go to the green mountains, then go;
official positions come and go by themselves."
How can one be indifferent to rank and status?
Once, I saw someone inscribe on a wall:
"When will one's efforts for livelihood be sufficient?
To be at leisure before old age is true leisure."
This is different from the saying, "One day observing the list of appointments,
three years harms the Daoist heart."
Dí Zūndù's Poetry
Dí Zūndù (狄遵度) wrote poetry,
taking Lǎo Dù (老杜) as his model.
He once composed an elegy to offer sacrifices at the tomb of Lái Yáng (來陽).
Suddenly, he dreamt that Zǐměi (子美) was reciting more than ten poems,
which were unknown to the world.
When he awoke,
he remembered them vaguely,
enough to complete a poem.
He wrote "Jiā Chéng" (佳城), which goes:
"The beautiful city is luxuriant and shrouded in cold mist,
Lonely chicks and suckling beasts cry out on the desolate path.
At night, I lie with the Northern Dipper hanging cold by my pillow,
Trees shed leaves, frost arches, wild geese link the sky.
Lone clouds drift west with the setting sun,
Travelers going east follow the long river.
Heaven and earth have not yet been destroyed, and I am still here,
Would I discuss lifespan with mayflies?"
From "Night at" onwards,
was what Zǐměi (子美) recited.
After more than a year,
Zūndù (遵度) passed away,
at the age of twenty-six.
Braiding Bamboo Bridges to Save Ants
The two Sòng (宋) brothers were young.
A Hu (胡) monk said:
"The younger Sòng (宋) will one day top the empire,
and the elder Sòng (宋) will not be far behind."
More than ten years later,
the monk exclaimed to the elder Sòng (宋):
"Your spiritual demeanor has suddenly changed,
as if you could save millions of lives."
He replied:
"How could a humble scholar have such power?"
The monk said:
"Try to recall."
Sòng (宋) said:
"There used to be an ant nest under the hall,
which was washed away by a torrential rain.
The ants swarmed around the nest,
and I playfully wove a bamboo bridge to help them cross."
The monk said:
"That's it.
The younger Sòng (宋) is taking the imperial examination this year,
and your success will certainly not be beneath his."
When the results were announced,
the younger Sòng (宋) indeed ranked first.
Empress Xiàn (憲) presided over the court,
and said that a younger brother should not precede an elder brother.
So she made the elder Sòng (宋) first,
and the younger Sòng (宋) tenth.
The Thatched Hut Monk
When Zēng Chǔgōng (曾楚公) resided in Quánnán (泉南),
there was a Thatched Hut Monk (草堂和尚),
over ninety years old,
whose precepts and conduct were pure and unblemished.
The duke and his wife often brought him clothes and food.
The monk said:
"I wish to be the son of the夫人 to repay you."
At that time, the夫人 was pregnant.
One evening,
she dreamt that the monk, parting the bed-curtain, entered.
The夫人 awoke in fright and gave birth to a son.
Then, the Thatched Hut Monk (草堂和尚) had already passed away in meditation,
and the son she gave birth to was precisely Lǔgōng (魯公).
Swallow Nests Exceeding a Foot Bring Auspiciousness
It is a common belief:
If swallows nest in a family's house,
and the nest opening faces inward,
and when it grows, it exceeds a foot in length,
it is auspicious.
Zhāng Gōng (張公) of the Jíxián (集賢) academy,
every year swallows nested in his main bedroom,
their length could accommodate a bolt of silk,
and all their openings faced inward.
After several years,
he was appointed to an important position.
Reciting the Diamond Sūtra
Zhāng Chíguó (張持國) recited the "Jīngāng Jīng" (金剛經) twice daily.
Every time he opened the scroll,
he would burn incense and sit upright.
He would not rise
until he had finished reciting the sūtra.
If spoken to,
he would not reply.
His family had always experienced many strange occurrences,
but when Chíguó (持國) was at home,
all was peaceful.
One day, his wife fell ill,
and in a trance, she saw several women harassing her.
His wife said:
"You cannot charm my husband,
so you only trouble me!"
The women said:
"He always recites the "Jīngāng Jīng" (金剛經),
how dare we approach?"
His wife said:
"Do I not also recite sūtras?"
They replied:
"Even if you recite it ten thousand times a day,
we would still not be afraid."
His wife then began to apply herself diligently,
and the strange occurrences ceased.
Fragrance of Hibiscus Flowers from the Mouth
When Ōu Gōng (歐公) was governor of Yǐngzhōu (穎州),
there was an official courtesan named Lú Mèiyí (盧媚兒) whose appearance was elegant and graceful,
and whose mouth always emitted the fragrance of hibiscus flowers.
A Shǔ (蜀) monk said:
"This person was a nun in her previous life,
reciting the "Fǎhuá Jīng" (法華經) for twenty years.
A single misguided thought
led her to this state."
Later, Ōu Gōng (歐公) asked the courtesan if she had ever read the "Fǎhuá Jīng" (法華經).
The courtesan said:
"Having lost myself to this profession,
I have no leisure for it."
Ōu Gōng (歐公) ordered the sūtra to be brought and shown to her.
At a glance, she could recite it,
as if she had always been familiar with it.
If given other sūtras,
she could not do so.
A Single Courier
The "Zuǒ Zhuàn" (左傳) says:
"The lord did not send a single courier
to inform me."
The commentary says:
"Lǐng xíng (行李) refers to a traveler."
Nowadays, people refer to luggage as lǐng xíng (行李),
which is incorrect.
Lǐ Líng's and Jiāng Yān's Letters
Dōngpō (東坡) said:
"Lǐ Líng's (李陵) 'Letter in Reply to Sū Wǔ' (答蘇武書),
its language is crude and shallow,
it was a forgery by someone during the Qí (齊) and Liáng (梁) dynasties.
Xiāo Tǒng (蕭統) did not realize it,
but Liú Zǐyuán (劉子元) alone knew."
According to the "Sòng Shǐ" (宋史),
Jiāng Yān (江淹), in prison, submitted a letter saying:
"This is why Zǐqīng (子卿) looked up to heaven and beat his chest,
weeping until his tears ran out and were followed by blood."
This directly quotes from Lǐ Líng's (李陵) letter,
thus it is clear that it was not written by someone from the Qí (齊) and Liáng (梁) dynasties.
As the years are now distant,
it is difficult to distinguish true from false,
and there are many such cases.
For example, regarding the "Xì Cí" (繫辭),
Ōu Gōng (歐公) still doubted it was written by Zhòngní (仲尼).
Jīnggōng (荊公) believed that the "Shī Xù" (詩序) was not the work of Zǐxià (子夏),
and that the "Lǐ Jì" (禮記) had many additions by Han (漢) Confucian scholars.
If this is the case for the Five Classics,
what about the rest?
Zhū Wēi (朱威) arbitrarily altered dozens of places in the main text of the "Zhōu Yì" (周易),
which largely shows his lack of judgment.
Jíbèi Bù (吉貝布)
Cotton from Mǐnzhōng (閩中),
its flowers are gathered to make cloth,
called "Jíbèi Bù" (吉貝布).
The "Nán Shǐ·Hǎinán Zhūguó Zhuàn" (南史·海南諸國傳) says:
"Línyì (林邑) and other countries produce 'gǔbèi' (古貝) trees,
their leaves are like goose feathers.
Spun into cloth,
it is no different from ramie cloth.
It is also dyed in five colors,
and woven into patterned cloth.
It is probably that the common folk pronounce 'gǔ' (古) as 'jí' (吉)."
Midnight Bell
Ōu Gōng's (歐公) "Shī Huà" (詩話) criticizes the Tang (唐) poet's line "at midnight, the sound of the bell reaches the traveler's boat,"
saying that midnight is not the time for bells to ring.
Some say that when a person dies, a bell of impermanence rings.
Perhaps the poet happened to hear this.
I once passed through Gūsū (姑蘇),
and stayed at a temple,
and heard a bell at midnight.
I asked the temple monks,
and they all said:
"It's the bell that divides the night,
what's so strange about that?"
Soon I heard the same in other temples.
Only then did I realize that "midnight bells"
exist only in Gūsū (姑蘇).
The Characters "打" and "不"
Are the common local errors nowadays limited to just the character "dǎ" (打)?
The character "bù" (不),
originally pronounced "fēn jiū qiè" (分鳩切),
is pronounced by everyone as "bū gǔ fǎn" (逋骨反).
I have thoroughly checked all rhyme dictionaries,
and there is no such sound.
Tōngyìn Zǐyú
Púyáng's "Tōngyìng Zǐyú"
is renowned throughout the world.
In that region, there is the Temple of Yìngtōng Hóu.
In front of it is a harbor,
and the fish from this harbor are the best.
Nowadays, people specifically look for large ones,
big enough to hold a seal,
calling them "Tōngyìn Zǐyú."
Jīnggōng also had a poem that said:
"Long fish on the chopping board, can hold three seals."
This is a popular傳聞 of error.
Lánzhǐ
Xúnzǐ says:
"The root of the Lánhuái is Zhǐ."
These are inherently two different things.
It also says:
"Crabs have six feet and two pincers."
Crabs actually have eight feet,
so it should not say six feet.
Xún Qīng
was a Chǔ person.
Both Lán, Zhǐ, and crabs are found in the Chǔ region.
Since the author used objects as metaphors,
they should have been able to distinguish the forms and natures of these objects.
I don't know how such errors occurred.
Zhèzhī
The "Zhèzhī Dance" was originally a play by the Tuòbá clan of the Later Wèi dynasty.
Later generations disdained it,
changing "Tuò" to "Zhè,"
and "Bá" to "Zhī."
Mimicking Ancient Poetry
The Wénxuǎn contains thirty "Mimicking Ancient" poems by Jiāng Wéntōng,
such as "Mimicking Xiū Shàngrén's Bedroom Feelings," which says:
"At dusk, the green clouds gather,
the fair lady has not yet arrived."
People today then use this as a story from Xiū Shàngrén's poetry.
Also, "Mimicking Yuānmíng's Pastoral Poetry" says:
"Sowing grain on the eastern hill,
seedlings fill the fields and paths."
Now this poem is also found in Yuānmíng's collected works,
all of which are errors.
Xiānglián Jí
Bǐtán says that the Xiānglián Jí was compiled by Hé Níng.
Later generations falsely attributed its authorship to Hán Wò.
This is a mistake.
In Táng Wú Róng's collection of poems,
there are "Harmonizing with Hán Zhìyáo Shìláng's Untitled Two Poems" which share the same rhyme as the untitled poems in Xiānglián Jí.
Wò's preface also fully records this matter.
Furthermore, I once saw a scroll of Wò's personally written poems,
and many of his poems such as "Niǎonà," "Duōqíng," and "Chūnjìn"
were in that scroll.
Wò's literary expression was elegant and refined,
which Níng could not match.
Níng said: "I have a Xiānglián Jí,
but it does not circulate in the world."
Níng enjoyed writing short verses.
When he became a chancellor,
he specifically ordered people to collect and burn them.
If so, Níng's Xiānglián Jí
consisted of frivolous and ornate short verses,
and what he meant by "does not circulate in the world"
was to cover up for himself.
How then can the current Xiānglián Jí be attributed to Níng?
Ōugōng Suspects Yì Is Not a Complete Work
Ōu Yǒngshú wrote the "Preface to the Illustrated Yì" saying:
"When I read Jīngjiě and saw it quote from the Yì:
'A difference of a hair's breadth,
leads to a mistake of a thousand miles,'
this passage is not in the current Yì.
I suspect the Yì is not a complete work.
Moreover, what Jīngjiě quotes,
according to Wáng Chōng's Lùnzhù, is an apocryphal text of the Yì.
Yǒngshú sought it in the Yìjīng,
which was a mistake.
Discussions on Jìn History
Jìn history contains an extreme number of falsehoods and fabrications,
some of which are gravely detrimental to moral teachings.
For example, Dèng Yōu journeyed with his own son and his brother's son.
At the time, bandits rose,
and Yōu feared he could not save both.
Wishing to save his brother's son,
he abandoned his own son.
When his son caught up,
Yōu tied him to the roadside and left.
If this is the case, Yōu destroyed natural human affection,
how can he be considered virtuous?
From the Liènǚ Zhuàn:
Wáng Hún saw Wáng Jì walking in the courtyard
and said:
"To have a son like this
is truly comforting."
His wife Zhōng Yǎn said:
"This daughter-in-law, having married a Cānjūn,
has produced more than just such a son."
What kind of words are these,
to be recorded in historical annals
and even called a "virtuous woman"?
Xiè Ān,
when the victory dispatch arrived, was playing chess with a guest.
Returning inside,
he unconsciously broke a clog tooth.
This was called "feigning composure to calm others."
When Ān crossed the sea,
the wind rose and waves surged.
Everyone else was terrified,
but Ān remained composed.
Also,
Huán Wēn wanted to harm Ān and Wáng Tǎnzhī.
Tǎnzhī held his hand-tablet upside down,
but Ān's expression did not change.
When Fú Jiān invaded,
he alone showed no fear.
In cases like these,
can it be called "feigning"?
Therefore, Jīnggōng's poem says:
"How contemptible are petty people,
easily startled and fearful by gains and losses.
They falsely claim a clog tooth broke,
I wish to excise it from the historical records."
This expresses deep resentment towards the blunders of historians.
Nánběi Shǐ
Lǐ Yánshòu compiled the Nánběi Shǐ,
and roughly achieved the style of historical writing.
Thus, his biography in the Táng Shū also states that it far surpassed the original books.
However, he was fond of narrating strange phenomena, auspicious omens, and prophecies,
which made it particularly cumbersome and vulgar.
For example, it says:
"Chén Zhǔ's name was Shúbǎo,
which, when read backwards, becomes 'Shǎofú' (lacking fortune)."
But how can vulgar, backward speech
be worthy of inclusion?
Many people indeed have the name Shúbǎo;
if we follow backward speech, would all of them be "lacking fortune"?
Also,
when Qí Wénxuān ascended the throne,
his reign title was "Tiānbǎo."
Breaking down the characters,
it becomes "one great person only ten,"
thus Tiānbǎo lasted exactly ten years before the emperor died.
Yet, Liáng Zhǔ Xiāo Guī, who succeeded to the throne, also had the reign title "Tiānbǎo,"
and it lasted for twenty-three years.
How unsubstantiated is this?
There are many such instances,
all of which could be entirely removed.
Lántíng Not Selected
Wáng Yòujūn's Lántíng, with "the sky is bright and the air is clear,"
is clearly an autumn scene,
and as such was not included in the Xuǎn.
However, "silk strings, bamboo pipes, wind instruments, string instruments,"
the phrase is also redundant.
Dù Yù's Stele
Dù Yù made two steles,
one he sank into the water,
fearing that after several centuries, if the water became dry land, the stele would emerge.
Yù only knew that valleys and hills change,
but did not know that stone can also wear away.
This is one interpretation.
However, for a deep valley to become dry land, it must first be filled with earth,
and only then become dry land.
Once the valley becomes dry land,
the stone would also be buried,
how could it still be seen?
This again shows a lack of understanding of physical principles.
Eight Years Younger Than Fúshēng, Two Years Older Than Tàigōng
Liáng Hào was eighty-two years old
when he passed the imperial examination as zhuàngyuán in the second year of Yōngxī.
His letter of thanks said:
"With white hair studying the classics,
eight years younger than Fúshēng;
Gaining a path to high office,
two years older than Tàigōng."
Later, he became the Imperial Librarian,
and died at over ninety years old.
Xiāofēng Sǎn
Wáng Jīnggōng once visited Cài Jūnmó
and was offered exquisitely prepared tea.
Jīnggōng took a pinch of "Xiāofēng Sǎn" from his pouch
and put it into the teacup,
drinking it along with the tea.
Jūnmó changed color.
Jīnggōng slowly said:
"Excellent tea flavor!"
Jūnmó burst into laughter
and also sighed at Jīnggōng's true nature.
Should be ordered according to Yuán Jiàng
Yuán Hòuzhī,
during the Xīníng reign, was the Zhī Fúzhōu.
An official reported a matter,
and the Duke asked how it should be handled.
The official replied,
"It should be done according to the original directive."
The Duke said,
"There has never been an original directive."
The official, startled, withdrew.
In the end, he was not punished.
The jealous wife of Fàn Sìchéng,
supervisor of wine in Fúzhōu.
His wife was beautiful and jealous.
One night,
it was Fàn's turn to sleep in the office.
A colleague playfully took a pair of slippers from a courtesan
and secretly placed them in Fàn's sleeping gear.
The next morning,
Fàn, carrying his bedding, returned home.
When his wife saw the slippers,
her expression became dejected.
She then clutched her heart and said,
"Heavens!
Has it come to this for me?"
She went into her room, hanged herself, and died.
There was also a man who served as the Cù in Húnán.
His wife gave birth to a son.
At first, he was very fond of the child.
One day, at a banquet,
he ordered courtesans to assist with the wine.
One courtesan was particularly intelligent and charming.
The Cù joked and laughed with her.
Suddenly, he saw an old soldier carrying two platters of raw meat before the Cù and his guests.
The Cù stared blankly and asked about it.
It was the flesh of his son.
It seems his wife, enraged by her husband's dalliance with the courtesan,
had personally butchered her son
and brought the meat as an offering.
A woman's jealousy is innate.
Even under threat of a naked blade, it does not change.
Therefore, the story in the *Xiaoshuo* about Tàizōng bestowing wine upon Fáng Jiǔlíng's wife
is still cited today.
The Six Tigresses, Sisters
In Yánpíng, there were six sisters of the Wú clan.
They were all jealous and fierce,
and were known at the time as "the Six Tigresses."
Among them, the "Fifth Tigress" was particularly extreme.
Throughout her life, she killed more than ten maids.
She married three times,
but none of her marriages worked out.
At midnight,
people often heard shouting and commotion in the main hall.
Everyone in the same room was afraid.
The Fifth Tigress, enraged, said,
"How dare these mad ghosts behave like this?"
She ordered the doors to be opened,
moved her bed to the central courtyard,
and slept alone with a blade in hand.
The entire night was silent.
People said that such was the awe-inspiring power of the Fifth Tigress
that even ghosts feared her.
Mistakenly Taking Zǎodòu Powder
Dèng Xiànchén, a physician from Shāyáng,
received a frantic knock at his door one night.
The person said,
"My home is ten *lǐ* from here.
My father is eighty years old
and suddenly fell ill with an abdominal ailment.
He is in a critical condition,
and I have come all this way to seek your help."
Dèng was tipsy
and hastily retrieved a packet of medicine from his satchel and gave it to him.
The person left in a hurry.
By dawn,
Dèng realized that the medicine was actually Zǎodòu powder.
Dèng was filled with regret,
believing the man's father would surely die.
Soon after, the man returned
and said,
"Thanks to your miraculous remedy,
my father has fully recovered."
He offered ten *qiān* as thanks.
It seems Dèng had given the medicine without thought,
but this person had taken it with utmost sincerity,
which is why the illness was cured.
Itchy Intestines Disease
Fù Shèrén suddenly contracted the disease of itchy intestines.
At its most severe,
he would often burst into uncontrollable laughter in front of others,
guffawing incessantly.
This disease was unknown to people in ancient times.
Lǐ Bóshí's Paintings
When Lǐ Bóshí visited the Qíji Courtyard,
he saw six horses presented by a foreign country
and painted them.
Soon after,
all six horses successively died.
People believed Lǐ's paintings were divine,
capturing their essence and spirit.
Four Poets Make a Riddle
Someone composed a poetic riddle that went:
"A beautiful woman feigns drunkenness and asks for support,
revealing her chest's frost-white skin.
She runs into the tent but cannot be found,
letting the wind and water fill the rivers and lakes."
These are the names of the four poets: Jiǎ Dǎo, Lǐ Bái, Luó Yǐn, and Pān Làng.
Some say it was composed by Wáng Jīnggōng.
Stealing Silk
A scholar was arrested for stealing silk.
The Tàishǒu ordered him to compose a *fù* to earn his release.
His ingenious reply was:
"Peering through the door, it was utterly empty—
my heart, oh, yearned for it.
Seeing profit and forgetting righteousness,
I rolled it up and kept it."
The *Fù* of "Zhāng Gōng Drinks Wine, Lǐ Gōng Gets Drunk"
Guō Fěi had talent and learning but was frivolous.
One night, he went out and was falsely accused by a drunken person.
The Tàishǒu questioned him.
Fěi smiled and said,
"The one who is 'Zhāng Gōng drinks wine, Lǐ Gōng gets drunk'
is me."
The Tàishǒu ordered him to compose "The *Fù* of Zhāng Gōng Drinks Wine, Lǐ Gōng Gets Druk."
Fěi recited:
"Events are unfathomable,
one should guard against the unforeseen.
How is it that when Zhāng Gōng drinks,
it is old Lǐ who gets drunk?
The elder from Qīnghé was enjoying the pleasure of cups and platters,
when the young master from Lǒngxī suddenly suffered the error of intoxication."
The Tàishǒu laughed and released him.
Brothers Visiting a Brothel
Lǐ Hànyīng, a Xiùcai, visited a brothel with his younger brother
and wrote on the wall before leaving.
A witty fellow wrote the ancient "Goose Poem" beside it, saying:
"Where are these two rows making a fuss with words?
From whose family are these fine brothers, a whole company?"
Abstaining from Desire to Prolong Life
Pú Chuánzhèng was the Zhī Hángzhōu.
A warlock requested an audience,
aged over ninety,
with the complexion of a baby.
The Duke asked him about the art of longevity.
He replied,
"My art is very simple and easy to practice:
merely abstain from sexual desire."
The Duke said,
"If that is the case,
then what is the benefit of living a thousand years?"
A White-Haired Old Man Becomes a Public Old Woman
There was a Lángguān
who, in his old age, acquired several maidservant-concubines.
With white hair at his temples, he had his wife and concubines pluck them alternately.
His wife, jealous of the younger concubines,
who were pleased by the maids,
removed his dark hairs.
His concubines, wishing him to appear younger,
removed his white hairs.
Before long, his chin and jaw were completely bare.
Also, the Jinshì Lǐ Jūyén plucked out all his white hairs.
His friend exclaimed in surprise,
"Yesterday, he was a white-haired old man;
now he is openly an old woman!"
Three Deer Make Bēn
Xuéshì Shí Fǔ once playfully said to Jīnggōng,
"Deer run faster than oxen.
Oxen are sturdier than deer.
Yet, three deer form the character 'bēn' (to run swiftly),
and three oxen form the character 'cū' (coarse, rough).
Why is their meaning contradictory?"
Jīnggōng smiled and did not reply.
The Shangguān's Brush, the Xiàguān's Mouth
Chén Yà's nature was humorous.
When he was Prefect of Rùnzhōu,
a certain Shàngguān Bì was among his staff.
Chén Yà trusted him deeply.
When his term was complete, and he was about to depart,
Chén Yà said,
"What advice do you have for me?"
Bì replied,
"Your talent and conduct, Lángzhōng, are faultless,
but your teasing goes too far."
Chén Yà laughed and said,
"You are Shàngguān Bì;
what about my 'xiàguān' (subordinate official) mouth?"
Bì laughed and left.
In the Scholar's Academy
Someone wrote in the Scholar's Academy:
"Lǐ Bóyáng pointed to a plum tree for his surname,
knowing it from birth."
Yáng Dànián saw it,
asked for a brush, and said,
"Mǎ Wényuān wrapped his corpse in horsehide,
ceasing only after death."
Clouds break, the moon comes, flowers play with shadows
Lángzhōng Zhāng Zǐyě was famous for his musical compositions.
Sòng Zǐjīng went to visit him,
first sending someone to playfully say,
"Shàngshū wishes to see the Lángzhōng of 'clouds break, the moon comes, flowers play with shadows'."
Zhāng Zǐyě called from behind a screen,
"Might you be the Shàngshū of 'spring's stir on the tips of red apricot branches'?"
Mocking the Niè surname
Guózi Bóshì Guō Zhōngshù
once mocked Sīyè Niè Chóngyì, saying:
"Close to the noble, entirely deaf;
collecting dragons, only deaf.
Though he has three ears,
alas, he cannot hear clearly."
Chóngyì replied,
"Do not mock my three ears;
it's far better than harboring two hearts."
Playfully written memorial
Kǒng Dàfū Sìzōng was the Administrator of Zhècáo,
and playfully wrote a memorial saying:
"My belly full of tea and soup for guests,
my eyes owed a thousand letters.
By the fire, I am like a lonely ghost;
by the gate, I am just like an old gatekeeper."
Riddle
Wáng Jīnggōng playfully composed a riddle:
"Round when drawn,
square when written.
Short in winter,
long in summer."
Jífǔ explained,
"In the Eastern Sea there is a fish,
without head and without tail.
Remove its spine,
and that is this riddle."
'Erlì' years are rare
There was a man of seventy,
whose wife was only thirty.
They had a son,
and Dōngpō playfully wrote a poem saying:
"The sage and good one is just at their 'erlì' years,
while the father has already reached the 'qīshí' years."
Writing the character 'wǔ' on the door
Lǐ Ānyì
called upon the wealthy man Zhèng Shēng,
who declined, saying he was out.
Ānyì wrote a large character '午' (wǔ) on the door and left.
Someone asked him the reason,
and he replied,
"A '牛' (niú, ox) without a '頭' (tóu, head)."
This also carried the meaning of the ancients who wrote '鳳' (fèng, phoenix).
My servant calls out 'Sītú'
Wén Lùgōng playfully said,
"I have never in my life as an official been able to catch up to one of my servants.
Before I entered the Western Bureau,
this servant was already called 'Púshè'.
By the time I became Púshè,
this servant had again been promoted to 'Sītú'."
Such was the common way of addressing them.
Ink Pool, Leather Shed
Wáng Sēngyàn's father, named Shīgǔ,
often called his inkstone "ink pool" (mòchí),
and his drum "leather shed" (pípéng).
While governing a prefecture in Lǐngnán,
a certain Lǐ Yàngǔ obtained an official position through tribute.
When he passed through the prefecture,
he requested an audience,
and his calling card read:
"Lǐ Mòchí Pípéng, Sīhù Cānjūn of Yǒngzhōu,
respectfully awaits your visit."
Yázhōu's geomantic position is heavy
Dīng Jìnggōng returned from Yázhōu,
and the guests at his table discussed which prefecture in the world was the most prominent.
The Duke said,
"Only Yázhōu's geomantic position is the heaviest."
The guests asked him why,
and he replied,
"Even a Chancellor serves only as the Sīhù Cānjūn of that prefecture;
how can other prefectures compare?"
Zhōngchéng hires a boat to return home, Lǎozhàng brings a horse to the pass
Shū Xìndào,
during the Yuánfēng era, incurred a fault and returned south.
At that time, Běn Lǎozhàng was summoned to reside in Huìlín Temple.
Someone asked about new events in the capital,
and he replied,
"Zhōngchéng Shū hired a passenger boat to return home,
and Běn Lǎozhàng rode a post horse to the pass."
'Wǒ Nóng' and 'Ěr Nóng'
Dù Sānsī,
a native of Wú,
was eloquent.
Lǐ Fáng of Xiāngyì playfully said,
"Regarding the saying 'ěr nóng wǒ nóng' in your immortal hometown,
from which classic does it come?"
He replied,
"It comes from the second chapter of 'Yìng Wǒ Lǐ'."
"'Yìng Wǒ Lǐ'"
is merely a term used when people address each other.
Xiùcai Kāng Le
Liǔ Miǎn was taking the imperial examinations,
and had many taboos,
calling "ān lè" (peace and happiness) "ān kāng" (peace and health)
to avoid the character "lè" which sounds like "luò" (fall/fail).
Suddenly, he heard the results were posted,
and sent his servant to check.
A moment later,
the servant returned,
saying,
"Xiùcai kāng le (the scholar has recovered/is healthy)!"
Bamboo Poem
A scholar from Qiántáng wrote a "Bamboo" poem and presented it to Dōngpō,
with lines saying:
"Leaves cluster like a thousand swords,
stems rise like ten thousand spears."
The Duke said,
"These bamboo leaves seem too few."
The man did not understand.
The Duke smiled and said,
"Ten bamboos produce only one leaf;
how can you say there are many?"
Qiú Lǎn and Méi Fú
People today call a county magistrate "Zìmín" (character-person),
a county clerk "Qiú Lǎn" (Qíu Lǎn, a famous ancient clerk),
and a county commandant "Méi Fú" (Méi Fú, a famous ancient commandant).
There was a boorish and vulgar man named Wáng Kàng,
who served as the Commandant of Wèishì.
He called the magistrate "Xuē Jiā" (Xuē Family).
Someone jokingly asked him,
"Do you know the meaning of 'Zì' and 'Lǎn'?
A county magistrate must be literate,
hence called 'Zì'.
A clerk examines documents with the magistrate,
hence called 'Lǎn'."
Kàng said,
"Then why is 'Wèi' called 'Méi Fú'?"
He replied,
"Their duties are vital and crucial,
a single (枚, méi) person of good fortune (福, fú).
Like yourself, you could be called 'Wáng Fú'."
Wáng Kàng once managed the stores of a rich family,
which is why he was mocked with this.
My younger brother died south of the Yangtze, my elder brother died north of the frontier
There was Lǐ Tíngyàn,
who presented a hundred-rhyme poem to a high official,
with lines saying:
"My younger brother died south of the Yangtze,
my elder brother died north of the frontier."
The high official felt pity and said,
"Your family has suffered such misfortune!"
Tíngyàn quickly replied,
"There is no such actual event;
I just wanted the couplet to be poignant and well-matched."
A moonlit night, inviting a neighboring monk for a casual chat
Xǔ Yìfāng's wife
prided herself on her integrity and purity.
Yìfāng once went out
and did not return until a year had passed.
His wife said:
"Since you departed,
I have merely kept the door closed and guarded myself."
Yìfāng sighed in admiration
and asked how she amused herself.
She replied:
"I occasionally compose small poems
to suit my mood."
Yìfāng was pleased,
took the poems to read them,
and found the first piece titled "Inviting a Neighboring Monk for a Chat on a Moonlit Night."
The "kǒu" (mouth radical) of the character "táng" (hall) was incomplete.
The Imperial Academy had a "Zhìlètáng."
Jǔrén residing there
often changed their names while awaiting appointment,
and some subsequently achieved fame.
A certain temple in Qiántáng was excellent,
but its monks were fond of lawsuits.
Shěn Ruìdá, while inspecting the monk's hall,
saw that the "kǒu" radical of the character "táng" was incomplete.
Playfully, he took up a brush and completed it,
and the disputes ceased.
Now, wherever a fire disaster occurs,
there is an urgent need for provincial and county plaques;
burning them brings relief.
Thus, one knows that prayers, exorcisms, and suppressing evil
may indeed have their reasons.
A Gourd, a Thousand Pieces of Gold
The tradition says:
"Losing a boat in midstream, a gourd is worth a thousand pieces of gold."
This is what is now called a "fúhuán" (floating ring),
which Zhè people call a "hú" (gourd).
Míngzhōu's Chāngguó County is on an island in the sea.
Now, the boats that travel back and forth have two rings,
which the boatmen call "hú."
Zhōng Kuí
Nowadays, people paint Zhōng Kuí at the beginning of the year to ward off evil.
Popular tradition attributes its origin to the time of Táng Mínghuáng.
During the Huángyòu reign,
a stele was unearthed,
which was the epitaph of Sòng Zōngquè's mother,
and it recorded that her sister's name was "Zhōng Kuí."
Also, the Běishǐ says:
"Yáo Xuān,
originally named Zhōng Kuí,
courtesy name Pìxié,
was born during the time of Wèi Dàowǔ."
There was also a Yú Jìng,
whose courtesy name was also Zhōng Kuí.
Considering their chronological order,
Xuān predates the others,
so it is known that it did not originate solely in the Sòng dynasty.
However, the characters "Kuí" and "Kuí" are different,
so there must be an error in transmission.
Orpiment
Ancient people wrote books using yellow paper,
dyed with pinyin: huángbò,
to ward off bookworms,
hence it was called "yellow scroll."
If there were errors,
they used orpiment to erase them,
because its color was similar to the paper.
Therefore, to approve or disapprove of someone's writing
is called "orpiment."
Wáng Mǎng's Prohibition on Duplicate Names
People of the Eastern Hàn dynasty did not have duplicate names.
Some say that during Wáng Mǎng's time, two-character names were forbidden.
This was likely due to the "qiān xí" (encroachment/imitation) practice.
Yàgǔxì (Startling Drum Play)
When Wáng Zǐchún first pacified Xīhé,
he taught the soldiers to perform yàgǔxì,
which subsequently became widespread.
The movements, dances, rhythms,
and the actors' lines
were all composed by Zǐchún.
Some say that Zǐchún, when arrayed against the Westerners,
ordered a hundred soldiers to dress as a yàgǔ troupe
and advance before the army.
The barbarians were all astonished at the sight,
whereupon the army advanced and fiercely attacked,
utterly defeating them.
Reciting the Gātē Gātē Mantra Backwards
Fishermen place monkey hair at the four corners of their nets,
and thus catch many fish.
They say that fish see it
as humans see brocade.
Someone saw a net cast for fishing,
but by focusing and silently reciting the Gātē Gātē mantra backwards seven times,
he could ensure no catch all day.
Swallow Meat as Bait for Fish
There was a fisherman who caught fish very easily.
He said he used swallow meat mixed with flour as bait.
However, people who eat swallow meat will surely be harmed by jiāolóng.
Fish and jiāolóng are both aquatic creatures,
so this theory is credible.
Zhāng Bǎibēi
Zhāng Bóyù could drink several dou of wine without getting drunk,
and was known as "Zhāng Bǎibēi" (Zhāng Hundred-Cups) to the world.
He would immediately suck in water to rinse his mouth,
saying:
"The poison of wine is in the teeth;
if it's rinsed away, it won't cause trouble."
Chén Kāngmín adopted his method
and could also drink up to one dou without getting drunk.
Tàiyīn Xuánjīngshí (Dark Essence Stone of the Great Yin)
There are more than ten kinds of salt,
and sea salt is the finest.
Next is jiěyán (lake salt),
but eating it causes many wind-related ailments.
The essence of salt is in the earth,
and after a long time, it condenses like crystal,
named "Tàiyīn Xuánjīngshí."
Its taste is bitter.
The Běncǎo says:
"Its taste is salty,"
which is incorrect.
Lǐ Tíngguī Ink
Lǐ Chāo, a master ink maker of the Táng dynasty, and his son Tíngguī,
crossed the river from Yìshuǐ
and settled in Shè.
Their original surname was Xī,
but in Jiāngnán, they were granted the surname Lǐ.
Tíngguī was originally named Tíngguī (邽).
Therefore, there are Xī Tíngguī inks
and Lǐ Tíngguī (邽) inks in the world.
Any made with the character "guī" (珪)
are fake.
His eldest son was Chéngkuān,
his second son Chéngyàn,
and Yàn's son Wényòng,
all capable of inheriting the craft.
During the Xiángfú reign,
Zhāoyìnggōng used Tíngguī (邽) ink for dyeing and decoration.
A nobleman once accidentally dropped an ink stick into a pond.
A month later, when he was drinking by the pond,
he dropped a gold implement.
He ordered a skilled diver to retrieve it.
The ink stick was also recovered,
its luster and color unchanged,
inside and out like new.
Lǐ Bì's Tea Poem
Tea's origin
was not well documented in ancient times.
The Běncǎo says:
Yìzhōu.
In the Táng dynasty, those from Méngshān, Gùzhǔ, and Qímén were considered superior,
still mixed with ingredients like su (Perilla) and jiāo (Sichuan pepper).
Hence, Lǐ Bì's poem says:
"The swirling foam transforms into a jade-green pond,
with added perilla, scattered like琉璃 (glass) eyes."
Thus, green color was valued.
They only spoke of "jiānchá" (boiling tea),
unaware of the subtleties of "diǎnshì" (whisking and tasting);
most of it was coarse tea.
Lù Yǔ's Chájīng comprehensively discussed those from Fújiàn, Quán, Sháo, and ten other prefectures,
saying only that their taste was excellent.
Now, Jiàn'ān is considered the best in the world.
Lìzhīpǔ (Treatise on Lychees)
It states that in the early Hàn dynasty, Nányuè King Wèi Tuó
used it as a local tribute.
During Emperor Hé's reign, the seven commanderies of Jiāozhǐ paid tribute with fresh lychees.
During the Tiānbǎo reign,
Fúzhōu sent them via post horses annually.
There was never any mention of those from Mǐnzhōng.
Now, those from Guǎngnán and Zǐkuí
are barely comparable to the inferior quality ones from Mǐnzhōng.
This means that the true lychee's fame did not begin to be noted until the Táng dynasty.
Now, Púyáng is considered the best in the world.
Taboo Against Eating Lamb Blood
Those who practice elixirs
are forbidden from eating lamb blood.
Even if one has taken medicine for decades,
a single consumption will cause all previous efforts to be lost.
Eye Ailments and Bathing Taboo
Those with eye ailments
must strictly avoid bathing,
as it can cause blindness.
Officials Taboo on "Wǎrì"
Officials often avoid the "wǎ rì"
when taking up official posts.
Many people do not understand the meaning of "wǎ."
Some say:
The character "jiǔ" somewhat resembles the character "wǎ."
The explanations from various scholars differ
and are mostly baseless.
Whenever one takes up an official post,
one must absolutely avoid the 4th, 7th, 16th, and 19th days of the month.
These are called the "Four Inauspicious Days."
Those who use these days
rarely come to a good end.
The term "xìmò jiānglái"
originated when Emperor Tàizǔ held an inner banquet
and ordered powdered food to be served,
hence it was called "tóushí" (first course).
Later generations, when banquets were about to end,
would serve this dish,
which was a deviation from the original sequence.
Also, at public banquets in zhōujùn,
when music was about to begin,
entertainers would exclaim "xìmò jiānglái."
This is because at imperial banquets, when music was presented,
it would first be initiated with stringed instruments,
and then harmonized with all other instruments.
Hence it was called "sīmò jiānglái" (silk music to come).
Now, wherever music begins with wind instruments,
not only is its name corrupted,
but its original meaning is also lost.
Avoiding Fire
There was a palace attendant named Sūn Gòngfèng.
A fire broke out in the hall,
and everyone scaled the walls and fled.
A wet nurse went straight through the flames and emerged,
her body unburnt,
and the infant still asleep and unaware.
People asked her,
and she replied:
"My husband said
that to avoid fire, one should close one's eyes
and rush out in a straight line.
If one's eyes are open,
one will surely suffocate and fall.
I used this advice,
so I came out unharmed,
and did not even feel my body treading through the blazing fire."
Rat Tears
If food is stored at night in a vessel,
and not covered tightly,
and a rat tries to steal the food but cannot get it,
it will run around the vessel,
and its tears will drip into the vessel.
Those who eat it will contract the "yellow sickness,"
their whole body becoming like wax,
and it cannot be cured by acupuncture or medicine.
Southerners Do Not Recognize Snow
There is no snow in Lǐngnán.
In Mǐnzhōng, only the four prefectures of Jiàn, Jiàn, Tíng, and Shào have it.
Thus, northerners mockingly say:
"Southerners do not recognize snow,
and compare it to willow catkins."
However, the willows in the south truly have no catkins.
Therefore, southerners not only do not recognize snow,
but also do not recognize willow catkins.
Fèngzhōu's Three Excellences
The hands of courtesans in Fèngzhōu, Shǎnxī, are all slender and white.
Their "cuìliǔ" (green willows, referring to eyebrows or waist)
are especially lovely.
Also, the wine from the public storehouse is excellent.
Hence, it is said in the world that Fèngzhōu has "three excellences,"
referring to hands, willows, and wine.
Lǐ Yù, a scholar from Xuānchéng, said:
"My hometown has four excellences:
lacquer, chestnuts, brushes, and honey."
A Scholar Seeks Shelter on Liǔlián Road
In Húnán, there were mischievous spirits who loved to kill people for sacrifice.
Scholars were offered as the highest sacrifice,
monks as the second,
and other people as the lowest.
There was a scholar traveling on Liǔlián Road.
At dusk,
a farmer said:
"There are fierce beasts ahead;
it's not advisable to travel at night.
There are residents in the woods nearby;
you can ask for shelter there."
He entered a desolate path
and suddenly saw a grand gate and a large mansion.
The host invited him into a room,
where the dishes were abundant and delicious.
When night fell,
a woman came out,
very beautiful.
The scholar flirted with her,
and she gladly responded.
They lingered for several days,
their affection intimate and close.
She privately said:
"Tonight they plan to murder you to sacrifice to the ghosts.
I am also from a good family,
but was abducted and brought here by them.
They sent me to serve you,
wanting to win your heart."
That night,
she and the scholar escaped through a gap in the wall.
By dawn, they had traveled forty *lǐ*
and reached a nearby county.
The county sent officials to arrest them.
The full extent of their crimes was discovered.
Dozens of people had been killed before and after.
The farmer who pointed the way was also part of their gang.
Thereupon, the whole family was executed according to law.
The scholar was awarded an official position for his efforts
and lived to old age with the woman.
Gu Poison
It is a custom in Mǐn and Shǔ to keep *gǔ* (poison).
The method:
first, gather a hundred insects in a vessel,
allow them to devour each other,
and after several months, when all are eaten
and only one remains,
it is then taken as the *gǔ*.
When its offspring is placed in food or drink,
it instantly kills people.
It is falsely claimed:
if many people are killed,
the *gǔ* owner becomes wealthy and prosperous.
Otherwise,
they will suffer misfortune instead.
Hence, foolish people persist in creating and keeping it.
Initially, when poisoned, one feels no difference.
Half a year later, the poison begins to take effect.
The *gǔ* multiplies gradually,
devouring the victim's intestines and stomach completely before they die.
At the time of death,
the victim is always able to reveal the name of the household that poisoned them.
Most victims are traveling merchants,
hence the matter is difficult to investigate.
Cài Jūnmò, serving as the grain transport commissioner,
busted several hundred households,
and thereafter it somewhat subsided.
Locals say:
"If a family has *gǔ*,
chickens should not be kept,
as they will be frightened and fly away."
Also, there is one creature that does not fear it:
only scorpions can control it.
White ginger lily can also cure its poison.
Liǔ Zǐhòu's "Poem on Planting White Ginger Lily" mostly describes this matter.
The *Běncǎo* (Materia Medica) says:
"Take three *zhīzi* fruits,
hide them in the collar of your clothes;
if you encounter poisoned food,
the *gǔ* will strike and make a sound itself."
Zhū Hǔcán
Each time a tiger eats a person,
an ear develops a notch.
On Xīshān in Tíngzhōu, there was a tiger
that was killed by an archer.
Both its ears were like saws.
The tiger's nature is very spiritual;
it does not eat people recklessly.
Perhaps it is due to predestination,
or past grievances.
Zhū Tài, a commoner from Wǔkāng,
was extremely filial to his mother.
He was seized by a tiger and carried away.
Zhū Tài loudly cried out:
"Tiger, if you violently kill me,
my mother will have no one to rely on!"
The tiger immediately released him.
Zhū Tài later recovered and was healthy as before.
The villagers called him "Zhū Hǔcán" (Zhū, the one spared by the tiger).
Centipede
Someone in the wilderness saw a centipede chasing a snake,
very urgently.
The snake, knowing its strength was inferior,
turned its body and opened its mouth towards it.
The centipede entered its mouth.
Soon the snake died,
and the centipede burrowed out from its side.
When the snake was cut open,
its intestines were already gone.
It is said, "jīqú (centipede) craves intestines."
Jīqú is a centipede.
Insect Enters Ear
Among the types of insects capable of entering human ears,
it is not only centipedes.
For instance, bedbugs,
which are also called "fire-head insects,"
and soapberry bugs
can all cause harm.
Someone suffered from a brainache
caused by insects eating away at it.
Someone advised him to use peach leaves as a pillow.
One night,
a *gǔ* worm emerged from his nose,
shaped like an eagle's beak.
People did not know its name.
Someone else had a centipede enter their ear,
and at its most extreme,
they would bang their head against a pillar
until blood flowed, unaware of it,
saying the itch was unbearable.
Centipedes entering the ear
often eat the marrow,
and even after it's gone, they can reproduce.
Whenever an insect enters the ear,
it is best to pour raw oil into it.
Water *Gǔ* Worms
Whenever eating at night, one must use a candle.
Chén Zhèngmǐn was greatly intoxicated,
and was about to drink water,
when he heard a sound in the water.
He quickly called for a candle to look at it.
He found a worm
shaped like an earthworm.
His attendants said:
"That is a water *gǔ* worm.
It enters the stomach and eats people's intestines."
Night Tiger
In Lǐngnán, there is a worm like an earthworm,
more than a *chǐ* long.
Its mouth is sharp like an awl.
It mostly comes out at midnight,
with half its body on the ground,
and the other half pointing in the air as it moves.
If someone accidentally touches it,
it goes straight into their heart and abdomen.
It eats the person until death,
then comes out.
Local people call it the "Night Tiger."
Planting Pines
Regarding all pines,
it is very easy to make them spread their branches widely like a canopy.
When planting, remove the large taproot of the pine,
leaving only the fibrous roots on the four sides.
Then none will fail to spread their branches.
Volume 47
End.
Painting Hán Tuìzhī
People in the world paint Hán Tuìzhī
with a small face and beautiful beard,
wearing a gauze hat.
This is Hán Xīzài of Jiāngnán.
There are contemporary inscriptions that are very clear about this.
Hán Xīzài's posthumous title was Wénjìng,
and he was called Hán Wéngōng.
Because of this, he was mistakenly identified as Hán Tuìzhī.
Not Understanding Mèngzǐ
Shèngměi, when young, once visited a high-ranking official,
and found him discussing the *Mèngzǐ* with guests,
without paying him much attention.
Suddenly, he asked Shèngměi:
"Have you ever read the *Mèngzǐ*?"
He replied:
"I have loved it all my life,
but I don't understand its meaning at all."
The host asked:
"What meaning don't you understand?"
He replied:
"I don't understand it from the beginning."
The host said:
"Please try to explain."
He said:
"It says Mèngzǐ 'did not see feudal lords,'
so why did he see King Huì of Liáng?" The man was astonished and had no reply.
A Rushing Horse Tramples a Dog to Death
In earlier years, scholars mostly valued parallel couplets in writing.
Mù Xiū and Zhāng Jǐng were the first to write in ancient prose.
The two gentlemen arrived at court,
waiting for dawn,
and happened to see a rushing horse trample a dog to death.
Each recorded the event
to compare their skill.
Mù said:
"The horse bolted,
and a yellow dog met its end under its hooves."
Zhāng said:
"There was a dog
that died beneath a rushing horse."
At that time, the literary style was newly changing,
and both men's words were clumsy and awkward,
yet they were considered skillful at the time.
Salt Law
Wáng Jūnxuàng, serving as the Commissioner of Finance,
requested a change to the salt law in Héběi.
Emperor Rénzōng replied in a rescript:
"I cannot bear for the soldiers and common people of Héběi to eat expensive salt."
The Commissioner of Finance immediately ceased and abandoned the proposal.
Guànquè Tower
Guànquè Tower in Hézhōng Prefecture
looks out upon Mount Zhōngtiáo in front
and down upon the Yellow River below.
Many poems by Tang people remain.
Lǐ Yì said:
"West of Guànquè Tower, a hundred-foot wall,
sandbars and cloudy trees are all boundless.
The music of the Hàn house follows the flowing water,
the mountains and rivers of the Wèi state are half in the setting sun.
A thousand years past still seems swift,
a single day of sorrow feels long.
Wind and mist combine in thoughts of returning home,
a distant gaze, though not spring, still saddens."
Wáng Wénhuàn said:
"The white sun follows the mountains to its end,
the Yellow River flows into the sea.
To broaden one's vision a thousand *lǐ*,
one must ascend another story."
Chàng Shī said:
"Remotely overlooking the flying birds,
towering above the worldly dust.
The sky's expanse encircles the flat plains,
the river flows through broken mountains."
Wáng Xiàng's Judgment
Ōu Gōng was serving as the Administrator of Chúzhōu.
Wáng Xiàng was a "Sanban Fengzhi,"
supervising a military post.
Within it, there was a scholar
who, because a student failed to provide tuition (*cìxiū*),
went personally to visit him.
The student closed his door and did not receive him.
The scholar sued him.
Wáng Xiàng's judgment read:
"One hears of coming to learn,
but not of going to teach.
Since the teacher has already condescended himself,
how can the student not elevate himself slightly?
Why collect two items to establish authority,
or involve two parties in a lawsuit?"
The scholar took the judgment to Ōu Gōng.
Ōu Gōng greatly praised his talent,
promoted and nurtured him,
and he eventually became a man of letters.
Wèi Yě's Poems
Wèi Yě of Shǔ
has a "Poem on Pínglù County, Shǎn Prefecture" that says:
"At Hánshí, flowers hide the county,
at Chóngyáng, chrysanthemums encircle the bay.
A single oar sound leaves the bank,
a few points mark the departure from the state."
Kòu Zhōngmǐn was garrisoned in the Northern Capital.
There was a courtesan whose demeanor was unrefined and clumsy;
locals called her "Unripe Zhāng Bā."
At a prefectural gathering,
Wèi Yě gifted her a poem saying:
"You are the 'Unripe Zhāng Bā' of the Northern Road,
I am the 'Ripe Wèi Sān' of the Western State.
Do not be surprised by my lack of smiles at the drinking table,
half-unripe and half-ripe, we are not yet acquainted."
Bái Lètiān's Poems
Whenever Bái Lètiān composed a poem,
he would have an old woman interpret it.
He would ask:
"Do you understand?"
If the old woman said:
"I understand,"
then he would record it.
If she said: "I don't understand,"
then he would revise it.
Therefore, the poetry of the late Táng period was close to being rustic and vulgar.
Five Horses
The world called the Grand Administrator the "Five Horses."
Some say the *Shī* states:
"Many flags, tall and narrow,
In the capital of Xùn.
Woven with plain silk,
With five fine horses."
Zhèng's commentary says of the *Zhōu Lǐ*:
The head of a zhōu sets up flags.
Hàn Grand Administrators were comparable to zhōu heads,
and by custom rode five horses,
hence the saying.
Others say:
In ancient times, four-horse chariots were used.
By the Hàn dynasty,
Grand Administrators added one horse when they went out.
This account is found in the *Hàn Guān Yí*.
A Riddle for Holding Chess Pieces
Shū Wáng was at Zhōngshān
playing chess with a Daoist priest.
The Daoist priest said:
"He also dares not move first,
and I also dare not move first.
Precisely because neither dares to move first,
there is also nothing to contend for,
and thus one can enter into the state of neither death nor life."
The Duke smiled and said:
"This is a riddle about holding chess pieces."
Dōngpō's Poems
Dōngpō composed a poem on *hǎitáng* that says:
"I fear the flowers will fall asleep deep in the night,
so I burn tall candles to illuminate their rosy blush."
This account is found in the *Yáng Fēi Wài Zhuàn*,
which says:
"Míng Huáng ascended the Chénxiāng Tíng
and summoned the Imperial Concubine.
The Concubine's face was flushed with wine, her makeup smudged,
her hair dishevelled and hairpin askew.
The Emperor laughed and said:
'Is this truly the Concubine's intoxication?
It is simply the *hǎitáng* having not had enough sleep!'"
He composed a poem on "Immortal Children" that says:
"Therefore, white silk is used to make immortal robes,
so no red ointment stains their heavenly purity."
This account is found in the second year of Chángshòu of Zétiān, when an imperial edict
ordered all nuns in the empire to wear robes of white silk.
A poem on "Olives" says:
"Waiting for the faint sweetness to return to the teeth and cheeks,
it has already yielded ten parts of sweetness to cliff honey."
The account of "cliff honey" is found in *Guǐ Gǔ Zǐ*, which says:
"Night-shining clear
is the firefly.
Hundred-flower sweet wine
is honey.
Cliff honey
is the cherry."
A poem "To a Candidate" says:
"In a lifetime, all things are sufficient,
what is lacking is only one death."
This account is found in the Liáng *Sēng Shǐ*,
which says:
"Shìzǔ summoned Bátuóluó.
When he arrived,
Shìzǔ jokingly said:
'The Mahāyāna did not come in vain from afar;
there is only one death left.'
Bátuóluó replied:
'This humble monk has been a guest of Your Majesty,
for thirty years.
What is lacking is only one death.'"
Lice Roaming the Prime Minister's Beard, Seen by the Emperor
When Wáng Jīnggōng entered the court,
a louse crawled up from his collar,
directly along his beard.
The attendants looked and smiled,
but the Duke did not notice.
After court was dismissed,
Wáng Yǔyù pointed it out to the Duke,
and moreover said:
"May I offer a word?"
The Duke said:
"What is it?"
Yǔyù said:
"Lice roamed the Prime Minister's beard,
and were seen by the Emperor."
Xǔ Wǒ
When Jiǎ Wèigōng was Prime Minister,
there was a Daoist alchemist surnamed Xǔ,
who never addressed people by name.
At the time, people called him "Xǔ Wǒ" (Xu Me).
The Duke urged him strongly,
and he entered the hall riding a donkey.
The gate guard stopped him.
Xǔ said:
"I seek nothing from the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister called me to come.
If it is like this,
I shall leave."
He did not dismount from the donkey and left.
The Duke sent someone to summon him,
but he never came.
The Duke sighed and said:
"Xǔ is but an ordinary man!
Precisely because he seeks nothing from others,
he cannot be compelled by power,
much less those who take on righteousness as their duty?"
Rúe Grass (Seven-Mile Fragrance)
Ancient people stored books,
using *rúe* to repel bookworms.
*Rúe*
is a fragrant herb.
What people today call "Seven-Mile Fragrance" is it.
Its leaves resemble pea shoots,
growing in small clusters.
Southerners pick it and place it under mats,
and it can remove fleas and lice.
When I was serving as Registrar of the Zhāowén Guǎn,
I obtained several plants from Lùgōng's home.
I transplanted them to the Secret Archives,
but they no longer exist today.
Many fragrant herbs have different names.
The so-called "lán sūn" —
*sūn* is *chāngpú*.
*Huì líng* —
*líng xiāng* is it.
*Sà* —
*báizhǐ* is it.
Huáng Zōngdàn's Eye Disease
Huáng Zōngdàn suffered from an eye disease in his later years.
Whenever he presented memorials,
he would first prepare the memorial's outline,
memorize it,
and then, before the Emperor,
display the outline and recite it.
His colleagues secretly swapped it with another document,
but Zōngdàn did not know.
When he was before the Emperor,
what he recited differed from the memorial's outline.
He returned home and requested to retire.
Bāo Xiàosù's Smile is Rarer than the Yellow River Clearing
Bāo Xiàosù governed Jīng,
renowned for his clear judgment.
There was a registered household who broke the law,
and was to be flogged on the back.
The clerk accepted a bribe,
and made an agreement with him, saying:
"Now, when you see the Yǐn,
you just cry out and defend yourself.
I will share your crime with you;
if you are flogged, I will also be flogged."
Afterward, Bāo brought the prisoner in for questioning,
and he indeed argued incessantly.
The clerk rebuked him, saying:
"Just receive the back flogging and leave;
why speak so much!"
Bāo thought he was abusing his power,
and flogged him in the courtyard.
He specially leniently treated the prisoner's crime,
only making him suffer the flogging.
He did not know he was being tricked.
Xiàosù was stern and rigid,
never showing a smiling face.
People said, "Bāo Xīrén's smile is rarer than the Yellow River clearing."
Carrying Manure and Playing Chess
Lín Bū lived on Gūshān in Hángzhōu.
He kept two cranes;
when released, they would fly into the clouds,
and after a long time, return to their cages.
Bū often floated a small boat to tour Xī Hú.
If a guest arrived,
a young attendant would invite the guest to sit
and open the cages to release the cranes.
After a long while,
Bū would return,
using the cranes' flight as a signal.
Bū was knowledgeable in many things,
but only could not play chess.
He often said:
"I, Bū, can do everything in the world
except carry manure and play chess."
The First to Strike Pays Money
Jū Zhēnqīng served as Governor of Rùnzhōu.
When commoners engaged in fights,
in addition to the original punishment,
he ordered the first to strike to pay money to the one who retaliated.
Common people were stingy with money,
so disputes ceased all day long.
They looked at each other,
none daring to strike first.
Strange Illness
In the world, there are those with strange illnesses.
Lǚ Jìnshū was administering Yǐngzhōu,
when he suddenly fell ill.
He merely shrunk,
and at his death was like a small child.
There was a certain Jiāng Yú,
who suddenly became illiterate.
Another person suffered from an eye condition,
seeing all straight objects as curved.
Yet another old woman,
ate without knowing satiety;
she ate a hundred steamed cakes,
and a *shí* of rice daily.
Zháséng,
whenever hungry,
would immediately need to eat something;
a slight delay would cause him to faint.
Smashing the Jar Painting
Sīmǎ Wēngōng, as a child, was playing with a group of children.
In the courtyard there was a large jar.
One child climbed it,
slipped, and fell into the water.
The other children ran away.
Gōng struck the jar with a stone,
and the water flowed out through the hole,
so the child did not die.
His act of saving a life was already evident in his childhood.
Between Jīng and Luò, many still create "Paintings of Children Smashing Jars."
Group Audience with Old Regulations
Candidates for imperial examinations from all over the realm,
upon reaching the capital, all had a group audience,
called "qúnjiàn" (group audience).
The ranks and rows were disorderly,
which troubled the officials.
In recent years, only the "jiětóu" (head candidate) was allowed to have an audience,
numbering several hundred.
The gatekeepers often said:
"There are three types of people whose ranks cannot be ordered:
examination candidates, foreigners, and camels."
Bear Den
Bears,
in the mountains for thousands of *lǐ*,
all have places to lie low and hide,
always in stone caves or hollow trees.
The mountain people call them "xióngguǎn" (bear dens).
Even a tiger,
if it ventures a hundred *lǐ* away, will lose its way.
The Whole City is Windy and Rainy Nearing Double Ninth
Pān Dàlín of Huángzhōu,
was skilled in poetry,
but very poor.
Xiè Wúyì of Línchuān wrote to ask:
"Do you have any new works?"
He replied:
"Every scene this autumn is a fine line,
but I regret being obscured by vulgar dust.
Yesterday I had a poem which said:
'The whole city is windy and rainy nearing Double Ninth.'
Suddenly the rent collector arrived,
and my mood was ruined.
Only this one line I send to you."
Those who heard it laughed at his impracticality.
Flower Poems Compared to Beautiful Women
Previous generations composed flower poems,
often comparing them to beautiful women.
For example:
"If taught to speak, they would overturn kingdoms;
even if heartless, they would move people."
Huáng Lúzhí's *Túmí* poem said:
"Dew-drenched Héláng trying *tāngbǐng*,
Sun-baked Xúnlìng lighting incense."
This compares them to handsome men.
Péng Yuáncái's *Hǎitáng* (Crabapple) poem said:
"After the rain, Consort Yáng bathed in the hot springs;
Thick dew, Héláng tried *tāngbǐng*."
His intention was even more skillful.
Poem on a Spring Day Event
Zhào Shīmín's *Chūnrì Jíshì* (Spring Day Event) says:
"Dew-covered flowers fallen to the ground weep morning sorrow,
Willows brushing the embankment play with spring's countenance."
Fànzhì's Poem
Fànzhì's poem says:
"Outside the city are earthen steamed buns,
The vegetable filling is inside the city.
Each person eats one,
Do not dislike it for being tasteless."
Huáng Lúzhí said:
"Since it's vegetable filling,
how can one know its taste anymore?"
He changed it,
saying:
"First pour wine on it,
and try to make it flavorful."
Sòng Dí's Paintings Originated from
Sòng Dí, a Yellow Lang of the Board of Revenue,
was skilled in landscape painting.
Among his most celebrated works,

were *Píngshā Yànluò* (Wild Geese Descending on a Level Sandbar), *Yuǎnpǔ Fánguī* (Sailboats Returning to a Distant Shore), *Shānshì Qínglán* (Mountain Market in Clear Mist), *Jiāngtiān Mùxuě* (River and Sky in Evening Snow), *Dòngtíng Qiūyuè* (Autumn Moon over Dòngtíng Lake), *Xiāoxiāng Yèyǔ* (Night Rain over Xiāo and Xiāng Rivers), *Yānsì Xiǎozhōng* (Morning Bell from a Misty Temple), and *Yúcūn Luòzhào* (Fishing Village in Evening Glow).
These were called the "Eight Scenes."
There was Chén Yòngzhī,
who also painted landscapes.
Dí said:
"Your painting is indeed skillful,
but lacks natural charm.
You should seek a decaying wall,
stretch plain silk over it,
and after a long time,
you will see that the earth of the decaying wall all forms images of landscapes.
The high parts become mountains,
the low parts become water,
the depressions become valleys,
the gaps become streams,
the prominent parts become close,
the obscure parts become distant.
With your heart pondering and your eyes imagining,
and your brush moving freely,
the scenes will naturally appear heaven-made,
not resembling human craft.
This is called 'living brushwork'."
From then on, Yòngzhī's paintings became supremely wonderful.
The River God, a Ghost of a Yuányòu Exile
Wáng Rónglǎo was an official in Guānzhōu.
When he retired,
on the day he was crossing the Guān River,
a wind arose and he could not cross.
The elders said:
"There is a rare item in your bag, Gōng.
This river god is extremely potent;
you should offer it."
Rónglǎo offered a jade fly-whisk,
but it was ineffective.
Then he offered a Duān inkstone,
and then a Xuān paper tiger,
but none were effective.
He had a fan with Huáng Lúzhí's cursive script,
inscribed with Wèi Yìngwù's poem:
"The spring tide, carrying rain, rushes faster in the evening,
At the wild ferry, no one is there, the boat drifts idly."
When he held it up as an offering,
before the incense and paper offerings were even collected,
a gentle south wind blew,
and with one sail, they crossed.
I say that the Guān River god must be the ghost of an exile from the Yuányòu era;
otherwise,
why such a profound fondness?
Snow Poem
Shèng Cìzhòng and Kǒng Píngzhòng were together in the academy,
and on a snowy night they discussed poetry, saying:
"We should compose lines unheard by others."
Píngzhòng said:
"Diagonal drag of the palace corner, a thousand *zhàng* dragon,
Lightly smeared on the wall waist, half a crescent moon."
Cìzhòng said:
"The line is very good,
but I regret that it is not grand enough."
Then he said:
"Looking at it, heaven and earth know no night,
Flying into gardens and forests, it is always spring."
Murals of Shòushèng Temple
Wáng Gǒng occupied Shǎnzhōu,
and gathered the best artisans from all over the realm
to paint the murals of Shòushèng Temple,
which were uniquely exquisite at that time.
There were eighteen painters in all,
and he had them all killed.
They were buried together in one pit
west of the temple,
so that such brushwork would never again exist in the world.
His cruelty was thus.
Even today, more than ten sections still remain,
their spiritual essence almost seems to leap forth.
Spending a Lifetime Amidst Wine and Meat
Liú Bàzi,
a native of Qīngzhōu,
walked with a crutch.
Every year he would go to Luòzhōng to see the flowers,
and stay at the Fàn family garden.
When the Elder Fàn saw him,
he immediately gave him twenty-four *jīn*,
saying:
"Bàzi, eat half a *jiǎo* (a sum of money, half of a larger amount)."
The Younger Fàn only gave him ten *jīn*,
saying:
"Bàzi, go eat a bowl of soup."
So he composed a poem:
"When Elder Fàn saw me, it was twenty-four,
When Younger Fàn saw me, it was a bowl of soup.
All within the four seas are brothers in life,
Spend a lifetime amidst wine and meat."
Cù Róng
Cù Róng is sometimes called "Cù Róng."
The *Hàn Shū* calls it "Gé Wǔ."
Although only a few pieces are used and they move in a single line,
there is still skill involved.
Xú Dézhān was good at moving them,
and thus became unrivaled.
His method:
one should always strive to have ample room,
and put the enemy in a dangerous position.
Sàn Lì
Ancient people used a "scattered brush" technique to write Lìshū,
calling it "Sàn Lì."
In recent years, Cài Jūnmó used a "scattered brush" technique to write Cǎoshū,
calling it "Sàn Cǎo,"
or sometimes "Fēi Cǎo."
Their methods all originated from "Fēi Bái,"
and also formed their own distinct schools.
If you offend me, I will show people your poem.
Shěn Dōngyáng's *Yě Shǐ* says:
In the Jìn dynasty, Huán Wēn was good friends with Yīn Hào when they were young.
Yīn Hào once wrote a short poem and showed it to Huán Wēn.
Huán Wēn said:
"You must be careful not to offend me,
if you offend me, I will show people your poem."
Holding chopsticks with the left hand
There were three guests, one of whom was a newly rich noble,
who stayed for a meal.
All three guests held their chopsticks with their left hands.
The noble said:
"Are all of you 'left-turning'?"
The guest replied:
"We naturally have to 'turn left,'
but as for you, how could you be a 'spoon-turning away person'?"
Jiànfú Sì Bēi
Fàn Wénzhèng was the prefect of Póyáng.
A scholar presented him with a poem,
which was very skillful.
He claimed that he had never eaten his fill in his life,
and that among the cold and starving in the world,
no one was more so than he.
At that time, Ōuyáng Shuàigèng's calligraphy of the *Jiànfú Sì Bēi* was very popular,
and an ink rubbing cost a thousand coins.
Fàn Wénzhèng had a thousand rubbings made,
and arranged for them to be sold in the capital.
The paper and ink were already prepared.
One night,
lightning struck and shattered the stele.
So people at the time said:
"A guest has come to make rubbings of the Jiànfú stele,
but no one rides a crane to Yángzhōu."
Dōngpō wrote a poem called *Qióng Cuò Quǎn*, saying:
"One night, thunder shattered the Jiànfú stele."
Qiū Lín Fù
Xú Zhòngmóu,
during the Huángyòu reign, was dismissed from his post as Judicial Commissioner of Guǎngdōng.
When he arrived at the palace,
the capital was experiencing heavy rain.
Zhòngmóu presented the *Qiū Lín Fù*,
which read in part:
"Continuous through the seventh and eighth months,
inundating large and small fields.
Hoping for clear weather, one prays to Buddha all day long,
and imperial audiences are canceled, with edicts transmitted overnight.
Mud fills the streets,
preventing passage by carts and horses;
waves level with bridge surfaces,
making passage by boats and ships difficult."
At that time, Jiǎ Wényuán and Chén Gōnggōng were in power.
They memorialized, saying:
"The balance of Yin and Yang is disordered,
and we ought to be impeached.
Yet the emperor's grace has not permitted it,
allowing minor officials to insult us with their words.
We have no face to lead the many officials."
The emperor was angered by Zhòngmóu,
and demoted him to supervise the wine tax in Shàowǔ.
Yù Lù Dà Jià
The Yù Lù [Jade Chariot]
was built by Táng Gāozōng.
From the Táng dynasty until now,
it has been to Tài Shān for the Dēngfēng ceremony three times.
Its other tours and inspections
are countless.
To this day, it remains strong and complete;
riding in it is as stable as a mountain,
a cup of water placed on it does not shake.
During the Qìnglì reign,
another Yù Lù was built,
but riding in it was shaky,
and it was eventually discarded.
During the Yuánfēng reign,
another one was built,
even more skillfully.
Before it was presented for imperial use,
while it was displayed in the grand courtyard,
the chariot shed happened to collapse,
and it was crushed and shattered.
So the Táng chariot was used again.
Its stability, convenience, and durability
across generations have made its construction method a mystery.
It is said that a divine being protects it.
If one walks behind other chariots,
it makes a steady sound.
Ghost Grabbing Foot
A certain Master of Records Lǐ was boating at night,
and was washing his feet over the side.
Suddenly, something from the water grabbed his foot.
Everyone tried to rescue him.
Lǐ cried out:
"The pain penetrates my bones,
it's unbearable,
I would rather die!"
Then he was dragged into the water.
The next day, his body was sought,
but not found.
Dreaming of Brothers All in the Hànlín
When Yuán Hòuzhī was young, he dreamed someone told him:
"In the future, several brothers will all be in the Hànlín Academy together."
Hòuzhī thought to himself that he had no brothers,
and doubted the dream was true.
During the Xīníng reign,
he was appointed an Academician.
At the same time, five people successively became Academicians:
Hán Chíguó
Wéi,
Chén Héshū
Yì,
Dèng Wényuē
Wǎn,
Yáng Yuánsù
Huì,
and Hòuzhī himself
(whose given name was Jiàng).
All their given names contained the radical "糸" (sī, meaning silk/thread).
Only then did he understand the saying about "brothers."
Zhāng Shòu Zhēn Zàn
Péi Dù once composed a self-eulogy for his portrait, saying:
"Your form is not tall,
your appearance is not striking.
Why are you a general?
Why are you a chancellor?
A piece of the spiritual platform [mind/heart],
cannot be depicted in painting."
Zhāng Shòu,
who was very handsome,
once had his portrait painted
and sent it to his elder brother.
Chancellor Táng modified Péi Dù's eulogy and sent it with the portrait, saying:
"Your form is very tall,
your appearance is very striking.
You are not a general,
you are not a chancellor.
A piece of the spiritual platform,
cannot be depicted in painting."
If asked, they don't know; but when used, they make no mistakes.
Scholars often used others' arguments when composing essays in response to challenges.
At the time, there was a saying:
"If asked, they don't know;
but when used, they make no mistakes."
Heaven made me dark
Wáng Jīnggōng suffered from asthma.
The medicine required Zǐtuán Shān Shēn (Ginseng from Zǐtuán Mountain),
which was unobtainable.
At that time, Xuē Shīzhèng returned from Hédōng,
and happened to have some.
He gifted a few ounces to the Duke.
The Duke refused to accept it,
saying:
"I have lived my whole life without Zǐtuán ginseng,
and have still lived until today."
He ultimately did not accept it.
The Duke's face was dark.
His disciples offered him face-washing powder,
asking him to wash his face.
The Duke said:
"Heaven made me dark;
what can face-washing powder do to me?"
The dwelling is built on the Qián Gāng, its appearance resembling the founding emperor.
Chancellor Wáng had achievements on the frontier,
and had long held a crucial position.
During Emperor Rénmiào's reign, a remonstrating official said:
"Your residence rests on the Qián Ridge,
and your appearance resembles the Founding Ancestor."
The Chancellor submitted a memorial requesting punishment, saying:
"My residence resting on the Qián Ridge
was bestowed by the imperial court;
my appearance resembling the Founding Ancestor
is naturally due to my parents."
The Emperor treated him even more favorably.
Chén Yà's Poems
Chén Yà's poem says:
"Waves calm, heaven meets reflections;
Mountains end, trees turn back their roots."
There is also his poem "Cherishing Bamboo" which says:
"Even if it grows out of the fence, I do not trim it,
letting it grow into a slender clump.
Year after year, in the height of summer,
every leaf is a cool breeze."
The Cat Bowed and Said "I Dare Not"
The ancestor of Gōng Miǎnzhòng of Póyáng,
in his household, many strange omens occurred:
Hens sometimes crowed at dawn,
dogs sometimes wore scarves and walked upright,
rats sometimes emerged in groups in broad daylight.
The family was frightened,
and summoned the sorceress Xú Ráo to treat it.
Xú Ráo sat opposite the stove,
with a cat lying beside her.
A family member pointed at the cat and said:
"Among all the strange things in our house,
the one that is not strange
is only this cat."
The cat suddenly stood up like a human, bowed its paws,
and said:
"I dare not!"
Xú Ráo was greatly alarmed and left.
A few days later,
both of his sons passed the highest imperial examinations.
Thus, it became known that strange omens are not necessarily all misfortunes.
Zhāng Tiānjúe's Cursive Script
Chancellor Zhāng loved masterly cursive script but was not skilled at it.
One day, he got an idea for a couplet,
asked for a brush, and wrote it down quickly,
then had his nephew transcribe it.
The nephew held what was written and asked:
"What character is this?"
The Chancellor looked at it intently for a long time,
but also couldn't recognize it himself,
and scolded:
"Why didn't you come and ask earlier?
You made me forget it!"
Not Familiar with the *Xiànghèjīng*
Yuāncái was pedantic, broad-minded, and liked the unusual.
He once kept two cranes,
and when a guest arrived,
he boasted:
"These are immortal birds.
All ordinary birds are oviparous,
but these birds are viviparous."
Before he finished speaking,
the gardener reported:
"A crane laid an egg last night."
Yuāncái shouted:
"How dare you slander the crane!"
A moment later,
the crane stretched its legs and lay on the ground,
and suddenly gave birth to an egg.
Yuāncái sighed and said:
"Even cranes deviate from the norm!
I was misled by Liú Yǔxī's *Jiāhuà*!
From now on,
except for the words of Buddha, Lǎozi, and Confucius,
everything else must be verified."
However, Yuāncái had simply not been familiar enough with the *Xiànghèjīng*.
Five Lifelong Regrets
Yuāncái once said:
"There are five things I have regretted in my life:
First, I regret that the Hilsa herring has too many bones;
second, I regret that kumquats are too sour;
third, I regret that water shield is cold in nature;
fourth, I regret that crabapple flowers have no fragrance;
fifth, I regret that Zēng Zǐgù could not write poetry."
Sūhéxiāng Wine
Grand Commandant Wáng Wénzhèng
was frail and often ill.
Emperor Zhēnzōng bestowed upon him a bottle of medicinal wine.
Wénzhèng drank it
and became well and strong.
The Emperor said:
"This is Sūhéxiāng wine.
For one *dǒu* of wine,
boil it with one *liǎng* of Sūhéxiāng pills,
and it will regulate the five *zàng* organs
and dispel all illnesses."
From then on, scholars and commoners imitated it.
Calligraphy from Jìn and Sòng Dynasties
Most of the extant calligraphy from people of the Jìn and Sòng Dynasties
are letters of condolence or inquiries about illness.
During the Zhēnguān era of the Táng Dynasty,
the acquisition of calligraphy from previous generations was very strict.
Calligraphy that was not related to condolences or inquiries about illness
all entered the imperial treasury.
What remained in the homes of scholar-officials
were all those that the imperial court did not acquire at that time,
which is why they have been passed down to this day.
The Scholar Who Used a Wet Nurse for Connections
Xǔ Huáidé was the Grand Marshal of the Palace Guard.
There was a *jǔrén* (舉人) who, through a wet nurse, sought to become his retainer,
and, trailing his gown, bowed in the courtyard.
Huáidé immediately sat down to receive him.
People said that Huáidé,
being a military
man,
did not understand proper etiquette,
and secretly advised him, saying:
"You should lower yourself slightly to receive him."
Huáidé said:
"I got the connections through the wet nurse;
a scholar who does this deserves only to be treated in such a manner."
Volume 48
End.
Qīnglóng and Báihǔ
For a residence, if there is flowing water on the left,
it is called Qīnglóng.
If there is a long road on the right,
it is called Báihǔ.
If there is a pond in front,
it is called Zhūquè.
If there are hills behind,
it is called Xuánwǔ.
This makes for the most auspicious land.
If these features are absent,
it is inauspicious.
Otherwise,
plant trees:
plant peach and willow to the east,
plum and jujube to the south,
gardenia and elm to the west,
and apricot to the north.
Residence Elevation
Generally, if a residence is lower on the east and higher on the west,
it brings wealth, nobility, and prominence.
If higher in front and lower in back,
it will have no descendants.
If higher in back and lower in front,
it will have many runaway cattle and horses.
Generally, if the land of a residence is desired to be flat,
it is called Liángtǔ;
if higher in back and lower in front,
it is called Jìntǔ;
living in both is auspicious.
If higher on the west and lower on the east,
it is called Lǔtǔ,
living in it brings wealth and nobility,
and virtuous people will emerge.
If higher in front and lower in back,
it is called Chǔtǔ,
living in it is inauspicious.
If high on all four sides and low in the center,
it is called Wèitǔ,
living in it leads to initial wealth followed by poverty.
Unsuitable Places for Residence
Generally, a residence should not be located at a street intersection,
nor at ancient temples, shrines, altars, or smelting sites,
nor where grass and trees do not grow,
nor at former military camps or battlefields,
nor directly where water flows,
nor at a mountain ridge's exposed point,
nor at the entrance of a large city gate,
nor opposite a prison gate,
nor at the mouth of a hundred rivers.
Residence with Waterways
Generally, if a residence has flowing water to the east that reaches rivers and seas,
it is auspicious.
If there is a major road to the east,
it leads to poverty.
If there is a major road to the north,
it is inauspicious.
If there is a major road to the south,
it leads to wealth and nobility.
Tree Orientation
Generally, all trees should face the dwelling,
which is auspicious.
If they turn their backs to the dwelling,
it is inauspicious.
Regarding the terrain of a dwelling,
if it is deficient in the mǎo-yǒu sector,
occupying it is natural and comfortable.
If it is deficient in the zǐ-wǔ sector,
occupying it is greatly inauspicious.
If it is deficient in the zǐ-chǒu sector,
occupying it leads to disputes.
If it is long north-south
and narrow east-west,
it is auspicious.
If it is long east-west
and narrow north-south,
it is inauspicious at first,
but auspicious later.
A radiant and lustrous appearance is auspicious.
For any human dwelling,
one with an abundant, moist, radiant, and yang qi
is auspicious.
One that is dry and lacks moisture
is inauspicious.
External and Internal Form and Configuration
The hills and ridges of a dwelling site
must embrace,
with the left and right mutually concealing,
head and tail joining,
the left looking to the right and the right looking to the left,
like a dragon or a tiger.
