It is also said:
“If there is a ‘running horse ridge’ (zǒumǎgāng) behind,
and a ‘horse-drinking pond’ (yīnmǎtáng) in front,
with the White Tiger (Báihǔ) following the mountains,
the Azure Dragon (Qīnglóng) entering the springs,
the Vermillion Bird (Zhūquè) beating its wings,
and the Black Tortoise (Xuánwǔ) ascending to heaven,
it is greatly auspicious.”
Each Burial Has Its Suitability
In ancient times, feudal lords were buried at the foot of connecting ridges,
grandees were buried on long plains,
and commoners were buried on flat ground.
Each had its suitability.
Wherever the Bright Hall (Míngtáng) is placed,
it must be stable and secure,
with all eight directions submitting,
guest and host returning and seeking refuge,
sitting four-square,
three corners rising,
from a distance appearing to prop up the sky,
and up close seeming to enter the springs.
The plants and trees grow large,
the soil is fertile and moist,
the dragon’s tail is like a pulled wheel or a dragged rope,
and the form is like embracing a child.
Places of Entry and Exit
The Fēngshuǐ Jué (風水訣) states:
“The place of exit is water,
and the place of entry is wind.
The qi脉 and water flow,
and the screening mountains (ànshān) all face this.
One should use the place where the qi脈 gathers.
Therefore, if the entry and exit of fēngshuǐ are improper,
it is the source of calamity.”
Five Unsuitable Types of Land
Generally, there are five unsuitable types of land:
A broken ridge
is the first.
Sand and gravel flowing backward
is the second.
Mountains appearing to resist an enemy
is the third.
Fēngshuǐ flowing back and forth,
doorways intersecting like arrows,
the Jade Table (Yù'àn) not rising,
the True Warrior (Zhēnwǔ) not soaring
is the fourth.
The four corners not extending,
the eight directions not growing,
transverse ridges and side mounds,
all without undulation,
and interlocking chains not connected
is the fifth.
Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Water Entry and Exit
For any dwelling,
if water flows out from beneath the gate,
wealth does not accumulate.
If wild water flows in,
it indicates decline and illness.
If water inside the dwelling intermingles,
it causes sudden death.
Nine Names for Water
There are nine names for water:
First is flowing water (liúshuǐ),
which connects to rivers and large streams.
Beyond sixty paces it is auspicious;
within sixty paces it is inauspicious.
Second is stagnant water (huángwū).
Third is sword-carrying water (dàijiàn).
Fourth is fighting water (dòushuǐ).
Fifth is arrow water (jiànshuǐ).
Sixth is clear blood water (qīngxuèshuǐ).
Seventh is chaotic water (luànshuǐ).
Eighth is guest water (kèshuǐ).
Ninth is rebellious water (nìshuǐ).
All of these are inauspicious.
White Tiger Ascending the Wall
If a dwelling has four corner roads on its four sides,
this is called the Heavenly Prison (Tiānyù),
which is inauspicious.
If the dwelling gate faces a lane's direct冲 (chōng),
this is called the White Tiger (Báihǔ),
which causes disability and illness.
If the dwelling is at a road fork,
this is called the White Tiger Guarding a Corpse (Báihǔ Yùshī).
If a northern road directly faces the dwelling,
this is called the White Tiger Ascending the Wall (Báihǔ Dēngqiáng).
Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Trees
Trees growing in the morning gate lead to death in the evening.
If there is an apricot tree to the east of the dwelling,
it is inauspicious.
If there is a plum tree to the north of the dwelling,
or a peach tree to the west of the dwelling,
all indicate lewdness and depravity.
If there is a willow tree to the west of the dwelling,
it leads to being punished and executed.
Planting willow trees to the east of the dwelling
benefits horses.
Planting date trees to the west of the dwelling
benefits cattle.
If there is a huái tree in the middle gate,
there will be wealth and nobility for three generations.
If there is an elm tree behind the dwelling,
a hundred ghosts will not dare to approach.
If there is a pomegranate tree in front of the hall,
it is auspicious.
Noble Mountains
Ordered Guard Mountains (Páiwèi Shān) resemble an array of guards.
Flag Staff Mountains (Jīngjié Shān) resemble newly sprouted bamboo shoots.
Wealth-Advancing Mountains (Jìncái Shān) are shaped like animal heads.
Screen Mountains (Píngzhàng Shān) resemble a standing desk.
Ornamental Pillar Mountains (Huábiǎo Shān) resemble a ceremonial scepter.
Guard Gate Mountains (Hàngmén Shān) have a horizontal blocking posture.
Bronze Fish Mountains (Tóngyú Shān) are shaped like a large bell.
Nine Palaces
Within the human head are the Nine Palaces (Jiǔgōng).
Above, they symbolize the Nine Heavens (Jiǔtiān);
below, they emulate the Nine Earths (Jiǔdì).
The body has nine orifices, yin and yang,
and also five cities and twelve towers,
golden halls and jade palaces.
Each palace has a deity
protecting the path of life.
One who meditates on the Nine Palaces (Jiǔgōng) and the Grand Unity (Tàiyǐ),
focuses the mind on the truth,
and it is as if they appear.
If just one palace is clearly perceived,
then a hundred evils will depart the body,
and all blessings will come.
Sound of Metal and Jade
If one suddenly hears the sound of metal and jade in the ears,
it means true qi is entering,
and the Way is about to be attained.
Divine Qi
Spirit (shén)
is the child of qi.
Qi
is the mother of spirit.
Form (xíng)
is the abode of spirit.
If qi is clear, spirit is clear.
If qi is turbid, spirit is clouded.
If qi is chaotic, spirit is weary.
If qi declines, spirit departs.
If spirit departs, form decays.
Humans take qi as the Way.
The Way takes qi as life.
If both life and the Way exist,
one can then live long and see far.
Internal and External Elixir
Lǎo Jūn said:
"Qì forms heaven and earth,
its transformations are unfathomable.
The Yang Dragon and Yin Tiger,
the Wood Elixir and Metal Essence, are two qì that intertwine and are refined to form
what is called the Outer Elixir.
Containing harmony and refining the hidden,
expelling the old and intaking the new,
ascending to the Níwán,
descending to the Dāntián,
cultivating and refining ceaselessly,
attending the Jiànggōng,
collecting the Five Qì,
to nourish the Hundred Spirits—
this is the Inner Elixir.
For cultivators of the Dao,
the Inner Elixir can prolong life,
and the Outer Elixir can lead to ascension to immortality.
When the Inner Elixir is perfected, the Outer Elixir will surely respond;
when the Outer Elixir responds, the Inner Elixir will surely be replenished.
However, neither alone suffices for ascension."
Six Qì
The six qì are:
xī governs the lungs,
hē governs the heart,
xū governs the liver,
hū governs the spleen,
chuī governs the kidneys,
xī governs the Sānjiāo.
The Sānjiāo emulates the thirty-six qì,
circulating through the six fǔ,
facilitating the flow of water and grain,
and regulating the body and spirit.
Nourishing the Spirit
To nourish the spirit,
one must first nourish qì;
to nourish qì, one must first nourish the brain;
to nourish the brain, one must first nourish jing (essence);
to nourish jing, one must first nourish blood;
to nourish blood, one must first nourish saliva;
to nourish saliva, one must first nourish water.
Regarding the Nine Reversions and Seven Returns,
speaking broadly,
one cycle takes one year;
speaking narrowly,
one cycle takes one day and one night.
Heaven descends and earth ascends.
From Yín to Shēn is the Seven Returns,
then arriving at Zǐ is the Nine Reversions.
Contemplation and Visualization
Of the essentials for immortals, none is greater than contemplation and visualization.
Contemplation means to preserve my spirit;
visualization means to visualize my body.
Close your eyes and see your own eyes;
collect your mind and see your own heart.
If the heart and eyes do not leave your body,
and do not harm your spirit,
then this is the gradual path of contemplation and visualization.
Nourishing Nature
The way to nourish nature is
to do a little labor,
but do not over-fatigue or strain beyond what you can bear.
Eat little and do not overeat;
always feel as if you are hungry while full,
and full while hungry.
Those who are good at nourishing their nature
eat only when truly hungry,
and drink only when truly thirsty.
After eating, one should walk
and rub the abdomen several hundred times with the hands.
At night, when sleeping, always practice keeping the mouth closed;
if the mouth opens, qì will be lost,
and evil will enter from outside.
Sleeping on your side with knees bent
benefits one's qì and strength,
and is better than sleeping on your back.
In spring, one should sleep late and rise early;
in summer and autumn, one should sleep at night and rise early;
in winter, one should sleep early and rise late.
Although it says rise early,
do not do so before the cock crows;
although it says rise late,
do not do so after sunrise.
Do not walk too long, stand too long, sit too long, lie too long, listen too long, look too long;
do not force yourself to eat;
do not force yourself to drink alcohol.
Do not drink too much;
if you drink too much, you will vomit quickly.
A person who nourishes their nature
does not spit far,
does not walk quickly,
does not listen intensely,
does not look intently,
does not sit for too long,
does not stand until tired,
does not lie until weary.
Wear clothes before feeling cold,
and remove them before feeling hot.
The Yellow Emperor's Miscellaneous Taboos
Daily taboos:
do not eat a full meal in the evening.
Monthly taboos:
do not get heavily drunk in the evening.
Annual taboos:
do not act contrary to principles in the evening.
Lifelong taboos:
do not have sexual intercourse by candlelight in the evening.
Salty injures the tendons,
sour injures the
bones,
satiety injures the lungs,
hunger injures qì.
Prolonged looking injures blood,
prolonged lying injures qì,
prolonged standing injures bones,
prolonged sitting injures flesh,
prolonged walking injures tendons.
Do not place a bed against a north wall;
do not sit facing north.
When sleeping at night, do not cover your head.
If someone has a nightmare, do not light a lamp to wake them,
they will surely die.
On the Yín day of the first month, burn white hair,
auspicious.
On a Yín day, cut fingernails;
on a Wǔ day, cut toenails.
Also burn white hair,
auspicious.
Exhalation and Inhalation
Exhaling means
expelling old qì,
also known as dead qì.
Inhaling means
taking in new qì,
also known as living qì.
Harmonizing Qì
Péng Zǔ said:
"The way to harmonize and guide qì is to
stay in a secret chamber with the door closed,
on a comfortable and warm bed,
with a pillow two and a half inches high.
Lie straight on your back,
close your eyes and hold your breath,
so that a feather placed on your nose does not move,
for three hundred breaths.
Your ears hear nothing,
your eyes see nothing,
your mind thinks of nothing.
If you do this, cold and heat cannot invade,
bees and scorpions cannot poison.
You will live three hundred and sixty years,
approaching the truly perfect person."
Night Sleeping
Upon waking at night,
one should tap the teeth nine times,
swallow saliva nine times,
and press the nose with the hands, left and right, up and down, dozens of times.
Preserving the Qì in the Heart
The Book of Immortals says:
"Always visualize a qì in your heart, as large as a chicken egg,
red inside and yellow outside,
it will ward off all evils
and prolong life."
It also says:
"Always visualize the heart as a fiery blaze like a dipper,
radiant and bright,
and a hundred evils will not dare to approach it."
Eye Twitching and Ear Ringing
The Book of Immortals says:
"If the eyes twitch and ears ring,
the heart pounds and face feels hot,
and there is inner melancholy in one's thoughts,
there will surely be disaster or misfortune.
One should secretly call out:
'Sīmìng Tōngtiān Zhēnrén,
continuously gather the life of a certain person with a golden rope,
so that this person may live for a thousand autumns without end.'
Chant this three times to stop the symptoms."
Recalling the Black-Clothed Person in the Eye
Always at cockcrow, visualize
that there is a person in each eye,
three inches tall,
dressed in black, standing.
Named 'Eye Light',
this allows one to see things thousands of miles away.
Prohibitions Regarding Movement and Stillness
Dàolín (《道林》) says:
"On the last day of the lunar month (huìrì), do not sing;
on the first day of the lunar month (shuòrì), do not weep.
When urinating or defecating, one must not look up at the sun, moon, or stars,
nor face northwest.
Do not wish to run with carts or gallop on horses,
cross over wells or straddle stoves.
Do not wish to lie on a high pillow and spit far,
pull a fan while sleeping,
or sit in a damp place facing the wind."
Dietary Prohibitions
Generally, people should eat small and frequent meals,
not a large amount all at once.
Do not eat too quickly,
as haste harms the spleen.
The proper way is to chew thoroughly until fine.
Do not rinse your mouth with hot water after eating cold food,
and do not rinse your mouth with cold water after eating hot food.
Always eat hot food first,
then cold food.
Excessive Drunkenness
Wine possesses great toxicity and great heat.
Great cold solidifies the sea,
yet only wine does not freeze;
thus is its extreme heat.
Drinking it causes confusion,
changing one's original nature;
thus is its extreme toxicity.
However, to relieve wind-cold,
promote blood circulation,
dispel evil qi,
and enhance the efficacy of medicine,
nothing surpasses wine.
But if one drinks to excess,
by the basinful and dipperful,
its toxic qi attacks the heart,
pierces the intestines, and corrodes the ribs.
This is the source of losing one's life.
Taking Yùquán
The Daoist Kuǎijīng (蒯京),
was one hundred seventy-eight years old and still very robust,
saying that he consumed yùquán every morning.
Yùquán (玉泉) means
the saliva in one's mouth.
Early in the morning, upon rising,
rinse the saliva until the mouth is full,
then swallow it,
and click the teeth fourteen times.
This is called "refining the essence."
Prohibitions in the Bedroom
When heaven and earth are dark and dim,
when the sun and moon suffer eclipses,
during fierce winds and heavy rains,
when thunder and lightning rage,
on the four seasons' eight festivals,
on the waxing and waning moon, new moon, and full moon,
when stars are out of their proper positions,
on one's natal day (běnmìng zhī rì),
on the days when Kuí and Gāng (魁罡) are on duty,
on the Liùjiǎzǐ (六甲子) days,
and on Liùdīng (六丁), Gēngshēn (庚申), Zǐmǎo (子卯) days.
Also forbidden are famous mountains and great rivers,
sacred trees and shrines,
Buddhist temples and ancient altars,
under the sun, moon, and stars,
and in front of lamps and candles.
Also, on the sixteenth day of the fifth month,
the time of the convergence of heaven and earth,
conjugal union is especially forbidden.
Hànshàng Tíjīn
Jiǎ Chéngshì (叚成式) and Wēn Tíngyún (溫庭筠) exchanged poems and maintained communication.
An Eastern Bian (東弁) person,
wrote five liánzhū (連珠) poems.
Dōngguǎn Gōng (東筦公) once arranged several flowers at night,
and wrote five "liánzhū" to replace playful words.
The first stated:
"I secretly think that the beautiful woman of the copper street
regrets being separated by dust and mud;
the plain maiden of the stone chamber
laments that immortal companions are easily parted.
Thus I know that the three-legged bird and the solitary luan
have always desired a mate;
the golden pheasant and jade swan
do not tire of forming groups."
The second stated:
"Her fame rivals Dàqiáo (大喬),
lamenting that the propitious date is yet undetermined;
her residence is near Xiǎoshì (小市),
regretting that reliable news is so mutable.
Thus I know that when night presses on and the watches lengthen,
the slanting Milky Way is languid when it turns;
when cold invades and dreams are broken,
the drifting clouds depart slowly."
The style of all five poems is the same.
Tíngyún's Poem
Wēn Tíngyún's (庭筠) poem says:
"Through the sparse window, whispered eyebrows pass."
Chéngshì's Poem
Jiǎ Chéngshì's (成式) poem says:
"Once saw a person by the stove,
dressed stylishly with a good figure.
Young men, full of talent under the flowers,
only capture the truth in their poems."
Yúnlán Paper
When Jiǎ Chéngshì (成式) was in Jiǔjiāng (九江),
he conceived the idea of making yúnlán (雲藍) paper.
Fish-roe Brocade and Phoenix Hairpins
Jiǎ Chéngshì's (成式) poem says:
"Green sleeves often brushing fish-roe brocade,
pale blue tassels long clinking against phoenix hairpins.
Knowing you wish to compose a poem of leisurely sentiments,
you must desire to transform yourself into embroidered shoes."
"Another kind of interest, the green tower has how many layers?
The setting sun slowly rolls up the winding rope.
I wish to cut deep red fish-roe brocade,
to seek light green damask with dragonflies."
Juéjù
A long couplet with two rhymes
is called a seven-character juéjù (絕句).
I Dare Not Speak
During the Five Dynasties (Wǔdài) period,
a guest of Fēng Yíngwáng (馮瀛王) lectured on the first chapter of the Dàodéjīng (《道德經》),
which contains "Dào kě dào,
fēi cháng dào" (道可道，
非常道).
The guest, seeing that the character Dào (道) was Fēng's (馮) name,
then said:
"I dare not speak (bùgǎshuō),
it can be said I dare not speak (kě bùgǎn shuō),
it is truly I dare not speak (fēi cháng bùgǎn shuō)."
The Great Shùn's Goodness Shared with Others
During the Zhìpíng (治平) era,
the provincial examination topic was "The Great Shùn's (大舜) Goodness Shared with Others" (大舜善與人同).
One examinee was rejected,
and felt very indignant.
His introductory paragraph (pòtí) read:
"In the past, there was the Great Shùn (大舜),
who was profoundly benevolent.
His Way (dào) permeated myriad generations,
and his goodness was shared with all people."
Someone commented to him:
"Comparing a urine pot to an oil drum,
it is fitting that you were dismissed."
Policy Question (Cètí)
There was a scholar named Yè (葉) from Qiántáng (錢塘) who became an official at the Imperial Academy (tàixué guān),
but lacked scholarship.
A jǔzi (舉子) pretended to write a policy question for Yè (葉), saying:
"The preface to the Xiàojīng (《孝經》) is difficult to understand in its meaning.
For example, which dynasty did Wéi Zhāowáng (韋昭王) rule?
Which mountain was xiānrú Lǐng (先儒領)?
Kǒngzǐ's (孔子) ambition was always present throughout the four seasons,
why did he uniquely say 'my ambition is in spring'?
Kǒngzǐ's (孔子) filial piety was always practiced throughout the four seasons,
why did he uniquely say 'autumn's practice is in filial piety'?
Since it says 'the Master passed away,'
then why is there 'Lǐ (鯉) hurrying across the courtyard'?"
Good at Taking Advantage
Someone who spoke
was good at taking advantage,
often saying:
"My quilt covers your quilt,
your felt mat spreads over my felt mat.
If you have money, we'll spend it together;
if I have no money, I'll spend your money.
When going up the mountain, you support my legs;
when coming down the mountain, I support your shoulders.
I know for certain I will die after you,
most likely you will die before me."
Grand Proclamation
A Prefect (tàishǒu), upon first taking office,
held a grand proclamation on the third day.
A musician (lèrrén) sang a jingle (kǒuhào), saying:
"Report to the officials and common people, they must celebrate!
The disaster star has retreated, the fortune star has arrived!"
The Prefect (tàishǒu) happily asked who had composed it.
He replied:
"This has always been the old custom of this prefecture."
Drinking Game
There were a Rú, a Dào, a Shì, and an Lì at a drinking party.
They played a game,
taking phrases whose first and last characters were the same.
The Rú said:
"Superiors influence inferiors with custom,
inferiors criticize superiors with custom."
The Dàoshì said:
"The Dào that can be spoken of,
is not the eternal Dào."
The Shì said:
"Form is precisely emptiness,
emptiness is precisely form."
The Lì said:
"The document itemized above,
respectfully submitted as before."
Playing a game at a wedding eve
On the eve of a village wedding,
there were a Xiùcai, a Cáolì, a Yīrén, and a Wūzhě gathered together.
They played a game,
linking verses based on their respective professions.
The Cáolì spoke first:
"Every day, formations are arrayed in sequence."
The Yīrén said:
"Medicines have warm, cool, cold, dry, and moist properties."
The Xiùcai said:
"Late at night, the young lady quickly arranges her makeup."
The Wūzhě said:
"Tàishàng Lǎojūn, quickly, quickly, quickly!"
Beating the Chest and Presenting
There was a rich but stingy man.
When his cousin was going to the capital, he announced his departure.
The man reluctantly gave him a thousand coins and a pot [of wine],
and wrote a note saying:
"One sinew,
one pot of blood,
the aforementioned are presented with a beaten chest,
I humbly implore the iron-hearted person to accept them."
Diverting Water to Irrigate Fields and Admitting Guilt
There was a stubborn commoner who, due to drought, secretly diverted someone else's water to irrigate his fields.
The owner caught him and brought him [to justice].
His confession of guilt said:
"I, the undersigned,
only because the heavens are dry and the *lǜlǚ* out of tune,
and deeply worried that the field sprouts would be flooded throughout the universe,
then stole someone's 'golden birth and beauty,'
causing that person's 'inch of time to be.'
Mindful that I did not know 'the first making of characters,'
I now humbly admit to 'comforting the people and punishing the wicked,'
and will fully obey whatever the local official decides."
Skirt Hem on Fire
There was a man of a tolerant and slow disposition.
One winter day, he was sitting around a brazier with someone.
He saw the person's skirt hem being burned by the fire,
and then said:
"There is something,
I have seen it for a long time,
I want to say it,
but I fear your temper is quick.
If I don't say it,
I fear you will be too much harmed.
So, is it right to say it?
Or is it right not to say it?"
The person asked what it was,
and he said:
"Your skirt is on fire."
The person then pulled up his clothes, extinguished the fire,
and became very angry, saying:
"You saw it for a long time,
why didn't you say so earlier?"
That man said:
"I said your temper was quick,
and indeed it is."
Pútái
East of Géchéng there is Pútái.
It is said that Qín Shǐhuáng passed through here
and twisted reeds to tie his horse.
To this day, the reeds still grow twisted.
Sìbǎogōng
Hàn Wǔdì decorated screens and curtains with various treasures,
set them up in Guìgōng,
and called it "Sìbǎogōng."
Tánqí
Hàn Wǔdì was fond of *cùjú*.
His attendants thought it was tiring.
The Emperor said:
"Choose something similar but less strenuous and present it."
So, *tánqí* was created and presented.
Some say it originated in Wèi Wéndì's palace as a dressing table game.
The Emperor was especially skilled at it,
able to flick the pieces with the corner of a handkerchief.
Someone else, with a lowered head, flicked them with a hemp scarf,
which was even more skillful than the Emperor.
The Heavenly Emperor's Face is One Foot Square
Jìn Zhōu Xīng died and then revived.
He said the Heavenly Emperor summoned him.
He ascended the hall,
looked up, and saw purple *qì* densely rising.
The face was one foot square.
He asked those around him:
"Is this the ancient Heavenly Emperor Zhāng?"
They replied:
"The ancient Heavenly Emperor ascended long ago;
this is merely the recent Heavenly Emperor Cáo Míngdì."
Língyúntái
When Língyúntái was first built,
all materials were weighed beforehand,
to ensure that their light and heavy properties were balanced.
Therefore, although it was tall and swayed with the wind,
it never collapsed.
When Jìn Míngdì ascended it, he feared it would tilt,
and ordered large timbers to support it.
Soon after, it crumbled.
Emperor Yuán's Bath
When Jìn Míngdì was Crown Prince,
he heard that Emperor Yuán was bathing.
He submitted a memorial saying:
"I humbly hear that a long bath is very tiring.
I wonder how Your Majesty's health is?"
The reply was:
"Removing dirt is very good;
my body is not tired."
Sìfèirì
Yè Xiān submitted a memorial to Sòng Wǔdì saying:
"I humbly understand that you will meet with the southern barbarians tomorrow morning.
Tomorrow is a Sìfèirì.
The first day of next month is good.
I wonder if you can follow that?"
The Emperor replied:
"Thank you for your diligence.
As for me, I never choose auspicious days."
Alas, My Feet!
Jiè Zǐtuī refused to come out.
Jìn Wéngōng set fire to the forest to force him out,
but he embraced a tree and died.
The Duke mourned him deeply,
then cut down the tree to make shoes.
Whenever he looked down,
he would shed tears and say:
"Alas, my feet!"
The address "Zúxià" originated from this.
Born Entrusted to a Gourd
Hú Guǎng was born in the fifth month,
which custom considered an inauspicious month.
His parents hid him in a gourd
and abandoned it by the riverbank.
A resident took him in and raised him.
When he grew up,
he had a great reputation.
His parents wanted to reclaim him.
He thought that abandoning his birth parents would harm righteousness,
and abandoning his adoptive parents would be ungrateful,
leaving him with nowhere to turn.
Because he was born entrusted to a gourd,
he took the surname Hú.
The Two Sons Neglected the Steamer
A guest visited Chén Tàiqiū.
His discourse was very sharp.
Tàiqiū ordered Yuánfāng and Jìfāng to cook rice to entertain the guest.
The two sons neglected the steamer
and secretly listened to the guest's words.
The rice fell into the pot and became gruel,
which they then served.
After the guest left,
Tàiqiū reprimanded them.
They fully explained the reason,
and recited the guest's words without omission.
Tàiqiū said:
"Gruel is fine;
why must it be rice?"
The "Ěr Rǔ" Relationship
Ní Zhèngpíng was not yet of age (had not reached twenty),
while Kǒng Wénjǔ was already over fifty.
They treated each other as "ěr rǔ" [informal 'you'].
As You Say, It Is Also Good
Sīmǎ Huī lived in Jīngzhōu.
Believing that Liú Biǎo would certainly cause trouble,
he sought to retreat and protect himself.
Whenever he spoke to others,
he would only say "good."
His wife reprimanded him for not distinguishing.
Huī said:
"As you say,
that is also very good."
He ultimately escaped disaster.
Ròujì
Wèi Língyúntái was extremely tall.
Wéi Dàn inscribed its plaque,
and his hair turned white that very day.
The plaque had some irregularities,
so workers were recruited to fix them.
There was a soldier from Qínxià
who climbed the structure wearing shoes,
as if walking on flat ground.
When asked,
he said:
"I have no special skill,
I just have a few inches of fleshy wings under each armpit."
Zǐgòng Was Gone for a Long Time, Divined the Dǐng Hexagram
Kǒngzǐ sent Zǐgòng out,
but he did not return for a long time.
A divination yielded the Dǐng hexagram,
but without feet.
The other disciples thought he would not return.
Yán Yuān said:
"If the Dǐng has no feet,
then perhaps he will come by boat?"
Indeed, he did.
Observing the Sunrise from the Stone Bridge
Qín Shǐhuáng built a stone bridge,
wishing to cross the sea to observe the sunrise.
A spirit drove stones into the sea,
but they did not move quickly,
so it whipped them.
All the stones turned red.
Mountains like Chéngyáng,
all stood up and tilted east,
appearing to rush towards it.
Bareheaded and Waking Up Late
Guǎn Níng was sailing across the sea when
his boat overturned.
Then he said:
"I once went bareheaded for a morning,
and woke up late for three mornings.
The transgression must be here."
This is the Stone-Eating Guest
Jiǎnwén was walking in the main hall,
and Yòujūn was behind him with Sūn Xīnggōng.
Yòujūn pointed at Sūn and said:
"This is the stone-eating guest."
Jiǎnwén said:
"How can you not know that there are naturally eloquent people in the world?"
Lǎozǐ Rode a Deer into the Womb
When Lǎozǐ was first born,
he rode a white deer into his mother's womb.
After he was born,
he had a broad forehead and large eyes,
sparse teeth and a square mouth,
ears with three openings,
a nose with two pillars,
his feet bore five characters,
and his hands held ten writings.
Cài Yōng Became an Immortal
Hàn Wáng Yuàn encountered a ghost,
who said that Cài Yōng had become an immortal,
flying back and forth,
very happy.
The Joy of Qióngyú
A qín decorated with seven treasures
was called the Joy of Qióngyú.
Half a Hero
Xùn said:
"Páng Tǒng is half a hero."
Everyone Stood to Greet Tàichū
Jǐngwáng wanted to kill Xiàhóu Tàichū,
but his mind was not made up.
He asked Ānwáng Fú:
"Is his talent enough to control him?"
Fú replied:
"Once, Zhào Yán was burying his son,
and when you came,
half the people stood to greet you.
When Tàichū comes,
everyone stands up.
From this, I know
you might not be his equal."
Then Jǐngwáng killed him.
Lofty like the Rising Morning Glow
During the Hǎixī period,
whenever the high officials gathered in the morning,
the court hall was still dark.
Only when Huìjīwáng arrived,
was he lofty like the rising morning glow.
Sick and Not Receiving Guests
Lǐ Yīng was sick and did not receive guests.
Only when Chén Zhònggōng came,
he rode in a carriage out the gate to welcome him.
Cài Yōng is the Reincarnation of Zhāng Héng
After Zhāng Héng died,
Cài Yōng's mother became pregnant.
At the time, people said that Yōng was the reincarnation of Zhāng Héng.
Pearl Shroud and Jade Casket
When the Hàn emperors and marquises died,
they all used pearl shrouds and jade caskets.
Lending Books is Ridiculous
Dù Yù wrote to his son:
"The ancient poem says, 'Lending books to others is ridiculous,
and returning borrowed books is also ridiculous.'"
Sleeping Soundly in the Commandery
Wèi Guàn said:
"When I was previously in Zhōngshān Commandery, I had nothing to do,
and simply slept soundly."
This Young Man is Very Wěiyí
People in Luòxià saw Liú Dàozhēn and said:
"This young man is very wěiyí."
Liú asked:
"Is this a good saying?"
They said:
"It is good."
Liú said:
"If it is a good word,
I wish your father were also wěiyí,
and your mother also wěiyí."
Commoner Excelling in the World
Yuán Shào saw Zhèng Jūn and said:
"I originally thought Zhèng Jūn was a famous scholar from Dōngzhōu,
but now he is an elder of the world,
excelling as a commoner in the world.
How could this be for no reason?"
Ge Cloth Turban and Feather Fan
Wǔhóu and Xuānwáng were preparing troops for battle.
Xuānwáng was in military attire overseeing affairs.
He sent someone to secretly observe Wǔhóu,
who was riding a plain carriage,
wearing a ge cloth turban,
holding a white feather fan and giving commands.
The three armies followed his every movement.
Xuānwáng sighed and said:
"He can be called a famous scholar."
Playing Go, a Letter Arrives Without a Son's Letter
Gù Shào, Administrator of Yùzhāng,
son of Yōng,
gathered his colleagues to play Go.
A letter arrived from outside,
but there was no letter from his son.
Although his expression remained unchanged,
he knew something had happened and gripped
the Go pieces, cutting his nails and palms until they bled.
When the guests dispersed,
he sighed and said:
"I am free from the burden left by Yánlíng,
how can there be the deep blame of losing my sight?"
Thus, he cut off his emotions and dispersed his sorrow as usual.
Lending a Hundred Hú of Salt
Shěn Jiè was guarding Fēng,
and his provisions ran out.
He borrowed a hundred hú of salt from Yáo Biāo.
Biāo was straightforward and upright.
Upon receiving the letter,
he did not reply.
He called his attendants and ordered them to dump a hundred hú of salt into the river,
saying:
"This shows I am not stingy,
but I regret to whom I am giving it!"
Mistakenly Calling His Father's Given Name
Zhūgě Kè mistakenly called Hán Wénhuǎng's father by his given name.
Huǎng said:
"Is it proper for a son to call his father by his given name in front of others?"
Kè replied:
"When threading a needle towards the sky,
if one does not see the sky,
it is not because one thinks little of the sky,
but because one's attention is elsewhere."
A Turtle Walks Without Choosing a Day
In the time of Sūn Quán,
someone captured a large tortoise
and intended to present it to the King of Wú.
At night, he moored in Yuèlǐ amidst a large mulberry tree.
The mulberry tree called out to the tortoise, saying:
“O diligent mysterious creature,
what is the matter with you?”
The tortoise replied:
“I traveled without choosing an auspicious day,
and thus encountered captivity.
However, even if all the firewood of the Southern Mountains were used,
it could not melt me down.”
The mulberry tree said:
“Zhūgé Yuánxùn will certainly cause you trouble,
and those who seek me will boil you.
What plan will you devise?”
The tortoise said:
“Do not speak too much,
disaster will soon befall you.”
When they arrived in Jiànyè,
Kè advised Quán to cook it.
The tortoise then stood up and rotted.
A Flourishing Family
Sūn Hào asked Chancellor Lù Kǎi:
“How many people from your family are serving in court?”
He replied:
“Two chancellors, five marquises,
and over ten generals.”
Hào said:
“How flourishing!”
Kǎi said:
“A ruler who is virtuous and ministers who are loyal make a flourishing state.
Fathers who are kind and sons who are filial make a flourishing family.
Currently, the government is chaotic and the people are suffering;
I fear ruin and downfall.
How dare your servant speak of flourishing?”
The Maid Accuses the Lord
Wáng Wǔzǐ’s attendants
once sought clothes from a maid in the gatehouse.
The maid wanted to commit adultery with him.
The man said:
“I dare not.”
The maid said:
“If you do not comply,
I will scream loudly.”
The man still did not comply.
The maid then cried out:
“Jiǎ wants to rape Jì!
Jì ordered him killed!”
The man fully recounted the previous situation,
but Wǔzǐ did not believe him.
The man said:
“Such injustice cannot be endured;
I shall accuse the lord before Heaven.”
Wǔzǐ suffered from illness for a whole year.
This man appeared and said:
“The lord must depart.”
Then he died.
The Foolish Dragon of Nine Mansions
In Luòxià, there was a cave
of unfathomable depth.
A woman, intending to kill her husband,
pushed him into the hole.
This man tumbled for a long time
before regaining consciousness.
He found another cave nearby,
and traveled over a hundred lǐ.
He felt that what he trod upon was like dust.
He smelled the fragrance of sticky rice
and found it delicious to eat.
Again he encountered something like mud,
which tasted similar to the dust he had just eaten.
He entered a city,
where, although there was no sun or moon,
the light surpassed that of the three luminaries.
Everyone wore feather garments
and performed extraordinary music.
In total, he passed through nine such places.
There was a tall man
who pointed to a sheep under a cypress tree,
knelt, and stroked the sheep’s beard,
obtaining two pearls.
The tall man took one.
The remaining pearl
he ordered the man to eat,
which greatly relieved his hunger.
When asked about the nine places,
he replied:
“Ask Zhāng Huà, and you will know.”
The man followed the cave out,
went to Huà and asked him.
He said:
“That which was like dust
was dragon's saliva from beneath the Yellow River;
the mud was mud from beneath Kūnlúnshān.
The nine places
are called 'Jiǔguǎn' by immortals.
The sheep was a foolish dragon.
The first pearl,
if eaten,
grants a lifespan equal to Heaven and Earth;
the next prolongs life;
the last pill
only satisfies hunger.”
The Parrot
Zhāng Huà had a parrot.
Each time he returned from an outing,
it would speak of the good and bad deeds of his servants.
One day,
it was completely silent.
Huà asked it the reason,
and it said:
“I was confined in a jar,
and had no means of knowing what happened outside.”
Suddenly it said:
“My dream last night was not good,
I ought to avoid going outside.”
Huà forced it to go to the courtyard,
and indeed it was attacked by a flying eagle,
barely escaping.
Pān and Shí Executed Together in the Eastern Marketplace
Shí Chóng and Pān Yuè were executed together in the Eastern Marketplace.
Shí Chóng said:
“The world kills heroes;
what have you done again?”
Pān Yuè said:
“The scholars are killed and fill the ravines;
the aftershocks have reached me.”
On No Ghosts
Sòng Dài, as the Inspector of Qīngzhōu,
prohibited sacrifices
and wrote "Wúguǐlùn" (On No Ghosts).
Later, a scholar came to Dài and said:
“You have cut off the blood offerings for our kind for over twenty years,
but because you had a black ox and a bearded courtesan,
we could not trouble you.
Now the courtesan has defected,
and the ox has died.
This allows us to control you.”
The next day, Dài died.
Lord Lúshān
Gù Shào, while serving as the Administrator of Yùzhāng,
prohibited sacrifices
and destroyed various temples.
When he reached the Lúshān Temple,
the entire commandery advised against it,
but he did not listen.
That night, someone walked before him,
resembling a fāngxiāng (exorcist),
and said he was the Lord of Lúshān.
Shào invited him in to sit
and discussed "Chūnqiū" with him.
When the lamp oil ran out,
he burned "Zuǒzhuàn" to continue the light.
The ghost wanted to overpower Shào,
but Shào's spiritual energy was very strong,
so the ghost became mild and submissive,
requesting the restoration of the temple.
Shào smiled and did not reply.
The ghost angrily said:
“Within three years, you will certainly decline,
and at that time, I will repay you!”
As predicted,
Shào indeed became gravely ill.
Everyone urged him to restore the temple,
but Shào said:
“How can evil overcome righteousness?”
He ultimately did not listen
and then died.
Jade Dew and Stone Marrow
Sōngshān has a large,
very deep cave.
In the early Jìn dynasty,
someone accidentally fell into the cave.
Inside was a thatched cottage,
where two people were playing wéiqí.
They gave the man a cup of white wine to drink.
He then walked past a fire well;
beside the well was something like green mud.
Eating it prevented hunger.
After about half a year,
he came out.
Zhāng Huà said:
“What you drank was jade dew (yùjiāng),
and what you ate was dragon-brain stone marrow (lóngnǎo shísuǐ).”
Jiǔyùnjǐu
Zhāng Huà and his friend drank Jiǔyùn liquor.
They were both quite merrily drunk.
Whenever Huà was drunk,
he would order his attendants to turn him over,
and then he would be completely at ease.
The next morning,
Huà suddenly thought that his friend must have died during the night.
He urgently inquired about it,
and indeed, his friend's belly was pierced,
and his intestines flowed beneath the bed.
This was because he had not been turned over.
Yīnshēng Lángjūn
The princes of the Ten Residences, who understood music,
would prepare for the emperor's visit to their courtyards,
welcoming the imperial carriage with music.
In the palace, they were called "Yīnshēng Lángjūn."
Jīntiáotuō
Wénzōng asked his chancellor,
"What is a tiáotuō?"
Before the chancellor could answer,
the emperor said,
"The Zhēngào mentions that Ānnī had golden tiáotuō as arm ornaments;
it is what is now called a bracelet."
The Zhēngào states that Lǜ'èhuá gave Yáng Quán one gold and one jade tiáotuō,
which is slightly different from this.
Étuǐzi
A jǔrén once presented a poem to Pèi Shī Wáng Zhìxīng.
Zhìxīng said,
"Don't you have é'tuǐzi?"
He was referring to crane's knees.
Dàozǐ Huà Lǘ
Wú Dàozǐ visited a monk.
The monk did not treat him with proper respect.
So, Dàozǐ painted a donkey on the wall and left.
That night,
all the furniture was crushed.
The monk invited Dàozǐ back,
pleaded with him,
and only then did Dàozǐ paint over the drawing.
Zhīlíng Huāyàng Bùtóng
Lú Shì failed the imperial examination.
He walked out of the capital gate
and stayed at an inn.
A man approached the fire
and recited,
"I have not yet become skilled in weaving brocade and silk,
haphazardly setting up looms and wrongly throwing shuttles.
Do not let the experienced weavers of the imperial workshop see this,
for they will mock me to death, just like my essays."
He then asked the man,
who said,
"My family business is weaving silk.
Before the recent turmoil,
we were affiliated with the imperial brocade workshop.
Recently, I tried to offer my meager skills to my former trade,
but everyone said, 'The patterns are different now.'
So, I am returning east."
Bǐguǎn Kè Cóngjūnxíng
Envoy Wáng's family had a brush handle
on which the "Cóngjūnxíng" was carved in the middle.
The horses, people, hair, houses, trees, mountains, and water
were all exquisitely rendered.
Each part was carved with one line from "Cóngjūnxíng."
It seemed almost beyond human skill.
It was said to have been carved with a mouse's tooth.
Zhùfēi Jìnshì
Dù Shēng passed the imperial examination from the post of Shíyí,
and was again appointed Shíyí.
He was called "Zhùfēi Jìnshì."
Lànzhēng Húlu
Zhèng Yúqìng invited his relatives and friends.
His attendants said,
"Inform the kitchen to steam it thoroughly and remove the hair,
but do not break its neck."
Everyone thought they would be serving steamed geese or ducks.
After a long while, the food was served:
a bowl of millet rice and
one thoroughly steamed gourd for each person.
The Duke ate with great relish.
Everyone else forced themselves to eat, and then stopped.
Jìbīngguó Xiāng
Chancellor Yáng invited Chancellor Cuī for a meal.
In the incense burner before them,
the smoke formed towers and pavilions.
It was said to be incense from Jìbīngguó.
Lín Xiǎowáng Tiè
Someone presented a book to Lǐ Déyù,
containing it in multiple layers of embroidered bags.
The Grand Commandant quite cherished it.
Lú Hóngxuān had a reputation for good calligraphy,
so he was asked to examine it.
He said,
"It is my tracing of Xiǎowáng Tiè."
Sòng Wǔ Tǎnshuài
During the summer, Dèzōng made a secret visit to Xīmíng Temple.
Sòng Jì was copying texts, wearing a kerchief and short trousers.
The emperor said,
"Sir,
could I have a bowl of tea?"
Jì replied,
"The water in the cauldron is just boiling,
you can pour it yourself."
The emperor then asked,
"What are you doing?
What is your surname and rank?"
Sòng said,
"My surname is Sòng,
I am the fifth son,
and I am sitting for the imperial examination."
Soon,
he heard someone call out "Guānjiā!"
Jì was terrified,
he knelt and waited to be punished.
One version states that
the emperor asked,
"How is your poem today?"
He replied,
"The Emperor's thoughts are unfathomable."
The emperor said,
"Sòng Wǔ is so straightforward!"
Later, when the Ministry of Rites announced the results,
the emperor asked if Jì's name was on the list.
The messenger returned, saying no.
The emperor said,
"Sòng Wǔ is straightforward again!"
Bùshícàixīn
Jiāng Mì did not eat vegetable hearts
for fear of harming life.
Xíng Zhì did not eat xiéhāo
because he disliked its name.
Tà'è Guǒtóu
Those who were appointed Zhongshū Shèrén directly,
bypassing the three usual steps,
were called "Tà'è Guǒtóu."
Bìdì Shù
It is popularly said that eating roasted soybeans mixed with pine needles is very delicious
and can be used as a method of escaping the world.
Xiáshí Yín
A scholar was delayed by wind at Xiáshí on the Hàn Jiāng
and recited a poem:
"I chose to stay at Xiáshí,
where autumn brings many winds and waves."
He could not continue for a long time.
Suddenly, a voice from the sky said,
"A night of rain in Jiānglíng,
breaking hearts with the Mùlán song."
Cìchì Yàozǐ
When Lǐ Ài was taking the imperial examination,
his diligence and quickness were unmatched,
earning him the nickname "Cìchì Yàozǐ."
Huángzéi Dǎ Hēizéi
During Xuānzōng's reign,
date cakes were sold in the capital.
They were made of yellow millet and black flour,
and it was said,
"The yellow bandits strike the black bandits."
This was a prophecy about the Cháo bandits.
Another account refers to the Cháo rebels.
Qǔ Qīngxiàng Wéi Zhuàngtóu
Xǔ Mèngróng and Sòng Jì were close friends as commoners.
Xǔ presided over the imperial examination,
and Sòng failed.
Xǔ invited Sòng to drink
and apologized to him.
In the midst of their drinking,
Xǔ declared loudly again,
"This year, for the country, I have selected a chancellor as the top graduate;
it is Yáo Sìqīng."
A few days later,
Yáo died.
Sòng went to see Xǔ and said,
"The nation is unfortunate;
Duke Yáo has passed away."
Yā Shān Zì
Ān Lùshān signed his name
by forming three pinches with his fingers.
Xī Shīzi Jiǎo
There was an actor in the Táng dynasty who went to the chancellor to complain about his official position.
After a long narration,
he was asked,
"What can you do in the music department?"
He replied,
"I have been performing the Xī Shīzi Jiǎo in the teaching section for thirty years."
The southeast of Yǒngníng Fāng in Cháng'ān is Jīnzhǎndì, which, if broken, can be restored. To the west of Ānyì Lǐ is Yùzhǎndì, which, once broken, cannot be made whole again.
Sìliù
The Sìliù style
originated with Xú and Yǔ.
Fén Xiāng Tàn Wán (Burning Incense and Drawing Lots)
When Xuānzōng was about to appoint a chancellor,
he would gather the names of three or four highly regarded individuals from both within and outside the court,
roll them into pellets,
place them on the incense altar,
cover them with an object,
burn incense and pray devoutly,
then draw a pellet to make the appointment.
Tú Guī (Marking and Returning)
When imperial edicts and commands contained provisions inconvenient for current affairs,
they would be marked out and returned,
which was called Tú Guī.
Mù Shì Jù Liáo Qì Tūn Tóng Liè (Looking Down on Colleagues, Swallowing Rivals with Pride)
When Lǐ Déyù was chancellor,
he showed no kindness in his demeanor towards others.
When he was later exiled to the south,
someone mocked him, saying:
“He looked down on all his colleagues, showing not an inch of kindness;
he swallowed his rivals with pride, cutting off all warmth.”
Lì Dézhèng (Erecting a Monument of Virtuous Governance)
During the reign of Xiànzōng,
the eunuch Tǔtú Chéngguàn wanted to erect a monument of virtuous governance for the emperor.
He had the stone smoothed and presented it for approval.
Lǐ Jiàng submitted a memorial, stating:
“A great ruler's virtue aligns with Heaven and Earth,
and his brilliance with the sun and moon.
There is no need to erect a monument to record his virtues,
lest it become a laughingstock to the world.”
The plan was thus abandoned.
Méng Huì Yě Yú (Grateful for the Favor, Also Foolish)
During the Táng dynasty, there was a eunuch
who learned to make paper cut-outs.
Someone gave him some firewood,
to which he replied:
“I am grateful for the favor, and also foolish, so much.”
Xiāng Gòng Jìnshì (Tributary Scholar from the Commandery)
During the reign of Wénzōng,
the Jìnshì degree holders were particularly numerous.
Scholars commented, saying:
“A Xiāng Gòng Jìnshì
is not worth a prefectural governor of an upper-grade prefecture.”
Liàn Tuǐ (Leg Training)
When Xīzōng was still a prince, he enjoyed playing Cùqiú (ancient football),
leading to the saying "Liàn Tuǐ."
Shǔkuí (Hollyhock)
Hollyhocks were used as torches,
and would not be extinguished in the rain.
Bǐng Juǎn Bīng Qiē (Pancakes Rolled with Ice and Sliced)
Thin pancakes were rolled with thick ice,
then cut with a knife,
splitting perfectly along the blade.
Píng Shì Hé Cǎo (What Kind of Grass is Píng?)
Wénzōng was widely read.
In Yányīng Hall, he asked his ministers:
“The Book of Odes says:
‘The deer cry ‘yōu yōu,’
eating the wild Píng grass.’
What kind of grass is this?”
Xuě Jué replied:
“According to the Ěryǎ,
Píng is Lài Xiāo.”
The emperor said:
“I read in the commentary to the Máoshī that
Píng has round leaves and white flowers,
growing in clumps in the wild.
It doesn't seem to be Lài Xiāo.”
Shī Fù (Poetry and Rhapsodies)
In the second year of Kāichéng (837 CE),
Vice Minister Gāo Kǎi presided over the imperial examinations.
The topics "Ní Cháng Yǔ Yī Qǔ Fù" (Rhapsody on the Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Robe Dance) and "Tàixué Shíjīng Shī" (Poem on the Stone Classics of the Imperial Academy) were issued.
The practice of writing poetry and rhapsodies in the examinations began from this point.
Juǎn Zhī Sìshíjiǔ (Volume 49)
End.
Rúlái (Tathāgata)
Rú is the essence of Lái,
Lái is the function of Rú.
One who is utterly and eternally self-identical is called Rú;
one who responds to things and comes is called Lái.
Lái
is the striking of gold;
Rú
is the vibration of jade.
Sān Jiào (Three Teachings)
The Yīn and Yáng of the Confucians,
the Being and Non-being of the Taoists,
and the Form and Emptiness of the Buddhists—
though their expressions differ, their ultimate meaning is one.
Shùn Fó (Shùn and Buddha)
Shùn acted from benevolence and righteousness;
he did not merely perform benevolence and righteousness.
Buddha acted from meditation and wisdom;
he did not merely perform meditation and wisdom.
Bāguà (Eight Trigrams)
Kǎn, in the true North,
is its fundamental nature,
the Buddha. Is there Yáng movement in the Yīn stillness?
Indeed, Yáng is born from Yīn within it.
As for Gèn,
it is that which brings all things to an end and begins all things.
Only Wénshū can embody this meaning.
Wénshū
is wisdom.
All things are not without wisdom,
and thus they mutually end and begin.
As for Zhèn,
all things are born and emerge.
Therefore it is said, "The Emperor emerges from Zhèn."
When spoken of as essence, it is spirit;
when spoken of as function, it is the Emperor.
Only Pǔxián can embody this meaning.
Aligned with Xùn,
affairs should be handled with purification and abstinence.
When undertaking matters,
one must purify the mind and guard against harm;
thus Xùn is taken as purification.
Lí
is when all things are flourishing and great like the Buddha,
whose dharma functions pervade the entire realm and possess brilliance;
thus it is said, "They meet in Lí."
As for Kūn,
it is the time of gathering and contraction,
like the Buddha gradually entering Nirvāṇa;
thus it is said, "To serve in Kūn."
Duì is the true West;
when all things are harvested and ripened,
there is much joy;
thus it is said, "To speak of joy in Duì."
As for Qián,
it is the place where Yīn and Yáng contend;
thus it is said, "To battle in Qián."
As for Kǎn,
it is the time of shedding all conditioned activity;
thus it is said, "To toil in Kǎn,"
then returning to ultimate stillness,
like one entering Nirvāṇa.
This speaks of how all things follow the natural principles of Heaven and Earth, Yīn and Yáng.
The way of the Confucians
reaches its apex here.
Sè Kōng (Form and Emptiness)
The Sè Kōng of the Buddhists
is identical to the You Wú (Being and Non-being) of the Confucians.
Form is Emptiness,
Emptiness is Form.
This is what Zhuāngzǐ meant by "You Wú Wú Yǒu" (Being and Non-being, Non-being and Being).
That which is within me is called Xíng (form/body);
that which is external is called Sè (form/color),
just as the Buddhists speak of Liùgēn (six sense organs) and Liùchén (six dusts).
Wúlòu Fǎmén (Path of Freedom from Defilements)
A Buddha
is one who commits no evil.
An immortal
is like a mountain, unmoving.
One who commits no evil
understands the way of day and night,
and thus realizes complete enlightenment.
To retreat and hide in secrecy
is what the Buddhists call the Wúlòu Fǎmén.
Guānyīn Rúlái (Guānyīn Tathāgata)
Their words of goodness are one despite different mouths,
truly not false, comparable to their Guān Zìzài (Avalokiteśvara).
Listen attentively to the Guānshìyīn of the Northern Buddha.
A Bodhisattva
is one who generously bestows and aids the multitude.
Prajñā
is akin to Zhuāngshēng’s Qí Wù Lùn (Discourse on the Equality of Things).
Rúlái and Bodhisattvas
are like Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Jì.
Xīn Sǐ (Death of the Mind)
No sorrow is greater than the death of the mind.
The Chan school calls this "Oh Heaven, Oh Heaven!"
Shēn Kǒu Qīngjìng (Purity of Body and Speech)
With a mind free from hindrances,
there is therefore no fear.
This can be achieved by those who are completely aligned with Heaven,
thus distancing themselves from delusion.
When the mind does not dwell on right or wrong,
and the mouth does not speak of gain or loss,
this is how one's body and mouth become pure.
To hold up the three-thousand-great-thousand worlds
is what Zhuāngshēng called "constricting the universe."
Form is not different from emptiness;
emptiness is not different from form;
form is precisely emptiness;
emptiness is precisely form.
This means forgetting one's liver and gall,
discarding one's ears and eyes,
and exhausting both inner and outer.
When the mind resides in the six emotions,
it is like a bird flying into a net,
shifting according to external things.
Zhuānglǎo says,
the past does not come,
and the future does not break off.
This is what Zhuāngshēng called "having no past or present."
Immeasurable and boundless,
this is why one dwells in an undifferentiated expanse,
hidden in a beginningless epoch,
and wanders through the ending and beginning of all things, yet never knows its limit.
Supreme and subtle,
this is what Lǎozǐ called "subtle, mysterious, and penetrating,"
profound and unknowable.
Its original nature is empty and still;
this is to constantly be without desire, so as to observe its subtlety.
A mind good and profound like this
is what is called "like clear, cold water."
Pure and without blemish or defilement,
this is what is called "cleansing the mysterious mirror,"
without flaws.
Great Compassion.
People take great enlightenment as their refuge; the world is deluded.
People are caught in the dust and toil of delusive thoughts, and do not awaken.
Though they live, they lose that by which they live.
This is what the enlightened lament,
and why the Buddhists are known for their great compassion.
Planting various good roots.
Gāoyáo sowed the seeds of virtue among the myriad people,
and the common people submitted to him.
This is like what the Buddhists call "planting various good roots."
Lǎozǐ cannot speak of benevolence and righteousness.
Lǎozǐ can speak of the Way and Virtue,
but cannot speak of benevolence and righteousness.
Indeed, people can be good at what is distant but not what is near,
good at what is high but not what is low.
How could Lǎozǐ not know that benevolence and righteousness are beneficial to the world?
I wish to speak extensively of the beauty of the Great Way,
hence I bring up benevolence and righteousness.
Transformation.
Transformation (變, biàn) refers to
the Way of Heaven;
transformation (化, huà) refers to
the Way of Earth, and that is all.
Who is capable of transformation?
Only the sage, perhaps?
Lǚ Wàng.
Lǚ Wàng is not sufficient to be called a sage;
he is merely a great worthy.
Wǎngliǎng.
When the spirit is unclear, it is called wǎng (魍);
when the essence is unclear, it is called liǎng (魎).
Zhengyi and Samādhi.
Daoists speak of zhēnyī (貞一);
Confucians speak of zhìyī (致一);
Buddhists speak of sānmèi (三昧).
Their meanings are interconnected.
To speak of one immediately implies two,
and then extends to three.
To speak of three is to be obscured in between.
It is merely a matter of repeatedly reflecting on it.
Mèngzǐ is good at establishing his words.
Mèngzǐ said:
"A noble person, when it comes to animals,
seeing them alive, cannot bear to see them die;
hearing their cries, cannot bear to eat their flesh."
This seems close to Buddhism.
He also said:
"The music of today is like the music of antiquity."
This is close to Lǎozhuāng.
Do you not see that Mèngzǐ is good at establishing his words?
Buddhism speaks of it deeply;
Confucianism speaks of it superficially.
The deep also shows its shallowness;
the shallow also shows its depth.
Mèngzǐ stopped his words here
out of consideration for the world and future generations.
Taboo names.
Tàishǐgōng's personal name was Tán (談),
so the Shǐjì has no character "Tán."
In the Jì Bù biography, Zhào Tán (趙談) was changed to "Zhào Tóng" (趙同).
Fàn Yè's father's name was Tài (泰),
so the Hòuhàn has no character "Tài."
Guō Tài and Zhèng Tài are both written as "Dà" (大).
Jì Ào's father's name was Chǔjīn (楚金),
so in his writings, he always replaced "jīn" (今) with "zī" (茲).
Hán Yù wrote a "Huìbiàn" (諱辯) for Lǐ Hè,
upholding the theory that "if a word is present, it does not constitute a taboo."
Therefore, Yù's father, Zhòngqīng,
was never tabooeed.
Cáo Zhì,
Sūn Zhí's son,
in a memorial, said:
"the trunk and roots (gànzhí, 幹植) are not strong,"
not avoiding the character "zhí" (植).
The Sānguózhì does not even avoid the names of its rulers,
saying: "merit is achieved by quán (權),"
which directly refers to Sūn Quán's name.
Wénjūn, Běimán.
King Wén (文王) can be referred to as "Wénjūn" (文君).
Zhāng Héng's rhapsody "Wénjūn is poised for me" is an example of this.
The Northern Di (北狄) can be referred to as "Běimán" (北蠻).
The "Xiongnu Zhuan" (匈奴傳) in the Shǐjì states: "Xiǎnyǔn and Hūnxù resided in the lower Běimán" (獫狁葷粥居下北蠻), which is an example of this.
The Two Canons (二典) can be referred to as the "Mó" (謨).
Mǎ Róng's "striking the resonating chime stones,
recorded in the Yú Mó" (載于《虞謨》) is an example of this.
The Yáodiǎn (堯典) can be referred to as the Tángshū (唐書).
In Wú's "Lù Kàng Zhuàn" (陸抗傳), "quiet words and arrogant defiance,
cautioned in the Tángshū" (《唐書》攸戒) is an example of this.
The Sháo (韶) can also be referred to as the Yǔyuè (禹樂).
The Shǐjì states: "Yǔ initiated the music of the Jiǔsháo" (禹興《九韶》之樂), which is an example of this.
The Three Kings (三王) can also be called Di (帝).
In the "Xià Jì" (夏紀) of the Shǐjì, "Emperor Zhòu" (帝紂) is an example of this.
Offering captives is not limited to people;
things can also be captives.
The Shū (書) says: "captured their treasures and jade" (俘厥寶玉), which is an example of this.
Fú (俘)
means to take.
Gài (匄)
does not only mean to beg for oneself;
giving to others can also be called gài.
Táng Chuānwáng said:
"take all good silk,
and give it to the palace residents" (匄諸宮入), which is an example of this.
Zhěn (胗)
does not only mean the pulse;
inspecting things can also be called zhěn.
The "Wáng Qiáo Zhào" (王喬詔) states: "the superior inspects and observes" (上方胗視), which is an example of this.
Xiǎng (餉)
is not limited to food and drink.
The commentary to the "Wèi Wénjì" (魏文紀) states:
"presented Sūn Quán with poems and rhapsodies" (以詩賦餉孫權);
Xú Xiàomù also has a "Poem in Reply to a Gifted Mirror" (答餉鏡詩), which is an example of this.
Cities and towns can also be called "bì" (幣).
The "Zhào Shìjiā" (趙世家) states: "with cities and towns, seventeen bì for our state" (以城市邑十七幣吾國), which is an example of this.
Shècè.
The Hàn dynasty's shècè (射策) was different from duìcè (對策).
According to the "Xiāo Wàngzhī Zhuàn" (蕭望之傳):
"Shè refers to writing difficult questions and doubtful points on bamboo slips,
and ranking them as grade A or B according to their difficulty,
without making it obvious.
The one who 'shoots' then interprets what they have picked.
Duì refers to making it explicit,
asking about political affairs and classical meanings,
and determining superiority or inferiority based on the literary style of their replies."
In the Jìn dynasty, Pān Jīng was invited by a province,
and during an audience, he was asked to draw a slip (wèn cè).
He drew the character for "unfilial" (不孝).
The Inspector said:
"Are you inviting an unfilial scholar?"
He replied:
"Today, to be a loyal minister,
one cannot be filial."
This is also a remnant practice of shècè.
Seal and Ribbon.
During the Hàn dynasty, official seals and ribbons
were not like today's golden-purple or silver-scarlet garments,
which are worn permanently by officials.
Rather, when one held a particular office,
one wore that seal and ribbon;
when dismissed, one removed them.
Hence, the Sāngōng presented their seals and ribbons [upon retirement].
Zhāng Huàn of the Latter Hàn said:
"I have been 'silver-moxa' ten times, both before and after."
"Silver"
refers to the silver seal.
"Moxa"
refers to the green ribbon.
"Ten times" means
he wore one for each office.
The seals were not very large.
The Prince of Huáinán said:
"A one-inch-square seal,
with a twelve-foot cord" — that is what it was like.
Women in the Jìn dynasty also had seals and ribbons.
Yú Tán's mother was granted a golden insignia and purple ribbon, which is an example of this.
Historical Writing
Zhāng Fǔ of the Jìn dynasty said:
"Sīmǎ Qiān narrated three thousand years of events
in five hundred thousand words;
Bān Gù narrated two hundred years of events
in eighty thousand words.
Historically, when historians wrote about the same event in two different biographies,
they would say:
'The account is in So-and-So's biography.'
The Jìnshū records a section of Yuān Chén and Zǔ Nà playing chess,
nearly two hundred characters long,
which appears in both biographies.
This makes the writing cumbersome."
Talent and Wisdom
What is inexhaustible in the world
is talent and wisdom.
Chén Píng once proposed six ingenious schemes,
but in his private residence, he deeply worried that misfortune would befall him.
Lù Jiǎ advised him to foster good relations with the Tàiwèi,
and also wrote down several matters concerning the Lǚ clan.
Píng followed his advice,
and eventually eliminated the Lǚ clan.
Thus, Jiǎ's wisdom and strategy were superior to Píng's.
When Liú Yàn managed finances and grain,
he alone was in charge.
During Shùnzōng's reign,
Lǐ Xùn took office,
and in one year, he calculated the revenue,
which matched Yàn's highest year.
The next year, it surpassed it.
The year after that,
it increased by another 1.8 million strings of cash.
And Chéng Yì's calculations
were even more precise than Xùn's.
Viewed from the perspective of talent in managing finances and grain,
Liú Yàn was inferior to Lǐ Xùn,
and Lǐ Xùn was inferior to Chéng Yì.
Tuìzhī Had Music and Took Elixirs
In Hán Tuìzhī's later years,
he enjoyed music and took mineral elixirs.
Zhāng Jí's "Eulogy" says:
"He brought out two maidservants,
who played the pípa and zither together.
Soon after, his illness gradually worsened,
and his wife attended to his medicine."
Bái Lètiān's poem "Thinking of Old Friends" says:
"Tuìzhī took sulfur,
and once sick, never recovered.
Wēizhī refined 'autumn stone,'
and though not old, died suddenly."
Tuìzhī once mocked people for not understanding the "literary drink,"
yet he himself was ruined by singing girls?
He wrote the epitaph for Doctor Lǐ,
warning people against taking mineral elixirs,
yet he himself ingested sulfur?
Contrasting Views
Yáng Yòu excavated graves,
while Táo Kǎn relocated them.
The two were diametrically opposite.
Wáng Róng loved accumulating wealth,
often holding ivory tallies in his hand;
Wáng Yǎn never spoke of money,
referring to it as "that thing over there."
The two were diametrically opposite.
Tánzhī wrote "On Abandoning Zhuāngzi,"
while Ruǎn Jí wrote "On Understanding Zhuāngzi."
They were also opposite.
The "On Abandoning Zhuāngzi" criticizes Zǐxiū but largely plagiarizes his words,
like bringing a spear into the house –
this is the greatest flaw in writing.
Chǔ Dà
Some might suspect that "Mr. Chǔ" refers to Chǔ Dà.
This is incorrect.
According to the Rúlín Zhuàn,
Chǔ Dà
was a disciple of Dǒng Zhòngshū.
The Píngzhǔn Shū states:
Chǔ Dà served as an envoy for Emperor Wǔ.
As for "Mr. Chǔ,"
he lived between the Āi and Chéng reigns.
The note in Wǔ Jì says:
"Mr. Chǔ's
given name was Shàosūn,
and he was a Hàn博士 (bóshì)."
Taboos in Writing
Cáo Zhí's "Seven Stimuli" speaks of food flavors, saying:
"Plucking fragrant lotus from a turtle's nest."
Zhāng Xié's "Seven Commands" says:
"The chicks from the cinnabar cave."
These two seem not to be items from a kitchen.
Generally, when writing, one must be aware of taboos.
Military Victories and Defeats
Military victories and defeats often arise from chance,
without a fixed calculation.
Xiè Xuán with eighty thousand men faced Fú Jiān's million-strong army;
their strength was clearly unequal.
If Fú Jiān had blocked the Féishǔi and arrayed his troops,
he would surely have ensured complete safety.
But he ordered his army to retreat,
and the troops fell into disarray and could not stand their ground,
thus he was defeated.
The world says Xiè Xuán was able to make Fú Jiān flee because of this.
Huán Wēn attacked Shǔ,
and was defeated at Guǎnqiáo.
The troops were scared and wanted to retreat,
but the drum officer mistakenly beat the advance drum.
Thereupon, they attacked,
Lǐ Shòu's army was utterly routed,
and he surrendered his state.
The world says Huán Wēn pacified Shǔ because of this.
Queen Mother's Maidservants
When the Queen Mother of the West met Emperor Wǔ of Hàn,
she had four maidservants at her side.
The Emperor asked their names,
and she replied:
"Dǒng Shuāngchéng, Xǔ Fēiqióng, Wǎnlíng Huá, and Duàn Ānxiāng."
Riding Cup
In the eastern sea, there was a man named Liú,
who was skilled at making wine.
In the height of summer, it could be sent a thousand *lǐ*,
and was called "Riding Cup."
Dreaming of Wife Sending a Poem
Sū Jiǎn passed the imperial examination.
He dreamt his wife sent him a poem that said:
"The Chǔ river's water is like a mirror,
all around white birds fly.
How many lands are there in Jīnlíng?
Once I leave, I know not when I'll return."
Dreaming of a Green-Clad Woman Demanding an Eye
The monk Chénggǎo dreamt of an envoy
leading a green-clad woman.
The envoy asked Gǎo for his eye,
speaking in a rather stern tone.
The man drew a knife
and first cut off Gǎo's right hand.
Gǎo said:
"I wish to exchange it for my left hand."
The man asked:
"What do you mean by left or right?"
Gǎo replied:
"I recently received the precepts,
so I wish to keep my right hand to adjust my cassock."
The man said:
"There's no need to cut off your hand again.
Since the master mentioned adjusting the cassock,
she has already returned."
He angrily rebuked the woman and told her to leave.
He further said:
"This woman
is a fish.
In his previous life, the master was a child of the Wáng family,
six or seven years old.
His family bought this fish,
which was still fresh and alive.
The master dug out its eye with his hand,
and that is why she has come to demand it now."
Poem on Gazing at Pénglái in the Rain
Jūn Fáng 夢出郊,
望巨浸中樓臺參差,
忽有二青衣棹舟至,
大呼曰：
「Zhāng Xiùcái 賦雨中望蓬萊山詩。 」
Jūn Fáng 賦曰：
「重簾垂密雨，
孤夢隔秋宮。
紅爐九華暗，
香消芳思融。
仙忻望不及，
鶴信遣誰通。
但云許玉斧，
寧知張巨公。 」
二童曰：
「凡世人爭合道神仙名字？ 」
俄巨獸哮吼波上,
風濤大作,
恐懼而覺,
婦人在鏡中
The daughter of Lǔ Sīyān from Jiāngnán,
one day as she was about to apply makeup,
suddenly saw a woman in the mirror,
with disheveled hair and bare feet,
holding an infant.
From then on, she saw her every day.
Sīyān asked her the reason,
and the woman said:
「In past years, I was taken by the Lùshì of Chāng County, who married me as a concubine.
A year later, I gave birth to this child.
Your daughter was the principal wife.
Later, the Lùshì went to a neighboring county,
and your daughter threw me and this child into a well,
filling it with stones.
She deceived her husband, saying that I had run away.
My family lodged a complaint with the authorities,
but it happened that your daughter died.
Although this is now a later incarnation,
she must certainly pay with her life. 」
Her daughter then died.
King Yánluó
Táng Yán'ānzhī served as the Jīngzhàoyǐn,
and was known for his strength and wisdom;
both common people and officials feared him.
One day,
he saw a god in armor and a quiver who bowed respectfully,
and said:
「The General of the Five Paths pays his respects.
I am now under a heavenly edict
to welcome you, Lord, to be King Yánluó,
replacing King Hán. 」
Yán'ānzhī died that very night.
Emperor Mínghuáng heard of this
and posthumously enfeoffed him as King Píngděng.
Línglóng, What Can Be Done About Old Age?
Shāng Línglóng
was a courtesan from Yúháng.
When Bái Gōng governed the prefecture,
he would sing with her daily, saying:
「Put away the Húqín,
cover the beautiful瑟,
Línglóng bows twice and stands ready to sing.
Do not think the prefect does not understand song,
listen as I sing of the yellow rooster and the white sun.
The yellow rooster urges the dawn, crowing before the hour of chǒu,
the white sun urges people to set after the hour of yǒu.
The red sash at the waist is not yet firmly tied,
the crimson face in the mirror is already lost.
Línglóng, Línglóng, what can be done about old age?
When the prefect finishes singing, you sing again. 」
At that time, Yuán Wēizhī was in Yuèzhōu.
He invited her with lavish gifts for more than a month,
having her sing all the songs she knew,
and composed a poem to send her off,
also sending it to Lètiān, saying:
「Do not let Línglóng sing my words,
my words are mostly poems sent to you.
She turns back to the riverside to arrange her returning oar,
when the moon sets and the tide is calm, that is the time to go. 」
Three Immortals
One autumn day on Wǔyí Shān,
Lǚ Zhēnrén, Zhōnglí Xiānshēng, and Wǔyí Jūn called out from the air, saying:
「Let all men and women be seated!
Command the drum master to beat the leading drum,
the pipe master Bāo Gōng Xī to play the horizontal flute,
the clapper master Hé Fèng'ér to strike the clappers,
the string master Dǒng Jiāoniáng to pluck the kǎnhóu,
Xiè Yīngfēi to pluck the chánglí,
a bǐcè.
Lǚ Āxiāng to pluck the round-bellied. 」
This was a pípá.
Presently,
they commanded a drinking game,
and a singer sang a beautiful human song,
the lyrics were:
「Heaven and earth, how rare our meetings;
The sun sets in the western mountains, evening birds fly home.
A hundred years pass in a flash, aspirations and desires unfulfilled;
The heavenly palace is so near, yet I regret not being able to follow. 」
The Whole Family's Joint Poem
Téng Tíngjùn,
on the road in Luòyáng, sought lodging at a farmhouse.
The host happened to be out.
Tíngjùn sighed, saying:
「Being a guest brings much hardship,
as dusk falls, there is no host. 」
Suddenly, an old man with thinning hair and worn clothes
came out and said:
「I just heard your poem, young sir.
Although Cáo Yún said 'a traveler always fears people',
I cannot pass by.
I am but a humble guest who sweeps the door for the whole family,
my surname is Má, my given name is Hé,
and my rank is Dà. 」
They went together to the western corner of the hall,
and saw in the main hall's upper pavilion
a wine jar and plates and ladles.
They sat together for a long time.
Then another guest came out
and said:
「Hé, please be quiet. 」
He said to Má Dà:
「We haven't finished our joint poem yet. 」
Má then wrote the topic, saying:
「A Joint Poem Composed Together at the Whole Family's Píngyuán Guǎn. 」
Má Dà's poem went:
「Since I became a neighbor to the whole family,
fragrance has filled my body.
I have no desire for purity,
but am useful for removing dust. 」
Qiě Yé said:
「Mine is seven characters per line,
and the rhyme is also different. 」
He then recited:
「In winter mornings, I often go to rely on the smoke and fire,
when spring comes, I return to raise my offspring.
I once sat at the brush-tip of Fú Wáng,
but lately I seek food at the whole family's door. 」
Tíngjùn still did not understand,
and composed a poem, saying:
「Tián Wén was called hospitable,
but how many such people are there?
If there were a Fēng Huān,
I would hope to be counted among the lowliest guests. 」
The two looked at each other and laughed, saying:
「How can you mock us? 」
They said:
「If you, Lord, stay at the whole family's door for one day,
you will be quite content. 」
Thereupon, they had a meal,
drinking dozens of rounds.
When the host returned,
and called Yánjùn,
the two men were nowhere to be seen.
He was sitting in the latrine,
next to a large bluebottle fly and a bald broom.
Tíngjùn had a feverish illness,
but from this point, he completely recovered.
Earth Immortal of Nányuè
The jinshi Zhào Yán obtained a soft screen painting from an artist.
It depicted a very beautiful woman.
Yán said:
「How can I make her come to life?
I wish to take her as my wife. 」
The artist said:
「This is a divine painting of mine.
Her name is Zhēnzhēn.
Call her name for a hundred days,
day and night without ceasing,
and she will surely respond.
Then drench her with wine made from the ashes of a hundred colored offerings,
and she will come alive. 」
Yán did as he was told,
and she indeed stepped down from the screen,
speaking, laughing, and eating as normal.
A year later, she gave birth to a son.
His friend said:
「This is a demon!
I have a divine sword that can slay her. 」
That evening,
Zhēnzhēn wept, saying:
「I am an earth immortal from Nányuè.
I was painted by a human,
and you then called me forth.
Since I did not thwart your wishes,
and now you suddenly doubt me,
I cannot stay any longer. 」
She took her son and ascended back onto the soft screen,
vomiting out the wine made from the ashes of a hundred colored offerings that she had drunk before.
Looking at the painting,
only an additional son had been added to it,
and both were merely paintings.
Green Skirts, Red Sleeves
In the early Jiànlóng period,
someone moored his boat in Bāxiá.
At night, he heard someone chanting, saying:
"Autumn paths are filled with yellow leaves,
The cliff reveals the roots of grass.
The cry of an ape suddenly breaks off,
Many traces of tears are on the traveler."
Throughout the night, he recited this over a hundred times.
There was also a certain Liáng Bóshēng,
who was studying in a ruined house.
He dreamed of a woman,
in a green skirt and red sleeves,
who called out, saying:
"Lord Liáng, please listen to my sorrowful verses."
The poem said:
"I chose the day to ascend the Gorges,
Autumn winds brought many waves.
A night of rain in Jiānglíng,
My heart breaks with the Mùlán song."
Chǔ Xiǎobō
The *jìnshì* Xiè Fěi resided in Bǎoyìng.
One evening, he went to the county bridge,
and suddenly saw a young woman emerge from a boat,
who said:
"I am
Chǔ Xiǎobō.
You may visit me in the boat."
She took out a poem from her bosom and said:
"Directly below the painted bridge is the orchid boat,
Snatching at the moon and rushing through the mist, it drifts at will.
A house full of gold and jade is useless,
Better to follow a youth and come and go as you please."
"My beauty and your talent are both impermanent,
You should no longer trouble yourself with such thoughts.
My home has its own clear stream water,
Only by drinking it will you know its lasting flavor."
Fěi went to a friend's house.
Late at night, he saw Xiǎobō again, leaning against the bridge pillar,
and playfully said to him:
"Wěishēng, why have you come so late?"
Fěi made as if to bow,
and walked calmly into the water,
unaware.
His servant plunged into the water to rescue him and pulled him ashore,
as if he were drunk.
He only woke up after more than a month.
His friend said:
"This is a rogue ghost."
He seized the poem and burned it.
Poem on a Paulownia Leaf
Shǔhóu Jìtú leaned against the Dàbēi Temple tower.
The wind blew a large paulownia leaf down,
on which was a poem saying:
"Wiping away green and lowering twin brows,
For the sadness in my heart.
Picking up a brush at the courtyard,
I draw a picture of lovesickness.
These characters are not written on stone,
These characters are not written on paper.
They are written on an autumn leaf,
Wishing to rise with the autumn wind.
All people with feeling under heaven,
All understand death by lovesickness.
All heartless people under heaven,
Do not know the meaning of lovesickness.
Those with feeling and those without,
I do not know where they will fall."
Several years later,
Jìtú chose a Rèn family woman for marriage,
and she said:
"That was the leaf written by me."
Mèng Shì Seduced by a Youth
Wàntrú in Wéiyáng,
was a great merchant,
trading abroad.
His wife, Mèng Shì, was strolling alone in the garden pavilion in spring,
and chanted:
"What a pity that during the spring season,
I still wander alone as before.
For no reason, several lines of tears,
Flow ceaselessly as I face the flowers."
Suddenly, a youth climbed over the wall and enticed her, saying:
"Floating life is like a temporary lodging,
How long is youth?
The abundant flowers are in full bloom,
yet yellow leaves are already falling.
The sorrows of human life,
Are surely more than a thousand kinds?
How can it compare to stealing a moment of joy?"
Mèng Shì composed a poem, saying:
"Whose young master is he,
Secretly deceiving himself in his heart?
He does not say it is ultimately impossible,
If possible, I fear the young master would know."
The youth replied to her, saying:
"The goddess matched with Zhāng Gù,
Wénjūn met Chángqīng.
When the time comes, if two are mutually agreeable,
It is enough to comfort a passionate heart."
From then on, he seduced her,
and took her to his own dwelling.
A year later,
her husband returned from abroad.
Mèng Shì worried and wept.
The youth said:
"I already knew he would come."
Having spoken, he soared up and left,
disappearing after a moment,
ultimately, it was unknown what kind of spirit it was.
Twenty-two Months in the Mother's Womb
The Grand Master of the Imperial Sacrifices, Guō Tǎn, said of himself:
"I remained in my mother's womb for more than a year without being born.
My family considered it an ominous marvel,
and administered many drugs to induce miscarriage,
but nothing happened.
A skilled acupuncturist said:
"Three needles will surely be effective."
He applied over a hundred needles in total,
but still nothing happened.
My parents knew it was hopeless,
and simply accepted fate.
At twenty-two months, I was born.
Both mother and child were safe,
and I also had few illnesses as I grew up.
Only, there were dozens of black spots on my chest,
which were the needle marks from that day.
How can human life be born or die by mere chance?
The Northern Marchmount Bestows Stone Geese
Yáng Yù,
was a person from Héshuò.
One day, he went out to the countryside.
An envoy came galloping from the north and asked:
"Are you not Yáng Yù?
The Northern Marchmount bestows a gift upon you,
you may kneel and receive it."
The envoy took out an object from his bosom,
wrapped in what seemed to be silk.
Yù returned home, burned incense, and opened it,
finding a pair of stone geese, one male and one female.
The one with the left wing covering the right was male,
and the one with the right wing covering the left was female.
Later, he had one son and one daughter.
The son became the Xuānhuī Envoy of the Zhōu dynasty,
and the daughter became the consort of Hàngāozǔ.
Red Lotus of Lúshān
During the Yōngxī reign,
Jūnfáng was moored at Kāixiān Temple on Lúshān.
Looking at the waterfall of Huángshí Yán,
a large red leaf drifted down.
He ordered a monk to quickly retrieve it.
It was a red lotus,
one leaf measuring three feet long,
and one foot three inches wide.
He had once read the *Lúshān Jì*,
which said, "The Pèishuǐ originates from the summit of Shuāngjiàn Peak.
There is a pond several hundred feet wide,
its depth immeasurable.
There is also Qīngyuán Pond,
where lotus flowers as large as cartwheels grow."
Now, this could be believed.
Jūnfáng then distributed this leaf to enthusiasts,
who ground it into a decoction and drank it.
Its lotus fragrance lingered for a night and did not dissipate.
Osmanthus Seeds in the Moon
Bái Lètiān's poem "On Língyǐn" says:
"Three hundred days in the prefecture,
Twelve times I entered the mountains.
I stayed because the osmanthus seeds fell,
I got drunk because the crabapples bloomed."
It also says:
"In the mountain temple, I search for osmanthus seeds in the moonlight,
From the city tower, I watch the tidal bore."
During the Xiángfú reign,
Jūnfáng was the magistrate of Qiántáng.
He stayed at Yuèlún Mountain Temple.
A monk reported, saying:
"Osmanthus seeds are falling on the pagoda."
He immediately went out and ascended the pagoda to look.
They were numerous, like smoke and mist,
twirling and settling,
scattering and falling onto the pagoda,
like morning glory seeds,
yellow and white interspersed.
When chewed, they had no taste.
Cattail and Wheat
A Daoist priest passed through the villages of Jǐzhōu.
He said,
"There is much cattail in the marsh.
Amidst the cattail, there is wheat that can be eaten."
The residents said,
"We have never known this."
The Daoist priest said,
"Gather ripe cattails and weave them into baskets.
Put two dòu of wheat into them and grind it.
Then both will become flour."
The villagers followed his instruction and tried it.
It was exactly the same as wheat flour,
but it was light and not firm.
The following year,
many people in Jǐyùn ate it,
saving the populace from hunger.
In subsequent years, it was no longer edible.
Dúgū's wife dreams of enjoying the moon.
During the Zhēnyuán era,
the jìnshì Dúgū Xiāshú lived in Cháng'ān.
He traveled to Shǔ for two years before returning.
