A few lǐ from the city,
as night fell,
he stopped at a Buddhist temple.
He then recited an old poem, saying:
"Closer to home, my heart grows more urgent;
I dare not ask those who come and go."
At midnight,
more than ten people arrived in the courtyard with wine vessels and musical instruments.
Xiāshú thought they were nobles,
so he hid and watched them.
Among them was a young woman,
standing sideways and looking unhappy.
Upon examining her,
it was his wife.
A young man raised his cup and said,
"May we hear the sound of jade and gold."
His wife, sorrowful and anxious,
as if she had no one to complain to,
sang:
"Tonight, alas,
my beloved has gone to the ends of the earth.
The garden breaks my heart, for I have seen its flowers three times."
One person said,
"Your beloved is not far;
why speak of the ends of the earth?"
Xiāshú was startled and enraged.
He picked up a large brick and threw it.
Silence. There was nothing at all.
He quickly rode home.
A maid in green announced that her mistress had awoken from a nightmare.
When Xiāshú reached the bedchamber,
his wife said,
"Just now, I dreamed of enjoying the moon with my sister-in-law.
We went out of Jīnguāng Mén,
towards a wild temple,
and were coerced by brutal men to sit and drink with them."
Her account was identical to what Xiāshú had seen.
Eight Precepts.
Xú Xuàn of Jiāngnán's eight precepts for safeguarding integrity:
First, knowing the arrogance of wealth and nobility,
therefore humble oneself and be lowly.
Second, knowing that fame and profit corrupt the self,
therefore adapt to circumstances and let destiny take its course.
Third, knowing that desires shorten life,
therefore observe virtue and refrain from them.
Fourth, knowing that overthinking dissipates intention,
therefore clarify the Way and maintain unity.
Fifth, knowing that excessive talk harms vital energy,
therefore forget words throughout the day.
Sixth, knowing that joy and anger harm the spirit,
therefore examine oneself and regulate oneself.
Seventh, knowing the falsity of play and amusement,
therefore preserve the spirit and delight in oneself.
Eighth, knowing that wine and food harm people,
therefore moderate taste and be frugal.
Volume 50
End.
Battle South of the City.
Zhāng Zhèngjiàn's "Zhàn Chéngnán" says:
"Clouds gather, two armies clash;
sword energy, the Seven Stars bright."
Bring Forth the Wine.
Liáng Zhāomíng's "Jiāng Jìn Jiǔ" says:
"The frivolous sons of Luòyáng,
the frivolous lads of Cháng'ān."
Longing.
Xú Líng's "Cháng Xiāngsī" says:
"Lóngchéng is far,
Yànmén is cold.
With much sorrow, I grow thinner still;
my girdle naturally loosens.
I yearn for you, but you are not seen now;
who will embrace my waist and look?"
Xiāng Jiāngzǒng's "Cháng Xiāngsī" says:
"The Xiāng River is deep,
Lǒngtóu chokes.
Within the red silk mosquito net,
the green zither's clear strings are silent."
Yù Jiē says:
"Longing,
long separation;
two hearts remember each other, yet cannot reach.
Sorrowful wind is desolate,
floating clouds gather.
Eyebrows like willow leaves fade,
in the rhomboid mirror they vanish."
Lù Qióng says:
"Longing,
long separation;
spring breeze sends swallows peeking into the curtain.
Opening cosmetic boxes, playing with flower branches,
the red chamber is filled with a thousand sorrows,
two streams of jade tears fall.
Hearts do not reflect each other,
gazing, how can one know?"
Thoughts of a Thousand Lǐ.
Wèi Zǔ's "Qiānlǐ Sī" says:
"Xì Jūn bid farewell to the Hàn realm,
Wáng Qiáng married a barbarian.
Sorrow comes like a fluttering banner,
tears fall like linked pearls.
No way to the wild geese of Shànglín,
only the wilderness of the border city is seen."
Luòyáng Road.
Lù Xì's "Luòyáng Dào" says:
"By the roadside, avoiding the dappled horse,
from within the carriage, gazing at the jade-like person."
Cháng'ān Road.
Chén Xuān's "Cháng'ān Dào" says:
"Cháng'ān opens its embroidered paths,
three roads lead to brocade gates.
Open carriages and military horses,

Deep favor grants temporary use of palaces,

Purple Chestnut Horse.
Liáng Yuándì's "Zǐliú Mǎ" says:
"Handsome youths of Cháng'ān,
with golden bridles and linked brocade coins.
Twisting blue silk reins,
shining coral whips."
Poem on Beautiful Women.
Liáng Jiǎnwén's "Měinǚ Piān" says:
"...born of jade, shining,
her blouse thin, like a light cicada.
Alluring charm follows her flowing gaze,
lingering coquetry follows her voice."
Southern Jiangnan Thoughts.
Liǔ Yùn's "Jiāngnán Sī" says:
"On the sandbar, picking white duckweed,
sunset over springtime Jiāngnán.
In Dòngtíng, a returning guest,
in Xiāngxiāo, meeting an old friend."
Three Wives' Charm.
Wáng Róng's "Sānfù Yàn" says:
"The eldest wife weaves fine silk and brocade,

The youngest wife alone has no duties,

Old master, please be seated for a while;

Liáng Zhāomíng says:
"The youngest wife alone has no duties,
her red makeup dewy and fresh."
Xiāngdōng Wáng says:

Song of the White Bronze Dagger.
Liáng Wǔ's "Bái Tóngchī Gē" says:

Yànyù Song.
Liáng Jiǎnwén's "Yànyù Gē" says:

Another Western Tune, "Yáng Pàn'ér Gē" says:

Song of the River Water.
Liáng Wǔdì's《Hézhōng zhī Shuǐ Gē》says:
"The water in Hédōng flows eastward;
a Luòyáng girl is named Mòchóu.
At thirteen, she could weave brocade;
at fourteen, she gathered mulberry leaves by the southern paths.
At fifteen, she married into the Lú family;
at sixteen, she bore a son like Āhóu.
The Lú family's beautiful house has cassia beams;
within, there is fragrant turmeric and liquid storax.
On her head, twelve rows of golden hairpins;
on her feet, silken shoes with five patterns.
A coral-framed mirror brilliantly reflects light;
flat-headed servants hold a pair of shoes.
What of her lifelong wealth and status is forgotten?
She regrets not marrying the eastern family's son earlier."
His《Qīngyáng Yuè》says:
"Green lotus leaves cover the green water;

Below are conjoined lotus roots;

"The shrike flies east, the swallow flies west;

Bìyù Gē
Sūn Chuò's《Qíngrén Bìyù Gē》says:

Táoyè Gē
Wáng Xiànzhī's《Qíngrén Táoyè Gē》says:

Rùcháo Qǔ

"Jiāngnán is a beautiful and elegant land;
Jīnlíng, the city of emperors.
Windingly it embraces green waters;
distantly rise vermilion towers."
Bēigē
Wáng Róng's《Bēigē》says:
"A tragic song can serve as weeping;
a distant gaze can serve as returning.
Wishing to return home, but no one is there;
wishing to cross the river, but no boat.
My thoughts are full but cannot be spoken;
inside my gut, carriages and horses turn."
Lǎo Shī
Yīng Qú's《Sānlǎo Shī》says:
"I saw a traveler on the road;
on the path, I saw three old men.
I stopped my carriage and asked the three old men;
how did you attain such longevity?
The eldest old man spoke first,
sleeping on his side, alone.
The middle old man spoke first,
measuring his stomach, restricting what he consumed.
The youngest old man spoke first,
sleeping at night without covering his head."
Cōngmǎ Xíng
Liú Xiàowēi's《Cōngmǎ Xíng》says:
"Colorful saddle pad, jade-carved saddle;
precious sword with gold-inlaid scabbard."
Dāngzhìjiǔ
Lù Jī's《Dāngzhìjiǔ》says:
"The three benefits are already luxuriant;
the four beginnings are just now resplendent."
Yuǎnyóu
Cáo Zhí's《Yuǎnyóu》says:
"A spiritual ao carries Fāngzhàng;
divine soldiers shake the towering mountains."
Mùlán Cùzhī
The crickets chirp,
Mùlán weaves at the window.
One hears no sound of the shuttle,
Only the girl's sighs.
Asked what she remembers,
The girl remembers nothing.
Last night I saw the conscription notice,
The Khagan is greatly conscripting troops.
Twelve scrolls of military records,
In each scroll is my father's name.
My father has no grown son,
Mùlán has no elder brother.
I wish to buy a saddle and horse,
And from this moment, go to battle in my father's stead.
At dawn, I bid farewell to my parents,
At dusk, I encamp by the Yellow River (Huáng Hé).
I hear no sound of my parents calling their daughter,
Only the splashing sound of the Yellow River (Huáng Hé).
At dawn, I bid farewell to the Yellow River (Huáng Hé),
At dusk, I encamp at Yānshān.
I hear no sound of my parents calling their daughter,
Only the whinnying of the Hú horses.
Ten thousand *lǐ* she journeyed for the war machine,
Crossing mountain passes as if flying.
Northern winds carried the golden armor,
Cold light shone on the iron coat.
Generals died in a hundred battles,
Valiant warriors returned after ten years.
Upon returning, she saw the Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ),
The Son of Heaven (Tiānzǐ) sat in the Bright Hall (Míngtáng).
Her merits were ranked twelve times,
Bestowed with hundreds of thousands of gifts.
The Khagan asked what she desired,
Mùlán did not wish to be a Minister (Shàngshū Láng).
I wish to ride a thousand-*lǐ* steed,
To send your daughter back to her hometown.
When her parents heard their daughter was coming,
They went out of the city wall, supporting each other.
When her elder sister (āyí) heard her younger sister (mèi) was coming,
She tidied her red makeup at the door.
When her younger brother (xiǎodì) heard his elder sister (zǐ) was coming,
He sharpened his knife, *huòhuò*, towards pigs and sheep.
I open my eastern chamber door,
I sit on my western room bed.
I take off my battle-time robe,
I put on my old-time clothes.
By the window, I arrange my cloud-like hair,
Facing the mirror, I apply yellow floral patterns.
Coming out the door, I meet my comrades,
All my comrades are astonished.
We traveled together for twelve years,
Yet no one knew Mùlán was a girl.
The male rabbit's feet kick,
The female rabbit's eyes are blurry.
When two rabbits run side by side on the ground,
How can one tell which is male and which is female?
Melody of Jiāngnán
The "Melody of Jiāngnán" says:
"In Jiāngnán, lotuses can be gathered,
How luxuriant are the lotus leaves!"
Funeral Song: Song of Hāolǐ
The ancient "Funeral Song" originated from the followers of Tián Héng,
Who sang to send off Héng.
One chapter speaks of the ephemeral nature of human life,
Like dew on garlic chives that dries up;
The second chapter speaks of a person's spirit returning to Hāolǐ after death.
During Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's time,
Lǐ Yánnián divided it into two melodies:
"Xièlù" (露) for sending off kings and nobles,
"Hāolǐ" for sending off officials and commoners.
It is also called "Wǎngē" (挽歌).
According to the "Zǔzhuàn" (左傳),
When Qí was about to battle Jǔ at Àilíng,
Gōngsūn Xià ordered his followers to sing "Yúbīn".
Dù's commentary says "funeral song,"
It did not begin with Tián Héng.
Mulberry on the Path
"Mulberry on the Path" is also called "Yàngē Luófū Xíng" (艷歌羅敷行).
The lyrics say:
"The moon rises in the southeast corner,
Shining on my Qín family tower."
A woman from Hándān, Qín Luófū,
Was picking mulberries on the path.
King Zhào ascended a terrace, saw her, and was pleased,
He prepared wine to seize her.
The woman was skilled at playing the zither,
And composed "Mulberry on the Path" to make it clear she would not comply.
Long Song, Short Song
"Long Song March" ("Chánggē Xíng"),
Composed by Emperor Wǔ of Wèi:
"Facing wine, one should sing,
How long is human life?"
Old sayings about "Long Song" and "Short Song"
Generally state that a person's lifespan is already fixed,
And should not be sought recklessly.
Dǒng Táo Xíng
"Dǒng Táo Xíng,"
Composed by wandering youths in the Later Hàn dynasty,
Foreshadowing the chaos of Dǒng Zhuó,
Who eventually fled.
Jìn Fù Xiūyì's "Lì Jiǔqiū Piān" (歷九秋篇),
Describes the longing of a husband and wife separated,
Stating it was modeled after "Dǒng Táo Xíng."
White Hair Song
Wénjūn composed "White Hair Song," saying:
"Clear like clouds on the mountain at dawn,
Bright like the moon between the clouds.
My beloved has two hearts,
Thus, I will part with him."
White Ramie Song
"White Ramie Song" (Bái Zhù Gē),
Praises the beauty of the dancers,
Suggesting to enjoy themselves while the opportune time lasts.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng ordered Shěn Yuē to change it to "Four Seasons Song" (Sì Shí Gē),
Such as "Orchid buds are varied,
Peach branches are half red,"
Which refers to spring.
Something I Miss
"Something I Miss" ("Yǒusuǒ Sī"),
Roughly says:
"The one I miss is in the great southern sea.
If you have another heart,
I will burn it and scatter its ashes to the wind."
Zǐyè Song
"Zǐyè Song,"
Created by a woman named Yè in the Jìn dynasty,
Its sound was excessively mournful.
Crows Cry at Night
"Crows Cry at Night" ("Wū Yè Tí"),
When Sòng Péngchéng Wáng Yìkāng was moved to Yùzhāng,
Wáng Yìqìng was then Governor of Jiāngzhōu,
They met and wept.
Emperor Wén heard of this,
And recalled him.
Greatly fearing,
His concubines heard the crows cry at night,
And knocked on the gate, saying:
"There should be an amnesty tomorrow."
When he was reassigned to Nánzhōu,
This song was then composed.
There is also "Wū Lóu Qǔ" (烏樓曲).
Stone City (Shíchéng),
When Sòng Zàngzhì was Administrator of Jìnglíng,
He saw a group of common people singing ballads on the city wall and composed this for them.
Mòchóu
In Shíchéng, there was a young girl named Mòchóu,
Skilled in singing ballads.
The lyrics say:
"Where is Mòchóu?
Mòchóu is west of Shíchéng.
A small boat with two oars,
Hurry to bring Mòchóu here."
Prince's Song
When Emperor Míng of Hàn was Crown Prince,
Musicians sang four chapters to praise his virtue.
The first was called "The Sun Shines Again" (Rì Chóngguāng),
The second "The Moon Re-wheels" (Yuè Chónglún),
The third "The Stars Re-radiate" (Xīng Chónghuī),
The fourth "The Sea Re-moistens" (Hǎi Chóngrùn).
Watering Horses in the Great Wall Grotto
The poem "Watering Horses in the Great Wall Grotto" ("Yǐn Mǎ Chángchéng Kū") says:
"Green, green are the grasses by the riverbank,
My endless thoughts go to a distant road."
Lamenting that her beloved wanders and does not return.
Composed by Cài Yǒng.
If Chén Lín's "cold water injures horse bones,"
Then it speaks of the Qín people's suffering during the construction of the Great Wall.
Qí Ode, Wú Melody
"Qí Ode March" ("Qí Ōu Xíng"),
Lù Shìhéng sings of the beauty of Qí land.
"Wú Melody March" ("Wú Qū Xíng"),
People of Wú sing of their land.
Gathering Guests in the Youth Field
"Gathering Guests in the Youth Field" ("Jiékè Shàonián Chǎng"),
Speaks of valuing righteousness over life,
And achieving fame and merit with generosity.
Singing Freely March
Bāo Zhāo said:
"Like dock weeds and mallow hibiscus,"
Referring to the court being prosperous,
And the ruler cherishing talent,
Why then should one depart by the road?
Mountain Pass Song
"Mountain Pass Song" ("Guānshān Qǔ"),
Laments separation.
Pheasants Fly at Dawn
《Zhì Cháo Fēi》 (Pheasant Flying at Dawn)
was composed during the time of Qí Xuān Wáng
by the hermit Dú Mùzǐ.
At seventy years old, he had no wife.
Seeing a male and female wild pheasant accompanying each other,
he took up his qín and sang of it.
Bié Hè Cāo
《Bié Hè Cāo》 (Parting Crane Melody)
was composed by Shānglíng Mùzǐ.
He had been married for five years without a child,
and his father and elder brothers were preparing to have him remarry.
His wife leaned against the door, weeping sadly.
Mùzǐ then, with a heavy heart, sang:
"Soon we shall part, like twin wings separated at the ends of the sky,
mountains and rivers vast, the road long and winding."
Shuǐ Xiān Cāo
《Shuǐ Xiān Cāo》 (Water Immortal Melody)
Bóyá learned the qín from Chénglián.
Master Chénglián said:
"My master, Fāng Zǐchūn, is in the middle of the Eastern Sea;
he can transform one's essence."
So he and Bóyá went together.
Arriving at Pénglái Shān,
he left Bóyá and said:
"I will go welcome my master."
He sailed away
and did not return for ten days.
Bóyá only heard the sound of water rushing into caves,
mountains and forests dark and distant,
and flocks of birds crying mournfully.
He sighed and said:
"My master will transform my essence."
He took up his qín and sang,
and suddenly understood the profound meaning.
Chénglián sailed back to welcome him,
and Bóyá then became the most skilled under heaven.
Gōng Wú Dù Hé
《Gōng Wú Dù Hé》 (My Lord, Do Not Cross the River) was originally 《Kōnghóu Yǐn》 (Kōnghóu Melody),
composed by Lìyù, the wife of Huò Zǐgāo, a ferryman in Cháoxiǎn.
Zǐgāo rose in the morning and punted his boat.
There was a white-haired madman,
with dishevelled hair and holding a pot,
who came out of the turbulent current and crossed.
His wife called out to stop him,
but it was too late,
and he drowned.
Thereupon, she took up her kōnghóu and sang:
"My lord, do not cross the river,
My lord, you have indeed crossed the river.
My lord, you fell into the river and died,
What shall I do with you?"
When the song ended,
she threw herself into the river and died.
Lìyù grieved for her,
and so she took her kōnghóu and transcribed the sound.
Those who heard it shed tears.
Kǎn Hóu
When Hàn Wǔdì destroyed Nányuè,
he sacrificed to Tàiyǐ and Hòutǔ.
He ordered the musician Hóu Huī to create a kǎn based on the qín,
meaning that its "kǎn kǎn" sound matched the rhythm.
Hóu
was the craftsman's surname,
hence it was called "Kǎn Hóu."
Later, the pronunciation was corrupted from "Xiàng" to "Kōng."
Dìng Qíng Shī
《Dìng Qíng Shī》 (Poem of Pledging Love)
was composed by Hàn Chǔ Qīn.
It speaks of a woman who cannot follow a man with propriety,
so she removes her clothes and cherished items,
and makes a pledge of profound love.
For example, a bracelet expresses profound devotion,
a finger ring expresses earnestness,
a pearl expresses earnestness,
a sachet expresses yearning,
a jumping bracelet expresses intimacy,
and a jade pendant pledges affection.
She believes this is the utmost,
and expects a meeting at Shānyīn, Shānyáng, Shānxī, and Shānběi.
But he never responds,
and so she regrets it herself.
Tóng Què Jì
《Tóng Què Tái》 (Bronze Sparrow Terrace),
also called 《Tóng Què Jì》 (Bronze Sparrow Entertainers),
recounts Wèi Wǔdì's dying wish that his palace entertainers
ascend the terrace on the first and fifteenth of each lunar month
to gaze towards his Xīlíng.
Later generations were saddened by his intention,
and composed songs about it.
Hé Huān Shī
《Hé Huān Shī》 (Poem of Joyful Union)
was composed by Jìn Yáng Fāng.
It speaks of how the tiger roars and the wind rises,
the dragon leaps and clouds float,
a magnet attracts a needle,
and a sun-mirror produces fire.
Voices resonate and respond,
like-minded people seek each other.
They always wish to eat grain from the same root,
drink from the same joined-branch cup,
wear clothing of the same twin-silk,
and sleep under the same seamless quilt.
When sitting, their knees must touch;
when walking, their hands must be clasped.
Like birds with one heart,
like fish with conjoined eyes.
Their bond can cut through metal and stone,
their closeness is stronger than glue and lacquer.
Zhāo Yǐn
《Zhāo Yǐn》 (Summoning the Hermits)
was composed by Xiǎo Shān for Hàn Huáinán Wáng Ān.
One cannot stay long in the mountains.
Later generations changed it to words of the king.
Zuǒ Sī wrote several pieces of 《Zhāo Yǐn》.
Wáng Kāngjū, in turn, wrote anti-《Zhāo Yǐn》.
The 《Huáinán》 book contains 《Xiǎo Shān》 and 《Dà Shān》,
referring to major and minor politics,
similar to the two 《Yǎ》 in the 《Shī》.
Dà Dāo Tóu
"Where is my husband now?"
Gǎo Zhēn refers to the husband.
It asks where the husband is now.
"On the mountain, another mountain"
"Heavy mountain"
forms the character "chū" (to go out),
meaning he has gone out and is not here.
"When will the big knife-head?"
The knife-head has a ring,
asking when he will return.
"The broken mirror flies up to the sky"
When the moon is full, he will come.
Lián Jù
Lián Jù (Linked Verses) originated from Hàn Wǔdì's Bólíang banquet.
Each person composed one line,
linking them to form a poem.
Seven-character poetry began here.
Qiè Huàn Mǎ
《Ài Qiè Huàn Mǎ》 (Exchanging a Beloved Concubine for a Horse)
was composed by Huáinán Wáng Ān.
Huí Wén Shī
Huí Wén Shī (Palindrome Poem),
when read backward,
all forms a coherent text.
Bǎi Nián Gē
《Bǎi Nián Gē》 (Song of a Hundred Years),
begins from childhood to old age,
successively describing the states of youth, vigorous adulthood, and old age.
One stanza for every ten years.
Lù Shìhéng alone extended it to one hundred and twenty.
Bù Xū Cí
《Bù Xū Cí》 (Pacing the Void Verses)
are sung in Taoist temples,
fully describing the ethereal beauty of immortals lightly ascending.
Pán Zhōng Shī (Poem on a Plate),
written in a coiled manner.
The poem says:
"Mountain trees are high,
crows cry sadly."
The end says:
"One should proceed from the center around the four corners."
Jiàn Chú
For example, Bào Zhāo's "Raise the banner and exit Dūnhuáng,
remove the foot soldiers and relay stations."
It merely contains the characters "jiàn chú"
but does not preserve its original meaning.
Fēng Rén Shī
Liáng Jiǎnwén's 《Fēng Rén Shī》 (Poem of the Fēng People),
where the upper line is a phrase,
explained by the lower line to form a text:
"Playing wéiqí, burning a worn-out jacket,
placing a piece, one knows the clothes are burning."
Wū Shēng Bā Jiǔ Zǐ
An ancient lyric says:
"A crow gives birth to eight or nine chicks,
sitting upright among the qín family's cassia trees."
It means the crow mother was originally in a mountain cave,
but came and was killed by the Qín family's pellet.
A yellow crane flies to the sky,
a carp is in a deep spring,
people catch and cook it.
Each life has its predetermined span.
Shí Qīng Bù Kě Wéi Fēi (In peaceful times, one should not commit evil)
The “Dōngmén Xíng” (East Gate Song) says:
“Setting out eastward from the gate,
I have no desire to return.”
This speaks of a scholar who, poor and restless in his abode,
draws his sword to depart.
His wife and children cling to his clothes, stopping him, saying:
“The times are peaceful,
one must not do evil.
We wish for gruel to eat,
not to seek wealth and status.”
Life is not a full hundred years.
The “Xīmén Xíng” (West Gate Song) says:
“Life is not a full hundred years,
yet one often harbors worries of a thousand years.
Days are short, suffering the long nights;
why not wander with a lit candle?”
Bāyú zhī Měi
When King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
he sang,
and had his musicians practice it.
It was called “Bāyú zhī Měi.”
Jūn Mǎ Huáng
“The lord’s horse is yellow,
the minister’s horse is grey.
The lord’s horse chases,
the minister’s horse is fine.”
This laments those who are unjustly exiled.
Míngjūn Gē
The “Wáng Míngjūn Gē” (Song of Wáng Míngjūn) begins with “I was originally a child of the Hàn house.”
Wáng Zhāojūn,
because of the Hàn taboo on the name “Zhāo,” had it changed to “Míng.”
Qīngshāng Qǔ
“Qīngshāng Qǔ” (Pure Commercial Melody)
is an old music from the Southern Dynasties.
After the Suí pacified Chén, a Qīngshāng Office was established,
and pieces like “Bāyú” and “Báizhù” were included.
Dà Xiǎo Chuíshǒu
“Dà Chuíshǒu” (Large Hanging Hands)
refers to dancing with hands hanging down.
There are also variations like “Xiǎo Chuíshǒu” (Small Hanging Hands) and “Dú Yáoshǒu” (Single Swaying Hand).
Xiéshǒu Qǔ
“Xiéshǒu Qǔ” (Hand-in-Hand Song)
speaks of holding hands and enjoying oneself,
fearing that the fragrant time will not linger,
and the emperor’s favor will cease.
Yèyè Qǔ
“Yèyè Qǔ” (Night After Night Song)
expresses sorrow for being alone.
“Yángchūn Qǔ” (Spring Song)
expresses sorrow for the times.
Lèchāng Gōngzhǔ
The wife of Xú Déyán, a Palace Attendant to the Chén crown prince,
was the younger sister of the Last Emperor,
and was enfeoffed as Lèchāng Gōngzhǔ.
As Chén was on the brink of chaos,
Déyán knew they could not stay together.
He said:
“With your beauty,
when the state falls, you will surely enter the house of a powerful family.
Our emotional bond is not broken;
I still hope we can meet again.”
So he broke a mirror,
each taking half.
He said, “On the fifteenth day of the first lunar month in the future, you must sell it in the market.”
When Chén fell,
his wife entered the house of Yáng Sù.
Déyán, wandering, reached the capital,
and on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, he sought her in the market.
There was an old servant selling half a mirror.
Déyán produced his half and matched them.
He inscribed a poem:
“The mirror and the person both departed,
the mirror returns but the person does not.
No longer the shadow of Héng'é,
only the bright moon’s radiance remains.”
Madame Chén received the poem,
and wept without eating.
Sù summoned Déyán
and returned his wife to him.
He ordered Madame Chén to compose a poem,
which said:
“Why such haste today?
The new official faces the old.
I dare not laugh or weep,
only now realizing how difficult it is to be human.”
Yǎoniáng
Yǎoniáng, a maidservant of Qiáo Zhīzhī of the Táng dynasty,
was kept by Wǔ Chéngsì.
Qiáo wrote a poem to reach Yǎoniáng,
tied the poem to her skirt belt,
and she threw herself into a well to die.
Chéngsì saw the poem,
and sent cruel officials to falsely accuse Zhīzhī,
ruining his family.
The poem said:
“Shíjīa’s Jīngǔ once again hears new songs,
ten bushels of pearls buy a beauty.
In former days, alas, you pledged yourself,
now singing and dancing win hearts.”
“Parting from you, leaving you, I ultimately cannot bear,
to no avail, I cover my sleeves, wounding my red powder.
A hundred years of separation in a high tower,
a generation’s beauty ends for you.”
This was the third month of the first year of Zàichū.
In the fourth month, he was imprisoned;
in the eighth month, he died.
Bǐngshī
To the left of Níngwáng’s residence lived the wife of a cake seller.
The Prince saw her once and was captivated.
He heavily compensated her husband and married her.
A year passed,
and he asked:
“Do you remember the cake seller?”
She remained silent, not answering.
He summoned her to see him.
She stared, tears streaming,
as if overcome with emotion.
Wáng Wéi was present
and wrote a poem:
“Do not, by present favor,
forget past kindness.
Gazing at the flowers, tears fill her eyes,
she speaks not with the King of Chǔ.”
Bīngshì Páozhōng Shī
During the Kāiyuán era,
padded robes were bestowed upon border troops,
made in the palace.
A soldier found a poem in his robe:
“A guest on frontier duty in the sandy wastes,
how can one sleep in such bitter cold?
This battle robe, made by hand,
I wonder whose side it will fall to.
Intentionally, I added extra thread,
emotionally, I put in more cotton.
This life is already passed,
let us form a bond in the next life.”
The soldier presented the poem to his commander.
The commander submitted it.
Emperor Míng showed the poem to all six palaces,
saying:
“If there is an author, do not hide it;
I will not punish you.”
A palace woman declared herself guilty unto death.
Emperor Míng pitied her,
and subsequently married her to the soldier who received the poem,
saying:
“I will form a bond with you in this life.”
Jì Nèi Shī
Zhū Tāo recruited soldiers,
without regard for family background,
ordering all to join the army.
There was a scholar whose demeanor was admirable.
Tāo asked his profession,
and he replied:
“I study to write poetry.”
Tāo immediately ordered him to write a poem for his wife,
the words were:
“Holding a brush to write poetry is easy,
shouldering a spear for frontier duty is hard.
Accustomed to the warmth of an embroidered quilt,
I fear the cold at Yànmén.
Wasted away, my belt is loose,
crying much, I soak the sandalwood pillow.
Try to keep your beautiful green brows,
turn and look at them as you paint your eyebrows.”
Tāo then ordered him to reply on behalf of his wife:
“Disheveled hair and thorn hairpin are rare in this world,
this plain skirt is still the dress from my wedding.
Sesame seeds are good to plant, but no one plants them;
it is time to return, why do you not return?”
Tāo then released him to return home.
Hán Hóng Tóng Xìngmíng
During the Dézōng era,
there was a vacancy for an imperial decree drafter.
The Secretariat submitted two names,
but the emperor’s brush did not mark them.
They requested again,
and the emperor wrote a note:
“Give it to Hán Hóng.”
At that time, there was another person with the same name as Hán Hóng,
who was the Inspector of Jiānghuái.
So both individuals were presented again.
The emperor again wrote a note:
“In the spring city, flying flowers are everywhere,
on Hánshí, the east wind sways the imperial willows.
At dusk, the Hàn palace passes wax candles,
light smoke disperses into the homes of the five marquises.”
He then wrote:
“Give it to *this* Hán Hóng.”
Dyeing Fingers to Inscribe Poetry
Lǐ Xiàngshēn was garrisoned in Huáinán,
and Zhāng Yòuxīn was dismissed from a commandery in Jiāngnán.
They feasted and drank with extreme delight.
Yòuxīn had once served as an official in Guǎnglíng,
and developed a deep affection for a singing girl,
but ultimately could not marry her.
By this time, twenty years had passed,
and she was still at the banquet.
Yòuxīn dipped his finger in wine
and inscribed a poem on a plate.
Lǐ ordered the singing girl to sing it to accompany the wine,
and the lyrics were:
"Clouds and rain parted ways twenty years ago;
Then I sought dreams and could not sleep.
Now, with white hair, we meet again,
Still ascending the tortoise-shell banquet of Xiāngwáng."
Zhāng's Wife Yáng Is Ugly
Zhāng Yòuxīn, a director of the Bureau of Military Affairs, was good friends with Yáng, the prefect of Chǔzhōu.
Yáng's wife, Lǐ Shì,
had virtue but no beauty,
yet Yáng never minded.
Zhāng once said to Yáng:
"I made a name for myself in my youth,
and only obtained a beautiful wife,
which satisfied my lifelong aspirations."
Yáng said:
"If you must seek this,
just let her share my preference,
and it will surely please your heart."
Zhāng believed him.
After marrying,
he was very displeased.
Yáng said:
"Why are you so foolish!"
Zhāng said:
"Having no estrangement with you,
I told you my feelings;
you misled me like this,
how can you call me foolish?"
Yáng recounted his own path of seeking fame and official positions,
saying:
"Is it not all the same as yours?"
He replied:
"Indeed."
"Then I obtained an ugly wife,
why should you not be the same as me?"
Zhāng Jūn asked:
"How does your wife compare to mine?"
He replied:
"Far worse."
Zhāng laughed heartily
and then returned to his former state.
After Zhāng had established his family,
he wrote a poem saying:
"A single peony bloom is worth a thousand gold,
I thought its color was always the deepest.
Today, the full railing blooms like snow,
all my life I've failed to appreciate the flower-viewing heart."
Sīkōng Is Used To It
Lǐ Sīkōng invited Liú Yǔxī for a drink.
He ordered a marvelous singing girl to sing to accompany the wine.
Liú composed a poem saying:
"Hairpins set, hair combed, court-style makeup,
a spring breeze melody, Dù Wéiniáng.
Sīkōng is used to it, a trivial matter,
it breaks the heart of every Jiāngnán prefect."
Lǐ presented the singing girl to him as a gift.
Peach Blossoms Still Smile in the Spring Breeze
Cuī Hù of Bólíng,
on Qīngmíng Day, wandered south of the capital city
and found a resident's villa.
He knocked on the door for a long time,
and a woman asked:
"Who is it?"
He replied with his surname and given name,
saying:
"I am seeking spring alone,
parched with thirst and seeking a drink."
The woman brought a cup of water,
leaning alone against a small peach tree,
showing remarkably deep affection.
Cuī took his leave.
The following year on Qīngmíng,
he suddenly thought of her,
and went directly to the place,
inscribing a poem on the door:
"Last year today, within this door,
human face and peach blossoms reflected red.
Where has that human face gone today?
The peach blossoms still smile in the spring breeze."
A few days later, he returned again
and heard crying from within.
When he asked about it,
an old man said:
"Are you not Cuī Hù?
My daughter has been disoriented as if she lost something since last year,
and after seeing the inscription on the left door,
she fell ill and died."
Cuī requested to enter and wept for her.
She was still solemnly on the bed.
Cuī lifted her head,
laid it on his lap,
and said:
"I am here,
I am here."
In a moment, she opened her eyes
and revived half a day later.
The old man was overjoyed
and gave his daughter to him.
Fán Sù and Xiǎo Mán
Bái Shàngshū's courtesan Fán Sù
was skilled in singing,
and Xiǎo Mán was skilled in dancing.
He once had a poem saying:
"Cherry-like Fán Sù's mouth,
willow-like Xiǎo Mán's waist."
He also wrote lyrics for "Yángliǔzhī" (Willow Branch), saying:
"A single tree, ten thousand branches in the spring breeze,
tenderer than gold, soft as silk.
In the southeast corner of Yǒngfēng Fāng,
to whom do they belong, deserted all day?"
Later, during Xuānzōng's reign, this lyric was sung,
and an order was given to take two willow branches from Yǒngfēng
and plant them in the Forbidden Palace.
Bái was moved that the emperor knew his name,
and further wrote a poem:
"Surely hereafter in the celestial patterns,
two more branches will be added to the brilliance of the Willow Mansion (star)."
Xǔ Fēiqióng
The poet Xǔ Hún dreamed of climbing a mountain;
there were palaces,
and people said this was Kūnlún.
He entered and saw several people drinking.
They invited him,
and he composed a poem saying:
"At dawn, I enter the Jasper Terrace, the dew air clear,
among those seated, only Xǔ Fēiqióng.
The worldly mind is not severed, karmic ties remain,
ten lǐ down the mountain, only the bright moon remains."
Another day, he dreamed again and arrived at that place.
Fēiqióng said:
"Why did you reveal my name to the human world?"
He immediately changed it to "The heavenly wind blows down the sound of ethereal music,"
and she said:
"Good."
Mountain Monk Does Not Recite Sutras
At the end of Dàhé,
an imperial edict commanded monks and nuns to be tested on sutra recitation;
those who failed would be forced to return to lay life.
Lǐ Zhāngwǔ was the Junior Prefect of Chéngdū.
There was a mountain monk who had lived in a meditation hermitage for years
and had never recited sutras.
Zhāngwǔ presented a poem to him, saying:
"The Southern School still allows expedient means,
how can there be any more sutras in the heart?
Go well, bhikṣu, by the clouds and waters,
what mountain's pines and cypresses are not green?"
The authorities excused him and let him go.
Lǐ Bái Teases Dù Fǔ
Lǐ Bái's poem teasing Dù Fǔ said:
"At the top of Fànkē Shān, I met Dù Fǔ,
wearing a bamboo hat at high noon.
I asked if he had become very thin since we parted,
all because of the hardship of composing poetry before."
Dù Mù Inscribes a Poem for a Chan Monk
When Dù Mù was in his early twenties, he passed the Imperial Examination.
He visited a temple with his peers.
A Chan monk sat alone wrapped in a coarse robe,
and his words were all profound and subtle.
He asked Dù Mù what profession he cultivated.
Those beside him boasted of Dù Mù's repeated successes,
and the monk smiled, saying:
"I don't know."
Dù Mù inscribed a poem saying:
"My home is in Dùqū by the south of the city,
two immortal cassia branches fragrant at once.
The Chan master knows not my name,
only now do I realize the profound taste of the empty gate."
Zǐyún
Dù Mù 杜牧 was appointed an Imperial Censor, assigned to a branch office in Luòyáng 洛陽.
Sītú Lǐ 李司徒, having been dismissed from his military governorship, was living in retirement.
He held a grand banquet,
with over a hundred female entertainers.
Dù Mù 杜牧 stared intently,
saying:
“I heard there was one named Zǐyún 紫雲;
which one is she?”
Lǐ 李 pointed her out.
Dù Mù 杜牧 said:
“Her reputation is well-deserved.
It would be proper for you to present her to me.”
Lǐ 李 bent over and smiled,
and all the entertainers turned their heads.
Dù Mù 杜牧 recited:
“In this splendid hall today, a silken banquet is spread;
Who summoned the Imperial Censor from his branch to be led?
Suddenly he spoke a wild word, startling all present;
Two rows of fair faces turned at once, their gaze intent.”
Three years later, during his revelries,
he wrote a poem:
“Drifting through rivers and lakes, with wine I roam;
A slender Chǔ 楚 waist, held in my palm, a home.
Ten years passed, a single dream of Yángzhōu 揚州 I woke from;
Earning the thin fame of a brothel, where my reputation has become.”
“With one oar, a hundred cups emptied from the wine-boat's store;
Ten years of youth, I have not wronged you, no more.
Today, beside a meditation couch, with silvering hair;
Tea smoke gently wafts amidst falling blossoms in the air.”
“Mínghé Piān” 明河篇
Sòng Zhīwèn 宋之問, during Empress Tiānhòu’s 天后朝 reign, sought appointment as a scholar of the Northern Gate,
but was not permitted.
He wrote the “Mínghé Piān” 明河篇, saying:
“The Bright River can be seen but not approached;
I wish to take a raft and seek a crossing.
And with the Weaver Girl’s shuttle-prop stone,
Visit again the fortune-teller of Chéngdū 成都.”
Zétiān 則天 said:
“It is not that I do not recognize Zhīwèn’s 之問 talent,
but he has an oral defect.”
This was because Zhīwèn 之問 had a tooth ailment,
and his breath was often foul.
Lǐ Shìzhī’s 李適之 Poem Upon Dismissal
At the end of the Kāiyuán 開元 era,
Chancellor Lǐ Shìzhī 李適之
had a very good reputation at the time.
Lǐ Línfǔ 李林甫 slandered and framed him, leading to his dismissal.
He wrote a poem saying:
“Avoiding the worthy, I first stepped down from the Chancellorship;
Delighting in the sages, I yet raise my cup to my lip.
I ask the guests at my gate,
How many came today?”
Línfǔ 林甫 grew even more enraged,
and he ultimately could not escape.
The Imperial Censor and the Singing Girl
In the early Dàhé 大和 era,
there was an Imperial Censor assigned to a branch office in Luòjīng 洛京.
There was a singing girl who excelled at singing.
The Defender-General Lǐ Féngjí 李逢吉 asked to see her once.
She came in grand attire.
Lǐ 李 ordered her to face his concubines.
Lǐ’s 李 forty-odd concubines
were all beneath her.
Once she entered,
she did not come out again.
After a night and a day, her whereabouts remained unknown.
She tearfully submitted a poem,
and Lǐ 李 merely smiled, saying:
“A very good poem.”
Then she was cut off.
She wrote:
“The Three Mountains are unseen, the sea is deep and vast;
How can immortal traces still be sought or cast?
When the green bird departed, the cloud path was broken;
Where Cháng'é 常娥 returned, the moon palace deep, a token.
Behind the gauze window, I secretly recall our spring love;
In the study curtain, who pities my lone night song above?
I suppose at this moment, the moon in the sky,
Should only shine on our two hearts, as we lie.”
Not Planting Peach and Plum Trees
Jiǎ Dǎo 賈島 first gained poetic fame,
but was arrogant and unruly in conduct,
and failed the examinations for a long time.
Péi Jìnggōng 裴晉公 dug a pond in Xīnghuà Lǐ 興化里
and built pavilions and terraces.
Jiǎ Dǎo 賈島, having just failed the examination,
wrote a poem in resentment and frustration inside a pavilion,
saying:
“A thousand homes were broken to make this one pond;
No peach or plum trees are planted, only roses beyond.
When rose blossoms fall after the autumn wind's sway,
Thorns fill your clothes, only then you will know, I say.”
Everyone disliked his insolence,
and he ultimately died without passing the examination.
Stepmother Abuses Children
During the Kāiyuán 開元 era,
a certain officer surnamed Zhāng 張 in Yōuzhōu 幽州,
married a woman from the Kǒng 孔 family,
who bore him five sons.
After she passed away,
his wife Lǐ 李 was fierce and jealous,
abusing the five sons,
whipping and beating them daily.
The sons, unable to bear their suffering,
reported it at the grave.
Their mother came out from the tomb,
caressed her sons,
and in sorrow and grief, inscribed a poem to Zhāng 張,
saying:
“Unwilling to become a stranger to you,
Tears always soak my kerchief as I weep.
Life and death now divide us in two,
There will never be a chance for us to meet.
The remaining cosmetics in the box,
I leave them for those who come after.
If you have affection for sons and daughters,
If not, then it is up to you, master.
If you wish to know where my heart broke,
The bright moon shines on this solitary grave, look.”
The military commissioner reported the matter to the emperor,
who ordered Lǐ 李 to be flogged one hundred times
and exiled to Língnán 嶺南,
and Zhāng 張 was suspended from office.
“Zhāngtái Liǔ” 章臺柳
Liǔ 柳,
a concubine of General Lǐ 李,
returned to Hán Hóng 韓翃.
Hán Hóng 韓翃 achieved fame the following year,
and was appointed an aide by Hóu Xīyì 侯希逸, the military governor of Zīqīng 菑青.
As the world was in turmoil,
he dared not take Liǔ 柳 with him,
leaving her in the capital.
For three years he was unable to return,
and sent a poem saying:
“Zhāngtái Liǔ 章臺柳,
Zhāngtái Liǔ 章臺柳,
Do your branches still sway as tenderly as they used to?
Even if your long boughs still hang as before,
They must have been plucked and broken by another’s hand, I’m sure.”
Liǔ 柳 replied:
“Willow branches,
In the fragrant season,
It is hateful that year after year they signal farewell.
A single leaf carried by the wind suddenly heralds autumn,
Even if you come, how could they bear to be broken?”
Later, Liǔ 柳 was abducted by the barbarian general Shāzhālì 沙叱利,
who kept her exclusively for his pleasure.
Hán Hóng 韓翃 accompanied Hóu Xīyì 侯希逸 to the court,
feeling dejected and unhappy.
An Imperial Guard commander, Xǔ Jùn 許俊,
rode his horse directly to Shāzhālì’s 沙吒利 residence,
took Liǔ 柳 onto his horse and rode away,
and immediately presented her to Hán Hóng 韓翃.
Luò Bīnwáng 駱賓王 Becomes a Monk
Sòng Zhīwèn 宋之問 arrived in Jiāngnán 江南
and visited Língyǐn Sì 靈隱寺.
He recited a poem as he walked:
“The Vulture Peak rises majestically,
The Dragon Palace hides in solitude.”
He had not yet completed the second couplet when
an old monk, lighting a long-burning lamp,
sat on a large meditation couch and
said:
“Young man, your poetic tune is quite arduous.
Why not say:
‘From its tower, behold the sun over the sea;
At its gate, hear the tide of Zhèjiāng 浙江 flee’?”
Zhīwèn 之問 was astonished,
and then continued:
“Osmanthus blossoms fall from the moon;
Heavenly fragrance floats beyond the clouds too soon.
Climbing vines, the pagoda is far;
Hollowing wood, the spring is distant, a star.
Frost is thin, flowers bloom anew;
Ice is light, leaves have not yet withered through.
Waiting to enter the Tiāntái Tiāntái road,
Watch me cross the stone bridge, my load.”
At dawn, he sought him out,
but he was no longer to be seen.
A monastery monk said:
“This was Luò Bīnwáng 駱賓王.
When Jìngyè 敬業 was defeated,
he and Bīnwáng 賓王 both fled.
The generals, fearing punishment,
sought out two similar individuals
and presented their heads. Thus, Jìngyè 敬業 became a monk on Héngshān 衡山,
and Bīnwáng 賓王 also shaved his head,
traveling extensively to famous mountains.”
Liú Xīyí’s 劉希夷 Poem
Liú Xīyí
once wrote a poem that said:
“This year the flowers fall, their colors change; next year when the flowers fall, who will still be here?”
He awakened and said:
“Is this not inauspicious?”
Then he wrote another poem that said:
“Year after year the flowers are similar;
year after year the people are different.”
He disliked this too.
Indeed, by the next spring, he passed away.
Zhǎngsūn and Ōuyáng ridicule each other.
Zhǎngsūn Wújì, seeing Ōuyáng Xún’s
ungainly appearance, ridiculed him, saying:
“Shoulders shrugged into a mountain character,
buried shoulders yet no head appears.
Who says that on the Qílín Pavilion,
they depict such a gibbon?”
Xún replied:
“A tight neck keeps arms warm,
a loose robe keeps the belly cold.
It is only because my mind is muddled,
that my face is round and full.”
Silver flowers combined with bronze nails
During the Kāiyuán reign,
Chancellor Sū Wèidào and Zhāng Chānglíng were both famous.
Zhāng once taunted Sū, saying:
“The reason my poetry is not as good as yours, Chancellor,
is because it lacks ‘silver flowers combined’ .”
Sū had a “Poem on Watching the Lanterns” that said:
“Fiery trees and silver flowers combine,
star bridges and iron chains open.”
Wèidào said:
“Though your poem lacks ‘silver flowers combined’ ,
it still has ‘bronze nails’ .”
Chānglíng's poem to Zhāng Chāngzōng said:
“In former days, Fúqiú Bó,
is now like Dīng Lìngwēi.”
Three things to fear in a wife
During the Zhōngzōng reign,
Péi Tán devoutly worshipped Buddhism.
His wife was fierce and jealous,
and Tán feared her.
He once said:
“There are three things to fear in a wife:
When she is young and beautiful,
she looks like a living Bodhisattva.
How can one not fear a living Bodhisattva?
When children fill the house,
she looks like the Nine-Son Demoness Mother.
How can one not fear the Nine-Son Demoness Mother?
When she reaches fifty or sixty,
with a little powder and rouge applied,
either blue or black,
she looks like a Kūbhāṇḍa.
How can one not fear a Kūbhāṇḍa?”
Lángzhōng and Yuánwài
Hè Shè playfully recited:
“A Yuánwài is always beautiful,
a Lángzhōng's prospects are not so good.
Who says that within the vermilion office,
they will turn into a mound of earth?”
Qiānguāng replied:
“Brocade tents are set up as needed,
golden censers burn at will.
I only regret that the Yuánwài position,
should not be listed among the stars.”
Skinned alive and swallowed whole
Lǐ Yìfǔ once wrote a poem that said:
“Carving the moon into a song-fan,
cutting clouds to make a dance-robe.
Pitying my own image of swirling snow,
I would gladly return to Luòchuān.”
There was a Zhāng Huáiqìng,
who was fond of stealing the writings of famous scholars.
He then wrote a poem saying:
“Naturally carving the moon into a song-fan,
awkwardly cutting clouds to make a dance-robe.
Looking in the mirror, pitying my own image of swirling snow,
when I came, I gladly returned to Luòchuān.”
At the time, people said:
“Zhāng Chānglíng is skinned alive,
Guō Zhèngyī is swallowed whole.”
Hermit Táo
Táo Hóngjǐng lived as a hermit on the southern side of Huàshān.
Emperor Gāozǔ of Liáng asked:
“What is there in the mountains?”
Hóngjǐng replied in a poem:
“What is there in the mountains?
On the peaks are many white clouds.
They can only please me,
they cannot be sent to Your Majesty.”
Mǎ Zìrán’s poem
Mǎ Zìrán’s poem said:
“Why bother to refine elixirs to maintain youth?
It’s not lively like a city, nor quiet like the mountains.
If people today seek the elixir of immortality,
a mind free from attachment to the environment is the great return.”
Yuán and Bái’s poems
Yuán Zhěn was a Censor,
investigating cases in Zǐtóng.
At that time, Bái Jūyì was in the capital,
and with other notable people, visited Cí’ēn.
They had a small drink under the flowers,
and he sent a poem to Yuán, saying:
“At flower time, we drank together to dispel spring sorrow,
drunk, we broke flower branches as wine tallies.
Suddenly I remember an old friend far away at the edge of the sky,
calculating the journey, you arrive in Liángzhōu today.”
On that very day, Yuán indeed reached Bāochéng,
and also sent a “Dream Journey” poem saying:
“I dreamt of you, my brother, by Qújiāng,
also wandering through the courtyards of Cí’ēn.
The post official called people to arrange horses and leave,
suddenly startled, I found myself in ancient Liángzhōu.”
Their souls met across a thousand li,
as if matching a tally.
The man in white recites a poem
Mǎ Zhí was appointed to Qiánnán,
but was quite unhappy.
Mooring his boat in a gorge,
on a moonlit night, he saw a man in white slowly walking along the dike,
reciting:
“Cutting bamboo to make a flute to play,
on the Phoenix Pond, phoenixes fly.
I trouble you to go further to Qiánnán,
this is precisely the time to fashion all beings.”
He sent someone to invite and inquire,
but the man was already gone.
Later, he entered the court from Qiánnán as Dàlǐ Qīng,
and subsequently became a Chancellor.
Bái Twenty and Wéi Nineteen
Liú Yǔxī once said:
“Bái Twenty (Bái Jūyì) greatly loved my ‘Shítóuchéng’ (Stone City) work, which says:
‘Mountains surround the old capital, still present;
tides strike the empty city, returning in solitude.’
I know I am not as good as Wéi Nineteen (Wéi Yīngwù)’s ‘The spring tide, brought by rain, rushes in the evening;
at the wild ferry, no one, the boat drifts itself.’ ”
Poem on ascending Yázhōu City
Lǐ Déyù’s poem on ascending Yázhōu City says:
“Alone I climb the high tower to gaze at the imperial capital,
even a flying crow would take half a year to reach it.
The green mountains seem to wish to keep me here,
circling the county city hundreds and thousands of times.”
Huíbō Cí (Round-wave lyrics)
During the Zhōngzōng reign,
Empress Wéi largely adopted the style of Empress Wǔ,
and the Emperor gradually feared her.
During an inner banquet, five rounds of “Huíbō Cí” were sung.
An entertainer said:
“Huíbō, at that time, oh oh,
fearing one's wife is also very good.
Outside, there is only Péi Tán,
inside, no one surpasses Old Lǐ.”
Recorded in the tooth-register, yet no crimson sash
Shěn Quánqī was punished for a crime,
but met with imperial grace.
Before his crimson sash was restored,
at an inner banquet,
he composed a “Huíbō Cí” :
“Huíbō, at that time, Quánqī,
exiled beyond the ridges, has returned alive.
My name and person have already been recorded,
but my robe and tablet have not yet regained their crimson color.”
Emperor Zhōngzōng immediately bestowed upon him a crimson fish-pouch.
Wáng Chuí
The "Yíngyáng Gē" was only for Wáng Chuí.
Barbarian dancers wore golden weiruí sashes.
Lóngxiāng Bō (Dragon-fragrance plectrum)
Yáng Fēi’s pípa
used a dragon-fragrance board as a plectrum.
Líshān
On Líshān, there are the Yǐnmǎ Quán (Horse-Drinking Spring), Jīnshā Dòng (Golden Sand Cave), and Yùhuá Fēng (Jade Flower Peak).
Yù Rúyì (Jade Scepter)
The Emperor felt uneasy, so
Luó Gōngyuǎn broke off a bamboo branch to make a yù rúyì and presented it.
Jīngāng Sāncáng took a seven-precious rúyì from his sleeve.
The one Gōngyuǎn presented
immediately turned back into bamboo.
Nísháng Yǔyī (Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Robe)
Palace entertainers wore seven-precious necklaces
and danced the “Nísháng Yǔyī Qǔ.”
When the music ended,
pearls and kingfisher feathers could be swept up,
immortal guests.
The Emperor (Shàng) obtained a white deer in the Fúróngyuán.
The hermit Wáng Mín
said: "It is a deer from the Hàn dynasty."
Then, from the fur near its antlers, a bronze plate was found,
which read:
"White deer from the Yíchūnyuàn."
The Emperor looked at it and called it "Xiānkè" (Immortal Guest).
Ānpò
Below the pine trees, there is red Fúlíng.
After remaining in the earth for a thousand years,
it turns into ānpò (amber).
Bōlí Bēi
Beside the Zhēng Hall, there is a stele from the Wèi dynasty's Wēnquán Táng.
Its stone is clear and translucent,
and in the palace, it is called "Bōlí Bēi" (Glass Stele).
Bào Xiè Shuō
There were frivolous people
who ridiculed Cáo and Liú as antiquated and clumsy,
calling Bào Zhāo a person from the era of Xī Huáng,
and Xiè Tiǎo peerless in ancient and modern times.
Yet, those who emulated Bào Zhāo ultimately could not achieve "rì zhōng shì cháo" (city market at noon),
and those who learned from Xiè Tiǎo barely managed "huáng niǎo dù qīng zhī" (yellow bird crossing green branches).
Bān Jiéyú Shī
The poems of Bān Jiéyú (or Bān Jiéhǎo) of the Hàn dynasty,
their origin lies with Lǐ Líng.
Her short piece "Tuánshàn" (Round Fan),
with its clear and graceful words and meaning,
deeply captures the essence of a common woman.
The section on the "Zhurú" (dwarf)
is enough to know its excellence.
If the school of Kǒng (Confucius) were to use poetry,
then Gōnggàn would ascend the hall,
Sī Wáng would enter the inner chamber,
and Jǐngyáng, Pān, and Lù could sit in the corridors.
The poems of Pān Ānrén
originated from Zhòngxuān.
The Hánlín (Academy) praised them as "fluttering like a soaring bird with feathers,"
"or a robe with fine silk gauze."
Xiè Kūn said:
"Pān's poetry is brilliant like spread brocade,
with no part that is not excellent.
Lù's writing is like sifting sand for gold,
often finding treasures."
I once said:
"Lù's talent is like the sea, Pān's
talent is like a river."
Érnǚ Qíng Duō Fēngyún Qì Shǎo
The poems of Zhāng Màoxiān
originated from Wáng Càn.
Their style is ornate and splendid,
their inspirations aspire to immortality,
and their use of words strives for beauty and refinement.
Although his fame was high in previous generations,
for a straightforward and enlightened scholar,
it is still regrettable that his "érnǚ qíng duō" (sentimentalities of love are many),
and "fēngyún qì shǎo" (heroic spirit is scarce).
Xiè Kānglè said:
"Though Zhāng Gōng may have a thousand chests [of treasures],
it is still just one body (style)."
The poems of Guō Jǐngchún
were modeled after Pān Yuè.
Their literary styles illuminate each other,
resplendent and delightful.
He first changed the plain and unadorned style of the Central Plains,
hence he is called the "first of the restoration."
The Hánlín considered them the pinnacle of poetry.
However, his "Yóuxiān" (Wandering Immortals) works
often contained passionate words,
deviating far from the profound Daoist philosophy.
He once said:
"Alas, a tiger's and leopard's bearing."
And also said:
"Folding wings, dwelling in thorny brambles."
These are expressions of frustrated ambition,
not the interest of transcendent immortals.
The poems of Táo Péngzé
originated from Yìng Qú,
and also harmonized with Zuǒ Sī's powerful style.
His literary style is concise and tranquil,
without lengthy words.
Whenever one reads his writings,
one imagines seeing the person himself.
As for lines like "Huān yán zuì fū jiǔ" (Joyfully speaking, I get drunk on wine)
or "Rì mù tiān wú yún" (At dusk, the sky is without clouds),
are their grace and elegance
merely the language of a farmer?
He is the patriarch of reclusive poets, ancient and modern.
Huìxiū
Tāng Huìxiū said:
"Xiè's poems are like lotuses emerging from water,
Yán's poems are like embroidered brocade and carved jade."
Wǔxián Shī
The poems of the five worthies: the two Wángs, Yuán, and the two Xiès,
their origin lies with Zhāng Huá.
Their talent and strength were relatively weak,
striving for clarity and simplicity,
thus acquiring a graceful and spiritual charm.
Assessing their true merits,
the Yùzhāng and Púshè
should be able to contend on equal terms.
The Zhēngjūn and Tàiwèi
could be entrusted with following in the second carriage.
The Zhēnglǔ is outstanding,
almost wishing to pass ahead of the Huáliú.
Yùzhāng Tàishǒu is
Xiè Zhān.
Púshè is
Kūn.
Zhēngjūn is
Wáng Huī.
Tàiwèi is
Yuán Shú.
Qiūhuái Dǎoyī Zhī Zuò
Xiǎo Xiè's (Xiè Xuānhuī's) talent and quick wit were abundant.
□It is regrettable that his "orchid and jade" withered early,
and his long rein was not yet galloped.
As for his "Qiūhuái" (Autumn Thoughts) and "Dǎoyī" (Pounding Clothes) works,
even Língyùn's sharp thoughts,
how could they surpass them?
The poems of Xiè Xuānhuī
originated from Xiè Kūn.
They were slightly marred by excessive intricacy.
Within a single chapter,
there are both jade and stone.
However, his extraordinary chapters and exquisite lines
are enough to make Shúyuán stumble,
and Míngyuǎn change color.
Jìn Sòng Wú Shī Shǒu
During the Jìn and Sòng dynasties,
there were almost no master poets.
In the Yìxī era,
Xiè Yìshòu and Yīn Zhòngwén were considered the best among the splendid cavalry;
there was no competition.
Jǐn Cì Zuò Zhǎng
Sòng Jiāndiǎn Shì Qū Huìgōng
was an old friend.
The Great General repaired the Northern Residence and
appointed him as the work supervisor (zuò zhǎng).
At that time, Xiè Huìlián also held the post of Jìshì Cānjūn.
Gōng composed the poem "Shuāngzhěn" (Twin Pillows),
and Xiè said:
"You are indeed capable of poetry,
but I fear people may not highly regard it yet.
For now, it can be attributed to Xiè Fǎlǔ."
The Great General saw it, admired it,
and bestowed two rolls of brocade upon Xiè.
Xiè said:
"This poem was composed by the supervisor of works.
Please bestow the brocade upon him."
Bǎoyuè
Huìxiū was frivolous,
his emotion surpassed his talent,
and the world equated him with Bào Zhāo.
This might be like Shāng or Zhōu.
The two Hú, Yǔ and Bái,
also possessed a clear rhythm.
The "Hánglù Nán" was composed by Dōngyáng Chái Kuò.
Bǎoyuè once stayed at his home,
and it happened that Kuò died.
Consequently, he secretly appropriated it.
Kuò's son brought out the original manuscript
intending to dispute the matter,
but was stopped by a large bribe.
Qí Huìxiū Shàngrén was
from the Tāng clan.
Dàoxiàn Shàngrén was
from the Bái clan.
Shì Bǎo was
from the Yǔ clan.
Shī Fù
Tāng Xiū said to Wú Mài:
"My poems can be the father of your poems."
Xiè Guānglù said:
"Not so.
Tāng can be an elder half-brother."
Shī Yǒu Shēngqì
Yuán Gǔ, the magistrate of Zhūjì in Qí,
was a mediocre poet,
and often claimed to be skilled.
He once said:
"My poems have life (shēngqì);
they need someone to grasp them.
Otherwise,
they will fly away."
Língyùn's courtesy name was Kè'ér.
Dù Míngshī of Qiántáng
dreamt one night that someone from the East came and entered his lodge from the south.
That very night,
Língyùn was born in Kuàijī.
Ten days later,
Xiè Xuán died.
Because his family considered descendants hard to come by,
they sent Língyùn to Dù Yě
(sound: Yǎ),
a quiet chamber of a family devoted to the Dao.
He was raised there,
and returned to the capital at fifteen.
Hence his courtesy name "Kè'ér".
A single scale of a horned dragon, a single feather of a phoenix.
Zhāng Jìyīng's ode to yellow chrysanthemums,
Pān Zhèngshū's excellence in green profusion—
though they did not possess all beauties,
they each attained a single scale of a horned dragon
and a single feather of a phoenix.
Poetry should not value the use of allusions.
Indeed, composing words by comparing events
is merely ordinary discourse.
When chanting emotions and nature,
why use past events?
"I miss you like flowing water"
is a direct observation.
"On a high terrace, much sorrowful wind"
is also merely what is seen.
"At dawn, I ascend the ridge-top"
is especially devoid of allusions.
"The bright moon illuminates accumulated snow"
how could it come from classics and histories?
Excellent phrases, ancient and modern,
are mostly not patchworks or borrowings,
but come from direct observation.
During the Dàmíng and Tàishǐ eras,
literature almost resembled copying from books.
Recently, writers
have gradually made it a custom.
Consequently, poetry contains no empty phrases,
and phrases contain no empty words.
This constrained patching and mending
has severely damaged literature.
The Eight Defects
Liáng Shěn Yuē said:
"There are eight defects in poetry:
First is Píngtóu (level head):
The first and second characters must not have the same initial consonant as the sixth and seventh characters.
For example, in 'Jīnrì liáng yànhuì,
huānlè suī jù chén,'
'jīn' and 'huān' are both level tones.
Second is Shàngwěi (rising tail):
The fifth character must not have the same initial consonant as the tenth character.
For example, in 'Qīngqīng hé pàn cǎo,
yùyù yuán zhōng liǔ,'
'cǎo' and 'liǔ' are both rising tones.
Third is Fēngyāo (bee waist):
The second character must not have the same initial consonant as the fifth character.
For example, in 'Wén jūn ài wǒ gān,
qiè yù zì xiū shì,'
'jūn' and 'gān' are both level tones,
'yù' and 'shì' are both entering tones.
Fourth is Hèténg (crane knee):
The fifth character must not have the same initial consonant as the fifteenth character.
For example, in 'Kè cóng yuǎnfāng lái,
yí wǒ yī shūzhá.
Shàng yán cháng xiāngsī,
xià yán jiǔ líbié.'
'Lái' and 'sī' are both level tones.
Fifth is Dàyùn (large rhyme):
For example, if 'shēng' and 'míng' are rhymes,
the preceding nine characters must not include 'jīng', 'qīng', 'píng', or 'róng'.
Sixth is Xiǎoyùn (small rhyme):
Excluding one character of the main rhyme,
among the nine characters, no two characters may share the same rhyme.
For example, 'yáo' and 'tiáo' should not be in different lines.
Seventh is Pángniǔ (side initial),
Eighth is Zhèngniǔ (main initial):
Within ten characters,
if two characters have the same initial consonant, it is a Zhèngniǔ.
If they do not belong to the same initial but have the same initial consonant, it is a Pángniǔ.
For example, 'liú' and 'liù' are Zhèngniǔ;
'liú' and 'liǔ' are Pángniǔ.
Of these eight types, Shàngwěi and Hèténg are most taboo,
while other defects are also generally avoided.
Wénzhōngzǐ discusses poetry
Suí Xué asked over a hundred times for the method of poetry,
but Wénzhōngzǐ did not answer.
Suí Xué then asked Xuē Shōu:
"I have discussed Chénliú above,
and Shěn and Xiè below.
I have categorized the four tones
and distinguished the eight defects.
Perhaps the Master has not understood?"
Xuē Shōu replied:
"The Master's discourse on poetry
illuminates the principles of the Three Mainstays above,
and reaches the nature of the Five Constants below.
A noble man expresses his aspirations through it,
and a sage observes the changes through it.
Now you are busily occupied with superficialities;
this is what the Master finds objectionable."
The Six Couplets
Táng Shàngguān Yí said:
"Poetry has six couplets:
First is Zhèngmíngduì (direct name couplet),
such as 'heaven' and 'earth', 'sun' and 'moon'.
Second is Tónglèiduì (same category couplet),
such as 'flower', 'leaf', 'grass', 'bud'.
Third is Liánzhūduì (string of pearls couplet),
such as 'xiāoxiāo' and 'hèhè'.
Fourth is Shuāngshēngduì (double initial couplet),
such as 'huáng huái' (yellow sophora) and 'lǜ liǔ' (green willow).
Fifth is Diéyùnduì (repeated rhyme couplet),
such as 'pánghuáng' (to wander) and 'fàngkuàng' (unrestrained).
Sixth is Shuāngnǐduì (double simile couplet),
such as 'spring trees' and 'autumn ponds'.
He also said poetry has eight couplets:
First is Fāngmíngduì (directional name couplet),
such as 'sending wine to the southeast,
welcoming a zither from the northwest.'
Second is Yìlèiduì (different category couplet),
such as 'wind weaves characters in the pond,
insects bore patterns on the leaves.'
Third is Shuāngshēngduì (double initial couplet),
such as 'autumn dew fragrances beautiful chrysanthemums,
spring breeze perfumes lovely orchids.'
Fourth is Diélèiduì (repeated category couplet),
such as 'wandering with a thousand kinds of thoughts,
procrastinating with a single mind.'
Fifth is Liánmiánduì (continuous couplet),
such as 'the remnant river, the river like a belt;
the first moon, the moon like eyebrows.'
Sixth is Shuāngnǐduì (double simile couplet),
such as 'discussing the moon, eyebrows surpass the moon;
speaking of flowers, cheeks excel the flowers.'
Seventh is Huíwénduì (palindrome couplet),
'qíng xīn yīn déyì, déyì suì xīn qíng'
(Feelings anew because of satisfaction, satisfaction then new feelings) is this.
Eighth is Gégōuduì (separated line couplet),
'longing and remembering again,
night after night tears wet my clothes.
Sighing in vain and weeping in vain,
day after day you have not returned' is this.
Sūn Yì discusses poetry
Sūn Yì said:
"From the Hàn dynasty, Wéi Mèng and Lǐ Líng were the originators of four and five-character verse.
During Jiàn'ān, Cáo and Liú were the peerless masters.
Ruǎn Jí's 'Yǒnghuái' and
Cì Xī's 'Bǔwáng'
largely grasped their essence.
The literature of Yǒngmíng was scattered and disparate,
merely describing objects and colors,
entirely lacking in inspiration and sentiment.
Later, poets competed to establish alternative styles,
taking incomprehensibility as profound charm,
and difficult characters as novelty.
Attacking unorthodox doctrines,
this is indeed excessive."
Jiǎorán discusses poetry
Shì Jiǎorán said:
“Poetry has four 'not-s,' four 'depths,' two 'essentials,' two 'losses,' four 'separations,' six 'delusions,' seven 'extremes,' and seven 'virtues.'”
The “four 'not-s'” mean: spirit high but not straining,
strength vigorous but not angry,
emotion abundant but not obscure,
talent ample but not scattered.
The “four 'depths'” mean: atmosphere deeply permeates form and structure,
conception deeply influences function and effect,
use of meter without stagnation deeply penetrates sound and antithesis,
use of allusions without obscurity deeply relates to analogy and comparison.
The “two 'essentials'” mean: strength must be complete but not harsh and jerky,
and spirit must be full but not overbearing.
The “two 'losses'” mean: although one wishes to abandon artifice and value straightforwardness,
divine thought cannot be straightforward;
although one wishes to abandon words and value meaning,
eloquent beauty cannot be forsaken.
The “four 'separations'” mean: desiring to express emotion yet departing from deep obsession,
desiring to incorporate history yet departing from pedantry,
desiring to be lofty and unrestrained yet departing from broad eccentricity,
and desiring to be soaring yet departing from frivolousness.
The “six 'delusions'” mean: taking grand emptiness as lofty antiquity,
taking slowness as ease and relaxation,
taking strangeness and disparity as novelty,
taking mistaken intention as unique excellence,
taking over-ripeness as subtle obscurity,
taking weak spirit as easiness.
The “seven 'extremes'” mean: to be extremely perilous yet not reclusive,
to be extremely unique yet not divergent,
to be extremely poignant yet traceless,
to be extremely close yet distant in meaning,
to be extremely unrestrained yet not wandering,
to be extremely beautiful yet natural.
The seven 'virtues' are: discerning form, lofty antiquity, elegant beauty, spirited charm, vitality, substantive structure, and style.
Three Thefts
Poetry has three thefts:
stealing words is the dullest thief,
as in the attributed line to Chángyú, “The sun and moon illuminate heaven's virtue.”
Though stealing ideas and events can be overlooked,
the emotion cannot be excused,
as in Liǔ Hún's lines: “Tiny ripples rise on Tàiyè Lake,
autumn on the tall trees of Chángyáng.”
and Shěn Quánqí's: “The lingering heat recedes from the small pond,
the cool of evening returns to the tall trees.”
Stealing momentum shows skillful talent and precise intention,
with no discernible trace,
it is the poet's art of stealing a white fox fur coat,
as in Jī Kāng's: “My gaze follows the returning wild geese,
my hand strums the five-stringed qín.”
and Wáng Chānglíng's: “My hand carries twin carp,
my gaze follows the wild geese for a thousand li.”
Bái Lètiān's Poetry
Bái Lètiān's admonitory poems excel in stirring,
his leisurely poems excel in letting go,
his melancholic poems excel in poignancy,
his lǜshī of over a hundred words excel in richness,
his five-character and seven-character poems of under a hundred words excel in emotion.
Poetry's 'Knot'
Poetry takes sound and meter as its 'knot' (vital point),
imagery as its bones,
and structure as its marrow.
Refining Lines
Refining lines is not as good as refining characters,
refining characters is not as good as refining intention,
refining intention is not as good as refining structure.
Natural Lines
There are natural lines,
lines divinely aided,
easy lines,
and painstaking lines.
Easy lines are composed spontaneously,
painstaking lines are obtained through deep thought.
Four Couplets
The first couplet is called 'breaking the topic,'
like a gale rolling up waves,
threatening to engulf the sky.
The second couplet is called the 'jaw couplet.'
The third couplet is called the 'neck couplet,'
and must have every character in antithesis.
The fourth couplet is called the 'closing couplet,'
which should be like a stone released from a high mountain,
once it's gone, it doesn't return.
Comparisons
Poetic comparisons:
Sun and moon compared to the ruler and empress,
dragon and heaven compared to the ruler's position,
rain and dew compared to moral beneficence,
thunder and lightning compared to penal majesty,
mountains and rivers compared to the nation,
yīn and yáng compared to ruler and minister,
metal and stone compared to loyalty and valor,
pine and bamboo compared to integrity and righteousness,
luán and phoenix compared to a jūnzi,
swallows and sparrows compared to petty people.
Fan Antithesis
When the first line and the third line are in antithesis,
and the second line and the fourth line are in antithesis,
as in:
“Last year beneath the flowers, we lingered and drank,
in the warm sun, tender peaches, orioles sang chaotically.
Today by the river, we part easily,
in pale mist and withered grass, horses frequently neigh.”
This is called 'fan antithesis.'

Bìluò Stela
In Jiàng Prefecture, there is a stela
with over a thousand characters in seal script,
which Lǐ Yángbīng loved.
Within it are the two characters “Bìluò,”
hence it is called the “Bìluò Stela.”
Later, an expert recognized it and said:
“In the thirteenth jǐ of the Táng Dynasty,
the dragon-star gathered at Guō Zhuāng.
Aizi Lǐ Xùn and others created a venerated Daoist image for their mother.”
Yuán and Bái's Thousand Replicated Poems
When Yuán was governor of Zhèdōng,
and Bái was prefect of Sūtái,
they set up post stations to deliver poetry scrolls.
It is said:
“Whenever there was a moon, we enjoyed it together;
there was no cup we didn't share.”
Their lines all secretly matched.
Empty Beam, Falling Swallow Mud
When Suí Yángdì composed poetry,
and required rhyming with the character “ní,”
all his ministers found it difficult to follow.
Xuē Dàohéng arrived later,
and in his completed poem, he had the line “empty beam, falling swallow mud.”
The Emperor resented him for surpassing himself,
and executed him on some pretext.
At the execution, he asked:
“Did you get 'empty beam, falling swallow mud'?”
Heavy Four Granted Scarlet
Mínghuáng played cáizhàn with Yáng Fēi,
and when about to roll "North,"
only a heavy four could win.
He repeatedly called out,
and indeed, a heavy four appeared.
The Emperor was delighted,
looked at Gāo Lìshì,
and ordered him to be granted scarlet robes.
Because of this, it was never changed.
Fetal Hair Brush
During the Southern Dynasties, there was an old woman skilled at making brushes,
and those made from fetal hair were particularly excellent.
There was also a brush maker named Tiětóu,
who could polish handles like jade.
Light of the Golden Áo
When Yú Dí was in Nánhǎi,
at midnight, it suddenly became as bright as dawn,
like the sun had just risen,
then suddenly it turned dark again.
He asked around Lǐngnán, and everyone said it was the same.
After more than a month, a foreign merchant said:
“On such and such a night of such and such a month,
I was traveling on the water with the wind,
when there appeared a great golden áo,
whose size was immeasurable.
The light from its two eyes shone brilliantly,
making the entire sea as bright as day.
A moment later, it disappeared.”
Only then was it known that it was the light illuminated by the golden áo.
Sēnggā as an Incarnation of Guānyīn
Master Sēnggā,
a man from the Western Regions,
whose surname was Hé.
He came to Sīzhōu Línhuái County in the early Táng Dynasty,
begged for land and erected a marker.
Beneath the marker, an inscription for an ancient temple and a golden statue were excavated,
bearing the characters “Pǔzhào Wángfó.”
So, a temple was built there.
Zhōngzōng asked Master Wànhuí who he was,
who replied:
“An incarnation of Guānshìyīn.”
Winter Melon Gùzi
After the *jìnshì* Cuī Yá and Zhāng Hù failed the imperial examination,
they traveled around Jiāng-Huái.
Whenever they were invited to a banquet,
they would declare themselves as chivalrous individuals.
Cuī Yá composed a poem titled "The Knight-Errant," saying:
"On the Tàiháng Ridge, three feet of snow;
In Cuī Yá's sleeve, three feet of iron.
If one day I meet a determined person,
I will leave home and bid farewell to my wife and children."
The two mutually praised each other.
Zhāng Hù presented a poem to the *láopénshǐ*,
who gave his son, named Dé Yàn, a minor position as a *cáo* official,
and he was nicknamed "Winter Melon."
Someone jokingly said:
"Your distinguished son is not suited for this position."
Zhāng Hù replied:
"A winter melon is just right to come from Hù's son."
Chūn'ér and Guìzǐ
Zhāng Hù had two sons:
one was Chūn'ér,
the other Guìzǐ.
He had a poem that said:
"Chūn'ér circling the trees in the spring garden,
Guìzǐ seeking flowers in the moonlight."
Water of Dàmíng Temple
Yá Hǎi, the *zhīshǐ* Bān Méng, visited Dàmíng Temple.
He saw a poem inscribed on the wall, which read:
"One person, dignified and grand,
Two luminaries, shining brightly.
The spring is deep by one *chǐ*,
A dot emerges beside the ice.
Two people connected,
Not lacking on one side.
Three beams, four pillars burning fiercely,
Add a double hook, two days complete."
Bān Méng said:
"'One person' is the character '大' (dà, big).
'Two luminaries' is the character '明' (míng, bright).
'The spring is deep by one *tiān*'
refers to '寸土' (cùn tǔ, an inch of earth),
which forms the character '寺' (sì, temple).
'A dot emerges beside the ice' is the character '水' (shuǐ, water).
'Two people connected' is the character '天' (tiān, heaven).
'Not lacking on one side' is the character '下' (xià, under).
'Three beams, four pillars burning fiercely' is the character '無' (wú, none).
'Add a double hook' is the character '比' (bǐ, compare).
Thus, 'The water of Dàmíng Temple is incomparable under heaven.'"
Shaping a round bamboo staff
When Lǐ Déyù was garrisoned in Zhèyòu,
he visited Gānlù Temple.
He gifted an old monk a bamboo staff,
saying:
"This is a bamboo given by a person from the kingdom of Dàyuān,
and it is the only one of its kind that is square."
Several years later,
he again took charge of Zhūfāng.
Upon arriving at the monastery,
he asked where the staff was.
The monk replied:
"I still treasure it to this day."
The duke requested to see it,
but it had been made round and lacquered.
From then on, the duke never looked at that monk again.
Moonlit night pavilion overlooking the river
In the summer moonlight at Gānlù Temple,
several people came from the west,
and went directly to the Wàngjiāng Pavilion.
They ordered wine and recited:
"Zhào Yīnéng could compose,
Zōu Yáng would offer poems.
What a pity the waters of the Western River,
Cannot save the fish in the rut."
Next, they said:
"How magnificent the scales that cross the sea,
How grand the wings that touch the sky.
Once they lose their auspicious conditions,
They turn into food for ants and crickets."
After reciting, they suddenly dispersed.
All the monks are scoundrels
A guest arrived at Qīnglóng Temple in the capital,
but the temple monks had no time to entertain him.
Another day he came again,
but was also hindered by other matters.
The guest grew angry,
and inscribed a poem on the gate, saying:
"The enshrined dragon goes to the Eastern Sea,
The sun and moon hide, slanting westward.
Jìngwén is not here now,
Broken stones fall into quicksand."
The monks all did not understand its meaning.
A *shāmí* explained:
"'The enshrined dragon goes' contains '合' (hé, to join/all).
'The sun and moon hide' contains '寺' (sì, temple).
'Jìngwén is not here' contains '苟' (gǒu, if/careless/scoundrel).
'Broken stones fall into quicksand' contains '卒' (zú, soldier/to die/finally/scoundrel).
This is an insolent remark."
Alchemy
The *hùjūn* Lǐ Quángāo
had a Daoist priest who claimed to be skilled in alchemy.
He said:
"You can find a cauldron
that can hold twenty *liǎng* of gold.
Every day, medicine will be administered,
and once the firing is complete, it will be replaced.
Do not worry about the time;
it will cycle endlessly."
Lǐ Quángāo was pleased with this proposal.
He had a golden belt that could reach the required amount.
After applying the fire,
he checked it daily.
When the day was complete,
he purified himself and opened it.
The golden color shone brightly,
and Lǐ Quángāo believed him.
Within three days, it was replaced again.
One day,
the Daoist priest did not come.
He opened the furnace to look,
and the gold was gone.
Paper butterflies
During the Xiántōng era,
there was a *jìnshì* Zhāng Cí who, after failing the examination,
traveled extensively in Jiāng-Huái.
He possessed Daoist arts,
cultivating *qì* and abstaining from grain.
He had a poem that said:
"What can be done about the golden crow (sun),
It flies ceaselessly overhead.
In the slow red furnace, medicine is born,
How can a jade-like countenance be preserved?
This year, flowers bloom on branches,
Next year, leaves fall from trees.
Better to simply drink wine,
Morning and evening, again and again."
When people invited him to drink,
he would cut three or twenty paper butterflies,
and blow on them with his *qì*,
causing them to fly in formation.
Later, he ascended in Jiāngnán,
leaving a poem that said:
"Zhāng Cí, Zhāng Cí, he does not linger,
All the classics of the world are within his belly.
His body floats aimlessly in the human realm,
His heart sways and moves beyond the heavens."
Zīzhōu offers a dragon
Zīzhōu offered a dragon to the Wéitiān Hall.
It was over ten feet long,
with all its scales and armor intact.
The duke placed it in Dàcí Hall for three days,
where it was suffocated by smoke and died.
The national history lacks records of this event.
What kind of omen was this?
Black and white *qì* in the Yángzǐ River
Lǐ Kèxiào ascended Mount Běigù on a moonlit night.
There was a black *qì*, like a dike,
emerging from the sea gate,
stretching across the middle of the Three Rivers.
There was also a white *qì*, like a rainbow,
emerging from Jīnshān,
intersecting with the black *qì*.
It was unknown whether it was sea monsters or *qì*.
Ten days later, the *shàngshū* Yù Wěi died.
Later, in the Yángzǐ River,
turtles and soft-shelled turtles floated downstream, filling the river,
all without heads.
At that time, Chancellor Hán died in the city.
A prime minister who saves the world
Yáo Chóng 姚崇 asked the Retainer Qí Hàn 齊澣,
“When I serve as prime minister,
what kind of people am I comparable to?
How do I compare to Guǎn Zhòng 管仲 and Yàn Yīng 晏嬰?”
Hàn 澣 replied,
“Guǎn 管 and Yàn 晏 established laws,
and although these laws might not extend to later generations,
they were effective during their lifetimes.
The laws that you, Prime Minister, established previously
have now all been changed.
In this respect, you are not their equal.
Prime Minister, you can be called a prime minister who saves the world.”
The Duke said,
“Is a prime minister who saves the world easily found?”
Ancient matters asked to Zhòng Shū 仲舒
Qí Hàn 齊澣 was good at understanding contemporary affairs,
and Gāo Zhòngshū 高仲舒 was good at understanding ancient matters.
Yáo Chóng 姚崇 said,
“If you want to know about ancient matters, ask Zhòng Shū 仲舒;
if you want to know about contemporary matters, ask Qí Hàn 齊澣.
Then there will be no failed governance.”
Spirit Shakes the Sash
The Hànlín Yuàn 翰林院 had a hanging bell
to provide warning in case of emergencies at night.
When documents were to be sent in or out,
a cord was pulled to replace a verbal summons.
During the Chángqìng 長慶 era,
when Zànhuáng 贊皇 was an academician,
there was warfare in Héběi 河北.
The bell frequently made a sound,
but no person was ever seen.
When the sound was urgent, the military situation was urgent;
when the sound was slow, the military situation was slow.
This never erred.
Yuán Xiāng 元相 was also in the academy,
and Yuán’s 元 poem contains "spirit shakes the sash," which refers to this.
My Late Father Holding a Torch
During the Zhēnyuán 貞元 era,
Secretary Xún 荀尚書 was at a village villa.
One night, he went out and lost his way.
Suddenly, a torch fire led the way forward.
When he arrived at his gate,
he saw the person holding the torch;
it was his late father.
Spirit Announces Fortune or Misfortune
Dòu Cān 竇參 was the magistrate of Púqí 蒲圻.
There was a spirit shrine,
which he wanted to demolish.
He dreamt that a spirit said,
“The reason I have not been able to harm you
is because you will one day hold the position of prime minister.
Please spare me for now,
and I can foretell your fortune or misfortune.”
After he awoke,
he entered the spirit shrine to offer sacrifices,
treating the spirit as his elder brother.
Later, whenever a transfer of office was imminent,
the spirit would report it beforehand.
When the spirit wished to meet,
he would first arrange a lavish meal in an empty room,
surrounding it with silk screens.
Those on either side would hear the sound of two people laughing and talking.
When Cān 參 was later demoted to Prefectural Assistant of Liǔzhōu 柳州,
the spirit said,
“You should manage your household affairs.
In two or three days, an envoy from the north will arrive,
and you will not be spared.”
A few days later, the imperial messenger arrived,
and indeed there was a subsequent decree.
Jade Fish Tally
During the Zhēnyuán 貞元 era,
Sīxūn Lángzhōng Lǐ Dí 司勛郎中李迪 returned home after court.
