He dreamt of a yellow-clad man leading him outside the door,
where someone said,
“Do not come until the jade fish tally descends.”
Later, on the Dragon's Tail Path in the court hall,
he saw a jade fish,
which he played with until he reached home.
Indeed, he died a few days later.
Chicken Master
Fèi Jīshī 費雞師 (Fei the Chicken Master):
Whenever a sick person came to him,
he would take a chicken and go with them,
then recite incantations and scold the chicken,
ordering it to enter the sick person's place.
If the chicken entered and died,
the sick person would immediately recover.
If the chicken came out,
the sick person would not recover.
At the time, he was called "Chicken Master."
Wù and Dīng Combined Pass the Exam
Zhào Huàchéng 趙化成, when he first sat for the civil service examination,
dreamt of a black-clad man who said,
“Your name is Huàchéng 化成.
The character ‘chéng 成’
is composed of wù 戊 and dīng 丁.
You must pass when wù 戊 and dīng 丁 combine.”
Indeed, he passed the examination that year.
Púsàmán 菩薩蠻 Lyrics
Lú Jiàng 盧絳 dreamt he was drinking sugarcane juice.
A woman in white sang the lyrics of "Púsàmán 菩薩蠻."
After singing, she said,
“Later, we shall meet at Gǔzǐ Pí 崮子陂.”
Later, when Jīnlíng 金陵 was pacified,
the imperial court assembled the troops to descend into formation at Gǔzǐ Pí 崮子陂 outside Chānghé Mén 閶闔門.
Changing the Teacup
Chén Yǒng 陳永, the Gate Supervisor of Jiāngnán Nèimén 江南內門, lost an important document.
A shaman, whose divinations were quite accurate,
was asked about it.
He said,
“The document is on the shelf on the east wall.”
Chén 陳 saw a teacup before the spirit,
and initially thought of exchanging it.
As he left the door,
the shaman said,
“Tell him not to forget the teacup.”
The cup
Chén 陳 subsequently found the document,
which was indeed for exchanging the teacup.
Ancient Mirror, Stone Figures
Xú Xuàn 徐鉉 obtained a mirror.
When he looked into it, he only saw one eye with a bear.
People from the mountains and wilds liked to collect unusual objects,
such as stone turtles, stone peaches, and stone dates.
He once dreamt that a person introduced himself, saying,
“My surname is Shí 石,
and I depend on you.”
Later, he obtained a stone figure,
over a foot long,
complete with eyebrows and eyes.
In this age, there are stone swallows, stone crabs, and the like.
Also, pine trees can transform into stone.
Lǒngzhōu 隴州 has fish-shaped stones
which, when placed among books, can ward off bookworms.
Mágū 麻姑 of Fāngzhàng Shān 方丈山
Wáng Bǎoyì 王保義, while serving as Xíngjūn Sīmǎ 行軍司馬 for Gāo Cónghuì 高從誨 in Jīngnán 荊南,
had a daughter who would not eat meat or blood.
At five years old, she understood scriptures like the Huángtíng Jīng 黃庭經.
When she grew up,
she dreamt of crossing water and climbing a mountain,
where she saw golden and silver palaces,
which were said to be "Fāngzhàng Xiān 方丈仙."
There were about ten female immortals,
one of whom was named "Mágū 麻姑."
They bonded as sisters
and taught her several pipa pieces.
From then on, they met every few nights,
and in over a year, she learned more than a hundred pieces,
the most exceptional of which was "Dú Zhǐ Shāng 獨指商,"
played with one finger for the entire piece.
She again dreamt that Mágū 麻姑 said,
“I will invite you soon.”
The next day, there were auspicious clouds, cranes, and music in the courtyard,
and the girl suddenly died.
Golden Shuttle on the Melon on Qīxī 七夕
The Dīng 丁 family in Càizhōu 蔡州 was skilled in needlework.
Every Qīxī 七夕, they would pray with wine and fruit.
Suddenly, they saw a meteor fall into the feast.
The next day, they found a golden shuttle on the melon.
From then on, their cleverness increased.
Submitted.
Kite Poem
Chén Jìdá 陳繼達 was originally a military man,
unlettered.
He dreamt someone made him drink over a liter of black ink,
and he immediately became literate.
He composed a "Kite Poem," saying:
“If one can understand the favors and disgraces of life,
it is just like a fluttering paper owl.
It is only sent up to the sky by the wind;
without wind, there will always be a time for it to come down.”
Consuming Shú 朮
It is said that when consuming shú 朮, one should avoid sparrows and pigeons.
This is not referring to doves and pigeons,
but rather to clams and oysters.
Outer Aide Dāo Yǎn 刀衍 had long consumed shú 朮.
After eating clams, he suffered from bloody diarrhea,
but eating doves and pigeons caused no ill effects.
Once, sparrows fighting fell into a basin of water.
Within ten days, they all transformed into clams.
Later, when dead sparrows were thrown in,
they did not transform.
Sparrows and clams are of the same kind of qi.
Greasy Head, Sweaty Embroidered Pillow
A courtesan in Jiēzhōu,
was taken in by a traveling envoy.
One day, when the man was out,
the courtesan was sleeping alone in the hall, resting on an embroidered pillow.
Suddenly, she saw a woman,
who grabbed the courtesan by the head and ordered her to rise,
saying:
"Your greasy head is sweating on his embroidered pillow."
The courtesan hit her,
and she ran to the east of the hall and disappeared.
Celadon Bowl
The abbot of Xiàyuàn in Bādōng,
found a celadon bowl by the water and
brought it back.
He placed cut flowers before the Buddha statue,
and the next day the bowl was full of flowers.
He then placed a little rice in it,
and overnight the bowl was also full of rice.
The same happened when he placed coins, gold, and silver in it.
From then on, the monastery became rich and prosperous.
When the abbot was old,
one day he crossed the river to inspect some fields,
and took the bowl from his bosom and threw it into the middle of the current.
His younger brother was astonished.
The master said:
"When I die,
will you all be able to carefully manage and uphold yourselves?
I abandon it,
not wishing it to increase your karmic burdens."
The abbot died soon after.
Crane Named Dāngē
The Daoist Zhào Zìrán from Fènghuángshān in Chízhōu,
dreamed that Yīn Zhēnjūn gave him a branch of cypress leaves.
He ate nine folds of it,
and thereafter he did not eat,
and his spirit and energy were extraordinary.
He wrote a poem saying:
"I once wished to dwell on mountain islands,
idly sleeping in the cold Jade Grotto.
Dāngē sometimes leads the dance,
coming and going, riding a cloudy luán."
Someone asked:
"Why is it named Dāngē?"
He replied:
"It is a crane."
Fish That Swallowed a Boat
Lǐ Chóngguī saw a large fish on a sandy island in the sea.
He cut open its belly,
and found a small boat,
along with three dead people,
their clothes still intact.
Immortal's Bone-Changing Coffins
On Wǔyíshān in Jiànzhōu,
there suddenly appeared the sound of celestial music,
its melody resembled "Welcoming the Immortal Guest" but had no rhythm.
There are many immortal's bone-changing coffins in the mountains,
located on precipitous cliffs.
True Chrysanthemum, Wild Chrysanthemum
The people of Shǔ plant many chrysanthemums,
as their shoots can be used in vegetables,
and their flowers as medicine.
Gardens and vegetable patches all cultivate them,
and they are sold everywhere in the marketplaces.
People from the countryside often gather wild chrysanthemums for apothecaries,
which is quite a grave mistake.
True chrysanthemum prolongs life,
while wild chrysanthemum causes diarrhea.
As Zhāng Huá said:
"Huángjīng prolongs life,
Gōuwěn kills people."
Hair Five Chǐ Long
Lǐ Shānfǔ had a beautiful appearance,
and his hair was over five chǐ long.
After every washing,
he had two maids hold a golden basin to catch it while he combed it.
A guest came to visit,
saw him combing his hair,
and rushed out,
mistaking him for a woman.
Shānfǔ called out to him repeatedly,
and only then did the guest realize his mistake.
Ten-Color Stationery
Xuē Tāo of Chéngdū was a rare beauty among courtesans.
When Yuán Wēizhī governed Shǔ,
she often accompanied him at banquets and smiled.
Later, Master Yuán sent her a poem on sōnghuā paper, saying:
"After parting, my thoughts of you are separated by smoke and water,
calamus flowers bloom high among the five-colored clouds."
Xuē planted calamus by Huànhuā Xī,
hence this line.
Sōnghuā paper, Jīnshā paper, Liúshā paper, Cǎixiá paper, Jīnfěn paper, and Lóngfèng paper from Shǔ,
have all been discontinued in recent years;
only the ten-color stationery still exists.
Dog Classic
Zhēnbái Xiānshēng Táo Hóngjǐng said:
"Péi Zhēnjūn liked to keep white dogs and white chickens.
The dog was named Báilíng,
and the chicken was named Báijīng.
For scholars of the Dao who live in mountains and forests,
these can ward off evil.
The Dǒugjīng says:
'If a household keeps a dog,
a pure white one is ominous.'
What Zhēnjūn said is certainly not a mistake.
What the Dǒugjīng says applies to common households."
Dream of Swallowing a Golden Tortoise
Liú Zàn's literary thoughts were very slow,
so he sincerely prayed to the celestial phenomena for literary talent.
One night,
he dreamed he swallowed a golden tortoise about the size of a coin,
and thereafter he had great literary inspiration.
During the Mèng dynasty, he served as an academician,
and had a collection titled Yùtáng Jí.
One day,
he vomited a golden tortoise into the water,
and died not long after.
Offering Food
Chén Yuánzhí enjoyed offering food as a hidden virtue,
and all birds and insects received his kindness.
Whenever he ate on the Jīnyuán,
hundreds of birds flew around him, singing.
One night,
he dreamed a man in scarlet robes said:
"You have accumulated hidden virtue for all creatures.
Your lifespan was originally not to exceed forty,
but it has been extended to ninety-nine years."
Monkey's Revenge
Someone kept a mother monkey and her baby.
One day, a kite flew down and attacked the baby,
pecking its brain in front of its mother,
and eating its marrow.
The monkey cried mournfully,
and did not eat for three days.
It went into the kitchen,
took a piece of meat,
placed it on its head,
and went to the central courtyard,
as if waiting for something.
Soon after, a kite indeed came to snatch the meat.
The monkey used both hands to tear its wings,
and gnawed its brain.
Everyone was greatly pleased.
Rénzōng's Tolerance for Admonishment
Bāo Zhěng was an upright remonstrance official,
whose critical words and righteous opinions
stirred the court and the common people.
Rénzōng said:
"Loyal and straightforward words are bitter to the mouth and harsh to the ear,
but they are indeed beneficial.
Even if they are not beneficial,
they do no harm.
Why must one reject and blame them?"
Prime Minister's Ward, Assistant Minister's Hamlet
In Xīluò, there were five prime ministerial residences,
belonging to Wén Lùgōng, Fù Xiàng, Wáng Xiàng, and the two Zhāng Xiàng.
The proverb says:
"There is a Prime Minister's Ward, an Assistant Minister's Hamlet."
Jade Cups
When Hán Wèigōng was the governor of Běidū,
someone presented him with two jade cups.
The duke rewarded him with a hundred gold pieces.
He then hosted a banquet, inviting distinguished guests,
and specially set up a table,
placing the cups upon it,
intending to pour wine and offer it to all the seated guests.
Suddenly, an officer accidentally bumped the table, knocking it over,
and both jade cups shattered.
Everyone seated turned pale,
and the officer prostrated himself on the ground, awaiting punishment.
The duke's expression remained unchanged,
and he said:
"Objects break sometimes.
It was an accident on your part,
not intentional.
What crime is there?"
Lái Gōng's Qiàntáo
Kòu Lái dreamt of a beautiful woman named Qiàntáo.
Later, an old woman brought her daughter,
and the Duke visited her.
The old woman said:
"My daughter does not see guests."
The Duke said:
"You should try calling her."
After a short while,
she came out and bowed, saying:
"This is my lord."
The Duke realized what he had dreamt earlier,
gave the old woman one hundred pieces of silver,
and bought the girl as his concubine.
Her words were often helpful.
Later, when the Duke was stationed in the north gate (Běimén),
there was not a single day without banquets.
There was a skilled singer,
to whom the Duke gave a bolt of silk,
but he was not yet satisfied.
Qiàntáo composed a poem that said:
"One clear song, one bolt of silk,
yet the beauty still seems to find it too little.
Unaware that under the weaver girl's window,
how many times the shuttle was thrown to weave it into being?"
Later, when the Duke was demoted to Léizhōu,
Qiàntáo wept and said:
"I have no extraordinary merit to ascend to an immortal,
but I have a minor accomplishment that prevents me from entering the realm of ghosts.
In a previous life, I was a disciple of an immortal and a knight-errant.
There was once a high official who was poisoned by his maidservant.
I went to execute her,
but I was not careful enough;
she had been pregnant for several months.
Thus, I killed two people with one execution,
and for that, I was condemned to re-enter transmigration.
Due to a karmic affinity,
I became your maidservant.
Now I am about to leave.
You are destined to be the lord of the underworld,
the King of Jambudvīpa (Yánfú Tí).
The heavenly decree is about to descend;
you should prepare for what comes next."
The next day, Qiàntáo indeed died.
The Duke also passed away not long after.
Míng Huáng
Táng Yáng Fēi dreamt of traveling with Míng Huáng to Líshān.
Upon arriving at Xīngyuán Post Station,
they were about to eat
when the imperial concubine (hòugōng) suddenly reported a fire.
In a hurry, they exited the station,
and looking back, all the wooden structures of the station were engulfed in flames.
Suddenly, there were two dragons.
The Emperor rode a white dragon,
flying swiftly;
the concubine rode a black dragon,
moving very slowly.
There was no one on their sides,
only a disheveled, black-faced creature,
whose appearance was not human-like.
Seeing the Emperor go far away,
it touched a perilous peak,
and sank into the mist.
Opening her eyes, she was alone in a room.
The black-faced creature said:
"I am the spirit of this peak.
A rider came to bestow upon the concubine the title 'Queen Mother of Sericulture of Yìzhōu'."
Suddenly, she awoke from her dream.
The next day,
news of the rebellion in Yúyáng arrived,
and the concubine was hanged to death at Mǎwéi.
The Emperor said:
"The dream has now come true.
Traveling with me to Líshān,
'lí' (驪) is homophonous with 'lí' (離, to separate).
The fire started while we were about to eat,
a sign of losing food.
Fire
is the essence of war.
All the wooden structures of the station were burned;
'yì' (易) is homophonous with 'yì' (驛, post station),
adding 'mù' (木, wood) next to it forms the character 'Yáng' (楊).
My riding a white dragon
is a symbol of traveling west;
her riding a black dragon
is the principle of darkness.
Traveling alone without assistance from either side,
'one rider' (yī qí)
refers to a horse.
The peak spirit is a mountain ghost.
Did she indeed die at Mǎwéi?
She was to be granted the title 'Queen Mother of Sericulture of Yìzhōu'.
Sericulture (yǎng cán)
is for producing silk.
Adding 'sī' (絲, silk) next to 'yì' (益) forms the character 'yì' (縊, to hang)."
In the dream, she arrived at a place
titled "Dōngxū Fǔ",
and then another courtyard
titled "Tàiyī Yùzhēn Yuánshàng Fēi Yuàn".
Entering, she saw Tàizhēn,
separated by a mica screen.
They sat facing each other, but her form was not visible.
The Emperor said:
"Do you miss me?"
The concubine said:
"Humans are not wood or stone;
how could they be without feelings?
On another day, we shall together straddle the dark glow and floating shadows to roam in Yùxū."
The Emperor said:
"The jade sea is boundless,
the path to the immortal mountains is cut off.
How can we communicate?"
The concubine said:
"If you meet the noble person (shàngrén) of the Wild Goose Mansion (Yàn Fǔ),
you can send a message through him."
After the Emperor awoke,
he composed a poem that said:
"The wind was fierce, clouds startled, rain did not form;
waking, the immortal dream was very clear.
At that time, I bitterly regretted the shadow of the silver screen,
which blocked the immortal concubine, letting me only hear her voice."
Later, remembering the words of the noble person of the Wild Goose Mansion,
indeed, a Dàoshì from Hóngdū, having found a bejeweled casket and private words on an immortal peak at sea, returned.
The Jade Emperor Bestows Cooling Elixir
Lǚ Huì was offered an appointment but
was exiled to Ānzhōu due to his straightforward remonstrance.
One day, as he sat alone in a small pavilion,
he closed his eyes and immediately had a vision:
A boy in green clothes said:
"The Jade Emperor (Yù Dì) is traveling south to Yánzhōu,
and summons you to accompany him
to correct the numerous immortals."
From then on, he ate heavenly food
and traveled in the Purple Palace (Zǐfǔ).
Yánzhōu was bitterly hot,
so the Supreme Emperor (Shàng Dì) bestowed upon the Duke a pellet of cooling elixir.
The Duke bowed, accepted the gift, and swallowed it.
His throat felt like ice and snow.
The Duke knew he would not be long in this world.
There was Zhū Míngfù,
who on the Xiāngjiāng road saw several hundred golden-armored officers and soldiers,
riding jade-horned blue deer.
Míngfù bowed and said:
"Are you immortals?"
They smiled but did not answer,
and extemporaneously composed a poem that said:
"Merit and good deeds are occasionally recorded in the Jade Palace (Yù Què),
while countless caps and robes are buried in dust.
I now follow the Emperor as a supervisor and corrector.
Who else would dare to stand firm in the Censorate (Bǎitái)?"
Death of the Soldier who Sold Medicine
In Guǎnchéng there was a Daoist
wearing a robe of blue cloth,
carrying a small basket.
He merely said he sold medicine for sudden death.
There was a bowman named Lǐ,
who said:
"I heard that Mr. Lǚ conceals his true identity among people.
This person sells medicine,
but for days no one has bought any.
Could it be that he uses the Way to transform people?"
He immediately went and asked:
"Everyone fears death,
so how could there be any buyers?"
The Daoist sighed and said:
"My medicine has seven pills.
Take them and you will die instantly.
It only costs seven gold coins."
Lǐ said:
"I am not afraid of death."
He offered seven gold coins
and requested one dose of the medicine.
The Daoist opened his gourd and took out the medicine,
which was all deep red.
He said:
"You will surely die.
You should make arrangements for your affairs."
Lǐ received the medicine
and hesitated, not daring to take it.
By dawn, he thought again:
"Seven pills will cause instant death?
How can that be possible?"
Thereupon he took and swallowed them.
When they dissolved, they were seven pieces of what common folk call "farting beetles" (pì pán chóng).
He then cursed, saying:
"The Daoist tricked me!"
He immediately went to question him.
The Daoist smiled and said:
"The previous medicine is all gone.
I should give you other medicine."
He again opened his gourd and took out seven pills,
all brown.
Lǐ immediately took them.
The Daoist said:
"We will meet another day between Huái and Zhè."
He bowed deeply and left.
From then on, Lǐ found all food and drink foul and unbearable.
He drank only a few cups of wine daily.
Taking His Wife Away.
At Chìgāngdiàn, south of Fēngqiūxiàn,
every night there was a strange occurrence.
It constantly called out, "Take your wife away."
Travelers were afraid and dared not pass.
A courier, Zhāng Dé, was carrying an urgent dispatch
and dared not delay.
Late at night,
an old woman emerged from the grass
and said:
"Take your wife away."
Dé, who was naturally bold,
shouted sternly:
"I'll take you!
Get on my back."
The old woman happily stepped forward.
Dé grabbed her two feet
and tied them to his waist with a rope.
After traveling several *lǐ*,
the old woman said to put her down.
Dé did not respond.
The old woman pleaded ceaselessly.
Soon her voice became very low,
and her body also grew light.
When they reached the next post station,
he lifted her to look,
but found only a piece of an ancient, rotten coffin board tied there.
When he burned it,
the stench spread for several *lǐ*,
and there was a chirping sound.
The strange phenomenon then ceased.
Lǐ Bái Seen on Sōngshān.
Bái Guīnián arrived at Sōngshān.
From afar, he saw the Eastern Peak,
where ancient trees' canopies almost swept the ground.
He walked to its side,
where ritual vessels were arranged.
A man came forward and said:
"Lǐ Hànlín summons you."
Guīnián hurried forward.
The man, dressed in a loose robe and wide sash,
with a refined and brilliant complexion,
said:
"I am Lǐ Bái of Táng.
Your ancestor is Bái Jūyì.
Although we were not of the same generation,
we were contemporaries.
People say our Ways are alike,
so now we visit each other.
I myself achieved water-deliverance (shuǐjiě),
and have been wandering among mountains and rivers.
Thinking of my homeland,
I returned west to the peaks of Sōng.
The Emperor sent a decree to the heavens,
and I was appointed here.
I have been in charge of memorials for a hundred years now.
Recently I passed Tóng,
and coincidentally encountered a lyric that said:
'Mistakenly entered the deep grotto of the Peach Blossom Spring,
a wondrous song and dancing phoenix.
Always remember the moment of parting,
the bright moon, fallen flowers, and heavy mist.
Like a dream,
like a dream,
seeing you off at the gate with tears.' " Guīnián asked:
"Where is my ancestor now?"
He replied:
"He is at the Terrace of Merits and Virtues,
following his former aspirations."
He then produced a scroll and gave it to Guīnián, saying:
"Read this, and you can understand the language of birds in the nine heavens
and the speech of beasts on earth.
If you cultivate more merits and virtuous deeds,
you can attain immortality."
Later, Guīnián traveled to Lùzhōu.
The Grand Protector, knowing he possessed unusual skills,
summoned him for questioning.
Two sparrows chirped and flew past the courtyard.
The Grand Protector asked:
"What are they saying?"
He replied:
"In a civilian's idle granary west of the city,
there is leftover grain on the ground.
They are going to share it."
He sent someone to verify it,
and it was true.
Then he saw a stable horse raise its head and neigh,
and asked:
"What is this one saying?"
He replied:
"The feed in the trough is hot
and cannot be eaten."
It was near Qīngmíng,
and an officer was driving more than twenty sheep.
He said:
"The last sheep won't move.
Whip it to make it move."
The Grand Protector asked:
"The sheep won't move.
Is there a reason?"
He replied:
"The sheep says a lamb in its belly is about to be born.
It wants to give birth before it dies."
The Grand Protector then kept the sheep for over a month,
and indeed it gave birth.
Guīnián then wandered outside the mundane world,
and occasionally someone would see him.
The巡察 General and the Jīn Guāngmíng Jīng.
Chén Yáozī moored his boat at Sānshān Jī.
An old man said:
"Tomorrow afternoon there will be a great wind.
Your boat will surely capsize.
You should be careful."
The next day, the sky was clear,
with not a cloud for ten thousand *lǐ*.
The boatmen wanted to depart
and requested to untie the ropes.
The Duke said:
"Wait a little longer."
All the other boats left the shore at once.
The Duke made an excuse,
and by noon, the sky was still calm.
Suddenly, dark clouds rose at the horizon,
and a violent windstorm arrived,
breaking trees and sending sand flying.
The raging waves were like mountains.
Many of the other boats sank.
The Duke was astonished and exclaimed.
He then saw the old man again, who said:
"I am also not human.
I am the Patrol General (Yóuyì Jiàng) of this river.
Because you will one day hold the position of Prime Minister,
I naturally had to inform you."
The Duke asked:
"How can I repay your kindness?"
The old man said:
"I originally seek no reward.
When a noble person like yourself arrives,
the dragon gods naturally ought to protect you.
I wish to obtain one copy of the *Jīn Guāngmíng Jīng* (Golden Light Sutra).
I can then, by its power, receive a promotion."
The Duke agreed.
When he arrived in the capital, he sent someone to Sānshān Jī
to cast three copies of the *Jīn Guāngmíng Jīng* into the water.
He dreamt of the old man, who said:
"I only wished for one,
but you granted three.
I have been promoted several ranks."
He bowed twice and departed.
Regarding matters in the Hùn Yù
A citizen named Qiū Xìn suddenly died.
After spending a night, he revived.
He said:
“Initially, I saw an official pulling something out of my mouth,
and then my breath ceased.
I was thrown outside the gate.
I bowed my head and entered the gate,
seeing my corpse lying in the hall below.
Another official said:
‘Do not let his breath completely cease.
This is merely for an interrogation.’
A soul was left to guard the corpse.
Shortly after, I arrived at a place
that resembled a government office,
and was ordered to proceed to the Hùn Yù for questioning.
I entered a thorny gate.
The ground was so foul and stinking that it was unbearable to approach.
There was tangled hair on the ground.
An official struck a hair bun with a staff and said:
‘Qiáo Chéng!’
Immediately, a head emerged and responded.
The official said:
‘You were just about to say that on a certain date, month, and year, you killed twelve sheep and pigs.
It was Qiū Xìn who sent you to kill them.
Now, respond to Xìn.’
Xìn recognized the voice;
it was Qiáo Èr Láng from the south of the prefecture.
His face was so ugly that it was unrecognizable.
He called out to Xìn, saying:
‘My sins fill heaven and earth.
Please, for me, divide the number twelve
to reduce my transgressions.’
Xìn replied:
‘Yesterday, many households offered sacrifices to the gods,
and I was indeed in charge of it,
but I merely purchased from you;
I did not send you to kill them.’
His head then sank back into the filth.
The official said:
‘You are innocent.
You should return.’
Xìn asked when this person could be released.
The official said:
‘He has killed tens of thousands of pigs and sheep.
He must endure this suffering for thousands of years
before he can be reborn.
Then his flesh will be cut off to repay those he killed.
Dying and being reborn,
being reborn and dying again,
even after thousands of generations,
the repayment will not be complete.”
The poems of Lǐ Hòu Zhǔ
Lǐ Zhǔ of Jiāngnán had double pupils in one eye.
He was devoted to drinking through long nights,
and was supplied three *shí* of wine daily within his palace.
Tài Zǔ ordered that he not be given wine.
He memorialized, saying:
“If not,
how can I pass the days?”
So, the supply was restored.
Lǐ Zhǔ’s appearance was exceedingly beautiful.
Tài Zǔ said:
“You are not of noble appearance;
you are merely a Hanlin Academician.”
There is a poem that says:
“My temples have gained new white streaks in recent days,
the chrysanthemums are still yellow as they were last year.”
Another line says:
“Bluebirds do not carry messages from beyond the clouds,
the fragrant emptiness forms sorrow in the rain.”
Both express a lack of contentment,
with the grief of a lost nation.
A poem at his deathbed says:
“After myriad ages, all culminates in one intoxication,
in the land of death, the burial ground has high plains.”
“The day my heart agrees is the time your fate will prosper”
Táng Zhuāng Zōng had imperial guards who accompanied him,
who begged for promotions and appointments for their merits.
The Emperor ultimately did not accept their requests.
Lǐ Cíyuán recounted their contributions for them.
The Emperor said:
“I also know that Qìng Báo has military merits,
but whenever I see his face, I feel angry.”
He then cited a poem by Táng Tài Zōng, saying:
“The day my heart agrees,
is the time your fate will prosper.”
Xuē Lín’s poem
Xuē Lín’s poem says:
“Pavilions near water are the first to catch the moon,
flowers and trees facing the sun are quick to meet spring.”
“Solo Falcon Striker”
Wáng Sù served as Xiàn Tái.
His demeanor was very forceful,
earning him the moniker “Solo Falcon Striker.”
Chosen by dice
Dīng Wèi was appointed Cān Zhèng.
Yáng Yì congratulated him.
He said:
“It was merely a choice by dice.
What is there to speak of?”
“True Salt and Iron”
Chén Shù served as Sān Sī Shǐ.
He was skilled in strategy.
Tài Zōng personally inscribed on a palace pillar:
“Chén Shù, the True Salt and Iron.”
“Mountain of Blood”
Zhēn Zōng, when residing in Zhū Dǐ,
once built an artificial mountain,
which was exquisitely crafted.
He hosted a banquet and invited his officials.
Yáo Tǎn said:
“This is but a mountain of blood gathered from the toil of the people.”
The Emperor demolished it,
and wrote the *Rú Xíng* on its wall.
Boxed meals
Dù Hào was widely learned.
Zhēn Zōng asked when boxed meals originated.
Hào replied:
“When Hàn Jǐng Dì was crown prince,
Wén Dì said:
‘The Crown Prince’s meals must be varied.
Order the Grand Provisioner to prepare two boxes,
and bestow them upon him.’
This was its beginning.”
Wearing patched robes to raise lice
Chá Dào had a simple and ancient nature.
In his youth, he lived in Láng Shān Temple.
He personally undertook chores like fetching firewood and water,
to provide for the monks.
He did not wash his patched robes,
in order to raise fleas and lice.
He rose to the position of Lóng Tú Gé Dài Zhì.
Tài Zǔ's cap
During a hot month, Tài Zǔ was cooling off in the imperial garden.
He summoned Academician Dòu Yí to draft an imperial edict.
Upon reaching the garden gate,
Dòu Yí saw Tài Zǔ with his cap pushed back,
sitting barefoot.
Yí stood back and did not advance.
Tài Zǔ smiled slightly,
and immediately ordered for his imperial robes.
Yí memorialized, saying:
“Your Majesty has just ascended to the great position.
It is fitting to set an example for the world with proper etiquette.
I fear that valiant heroes, hearing of this, might lose their resolve.”
Tài Zǔ straightened his demeanor and thanked him.
After this, when facing close officials,
he never appeared without his cap and belt.
Key to the Northern Gate
Guān Lái Gōng was guarding the Northern Gate.
A Khitan envoy passed by,
and the envoy said:
“The Grand Councilor is highly esteemed.
Why is he not in the Central Secretariat?”
He replied:
“His Majesty believes that the court is peaceful,
and the Northern Gate is a key strategic point,
which cannot be entrusted to anyone but me.”
Heavenly Scroll Descends on Lóng Tú Gé
When the Heavenly Scroll first descended,
all the officials memorialized with congratulations,
their words overflowing with praise.
However, Dài Zhì Qī Lún alone said:
“Such an event has not occurred for ages.
We should not rely on it as an omen of good fortune.
Instead, we should be vigilant, afraid, examine ourselves, and cultivate virtue,
to respond to the will of Heaven.”
Dīng and Guān encounter
Guān Lái Gōng was demoted to Hǎi Kāng.
Dīng Jìn Gōng was punished and sent to Zhū Yá.
He borrowed a route from Guān Lái Gōng and said:
“My exile and banishment are truly unjust.
Now Dīng is coming,
and some of my servants are strong-willed.
They will certainly seek revenge.
We must guard against this.”
So, he gathered them to play dice and chess.
When he heard that Dīng had left the border,
he dismissed them.
Oleander screen
Lú Xiàngguó had an unmarried daughter,
whose nature was solitary and lofty.
Every evening,
she would travel through the air with a Daoist priest
for worldly pleasures.
Her mother became aware of this
and informed the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister said:
"My daughter's nature is pure and detached;
she must be a celestial immortal."
He then asked about the contents of her room.
The daughter said:
"On the north wall of the hall, there is a screen with oleander flowers."
The Prime Minister said:
"Tonight, use a needle to pass a thread through it."
The next day,
the duke ordered both markets to borrow oleander flower screens,
and to write the street and alley names and surnames on each.
By noon,
there were over eight hundred items.
The one with the needle and thread passed through it
was inscribed:
"Tōnghuàfāng,
surname Zuǒ Yuánfǎng."
The Prime Minister immediately summoned him.
When the Daoist priest arrived,
he sat down and placed wine,
then threw the cup onto a beam.
The Prime Minister looked up,
and suddenly the Daoist priest disappeared.
He returned to check on his daughter,
and she was also nowhere to be found.
He searched for many years but never found her,
and no one understood why.
The 'White Pills Formula'
Qīngdùlǐ Lǎoshì, who had inherited medical skills
and excelled at playing the qín,
claimed to have attained Jī Kāng's mastery.
One day, due to drunkenness, he accidentally fell into a dry well
and reached a cave entrance,
inscribed:
"Xuándūdòng."
He saw a Daoist priest,
who made Lǐ play the qín,
performing the melody "Guǎnglímgsàn."
The Daoist priest said:
"This is your own composition;
Shúyè is your previous incarnation."
He ordered him to be served stone marrow to drink,
and then pulled a plain book from a stone beam.
When it was unrolled and examined,
it was the 'White Pills Formula for treating thirty-six types of wind illnesses.'
The Daoist priest said:
"Take this back to formulate,
and widely treat people in the world.
When your merit is complete, return here."
He ordered Lǐ to close his eyes,
and he found himself outside the north gate of Qīngzhōu.
When he arrived home,
his wife had already completed her mourning.
It was the third year of Qiánfú.
He then compounded the medicine,
and all who took it were cured.
A few years later, he lost his appetite
and stopped eating grains.
He then sought out the dry well,
and one day he did not return,
having also found the path and returned to immortal status.
End of Volume 52.
Yǔ Shēns Arithmetic
Yǔ Shēn of Qí was supremely skilled in arithmetic.
Wǔxiàngōng Xiāo Kuǎn was gravely ill with a stomach ailment
and asked Shēn:
"Will there be no joy?"
He replied:
"The planet Zhēnxīng is in Xiāngyáng and Jīngzhōu.
From a young age, you were blessed as a magistrate,
and will die in a chaotic era.
Your fame rivals that of Yī and Huò;
what regrets could there be?"
The duke said:
"The bewildered ruler is tyrannical and cruel;
people yearn for Yáo and Shùn.
My regret is not seeing the world cleared and tranquil,
and the horses rested on Huàshān."
He sighed and died.
Tower Drums
Lǐ Chóng of Qí served as the Inspector of Yǎnzhōu.
There were robbers in the prefecture.
Chóng then set up a tower in each village,
with a drum suspended in each tower.
When a robbery occurred,
the drum would be beaten furiously.
The first villages to hear it
would beat their drum once,
and those who heard it next would beat theirs in turn, making a rhythm.
In a short while,
the sound spread a hundred Lǐ.
They would lie in wait at strategic points,
and none escaped capture.
The placement of drums in various prefectures
began from this time.
It was then called "Wòhǔ."
Gambling the Administrator of Xuānchéng
Sòng Wéndì was skilled at playing yì (go).
He gambled with Yáng Xuánbǎo for the position of Administrator of Xuānchéng,
and an imperial edict was issued that very day.
People considered it a frivolous waste.
Dīnggōngténɡ Wine
Xiè Shúrang of Qí's mother suffered from wind-illness.
A voice from the air said:
"If you make wine from Dīnggōngténɡ,
she will recover."
Later, he sought it until he reached Yídū Jùn,
and saw a public woodcutter in the mountains
who said:
"This is Dīnggōngténɡ;
it is especially effective for treating wind-illness."
He then gave him four pieces
and also showed him how to infuse it in wine.
His mother's illness indeed improved.
Lingering After Parting
Wáng Yuánjǐng was sent as an envoy to Liángzhōu.
Xiàochuò saw him off,
weeping.
Yuánjǐng had no tears,
and thanked him, saying:
"Do not blame me for lingering after parting."
Princess Cháng's Embroidered and Feather-Inlaid Bodice
The Princess Cháng of Wèi Guó often wore a bodice adorned with appliqué embroidery and feather inlay.
Tàizǔ said:
"From now on, do not adorn yourself like this again."
The Princess smiled and said:
"How many kingfisher feathers are used?"
The Emperor said:
"If the imperial family wears this,
the palace and imperial relatives will imitate it,
driving up the price of kingfisher feathers.
Small commoners, seeking profit, will harm life;
truly, this is due to you.
You grew up in wealth and nobility;
you ought to remember to cherish your blessings."
The Princess said:
"Cannot the imperial family use gold to adorn a shoulder-borne palanquin?"
Tàizǔ said:
"With the wealth of the four seas,
even if I adorned all the palace halls with gold and silver,
I could still manage.
But I am merely a guardian of wealth for the Son of Heaven;
how can I use it arbitrarily?"
Bestowing Wine upon Liú Chǎng
Liú Chǎng was skillful;
he personally wove a pearl saddle and bridle
in the shape of playing dragons.
Tàizǔ said:
"If you applied this mind to diligently manage the people's affairs,
would that not also be good?"
When Chǎng was in his kingdom,
he frequently placed poison to kill his officials.
Tàizǔ visited Jiǎngwǔchí.
Before the accompanying officials had assembled,
Chǎng arrived first.
Tàizǔ summoned him and bestowed a cup of wine.
Chǎng suspected it
and, holding the cup, wept, saying:
"Your servant resisted the imperial court,
a crime for which there is no pardon.
Since Your Majesty treats me as one who will not die,
I wish to be a commoner of Dàliáng
and witness the prosperity of peace."
Tàizǔ said:
"I open my true heart to people;
how could such a thing be?"
He took the wine and drank it himself,
then poured another cup and bestowed it upon Chǎng.
Later, Chén Hóngjìn returned to the capital from Zhāng and Quán,
Qián Jiāo came to court from Wúyuè,
and the Later Lord of Jiāngnán was among the same ranks.
Chǎng, attending the banquet,
said:
"Among these few,
I was the first to return to the court.
I wish to hold a staff and be the leader of all the surrendered kings."
Tàizǔ laughed heartily.
Bestowing Fifty Thousand Taels of Silver upon the Last Lord of Jiāngnán
During the Kāibǎo era,
Zhào Pǔ held supreme political power.
The Latter Ruler of Jiāngnán sent Zhào Pǔ fifty thousand taels of silver.
Zhào Pǔ declined.
Tàizǔ said,
"The dignity of a great nation
must not be weakened by itself.
You should make them unable to fathom your intentions,
so it must not be refused."
Soon after, the Latter Ruler sent his younger brother, Cóngshàn, to present tribute.
In addition to the usual gifts,
he secretly brought white gold in the same amount as was previously offered to Zhào Pǔ.
The monarch and ministers of Jiāngnán were greatly astonished and convinced,
impressed by the Emperor's magnificent demeanor.
Fire in the Imperial Wine Brewery
During Tàizǔ's time,
there was a fire in the Imperial Wine Brewery.
All the supervising officials and dozens of others were executed in the marketplace.
The soldier who started the fire was bound and thrown into the flames.
From then on, all government departments were meticulously orderly.
Yǒngchāng Líng
Tàizǔ was born in Jiāmǎyíng, Luòyáng,
and loved its local customs and climate.
At the beginning of his reign, he began constructing palaces and other buildings,
with the intention of moving the capital.
In the ninth year, he made four trips to the suburbs for sacrifices,
but many of his palaces and guards were in uneasy circumstances,
or experienced strange phenomena,
so he returned east.
He sighed,
"I cannot live here during my life,
but I shall be buried here when I die."
He ascended the watchtower and fired a whistling arrow,
pointing to the spot and saying,
"I shall be buried here later."
Yǒngchāng Líng is that very place.
Praying for Rain at the Five Sacred Mountains
In the summer of the second year of Zhìdào,
there was a drought.
The Emperor dispatched eunuchs to the Five Sacred Mountains to pray for rain.
A scholar drafted the prayer,
which the Emperor personally wrote out.
Incense was set up according to the direction of each mountain,
and the eunuchs were sent off after bowing twice.
Wáng Yǔchēng memorialized, "The Five Sacred Mountains are regarded as equivalent to the Three Ducal Ministers.
The Emperor personally inscribed the prayer tablet,
which exceeds the proper rites and ceremonies.
There is no reason for him to write it personally."
The Emperor replied,
"Chéng Tāng cut his hair and nails
to pray at the Sānglín altar.
He had nothing to spare.
How much more should I, when pleading for the lives of the common people,
be unwilling to sacrifice the effort of writing?"
Hǎidōngqīng
In the coastal forests of Dēngzhōu there were falcons,
which flew from Gāolì across the coast in a single night.
They were called Hǎidōngqīng.
During the Chúnhuà era,
Zhào Bǎozhōng presented one as a tribute.
The Emperor said,
"I have long since ceased hunting,
and have released all my hawks and hounds.
I have no use for this.
I now bestow it upon you, my lord."
One Buddha is Born
Tàizōng placed particular importance on the appointments of officials, both internal and external.
He once said,
"I hear that when the imperial court appoints a Shèrén,
relatives and friends congratulate each other,
and the saying goes, 'One Buddha is born.'
How can this be taken lightly?"
He also said,
"The office of Xuéshì is pure, vital, and weighty.
I often regret that I could not hold such a position."
Fēibái
Tàizōng was skilled in Fēibái calligraphy.
His large characters were several feet square,
and he was particularly adept at small cursive script.
He once said,
"As I rule the world,
what need do I have for brush and ink?
It is just that my heart loves it,
and I cannot give it up."
Three Gō Chess Formations
Tàizōng once created three Gō chess formations:
one was called the 'Lone Flying Swan Formation' (Dúfēi Tiān'é Shì),
the second was the 'Facing a Thousand Miles Formation' (Duìmiàn Qiānlǐ Shì),
and the third was the 'Retrieving a Bright Pearl from the Great Sea Formation' (Dàhǎi Qǔ Míngzhū Shì).
All were devised by the Emperor.
Nineteen Characters for Gō Chess Diagrams
The ancient method of Gō chess diagrams
used the four tones (píng, shàng, qù, rù) to mark the four corners,
making them mixed and difficult to distinguish.
Xú Xuàn changed it to nineteen characters:
one, heaven (tiān);
two, position (wèi);
three, talent (cái);
four, seasons (shí);
five, elements (xíng);
six, palaces (gōng);
seven, dippers (dǒu);
eight, directions (fāng);
nine, provinces (zhōu);
ten, suns (rì);
eleven, winter (dōng);
twelve, months (yuè);
thirteen, intercalary (rùn);
fourteen, pheasants (zhì);
fifteen, full moon (wàng);
sixteen, prime ministers (xiàng);
seventeen, sheng (shēng);
eighteen, pines (sōng);
nineteen, guests (kè).
This was very simple and convenient.
Attendant Jiǎ Xuán
Tàizōng was a top-ranked Gō player.
The Attendant Jiǎ Xuán
was at that time compared to Wáng Jīxīn.
Jiǎ Xuán was addicted to alcohol
and died of illness.
The Emperor lamented his loss.
Pān Shènxīu was also skilled at Gō,
and offered a poem saying:
"Now I have attained the immortal's techniques,
yet still fear the monarch's four-way handicap."
Féng Dào's Mission to the Tartars
During the Tiānfú era of the Jìn dynasty,
a memorial was submitted regarding the title of the 'Treasure Stratagem and Military Garment' (Bǎocè Róngyī).
One of the grand councilors was to be sent as an envoy.
Zhào Yíng, Sāng Wéihàn, and Wén Sōng were all afraid of undertaking the mission.
Féng Dào requested paper and wrote,
"Dào will go."
He sent someone to tell his wife and children that he would not return home.
Within a few days, he departed northward.
The Tartar ruler, knowing Féng Dào had a great reputation,
detained him
and bestowed upon him a 'bull's head' and an ivory tablet as special honors.
Féng Dào wrote a poem saying:
"The bull's head is especially granted,
and an ivory tablet I am allowed to hold."
Whenever Féng Dào received gifts,
he bought firewood and charcoal with them.
He said that the northern lands were bitterly cold,
which an old man could not endure,
so he must prepare for it.
The barbarians were somewhat moved by his intentions
and eventually sent him back.
Féng Dào submitted three memorials requesting to stay,
but they insisted on sending him away, so he finally left,
after staying for more than a month.
Once he set off,
he lingered at every stop,
taking two months in total to leave their territory,
then he swiftly returned.
His attendants said,
"Having returned alive,
we regret not having wings to fly,
why did you, sir, delay at every stop?"
Féng Dào replied,
"The barbarians are full of deceit.
If we had rushed back,
with their strong legs, they could have caught up in a single night.
How could we have escaped?
But by moving slowly, they would be unable to predict our intentions."
Upon his return, Féng Dào wrote a poem saying:
"This day last year I served the Emperor,
only for the court, not for my home.
On the imperial hall, the Son of Heaven shed tears with one cup,
at the gate, the people sighed at the double envoys.
In the desolate north, winter brought constant snow,
in the rabbit's park, spring returned with flowers everywhere.
Above and below, like flesh and bone,
how many bodies lie buried under wind and sand? "
While among the Tartars, Féng Dào wrote a poem saying:
"By day I wear four padded coats to hide my hands,
by night I cover myself with three quilts, fearing to expose my head."
Such was the bitter cold.
Lú Duōxùn Attacked Zhào Pǔ's Shortcomings
Dòu Yí,
during the Kāibǎo era, was a Hànlín Xuéshì.
At that time, Zhào Pǔ held sole power,
and the emperor wanted to know his faults.
One day,
he summoned Yí,
speaking of Pǔ's unlawful actions,
and also praising Yí's talent and prestige.
Yí spoke glowingly of Pǔ as a long-serving old official,
public-spirited, loyal, honest, and upright.
The emperor was displeased.
Yí returned,
set out wine, and said:
"I will certainly not become a prime minister,
nor will I be banished to Zhūyá.
My family can be preserved."
Soon after, Academician Lú Duōxùn was summoned,
who then attacked Pǔ's shortcomings.
Pǔ was dismissed
and sent to govern Héyáng.
Duōxùn then became a Cānzhī Zhèngshì
and served as prime minister.
Later, Pǔ was reinstated as prime minister,
and Duōxùn was exiled to Yázhōu.
His words were proven true.
Neighbors encroaching on an old residence
Yáng Jiè served in Shǔ,
reaching a high official position.
After returning to Táng with Wáng Yǎn,
he retired and went back to Cháng'ān.
Much of his old residence had been encroached upon by neighbors.
His sons and nephews wanted to complain to the authorities.
Jiè wrote on the back of their petition:
"My four neighbors encroach upon me, and I let them;
ultimately, one must think of a time when there was nothing.
Try going up to the base of the Hányuán Diàn,
where autumn winds and autumn grasses are scattered widely."
His sons and nephews dared not speak again.
Someone else snoring beside one's couch
During the Kāibǎo era,
the imperial army besieged Jīnlíng.
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ sent Xú Xuàn to the court,
who, when received in the side hall,
earnestly stated that Jiāngnán's service to the great power was very respectful,
merely that he was unwell and unable to attend court,
not daring to refuse the edict.
Tàizǔ said:
"No need for many words.
What crime has Jiāngnán committed?
It's just that the whole world is one family,
and how can I allow others to snore
beside my couch?"
Xuàn returned to report.
Not long after, the city fell,
and he returned to court with the Hòuzhǔ.
Xuàn was straightforward by nature.
Seeing literati and officials wearing coarse cloaks in cold weather,
he said:
"Since the Hu barbarians brought chaos in the Central Plains,
this custom has not changed.
Wearing felt and fur
is truly bothersome for many people."
One day,
seeing his son-in-law also wearing a fur coat,
he admonished him, saying:
"Wú Láng is of a superior class,
how can he imitate this?"
Shú said:
"It's bitterly cold in the morning,
and many in court wear them."
Xuàn said:
"Gentlemen of integrity
have never worn them."
This was a reference to himself.
Yúyáng Sǎn
Xú Xié served in Jiāngzuǒ,
rising to Zhōngshū Shèrén.
When he was collating secretarial documents,
Wú Shú was a Jiàolǐ.
In ancient yuèfǔ poems, there was the character "摻" (sǎn),
but Shú often changed it to "操" (cāo),
which was a variation in zhāngcǎo script.
Xié said:
"This cannot be generalized.
For example, Yúyáng Sǎn,
its pronunciation is 'qī jiàn fǎn' (the initial of qī, the final of jiàn),
meaning 'three drum beats'.
Ní Héng wrote the 'Yúyáng Sǎn Zhuāgǔ Gē' (Song of Yúyáng Sǎn Drum Beats), saying:
'The border town opens late, Yúyáng Sǎn,
yellow dust swirls, and the white sun dims.' " Shú smiled and submitted.
Also, once, he went to Qīngshǔ Gé.
The ground in front of the pavilion, after rain,
had grass growing in the brick cracks.
It was weeded out but grew back.
Xié said:
"The Lǚshì Chūnqiū says:
'No miscellaneous trees grow beneath cinnamon branches,'
because its taste is acrid and pungent."
The Hòuzhǔ ordered several dou of cinnamon dust to be brought,
evenly spread in the cracks.
After a night, all the grass died.
His extensive knowledge was like this.
Red crow and white rabbit
Qián Zhāoxù was the prefect of Tōnglì Jūn.
In the early days of Zhìdào,
a red crow and a white rabbit were captured.
He submitted a memorial, saying:
"The crow is the essence of yang,
and the rabbit is of the yin category.
This shows the prosperity and flourishing of the fire virtue,
and is a sign of the taming and submission of the west (metal)."
Prayer
Tàizōng composed a prayer himself,
but could not complete it.
He ordered Hànlín Xuéshì Qián Ruòshuǐ to draft it, saying:
"The great benevolence of the Heavenly Emperor,
though this humble self bears it;
the lives of the common people
are overseen by the enlightened spirits."
The emperor was pleased and said:
"I have thought about this for a long time,
but could not find the words."
Staff record
Dǎng Jìn,
a northern Róng person.
In the early days of the dynasty, he was a cavalry commander,
and illiterate.
The emperor suddenly asked about the number of people in the army.
Previously, military officers would meticulously write down the number of soldiers and weapons they commanded
on the sticks they carried,
which were called "zhàngjì" (staff records),
like "hùjì" (tablet records).
Jìn merely held up his stick and replied:
"It's all here."
In the markets of the capital,
there were those who kept hawks and falcons.
Jìn would always release them,
cursing:
"If you can't buy meat to provide for your parents,
why feed it to birds and beasts instead?"
Tàizōng, when he was the Prince of Jìn,
had hawks and falcons.
Jìn suddenly saw them,
questioned and reprimanded, wanting to release them.
The stableman said:
"The Prince of Jìn ordered them to be kept."
Jìn immediately gave him money to buy meat,
saying:
"You must watch carefully,
don't let them be harmed by cats or pigs."
Once, he suffered from a sore.
His guests and subordinates came to visit,
and Jìn was covered in a brocade quilt.
One attendant whispered:
"He's rotten."
Jìn ordered his attendants to quickly seize the official,
slapped his cheek and cursed:
"I am a genuine Khitan,
what 'Xī' is there?
A small sore on the leg,
how can it be rotten?"
He meant that the Xī were of low status.
Passing through the market,
he saw someone tied up and punished.
He asked:
"What did you say?"
The actor replied:
"I was talking about Hán Xìn."
Jìn angrily said:
"You speak of Hán Xìn to me,
when you see Hán Xìn, you should speak of me!
This is a two-faced person!"
He immediately ordered him to be beaten with a staff.
Jìn's given name was Jìn,
but he was often called Huī.
Someone took issue with this,
and he said:
"I just follow whatever is convenient for me."
On eating fish
Liú Jí 護治京東 (hù zhì Jīngdōng).
The river overflowed its banks.
At that time, Zhāng Qùhuá was the zhuǎnyùnshǐ (transport commissioner).
He was on an inspection tour
and dined together (with Liú Jí),
with sliced carp as a dish.
Zhāng Qùhuá said:
"Southerners eat fish,
and are not at all bothered by its fishy smell."
He intended to belittle southerners.
Liú Jí replied:
"Your Excellency the Transport Commissioner, as a top scholar in the jìnshì (metropolitan graduate) examination,
have you never read books?
The 'Shàngshū' (Book of Documents) says:
'Yǔ (禹) dredged the nine rivers,
and there were fish and turtles;
he had people eat them fresh.'
The 'Yì' (Book of Changes), Gòu (姤) hexagram, line nine-two says:
'Wrapped are the fish,' and 'Righteous gentlemen hunt and fish.'
The 'Zhōulǐ' (Rites of Zhou) says:
'The xiànrén (獻人, official in charge of tribute)
is responsible for offering tribute seasonally,
building weirs.'
The 'Shī' (Book of Poetry) records excellent fish.
The 'Xiǎoyǎ' (Minor Odes) says:
'Roasted turtle and sliced carp.'
The 'Guófēng' (Airs of the States) says:
'Indeed, the bream of the Hé (河).'
The 'Zàijì' (載記, Records) says:
'When floods descend,
fish and turtles are not offered.
Fish and turtles not properly killed
are not sold in the market.
Those who live in the mountains
do not use fish and turtles as gifts.
In the third month,
the Son of Heaven travels by boat
to offer tuna in the ancestral temple.
In early autumn,
the Son of Heaven eats rice and fish.
Furthermore, for those who eat fish,
remove the 'yǐ' (乙, fish-gall bladder).'
Kǒngzǐ (孔子),
a person from Lǔ (魯),
said:
'Rotten fish should not be eaten.'
Zhào Yīn (趙厧),
a person from Jìn (晉),
ate fish.
Tián Wén (田文),
a person from Qí (齊),
all his senior guests ate fish.
Zǐchǎn (子產),
a person from Zhèng (鄭),
was offered fish by someone.
Zǐgōng (子公),
also a person from Zhèng,
carved a turtle and dipped his finger in the cauldron.
Great Shùn (舜) fished at Léizé (雷澤),
Lǚ Wàng (呂望) fished at Wèibīn (渭濱).
Why must they all be people from the southern states?"
Zhāng Qùhuá's expression fell,
and he could not reply.
Dīng Jìngōng (丁晉公) Meets Lǚ Dòngbīn (呂洞賓)
When Dīng Wèi (丁謂) was the tōngpàn (通判, assistant prefect) of Ráozhōu (饒州),
Lǚ Dòngbīn met him
and said:
"Your appearance is quite similar to Lǐ Déyù (李德裕).
In the future, your wealth and status will also be like his."
He also called on Zhāng Bó (張泊)
and left a poem saying:
"Success will be achieved in the 'broken melon' year."
People commonly refer to "broken melon" as two eights, meaning sixteen,
but he died at the age of sixty-four.
Lǚ Dòngbīn had a self-penned verse saying:
"In the morning I bid farewell to Bǎiyuè (百越), in the evening to Sānwú (三吳),
A green serpent in my sleeve, my courage bold.
Thrice I entered Yuèyáng (岳陽), unrecognized by people,
Chanting loudly, I flew across Dòngtíng Hú (洞庭湖)."
There were also these lines:
"The sea-drinking turtle, no one recognizes,
The mountain-burning talisman, ghosts find hard to see.
Within a single grain of millet, a world is hidden,
In a two-sheng pot, mountains and rivers are cooked."
The Qiānzìwén (千字文)
The 'Qiānzìwén' (Thousand Character Classic) is titled:
"By imperial edict, Yuánwài Sànqí Shìláng (員外散騎侍郎) Zhōu Xìngsì (周興嗣) rhymed it."
The character "chì" (勑) is merely a scribal error for "Liáng" (梁);
at that time, imperial decrees were not yet referred to as "chì."
It was not until the Xiǎnqìng (顯慶) reign of the Táng (唐) dynasty
that it was stipulated that decrees not passing through the Fènggé (鳳閣) and Luántái (鸞臺) could not be called "chì."
Writing Edicts on Wú (吳) Silk Undershirts
Towards the end of the Táng dynasty, there were imperial edicts written in red ink,
mobilizing troops from various fāngzhèn (方鎮, military governors).
This was presumably to demonstrate trust in times of crisis.
Zhāozōng (昭宗) wrote an edict on a Wú (吳) silk undershirt,
sending it by secret path to Qián Liú (錢鏐),
informing him of the nation's peril.
The Liùtiě (六帖)
Bái Jūyì (白居易) compiled the 'Liùtiě' (Six Compilations).
He used several thousand pottery jars,
each titled with a category,
and arranged them on a seven-tiered shelf in his study.
He ordered his students to collect relevant facts and throw them into the jars.
He then inverted them to copy and compile the book.
Therefore, the recorded events are not in chronological order.
Otters Sacrificing Fish
According to an old saying, Lǐ Shāngyǐn (李商隱), when composing essays, often consulted numerous books,
which were stacked like fish scales.
At the time, this was called "otters sacrificing fish."
Lǐ Shāngyǐn (李商隱)'s Use of Huīdīng (灰釘)
Liú Cuò (劉錯) wanted to annotate Lǐ Shāngyǐn's 'Fánnán Jí' (樊南集).
There was a letter written on behalf of Wáng Yuánmào (王元茂) to Liú Shèn (劉慎) saying:
"Funeral preparations reached the tombs,
the time for flying and fleeing is cut off;
Throwing down weapons and scattering on the ground,
the hope of huīdīng (灰釘) is exhausted."
He only regretted not knowing the meaning of "huīdīng" (灰釘).
It refers to Dù Dú (杜篤)'s 'Lùndū Fù' (論都賦) of the Hàn (漢) dynasty, which says:
"Burn Kāngjū (康居),
turning precious things to ash.
Strike the whistling arrow,
nail the deer snare."
Lǐ Shāngyǐn's (李商隱) ornate style was like this.
The Duck That Could Speak Human Language
Táng (唐) dynasty's Lù Guīméng (陸龜蒙) was cunning and resourceful.
He lived in Lìzé (笠澤).
An eunuch from Cháng'ān (長安) was sent to Hángzhōu (杭州).
His boat passed by Lù Guīméng's (陸龜蒙) residence.
He shot a green-headed male duck,
breaking its neck.
Lù Guīméng (陸龜méng) cried out loudly:
"This duck is good at speaking human language!
It was to be presented to the Son of Heaven.
Now I will take this dead duck to the authorities and report it myself!"
The eunuch was terrified,
and only stopped after generously offering gold and silk.
He asked:
"What did this duck say?"
Lù Guīméng (陸龜méng) replied:
"It always called its own name."
Poem Titled "Cuìwēi" (翠微)
Cuìwēi Sì (翠微寺) is on the summit of Lǐ Shān (驪山).
It was formerly an imperial palace.
Emperor Táng Tàizōng (唐太宗) sought refuge from the summer heat here.
Later, someone inscribed a poem saying:
"Cuìwēi Sì was originally Cuìwēi Gōng (翠微宮),
With dozens of layers of pavilions and terraces.
The Son of Heaven no longer comes, the monks have also left,
A woodcutter occasionally fells a pine branch."
Erecting a Golden Rooster on Amnesty Day
Sòng Xiàowáng (宋孝王) asked Sītiān Yīngzhī (司天膺之) about the practice of erecting a golden rooster on amnesty days in the later Wèi (魏) and Běiqí (北齊) dynasties.
Yīngzhī (膺之) said:
"According to the celestial prognostication in the 'Hǎizhōng Xīngzhàn' (海中星占),
the movement of the Tiānjī Xīng (天雞星, Celestial Rooster Star) indicates an amnesty.
On amnesty days in Běiqí (北齊),
the military arsenal was ordered to set up a golden rooster to the right of the palace gate,
and beat drums a thousand times to proclaim the amnesty.
The practice of erecting a golden rooster
is said to have originated with Lǚ Guāng (呂光) of Xīliáng (西涼).
Investigating its meaning,
the west governs Duì (兌) hexagram,
Duì (兌) represents a marsh.
The rooster is the spirit of Xùn (巽) hexagram,
and Xùn (巽) represents command or decree.
Therefore, these two objects were combined to form its shape,
raised on a long pole,
so that everyone could see it."
Up the Slope, Down the Slope
Lǐ Wénzhèng (李文正) ordered that the jiànyì (諫議, remonstrance official) be called "pōbài" (坡拜, slope bow).
This is because, according to old Táng (唐) usage, one entered the position of "jiànyì" from outside,
and their rank was above that of gěishè (給舍, palace attendants).
After a year, they would be promoted to gěishìzhōng (給事中, Supervising Secretary),
and after another year, to shèrén (舍人, Palace Attendant).
Hence, some would mock the jiànyì (諫議) saying:
"You are now 'up the slope,'
but later you will 'go down the slope' again."
Liú Jūn's (劉君) 'Jiāhuà' (佳話, Good Stories) records that
when someone was first appointed jiànyì (諫議),
a gěishè (給舍) jokingly said:
"Who suddenly ranks above me?"
The other replied:
"If I am untalented,
why don't you pull me down?"
This implies promotion.
Failing One's Eyes and Mouth
A proverb says:
"Not visiting Cháng'ān (長安) is a disservice to one's eyes;
not visiting Liǎngzhè (兩浙) is a disservice to one's mouth."
Tàipíng Xīngguó (太平興國)
Tàizōng changed the reign title to Tàipíng Xīngguó.
Those who knew said, "The character 'Tàipíng' (太平) is composed of 'yī' (一), 'rén' (人), and 'liùshí' (六十) (meaning 'one person sixty')."
Tàizōng lived to be sixty-nine.
Since the reign title was changed within those years,
it also corresponded to that number.
Língqí Jīng
The 《Língqí Jīng》 is a method from Huángshí Gōng.
Jiāng Mì of Southern Qí once used qí (chess pieces) to divine the hexagram of 'gold benefitting a jade cup.'
The Five Elements section of the Táng 《Jīngjí Zhì》 contains a one-volume work titled 《Shísān Língqí Jīng Bǔ》,
which indicates its ancient transmission.
However, when a matter was divined twice,
it ultimately did not prove true.
Navel Rupture
Wáng Quán, a Palace Assistant Secretary, was fond of wine.
Suddenly, his navel ruptured with a sound.
He held a basin to it,
and obtained over a dou of clear wine before he died.
Zhōu Shìzōng Composes Poetry
Zhōu Shìzōng once composed a poem
and showed it to the academician Dòu Yǎn, saying:
"Can this be circulated?"
Yǎn replied:
"Poetry is a specialized field of study.
If one exerts great effort in refining it,
it will interfere with urgent state affairs.
If the refinement is not thorough,
it will not be entirely good."
Shìzōng understood his meaning
and consequently wrote no more poetry.
Suffering in Hell
Someone doubted that the duration of suffering in hell described in Buddhist scriptures was too long.
The Duke said:
"Legal texts mention exile three thousand lǐ,
the distance is very far.
Penal servitude for three years,
the days are very long.
At the beginning of committing a crime,
it is merely for an instant."
Not Deceiving Spirits
Zhū Zhēn, a recluse from Jiāngnán, said:
"The world says 'do not deceive spirits,'
but if one does not deceive one's own heart,
then one does not deceive spirits."
Three Abundances
Scholars should cultivate three abundances:
much reading,
much discussion,
and much writing.
Among these three abundances,
discussion is the most difficult.
Poem on "Heavenly Rooster Playing in Gentle Breeze"
Zhāng Bì of Jiāngnán was in charge of the imperial examinations.
The test poem was "Heavenly Rooster Playing in Gentle Breeze."
Bì merely used poetic lines from the 《Wénxuǎn》 as topics,
without ever investigating their origin.
A presented scholar named Zhāng stated to the chief examiner,
saying, "The 《Ěryǎ》 mentions 'hàn' (鶾),
and the 《Píyǎ》 mentions 'heavenly rooster.'
Which is correct, I do not know?"
Bì was unable to answer.
He hastily took out the two dictionaries, 《Ěryǎ》 and 《Píyǎ》, to check and tell him.
Comparing Imperial Edicts
Zhāng Qùhuá, while serving as a Supervising Remembrancer,
submitted a memorial saying:
"Currently, the drafter of imperial edicts, Zhāng Dàn, is untalented.
I wish to compete with him."
An imperial edict ordered the Central Secretariat to administer a test.
Dàn indeed did not succeed.
Qùhuá was promoted to Rectifier of Omissions,
and Dàn was dismissed from drafting imperial edicts.
Qùhuá had a reputation at the time.
Although he won,
he was despised by upright public opinion.
And Dàn should also have retired gracefully.
How could he contend with a newly successful scholar?
This was also a mistake.
Two Bureaucrats Composing Poetry and Rhapsody
During the Kāiyùn reign of the Jìn dynasty,
an imperial edict commanded officials of the two bureaus (Chancellery and Secretariat) to each compose one poem and one rhapsody,
to be submitted to the Ministry of Rites
as an examination topic.
Lǐ Yì alone said:
"Yì knows only a limited number of characters.
He relies on others to accomplish things.
If he were made to wear a white robe and enter the Ministry of Tribute (for examination),
he would certainly fail.
How can he compose essays to serve as a model for the world?"
He ultimately refused to compose them.
Heavy Headgear
Heavy headgear refers to
a large-brimmed cap.
It was originally the attire of country folk and mountain recluses,
made of black fabric.
Emperor Xiàowén of Later Wèi, after moving the capital from Yúnzhōng to Dài,
bestowed it upon his officials.
Since the Five Dynasties,
only censors wore it.
At the beginning of the Chúnhuà era,
chancellors, academicians, and officials of the Censorate were all ordered to wear it.
Lú Yánràng's Poetry
Lú Yánràng of Táng composed poetry that was shallow and simple.
Only Wú Róng greatly esteemed his works,
saying they would surely achieve lasting fame.
In "Staying at Dōnglín," he wrote:
"Two or three streaks of lightning wishing for rain,
seven or eight stars still in the sky."
In "Expressing My Feelings," he wrote:
"My calling card has moss growing under the five gates,
my house servant is bone-thin in the six streets."
In "Xúan the Monk," he said:
"The high monk speaks clearly, his teeth without water;
the old crane flies ably, its bones carrying wind."
In "Night of the Sixteenth of the Eighth Month," he wrote:
"Only a small error of fate,
should consume not much light."
In "To Someone," he wrote:
"Having settled one character in my chant,
I've twisted off several whiskers."
There are also lines like "On the tree, an admonishing 'gāo zhōu pī jiá' bird,
between the windows, a knocking 'bì bó kòu tóu' insect."
Five Birds Named as Guests
Lǐ Fǎng admired Bái Jūyì's poetry.
In his garden, he kept five birds,
all named as guests:
the white pheasant was called 'Jiākè' (Excellent Guest),
the egret 'Báixuěkè' (White Snow Guest),
the crane 'Xiānkè' (Immortal Guest),
the peacock 'Nánkè' (Southern Guest),
and the parrot 'Lǒngkè' (Lǒng Guest).
He also admired Bái Jūyì's "Gathering of Seven Elders,"
and gathered Sòng Qí and eight others
to form the "Gathering of Nine Elders."
Recording Poems
From the Xī dynasty (雍熙) until now, thirty years have passed.
Those who could write poetry are now briefly recorded.
Yáng Huīzhī (楊徽之) in "Huì Wàng" (會望) said:
"Vast and distant, where do the misty weeds end?
Waving and swaying, the wind-blown willows cannot bear to hang."
In "Jiāng Xíng" (江行) he said:
"New frost dyes the maple leaves,
The bright moon lends its light to the reed blossoms."
In "Jiāyáng Chuān" (嘉陽川) he said:
"The Green Emperor (Qīngdì) has already made spring ageless,
Why does the Moon Goddess (Sù'é) begrudge the moon remaining ever full?"
In "Yuán Yè" (元夜) he said:
"Clouds return to the myriad-year-old trees,
The moon fills the nine-layered city."
Xú Xuàn (徐鉉) in "Bìng Zhōng" (病中) said:
"Frantically writing characters towards the empty space,
The whole world is turbulent, do not ask the way."
Liáng Zhōuhàn (梁周翰) in "Chū Jū" (出居) said:
"After a night's rain, vegetable sprouts unfold,
In several places on the spring mountain, the fragrance of tea banners rises."
Zhèng Wénbǎo (鄭文寶) in "Chūn Jiāo" (春郊) said:
"A road of a hundred grasses and a thousand flowers,
A sky of slanting wind and fine rain."
In "Sòng Bié" (送別) he said:
"The floral light in Dùqǔ (杜曲) is rich like wine,
The spring scenery at Bālíng (霸陵) is older than people."
In "Sòng Rén Qù" (送人去) he said:
"The full sail and western sun hasten the journey,
Overnight the east wind scattered the Chu plums."
Liú Shīdào (劉師道) in "Jì Bié" (寄別) said:
"At Nánpǔ (南浦) the green spring grass is not yet injured,
Going north, I am still ashamed of the startled morning apes."
In "Xiào Shì" (咲世) he said:
"Wild horses fly past the window,
Vinegar flies dance in the urn like the sky."
Lǐ Zōng'è (李宗諤) in "Chūn Jiāo" (春郊) said:
"A stream of evening green floats with mandarin ducks,
Ten thousand trees of spring red call with cuckoos."
Lǐ Wéi (李維) in "Zhǔ Gōng Tíng" (渚宮亭) said:
"The fragrant grasses of the old palace remain,
Past events flow away like the evening river."
In "Sòng Rén Yuèzhōu" (送人越州) he said:
"The wind-blown firewood of the Ruòyé (若耶) road,
The frosty tangerines of Dòngtíng (洞庭) in autumn."
Dīng Wèi (丁謂) in "Sòng Zhāng Nán'ān" (送章南安) said:
"Plum blossoms across the mountain pass road,
Peach leaves float on the boat crossing the river."
In "Bājiāo" (芭蕉) he said:
"The sealed green memorial is first opened,
The green phoenix seeking its mate just spreads its tail."
Sū Wéi (蘇為) in his poem "Hú Tíng" (湖亭) said:
"How boundless the green spring waves,
White birds fly freely."
Yàn Shū (晏殊) said:
"The poetic bones of Dōngyáng (東陽) are lean,
The parting soul at Nánpǔ (南浦) fades away."
Qián Zhāodù (錢昭度) in "Cūn Jū" (村居) said:
"Yellow wasps leave their court as the sea tide rises,
White ants fight fiercely as mountain rain comes."
In "Zì Yǒng" (自詠) he said:
"My stern guts despise bamboo leaves,
My old illness fears water caltrops."
In "Chūn Zhòu" (春晝) he said:
"People return to Empress Hàn's (Hàn Hòu) golden palace,
Swallows are in Lú Jiā's (盧家) white jade hall."
In "Dēng Lóu" (登樓) he said:
"The distant water cleanses the forest's colors,
Faint clouds arise in the setting sun."
Qián (錢) and Liú (劉) change poetic style
In recent years, Qián Wéiyǎn (錢惟演) and Liú Yún (劉筠) were the first to change poetic style.
Wéiyǎn (惟演) in "Tú Zhōng" (途中) said:
"The intention of snow has not formed, clouds touch the ground,
The autumn sound is ceaseless, geese connect the sky."
He also said:
"At the guest pavilion, I'm tired of hearing discussions of long and short,
How can village wine distinguish saints and sages?"
In "Sòng Sēng" (送僧) he said:
"A lone wisp of smoke rises from the monk's couch,
The traveling clothes are cool from dream rain."
Poems by two monks
The Chu (楚) monk Huìchóng (惠崇) in "Sī Dōng Sì Lín" (思東寺林) said:
"Birds return to the cedars, snow falls,
The monk meditates, stones sink into clouds."
In "Sòng Lǐ Kān" (送李堪) he said:
"Autumn sounds stir the myriad trees,
The evening light rises over a thousand mountains."
The Shu (蜀) monk Xīzhòu (希晝) in "Dá Huáng Guìzhōu" (答黃桂州) said:
"The arriving letter meets a scarce year,
The departing dream traverses perilous peaks."
In "Guǎngnán Chén Zhuǎnyùn" (廣南陳轉運) he said:
"Spring emerges beyond Guìlǐng (桂嶺),
People are west of the sea gate."
Luòlú Tǐ (轆轤體) call and response couplets
From Shùn's (舜) creation of songs,
Gāoyáo (皋繇) proclaiming words and re-singing,
and Bǎiliáng (柏梁) linked verses,
Yán Yánnián (顏延年) harmonizing with Xiè Jiān (謝監) and Xiè Xuānhuī (謝玄暉),
there were pieces like "Harmonizing with the Ascent of Sun Quán's (孫權) Old City at Wǔchāng (武昌)."
In Liáng Hésùn's (梁何遜) collected works, there are many linked verses.
Táng Yuánzhěn (唐元稹) composed twenty pieces titled "Chūn Shēn" (春深),
all using the four rhymes jiā (家), huā (花), chē (車), xié (斜).
Liú (劉) and Bái (白) changed them,
also using these four characters.
Lìnghú Chǔ (令狐楚) harmonized poems,
rhyming several times.
For linked verses,
sometimes two lines, sometimes four lines,
there is also one person providing a line,
and another providing the corresponding line.
This is called the Luòlú Tǐ (轆轤體) (windlass style).
The five characters of brushwork
Qián Ruòshuǐ (錢若水) said that among the ancients skilled in calligraphy who mastered brushwork,
Táng Lù Xīshēng (唐陸希聲) obtained it.
There were five characters:
piě (撇), yā (押), gōu (鉤), gé (格), dǐ (抵).
Using the brush like fishing,
then the strokes are vigorous,
which is called zhěngdēng bǐ (撜鐙筆).
Xīshēng (希聲) said:
"In the past, the Two Wángs (二王) both transmitted this method."
Xīshēng (希聲) passed it to the monk Biànguāng (辯光),
who entered Cháng'ān (長安) as a Hanlin (翰林) attendant.
Xīshēng (希聲) had not yet achieved prominence,
and sent a poem saying:
"Dragons and snakes beneath the brush seem to possess spirit,
Thunder and rain from the celestial pond change in an instant.
I tell the person who once had hands not chapped,
He should remember the people washing silk by the riverside."
Biànguāng (辯光) then introduced Xīshēng (希聲) to powerful favored officials,
who later became prime minister.
Dāo Yǎn (刀衍) said that the Southern Táng (江南) later ruler (hòuzhǔ) obtained this method,
and his calligraphy was extremely vigorous.
He added two more characters,
saying:
"dǎo (導) and sòng (送)."
Using medicine based on deficiency and excess
Chén Zhāoyù (陳昭遇) was skilled in medicine,
and never read books.
He returned to court with Liú Chǎng (劉鋹).
Carrying his medicine bag,
he saw hundreds of people daily.
He silently recognized the symptoms of wind, fatigue, and cold,
then observed their age, physical condition (deficiency or excess),
and prescribed decoctions according to ancient formulas.
Few did not recover.
He had never actually consulted pulse diagnosis texts.
The world considered him a divine physician.
This is what Zhuāng Zhōu (莊周) called "xuánjiě" (懸解) (spontaneous understanding),
and Tóng Guò (童過) called "reading a book a hundred times and the meaning reveals itself."
Blind in one eye
When Qián Liú (錢鏐) was old,
he became blind in one eye.
A certain Imperial Physician (guóyī) Wú (吳) from the central court said:
"It is better not to treat this;
it will prolong your life by five to seven years.
If the membrane is removed and the cataract cleared,
the eye will return to its former state,
but there is a worry of diminishing good fortune."
Liú (鏐) said:
"It is enough for me not to be a one-eyed ghost underground."
The physician treated him,
and his sight was restored.
He rewarded the physician with gold and silk totaling fifty thousand strings of cash.
Soon after, Liú (鏐) died.
Building the Tàiyī (太一) Palace
During the Tàipíng Xīngguó (太平興國) reign,
the Daoist adept Chǔ Zhīlán (楚芝蘭) reported:
According to the "Tàiyī Jīng" (太一經),
the Wǔfú Tàiyī (五福太一) is the Nine Noble Gods of Heaven.
It travels through the five palaces,
shifting every forty-five years.
Now it is due to enter the Wú (吳) region.
Where the Wǔfú (五福) arrives,
the people receive its blessing.
A palace should be built in Sūzhōu (蘇州).
Tàizōng (太宗) followed this advice.
After the palace was completed,
Zhīlán (芝蘭) again reported that worshipping Tàiyī (太一) in Wú (吳)
would only benefit the people of Wú (吳).
It should be moved and built in Sūcūn (蘇村), thirty lí south of the capital.
So, a new palace was rebuilt,
with ten halls,
named:
"Jūnqí Tàiyī (君棊太一), Chénqí Tàiyī (臣棊太一), Mínqí Tàiyī (民棊太一), Jiǔqì Tàiyī (九氣太一), Dàyóu Tàiyī (大游太一), Xiǎoyóu Tàiyī (小游太一), Shíshén Tàiyī (十神太一), Tiāntàiyī (天太一), Dìtàiyī (地太一),"
and together with the Wǔfú (五福), making eighteen.
The palaces in Luòyáng (洛陽) resemble the Tuşita (Dōushuài) Heaven Palace.
During the Western Jìn dynasty,
a Hú monk arrived in Luòyáng.
Upon seeing the palace,
he sighed,
“This truly is the Tūshuài Heaven palace,
but it was built by human effort,
not by spiritual power.”
When he was about to die,
he bid farewell to his disciples, saying:
“Mountains, rivers, and all under heaven will perish,
much less the human body;
how can it last long?
But if one can focus the mind on purity,
and cast aside the three poisons,
even if the physical forms differ,
their gathering will surely be the same.”
Destroying bronze Buddhas to cast coins.
Zhōu Shìzōng destroyed bronze Buddha statues to cast coins,
saying:
“Buddhism holds that one should not spare one’s head, eyes, marrow, or brain,
if it benefits sentient beings.
How then
can I cherish bronze statues?”
The Great Compassion bronze statue in Zhènzhōu was very efficacious.
When it was being destroyed,
an axe broke it open from its chest.
Later, Shìzōng campaigned north,
and a carbuncle erupted on his chest.
Everyone said it was karmic retribution.
Tàipíng Xīngguó Temple,
formerly Lóngxīng Temple,
was converted into a granary by Shìzōng.
At the beginning of the dynasty,
the abbot repeatedly beat the drum to request its restoration as a temple.
The emperor sent an imperial envoy with a sword, ordering him to behead the monk,
and instructed him:
“If he is afraid, then behead him.
But if he shows no fear at the execution,
then do not behead him yet.”
When the monk was questioned,
his expression was composed,
and he offered his neck for execution.
The emperor was deeply moved,
and restored it as a temple.
He also repaired the old Fēngshàn Temple, making it Kāibǎo Temple.
People from the Western Lands do not eat meat.
At the beginning of the Dàzhōng Xiángfú era,
the Western Regions monk Juéchēng came and said:
“Upon entering this country, I saw pigs and sheep slaughtered,
and meat hanging in the markets,
which was very unbearable to watch.
I see that the people of this land have quite evil hearts.
Those people from the Western Lands
do not eat meat at all.”
The emperor summoned him and asked what he desired.
He only requested a golden kaṣa,
to be placed at the vajra throne, and that was all.
Lǐ Fú becomes the Prefect of Chūnzhōu.
Lú Duōxùn was demoted to Zhūyá.
Counselor Grandee Lǐ Fú happened to be the Prefect of Kāifēngfǔ.
He sought an audience with Zhào Pǔ,
and said that although Zhūyá was overseas,
its climate and soil were not particularly bad,
and most exiles survived.
Chūnzhōu was in the interior,
but those who went there inevitably died.
He hoped for a reconsideration of the previous order,
to outwardly display leniency,
rather than condemning him to death.
Pǔ nodded in agreement.
After more than a month,
Fú was demoted to Xuānzhōu for an offense.
The emperor’s anger had not subsided,
and he ordered his demotion to beyond the mountain passes.
Pǔ fully recounted the previous matter,
so Fú was made Prefect of Chūnzhōu,
and died upon arriving at the prefecture.
Poems by Scholar Zhū.
The scholar Zhū Zhēnbái from Jiangnán was good at satirizing and chanting.
His poem on the hedgehog says:
“Moving like a pincushion,
lying like a chestnut burr.
Do not mock it for being so big,
who would dare throw a punch?”
He once paid a visit to a nobleman
who did not treat him courteously.
In the main hall, there was a lattice screen.
Zhēnbái inscribed a poem on it, saying:
“The barrier of the Way is no barrier at all,
the words are blurred yet not blurred.
With eyes all over its body,
does it know how to recognize people?”
His poem titled “On a Coffin” says:
“Eventually, it will be needed,
but not for you yet.”
His poem “On the Moon” says:
“Seen at Dāngtú, seen at Dāngtú,
seen at Wúhú, seen at Wúhú.
On the fifteenth night of the eighth month,
it resembles a fan without a handle.”
Xú Xuàn's fondness for spirits and deities.
Xú Xuàn did not believe in Buddhism,
but was extremely fond of tales of spirits and deities.
The Middle Lord of Jiangnán ordered him to read the “Śūraṅgama Sūtra,”
which contains profound principles.
After more than ten days,
he said:
“Your servant has read it several times,
and sees that its discourse on emptiness
is like pouring from one vessel
and into another.
I do not understand its meaning at all.”
Xuàn dedicated himself to collecting tales of the supernatural,
compiling the “Jī Shén Lù.”
He once presided over selection of officials.
Candidates would cunningly speak of the supernatural,
using it for personal gain.
The commoner Kuǎiliàng
was fond of exaggerating,
and Xuàn housed him in his residence.
Many of the stories in “Jī Shén Lù”
were narrated by Liàng.
Liàng once offended Xuàn,
who became very angry
and refused to speak to him.
One day, Liàng suddenly said:
“There was a strange person
with fleshy wings who flew out of the hall
and ascended to the main chamber.”
Xuàn immediately rejoiced
and ordered it to be recorded.
Someone once said to Xuàn:
“You disdain and reject the teachings of the Buddha.
Could Gautama not be a yellow-faced deity?”
Xuàn smiled and did not reply.
The hand that built the Wǔfènglóu.
Hán Pǔ and Hán Jì
both possessed literary talent.
Jì once slighted Pǔ,
telling people:
“My elder brother’s writing
is like a straw hut with rope hinges,
merely providing shelter from wind and rain.
My writing
is the hand that builds the Wǔfènglóu.”
Pǔ secretly overheard his words,
and happened to obtain Shǔ paper.
He sent a poem to Jì, saying:
“Ten styles of barbarian paper from Yìzhōu,
sent fresh from Wǎnxī Tóu.
Elder brother finds this entirely useless,
but it can help you repair your Wǔfènglóu.”
The poem “Yè Jīnmén.”
Chéng Yoùwén of Jiangnán, who was Dàlǐ Qīng,
was fond of composing lyrics.
He once wrote the tune “Yè Jīnmén,”
with the line: “Wind suddenly rises,
ruffling a pond of spring water.”
Later, due to a delay in official documents from Qín,
the Middle Lord said:
“Sir, why don’t you go and try?
What would be lacking for you from a pond of spring water?”
