Seeking a letter of goodwill.
During the Kāibǎo era,
Yēlǜ Cóng, the barbarian Prefect of Zhóuzhōu, sent a request to the Prefect of Xióngzhōu for a letter of goodwill, saying:
“Officials should not communicate outside the border,
and words are thus inappropriate;
but if the matter benefits the state,
it is permissible to act independently.”
Its literary quality was quite remarkable.
Bùdòngzūnyuàn.
When Lǐ Tāo was a commoner,
there was a Buddhist temple at Níshuǐguān,
called “Bùdòngzūnyuàn,”
and
it contained a monk who never left the temple.
Not long after,
the temple was destroyed by fire,
and the monks dispersed.
Tāo wrote a poem:
“The meditation guest has fled,
the Bùdòngzūn has moved.
The topsy-turvy affairs of the world,
eighty-four thousand gates.”
Volume 53
End.
No empty reputations under these names.
Xūe Dáohéng was sent on a mission to Chén,
and composed the poem "Rén Yuē," saying:
"It's only seven days into spring,
but already two years since I left home."
The southerners mocked him, saying:
"What kind of language is this?"
When he then said:
"Man returns after the falling geese,
thoughts arise before the flowers,"
they then said:
"A renowned name truly has no empty scholar."
Records on the Powder Tray
Gāo Jiá of the Suí dynasty was a Grand Minister of the Right.
He would often fill a tray with powder
and place it by his bed.
Whenever he thought of an official matter,
he would write it on the tray.
By morning,
he would transcribe it
and implement it at court.
Can You Still Make "Empty Beam Swallow Mud"?
Yángdì was skilled at writing
and disliked others surpassing his work.
Xūe Dáohéng thus incurred his displeasure.
When Yángdì had him executed,
he said:
"Can you still make 'empty beam fallen swallow mud'?"
The Emperor composed "Yàn Gē Xíng,"
and all the literati harmonized with it.
Wáng Zhòu alone did not humble himself before the Emperor,
and the Emperor frequently suppressed him.
Zhòu was eventually harmed.
The Emperor recited Zhòu's striking line and said:
"'The courtyard grass, unattended, turns green at will' –
can he still compose such words?"
Mirror Sound
Sū Wēi had a mirror.
When a solar eclipse was complete,
the mirror also became dim and black, seeing nothing.
When the eclipse was half complete,
the mirror was also half dim.
Later, there was a sound in the cabinet like a qìng (stone chime),
and upon searching, it was the sound of the mirror.
Soon after,
his son Kuí died,
and there was no more sound.
When Wēi fell from power,
his whereabouts became unknown.
Fēngdū Market
Luòyáng's southern market
was the Suí Fēngdū market.
When the outer wall was first being built,
a tomb was unearthed.
Inside the coffin was a flat stone,
with vermilion writing that stated:
"Divination said to reside in court;
the tortoise said near the market.
In five hundred years,
it will be seen here."
Upon checking the years and months,
it corresponded to the second year of Huángchū.
Dream of a Great Flood
Suí Wéndì dreamed of a great flood submerging the city,
so he moved to Dàxīng.
A diviner said:
"The great flood
is the name of Táng Gāozǔ."
Lady's Army
Píngyáng Gōngzhǔ heard that Gāozǔ had raised an army of righteousness in Tàiyuán,
so she gathered fugitives to welcome the army.
At the time, it was called the "Lady's Army."
Register of Characters
Lǐ Shǒusù was particularly skilled in genealogy;
people called him "the living register."
Yú Shìnán composed the "Rénwù Zhì."
Beautiful Women Eating Milk
After Hóu Jūnjí was executed,
his household was inventoried.
Two beautiful women were found,
whose beauty was unparalleled.
They regularly ate human milk instead of grain.
Rogue Bandit
Lǐ Jì often said:
"When I was twelve or thirteen, I was a rogue bandit,
killing anyone I met.
When I was fourteen or fifteen, I was an unstoppable bandit;
anyone who displeased me,
I would kill.
When I was seventeen or eighteen, I was a good bandit,
killing everyone on the battlefield.
At twenty, I became a great general,
using military force to save people from death."
Several Hú of Blood
Qín Shúbǎo was often ill in his later years.
He said:
"I grew up amidst military campaigns,
fought over two hundred battles,
and shed no less than several hú of blood.
How could I not be ill?"
Walking Secretary
Tàizōng once went out on an excursion.
The officials requested to carry a duplicate of the archives to follow him.
The Emperor said:
"No need.
Yú Shìnán is here;
he is my walking secretary."
Owl's Cry and Official Promotion
An owl cried early in the morning in the tree in Zhāng Cuògèng's courtyard.
His wife thought it was inauspicious
and repeatedly spat at it.
Zhāng said:
"Quickly sweep and clean,
I am about to be promoted."
Before he finished speaking,
the well-wishers were already at the gate.
Western Regions Buddhist Monk
During the Zhēngguān era,
a Buddhist monk from the Western Regions was presented,
whose incantations could cause people to die and revive.
Tàizōng ordered brave and strong men from the flying cavalry to test him.
They died as he said,
and revived as he said.
Chuán Yì said:
"This is an evil art.
Evil cannot overcome righteousness.
If he were to cast a spell on your servant,
it certainly would not work."
The Emperor summoned the monk to cast a spell on Yì,
who initially felt nothing.
After a moment,
the Buddhist monk himself fell down,
as if struck,
and did not revive again.
Diamond
There was a Brahman monk
who claimed to possess a Buddha's tooth,
which could break any hard object it struck.
People flocked to see it like a market.
Chuán Yì said to his son:
"I have heard that a diamond is extremely hard,
nothing can withstand it,
but only an antelope horn can break it.
You go and test it."
Indeed, it shattered upon contact.
Tàizōng's Lamentation
Chǔ Suìliáng composed Tàizōng's lamentation text.
Upon returning from court,
his horse mistakenly entered a private residence, and he did not notice.
Golden Mat
Hóu Jūnjí conquered Gāochāng
and obtained a golden mat,
which was extremely exquisite,
and not found in the imperial treasury.
Three Regrets
Xūe Yuánchāo said:
"My wealth and honor are beyond measure,
yet I have three lifelong regrets:
not being promoted through the imperial examination for jinshì,
not being able to marry a woman from the Five Great Clans,
and not being able to compile the national history."
Patrolling the Embankment, Strolling in the Moonlight, and Chanting Poetry
Gāozōng inherited the aftermath of the Zhēngguān era,
and there was peace throughout the land.
Shàngguān Yí alone managed state affairs.
He would enter court at dawn,
patrol the Luòshǔi embankment,
stroll in the moonlight with his reins slackened,
and chant poetry, saying:
"The vast river flows silently,
I urge my horse across the long isle.
Magpies fly as the mountain moon lightens to dawn,
cicadas chirp in the wild autumn wind."
The assembled officials regarded him as an immortal.
Eunuch Flying a Kite
Yáng Dégàn was the Magistrate of Wànnián.
A eunuch was flying a kite
and disregarded people's crops.
Dégàn apprehended him and beat him with a staff.
The eunuch tearfully reported this to Gāozōng.
The Emperor said:
"You know well that this fellow is fierce,
why did you bother his common people?"
He did not pursue the matter.
A Hu-headed, barbarian-faced
Jiǎ Jiāyǐn, at seven years old,
was summoned for an audience as a child prodigy.
Xú Jì said:
"This child has a barbarian face,
how can he be so intelligent?"
Jiāyǐn said:
"A Hu-head can still be prime minister,
why should a barbarian face impede intelligence?"
Xú Jì's appearance resembled that of a Hu.
Concealing Names
Empress Wǔ, finding that many selections by the Ministry of Personnel were unreliable,
ordered that on the examination day, candidates should conceal their names,
and be graded blindly to determine their ranks.
The system of concealing names for judgments began then.
A Bundle of Silk Thread
Zhāng Chāngyí and his brothers,
relying on the favor of Yìzhī and Chāngzōng,
lived in excessive luxury.
Someone wrote on their gate:
"A bundle of silk thread,
how many days can it be wound?"
Chāngyí immediately wrote beneath it:
"One day is enough."
Before long, disaster struck.
Shěn Sānxiōng's Poetry
Shěn Quánqī presented his poetry to Zhāng Yàngōng.
Yàngōng said:
"Shěn Sānxiōng's poetry
must be given first place."
Brocade Robe
Empress Wǔ toured Lóngmén
and commanded her officials to compose poems,
promising a brocade robe to the first to finish.
The Left Scribe Dōngfāng Qiú had already received the award,
when Sòng Zhīwèn's poem was also completed.
Its literary quality and reasoning were both excellent,
so the brocade robe was taken from the former and given to him.
No Such Writing in Three or Two Hundred Years
Cuī Róng composed the elegy for Empress Wǔ,
and then fell ill and died.
People at the time believed there would be no such writing for three or two hundred years.
Dìng Kūnmíng Chí
During Emperor Zhōngzōng's reign,
Princess Ānlè requested Kūnmíng Chí.
The Emperor said:
"Since previous generations,
it has not been given to people."
The princess was displeased,
and consequently conscripted a large number of laborers
to dig another pond,
which she named:
"Dìng Kūnmíng Chí."
When it was completed,
Emperor Zhōngzōng went to view it,
and ordered high officials to compose poems.
Lǐ Yuèzhī said:
"May one only momentarily contemplate the ease of the recluse,
and not cause the poets of the time to toil."
Accusing a Son of Unfilial Conduct
When Lǐ Jiézhī was the Administrator of Hénán,
a woman accused her son of being unfilial.
The son wept and could not defend himself,
only saying:
"I have offended my mother,
and willingly accept death."
The mother insisted on having him killed.
Lǐ Jiézhī said:
"You may buy a coffin and retrieve your son's corpse."
He then sent someone to follow her.
The woman went out
and said to a Daoist priest:
"The matter is settled."
Soon, the coffin arrived.
Lǐ Jiézhī ordered the Daoist priest to be arrested.
It turned out the priest had a private affair with the woman,
and had always been constrained by the son,
which was why they wished to eliminate him.
Lǐ Jiézhī beat the mother and the Daoist priest to death,
and used the coffin to carry the mother's corpse home.
Zhāng Dǐ
When Cuī Shí was Chancellor of the Secretariat,
Zhāng Jiāzhēn was a Gentleman of the Secretariat.
Cuī Shí held him lightly,
often calling him "Zhāng Dǐ" (literally, "Zhāng the bottom/lowly").
Later, during a discussion of affairs,
Zhāng Jiāzhēn surpassed everyone.
Cuī Shí exclaimed:
"Zhāng Dǐ is actually a man like us!
This is indeed his rightful place."
Observing the Ministries Tower
Cuī Rìzhī regretted not holding one of the eight high positions.
When he became Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices,
he built a tower in his official hall
that directly overlooked the Imperial Secretariat (Shàngshū Shěng).
At the time, it was called "Master Cuī's Observing the Ministries Tower."
Jade Trees Verdant
The county of Yúnyáng had many former sites of Hàn imperial palaces.
There was a tree resembling a locust tree but with fine leaves,
which scholars called a "jade tree."
Yáng Zǐyún's "Gānquán Fù" mentions "jade trees verdant."
Later, Zuǒ Sī considered this "jade tree" to be a false claim of a rare wonder,
and not truly accurate.
Jìn Ever-burning Lamp
In a temple in Jiānglíng County, there was a Jìn ever-burning lamp.
Over the years,
the flame was blue and not hot.
When Emperor Wén of Suí pacified Chén,
he was already surprised by its antiquity.
Suǒ Jìng's Calligraphy
Wáng Lì,
the uncle of the Right General (Wáng Xīzhī),
obtained a sheet of Suǒ Jìng's calligraphy.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
he folded it four times and carried it in his clothes to cross the Yangtze River.
Concealing the Awkwardness for Duke Wèi
Wèi Shōu,
a luminary of the Northern Dynasties,
when Xú Líng was sent as an envoy to Qí,
Wèi Shōu compiled his writings and gave them to him,
intending for them to be disseminated south of the Yangtze.
Xú Líng, upon crossing the Yangtze, sank them,
saying:
"I am concealing the awkwardness for Duke Wèi."
Língyùn's Beard
Xiè Língyùn of Jìn had a beautiful beard.
Before his execution,
he donated it to the Jíhuán Temple in Nánhǎi as the beard of Vimalakīrti.
False Mask
Gāo Qí's Prince of Lánlíng, Chánggōng, was fair and resembled a woman.
So he wore a false mask
when facing enemies.
When fighting the Zhōu army,
his bravery surpassed all three armies.
The people of Qí admired him,
and composed a dance to imitate his gestures of command and combat.
This is the origin of the mask.
Tàyáoniáng
Towards the end of the Suí dynasty, there was a man in Héjiān who blew his nose and got drunk,
calling himself "Lángzhōng."
Whenever he was drunk, he would beat his wife.
His wife was beautiful and a good singer.
Whenever she sang sorrowful and resentful songs,
she would sway her body.
Enthusiasts made a false mask to depict her appearance,
calling it "Tàyáoniáng."
This is now transformed into "Róngniáng."
Qiānqiū Jié
The fifth day of the eighth month,
Emperor Míng's birthday,
was called "Qiānqiū Jié."
Princes and imperial relatives presented golden mirrors and sashes,
while officials and commoners tied "dew-catching silk pouches"
and exchanged them as gifts.
Shuǐdiào Gē
Emperor Yáng of Suí excavated the Biàn Hé
and personally composed the "Shuǐdiào Gē."
Āpó Tángzhǔ
When Emperor Yáng feasted his officials,
he referred to Emperor Gāozǔ of Táng, whose face was wrinkled,
as "Āpó" (old woman).
When Gāozǔ returned,
he was displeased,
and told Empress Dòu.
The Empress said:
"This is an auspicious omen.
You are enfeoffed in Táng,
and 'Táng' (唐) is homophonous with 'táng' (堂, hall).
So 'Āpó' means 'mistress of the hall' (tángzhǔ). "
Gāozǔ was greatly pleased.
Ball Court
Wǔ Chóngxùn poured oil on the ground
to build a ball court.
Minister of Agriculture Selling Vegetables
During Emperor Gāozōng's time,
the Minister of Agriculture wished to sell surplus winter vegetables.
He presented a handwritten imperial edict in ink to the Executive Censor Sū Liángsì.
Sū Liángsì replied:
"Gōngyí, when serving as prime minister of Lǔ,
still pulled out mallows from his garden.
How much more so should one not engage in selling vegetables
when ruling over all nations?"
The matter was consequently not carried out.
Drunken Monk Painting
Zhāng Sēngyáo made "The Painting of Drunken Monks."
Daoists often used this to mock monks.
So the monks gathered several hundred thousand cash,
offered a painting and established a precedent,
making "The Painting of Drunken Daoists."
Both are now circulated in the world.
Reporting an alarm for your honorable father
Xǔ Jìngzōng impeached and had his son, Áng, exiled to Língnán.
When Jìngzōng died,
scholar Yuán Sīgǔ debated his posthumous title, saying "error" (謬).
Áng's son, Yànbó, was about to strike him among the crowd.
Yuán said:
"Today I am avenging your honorable father,
why are you angry instead?"
Yànbó was ashamed and stopped.
Seeking life or seeking death
Empress Wǔ was planning to execute people.
Dàlǐ Qīng Hú Yuánlǐ, following her command, sought to entrap people unto death.
Lǐ Rìzhī changed the judgment,
but Yuánlǐ refused three times.
Yuánlǐ said:
"As long as Hú Yuánlǐ is here,
this person cannot seek life."
Rìzhī said:
"As long as Lǐ Rìzhī is here,
this person cannot seek death."
In the end, he was spared.
Coffin at Xiákǒu
General Wáng Guǒ
saw a coffin on a cliffside at Xiákǒu,
about to fall.
He moved it to a flat place
and found an inscription saying:
"Three hundred years hence, water will carry me away;
on the verge of falling, I meet Wáng Guǒ."
Wéi Xùn
Xùn was three years younger than Lù Jī's entry into Luòyáng,
and two years older than Chóng'ěr's accession to the throne.
He presented himself to the late Shàngshū Liú Gōng, a man of twenty-eight *zhàng*.
He recorded what was discussed,
which later became a topic of conversation.
In the tenth year of Dàzhōng
Wéi Xùn, the Shàoyǐn of Jiānglíng, narrated this.
Zhāng Xún's poem
Zhāng Xún defended Suīyáng,
writing a poem that said:
"Combat is bitter since spring began,
the lonely city grows more perilous each day.
The encirclement matches a lunar halo,
the divided defense is like a fish-scale formation.
Often vexed by rising yellow dust,
at times we wave white feathers.
Bandaging wounds, still we sally forth,
drinking blood, again we ascend the ramparts."
His poem "Hearing the Flute at Night" says:
"Unable to discern the color of wind and dust,
how can one know the heart of heaven and earth?"
Zhìgōng's prophecy
Zhìgōng Dàshī of the Liáng dynasty said:
"A two-horned woman in green clothes,
turning her back on the great *háng* to invite the king,
a 'one-stop' month will surely perish."
"Two-horned woman" is the character Ān (安);
"green clothes" is Lù (祿);
"great *háng*" (大行) is a mountain;
"one-stop" (一止) is the first month (正月).
Indeed, it perished in the first month.
The character *táng* in the annotation of a poem, but no *gāo* character in the Six Classics
Sòng Kǎogōng's poem says:
"On horseback I encounter Hánshí,
the spring light reveals no *táng* (malt syrup)."
Zhèng Jiān's annotation to the *Máo Shī* at the place describing playing the flute says:
"This is the item found at homes selling *táng* today."
In the Six Classics, only this annotation contains the character "táng" (餳).
On the Double Ninth Festival,
I intended to rhyme a poem with the character "gāo" (餻).
As the Six Classics do not contain the character "gāo",
I dared not do it.
The Five Watches
The Five Watches are
Jiǎ, Yǐ, Bǐng, Dīng, Wù,
passing from one to another.
Only the first watch (一夜) and the midnight watch (子夜)
are not clear.
Three Dukes Entering the Market
Sītú Dù often said:
"After I retire from office,
I must buy a small horse.
After eating my fill,
I will ride it.
Wearing a coarse cloth tunic,
entering the market to watch the spinning bells and puppets will be enough."
Later, after resigning, he indeed carried out his wish.
An advising official submitted a memorial saying:
"It is improper for a Duke to enter the market."
The Duke said:
"This was already in my plan."
Steamed *húmèi* is indescribably delicious
Liú Yàn entered court at the fifth watch.
It was cold then.
On the way, he saw a place selling steamed *hú* (barbarian buns),
with a rich aroma wafting.
He sent someone to buy some,
and ate it, hidden beneath his robe and wrapped in his skirt,
saying to his colleagues:
"It's indescribably delicious."
Selling cakes and singing
At the entrance of the alley where Shìláng Liú Bóchú lived,
there was a cake seller.
Early in the morning, passing his door,
one would always hear singing by the stove.
Liú Bóchú called him over, gave him ten thousand coins,
and told him to increase his capital,
saying:
"Use *húbǐng* (foreign cakes) to repay me."
Later, passing his door,
no singing was heard.
He called him over and asked:
"Why did you stop singing so suddenly?"
He replied:
"As my capital has grown large,
my calculations have become coarser,
and I have no time to sing."
Yǔwén Róng, the Hundred-Day Prime Minister
In the Yǒnghuī era,
Lú Qíqīng died suddenly.
When he revived,
he recounted seeing his maternal uncle acting as a judge in the underworld.
An official pushed a case forward and said:
"Yǔwén Róng is to be Prime Minister."
His uncle said:
"How can Róng be fit to be Prime Minister?"
The official said:
"The heavenly decree has already been issued,
the duration is up to the judge."
So his uncle judged it to be one hundred days.
After he was appointed,
he was indeed dismissed after one hundred days.
Holding this scale to weigh the world
When Shàngguān Zhāoróng's mother was about to give birth,
she dreamed someone gave her a scale,
saying:
"Hold this scale to weigh the world."
Madam Zhèng hoped it would be a boy,
but when Zhāoróng was born,
her mother said:
"To weigh the world,
how could it be a girl?"
She gurgled as if responding:
"It is."
Sòng Zhīwèn begged for Liú Xīyí's poem
Liú Xīyí's poem said:
"Year after year, flowers are alike,
year after year, people are different."
Sòng Zhīwèn deeply loved this line.
He pleaded tearfully for it, but Xīyí refused to give it.
Zhīwèn grew angry
and crushed him to death with a sack of earth.
Sòng Zhīwèn did not die a natural death;
this was heavenly retribution.
Cranes and cormorants
It is commonly believed that only cranes are born from the womb (viviparous),
which is why the rhapsody says "a viviparous immortal bird."
However, people do not know that cormorants are also viviparous.
If it is because cormorants eat fish,
unlike cranes,
I have now seen crane keepers
feeding them foul and smelly things, worse than what cormorants eat.
If it is because their color is blacker than cranes,
then a white crane lives a thousand years
before transforming into a black crane.
A gentleman dislikes residing in a low place;
is this perhaps what is meant by cormorants?
Chén Biāo's poem on "Mallows" says:
"How much can it contend with peonies?
It is disliked precisely because it is common."
This also refers to cormorants.
Spinach
Bōléng spinach,
comes from Western countries.
A monk came from Bōléng bringing its seeds.
Some say it was Pōléng who brought them;
this is a phonetic error.
Chādǎ
Fàn Xīcháo went to govern Tàiyuán,
and bid farewell to the vice minister in the Imperial Secretariat, saying:
"If the vice minister has any matter,
just give the order.
If I don't respond the second time,
please forgive me.
If I don't respond by the third time,
then the vice minister may proceed to chādǎ."
Chā refers to
the shaft used by arrow makers.
Dǎ
means to damage and discard arrows,
Zhūgě Cài
Wherever Zhūgě stayed,
he exclusively planted turnips (mànjīng).
The first reason was that they could be eaten raw as soon as their sprouts appeared.
That's one.
The second was that the mature leaves could be boiled.
That's two.
The third was that they grew abundantly with prolonged cultivation.
That's three.
The fourth was that there was no regret in discarding them.
That's four.
The fifth was that they were easy to find upon return.
That's five.
The sixth was that they could be dug up and eaten in winter.
That's six.
In Shǔ, they are called "Zhūgě Cài."
Cuī Qún's Extraordinary Intelligence
Hán Shíyī Yù was truly too frivolous.
He said to Lǐ Chéng:
"I have been acquainted with Grand Chancellor Cuī Qún for many years,
and he is truly intelligent beyond others."
Lǐ asked:
"In what way is he beyond others?"
Hán replied:
"Having been acquainted with Yù for over thirty years,
he has never discussed literature with Yù.
This is what makes him beyond others."
Hán Yù's Edict
When Hán Yù was first demoted,
Secretariat Director Xí composed the edict for him,
which read:
"He achieved scholarly success early,
and also had a reputation."
After Xí passed away,
a friend said:
"How could Xí Yuánlì's children and nephews
suffer from 'yin-poison' cold-damage and
eat unclean things?"
Hán replied:
"Xí Shíbā was too late in eating unclean things."
Someone asked:
"Why?"
He said:
"His words were not appropriate."
This was because he resented the edict saying "and also had a reputation."
The Prime Minister's Wife of Eighteen Years
When Yuán Zài was defeated,
his wife, Lady Wáng, said:
"I am the daughter of a Military Governor,
and a prime minister's wife for eighteen years.
Today, my husband has committed a crime;
I am willing to die.
But to make me a common slave,
is worse than death."
The presiding official reported this,
and she was soon granted death.
The Prime Minister's Night Ritual
When Wáng Jìn was imprisoned,
the interrogation read:
"As a prime minister,
what did you seek in your night rituals?"
Wáng replied:
"Whether you know or not,
I deserve to die."
Begging for a Quick Death
Yuán Zài, in the Buddha hall of Wànnián County,
met the presiding official
and begged for a quick death.
The official said:
"It is not strange that the Grand Chancellor receives some dirt today."
Then he took off a dirty sock,
stuffed his mouth with it, and he died.
The Prime Minister's Stele
Dù Péngjǔ's father once dreamt of a large stele,
which was said to be the Prime Minister's Stele.
Those who had already served had their names filled with gold;
those who had not yet served had their names carved on the stele.
Dù asked:
"Are there any from the Dù family?"
He replied:
"Yes,
feel free to look."
Beneath his surname was a bird
with a trailing foot radical,
but he forgot the character.
So he named Péngjǔ, saying:
"If you do not become a prime minister,
then for generations, your sons will be named with the bird radical
and a trailing foot radical."
When Péngjǔ later had a son,
he named him Hóngjiàn.
Three Platforms
During the Northern Qí, Gāo Yáng destroyed the Bronze Sparrow Terrace
and built three platforms.
Palace women would clap their hands and call 'Up to the platform!'
then deliver wine.
During the reign of Empress Zétiān,
Prefect Dèng Hóngqìng presented three platforms of wine.
Dàozhōu Cānjūn and Húzhōu Wénxué
Yáng Guózhōng held a gathering of his relatives.
At that time, the official in charge of the Civil Office selections wished to make a great jest.
He called the names of the selected candidates,
led them into the central courtyard,
and without asking about their qualifications or seniority,
assigned the short ones
to be Military Supervisors of Dàozhōu;
and those with beards
to be Literary Officials of Húzhōu.
There was great laughter behind the curtains.
Sages of the Three Teachings
On Dèzōng's birthday,
discussions of the three teachings were held in the inner palace.
After everyone finished speaking,
the monk Jiànxū said:
"Your servant requests to address a matter.
Xuányuán Huángdì
is the founder of our Táng dynasty.
Wénxuān Wáng
is a sage of ancient and modern times.
Shìjiā Rúlái
is a sage of the Western Paradise.
And His Majesty the Emperor
is a sage of Jambudvīpa (Nánshàn Bùzhōu)."
The Easy Road to Shǔ
Lù Chàng visited Wéi Gāo
and composed "The Easy Road to Shǔ," saying:
"The road to Shǔ is easy,
easier than walking on level ground."
Gāo was greatly pleased.
Bǎozhāng Jí
Empress Wǔ asked Wáng Fāngqìng:
"Are your family's old writings preserved?"
Fāngqìng collected calligraphic works from over twenty people, including Yòujūn,
commissioned Cuī Róng to write a preface,
and it was given the name "Bǎozhāng Jí."
Poem for Xiàng Sī
Jìjiǔ Yáng's poem "For Xiàng Sī" says:
"Each time I see your poems, they are always good;
now I observe your character surpasses your poetry.
I have never been one to hide people's virtues in my life,
so wherever I meet someone, I speak of Xiàng Sī."
Borrowed Boat Post
Wáng Nèishǐ's "Borrowed Boat Post"
was treasured by Lú Shàngshū.
Zhāng sighed and returned it.
Tiger Bones for Rain
When there was severe drought in the south,
tiger bones were thrown into places with dragons, and rain would immediately fall,
enraging the dragons.
Woman with an Unlucky Demeanor
Wáng Shēng had a sister,
of national beauty.
Dèzōng took her into the palace,
but she did not enjoy the imperial gardens.
The Emperor said:
"A woman with an unlucky demeanor."
So he sent her out.
He ordered her brother
not to marry her to a jinshì or court official,
but to let her be married to a military commander's personal attendant.
Later, due to unforeseen circumstances,
Brocade in the Well
Fèi Xùn took the *jìnshì* examination.
He dreamt of being clothed in brocade within a well.
Upon waking,
he rejoiced to himself, saying:
"I shall pass the examination and return to my hometown in brocade clothes!"
Someone else said:
"This is not a good dream.
Being clothed in brocade in a well
is a sign that your literary talents will not become manifest."
The next spring, he indeed failed the examination.
Concerning dream interpretation:
If a person's *zàngqì* is predominantly *yīn*, they dream frequently.
If their *yáng* is strong, they dream rarely;
even if they dream, they don't remember it.
Blind people have no dreams,
and foolish people have few dreams.
There was a scholar who could interpret dreams.
Someone would invent a dream
and ask him to interpret it,
and all his interpretations were accurate.
Another day, the scholar was told:
"I actually have no dreams;
what I told you before I invented
just to test you.
Why were all your interpretations accurate?"
He replied:
"Intent takes form in words,
and fortune or misfortune follows."
There was a pious
layman, Wáng Yù,
who was devoted to Chan studies.
In his later years, he said to his fellow practitioners:
"I shall pass away on a certain day."
A monk said:
"Penetrating the formless,
unhindered in the ten directions,
even reaching a state of no-mind,
is not yet considered complete;
how much less so for those with thoughts?"
Placing a Thousand Gold to Pray to Sūn Zhēnrén.
In Méizhōu, a commoner couple
had only one son in their middle age.
When he reached adulthood,
he became increasingly thin and emaciated.
The father placed a copy of the *Qiānjīn Fāng* in an upstairs chamber of their residence,
burning incense day and night,
looking towards Mount Éméi and praying to Sūn Zhēnrén,
begging for protection and rescue.
One night,
he dreamt of an old man in white clothes who said:
"When your son was born,
he received less vital energy (*qì*) from his parents.
I will now instruct you:
each morning, let both parents breathe out their breath
and have your son open his mouth and swallow it.
If you do this for three days,
your son will recover."
He then followed the instruction with focused mind.
Immediately, the son became strong and able to eat,
and all his ailments completely vanished.
Later, he donned a brown robe and entered the Dao,
serving the True Person diligently.
Meat *Zhī*
In Shǔ, there was a village man selling a white toad.
It was very large,
with two eyes like cinnabar.
Everyone said it was "meat *zhī*."
A medicine worker bought it,
fearing it would escape.
He placed a large stone mortar on the ground and covered it with a white cloth.
By dawn,
the stone mortar was transparent like a lantern.
The medical worker was astonished.
He fasted, bathed, carried his cauldron and the toad,
and left his home to enter Qīngchéng Mountain.
His fate is unknown.
White Toad
There was a Xiān Yú Xī,
who was drinking at Wànsuì Lake on the third day of the third lunar month.
He saw a small white toad by the grass,
and so he picked it up.
At the same banquet, there was a person named Liú,
who snatched it and swallowed it.
Xī jokingly said:
"Your Excellency swallowed this white toad;
if you manage to achieve the Dao,
you'll just be a bandit!"
After swallowing it,
he hastily drank water,
and was dizzy and unwell for more than ten days,
only recovering after medical treatment.
I once read in *Bàopǔzǐ·Nèipiān* that it says:
"Meat *zhī*
is a ten-thousand-year-old toad.
It has horns on its head,
red eyes,
cinnabar patterns under its chin,
and is heavy but jumps nimbly.
If taken at noon on the fifth day of the fifth month
and dried in the shade,
its left foot can draw water from the ground to form a spring.
Carrying it wards off weapons.
If an enemy shoots with bows and crossbows,
they will all wound themselves instead."
Today's people swallow it raw or eat it cooked,
which is utterly foolish.
Even if a white toad were meat *zhī*,
the internal organs of common people are full of foul impurities;
if these attack a spiritual creature,
how can any person remain whole?
Eel, Toad, Softshell Turtle
Eel, toad, and softshell turtle –
the large ones of these three creatures
are poisonous and can kill.
Even small toads
can cause urinary retention
and painful distension below the navel,
sometimes leading to death.
It is advisable to throw fresh fermented soybeans into freshly drawn water,
soaking them until the bean water is concentrated,
and drinking it will bring immediate relief.
Earth Pulp Detoxification
There was a temple monk who bought wild mulberries;
some were black with spots,
some were yellowish-white and red.
They were eaten as a communal meal.
All the monks suffered vomiting and diarrhea,
and some died.
A medical worker said:
"Dig a pit in the ground,
pour freshly drawn water into the pit,
stir it until it clarifies,
and call it 'earth pulp.'
Drinking it will immediately neutralize the poison."
Mushrooms that grow on trees are called *xùn*,
and those that grow on the ground are called *jūn*.
They all grow from stagnant, humid vapor.
There are also those that grow on rotten wood and poisonous snakes,
which are large and brilliant.
People mistakenly take them for spiritual *zhī*,
eat them, and die quickly.
Checking Deceased Names Against a Register
Ài Yánzuò, a dyer from Chéngdū,
was captured by bandits
and forced to make lacquerware.
Suddenly, he heard that imperial troops were arriving.
Yánzuò climbed a tree
and hid among the dense leaves,
witnessing the searching, capturing, and slaughtering.
At night,
he descended the tree
and lay among the piled corpses.
In the middle of the night,
he heard shouting,
somewhat resembling that of generals and officers.
There were dozens of people,
all without torches,
their forms unseen.
Only the sound of them checking against a register
and calling out names was heard.
The stiff corpses, upon hearing their names called,
each rose and responded,
except Yánzuò, whose name was not called.
He then realized that the suppression of rebellion and punishment of traitors
was carried out by Heaven's command,
and no one was mistakenly killed.
The Yi Woman's Unyielding Spirit
In the *jiǎwǔ* year,
the imperial army captured Yìzhōu,
and the troops were stationed at Hóngyǎ.
A soldier captured an Yi woman
who was quite beautiful and said she had a husband.
The soldier wanted to assault her,
but she clasped her arms, crossed her knees,
and sat on the ground with bowed head.
The soldier grew angry
and threatened to cut off her neck,
but the woman's heart utterly refused to yield.
Decorating Merit Paintings
Zhāng Guāng praised the merits of mounting and painting.
He was captured by bandits,
and though struck several times with swords, his neck was not severed.
Lying among piled corpses,
at midnight,
he saw an old monk who said:
"You have put your heart into the merits of mounting and painting throughout your life,
so I have come to save you."
After speaking,
he opened his eyes and felt no suffering.
Bōluó Huā
The Bōluó flower in Éméi Shān.
Its bud is as large as a fist,
and its leaves resemble loquat leaves.
When there are more than twenty leaves,
three clusters
of flowers,
three
to ten-plus blooms.
It withers only after a month.
A monk from the Western Regions said:
"It is also so in Central India."
Transformation into a Tiger
Hǎo Èr, a villager from Língchí Xiàn,
made a living as a doctor and diviner.
At home, he had a painting called "Huà Hǔ Tú" (Painting of a Tiger),
and every day he would sit intently,
staring at it tirelessly,
completely forgetting human affairs.
When people called for medical treatment,
he would simply use the tiger painting as a charm and give it to them as medicine.
Within a few years,
his house was full of such hangings,
and he only liked to eat raw meat.
Later, he transformed into a tiger.
Old Monk Transforms into a Tiger
A person from Chéngdū surnamed Xú,
arrived at a village
and saw an old monk in a pit,
who said:
"Last night I entered the village to preach,
and on my way back, I mistakenly fell into this pit.
I hope the benefactor will show compassion and rescue me."
The villagers collectively opened the pit and brought him out.
He leaped a few steps,
transformed into a giant tiger, and left.
Tiger's Majesty
A hunter from Yǒngkāng Jūn, named Xué Quēkǒu,
was able to stab tigers.
He said:
"A tiger has a majestic bone,
shaped like the character '乙' (yǐ),
about three inches long,
located beneath the skin on both sides of its ribs.
If one obtains it and wears it when confronting officials,
one can command the crowd.
A tiger generally only emits light from one eye when looking,
and sees with the other eye.
Those who are killed by a tiger or drown
have their souls called 'Chāng Guǐ'.
Whenever there is a lunar halo,
tigers will mate.
When a tiger eats a dog, it will surely become drunk;
the dog,
is the tiger's wine.
A tiger never harms a drunk person.
Once, a villager,
drunk, slept by a cliff.
A tiger came and sniffed him,
its whiskers accidentally went into the drunkard's nose,
causing a loud sneeze.
The tiger was startled and leaped,
falling off the cliff and dying."
Burying Silkworms and Selling Mulberry
The Lǐ family in Xīnfán Xiàn
raised many silkworms.
When they were about to mature,
mulberry leaves became very expensive,
so they buried the silkworms and sold their leaves,
making a great profit.
Consequently, they bought meat and flour to make steamed buns (mántóu).
When they ate them,
upon tearing open each one,
there was a silkworm inside.
From then on, their family suffered losses and deaths.
For silkworms
are spiritual creatures that clothe the world.
That ignorant people would bury them
resulted in this retribution.
Killing Living Beings and Being Unfaithful
Sūn Zhīwēi painted Buddhist and Daoist figures,
and abstained from meat and wine.
There was a sorceress who could recognize the forms of ghosts.
Zhīwēi asked her,
and she said:
"There are several kinds of ghosts.
Those with good fortune and virtue
are vibrant and clear-minded,
and can converse with people directly.
Those with meager fortunes
are weak in spirit and withered in essence,
and must rely on someone else to convey their words.
Currently, on the path, humans and ghosts are half and half,
but people themselves cannot distinguish them."
Zhīwēi asked:
"Among the sins, what is most heavily regarded in the underworld?"
She replied:
"Killing living beings and being unfaithful.
What is most revered
is Buddhism."
Practicing the Yùquán Method
Dù Dǐngshēng practiced the Yùquán method
to expel the Three Corpses,
strengthen teeth and hair,
and cure a hundred ailments.
Yùquán
refers to the bodily fluids from the two脉 (mài) under the tongue.
Every morning upon rising, one sits down,
closes the eyes and clears the mind,
clicks the teeth fourteen times (two sevens),
rinses until the mouth is full,
then swallows it,
mentally guiding it once to the Qìhǎi (sea of qi) below the navel.
After a long time,
it will naturally sound like trickling water flowing down into a deep abyss.
Doing this,
harmonizes the hundred脉 (mài).
Therefore, the "Huángtíng" says:
"Clear water from the Jade Pool irrigates the spiritual root."
It also says:
"Rinsing and swallowing the spiritual fluid prevents calamities." This is it.
The Stepmother Swallow Harms the Chicks
After their official duties, the palace literary officials
each recounted things they had seen and heard in their lives.
Academicians (Xuéshì Chéngzhǐ) Wáng Rényù and Zhāng Hàng spoke about Fàn Zhì:
"Two swallows nested beneath their house,
raising several chicks,
which had already been fed.
The female was caught and eaten by a cat.
The male chirped for a long time before finally leaving.
It then paired with another swallow,
feeding the chicks as before.
Within a few days,
all the chicks fell to the ground,
writhing as if paralyzed.
The children cut open their bellies to look,
and found them filled with caltrop seeds in their crops.
It was indeed harmed by the second mate (stepmother).
Indeed, all creatures with blood and breath
are never without feelings of hatred, love, jealousy, and envy."
Donkeys as Foals
Donkey foals,
follow their mothers.
Some are in front,
some are beside their mother,
some are behind;
this depends on their birth time.
Those born at the beginning of the month are in front,
those born in the middle of the month are in the middle,
and those born at the end of the month are at the back.
Encountering a Tiger on Shāngshān
The roads in Shāngshān had many fierce beasts.
A group of donkeys was traveling early in the morning,
when the donkeys suddenly became startled.
A tiger leaped out from a thicket,
seized a man, and carried him off.
Those traveling together dared not look back.
After a short while (the time it takes to eat a meal),
the seized man returned,
saying:
"The tiger carried me to the top of a cliff.
In front was a ten-thousand-fathom clear stream,
and to the south of the stream was a cave.
At the mouth of the cave, several small tigers looked out,
as if waiting for something.
The tiger roared, calling its cubs.
I stealthily stretched out my leg, and with all my might, stomped on the tiger's back.
The tiger lost its footing and fell into a deep ravine.
It could not climb up again.
That is how I escaped."
Drunk Entering a Tomb
In Yǎnzhōu, there was a commoner's family burying their parents.
All their relatives by marriage arrived.
One son-in-law, in his drunkenness, followed the coffin into the tomb.
The landowner did not know this,
and immediately sealed it up and left.
The next day,
the family returned to the tomb,
and faintly heard cries from within.
They opened it up and brought him out.
He said:
"After sobering up,
I felt myself in a dark room.
I raised my hand to feel the walls
and only then realized I was in the tomb.
Suddenly, I heard a man and an old woman whispering, saying:
'We've been in this temporary lodging for a long time;
now we are happy to be settled.'
It was as if they were congratulating each other.
Then one said:
'How can there be the scent of a living person?
Get a light to see.'
Then a torch appeared beside the coffin,
illuminating me.
They then said:
'Burn him!'
When they said 'burn,' torches gathered around,
burning my beard and hair to cinders,
and burning my skin,
but I did not feel much pain.
It stopped after a short while."
Stories of the Yùshǐtái
According to stories of the Yùshǐ,
when officials came to pay respects,
there was no usher.
Suddenly, they would all bow together at the foot of the stairs,
and silently withdraw.
This was called "ghost audience" (guǐcān).
Also, when three cases were judged,
the judgment would say:
the two characters "jìzī" (記資).
Their meaning was not understood,
nor was their origin known.
Poisoned by Turtles
Someone caught over ten turtles from a river,
very plump and tender.
They were cooked and stewed,
and the whole family ate them together.
That evening, all of them died;
not a single person escaped.
They were indeed poisoned by the turtles.
Aquatic creatures found on land
are certainly to be suspected.
A gentleman should be cautious about what he eats and drinks.
Yǔ's Footprints on Shàngxiāofēng
On Lúshān, there is Xiāofēng,
about a thousand rén high.
On it are ancient traces,
said to be where Great Yǔ moored his boat
when he controlled the floods.
Holes were chiseled into the rock
to tie cables there.
There is a cliffside stele with
tadpole-script characters,
faintly visible.
Taro Wall
A monk in a temple on Gézàoshān
devoted great effort to planting taro,
harvesting an extremely large amount each year.
He pounded it into a paste,
and built ditches into walls with it.
Later, when there was a great famine,
only the forty-odd monks of this temple ate from the taro ditches to survive the harsh year.
Predicting Floods and Droughts
On the night of Shàngyuán,
set up a pole one zhàng tall in the courtyard.
Wait until noon by moonlight;
if its shadow is seven chǐ,
it will be a great harvest.
Six chǐ,
a small harvest.
Nine chǐ or one zhàng,
there will be floods.
Five chǐ,
a drought year.
Three chǐ,
a great drought.
Also, on the first day of the first month,
check the cattle under the ox shed:
if all are lying down, the five grains will have difficulty forming seedlings.
If half are lying and half are standing,
the year will be average.
If all the cattle are standing,
then the five grains will ripen.
If it rains on jiǎzǐ in spring, there will be much drought;
if it rains on jiǎzǐ in autumn, there will be much flooding.
Nineteen Turtles Beg for Life
At Cūi Tuō Shàngshū's house,
he was entertaining guests.
That night, he dreamt of nineteen people,
dressed in green-blue silk robes,
bowing and begging for life.
After he awoke,
he saw turtles swimming in a vessel of water.
He counted them,
and there were exactly nineteen, big and small.
He then went to the water's edge and released them.
Zhāng Shǒuzhōng's Poems
The last line of Zhāng Shǒuzhōng Xiùcái's poem "Butterflies" says:
"If tonight you rest on the fragrant grass path,
please convey my secret feelings to the noble young man."
He also said:
"Fated for misfortune, Sū Qín frequently left his state;
full of emotion, Pān Yuè quickly grieved for autumn."
This is the dividing line for the fútóu.
Wáng Shěnzhī, the military governor of Mǐn, had a nephew who was good at witty conversation.
There was a scholar whose complexion was quite dark.
When he fell asleep drunk,
Wáng inscribed on his forehead with a red brush:
"This is the dividing line for the smile."
Rose Poem
Lǐ Jìlán's daughter,
at six years old,
composed a poem "Rose," saying:
"For a long time, it has not been trained on a trellis;
my feelings are tangled and confused."
Her father said:
"This girl will surely become an immoral woman."
It turned out as he said.
Yán Lǔgōng's Post-Mortem Liberation
More than ten years after Yán Lǔgōng suffered misfortune,
a family servant saw him in Luòzhōng, dressed in a white shirt and holding an umbrella,
returning to a vegetable garden on the city's edge.
There were several dilapidated houses.
The servant followed him in and bowed.
The Duke took ten ounces of gold from his bosom,
to send to his family,
and warned the servant not to tell anyone.
The Duke's son went to the aforementioned place,
but only saw a landscape overgrown with weeds.
People at the time all said:
"Lǔgōng attained the Dao through post-mortem liberation."
Rats Pilfering Granaries
During the Tiānfù era,
there was a great famine in Lǒngyòu.
That year's autumn harvest was very abundant,
but just before reaping,
more than half of it had no grain heads.
Someone went into the fields, broke open rat holes and searched,
and found a great deal.
Thus, every family dug up holes,
with some finding five or seven hú.
This was passed down and called "rats pilfering granaries" (jiératscāng).
People in the villages all went to the fields to forage for food,
saving many lives.
Essence of Fire
Rèn Zàn, a Hanlin Academician of the Liáng dynasty,
held office for several years
still wearing a vermilion ribbon.
He inscribed a poem on his desk.
The Liáng ruler learned of it
and commanded that he be bestowed a purple robe and a golden seal.
The poem said:
"For several years, I have been honored within the court,
the color of my official's robe stands out clearly.
Rèn Zàn, courtesy name Xīdù,
knows you are the essence of fire."
Chanting the Great Compassion Mantra
Ouyáng Càn of Xú was walking on a road and encountered rain.
It was already dark.
He saw a giant object, over a zhàng long,
appear before him.
Càn concentrated on chanting the "Dàbēizhòu."
The demon could not approach,
and the rain also gradually stopped.
Painting Chickens
In Jiāngnán, there was a Daoist priest named Lì Guīzhēn.
He once visited Xìngguǒguān in Hóngzhōu.
The statues inside were made of clay and hemp from the Xuánzōng era,
and sparrows and pigeons defecated on them.
Guīzhēn painted a chicken on the wall;
its brushwork was extraordinary.
From then on, no birds or sparrows rested there again.
Snake Fungi
The common people of Húnán
found a very large mushroom
in the countryside
and presented it to the Prefect.
A monk said:
"This object is very poisonous,
be careful not to eat it."
So they dug around where it was found,
and there were over a thousand hibernating snakes.
Fabricated Couplets
Zhāng Jié was a witty man
who could compose fabricated couplets.
He once sat in a group of three,
and recited:
"Three men sit like tripod legs,
all night long they wag their heads and hum."
He also said:
"A clapper hangs from the soapberry tree,
a tea whisk dangles from the gourd trellis."
Once he angered a military officer.
Zhāng Jié said:
"Since the lord wishes to throw punches,
this humble one cannot bear the fright."
Playing the Shēng to Summon Wind
A frivolous person
ordered a musician to play the shēng,
saying:
"No need to perform a tune,
I want you to summon the wind."
A Handful from Heaven
In the Xīngyuán era, there was a southern road leading to Bāzhōu.
The top of its precipitous cliff
was called "Lonely Clouds' Two Corners."
A proverb said:
"Lonely Clouds' Two Corners,
a handful from heaven."
Goose Slaves
Geese roost in the sandbars of rivers and lakes,
numbering in the thousands.
The large ones stay in the middle,
ordering "goose slaves" to surround them and guard against hunters.
Chén Shú's Poem
Chén Shú composed a poem with a monk, saying:
"Moving like a single-wheeled cart,
always fearing the great road will overturn.
Still like a round-bottomed vessel,
always fearing other objects will strike.
Since moving and still are thus,
how can one not depart from the mundane?"
Volume 54
End.
The Emperor Asks about Lǚ Zhēn's Health
In the early Xīníng era,
Lǚ Zhēn was the Prefect of Jīng.
When he entered the imperial hall,
Zhōu Yuē, the Judicial Assistant of the prefecture, followed him.
The Emperor suddenly asked:
"Is Your Excellency in good health?"
He replied:
"Nothing is wrong."
After a moment, he asked again:
"Are you truly without ailment?"
He said:
"This subject dares not force it."
At that time, Lǚ Gōng's complexion showed no trace of deficiency.
As Lǚ was about to withdraw, the Emperor again asked Zhōu Yuē:
"What do you think of Lǚ Zhēn?"
He replied:
"In this subject's observation of Zhēn,
he also seems to have nothing wrong."
When Lǚ exited the palace gate,
he felt deeply suspicious,
straightened his headscarf, wiped his face,
and asked for a mirror to examine himself.
He asked Zhōu:
"Do you truly see Zhēn as having nothing wrong?"
He said:
"Lóngtú, do not doubt yourself,
your complexion is calm and peaceful."
A few days later,
he indeed fell ill and did not recover.
From this, we know that the sagacious wisdom of the Emperor is not something ordinary perception can match.
Star Name Zhōubó
In the second year of Jǐngdé,
a giant star appeared west of Tiāndī,
its light like a golden pellet.
No one recognized it.
Zhōu Kèmíng, the Director of the Bureau of Astronomy, said:
"According to the 'Tiānwén Lù,'
the star observed in Jīngzhōu
is named Zhōubó.
The saying goes:
'Its color is golden yellow,
its light brilliant.
In the country where it is seen,
there will be peace and prosperity.'
Also, according to 'Yuánmìng Bāo,'
its meaning is 'Virtue Star.'"
At that time, there was a triumphal return from Chányuān,
and the whole realm was pacified,
which suited the appearance of this star.
Lǐ Jiànzhōng's Poems
Lǐ Jiànzhōng was skilled in cursive and clerical scripts,
and his poems were clear and simple,
like the man himself.
He had a poem "Looking at the Lake Tower in Hángzhōu" which said:
"Where small boats idly push off,
the lake and sky scene is also subtle.
Spring waves are endlessly green,
white birds fly freely.
The setting sun on the distant lonely sandbar,
light mist around the sparse ancient temple.
Sometimes I carry a pot of wine,
lingering until the cool evening to return."
His "West Lake" poem said:
"Rising mist and heavy spring air,
the moon held deep in the night's traces."
He always loved to recite four lines from the "Léngyán Jīng" which said:
"How can one who hears and holds the Buddha,
not hear the hearing itself?
Once the root of delusion is removed,
dust vanishes and enlightenment is perfectly pure."
He would chant these lines in all his daily activities.
Xiè Língyùn Reincarnated as Biān Hào
When Biān Hào of Jiāngnán was first born,
his father suddenly dreamt that Xiè Língyùn came to visit with his calling card,
introducing himself as the former Prefect of Yǒngjiā,
with a long beard and elegant demeanor,
clear bones and an alert spirit,
his clothes and scarf
light as smoke and mist.
He said:
"I wish to entrust myself to you as father and son.
Previously, I was residing on Fēiláifēng in Zhèxī,
translating the 'Jīngāng Jīng.'
There were places not quite conforming to the Buddha's intent,
and I wish to be born into your family to revise them.
Be careful not to feed me meat or fish.
At seven years old,
allow me to leave home to become a monk,
to complete the previous sutra."
After the dream ended,
Hào was born,
resembling the person in the dream.
His father loved him,
and his pet name was Kānglè.
As he grew up, he was intelligent and sensitive,
and insisted on leaving home to become a monk.
His father did not agree,
and forced him with meat.
When he came of age,
he was forced to marry.
Later, the ruling lord loved his erudition,
and repeatedly employed him.
However, he was soft-hearted and indecisive,
only fond of Buddhism.
Initially, when he campaigned to pacify Jiànzhōu,
he only sought to save lives;
people called him "Biān Luóhàn."
When he was appointed to Xiāngtán,
he was called "Biān Púsà."
When he was made commander of Tán,
policies came from many sources,
with no decisive authority,
causing disappointment among the people of Chǔ,
who called him "Biān Héshàng."
Selecting Three Filial Scholars to Discuss Classics
Zhēnzōng enjoyed discussing classics.
One day, he ordered Féng Yuán to discuss the "Yì,"
saying:
"I wish to select three scholars of pure filial piety,
dressed in casual clothes and wearing caps,
sitting side by side with classics.
In their leisure, I would offer tea and fruits,
and they would engage in full discussions,
doing away with the formal procedures of presenting arguments."
Féng Yuán recommended Chá Dào, Lǐ Xūyǐ, and Lǐ Xíngjiǎn.
Zhēnzōng immediately summoned them,
and arranged for them to attend him,
happily saying:
"I have gained clarity!"
Fàn Guǒ Presents a Poem
Tàizōng was the governor of Bìngzhōu,
and returned triumphantly.
Fàn Guǒ, as a county magistrate,
presented a poem with the lines: "A thousand li of territory comes from the west of the Zhé,
one sound of gongs and drums descends upon Hédōng."
Xīzhāi Rùnbǐ
Lǐ Hàn passed the imperial examination on the same榜 as Hé Níng.
Later, he and his chief examiner were both appointed academicians.
When Hé Níng became a chancellor,
Lǐ Hàn was a Grand Scholar-Counselor (Chéngzhǐ).
It happened that he was assigned to draft edicts.
The next day,
in the Yùtáng, he boldly opened Chancellor Hé's old chamber,
and took all the paintings, artifacts, and curiosities.
He left a poem saying:
"My chief examiner ascended to high office and returned to the Fènggé,
This student drafts edicts and presides over the áotóu.
The old chamber in Yùtáng has many treasures,
Can they not serve as 'ink-money' for Xīzhāi?"
Wǔzǐ Dēngkē
Dòu Yǔjūn had five sons:
Yí, Kǎn, Chēng, Yǎn, and Yǎn.
They successively passed the imperial examinations.
Féng Yíngwáng presented a poem to Dòu Yǔjūn saying:
"One ancient Cinchona tree grows old,
Five branches of fragrant osmanthus bloom."
Fáng Xiàng Cāngtóu
When Shí Xīzài was young,
he met an old man on a road in Sōngyáng.
The man said:
"You are truly a chancellor for times of peace.
When I was young, I was a page (cāngtóu) in charge of books for Fáng Xuánlíng, a chancellor of the Táng dynasty.
You greatly resemble Chancellor Fáng."
He then exhorted him, saying:
"Serve the true lord well."
After speaking, he vanished.
Later, Shí Xīzài became a secretary to Tàizōng,
and seven years after the emperor's accession, he was appointed Píngzhāngshì.
Chénghuáng Dūxiū Yílíng Xiànyǔ
In the early Bǎoyuán era,
Sòng Zhèngjī was the prefect of Xiázhōu.
One night,
he dreamed that an official said:
"The Chénghuáng God has sent me to supervise the repair of the Yílíng County yamen,
it should not be delayed."
He dreamed this for three consecutive nights.
The next day, it was reported
that Ōuyáng Yǒngshū had been demoted to be the magistrate of Yílíng.
Sòng Zhèngjī was moved by his dream,
and treated him with extraordinary deference.
Ōuyáng Yǒngshū became even more diligent and humble in his work.
Whenever he submitted a report,
he would always stand with his tablet (hu) in the courtyard,
and when Sòng Zhèngjī entered the door,
he would first descend the steps to greet him.
Yáng Dànián Zuòshī Yùyàn
At twenty-one, Yáng Dànián became a Guānglùcéng.
In the third month,
a banquet was held in the imperial garden,
but he was not allowed to attend.
He presented a poem to the academicians (guǎnzhí) saying:
"I hear those who wear court flowers have their temples full of red,
Silk and pipes in the Shànglín serve the 'double pupil'.
Pénglái is close at hand, yet there is no way to reach it,
Only now do I believe immortals and mortals are truly different."
The emperor heard it,
and on that very day appointed him to the Jíxiányuàn,
ordering him to attend the evening banquet.
Huáiyù Shānrén
Yáng Dànián's ancestor, Wén Yì,
served as the magistrate of Yùshān during the Later Táng dynasty.
A Daoist priest came to visit,
calling himself "Huáiyù Shānrén."
Soon after, he disappeared,
and Yáng Dànián was then born.
Later, at thirty-seven, he became an academician.
While napping in the Yùtáng,
he dreamed of the Daoist priest calling himself "Huáiyù Shānrén,"
who took out a tablet from his sleeve,
on which was written "thirty-seven."
Yáng Dànián exclaimed in surprise,
"Is this not my destined number?"
The Daoist priest smiled faintly,
and then asked,
"Can it be extended?"
The Daoist priest commanded a brush and only added a cycle of twelve years,
making it "forty-nine."
When he reached that age, he indeed died.
Tóngjiǎ Tóngxiūqī
Lǐ Jùn and Lǐ Zōng'è were of the same clan and born in the same sexagenary cycle (tóngjiǎ),
with Lǐ Jùn being born one day later.
Their joys and sorrows were always shared.
When Lǐ Zōng'è died,
Lǐ Jùn passed away one day later.
Bǎoshǒu Ménfá
Zhēnzōng said to Lǐ Zōng'è:
"Among the families of chancellors and generals in our dynasty,
their lineage has not declined.
Only Chancellor Fǎng
and General Cáo Bīn have achieved this.
I hear that your family is even more harmonious and orderly.
I wish that the foundation established by the two saintly emperors
could also be like your family,
preserving their family's standing."
Sìshuǐ Fāyuànwén
Lǐ Zōng'è reported that corpses floated down the Biànqú river, covering it,
and were exposed on sandbanks.
The emperor was saddened,
and personally composed the 《Sìshuǐ Fāyuànwén》,
commanding it to be carved on a stone tablet at Huáitíng.
Annually, one hundred strings of cash were allocated
to hold fasting rituals and Daoist services, each lasting seven days,
and officials were given money to collect and bury the bodies.
The imperial composition roughly states:
"Alas!
Above the sandbanks and shoals,
birds of prey compete for food.
Among the islands and islets,
fish and turtles vie for sustenance.
Your evil karma was not created by others,
your misfortunes stem entirely from yourselves.
Those in officialdom,
relied on their power to oppress the people;
those among the people,
deceived their consciences and violated the law.
May this cleansing wash away their sins,
and may each ascend to rebirth.
Understand the principle that all Buddhas are fundamentally empty,
and embody the supreme truth of ultimate void."
Wáng Yǔchēng Shībiǎo
Wáng Yǔchēng once wrote the 《Èrchù Fù》 to express his aspirations.
Later, he became a Draft Official (Zhīzhìgào),
but offended the contemporary chancellor,
and was sent out to govern Huángzhōu.
Sū Yìjiǎn, whose imperial examination list included more than three hundred successful candidates such as Sūn Hé, memorialized, saying:
"Yǔchēng is a seasoned scholar in the imperial academy (jìnlín),
and has repeatedly been a banished official.
Your subject wishes to have the students from this imperial examination escort him out of the city."
The memorial was approved.
Wáng Yǔchēng wrote a poem in thanks, saying:
"How honored I am to have you line up and see me off,
An old crane riding a carriage, I am ashamed before the valley warblers.
Thrice entering the Chéngmíng Hall, I did not know how to conduct myself,
Watching others release their students from under their patronage."
At that time, relatives and friends followed the prevailing likes and dislikes,
and dared not approach him.
Only Dòu Yuánbīn held his hand,
and wept at the palace gate (gémén), saying:
"Heaven!
Is this not fate?"
Later, he thanked him with a poem, saying:
"Only Dòu Yuánwài from Nánjīng,
Shed tears for me before the palace gate."
Not long after arriving in the prefecture,
two tigers fought in the territory,
one died.
County chickens crowed at night.
There was winter thunder and hail.
The Directorate of Astronomy (Sītiān) memorialized that the local governor bore the blame,
and immediately ordered his transfer to Qízhōu.
His memorial of thanks stated:
"The questions about ghosts and spirits in Xuānshì,
I do not expect to return alive;
The writings on Feng and Shan sacrifices in Màolíng,
I only anticipate after my death."
Within a month, he died.
Tàizōng once admonished him, saying:
"You are intelligent,
and your literary talent is no less than Hán Yù and Liǔ Zōngyuán,
but you are too unyielding to tolerate others,
many people thwart you,
making it difficult for me to protect you."
Lǐ Hán Shūcí
Lǐ Gǔ and Hán Xīzài were early companions at their desks (tóng bǐyàn).
When they parted, they agreed:
"Each of us will choose our lord based on our talent and destiny."
During the Xiǎndé era, Lǐ Gǔ served the Zhōu dynasty,
as a Píngzhāngshì.
Hán Xīzài served Lǐ Xiānzhǔ of Jiāngnán,
as a Guāngzhèngdiàn Xuéshì.
Hán Xīzài sent a letter to Lǐ Gǔ saying:
"If Jiāngnán truly makes me its chancellor,
I will lead a mighty army to conquer the Central Plains."
Lǐ Gǔ replied:
"If the Central Plains truly makes me its chancellor,
subduing Jiāngnán will be as easy as taking something from a bag."
Later, Lǐ Gǔ indeed became a chancellor,
and personally led a campaign against Jiāngnán,
but Hán Xīzài had already died.
Chěng Yì Shāng Shēng
Rénzōng read the *Wǔdài Shǐ* (History of the Five Dynasties).
When he reached the part where Zhōu Tàizǔ, by the water, drew his bow and shot two wild ducks,
piercing both with one arrow,
his courtiers praised him and offered congratulations.
The Emperor closed his book and said,
"Displaying skill to harm living beings
is not something I enjoy."
The palace eunuch Zhèng Zhāoxìn, who managed internal affairs for fifteen years,
often warned,
"Moving, living creatures
must not be cooked without permission."
He deeply abhorred killing.
Ten couplets by Yáng Huīzhī inscribed on the imperial screen.
Yáng Huīzhī:
Tàizōng, hearing of his poetic fame,
demanded all his writings,
selected ten couplets from his collection,
and had them inscribed on the imperial screen.
Mào Zhí escapes death.
When Zhāng Mào Zhí was young, he bought melons in a garden.
An old man, leaning on his hoe, squinted and said,
"You will soon have your neck severed.
When the blade descends,
if it is too quick, you will die;
if it is slightly slow, you will live.
If you truly escape,
you will enjoy wealth and honor."
Not long after,
Mùróng Yànchāo occupied Yǎn,
and conscripted all the defenders to guard the ramparts.
When the Zhōu army defeated the enemy,
those who defended the city were all beheaded.
When it came to Mào Zhí,
the executioner with the blade said,
"Your hair is very long and black.
It would be a pity for it to be stained with neck blood.
You may cut it first."
Mào Zhí slowly tidied his hair
and thus escaped.
Later, he became a Zhī Zhìgào.
The Master of Fēngdū Guàn.
Wáng Xiǎn, when young, served Tàizōng as an attendant.
A barefoot Daoist priest examined his features and said,
"This child is destined to become a general and prime minister,
but lacks hidden virtues."
When he grew up,
Tàizōng said,
"You are not a scholar,
and are entirely lacking in learning.
If you achieve wealth and honor someday,
you will inevitably face a wall."
He took out three chapters of *Jūnjiè* (Military Precepts) and ordered him to recite them.
During the Xiánpíng reign,
he was sent out with an army to Dìngzhōu,
with full authority to act as he saw fit.
Suddenly, a Daoist priest requested an audience,
introducing himself as the Master of Fēngdū Guàn.
When he smiled, the corners of his mouth reached his ears,
and his disheveled hair resembled a wild boar's bristles.
He said,
"Yesterday, the Lord on High decreed that twenty thousand barbarian souls be brought to this temple,
to die by your hand.
If you indeed kill them,
your merit will surpass the world,
but your life span will be reduced by twelve years.
Please decide between these two outcomes."
Xiǎn considered him insane
and shouted for him to leave.
A few days later,
the Qìdān led tens of thousands of cavalry to hunt in the territory of Wēishèng Jūn.
Xiǎn led his troops to ambush them
and greatly defeated them,
beheading twenty thousand heads.
When the victory report reached the court,
he was summoned to be a Shūxiàng.
He died after several years.
The rise and fall of lord and minister are limited.
Liú Chāngyán,
during Tàizōng's time, was a Qǐjū Láng.
He was good at strategizing
to align with the emperor's intentions.
Before long,
he became a Jiànyì Zhī Mìyuàn.
The opportunities for a lord and minister to flourish or decline are limited.
One day,
the emperor's favor suddenly dissolved.
He said,
"Liú Mǒu's reports and replies
are all spoken with a southern accent,
and I cannot understand a single word."
Granted money to repay debts.
Lǐ Wénjìng Gōng Hàng,
when he first became a Zhī Zhìgào,
Tàizōng knew he was poor
and owed a lot of interest money to people.
He said,
"How much is Hàng's salary
as a Zhìgào?
How could he possibly have time to repay debts?"
He specially granted him one million cash
to repay them.
Later, when he became prime minister,
during a time of great peace with nothing to do,
he dismissed all petitions and proposals for reform,
saying to his close associates,
"I have no other way to repay the country
than by ensuring peace for the common people."
Mr. Ice Pot.
Tàizōng ordered Sū Yìjiǎn to lecture on *Wénzhōngzǐ*.
There was a passage about "Yáng Sù leaving his son a recipe for 'stem-soup and preserved provisions'."
The Emperor then asked,
"What food item is most precious?"
He replied,
"There is no fixed taste for things;
that which suits the mouth is precious.
I only know that pickled vegetable juice is delicious.
I recall one evening it was extremely cold.
I hugged the stove and drank heartily.
In the middle of the night, my mouth was dry.
In the moonlit courtyard,
amidst the lingering snow,
an earthenware pot of pickled vegetables was overturned.
I munched on several roots.
At that moment, I felt that even the immortal cuisine of the upper realm,
phoenix meat and egret embryos,
might not surpass it.
I have often wanted to write a *Biography of Mr. Ice Pot* to record this event,
but have been too busy to do so."
The Emperor smiled and agreed.
Song for Curing Black Moustache and Firm Teeth.
Zhāng Shīzhèng, at fifty,
already had sparse and loose teeth.
Ten-plus years later,
he could cut large chunks of meat
as sharply as with a knife.
He once obtained a prescription,
which recounted:
"Yuánhéng, during the Tiānshèng era,
ascended the summit of a mountain.
Below the old foundation of the Míngxīng Guǎn,
he found a broken stele,
on which ancient characters were vaguely discernible.
It was a 'Song for Medicine to Cure Mouth and Teeth and Blacken Whiskers,'
which read:
'Pig's teeth, soap beans, and fresh ginger,
western coptis, and Sichuan rehmannia.
Mulberry twigs, Eclipta prostrata, and Sophora japonica fruit,
Asarum, and lotus calyx
(This refers to the heart of the lotus leaf, cut.)
should be in equal parts.
Burn and calcine them with an equal amount of green salt,
then grind finely; this powder is best used.
Brush teeth to make them firm and blacken whiskers and temples.
Who would know such an immortal prescription exists in the world?'"
Governing the Prison of Killing.
Shào Cuì Guān Wèizōng carved blocks to print Guānyīn images.
Wáng Yuányì Dàizhì wrote an essay saying:
"Gǒng Yànfǔ of the Ministry of Justice
dreamed that two scarlet-robed officials summoned him into a great mansion."
There was a purple-robed official at a desk;
this was the king.
Under the eaves, prisoners' eyes were being gouged out with sand basins
and ground;
others had their arms cut off and ears severed,
beyond recognition.
After a while,
an official arrived,
scolding Gǒng and ordering him to undress.
Gǒng protested that he was an official and had committed no crime.
The official angrily said,
"This is the prison for killing living beings.
How could your official status matter?"
Gǒng, in distress, called out the name of Guānyīn,
and all the prisoners echoed him.
The mutilated were made whole,
and the bound were released.
Gǒng then woke up.
Tàiwèi Zǎn understands people.
Zǎn Jū-rùn (太尉) Grand Commandant Zǎn Jū-rùn was illiterate.
Every time he handled official documents,
he would hold a large brush in his left hand
and draw a long stroke.
Even cunning and deceitful clerks,
when attempting to imitate it, would surely fail.
Shěn Lún (沈倫) was in the staff quarters,
and he often said:
"Investigator Shěn walks with such dignity and gravity,
as if treading in the ancestral temple;
he will surely become a prime minister."
He strongly recommended him to Tàizǔ (太祖),
and indeed, he later became a prime minister.
Because Shěn knew Zǎn was unlettered,
he invited all his children and grandchildren to his home,
built a school to educate them as if they were his own children,
to repay his kindness in recognizing talent.
Tàizǔ (太祖) Attacks Shǔ (蜀)
Tàizǔ (太祖) was keen of hearing and far-sighted.
Someone came from Shǔ (蜀),
and he asked:
"What is happening beyond Jiàn (劍) Pass?"
The person replied:
"I only heard that everyone in the cities and towns is reciting the 'Poem of Bitter Heat,' saying:
'The oppressive heat and stifling humidity have no escape;
when will the cool breeze arrive?'" The emperor said:
"The people of Shǔ (蜀) wish for my arrival."
At that time, Jīng-Chǔ (荊楚) had already been conquered,
and Mèng Chǎng (孟昶) feared the "lips-and-teeth-without-each-other" (mutual destruction) situation,
but there was no justifiable reason for a western campaign.
Chǎng (昶) dispatched a wax-sealed letter via a secret route to Tàiliáng (太涼),
to ally with Liú Jūn (劉鈞) for support,
but it was intercepted by the imperial court.
Tàizǔ (太祖) said:
"Now there is a legitimate reason to raise an army."
He ordered Wáng Quán-bīn (王全斌) to attack it.
Chǎng (昶) was captured and brought to the imperial court.
General Wáng Rén-shàn (王仁贍) returned first,
requesting an audience.
Fearing his own misdeeds might be exposed,
he enumerated the avarice and corruption of Quán-bīn (全斌) and others.
Tàizǔ (太祖) smiled and said:
"Taking Lǐ Tíng-guī's (李廷珪) courtesan,
and arbitrarily opening the Fēngdé (豐德) Treasury to take gold and jewels,
who was this again?"
Rén-shàn (仁贍) was terrified.
The emperor said:
"Among those who went on this campaign, the only one who was upright, modest, and cautious
was Cáo Bīn (曹彬) alone."
Court officials requested a thorough investigation and punishment of the generals and soldiers who participated in the conquest of Shǔ (蜀),
but the emperor released them all.
The Tattooed Man Becomes Emperor
There was an old man named Chái Wēng (柴翁) from Wèi (魏),
whose daughter was in the imperial harem of Táng Zhuāng-zōng (唐莊宗).
When Míng-zōng (明宗) entered Luò (洛),
she was dismissed from the palace.
Her parents welcomed her,
and her trousseau was valued at one hundred thousand,
half of which she gave to her parents,
telling them to return,
saying:
"I saw a team leader in the post station, dark-skinned, with a tattooed neck like a sparrow,
he is a person of extreme nobility,
and I wish to serve him."
Her parents could not dissuade her.
When asked,
it was Guō Wēi (郭威).
One day,
she said to Guō (郭):
"Your nobility is beyond words.
I have five million in wealth,
and I wish to offer it to you to further your career."
Zhōu Zǔ (周祖) (Guō Wēi (郭威)) thus used her wealth to become a military commissioner.
Chái Wēng (柴翁) knew about matters of the underworld.
One day,
he suddenly laughed loudly,
and when his wife asked him why,
he just kept laughing.
So she gave him wine to drink,
and when he was very drunk,
he finally said:
"The tattooed man will become the Son of Heaven."
Mercury and the Drafting Official
Xiàhóu Jiā-zhèng (夏侯嘉正),
during Tàizōng's (太宗) time, was a censor,
and spoke forthrightly at the academy.
He delighted in alchemy,
and once said:
"If I could obtain half an ounce of silver from mercury,
and serve as a drafting official for one day,
my life would be complete."
Both wishes remained unfulfilled when he died.
Guessing Games
Dīng Wén-guǒ (丁文果) was good at guessing games.
Tàizōng (太宗) placed an object in a container,
and Wén-guǒ (文果) said:
"Flowery, flowery, full of bloom,
picking flowers in the mountains.
Though without official rank,
it attends court twice a day."
When it was opened,
it was a bee.
Again, another object was taken,
and he was asked to guess.
Wén-guǒ (文果) said:
"It has a head and feet,
if not stone, then jade.
Wishing to retract its head,
it cannot pull it into its belly."
It was a stone tortoise used as a paperweight.
The Ode of the Four Barbarians Coming to Court
Qián Xī (錢熙),
a man from Quán (泉),
presented "The Ode of the Four Barbarians Coming to Court" (《四夷來王賦》).
Tàizōng (太宗) promoted him to an academy position.
The officials requested to test him,
but the emperor said:
"The former *jìnshì* (進士) whom the officials wish to test,
Zhào (趙) personally selected him."
Yuán Hòu-zhī's (元厚之) Poem
Yuán Hòu-zhī's (元厚之) literary style was mature and did not decline with age.
His "Recalling Old Travels in Jīng-nán (荊南)" (《懷荊南舊遊》) says:
"Last year I was drunk amidst a cluster of crabapples,
now I hear new branches bloom with old reds.
Last night I dreamt of drinking beneath the flowers,
unaware my body was in the Jade Hall."
Zēng Lǔ-gōng (曾魯公)
Zēng Lǔ-gōng (曾魯公), nearing eighty,
still possessed vigorous brushwork.
Zēng Zǐ-xuān (曾子宣) was demoted to serve as governor of Pán-yáng (番陽).
His handwritten letter said:
"The whirlwind is still far,
not ceasing for six months.
Waxing and waning follow the Dao,
in seven days, it will naturally return."
Chén Xī-yí's (陳希夷) Admonition to Zhǒng Fàng (種放)
Chén Tuán (陳摶) lived in seclusion on Huà Shān (華山).
As a child, he played by the Wèi Shuǐ (渭水).
A blue-clad old woman embraced him,
and suckled him, saying:
"I will make you free from desires and cravings,
and your intelligence will surpass others."
The master once admonished his disciple Zhǒng Fàng (種放), saying:
"One day you will meet an enlightened ruler,
and your name will shake the imperial court.
Name,
throughout ancient and modern times, is a beautiful vessel,
but the creator deeply resents it.
There is no perfect reputation between heaven and earth;
your name will be tarnished by something."
In his later years, Fàng (放) became excessively extravagant,
accumulating properties that filled the area between Yōng (雍) and Hào (鎬),
thereby losing his integrity.
Dǎng Jìn (党進) Showing Off His Learning
Dǎng Jìn (党進) was illiterate.
When the imperial court sent him to defend Qiū (秋) in Gāo-yáng (高陽),
he insisted on making a speech on the day of his departure.
The palace gate officials said:
"Grand Commandant is a frontier minister,
there is no need for such formality."
Jìn (進) was stubborn and fierce,
insisting on delivering it.
Jìn (進) knelt forward,
unable to utter a single word for a long time.
Suddenly, he looked up at the emperor's tablet,
and loudly declared:
"I heard that in ancient times,
the customs were simple and unadorned.
May Your Majesty take good care of yourself."
The guards covered their mouths.
Later, his attendants asked:
"Grand Commandant, why did you recite those two lines?"
Jìn (進) said:
"I often see literati love to show off their learning,
so I also showed off two lines,
to let His Majesty know that I read books."
The Father as a Subordinate Official
Líng Cè (凌策) was a Vice Minister,
his father had once been a subordinate official (*suǒyóu* 所由) of a garrison.
When Cè (策) was just a boy,
his father brought him to pay respects to Ān Hóng-jiàn (安鴻漸),
begging him to give him a name.
Hóng-jiàn (鴻漸) was humorous and frivolous,
so he named him "Jiào-zhī" (教之, "teach him").
This implied he was "born of *suǒyóu*" (所由生, "born of a subordinate official").
After Cè (策) grew up,
he largely managed to avoid the implications of this name.
Price of Tang Wine
Zhēnzōng once asked a close minister:
"What was the price of wine in the Táng dynasty?"
No one could answer.
Dīng Jìngōng said:
"Thirty [cash] per shēng."
The Emperor said:
"How do you know that?"
He replied:
"Dù Fǔ's poem says:
'Hurry and come drink a dòu with me,
I have three hundred bronze cash.'
From this, we know one shēng was thirty."
The name Cìgōng in the court roster
Liáng Shì, accompanying Lú Nánjīn, the judge of the court, ascended to the imperial hall.
In the court roster, there was a name Cìgōng.
Rénzōng asked:
"Why is he named Cìgōng?"
Nánjīn, being skilled in law, could not answer.
Shì said:
"Huáng Bà of the Hàn dynasty
had the courtesy name Cìgōng."
The Emperor asked:
"Who are you, my lord?"
He replied:
"I am Liáng Shì, a deliberative official."
The Emperor further asked which Liáng family he belonged to.
He replied:
"My grandfather, Háo, and father, Gù,
both passed the first class of the imperial examinations."
The Emperor said:
"No wonder your face resembles Liáng Gù so closely."
On another day, Shì reported:
"My father and grandfather served Tàizōng and Zhēnzōng respectively;
how does Your Majesty know of them?"
The Emperor said:
"In the Tiāntóng Pavilion, there are busts of famous ministers.
I have looked at them very closely."
Later, Shì was appointed as a Recorder and Drafter of Imperial Edicts,
and eventually to Hanlìn Grand Academician.
All his appointments were issued by imperial rescript.
In less than ten years, he reached the position of Grand Councillor.
The 'Bǐtán' records a public affair:
Páng Zhuāngmǐn,
Passed over for Ziwei, held back for Dianyuan
Zhāng Qùhuá, a first-class scholar from the Academy,
submitted a memorial saying:
Zhāng Dàn and Lú Duōxùn, Drafters of Imperial Edicts,
and Shī Wán, a court official,
are shallow in literary learning.
I wish to compare their merits and demerits.
Tàizǔ immediately summoned Dàn and his group,
and held a re-examination before the imperial presence,
entrusting Táo Gǔ with the assessment.
The Emperor selected Duōxùn as qualified,
and dismissed the rest.
At that time, the saying referred to Dàn as "the Passed-over Zǐwēi"
and Wán as "the Held-back Diànyuàn."
Qùhuá was appointed Right Remonstrance Official,
which was criticized by scholars.
He was not promoted for sixteen years thereafter,
falling behind even those who advanced normally.
The 'Tányuàn' also records:
Father Shào and Mother Chén
Shào Yè, when governor of Guǎngzhōu,
dug an inner river to berth boats and ships,
so they would not be harmed by typhoons.
Chén Shìqīng replaced him,
and memorialized to request exemption from the local harm of buying salt based on population.
The people of Wǔyáng then had clothing and food.
The people of Guǎngzhōu sang:
"Father Shào and Mother Chén,
relieved us of two hardships."
Dream of six seals hanging from a sword tip
Zhāng Guāiyá, when garrisoning Yì,
repeatedly requested to replace Wáng Wénzhèng to memorialize for the dismissal of Líng Cè.
While young, he once dreamed that someone hung six seals from the tip of a sword and gave them to him.
Afterwards, he held six appointments outside Jiàn.
Tàizōng asks about the character 'Yǐn'
Líng Cè appointed Yáng Yǐn as the Assistant Prefect of Yì.
When his name was submitted to the Emperor,
Tàizōng did not recognize the character 'Yǐn'
(pronounced xún).
He issued an edict asking for the reason behind the name.
He replied:
"My late father named him;
I do not know the reason.
My elder brother is Fén, and my younger brother is Tuì,
all beside 'chóng.'
Now that I am an orphan,
I dare not presumptuously change it."
The Emperor asked:
"What is the meaning of Yǐn?"
He replied:
