"I heard it means a book-borer with wings,
also called a silverfish."
The Emperor said:
"The ancients named their children after the sun, moon, mountains, and rivers.
Even if there was a hidden ailment, they feared that the appellation would be inappropriate.
Now, to name one's child after such a trivial creature,
what is the meaning of that?"
The Emperor's brush specifically removed the 'chóng' radical,
and simply bestowed the name 'Tán.'
Hú Dàn borrows valuable artifacts for money
Hú Dàn, a grand supervisor,
was sent out to govern Míngzhōu.
In the same year, Dǒng Yǎn, a Palace Censor, governed Yángzhōu.
They stayed together very happily.
When Hú Dàn entered the back hall,
courtesans were brought out to serve at the banquet,
and all the food containers were precious artifacts from the imperial court.
Dàn said:
"It is rare for people to meet like this in life.
Tomorrow, could you honor my humble boat with a few cups of wine?"
He also said:
"Being poor, I have never seen such precious artifacts.
Could I borrow them briefly
to show off to my wife and children?"
Dǒng, having stored them all in a trousseau,
sent them to his boat.
The next day, at the fifth watch,
Hú Dàn departed without notice.
When he arrived in Yúháng,
Xuē Yìng, a grand remonstrance official,
who was also a successful candidate from the same examination year,
first asked if he had seen his fellow examination candidate Dǒng when he passed through Wéiyáng.
Dàn replied:
"Looking at his talent and character, he is an outstanding and exceptional man,
but he is merely greedy by nature."
One day, Dàn said to Yì:
"Lend me two thousand string of cash
to build a villa by Jiànhú.
As soon as my term in Yín is over,
I will retire due to illness
and fish in Yuèxī in a small boat."
Xuē had no choice
and gave him three hundred taels of silver.
Later, Wáng Jì'ēn, the Drafter of Imperial Edicts, pacified Shǔ.
He bribed Dàn with several thousand taels of silver
to commission a commendatory edict.
The matter failed,
and Dàn was demoted to Xúnzhōu,
and given a *jué* ring in the imperial palace.
Nurturing the people and having few desires
Wáng Zhāosù's learning and conduct surpassed his era.
He lived as a widower, abstaining from desires for forty years,
his complexion like fresh cinnabar.
Tàizōng summoned him.
He sat and lectured on the *Qián Guà*.
When he reached "The flying dragon is in the sky,"
he adjusted his cap, bowed profoundly, and changing his expression, said:
"This is precisely Your Majesty today."
He was kept in the palace for over a month.
The Emperor inquired about the art of governing the world and cultivating one's health.
Zhāosù said:
"To govern the world, nothing is better than nurturing the people;
to cultivate one's health, nothing is better than having few desires."
The Emperor wrote his words on the imperial screen.
Urgent report from Xīhé
In the Qìnglì era,
the imperial army suffered a defeat in Xīhé.
Several high-ranking generals were captured by the barbarians.
An urgent report had arrived ten days ago,
but the high ministers deliberately delayed it.
The Emperor was in the Huàchéng Hall.
An old soldier, holding a broom, sighed:
"What a pity for Grand Commandant Liú!"
The Emperor was surprised and asked him.
He replied:
"Does Your Majesty not know that Grand Commandant Liú and five or six other generals were killed at the same time?"
He immediately untied his belt, wrote on it, and presented it,
saying:
"My entire Xīhǔyì camp in Yíngzhōu was destroyed,
and my son-in-law also perished.
This is an urgent report from my family."
The Emperor immediately summoned the executive officials to examine it.
The high ministers then reported that they had received news but had not yet confirmed it,
and were waiting for details to arrive day and night before reporting,
requesting the Emperor to relieve his anxiety.
The Emperor sternly said:
"The matter has come to this,
and you still speak of requesting to relieve my anxiety?
You are cruel people!"
The Grand Councillor then requested to retire.
Tàizǔ executes the slanderers
During the *Kāibǎo* era,
someone memorialized the
*Tàizǔ* saying: "Prince
*Jìn*'s divine countenance is extraordinary,
and I fear that people's sentiments will attach to him.
As the Capital Prefect,
he acts recklessly and unrestrainedly,
and his officials bend the law to curry favor with the powerful.
Your Majesty should plan for this." The Emperor
angrily said:
"I and my brother, Prince *Jìn*, have built this nation in harmony and peace,
and we maintain a relationship of respect and filial piety.
One day, I intend to let him manage all the affairs of the realm.
How dare a petty person try to separate my limbs?"
He immediately ordered the accuser to be executed.
*Gāoyángguān*'s Memorials
*Tàizōng* succeeded to the throne,
and *Gāoyángguān* presented a memorial:
"An ominous aura arose at night,
stretching across the northern land.
The border situation is quite unstable."
The Emperor summoned *Xiàng Mǐnzhōng* to discuss it.
*Xiàng* reported: "*Cuī Hàn* holds the *Jié* at *Gāoyáng*,
and he is arrogant and unrestrained due to his accomplishments.
Your Majesty should recall him and execute him
to suppress the ominous aura."
The Emperor said:
"What kind of talk is that?
*Hàn* was promoted from the ranks due to his ability,
and thus was appointed a *Jié*.
I estimate he will not let me down."
The Emperor sent a literary official to declare consolation and greetings,
and the ominous portent dissipated on its own,
and the border areas became peaceful.
*Táo Gǔ*'s "Luan Glue Tune"
In the early days of the dynasty, the court sent
*Táo Gǔ* as an envoy to *Jiāngnán*,
under the pretext of delivering a letter,
but actually to spy.
Chancellor *Lǐ Gǔ* sent a letter to *Hán Xīzài* saying:
"The 'Mr. Five Willows' is extremely arrogant;
treat him well."
*Gǔ* arrived and
it was indeed as *Lǐ* had said.
*Xīzài* said: "*Táo Xiùshí* is not a man of integrity,
his moral defenses can be breached."
He then had him stay overnight.
After he finished copying the books of the Six Dynasties,
he was kept at the guest house for half a year.
*Xīzài* sent the singing girl *Qín Ruòlán* to pretend to be a postal station attendant's daughter,
dressed in ragged clothes with a bamboo hairpin,
holding a broom and sweeping.
*Gǔ* saw her and was pleased,
and thus broke the vow of "being cautious when alone,"
writing a small *qu* (song-lyric) for her.
A few days later,
Lord *Lǐ* hosted a banquet in the *Qīngxīn Táng*,
ordering a large glass *zhōng* (cup) to be filled and offered to him.
*Gǔ* steadfastly ignored it.
*Lán* was brought out to the banquet
and sang the previous *qu* to accompany the wine.
*Gǔ* was greatly ashamed,
fell head over heels and vomited on the mat,
but was still not allowed to leave.
He was greatly despised by Lord *Lǐ*.
The lyric was titled "Good Scenery" and went:
"A good marriage,
a bad marriage,
I only got one night's sleep at the postal station,
farewell, immortal.
The pipa has played all the tunes of lovesickness,
but true understanding is rare.
When will the 'luan glue' mend the phoenix strings?
What year will that be?"
When he returned to the capital,
the "Luan Glue" tune was already widely known,
and because of this, he was not greatly employed thereafter.
Changing Ancient Poems
*Wēn Gōng* said:
"*Wèi Yě*'s poem says:
'No overnight fire in the leaf-burning stove,
a dying lamp by the window for reading.'
Common people change 'leaf' (*yè*) to 'medicine' (*yào*)."
*Lǔzhí* said:
"Old *Dù*'s poem says:
'Yellow *dú* has no sprouts, mountain snow is abundant.'
Yellow *dú* refers to a small taro root.
Common people change it to 'yellow essence' (*huángjīng*).
Just like *Yuānmíng*'s poem:
'Leisurely I see the southern mountain,'
common people change it to 'gazing at the southern mountain.'"
Names of Two Birds
*Tuìzhī*'s poem says:
"Wake me up when the window is fully bright,
urge me home before the sun sets in the west."
*Lǔzhí* said:
"These are the names of two birds.
'Urge home' (*cuīguī*) is the cuckoo (*zǐguī*).
'Wake up' (*huànqǐ*) sounds like winding silk,
round and clear,
especially singing at dawn in spring.
People in *Jiāngnán* call it 'spring wake'."
Lying Sideways
*Wáng Jīnggōng* said:
"Red and purple have no leaves to shelter their splendid forms,
yellow chrysanthemums scatter their fragrance and fall to the roadside dust.
In late autumn, the green officials can barely protect themselves,
when the sun is high, the green maiden still lies sideways."
He also said:
"Trees fall, and hills and ridges present themselves,
water returns, and islets lie sideways."
*Shāngǔ* said:
"'Present themselves' (*zìxiàn*) and 'lie sideways' (*héngchén*) are found in *Xiāngrú*'s *fù* (rhapsody)."
The *Léngyán Jīng* also says:
"When lying sideways,
the taste is like chewing wax."
The "奪胎換骨" Method
*Huáng Lǔzhí* said:
"Poetic meaning is boundless,
but human talent is limited.
To pursue boundless meaning with limited talent,
even *Shàolíng* and *Yuānmíng* could not excel.
However, without changing the meaning
but creating new phrasing for it,
is called the 'changing bones' (*huàngǔ*) method.
To appropriate its meaning and describe it,
is called the 'snatching the fetus' (*duótāi*) method.
For example, *Zhèng Gǔ*'s 'October Chrysanthemum' says:
'Because people's hearts are different today,
the autumn fragrance may not necessarily wither in a single night.'
This meaning is excellent,
but its flaw is that the 'qi' (spirit) is not long enough."
*Zēng Zǐgù* said:
"A poem should allow people to grasp its meaning at a glance,
yet leave them with lingering thoughts."
*Jīnggōng*'s 'Chrysanthemum Poem' says:
"After a thousand flowers and a hundred plants have withered,
only then is a recluse seen holding a single branch."
*Dōngpō* then said:
"All things eventually turn into dreams,
cease, cease!
Tomorrow's yellow flowers will even sadden the butterflies."
Another example is *Lǐ Bái*'s poem:
"Birds fly endlessly in the emerald evening sky."
He also said:
"At the end of the azure sky, a lone swan disappears."
However, its flaw is as discussed before.
*Shāngǔ*'s poem says:
"I don't know how wide the horizon is,
white birds are all gone, and the azure sky returns."
All such examples
are of the 'changing bones' method.
*Gù Kuàng*'s poem says:
"One parting, twenty years have passed,
how many partings can a person endure?"
*Jīnggōng* said:
"One day at your house holding wine cups,
six years of waves and dust.
I don't know on the road by *Wūshí Jiāng*,
how many times will we find each other in old age?"
*Lètiān*'s poem says:
"Facing the wind, an autumn tree at its peak,
toasting wine, a long-lived body.
A drunken face like frosty leaves,
though red, it is not spring."
*Dōngpō* said:
"Children mistakenly rejoice in rosy cheeks,
with a smile, how would they know it's red from wine?"
All such examples
are of the 'snatching the fetus' method.
*Lǐ Géfēi*'s Essay
*Lǐ Géfēi* said:
"*Zhūgé Kǒngmíng*'s 'Memorial on Sending Out the Army',
*Lǐ Lìngbó*'s 'Memorial of Pleading',
*Liú Bólún*'s 'Eulogy for Wine',
*Táo Yuānmíng*'s 'Returning Home'
all flow out naturally as from one's heart and lungs,
showing no traces of axe or chisel."
Thus it is known that *qì* (spirit/vitality) is paramount in writing.
Old *Dù*'s poetry surpasses others
in its sincerity and truthfulness.
For example, *Yùchuān Zǐ*'s poem says:
"Last night, returning from a village drink,
I stumbled three, four, five times.
Caressing the green moss,
don't wake them, startling you."
*Jīnggōng* adopted its meaning
and composed a 'Fan Poem' saying:
"A precious moon disk refined by an jade axe,
beside the moon, a maiden rides a luan.
The clear sky, wind, and dew are not of the human world,
disheveled hair and askew hairpin make it especially cold."
Xiù Guānxī's Words
Fǎyún Xiù Guānxī
said to Huáng Lúzhí:
"You compose lewd songs and short lyrics;
you should stop."
Lúzhí said:
"These are merely words in the air,
neither murder nor theft.
How could I be condemned to the evil realms for this?"
The Master said:
"You use perverse words to stir people's lust,
causing them to transgress ritual and defy prohibitions.
Your sin is not merely falling into the evil realms."
Lúzhí thenceforth stopped composing lyrics.
Lǐ Bóshí was skilled at painting horses.
The Master said:
"Bóshí is a grandee
yet makes a living by painting,
which is already shameful.
And furthermore, he paints horses."
Bóshí retorted angrily:
"Surely this will not corrupt people's minds and cause them to fall into the evil realms?"
The Master said:
"You have pursued this occupation for a long time,
thinking of their forms,
seeking their divine swiftness,
keeping them in your mind incessantly.
One day, when your eyesight fails,
you will undoubtedly be reborn as a horse."
Bóshí was astonished and said:
"How can I atone for this fault?"
The Master advised him to paint Guānshìyīn.
Phrases Beyond Imagery
Many Táng monks composed excellent verses.
They compared things metaphorically,
without explicitly naming a specific object.
This is called a "phrase beyond imagery."
For example, Wú Kě's poem says:
"Listening to the rain, the cold night ends;
closing the gate, fallen leaves are deep."
Here, fallen leaves are compared to the sound of rain.
Another example says:
"Faint sunlight descends upon tall trees;
distant fires enter the autumn mountains."
Here, faint sunlight is compared to distant fires.
The marvel lies in describing their function without naming them.
Full City of Wind and Rain Near Double Ninth
Pān Dàlín was skilled at poetry,
but very poor.
Xiè Yuányì wrote a letter asking if he had any new works.
He replied:
"The autumn scenery,
every single item, is a beautiful line,
but I regret being obscured by vulgar concerns.
Yesterday I got a line:
'Full city of wind and rain near Double Ninth.'
Suddenly the rent collector arrived,
and it spoiled my mood.
Only this single line I send to you."
Those who heard it laughed at his eccentricity.
Fourteen-Character Master Title
Dàoqián had a line of poetry:
"From beyond the woods, faintly comes the sound of a loom,
knowing there is a household amidst the verdant peaks."
Dōngpō said:
"This is my master's fourteen-character master title."
Bamboo Poems
The monk Qīngshùn Yírán of Xīhú
often wrote "Bamboo Poems," saying:
"An inch of land in the city is like an inch of gold;
in my secluded studio, I planted only ten bamboos.
Spring wind, be careful not to make your children and grandchildren grow too tall,
lest they break the green moss before my steps."
He also had a poem "Under the Grove" that says:
"Long have I wandered under the grove,
and understood the grove's delight.
Let its green shade flourish;
it hinders not the passing clear breeze.
At leisure, I sleep on a stone;
I know not the count of fallen leaves.
A bird suddenly flies in,
and breaks the secluded silence with its cry."
Kūn Style
When poetry reached Lǐ Yìshān,
it was called "a bottleneck in literature,"
because his allusions were obscure and recondite.
It was then known as the Kūn style.
Jīnggōng in his later years
sometimes also admired it,
as in his "Clouds" poem:
"May I ask if the fire city should be explored with a whip,
or if it is better to listen to the clouds in the dwelling through the window?"
Holding the Chess Riddle
Jīnggōng was at Zhōngshān,
and while playing chess, he composed a few lines:
"Neither dares to go first;
neither dares to go first;
thus there is no contention,
and therefore one can enter neither death nor birth."
The Duke laughed and said:
"This is a riddle about holding chess pieces."
Mò Hàodàng
Old Dù's poem says:
"White gulls disappear into the vast expanse (mò hàodàng)."
Now it is mistakenly written as "wave (bō)."
Jīnggōng said:
"The Daoist came from the northern mountain,
asking the pines on my eastern ridge.
He pointed his finger at the roof ridge,
saying, 'It is now this tall.'"
Now it is mistakenly written as "asking the pines to prune the eastern ridge."
This and "bō hàodàng" should be considered together.
Zhāng Tiānjú's Cursive Script
Chancellor Zhāng was fond of cursive script,
but was not skilled at it.
One day he received a poem,
asked for a brush, and hastily filled the paper with writing.
He asked his nephew to transcribe it.
At a particularly difficult and unusual spot,
the nephew was at a loss and stopped.
Holding the writing, he asked:
"What character is this?"
The Chancellor stared intently,
then chided:
"Why didn't you come and ask earlier,
making me forget it!"
Dōngpō's Poems
Dōngpō composed a poem on "Crabapples," saying:
"I only fear that late at night the flowers will fall asleep,
so I burn high silver candles to illuminate their crimson faces."
This incident is found in "An Unofficial Biography of Consort Yáng," which says:
"Consort [Yáng] had not yet sobered from the morning wine.
Emperor Míng laughed and said:
'Is this truly Consort [Yáng] drunk,
or merely the crabapple not yet having had enough sleep?'" He composed a poem on "Buddhist Nuns," saying:
"They should take white silk to make their spring clothes."
This incident is found in an imperial decree:
"All nuns in the empire should use white silk for their clothes."
He composed a poem on "Olives," saying:
"Already it loses to cliff honey in sweetness by a full measure."
This incident is found in "Guǐ Gǔzǐ," which says:
"'Illuminating the night' [refers to] a clear firefly.
'Hundred flowers' [refers to] sweet honey.
'Cliff honey' [refers to] cherries."
Taìzǔ's Far-Sighted Strategy
One day, Emperor Shénzōng was walking in the imperial garden
and saw someone herding sows and piglets.
He asked:
"What are these used for?"
The reply was:
"They have been kept since the time of our ancestors;
we do not know what they are actually used for."
The Emperor pondered for a long time,
then issued an edict to the relevant officials:
"From now on, no more pigs are to be kept within the palace."
A few months later,
imperial guards suddenly captured an evildoer
who urgently needed to be sprinkled with pig's blood,
but none could be obtained in the palace.
Shénzōng then realized that Taìzǔ's far-sighted strategy had extended even to this.
Dīng Jìngōng's Poem
Dīng Jìngōng's poem "Overseas" says:
"The grass that dispels worries—what worries does it have?
The flower named 'laughing'—at whom does it smile?"
The world considered this skillful.
Dōngpō said:
"Flowers, not knowing faces, always smile;
birds, not knowing names, merely call out by themselves."
One then realizes how far apart their talents and abilities were.
Cuī Huī's "Head-Piece" Lyrics
Qín Shàoyóu (秦少游) had a *cí* (詞) poem which said:
"Ten thousand fallen blossoms, sorrow like the ocean."
Juéfàn (覺範) composed a *fù* (賦) on Cuī Huī's (崔徽) head,
using Shàoyóu's (少游) rhyme, saying:
"Half a body beyond the screen,
waking to faded crimson lips.
Spring thoughts in disarray,
a fragrant heart shattered.
Only the jade hairpins remain,
the tassel belt is nowhere to be seen.
Let me ask,
who among today's beauties is worthy to face her refined charm?
We once met at the Xiāngpǔ (湘浦),
my hand lifting her light silk canopy.
I doubt it was a dream,
for it seems present still.
The spring of life easily ends,
a single affection is hard to change.
How many things,
all followed hatred far to connect with the cloud-sea."
Xiè Wúyì (謝無逸) wrote a poem.
Jīnggōng's (荊公) daughter,
Wú Ānchí's (吳安持) wife,
was skilled in poetry.
She once sent a poem to Jīnggōng (荊公) saying:
"The west wind does not enter the small window gauze,
the autumn air should pity me for missing home.
Gazing as far as the eye can see, a thousand *lǐ* (里) of mountains and rivers, a thousand *lǐ* (里) of sorrow,
still with tears I look at the yellow chrysanthemums."
He replied:
"A single green lamp reflected on the window gauze,
better to read the *Léngyán* (楞嚴) Sūtra, do not long for home.
If one can understand all conditions as illusory,
in the world there is only the marvelous lotus flower."
Bamboo shoots named "young shoots"
Lǎo Dù's (老杜) poem says:
"Bamboo roots and young shoots, unseen by anyone."
A Táng (唐) dynasty poem "Eating Bamboo Shoots" says:
"Young shoots shed their brocade swaddling,
side-by-side, jade-like, fragrant, and smooth."
Thus, it is clear that "young shoots" refers to bamboo shoots.
Zànníng's (贊寧) *Zájì* (雜記) says:
"At the base of bamboo roots, there are rats,
as large as cats,
their color resembling bamboo,
named 'bamboo pig,'
also named 'young shoot' (稚子)."
Poem on the Northern Expedition
Lǎo Dù's (老杜) poem *Běizhēng* (北征) says:
"Did not hear of Xià (夏) and Shāng (商) decline,
but personally executed Bàosì (褒姒)."
The meaning implies that Mínghuáng (明皇), having seen the decline of Xià (夏) and Shāng (商),
was able to regret his past and
order his imperial concubine to die.
Liú Yǔxī's (劉禹錫) poem *Mǎwéi* (馬嵬) says:
"The imperial army executed the treacherous soldiers,
the Son of Heaven pitied the enchantress.
All the officials stood by the door screen,
the nobleman pulled the Emperor's robe."
Bái Lètiān's (白樂天) *Chánghèngē* (長恨歌) says:
"The six armies would not advance, what could be done?
The graceful beauty died before the horses."
This implies that the imperial army forced the imperial concubine,
singing of Lù Shān's (祿山) rebellion.
How far this deviates from Lǎo Dù (老杜) is like a thousand *lǐ* (里)!
Eulogy for the Eldest Princess
Shénzōng (神宗) composed the *Qínguó Dàzhǎnggōngzhǔ Wǎnací* (秦國大長公主挽詞) saying:
"The sea is vast, the road to the three mountains,
the fragrant carriage is surely not returning.
The deep tent is empty of kingfishers,
the cold pendant has lost its pearls and jades.
The bright moon lingers over the singing fan,
the lingering glow scatters the dancing clothes.
The carriage returns from the capital gate,
the old grass naturally turns green in spring."
And also said:
"At dawn, departing on the road west of the city,
the spirit carriage appears even more distant.
The spring wind chills the Lǔguǎn (魯館),
the bright moon cuts off the Qínxiāo (秦簫).
Dust enters the silk robe, darkening it,
fragrance disperses with the jade inscription.
The fragrant soul flies to the northern islet,
how can it be summoned again?"
And also said:
"Dust originates from heaven and abyss,
grace deepens from national love.
Though songs and bells remain in the palace,
peach and plum blossoms do not make a spring.
Water flows crookedly, yet still soaks the ground,
the tall building is also separated by Qín (秦).
The small city of Kuàijī (會稽),
no longer has people offering pearls."
The Poems of the Four Masters
Wáng Jīnggōng (王荊公) compiled the poems of Lǐ Tàibái (李太白), Dù Zǐměi (杜子美), Hán Tuìzhī (韓退之), and Ōu Yǒngshú (歐永叔),
into *Sìjiājí* (四家集),
placing Ōugōng (歐公) above Tàibái (太白).
Gōng (公) said:
"Tàibái's (太白) words are swift and quick,
but nine out of ten lines speak only of women and wine."
Poem on a Fishing Net Stone
During the Jiāyòu (嘉祐) era,
a fisherman at the riverside caught a stone with his net.
A poem was carved on it, saying:
"Raindrops on empty steps at dawn,
no intention of changing the evening's fragrance.
The flowers on the wellside *tóng* (桐) tree have all fallen,
half of them on the silver bed."
A well curb.
No one knows who wrote it.
Ink Plum Blossoms
Huāguāng Rénlǎo (花光仁老) from Héngzhōu (衡州) painted plum blossoms with ink.
Huáng Lúzhí (黃魯直) observed them and said:
"Like the tender cold of an early spring morning,
walking by the water's edge amidst fences on Gūshān (孤山),
only lacking fragrance."
The Dragon Maiden of Wúchéng (吳城)
When Huáng Lúzhí (黃魯直) set off from Jīngzhōu (荊州) pavilion,
there was a *cí* (詞) poem between the pillars that said:
"Curtains rolled, leaning alone on the curved railing,
clouds spread across the boundless evening sky,
tearful eyes never cleared,
home is at the head of Wú (吳) and tail of Chǔ (楚).
A few snowflakes scatter and fall,
startling the sand gulls with a splash,
just as a poetic line was about to be completed,
it vanished into the smoky mist."
Lúzhí (魯直) said mournfully:
"It seems to be spoken for me.
I don't know who wrote it,
the brushwork resembles that of a woman,
and it has the line 'tearful eyes never cleared,'
I suspect it's a ghost."
That night,
a woman appeared in Lúzhí's (魯直) dream and said:
"My home is on Wúchéngshān (吳城山) in Yùzhāng (豫章).
I came here on a passenger boat,
fell into the water and died,
but was not recovered.
I felt moved on the Jiangtíng (江亭) and wrote this,
never expecting you to recognize it."
Lúzhí (魯直) woke up in surprise and said:
"This must be the little Dragon Maiden of Wúchéng (吳城)."
Peony Gāthā
When Tàizǔ (太祖) was about to punish Jiāngnán (江南),
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ (李後主) wished to resist the imperial army.
Fǎyǎn Chánshī (法眼禪師), observing the peonies in the imperial palace,
composed a *gāthā* (偈) to satirize him, saying:
"Wearing felt, facing the fragrant thicket,
our interests have always been different.
My hair turns white from today,
the flowers were red last year.
Their beauty sways with the morning dew,
their fragrance follows the dawn wind.
Why wait until they wither and fall,
before they become like emptiness?"
Hòuzhǔ (後主) did not understand,
so the Master crossed the river.
Bái Lètiān's (白樂天) Poems
Whenever Bái Lètiān (白樂天) composed a poem,
he would have an old woman explain it.
He would ask:
"Do you understand?"
The old woman would say:
"I understand."
Then he would record it.
If she did not understand,
he would revise it again.
Therefore, the poetry of the late Táng (唐) dynasty
is close to being crude and vulgar.
Dōngpō's (東坡) *Cí* (詞)
Dōngpō (東坡) and Shàoyóu (少游) drank a farewell toast,
and composed *Yú Měirén* (虞美人) saying:
"Waves crash against the pillow at dawn over the long Huái (淮) River,
a sliver of moon peeks at people.
The emotionless Biànshuǐ (汴水) flows eastward by itself,
carrying only a boat of farewells towards Xīzhōu (西州).
Amidst bamboo shade and flower islands, we once got drunk together,
the wine was not more than the tears.
Who taught that discernment should be in the dust?
Brewing up a scene of vexation."
It is traditionally said that this *cí* (詞) was composed by Hè Fānghuí (賀方回),
which is incorrect,
it was composed by Dōngpō (東坡).
Huátíng Chuánzǐ Héshàng's (華亭舡子和尚) Gāthā
Huátíng Chuánzi Héshàng had a gātā that said:
"A thousand-foot fishing line hangs straight down,
one ripple barely stirs, ten thousand follow.
The night is still, the water cold, the fish do not bite,
the boat returns full, carrying only the bright moon."
Huáng Lúzhí sang a chángduǎnjù that said:
"One ripple barely stirs, ten thousand follow,
a straw cape and hat, one fishing line,
the golden scales are deep within,
a thousand feet must still hang down.
Swallowing and then spitting,
believing and then doubting,
slow to take the hook.
Cold water, still river,
green mountains fill the eyes,
returning with the bright moon."
Lǎo Dù's poem
Lǎo Dù's poem says:
"Called by the Son of Heaven, he would not board the boat."
舡 (chuán),
is a local dialect word,
it is merely a lapel button.
"Every household keeps a black ghost,"
people in the Chuān Shǎn Lù region often worship black barbarian ghosts.
Common people do not understand,
so they interpret it as keeping livestock,
thus Shěn Cúnzhōng mistakenly identified the black ghosts as cormorants.
"Late at night, still holding a candle,
fearing it is still a dream."
If read with a falling tone,
its meaning is lost.
Lǐ Yuányīng's poem
Lǐ Yuányīng lost his wife,
and wrote a chángduǎnjù:
"Last year we met in the deep courtyard,
beneath the haitáng, once sang 'Jīnlǚ'.
After the song, flowers like rain,
on her emerald silk robe,
countless red speckles.
This year, revisiting the place where we held hands,
objects remain but the person is gone, late spring.
Looking back at the Qīngmén road,
scattered red catkins,
chasing the east wind away."
Yuányīng also died soon after.
Shí Mànqīng fell from his horse
Shí Mànqīng loved to joke.
Once, when he went out,
his groom lost the reins,
the horse was startled,
Mànqīng fell to the ground.
His attendants quickly helped him back onto the saddle,
Mànqīng slowly said:
"Luckily I am Scholar Shí,
if I were Scholar Wǎ,
wouldn't I be shattered?"
The Daoist priest's liver mántou
Juélián Chánshī was good at poetry,
Ōu Gōng said:
"This Daoist priest makes liver mántou."
Someone asked why,
and he replied:
"There is not a trace of vegetable flavor in it."
Rénzōng kept him at Jìngyīn Chányuàn,
where he wrote a gātā that said:
"Yáo's benevolence is as vast as heaven,
grant the lonely and poor freedom to fly."
This was his poem.
Pō Gǔ Qín Sāngōng's poems
Qín Shàoyóu's poem "Blaming Léizhōu" says:
"The southern lands are hot all year round,
a sorrowful person's days and nights are long.
Settling this body like an unmoving stone,
for a moment, forgetting one's hometown."
Huáng Lúzhí's "Blaming Yízhōu" says:
"Old age appears on the face daily,
joyous feelings leave the heart daily.
Today is already not like yesterday,
the future will not be like today."
"A light gauze headscarf,
a short bamboo mat, a six-foot bed.
No guests, the days are tranquil,
with wind, cool all night."
Shàoyóu was sentimental,
hence his poems were leisurely.
As for Dōngpō, he said:
"My entire life, everything is sufficient,
what I lack is only one death."
His heroic and ambitious spirit,
is admirable and inspiring.
Huājiǔ poem
Prime Minister Zhāng Qíxián's poem "Reply to the Western Capital's Garrison Administrator for the Gift of Huājiǔ" says:
"With flowers but no wine, the head is too lazy to lift,
with wine but no flowers, the eyes are weary to open.
How good it is on a day of no affairs in Xīyuán,
Luòyáng's flowers and wine arrive all at once."
Stealing poetry
Wèi Zhōufǔ sent a poem to Chén Yà,
which contained a couplet borrowed from an ancient poet,
and Yà did not show courtesy.
Zhōufǔ then sent another jueju that said:
"Having nothing to do but eat one's fill,
how can it compare to composing new verses by the window?
Literary works largely share similar themes,
I am just said to love stealing poems."
Yà replied with the same rhyme:
"Ancient sages are indeed blameworthy,
I would not dare say you love stealing poems.
It's unbearable how ancient people are so clever,
they stole a couplet of poetry in advance."
Chén Yà passes the imperial examination
Chén Yà was orphaned young,
and raised in his uncle's home.
His uncle was a physician,
people called him "Yátuī."
When Yà passed the imperial examination,
everyone congratulated him,
and his uncle had a poem that said:
"Zhāng Gōng drinks wine, Lǐ Gōng gets drunk,
people have always said this, and it's true.
Chén Yà newly passed the imperial examination this year,
the whole city congratulates Lǐ Yátuī."
Flat as a scale, bright as a mirror
Shuāng Jiàn served as a Qianpan in Méngzhōu,
his colleagues sometimes praised their county magistrate as "flat as a scale,
bright as a mirror."
Jiàn said:
"Then the clerk ran into the hall,
broke the mirror,
and snapped the scale."
Sūn Shān passes the examination
Sūn Shān barely made it onto the list of successful candidates.
A fellow examinee entrusted Shān to inquire about their results,
and Shān said:
"The end of the list of successful candidates is Sūn Shān,
my friend is even beyond Sūn Shān."
Later, Shān achieved fame through an imperial grace list,
and wrote a poem that said:
"A jinshi alongside Pángǔ on the list,
the Tànhuāláng in Fúxī's hands."
He also said:
"Fortunately, by the emperor's grace, I was accepted,
this time I will enter the yellow springs with a smile."
Explaining the Yìjīng
During Xiánpíng,
a magistrate of the district,
invited Mr. Huángzhōu to lecture on the Yìjīng.
When he reached the "Kuí Guà," to "The ninth line in the upper position sees a pig carrying mud,
loading a cart with ghosts."
He said:
"The lower yin has the meaning of carrying the upper,
and ghosts are accumulated yin."
Sūn Shān said:
"Loading a cart with ghosts,
is King Yánluó's moving his family and small belongings."
One day, when explaining the "Shìhé Guà,"
to "Thunder and lightning combine to make a display,"
the先生 said:
"First a flash of lightning,
then a clap of thunder,
therefore they combine."
Shān said:
"I will go home now."
The先生 asked:
"Why?"
Shān said:
"Bad weather."
One day, when lecturing on the Lúnyǔ, "The Jìshì offered sacrifices to Mount Tài,"
as the most revered of the Five Sacred Mountains.
Shān said:
"Since Mount Tài is the most revered of the Five Sacred Mountains,
the Kitchen God must be the head of a household."
Mocking Rèn Gǔ's poem
Rèn Gǔ, seeking fame, hid himself in the mountains and waters of Yī and Luò,
hoping for an invitation to no avail.
Secretly, he went to the capital to visit friends.
A court official mocked him, saying:
"The cloud-forest must wonder why the crane letter is late,
coming to the capital by day to inquire about affairs.
From now on, you must close your eyes when you see mountains,
for they have deceived you for too long."
Jìaofāng entrance verses
During the reign of Táng Zhāozōng,
the situation was controlled by Zhū Quánzhōng.
One day at a banquet,
a performer from the Bureau of Music looked at the imperial bulletin and said:
"Fortunately,
only one
is born every five hundred years;
if one were born every year,
how would the imperial court be able to cope?"
Two Poems by Yáng Xuě
The scholar Wáng Miǎn's poem "Ode to the Goat" goes:
"Two soap-pod-like horns on its head,
a tuft of whiskers beneath its chin.
Who knows from what land this saintly one comes,
scattering rosary beads as it walks on its hindquarters?"
He also wrote a poem "Snow," which goes:
"Heaven burns and drops bean stalks' ash,
making black plums turn white blossoms.
Taoist priests transform into silver shawms,
nuns become jade tea mallets."
Pí and Guī Mock Each Other
Pí Rìxiū visited Guī Rénshào,
who feigned illness and did not come out.
Rìxiū, using Guī's surname, wrote a poem mocking him:
"Hard bones and stubborn form, for how many autumns?
This stinking corpse, how unrefined it is!
Only after death will it be thoroughly explored,
simply because it wouldn't show its head back then."
Rénshào retorted with a poem:
"Several sharp pieces cut and pieced into a ball,
refined in fire and kneaded in water.
A packet of idle air, known to be ever-present,
inviting kicks and punches, never ceasing."
Rearing Silkworms in the Twelfth Month
A clerk from Héběi province saw his district magistrate and said:
"There is a matter of great convenience,
the common people harvest wheat and rear silkworms in the fifth month,
all at once a great toil.
I wish to have them rear silkworms in the twelfth month."
The magistrate said:
"That is indeed true,
but I fear there will be no mulberry leaves in the twelfth month."
The clerk said:
"I humbly submit for your arrangement."
Chén Yà's Poems
There was a monk who,
during a drought,
sought rain in the market.
Chén Yà wrote a poem using names of medicinal herbs and presented it to him:
"If the rainless period lasts through half a summer,
you and the master will turn into bitter gourds."
In Shòuzhōu, there was a stout courtesan leader.
Yà asked her where she was from,
and she replied:
"I am originally from Féishàng."
Yà laughed and said:
"I would call you a Féixià person."
Yà himself wrote "A Self-Eulogy," which goes:
"A mouth as if mute,
no intention to do evil.
At heart, originally nothing,
on the outside, many sharp angles."
There was a servant named Huáng Xīng,
who cooked ingredients in the outer kitchen,
placing pig trotters among them.
A young maidservant, like a monk, secretly ate them.
Xīng sued her before the official,
who said:
"This exactly matches the old poem:
'Like a monk passing by the kitchen early in the morning,
stealing the trotters from Huáng Xīng's ingredients.'"
A Congratulatory Memorial for the Four-Chamber Grand Guardian
Lǐ Yuán wrote "A Congratulatory Memorial for the Four-Chamber Grand Guardian," which goes:
"We humbly acknowledge that Your Excellency, the Grand Guardian,
having just departed from the ranks of the Five Capitals,
has immediately transferred to the office of the Four Chambers.
Your purple robe sweeps the ground,
your ivory tablet rests on your chest.
Holding a golden bone standard in hand,
sitting in a silver-framed chair.
In olden days, only one person held your horse,
now about ten people cry out to clear your path.
Judging by this prestige,
in the end, you must become a Grand Commandant;
you should also remember old acquaintances,
and above all, do not beat the long-term retainers."
Observing Your Bearing, You Must Not Be Very Exalted
There was a nobleman with a strong personality.
He once played chess with a subordinate official and said:
"Observing your bearing,
you must not be very exalted,
please sit in the west corridor."
Then he had an inkstone brought,
and as he made his moves, he loudly called out "Nuo!"
but forbade any sound when capturing a piece.
Poem on Seeing Off a Guest
Gāo Áocáo's poem "Seeing Off a Guest" goes:
"Seeing you off and seeing you off again,
seeing you off to the bridge head.
Piled high are two eyes' tears,
packed full is a chest of sorrow."
Fake Locusts
Jiǎ Huángzhōng was a chancellor,
and Lú Duōxùn was a consultant.
One day,
there were locust nymphs in the vicinity of the capital.
Lú said:
"Those things there
are Jiǎ Huángchóng (locusts surnamed Jiǎ)."
Jiǎ said:
"I also heard they do not harm crops,
but Lú Duō Sǔn (Lú, who does much harm) only."
Xuānshuǐ
Shí Cānzhèng was in the Central Secretariat Hall.
One chancellor said:
"Bring Xuānshuǐ."
Shí asked:
"What is that?"
He replied:
"The water from the Xuānhuī Institute is sweet and cool."
Shí Gōng said:
"If so, the water from the Sīnóng Temple
should be called 'Nóngshuǐ.'"
Messily Written Exam Paper
Kǒng Dēng was not a scholar.
During the Zhìpíng era, he came to the capital for the imperial examinations,
ashamed to submit a blank paper,
so he messily wrote on the exam paper:
"Three days of thunder,
five days of lightning,
ten days of rain.
Tàishān does not disdain specks of dust,
the great sea does not argue over ladles.
When people fawn,
I too go along.
It's good to feed horses on the roof,
their urine and feces flowing down both sides.
It's good to open a pawnshop on top of a banner pole.
The answer is 'high and dry,
must not come down yet.'
Still waiting for advice,
he also wrote a copy of Yīzhōu,
and at the end said:
"From here to passing the exam is ten thousand eight thousand li."
And also said:
"I, a Taoist, have done this thing;
I've bought a pair of straw sandals for a long journey."
The examination hall posted a notice for his arrest.
Dēng fled home.
A Sage of the Kong School
Yáng Qiú submitted a memorial to Grand Minister Chén Yà, saying:
"We humbly acknowledge that Your Excellency,
a renowned family of poetry and rites,
is a sage of the Kong School."
The official playfully replied with a poem:
"Having received your long letter,
how shall I interpret its meaning?
Please look at the clothes on my body,
there are no scorpions in my trousers."
Also,
a poem mocking a person with a black face said:
"Laughing like a cracked black plum,
crying like oozing drum juice.
A sticky note between the brows,
above that is a headscarf."
Opposite Couplets
A prefectural assistant once made an opposite couplet at a banquet, saying:
"When it's hot, there's no need for soup in a soup bowl."
A courtesan replied with a couplet:
"When the hall is cool, there's no use for a fan on a fan cart."
Mòjué
Ōu Gōng returned and said:
"The record says:
'Pointed-brim hats are worn by humble commoners,
short-booted soldiers are Mòjué troops.'"
The Duke said:
"I don't know what Mòjué means."
I once heard an old scholar say, "Pointed-brim hats are peculiar and pressed,
shallow-faced hemp shoes are worn by lièquè tea-drinkers."
Therefore, I have kept both explanations.
Two Scholars' Poems
A student from Héshuò and a student from Luòyáng were drinking together and composing poetry.
The Héshuò student said:
"In past years I often went east of Luòyáng,
year after year just watching the red flowers.
This year I do not see the face of the flower branches,
but the flowers are red where they were red in the past."
The Héshuò student said:
"In past years I often went north of Běijīng,
year after year just watching the radishes.
This year I do not see the face of the radishes,
but the radishes are radishing where they radished in the past."
Lǐ Zhōng Transforms into a Tiger
The gentleman Lǐ Zhōng from Jiànzhōu had been ill for a long time.
When his son returned from the market with medicine,
his father's jowls dropped and saliva flowed,
his appearance like a tiger's.
The son ran out
and closed his room.
Soon he heard roaring sounds,
and peering through a hole in the wall,
he saw that it was a real tiger.
The "Jade Tree Song"
At the end of the Táng dynasty, there was a man from Yíchūn named Wáng Gǔ,
who was famous for his poetry.
He once composed the "Yùshù Qǔ" (Jade Tree Song),
its lyrics saying:
"Rulers and ministers are still lost in a drunken dream,
but one side has already lost the sun and moon of Chén."
He once encountered some ruffians in the marketplace who beat him.
Wáng Gǔ cried out loudly:
"You rascals, do not be rude!
I am the one who chants the 'Yùshù Qǔ'!"
The ruffians were ashamed and apologized, then withdrew.
Yǐnniáng Taught the Art of Stabbing and Striking
In the Táng dynasty, there was a great general of Wèi, Niè Fēng.
He had a daughter who was ten years old,
named Yǐnniáng.
She was suddenly abducted by a mendicant nun.
Her parents did not know where she had gone,
and wept day and night.
Five years later,
the nun returned Yǐnniáng,
saying:
"Her training is complete."
Her parents inquired about what she had learned.
She said:
"The nun took me to a cave in a cliff.
She gave me a pill to take,
made me hold a sword,
and taught me the art of stabbing and striking.
After one year,
I could stab monkeys and gibbons as if flying,
and tigers and leopards as if they were nothing.
After three years,
I could fly and stab hawks and falcons.
After four years,
she would take me into the city,
point to someone,
recount their transgressions and evils,
and say:
'Bring me their head.'
And as soon as she spoke, the head would arrive.
She would then use medicine to dissolve it into water.
Five years later,
she suddenly said:
'A certain high official,
his crimes are full,
he deceives the ruler and oppresses the people.
Bring me his head.'
Yǐnniáng accepted the command and went,
hiding on a beam in the high official's residence.
After a short while,
she returned with his head.
The nun was furious and said:
'Why are you so late?'
Yǐnniáng said:
'Because I found the person amusing and lovely to play with,
I didn't want to act immediately.'
The nun scolded her, saying:
'From now on, when you encounter such people,
first cut off what they love,
then decide.
Your skill is complete,
you may return.'
So she returned home."
The Tiger of Héngshān
During the Chángqìng era,
there was a recluse named Mǎ Zhěng at a retreat on Héngshān.
He saw an old monk with an ancient face and bushy eyebrows.
The monk borrowed Mǎ Zhěng's servant to carry money to the market down the mountain to buy salt and cheese.
Initially, Mǎ Zhěng did not know where the old monk was going.
A mountain dweller named Mǎ Shào arrived later,
saying he had encountered a tiger on the road
that ate a servant.
After eating, it immediately shed its striped coat
and put on a monk's robe.
Upon closer inspection, it was indeed the old monk.
After a short while,
the monk returned, his mouth still bloody.
The two were horrified
and conspired together.
They tricked the monk, saying:
"There is a monster in the temple well."
The monk went to peer into the well.
The two men used their combined strength to push him into the well,
pressing him down with a large stone,
and then hurried down the mountain.
It was already dusk.
They saw dozens of people,
some monks, some Daoists, some men and women,
all furiously saying:
"These two thieves killed our Chan master!
We have come to pursue and capture them."
The two questioned the hunters:
"Who are these people?"
The hunters said:
"These are chāngguǐ (tiger-ghosts).
They were people eaten by the tiger in the past.
Once they become ghosts,
they serve the tiger."
The two then sternly reprimanded the ghosts, saying:
"You are truly despicable ghosts!
Alive, you were food for the tiger.
Dead, you served the tiger.
Now that it has fortunately perished,
do you still cry and wail after it?"
One ghost replied:
"We were indeed eaten by the tiger,
and we should engrave in our hearts to repay this injustice.
However, we never knew that the one called the Chan master was actually a tiger."
Volume 55
Ends.
Dù Shī Cures Illness
There was a person suffering from malaria.
Dù Zǐměi (Dù Fǔ) said:
"Reciting my poems can cure it."
He then ordered them to recite "As night deepens, I light another candle,
facing each other as if in a dream."
The malaria was as before.
He then ordered them to recite "Zǐzhāng's skull, blood smeared and muddled."
The illness indeed immediately improved.
Comparable to Táoyuán
Xiànzōng praised Róng Yù's poems, saying:
"If this person were here,
he could be compared to Wǔlíng Táoyuán (Peach Blossom Spring),
for his verses."
Spring Day Gets Spring Clothes
Liǔ Gōngquán accompanied the imperial carriage.
The Emperor said:
"I have a happy event.
Border clothes have long not been issued in time,
but this year, in the second month, all have been distributed.
You may compose a poem to celebrate."
Liǔ Gōngquán said:
"Although there was no war last year,
they have not yet returned this year.
How can imperial grace be repaid?
On a spring day, spring clothes are received."
Diving for a Dragon and Obtaining a Pearl
Yuán Zhěn, Liú Yǔxī, and Wéi Chǔkè
gathered together at Lètiān's (Bái Jūyì's) residence.
Each composed a "Huái Gǔ" (Nostalgia for the Past) poem about Jīnlíng.
Liú's poem was completed first.
Bái Jūyì said:
"Four people dove for a dragon,
and you obtained the pearl first.
What use are the remaining scales and horns?"
The three gentlemen then stopped composing.
Poetry Gourd
Táng Qiú loved to compose poetry.
He rolled his manuscripts into balls
and stored them in a large gourd in the river,
saying:
"If they do not sink,
those who find them will then know my painstaking effort."
They flowed to Xīnqú.
Someone who knew him said:
"This is the poetry gourd of the recluse Táng."
They retrieved it,
and his poems were then transmitted.
His poem "Tí Yǐnjū" (On Dwelling in Seclusion) says:
"A few drops of stone-spring rain,
a stream of frost-leaf wind.
My work is in the green mountains,
my Dao is perfected in doing nothing."
Yearning for the Spring Scenery of Jìnghú
Yuán Zhěn (元稹) was an imperial inspector in Zhèdōng (淅東),
and was fond of the courtesan Liú Cǎichūn (劉採春).
Yuán Zhěn (稹) once had a poem that said:
"Hesitating, I have not yet returned,
it is not because I am in love with perch."
Someone annotated it, saying:
"It's because he loves the spring colors of Jìnghú (鏡湖),"
referring to Liú Cǎichūn (劉採春).
Zhèng Zhègū (鄭鷓鴣)
Zhèng Dūguān (鄭都官) had a "Partridge Poem" (《鷓鴣詩》),
and was at the time called "Zhèng Zhègū (鄭鷓鴣)."
Ruìjǐnkē (瑞錦窠)
The Secretary of the Ministry of Rites was in charge of literary composition within the province,
and was called Ruìjǐnkē (瑞錦窠).
Huáixī Bēi Màozi (淮西碑帽子)
Liǔ Zǐhòu (柳子厚) said that Hán Tuìzhī's (韓退之) "Stele for Huáixī" (《淮西碑》) still had a "hat" (preamble).
"If I were to compose it,
I would directly speak of the military campaign against the rebels."
He also said:
"Left for meals, right for porridge,
how is that like my 'Ode to Pacifying Huáixī' (《平淮西雅》) which says 'looking up to father, looking down to son'?"
Catching the gist of the words
A Tang dynasty poetry monk was skilled in discussing poetry,
especially good at catching the gist of the words.
Zhāng Shuǐbù (張水部) one day got a line saying:
"Often when sending someone off,
I recall the time I left home."
He thought no ancient had ever said it.
The monk said:
"There is one who said it:
'Seeing other people's peach and plum trees,
I remember the spring in my old garden' is it."
Lètiān zhī Gōng (樂天之宮)
A merchant guest crossing the sea encountered a storm,
and landed at a palace gate.
He said it was "Lètiān zhī Gōng (樂天之宮)."
Bái (白) heard this,
and then composed a poem:
"Recently someone returned from overseas,
seeing a tower deep within the sea mountains.
Inside is an immortal shrine with one room,
all saying this awaits Lètiān (樂天) to come."
He also said:
"I study the Buddhist gate, not immortality,
I fear your words are a false傳.
The sea mountains are not where I will return,
if I return, I must return to Tuṣita Heaven (兜率天)."
Poet Tiger
Luó Yè's (羅鄴) "Peony" poem says:
"When all spring reds have fallen, then the flowers are seen,
a canopy shields them from light sun, guarding their fragrant glow.
Buying and planting them in ponds and gardens, fearing there's no space,
how many families will see their descendants [enjoying them]?"
Everyone called him a poet tiger.
Sòng Zhīwèn (宋之問),
during Empress Wǔ's (天后) reign, sought to be a Northern Gate Scholar,
but was not allowed.
He then wrote "Ode to the Milky Way" (《明河篇》) to express his feelings,
saying:
"The Milky Way can be seen but not approached,
I wish to ride a raft and ask for a ford.
And take the Weaver Girl's loom stone,
to visit the fortune-teller of Lín'áng (臨卬)."
Empress Wǔ (天后) said:
"It's not that I don't know his talent,
but he has a flaw in his mouth."
Zhīwèn (之問) had a tooth ailment,
hence his bad breath.
This is already recorded in "Běnshì Shī" (《本事詩》).
Mílóu (迷樓)
During Emperor Yáng of Sui's (隋煬帝) time,
Xiàng Shēng (項昇) from Zhejiang presented new palace plans,
and the Emperor loved them.
He ordered the construction in Yángzhōu (楊州) according to the plans.
Once completed,
he visited it and said:
"Even true immortals wandering here
would get lost."
So it was named "Mílóu (迷樓)."
Sānhuā Mǎ (三花馬)
Hán Gàn (韓幹) painted "Reviewing Horses" (閱馬圖) and imperial horses,
all featuring Sānhuā Mǎ (三花馬).
Sānhuā (三花) means trimming the mane into three braids.
Bái Lètiān's (樂天) poem says:
"Dance robes are cut with four leaves,
horse manes are trimmed with three flowers."
Candidates first lighting three candles
According to Tang regulations:
When candidates took exams,
once dusk fell,
they were allowed to light three candles.
Wéi Yǒngyí (韋永貽) finished his exam early on the day,
and wrote a poem:
"Three candles extinguished, the bell just starting to chime,
the nine-times refined elixir formed, but the cauldron not yet opened.
Sun and moon gradually sinking, people bustling about,
not knowing who is the exiled immortal arriving."
Qūchén Sī (麯塵絲)
Yáng Jùyuán's (楊巨源) poem says:
"The willows by the river are like Qūchén Sī (麯塵絲)."
Yán Qǔ (鹽曲)
Jiāozhǐ (交趾) has "Huángdì Yán Qǔ" (《黃帝鹽曲》).
According to Tang records, there are "Tūjué Yán" (《突厥鹽》), "Āquè Yán" (《阿鵲鹽》), etc.
Shī Jiānwú's (施肩吾) poem says:
"The frantic Chǔ (楚) guest sings into snow,
the charming and lazy Wú (吳) girl's smile is salt."
Drinking inkstone water
During the Ministry of Rites examination,
no tea or soup was provided,
only inkstone water to drink,
all mouths were blackened.
Applying makeup and powders, stacking up dead people
Xú Zhòngyā (徐仲鴉) and Lǐ Jiǔgāo (李九皋) were both good at poetry.
Xú's (徐) poetry was rich and beautiful,
Lǐ (李) often used allusions.
Lǐ (李) said to Xú (徐):
"Your poetry is like a beautiful woman,
skilled at applying makeup and powders."
Xú (徐) said:
"You are like a vendor of funerary objects,
merely stacking up dead people."
Autumn Sound Poem
Xú Kǎi (徐鍇) wrote "Autumn Sound Poem" (《秋聲詩》):
"Well phoenix trees drop onto the steps,
distant frontier geese fly across the sky.
Raindrops age the moss,
wind blows the ivy red."
Fishing Old Man Picture
The "Jiangnán Fishing Old Man Picture" (《江南釣叟圖》) is widely circulated,
on which are two "Fisherman's Songs" (《漁父詞》).
There is a line "a single hook lightly made of silk floss."
Chángnián Sānlǎo (長年三老)
In Chuānxiá (川峽), the boatmen and polemen are called Chángnián Sānlǎo (長年三老).
Old Dù's (老杜) poem says:
"Amidst the songs of the Chángnián Sānlǎo (長年三老),
high waves on the shoals in broad daylight."
Water bird
Pìtí (鷿鵜) is a water bird.
Its fat, when applied to blades and swords,
prevents rust.
An ancient poem says:
"Horses chew alfalfa leaves,
swords gleam with pìtí (鷿鵜) fat."
Back-beating Poem
Lú Yánràng's (盧延讓) "Lament for a Border General" (《哭邊將》) poem says:
"It was naturally caused by lead poisoning,
not injury from cannon stones.
Many official documents on his body,
great resentment for the sores on his back."
People called it a back-beating poem.
Èr Rǔ Gē (爾汝歌)
Sūn Hào (孫皓) surrendered to Jìn (晉),
and was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Guīmìng (歸命侯).
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) asked:
"I hear the southerners like to compose Èr Rǔ Gē (《爾汝歌》),
are you somewhat capable?"
Hào (皓) raised his cup and sang:
"Once I was your neighbor,
now I am your subject."
Dìsān Tīng (第三廳)
"The village elder today is not in good spirits,
due to lack of a bottle of wine for curing deafness.
Disturbing the Jade Hall is almost complete,
indistinctly approaching the Dìsān Tīng (第三廳)."
Zhōngshān Gōng (鍾山公)
Hòu Táng's Lǐ Jiànxūn led an army to Línchuān,
and upon his return, was appointed Sīkōng.
He repeatedly submitted memorials requesting retirement,
styling himself Zhōngshān Gōng.
The emperor issued an edict appointing him Sītú,
but he declined to take office.
The scholar Tāng Yuè wrote a congratulatory note to him.
Jiànxūn replied with a poem, saying:
"Since the Sīkōng position is yet ungranted,
how dare I act as Sītú?
Fortunately, I have the title of Shān Gōng,
why am I not addressed as such?"
Previously,
Sòng Qíqiū retired to Jiǔhuá.
Before a year had passed,
he was summoned once and rose to office,
which was criticized by the public at the time.
Someone, comparing Jiànxūn to Běi Sòng,
composed a poem, saying:
"Peach blossoms and flowing water must be trusted,
not like Liú Láng, who goes and comes back."
Jiǎ Zhì's Poem on Xuē Yáoyīng
Yuán Zài took Xuē Yáoyīng as his concubine,
providing her with a golden silk canopy and a dust-repelling mattress,
and clothing her in dragon silk robes.
Jiǎ Zhì's poem says:
"Afraid to dance, her light garment feels heavy;
smiling, her peach-like face seems to open.
Only then did I realize that Emperor Chéng of Hàn
vainly built the Wind-Sheltering Pavilion."
Hé Xùn's Poetic Ability
Hé Xùn could compose poetry at the age of eight.
Shěn Yuè said:
"Every time I read your poems,
I repeat them three times a day without ceasing."
Hence, Lǐ Yìshān's poem says:
"Tell Hé Xùn to stop composing linked verses,
lest the person named Shěn in Dōngyáng waste away."
Tàibái Enters the Moon
Lǐ Tàibái made three attempts to revise Ci Xuan (Collected Lyrics), but dissatisfied,
he burned them all,
keeping only "Hèn Bié Fù" (Rhapsody on the Sorrow of Separation).
When Lù Shān rebelled,
he wrote in "Hú Wú Rén" (No Barbarians Left) saying:
"When Tàibái enters the moon, the enemy can be destroyed."
When Lù Shān died,
Tàibái entered the moon.
Dù Shī
Yáng Dànián disliked Dù Fǔ's poetry,
calling him a "village pedant."
Once, a villager pressed Dànián with Dù Fǔ's poetry, saying:
"Please try to complete this line of Dù Fǔ for me."
He then recited "The traveler on the Jiāng and Hàn rivers longs to return home,"
and as Dànián was about to compose the couplet,
the villager slowly said:
"A useless scholar in the universe."
Dànián was silent.
Ōu Gōng also did not particularly love Dù Fǔ's poetry,
but considered Hán Tuìzhī peerless.
Tuìzhī, in the literary world of the Táng Dynasty,
never humbled himself,
except when praising Lǐ Bái and Dù Fǔ without ceasing.
Ōu Gōng's displeasure with Zǐměi
is incomprehensible.
Yet he admired and appreciated Lǐ Bái;
perhaps it was because Tàibái's soaring and dynamic style
was easier to be moved by?
Zhāng Wénchāng's Poem on a Horse
Zhāng Wénchāng's yuèfǔ lyrics are elegant and deeply subtle,
and his five-character poems are also plain and lovely.
However, his seven-character poems contain more praise than literary expression.
His "Xiè Mǎ Shī" (Poem Thanking a Horse) says:
"Just leaving the splendid stable, its hooves hesitate;
first arriving at a poor home, it raises its eyes in alarm."
This horse was slow and unable to move, and easily startled.
Poetry of Motion and Stillness
There is a poem with the line "When the wind settles, flowers still fall,"
which Wáng Jīnggōng paired with "Birds chirping make the mountain even more secluded."
The upper line has motion within stillness,
and the lower line has stillness within motion.
Deep courtyard, apricot blossom rain
Wáng Jīnggōng said:
"A branch of pear blossoms, spring bearing rain,"
"Peach blossoms falling wildly like red rain,"
"At dusk, the pearl curtain rolls up, revealing the western mountain's rain,"
all are striking lines.
However, none are as excellent as "Deep courtyard, apricot blossom rain,"
where the words end, but the meaning does not.
Fàn Xīwén's Poem
Fàn Xīwén's poem "Zèng Diàozhě" (To a Fisherman) says:
"People coming and going on the river,
all love the delicious perch.
See how your single leaf-like boat
appears and disappears amidst the wind and waves."
Also, his "Guān Dù" (Observing Crossing) poem:
"One oar light as a leaf,
bystanders too are drained of spirit.
Another time on flat ground,
do not forget those in peril."
Wénxǐ Banquet Awarded Poem
Tàizōng was fond of literature.
Each time scholars passed the imperial examination,
he would bestow upon them an imperial poem at the Wénxǐ banquet,
which became a custom.
Rénzōng composed even more poems.
One says:
"When a humble scholar meets a prosperous era,
how should he repay the country?"
Butterfly Poem
Xiè Xuéshì's "Húdié" (Butterfly) poem says:
"Madly following willow catkins, sometimes seen;
dancing into pear blossoms, nowhere to be found."
Lǐ Shì Gōngzhōng Shī (Palace Poem by the Lǐ Clan)
Ōu Gōng said:
"Poetry originates from the heart;
poverty, wealth, sorrow, and joy
are all tied to one's emotions."
A palace poem by the Lǐ clan of Jiāngnán says:
"The curtained sun has risen three zhàng high, piercing through;
in the golden censer, fragrant beasts are successively added;
the red brocade floor covering wrinkles with each step.
The beauty finishes her dance, her golden hairpin slides;
feeling ill from wine, she picks and sniffs a flower bud;
from a distant hall, the faint sound of flutes and drums plays."
This is different from the scholar's poem: "Trying to pick wild vegetables and boil them with their roots,
then chop green firewood and burn it with its leaves."
Qiū Jùn's Poem
When Qiū Jùn arrived in Shānyáng,
the prefect invited him to a banquet.
Jùn's poem says:
"It makes all women's faces in the world ugly,
and truly captures the hearts of gentlemen in the world."
Tiáoyuán Dì Yǎngbìng Fāng (The Place of Governance Becomes a Recuperation Ward)
Wáng Suí became prime minister and fell gravely ill,
especially favoring Buddhism.
Someone mocked him, saying:
"Who says the place of governance
has become a recuperation ward?
One only sees monks filling the rooms,
how can one know the house is ablaze?"
Wèi Yě's Poem
Wèi Yě lived in seclusion on Huàshān.
Zhēnzōng repeatedly summoned him,
but he did not come.
He left a poem inscribed on a wall and departed,
saying:
"When washing the inkstone, fish swallow the water;
when brewing tea, cranes avoid the smoke."
The envoy returned,
and reported with the poem.
The Emperor said:
"Yě will not come."
Three Times in the Hànlín Academy
Liú Zǐyí entered the Hànlín Academy three times.
His poem says:
"What flavor do the three stolen蟠桃 peaches attain?
Reaching the top of the Aó head, the situation becomes more solitary."
Jiāngnán Qǔ (Southern Songs)
When Guān Láigōng was young,
he once composed a "Jiāngnán Qǔ," saying:
"Spring ends in Jiāngnán, my heart breaks with parting;
duckweed fills the sandbar, but the person has not returned."
He also said:
"At dusk, when I gaze over Jiāngnán,
my sorrow is endless, like the spring water."
His sentiments were all sorrowful,
and in his later years, he indeed moved south.
Jiāngshān Liú Rén (Rivers and Mountains Retain People)
Sū Zǐměi was long frustrated.
He ascended the Chāngmén gate in Sūzhōu,
and inscribed:
"Time passes swiftly, all like a dream;
the scenery is bleak, and autumn changes again.
My home is beneath the Fènghuáng city gates,
why do the rivers and mountains insist on keeping me?"
He also wrote next to it:
"Do the rivers and mountains retain people?
Or do people retain the rivers and mountains?"
Xiāng Líng Gǔ Sè Shī (Poem on the Xiāng Spirit Playing the Zither)
Qián Qǐ was staying overnight at an inn.
Outside the window, someone recited:
"The person in the曲 (melody) is unseen,
On the river, several peaks are green."
Later, during the palace examination for the poem 《Xiāng Líng Gǔ Sè》 (Xiāng Líng Playing the Se),
he had long struggled to find the concluding lines.
He then used this couplet to complete it,
and consequently was chosen as the魁 (chief/top scorer).
A scholar from Mǐn's poetic prose
During the Zhēn Zōng Emperor's reign,
a scholar from Mǐn was taking the examination for the 《Tiān Dé Qīng Míng Fù》 (Rhapsody on the Purity of Heavenly Virtue).
He began the essay by saying:
"How is the Way of Heaven?
The more one looks up, the higher it seems."
The examination supervisor was also a person from Mǐn,
and so he was selected.
Another Jīng Nán (Jingnan) scholar composed a poem on snow,
beginning with the character "先" (xiān),
and the concluding line was:
"Before the twelve peaks, the heavens slowly turn."
Poets' use of "也"
Poets' use of the character "也" (yě)
was originally all pronounced "yè".
Dù Fǔ said: "青袍也自公" (qīng páo yè zì gōng – the green robe is also for public service),
Yuán Zhěn said: "也向慈恩寺裏遊" (yè xiàng Cí'ēn Sì lǐ yóu – also traveled within Cí'ēn Temple).
People today read it as it is written (i.e., pronounce yě),
which is incorrect.
The Qìdān poem
Diāo Yuē's poem during his mission to Qìdān said:
"The Yālìbì presides over the feast,
The Hèbázhī inspects the rooms.
For the farewell, three pǐzhì,
As a gift of honey, ten pílí."
These all recorded actual events.
Yílìbì
is an official title,
like a chief administrator in China.
Hèbázhī
is like a chamberlain.
Pǐzhì
are small wooden jars made of colored silk-wood,
like yellow lacquer.
Pílí
are all like large rats;
the Di (northern barbarians) considered them precious food.
Night banquet poem
Shī Jiānwú's 《Yè Yàn Shī》 (Night Banquet Poem):
"Curved railings like a painting, bought and sleepless,
From the jade brazier at night, agarwood smoke rises.
A line of twelve beautiful maidens, like immortals,
Their rosy faces about to smile, like blooming peach blossoms.
In the green window, they playfully preen and wash late,
Unaware outside that the Milky Way has turned.
Scolded and punished by her lover with a glass cup,
The wine enters her four limbs, soft as red jade."
Three drafts of "Sour Prose"
Qián Xī,
during the Tàizōng Emperor's reign, presented the 《Sì Yí Lái Wáng Fù》 (Rhapsody on the Submission of the Four Barbarian Tribes),
and was promoted to a post in the academy.
He once composed the 《Sān Zhuó Suān Wén》 (Three Drafts of Sour Prose),
which roughly states:
"At Wèichuān, where the water is emerald,
early one abandons those who fish for the moon;
On Shānglǐng, where mountains are green,
one does not follow those who sleep among the clouds."
And: "Year after year failing the examination,
the spring breeze merely weeps for the migrating orioles;
Wandering everywhere,
the night rain vainly grieves for the separated wild geese."
When he died,
Lǐ Qìngsūn cried over him, saying:
"No one recites the exquisite Rhapsody on the Four Barbarian Tribes,
but the Three Drafts of Sour Prose is renowned throughout the world."
Rhapsody on the Wōwā Horse
Qiáo Yí submitted for examination the 《Wōwā Mǎ Fù》 (Rhapsody on the Wōwā Horse):
"Four hooves drag silk,
turning the startling waves of the vast desert sea;
A single snort creates wind,
scattering the shattered leaves of the Hu mountains below."
Felling the huái trees along the road to the two capitals
During the Zhēnyuán period,
the Ministry of Revenue wanted to cut down the huái (locust) trees along the road to the two capitals for firewood,
and plant small peach trees instead.
The Wèinán (Weinana) County Magistrate Zhāng Zào submitted a petition stating:
"Where Shào Bó rested,
even that should not be cut down;
Where the former emperor once traveled,
how could it be appropriate to fell them?"
Thereupon, the plan was stopped.
A guest addresses Zhāng Sānyǐng
A guest said to Zhāng Zǐyě:
"People all call you Zhāng Sānzhōng,
referring to 'matters in the heart,'
'tears in the eyes,'
and 'a person in mind'."
He replied:
"Why not call me Zhāng Sānyǐng (Zhāng Three Shadows)?
'The clouds part, the moon comes, flowers play with shadows,'
'Delicate and languid, unwilling to rise,
the curtains are pressed by flower shadows,'
'No one on the willow path,
falling catkins leave no shadow.'
These are the lines I am proud of throughout my life."
Poem on grass
Lín Bū's poem on grass said:
"Every year at Jīngǔ,
who commands the wild growth of spring colors?
Where the remaining flowers fall,
the ground is full of smoke and rain.
Again, a farewell song,
at the long pavilion at dusk,
the noble son departs,
countless lush grasses on roads north, south, east, and west."
Tàizōng's poem
At Shǎnfǔ, Táng Zhāozōng had a poem that said:
"How can there be a hero,
to welcome me back to the great palace?"
At Xiāoyáo Bridge, the Tàizōng Emperor had a poem that said:
"Formerly, I rode a single horse and departed,
now I drive ten thousand chariots and return."
The circumstances are not comparable.
Increased salary for three-class attendants
According to the old system:
Attendants of the three classes
received a monthly salary of seven hundred (coins)
and half a catty of meat.
During the Xiángfú era,
someone inscribed on a wall:
"The attendants of the three classes are truly pitiable,
their lowliness and hardship are well known.
When will seven hundred coins' pay make them rich?
When will half a catty of mutton make them fat?"
The imperial court then increased their salary.
Elegy for Chānglíng
Lǐ Wénzhèng submitted an 《Chānglíng Wǎncí》 (Elegy for Chānglíng) that said:
"How many times did he offer jade to the Supreme Emperor,
from the imperial tower, he received kings who surrendered three times."
Having a salary to fatten one's wife and children
During the Rénzōng Emperor's reign,
a high official's poem said:
"Having a salary to fatten one's wife and children,
but no benevolence extends to officials and common people."
(Someone) jokingly said:
"On the main road, I met a heavily laden cart,
with a very heavy load,
the lean ox suffering greatly.
Is it not your wife and children?"
Gazing at peach and plum blossoms from a flower vendor's shoulder pole
Imperial scholars and officials were tied up with duties,
rarely having leisure or outings,
to the point of having lines like: "Gazing at peach and plum blossoms from a flower vendor's shoulder pole,
Listening to music from atop a wine shop."
Morning worship at Shényù Hall
Shényù Hall in Xījīng (Western Capital)
was ten lǐ from the city.
Morning worship often involved suffering from early rising.
The Deputy Prefect would offer three rounds of imperial wine,
and they would withdraw without exchanging a single word.
His poem said:
"Walking ten lǐ while still dreaming,
Drinking three cups without exchanging a word."
Méi Shèngyú's poem
Méi Shèngyú's poem includes "Yǒng Hétún" (Ode to the Pufferfish):
"On spring islets, reed shoots grow,
On spring banks, poplar catkins fly.
The pufferfish at this time,
is too precious to count among fish and shrimp."
The opening lines already fully express the pufferfish's excellence.
Sū Zǐzhān obtained a barbarian cloth bow-cover sold by the southwestern barbarians;
its pattern was woven with Shèngyú's 《Chūn Xuě Shī》 (Spring Snow Poem),
showing how respected his name was even among the barbarians.
The followers not loved by Zhèng Dūguān
The Wú (Wu) monk Zànníng,
in the early days of the dynasty, served as the Monk Registrar.
Ān Hóngjiàn mocked him, saying:
"The followers not loved by Zhèng Dūguān
constantly form groups for chanting."
Níng replied:
"The kind of people Qín Shǐhuáng (Qin Shihuang) hadn't buried alive yet
often form crowds."
Zhèng Gǔ's poem said: "I love monks but not purple-robed monks."
Dù Fǔ's Collected Works
Chén Cóngyì’s poems resembled those of Bái Lètiān.
Ever since Yáng and Liú started singing in harmony,
and the *Xīkūn* collection circulated,
later poets vied to imitate them.
This change in the *fēngyǎ* style
was called the “Kūn Tǐ.”
Lord Chén once by chance obtained an old copy of Dù’s collected works.
Many characters were missing or incorrect.
Up to "身輕一鳥" (a body light as a bird),
one character was missing below.
He and several guests each used one character to fill it in.
Some said "疾" (swift),
some said "落" (descending),
some said "起" (ascending),
some said "下" (down).
Later, he obtained another copy,
which read "身輕一鳥過" (a body light as a bird passing).
Lord Chén sighed in admiration, saying:
"Though it is just one character,
none of you gentlemen could reach that!"
Nine Monks’ Collection
In this dynasty, there were nine famous monk-poets.
Their collection was titled *Jiǔ Sēng*.
One was called Huìchóng;
I forget the names of the others and their poems.
One poem says:
"Horses graze on land where they descended,
eagles circle above clouds after battle."
Another says:
"Spring is born beyond the Guìlǐng mountains,
people live west of Hǎimén."
The *Jìnshì* Xǔ Tóng,
a man of outstanding talent,
once gathered the monks to compose poems on assigned topics.
He stipulated:
"Do not use anything from this particular family."
(These were categories like mountains, water, wind, clouds, bamboo, rocks, flowers, grass, snow, frost, stars, sun, birds, fowl.)
All the monks laid down their brushes.
When Tóng passed the imperial examination,
people at the time mocked him, saying:
"Zhāng Kāng wraps up his horse,
Xǔ Tóng noisily arrays his wife." This is it.
Jiāo and Dǎo’s Poetry
Mèng Jiāo and Jiǎ Dǎo died in poverty due to their poetry.
Mèng’s *Yíjū* says:
"Borrowing a cart to carry furniture,
the furniture is less than the cart."
This means there was absolutely nothing at all.
His *Xiè Tàn* says:
"Warmed a bent body into a straight body."
Unless one had personally experienced it,
one could not utter this line.
Jiǎ said:
"Though there are hairs by my temples,
they are not enough to weave a winter coat."
Even if they could be woven,
how much would there be?
Also, his *Cháo Jī Shī* says:
"Sitting, I open the xilín zither,
cold snaps two or three strings."
It’s not just enduring hunger;
how could such cold be endured?
Zhōu Pǔ’s poems,
forged for months and refined for seasons,
even before completion,
were already widely circulated.
One says:
"The wind warms, bird sounds fragment;
the sun rises high, flower shadows deepen."
Another says:
"In the morning, mountain birds clamor;
after the rain, apricot blossoms are sparse."
Méi Shèngyú on Poetry
Méi Shèngyú said:
"For a poet, if the ideas are new and the words are skillful,
achieving what previous poets have not said,
it is excellent.
It must depict difficult-to-describe scenes
as if they are right before one's eyes.
It must contain inexhaustible meaning,
apparent beyond the words.
Jiǎ Dǎo said:
'Bamboo basket gathers mountain fruits,
clay pot carries stone spring water.'
Yáo Lìng said:
'Horses follow mountain deer to graze,
chickens chase wild birds to fly.'
These all describe the desolate condition of an official in a mountain town.
But they are not as skillful as 'The county is old, locust roots emerge;
the official is clean, the horse's stomach is high.'
If Yán Wéi's 'Spring water overflows the willow pond,
evening sun lingers in the flower dell,'
then are not the natural scenery and object states right before one's eyes?
Wēn Tíngyún's 'Chicken crow at thatched inn under moon,
human footprints on plank bridge in frost,'
and Jiǎ Dǎo's 'Strange birds cry in the wild,
setting sun frightens travelers,'
then are not the hardships of the road,
the sorrow of an exile, and the longing of a traveler apparent beyond the words?"
The Sleepyhead *Zhuàngyuán* Passes
Lǚ Wénmù, during a brief trip to a county,
encountered Hú Dàn, who was with his father, the county magistrate.
A guest praised Lǚ,
quoting his poem:
"Trimmed the cold lamp to its end, but dreams did not come."
Hú laughed and said:
"He is merely a sleepyhead!"
The common saying turned into *kē*.
The next year, Lǚ passed the *jiǎkē* examination.
He sent a message to Hú, saying:
"The sleepyhead has passed the *Zhuàngyuán* examination!"
Hú replied:
"Wait until next year when I pass as the first person;
I will concede you one point only."
In the next list, he indeed came first.
Poem Gifted to a Fisherman
There is a poem *Zèng Yúfù* that says:
"Before my eyes, I see no affairs of court or market;
in my ears, I only hear the sound of wind and rain."
Commentators said:
"He suffers from *gānshèn fēng* (liver-kidney wind syndrome)."
Another line: "Searched all day and could not find it,
sometimes it comes on its own."
Originally referring to the difficulty of finding good lines,
it was said: "This is someone who has lost a cat."
King Téng's Butterfly Painting
Wáng Jiàn's *Gōng Cí* (Palace Lyrics), a hundred poems,
mostly recount events within the Tang imperial palace
that are not recorded in historical chronicles or popular novels,
such as:
"For several days there were no summons within the palace,
news circulated of King Téng's 'Butterfly Painting'."
King Téng, Yuán Yīng,
was the son of Gāozǔ.
The *Mínghuà Lù* (Records of Famous Paintings) briefly mentions his skill in painting.
Poetic Flaws in Lines
Poets eagerly seek good lines,
sometimes leading to illogical reasoning,
which is also a poetic flaw.
For example, "In my sleeve, remonstrance drafts go to court;
on my head, palace flowers return from the banquet."
There is no reason to directly use rough drafts for remonstrance memorials.
"Below Gūsū Terrace, Hánshān Temple;
at midnight, its bell tolls reach the traveler's boat."
What about the fact that the third watch is not the time for striking bells?
Jiǎ Dǎo's *Kū Sēng* (Mourning a Monk) says:
"Painted and kept his walking image,
burned his seated meditation body."
At the time, it was interpreted as burning a living monk to death.
If "Steps follow green mountain's shadow,
sits learning from white pagoda's bones,"
and "Alone walks the潭底 shadow,
counts breaths by the tree's body,"
what is the difference between refined and coarse?
Xiè Bóchū’s Poetry
Xiè Jǐng Bóchū from Mǐn,
during the Tiānshèng era,
was famous for his poetry.
When I was exiled to Yílíng,
he sent me a long rhyming poem,
which included:
"The magistrate's robe color is green like river waves,
the scholar's writings are like Shu brocade spread out.
A foreign land transformed into a valley of elegance,
distant people vied to recognize the 校儲郎.
A lower kingdom found it hard to retain the golden horse guest,
new poems are passed to the bamboo branch maiden."
Another poem says:
"Self-planted yellow flowers add to the wild scenery,
newly moved tall bamboos listen to autumn sounds."
"Garden trees change leaves, plums are first ripe,
ponds are deserted, swallows learn to fly."
Lord of the Hibiscus City
After Shí Mànqīng died,
some people vaguely saw him.
He said:
"I am appointed as an immortal,
the Lord of the Hibiscus City."
He rode a green mule,
flying like the wind.
Later, he descended upon the home of a *jǔzǐ*,
leaving a poem that said:
"Oriole's song does not grow old with spring's light,
flower's shadow always follows the long day's foot."
Listening to the Wind, Listening to the Water
Wáng Jiàn's 《Níshang Cí》:
"Disciples in song keep one hue,
listening to wind, listening to water, creating the Níshang."
Today there are two tunes, 《Wàng Yíng》 and 《Xiàn Xiān Yīn》,
which are echoes of it.
Unsure what "listening to wind, listening to water" refers to,
Zhào Shīmín's poem
Zhào Shīmín, a Dragon Diagram,
his poem says:
"In wheat season, morning air is mild,
in summer's locust shade, noon is cool."
Discussing Hán Tuìzhī's poetry
Hán Tuìzhī's literary power was applicable everywhere.
He once considered poetry a minor matter of writing,
hence he said:
"A passionate guest who fears wine,
a poet by the way."
I alone admire his use of rhyme.
When rhymes are broad,
waves overflow,
spilling into adjacent rhymes,
unrestrained by common patterns,
such as in 《Cǐ Rì Zú Kě Xī》 and similar works.
When rhymes are narrow,
skill is revealed through difficulty,
the more perilous, the more ingenious,
such as in 《Bìng Zhōng Zèng Zhāng Shíbā》 and similar works.
It's like a skilled driver:
on wide roads and broad paths,
he drives freely and unrestrained,
going wherever he pleases.
Yet even at winding streams and ant hills,
his pace is appropriate,
without stumbling or falling.
Méi Shèngyú said:
"Méng Shǐ said that Tuìzhī's character was stubborn;
if broad rhymes were sufficient for him,
he would still often stray into adjacent ones.
Narrow rhymes are hard to use alone,
yet he would not stray,
isn't this because of his obstinate nature?"
dàyù Hòupǔ Tāng
There are still omissions in the 《Shīhuà》.
Although Ōuyáng Wénzhōng Gōng's literary fame is unattainable,
his record of events is one of them,
so I dare to continue it.
The Wéndé Diàn was
the place for daily court audiences.
After the prime ministers finished presenting their matters,
they would come to line up,
often until the sun was high.
The court guards liked to offer Hòupǔ Tāng to the court officials.
Someone jokingly wrote a poem:
"The paulownia shadows beneath the courtyard are worn out from standing,
all the Hòupǔ Tāng on the streets has been consumed."
Huìchóng's poem
Huìchóng's poem has "The sword is still, the dragon returns to its scabbard;
the flag is idle, the tiger circles the pole."
What he was especially proud of was,
"The river divides, the ridge's force is broken;
spring enters, the burn marks are green."
Someone said he committed plagiarism,
and he replied:
"'The river divides, the ridge's force' is Sīkōng Shǔ;
'spring enters, the burn marks' is Liú Chángqīng.
It's not that my senior brother often plagiarizes the ancients,
but that the ancients' poetry lines plagiarized my senior brother."
Pān Làng once teased him, saying:
"You should be worried about prison matters;
I dreamed you bowed to me,
surely you're not returning to secular life?"
Chóng replied:
"Huìchóng bowing,
means the monk has fallen;
Scholar, aren't you going to the island of monks?"
Lǜ Tīng Jūn Shēng Shī
Téng Yuánfā just before the imperial examination wrote 《Lǜ Tīng Jūn Shēng Shī》:
"Outside the cessation of arms in myriad nations,
amidst the triumphal songs of all living beings."
Bào Gūyàn
Bào often served as judicial assistant in Hénán Fǔ.
He once offended the prefect Xuē Yìng,
and offered the poem 《Gū Yàn》:
"The weather is cold, rice and grain are scarce;
for a thousand miles, the lone one is hard to advance.
I don't mind filling your kitchen,
to bring a message from the border."
Xuē greatly admired it,
and he was then called "Bào Gūyàn."
Wèi Yě's poem
Wèi Yě was not well-known when he was young.
His poem 《Tí Hú Shàng Sì》 says:
"Several sounds of oars leaving the shore,
a few points of mountains from another prefecture."
A scholar saw it and was greatly surprised,
and presented him with a poem:
"No wonder his name is 'Wild' (Yě),
for his nature is always uncommon.
Borrowing a cap to visit me,
I turn over my shoes to welcome you."
From then on, people began to value him.
He has a poem 《Zèng Xiān Gōng》 that says:
"Though literature is ancient like appearance,
the Dao is not poor like the family."
Cùjú poem
Dīng Jìnggōng was fond of cùjú in his youth,
and wrote a poem:
"Eagles and falcons soar with double eyes,
dragons and snakes coil around four limbs.
Stepping on it for several steps,
standing on tiptoe for a long time afterward."
Chén Wénhuì's poem
Chén Wénhuì Gōng's poem says:
"Flat waves vast, mist hazy,
wild rice just ripe, willows yellow.
