Moored boat tied to the bank, unable to bear leaving,
autumn wind, slanting sun, fragrant perch."
It also says:
"Rain-netted spider silk broken,
wind-blown branches shake birds' dreams."
Zhāngxiàn Tàihòu's elegy
When Zhāngxiàn Tàihòu ascended to heaven,
Shí Mànqīng presented an elegy that said:
"The Zhen trigram emerges, the Kun trigram transforms,
Qian completes, the Great Ultimate is empty."
Shí Mànqīng's couplet
Lǐ Chángjí's song says:
"If Heaven has feelings, Heaven too will age,"
Shí Mànqīng's couplet:
"If the Moon has no resentment, the Moon will always be round."
Liú Gài's poem
Liú Gài had integrity,
and wrote a poem:
"In past years I was a guest in Xiāoxiāng,
haggard, I returned from Dōngqín but could not settle.
Sometimes I see beautiful streams and mountains from the west window,
how can I still remember Chǔ Qīng?
Reading books misled me for forty years,
sometimes I myself pat the railing."
Hán Wèigōng's poem
In the early Xīníng period,
Wèigōng retired from prime ministership,
guarding the northern gate.
Many new appointees insulted him.
He wrote a poem:
"Flowers gone from the morning thicket, bees and butterflies in disarray;
rain evenly falls on the spring garden, the well-sweep idle."
It was praised for its subtle grace.
Eunuch Wáng Shēn's palace poem
In the early Yuánfēng period,
the eunuch Wáng Shēn,
emulating Wáng Jiàn's palace poems,
wrote:
"The Grand Empress Dowager's birthday, solemn and honored,
offering longevity in the palace before the fifth watch.
The Son of Heaven holds the cup and bows again,
attending the Benevolent Empress Dowager until dawn."
Enjoying flowers and fishing
In the spring months of the Yuán Dynasty,
the two chancellories, two secretariats, and three academies were often summoned to the imperial garden to enjoy flowers and fish.
Since Zhào Yuánhào's rebellion,
and the war on the western frontier,
this practice had been suspended for a long time.
In the late Jiāyòu period,
the old custom was restored, and officials harmonized with imperial poems.
Hán Wèigōng's poem says:
"Light clouds hold rain to greet the imperial procession,
the chill retains spring within the longevity cup.
Twenty years ago, I attended such a banquet,
today, as a high official, I am happy to join again."
The eunuch Rèn Shǒuzhōng said:
"Hán Qí's poem satirizes Your Majesty."
Rénzōng was startled,
and Shǒuzhōng said:
"It satirizes Your Majesty for feasting too frequently."
Medicinal name poem
Chén Yà Lángzhōng composed a hundred poems using medicinal names.
His 《Shàng Yuán Yè》 says:
"Just look at the ox's neck in front of the cart,
of ten families, five have lost their hides."
Suōyī Qīxī, two poems
Yáng Pǔ 善 for poetry,
not an official.
Tài Zōng summoned him for an audience,
and he recited a poem on 'Straw Raincoat' on the spot, saying:
"Madly shed after a spring drunken spell at a wine shop,
randomly piled at a fisherman's hut when the evening clears."
His poem 'Qī Xī' said:
"Year after year, talent is begged and given to people,
not realizing that people already have too much talent."
Poem about the Beacon Mound
Liú Zǐyí and Xià Yīng Gōng were both in the Hànlín Academy.
Yīng Gōng became the Vice Commissioner of Military Affairs,
feeling quite displeased,
he composed the 'Poem about the Beacon Mound', saying:
"Emptyly displaying a sturdy appearance facing the official road,
many people take the shortcut."
Poem for the Yǐn Yīng Lecture on Arts
The *jìnshì* Dīng Yǎn, in his examination for the 'Yǐn Yīng Yán Jiǎng Yì Shī', wrote:
"The former glory of the White Tiger is obscured,
the old affairs of Jīn Huá are made light of.
It is not that there is no awakening without intention,
but that the intention is for the common people."
Zhèng Gōngbù's Poem
Zhèng Gōngbù's poem contains the lines: "The floral light of Dù Qū is thick like wine,
the spring scenery of Bà Líng is older than man,"
which are truly rare lines.
Teased to Death
When Méi Shèngyú passed away,
Sòng Zǐcái chose a day and said:
"Recently, I saw Shèngyú's face was particularly lustrous,
I thought it indicated robust health,
but did not know it was an ill omen."
At that time, Hán Qīnshèng Zōngyàn's face was also lustrous,
and Shěn Wéntōng pointed and said:
"Next it will be Qīnshèng."
Everyone blamed him for his blunt rudeness.
Not many days later,
Qīnshèng indeed died.
I said to Wéntōng:
"Although you did not curse him,
it was also teasing him to death."
Poems by Yán and Dù
Méi Shèngyú loved Yán Wéi's poem:
"The spring water in the willow pond flows slowly,
the evening sun in the flower dell lingers."
Good it is, yes,
but comparing it closely,
if the evening sun lingers, the flowers are abundant;
but if the spring water flows slowly, it is not abundant.
Like Old Dù's "Deep mountains hasten short days,
tall trees are prone to high winds."
This has no flaws.
Wáng Yuánzhī's Memorial
Wáng Yuánzhī's poem 'Exiled to Huáng Zhōu' says:
"Again for a governor I go to Huáng Zhōu,
still a court official, white hairs sprout."
His memorial to the throne said:
"All counties have bountiful harvests,
there is truly no public business.
My family is well-fed and warm,
all thanks to Your Majesty's grace."
Yuánzhī was at court and could not get along with the Grand Councilor.
He wrote 'Poem on the River Porpoise' to satirize its stoutness, saying:
"It consumes fish and shrimp, quite plump and fat."
And also:
"The river clouds are vast, rain is coming,
heaven's intent for rain has nothing to do with you."
It is a common saying:
"When the river porpoise appears,
it can bring wind and rain."
A Dullard
Poetry prioritizes meaning,
with literary expression secondary.
If the meaning is profound and elevated,
even if the literary expression is plain and simple,
it is naturally a remarkable work.
Lú Tóng's poem has the line:
"A dullard,"
if not for the meaning of the entire piece,
one would naturally cover one's mouth in shock.
Pān Làng's Poem
Pān Làng's poem 'Returning to Qián Táng' says:
"A long-term sojourner sees white hairs,
a lone skiff returns to Tóng Lú.
The new moon has no bright illumination,
the setting sun has residual glow.
The wind and water at Yú Pǔ are swift,
the smoke and fires on Lóng Shān are faint.
From time to time, geese are heard on the sand,
one by one flying away from people."
This poem is no less than Liú Chángqīng's.
Over Forty Years Old, a Stalwart
Wáng Yìróu Shèngzhī,
young and stubborn,
would not humble himself.
Zhāng Yàn Shúwén was older,
and always took the seat of honor whenever they gathered.
It was traditionally said that Wáng Zhìxìng, the military governor of Xú Zhōu, wrote the poem:
"Over forty years old, a stalwart."
Shèngzhī secretly inscribed this line on the screen behind Shúwén's seat.
My Clan is Renowned Throughout the Realm
Lǐ Xún Gōngsù once composed a poem for a kinsman, saying:
"My clan is renowned throughout the realm."
Wáng Shèngzhī commented:
"One residing in Gān Quán is renowned for singing,
one selling medicine is renowned for his wooden ox,
one playing *wéiqí* is renowned for his bluntness,
one making headwear is renowned for his obstinacy,
one writing poetry is renowned for his broad-mindedness."
These several people were all famous residents of the capital.
A courtesan named Lǐ lived in Gān Quán,
skilled in singing.
Lǐ Mùniú sold medicine.
Lǐ Hānzi played *wéiqí*,
a national master without peer,
yet his mind was muddled.
Huáng Jué's Poem Gifted to Méi Chāngyán
Méi Chāngyán was sent out to govern Bìng Zhōu,
Huáng Jué presented him with a poem, saying:
"Departing temporarily to open the banner of *píhǔ* (fierce warriors),
returning, you must occupy the Phoenix Pool (a high official position).
There is not a single white hair on your temples,
to govern the common people is truly not late."
Encountering Lǚ Dòngbīn
Huáng Jué saw a Daoist priest at a traveler's inn,
they drank together.
The Daoist raised his cup, dipped it in water, and wrote the character "Lǚ".
Jué then realized he was Dòngbīn.
He took out seven large coins and three small coins from his bosom,
and said:
"The number cannot be increased."
He gave him a piece of medicine several inches long,
saying, "Grind and take this with wine on New Year's Day,
and you will be free from illness for one year."
Jué followed his instructions,
and when he reached over seventy years old,
the medicine was also nearly used up.
He wrote a poem saying:
"The calendar by the bed has few days left,
counting on fingers, next year will be seventy-three."
He indeed died that year.
The Officials of the Academies Have Torn Me to This State
People do not understand Lǐ Shāngyǐn's poem 'Jǐn Sè';
some say it refers to the name of a maidservant in Lìnghú Chǔ's household.
Yáng Dànián, Qián Wénxī, Yàn Wénxiàn, and Liú Zǐyí all took Yìshān as their poetic master,
and their style was called "Xī Kūn Tǐ".
Later scholars often plagiarized Yìshān's poetic lines.
At an imperial banquet,
an actor played Yìshān,
his clothes ragged and worn,
and he told people:
"[Alas!] I have been torn to this state by the officials of the academies."
Zǐyí painted a portrait of Yìshān,
and wrote his poems to its left and right,
revering him to this extent.
Following Rhyme, Using Rhyme, Adhering to Rhyme
In the Táng Dynasty, when poets composed accompanying poems,
there were *cìyùn*, *yòngyùn*, and *yīyùn*.
The latter, *yīyùn*,
simply means being in the same rhyme group.
*Yòngyùn* means using the other's rhyme,
but not necessarily in the same order.
Hán Lìbù's accompanying poem to Huángfǔ's 'Lùhún Shān Huǒ' is an example.
Many people nowadays do not understand this.
Liú Chángqīng's 'Yúgān Lǚshè':
"Withered and fallen, the evening sky is vast,
red maples, frosty leaves are sparse.
The lonely city gate closes towards the water,
a lone bird flies away from people.
At the ferry crossing, the moon just rises,
from the Yè family, fishermen return.
My heart yearns for home, about to break,
where are people pounding winter clothes?"
Zhāng Jiè's 'Sù Jiāng Shàng':
"At the Chǔ station, south of the ferry crossing,
late at night, few travelers come.
The bright moon reveals the rising tide,
the calm river feels the gulls flying.
The traveler's inn is now far,
this journey is yet to end.
Long away from home, without news,
again hear the pounding of winter clothes."
The two poems resemble *cìyùn*,
both are remarkable works.
Tang Poets Measuring Their Strength to Become Renowned Masters
The *Guǎnzi* says:
"Do not attempt too many tasks,
nor aim to begin and end everything."
This means scholars value achieving success.
Tang people, when composing poetry,
all measured their own strength,
pondering deeply for decades,
and each became a renowned master.
Today's people have achieved little,
yet look down upon their predecessors.
Dù Shī says:
"One realizes even more how the skilled craftsman's heart suffers uniquely."
How could this apply only to painters?
Ruì Yè
Wáng Lún's daughter from Háilíng,
was possessed by a ghost,
and claimed to be an immortal.
She produced dozens of styles of calligraphy,
their names, forms, and styles never repeating.
Among those used by the immortals,
there was a poem about snow that said:
"Why does Cháng'é mock those who are not present?
Auspicious leaves scatter and fall into the human world."
It was said there is an auspicious tree in heaven,
whose flowers have six petals.
She called Wáng Lún "Qīngfēi Rúzi" (a pure non-Confucian),
who did not understand its meaning,
and presented a poem saying:
"You are the autumn paulownia,
I am the spring breeze.
The spring breeze can change the autumn paulownia,
but the autumn paulownia does not recognize the spring breeze's face."
A poem *Tí Jīnshān* said:
"Wind-driven waves churn like snow,
rocks at the mountain's foot coil like dragons."
Xīshān Poems
At Xīshān in Hóngzhōu,
many visitors left poems.
A monk reported to the prefect, saying:
"The poems are all bad;
why not remove them?"
The prefect, startled, asked:
"Are the monk's poems any good?"
The monk then recited:
"Hóngzhōu's Tàibái Fang,
its layered greenness borders the sky.
For ten thousand ages it blocks the new moon,
half the river loses the setting sun."
Fúzhōu Monk Poets
The mountain poems of Fúzhōu contain many excellent lines,
such as: "Clouds withdraw a thousand peaks' rain,
the tide expands half the river's sky."
"Poetry becomes obscure when guests are tested with unusual themes,
chess players make low moves when giving handicaps."
When Old Age Desires to Rely on Monks, in Urgency One Embraces the Buddha
Prime Minister Wáng was fond of jests.
He once said:
"In old age, I wish to rely on monks."
Someone replied:
"When urgent, one embraces the Buddha's feet."
The Prime Minister said:
"'When old age desires to rely on monks,'
is an ancient poem."
The guest replied:
"'When urgent, one embraces the Buddha's feet,'
is also a common saying, a complete phrase.
Moreover, taking 'head' (頭) from above,
and 'feet' (腳) from below,
isn't that a precise couplet?"
Yáng È's Poems
Yáng È from Shǔ's poem *Shòulí Xuānshì* says:
"I wish to stand before the enlightened emperor,
and ask the people of Luòyáng."
His poem *Tí Líshān* says:
"Travelers ask about the palaces,
plowmen find pearls and jades."
Huāruǐ Fūrén's Poems
During the reign of Mèng Shǔ,
Huāruǐ Fūrén's poems were mostly similar to Wáng Jiàn's palace lyrics.
One says:
"The kitchen boat brings food to taste new dishes,
all those seated are attendant officials.
At noon, the palace proclaims a request for finely sliced fish,
from beyond the flowers, fishermen are urged to come."
Another says:
"At the beginning of the month, money for buying flowers is distributed,
the palace is filled with thousands of maids.
When called by name, many do not answer,
blushingly they rush past the imperial bed."
How Can a Wild Hawk Have Corvée Labor?
Many scholars of the classics in Shāndōng did not understand literature.
Once, two classicists serving as officials in the same county,
suddenly cited Zhèng Gǔ's poem:
"Even in the deepest parts of the mountains,
there should be no way to avoid the king's corvée."
One of them sighed and said:
"This poem is mistaken.
How can a wild hawk ever have corvée labor for the king?"
The other explained:
"How could the ancients err in what they composed?
This year, they must have been conscripting feathers."
Chìsōng's Poem to Zhāng Liáng
Yáng Ānguó, a Hanlin Academician,
wished to seek an external official post due to old age.
He told people:
"The poem Chìsōngzi gave to Zhāng Liáng says:
'It is better to return early to the mountains in leisure,
to avoid serving the ruler to no avail.'
I am just like that."
Five Regional Pronunciations
Sīmǎ Jūnshí discussed the names of the nine flags;
旗 (qí) and 旂 (qí) are similar.
How are they distinguished by pronunciation?
In *Xiǎoyá*:
"The courtyard torch faces the dawn,
one speaks of observing its 旂."
In *Zuǒzhuàn*:
"Dragons and tigers crouch in the constellation Chén,
taking the name's 旂."
However, 旂 as in 'wèi qí' (尉旂) should be pronounced like 'qín' (芹).
People from Guānzhōng, when saying 清 (qīng) as in 'clear,'
do not change the character 晴 (qíng).
But for 青 (qīng) as in 'dān qīng' (丹青, vermilion and cyan),
it is pronounced like 'qī' (萋).
Also, they pronounce 中 (zhōng) as 'zhēng' (烝),
and 虫 (chóng) as 'chén' (塵).
They do not know that 旂 was originally pronounced 'qín' (芹),
and due to regional accents, it changed,
just like 青 (qīng) being pronounced as 'qī' (萋).
If regional pronunciations are this varied,
people from Mǐn pronounce 高 (gāo) as 'gē' (歌),
people from Jīngchǔ pronounce 南 (nán) as 'nán' (難),
and 荊 (jīng) as 'jīn' (斤).
Even literati composing songs and poems
often do not realize this.
Medicinal Name Poems
Chén Yà's medicinal name poem *Yǒng Báifà* says:
"If a Daoist's head turns white early,
Lǎojūn should have had black hair back then."
"Chess pieces, in cold weather, are exhaled upon before moving,
clothes, because of spring thinness, are cut from shrunk gauze."
Chéngwù Láng Opposes Yíngshuāng Tù
Shí Shàochuán Zhōnglì
received a visiting card from 'Chéngwù Láng' (承務狼).
Shí, delighted, said:
"I have sought this couplet for thirty years,
and now I have it.
'Yíngshuāng Tù' (迎霜兔, frost-welcoming rabbit) can be paired with 'Chéngwù Láng' (承務狼, wolf of official duty)."
Upon seeing this, Shàngguān Bì advised Shí to be careful with his words.
Shí angrily said:
"You are Shàngguān Bì (上官佖),
what can you do about my 'lower official' (下官) mouth?"
The Title 'Xiàguān'
Before the Jìn and Wèi dynasties,
those with states all referred to their officials and common people as subjects.
Sòng Xiàowǔ disliked the strength of the feudal lords,
and gradually diminished and deprived them of their privileges,
ordering them to use the title "xiàguān" (下官, lower official).
Even the title 'xiàguān'
was not to be taken lightly.
Nowadays, people use it as a general term.
Character Radicals and Prefectural Governors
There was a person who took the Jìnshì exam and was selected as the top candidate.
His associates, intending to insult him,
when that person was acting as the prefectural governor,
took character radicals as their guide,
saying:
"Jīn (金) yín (銀) chāi (釵) chuàn (釧) pù (鋪)." (gold, silver, hairpin, bracelet, shop)
The next person said:
"Sī (絲) mián (綿) chóu (紬) juàn (絹) wǎng (網)." (silk, cotton, pongee, silk, net)
The associates said:
"Guǐ (鬼) mèi (魅) wǎng (魍) liǎng (魎) kuí (魁)." (ghost, demon, goblin, monster, chief)
There is a folk riddle that says:
"Hit fast, it rounds fast;
hit slow, it rounds slow.
Divided into four sections,
sent to the kiln before night."
Initially, it seems to describe pottery,
but it actually refers to the prefectural governor (令).
Hù Láng
Nowadays, some people call a mǎnyú (駔𩦱, horse-dealer) a yá (牙).
Originally, they were called hùláng (互郎),
as they managed hùshì (互市, mutual markets).
Táng (唐) people wrote hù (互) as yá (牙),
because hù (互) resembles yá (牙),
and thus it was transformed into yá (牙).
Today, people write wàn (萬) as wàn (万),
and qiān (千) as piě (撇).
However, since numbers can be referenced,
the original characters can be preserved.
Otherwise, it would also be like hù (互) and yá (牙).
Yìlǎotíng (佚老亭)
Chén Wénhuì Gōng (陳文惠公) retired from his position as Prime Minister,
at nearly eighty years old.
He wrote a poem saying:
“My youthful days were spent wandering many paths;
In my white-haired years, I gained the most time.”
He named his pavilion “Yìlǎotíng (佚老亭)”.
Thereafter, when scholar-officials retired,
they often named their pavilions “Yìlǎo (佚老)”.
Wénhuì (文惠) was skilled in cursive script,
and described himself saying:
“No one before me,
no one after me.”
Mòjuébīng (末厥兵)
Ōu Gōng (歐公) recorded Táo Shàngshū’s (陶尚書) poem, saying:
“Pointy-hatted, base commoners,
Short-booted mòjuébīng (末厥兵).”
He did not understand its meaning.
I say that nowadays, we call a dog with a docked tail juéwěi (厥尾),
and clothing that is short in the back
is also called jué (厥).
This soldier just refers to their low and humble status.
However, people today do not connect mòjué (末厥) together,
otherwise it could also be a suitable match for the phrase bēifán (卑凡).
Hélóu (何樓)
People in the world refer to those who are false as Hélóu (何樓).
In the early days of the dynasty, there was a Hélóu (何樓) in the capital,
where all the goods sold below it were shoddy.
Thus, people used this to describe them.
Although the building has now been demolished,
the saying is still passed down.
Húsēngshī (胡僧詩)
Yú Jìng Shàngshū (余靖尚書) was an envoy to Qìdān (契丹),
and could speak the Hú (胡) language.
He had the captives compose a poem saying:
“Yèyán mòluó (夜筵沒羅)
means a grand feast.
Chén bài xǐ (臣拜洗)
means receiving a bestowal.
Liǎng cháo juéhé (兩朝厥荷)
means good relations.
Qíng gànqín (情幹勤)
means deep and profound.
Wēichén yǎcéng (微臣雅曾)
means to bow and dance.
Zhù ruòtǒng (祝若統)
means blessings and protection.
Shèngshòu tiěbǎi (聖壽鐵擺)
means as high as Sōng Gāo (嵩高).
Jù fúfè (俱弗忒).”
Meaning boundless.
The captive ruler laughed.
Xīdūshī (西都詩)
Sòng Cìdào (宋次道) once wrote the “Xīdūshī (西都詩)”,
where he paired “Yěhúluò (野狐落)” with “Wǔfènglóu (五鳳樓)”.
He said Yěhúluò (野狐落)
was the name of a Táng (唐) palace,
where palace women gathered.
Míng sì xìngshī (名似姓詩)
During Tàizōng’s (太宗) reign,
there were several jìnshì (進士) who had names similar to surnames.
Someone composed a poem about them:
“Guō Zhèng (郭鄭), Zhèng Dōng (鄭東), Dōng Yějìang (東野絳),
Mǎ Zhāng (馬張), Zhāng Xià (張夏), Xiàhóu Lín (夏侯璘).”
In the early Xīníng (熙寧) period,
there were scholars named Cuī Dù (崔度), Cuī Gōngdù (崔公度),
Wáng Sháo (王韶), and Wáng Zǐsháo (王子韶),
all of whom were truly enfeoffed.
There were also Zhāng Jūnchén (張君陳) and
Chén Jūnzhāng (陳君張).
The Táng (唐) person Dōngfāng Qiú (東方虯)
wanted to pair with Xīguān Bào (西關豹),
and there must have been someone who liked to compose couplets for him.
Shuō Huáng Cháo shì (說黃巢事)
A Daoist spoke of Huáng Cháo’s (黃巢) affairs,
and then said:
“Huáng Dà’s (黃大) later years came to this.”
Zhāng Āndào (張安道) said:
“Huáng Cháo (黃巢) had six brothers,
and Cháo (巢) was the youngest. ”
He also said:
“Huáng Liù (黃六) could still deceive people;
his deceptions were so numerous and varied.”
Shā jì shè zhū (殺祭社豬)
Zhāng Duān (張端) was the Sīlù (司錄) of Hénán (河南).
When the prefecture was to offer sacrifices to the earth god,
a pig was purchased and already presented to the Yǐn (尹).
The pig suddenly ran into Zhāng Duān’s (張端) house.
Duān (端) immediately killed it.
He reported this to the Yǐn (尹),
who summoned him and asked.
Duān (端) replied:
“According to the law, if a pig
enters a private house at night without cause,
the owner may kill it on the spot without penalty.”
The Yǐn (尹) laughed greatly
and had another pig bought.
Jiǔ rú Mǐng (酒如澠) zài běi yuē Dí (在北曰狄) Liú Xiànghàng (劉相沆) was an envoy to Qìdān (契丹).
A guest once said:
“Wine like Mǐng (澠) River,
restrains travelers but does not stop.”
No one could provide a couplet.
Liú (劉) immediately responded:
“In the north, it is called Dí (狄),
what harm is there in playing ‘Chūsài’ (出塞)?”
When Tàizǔ (太祖) ascended the throne,
street vendors used scented seals to mark characters that were too close to the emperor’s name.
They dared not speak it out,
but struck iron plates to silently convey it,
and this tradition has remained unchanged.
Ěr jì shū (耳寄書) Lù Jī (陸機) used Huáng’ěr (黃耳) to deliver a letter,
from Luò (洛) to Wú (吳),
crossing the Jiāng (江), Huái (淮), and Dàhé (大河) rivers, able to swim across water.
If this dog had supernatural powers,
it would be beyond words.
Some say:
The Lù (陸) family had a slave named Huáng’ěr (黃耳).
Those who did not know saw a dog named “Huáng’ěr (黃耳)”,
and thus assumed it was the dog.
Mèng Dōngyě shī (孟東野詩)
Lǐ Xízhī (李習之) praised Mèng Dōngyě’s (孟東野) poem: “Eating pickled vegetables, my intestines ache;
Forced to sing, my voice finds no joy.
Stepping out, there are immediate obstacles;
Who says heaven and earth are vast?”
This can be called truly understanding his music.
Today, five volumes of the “Jiāo Jí (郊集)” are circulated,
and there is also the “Jiǎn Yě Jí (減也集)”.
Its language is often cold and obscure,
leading to suspicion that the former five volumes were abridged and selected by famous scholars.
Dōngyě (東野) and Tuìzhī (退之) composed joint verses,
and if it was magnificent and skillful,
Tuìzhī (退之) might have refined it.
Volume 56
End.
Xīchí chànghè (西池唱和)
During Yuányòu (元祐),
the Mìgé (祕閣) gathered at Xīchí (西池) on the third day of the third lunar month.
Wáng Zhòngzhì (王仲至) wrote a poem,
and Zhāng Wénqián (張文潛)’s harmony was the most skillful,
saying:
“Gathered waves make a sound, yellow silk stirs;
Rolling wind has no strength, colorful banners droop.”
Qín Shàoyóu (秦少游) said:
“Curtains in a thousand homes, brocade hanging low.”
Zhòngzhì (仲至) laughed and said:
“Again, he wants to enter the xiǎoyòu (小右) tune.”
However, Shàoyóu (少游) had: “Yǐ fán Yìshǎo (逸少) shū chénjī (書陳跡),
Gēng shǔ Xiāngrú (相如) fù ‘Shànglín’ (上林).”
Which others found hard to match.
Shī bèi sìjǐng (詩備四景)
“Holding cold plum blossoms, shaking the snow petals;
Gracefully, gradually, green shade appears.
Through the window, last night, the rustling rain;
Already, there is the sound of autumn wind and falling leaves.”
Ōu Gōng (歐公) said:
“This poem contains scenes of all four seasons.”
Gù Tú (顧屠)
During Yuányòu (元祐),
Gù Zǐdūn (顧子敦) had the nickname Gù Tú (顧屠),
because of his stoutness.
Qián Mùfù (錢穆父) had nine sons.
Dōngpō (東坡) considered him Jiǔzǐmǔ (九子母) (mother of nine sons).
Later, he wrote a poem saying:
“The Nine Provinces envy your grand household,”
This was why.
And in “Sòng Zǐdūn (送子敦)”, he said:
“My friend Gù Zǐdūn (顧子敦),
both his body and courage are hard to surpass.”
He also said:
“Rubbing hands towards pigs and sheep,”
And also said:
“Lifelong hand that drafted imperial edicts,”
All these are butcher’s language.
Zǐdūn (子敦) was displeased.
Pō (坡) then replied:
“Take good care of your precious body,
my previous words were just a jest.”
The Lord of Chángbái Shān,
Ōuyáng Zhòngchún, dreamt of a Daoist who held a patent of appointment and said:
“The Supreme Emperor has appointed you the Lord of Chángbái Shān.”
After he died,
Dōngpō wept for him and said:
“Dead, he became the Lord of Chángbái;
His name is inscribed in the vermilion palace.”
Broom for Sweeping Away Sorrow, Ice for Sobering Up
Dōngpō considered the spring scenery of Dòngtíng a “broom for sweeping away sorrow.”
Shāngǔ considered crystal-clear minced fish a “sūxǐng jiǔbīng” (ice for sobering up).
A Little Spring Charm Is Enough to Stir the Heart
Jīnggōng served as Grand Councillor.
In the Hanlin Academy, there was a pomegranate bush,
Its branches and leaves were very luxuriant,
But it bore only one flower.
His poem said:
“Ten thousand branches with lush leaves, a single red spot;
A little spring charm is enough to stir the heart.”
Cháo Wújiù's Poetry and Prose
During the Yuánfēng era,
Cháo Wújiù's poetry and prose gained fame.
Chén Wúsì playfully wrote a poem saying:
“I hear your new writings are well-fashioned,
Like red pomegranates of Xiāngzhōu and flowers of Èzhōu.”
Chén Wúsì's Poetic Memorial
Chén Wúsì's essay "On Being Appointed" said:
“Leaning on old age, I hasten to the solemn imperial edict,
Walking slowly, I reach the propitious time.
How many words can truly be corrected?
How dare I resent the delay of ten years?
How could I assent to the error of the golden chariot?
How could I refuse the mockery of the wet nurse?
My former worries and fears are cut off,
The promise of Lùmén is not yet fulfilled.”
Someone said:
“Having only just obtained a 'zhèngzì' (corrector),
There's no need to speak of 'hastening to the solemn imperial edict.'”
Wúsì then wrote a memorial of thanks, saying:
“Though the name is an 'election for literary posts,'
It is actually a 'reserve for prime ministers and generals.'”
He also said:
“With a bald head and gaps in my teeth,
How dare I refuse the mockery of the wet nurse?
Fighting for shallow views and being lightly esteemed,
I increasingly fear the error of the golden chariot.”
Shāngǔ on Poetry
Shāngǔ said that one should not force poetry and prose by digging into the void,
But rather let them arise from the situation,
Then they will naturally be skillful.
Before composing each piece, first establish the main idea.
Long pieces require twists and turns, with meaning conveyed thrice, before a chapter is formed.
Soft Red Fragrant Dust
An elder once said that the wind and moon of Xīhú are not as good as the soft red fragrant dust of Dōnghuá.
Thus Dōngpō's poem said:
“Half-white, not ashamed of the hair hanging by my collar,
Still I cling to the soft red dust of the trailing carriage.”
Calligraphy and Poetic Style
Dōngpō said:
“Among calligraphers, none is finer than Yán Lǔgōng,
Yet the decline of calligraphy began with Lǔgōng.
Among poets, none is finer than Hán Tuìzhī,
Yet the change in poetic style began with Tuìzhī.”
The Magpie-robin Sings
Shāngǔ said:
“Reading the 'Monthly Ordinances' in the 《Zhōushū》:
'When the magpie-robin sings,
Slanderous people are at the side of the ruler.'
Then I understood old Dù's poem 'The Oriole' with the lines: 'If it chirps out of season,
There are slanderers at the ruler’s side.'”
Táo Yuānmíng's Poetry
Shāngǔ said:
“It is better for the rhythm to be disharmonious
Than for the lines to be weak.
It is better for the choice of words to be unskillful
Than for the language to be obscure.
This is Yu Kāifǔ's strength.
However, he had an intention to compose poetry.
As for Táo Yuānmíng,
He is what is called 'naturally fitting without need for rope or chisel.'”
Ghosts Speak Like Humans, Humans Speak Like Ghosts
“Bright moon, clear breeze,
A good night's gathering.
Stars and rivers shift,
Joy does not last forever.”
This is a ghost poem.
Shāngǔ said:
“This must have been composed by the Cáo Zǐjiàn of ghosts.”
He also said:
“In the palace of Hándān,
Metal, stone, silk, and bamboo pipes.”
These two lines are not only rarely composed by humans,
But also extremely difficult for those who know them to achieve.
Zhāng Wénqián said:
“In the old days, ghosts spoke like humans;
Now, humans speak like ghosts.”
Ordinary Folk
Chén Fǔ of Dānyáng,
Each year during the Qīngmíng Festival, when visiting graves,
Would go to the residence of Master Húyīn in Jiángshān,
And inscribed a poem there, saying:
“The pine pollen on North Mountain drifts and flowers on its own,
Below the capital, the wind is light, the wheat stalks lean.
My body is like the swallows of the old Wáng and Xiè families,
Once a year, I come to your home.”
Jīnggōng saw the poem and laughed, saying:
“I am teasing you for being ordinary folk.”
Poem Presented to Wáng Zhèngzhòng
Someone presented a long poem to Wáng Zhèngzhòng,
One couplet of which was:
“The dog-keeper transmits new rhapsodies,
The Rooster Forest discusses recent poems.”
Qín Shàoyóu's Poetic Omen
Qín Shàoyóu, after a textual revision appointment, was made Vice-Prefect of Hángzhōu.
In Chǔ, during a drinking session,
He wrote a poem saying:
“All my life I have owed sleep in monks' cells,
I fully intend to repay it everywhere now.”
The next month,
He was demoted to supervise the salt monopoly in Chǔzhōu.
Those who liked such things considered it a poetic omen.
Ultimate Treasure Elixir
Wáng Yǔyù's poems,
Were called “Ultimate Treasure Elixir,”
Because they frequently used precious items,
For example, gold would always be paired with white jade.
Someone forcibly composed rich and noble lines, saying:
“His leg veins turned into red tortoiseshell,
His eyes transformed into green lapis lazuli.”
Yàn Shūyuán's short lyric poem said:
“Dancing low, the moon over the willow tower heart;
Singing to the end, the wind beneath the peach blossom fan.”
Cháo Wúchù said:
“One who can compose such lines
Surely knows not to live in a three-family village.”
Túmí Poem
Hán Cūn Guó's poem on túmí flowers said:
“All my life I have loved this rich fragrance,
Looking up, I often welcome the falling catkins in the wind.
Always fearing spring's departure would leave lingering regret,
Its archetype is originally within the wine cup.”
Shāngǔ particularly loved Jīnggōng's lines: “Ponderously they give off rising heat haze,
Gracefully, a stream of flowers.”
He said it contained multiple meanings.
Wén Zhōuhàn's Poem
Dōngpō, upon seeing Wén Zhōuhàn's poem, said:
“It is not easy to compose such a work;
This poem can be used for two purposes.”
Bamboo Poem
Wáng Jiāo's "Bamboo Poem" said:
“Leaves hang like a thousand swords,
Stems rise like ten thousand spears.”
Dōngpō said:
“Ten bamboo poles,
With only one leaf.”
Rain Fists and Wind Mouths
Wáng Yǔxī had an old acquaintance with Dōngpō,
And once composed a "Poem Congratulating the Rain," saying:
“Rain fists beating the leaves follow the hand and depart,
Wind mouths blowing cool pursue people and arrive.”
Dōngpō said:
“How can Shíliù Láng compose a poem
So out of order?”
Yǔxī said:
“It was composed while drunk.”
Another day, he presented another scroll,
Dōngpō said:
“Are you drunk again?”
Old Dù's Avoided Character
Old Dù avoided the character "xián" (閑) in his family,
Yet in his poems, he says:
“Fluttering playful butterflies leisurely pass slowly.”
He also says:
“I also love the slightly frosted temples,
Retaining joy for a night of leisure.”
One version has "lán" (闌).
The character "xián" (閑) should be considered correct;
When composing, he probably did not avoid it himself.
Guō Gōngfù's Poem
Guō Gōngfù showed his poetry to Dōngpō,
first reciting it himself,
his voice resounding on all sides.
He asked Pō,
"How many points is this poem worth?"
Pō replied,
"It's a ten-point poem."
Xiángzhèng asked in surprised delight,
Pō said,
"Seven points for the reading,
three points for the poem."
Dōngpō also said,
"People like Guō Xiángzhèng only know that something with rhymes is a poem."
Cài Tiānqǐ's Poetry
Cài Tiānqǐ and Qín Shàoyóu's poetry said:
"We wish to be like Jiè and Shí,
to grow old at Hàn Gōng's gate."
Jīnggōng's Poetic Lines
Jīnggōng harmonized a folk song for someone,
one line said:
"Where the setting sun reaches, flowers are especially warm."
He also wrote a flower cake poem on behalf of a child,
regrettably it is not seen.
Lín Bū's Ode to Plum Blossoms
Wáng Jūnqīng said,
"'Sparse shadows slant across the clear shallow water,
Faint fragrance drifts in the moonlit dusk.'
This is Lín Bū's ode to plum blossoms,
but it could also apply to apricots, peaches, and plums."
Pō said,
"If so,
then apricot, peach, and plum blossoms would not dare to claim it."
Sū Zǐyóu's Poem Sent to Dōngpō
When Sū Zǐyóu was on a diplomatic mission to Shuòfāng,
he sent a poem to Dōngpō saying:
"Who brought our family's collected works past Yōudū?
Every time I see the Hú people, they ask about Dà Sū.
Don't let your writings stir up the barbarians,
lest it hinder your chatting and laughing while lounging by the rivers and lakes."
Mèng Jiāo's Poetry
Lǐ Xīshēng said,
"Mèng Jiāo's poetry is just like Cháo Cuò's character;
it's not that it's bad,
what harms it is its severity and straightforwardness."
Shāngǔ said:
"Writing poetry is like staging a play,
at first there's the arrangement,
then at the end there must be a joke,
only then is it an 'exit.'
This was probably said after reading Qín Shàoyóu's poetry,
disliking how his final verses had no conclusion."
Gulls in the Same Wave
Jīnggōng said,
"Regarding things like 'gulls are not startled,'
how should one phrase it well?"
Shāngǔ said,
"Gulls in the same wave."
Jìzhāi's Poetry
Shàoyóu utterly disliked Shāngǔ's poem 'Harmonizing Jìzhāi,' which said:
"Great ambition, yet cautious in small details."
Speaking of the affairs of Càizhōu,
few people understood it.
Courtesy Names All End in Fǔ
In the early Xīníng era,
when Jīnggōng was in power,
many courtesy names at the time ended with "fǔ,"
and many signatures used circles.
A saying at the time went:
"Courtesy names all end in fǔ,
Flowery scripts are all ringed."
Dúlèyuán Poetry
Dōngpō wrote a poem about Wēn Gōng's Dúlèyuán.
The first four lines
already describe it completely.
It said:
"Green mountains above the house,
Flowing water below the house.
Within it, a five-mǔ garden,
Flowers and trees are lush and wild."
This can already be depicted in a painting.
Poetry Values Roundness and Maturity
Xiè Tiǎo said,
"Good poetry is round, beautiful, and flowing like a thrown pellet."
Therefore, Dōngpō said,
"Within it are clear, round lines,
Bronze pellets flying like sling-shots."
Indeed, poetry values roundness and maturity.
However, roundness and maturity often err on the side of plainness and ease,
while ruggedness and stiffness often err on the side of dryness and barrenness.
If one can avoid losing both extremes,
then one can rival ancient authors.
Xiè Shīhòu's Poetry
Shāngǔ said Xiè Shīhòu's poetry greatly resembled Lǎo Dù's,
such as "Wearing clothes inside out to greet outside the door,
Calling all children to bow before the lamp."
If compiled into Lǎo Dù's poetry collection, there would be no shame.
Turtle Pedestal on the Treetop
Dōngpō's poem for Chéng Jūn's Guīzhēntíng said:
"Soon you will see a thousand-character elegy,
with a turtle pedestal visible on the treetop."
A pedestal is a turtle's base,
it should not be seen on a treetop.
Dōngpō's Poem Thanking the Emperor's Calligraphy
Sūn Shēnlǎo laughed at Dōngpō's poem "Thanking the Emperor for Bestowed Calligraphy," saying:
"What sense does it make
to directly mention the victory report from Shǎnxī at the end?"
Satirizing Mǐ Yuánzhāng
Dōngpō's colophon on the books collected by Mǐ Yuánzhāng said:
"Drawing a cake on the ground may not resemble it,
but it makes foolish children drool."
He also said:
"Embroidered pouches and jade scrolls come without feet."
Shāngǔ harmonized, saying:
"The hundred family editions are vaguely similar,
like the moon traveling in the sky seen in all waters."
He also said:
"The clumsy one who steals a hook immediately breaks a foot."
Both refer to Yuánzhāng's obsessive cleanliness and his fondness for snatching other people's paintings.
Olive Poem
Dōngpō's 'Olive Poem' said:
"Numerous green fruits fall onto red salt."
Olive trees are tall and difficult to pick;
if salt is rubbed on the trunk itself,
its fruits will fall naturally.
Southerners boast about dates, saying:
"By the time you taste their aftertaste,
I've already finished the sweetness."
Planting Bamboo in the Imperial Library
Lǐ Gōngzé planted bamboo in the imperial library,
jokingly saying:
"Later generations, pointing at this bamboo, will surely say Lǐ Wénzhèng planted it by hand."
Liú Gòngfù laughed, saying:
"Wénzhèng not only knows how to tie pens,
but also how to plant bamboo?"
At that time, there was a pen craftsman who imitated Wénzhèng,
hence the remark.
Cannon-Cart Clouds
Boatmen observe clouds;
if cannon-cart clouds arise,
they immediately avoid them,
as a great wind will suddenly arrive.
Dōngpō had a line saying:
"Today the river's sky is ominous,
Cannon-cart clouds rise, the wind is about to start."
Zhāng Wénqián had a line saying:
"Gladly facing mountain colors like idle eyebrows,
Sorrowfully facing river clouds rising like cannon-carts."
Ōugōng's Poetry
Ōugōng's poem said:
"White hair hangs at both temples,
Seven gold rings around the waist."
It also said:
"A precious belt with ten thousand studs, seven rings around the waist."
Liú Gòngfù said:
"When did Yǒngshú ever mention this belt of his?"
Drought Poem
Zhāng Wénqián's 'Drought Poem' said:
"Zhào Dùn at the edge of the sky is even more fearsome,
Wǔ Hóu at the bottom of the water is sound asleep."
This poem was considered almost as good as Yáng Xún's Ròujūn.
Dōngpō on Poetry
Dōngpō said:
"Whenever a person creates writing,
they must be able to pull tens of thousands of pounds with their brush tip,
only then can they speak of writing."
Ōugōng said:
"When inspiration strikes, the brush strength is worth a thousand gold."
Sand Poem
Someone presented his name card to Jīnggōng, saying:
"I am the poet Lóng Tàichū."
At that time, an old soldier was cleaning copper vessels with sand.
The Duke said:
"You can write a sand poem."
Tàichū recited immediately:
"Vast and yellow, emerging from the frontier,
Distant and white, spreading over the banks.
Birds pass, the wind calms the seal script,
Tide returns, the sun shines on the stars."
Mocking Wáng Yǔyù's Poetry
After Wáng Yǔyù 王禹玉 passed away,
an anonymous person mocked him, saying:
"Tàigōng 太公 was tormented by his descendants;
after his death, he had no reputation, only money.
He obsequiously submitted to Wáng Jièfǔ 王介甫,
and strangely impressed Sòng Zhāoxuān 宋昭宣.
He once said that a well's mouth is difficult to play with,
and he sat alone in the Zhōngshū 中書 for countless years.
Recently, the Eastern Prefecture has had no land,
so he should receive full compensation, not merely power."
When Wáng Yǔyù's 王禹yù's family members passed by the Yǎmén 衙門,
they pointed out that it was Zhāng Shānrén 張山人 who wrote the poem.
"I have written many seventeen-character poems in my life,
but a poem with such a theme as that, I could not compose."
The fǔyǐn 府尹 smiled and sent them away.
Sū Dōngpō's 蘇東坡's preface to Shāngǔ's 山谷's poetry
Sū Dōngpō's 蘇東坡's preface "Xiè Jīndài Ānmǎ" 《謝金帶鞍馬》 is a "Sòng Qióng Wén" 《送窮文》 in the four-six prose style.
Huáng Shāngǔ's 黃山谷's poem "Límáo Bǐ" 《狸毛筆》 is a "Máo Yǐng Zhuàn" 《毛穎傳》 in verse.
Pān Bīnlǎo's 潘邠老's poems,
often resemble Dù Fǔ's 杜甫's,
and he continued to do so incessantly.
It would be difficult for Dù Fǔ 杜甫 to survive.
If Dù Fǔ 杜甫 were to be reborn,
he would have to squabble with Pān Shí 潘十.
The character sān 毿 in poetry
When Sū Dōngpō 蘇東坡 returned from overseas,
he wrote a poem
using the character sān 毿.
Lǐ Duānshū 李端叔 harmonized it, saying:
"I see my students again, do they recognize me?
My snow-white beard and frosty temples hang down softly (sānsān 毿毿)."
There was a person with keen insight
who could see people's past and future lives.
Suddenly, a wicked youth appeared before him.
That person said:
"There is already a peeling sound on his head,
and his waist is about to become flabby (sānsān 毿毿)."
Chén Wúyǐ 陳無巳 said:
"I wanted to harmonize it, saying:
'Do not let your waist become flabby (sānsān 毿毿) below.'"
Qín Shàoyóu's 秦少游's impromptu poem
When Lǚ Shēngōng 呂申公 was in Yángzhōu 揚州,
during the Mid-Autumn Festival,
he ordered Qín Shàoyóu 秦少游 to compose an impromptu poem.
It contained the lines: "Banners and pennants illuminate the sea in the autumn colors,
drums and trumpets echo to the heavens in the bright moon."
However, that evening turned slightly cloudy.
Shàoyóu 少游 composed another one, saying:
"It is simply that our lord has much benevolence and love,
turning back the autumn colors to create a spring gloom."
Sòng Yù 宋玉 and Qū Yuán 屈原
Ōuyáng Wénzhōng Gōng 歐陽文忠公 called himself "Liùyī Jūshì" 六一居士.
Wáng Jīnggōng 王荊公 called himself "Chǔ Lǎo" 楚老.
Today's poetry critics, when mentioning Liùyī 六一 and Chǔ Lǎo 楚老,
refer to these two great masters.
Liùyī 六一 said:
"Qū Yuán's 屈原's 'Lí Sāo' 《離騷》 makes one's head feel muddled when reading it,
yet if one extracts a line or two and savors it repeatedly,
it is no different from the 'Fēng' 《風》.
Sòng Yù's 宋玉's poetry, compared to Qū Yuán's 屈原's,
sometimes shows signs of being superior."
Clear breeze and bright moon have constant light, fresh as new
Chǔ Lǎo 楚老 said:
"All the good words in the world
have already been spoken by Dù Fǔ 杜甫.
All the common
words in the world
have already been spoken by Bái Lètiān 白樂天."
However, Lǐ Zànhuáng 李贊皇 said:
"It is like the clear breeze and bright moon;
they are always present throughout the four seasons,
yet their light and scenery are always new."
So, it seems there is no lack of them.
Ōu's 歐 poetry is like a jade candle
Chǔ Lǎo 楚老 said:
"Ōu's 歐 poetry is like a jade candle."
Yè Zhìyuǎn 葉致遠 said:
"Could it be that all four seasons are harmonious,
and every part of the scroll is like flowing water?"
The Duke said:
"Zhìyuǎn 致遠 can be said to be a good judge.
It is a pity that Ōuyáng Gōng 歐陽公 did not hear it during his lifetime."
Wáng Jiàn's 王建's Palace Poems
Regarding Wáng Jiàn's 王建's "Gōngcí" 《宮詞》,
Jīnggōng 荊公 particularly loved the lines: "Searching for fading red among the tree-tops and tree-bottoms,
one petal flying west, one flying east.
It is simply that the peach blossoms are eager to bear fruit,
mistakenly making people resent the five-watch wind."
Red fades, fragrance moistens, entering the plum rains season
Wáng Jūnyù Mìxué 王君玉密學 had ten "Wàng Jiāngnán" 《望江南》 poems,
calling himself a banished immortal.
Chǔ Lǎo 楚老 intensely loved his line: "Red fades, fragrance moistens, entering the plum rains season."
The poems of Fēng 馮 and Guān 冠, two dukes
Fēng Chánglè 馮長樂, at seven years old,
recited a "Zhì Pǔ" 《治圃》 poem, saying:
"Flowers already fallen to the ground should be swept away,
but grass not yet touched by frost should not be flattened."
His benevolent nature,
preserving all living beings' lives,
was already evident here.
Guān Láigōng 冠萊公, at eight years old,
recited a "Huá Shī" 《華詩》, saying:
"There is only Heaven above,
no other mountain can be its equal."
His teacher said to Láigōng's 萊公's father:
"How can your esteemed son not become a prime minister!"
Depicting objects and expressing emotions
The poet's skill
lies entirely in depicting objects and expressing emotions.
The emotion's abode is color,
and color's comparison is flower.
For example, the Táng 唐 people's "Mǔdān" 《牡丹》 poem says:
"Red blooms late at Xīzǐ's 西子's makeup tower,
green reveals itself at Má Gū's 麻姑's water palace in spring."
If one changes 'spring' to 'autumn,'
it would completely be a lotus flower line.
Lín Héjìng's 林和靖's "Méihuā" 《梅花》:
"Sparse shadows slant across clear, shallow water,
faint fragrance floats in the dusky moon."
This is similar to a wild rose.
The Sān Hán 三韓 envoy's Jīnshān 金山 poem
During the Xīníng 熙寧 era,
Pú Yǐnliàng 朴寅亮, an envoy from Sān Hán 三韓, composed a "Jīnshān Shī" 《金山詩》.
Its preface formerly stated regarding the previous and subsequent poems:
"People do not see the mountain as gold."
It says:
"Ten thousand layers embrace the peak, the sky leans like a pestle,
a single fishing rod with the setting sun, water floats gold."
Waterfall poem
Xú Níng's 徐凝's "Pùbù" 《瀑布》:
"A single strip breaks the green mountain's color,"
is truly not as good as Fàn Wénzhèng's 范文正's "A white rainbow descends to drink in the ravine,
a long sword stands leaning against the sky."
A monk debated that Xú's 徐 poem did not show the waterfall,
and spontaneously recited:
"The earth's axis cannot fully roll it up,
heaven's loom continuously releases it."
This captures the form but not the force,
how is it different from the Sān Hán 三韓 envoy saying "the gold mountain does not show gold"?
This is the flaw of seeking too much beyond the intention.
Poems composed by imperial order
In the "Jiù Shǐ" 《舊史》, Liǔ Gōngquán's 柳公權's "Yìngzhì Liánjù" 《應制聯句》 states:
"The gentle southern breeze comes,
making the palace halls slightly cool."
However, when fearing the heat in a grand hall,
the arrival of the southern wind would not only bring a slight coolness.
The "Xīn Shǐ" 《新史》 changed it, saying:
"The palace rafters produce lingering coolness."
This is because the curved rafters and clustered purlins
catch the wind powerfully and swiftly.
These two characters contributed to the refinement of the wording.
Profound search reaching the utmost
When people think deeply about classical studies,
they often cannot express their emotions fully.
Only in poetry can one conduct a profound search to reach the utmost,
which is what is meant by "one should seek it by entering the sea."
A Táng 唐 person said:
"The lines are obtained in the middle of the night,
the heart returns from beyond the heavens."
Pénglái Xiān 蓬萊仙
There was a Pénglái Xiān 蓬萊仙,
whose words were extremely emotional.
Táo Yīnjū 陶隱居 said:
"To be a talented ghost
is still better than a dull immortal."
Changing "hèn" to "xìng"
When Xiāo Chǔcái was the magistrate of Lìyáng County,
Zhāng Guāiyá was the prefect.
One day, he was invited to a meal,
and saw on Guāiyá's desk a quatrain that read:
"I only regret that in times of great peace there is nothing to do;
the old Grand Secretary in Huáinán is idly killing time."
Xiāo changed the character "恨" (hèn, regret) to "幸" (xìng, fortunately).
Guāiyá came out and looked at the draft, saying:
"Who changed my poem?"
His attendants told him the truth.
Xiāo said:
"It was to preserve your life, sir.
Your achievements are great and your position high;
this is a time when treacherous people are watching with sidelong glances.
Moreover, the empire is unified;
why do you alone 'regret' peace?"
Guāiyá replied:
"Brother Xiāo,
you are my teacher for a single character."
Dirges for Tàilíng
The emperor composed five dirges for Tàilíng:
"When the military tent first planned the night,
the cloud chariot suddenly departed for the Emperor's land.
A hundred deities accompanied Yǔ's burial,
three years of mourning were observed like for Yáo.
The North Star is linked with the dragon robe,
the west wind scatters the wild geese's formation.
Only eternal deeds remain,
their continuation I shamefully undertake, O 'doubled light'."
"The immortal's appointment at Gūyè was early,
the dream of Huáxū is already past.
The court depended on the Holy Mother,
the foundation of the enterprise was entrusted to a young person.
The sun turns the shadow of the bronze壶 (hú),
heaven shifts the spring of the jade throne.
At the nine gates, flutes and drums sound,
sadly moving the dust of the imperial carriage."
"Favoring the wise, heaven grants spirit,
resourcefulness and unique strategy.
Dust flows into the hidden treasury,
the key is to the Surrender Tower.
The wind is swift, the wagtail plain late,
frost is cold, the wild geese roost in autumn.
The imperial robes are now in the bedchamber,
I still think of the early morning requests."
"Again seated in the central heaven,
still thinking of the warm jade complexion.
On the jade steps, flowers fall of their own accord,
the shadow of the precious fan remains empty.
Deeply moved by the kinship sorrow,
respectfully receiving the hereditary grace.
Wishing to fulfill the aspiration to commemorate,
forever to inherit the reverence for Yùlíng."
"Remembering the day when the royal mansion opened,
the six dragons once stayed and flew.
In the jade palace, spring was initially eternal,
on the golden plate, the dew had not yet dried.
The bramble roots were flourishing together,
the cherry blossoms shone with each other.
Today, inheriting the foundation,
I recall past events, finding them not wrong."
Crediting Xiāo Guī for merit, grace beginning with Wěi
In the early Xīníng era,
when Zhāng Shàn, a Grand Secretary, achieved a position in the two ministries,
he sent a congratulatory poem to Wáng Jīnggōng.
Jīnggōng replied with a matching poem that read:
"My merit credits Xiāo Guī, ashamed of the Hàn court;
my grace begins with Wěi, making the Yān Terrace renowned."
Lù Nóngshī said:
"'Xiāo Guī and Cáo Suí', Gāo Dì ranked Xiāo Hé first in merit,
but to say 'grace begins with Wěi'
initially has no 'grace' character."
Jīnggōng laughed and said:
"Hán Tuìzhī's 'Couplet on Cockfighting'
says: 'grateful and ashamed, beginning with Wěi'
—if there were no basis,
how could it be paired with the character 'gōng' (merit)?"
Poem Remembering Lín
Zhāng Chuíyá, when young, studied with the recluse Chuán Lín.
After Chuíyá became prominent,
he sought Lín for thirty years
but could not find him,
so he wrote the 'Poem Remembering Lín', which said:
"Send this to Cháo and Yóu, do not laugh at me;
in this life, I will never envy the light and fat."
In his later years, he was defending Huāqiū.
Someone wearing coarse clothes and riding a donkey knocked at the gate, loudly shouting:
"Tell the Grand Secretary
that Chuán Lín from Qīngzhōu has arrived."
The official in the pavilion rushed to report this.
Chuíyá said:
"Master Chuán is a man of the world;
who are you to dare call his given name?"
Lín laughed and said:
"Having been apart from you for a lifetime,
yet still of the same mind,
do you really know that I exist in this world?"
Chuíyá asked why he had hidden himself before and was appearing now.
Lín said:
"You are about to depart;
I came to tell you."
He added:
"You also know this yourself."
Lín said:
"If you know, what more is there to say?"
A month later,
Chuíyá passed away.
Zhuàngyuán Entering the Grand Council
In this dynasty, those who became Zhuàngyuán and then entered the Grand Council were:
Lǚ Wénmù Méngzhèng, Wáng Wénzhèng Céng, Lǐ Wéndìng Dí, and Sòng Yuánxiàn Xiáng.
When Yuánxiàn was appointed,
Shí Yángtǐ, a drafter of imperial edicts, congratulated him with a poem that said:
"Forty-three dragon heads sat at court,
only four reached the yellow doors."
The Vice Privy Councillor, Wáng Bóyōng Yáo, said:
"Why didn't you say 'already four people',
but insist on 'only'?"
This is because Bóyōng succeeded Yuánxiàn as the most brilliant scholar in the realm,
but he passed away in his position not long after.
From the Qìnglì era until now,
there have been no more who, having excelled among scholars, then received a grand appointment.
Du Fǔ's Poem's "Tiānquè" Character
Dù Zǐměi's poem "Staying at Lóngmén" reads:
"The celestial gates (tiānquè) are pressed by the celestial bodies,
lying in the clouds, clothes are cold."
Jīnggōng said:
"'Què' (阙) should be 'yuè' (阅)."
However, Wéi Huán's 'Dōngdū Jì' (Record of the Eastern Capital) says:
"Lóngmén is called the Twin Towers (shuāngquè),
because it stands opposite the imperial palace,
like celestial gates (tiānquè)."
This is a poem about staying at Lóngmén;
what doubt is there in using the character 'què'?
Níshang Lyric
Ōugōng discussed Wáng Jiàn's 'Níshang Cí' (Níshang Lyric):
"Among the disciples' section, one color remained,
listening to the wind and water to compose 'Níshang'."
He regretted not understanding "listening to the wind and water."
A Tang dynasty 'Xīchéng Jì' (Record of the Western Cities) states:
"The king of the state of Qūcí and his musical subjects,
listened to the sounds of wind and water in the great mountains,
harmonized and tuned them into melodies.
Later, foreign tunes entered China,
such as 'Yīzhōu', 'Liángzhōu', and 'Gānzhōu',
all originated from Qūcí."
This explanation is close,
but it doesn't mention 'Níshang' specifically.
Zhèng Yú's annotation to his 'Jīnyángmén Shī' (Poem on Jīnyáng Gate) says:
"Yè Fǎshàn led Mínghuáng to the moon palace.
Upon returning, having heard the music,
he transcribed half of it.
Coincidentally, Xīliáng Prefecture presented the 'Póluómén' (Brahmin) tune,
whose melodies were similar.
So, the two were combined
to create the 'Níshang Yǔyī' (Rainbow Skirt and Feathered Robe)."
Thus, it is known that 'Níshang' also came from the Western Regions.
Jīnggōng Obtained the Phraseology of Lísāo
During the Yuánfēng era,
Jīnggōng was in Jīnlíng,
and Dōngpō traveled north from Huángzhōu,
spending days associating with Jīnggōng.
Jīnggōng sighed and said:
"I wonder how many more centuries will pass
before there will be another person like this."
He showed Dōngpō his recent compositions,
saying:
"'If accumulated plums are like white night,
and honored peaches gleam like day' —
since Qū and Sòng passed away,
over a thousand years,
there has been no return of the phraseology of 'Lísāo',
but now I see it."
When Dōngpō reached Yízhēn,
he sent a poem to Wáng Shèngzhī, the prefect of Jīnlíng, which included the lines:
"Many peaks cleverly obstruct the sun,
the distant border almost floats in the sky."
Jīnggōng then stroked his desk and said:
"In my entire life of composing poetry,
I have never written these two lines."
Wáng Jūnyù's Poem
Wáng Jūnyùqí's 《Qiūlián Shī》 (Autumn Lotus Poem) says:
"Silkworms chill, ice cocoons thin;
Bees old, dew chambers empty."
His 《Wén Jué》 (Hearing the Horn) poem says:
"Geese from Lǒng fall, startled by the sky in the water;
Soldiers on campaign look at each other, the moon like frost."
He also has a poem that says:
"Fish, cold, do not eat the hook in the clear pond;
Egrets, still, frequently startle the small pavilion's game of chess."
Jūnyù once said:
"Poets might as well occasionally use common language;
it particularly shows skill.
Snow that has not melted,
common folk call 'dàibàn' (waiting companion).
For example, it says, 'Dàibàn cannot endure the cold of paired tiles,
shyness of light often fears the slanted jade hook.'
'Dàibàn' and 'xiūmíng' (shyness of light) are both common terms."
Test for a court position poem
Wáng Zhòng Wáng Qīnchén's poem for testing for a court position says:
"Ancient trees cast shade on the Bái Yù Táng,
Long-lived ones come here to test their writing.
As the sun slants, the 《Chángyáng Fù》 is finished,
Idly brushing dust towards the painted wall."
Wáng Jīnggōng changed it to "奏賦《長楊》罷" (finished presenting the 《Chángyáng》 ode),
saying:
"The phrasing is stronger this way."
Líbétǐ (Separation and union style)
The 《Yàomíng Shī》 (Medicinal Herb Name Poems) originated from Chén Yà;
this is not true.
The líhétǐ already existed in the Eastern Hàn,
and only in the Táng did the name 《Yàomíng》 become prominent.
For example, Zhāng Jiè's "By the riverbank at year's end, a meeting place,
Yellow leaves, before the frost, branches of bànxià.
At midnight, reciting poems towards the pines and osmanthus,
All matters in my heart, you know well" is an example.
Jíjù (Collected lines)
Jíjù existed since the beginning of the state,
but it was not until Shí Mànqīng used it for literary amusement
that it became widely recognized.
《Xiàdì Ǒuchéng》 (Accidentally Composed After Failing the Examination) says:
"All my life, I've gained no power from literature,
Wishing to ascend to the blue clouds, but without a cause.
The sagely ruler does not trouble to summon from a thousand li,
Why does Cháng'é begrudge a single branch of spring?
Though a phoenix decree descends, bestowing a fate,
One also establishes oneself amidst a thicket of jackals and tigers.
Crying until blood flows, to no avail,
Who is that, wearing vermillion and riding a horse?"
It also says:
"Year after year, ambition rushes,
Making wedding clothes for others.
Looking up at the sky, laughing loudly, I step out the door,
Alone facing the east wind, dancing a single turn."
Yìhèmíng (Inscription for Buried Cranes)
The 《Yìhèmíng》 on Jiāoshān,
composed by Huáyáng Zhēnyì;
Ōu Gōng said it was Gù Kuàng's daoist name.
Sū Zǐměi's poem says:
"In Shānyīn, the goose-exchange scripture is unseen,
In Jīngkǒu, only the 《Yìhèmíng》 is transmitted in vain."
It is truly written by Yòujūn.
《Táo Yǐnjū Wàichuán》 (Unofficial Biography of Recluse Táo) says:
"The recluse,
styled Huáyáng Zhēnrén,
later styled Huáyáng Zhēnyì."
Therefore, it is beyond doubt that the 《Yìhèmíng》 is by the recluse.
Zhèng Qián did not see the Eight Lamentations Poem
《Shùxuān Lù》 says:
"Dù Zǐměi was proud of his poetry.
When Zhèng Qián's wife suffered from malaria,
he ordered her to recite his poem, 'The curly beard resembles Tàizōng,
Its color reflects the spring beyond the frontier.'
The malaria ghost would then avoid her."
This is the opinion of a vulgar person from the late Táng.
'The curly beard resembles Tàizōng' is from the 《Bā'āi》 (Eight Lamentations) poem,
referring to Rǔyáng Wáng Jìn.
Jìn died before Qián,
and the 《Bā'āi》 poem was written by his peers after Qián's death.
Thus, it is clear that Qián did not live to see this poem.
Hé Xùn and others' poems and odes
Hé Xùn's poem says:
"Thin clouds emerge from the cliffs,
The crescent moon rises from the slopes."
Shǎolíng, however, says:
"Thin clouds emerge from the cliffs,
A lone moon tumbles in the waves."
Although, due to repeated use, it became more exquisite.
《Yùtái Jí Xù》 (Preface to the Collection of Jade Terraces) says:
"The golden star contends for brilliance with Wùnǚ,
The musk moon competes for beauty with Cháng'é."
A Northern Qí stele says:
"Floating clouds and mountain pines spread a canopy,
Autumn moon and cliff osmanthus share a cluster."
Yú Zǐshān's 《Mǎshè Fù》 (Horse Archery Ode) says:
"Falling flowers and auspicious canopies fly together,
Willows and spring banners are one color."
Wáng Bó says:
"Falling mist and lonely wild geese fly together,
Autumn waters and the long sky are one color."
Xuē Féng originally said:
"Wild flowers contend with the evening glow for redness,
Strange rocks and cold streams share greenness."
Shā Fēngjǐng (Spoiling the scenery)
Lǐ Yìshān's 《Zázǎn》 (Miscellaneous Compendium),
one section says:
"Shā fēngjǐng,
refers to washing feet in clear springs,
Waving banners over flowers,
Building a tower with its back to the mountain,
Burning a qín and boiling a crane,
Drinking tea with flowers,
And shouting before descending."
Yàn Yuánxiàn presented to Jīnggōng,
all using the language of shā fēngjǐng.
Lamenting Dù Zǐměi's poem
A Táng dynasty poem lamenting Dù Zǐměi says:
"Odes surpass the 《Sāndū》,
Poems should be sought from the two 《Yǎ》."
This implies that Shǎolíng's poetic discipline distantly inherited that of the Zhōu poems.
"White rice for the slave, green fodder for the horse,"
though it does not explicitly state the master,
yet treating the slave and horse in such a manner,
the master can be inferred,
which is similar in meaning to "I cut the thorny brambles,
And feed my horses.
I cut the willow branches,
And feed my colts."
Also, "The small city is over ten thousand feet tall,
The large city is not as good as iron,"
implies that a small city is hard to make tall,
and a large city is hard to make strong.
This accurately captures the ancient practice of authors providing mutual elucidation in their writings.
Poems entirely in píngshēng (level tones)
Yàn Yuánxiàn said to Méi Shèngyú:
"In ancient verses, some use entirely píngshēng,
The characters are smoothly placed,
like 'The withered mulberry knows the sky wind.'
I regret not having seen a poem entirely in zèshēng (oblique tones)."
Shèngyú then composed a poem in five-zèshēng style, saying:
"The moon emerges from the mouth of the broken bank,
Its shadow illuminates the back of another boat.
And I drink alone with my wife,
Far better than facing vulgar guests."
Hǎilì (Sea Standing)
Dù Shǎolíng's "Clouds of the nine heavens hang low,
Waters of the four seas all stand."
Dōngpō's 《Yǒuměi Táng》 poem:
"Black winds from beyond the sky blow the sea to stand,"
is derived from this.
Composing poems in a dream
Zhāng Dǎn,
during the Xīníng reign, dreamed he was walking in a vast sky,
hearing celestial winds and ocean waves,
their sounds shaking the forests.
He then saw towers and pavilions in the sea,
hundreds of people in jade and pearl ornaments bowed to Dǎn,
offered paper, requesting a composition,
the brushes and inkstones were all of green jade,
and they warned him:
"The writings here
must be like hidden rising phoenixes,
often competing in skill with Zhīnǚ's loom;
anything beyond this is merely human language."
Dǎn's poem says:
"Celestial winds scatter the glow of Chìchéng,
Dyeing out a myriad of cloud-connected trees in bloom.
Mistakenly entering a drunken dream, losing the way back,
Others should laugh at me for forgetting to return home."
An immortal said:
"Your poem is excellent,
but it cannot avoid being close to the mundane."
A cup of wine was offered,
extremely sweet and cold.
Suddenly, he felt himself falling into a ten-thousand-ren mountain and awoke.
Turning into a three-day rain
Sòng Qí and Shěn Yìlún were both in the Huánggé.
After a long drought, it rained,
but then would not stop.
Qí said:
"It turned into a three-day rain,"
Yìlún replied:
"It tuned out a city full of mud."
Dòngtíng Poem
Dòngtíng is the most magnificent sight under Heaven.
Ancient poets wrote, for example: "Water embraces human reflections broadly,
Mountains rise high above the terrain."
And also: "Looking around, I doubt there's any land,
Suddenly there's a mountain in midstream."
None is like Mèng Hàorán's: "Mist steams over Yúnmèng Zé,
Waves stir Yuèyáng Chéng."
As for Dù Zǐměi,
he wrote:
"Wú and Chǔ are split apart in the southeast,
Heaven and Earth float day and night."
Tàibái's Lost Works
Lǐ Tàibái's lost works say:
"Sheer cliffs like cut melons,
Mist light breaks green on the cliffs.
The Heavenly River flows from their midst,
White clouds swell the rivers and valleys.
Jade tablets stir with writings,
Not to be read by worldly eyes.
I gather my body and soar to the azure sky,
Pine winds brush my feet."
It also says:
"I lift my sleeve to reveal my bangle,
Beckoning me to eat sesame seeds."
Poem on Fēngdǐng Sì
Fēngdǐng Sì in Qízhōu's Huángméi Xiàn,
is in the middle of the water,
encircled by ten thousand prostrate mountains.
Zēng Fù was the magistrate;
he went up there on business
and saw a plaque on a beam,
dark with dust and flaking powder.
After wiping it clean and reading it,
it turned out to be a poem by Tàibái:
"Staying the night at Fēngdǐng Sì,
I raise my hand to touch the stars.
I dare not speak loudly,
Lest I startle the people in Heaven."
It is commonly believed to be a poem by Yáng Wéngōng in his youth,
but this is a mistake.
Téng Wáng Zhànrán
Ōugōng recorded Wáng Jiàn's "Gōngcí" (Palace Poems) as saying:
"For several days there were no summonses in the palace,
Word came of Téng Wáng's 'Butterfly Painting'."
It is famous,
but Zhànrán was not Yuán Yīng.
Laying Brocade at the Bottom of the Pond
Wáng Jiàn's "Gōngcí":
"Emerald beauties locked in the Yúǎo Gōng,
The former emperor never passed by where they were.
Now there's no need to lay brocade at the bottom of the pond,
Water caltrops and foxnuts are gradually accumulating."
Lǐ Shí's "Kāichéng Chéngzhào Lù" (Record of Receiving Edicts in Kāichéng),
recorded Wénzōng discussing Dézōng's extravagance, saying:
"I heard that old palace women in the Forbidden City, whenever drawing spring water,
would first lay brocade at the bottom of the pond."
Thus we know that Wáng Jiàn's poems all recount facts,
and are not empty words.
Poem on a Tiger Painting
Wáng Jièfǔ, Ōu Yǒngshú, and Méi Shèngyú sat together, each given the task of writing "A Poem on a Tiger Painting."
Jièfǔ finished first,
and then inscribed Dù Fǔ's "Song of the Painting of a Falcon."
The Later Lord's Long and Short Verses
The Later Lord of Southern Táng composed long and short verses during the siege of his city,
but before they were finished, the city fell:
"Cherry blossoms have all fallen, spring has departed,
Butterflies turn golden dust, flying in pairs,
Cuckoos cry under the small moon, west of the tower.
Curved jade railings and bamboo screens,
Sadly rolled up the golden mud.
The gates and alleys are desolate, people gone,
Looking back, lingering smoke and low grass blur."
The Recluse of Fāngchéng
Fàn Qiānshú resided in Fāngchéng.
There was a recluse who claimed to have been an old white-haired villager in the past,
who met a master who taught him a divine medicine,
and his complexion became like fresh vermilion.
When he announced his departure,
he left a poem saying:
"Do not be surprised that I return early, leaning on my staff,
My home mountain idly holds a stream of clouds."
Poems by Three Monks
Monk Qí Sì's poem says:
"Spring is deep, guests visit the temple,
Flowers fall, the monk closes his door."
Huìchóng said:
"Morning wind carries the distant chime of the qìng,
Evening snow deepens into the corridor."
The Mǐn monk Kě Rén's poem says:
"One bowl defines my life,
Following fate through the years.
Every mountain has a temple,
Where is not home?"
Old Wild Fox Spirit
Wáng Jīnggōng saw Dōngpō's "Jì Zuìbáitáng" (Record of the Drunken White Hall) and said:
"This must be a discussion of the merits and demerits of Hán Yù and Bái Jūyì."
Dōngpō said:
"It is not as good as Jièfǔ's 'Jì Chǔzhōu Xué' (Record of Chǔzhōu Academy),
which is merely an essay on schools."
However, the two gentlemen admired each other's superior qualities.
Dōngpō was serving at Xītàiyī Temple
and saw a former inscription by Wáng Jīnggōng:
"Willows and cicadas chirp, green shades deepen,
Lotus flowers in the setting sun, red grows rich.
Thirty-six ponds of spring water,
White-haired, I long to see Jiāngnán."
He gazed at it for a long time,
and said:
"An old wild fox spirit indeed!"
Pí Guāngyè's Poem
During the time of King Qián Liú of Wúyuè,
Prime Minister Pí Guāngyè had a poem that said:
"Travelers break willow branches with light catkins,
Swallows carry mud with fallen flowers."
Everyone competed in praising it.
Péi Guāngyuē spoke up loudly, saying:
"These two lines are unbalanced and not skillful.
Willows should have catkins,
but mud may not have flowers."
Bamboo Forest Bird
Shàolíng's "Qīgē" (Seven Songs) says:
"Alas, the fourth song, oh, the fourth performance,
The bamboo forest weeps for me in the clear day."
Later annotators of the poem changed it to "forest apes."
During the Chóngníng era,
a guest from Tóngzhōu brought a caged bird,
the size of a sparrow,
its color bright green,
and it sang well.
When asked its name,
he replied:
"It is a bamboo forest bird."
Poem on the Tombs of Zhōu
Lǐ Hándān had a poem titled "On the Three Tombs of the Zhōu Dynasty."
His "Gōngdì Líng" (Tomb of Emperor Gōng) said:
"They played with plows and pulled carts, urged by drums,
Unaware that outside the gate, spears had been turned back.
Wild brambles and broken mounds are about three feet high,
Who says Fánglíng came with half a guard?"
He was impeached by his enemies
and punished for slander.
Chanting and Harmonizing at the Ministry of Rites
In the early Jiāyòu era,
Ōuyáng Yǒngshú, Wáng Yǔyù, Méi Gōngyí, Hán Zǐhuá, and Fàn Jǐngrén together presided over the spring examinations.
There was a "Lǐbù Chànghé Jí" (Collection of Chants and Harmonizations from the Ministry of Rites).
Méi Shèngyú was a subordinate at the time,
and had a poem that said:
"Ten thousand ants battle fiercely, the spring day is long,
Five stars shine brightly, the night hall is deep."
The examination candidates jokingly said:
"The chief examiner considers himself a star,
and we are the ants.
This is the humility of the examination official."
Lǚ Dòngbīn
Zhōng Ruòwēng, the transmission master of Píngliáng,
had a Daoist practitioner request an audience.
His disciple, a shepherd boy, led a yellow calf and stood in the courtyard.
Ruòwēng found this unusual,
and pointed at the shepherd boy, saying:
"Can this Daoist write a poem about this?"
He smiled and said:
"No need for me to speak,
this child can do it."
Then he wrote in large characters:
"Grass spreads across the field for six or seven li,
A flute plays three or four notes in the evening breeze.
Returning, I eat my fill after dusk,
And lie down in the bright moonlight without taking off my coir raincoat."
After he left,
people in the prefecture saw the Daoist carrying two large jars,
singing loudly as he left the city gate.
They traced him but he was gone.
The jars had two mouths;
could it be Lǚ Dòngbīn?
Fèngzǐ
"Poem Mocking Clay Geese" says:
"Little geese peck with their yellow beaks,
Fèngzǐ are slender with delicate powdered waists."
Cuī Bào's "Gǔjīn Zhù" (Ancient and Modern Annotations) says:
"Large butterflies are called Fèngzǐ."
Wáng Yuánzhī's Couplets
Wáng Yǔchēng Yuánzhī's father was originally a miller.
Bì Wénjiǎn Shì'ān was a prefectural official.
When Yuánzhī was seven years old,
he delivered flour on behalf of his father.
Upon arriving at the government office,
he stood in the courtyard.
Wénjiǎn was just then instructing his sons to compose a couplet,
saying:
"A talking parrot can hardly compare to a phoenix."
Yuánzhī boldly said:
"A spider, though clever, is not as good as a silkworm."
Wénjiǎn said:
"Your spirit is full,
and you will soon be famous in the world."
Later, he walked with the Duke in the imperial court.
Wáng Jīnggōng's Poetry
Wáng Jīnggōng said:
"How could Lǐ Hàn have known Hán Tuì
zhī?
He compiled his writings
without distinguishing good from bad,
which cannot be shown to one's descendants,
let alone passed down to future generations?"
Regarding this, his disciples
had a certain intention.
His writings still lack good editions.
Such as, "As spring wanes, leaves are dense, flower branches are few;
Awakened from sleep, much tea, few wine cups."
"Our Emperor is heroic, surpassing Guāngwǔ;
The senior general's prestige rivals Wěi Xiāo."
These are all poems by Wáng Yuánzhī.
《Jīnlíng Dúzhuó》 (Solo Drinking in Jīnlíng):
"Snowy waves from the West River reach the sky's edge."
《Jì Liú Yuánfù》 (Sent to Liú Yuánfù):
"A Hanlin scholar exiled from Penglái Palace."
These are poems by Wáng Jūnyù.
"By the ford, thousands of trees with vibrant flowers,"
"At the world's end, the sea gate lies across Běigù,"
"Unknowing if a vermilion door locks a beauty,"
These are all poems by Wáng Píngfǔ.
Autumn Blooms Don't Fall Like Spring Flowers
During the Jiāyòu reign, Ōugōng
saw Wáng Jīnggōng's poem: "Dusk, wind and rain darken the garden;
Fading chrysanthemums scatter, covering the ground with gold."
He laughed and said:
"All other flowers fall,
only chrysanthemums wither on their branches."
He then playfully said:
"Autumn blooms don't fall like spring flowers;
Report this to the poet, look carefully."
Jīnggōng heard this and said:
"How could he not know that the 'Chǔcí' says 'eating the fallen petals of autumn chrysanthemums'?
Ōuyáng's lack of study is a fault."
Planting Red Plum Trees
Red plum trees uniquely flourished in Gūsū.
Yàn Yuánxiàn first transplanted them to his residence on Xīgāng.
One day, a noble bribed the garden official
and obtained a branch to graft,
whereupon there were two such trees in the capital.
The Duke once drank with guests beneath the flowers,
composing a poem which said:
"If they bloomed two or three months later,
Northerners would surely mistake them for apricot blossoms."
A guest said:
"Your poem is certainly good,
but why are you so dismissive of the Northern custom?"
The Duke smiled and said:
"How could those bumpkins be otherwise?"
Wáng Jūn heard of the flower theft,
and sent a poem to the Duke:
"By the north of Guǎnwá Palace, an old spirit,
Powder-thin, jade-cold, with new dewy buds.
The garden official inexplicably stole a branch,
From then on, Fèngchéng has its servant."
Loving Literary Drinking is the Same Category as Commoners Buying Wine
Dōngpō spoke of Hán Tuìzhī's poem:
"Many rich young men in Cháng'ān,
Their tables laden with fragrant meat.
They don't understand literary drinking,
Only capable of intoxicating red skirts."
When it says "Charming beauties dance on the mat,
Clear eyes shoot forth like swords and spears,"
then one knows that this old man's passion for such things was not shallow.
Zhāng Wénqián jokingly replied:
"Those who love literary drinking
are in the same category as commoners buying wine."
Yuánfù's Second Marriage
Liú Yuánfù Chǎng remarried.
Ōugōng playfully sent him two quatrains:
"Who among peers in life's endeavors came first?
With a stroke of the brush, literature spread throughout the land.
Tomorrow, the capital's paper should surely be precious,
As curtains open, fans part, revealing the new chapter."
"How long is a thousand years for immortals?
In this fleeting world, one is startled by busy days and months.
Let the new flowers in the grotto not laugh at him,
Liú Láng is now the old Liú Láng."
Yuánfù was displeased.
Secretary Wáng's Stolen Willow Poem
During the Jiāyòu reign,
when admiring flowers and fishing,
Wáng Jièfǔ, as the drafter of imperial edicts, was seated at the end.
The Emperor presented a poem, and the ministers were to compose a reply.
When it reached Jièfǔ,
it was almost dusk.
Eager to present it to the Emperor,
he had the phrase "Pīxiāng Diàn"
but no couplet.
Zhèng Yìfū Xiè, who sat next to him,
said:
"It should be paired with 'Tàiyè Chí'."
He tapped on his poem, saying:
"The vermilion chariot stays at Pīxiāng Diàn,
Wine cups are sent by Tàiyè Chí."
The next day, it was widely rumored in the capital that Secretary Wáng had stolen Zhèng's "waves turned in Tàiyè,
curtains rolled up in Pīxiāng."
Jièfǔ bore a grudge.
Dōngpō Teases Chén Jìcháng's Fear of His Wife
When Dōngpō was exiled to Huángzhōu,
he befriended Chén Zào Jìcháng.
Jìcháng considered himself well-versed in Zen studies.
However, his wife Liǔ Shì was quite fierce.
Jìcháng feared her.
When guests arrived,
she would sometimes scold without stopping,
her voice reaching outside.
Dōngpō then playfully wrote a poem:
"Who is like the worthy recluse of Lóngqiū,
Discussing emptiness and existence, sleepless through the night?
Suddenly he hears the roar of the Hédōng lioness,
His staff falls from his hand, his mind bewildered."
Jade Grinder's Southern Delicacy
Yè Hǎizhìyuǎn had a poem "Shìchá" (Testing Tea) which said:
"Ground into celestial dragons and phoenixes,
Brewed into earthly crabs and shrimps."
A witty person jokingly said:
"This is not testing tea,
but a jade grinder's poem tasting Southern delicacies."
Péngmén Wall Inscription
On a wall in Péngmén there was a couplet:
"A single dove calls in the noonday quiet,
A pair of swallows chat in the spring clear."
Dōngpō said:
"This is an excellent line by a Tang poet."
Two Candidates Arrested
Shí Mànqīng was at the Hanlin Academy.
At the fifth watch, rushing to court,
he saw two candidates tied up at the police station.
Mànqīng asked what happened.
The official said:
"Yesterday, in the neighborhood, there was a wedding.
The two young men made a hole to peek through,
and were caught after midnight."
Mànqīng strongly interceded for their release,
reciting a poem composed of collected lines:
"Sí Kōng, when you approach Rǔ, you must know;
Beneath the moon, who else knocks at the door?
How intolerable, that pair of poor-sighted eyes,
What seemed an advantage turned out to be a disadvantage."
Birthday Poem
Zhōu Bāngyàn Měichéng's poem "Shàng Jiāgōng Shēngrì" (Presented to His Excellency on His Birthday) said:
"His influence extends beyond the mountains and rivers of the 'Yǔgòng',
The man is within the Rites and Music of Zhōu Gōng."
Planting Flowers in a Secluded Valley
When Ōugōng was the Prefect of Chúzhōu,
he instructed his staff to plant flowers in the secluded valley of Lángyá.
A subordinate asked for the names of the varieties in a memorandum.
The Duke wrote at the end of the paper:
"Light and dark, red and white, should be interspersed,
Before and after, they must still be planted in order.
I wish to bring wine there in all four seasons,
Let not a single day pass without flowers blooming."
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ's Long and Short Verses
After Lǐ Hòuzhǔ of Southern Táng submitted to the court,
he constantly longed for his Jiang-state,
and also thought of his scattered concubines.
His *chángduǎn jù* (long and short verses) say:
"Outside the curtain, the rain patters,
The spring will soon be over.
My silk quilt cannot withstand the cold of the fifth watch.
In dreams, I know not I am a guest,
For a moment, I indulge in joy.
Alone, do not lean on the railing,
Infinite rivers and mountains.
Easy to part, difficult to meet again.
Flowing water, falling flowers, spring is gone,
Between heaven and earth."
Not long after, he passed away.
The Singer Zhuǎncūn Yīng
Wáng Shēn Jìnqīng, the Commandant,
after the loss of the Shǔ Kingdom,
was demoted to Jūnzhōu.
All his maidservants were driven away.
There was a singer named Zhuǎncūn Yīng,
whose whereabouts were unknown.
Two years later,
passing through Rǔyīn by the market tower,
he heard a deeply mournful weeping.
When asked,
it was Zhuǎncūn Yīng.
He obtained the lines:
"The fair lady now belongs to Shāzhìlì,
The righteous knight now has no guests like Gǔ Yāyá."
Someone completed the poem,
its lines read:
"For years, drifting to the ends of the earth,
Returning from a myriad *lǐ*, both temples are gray.
Green sleeves, faint fragrance, only tears moisten,
Where in the misty blue towers does she now reside?
The fair lady now belongs to Shāzhìlì,
The righteous knight now has no Gǔ Yāyá.
Turning back, sound and trace are both utterly lost,
Zhuǎncūn Yīng, cease chirping among the Qìnyuán flowers."
Lǔzhí's Poetry
Huáng Lǔzhí could compose poetry at the age of eight.
His poem "Sending Someone to Take the Imperial Examination" says:
"Sending you back before the enlightened ruler,
If asked about the old Huáng Tíngjiān,
He has been exiled among men for eight years now."
Làikě and Shòuqúan
The monk-poet Jǔkě suffered from a severe illness;
people called him Làikě.
Shànquán was also skilled in poetry,
with a clear and gaunt appearance;
people called him Shòuqúan.
Kě's poem includes "Hoarfrost makes all the trees fall,
Revealing all the autumn of the Western Mountains."
Quán said:
"At the valley mouth, the sun has not yet slanted,
Several peaks cast evening shadows."
Qiū's Poem to Her Husband
The daughters of the Court Gentleman Qiū Shùnzhū
were all skilled in literature and poetry.
His second daughter's poem to her husband says:
"Behind the curtain, a lone lamp makes dawn feel late,
Sleeping alone, I retain the overnight makeup on my brows.
On the coral pillow, a lingering dream startles,
Recognizing the moment Xiāo Láng's horse passes by."
Yáo Sìzōng was the prefect.
Zhāng Yuán, who had a reputation for wildness in Huázhōu,
was implicated in a crime during the Tiānshèng era and spent his life in confinement,
expressing himself through poetry.
For example, his "Ode to Snow" poem:
"Three million jade dragons vanquished,
