Their broken scales and shattered armor fill the sky."
His "Ode to a White Eagle":
"With a mind to snatch the rabbit on the moon,
It intentionally flies with white clouds towards the edge of the sky."
His "Kōngtóng Shān" poem says:
"Shattering the Hèlán rocks,
Sweeping clean the dust of the Western Sea.
A commoner can discern this,
Alas, to be a destitute fish."
The Duke said:
"If this man is not taken in,
we will lose a Zhāng Yuán."
Therefore, he recommended him for an official post.
Poem while Accompanying the Emperor
Zēng Zǐkāi composed a poem "Accompanying the Emperor,"
rhyming with *xīn* (辛), repeatedly without ceasing.
Dōngpō was weary of it,
and responded, saying:
"After reading your poem, what does it resemble?
Pounded ginger and cinnamon, with an excess of pungency (*xīn*)."
He then asked his guest:
"Do you understand this?
It means the first line is too spicy."
Yáng Luán's Poem
It is popularly believed that Ōu Gōng presided over the imperial examinations,
and a candidate asked if Yáo and Shùn were two different people.
Ōu Gōng replied:
"There's no need to use them."
This was actually a conversation between Tāng Yuè and Yáng Luán of Southern Táng,
recorded in Zhèng Wénbǎo's *Jiāngbiǎo Zhì*.
It also records Luán's poem:
"By day, the rice plate is covered with flies,
At night, mosquitoes swarm into a mass again.
Every time after midnight, when people are quiet,
They surely come to bite Yáng Luán on the head."
Liǔzhī and Jiàngtáo
*Táng Shī Lín* says:
"Tuìzhī's concubines
were named Liǔzhī and Jiàngtáo.
His 'Quatrain at Shòuyáng Post Station when Sending Wáng Tíngcòu' says:
'I see no garden flowers or street willows,
Only the round moon above the horse's head.'
When he returned,
Liǔzhī had run away.
He also had a poem 'First Return to Zhènzhōu':
'Since our parting, the willows by the street,
Are swayed wildly by the east wind, as if to fly.
Only the small peach trees in the garden remain,
Keeping their flowers unbloomed, awaiting their lord's return.'
From then on, his affection was entirely for Jiàngtáo."
The Luófú Immortal
Recently, someone traveling to Luófú
stayed overnight in a cave valley.
In the middle of the night,
he saw a person without clothes,
but with dark blue fur covering his body.
He believed it must be an immortal,
so he bowed twice and asked about the Way.
That person paid him no heed,
let out several long whistles,
their sound shaking the forest trees,
and sang a poem:
"When clouds come, ten thousand peaks move,
When clouds go, the sky's color clears.
Two or three long whistles,
The empty mountain, the autumn moon white."
Inner Court Banquet Poem
Zhāng Jiè's "Inner Court Banquet on Cold Food Day":
"Morning light and auspicious aura fill the palace towers,
Colorful banners and fish-dragon flags are dense on all sides.
From the imperial kitchens beneath the corridor, cold food is distributed,
In front of the hall, fragrant riders chase a flying ball.
A thousand officials, though all drunk, are still made to sit,
A hundred performances are all presented, not yet allowed to cease.
All rejoice, receiving grace, leaving deep in the night,
The Imperial Guard dares not question their passage."
Thus, it is known that the Táng dynasty also held banquets for officials on Qīngmíng,
all serving cold food,
and that they concluded late at night.
Chǔmò's Poem
*Wúyuè Jìshì* records:
"The Yuè monk Chǔmò
had extraordinary lines in his poetry.
He once said:
'Reaching the river, the land of Wú ends,
Across the bank, the mountains of Yuè are many.'
Luó Yǐn saw it and said:
'These are my lines, lost for a long time,
and now obtained by a Wú beggar.'" End of Volume 57.
End.
Xiāo Hé and the Worn-Out Brush
The Hàn Chancellor Xiāo Hé was skilled in seal script (*zhuàn*) and official script (*chōu*),
and often used a worn-out brush.
Eight-Angled Dangling Bristles
Cài Yōng entered Sōngshān,
to study calligraphy in a stone chamber.
He obtained a plain book
with eight-angled dangling bristles,
which described Lǐ Sī, Shǐ Chōu, and others' brushwork methods.
Yōng cried out with joy,
and often told people he had marvelously grasped its principles.
He personally wrote the "Five Classics" at the Imperial Academy,
and spectators were as numerous as those in a marketplace.
Five-Spirit Elixir
Zhōng Yáo saw Cài Yōng's brushwork methods at Wéi Dàn's seat,
beat his chest for three days,
and consequently vomited blood.
The Crown Prince saved him with the Five-Spirit Elixir,
and he survived.
Yáo earnestly sought the methods, but they were not given to him.
When Dàn died,
Yáo ordered someone to secretly dig up his tomb,
and thus obtained them.
Sòng Yì's Calligraphy
Sòng Yì, a disciple of Zhōng Yáo,
whenever he painted a *pī* (downward stroke to the left),
would often snap his brush three times.
When he made a *gē* (hook stroke),
it was like a hundred *jūn* crossbow.
When he made a dot,
it was like lifting a high rock and letting it fall.
When he made a *qiān* (pulling stroke),
it was like a century-old withered vine.
When he made a free-flowing stroke,
it was like a startled snake passing through water.
Intention Precedes the Brush
Indeed, when one desires to write, one must first grind ink dry,
concentrate the spirit and think quietly,
imagining the size, tilt, straightness, and vibration of the characters.
Let the sinews and veins connect,
the intention precede the brush,
and the character reside in the heart,
then proceed to write the characters.
Xīzhī Learns Calligraphy
Wáng Xīzhī in his youth studied the calligraphy of Madame Wèi.
When he crossed the Jiāng River northwards,
he saw the calligraphy of Lǐ Sī and others.
He went to Xǔ,
and saw the calligraphy of Zhōng Yáo and Liáng Míng.
He went to Luò,
and saw the calligraphy of Cài Yōng,
and also saw the "Zhāng Yuè Stela".
Only then did he realize that studying Madame Wèi's calligraphy
was a waste of years and months.
Consequently, he took many stelae as his teachers and learned from them.
At that time, he was fifty-two years old.
Brush Array
The Right General's "Brush Array Diagram" says:
"Paper,
that is the battle array.
The brush,
that is the sword and shield.
Ink,
that is the armor.
Water and inkstone,
that is the city walls.
The heart and mind,
that is the general.
Structure,
that is strategy."
Character Size
Compress large characters to make them appear small,
and expand small characters to make them appear large,
then naturally, looseness and tightness will be appropriate.
Horizontal strokes should be straight,
like a long boat cutting across a small islet.
Vertical strokes should be upright,
like spring bamboo shoots emerging from a cold valley.
Character Flaws
When learning to write characters, one must follow the forms of correct methods,
and not be wide at the top and narrow at the bottom,
for this makes the head heavy and the tail light.
If too dense, it resembles being afflicted by a wasting disease;
if too sparse, it resembles a bird drowned in water.
If too long, it resembles a dead snake hanging on a tree;
if too short, it resembles a crushed toad.
Misplaced Dots and Strokes
A misplaced dot,
is like a beautiful woman without eyes.
A misplaced stroke,
is like a strong man without a wrist.
Imprinting Clay and Drawing Sand
Zhāng Chángshǐ said:
"The marvel of skillful writing,
lies in the circular rotation of holding the brush,
do not let it be rigid or constrained.
Next,
the layout should be appropriate.
Next,
the paper and brush should be excellent.
Next,
changing methods to suit one's inclination,
transcending rules and regulations.
When all five are complete,
then one can be equal to the ancients."
My old uncle Yàn Yuǎn said from south of the Chǔ River:
"Using the brush should be like stamping an impression in clay,
and like a awl drawing in sand,
making it concealed and extended,
so the strokes are deep
and firm,
without
blunting its tip.
One should always desire to penetrate through the back of the paper,
entering the wood seven fen deep."
Wáng Yì, at the age of twelve,
saw the brush treatises of earlier generations,
and his calligraphy greatly improved.
Madame Wèi said:
"This child must have seen the secrets of brush usage,
his calligraphy already possesses the wisdom of an elder."
She then shed tears and said:
"This child will surely surpass me."
During the reign of Emperor Jìn,
the "Eulogy for the Northern Suburbs" was rewritten,
and when the artisans planed it,
the characters had penetrated seven *fen* deep into the wood.
Brush Treatises
Cáo Xǐ wrote "Treatise on the Brush",
Zhāng Zhī wrote "Treatise on the Heart of the Brush",
Zhōng Yáo wrote "Treatise on the Bones of Calligraphy",
Wáng Xīzhī wrote "Brush Array Diagram".
Brush, Inkstone, Paper, Ink
For brushes, take rabbit hair from the autumn months of August or September, from the steep cliffs of Chongshān,
the brush head should be one *cun* long,
the handle five *cun* long,
with a sharp tip and a long waist.
For inkstones, take new stone that is moist and slightly rough,
with colors that blend.
For ink, take pine soot from Lúshān,
and deer antler glue from Dàijùn.
For paper, take that from Dōngyáng, like fish roe, supple and smooth and clean.
Then, calmly unfold your thoughts,
and with a flourish of your sleeve, create;
whether cursive or regular script, with all its curves,
all should be delivered with the strength of one's entire body.
Beginners must first practice writing large characters,
and not small characters.
Ink Pig
Any calligraphy that has too much flesh and too little bone
is called an "ink pig".
Therefore, it is known that those with abundant strength and rich sinews succeed,
while those without strength and sinews are flawed.
Chángshì Ascends the Bed
Tàizōng made *fēibái* calligraphy,
and his ministers eagerly competed to take it from the emperor's hand.
Liú Jì ascended the imperial bed,
and reached out to get it.
Tàizōng laughed and said:
"In the past, I heard of a concubine drunk in a carriage;
today, I see a Chángshì ascending the bed."
Drawing on a Quilt
Zhōng Yáo instructed his son, saying:
"I have studied calligraphy for thirty years;
when lying down, I would draw on my quilt,
causing it to wear through."
More Marvelous Within Marvelous
Yú Shìnán's calligraphy
was elegant and forceful in its form,
with extraordinary demeanor,
capable within capability,
marvelous within marvelous.
Gold Born, Jade潤 (Moist)
Chǔ Suíliáng's calligraphy,
had gold born within the characters,
and jade moisture between the lines.
Ancient Fat, Modern Thin
Zhāng Chángshǐ said:
"Xiànzhī is called 'ancient fat',
Zhāng Xù is called 'modern thin'."
Regular, Running, Running-Cursive
Running script is neither cursive nor regular;
it departs from squares and traces circles, combining regular script and bearing characteristics of cursive;
it is called running-cursive.
In the Later Hàn dynasty, Xú Ān searched through various historical records
and found twelve forms of script,
all resembling divine shapes.
He also added twenty-two forms,
making a total of fifty-six types of script.
Fifty-six Types of Script
It says:
Tài Hào Páo Xī Shì obtained the auspicious omen of a brilliant dragon,
and created the Dragon Script (Lóngshū).
Shén Nóng Shì, inspired by the ears of fine grain,
created the Spike Script (Suìshū).
Huáng Dì commanded Cāng Jié to create characters based on bird tracks,
making the Bamboo Seal Script (Zhúzhuànshū).
He also, seeing auspicious clouds,
created the Cloud Script (Yúnshū).
Shào Hào created the Golden Heaven Phoenix Script (Jīntiān Luánfèngshū).
Gāo Yáng Shì devised the Tadpole Script (Kēdǒushū).
Gāo Xīn Shì created the Immortal Figure Script (Xiānrénxíngshū).
Dì Yáo, inspired by a divine turtle carrying a diagram,
created the Turtle Script (Guīshū).
Xià Hòu Shì created the Bell-Cauldron Script (Zhōngdǐngshū).
During the time of Chéng Tāng,
the immortal Wù Guāng created the Inverted Rampset Seal Script (Dàoxiè Zhuànshū),
and Shǐ Yì created the Tiger Script (Hǔshū),
as there were tigers that did not harm people.
King Wén of Zhōu saw a red sparrow carrying a book gather at his door,
and King Wǔ saw a red bird enter his chamber,
hence they created the Bird Script (Niǎoshū).
The matchmaker of Zhōu created the Filling Script (Tiánshū),
used to inscribe imperial palaces.
During the time of King Xuān,
Shǐ Chōu created the Great Seal Script (Dàzhuànshū),
and also the Repeated Seal Script (Fùzhuàn).
The Staff Script (Shūshū)
was the responsibility of Bó Shì;
thus, civil officials recorded on tablets (hù),
and military officials recorded on staffs (shū).
The Small Seal Script (Xiǎozhuàn)
was created during the Zhōu dynasty;
the Immortal Seal Script (Xiānrénzhuàn)
existed in ancient times;
Lǐ Sī reformed it into the Seal Script (Zhuàn),
which was pictographic.
When a qílín was captured during a western hunt,
Zhòng Ní turned his sleeve and wiped his face, saying:
"My Way has reached its end!"
His disciples then created the Qílín Script (Qílínshū).
Sīmǎ Zǐwéi, due to the retrograde motion of Mars,
created the Revolving Constellation Script (Zhuǎnxiùshū).
Lǔ Qiū Hú's wife, while playing with silkworms,
created the Insect Script (Chóngshū).
During the Six Kingdoms period,
this was used for confidential letters.
Lǐ Sī created the Fine Seal Script (Xìzhuànshū),
and also the Small Seal Script (Xiǎozhuàn),
which Shǐ Huáng used for prayers on famous mountains.
He also created the Carved Talisman Script (Kèfúshū),
used for inscribing seals.
In the Qín dynasty, Chéng Miǎo, in prison, transformed the Great Seal Script into the Clerical Script (Lìshū);
the ancient common clerical script
is what is now called the Bāfēn.
Xiāo Hé created the Signature Script (Shǔshū),
for inscribing the Azure Dragon and White Tiger Twin Gates (Cānglóng, Báihǔ Èrquè).
The Draft Script (Gǎoshū)
is a form of running script (cǎoxíng);
Dǒng Zhòngshū wished to speak of disasters and anomalies,
but Zhǔfù Yǎn stole and presented it.
Sīmǎ Xiāngrú, mimicking the four seasons,
created the Climate Script (Qìhòushū).
The Auspicious Ganoderma Script (Zhīyīngshū)
was used as a talisman during the Six Kingdoms period;
the Glorious Ganoderma Script (Yīngzhīshū)
was named so because the Hàn dynasty sang the "Song of the Ganoderma Chamber" (Zhīfáng zhī Qǔ).
The Gold Inlaid Script (Jīncuòshū)
was the name of an ancient coin.
The Shàngfāng Great Seal Script (Shàngfāng Dàzhuàn)
was described by Chéng Miǎo,
and later generations embellished it into a standard.
The Crane Head Script (Hètóushū) and the Undulating Wave Script (Yǎnbōshū)
were both used for imperial edict tablets,
which were the Hàn dynasty's one-foot-one bamboo slips.
The Mosquito Leg Script (Wénjiǎoshū)
was also for imperial edict tablets.
The Hanging Haze Seal Script (Chuíxiá Zhuàn) and the Hanging Needle Seal Script (Xuánzhēn Zhuàn)
were both favored by Emperor Zhāng of Hàn,
who created the Grass Script (Zhāngcǎoshū);
Wéi Dàn called it the "Sage of Grass Script."
Cài Yōng, while serving at the gate,
saw a servant making characters with a whitewash brush,
and upon returning, created the Flying White Script (Fēibái).
Zhāng Zhī created the One-Stroke Script (Yībǐshū).
Wáng Cìzhòng created the Bāfēn Script (Bāfēnshū).
Lǔ Zhōng dreamed of a snake coiling around his body,
and created the Snake Script (Shéshū).
The Running Script (Xíngshū)
is a slightly smaller version of regular script.
Zhōng Yáo's Running-Draft Script (Xíngyāshū).
Wèi Héng created the Scattered Clerical Script (Sànlì),
which is similar to Fēibái.
Wáng Xīzhī created the Dragon Claw Script (Lóngzhǎoshū).
Draft, Running, and Clerical Scripts,
Zhōng Yáo transformed them,
and the Two Wángs (Èr Wáng) further transformed them,
resulting in the Eight Styles of Script (Bātǐshū).
Wáng Sēngchǔ created the Melon Script (Guāshū).
The Ghost Script (Guǐshū) refers to
someone who was struck dead during the Yuánjiā era of Sòng,
and had characters resembling seal script on his arm.
There were also Foreign Barbarian Scripts (Wàiguó Húshū), and Indian Scripts (Tiānzhúshū).
Hédōng Sān created the Flower Script (Huāshū).
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng evaluated the calligraphy of twenty-eight individuals from the late Hàn to the Liáng dynasty.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng evaluated calligraphy, saying:
Zhōng Yáo's calligraphy is like a crane soaring in the clouds,
or a flock of ducks playing in the sea.
Wáng Xīzhī's character strokes are heroic and expansive,
like a dragon leaping through the gate of heaven,
or a tiger reposing in a phoenix pavilion.
Zhāng Zhī is like Emperor Wǔ of Hàn's fondness for the Dao,
floating in the void, wishing to become an immortal.
Cài Yōng's bone structure is penetrating and clear,
as if endowed with divine spirit.
Wéi Dàn is like a dragon's might and a tiger's roar,
a sword drawn and a crossbow strung.
Xiāo Zǐyún is like a perilous wind obstructing the sun,
a solitary pine with a single branch;
Jīng Kē carrying a sword,
a brave warrior drawing a bow,
a mighty man hunting tigers and sheep.
Xīn is like a maid of a literary family becoming a madam,
her manners shy and hesitant,
ultimately not truly resembling one.
Lǐ Zhèndōng is like a lotus emerging from water,
its brilliance fresh and clear.
Wáng Xiànzhī stands out from the crowd,
unparalleled by anyone,
like a young man from the Hésuò region,
his demeanor radiant and pleasing,
his whole being exuding charm,
irresistible.
Suǒ Jìng is like a whirlwind suddenly rising,
or a raptor suddenly taking flight.
Wáng Sēng's calligraphy is like the sons and brothers of the Wáng and Xiè families,
though their attire is not always proper,
they possess a refreshing and elegant strength.
Yán Jiù is like offering fruit from a poor family,
lacking in rare delicacies.
Ruǎn Yán is like a fruit losing its quality during travel.
Wáng Bāo's style is poignant and flowing, but the world does not match his appearance.
Shī Yí is like a hovering feather yet to rest,
lifting its wings to depart far.
Zhōng Huì has twelve kinds of unexpected wonders.
Táo Yǐnjū is like a young child from Wúxīng,
whose form is not yet fully developed, but whose bone structure is sharp and lively.
Although Xiāo Shí has a family style,
its elegance and force are weak.
Wáng Bīnbīn is unrestrained and sharp.
Fàn Huáiyuē's regular script is powerful,
but his running script is ineffective.
Wú Shī is like an old man from Xīntíng,
who, upon passing through Yángzhōu,
immediately developed a distinctive accent and manner.
Liǔ Hún has not fully grasped the essence.
Xī Yīn has grasped the essence very thoroughly,
but his thinness carries a sense of timidity.
Xú Wéi is like a scholar-official from Nángāng,
not lacking in demeanor.
Yuán Shānsōng's calligraphy is like a Daoist priest from a deep mountain,
who retreats upon seeing people.
Zhāng Sī is like an eloquent debater facing a crowd.
Bù Shào also has a distinctive family style.
Tadpole and Lacquer Scripts
King Gōng of Lǔ of Hàn destroyed the residence of Kǒngzǐ,
and a woman from Hénèi demolished the tomb of Lǐ Ěr (Lǎozi),
each finding ancient texts.
People at the time did not understand them,
and called them Tadpole Scripts (Kēdǒushū).
During the Tàikāng era of Jìn,
a farmer in Jíjùn uncovered the tomb of King Ānxī of Wèi,
obtaining bamboo slips with Lacquer Script (Qīshū).
Gourd History
During the Liáng dynasty, a monk crossed south,
carrying a gourd
containing Bān Gù's original text of the Hànshū.
The prefect of Xuānchéng, Xiāo Chēn, obtained it,
and called it "Gourd History" (Hùshǐ).
Falling Jade and Dripping Pearls
Liáng Shēngqīng's small seal script is like falling jade and dripping pearls.
White Jade Tower Records
When Lǐ Hè was about to die,
a man in scarlet robes drove a red *qiú*,
holding a tablet
inscribed with what looked like ancient seal script
or the ancient characters of thunderbolts.
He said he was summoning Hè.
Hè was unable to read it.
He went down the steps and kowtowed,
saying that Āmí was old and sick
and did not wish to go.
The man in scarlet robes said:
"The Dì has completed the Bái Yù Lóu,
and has urgently summoned you to write a record.
Life in Heaven is rather joyful and not hard."
A short while later, he breathed his last.
When Hè was learning to speak,
he called his *tàifūrén* "Āmí."
Thunderbolt script:
During the Yuánjiā reign of the Sòng dynasty,
someone in Jīngkǒu was struck dead by lightning.
On his arm were four vermilion characters written by a thunderbolt.
The four characters said:
"Killed by the karmic nexus."
Broken into ghost script:
Xiè Ān interpreting script:
Xiè Ānshí learned regular script from the Yòujūn.
The Yòujūn said:
"You are an interpreter of script,
and you know how difficult it is to interpret script."
Ānshí did not value Xiànzhī,
and when he obtained Xiànzhī's script,
he tore it into pieces of patterned paper.
Lady Wèi's script:
Lady Wèi's regular script entered the category of exquisite works,
like water in a jade pot,
or the moon on a jasper terrace,
graceful as a fragrant tree,
serene as a clear breeze.
Wáng Zǐjìng, at five years old,
often visited her with his elder brothers.
Lady Wèi wrote "Dàyǎ Yín" and bestowed it upon him.
*Lèyì Lùn*:
Princess Tàipíng of the Táng dynasty loved the *Lèyì Lùn*.
Zétiān gave it to her.
The Princess placed it in a woven bag within a chest.
When her property was confiscated,
an old woman from Xiányáng stole it away.
When county officials searched for it,
the old woman, in fright,
threw it into the stove.
Its fragrance was smelled for several days.
Discourse on Yòujūn's script:
Lǐ Sìzhēn, discussing Yòujūn's script, said:
"Ten thousand characters are not alike,
because its variations are hard to match.
When writing *Lèyì* and *Tàishǐ Zhēn*,
the forms are all upright and proper,
with the image of loyal ministers and virtuous women.
In *Gàoshì Wén* and *Cáo É Bēi*,
the appearance is sorrowful and worn,
with the image of filial sons and obedient grandsons.
In *Xiāoyáo Piān* and *Gūyàn Fù*,
the traces are distant and the interest high,
with the image of transcending the mundane and embracing simplicity.
In *Huàxiàng Zàn* and *Luòshén Fù*,
the posture and demeanor are elegant and beautiful,
with the image of dignified solemnity.
This is what is called achieving meaning,
not merely delighting in personal unique beauty."
Minor Sage:
The Yòujūn wrote *Lèyì Lùn* for Zǐjìng.
Later he said:
"This script is bestowed upon Guānnú."
He meant that he could reach the marvelous and enter the realm of the sage,
his sinews and bones no less than his father's.
Therefore, he was called the "Minor Sage."
Guānnú
was Zǐjìng's childhood name.
Zǐjìng's *Luòshén Fù*:
The Yuè family possessed a copy of *Luòshén Fù*,
which was Zǐjìng's small regular script,
written on bird-silk bordered paper.
Buying jade, gaining a lamb:
Yáng Xīn received instruction from Xiànzhī.
Shěn Yuē said:
"After Zǐjìng,
he can stand alone."
People said: "Buying jade, gaining a lamb,
one's hopes are not lost."
The *gē* stroke in the character *jiǎn*:
Emperor Tàizōng of Táng excelled at clerical script.
He studied under Yú Shìnán
and often had difficulty with the *gē* stroke.
One day, when writing the character "戩",
he left its right side empty.
Shìnán took the brush and filled it in.
The Emperor showed it to Wèi Zhènggōng and said:
"I have learned from Shìnán
to exhaust his method.
Please examine it."
Zhènggōng said:
"When a great brush faces a pond,
all forms cannot escape its shape.
It is not something that a subject's writing can emulate.
Looking up at Your Majesty's sacred work,
only the *gē* stroke in the character "戩"
is quite close to the original."
The Emperor deeply praised the Duke's profound discernment.
Monk Jié:
The Suí dynasty monk Jìngtuō was skilled in regular script.
With a large brush, he wrote characters a *fāngzhàng* in size.
They were naturally vigorous and powerful.
At the time, he was called "Monk Jié."
Three styles:
Zhōng Yáo had three styles:
The first was called *Míngshí*,
referring to regular script.
The second was called *Zhāngchéng*,
referring to *bāfēn* script.
The third was called *Xíngyā*,
referring to running script.
Immortal of Flying White:
Lǐ Sìzhēn said:
"Wáng Yìshǎo's flying white script is like mist in a valley unfurling and receding,
or smoke in the sky illuminating and dazzling.
Long swords stand straight and lean against the heavens,
swift arrows dart fleetingly into nothingness.
He can be called the 'Immortal of Flying White'."
Platform of Marvelous Steps and Precious Traces:
When Emperor Wén of Suí pacified Chén,
he obtained over eight hundred scrolls of calligraphy and painting in the Guānwén Diàn.
Later, he built two platforms.
The eastern one was called "Miàojiē,"
housing ancient and modern masterworks of calligraphy;
the western one was called "Bǎojì,"
collecting famous paintings from antiquity.
Obtaining the Yòujūn's flesh:
The Suí dynasty monk Zhìguǒ said that the meditation master Yǒng Chánshī Heshàng obtained the Yòujūn's flesh,
while Zhìguǒ obtained the Yòujūn's bones,
hidden within the flesh.
Obtaining an immortal's hand in calligraphy:
When a calligrapher first changed the Yòujūn's running script method,
with pauses, rises, and returns,
Lǐ Yángbīng called it "obtaining an immortal's hand in calligraphy."
Sage of Cursive:
Cuī Yuàn excelled at *zhāngcǎo* script.
Wáng Zǐjìng said:
"He is exactly like Zhāng Bóyīng."
Wáng Yǐn called him the "Sage of Cursive."
Profound and Vigorous:
Wú Huángxiàng excelled at running and cursive script.
He was known as "profound and vigorous."
Silver Hook and Scorpion Tail:
Suǒ Jìng's cursive script was unrivaled in his generation,
named "Silver Hook and Scorpion Tail."
Selling letters for wealth:
Zhāng Xù said:
"A lonely tumbleweed sways by itself,
startled sand flies up on its own.
The ultimate of cursive sages is in this!"
There was a poor scholar who was Xù's neighbor.
He would send Xù several letters a day
and obtain his written replies.
He then sold them in the market,
thereby acquiring wealth.
Emulating Summer Clouds:
Monk Huáisù said of himself that he possessed the *sānmèi* of the cursive sage.
He also said:
"I observe the many strange peaks in summer clouds,
and always emulate them.
Summer clouds change with the wind,
and thus have no constant form."
Zhèng Qián's Three Excellences:
During the Kāiyuán reign, Zhèng Qián
would present poems, calligraphy, and paintings.
Emperor Mínghuáng would personally inscribe:
"Zhèng Qián's Three Excellences."
Qián's cursive script was like wind sweeping away clouds and gathering them,
or the evening glow urging the moon to rise,
large and small perfectly balanced.
Shì Yàqī was good at cursive script.
He said of himself:
"My calligraphy is neither too large nor too small,
it attains the middle way.
Like birds flying out of a forest,
or startled snakes entering grass.
Calligraphy that changes through mastery is exemplified by
Wáng changing Zǐyún's style,
Ōu changing Yòujūn's style,
and Liǔ changing Ōuyáng's style.
Zhìyǒng Chánshī, Chǔ Suìliáng, Yán Zhēnqīng, Lǐ Yōng, Yú Shìnán, and others,
all gained proficiency in calligraphy,
then transformed their own styles,
and all achieved lasting fame.
If one adheres to rules without change,
it is called 'slave calligraphy'."
Planting Banana Trees
Lù Yǔ's "Biography of Huáisù" states:
"He was unrestrained and paid no attention to minor details.
He drank wine to nourish his nature,
and wrote cursive script to express his aspirations.
When he was tipsy and inspired,
he would write on any temple wall, village wall, clothing, or utensil.
Being poor and without paper,
he planted over ten thousand banana trees,
to provide for his brushwork.
He also lacquered a plate and a square board,
and wrote on them until both the plate and board were worn through."
Ancient Hairpin Foot and House Leakage Mark
Yán Lǔgōng and Huáisù studied cursive script together under Guō Bīngcáo.
Someone asked:
"Zhāng Chángshǐ saw Gōngsūn Dàniáng's sword dance,
and grasped the forms of rising, falling, circling, and soaring.
Does Bīngcáo have such a thing?"
Huáisù responded with "ancient hairpin foot."
Lǔgōng said:
"What about the 'house leakage mark'?"
Huáisù embraced Lǔgōng's leg and slept.
Lǔgōng asked again:
"Master, what did you gain?"
He replied:
"Poor me, when I studied Master Xià Yún's writings,
I encountered cracked walls on the road,
each one natural."
Yìshǎo Specializes in the Character 'Yǒng'
The "Jìnjīng" states:
"The Eight Principles originated at the beginning of clerical script characters."
Lǐ Yángbīng said:
"Wáng Yìshǎo was skilled in calligraphy,
and for fifteen years,
he particularly specialized in the character 'yǒng,'
because its eight strokes' momentum
can apply to all characters."
The character 'yǒng' has eight strokes.
Crane Head and Mosquito Leg
The "crane head" and "mosquito leg" two scripts
were both used on Hàn imperial decrees,
each being pictorial.
Burying Jade and Embedding Fragrance
During the Wáng Shǔ period,
when Qínzhōu was building its city walls,
a stone inscription in a tile coffin read:
"Wáng Shì, wife of Zhāng Chóng, governor of Wèizhōu during the second year of Suí Kāixuān."
The inscription contained the phrases: "Deeply burying jade,
and luxuriantly embedding fragrance."
Brush Tiger
Dòu Quán called Lǐ Yángbīng's seal script "brush tiger."
He also created small seal script,
and praised it, saying:
"The prime minister's style,
his divine thoughts are profound.
Hairpins bend like jade,
tripods hang like gold."
One-Stroke Script
Zhāng Zhī's cursive script,
with its continuous qi and脉 (脈),
unbroken across lines,
was called "one-stroke script."
Kǒng Jìngtōng was also skilled in cursive script,
able to write one line in one continuous stroke, but that was all.
Eight-Part Script
Cài Wénjī said:
"My father said that clerical script takes eight parts and keeps two,
while seal script takes two parts and keeps eight,
hence it is called eight-part script."
Zhāng Huáiguàn said:
"Bójiē's characters gradually dispersed as if forming the character 'bā' (八),
hence it is called eight-part script."
Letter to Grandee Lǐ
Lǐ Yángbīng's letter to Grandee Lǐ states:
"My aspiration lies in ancient seal script.
From heaven, earth, mountains, and rivers, I grasp the constant forms of squareness, roundness, flow, and stillness.
From the sun, moon, and stars, I attain the degrees of longitude, latitude, and brilliant rotation.
From clouds, mist, grass, and trees, I derive the forms of spreading, scattering, nurturing, and sprawling.
From attire, crowns, cultural artifacts, I learn the manners of bowing, yielding, and circling.
From hair, eyebrows, mouth, and nose, I discern the divisions of joy, anger, sorrow, and cheerfulness.
From insects, fish, birds, and beasts, I comprehend the principles of bending, stretching, flying, and moving.
From bones, fur, teeth, and tusks, I capture the momentum of pulling, swinging, chewing, and gnawing.
With a flick of the hand, myriad changes occur;
whatever the mind desires is accomplished.
I often lament that the remaining texts from Kǒng Wèibi [Kong's wall]
and the old bamboo slips from Jí Zhǒng [Jí Tomb]
are from too ancient times,
and errors abound."
Self-Engraved
Lǐ Yōng's calligraphy
was often self-engraved,
and he frequently used fictitious names for the engravers,
such as Fúlíng Zhī, Huáng Xiānhè, and the like.
Drawing on the Stomach with a Hand
Wáng Shàozōng said:
"When writing calligraphy, and encountering ink,
one practices like Yú Qī, drawing on his stomach with his hand while in bed."
Ding Inscription
When Emperor Xuān's sweet dew descended on Huàshān's Xiānzhǎng Peak,
a ding was cast to collect the dew,
and an inscription was carved, saying:
"All nations submit with tribute,
long-lasting cast divine
ding receiving heavenly wine."
Calligraphy Extremes
Yú Shìnán had five extremes,
Zhōng Zhàojīng three extremes,
Zhèng Qián three extremes,
monk Hóng Yǎn four extremes,
Lǐ Yōng six extremes,
all were skilled in calligraphy, which constituted one of their extremes.
Five-Colored Paper
Xiāo Chéng collected wild hemp and paper mulberry,
and made five-colored, variegated paper.
Discourse on Calligraphy
Guō Zhōngshù's discourse on calligraphy states:
"Small seal script scattered and eight-part script was born;
eight-part script broke and clerical script emerged;
clerical script went astray and running script was made;
running script became wild and cursive script was deified.
From clerical script downwards,
I do not wish to observe."
Praise for the Character 'Xiāo'
Lǐ Yuē's wall inscription, "Praise for the Character 'Xiāo'," says:
"Splashing, surging with momentum,
magnificent and mighty in spirit.
A startled whale in Kūnchí,
fighting dragons at Mèngmén."
It also says:
"Embracing purity, daily clean,
containing essence, internally fused.
Transcending doubt beyond the worldly,
all within the compass.
Art reaching the utmost of creation,
its comparisons are endless."
Six Principles
Painting has six principles:
First, spirit resonance and vivid movement;
second, bone structure using the brush;
third, responding to objects by depicting their forms;
fourth, suiting colors to their categories;
fifth, planning and placement of elements;
sixth, transmission through copying and imitation.
Forced Naming: The First
Lù Kòngwēi thoroughly understood the essence of painting,
his characters transcended words and images,
encompassing past and future,
standing unique throughout history.
For the highest grades and above,
there is no place for words.
Forcibly giving it a name,
it is reluctantly designated as 'the first.'
Ascending the Tower and Removing the Ladder
Gù Kǎizhī built a multi-storied tower as his painting studio.
During strong winds and heavy rains,
blazing heat and bitter cold,
he would not put brush to paper.
When summer and winter had passed,
and the world was bright and clear,
he would then dip his brush,
ascend the tower, and remove the ladder,
rarely seen by his wife and children.
Moving Pictures
Liú Shàozǔ's copies and imitations were so precise
that he was at the time called "moving pictures."
However, he recounted rather than created,
which is not what painting primarily values.
Mùyàn tú
Gù Gōng's application is exquisite and subtle,
his spiritual heart immeasurable.
He left his mark in calligraphy and painting;
his spirit and vitality fluttered as if above the clouds,
not to be sought within mere pictures.
To stand as his equal
one would not find such a person.
The Mùyàn tú is like a roc soaring and a dragon leaping,
disappearing into the Milky Way,
which scales or feathers cannot pursue.
Lù Gōng's brushwork is wondrous and penetrates the spirit;
his movements are in harmony with the divine.
His splendid paintings are vigorous and sharp,
like a drill or a knife.
His Shìxián tú, when compared to the Mùyàn,
is not merely a slight difference in quality.
The Reincarnation of Sēngyóu
I once discussed painting with Wú Hùcáo Dàozǐ
and did not notice the passage of the entire day.
This gentleman's talent is far-reaching and his thoughts profound;
when he puts brush to paper, it is as if there is divine assistance.
For two hundred years, he has had virtually no equal.
He is therefore the reincarnation of Zhāng Sēngyóu.
Painting on Fans
Xiāo Yù often painted on fans,
depicting mountains.
Within a mere foot,
one could behold a thousand li's distance.
Within a square inch,
one could discern the steepness of a thousand zhàng.
A Bed on Top of a Bed
Máo Léng,
Hùiyuǎn's son,
was quick and fluent, with ample skill,
but his true artistry was insufficient.
He was good at composition,
sketchy yet not cumbersome.
If compared to his father,
it would be like putting a bed on top of a bed.
Illness of Qīngxián
Yuán Zhì,
the youngest son of the former,
was handsome and spirited,
not diminishing his family's reputation.
Starting from the age of aspiring to study,
he already suffered from qīngxián.
Formerly, I saw his brushwork was vigorous and strong,
indistinguishable from his father's paintings.
Wáng Zǐjìng's Painting
Wáng Zǐjìng was painting on a fan,
when he accidentally dropped his brush.
He then turned it into a spirited bird and a reclining ox,
absolutely marvelous.
In ancient times, Gāo Xiàoxíng, the King of Guǎngníng in Northern Qí, painted eagles and falcons in a hall.
Spectators barely knew it was a painting.
Doves and pigeons, seeing it from afar,
were all terrified.
Wáng Zǐjìng also transcribed the Bó Niú Fù onto a fan.
The Sage of Painting
Yáng Zǐhuá of Northern Qí painted horses on a wall;
every evening, they would kick, bite, and whinny,
as if demanding water and grass.
He also painted dragons on plain silk;
when unrolled or rolled up, clouds and mists would gather and disperse.
Shìzǔ called him "the Sage of Painting."
A Roof on Top of a Roof
Zhèng Fǎlún of the Suí dynasty had meticulous brushwork.
Compared to his elder brother,
it would perhaps be like building a roof on top of a roof.
Zhànrán's Bees and Butterflies
Sì Téngwáng Zhànrán painted a scroll of bees, butterflies, and sparrows.
He exhausted all the subtle principles.
Transformations of Hell
Wú Dàoxuán,
courtesy name Dàozǐ,
after finishing his paintings of the Transformations of Hell,
all the people of the capital came to view them.
They were all terrified of sin and cultivated blessings.
Butchers and wine sellers in both markets, and fish vendors, did not gather customers.
Three Men Each Show Their Skill
During the Kāiyuán era,
the Emperor journeyed to Dōngluò.
Wú Dàozǐ met with General Péi Wú and Palace Secretary Zhāng Xù.
Each displayed his skill:
Péi performed a sword dance,
while Zhāng and Wú each wrote and painted a wall.
Jiālíng Landscape
Emperor Míng suddenly longed for the Jiālíng landscape in Shǔ.
So he ordered Wú Dàoxuán to go and depict it via post-station.
Upon his return,
he reported:
"Your servant has no drafts;
they are all remembered in my mind."
He was then commanded to paint them in the Dàtóng Palace.
The three hundred li of Jiālíng River landscape
were completed in one day.
At that time, there was General Lǐ,
who also painted in the Dàtóng Palace,
taking several months to complete.
Emperor Míng said:
"Sīxùn's months of work
and Dàoxuán's one day's achievement
are both extremely marvelous."
Five Dragons
Wú Dàozǐ painted five dragons inside the palace;
their scales and armor seemed to fly.
Whenever a great rain was imminent,
smoke and mist would arise.
Portraits
Zhōu Fǎng exhausted the marvels of painting.
Zhào Zòng, Assistant Minister and son-in-law of Guō Lìnggōng,
once commissioned Hán Gàn to paint his portrait,
and then invited Fǎng to paint one.
He could not determine their superiority.
When Madame Zhào Guó returned to visit her parents,
Lìnggōng asked who painted this picture.
She replied:
"Zhào Láng."
He then asked:
"Which one is most similar?"
She replied:
"Both paintings are similar;
the latter painter is better.
The former painting merely captured Zhào Láng's appearance,
while the latter captured both his spirit, essence, and character."
Lìnggōng then asked who the latter painter was.
She replied:
"Zhōu Chángshǐ."
Thus, the superiority of the two paintings was determined.
Furthermore, Zhōu Fǎng's paintings of women and children were unmatched in ancient and modern times.
On the left side, the luán (mythical bird),
and modern cut-branch flowers ranked first.
Wáng Mò
Wáng Mò was skilled at ink splashing;
at the time, he was called "Wáng Mò."
He was good at painting landscapes, pine trees, cypress trees, and various other trees.
After becoming tipsy from wine,
he would first splash ink,
kick with his feet and wipe with his hands,
shaping it into mountains, rocks, and trees according to its form.
Responding to his heart and following his will,
he instantly created nature.
Snow and mist wept over it,
wind and rain swept over it,
without revealing any traces of ink stains.
Flowers and Birds
Wéi Luán's flowers and birds were exquisite and subtle.
Hermit Xiāo Yuè was skilled at bamboo,
a single color with elegant charm.
Pine and Rocks
Wéi Yǎn's pine and rocks.
His paternal uncle was skilled at dragons and horses;
his father, Luán, was skilled at landscapes, pines, and rocks.
Yǎn was skilled at immortal monks, ancient pines, and unusual rocks.
People knew he was good at horses,
but did not know he was even more skilled at pine and rocks.
Within a foot, a thousand zhàng;
many trunks clustered with shadows,
smoke and mist bursting forth,
wind and rain howling.
Their winding forms resembled overturned canopies,
their twisting shapes were like coiling dragons.
Left Province Wall Paintings
Bì Hóng became Gěishìzhōng in the second year of Dàlì,
and painted pine and rocks on the wall of the Left Province Hall.
All those who loved such things wrote poems to praise them.
Skilled in Calligraphy and Painting
Wáng Xù, King of Jiāngdū,
son of Huò Wáng Yuánguǐ,
also a nephew of Tàizōng.
He had many talents and skills,
and was skilled at calligraphy, painting, saddles, and horses.
Wáng Zǎi Transcends Form
Wáng Zǎi painted landscapes and trees,
transcending physical form.
Wéi Lìnggōng treated him as an honored guest.
Six Canons Fully Equipped
Yáng Qìzǐ,
a man from the Suí-Táng interregnum,
rose to the office of Shàng Yítóng.
The Six Canons were fully equipped in him;
but if one looks at his 'bone-spirit',
he was inferior to Yán Lìběn.
Presenting Loquats
Táng Tàizōng
wrote: “The envoy has arrived,
and I have received the loquats you sent.
I am deeply pleased and comforted.
These excellent fruits are a rare delicacy,
I appreciate their seasonal freshness.
However, the journey is long,
there is no need to send more.”
Duànshǒu
Gāozōng
wrote: “The envoy has arrived,
and I learned that Xuántáng is complete.
Having obtained early offspring,
I am deeply comforted.
I don’t know when all the works will be finished with Duànshǒu.”
Zhīfàzhěnwēi
Yǔ Liàng
wrote: “Liàng reports,
I have received the imperial edict and a memorial in a box.
First, I made Zhīfà for Tízi,
but there is no model.
If there is one,
it can be temporarily given to her.”
Wùyìquán
Jì Zhān
wrote: “Zhān reports,
since I received your letter yesterday,
Yì is even poorer,
and has nothing to express his intentions with.
Two dòu of flour,
this is what is meant by ‘the object is small but the intention is complete’.”
Yuèyì Lùn
Yú Shìnán
wrote: “My esteemed brother's 'Yuèyì Lùn'
truly surpasses the master.
I am immensely delighted.”
Qiúchìjiàn
Liǔ Gōngquán
wrote: “I received your honored message,
and understand that it has been presented.
My humble heart is both joyful and apprehensive.
Your kindness in asking what I need
fills me with overwhelming gratitude.
If there is a season for Chìjiàn,
please send three liǎng,
to help my declining health.
Not fully expressed.
Gōngquán’s respectful report.”
Wénzi Wéi Zōulǔ
Lǐ Sī
wrote: “Farming and weeding were used to govern the fields,
and within a year, success was achieved.
The law made Wénzi the Zōulǔ.”
Píngshū
Sēng Huáisù
wrote: “Yòujūn said:
‘My regular and cursive scripts surpass Zhōng,
and my cursive script is certainly no less than Zhāng’s.’
I believe his regular script is not as good as Zhōng’s,
and his cursive script is not as good as Zhāng’s.”
Juīmián
Wáng Xīzhī
wrote: “I just received your letter,
and know that you asked about my desires.
I heard the words with great dissatisfaction.
I was sleeping peacefully at home,
unaware of your arrival.
I regret not having met you for a moment.
Xīzhī’s humble greeting.”
Qiáozhōu Sūn
Wáng Xīzhī
wrote: “Qiáo Zhōu has a grandson,
who is lofty and does not go out.”
Jūnpíngděng Yǒuhòufǒu
Xīzhī
wrote: “My dear sir,
do Yán Jūnpíng, Sīmǎ Xiāngrú, and Yáng Zǐyún
all have descendants?”
Rénwù Miǎorán
Xīzhī
wrote: “Cài Gōng is critically ill.
Having seen Rénzǔ on the twenty-sixth for his illness,
he became even more critically ill,
which is deeply concerning.
Today, notable figures are few and far between,
which makes one disheartened.”
Fēibái Jiāzào
Xīzhī
wrote: “Fēibái is truly excellent.
When one hastily seeks it,
one is almost exhausted,
let alone making small progress.”
Qiú Lángdú
Xīzhī
wrote: “My younger sister-in-law is not well
and needs Lángdú,
but it cannot be found in the market.
If you happen to have some,
please share three liǎng.”
Éqún
Wáng Xiànzhī
wrote: “I do not know the situation of the various families in Hǎiyán, their ups and downs,
this is a constant worry.
Liú Dàoshì’s goose flock
has also returned.”
Juàn zhī Wǔshíbā
End.
Liángtián Chúléi
Cài Hóng went to Luòzhōng,
and someone asked what the registered surnames in Wúzhōng were doing.
He replied:
“The gentlemen in Wúzhōng take paper as fertile land,
pens as hoes and plows,
ink as crops,
and righteousness and reason as a bountiful harvest.”
Yòujūn Bǐ
Zhūgě Shì of Xuānzhōu was skilled at making brushes.
Liǔ Gōngquán sought them.
He first gave two brushes,
and said to his son:
“If Scholar Liǔ is a skilled calligrapher,
he will keep these brushes.
Otherwise, he will return them,
and then give him ordinary brushes.”
Not long after,
Liǔ returned them as they were not suitable for his use and requested others.
So, he was given ordinary brushes.
The two brushes given earlier
could only be used by Yòujūn.
Bànmiàn Xiàobànmiàntí
Jiǎ Bì dreamed of having his head exchanged.
The next day, everyone who saw him was astonished,
for he could laugh on one side of his face
and cry on the other.
Bǐxiān
At the end of the Shíjìn dynasty,
a recluse in Rǔzhōu made ten brushes every night
and sold them in the morning.
Later, he moved away and his whereabouts were unknown.
Decades later,
people saw him again.
His complexion was as before,
and he was called “Bǐxiān.”
Sìshí Lìng
Cuī Shí’s 'Sìshí Lìng':
“In the first month, when the inkstone thaws,
children begin primary school.
In the eleventh month, when the inkstone water freezes,
they are commanded to read the 'Lúnyǔ'.”
Xiě Huáyánjīng
During the Yǒnghuī era,
a monk in Dìngzhōu wanted to copy the 'Huáyánjīng'.
First, he planted paper mulberry trees using agarwood water,
and used them to make paper.
Jiàngluójiān
Zhāng Zhòngshū was in Guǎng.
During a long rain,
he made many Jiàngluójiān.
Quèzhuì Fāngcùnzhǐ
During the Dàzhōng era,
Kǒng Wēnyù was demoted to Sīmǎ of Léizhōu.
A magpie dropped a square inch of paper from above,
which had the characters “Bǔquē” on it.
Not long after, he was indeed reinstated.
Bēigǔténg Wén
Shū Yuánxú wrote 'Bēi Yǎn Xī Gǔténg Wén',
its outline states:
“Yǎn Xī has many ancient wisteria trees,
which die in early spring.
The people on the banks of the stream say
that there are many paper makers in the stream,
who fell trees indiscriminately.
Today, the number of scholars who claim to be skilled in writing
is greater than that of trees and bamboo.
Who among them does not write on Yǎn Xī wisteria?
Even if the whole world were a stream,
it would still not be enough,
let alone one stream?
I say that those who wrote then and now
all died by means of Yǎn Xī wisteria.”
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ (李後主) was attentive to writing instruments.
The Chéngxīntáng (澄心堂) paper, Lǐ Tíngguī (李廷珪) ink, and Lóngwěi (龍尾) stone inkstones he used
were considered the finest under heaven.
Yòujūn's (右軍) "wind-character" inkstone.
An old man in Kuàijī (會稽) said:
"A descendant of Yòujūn (右軍) possesses a 'wind-character' inkstone,
over a foot in size,
perfectly red in color.
When used, it is no less effective than Duān (端) stone.
It is said to have been used by Yòujūn (右軍).
Shí Tāngxiū (石湯休) acquired it for twenty thousand cash."
Hóngsī (紅絲) Stone.
Qīngzhōu (青州) hóngsī (紅絲) stone
has an outer skin.
When ground, its grain appears.
Red and yellow intermingle.
For those with a yellow grain,
their 'silk' is red;
for those with a red grain,
their 'silk' is yellow.
It must be adequately watered
before it can be used,
otherwise, it will be dry and thirsty.
Táng Yànlóu (唐彥猷) greatly admired this inkstone,
believing its ink-emitting quality was no less than Duān (端) stone.
Cài Jūnmó (蔡君謨) also said:
"Duān (端) stone is lustrous and smooth.
Only those with '鋩' (spikes/sharpness) are particularly good at emitting ink.
Shè (歙) stone often has '鋩',
but only those with a greasy texture are good.
For extraordinary objects,
their uniqueness must differ from their kind."
Fèngzhū (鳳硃) Stone.
Sū Zǐzhān (蘇子瞻) said:
"I am fond of Fèngzhū (鳳硃) stone,
but rarely find genuine ones.
Táng Yànlóu (唐彥猷) considered Qīngzhōu (青州) hóngsī (紅絲) stone to be supreme,
but perhaps it is only suitable for making dice bowls."
Duānyàn (端硯).
Sū Gōng Yìjiǎn (蘇公易簡) said:
"Liǔ Gōngquán (柳公權) ranked green stone as first,
that from Jiàngzhōu (絳州) as second,
without mentioning Duān (端) stone at all."
It is widely believed that in Duānxī (端溪),
there is an abundance of charming moss.
When craftsmen carve stone into inkstones,
they pack it with this moss.
Thus, it can travel from Lǐngbiǎo (嶺表) to Zhōngxià (中夏) without damage.
Some say:
"The stone from the water is blue in color;
the stone from halfway up the mountain is purple;
the stone from the absolute summit
is even more lustrous, and those the color of pig's liver are best.
Where water is stored, if there are white, yellow, or red spots,
they are called qúyùyǎn (鴝鵒眼, mynah bird eyes).
If the vein texture is yellow,
it is called jīnxianwén (金線紋, gold thread pattern).
The mountain is called Fǔkē (斧柯).
In ancient times, when people collected stone for inkstones,
they would surely sacrifice a sheep in its pen,
otherwise, thunder and lightning would strike,
and they would lose the location of the stone."
Qúyùyǎn (鴝鵒眼).
Duān (端) stone with 'eyes' is the most precious,
called qúyùshí (鴝鵒石, mynah bird stone).
The patterns are exquisite,
like knots in wood.
Nowadays, those who do not know
mistakenly consider them a defect in the stone.
Alas, how lamentable!
Stones come from the upper and lower caves,
and Xīkēng (西坑).
The latter are all inferior.
Only the upper cave has 'eyes',
and the finest among these are green, blue, and yellow in three colors,
with many layers.
From the outside to the center, there are usually nine layers.
The larger ones are particularly rare.
Sometimes they are arranged in the inkstone
in the shape of the Big Dipper or the Scorpio constellation.
Local people judge the price by the number of 'eyes'.
Those appearing outside the inkwell
are called gāoyǎn (高眼, high eyes);
those inside are dǐyǎn (底眼, bottom eyes).
Gāoyǎn (高眼) are particularly esteemed,
as they are not stained by ink
and can always be seen.
Some say:
"Offer a medium sacrifice when extracting the stone."
Old folks say this is not the case.
Some say:
"Stone with 'gold threads' is beautiful."
This is a distorted view.
Zǐshí (子石).
Among Duān (端) stone, zǐshí (子石, 'child stone') is considered superior,
growing within large stones.
It is essentially fine stone.
Common folk mistakenly call it zǐshí (紫石, purple stone).
It is also considered good if it retains water without loss.
Having valuable 'eyes'
is a defect in the stone.
Government officials submit it as annual tribute,
above other inkstones.
However, only one or two out of ten are good at emitting ink;
they merely serve as curiosities.
Duānxī (端溪).
Duānxī (端溪) has Fǔkē (斧柯), Cháyuán (茶園), and Jiāngjūndì (將軍地).
All are from Duānxī (端溪),
but those from Fǔkē (斧柯)
are no larger than three or four fingers,
weighing one or two *hē* (呵).
Their moisture drips,
truly a rare find.
Cháyuán (茶園) is second,
and Jiāngjūndì (將軍地) is again second.
Huóyǎn (活眼) and Sǐyǎn (死眼).
Sū Yìjiǎn (蘇易簡) wrote the *Wénfáng Sìpǔ* (文房四譜, Four Treasures of the Study),
which states:
"Among the four treasures, the inkstone is paramount.
Brushes, ink, and paper can all be acquired at any time,
but the only item that can accompany one throughout life
is the inkstone."
The *Pǔ* (譜) records over forty grades,
with Qīngzhōu (青州) hóngsī (紅絲) stone as first,
Fǔkēshān (斧柯山) as second,
and Lóngwěishí (龍尾石) as third;
the rest are in the middle to lower grades.
Even the inkstones from Tóngquètái (銅雀臺) and tile inkstones are listed in the lower grades,
merely preserved as ancient objects.
Duān (端) produces four types:
Yánshí (岩石, rock stone) is first,
Shíwū (石屋, stone house) is second,
Xīkēng (西坑) is again second,
and Hòulì (後歷) is the inferior rock,
twenty *lǐ* (里) distant from Xīkēng (西坑).
Seven *lǐ* (里) from Hòulì (後歷),
what is produced is strikingly different.
This is like Ān (安) producing tea,
and Běiyuàn (北苑) and Hèyuán (壑源) being ten-odd *lǐ* (里) from Shāxī (沙溪),
yet their quality varies greatly.
Yánshí (岩石) is further divided into upper and lower,
and there is also the distinction between huóyǎn (活眼, 'living eyes') and sǐyǎn (死眼, 'dead eyes').
Circular and layered,
with yellow and black interspersed,
with a dark essence inside,
crystal clear and lovely,
are called huóyǎn (活眼).
Those whose four sides are soaked,
not very bright,
are called lèiyǎn (淚眼, 'tear eyes').
Those with a basic shape,
identical inside and out,
completely lacking luster,
are called sǐyǎn (死眼).
Huóyǎn (活眼) are superior to lèiyǎn (淚眼),
lèiyǎn (淚眼) are superior to sǐyǎn (死眼),
and sǐyǎn (死眼) are superior to having no eyes.
Lóngwěixī (龍尾溪).
Shè (歙) stone comes from Lóngwěixī (龍尾溪),
valued for its jīnxīng (金星, 'gold stars').
When I was young, I obtained a jīnkēng (金坑, 'gold pit') ore stone,
which was hard and good at emitting ink.
Duānxī (端溪) values the northern cave as superior,
and Lóngwěi (龍尾) values depth as superior.
Lóngwěi (龍尾) is superior to Duānxī (端溪) in that it became valued later than Duān (端) stone.
It only became prized after Duān (端) stone emerged.
Lǐ Hè's (李賀) Poem.
Yǒngshú (永叔) believed Duānxī (端溪) emerged later,
but this is not true.
Lǐ Hè (李賀) has a poem *Duānxī Qīnghuā Shíyàn* (端溪青花石硯, Duānxī Blue Flower Stone Inkstone) that says:
"Crimson wine, Chánghóng (萇弘) swallowed bloodstains,"
referring to qúyùyǎn (鴝鵒眼),
indicating Duān (端) stone had been used as inkstones for a long time.
Various Zhōu Inkstones
The inkstones from Zīzhōu are made of Jīnquèshí (Golden Sparrow Stone).
Their color is deep purplish-blue,
and when tapped, they sound like gold and jade.
There is also Qīngjīnshí (Blue Goldstone),
which makes no sound when tapped,
but grinds ink well.
From Qīngzhōu comes Zǐjīnshí (Purple Gold Stone),
whose form resembles the Xīkēng stone from Duānzhōu,
and it grinds ink even better.
The purple stone from Yǒngfú Xiàn in Jízhōu
also resembles Xīkēng stone.
From Chí Mù Dǎo in Dēngzhōu, there is stone
with wavy patterns and golden specks on it.
The corner stone from Jiàngzhōu
is the color of a white ox horn.
The Dàtuó stone from Guīzhōu
is a river stone found in the Jiāng River,
and it is used in Chuānxiá.
Entering Sùzhōu, Lèshí (Music Stone) is produced.
It is smooth, oily, and grinds ink well,
but it lacks stone veins.
Wànzhōu has Xuánjīnyá stone,
and also Cídòng stone.
The Táohé River produces green stone,
which is warm and brings out the ink,
but it doesn't withstand prolonged grinding.
The Dānshí from Láoshān
is smooth, lustrous, firm, and oily.
Ancient tile inkstones are found in Xiāngzhōu from the Wèi Tóngquè Tái;
local people, when digging the earth,
often find them.
Chéngní from Guózhōu,
when people in the Táng dynasty graded inkstones,
it was considered the best,
but today it is rarely used.
In Zézhōu, the Daoist Lǚ Wēng made Chéngní inkstones,
which were as firm and heavy as stone.
When touched by hand, a halo would immediately appear,
and the character "Lǚ" was inscribed on them.
The stone from Qīngtānzhōu and Yǒng inkstones
are all grinding inkstones.
Liǔ Gōngquán considered them the best,
but this must have been before he saw Xī stone,
and so he regarded them as superior.
Inkstone Rhapsody
Chuán Xuán's "Yàn Fù" says:
"Wood is valued for its softness,
stone is beautiful for its moist firmness.
Daoist friends use floating rafts as inkstones,
which shows that ancient times also had water inkstones."
Bronze Inkstones and Clam Inkstones
Liú Cōng said to Jìn Huáidì:
"Recently, you presented me with a bronze inkstone made of mulberry wood."
Yuán Tuǎn presented Yú Yì with a clam inkstone.
Crystal Inkstones
Dīng Shù had a crystal inkstone,
only about four inches in size,
shaped like the character "fēng".
When used with ink, it did not reflect light,
and it ground ink as well as Xī stone.
Jade Inkstones
Lǐ Chōngbó, the Liúhòu of Zhèntóng, obtained jade material,
and carved it into a round inkstone.
It ground ink delightfully.
Green Jade Inkstones
Xǔ Hànyáng's brush had a white jade handle,
and his inkstone was made of green jade,
with a glass case.
Iron Inkstones
In Qīngzhōu, inkstones are made of refined iron,
which grind ink very well,
and have handles for holding.
Jìn Sāng Wéihàn cast raw iron inkstones.
Lacquer Inkstones
Jìn Yí Kuáng,
when the crown prince married his consort,
there was a lacquer inkstone.
Bamboo Inkstones
The "Yìwù Zhì" says:
"In Guǎngnán, inkstones are made of bamboo."
Cleaning Inkstones
All inkstones must be cleaned once a day.
Even if that's not possible,
the water must be changed daily.
For washing, a small felt pad or paper should be used.
If used for a long time,
the stone surface will become stained and dirty.
Then, grind and wash it with bran charcoal,
and it will be like new again.
In bitter cold, fine inkstones should not be used,
as the stone texture freezes,
and the ink will have less luster.
The Inkstone of Dìhóng Shì
The Yellow Emperor obtained very fine jade,
and fashioned it into an "Ink Sea".
On it were inscribed the characters:
"The Inkstone of Dìhóng Shì."
Also, the "Tài Gōng Jīnkuì Yàn Shū" says:
"When stone and ink adhere,
evil thoughts and slanders will not be revealed white."
From this, we know that inkstones have a long history.
An inkstone (yàn)
is for grinding (yán),
it can grind ink to make it smooth and moist.
Confucius's Inkstone
Wǔ Wěi's "Cóng Zhēng Jì" says:
"In the Confucius Temple in Lǔguó, there is one stone inkstone,
very ancient material,
an item Confucius used in his daily life.
The carriage requested by Yán Lù is also preserved."
Yànxī
The "Yǒngjiā Jùn Jì" says:
"Yànxī, a ridge, has many stone inkstones."
The "Shù Yì Jì" says:
"On a slope in Dòngtíng Hú, there are Fàn Lǐ's stone bed and stone inkstone."
A Chest of Worn-out Inkstones
An ancient person learned calligraphy from a master.
After several years, he thought his skill was perfected,
and he bade farewell and left.
The master said:
"I have a chest of items,
which can be delivered to a certain place."
Upon reaching the foot of the mountain,
there was no one to deliver them to.
The seal on the package was also not very tight,
so he opened it.
Inside were dozens of inkstones, all worn down with holes from grinding.
He then realized these were the ones the master had used for many years.
So he returned to the mountain, devoted himself to study,
and only completed his art when his hair turned white.
Repairing a Hundred Broken Inkstones
During the Shí Jìn period,
in Guān Yòu, there was a recluse named Lǐ,
who could paint four badgers,
and also repair Duān inkstones that were broken into a hundred pieces.
He would take them home, and within ten days, they would be restored to their original state,
as if newly carved,
with hardly any flaws or defects.
No one in the world knew his method.
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ's Green Stone Inkstone
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ obtained a green stone inkstone.
In the inkwell, there was a yellow stone,
like a pellet,
and water was always full.
Even when used all day, it did not diminish.
He always kept it with him.
Later, when he returned to court,
Táo Gǔ saw it and found it extraordinary.
The inkstone was too large to carry,
so he took the stone pellet.
After he left, the king pulled his hand, shook his arm, and mounted his horse.
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ offered precious playthings as thanks,
but Táo did not accept.
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ said:
"Only this inkstone can produce water;
all other inkstones are unusable."
Táo tried dozens of inkstones,
and none produced water.
Lǐ Hòuzhǔ begged him bitterly,
but could not persuade him,
and said:
"Then I must smash it."
When the stone broke,
a small fish jumped onto the ground,
and immediately died.
From then on, the inkstone lost its luster and moisture.
True Material and Original Nature
Inkstones should be made of stone,
mirrors should be made of bronze;
this is their true material and original nature.
Using a tile as an inkstone
is like using iron as a mirror.
Memorial on Accepting an Inkstone and a Bronze Pen Holder
Yǔ Jiānwú's "Xiè Yàn Tóng Bǐgé Qǐ" says:
"The smoke-ground green stone [inkstone]
has already trod the altar of Kǒng Shì;
the bronze dragon [pen holder] for inserting brushes
still laughs at Wáng Shēng's wall."
Stone Inkstone Rhapsody
Lí Péng’s《Shí Yàn Fù》says:
“Carved and ground,
its smoothness is like a whetstone.
Desiring to grind fine ink and dip the brush,
it resides in emptiness and measures the water.
Water follows the halo and returns in a circle,
ink floats with a sheen and rises dark.
Bright yet unblended,
this is why it is used.
Entering without change,
thus it is deemed beautiful.
The finished vessel esteems antiquity,
evoking Quèlǐ with the Uncrowned King;
imitating recent methods and enhancing the contemporary,
it equals the Intendant of Kuàijī.”
It also says:
“A fist-sized stone is taken for its firmness,
a spoonful of water is taken for its purity.”
It also says:
“Facing this great craftsman,
among the grand brushes.
Valued on the morning of ‘killing the green’ (editing bamboo slips),
put to use on the day of ‘drafting profound texts’.”
Yàn Shī
Monk Guànhyū’s《Yàn Shī》says:
“With humble heart, long nourished by moisture,
placed in the case, it finds greater peace.”
Shí Xūzhōng Zhuàn
Wén Sōng’s《Shí Xūzhōng Zhuàn》says:
“Shí Xūzhōng,
courtesy name Jūmò.
Of square and round bearing,
with a tranquil core.
Possessing the capacity of vast, boundless waters,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Jímò.
With Xuānchéng’s Máo Yuánruì, Yàn’s Yì Xuánguāng, and Huáyīn’s Chǔ Zhībái,
all shared the same origin (profession).”
Lóngnǎoxiāng
Lóngnǎoxiāng comes from the country of Bōlǜ.
The tree resembles a pine,
with the fragrance of fir wood.
Dried resin is called “Lóngnǎoxiāng,”
clear resin is called “Bōlǜgāo,”
and the most exquisite kind of seed is Méihuā Lóngnǎo.
Incense herbs are called “Bōlǜ.”
Xiāngpízhǐ
The Zhànxiāng tree from Lǐngbiǎo,
its trunk resembles a giant mulberry,
its leaves resemble orange peel.
It can be made into paper,
named Xiāngpízhǐ,
ash-white.
Jiàngzhēnxiāng
《Xiān Zhuàn》says:
“Jiàngzhēnxiāng,
when burned, attracts cranes.”
Lónglínxiāng
Yèzixiāng,
which is the thinner kind of Zhànxiāng,
also called “Lónglínxiāng.”
Yànwěixiāng
The orchid leaf,
pointed and long.
Has red and white flowers,
commonly called Yànwěixiāng.
Boiled water for bathing cures wind-illness.
Mǎtíxiāng,
is Dùhéng.
Its leaves resemble mallow,
shaped like a horse’s hoof.
Daoists consume it to make the body fragrant.
Lóngxiánxiāng
Lóngxiánxiāng comes from the country of Wénshí.
The people of that country watch for islands;
when strange birds gather and hover above the forest,
and schools of fish swim below,
then a latent dragon spews forth its saliva,
floating on the water.
Boatmen who manage to retrieve it
become immensely wealthy.
Its saliva is like glue.
Yìguóxiāng
Bìhánxiāng, Bìxiéxiāng, Jīnfèngxiāng,
all offered by foreign countries.
Shénxiāng
During the reign of Hàn Wǔdì,
the country of Yuèzhī presented Shénxiāng as tribute.
When burned in the palace,
all those suffering from epidemics recovered.
Within a hundred Lǐ of Cháng’ān,
its fragrance was perceived,
lasting for nine months without ceasing.
Jiǔhéxiāng
《Sāndòng Zhūnáng》says:
“Celestial maidens hold the celestial incense,
and in a jade censer burn the Jiǔhéxiāng.”
Passing over an incense burner on the way to the latrine
Liú Jìhé of Xiāngyáng was fond of incense,
and always, on his way to the latrine,
would pass over an incense burner.
Master of Records Zhāng Tǎn said:
“People call you a vulgar man,
and it is not without reason.”
Jìhé said:
“When Xún Lìngjūn visited someone’s home,
the fragrance lingered for three days.
What about me then?”
Tǎn said:
“A ugly woman imitating a frown,
those who see it will surely flee.
Do you want me to run away?”
Xiāngzhuàn
In recent times, Xiāngzhuàn are made;
their patterns are only the twelve terrestrial branches,
divided into a hundred kè.
They burn for exactly one day and night.
Ruǐxiāng
Use half a jīn of Xuánshen,
boil it dry in a silver vessel,
then stir-fry until a slight smoke appears.
Four liǎng of Gānsōng,
two qián of báitán,
two qián each of raw shèxiāng and rǔxiāng.
Grind them with honey,
and form pills the size of a chicken’s head.
Rùyìn
All incense must be placed in a yìn,
it is crucial for proper drying and humidifying.
After compounding,
store in a sealed container,
seal with wax paper,
and bury underground in the house for over half a month.
Xūnyīxiāng
When perfuming clothes,
place a small bucket of hot water on a fumigating basket,
cover it with the clothes to moisten them,
then the fragrance will penetrate the clothes.
Xiānghòupǔ
The《Shū》states: “Utmost governance has a fragrant reputation,”
and “Bright virtue alone is fragrant.”
Conversely, it says: “A foul smell reaches above.”
The《Zhuàn》uses the room of Zhīlán
and the fish market
to distinguish between good and evil.
The《Lísāo》uses Lánhuì and Dùhéng for gentlemen,
and dung heaps and Xiāoài for petty people.
A gentleman cleanses himself like snow,
and weighs himself with righteousness and morality,
possessing an infinite reputation.
My compilation of a fragrance manual
also shares this intent.
Bèicǎo Fùjí
Sòng Jǐnggōng burned exotic incense on his terrace.
A countryman, carrying straw and bearing a satchel,
knocked at the gate and entered.
This was Zǐwéi,
whose family had for generations managed the celestial department.
Bǎixiāng
Hàn Wǔdì built the Bǎiliáng Tái,
using cypress (bǎi),
its fragrance was smelled for dozens of Lǐ.
Rìdī Zìhéxiāng
Jīn Rìdī, upon entering service,
desired his clothes to be fragrant and clean,
changing his Hú-lǔ (barbarian) scent.
He personally blended an incense.
Wǔdì was indeed pleased by it.
Wèi Wǔ Jìn Xūnxiāng
Wèi Wǔdì issued an order saying:
“The world is newly settled,
I immediately forbid the use of incense in my household.”
Zōngchāo Xiāng
Zōng Chāo once performed a ritual on an open altar.
The incense in his box ran out,
but naturally filled the censer to overflowing,
and smoke issued forth without fire.
Wǔfāng Xiāngchuáng
Suí Yángdì, in front of the Wénpíng Diàn, had two side halls,
each with twelve rooms.
In these twelve rooms,
in front of each of the twelve precious cupboards,
five directions of incense beds (Wǔfāng Xiāngchuáng) were set up,
adorned with gold, jade, pearls, and kingfisher feathers.
Whenever the emperor’s carriage arrived,
palace women would carry incense censers and walk in front of the imperial carriage.
Chénxiāng Táng (Aloeswood Hall)
Yáng Sù built a Chénxiāng Táng in his residence.
Shī Bóshān Xiānglú (Lost Bóshān Incense Burner)
Lú Shì of Kuàijī
lost a Bóshān incense burner.
Wú Tài divined it, saying:
“Though this object’s material is metal,
its treasure resembles a mountain,
it has trees but is not a forest,
it has holes but is not a spring.
When Hélǘ rose,
it was seen emitting green smoke.
This is an incense burner.”
Xiāng Zhōng Jì Shè (Musk is Forbidden in Incense)
Musk is especially forbidden in incense.
When Zhèng Zhù of Táng went to Hézhōng,
his concubines, over a hundred riding,
emitted a fragrance for several *lǐ*,
repugnant to people’s noses.
That year, from Jīngzhào to Hézhōng,
all the melons along the way perished;
not a single stem was harvested.
Xiè Chén Ní Bì (Aloeswood Dust for Plastering Walls)
When Zōng Chǔkè of Táng built a new residence,
he used aloeswood and red powder to plaster the walls,
so that when the door opened, a fragrant aroma burst forth.
Also, during the reign of Táng Jìngzōng,
Pōsí offered aloeswood materials for a pavilion.
The Remonstrance Official Lǐ Hàn admonished, saying:
“To make a pavilion of aloeswood,
how is it different from Yáotái or Qióngshì?”
Xiāng Yīng (Fragrant Streamer)
Fragrant streamers are made of five colors.
When a woman visits her husband’s parents,
she first holds a fragrant streamer to consult them.
Cì Lóngnǎo (Bestowing Dragon's Brain (Borneol))
Yuánzōng held a night banquet,
and bestowed several *jīn* of dragon's brain, contained in a glass vessel,
upon his assembled officials.
Féng Mì said:
“I request permission to emulate Chén Píng as chancellor;
from the prime minister down,
all knelt to receive it.”
When half of it still remained,
he then bowed, holding it, saying:
“An imperial edict bestows this upon the Recorder Féng Mì.”
Yuánzōng laughed and granted it.
Sānqīng Tái (Three Pure Ones Terrace)
Wáng Chǎng, King of Mǐnguó, erected the Sānqīng Tái.
It had three layers,
with statues cast in gold.
Daily, several *jīn* of dragon's brain, chónglù, and other incenses were burned.
Wǔsè Xiāngnáng (Five-Colored Sachet)
Shǔ Wén Dàn, at the age of five,
said to his mother:
“There is a five-colored sachet
up in the apricot grove,
I wish you would retrieve it.”
This was Dàn’s previous life, at the age of five,
when he lost his footing and fell into a well.
Now he was reborn.
Dìshàng Xiéqì (Earthly Evil Qi)
The evil *qì* of demons on earth
rises straight up to the heavens for forty *lǐ*.
People burn qīngmù, chónglù, and ānxī jiāo in their sleeping chambers
to ward off foul odors
and repel evil and defiling mists.
Thus, celestial beings, jade maidens, and the Great One Emperor descend with the fragrant *qì*.
Sānbān Chī Xiāng (Sānbān Eats Incense)
The Sānbān Yuàn oversaw over eight thousand emissaries,
who performed duties externally,
and several hundred of whom were constantly in the院when retired.
Every year on Yuánjié,
they pooled money to provide meals for monks,
and presented incense boxes to wish for the Emperor’s longevity,
which was called “incense money.”
The saying in Jīngshī goes, “Sānbān eats incense.”
Wēi Xiāng (Aromatic Herb)
Also named Wēiruí.
When the king's rituals are complete,
it grows in front of the palace.
It also says:
If the king loves human life, it will grow.
Qiānbù Xiāng (Thousand-Pace Fragrance)
Nánhǎi presented qiānbù xiāng.
Wearing it, one could be smelled from a thousand paces away.
Today, there is a qiānbù cǎo in the coastal regions,
which is its species.
Shuǐ Shè (Water Musk)
During the Tiānbǎo era,
a hunter caught a shuǐ shè.
The navel musk was all water.
Each time it was extracted by piercing with a needle,
its fragrance was twice that of meat musk.
Wénshí (Patterned Stone)
Biànshān is in Húzhōu.
Under the mountain is priceless incense.
An old woman picked up a wénshí,
whose luster was delightful.
It accidentally fell into fire,
and an unusual fragrance was smelled far and near.
She collected and treasured it.
Each time it was thrown into fire,
the unusual fragrance was as before.
Qiángwēi Shuǐ (Rosewater)
In the fifth year of Zhōu Xiǎndé,
the Kingdom of Kūnmíng offered fifteen bottles of rosewater,
said to have come from the Western Regions.
When sprinkled on clothes,
the scent remained even after the clothes wore out.
Fǎnhún Xiāng (Soul-Returning Incense)
Xītiān Zhǔbù Xú Zhào met Sū Shìzǐ Dé Gē,
who claimed to be skilled at blending soul-returning incense.
He held an incense burner,
and took a packet from his bosom,
like white sandalwood powder,
which he scooped into the burner.
The smoke curled upwards,
even more intensely than dragon's brain.
Dé Gē chanted softly:
“Xú Zhào of Dōnghǎi wishes to see his ancestors’ spirits;
may this incense smoke serve as a guide.”
He then saw all his parents and great-grandparents.
Dé Gē said:
“However, if they have been gone for eighty years
or more, they cannot be brought back.”
Xūnlú Míng (Inscription for an Incense Burner)
Liú Xiàng of Hàn’s “Xūnlú Míng” says:
“Sūhé fills the air,
not smoke, but like clouds.
Sometimes dense, then thin,
now gathering, then dispersing.
With weak fire, it is hard to exhaust;
with long wind, easy to perceive.
Who says it is the power of the Way?
It is diffused by compassion.”
Shè Liáo Dì Dú (Musk Cures Earth Poisons)
《Běncǎo》 says:
“Musk deer resemble roe deer,
they often eat cypress leaves,
and also like to devour snakes.
In the fifth month, when musk is obtained,
snake skin and bones are often found,
thus musk cures snake venom.”
Chénjiān Xiāng (Aloeswood & Jiānxiāng)
《Tányuàn》 says:
“One tree produces three grades of incense:
called chén (aloeswood),
called jiān,
and called huángshú.”
《Juànyóu Zálù》 says:
“Aloeswood trees are especially abundant in the coastal prefectures of Lǐngnán.
The large ones require an arm’s embrace,
and mountain people sometimes use them for roof purlins and rice steamers.
Only one or two in a hundred have fragrance,
because the wood only forms resin when it absorbs water,
mostly found in broken, peeling, or dead trunks,
or as jiān or huángshú.
Those that die naturally are called shuǐpán xiāng.
Gāo and Dòu prefectures produce jiéxiāng (formed incense).
Mountain people, seeing crooked trunks and slanted branches of fragrant wood,
would surely cut a hollow with a knife,
and after a year of rainwater soaking,
incense would form.
They would then saw and retrieve it,
scraping off the white wood.
The incense formed into mottled spots,
also called zhègū bān (partridge spots).
The best chén (aloeswood)
is in Qióng, Cuī, and other prefectures,
commonly called jiǎochén.
This is obtained from underwater,
suitable for fumigation.
Huángchén (yellow aloeswood)
is obtained from dead wood,
suitable for medicine.
Huánglàchén (yellow wax aloeswood) with luster is rare.”
According to《Nán Shǐ》, it says:
“When placed in water, it sinks,
hence the name chénxiāng (sinking incense).
The next one that floats
is jiānxiāng.”
Rǔxiāng (Frankincense)
《筆談》(Bǐtán) states:
"Frankincense was originally named Dǒnglù.
Because it drips down like a nipple,
it is called 'nipple incense' (rǔtóuxiāng).
That which melts and settles on the ground
is called 'couch incense' (tàxiāng),
and the next best is 'ridge incense' (dòngxiāng).
Below that is 'cake incense' (bǐngxiāng),
which is often mixed with impurities to form large lumps,
resembling pitch."
Clove (jīshéxiāng).
《曰華子》(Yuēhuázǐ) states:
"Clove treats bad breath,
which is why the court officials (sānxǐnglángguān) would hold incense in their mouths when presenting memorials."
Five Incenses (wǔxiāng).
《雜修養方》(Záxiūyǎngfāng) states:
"On the first day of the first month,
boil water with five kinds of wood to bathe,
making one's hair remain black until old age."
Xú Kǎi's (Xú Kǎi) commentary states:
"Daoists consider Aquilaria agallocha (qīngmùxiāng) to be the five incenses,
also called the five woods (wǔmù)."
Dūliáng Incense (Dūliángxiāng).
Its shape is like patchouli (huòxiāng).
An ancient poem says:
"In the bó-incense burner, a hundred blended incenses,
turmeric (yùjīn), storax (sūhé), and Dūliáng."
Blended Incense (héxiāng).
Jiǎ Tiānxī (Jiǎ Tiānxī) created 'Intentionally Blended' (Yìhé),
which is pure, beautiful, tranquil, and distant,
naturally possessing an air of wealth and nobility.
It makes other people's incenses
seem quite cold.
'Intentionally Permissible' (Yìkě) incense.
It was originally named 'Appropriately Loved' (Yí'ài).
Some say:
"This is an incense from a palace in Jiāngnán."
There was a beauty whose courtesy name was "Yí Shèn'ài" (Yí Shèn'ài),
so this incense was named "Yí'ài."
Shāngǔ (Shāngǔ) said:
"The incense is truly extraordinary,
but its name has a 'rouge-and-powder' air."
It was renamed "Yìkě."
'Laughing Orchid' (Xiàolán).
The Wú (Wú) monk Qìngyí (Qìngyí) made 'Laughing Orchid' incense.
I said:
"Is this not what Hán Wèigōng (Hán Wèigōng) called 'Dense Plum Blossom' (Nóngméi),
and Shāngǔ (Shāngǔ) called 'Hidden Spring' (Cángchūn)?"
Its method uses agarwood (chén) as the sovereign,
clove (jīshé) as the minister,
dust from Běiyuàn (Běiyuàn),
costus root (guìchàng),
the essence of twelve leaves,
white lead (qiānhuá) powder,
and cypress musk (bǎimù) navel as assistants,
with the liquid of a hundred flowers as the envoy.
One stick, about the size of a finger,
is fragrant and dense,
as if smelling orchids from nine cultivated fields,
and gathering fragrant thoroughwort from a hundred acres.
'Pure and True Incense' (Qīngzhēnxiāng).
Dīng Jìngōng's (Dīng Jìngōng) 《清真香歌》(Qīngzhēnxiānggē) states:
"Four liǎng of pine resin, half a fēn of musk,
mixed with honey and rolled into pellets like bullets.
When burned in a golden censer, it resembles a flower heart,
exhaling fragrance into the morning breeze, as I recently saw in Shěn (Shěn)'s (family collection)."
I stood by the incense manual,
regretting its incompleteness.
Desiring to expand and correct it,
I compiled the 《後譜》(Hòupǔ),
dividing it into five sections.
Wine Manual (Jiǔpǔ).
《說文》(Shuōwén) states:
"Tú (Tú),
is wine yeast.
Lǐ (Lǐ),
is wine fermented overnight.
Láo (Láo),
is wine with dregs.
Zhòu (Zhòu),
is double-fermented wine.
Lí (Lí),
is thin wine.
Zuì (Zuì),
is ceremonial wine."
Wine named 'Joyful Elder' (Huānbó).
Wine is 'Joyful Elder',
its meaning is found in 《易林》(Yìlín).
Regardless of noble or humble, wise or foolish,
Chinese or barbarian, all enjoy and delight in it.
Róng Wine (Róngjiǔ).
Pí Rìxiū's (Pí Rìxiū) poem says:
"Tomorrow morning, there will be something to fulfill your trust,
three bottles of Róng wine sent by night boat."
Róng wine
is a wine name from outside the Jiāng (Jiāng) region.
Wine Flag (Jiǔqí).
《韓非子》(Hán Fēizǐ) states:
"A Song (Sòng) man sold wine and hung his banner very high."
The existence of flags in wine markets
first appears here.
Some call them "lián" (lián).
Liú Báiduò (Liú Báiduò).
Liú Báiduò (Liú Báiduò) from Jiāngdōng (Jiāngdōng) was good at brewing wine.
In the sixth month, he would fill jars with wine
and place them in the sun.
After ten days, the taste would remain unchanged and become even more fragrant and delicious,
making people deeply drunk.
Court officials would send it to each other over a thousand li,
calling it "Crane Goblet" (Hèshāng),
also known as "Donkey-Riding Wine" (Qílǘjiǔ).
Drunken Sage (Zuìshèng).
Lǐ Bái (Lǐ Bái), whenever drunk,
never made a mistake in writing.
People therefore called him "Wine Sage" (Jiǔshèng).
Bái Lètiān (Bái Lètiān) called himself "Drunken Magistrate" (Zuìyǐn).
Pí Rìxiū (Pí Rìxiū) called himself "Drunken Scholar" (Zuìshì).
Letter from Zǔ Táizhōu (Zǔ Táizhōu).
Jìn (Jìn) dynasty's Zǔ Táizhōu (Zǔ Táizhōu) wrote a letter to Wáng Jīngzhōu (Wáng Jīngzhōu):
"The ancients considered wine a warning.
I wish you would set aside cups and abandon goblets,
burn wine jars and destroy wine bottles.
Execute Yí Díchí (Yí Díchí) at Yǔshān (Yǔshān),
and banish Dù Kāng (Dù Kāng) to Sānwēi (Sānwēi)."
Kūnlún Goblet (Kūnlúnshāng).
Wèi (Wèi) dynasty's Jiǎ Jiāng (Jiǎ Jiāng) had a slave
who was skilled at distinguishing water.
Once, while traveling by boat in the middle of the Yellow River (Huánghé),
he used a gourd to collect seven or eight sheng of water from the river source.
After a night, its color became like crimson.
He used it to brew wine,
named "Kūnlún Goblet,"
whose aroma and taste were exquisitely wonderful.
Pánruò Tāng (Pánruò Tāng).
Northern monks called wine "Pánruò Tāng"
to evade legal prohibitions with euphemistic terms.
Lying in Rice Straw (Wòshǔráng).
Anyone who lies drunk in rice straw
will surely contract leprosy.
If one drinks tea when drunk,
it will surely cause bladder qi (pángguāngqì).
Eating too much salty food often leads to diabetes (xiāozhōng).
Burl Wood Cup (Yǐngmùbēi).
《松陵唱和》(Sōnglíngchànghé) contains a poem titled 《癭木盃》(Yǐngmùbēi),
which was made from wood knots.
Bamboo Root (Zhúgēn).
Old Dù's (Dù) poem says:
"Drunk, we end up lying together on bamboo roots."
This implies using bamboo roots as drinking vessels.
Lotus Seed Cup (Liánzǐbēi).
Táng (Táng) people particularly favored lotus seed cups.
Bái Gōng (Bái Gōng) mentions them in his poems.
During the time of King Mù of Zhōu (Zhōu Mùwáng),
there was a cup named "Ever Full" (Chángmǎn).
Pomegranate (Ānshíliú).
The kingdom of Dùnsūn (Dùnsūn) has pomegranates.
Its juice is left in a basin for several days,
becoming fine wine.
Wine Laws (Jiǔlìng).
A drinking game said:
“Lord Méngcháng's (Mèngcháng) three thousand retainers,
are 'people of the same kind' (Tóngrén);
one hundred thousand sheep at the Huángshǔi (Huángshuǐ) ford,
