are 'not yet crossed, small livestock' (Wèijì Xiǎoxù). ”
It also said:
“Chú Ní (Chú Ní) bumped into the locust tree,
and died to become a ghost by the tree;
Yù Ràng (Yù Ràng) swallowed charcoal,
eventually becoming ash beneath the mountain. ”
It also said:
“Yǔ (Yǔ) of Xià (Xià) saw rain falling,
and sent Lǐ Mù (Lǐ Mù) to deliver wooden clogs to Xiāo Hé (Xiāo Hé);
Xiāo Hé (Xiāo Hé) said, 'What is the need (hé xiāo)?'
Tián Dān (Tián Dān) settled the reclaimed fields,
and sent Gòng Yǔ (Gòng Yǔ) to deliver the 'Tribute of Yǔ' (Yǔ Gòng) to Lǐ Dé (Lǐ Dé);
Lǐ Dé (Lǐ Dé) said, 'I've got the principle (dé lǐ).' ”
It also said:
“In the temple, monks feeding cows eat grass;
in the monastery, Daoists cooking vegetables provide firewood. ”
It also said:
“Ascending the mountain to gather huánglíng (huánglíng),
descending the mountain, I met an old man,
who recited:
‘White hair scratched grows even shorter,
almost unable to hold a hairpin.’
Ascending the mountain to gather jiāoténg (jiāoténg),
descending the mountain, I met a drunken foreign monk,
who said:
‘In what year did I drink the 'wine of the voice-hearers' (shēngwén jiǔ),
that even now I am still drunken and not awake?’ ” Juǎn zhī Wǔshíjiǔ (Juǎn zhī Wǔshíjiǔ) ends.
Three poles of sun
During the Yǒngmíng (Yǒngmíng) era,
when the sun was three poles high,
it had a variegated color, yellow, and a red halo.
Three-qi (qì) star
The three-qì (qì) star governs sweet dew;
if it is bright and moist, sweet dew will descend.
Water shield and turtle
Water shield soup is exceedingly delicious;
people in Jiāngdōng (Jiāngdōng) call it "water shield and turtle" (chúnguī).
Hurricane
In the autumn and summer in the Nánhǎi (Nánhǎi) region,
when clouds have a halo like a rainbow,
it is called a "hurricane mother" (jùmǔ),
and there will certainly be a hurricane.
Three-Wéi (Wéi) dew
Among beautiful waters,
there is the dew of Sānwéi (Sānwéi).
Wénzhāng (Wénzhāng) Ridge
Guìzhōu (Guìzhōu) has Wénzhāng (Wénzhāng) Ridge;
Fúzhōu (Fúzhōu) has Jǐnxìu (Jǐnxiù) Islet.
Bright brocade secures celestial deer,
new twill weaves phoenixes.
Celestial Green Youth
Zhào Xù (Zhào Xù) lived in seclusion in Guǎnglíng (Guǎnglíng);
a woman wearing a dress of six-denier mist-gauze,
treading on five-colored patterned shoes,
said:
“I am the Celestial Green Youth (Tiānshàng Qīngtóng);
it is my fate to be your partner.”
In the middle of the night, he again heard another woman outside,
calling out "Lady Qīng (Qīng Fūrén),"
and tapping a pillar, she sang:
“Moon-dew flutters, the Milky Way slants,
alone I journey gracefully in a cloud-chariot.
The immortal gentleman alone invites the Lord Green Youth (Qīngtóng Jūn),
to form affection under a silken canopy with intertwining flowers.”
Xù (Xù) arose to greet her,
and she said:
“I am Éméi (Éméi);
hearing of your gathering with Green Youth (Qīngtóng),
I came to catch the fugitive.”
After they parted,
she bestowed upon him great secret teachings,
emphasizing that "with a dead heart one can achieve longevity,
and by preserving essence one can attain spirit."
Maiden wind
When Guǎn Lù (Guǎn Lù) passed through Qīnghé (Qīnghé),
there was a great drought.
Lù (Lù) said:
“It will rain tonight.
Already there is a maidenly breeze in the trees,
and yin birds are harmoniously singing among the trees;
then a youthful breeze will rise,
and birds will fly in disarray.
Its manifestation is imminent.”
In a moment,
winds and clouds gathered from all four directions,
and there was heavy rain.
Branch-washing rain
Heavy rain in the sixth month
is called "branch-washing rain" (zhuó zhī yǔ).
Salted fish not brought to the cutting board
Crown Prince Fā (Fā) desired a legacy,
and had a fondness for salted fish,
but the Duke (Gōng) did not allow it even in the rain.
King Wén (Wén) said:
“Fā (Fā) is fond of salted fish,
why not give it to him?”
The Grand Duke (Tàigōng) said:
“According to ritual,
salted fish are not brought to the cutting board.”
Green flies as mourners
Yú Fān (Yú Fān) was banished to the south,
and regretted his fall into obscurity on the sea-coast,
saying that he had no one to speak with in life,
and would have green flies as mourners in death.
Ninety thousand sheets of paper
When Wáng Yòujūn (Wáng Yòujūn) was the Internal Scribe of Kuàijī (Kuàijī),
Xiè Gōng (Xiè Gōng) asked him for paper.
Upon inspecting the storehouse,
there were ninety thousand sheets,
all of which he gave to him.
Ascending Immortal Bridge
Ten lǐ (lǐ) from Shǔchéng (Shǔchéng) is the Shēngxiān (Shēngxiān) Bridge.
When Sīmǎ Xiāngrú (Sīmǎ Xiāngrú) first entered Cháng'ān (Cháng'ān),
he inscribed:
“Unless I ride a vermilion chariot drawn by four horses,
I will not pass beneath this.”
Shooting a dogwood
Guō Pú (Guō Pú) sought refuge in Xīnxī (Xīnxī).
Someone asked Pú (Pú) to guess an object,
and Pú (Pú) said:
“You are like 'red-containing' (chíhán),
containing a 'dark pearl' (xuánzhū).
Based on these words,
it must be a dogwood (zhūyú).”
Male and female birds
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ) asked Dōngfāng Shuò (Dōngfāng Shuò):
“How does one know the male and female of birds?”
He replied:
“The male's left wing overlaps the right,
and its voice is high;
the female's right wing overlaps the left,
and its voice is small.”
Dew-collecting basin
Emperor Wǔ (Wǔ) of Hàn (Hàn) made a bronze dew-collecting basin,
twenty zhàng (zhàng) high,
with an immortal's palm on top to collect dew and jade dust,
intending to seek immortality with it.
Avoiding the character tán
Sū Tǐng (Sū Tǐng) was five years old.
When Péi Tán (Péi Tán) visited,
his father tested him by having him recite Yǔ Xìn's (Yǔ Xìn) 'Rhapsody on Withered Trees' (Kūshù Fù).
Tǐng (Tǐng) somewhat avoided the character "tán" (談),
and changed its rhyme, saying:
“In former years, willows were transplanted,
gracefully by the Yin of Hàn (Hàn).
Now seeing them withered and fallen,
sadly by the river banks.
If trees are thus,
how can humans endure?”
Three goblets
Liú Biǎo's (Liú Biǎo) disciples called the goblets "three elegant ones" (sānyǎ).
The largest was called Bóyǎ (Bóyǎ),
holding seven shēng (shēng);
the next was Zhòngyǎ (Zhòngyǎ),
holding six shēng (shēng);
and the next was Jìyǎ (Jìyǎ),
holding five shēng (shēng).
Yuánzhēnzǐ's (Yuánzhēnzǐ) fishing song
Xiànzōng (憲宗) sought the Fishermen's Songs of Xuánzhēnzǐ (玄真子).
Lǐ Déyù (李德裕), as the Prefect of Rùnzhōu (潤州),
obtained them.
Xuánzhēnzǐ (玄真子)
was Zhāng Zhìhé (張志和),
who styled himself "Smoky Wave Angler."
The songs say:
"White egrets fly by Xīsài (西塞) Mountain,
peach blossoms flow in the water, mandarin fish are fat.
A green bamboo hat,
a green coir cloak,
in the spring river's fine rain, there's no need to go home."
The second says:
"The fisherman at Diàotái (釣臺) wears coarse cloth as a fur coat,
in the rain, three or three small boats.
Able to ply the oars,
accustomed to riding the current,
the white waves of the long river never cause worry."
The third says:
"An old fisherman in the bend of Zhèxī (霅溪),
with a small boat as his home, west then east.
River snow,
wind by the bank,
smiling in his lotus leaf clothes, unafraid of poverty."
The fourth says:
"Along the river, near houses, I rejoice with people,
sharing bamboo rice and wild rice stem soup.
Maple leaves fall,
reed flowers wither,
drunkenly moored in my fishing boat, I feel no cold."
The fifth says:
"The moon is perfectly round over Qīngcǎo (青草) Lake,
the fisherman of Bālíng (巴陵) sings his oar songs in succession.
Fishing reels,
punt-like boats,
finding joy in the waves, no need for immortality."
Luán'gāng (鸞岡) and Hèlǐng (鶴嶺)
Xīshān (西山) has forty-two arhats,
and twelve true immortals,
based on the beauty of Luán'gāng (鸞岡) and Hèlǐng (鶴嶺).
Shǔróng (黍容)
Zōu Yǎn (鄒衍) was in Yān (燕),
where there was a valley,
beautiful but cold,
where no grain grew.
Master Zōu (鄒子) blew on the pitch-pipes and Yang energy was born,
and to this day it is called Gǔshǔ (谷黍).
Fùzǐ (附子)
At one year old, it is called Cèzǐ (測子);
at two years old, Wūtóu (烏頭);
at three years old, Fùzǐ (附子);
at four years old, Wūzhuó (烏啄);
at five years old, Tiānxíong (天雄).
Butcher from Fēngpèi (豐沛)
The Grand Emperor did not enjoy Guānzhōng (關中),
longing for his hometown.
Gāozǔ (高祖) moved butchers from Fēngpèi (豐沛) who sold wine and made cakes to Xīnfēng (新豐).
Songs shake the梁塵 (Liángchén)
During the Hàn (漢) dynasty, a skilled singer from Wú (吳), Duke Yú (虞公),
made his voice shake the dust on the beams.
Lí Palace and Bié View
Qín Shǐhuáng (秦始皇) built one hundred forty-six Lí Palaces (離宮) and Bié Views (別觀) in his Shànglín (上林) Park.
Dividing winds to send boats
Travelers praying at Dòngtíng (洞庭) Lake
could divide the winds to send boats north and south.
Fèngzhào (鳳詔)
Shí Hǔ (石虎)'s imperial edicts were written on five-colored paper,
placed in the mouth of a wooden phoenix,
which flew down to the platform,
so they were called Fèngzhào (鳳詔).
Xīnchéng (新城) rice
The glutinous rice of Xīnchéng (新城)
could be smelled five *lǐ* away.
Cǎozhōngrǔ (草鍾乳)
Chives are warm in nature,
and are called "Cǎozhōngrǔ (草鍾乳)."
In Yōuzhōu (幽州) dialect,
a yellow bird is called a "huángyīng (黃鶯)."
The sky can lean on a pillar
After a hundred generations,
the earth will be higher than the sky.
After a thousand generations,
the sky can lean on a pillar.
Tiānxīn (天心) and Yuèxié (月脅)
Huángfǔ Shí (皇甫湜) described the wonder of poetry and prose as:
"Penetrating the heart of the sky (Tiānxīn),
emerging from the ribs of the moon (Yuèxié)."
Cuī Jīn Zhuàn Yù (炊金饌玉)
Luò Bīn (駱賓) referred to a sumptuous feast as "Cuī Jīn Zhuàn Yù (炊金饌玉)" (cooking gold and preparing jade).
Ruìyún (瑞雲)
The color of clouds is called Yù (矞).
Yù (矞)
is an auspicious cloud (Ruìyún).
Mùyāo (木妖)
During the Tiānbǎo (天寶) era of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
when palaces and residences were built,
using extreme amounts of wood,
those who knew called it "Mùyāo (木妖)" (wood demon).
Yàn Míng Jiélín (硯名結鄰)
Lǐ Wèigōng (李衛公) of the Táng (唐) dynasty collected many inkstones,
the most exquisite of which
was named "Jiélín (結鄰)" (forming a neighborhood),
meaning it became a neighbor to him.
Jiǔdǐngpán (九飣盤)
When the imperial kitchen of the Táng (唐) dynasty presented food,
nine plates were used for arrangement,
called Jiǔdǐngpán (九飣盤).
Jiūchē Zhúmǎ (鳩車竹馬)
Wáng Yuáncháng (王元長) said:
"A child of five years plays with a dove cart (jiūchē);
at seven years, he plays with a bamboo horse (zhúmǎ)."
Húláng (壺郎)
The official in charge of the water clock was called "Húláng (壺郎)."
Lù Lǐ (陸俚) composed a rhapsody,
Pān Yuè (潘岳) called a measure-scoop "Jīnqí (金祈),"
which is now a bronze dipper.
Bājí (八極)
The Middle Kingdom is
one eighty-first of the world,
surrounded by sea.
There are nine such (lands),
surrounded by a great ocean,
collectively called Bājí (八極) (the eight extremes).
Nítáng (猊糖)
Sugar shaped like a suānní (狻猊)
is called "Nítáng (猊糖)."
Four nipples
King Wén (文王) had four nipples on his body.
*Chūnqiū Yuánmìngbāo* (春秋元命苞)
Dreaming of cooking in a mortar
Zhāng Zhān (張瞻) dreamt of cooking in a mortar;
interpreting it, he lost his wife.
Cooking in a mortar
means having no wife.
Qībǎozhuāngyángōng (七寶莊嚴公)
After Lǐ Déyín (李德林) of the Suí (隋) dynasty completed the compilation of laws and regulations,
he was bestowed a nine-ring belt.
Later, he presented the "Strategy for Pacifying Chén (陳)."
Emperor Wén (文帝) said:
"Once the task is accomplished,
I shall adorn the Duke with seven treasures (qībǎo zhuāngyán gōng)."
Jīnbō Yùyè (金波玉葉)
The moon is like golden waves first reflecting in the sky,
clouds are like jade leaves suddenly stirred by the wind.
Shényàn Guǐwán (神燕鬼丸)
Gold foil depicts divine swallows (Shényàn),
vermilion paste prints ghost pellets (Guǐwán).
Butterflies descend upon Emperor Wǔ's (武帝) temple
On Liángshān (梁山) there is a temple to Emperor Wǔ (武帝) of Hàn (漢),
where sacrifices are still offered to this day.
Often, two or three hundred butterflies descend upon the temple,
enjoying the food.
They are not startled when approached,
and leave in a swarm only after the meal is cleared.
At the time, they were believed to be Emperor Wǔ's (武帝) attendants,
and whoever caught them would surely fall ill.
*Zhōuyì* (周易) divination for names to be killed
Jiāo Mǐn (焦敏) of Jìnzhōu (晉州) was known for being ill-informed.
He claimed that the imperial academy's printed edition of the *Jiǔjīng* (九經) was not authentic.
The scholars all said:
"Although this originated in the Five Dynasties,
it was meticulously proofread by many scholars,
and is certainly an authentic edition."
Mǐn (敏) said:
"Gentlemen, you haven't looked closely at all.
Take the *Zhōuyì* (周易), for example,
why are all the names divined to be killed?"
Handkerchief
Emperor Wǔ (武帝) of Liáng (梁) strangled Dù Léng (杜稜) with a handkerchief;
Léng (稜) passed out.
Viewing official appointments harms the Daoist mind
Yáo Hé (姚合) of the Táng (唐) dynasty wrote in a poem:
"One day I viewed the official appointments,
for three years my Daoist mind was harmed.
Mountains are best climbed through snow,
poetry is best recited with the wind.
Wild guests dislike knowing official seals,
family members laugh at selling a zither.
One should just let the days pass,
realizing that mistakes run deeper."
Cǐguī (子規) poems
Dù Xúnhè's 《Zǐ Guī》 poem says:
"The Chǔ sky is vast and the moon forms a wheel,
The sounds of Shǔ's soul seem to tell people.
Crying until blood flows is useless,
It's better to seal one's mouth and pass the spring."
One Kuí is enough.
Duke Āi of Lǔ asked Kǒngzǐ:
"I have heard that Kuí has one foot,
different from others;
is it true?"
Kǒngzǐ replied:
"In the past, Zhònglí promoted Kuí,
and then wanted to find more people to assist him.
Shùn said:
'Music
is the essence of heaven and earth,
only a sage can master it.
To set the six pitches,
harmonize the five tones,
understand the essence of music,
and thus communicate with the eight winds.
Kuí can do this,
one [like him] is enough.'
He does not have one foot."
Disturbing the spring breeze, never ceasing.
Luó Yǐn's poem says:
"A cluster of green smoke locks the jade tower,
Half hanging by the railing, half over the ditch.
Next year there will still be new branches,
Disturbing the spring breeze, never ceasing."
Carrying
carrying a satchel and entering,
carrying and returning.
Dà Zǔ
Duàn Gānmù,
the Dà Zǔ of Jìn.
Fighting ducks.
Zhāng Jiè's 《Jìn Yǒurén》 says:
"I remember the days in Jiāngnán,
wandering together during the third month.
Picking tea and seeking distant streams,
fighting ducks towards the spring pond."
Kē's mother chooses neighbors.
Mèng Kē lived alone with his mother when he was young.
They lived near a cemetery,
and Kē playfully enacted burials.
His mother said:
"This is not a suitable place to live."
They left,
and lived by the market.
He again playfully enacted merchants.
His mother left,
and they lived by a school.
He then performed the rituals of bowing, yielding, advancing, and retreating.
His mother said:
"This is truly a suitable place to live."
Thus he became a scholar of Confucianism.
Qiú.
Wéi Zhuāng's 《Fūzhōu Hánshí》 poem says:
"Long days stretch on with nothing to do,
I hear the sound of kicking a 'qìqiú' from beyond the wall."
Mílè shares a niche.
Chǔ Suìliáng's letter says:
"I hear you have long abandoned the dust and dirt,
and share a niche with Mílè.
One meal of vegetarian food,
eight hours of Zen chanting."
Six-petaled flower.
Sòng Jiāngxiàwáng Yìtài,
on New Year's Day, caught snow with his clothes,
and made six-petaled flowers,
presenting them as an auspicious omen.
Loose belts in court.
A Táng proverb says:
"When one person is in court,
a hundred people loosen their belts."
Meaning that when one person is noble, their relatives and friends are all honored.
Welcoming the lengthening of days on the solstice.
Cáo Zhí said:
"Presenting shoes on the winter solstice
is for welcoming blessings and treading on length."
Goose Pagoda.
When the Buddha was in the world,
a bhikṣu saw a flock of geese flying in the sky,
and thought:
"These geese can suffice for my expenses."
The geese then fell to the ground.
The Buddha said:
"This is the goose king,
it should not be eaten rashly."
So he had a pagoda built for it.
Secret Yè.
Sòng Zhīwèn said:
"The secret yè of the western city,
the immortal stream of the northern forbidden area."
Golden spatula scraping the film.
Emperor Wén of Wèi suffered from an eye disease;
he ordered Huà Tuó to scrape the film with a golden spatula.
Lǐ Hè's connected eyebrows.
《Lǐ Hè Xiǎozhuàn》 says:
"Hè had connected eyebrows and long fingers,
he composed poetry diligently and wrote quickly."
White-haired child.
Péi Sì said:
"Táng Suī, with white hair, enlightened Qín;
Gān Luó, a mere child, served Zhào."
Official fields, public office fields.
During the Kāihuáng era of the Suí dynasty,
officials from dukes and ministers down were granted official fields.
Those from the first to fifth ranks
were also granted public office fields.
Flower Maiden.
《Nányuè Fūrén Zhuàn》 mentions a female Daoist, Huáng Xūchè,
who was over eighty years old,
but had the appearance of an infant,
and was called "Huā Gū."
The Fūrén appeared to her in a dream,
and later she too ascended to heaven.
Two back-facing ministers.
During Emperor Xuān's time,
in a stone chamber in Shàngjùn, there were bound and shackled ministers facing each other,
said to be the two back-facing ministers.
Zhān and the two back-facing ministers killed Yàyā.
The emperor grasped their feet.
Four friends.
《Zuìyín Xiānshēng》:
"It is said that Sōngshān monk Rúmǎn was his friend in the Buddhist gate,
Píngquán guest Wéi Chǔ was his friend of mountains and waters,
Liú Mèngdé was his friend in poetry,
and Huángfǔ Míngzhī was his friend in wine."
Poem of a poor girl.
Táng Qín Tāoyù's 《Yǒng Pínnǚ》 poem:
"A humble family has not known the fragrance of fine silks,
Intending to entrust a good match, I hurt myself even more.
Who loves elegant and refined tastes?
Everyone pities the frugal makeup of the times.
Dare to boast of slender fingers,
But not to compete in drawing long eyebrows.
I regret that year after year I hold the needle and thread,
Making wedding gowns for others."
Lament of the Spring Palace.
Dù Xúnhè's 《Chūngōng Yuàn》 poem says:
"Early on misled by beauty,
I feel lazy to put on makeup before the mirror.
Favor is not in appearance,
How can I, a concubine, adorn myself?
The wind is warm, bird songs are scattered,
The sun is high, flower shadows are heavy.
Year after year, the girls of Yuèxī,
Miss each other while picking lotus flowers."
Bamboo poem.
Luó Yè's 《Zhú》 poem says:
"Peach and plum should laugh at being late."
Sun and moon are not round.
《Lùn Héng》 says:
"The sun and moon are not round
because they are far from humans."
Lóngbó Guó.
《Hétú Yùbǎn》 says:
"Ninety thousand li north from Kūnlún one reaches Lóngbó Guó,
where people are thirty zhàng tall,
and live eighteen thousand years before dying."
Dàjiā.
The Son of Heaven has no outside,
taking the world as his home,
hence he is called Dàjiā.
Serving Heaven as father,
Earth as mother,
the sun as elder brother,
the moon as elder sister.
Sun Territory.
The Son of Heaven's territory is a thousand lǐ square,
like the circular path of the sun and moon,
hence it is called "Rìjī,"
also called "Rìwéi."
Four books for ruler and ministers.
There are four types of documents issued by the Son of Heaven:
called cèshū,
called zhìshū,
called zhàoshū,
and called chéngshū.
There are also four types of memorials submitted by all officials to the Son of Heaven:
called zhāng,
called zòu,
called biǎo,
and called yì.
When playing the qín,
the rapid rotation of fingers is called xièxíng (crab walk);
the sideways turn of fingers is called luánmíng (phoenix cry).
If only fingernails are used, the sound is dry and full of melancholic thoughts;
if only flesh is used, the sound is heavy, turbid, and uneven.
Wòshítái
King Zhāo of Yān was fond of immortals.
The immortal Gān Xū ascended Wòshí zhī Tái with the king.
Guǐgǔ Xiānshēng
was a person of the time of Duke Píng of Jìn.
He dwelled in seclusion in Guǐgǔ,
hence he was given that appellation.
His surname was Wáng, and his given name was Xǔ.
He once taught the art of diplomacy (zònghéngshù) to Sū Qín and Zhāng Yí.
Later, he attained immortality.
Ròuzhī
The jìnshì Xiāo Jìngzhī,
when digging the ground, obtained an object
resembling a human hand,
fat and moist,
and slightly reddish in color.
He cooked and ate it.
Later, he met a strange person who said:
"You have tasted the elixir of immortality."
Then he was informed:
"It is ròuzhī;
those who eat it attain longevity."
Hànjiāng Jiěpèi
Zhèng Jiāofǔ met two women by the Hàn Jiāng and conversed with them.
They untied their precious Dàmíngzhū and gave it to Jiāofǔ.
Soon after, they disappeared,
and the pearls were also gone.
Xīliáng Guāndēng
Emperor Míng of Táng used Yè Fǎshàn's magic
to go from his palace to Xīliáng Fǔ on the Yuánxiāo night to view the lanterns,
and pawned an iron rúyì for wine before returning.
When he sent an envoy to retrieve it, it was not a falsehood.
Chóuchéng
"Attacking the Chóuchéng of sorrow never breaks it;
sweeping the Chóuchéng of sorrow never opens it.
Closing the door to drive away sorrow,
sorrow still refuses to leave.
Hiding deep to avoid sorrow,
sorrow already knows where one is."
It also says:
"What can cook sorrow until it is done?
What can burn sorrow until it ignites?"
It also says:
"Often loosening one's belt
especially damages one's complexion."
This refers to the ghost of sorrow.
It also says:
"Let one inch of heart
be able to contain ten thousand hú of sorrow."
Yǎnjié
Drunk eyes are called "yǎnjié."
Yáoméiyǔ'ěr
Yáo had eight-colored eyebrows,
and Yǔ had three-holed ears.
In Yáo's time,
meat naturally grew in the kitchen,
thin like a fan.
Shaking and fanning it produced wind,
preventing food from spoiling.
It was called shàfǔ.
Qīwěi
First is the Yìwěi,
second is the Shūwěi,
third is the Shīwěi,
fourth is the Lǐwěi,
fifth is the Yuèwěi,
sixth is the Xiàojīngwěi,
seventh is the Chūnqiūwěi.
Wǔhú
Wǔhú is
another name for Tàihú,
because it spans over five hundred lǐ in circumference,
hence it is called "Wǔhú."
According to the Yángzhōujì:
"Tàihú is also named Guāntíng,
also named Zhènzé,
and also said to be Dòngtíng."
According to the Jīngzhōujì, it says:
"Guāntíng is none other than Pénglǐ Zé,
called Péngzé,
also named Qīngcǎohú,
named after Qīngcǎo Shān."
Zàn Lántíngjì
Xiāo Yì acquired the Lántíngjì by trickery.
It was written by Wáng Yòujūn,
using a rat-whisker brush and silk paper,
totaling three hundred and twenty-four characters.
Mínghuáng Yǐyǒushēng
Emperor Míng of Táng was born in the Yǐyǒu year and loved cockfighting,
which was a sign of impending chaos.
Bòmíng Jiējiǎo
In the fourth year of Zhēnyuán,
the Ministry of Personnel reported:
Since the time of difficulties,
documents have been lost,
and some people falsely impersonate officials,
or commit fraud.
Those who presented themselves as officials in separate districts
were called "bòmíng."
Those who took over the positions of deceased persons
were called "jiējiǎo."
Dàoshì Chángchímǎn
The Prince of Rǔyáng was drinking with Yè Jìngnéng.
Yè said:
"I have a disciple who can drink;
I should let him pay his respects."
The next day,
someone announced himself
as the dàoshì Chángchímǎn.
Upon seeing him,
he was a dwarf
who spoke of the dao of primeval chaos.
He was given wine,
and after about five dòu,
he suddenly fell over drunk.
Tiǎocài Shī
Lù Guīméng's poem "Tiǎocài" says:
"While resting, the shadows of nephews and uncles often shift;
often plucking, one sees the hearts of the uncle and aunt."
Fùkē
In Jiāngnán, frivolous talk is called "fùkētán."
The Three Sovereigns walked,
the Five Emperors trotted,
the Three Kings galloped,
the Five Hegemons sped.
Yīguóxiāng
The Chìtǔ Guó was in Háinán,
producing an extraordinary fragrance.
Each time a pellet of incense was burned,
its scent could be perceived for several hundred lǐ,
and it was called "Yīguóxiāng."
Tiānquèshān
Emperor Yuán of Jìn wanted to erect gate towers in front of the palace,
but opinions were divided.
Wáng Dǎo pointed to Niútóushān as Tiānquèshān,
thus avoiding the need to erect separate gate towers.
Lóugū
Yú Zǐrán met a debater
who called himself Lúgōu.
Later, upon verification,
it was actually a lóugū.
Luòdiāo Duāngōng
In his youth, Táng Gāopián was a Sīmǎ Zǒngbīng.
While on inspection, he saw a pair of eagles
and said:
"If I am to become noble,
I shall shoot both."
Indeed, his arrow struck both eagles,
hence he was called "Luòdiāo Duāngōng."
Nǚzhǔ Wǔzhǔ
During the Zhēngguàn reign,
a "Secret Record" (Mìjì) stated:
"After three generations of Táng,
there will be a female ruler, a Martial King (Wǔwáng), who will possess the empire."
Tàizōng secretly summoned Lǐ Chúnfēng and questioned him about it.
Chúnfēng said:
"That person has already been born in Your Majesty's palace.
From now, in forty years, she will possess the empire,
and slaughter your descendants almost completely."
Tàizōng said:
"What if I kill those who are suspicious,
how about that?"
He replied:
"It is Heaven's command;
there is no way to avoid it.
The king cannot be killed,
and it would wrongly implicate the innocent.
Moreover, according to the divination, she is already grown,
and perhaps she is one of Your Majesty's close relatives.
After another forty years, she will decline;
when old, she will be benevolent,
so she might not harm many of Your Majesty's descendants.
If she were killed now,
she would become an enemy.
If she were to be reborn young and strong,
the harm would be even greater."
So, he stopped.
Chē Wǔzǐ's (Chē Wǔzǐ) wife was jealous.
Chē Wǔzǐ's (Chē Wǔzǐ) wife was extremely jealous.
Chē Wǔzǐ (Chē Wǔzǐ) called his father and elder brother to stay overnight.
He hung a crimson skirt on a screen.
His wife drew a knife and went straight to the bed,
pulled back the covers,
and found it was her elder brother.
She was ashamed and withdrew.
Huázhǔ (Huázhǔ) Rainbow Stream
The "Sea Chart" (Hǎitú) says:
"A great star, like a rainbow,
streamed down to Huázhǔ (Huázhǔ).
Nǚjié (Nǚjié) was moved and gave birth to Báidì Jīntiānshì (Báidì Jīntiānshì).
Shǎohào (Shǎohào).
Consort Fùbǎo (Fùbǎo) saw a flash of lightning around the pivot of the Northern Dipper (Běidǒu Xū),
and was moved to give birth to the nine sons of Huángdì Xuānyuánshì (Huángdì Xuānyuánshì)."
It will rain tonight.
The "Biography of Guǎn Lù" (Guǎn Lù Zhuàn) says:
"At the time, there was a great drought.
Guǎn Lù (Guǎn Lù) said:
'It will rain tonight;
there is already a gentle breeze among the trees.'
Soon after, it indeed rained."
River Spirit
The "River Chart" (Hétú) says:
"The essence of the river ascends to become the Heavenly River (Tiānhé)."
Nine Mountains
The "Lǚshì Chūnqiū" (Lǚshì Chūnqiū) says:
"What are the Nine Mountains (Jiǔshān)?
Kuàijī (Kuàijī), Tàishān (Tàishān), Wángwū (Wángwū), Shǒuyáng (Shǒuyáng), Tàihuá (Tàihuá), Qíshān (Qíshān), Tàiháng (Tàiháng), Yángcháng (Yángcháng), Mèngmén (Mèngmén)."
Crystal Pillars
The "Wèilüè" (Wèilüè) says:
"The country of Dàqín (Dàqín) uses crystals (shuǐjīng) as pillars for its houses."
Stammering
The "Guǎnzǐ" (Guǎnzǐ) says:
"I fear matters and dare not undertake them;
I fear words and do not speak them.
Therefore, it is called 'old stammering' (lǎo chī)."
Urgent Robbery
Ruǎn Jiǎn (Ruǎn Jiǎn) of Chénliú (Chénliú) was the Prefect (Lìng) of Kāifēng (Kāifēng).
There was a robbery.
An official reported:
"It is very urgent!"
Jiǎn (Jiǎn) was playing go and humming loudly.
The official said:
"The robbery is urgent!"
Jiǎn (Jiǎn) said:
"The 'robbery' on the board is also very urgent."
Whip Rotted and Saddle Decayed
The "Yuàn Yuē" (Yuàn Yuē) says:
"Someone was walking in the mountains
and saw two old men playing chūpú (chūpú) in a cave.
They had propped their horsewhips on the ground.
When he observed them,
soon the whips were rotted and the saddles decayed."
Red Jade Flute
The "Sānshíguó Chūnqiū" (Sānshíguó Chūnqiū) says:
"Hú Ān (Hú Ān) of Liángzhōu (Liángzhōu) plundered the tomb of Jìn Wénwáng (Jìn Wénwáng) Zhāng Jùn (Zhāng Jùn).
He saw Jùn's (Jùn's) appearance as if alive,
and obtained a red jade flute (chìyù xiāo) and a purple jade flute (zǐyù dí)."
Mourning a Neighbor's Daughter
Wáng Yǐn's (Wáng Yǐn) "Jìnshū" (Jìnshū) says:
"Ruǎn Jí's (Ruǎn Jí) neighbor's daughter died before marriage.
Jí (Jí) went to mourn her with utmost sorrow."
Selling a Dog to Marry Off a Daughter
Wú Yǐnzhī (Wú Yǐnzhī) of Jìn (Jìn) was about to marry off his daughter,
so he led a dog to sell it.
